papers.abstract: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.
authors: Xueyang Yu, Yifan Jing, Taiming Lu, Linrong Cai, Zhipeng Cai, Yunyang Xiong, Gabriel Sarch, Zhuang Liu
bullets: Evaluates whether models can describe and use a generated image to answer visual questions.
Tests 13 vision-language model–image generator pairs across ten tasks.
Generation reduces mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine tasks.
BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B each lose accuracy on eight tasks; VSTAR drops 10.47 points with generation.
Results vary across repeated edits: ChartQAPro and MathVista remain below baseline, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of generated images as helpers for VLM visual reasoning; fits multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
papers.tldr: Generated helper images generally hurt rather than improve visual reasoning, though repeated edits can help on some tasks.

papers.abstract: Visual context is a powerful cue for object recognition: scenes inform what, where, and at what scale objects are likely to appear. Yet over-reliance on context becomes a failure mode when models predict objects based on their typical neighbors rather than the objects' own visual features, which we call typicality bias. While extensively studied in the pre-Transformer era, it has often been assumed that architectural and scale improvements would naturally solve it, and a systematic diagnostic across the modern vision stack remains absent. We provide such a diagnostic framework. We measure typicality bias via normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs, and introduce STRANGE-Bench (Synthetic Typicality-RANked Grounded Evaluation Benchmark): a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark spanning 17 sub-tiers from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs. Across five model families (specialist detectors, open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised, vision-language, and multimodal large language models) and three recognition tasks (supervised detection, open-vocabulary detection, and classification), the bias is prevalent: gaps of 5-11 p.p. persist when objects appear outside their typical company, and do not consistently shrink with scale. To mitigate it, we turn to data augmentation: existing augmentations are designed for visual diversity, not for breaking co-occurrence shortcuts, and sample from the very distribution that produces typicality bias. We propose Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), a simple sampling rule for paste-based augmentations that uses the NPMI signal to tilt the training-time co-occurrence distribution toward atypical partners. AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 p.p. on natural-image COCO splits and 23.0 p.p. on synthetic STRANGE-Bench across three model families, without sacrificing overall performance.
authors: Siddhartha Gairola, Jiahao Xie, Anna Kukleva, Francesco Locatello, Bernt Schiele
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic framework for measuring typicality bias using normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs.
Presents STRANGE-Bench, a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark with 17 tiers ranging from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs.
Finds persistent 5–11 percentage-point recognition gaps for atypical object contexts across five model families and three tasks; scaling does not consistently resolve the bias.
Proposes Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), which uses NPMI to pair objects with atypical partners during paste-based augmentation.
AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 points on COCO splits and 23.0 points on STRANGE-Bench without sacrificing overall performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the STRANGE-Bench generation pipeline, illustrated with outputs of the actual build. (1) Typicality-based sampling: partners are drawn by their COCO NPMI with the anchor, high for the typical arm and low or never co-occurring for the atypical arm. (2) Layout and caption: a planner places the categories in a layout and writes a caption from it; each category keeps its color in panels 2 and 3. (3) Rendering and annotation: SD 3.5 Large renders the caption up to three times until SAM3 finds every category, and the boxes of the SAM3 masks are the annotations. (4) Audit: Grounding DINO rejects scenes with unintended objects (here, a laptop), and SAM3 and OWLv2 turn the remaining ones into ignore regions or drop the scene. (5) Assembly: typical and atypical sub-tiers at each contextual load k, plus Tnever, form STRANGE-Bench.

Figure 1: Typicality bias across the modern vision stack. Left: Three anchor classes (target object categories we examine): skateboard, dog, and cow, shown in their typical company (top row: with a person, with a frisbee, with a bird) and in atypical surroundings (bottom row: with a cat, with a spoon, with a clock). Right: Each model’s score on the anchor classes in COCO val images where they appear with typical vs. atypical partners (NPMI quintile splits, §3.1). The performance gap ∆ = (Typical – Atypical) persists across all five model families and three tasks we examine, ranging from ∆ = 5.4 p.p. (Co-DINO Swin-L) to ∆ = 11.0 p.p. (OpenCLIP).

Figure 5: Per-tier typicality gap including T6. Fig. 4 with the five-partner tier T6 and an Avg group (each model’s mean over T1 to T6) added. T6 layouts come from a rule-based layout solver, while those of T1 to T5 mostly come from Qwen, so T6 differs from the other tiers in layout source as well as in k.

Figure 2: NPMI signal on COCO train2017 and example STRANGE-Bench scenes. Left: The 80×80 NPMI matrix over object categories computed from COCO train2017 (Sec. 3.1). Hot (red) cells correspond to high-NPMI (typical) pairs, cool (blue) cells to low-NPMI (atypical) pairs, and black cells to category pairs that never co-occur in training. Right, top row (T5): three typical STRANGE-Bench (Sec. 3.2) scenes (green border: anchors knife, baseball bat, tv) and three atypical scenes (red border: anchors fork, skis, fire hydrant); the anchor class is shown in blue below each panel. Anchors differ across columns and are matched only by NPMI tier, not by identity. Right, bottom row (Tnever): STRANGE-Bench scenes for anchor classes bench, skateboard, suitcase, zebra, microwave, and book, each paired with partners that never co-occur with the anchor in COCO train2017.

Figure 4: Typicality bias is universal across modern vision models. Per-tier typicality gap ∆ = MT−MA on STRANGE-Bench for six models. The gap grows at every tier for the DINOv3 ViT-B linear probe (up to ∆ = 37.2 at T5), CLIP and OpenCLIP. Co-DINO R-50 rises to about 8.0 by T3 and stays there. The LLaVA-OV gaps (F1 macro) are smaller.

Figure 6: Pretraining data and model capacity on STRANGE-Bench. Adding capacity on the same pretraining data (solid lines) lowers the gap in both families; adding pretraining data at ViT-B capacity (curved arrows, gray band) raises it. ∆1-5: mean typical minus atypical over T1 to T5, against the image-encoder parameters; dot area grows with the logarithm of the number of pretraining images. CLIP and OpenCLIP: zero-shot mAP; DINO: linear probe on COCO, F1micro.

Figure 19: Rating interfaces of the user study. (a) Quality audit: the annotated boxes are drawn so that box correctness can be judged, and the instructions ask raters to judge the rendering, not the plausibility of the object combination. (b) Free listing: no boxes are drawn and the anchor is never named. (c) Pair plausibility: two class names, no image.

Figure 20: Free-listing answers on Tnever scenes. Eight of the 100 Tnever scenes of the free-listing task, as the raters saw them. Below each scene: the intended classes (anchor in bold) and how many of the four raters listed the anchor. In the two misses the raters named a similar class.

Figure 18: Spatial layout. Box-center density per sub-tier on a 32×32 grid (normalized to image coordinates). Centers lie below the image center on average in every sub-tier, with the same distribution in the typical and atypical sub-tiers at each k; the single anchors of T1 sit near the horizontal center.

Figure 7: NPMI matrix on COCO train vs. COCO val (80×80 categories, same train-frequency ordering, black = never co-occur; the diagonal is black by construction). Left: on train2017, 982 of the 80 · 79 = 6,320 off-diagonal cells are zero (15.5%): a small minority of category pairs never co-occur in training. Right: on val2017, the empty-cell fraction jumps to 49.1% (3,104 zero cells), more than 3× the training fraction. The added zeros are structured: the empty-cell rate is highest in the lower-right long-tail× long-tail quadrant (78.5% vs. 39.5% elsewhere), exactly the regime where typicality bias is expected to be strongest. For nearly half of all category pairs the natural val set provides no signal at all, irrespective of how we slice it; this is the structural coverage hole that motivates the synthetic STRANGE-Bench evaluation (§C).

Figure 17: Object-scale balance. Per-sub-tier boxplot of relative bbox area (% of image). Median absolute difference between the typical and atypical sub-tiers at fixed k: 0.66, 0.37, 0.47, 0.65, 0.15 pt for k=1, . . . , 5 (T2 to T6), 0.09 pt for the small-anchor pair, and 3.0 pt for T1. Sub-tiers right of the dashed line are outside the main grid.

Figure 16: Tier semantics. Per-sub-tier distribution of intended-pair NPMI on COCO-train. Typical and atypical sub-tiers have the expected sign and are separated at every quartile. Pairs that never co-occur have no NPMI and are not shown: the never-co-occurring sub-tiers, and in the atypical sub-tiers the share in the last column of Tab. 33. Sub-tiers right of the dashed line are outside the main grid.

Figure 12: Anchor: traffic light. Same layout as Fig. 10. Typical contexts pair it with street scenes and vehicles; atypical / never contexts displace the traffic light into indoor or natural scenes (bedroom, beach, grassland).

Figure 9: Random samples of the six sub-tiers outside the main grid. One column per sub-tier, drawn at random as in Fig. 8: T6 (k = 5) and the k = 1 pair with a small anchor (three typical scenes above three atypical ones), and the never-co-occurring cliques with k = 3 and k = 4 (App. A).

Figure 11: Anchor: cow. Same layout as Fig. 10. Notice how the cow appears in pasture / farmland contexts on the typical side, while on the atypical / never side it shares the scene with out-of-place objects (toilet, snowboard, microwave) or, at T1, an unusual background.

Figure 13: Anchor: fire hydrant. Same layout as Fig. 10. Typical pairings include vehicles and other street objects (car, stop sign, parking meter); atypical / never pairings place the fire hydrant next to animals and household objects (bear, giraffe, oven, toaster).

Figure 14: Anchor: airplane. Same layout as Fig. 10. Typical pairings usually appear on runways or airfields with related vehicles and luggage (truck, suitcase); atypical / never pairings put the airplane next to food, animals, or household objects (banana, elephant, toilet).

Figure 15: Anchor: bear. Same layout as Fig. 10. Typical pairings are forest / park scenes; atypical / never pairings move the bear to beaches, snow, or studio backdrops next to household objects (laptop, hair drier, toothbrush).

Figure 10: Anchor: zebra. Two typical (green) and two atypical (red) scenes per tier and four Tnever scenes (purple) with this anchor, drawn at random; the partner classes are listed below each panel. Top to bottom: the anchor alone with a natural or unusual background (T1); T2 to T5 add 1 to 4 typical or atypical partners; Tnever adds one or two partners that never co-occur with the anchor. The zebra stays visually consistent; the surrounding scene shifts as we sweep partner-count and pair-typicality.

Figure 8: Random samples across the main tiers. Three typical (green) and three atypical (red) scenes per tier, for T1 with natural and unusual background, and six Tnever scenes (purple), drawn uniformly at random and not curated; the anchor class is below each panel. Across panels, partner-count k∈{0, 1, 2, 3, 4} and partner typicality (typical / atypical / never) jointly drive the contextual variation.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic of typicality bias across vision-language and multimodal LLMs; introduces benchmark and co-occurrence-aware augmentation.
papers.title: Stranger Things: When Objects Appear Without Their Typical Neighbors
papers.tldr: Modern vision models rely on objects’ typical neighbors, but NPMI-guided atypical sampling substantially reduces this context bias without hurting overall performance.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal place recognition (CMPR) matches natural language descriptions against databases of geo-tagged reference images, enabling localization without visual queries. Despite its potential for language-guided navigation, existing vision-language models lag far behind visual place recognition (VPR) baselines, even after task adaptation. Unlike general-purpose text-to-image retrieval, place recognition relies on subtle local cues to distinguish visually similar locations. We therefore hypothesize that a primary bottleneck in CMPR is capturing fine-grained correspondences between image regions and text details, which requires higher visual token granularity, strong text representation capacity, and local cross-modal matching. To address this challenge, we propose CrossPlace, a two-stage CMPR framework. Stage 1 performs global retrieval by pairing a jointly aligned DINOv2-B/14 visual backbone with a progressively fine-tuned BGE-Large text encoder, while Stage 2 refines top candidates using a lightweight token-level cross-attention reranker. Through systematic analysis, we isolate the drivers of retrieval accuracy and show that visual token density provides the largest performance improvement, while text encoder capacity and task fine-tuning offer complementary gains. To evaluate robustness under realistic conditions, we also extend CMPR evaluation to city-scale and severe weather and illumination settings. Across all existing and new benchmarks, CrossPlace achieves double-digit Recall@1 improvements over prior cross-modal methods, closes the gap to unimodal text retrieval, and narrows it to unimodal VPR. Code and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/oferidan1/CrossPlace
authors: Ofer Idan, Dan Badur, Yoli Shavit
bullets: CMPR matches natural-language descriptions to geo-tagged reference images, but trails visual place recognition because subtle local details are difficult to align.
A two-stage pipeline first performs global retrieval with DINOv2-B/14 and a fine-tuned BGE-Large text encoder, then reranks candidates with lightweight token-level cross-attention.
Analysis identifies visual token density as the largest accuracy driver, with text capacity and task fine-tuning providing complementary gains.
Evaluation includes existing benchmarks plus city-scale and severe weather/illumination conditions.
CrossPlace reports double-digit Recall@1 gains over prior cross-modal methods and narrows the gap to unimodal VPR.

papers.selection_reason: Cross-modal place recognition for language-guided localization; fine-grained image-text spatial matching.
papers.title: Towards Closing the Performance Gap in Cross-Modal Place Recognition
papers.tldr: CrossPlace improves cross-modal place recognition by combining high-resolution visual tokens, a stronger text encoder, and token-level reranking to better match fine-grained image–text cues.

papers.abstract: We introduce BOP-Refer, the first benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of everyday and industrial objects sourced from 9 diverse BOP datasets. We pair images from these datasets with VLM-generated and human-verified referring expressions, and derive accurate ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes of the referred objects from their 3D models and 6DoF pose annotations. Our systematic evaluation of 17 frontier VLMs across the major proprietary and open-weight families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, Gemma) shows that the best model, Gemini 4 Carbon, reaches 72.6% AP_IoU2D in 2D but only 12.4% AP_IoU3D in 3D, despite the more lenient IoU thresholds in 3D. The predicted 3D boxes are usually centered on the target objects in the image but often off in depth by more than the object's size, suggesting that metric scale estimation, which needs reliable object size priors, is currently by far the main source of error.
authors: Tomas Hodan, Vineet Bhat, Martin Sundermeyer, Jonathan Tremblay, Yash Patel, M\'ed\'eric Fourmy, Stephen Tyree, Junwen Huang, Varun Burde, Martin C\'ifka, Eric Brachmann, Vincent Lepetit, Stan Birchfield, Jiri Matas, Carsten Rother
bullets: Introduces a benchmark covering everyday and industrial objects from 9 diverse BOP datasets.
Pairs images with VLM-generated, human-verified referring expressions and derives 2D/3D ground-truth boxes from object models and 6DoF poses.
Evaluates 17 proprietary and open-weight VLMs across Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, and Gemma families.
The best reported model achieves 72.6% 2D AP but only 12.4% 3D AP, even with more lenient 3D IoU thresholds.
3D predictions are generally image-centered but often have large depth errors, indicating metric scale and object-size priors as the main limitation.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can generate images that satisfy complex prompts, yet often produce images that omit requested objects, attributes, or relationships. We ask if models can more reliably generate text-aligned images by redistributing probability toward their more successful outcomes. We propose TrailMix, a training-free method that uses the base model's distribution of possible outcomes to adaptively guide generation toward better text alignment. During denoising, TrailMix generates inexpensive lookahead images from parallel trajectories (trails) and scores their alignment with the prompt using an external judge. The resulting distribution of reward scores allows us to estimate how strongly to steer generation toward a desired alignment level. We use these estimates to reweight and resample trajectories, favoring more promising outcomes. Across three text-to-image benchmarks, TrailMix outperforms existing baselines, with particularly strong gains on rare multi-object compositions. We further extend TrailMix to targeted image editing and introduce SEAM-Bench (Semantic Editing and Attribute Maintenance), a systematic benchmark evaluating whether semantic edits preserve other image content. Experiments on SEAM-Bench and existing benchmark PIE-Bench demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach for controlled image editing. Our results show how a model's own possible outcomes can inform reliable and controllable generation.
authors: Abinitha Gourabathina, Sana Tonekaboni, Marzyeh Ghassemi, Akbar Rafiey
bullets: Addresses missing objects, attributes, and relationships in diffusion-generated images.
Generates inexpensive lookahead images from parallel denoising trajectories and scores prompt alignment with an external judge.
Adaptively estimates steering strength, then reweights and resamples trajectories toward better-aligned outcomes.
Outperforms existing baselines across three text-to-image benchmarks, with especially strong gains on rare multi-object compositions.
Extends to image editing and introduces SEAM-Bench to evaluate semantic edits while preserving other content; also performs effectively on SEAM-Bench and PIE-Bench.

papers.abstract: Scene rearrangement is an essential task for 3D content creation applications, requiring generation of diverse, aesthetic and functional scene rearrangements. We present SceneDesigner3D, an agentic evolutionary search method for 3D indoor scene rearrangement that systematically explores the design space of 3D scenes and generates multiple solutions according to common interior design principles. Given an input scene and a text prompt, SceneDesigner3D represents the rearrangement as an editable program and evolves a population of candidate layouts. Starting from distinct design ideas, a VLM agent mutates the programs by refining promising candidates, exploring new rearrangement strategies or redesigning from scratch, while verifying the layouts for physical validity. Proposals are scored by a VLM judge for adherence to the input prompt and satisfaction of design principles such as balance, zoning and emphasis, as well as numerically computed principles such as circulation and clutter. An archive of top-performing, structurally varied candidates further increases diversity of rearrangements. Experiments on the SAGE-10k and SceneSmith datasets show that SceneDesigner3D improves prompt adherence and computed design principle scores over baselines by up to 5.1% and 15.2%, respectively. Code will be made publicly available.
bullets: Represents scene rearrangements as editable programs and evolves populations of candidate layouts.
A VLM agent mutates candidates through refinement, exploration, or redesign from scratch, with physical-validity checks.
A VLM judge scores prompt adherence and qualitative principles, while numerical metrics assess circulation and clutter.
An archive preserves high-performing, structurally diverse solutions.
Experiments on SAGE-10k and SceneSmith report up to 5.1% better prompt adherence and 15.2% better computed design-principle scores than baselines.

Each candidate is judged by a VLM against its parent on the prompt requirements and design principles, and combined with numerically computed principles into its fitness. An archive keeps diverse candidates as inspiration for future iterations, giving diverse layouts that follow the prompt and design principles.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing scene understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to interpret queried targets in relation to nearby objects and surrounding structures, which serve as spatial references or define the scope of an answer. However, standard answers and bounding boxes often leave these contextual relationships implicit. Thus, we construct GeoContext-5K to make them explicit in 5,394 training pairs for visual question answering (VQA), with spatial cues, visual facts, and supporting regions. GeOPD uses these annotations for on-policy distillation, guiding a frozen teacher with region marks on the full image and a visual fact while preserving surrounding spatial references. It prioritizes teacher corrections that agree with the shift in the student's next token distribution when evidence is restored. A complementary objective weights the contrast between the student's scores on the two views by how much masking lowers the teacher's log probability for the same sampled token. Experiments on five remote sensing VQA benchmarks show that GeOPD outperforms the evaluated open-source MLLMs and matched post-training baselines, improving over the 4B and 9B base models by 5.81 and 2.97 percentage points on average. The dataset and code will be publicly released at https://github.com/YeeCharm/GeOPD.
authors: Yichang Luo, Hourun Zhu, Shixiong Liu, Kan Wei, Shi Liang, Yidan Zhang, Lei Wang
bullets: GeoContext-5K contains 5,394 VQA training pairs with spatial cues, visual facts, and supporting regions.

It prioritizes teacher corrections supported by changes in the student’s next-token distribution when evidence is restored.
A contrastive objective uses how masking affects the teacher’s token likelihood to weight student-view comparisons.
Across five remote-sensing VQA benchmarks, GeOPD improves over 4B and 9B base models by 5.81 and 2.97 percentage points on average, respectively.

papers.abstract: Poetry-to-video generation requires more than translating text into visual scenes. Poetic language is highly compressed, often depends on historical and cultural knowledge, and frequently conveys meaning through metaphor, imagery, and other non-literal expressions. We introduce PoVi, a benchmark and agentic framework for grounded poetry-to-video generation, evaluating semantic grounding, discourse coherence, and audiovisual realization. PoVi reconstructs poem semantics into an evidence-bounded representation and progressively transforms them into narration, interpretation, character assets, and shot-level visual plans, followed by narration-aligned video generation. Across three planning backbones and four video generators, PoVi consistently improves over single-call generation, with the largest gains on implicit background knowledge and metaphorical relations. PoVi provides a testbed for studying knowledge-grounded, long-horizon multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.
authors: Yuxia Zhu, Shiying Zhang, Lingzhuang Sun, Song Yang, Siheng Wu, Xinglong Xu, Sizhe Qiu, Hao Liang, Cheng Tan, Asher Qin, Wentao Zhang
bullets: Targets the challenges of compressed poetic language, implicit background knowledge, and figurative meaning in poetry-to-video generation.
Builds an evidence-bounded semantic representation, then progressively creates narration, interpretations, character assets, and shot-level plans.
Generates videos aligned with narration and evaluates semantic grounding, discourse coherence, and audiovisual realization.
Across three planning backbones and four video generators, consistently outperforms single-call generation, especially for implicit knowledge and metaphorical relations.
Provides a testbed for long-horizon, knowledge-grounded multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.

papers.abstract: Non-invasive brain-to-text seeks to recover language from brain activity without surgery. A central challenge is turning learned brain-language representations into accurate word predictions. We present MEG2text, a decoding system that combines corrected training and evaluation, brain-text alignment, a class-balanced word readout, and target-word language-model fusion. On LibriBrain100's word-ranking task, MEG2text reaches 64.12% mean Top-10 balanced accuracy, improving on published MEG-XL by 16.92 percentage points across four corpora, with gains on each corpus. Controlled comparisons show that both implementation corrections and a learned readout contribute to this improvement. Candidate-level analysis reveals that some words receive informative scores yet consistently lose to competing candidates, while an identical-feature comparison shows that learning the classification rule improves decoding without changing the representation. These findings identify the decoding rule as a consequential part of non-invasive brain-to-text and show how system improvements can make better use of aligned neural features.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting aligned brain-language representations into accurate word predictions.
Uses corrected training and evaluation, brain-text alignment, a class-balanced word readout, and target-word language-model fusion.
Achieves 64.12% mean Top-10 balanced accuracy on LibriBrain100’s word-ranking task, 16.92 percentage points above published MEG-XL across four corpora.
Controlled comparisons indicate that implementation corrections and the learned readout both contribute to the gains.
Candidate analysis suggests the decoding rule affects performance even when neural representations remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: Answering a knowledge-based visual question requires first recognizing the entity in the image and then recalling knowledge about it. Thinking vision-language models (VLMs) reason for thousands of tokens before answering, yet it remains underexplored how well such thinking VLMs perform each of these two steps. We therefore analyze thinking VLMs on this task and make two key observations. (1) Recognition is the bottleneck, since 76.3% of errors across four models on ViQuAE stem from misrecognizing the entity, and 84.9% of these failures are resolved once the entity name is provided in the question. (2) Recognition is driven by entity-recall clues rather than by general descriptions of the image. An entity-recall clue is a distinctive visual detail that helps the model recall the entity, such as keys, a traditional attribute of Saint Peter. Based on these findings, we propose ClueRL, a reinforcement learning approach that extends Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with an advantage localized to the entity-recall clue in the thinking trace. Rather than injecting new entity knowledge, ClueRL changes how VLMs think: it leads them to attend more closely to visual details and spot these clues, helping them use the knowledge they already have. Consequently, it outperforms both GRPO and a perception-reward baseline on three entity recognition benchmarks. Moreover, this clue-seeking behavior generalizes beyond entity recognition, the only task used for training. Since recognition is the bottleneck, the gains carry over to knowledge-based visual question answering. They even extend to general multimodal reasoning, raising Qwen3.5-4B by 4.4 and 4.0 points on the ScienceQA and MMMU subsets of MMStar, respectively.
authors: Kyungmin Min, Soyeon Kim, Junseok Kim, Kyomin Jung
bullets: Entity recognition is the main bottleneck: 76.3% of errors across four models on ViQuAE come from misidentifying the entity.
Most recognition failures are resolved when the entity name is supplied, indicating that models often possess the needed knowledge but fail to identify the visual entity.
Recognition depends on entity-recall clues—distinctive details such as Saint Peter’s keys—rather than generic image descriptions.
ClueRL extends GRPO with an advantage focused on entity-recall clues in the reasoning trace, without adding entity knowledge.
It outperforms GRPO and a perception-reward baseline on three entity-recognition benchmarks and improves knowledge-based VQA and broader multimodal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Generative driving planners may produce trajectories that appear feasible at their reference points but violate environmental constraints over the full vehicle body. We propose FeaXDrive2, an end-to-end generative planning framework that enhances vehicle-embodied spatial feasibility (VESF) through body-scene spatial grounding. The proposed method constructs spatial queries from actual vehicle-body corners and dynamically updates visual sampling locations using evolving trajectory estimates across Flow steps. Retrieved local visual features condition subsequent Action Flow-DiT velocity predictions, allowing trajectory generation to guide spatial information retrieval. Rollout-Consistent Safety Fine-Tuning (RC-F) combines high-risk trajectory supervision with reference behavior preservation, followed by planning-supervised VLM-Action Alignment. Vehicle-geometry counterfactual analysis reveals safety differences under identical trajectories but varying vehicle geometry. On NAVSIM, FeaXDrive2 reduces at-fault collisions by 36.5% relative to the base planner and improves PDMS from 87.0 to 88.8. Under NAVSIM v2 evaluation, EPDMS increases from 86.5 to 88.3. Ablation and body-clearance analyses further demonstrate the safety benefits of body-scene spatial grounding.
authors: Bo Leng, Baoyun Wang, Wenxin Wen, Ming Liu, Weiqi Zhang, Ran Yu, Chongfeng Wei, Zhuoren Li, Lu Xiong
bullets: Addresses collisions caused by evaluating feasibility only at trajectory reference points rather than across the vehicle body.
Builds spatial queries from vehicle-body corners and updates visual sampling locations as trajectory estimates evolve during Flow steps.
Uses retrieved local visual features to condition Action Flow-DiT predictions, enabling trajectory-guided spatial retrieval.
Adds Rollout-Consistent Safety Fine-Tuning and planning-supervised VLM–Action Alignment.
On NAVSIM, reduces at-fault collisions by 36.5% and improves PDMS from 87.0 to 88.8; NAVSIM v2 EPDMS rises from 86.5 to 88.3.

papers.abstract: Dense global attention is crucial for capturing cross-view geometry in visual geometry foundation models, yet its quadratic complexity limits efficient inference on long image sequences. Existing sparse attention methods primarily select entries of the global attention matrix based on attention probabilities and construct masks independently across layers, overlooking value redundancy and cross-layer information reuse. By analyzing attention distributions and clustering value representations across layers, we reveal two forms of \emph{cross-layer consistency}, characterized by highly similar attention probability distributions and localized changes in value redundancy structures. Building on these observations, we propose \textbf{DuCo}, a training-free sparse attention framework that exploits historical attention information and value redundancy for efficient geometric inference. Specifically, DuCo leverages historical attention information to estimate current-layer dense attention probabilities and introduces value clustering to exploit redundancy, with clusters efficiently refined through local updates across layers. Both factors are integrated through probability-weighted value distortion to jointly optimize four cluster representation states under an attention budget for sparse mask construction. Experiments across three visual geometry foundation models and five benchmarks demonstrate favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-offs.
authors: Liangyu Xiang, Junyu Gao, Xiaofeng Wang, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Dense global attention captures cross-view geometry but has quadratic cost on long image sequences.
DuCo estimates current attention from historical layers and reuses clustered value representations with efficient local updates.
Probability-weighted value distortion jointly optimizes cluster states under an attention budget to construct sparse masks.
Experiments on three visual geometry foundation models and five benchmarks show favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.

papers.abstract: It is commonly accepted that high-level concepts are represented linearly in the representation space of large neural networks. For Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs), finding those interpretable directions in visual representations is important for interpretability. To find them, the classical approach is to train a linear classifier on the representations, but it needs a large amount of labels and only recovers what can be read from the representations, not what the model actually uses. In this paper we start from the following insight: The LLM Decoder of an LVLM is also a classifier whose classes are the possible next tokens. So we use its first-order Taylor expansion as a linear classifier. Hence, we introduce Decoder-as-a-Probe (DaP), which significantly outperforms classical probing and steering baselines especially when training data is sparse. (1) It verbalizes what an LVLM perceives in a given image. (2) It can surgically change the perception of the LVLM about specific attributes (e.g. change only the color, the clothes worn or the action done). Due to its simplicity and data efficiency, we believe DaP can serve as a plug-and-play tool for LVLM research, such as interpretability, hallucination mitigation or instruction tuning.
authors: Adhemar de Senneville, Xavier Bou, J\'er\'emy Anger, Rafael Grompone, Gabriele Facciolo
bullets: Addresses the need to identify interpretable directions in LVLM visual representations without large labeled datasets.
Approximates the decoder with a first-order Taylor expansion, treating it as a linear classifier over next-token classes.

Outperforms classical probing and steering baselines, particularly when training data is sparse.
Proposed as a plug-and-play tool for interpretability, hallucination mitigation, and instruction tuning.

papers.abstract: Almost every short-video upload now passes through a classifier that fuses video, speech, and on-screen text into one decision about whether it may be seen. It moderates every language community on the platform at once, and fairness across them is judged, if at all, from one accuracy score. That score is compatible with error falling almost entirely on one language group. An audit that goes looking reads the model's decisions, the last stage of a long pipeline and the one whose test has the fewest items. We ask where in a fused pipeline a subgroup asymmetry can be detected at all: in what the classifier may read, in what its branches encode, or in what it decides. We answer this with a post-hoc audit of a published TikTok classifier, holding all three stages to one significance standard using only its logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features, with source language as the subgroup axis. The asymmetry is significant at the stage deciding what the model may read, and again in what the text branch encodes. At the earlier stage, a language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English one, for reasons of segmentation, not verbosity. The asymmetry is undetectable at the decision, where the smallest subgroup leaves twelve items to test. An audit reading only decisions looks where its evidence is thinnest; the same test staged upstream recovers a disparity the decision-level view returns as noise.
bullets: Audits a fused video, speech, and text moderation pipeline using logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features.
Tests three stages under one significance standard, with source language as the subgroup axis.
Finds significant asymmetry in what content the model may read and in the text branch’s representations.
A language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English clip due to segmentation, not verbosity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The audited pipeline and the three stages at which we test it. A clip enters MTikGuard as a raw video file; extraction yields sampled frames, a Whisper transcript, and an EasyOCR string concatenated into one text field, a language-blind cap decides how much of that field survives, two encoders represent what is left, and a fusion layer emits one label. The audit taps three of these links and holds all three to the same significance standard. The item counts show why they are not equally testable. The cap and the encoders can be tested over every clip, while a false-positive rate exists only over a subgroup’s true-PASS items, which leaves twelve in the smallest subgroup.

Figure 3: What a language-blind token cap does to each subgroup. (a) Fused-text length per clip (log scale) against the pipeline’s 64-word-piece cap, where everything above the line is discarded before the classifier reads it, with the median share each subgroup keeps printed above. (b) The cause is segmentation: median word pieces per character with bootstrap 95% intervals, Vietnamese separated from English while the volume of text extracted does not differ. Tests (Holmadjusted within the four-test family): truncated at all, Fisher p = 0.21; retained fraction, Mann–Whitney p = 0.014, padj = 0.042; word pieces per character, p = 3 × 10−4, padj = 0.001; extracted volume, p = 0.18. The undetected-language subgroup is the most fragmented and most truncated, and its wide interval is the same small-subgroup problem that defeats the comparison in Section 5.1.

Figure 1: The case the audit is built to surface. Two creators upload near-identical borderline clips, one narrated in English and one in Vietnamese, to the same classifier and receive opposite outcomes. One aggregate accuracy score is reported whichever way the errors fall, whether they are spread evenly across the language groups or concentrated almost entirely on one, so only disaggregation separates the two situations.

papers.selection_reason: Conducts a fairness audit of a fused multimodal moderation pipeline (video, speech, text), identifying where subgroup asymmetry enters the decision-making process.
papers.title: Where Does the Asymmetry Enter? Staging a Fairness Audit Across a Fused Multimodal Moderation Pipeline
papers.tldr: A staged fairness audit finds that language-based asymmetry enters upstream—in content access and text encoding—while decision-only audits miss it because their evidence is too sparse.

papers.abstract: AI wearables, such as smart glasses, extend the context available to agents beyond digital environments to users' physical surroundings. With these devices, computer tasks can originate from users' ongoing activities rather than solely from explicit instructions. Through first-person observations, agents can identify objects and activities relevant to user requests and ground digital tasks in the surrounding context. We call this interaction paradigm Ego Use. However, first-person observations are limited by the wearer's viewpoint and may provide incomplete or ambiguous evidence of ongoing activities. As new observations arrive, agents may need to revise their understanding of the physical context and user intent, and reassess whether prior digital actions remain valid. Whether current agents can reliably handle these changes remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce EgoUseBench, a benchmark for evaluating Ego Use across three interaction settings with different levels of first-person context. Computer-Use relies on explicit instructions, Offline Ego Use provides prerecorded first-person context before execution, and Online Ego Use provides continuous observations as user intent evolves. Based on over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings, we construct 693 tasks across the three interaction settings. To capture task evolution, we track first-person observations, user requirements, and website state separately. We further group tasks by how information changes during execution, resulting in three types: Graft (revised user requirements), Refresh (new first-person observations), and Clarify (agent-initiated information seeking). We evaluate advanced models and find that average success rates in Online Ego Use are 26.3% lower than in Computer-Use. This result reveals the difficulty of keeping task execution aligned with evolving first-person context and user intent.
authors: Yurun Chen, Biao Yi, Qihang Yu, Keting Yin, Shengyu Zhang
bullets: Introduces three settings: explicit-instruction Computer-Use, prerecorded Offline Ego Use, and continuously observed Online Ego Use.

Groups evolving tasks into Graft, Refresh, and Clarify based on how information changes.

papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates separately trained domain specialists into a single unified model. Existing methods focus on refining the distillation procedure while initializing the student from a base model or a multi-domain SFT checkpoint, which leaves capability integration largely to distillation itself. Instead, we treat the starting point as a design variable and propose Unified MOPD (Uni-MOPD), which pairs a strong start with a simple recipe: a training-free uniform merge of specialists from the same base model initializes the student, and short MOPD with uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL refines it. Across five multimodal domains and 19 benchmarks, our study establishes three findings. (1) The starting point matters more than subsequent training choices: before any training, the uniform merge already matches the score that the base model reaches after 200 MOPD updates, and after short distillation it matches higher-scoring, search-based starts. (2) Short MOPD recovers most of the capabilities the merge leaves unintegrated; it improves every domain, with the largest gains where the domain teacher still leads. (3) From a strong start, uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL match or exceed every evaluated sampling strategy and divergence, without schedules, per-token weighting, or truncation hyperparameters. Uni-MOPD outperforms Open-MOPD at the same training budget while training 3.3 times faster than its released code. We will release the training framework, specialist checkpoints, and unified student.
authors: Wenzheng Chang, Taiqiang Wu, Yuqi Xu, Yongfu Zhu, Zelin Peng, Ji Zhao, Shuai Dong, Wenpu Liu, Caoyuan Ma, Xuehui Wang, Ziyue Wang, Weichu Xie, Haiyuan Wan, Ngai Wong, Tong He, Wenqi Shao, Jiaqi Wang
bullets: A training-free uniform merge of specialists from the same base model provides a strong initialization.
Short MOPD with uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL recovers capabilities left unintegrated by the merge.
The approach improves performance across all five multimodal domains and 19 benchmarks, especially where teachers remain stronger.
From a strong initialization, simple uniform sampling and reverse KL match or exceed evaluated alternatives without extra schedules or weighting hyperparameters.
Uni-MOPD outperforms Open-MOPD at the same training budget and trains 3.3× faster than its released implementation.

papers.abstract: Robust image-text retrieval aims to maintain accurate cross-modal matching when image or text queries are incomplete, supporting reliable information access in real-world applications. However, existing methods typically focus on adapting to distribution shifts, without adequately addressing candidate discrimination for incomplete queries and ranking instability. To this end, we propose semantic projection and alignment with relational constraints (SPARC), which elicits latent multimodal knowledge from frozen encoders to improve candidate discrimination and ranking stability. Specifically, we first devise a semantic calibration module on a product of spheres that refines incomplete visual and textual features through tangent-space updates, maintaining the unit-sphere structure used for cosine similarity. Second, we introduce a robust semantic guidance module that combines latent multimodal knowledge encoded in complete image-text features with cross-modal semantic anchors to promote semantic alignment of the calibrated features. Finally, we introduce a matching relation constraint module that fuses original query features with their calibrated counterparts and applies a soft ranking constraint to penalize reductions in initially positive matching margins, thereby limiting ranking perturbations. Extensive experiments on Flickr30K and COCO demonstrate that SPARC outperforms competing methods under various image occlusion and word deletion settings, while achieving consistent gains across different pretrained backbones.
authors: Zhongkuan Mao, Wenzhuo Zhao, Haidong Chen, Shangze Li, Yidong Wang, Jinhe Bi, Yunpu Ma, Junfeng Fang, Fei Shen, Tat-Seng Chua

Refines incomplete visual and textual features with tangent-space updates on a product of spheres.
Uses complete image-text features and cross-modal anchors to guide semantic alignment.
Applies a soft matching-relation constraint to preserve initially positive ranking margins.
Outperforms competing methods on Flickr30K and COCO across corruption settings and pretrained backbones.

papers.abstract: Pretrained visual representations improve diffusion-transformer training, yet exploiting both global context and local spatial structure requires deciding which semantic states to model and how to access them. We introduce Semantic State Reading (SSR), which jointly denoises image latents, a global CLS token encoding image-level context, and a compact patch state preserving spatial correspondence. SSR couples this global-local modeling with distinct reading paths: local states are fused with corresponding image tokens at the input, while independent projections inject the current global state into every transformer block. Both semantic scopes thus remain accessible throughout denoising. Ablations show complementary benefits from local-state modeling and repeated global reading, and semantic-trajectory interventions alter image layout under a fixed class label. On ImageNet $256 \times 256$, SiT-XL/2 with SSR reaches or surpasses the reference FIDs of SiT, REPA, and Representation Entanglement for Generation (REG) with $100\times$, $40\times$, and $2\times$ fewer training iterations, respectively. SSR achieves unguided FID 1.78 at 2M iterations and FID 1.34 with classifier-free guidance alone. Combining classifier-free guidance with autoguidance yields FID 1.31 at 1M iterations, achieving the best FID in our main comparison table.
authors: Guanxi Lai, Zixuan Li, Zhiwei Li, Qi Li
bullets: Jointly denoises image latents, a global CLS state, and compact spatially aligned patch states.
Fuses local semantic states with corresponding image tokens and injects global context into every transformer block.
Ablations show complementary gains from local-state modeling and repeated global-state reading.
Semantic-trajectory interventions can change image layout while keeping the class label fixed.

On ImageNet 256×256, it reports FID 1.78 unguided, 1.34 with classifier-free guidance, and 1.31 with combined classifier-free guidance and autoguidance, using fewer training iterations than cited baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Comparison between REG and our Semantic State Reading (SSR). (d) During inference, SSR jointly generates image, local and global states from random noise, retaining spatial input fusion and per-layer CLS injection at every sampling step. papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) with general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offers a flexible alternative to task-specific navigation policies, while reliable long-horizon execution remains challenging. Agents must track navigation progress, detect discrepancies between commanded and actual motion, and recognize when movement has passed relevant landmarks or entrances. We present Navigent, an agentic VLN framework built around a frozen MLLM and a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC). GEC performs two complementary checks: action-to-motion consistency, which evaluates measured displacement against commanded movement, and motion-to-landmark consistency, which tracks agent-selected visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates. Detected discrepancies interrupt the remaining action sequence and trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery. Historical visual memory supports progress tracking across extended routes. An offline self-improvement procedure further analyzes successful and failed training trajectories to refine navigation prompts and GEC logic while keeping model weights fixed. On the R2R-CE validation-unseen split (1,839 episodes) and RxR-CE validation-unseen split(3,669 episodes), Navigent achieves 84.0%/86.0% SR and 72.9%/69.1% SPL, respectively, demonstrating the value of geometry-grounded execution verification for reliable agentic navigation. Project Page: https://marslab-navigent.github.io/navigent.github.io/ Code: https://github.com/MarsLab-Navigent/Navigent
authors: Xinyu Zhou, Weiren Cai, Yitong Chen, Shenghai Yuan, Zihang Mu, Boyu Ma, Jiahua Dong, Yanshuo Lu, Jiaqi Bai, Jianfei Yang

Uses a frozen multimodal large language model with a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC).
GEC checks action-to-motion consistency and motion-to-landmark consistency using visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates.
Detected discrepancies trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery; historical visual memory tracks progress.
Reports 84.0%/86.0% success rate and 72.9%/69.1% SPL on R2R-CE/RxR-CE validation-unseen splits, respectively.

papers.abstract: Code-driven video generation asks a coding agent to write and run rendering programs. This gives exact control over typography, data visualizations, synchronized audio, and multi-shot scenes, and it leaves an editable project behind. A program that exits cleanly can still render overlapping labels, a camera aimed away from its subject, broken object interactions, or narration that drifts out of sync, and none of these raise a runtime error. Feeding rendered frames and audio back into the coding session bloats its long-horizon context, while critiquing only the finished full-resolution render turns early design mistakes into costly rewrites. We introduce VibeVideoAgent, a training-free framework that lets coding agents inspect their drafts throughout production. Multimodal perception runs in short-lived contexts kept apart from the coder and returns compact, grounded Findings. Seven primitives operate on a unified multi-clock representation of assets and drafts: they explore media from coarse to fine, verify quoted requirements with evidence from every required modality, compare a draft with a reference or an earlier revision on separate clocks, and measure stream signals locally. A lightweight staged protocol has the agent test its riskiest decision on a minimal preview first. On all 239 VibeVideoBench tasks, with matched agent runtimes and a fixed perception model, VibeVideoAgent improves holistic audiovisual quality (L3) for Claude Opus 5.5 (4.03 -> 4.43, while L2 rubric compliance rises from 98.87% to 99.35%), GPT-6 Astra (4.03 -> 4.27), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (3.97 -> 4.10), with the largest gains in audio-visual synchronization (up to +0.56). Controlled ablations show that each component contributes, and trajectory audits show that the granularity of code edits governs the trade-off between rubric adherence and perceptual quality.
authors: Xuanyu Zheng, Luoyuan Zhang, Yancheng Long, Haoyang Xu, Muxi Diao, Yuzhe Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao
bullets: Addresses perceptual failures that produce valid code but flawed videos, such as occlusion, poor camera framing, broken interactions, and audio drift.
Uses short-lived multimodal perception contexts that return compact, grounded findings without bloating the coding agent’s long-horizon context.
Introduces seven primitives over a unified multi-clock representation to inspect media, verify requirements, compare revisions or references, and measure local stream signals.
A staged protocol tests risky design choices on minimal previews before committing to costly full renders.
Across 239 VibeVideoBench tasks, it improves holistic audiovisual quality and especially audio-visual synchronization for three evaluated agents; ablations indicate all components contribute.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture of VibeVideoAgent. (a) A three-clock Media specification 𝜎 addresses assets, stills, partial previews, and full renders, with crop-before-scale magnification and source-file hashing. (b) Seven stack-agnostic primitives explore media from coarse to fine, verify sourced requirements across modalities, compare two media on separate clocks, and probe signals without model calls, returning grounded Findings 𝑓𝑡 to an auditable ledger. (c) A staged protocol gates planning and then guides preview, assembly, repair, and delivery checks.

Figure 4. End-to-end authoring with VibeVideoAgent. (a) The recorded W0448 run with real frames. (2) stage=assembly checks catch silent staging bugs in v1.mp4 even though the render exited cleanly: the backpack is held in hand, and in the Family beat no lid closes while the child already stands in the doorway. (3) compare_media(finding_id, media) confirms a targeted render.py patch across shifted clocks. (4) Deterministic probe_media checks finalize the seamless red-button loop. Raw frames stay inside short-lived Gemini 3.8 Flash calls, whose Findings are 5.5× smaller than the media they perceive. (b) Without engine-specific adapters, the same seven primitives serve an interactive 3D WebGPU system (W0154, +71.1 pp L2 under the Argon judge), a long-form paper explainer with synchronized narration (PA02, 12.0× smaller payload), and reference-guided reconstruction of motion and audio (R0009, Flash-judged L3 3.60 → 4.80).

Figure 1. Closing the perceptual loop in code-driven video generation. (a) A conventional coding agent either ships unchecked renders, so visual, spatial, and sync bugs survive a clean exit code, or puts raw frames and audio into its context 𝐶𝑡 and critiques only the final video, which leads to whole-project rewrites. (b) VibeVideoAgent keeps raw media out of 𝐶𝑡 : a stateless VLM worker Φ and local probes Ψ return compact, grounded Findings 𝑓𝑡 at every stage, from a minimal preview to final delivery.

It also separates an over-specific observable it wrote for R_farewell (marked fail*) from the satisfied prompt_quote. It then patches render.py, confirms both repairs with dual-clock compare_media, and finishes with decode and seam probes, leaving R_end_zoom as uncertain. The bottom row reports perception cost, context compression, and the Flash-judged outcome against the native Opus 5.5 baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a framework (VibeVideoAgent) for code-driven video generation that uses multimodal perception to close the perceptual loop. This fits the Multimodal Foundation Models category as it involves agents combining vision and language for generation tasks.
papers.title: VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation
papers.tldr: VibeVideoAgent improves code-driven video generation by giving coding agents compact, staged, multimodal feedback throughout production instead of only after rendering.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate impressive multimodal capabilities, yet suffer from hallucination - generating factually inaccurate content. Contrastive Decoding (CD) mitigates this by contrasting amateur and expert branches at the logit level. However, our investigation reveals that such logit-level interventions fundamentally compromise generation coherence, necessitating restrictive penalty constraints unrelated to hallucination suppression. We introduce Attention Contrastive Decoding (ACD), a training-free plug-in that complements logit-level CD by relocating part of the contrastive operations to the attention mechanism. Operating at an earlier stage of the forward pass, ACD performs smooth semantic-preserving interventions through an Adaptive Subtraction Strategy (ASS), which attenuates hallucination-associated attention patterns while amplifying critical visual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that combining ACD with existing CD methods (e.g., VCD+ACD) produces substantially more coherent outputs with further reduced hallucinations, eliminating restrictive penalties while enabling trustworthy multimodal generation.
authors: Yujia Chen, Rui Sun, Huayu Mai, Wangkai Li, Zhangyu He, Bingzhou Wang, Aibing Li, Wenzhang Sun, Tianzhu Zhang
bullets: Logit-level Contrastive Decoding can harm coherence and requires restrictive penalty constraints.
ACD is a training-free plug-in that complements existing contrastive decoding methods.
Its Adaptive Subtraction Strategy adjusts attention patterns to suppress hallucination-related signals and emphasize important visual information.
Combining ACD with methods such as VCD reportedly yields more coherent outputs and further reduces hallucinations.
The approach targets trustworthy multimodal generation without restrictive penalties.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed framework (VCD + ACD). (a) Attention Contrastive Decoding (ACD). Given an image v and its perturbed counterpart v′, ACD computes parallel attention maps Aclean

Figure 1. (a) VCD mitigates hallucinations by subtracting hallucination-induced distributions from original outputs. (b) However, logit-level subtraction disrupts linguistic coherence compared to vanilla decoding .

Figure 3. Visualization of the Adaptive Subtraction Strategy (ASS). (a) Input image. (b) Clean attention correctly focuses on the person. (c) Under hallucination induction, attention drifts to background noise. (d) Attention after ASS. The red box marks a Case 1 region (Aclean > Anoisy): ASS amplifies the clean signal by (1+α), producing sharper focus than (b). The yellow box marks a Case 2 region (Anoisy ≥Aclean): ASS suppresses spurious activation via contrastive subtraction. The resulting map (d) achieves a higher signal-to-noise ratio than the original clean state (b), widening the margin between object and background.

Figure 5. Absolute performance across α values. Top: VCD (α ∈ [0.5, 1.5]); Bottom: VCD+ACD (α ∈ [0.05, 0.25]). Green stars indicate optimal configurations. VCD exhibits substantial variation while VCD+ACD maintains tight performance bounds.

Figure 7. Layer-wise cosine similarity between clean and noisy stream hidden states (LLaVA-1.5-7B, 32 layers). Text tokens maintain consistently higher similarity than visual tokens. Divergence peaks at middle layers and partially recovers in deeper layers, confirming bounded propagation.

papers.abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide transferable numerical forecasting priors. However, forecast-relevant information may be conveyed in text without being reflected in the observed series. Many multimodal forecasting methods integrate such context through model inputs or intermediate representations. We investigate a complementary mechanism: text-conditioned parameter adaptation. We propose Context-to-LoRA for Time Series (C2LoRA-TS), which encodes text and generates temporary Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) updates for selected weight matrices of a frozen TSFM. Both the numerical backbone and text encoder remain frozen, and the method exactly recovers the frozen TSFM output when context is absent. Evaluated on Time-MMD across nine domains and three TSFM architectures, C2LoRA-TS achieves lower aggregate forecasting error than the frozen-TSFM and Static LoRA baselines for every architecture and seed. Replacing the instance-specific text with a single globally fixed context degrades performance for every architecture. These results support text-conditioned parameter generation as a viable strategy for multimodal forecasting with frozen TSFMs.
authors: Kunqi Li, Bin Liang, Zhidong Li
bullets: Addresses forecast-relevant information present in text but missing from observed time series.
Encodes text into temporary LoRA updates for selected weights while keeping the TSFM and text encoder frozen.
Exactly recovers the frozen TSFM output when no context is available.
On Time-MMD across nine domains and three TSFM architectures, it lowers aggregate error versus frozen-TSFM and Static LoRA baselines for every architecture and seed.
Globally fixed text context performs worse than instance-specific context, supporting adaptive parameter generation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Method overview. The numerical history is processed by a frozen TSFM, while a frozen text encoder followed by normalized mean pooling maps the textual context to a vector embedding zT . For each selected frozen transformation Wℓ,0, hypernetworks gAℓ and gBℓ generate the low-rank adaptation factors Aℓ(zT ) and Bℓ(zT ). For each forecast, the factor pair defines the rank-bounded update ∆Wℓ(zT ) = mTBℓ(zT )Aℓ(zT ), which is applied during the TSFM forward pass and vanishes when context is absent.

papers.tldr: C2LoRA-TS improves frozen time-series foundation models by generating text-conditioned, instance-specific LoRA updates for multimodal forecasting.

papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) in real-world systems must handle unpredictable modality missingness caused by sensor failures, privacy masking, and unstable transmission. Existing methods either learn reliability-aware representations or reconstruct missing inputs, often using a single flattened encoder output. This overlooks deep encoders' semantic hierarchy and intra- and inter-modal interactions, causing semantic averaging and ill-posed mappings. We propose Hierarchical Semantic Learning (HSL), a framework that exploits semantic hierarchy for robust MSA with missing modalities. Hierarchical Semantic Decoupling exposes low-, mid-, and high-level feature streams from each modality encoder. Cross-Modal Cross-Level Semantic Reconstruction performs ladder-style recovery, using high-level semantics from observed modalities as global anchors to progressively reconstruct mid-level structures and low-level details of missing modalities. To stabilize cross-level reconstruction, Hierarchical Cascade Error Supervisor applies prototypical contrastive regularization to observed and reconstructed features, enforcing level-specific semantic consistency and limiting error propagation. Finally, Hierarchical Interactive Fusion captures dense interactions across modalities and semantic levels to produce robust predictions under diverse missingness patterns. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, IEMOCAP, and CH-SIMS show that HSL outperforms baselines in most missing-modality settings.
authors: Chunlei Meng, Rong Fu, Zhan Chen, Yi Liu, Zhuo Zou, LiDa Xu, Chun Ouyang, Zhongxue Gan
bullets: Addresses modality loss from sensor failures, privacy masking, and unstable transmission in real-world MSA.
Decouples each modality into low-, mid-, and high-level semantic feature streams.
Reconstructs missing modalities from high-level anchors through mid-level structures to low-level details.
Uses prototypical contrastive regularization to enforce level-specific consistency and reduce error propagation.
Outperforms baselines in most missing-modality settings across CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, IEMOCAP, and CH-SIMS.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the Hierarchical Semantic Learning (HSL) framework, illustrated with a missing acoustic modality. HSL consists of four components: HSD decomposes each observed modality into low-, mid-, and high-level semantics; CM-CLSR reconstructs missing mid-/low-level features from high-level cues via the Semantic Injection Decoder (SID); HCES regularizes level-wise reconstructions using a contrastive loss; and HIF fuses all hierarchical features with a Transformer to produce the final prediction. Solid arrows indicate data flow, and dashed arrows indicate supervision.

papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical Semantic Learning framework for robust multimodal sentiment analysis that handles missing modalities through cross-level reconstruction and contrastive regularization.
papers.title: Hierarchical Semantic Learning for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Missing Modalities
papers.tldr: HSL improves multimodal sentiment analysis under missing modalities by reconstructing modality features progressively across semantic levels and fusing cross-modal interactions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language agents act on native-resolution renders of multi-element pages, where one perturbed photo or a few altered text strokes can redirect the decision. Any content provider can craft such a perturbation on the open model behind the agent, so a plug-in purifier is the natural first line of defense. Yet diffusion purifiers were designed and evaluated at the fixed resolution of the diffusion model on classifier or natural-image benchmarks, and defense evaluations for agents test JPEG, blur and noise but no diffusion purifier. We present the first study of adversarial purification at the agentic level, for an agent built on Qwen3-VL-8B: purifiers run at native resolution on multi-element inputs, face grey-box attackers who know the agent's model but not the defense, and are compared at matched clean cost. We show that treating agentic inputs as classifier inputs misleads both evaluation and design. Resizing the input to the resolution of the diffusion model, as existing purifiers do, raises the TextVQA clean cost of the Divide-and-Conquer purifier (DC) from 4.0 to 35.7 points. On web-shop pages, DC keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy against web-hardened perturbations, where cheap input transformations at matched clean cost keep at most 40.0%, and this robustness comes from the global noise level: input-estimated masks and noise levels add none. These findings hold on a disjoint held-out set and on a second VLM and yield three requirements for defenses, we release the protocol.
authors: Yan Lin, Zhongliang Guo, Jingyu Lin, Daizong Liu
bullets: Native-resolution, multi-element agent inputs can be redirected by perturbing a single photo or a few text strokes.
The study evaluates purifiers for Qwen3-VL-8B against grey-box attackers at matched clean cost.
Resizing inputs to the diffusion model’s resolution substantially increases the Divide-and-Conquer purifier’s TextVQA clean cost, from 4.0 to 35.7 points.
On web-shop pages, Divide-and-Conquer achieves 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy, versus at most 40.0% for cheap input transformations at matched clean cost.
Global noise level drives the robustness; input-estimated masks and noise levels add no benefit, with findings replicated on held-out data and a second VLM.

papers.title: Agentic-Level Adversarial Purification: Revisiting Diffusion Purifiers on Native-Resolution Agentic Inputs

papers.abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) are designed to represent the temporal structure of audio and video, yet it remains unclear how effectively they use this temporal information to relate sounds to visual events. To examine this, we probe an AV-LLM on an audio-visual synchronization task by shifting the audio so that the queried sound overlaps a different visual event. We observe that the model still favors the originally aligned event over the newly aligned one, indicating limited sensitivity to changes in audio-visual temporal alignment. To address this, we propose Modality-Shift Contrastive Decoding (MSCD), a training-free decoding method that emphasizes audio-visual temporal alignment in model predictions. MSCD contrasts logits under preserved and disrupted temporal alignment to favor predictions supported by aligned audio and video. We disrupt this alignment by temporally shifting either the audio or the video, while keeping the other modality fixed. Extensive evaluations with two AV-LLMs across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MSCD for temporally grounded audio-visual understanding. In particular, MSCD improves accuracy over the base models on Daily-Omni by 2.2 and 2.8 percentage points for OmniVinci and video-SALMONN 2+, respectively, suggesting that emphasizing temporal alignment can also benefit broader audio-visual understanding.
authors: Minyeong Jeong, Yeonju Kim, Yong Man Ro
bullets: AV-LLMs may favor originally associated visual events even when audio is shifted to overlap a different event, revealing limited temporal-alignment sensitivity.
MSCD is a training-free decoding method that compares logits under preserved versus disrupted audio-visual alignment.
Alignment is disrupted by shifting either the audio or video while keeping the other modality fixed.
Evaluations on two AV-LLMs across three benchmarks show improved temporally grounded understanding.
On Daily-Omni, accuracy increases by 2.2 and 2.8 percentage points for OmniVinci and video-SALMONN 2+, respectively.

papers.title: Modality-Shift Contrastive Decoding for Temporally Grounded Audio-Visual Understanding

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at static visual understanding and are increasingly applied to spatial planning, where a model interprets a visual layout and outputs an action sequence to reach a goal. Grid games are a common testbed for this ability because their rules are explicit and a solver can verify every move. Yet existing benchmarks mostly report end-to-end success rates, which hide whether a failure stems from visual perception, rule application, or multi-step planning. We introduce GridProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that 1) locates the failing stage between visual perception and planning and 2) verifies the diagnosis by targeted fine-tuning. On Sokoban, GridProbe pairs end-to-end solving with four probes (recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state tracking) and gives every board both as an image and as an equivalent text grid. Evaluating seven MLLMs on Sokoban and a maze game reveals distinct bottlenecks behind similar success rates: proprietary models are limited by multi-step planning, whereas open-source models are limited by rule application or by visual grid indexing, i.e., counting rows and columns. Planning failures also hide perception failures: when planning is easier, the visual cost of the same model grows from 7.6 to 37.7 points. The diagnosis identifies what to train: fine-tuning only the vision module of the perception-limited model on board reading raises its interactive Sokoban success 3.5-fold (5.8% to 20.4%) and transfers zero-shot to the unseen maze game (single-turn success 13.8% to 67.1%), whereas the same data does not help a rule-limited model and training on solver solutions brings no gain. We will release the benchmark and code at https://github.com/suat-llm/GridProbe.
authors: Luoxi Zhang, Tianyi Tan, Jiawei Liu, Xingyu Zeng, Min Yang, Shiwen Ni
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic benchmark for separating perception, rule application, and planning failures in visual grid games.
Combines Sokoban solving with recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state-tracking probes, using both image and equivalent text-grid inputs.
Across seven MLLMs, proprietary models mainly struggle with multi-step planning, while open-source models struggle with rule application or visual grid indexing.
Targeted vision-module fine-tuning improves a perception-limited model’s Sokoban success from 5.8% to 20.4% and transfers to an unseen maze game, while solver-solution training provides no gain.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a diagnostic benchmark to analyze failure modes in Multimodal LLMs during spatial planning tasks, providing insights into the gap between visual perception and planning in embodied agents.
papers.title: Lost in the Grid: Where Multimodal LLMs Fail Between Seeing and Planning
papers.tldr: GridProbe shows that similar MLLM planning failures can arise from different bottlenecks—visual grid indexing, rule application, or multi-step planning—and diagnoses which component to train.

papers.abstract: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.
authors: Luoxi Zhang, Jiawei Liu, Yanlin Luo, Peiyang He, Junlin Zhu, Chun To Choi, Yang Xiong, Jiang Wu, Xingyu Zeng, Min Yang, Shiwen Ni
bullets: Introduces a three-way benchmark: Answerable, Guessable, and Unanswerable.
Contains 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, with controlled wording and visual-input perturbations.
Evaluation of 10 Video LLMs attributes failures mainly to insufficient evidence-sufficiency judgment, not evidence perception.
Targeted guess-level supervision increases appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals.
Conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions, highlighting the need for graded supervision.
