papers.selection_reason: Introduces a diagnostic benchmark for Video LLMs to handle partial evidence, addressing critical challenges in spatial reasoning and understanding within multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Out of Sight, Not Out of Clues: Can Video LLMs Guess from Partial Evidence?
papers.tldr: ClueProbe shows that Video LLMs often perceive partial visual clues but fail to judge when evidence supports a cautious guess rather than a definite answer or refusal.

papers.abstract: Humans can recognize novel concepts from only a few observations by identifying defining visual attributes and eliminating alternative interpretations. However, a single observation is consistent with multiple possible concepts, and accurate visual perception alone is insufficient to determine the intended interpretation. Negative evidence can reduce this ambiguity by eliminating competing hypotheses. Inspired by Quine's gavagai problem, we introduce the Gavagai Benchmark to evaluate whether vision-language models can identify the attributes defining a novel concept from positive and negative examples. The benchmark consists of synthetic images depicting novel combinations of visual attributes and real images of newly described species. Using these datasets, we examine how models use negative examples to identify novel concepts and analyze the respective roles of visual perception and reasoning. Several models struggle even when correct attributes are provided, while others show large gaps when ground-truth attributes are replaced with model predictions. These diagnostic comparisons highlight challenges in both attribute perception and inference from limited evidence.
authors: Katsuya Ogata, Kazuya Nishimura, Yuta Nakashima
bullets: Evaluates concept learning under highly limited positive and negative evidence.
Uses synthetic images with novel attribute combinations and real images of newly described species.
Separates visual attribute perception from reasoning by comparing ground-truth and model-predicted attributes.
Finds that some models struggle even with correct attributes, while others degrade substantially when predicting attributes themselves.
Highlights the importance of negative evidence for eliminating competing interpretations.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for VLM concept learning from positive and negative examples, probing perception and reasoning.
papers.title: What Makes a Gavagai? Learning Visual Concepts from One Positive and Few Negatives
papers.tldr: The Gavagai Benchmark tests whether vision-language models can infer novel visual concepts from one positive and a few negative examples, revealing weaknesses in both attribute perception and reasoning.

papers.abstract: Overall part-discrimination accuracy can conceal failures when image position favors the wrong bilateral part. We examine whether dense descriptors distinguish the correct part under this conflict and whether their discrimination scores help select matching coordinates. We evaluate position agreement and conflict within the same target images and annotated part pairs, using a bounding-box-side score to define the conditions. We compare the original descriptors with their even and odd components under horizontal reflection, examine feature upsampling with the backbone and adapters fixed, and test candidate-selection rules based on odd scores. On SPair-71k, odd discrimination accuracy falls from 86.66% under agreement to 19.63% under conflict for frozen DINOv2, compared with 95.27% to 86.16% for MARCO. With MARCO's input geometry fixed, odd accuracy in box-side conflict was 34.12% on the native grid and 88.84% after learned upsampling and pooling back to that grid. Odd-score rules improve on the original hard-peak matchers overall for DINOv2 and DINOv3 and on conflict queries for MARCO. With MARCO's soft decoder fixed, reranking the cosine peaks changes mean per-pair PCK by +0.47 pp. For supervised GeoAware-SC, using the odd score to select the localization window center yields only 15 net additional correct matches, with 330 corrections and 315 introduced errors. Evaluating discrimination under position conflict reveals failures hidden by aggregate accuracy. Reporting corrections and introduced errors separately also shows whether a discriminative score produces useful matching decisions.
bullets: Aggregate part-discrimination accuracy can hide errors when image position favors the wrong bilateral part.
The study compares descriptor behavior under horizontal-reflection agreement versus conflict, including even/odd components, upsampling, and odd-score-based candidate selection.
On SPair-71k, frozen DINOv2 odd accuracy drops from 86.66% with position agreement to 19.63% under conflict; MARCO drops from 95.27% to 86.16%.
For MARCO, learned upsampling raises conflict accuracy from 34.12% on the native grid to 88.84% after pooling back to that grid.

Odd-score rules improve some hard-peak matching results, but localization gains are limited: MARCO reranking changes PCK by +0.47 percentage points, while GeoAware-SC yields 330 corrections and 315 introduced errors.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates left-right spatial discrimination in dense descriptors, relevant to spatial understanding in vision models.
papers.title: When Position Favors the Wrong Part: Evaluating Left-Right Discrimination in Semantic Correspondence
papers.tldr: Position-conflict testing exposes hidden failures in dense descriptors, while odd-symmetry scores can improve matching selectively but do not consistently yield better localization.

papers.abstract: Multimodal drafts learn from multimodal (MM) and text-only (TXT) supervision, yet their effects on alignment and how to combine them remain unclear. We diagnose draft-target alignment through paired predictions with and without visual input, decomposing distributional error into text-conditioned and visual-response components. Drafts with similar text-conditioned alignment can still differ markedly in visual-response risk and acceptance. Controlled continuation training shows that high-risk groups outperform random and low-risk groups, and visual-response risk guides MM training more effectively than aggregate risk. Building on these diagnostics, we propose MNRS-Joint, which configures joint supervision from a given draft's component-risk distributions, using modality-specific mean risks to determine the MM:TXT mixture. Across three warm-ups, its distinct mixtures fall in high-performing regions of the ratio sweeps. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, MNRS-Joint improves mean accepted length from 3.35 to 3.53 and mean speedup from $2.04\times$ to $2.16\times$ over composition-matched random training under greedy tree decoding. The gains also hold under stochastic chain decoding.
authors: Haozhe Du, Runze Liu, Jiaming Fan, Yitong Tao, Shuxia Lin, Chonghan Liu, Daming Cao, Xu Yang
bullets: Decomposes alignment error into text-conditioned and visual-response risks using predictions with and without visual input.
Finds that visual-response risk better identifies training groups and guides multimodal training than aggregate risk.
Introduces MNRS-Joint, which sets the MM:TXT supervision ratio from modality-specific mean risks.
Across three warm-ups, its selected mixtures perform well; on LLaVA-1.5-7B, accepted length rises from 3.35 to 3.53 and speedup from 2.04× to 2.16× versus composition-matched random training.
Improvements also hold under stochastic chain decoding.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses alignment in multimodal draft training and proposes joint supervision for LLaVA-style models.
papers.title: From Diagnosing Alignment to Joint Supervision in Multimodal Draft Training
papers.tldr: A risk-based diagnostic of multimodal draft alignment leads to MNRS-Joint, which selects MM:TXT supervision mixtures and improves draft acceptance and decoding speed.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance through instruction tuning, yet adapting them to sequential tasks requires Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT). Existing replay-free methods expand prompts or routed LoRA experts across multi-layer decoders, incurring heavy parameter and routing overhead while shifting internal feature distributions. Instead, we identify the final linear layer of the vision-language projector as a high-capacity, coordinate-stationary bridge, where sequential updates easily induce interface drift by displacing historical visual tokens. While low-rank subspace adaptation offers a compact remedy, selecting directions solely from historical statistics or task gradients sacrifices plasticity or stability, and unconstrained multi-step updates still accumulate large drift. To resolve both issues, we propose Projector Refinement through Optimized Update Directions (PROUD), a continual subspace optimization framework for the terminal projector layer. At task onset, PROUD combines retained input statistics with initial gradients to analytically extract a metric-orthonormal subspace maximizing first-order task gain under a drift budget. During training, it regularizes updates within this fixed subspace via an exact Frobenius penalty before losslessly merging them with zero inference or routing overhead. Experiments on UCIT and CoIN across MLLM backbones show that PROUD outperforms recent replay-free baselines in continual accuracy while curbing forgetting with a fraction of trainable parameters.
authors: Hao Yu, Quan Cheng, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Targets interface drift in the projector’s final linear layer, where sequential updates can displace historical visual-token representations.
Analytically selects a metric-orthonormal subspace using retained input statistics and initial task gradients under a drift budget.
Constrains training updates to this fixed subspace with an exact Frobenius penalty, then merges them without inference or routing overhead.
Experiments on UCIT and CoIN across MLLM backbones report higher continual accuracy and less forgetting than replay-free baselines, using fewer trainable parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PROUD. Frozen upstream layers keep the final projector’s input features stationary. At each task, historical statistics and the initial task gradient select a metric-orthonormal input basis. The basis stays fixed while the outgoing factor is trained; its update is merged before the next task.

Figure 4. Subspace direction quality and cumulative drift on UCIT. (a) Held-out loss reduction under matched drift budgets and (b) whitened gradient capture during fixed-basis training on VizWiz-caption. (c) Mean interface displacement D̄t on earlier tasks. PROUD achieves the largest loss reduction, sustains high gradient capture, and minimizes cumulative drift.

Figure 5. Impact of adaptation placement on UCIT. Final accuracy across vision-encoder, projector, and language-decoder sites under a matched trainable parameter budget. Terminal-projector adaptation approaches its joint-training reference shown by the dashed line and outperforms encoder or decoder tuning.

Figure 6. Answer-format retention on CoIN and IconQA. (a) ScienceQA accuracy across eight CoIN stages. PROUD avoids the severe accuracy fluctuations of baselines. (b) Qualitative example where unconstrained adaptation violates the requested word format (11:15), whereas PROUD preserves quarter.

(b) Held-out whitened gradient capture versus final accuracy and backward transfer (BWT) across rank-128 subspaces. PROUD combines high whitened gradient capture with minimal forgetting.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for continual instruction tuning of multimodal LLMs by optimizing the projector subspace, addressing both Multimodal LLMs and Continual Learning.
papers.title: Projector Subspace Optimization for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
papers.tldr: PROUD enables replay-free multimodal continual instruction tuning by optimizing a compact, drift-controlled update subspace in the vision-language projector.

papers.abstract: Given a continuous RGB-D stream and a language request, streaming 3D affordance grounding requires an agent to decide when to respond and where to locate the requested functional part using only observations available so far. Existing 3D affordance grounding methods typically assume complete scene observations, while streaming vision-language models lack fine-grained 3D functional grounding. Our goal is to jointly determine response timing and functional-part localization during continuous scene observation. We propose StreamAff, an evidence-guided response strategy that makes both decisions from the grounding model's own visual evidence. The model scores the visual patches of the frames it reads: their combined support, weighed against a wait option, decides when to respond, and the highest-scoring patch selects the frame to ground in. A conditional look-back policy lets the model answer from an earlier observation at the moment of the request or wait for new evidence, and zoom-and-refine grounding segments the part named in the answer on the 3D points of the selected frame. We further introduce StreamFun3D, a benchmark derived from real-world 3D scenes that evaluates response timing and grounding across four evidence settings: Current, History, Future, and Unobserved, together with StreamIoU, a metric that credits a mask only when the response is timely and grounded in a valid source frame. We adapt offline 3D affordance grounding methods and build external-decider baselines that pair vision-language models with our mask decoder. StreamAff achieves 30.14% StreamIoU on 15-second streams, a 40.6% relative improvement over the strongest of these baselines.
authors: Wenting Luan, Weilong Yan, Siqi Lu, Ming Li, Beibei Lin, Yongbin Zheng, Robby T. Tan
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline 3D affordance grounding and streaming vision-language interaction.
Uses visual-patch evidence to weigh responding now against waiting for more observations.
A conditional look-back policy can select an earlier frame or wait for new evidence.
Zoom-and-refine grounding segments the named functional part in the selected frame’s 3D points.
Introduces StreamFun3D and StreamIoU; StreamAff improves 40.6% relatively over the strongest external-decider baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of StreamAff. RGB-D observations are stored as 3D-aware visual tokens. When to respond: at request step q = 11, the current frame yields WAIT (p∅ = 0.99); looking back over all 12 observed frames lowers p∅ to 0.06, triggering a response at the same step. Scores denote probability masses in this look-back read. Where to ground: the outlined top-scoring patch selects an earlier frame (i⋆ = 4). The model answers from the look-back read and uses its part phrase to segment that frame’s 3D points. Zoom re-encodes phraseselected windows at higher resolution and adds their features to the frame’s 3D features; Refine corrects the decoder mask voxel-wise.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison. Streaming (a,b): all methods see only arrived frames. StreamAff responds on time by retrieving past evidence (a) or waiting for visibility (b); Qwen3-VL deciders respond late or mask the wrong object. Offline (c,d): masks are shown on the 3D points of the same valid source frame. StreamAff better isolates target parts using only frames available at response, while Fun3DU and T-FunS3D use full streams. Yellow: annotated part; green: StreamAff; magenta/blue: baselines.

Figure 2. Construction and evidence settings of StreamFun3D. (a) Construction of a grounded streaming sample. (b) Examples of the four evidence settings. Green marks valid source frames and target parts.

Table 2. Results on the SceneFun3D evaluation sets of StreamFun3D. Cells report mIoU / StreamIoU (%). mIoU ignores timing; StreamIoU (Eq. (1)) additionally requires the correct response step and a valid source frame. Wait denotes the correct-wait rate (%) on Unobserved requests. Best and second-best scores are highlighted per metric.

Table 3. Results on ScanNet++. Each cell reports mIoU / StreamIoU (%) on 220 answerable requests, with the same protocol as Tab. 2; Wait is the correct-wait rate (%) on 74 Unobserved requests from 56 scenes. Best and second-best results are highlighted per metric.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses streaming 3D affordance grounding for embodied agents, combining spatial reasoning with temporal decision-making, directly relevant to Robot Learning and Manipulation and Spatial Intelligence.
papers.title: When to Respond, Where to Ground: Streaming 3D Affordance Grounding
papers.tldr: StreamAff jointly decides when to answer and where to ground a requested functional part in continuous RGB-D streams, achieving 30.14% StreamIoU on 15-second streams.

papers.abstract: Foundation models (FMs) have advanced visual understanding and generation by providing semantically rich representations. However, this role of FMs remains underexplored in human motion. Large motion datasets offer diverse movements at scale, but often lack action labels for systematically evaluating learned representations on understanding tasks. Skeleton datasets enable such evaluation through established recognition protocols, yet are typically smaller and focus on predefined actions captured in controlled environments. To combine these strengths, we present MoSk, to the best of our knowledge, the first Motion-Skeleton foundation model to integrate motion and skeleton datasets. MoSk learns shared representations through self-supervised masked motion modeling. We incorporate joint-name embeddings to provide a common anatomical reference across various skeleton formats. A cross-attention decoder reconstructs masked motion from the encoder's features, with joint-name embeddings specifying the target joints. Experiments demonstrate strong action-recognition performance across diverse settings, including linear evaluation and fine-tuning. MoSk also substantially improves motion generation across multiple backbones through representation alignment, reducing FID on MotionMillion by up to 9.75 for unconditional generation and 3.83 for text-to-motion generation.
authors: Yun Chen, Munchurl Kim, Jeonghyeok Do
bullets: Addresses the gap between large, diverse motion datasets and smaller, labeled skeleton datasets.
Uses self-supervised masked motion modeling with joint-name embeddings to align different skeleton formats.
Employs a cross-attention decoder to reconstruct masked motion conditioned on target-joint identities.
Achieves strong action-recognition results under linear evaluation and fine-tuning.
Improves generation across multiple backbones, reducing FID by up to 9.75 for unconditional and 3.83 for text-to-motion generation.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MoSk. (a) MoSk learns from a combined corpus of motion and skeleton sequences with different joint sets through masked modeling. Joint-name embeddings provide a shared anatomical reference across these formats, while masked modeling encourages the encoder to capture spatial and temporal motion structure. Decoder queries combine a shared learnable vector with joint-name embeddings to specify which joints to reconstruct from the encoded context. Each encoder/decoder block contains attention (MSA/MCA) and feed-forward (FFN) layers, each preceded by layer normalization (LN) and paired with a residual connection. (b) MoSk’s frozen encoder (except during semi-supervised and full fine-tuning) supports action recognition via a classification head and guides motion generators via training-time feature alignment. Snowflakes and flames denote frozen and trainable modules, respectively.

Figure 5. Unconditional generation on HumanML3D and MotionMillion. MotionJiT samples generated with and without MoSk representation alignment share the same sequence length and initial noise. Insets highlight foot contacts, with sliding marked in red (foot height below 5 cm and displacement above 1.67 cm per frame). Labels report foot-skating rate (%) and mean joint jerk (m/s3).

Figure 6. Additional unconditional generation on HumanML3D and MotionMillion. Paired samples show reduced foot sliding with MoSk. Foot-contact insets and metric labels follow the conventions in Fig. 5.

Figure 8. Inputs from motion datasets. Each row shows seven frames after conversion from motion features to MoSk’s unified input format, together with the corresponding text description. MoSk uses only joint positions during self-supervised training. Red and blue mark anatomical left and right, dotted lines trace pelvis trajectories, and grid spacing is 0.5 m.

Figure 3. Text-to-motion generation on MotionMillion and RoMo. We compare MotionJiT with and without MoSk representation alignment using identical captions, sequence lengths, and initial noise. Insets zoom in on foot contacts, with sliding marked in red (foot height below 5 cm and displacement above 1.67 cm per frame). Labels report foot-skating rate and mean joint jerk (m/s3).

Figure 1. Motivation. Motion datasets are large and diverse but often lack recognition protocols. Skeleton datasets provide such protocols but have limited scale and action coverage. MoSk integrates both sources into a unified corpus and is trained as a motion foundation model for both understanding and generation.

Figure 9. Kinect v2 inputs. The examples show joint sequences after conversion to MoSk’s unified input format, retaining the 25-joint layout and relative positions between people. Orange and teal mark anatomical left and right for the second person. ETRI LivingLab is shown for reference and excluded from MoSk’s self-supervised training. Other visualization conventions follow Fig. 8.

Figure 10. Inputs with unseen skeleton layouts. The examples show joint sequences after conversion to MoSk’s unified input format, retaining the original Kinect v1 (20 joints) and OpenNI (15 joints) layouts. These datasets are used only for downstream evaluation, and their joint layouts are unseen during MoSk’s self-supervised training. Visualization conventions follow Figs. 8 and 9.

Figure 7. Additional text-to-motion generation on MotionMillion and RoMo. Each example shows the conditioning caption, its groundtruth reference motion, and MotionJiT generations with and without MoSk representation alignment. Insets and metric labels follow Fig. 5.

Figure 4. Construction of the NTU training corpus. (a) NTU-60 is a subset of NTU-120, and their X-Sub protocols assign common subjects to the same training and test splits. NTU-60 X-View separates training and test clips by camera, whereas NTU-120 X-Set separates them by recording setup. (b) MoSk therefore uses only NTU-120. papers.selection_reason: Introduces a Motion-Skeleton foundation model for human motion, a core component of embodied AI, and demonstrates strong performance in action recognition and generation.
papers.title: MoSk: A Unified Motion-Skeleton Foundation Model for Human Motion Understanding and Generation
papers.tldr: MoSk is a unified foundation model that learns transferable human-motion representations from motion and skeleton data for both understanding and generation.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised cross-modal homography estimation is challenging because appearance differences obscure shared geometric structures. Separating modality transfer from homography estimation helps reduce these differences, but accurate alignment still requires effective geometric representations and consistency constraints on the two subtasks. We propose GeoCo (Geometry-Aware and Consistency-Constrained Homography Estimation), a framework that addresses these two requirements without cross-modal transformation labels. Its homography estimator, RVHomo, adapts hierarchical features from a frozen vision foundation model (VFM) and fuses them with local CNN features to capture structural context and spatial detail. Two geometric consistency constraints encourage modality transfer to preserve geometry and homography predictions to remain consistent under synthetic geometric transformations. Through two-stage progressive distillation, we further obtain GeoCo-D, which uses the lightweight RVHomo-D estimator. An intermediate model first learns to perform cross-modal matching without modality transfer, then transfers prediction and feature knowledge to the student, eliminating online VFM extraction. Experiments on GoogleMap, OPT-SAR, FSD, and VIS-IR show that GeoCo reduces mean average corner error by 17.4-46.7% relative to the best-performing baseline on each dataset. GeoCo-D also outperforms all compared baselines while using 98.5% fewer parameters and 70.4% fewer FLOPs than the complete GeoCo teacher.
authors: Zhuoran Yang, Junchen Yu, Runmin Zhang, Linshan Li, Chenghao Zhang, Hui-liang Shen, Si-Yuan Cao
bullets: Addresses appearance gaps between modalities that obscure shared geometric structure during homography estimation.
RVHomo fuses hierarchical features from a frozen vision foundation model with local CNN features to capture both context and spatial detail.
Geometric consistency constraints enforce geometry preservation during modality transfer and prediction consistency under synthetic transformations.
Progressive distillation produces GeoCo-D, which avoids online foundation-model feature extraction through a lightweight estimator.

Across four datasets, GeoCo reduces mean average corner error by 17.4–46.7% versus the strongest baseline per dataset; GeoCo-D uses 98.5% fewer parameters and 70.4% fewer FLOPs than the teacher while outperforming compared baselines.

papers.abstract: Understanding manga requires connecting who appears and who speaks with the events, character states, and relationships that unfold across panels. We study manga visual parsing through local story understanding: analyzing each double-page spread independently to capture and organize its story information in a reusable structured representation. We propose MangaParser, an agentic reading framework that jointly performs character clustering, speaker diarization, and speaker-to-character binding within a shared multimodal conversation, without additional training or fine-tuning. The agent uses structured story memory to guide character and speaker identification, inspecting relevant image regions when uncertain and refining its predictions and story records together as evidence accumulates. Quantitative evaluations show that our parser substantially outperforms manga-specific models across multiple backbones. Parsing examples illustrate how a unified representation links the character and speaker predictions with narrative content and supporting evidence. We further test reusability through story question answering using outputs generated before the questions are provided. The results confirm output reusability, offering a foundation for manga translation, content retrieval, and question answering.
authors: Yingxuan Li, Jiafeng Mao, Arata Furukawa, Mayu Otani
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting who appears and speaks with events, character states, and relationships across manga panels.
Uses an agentic multimodal conversation to jointly perform character clustering, speaker diarization, and speaker-to-character binding.
Maintains structured story memory, selectively inspects image regions, and refines predictions as evidence accumulates.
Outperforms manga-specific models across multiple backbones in quantitative evaluations, according to the abstract.
Its parsed outputs support downstream story question answering and applications such as translation and content retrieval.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence concerns both scene structure and its temporal evolution. Yet a semantically correct description can conceal a quantitative error: recognizing that objects are approaching does not determine their closing speed or whether they will meet. Such errors are critical in collision avoidance, trajectory tracking, and reactive grasping, where actions depend on motion magnitude, timing, and relative geometry. We study quantitative kinematic understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs): resolving motion magnitude, rate, reference-frame dependence, and future spatial evolution from visual evidence. We introduce the Quantitative Kinematics Benchmark (QK-Bench), comprising 2,341 multiple-choice QA pairs from 379 videos and 17 tasks spanning Object-Centric Kinematics, Camera Ego-Motion Kinematics, and Multi-Object Kinematic Relations. Hidden geometric and temporal signals support trajectory construction and filtering, while fixed kinematic rules map physical quantities to verifiable answers, including categorical labels. Trajectory and question validation ensure target reliability and sufficient visual support in the sampled frames. All models receive a unified monocular RGB input. Evaluations of proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest model achieves only 41.2\% overall accuracy, and spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage. These findings indicate that current advances in spatial intelligence do not reliably transfer to quantitative kinematic understanding.
authors: Lennox Wei, Jiaqi Yao, Shixin Sun, Yuanzheng Zhang, Jianhua Han, Meng Tian, Shaohui Liu, Wangmeng Zuo
bullets: Introduces 2,341 multiple-choice questions from 379 videos across 17 quantitative kinematics tasks.
Covers object motion, camera ego-motion, and multi-object kinematic relations using monocular RGB input.
Uses validated trajectories, hidden geometric/temporal signals, and fixed kinematic rules to produce verifiable answers.
The best evaluated model reaches only 41.2% overall accuracy, while spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage.
Shows that general spatial intelligence does not reliably transfer to quantitative understanding of dynamic scenes.

papers.abstract: Free-text 3D grounding, segmenting in a CT volume the region described by one sentence of the radiology report, could link reports to images at scale, but it is unclear where current models fail. We analyse the publicly released VoxTell model on all 381 findings of the 200-scan ReXGroundingCT validation set, where it grounds 53.5% of findings. Its failures are rarely about which lesion or side is meant. No miss lies on the side opposite to the one named, and findings are almost never confused with one another. Instead, predictions are too large, land on a neighbouring lesion on the correct side, or are missing for small findings, and diffuse findings are rarely grounded. Removing location words halves performance, to the level of label-only prompting, and anatomical rules derived from the sentence never improve the full-sentence output. The same pattern holds on the hidden 300-scan test set. Further progress therefore depends on extent estimation and small-lesion sensitivity rather than on anatomical post-processing.
authors: Abdullah Arif Sheikh, Kamalaker Dadi, Raju S. Bapi
bullets: VoxTell grounds 53.5% of 381 findings in the ReXGroundingCT validation set.
Errors rarely involve the wrong lesion or opposite side; predictions are often oversized or shift to a neighboring lesion on the correct side.
Small findings are frequently missed, while diffuse findings are rarely grounded.
Removing location words halves performance, and anatomy-based post-processing does not improve full-sentence predictions.
The same failure pattern appears on the hidden test set, emphasizing extent estimation and small-lesion sensitivity as priorities.

papers.selection_reason: Error analysis of free-text 3D grounding in CT volumes, directly relevant to spatial language grounding and 3D-aware multimodal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Visual process reward models (PRMs) can detect calculation errors yet assign high scores to steps that misread visual relations. Supervision based on subsequent answer success does not directly establish whether a step's relational claim holds. To strengthen visual-relation verification, we first build an automated pipeline that programmatically verifies each claim and identifies the required objects, relations, and image regions. It produces RelProcessTrain and RelProcessBench (RPB), which tests whether scores respond appropriately to relational evidence through controlled image edits and step rephrasings. Building on this pipeline, we further introduce RelPRM, a visual-relation-oriented method for process reward modeling with two training mechanisms. Relation-evidence self-distillation constructs views preserving necessary objects, relations, and dependencies, reducing the burden of finding decisive evidence in complex scenes and transferring reliable evidence-assisted judgments to full images. Relation-evidence-driven consistency training encourages appropriate score changes when relation edits reverse a step's truth, stability under irrelevant edits, and similar score changes across paraphrases. At inference, RelPRM directly scores the current step using only the original image and reasoning context. RelPRM achieves 66.2% on VisualProcessBench (VPB) and 68.4% on RPB, gains of 4.2 and 9.9 percentage points over VisualPRM-8B. These results show that training for visual relations improves both relational verification and step assessment across broader multimodal reasoning tasks.
authors: Zhaoxing Zhang, Ziqiu Gui, Cheng Chen
bullets: Addresses PRMs that reward steps making incorrect claims about visual relationships despite correct final answers.
Builds an automated verification pipeline and releases RelProcessTrain and the relation-focused RelProcessBench (RPB).
Uses relation-evidence self-distillation and consistency training to promote sensitivity to relevant relation changes, robustness to irrelevant edits, and paraphrase stability.
Scores each reasoning step at inference using only the original image and reasoning context.
Reaches 66.2% on VPB and 68.4% on RPB, improving over VisualPRM-8B by 4.2 and 9.9 percentage points, respectively.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies increasingly operate without explicit HD maps at inference, raising the question of what road knowledge they actually internalize. To probe this knowledge through model outputs, we introduce Road-KSU, a framework that automatically converts HD maps and actor annotations into a road-centric scene graph. From this, we derive road-focused question answering and reasoning targets, complemented by map-based trajectory compliance metrics. Pairing Road-KSU with geographically disjoint splits yields a $2 \times 2$ evaluation crossing output modality (language vs. action) with place familiarity (seen vs. unseen roads). On NAVSIM, 95% of test samples lie within 10m of a training sample, and scores of 13 published planners on turns rise steeply with the number of training drives through the test location, pointing to memorized road geometry. Retraining on geographically disjoint splits and probing with Road-KSU confirm that action-space performance degrades most on unfamiliar turns, with failures dominated by geometric compliance. Language accuracy, however, drops on road-centric VQA on straight and curved roads alike, and remains stable on dynamic scene content. Scaling the training data further reveals a double dissociation: more drives through the same places improve driving on unseen roads but leave road question answering unchanged, whereas spreading a fixed data budget over more places increases road question answering with little change in driving performance. These findings show that improved driving scores need not imply broader road understanding on unseen roads, and identify geographic diversity as key to transferable road knowledge.
authors: Lena Wild, Christian Helten, Katie Z Luo, Jakob Thumm, Rafael Valencia, Patric Jensfelt, Marco Pavone

On unfamiliar turns, action failures are mainly geometric; language accuracy falls on road-centric questions but remains stable for dynamic-scene content.
More drives in the same places improve driving on unseen roads without improving road QA, while broader geographic coverage improves QA with little driving change.

papers.title: Off the Driven Path: Transferable Road Understanding in Driving VLAs
papers.tldr: Driving models can memorize road geometry, while transferable road understanding depends more on geographic diversity than simply adding more drives in familiar places.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a new paradigm and method for giving large language models spatial understanding. Standard language models operate exclusively over discrete words (secondary representations of things rather than continuous space itself), forcing them to guess geometry verbally. Whereas most multimodal approaches equate spatial grounding with camera images or video frames, spatial structure itself is not a picture: it consists of coordinate frames, solid boundaries, and how objects move and relate to each other in continuous space. Motivated by this distinction, we place continuous object tokens combining pose (position, orientation, and scale) and signed-distance shape embeddings alongside word tokens inside a single uninterrupted transformer sequence, allowing language and geometry to attend to each other as object scenes are built and updated step by step. Control tokens switch output automatically between natural-language words and continuous object state updates to a persistent object workspace, while an attention mask blocks earlier prose when generating the answer, so responses must be read directly from settled geometry. To prove this method works, we attach a narrow parallel spatial stream (+4.4% weights) alongside unfrozen Qwen3-1.7B layers. In our two-dimensional tests, the model spawns and transforms multi-object scenes from English descriptions, transfers shapes to held-out nouns, and relies causally on the workspace to answer spatial questions.
bullets: Motivates continuous geometric representations—poses, boundaries, and relations—as distinct from image-based spatial grounding.
Interleaves word tokens with continuous object tokens encoding pose and signed-distance shapes in one transformer sequence.
Uses control tokens and a persistent object workspace to alternate between language generation and geometric scene updates.
An attention mask forces answers to be derived from the settled workspace rather than earlier prose.
In 2D tests, the model constructs and transforms multi-object scenes, transfers shapes to unseen nouns, and causally uses the workspace for spatial questions.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the spatial workspace paradigm. Words and continuous objects share a single sequence through the language model (treated as a black box). Each object combines a 5-element pose (𝑥, 𝑦, cos 𝜃, sin 𝜃, 𝑠) with a 32-element signed-distance shape embedding ®𝑧32 compressed from its 128-point outline [13], projected by𝑊in into object embeddings ®𝑒obj alongside word embeddings ®𝑒𝑤 projected by𝑊emb. Control tokens switch between natural language (Word Head) and object representation (Object Head). Emitting the <LOOK> token masks the entire prior sequence so the model can only read the current geometry from the object workspace.

Figure 6. Coordinate-free scene layout. The user prompt contains only relative natural-language statements with no coordinates or sizes; the model constructs a 2 × 2 workspace layout across four held-out nouns and answers from <LOOK>.

Figure 2. Parallel spatial stream and attention mask on Qwen3-1.7B [12]. (a) Across each of the 28 pretrained layers, a 256-dimensional parallel spatial block runs alongside the 2048-dimensional language stream (+4.4% added parameters). Language features are down-projected from 2048 to 256 dimensions so language and geometry enter each spatial block at equal width, and spatial updates are projected back into upper language layers (ℓ ≥ 6) through zero-initialized cross-projections (𝐵 = 0). (b) Attention visibility across the sequence: text tokens attend causally, object tokens within the same <STEP> or <LOOK> block attend to each other bidirectionally, and <LOOK> blocks all earlier text and intermediate steps.
Figure 4. Assembling scattered held-out nouns across translations and rotation. Dotted outlines and arrows mark the previous step; dark dashed outlines on <LOOK> show exact target polygons.

papers.selection_reason: Integrates continuous geometric tokens into an LLM for spatial reasoning, directly relevant to spatial intelligence.

papers.tldr: The paper introduces a language–geometry transformer that builds and updates continuous 2D object scenes directly alongside text, enabling spatial reasoning without images.

papers.abstract: Understanding large-scale 3D urban scenes requires representations that capture both multi-scale geometric structures and complex spatial relationships. However, existing 3D vision-language methods primarily emphasize global semantic alignment or object-level representations, leaving structured relational modeling underexplored within unified contrastive and generative frameworks. In this paper, we present 3D CoCa v3, a scene-graph-enhanced contrastive and generative framework for urban 3D scene understanding. Our framework features a Pyramid Vision Encoder for multi-scale geometric representation learning and a language-model-based decoder with question-guided caption retrieval and visual cross-attention. We further introduce MSG-based relational descriptions to enrich contrastive 3D-language alignment with structured spatial relationships. To support semantic and relational supervision, we construct City3D-9.6K, a multi-view urban vision-language dataset with aligned visual-geometric observations, scene captions, and scene graphs. Extensive experiments on City-3DQA demonstrate that 3D CoCa v3 achieves 88.35% and 64.79% overall top-1 accuracy on the sentence-wise and city-wise splits, surpassing 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points, respectively. Furthermore, 3D CoCa v3 achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, demonstrating its effectiveness in urban spatial reasoning and geometric understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/3DCoCav3.
authors: Nannan Zhang, Ting Huang, Zeyu Zhang, Haoyu Chen, Yanjie Zhu, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses limited structured relational modeling in existing 3D vision-language methods.
Uses a Pyramid Vision Encoder, a language-model decoder with question-guided caption retrieval and visual cross-attention, and MSG-based relational descriptions.
Introduces City3D-9.6K, a multi-view urban vision-language dataset containing geometric observations, captions, and scene graphs.
On City-3DQA, reaches 88.35% sentence-wise and 64.79% city-wise top-1 accuracy, improving over 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points.
Achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, indicating strong urban spatial reasoning and geometric understanding.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in Japanese-language settings, yet multimodal safety evaluation has been largely English-centric. We extend the Multimodal Safety Test Suite (MSTS) of R\"ottger et al. (2025) to Japanese as the 12th language, contributing 320 machine-translated and post-edited cases with reference answers plus 82 culturally localized Japanese images. We introduce an evaluation framework that (i) extends MSTS's 3-class safety grouping with a 5-point scale that also rewards useful (not just safe) responses, and (ii) separates image recognition from safety judgment to isolate recognition errors. Using this framework, we evaluate five modern Japanese VLMs (Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5, InternVL3, LLM-JP-4-VL, Qwen3-VL) against human evaluation, and find substantial variance in the safety readiness across the models. Finally, we evaluate two LLM-as-a-Judge models and find that providing a reference answer improves agreement with human safety judgments, though recall for detecting unsafe responses remains limited, underscoring the difficulty of automating multimodal safety evaluation. The dataset created for our study will be released upon publication.
authors: Su Myat Noe, Hisami Suzuki, Kouta Nakayama, Naoaki Okazaki

Reference answers improve LLM-as-a-Judge agreement with humans, but unsafe-response recall remains limited.

papers.abstract: Diagnosis of congenital heart disease (CHD) requires understanding the spatial relationships between cardiac structures, which clinicians assess by scrolling through CT or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) slices and rotating 3D reconstructions. Although automated methods have advanced cardiac segmentation, identifying congenital heart defects from volumetric scans remains an open challenge. The two existing approaches rely on handcrafted diagnostic rules limited to static anatomical abnormalities. We introduce CHD-Bench, the first benchmark for interactive CHD diagnosis, defining a multi-label task and evaluation protocol over 247 CT and MRI scans from three cohorts covering 38 CHD types. We also present CHD-Harness, open-source software that runs a VLM in a 3D Slicer environment through 22 tools, manages each examination, and records the resulting diagnosis and supporting views. We evaluate off-the-shelf medical, open weight, and closed weight VLMs and compare them with a 3D CNN classifier and published rule-based results. Gemini 4 Argon with CHD-Harness achieves the highest macro F1 across all three cohorts (0.63, 0.63, and 0.43). Allowing for interactive examination raises its macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views. These results establish CHD-Bench and CHD-Harness as a foundation for developing and evaluating VLMs for interactive CHD diagnosis.
authors: Gautham Krishnan P, Shrisharanyan Vasu, Aniketh Vijesh, Rajagopalan Rameshbabu, Harikrishnan Anil Maya, Sarin Xavier, Mahesh Kappanayil, Gilad Gressel
bullets: Introduces a multi-label interactive CHD diagnosis benchmark spanning 247 CT/MRI scans, three cohorts, and 38 CHD types.

Compares medical, open-weight, and closed-weight VLMs with a 3D CNN and rule-based methods.
Gemini 4 Argon with CHD-Harness achieves the highest reported macro F1 across cohorts: 0.63, 0.63, and 0.43.
Interactive examination improves macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views; broader clinical generalization remains outside the reported scope.

papers.abstract: Wearable assistants must localize interface elements from camera observations when direct screenshot access is unavailable, yet existing GUI grounding benchmarks primarily evaluate native screenshots. We introduce GlassGround, a new benchmark that pairs native screenshots with wearable camera observations while holding GUI states, instructions, and targets fixed. GlassGround contains 3,250 tasks across Android and iOS, captured using four wearable devices under four viewing conditions. Across ten open-source models, mean grounding accuracy drops from 94.8% on screenshots to 48.5% on camera images. Further analysis reveals that changes in target scale, screen geometry, and background cannot fully explain this performance degradation. We then study two ways to narrow this gap. At inference time, local zooming and screen rectification help but leave most of the gap. For training-time adaptation, we build on GlassGround's paired-view design and introduce PairDistill, a baseline that aligns target representations across views alongside coordinate supervision. Trained on independently collected data and using no screenshots at inference, it improves camera-image accuracy by 9.4 and 12.2 points on two backbones and transfers to unseen devices and operating systems. Combined with local zooming, it reaches 69.6% and 64.4%, but does not close the gap. The GlassGround dataset and code are available at https://github.com/yunnw/GlassGround.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in visual reasoning, but extended generation over large visual contexts remains computationally expensive. During autoregressive decoding, visual attention is recomputed for every generated token, even when consecutive tokens rely on similar visual evidence. We introduce VAPOR (Visual Attention Persistence with On-demand Refresh), a training-free framework that reduces this redundancy by reusing visual attention outputs across decoding steps and refreshing them when needed. VAPOR caches the visual attention output while continuing to update textual attention at every step, helping reduce visual grounding drift during extended reasoning. To decide when to reuse cached outputs, VAPOR estimates visual attention mass using a low-rank approximation. It also uses prefill-based attention consistency and cache age to make independent Persist and Refresh decisions for each attention head. VAPOR retains the full visual key-value (KV) cache, so all visual tokens remain available when new evidence is needed. Experiments on eight image and four video reasoning benchmarks across two MLLM families show that VAPOR improves accuracy over dense attention on nearly all benchmarks while achieving 1.11-1.21x decoding speedups. Compared with the strongest state-of-the-art acceleration baseline in each setting, VAPOR further improves accuracy by 0.35-2.15 percentage points while achieving comparable or lower decoding latency. Our code is available at https://github.com/Su-my/VAPOR.
authors: Mingyu Su, Wei Wu, Erle Zhu, Chengxing Xie, Deyao Hong, Hongning Wang
bullets: Targets the high cost of recomputing visual attention for every generated token in long visual-context reasoning.
Uses a training-free cache of visual attention outputs while continuing to update textual attention at each step.
Makes per-head Persist/Refresh decisions using low-rank visual attention estimates, prefill consistency, and cache age.
Retains the full visual KV cache so all visual tokens remain accessible when new evidence is needed.
Across image and video benchmarks, improves accuracy over dense attention while delivering 1.11–1.21× decoding speedups.

papers.abstract: A cart can follow its reference trajectory while its cargo floats above the deck. Asset4D-Bench tests whether coding agents recover objects, motion and interactions from visual references as editable Blender scenes. Its 114 conditions span image editing, video reconstruction with matched full or partial starter assets, and independently selected from-scratch tasks. We independently reopen projects and measure them against native reference states. The 228 archived scores include original delivery outcomes and versioned measures of scene quality. On 24 from-scratch tasks, each model earns full dynamics credit on 14. Of these, three GPT-6.1-Sol and eight GPT-6-Astra reconstructions earn zero relation points. Under the fixed scoring weights, relations contribute 5.15 points to the 6.50-point Sol-minus-Astra difference in mean recovered fidelity. Differences in execution and recovery policy across archived runs preclude a causal estimate of starter-asset effects.

Relation errors accounted for most of the reported mean-fidelity gap between GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra under the fixed scoring weights.
Archived execution and recovery differences prevent causal conclusions about the effect of starter assets.

papers.abstract: Visual language models (VLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities across various multimodal tasks, but they remain susceptible to hallucinations, undermining their reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks primarily focus on identifying hallucinations and describing their manifestations, often neglecting their underlying causes. Specifically, multimodal hallucinations can stem from two distinct failure modes: text modality bias (TMB), reflecting an over-reliance on misleading text input; and language prior (LP), reflecting a reliance on previously learned knowledge. To differentiate these failure modes, we propose VTK-Bench, a benchmark that explicitly separates three information sources: visual information (V), textual information (T), and prior knowledge (K). By establishing mutually exclusive answers corresponding to V, T, and K, VTK-Bench enables fine-grained attribution analysis of model responses. Furthermore, we introduce discrete attribution and soft attribution metrics to characterize information source preferences. Extensive experiments on 11 representative open-source VLMs show that LP is more prevalent than TMB in most evaluated models. Notably, TMB decreases substantially with model scaling, whereas LP exhibits relatively limited improvement and remains the dominant failure mode. These findings highlight the importance of different information source preferences for a deeper understanding of multimodal hallucinations.
authors: Yao Lu, Yuhang Zheng, Yaxin Gao, Zhe Tang, Zhaowei Zhu, Jiaheng Wei, Yunhao Wang, Shanqing Yu, Qi Xuan
bullets: Separates three information sources: visual input (V), textual input (T), and prior knowledge (K).
Uses mutually exclusive answers to attribute model responses to V, T, or K.
Introduces discrete and soft attribution metrics for measuring information-source preferences.
Evaluates 11 open-source VLMs and finds language-prior errors more prevalent than text-modality bias.

papers.abstract: Hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often arise from visual assumptions that go unchecked. Self-reflection, multi-agent debate, and counterfactual verification can reinforce erroneous conclusions when they rely on the same unverified visual assumptions. External visual tools can provide verifiable evidence, but models may select the wrong tools, supply incorrect parameters, or ignore or contradict the evidence they obtain. In this work, we propose EVA, an Evidence-seeking Visual Agent that reframes multimodal reasoning as an explicit process of evidence acquisition and verification. At the core of EVA is a unified evidence-grounded execution pipeline designed to address the above challenges through two tightly coupled mechanisms. First, we introduce Iterative Tool Replanning, which dynamically refines tool selection and parameters based on intermediate observations, improving the reliability of tool usage. Second, we develop Evidence Consistency Verification, an answer validation mechanism that improves alignment between the final prediction and the collected evidence, mitigating evidence--reasoning inconsistencies. In addition, to balance robustness and efficiency, EVA incorporates Selective Evidence Routing, an adaptive fast--slow reasoning strategy that determines when external evidence is necessary. Visually straightforward queries are handled via direct reasoning, while complex or high-risk cases trigger tool-based evidence acquisition. By jointly addressing how to reliably acquire evidence and how to use it consistently, EVA transforms multimodal reasoning from passive answer validation into explicit evidence-backed decision making. Experimental results demonstrate that EVA achieves significantly improved reasoning reliability over direct VLM inference and multi-agent methods, while maintaining efficiency through selective tool invocation.
authors: Ting Lei, Yu Chen, Yang Liu
bullets: Targets unchecked visual assumptions and failures in tool selection, parameterization, and evidence use.
Uses Iterative Tool Replanning to refine tools and parameters from intermediate observations.
Applies Evidence Consistency Verification to align final predictions with collected evidence.
Employs Selective Evidence Routing: direct reasoning for simple queries and tool-based verification for complex or high-risk cases.
Reports improved reasoning reliability over direct VLM inference and multi-agent methods while preserving efficiency through selective tool use.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of EVA. EVA first performs Selective Evidence Routing to determine whether external evidence is required. papers.abstract: Multimodal memory enables long-horizon vision-language agents to preserve and retrieve past experiences. While prior research has focused on memory construction and retrieval, effectively using the provided memory remains a challenge for vision-language models (VLMs). We find that VLMs often fail to answer downstream questions even when sufficient multimodal evidence is provided. To investigate why VLMs struggle, we replace memory images with reference captions and observe substantial performance gains, suggesting difficulties in reading visual evidence directly. However, model-generated captions may omit critical information, limiting this approach in practice. These limitations motivate a closer examination of memory utilization, revealing failures in both evidence reading and downstream question answering. Building on this distinction, we propose \textbf{MemRU}, a two-stage training framework that improves evidence reading through supervised fine-tuning (Read SFT) and downstream evidence utilization through Group Relative Policy Optimization (Use GRPO). Experimental results demonstrate that our 8B model generalizes across three unseen multimodal memory systems, outperforming Qwen3-VL-32B and approaching GPT-5-mini.
authors: Junseok Kim, Kyungmin Min, Kyomin Jung
bullets: VLMs often fail to answer questions despite having sufficient multimodal evidence in memory.
Replacing memory images with reference captions substantially improves performance, exposing difficulty in directly reading visual evidence.
MemRU separates evidence reading from evidence utilization, training them with Read SFT and Use GRPO, respectively.
An 8B MemRU model generalizes across three unseen multimodal memory systems, outperforming Qwen3-VL-32B and approaching GPT-5-mini.
Generated captions can omit critical information, so caption-based memory use is not always reliable.

papers.abstract: Purpose: Figure retrieval from reference atlases in expert domains like forensic pathology, dentistry and geology must work without labels or training pairs, on content that often cannot leave local hardware, and on images outside the training data of image-text encoders. This work proposes a structure-aware pipeline that satisfies all three, retrieving figures through the page structure recovered by layout geometry and a local open-weight 8B VLM. Methods: A geometry-based pairing method is introduced, in which the model receives a schematic of the detected boxes and selects each picture's caption without access to pixels or text. Caption retrieval is evaluated on three private corpora (29 books, 10,421 figures, 218 queries) with blind human grading, against a lexical baseline, generated descriptions and five image-text encoders. Results: Geometric pairing was correct for 96%, 92% and 77% of pictures in the three domains, against 76%, 45% and 53% for the better of two document parsers. A hosted model given the schematic was equally accurate, while coordinates as text lost 22 points. Caption retrieval obtained an nDCG@5 of 0.85, 0.87 and 0.76, against 0.54, 0.51 and 0.27 for the best cross-modal encoder and 0.41, 0.28 and 0.30 for generated descriptions. Pairing errors carried over to retrieval. Conclusion: The proposed pipeline achieves accurate figure retrieval with small local models and no in-domain training, where general and biomedical image-text encoders fall far behind. Its geometry-only pairing is the most accurate of five methods and exposes no content, even to a hosted model. Code and prompts are released.
authors: Argyrios Zafeiriou, Dionysios Koulouris, Ilias Maglogiannis
bullets: Targets expert-domain figure retrieval under label scarcity, privacy constraints, and out-of-domain content.
Pairs figures with captions from layout-box schematics, without exposing image pixels or text to the model.
Evaluated on three private corpora spanning 29 books, 10,421 figures, and 218 queries, with blind human grading.
Geometry-based pairing reached 96%, 92%, and 77% accuracy across domains, outperforming document parsers.
Caption retrieval achieved nDCG@5 of 0.85, 0.87, and 0.76, substantially above the best cross-modal encoders; pairing errors limited retrieval.

Subsequently, near-duplicate drafts were removed on the query text alone, with no image, caption or retrieval result in view, leaving 58 queries in forensic pathology, 80 in dental and oral medicine and 80 in geology, spread over the topics of each domain. papers.title: Structure-Aware Multimodal Retrieval Under Data Scarcity, Privacy Constraints and Out-of-Domain Content
papers.tldr: A privacy-preserving, training-free pipeline uses page geometry and a local 8B vision-language model to retrieve figures accurately from specialized reference atlases.

papers.abstract: Most vision-language models (VLMs) specialize in offline video understanding; in contrast, their post-trained versions, streaming VLMs, can perform live interactions. We investigate whether streaming VLMs can replace their offline parent models on offline tasks. Such replacement could reduce deployment costs and improve efficiency. We propose Streaming Tax to systematically evaluate streaming VLMs on offline tasks. Our exploration spans three core dimensions: understanding, trustworthiness, and generalization across 15 benchmarks. Our findings reveal a critical gap between offline capability preservation and practical replaceability. This gap emerges at two stages: streaming adaptation can alter trustworthy behavior even when offline understanding is largely preserved, while the native streaming protocol can introduce further performance losses. Our analyses show that some of these losses arise from restricted access to historical visual evidence and failures to deliver usable responses. Importantly, regarding safety, streaming models often leave both harmful and legitimate requests unanswered rather than genuinely refusing unsafe ones. We then propose Stream++, a training-free plugin to improve streaming VLMs on offline tasks.
authors: Zhi Yang, Junzhou Chen, Jindong Wang
bullets: Evaluates streaming VLMs on offline tasks across understanding, trustworthiness, and generalization using 15 benchmarks.
Finds two sources of performance loss: streaming adaptation can change trustworthy behavior, and the native streaming protocol can limit visual history and response usability.
Shows that safety behavior often manifests as unanswered requests—including legitimate ones—rather than appropriate refusal of harmful requests.
Introduces Stream++, a training-free plugin designed to improve streaming VLM performance on offline tasks.

We pair six streaming children with five offline parents and compare parent offline (P ), child offline (C), and child native streaming (S), where applicable. papers.tldr: Streaming VLMs may preserve offline understanding but are not yet reliable replacements for offline models due to adaptation and streaming-protocol costs.

papers.abstract: Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. Standard post-training uses outcome reward models (ORMs) that supervise only the final decision, rewarding a confident answer regardless of whether the image supports one, while existing methods either tend to detect uncertainty post-hoc or assume an objective verdict always exists. We instead split multimodal reasoning into two stages: perception, where the model must factually describe the scene, and calibration, where it must judge whether that evidence is sufficient to commit to a conclusion. We introduce HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that scores each stage independently, rewarding agreement between evidence and expressed confidence rather than outcome correctness alone. Training with HumblePRM increases abstention due to uncertainty on ambiguous inputs considerably while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged. We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.
authors: Saket Reddy, Ke Yang, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: Targets a weakness of outcome-only reward models, which may favor confident answers even without sufficient visual evidence.
Splits reasoning into perception—describing the scene—and calibration—deciding whether the evidence supports a conclusion.
Uses a lightweight process reward model to score these stages independently and align confidence with observed evidence.
Increases uncertainty-driven abstention on ambiguous inputs while keeping accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged.
The improvement transfers to the larger Gemma 4 E4B edge model.

figures.caption: Figure 1: HumblePRM vs. ORM supervision on an ambiguous input. The perception step correctly describes how the capsules lack any labeling or context, but the calibration step declares the scene clearly safe and attempts to help without verifying that the capsules are really vitamins, potentially providing dangerous medical advice. The ORM scores only the outcome and cannot separate a misread image from a correctly read one that is miscalibrated, while HumblePRM scores each step independently and attributes the failure to calibration.

Table 3: Gemma 4 E4B study, testing whether the effect transfers across model family and scale. The training pipeline, reward models, and evaluation are identical to Table 2; only the policy backbone changes.

Table 7: Reward model training example for a clearly safe image paired with safe context, illustrating an incorrect perception step. The perception step wrongly identifies the image as blurry, and the calibration step then reasons validly from that false premise; because each step is scored conditional on the steps preceding it, the calibration step is labeled correct even though the trace as a whole is wrong. The PRM receives a label at every step separator, allowing the failure to be localized to perception, while the ORM receives one only at the final step.

Table 6: Reward model training example for an ambiguous image, with a correct perception step, calibration step, and response. The PRM receives a label at every step separator, while the ORM receives one only at the final step.

Table 8: Reward model training example for a clearly unsafe image, illustrating an incorrect calibration step. The perception step describes the scene faithfully, correctly identifying the shattered storefront and the explicit forced-entry indicator, but the calibration step overrides that evidence by inventing a benign professional intent and declaring the request permissible. The response then acts on that verdict. The ORM sees only that the trace ended badly, while the PRM sees a label at every step separator and attributes the failure to calibration rather than to perception.

Table 1: Composition of the two training datasets: 3,000 step-labeled traces for the reward models and 2,500 image–prompt pairs without CoT for the policy, spanning the same four input categories. Clearly safe, safe context pairs a benign image with a benign request, Clearly safe, unsafe context pairs a benign image with a harmful request, Clearly unsafe covers images that are explicitly harmful in and of themselves, and Ambiguous covers images whose visual evidence is insufficient to support either a safe or an unsafe verdict. Reward model traces are split by which stage is corrupted; CP/IP denote correct/incorrect perception, CC/IC correct/incorrect calibration.

Table 4: Help vs. abstain rates for Qwen and Gemma (positive class = abstain). TPR = ambiguous images where model abstains, TNR = clear safe images where model helps, FPR = clear safe images where model abstains (the over-abstention rate), & FNR = ambiguous images where model helps. In both families, the PRM model achieves much better TPR on ambiguous images with only a mild increase in over-abstention (FPR).

Table 5: Examples of intrinsically ambiguous images. Each image supports at least two plausible readings that call for different responses, one of which is unsafe, and nothing visible in the image settles which reading is correct.

Table 2: Qwen 3.5 2B policy model results. MSSBench measures accuracy on clear images; filtered MMSafetyBench measures the rate of abstention attributed specifically to visual ambiguity on ambiguous images. Both reward models are Qwen 3.5 0.8B trained on identical data, differing only in whether supervision is applied at every reasoning step or at the outcome alone.
Table 9: Comparison of ORM and PRM reasoning traces across three multimodal prompts, showing differences in perception and calibration steps and the resulting refusal or compliance behavior.

papers.abstract: Visual reasoning requires models to identify relevant visual evidence and use it to derive correct answers. Outcomebased reinforcement learning (RL) faces two key challenges in this regime: it yields no learning signal when perceptual errors cause all sampled responses to fail, and it broadcasts a uniform advantage across every token within a response. Conversely, while visual self-distillation offers dense guidance from evidence-centered image crops, student learning from token distributions alone often fails to elicit correct final answers. Motivated by an audit of training rollouts that exposes these complementary failure modes, we introduce ViCARD (Visual Credit Assignment with RewardGated Distillation), which integrates per-token visual supervision with verified correctness rewards. For each rollout group, we leverage a teacher with its input image cropped to the relevant visual area, and use this to provide per-token supervision to the student while also valuing correctness. If all sampled rollouts fail, ViCARD samples an additional crop-teacher answer and activates on-policy distillation only if that answer is correct. Together, these mechanisms provide fine-grained visual credit within informative reward groups and a learning signal for otherwise uninformative all-fail groups. Extensive comparisons across model scales demonstrate that ViCARD improves fine-grained visual reasoning performance over RL and distillation baselines, while retaining broad visual reasoning capabilities.
bullets: Addresses two RL limitations: all-fail rollouts yield no signal, and uniform response-level advantages obscure token-level credit.
Uses a teacher model on a relevant image crop to provide fine-grained visual supervision alongside correctness rewards.
For all-fail rollout groups, activates on-policy distillation only when an additional crop-teacher answer is verified correct.
Experiments across model scales show improved fine-grained visual reasoning over RL and distillation baselines while preserving broad visual reasoning.
Scope: relies on identifying relevant visual crops and verified teacher answers for corrective supervision.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Training framework of ViCARD. (1) Verified full-image rollouts determine supervision in (2): crop-to-full scores redistribute GRPO credit in mixed-reward groups, while a verified crop-teacher answer activates OPD in all-fail groups. In (3), teacher parameters, targets, and token weights remain fixed during student optimization on the current batch. The teacher parameters are then updated by EMA for the next rollout batch. Inference uses the full-image student. Solid arrows indicate training flow; dashed arrows indicate teacher scoring and updates.

Figure 1. Comparison between Vision-OPD, GRPO, and ViCARD. All methods train on full-image student rollouts. Vision-OPD matches crop-teacher distributions in (a); GRPO assigns a shared outcome advantage to response tokens in (b). ViCARD uses visual token weights in mixed-reward groups and verified OPD on original student rollouts when all answers fail in (c). Circle sizes indicate token weights; check marks and crosses denote correct and incorrect answers. Inference uses the full-image student alone.

Figure 7. Benchmark-wise performance differences. Accuracy differences between ViCARD and GRPO (blue circles) or Vision-OPD (orange diamonds) on the six fine-grained evaluation tracks for (a) Qwen3.5-4B and (b) Qwen3.5-9B. MME-RW denotes MME-RealWorld.

Points compare GRPO, OPSD, Vision-OPD, and ViCARD under the same regional training setting and evaluation protocol, with each score labeled above its marker. The vertical axis spans 60–80%. ViCARD achieves 75.17% at 4B and 75.44% at 9B.

Figure 10(d,e). Wrong-to-correct visual reasoning (continued). Panels (d,e) reuse the cases in Fig. 3(b,d). In the plate’s base group, one of eight responses is correct; the selected incorrect answer has A < 0, and the centered weight w = 1.127 increases the magnitude of the negative coefficient on “four”. The trained groups in panels (c–e) are 8/8 correct, giving A = 0 and w = 1. The plate crop is enlarged for display; scoring uses the supplied crop.

Figure 9. Complementary visual and reasoning capabilities in six 4B benchmark cases. Group A pairs ViCARD with Vision-OPD, group B pairs it with GRPO, and group C contains cases answered correctly only by ViCARD. HR-8K and MME-EN denote HR-Bench 8K and MME-RealWorld EN; numbers identify benchmark questions. Questions are shortened for display, and answers summarize the saved responses. Boxes and enlarged views highlight evidence for presentation; evaluation uses the original full images.

Figure 12. On-policy diagnostics during 4B ViCARD training. (a) Normalized token effective sample size, computed from pre-update actor/rollout probability ratios clamped to [0.5, 2]. (b) Sampled approximate KL after rescoring the same responses following each optimizer update. Dashed lines mark arithmetic means over updates 341–390. The curves cover 389 recorded updates and are disconnected at the missing update 100.

Figure 11. Token log-ratio distributions before and after training. Base Qwen3.5-4B and ViCARD independently generate eight responses for each of the same 200 training questions. We score reasoning tokens preceding the final answer, with equal mass per image and response. (a) CDF of the crop/full log-ratio ∆ on a symmetric log scale. (b) Tail probabilities of |∆| using evidence crops (solid) or area-matched random crops (dashed). These log-ratios are used to construct token weights.

Figure 6. Correct-answer overlap between GRPO, Vision-OPD, and ViCARD with Qwen3.5-4B. Labels show counts and percentages of all 32162 fine-grained visual questions. ViCARD provides complementary strengths from both baselines, capturing a large portion of the questions that GRPO and Vision-OPD can individually answer well.

Table 1. Main benchmark comparison, with ViCARD generally outperforming other methods. Accuracy (%) following VisionOPD [30]; bold marks each backbone’s best scores, including ties. Fine Avg. weights the six fine-grained tracks by sample count; holdout scores are separate. Dashed groups use a 27B teacher. −fallback removes the all-fail OPD branch. Settings are in Appendix B.

Table 5. Observed limitations of outcome-only and distillation-only training signals. We compare 1595 randomly selected training samples with uniquely matched records from both methods. kG and kO count correct responses out of eight full-image student rollouts in the GRPO and Vision-OPD runs. Rows report overlapping events with their respective denominators.

Table 2. Evaluation benchmarks and metrics following Vision-OPD [30]. The upper block contains six fine-grained tracks; the lower block contains four holdout tasks. Fine Avg. is ∑6 b=1 nbab/32162, where ab is accuracy (%) and nb is the sample count for each upper-block track. All scores are percentages; scoring follows the released evaluation code.

Table 4. Experimental configuration for ViCARD. The listed settings apply to Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B. Each batch contains 16 questions with eight student responses each (128 responses); training spans one epoch with 390 updates. Sequence centering follows token-weight clipping and preserves both mean one per response and the weight bounds. Verified fallback uses sampled-token JSD after a crop-teacher answer passes verification. Each EMA update mixes 95% of the previous teacher with 5% of the current student. Image-token budgets follow the backbone processor defaults with dynamic resolution. Training and evaluation both use non-thinking mode with the listed sampling parameters.

Table 6. Sensitivity of the observational audit. N is the number of matched questions in each cohort; kG and kO count correct GRPO and Vision-OPD responses out of eight, as in Tab. 5. Each rate cell reports the event count divided by the conditioning-set size, followed by the percentage. The final column conditions on kG ≥ 1, giving 292/1242 = 23.51% for all common questions; the corresponding rate over all 1595 questions is 18.31%. “No known truncation” excludes recorded GRPO truncations; truncation flags are unavailable for Vision-OPD. The subsets overlap.

papers.selection_reason: Visual credit assignment with reward-gated distillation for multimodal reasoning; directly targets multimodal LLM training and reasoning.
papers.title: ViCARD: Visual Credit Assignment with Reward-Gated Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: ViCARD combines verified outcome rewards with crop-based per-token visual distillation to improve multimodal reasoning, especially when standard RL provides weak or no learning signals.

papers.abstract: We propose the Audio-Visual Query Transformer (AVQFormer), a highly efficient architecture built upon a 2.7B parameter LLM featuring a fixed-length $K=16$ semantic alignment module, stabilized via Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training (ASCST) with Entropy Regularization. Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on global audio representations to compensate for inefficient, frame-based visual encoders. While our Phase 1 prompted evaluations demonstrate that the Multimodal Base Model achieves strong deep semantic alignment (scoring 0.889 on BERTScore F1), optimizing this architecture for legacy metrics reveals a performance gap. We explore this gap as a hypothesis we term temporal alignment friction: a conflict where global audio representations disrupt the chronological sequence of visual frames, leading to penalties under visually-focused evaluation metrics. Consequently, by stripping away the audio, our Video-Only ablation conforms more closely to this rigid syntax, achieving 63.0 CIDEr. While trailing larger models such as Qwen2.5-VL (67.4 CIDEr), this establishes a strong baseline for sub-3B parameter LLM-based models. This indicates that CIDEr, as applied to datasets such as MSR-VTT, may exhibit a bias toward visually grounded syntax, limiting its ability to fully capture multimodal semantic richness.
bullets: The work proposes a fixed-length (K=16) Audio-Visual Query Transformer built on a 2.7B-parameter LLM.
Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training with entropy regularization stabilizes reinforcement-learning optimization.
The authors hypothesize “temporal alignment friction”: global audio features can disrupt visual chronology and hurt visually focused metrics.
Removing audio yields 63.0 CIDEr, below Qwen2.5-VL’s 67.4 but providing a strong sub-3B baseline.
The results suggest CIDEr on datasets such as MSR-VTT may undervalue multimodal semantic richness.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overall model architecture. The system comprises three main stages: Frozen Encoders for perception, a Trainable Fusion module for cross-modal alignment, and a parameter-efficiently tuned LLM Decoder for generation.
