Figure 3. Model Performance Progression tracking progression from Phase 1 to Phase 2.

Table 1. MSR-VTT test set captioning performance comparing classical non-LLM architectures and LLM-Based Models (Adapted for Captioning). Metrics are abbreviated as follows: C (CIDEr), B@4 (BLEU-4), M (METEOR), R (ROUGEL), and BS (BERTScore F1). All values are taken directly from the respective original papers. Models are grouped by training paradigm: (i) classical captioning models optimized directly for n-gram metrics via supervised fine-tuning, and (ii) LLM-based multimodal models, including parameter-efficiently fine-tuned (PEFT) systems adapted for captioning and zero-shot baselines. All scores correspond to the MSR-VTT test split unless otherwise specified. This comparison highlights the structural gap between models explicitly optimized for syntactic metrics and modern LLM-based architectures, which are less commonly evaluated under such protocols.

The Multimodal Base model extracts auditory context (highlighted in italics), but is penalized because the visually-biased ground truths omit these events. papers.title: A Semantics-First Approach to Multimodal Video Captioning with Frozen Encoders and Stabilized Reinforcement Learning

papers.abstract: Degraded images make vision-language models answer wrongly. Using synthetic paired blur, noise, and low light, we trace which clean image states can still repair those answers from the vision encoder through the language model. In four encoder models, 12 to 23 ranked tokens recover half of the full-patch effect, whereas random orders require four to fifteen times as many; encoder-free Gemma needs 22.2 versus 53.1. Full-block repair expires at a model-specific language-model crossing. The matched reverse-direction intervention is algebraically identical to text-token restoration, so its gap from image restoration measures a redundancy band rather than an independent predictor. A clean-image gray-ablation crossing independently predicts held-out repair with 1.53-layer error, against 3.65 for shared depth. Gemma MMBench has the only large attention-to-repair point gap; Gemma GQA does not. Restormer provides a non-oracle consistency check on two models.
authors: Vishal Bhutani, Prasang Gupta, Sumanth Chundru, Kevin Paul
bullets: Synthetic blur, noise, and low-light degradations are used to trace repair from the vision encoder through the language model.
In four encoder models, 12–23 ranked tokens recover half the full-patch repair effect, while random ordering needs 4–15× more tokens.
Full-block repair ends at a model-specific language-model crossing; encoder-free Gemma requires 22.2 versus 53.1 tokens in the reported comparison.
A clean-image gray-ablation crossing predicts held-out repair with 1.53-layer error, outperforming shared-depth prediction at 3.65 layers.
The attention-to-repair gap is large for Gemma MMBench but not Gemma GQA; Restormer provides a non-oracle check on two models.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes image-token redundancy and repair in vision-language models; fits multimodal LLM understanding and token-efficiency insights.
papers.title: Measuring and Predicting Image-Token Repair Boundaries in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: The study identifies where and how image-token interventions can repair vision-language model errors, finding model-specific boundaries and a strong advantage for ranked over random token restoration.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing seen images from fMRI has advanced through diffusion models, but the current state-of-the-art Brain-IT pipeline still has a lossy bottleneck: its low-level branch outlines the figure well, yet the diffusion model that follows frequently mispaints colour, object identity and layout. We move one step backward and condition the refiner directly on the fMRI-derived low-level image, using six one-hidden-layer MLP heads (scene, main-subject category, count, colour, object, layout) to predict the content prompt that guides a frozen Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 model. On the 930 shared NSD concepts, scored with Brain-IT's own metric code on the same ground truth, NeuroRefine reaches a CLIP image cosine of 0.755 against 0.735 for Brain-IT enhanced and produces markedly sharper images, while the saturated 2-way identification is unchanged. The low-level image supplies an explicit spatial prior rather than a lossless layout: refinement trades some layout agreement (0.541 against 0.638) for semantic fidelity and texture. We then show that the standard panel is multi-factor: a high PixCorr can coexist with completely different content, so we read the low-level and semantic factors separately and quantify where they disagree. Finally, we trace the cortical sources of the prompt heads across subjects and report their causal lesion profile and the fMRI noise ceiling. Direction errors are left to future work.
bullets: Addresses Brain-IT’s tendency to misrepresent colour, object identity, and layout after low-level image reconstruction.
Uses six one-hidden-layer MLP heads to predict scene, subject category, count, colour, object, and layout prompts from fMRI-derived images.
Guides a frozen Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 model with these prompts on 930 shared NSD concepts.
Achieves a CLIP image cosine of 0.755 versus 0.735 for Brain-IT enhanced, with sharper reconstructions; 2-way identification remains unchanged.
Separately analyzes low-level and semantic factors, cortical sources, lesion profiles, and the fMRI noise ceiling.

(B) Content pathway: six independent MLP heads (scene, subject, count, colour, object, layout; 1024 units, GELU, dropout 0.3) predict structured content that is assembled into a content prompt. The frozen Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 editor takes the low-level image as an image condition and the content prompt as text, and returns a 1024× 1024 reconstruction (20 steps, cfg 4.0). Unlike Brain-IT (Beliy et al., 2026), which conditions its SDXL refiner on a caption, NeuroRefine conditions the refiner on the low-level image itself. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a refinement method for fMRI decoding using a VLM (Qwen) with six-head MLP conditioning, fitting Multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: NeuroRefine: Six-Head MLP Content Conditioning and Qwen Refinement for Faithful fMRI Decoding
papers.tldr: NeuroRefine improves fMRI image reconstruction’s semantic fidelity by using MLP-predicted content prompts to guide a frozen Qwen image editor, while trading off some layout agreement.

papers.abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that AI models converge toward a shared representation of the world, even when trained on different data modalities. Previous work has found evidence for the PRH in the activations of vision and language models. In this work, we ask whether vision and language models also converge in how they act on these representations: precisely, in how these internal representations affect the models' output. At a chosen layer of a transformer, the Jacobian lens gives every word in the vocabulary (or class in an image classifier) a vector in the hidden state: the vector that most increases the model's tendency to generate that word, at that position or later, or to predict that class. Collectively, these vectors make up what is referred to as the model's J-space. We find evidence of the PRH in J-space across vision and language models, and furthermore, we find that J-spaces mostly converge up to a rotation. That is, a single rotation, fitted on a subset of words, approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's, and so applies to words and classes it was not fitted on. A word's vector, rotated from a text-only language model's J-space into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model, changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added). Rotated into an image generator's text conditioning, a word's vector changes the object in the generated image. Rotated into an ImageNet classifier (trained without text), it raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa. This suggests that models converge not only in how they represent the world, but also in how they act on it.
bullets: Extends the Platonic Representation Hypothesis from internal activations to how models act on those representations.
Represents each output word or image class by a Jacobian vector in a model’s hidden-state space, called J-space.
Finds that J-spaces across vision and language models approximately align after fitting one rotation on only some words.
Rotated vectors transfer semantic effects across modalities, altering image understanding, generation, or classifier scores in the corresponding concept.
The evidence suggests cross-modal convergence in both world representation and model behavior, within the tested models and tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Explores convergence in Jacobian space between vision and language models, a core topic in multimodal foundation models and representation learning.
papers.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Jacobian-Space: Language and Vision Models Agree Approximately Up to a Rotation
papers.tldr: Vision and language models appear to share similar Jacobian-based output representations, which can often be aligned across models with a single rotation.

papers.abstract: Composing frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) skills under an agentic planner promises scalable long-horizon manipulation without long-horizon demonstrations, yet strong atomic skills routinely fail at seams even under a correct plan. Standard remedies reset the robot's pose or draft entry conditions in language, missing the physical cause we uncover via causal interventions: even after re-homing, a frozen VLA rigidly retraces its habitual trajectory and collides with displaced scene residue, whether or not it can see it. We propose the Skill Envelope, a policy-measured 3D geometric precondition capturing the volume a frozen skill sweeps during successful executions. Exploiting the insight that the rigidity making a frozen skill fragile at seams also makes its trajectory predictable in advance, we expose each envelope as two classical 3D tools (CHECK to detect blocking residue and FREE to locate safe placement regions), establishing a division of labor where VLAs execute in-distribution manipulation and code repairs out-of-distribution states. On LIBERO-Goal with frozen $π_{0.5}$, our zero-failure envelope predicts collisions at 0.946 AUROC (0.944 from one RGB-D view) and beats frontier VLMs on seam readiness (0.902 vs. 0.793); using it for skill ordering and code repair lifts success from 82.8% to 92.3% on two-step seams and from 29.7% to 93.8% on drawer-bearing 3-4 step chains, matching privileged world reset. Together, these results show that reliable VLA composition hinges on measuring a policy's physical workspace rather than guessing preconditions in language. Ongoing work closes the loop with autonomous LLM orchestration, synthesized free-object recovery, and cross-policy evaluation on cluttered benchmarks and real hardware.
bullets: Frozen VLAs can collide with residual objects because they rigidly retrace habitual trajectories, even after re-homing or when residue is not visible.
The method models each skill’s swept volume as a 3D geometric precondition and exposes it through CHECK for collision detection and FREE for safe placement.
On LIBERO-Goal with frozen π₀.₅, envelope-based collision prediction achieved 0.946 AUROC, or 0.944 from one RGB-D view.
Using envelope-guided ordering and code repair improved two-step seam success from 82.8% to 92.3% and 3–4-step drawer chains from 29.7% to 93.8%.
The approach is evaluated in simulation and remains limited by ongoing work on autonomous orchestration, cluttered benchmarks, and real hardware.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Geometric tools detect collisions from depth, outperform VLMs, and repair multi-step chains. (a) Real handoff (push the plate→ cheese in the bowl): top, CHECK flags the displaced plate (red) intersecting the next skill’s 3D envelope Ek (teal); bottom, FREE marks a safe zone outside both Ek and the following skill’s envelope Ek+1 (indigo: wine to rack) so moving the plate will not block the upcoming step (amber arrow illustrates planned free-object repair, Q2, Table II). (b) Pre-execution collision detection across 640 handoffs using only nominal-rollout overlap (no failure data): geometry detects collisions with both drawers (0.986) and free objects (0.847), and a single RGB-D camera nearly matches simulator state (0.944 vs. 0.946 AUROC). (c) Top: predicting whether the next skill will succeed on 429 handoffs, our envelope-based readiness model (0.902 AUROC) beats frontier VLMs prompted with images (Img) or BATON-style text rules (Text) by at least +0.110. Bottom: on 128 drawer-bearing 3–4 step chains, envelope-guided skill ordering and code repair (Plan+Fix) lifts full-chain success from 29.7% (Random+Home) to 93.8% (+64.1 pts), matching simulator World Reset (90.6%).

Fig. 2. Seam failures are primarily physical and policy-specific. (a) Comparing three interventions on the exact same transition and random seed of open middle drawer → push the plate (totals over 10 trials): returning the arm home (Re-homed) still collides 10 of 10 times; erasing the drawer from the policy’s camera input (View Reset, inset) leaves the physical collision unchanged (0/10 success, 10 of 10 collisions); only physically closing the drawer (World Reset) succeeds (10/10). (b) Top: on the same open drawer, push the plate’s 3D envelope intersects the drawer (red, 0/10), whereas turn on the stove sweeps clear (no overlap, 10/10). Bottom: across all nine skills that can follow open middle drawer (dashed green line: World Reset 9–10/10), our 3D overlap cleanly separates the six colliding skills (breaking five) from the three clear ones, whereas frontier VLM Qwen4-Max flags nearly every skill as blocked across 7 held-out trials per pair, even the completely unaffected turn on the stove.

papers.selection_reason: 3D geometric skill envelopes for composing frozen VLA skills in long-horizon manipulation, using policy-measured spatial preconditions and code-based repair.
papers.title: VLAs Execute, Code Recovers: 3D Skill Envelopes Bridge the Compositional Gap in Agentic Manipulation
papers.tldr: Skill Envelopes measure the 3D workspace swept by frozen VLA skills, enabling code to detect and repair physical seam failures in long-horizon manipulation.

papers.abstract: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, outperforming frontier VLM judges by 4.4%-12.8% while achieving at least 90% recall for both human approvals and rejections. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 5.0% to 68.0%. Across 15 models at their highest reasoning effort, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We fine-tune Qwen3.8-27B with group relative policy optimization (GRPO) using our verification programs as rewards, improving pass@1 from 30.31% to 52.19% on held-out instances. Our project page is at https://motion-graphics-bench.github.io/.
bullets: Introduces an expert-curated benchmark of 100 static-SVG motion-editing instances derived from real-world Lottie designs.
Verification programs support multiple valid implementations and achieve 93.3% agreement with human judgments, outperforming VLM judges by 4.4–12.8 percentage points.
Across 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 5.0% to 68.0%; common failures involve poses, motion trajectories, and event coordination.
Using verification programs as GRPO rewards improves Qwen3.8-27B pass@1 from 30.31% to 52.19% on held-out instances.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and GRPO fine-tuning for LLM-based motion graphics generation from images and language; relevant to multimodal and temporally structured visual generation.
papers.title: MotionGraphicsBench: Evaluating Motion Graphics Generation with Programmatic Verification
papers.tldr: MotionGraphicsBench evaluates whether LLM-generated SVG animations satisfy spatial, visual, and temporal prompts using deterministic, human-readable verification programs instead of reference matching or VLM judges.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for long-horizon robot autonomy, enabling robots to reason about objects, their spatial relationships, and past observations across time. However, existing object-centric semantic maps are primarily designed for static environments and rely on an append-only point integration strategy, where newly observed points are accumulated but previously integrated points are rarely reevaluated. Consequently, perception errors accumulate over time, and outdated points persist after objects move or disappear. Although recent dynamic mapping methods update object-level representations in changing scenes, they do not explicitly revise noisy or obsolete points within each object. We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object representations through probabilistic point-level confidence updating. Each object point maintains a confidence score that is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: consistent observations reinforce reliable points, while inconsistent segmentation masks, depth measurements, and visibility cues suppress spurious and outdated points. Combined with object tracking and re-identification to preserve instance identities under motion and relocation, our framework enables object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated. Experiments demonstrate improved mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet, show robustness in dynamic environments and under perception noise, and provide an effective spatial memory for object navigation and embodied question-answering with success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and stale points caused by append-only mapping in dynamic scenes.
Updates each point’s confidence using multi-view temporal evidence from segmentation, depth, and visibility consistency.
Combines point refinement with object tracking and re-identification to maintain identities through motion and relocation.
Improves mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet.
Supports downstream object navigation and embodied question-answering, with reported success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed dynamic semantic mapping framework. Given posed RGB-D observations, openvocabulary detections are generated and associated with object instances in the 3D semantic map. For each association, we perform a visibility-based point confidence update. Points supported by current detections, such as the green points on the table, receive higher confidence. In contrast, inconsistent outlier points, such as red points mistakenly fused into a bed instance due to previous segmentation errors, are down-weighted when later observations identify them as pillows. Points belonging to removed objects are identified through visibility reasoning, assigned lower confidence, and eventually pruned. Unobserved points in the current frame, shown in gray, remain unchanged until more evidence is collected in later frames. The semantic map is updated online in this frame-by-frame manner, while periodic instance-fragment merging reduces duplicate instances and re-identification preserves object identities when objects are relocated and re-observed at new locations.

Fig. 6: Example of handling under-segmentation. A pillow is initially fused into the chair instance due to undersegmentation. Once the pillow is correctly segmented in later frames, our method adds it as a separate instance and gradually removes the corresponding points from the chair instance through confidence updates.
Fig. 7: Example of in-view object tracking. Our method tracks the moving bowl in images and updates its location in the semantic map while preserving the same instance ID.

Fig. 5: Example of object fragment merging. A table is initially reconstructed as two separate instances due to temporally disconnected partial observations at 1s and 10s. As more observations become available at 12s, our method merges the fragments into a complete object instance.

Fig. 1: Dynamic open-vocabulary semantic mapping. Our method maintains a refinable object-centric 3D semantic map through point-level probabilistic updates. It handles dynamic objects that newly appear, move within the robot’s view, or are relocated out of view and later re-identified.

Fig. 9: Examples of object navigation and EQA tasks executed on the Spot robot. Our semantic map serves as an online memory that helps the LLM localize target objects, plan embodied skills, and answer questions.

Fig. 4: Example of handling incorrect detections. A plastic bag is mistakenly detected as a pillow, creating a false instance in the map. Our confidence update mechanism accumulates positive evidence for consistently detected objects and negative evidence for unsupported instances, eventually removing the false pillow while preserving the true one.

papers.selection_reason: Online refinable 3D semantic mapping as spatial memory for object navigation and embodied QA.
papers.title: Point-Level Refinable Semantic Mapping for Spatial Understanding
papers.tldr: An online semantic-mapping framework refines object-level 3D maps point by point, removing noisy or outdated information as environments change.

papers.abstract: High-resolution Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) preserve critical, fine-grained visual details by encoding a global thumbnail alongside multiple local crops. However, the resulting thousands of vision tokens introduce severe computational bottlenecks during Large Language Model (LLM) inference. Existing token pruning methods rely primarily on query-agnostic visual saliency, while current query-aware approaches either operate at a coarse crop-level resolution or compute token relevance too late, after vision tokens have already entered the heavy LLM layers. To address this, we propose a training-free, hierarchical token pruning framework that utilizes query guidance prior to executing any LLM blocks. Our top-down hierarchy first operates at the instance-level, dynamically scaling the vision token retention ratio of each sample based on its visual complexity. Next, at the crop-level, we distribute this sample budget across local crops using sentence-level cross-modal similarity. Finally, at the token-level, we exploit projected vision tokens alongside textual query token embeddings in the shared space to measure fine-grained alignment, applying a text-debiasing normalization to produce high-fidelity query scores. These query-guided budgets and scores are fused with local and global visual saliency metrics to select the most critical vision tokens. Extensive experiments on LLaVA-NeXT-7B demonstrate that our plug-and-play framework retains 98.0% and 94.8% of unpruned performance at 25% and 10% vision token retention, respectively. Notably, at 25% retention, our method delivers a 2.0x inference throughput speedup and even surpasses the unpruned baseline on POPE by 0.7 points.
bullets: Addresses the computational bottleneck caused by thousands of vision tokens from global thumbnails and local crops.
Dynamically allocates retention budgets across samples, crops, and tokens using visual complexity and query-aware cross-modal alignment.
Combines query-guided scores with local and global visual saliency to select critical tokens before any LLM blocks execute.
On LLaVA-NeXT-7B, retains 98.0% and 94.8% of unpruned performance at 25% and 10% token retention, respectively.
At 25% retention, achieves a 2.0× inference throughput speedup and exceeds the unpruned baseline on POPE by 0.7 points.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of our training-free token pruning framework for high-resolution LVLMs. An input image is processed into a full-image view and multiple sub-images, which are passed through a Visual Encoder and Projector to produce visual tokens (V ). A text query is tokenized into embeddings (E). The pruning process consists of three main stages: (1) Adaptive Budget Allocation: A two-level budget is computed. At the Sample-level, a token retention ratio (Rj) is dynamically set for each image based on its visual token diversity (Hj). At the Crop-level, this budget is distributed among the sub-images based on the query-crop relevance. (2) Query Score Algorithm: A fine-grained relevance score is computed between the query embeddings (E) and the visual tokens (V ). Raw cross-modal similarities are standardized using a text-debiasing z-score to produce a robust query score (qsi) for each token. (3) Fuse & Select: The final token selection score is calculated by fusing the Query Score with two visual saliency cues: a local score from the sub-image’s own [CLS] attention (ai) and a global score derived from the full-image view (gi). The top-bi tokens are selected and fed to LLM for inference.

Fig. 2: Adaptive per-sample budget allocation on POPE examples. Our query-aware framework dynamically scales token retention according to scene complexity. The visually redundant snow scene (left) retains only 516 of 2,880 visual tokens, whereas the cluttered baseball scene (right) dynamically allocates 860 tokens to preserve fine-grained details needed for accurate question answering.

Fig. 1: Pruning masks on a POPE sample at a 25% retention ratio. GlobalCom2 uses an image-only mask that is unchanged by the query; for the chair question shown here, it removes most chair evidence before the LLM and answers incorrectly. Our query-aware mask retains the relevant chair tokens and answers correctly.

Avg. is the mean score relative to the unpruned model. Baseline results without a mark are taken from GlobalCom2 [11]; ∗ denotes results obtained by running the released code. The best and second-best results among pruning methods are in bold and underlined.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free hierarchical token pruning for high-resolution LVLMs directly targets token pruning/eviction efficiency and multimodal LLM inference.
papers.title: Hierarchical and Query-Aware Visual Token Pruning for High-Resolution LVLMs
papers.tldr: A training-free hierarchical method prunes high-resolution LVLM vision tokens using query relevance and visual saliency before LLM inference, substantially reducing computation while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Generating 3D-consistent novel views from 2D diffusion models remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. In this work, we introduce a framework that enhances geometric alignment for monocular view synthesis under drastic camera changes by jointly generating a target view and its corresponding depth map. By conditioning the diffusion pipeline on the single source image, source depth, and target camera rays, our approach forces the model to inherently reason in 3D space even under extreme viewpoint shifts. To guarantee spatial fidelity, we propose a novel per-pixel depth consistency constraint, which verifies and enforces 3D consistency across generated views. Our framework establishes a robust pipeline for geometrically consistent view synthesis, yielding superior visual accuracy and spatial alignment compared to current state-of-the-art methods. With this work, we pave the road towards robust 3D world models capable of understanding complex environments from a single view image.
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in 2D diffusion models under large camera viewpoint changes.
Conditions diffusion on a source image, source depth, and target camera rays to encourage 3D reasoning.
Introduces a per-pixel depth consistency constraint to preserve spatial fidelity across views.
Reports superior visual accuracy and spatial alignment compared with existing state-of-the-art methods.
Targets robust single-image understanding for future 3D world models.

figures.caption: Figure 3 ESC Framework. The framework extends Qwen MM-DiT with depth information and Plücker rays conditioning by leveraging LoRA adapters and a Ray ControlNet. At inference time, we leverage PCC-based sampling to enforce improved generated scene geometry.

Figure 2 PCC computation pipeline. The source view (a) is from the original scene, while the target view (f) has been modified: a red sphere is added and a yellow sphere is removed. Top row (∆t, detectingmissing geometry): the source depth (b) is unprojected to 3D and reprojected into the target camera frame (c); black regions indicate pixels outside the reprojection coverage. Where the yellow sphere was removed, target camera rays pass through and hit the cubes in the back instead of striking the sphere surface, producing large positive ∆t values. These inconsistent pixels are highlighted in red (e), with nf = 13703 pixels exceeding the error threshold δ. Bottom row (∆s, detecting hallucinated geometry): The modified target depth is reprojected back into the source frame (h). The added red sphere reprojects into a region with no corresponding geometry in the source perspective, yielding large positive ∆s values and nb = 8581 inconsistent pixels (j). The final PCC score of 0.0232 quantifies the overall geometric disagreement between the two views.

Figure 9 Effect of frame gap onmodel performance. Performance consistently degrades across all models as the frame gap increases. Nevertheless, our method outperforms all baselines at every frame-gap setting on all metrics except PSNR and SSIM, for which LagerNVS achieves the best results.

Figure 1 Novel view synthesis highlights. Given a single input view, its corresponding depth map, and Plücker ray conditioning, our method generates novel views that remain 3D-consistent with the target across challenging datasets (DL3DV, RealEstate10K, T&T) and selective in-the-wild scenes. For the datasets, we illustrate a single novel view generation alongside the ground-truth target, whereas for the in-the-wild setting, we demonstrate two distinct novel view generations.

Figure 5 Best-of-N novel-view synthesis. Each row shows the source view (blue border), ground truth (green border), the PCC-selected best sample (orange border), and five additional candidates (orange border) from the same Best-of-N pool.

Figure 4 Qualitative comparison on novel view synthesis. For each scene we show the input source view (blue border), the renderings produced by the baselines (gray border: PhotoNVS, VIVID, OVIE, GLD, LagerNVS), our ESC variants (orange border: ESC-Shadow, ESC-Base, and the geometry-guided ESC-PCC-BoN (Best-of-N)), and the ground-truth target view (green border). Top: an outdoor scene from DL3DV. Middle: an indoor scene from RealEstate10K. Bottom: the Barn scene from Tanks & Temples. Our variants reproduce scene geometry and fine detail more faithfully than the baselines, with ESC-PCC-BoN best matching the ground-truth target.

Figure 6 Metric correlation analyses. Per-view correlation between PCC and 2D metrics across both experiments. Each point represents a single (variant, view) pair. Red: scale jitter experiment—PCC correlates strongly with all 2D metrics (r=−0.84 for PSNR, −0.90 for SSIM, +0.83 for LPIPS), since geometric distortion simultaneously changes appearance. Blue: occlusion experiment—correlations weaken substantially (r=−0.24 for PSNR, −0.30 for SSIM, +0.22 for LPIPS), as views with large visual differences (high LPIPS, low PSNR) maintain low PCC because each scene is internally 3D-consistent. The strong-to-weak correlation shift between experiments demonstrates that PCC and 2D metrics measure fundamentally orthogonal properties.

Figure 8 Geometrically inconsistent point detections in a counterfactual scene. The real pair depicts a 3D-consistent scene in which all objects remain stationary as the camera moves between the two viewpoints. The edited pair shares the same source image (same left image), and its target image (right image) is rendered from the same camera viewpoint as in the consistent pair. However, one or more objects are displaced in the second’s target, producing a counterfactual scene that is incompatible with the 3D structure observed in source. By projecting the point cloud derived from each image into the other view, the PCC-based procedure identifies points whose projected geometry is inconsistent with the modified scene. These inconsistencies are highlighted as red and blue pixels, corresponding to inconsistencies detected by the forward and backward projections, respectively.

Figure 11 OneBlender +Kubric scene rendered fromall 15 grid viewpoints, with ground-truth disparity overlaid. Each tile shows the rendered RGB view; the bottom-right is the corresponding ground-truth depth converted to inverse-depth (disparity). Rows / columns follow the shared yaw × pitch grid (yaws {−90◦,−45◦, 0◦,+45◦,+90◦}, pitches {−20◦, 0◦,+20◦}).

Figure 12 Scale jitter experiment. Baseline (top) with no jitter, and two variants where each object is randomly scaled by ±5% and ±20%. All metrics degrade together: PCC increases (worse 3D consistency), while PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS decrease (worse visual similarity). Unlike the occlusion experiment, scale jitter is detectable by all metrics since it changes both geometry and appearance uniformly.

Figure 14 Ground-truth versus DA3-estimated geometry for a two-view pair. We visualize three distinct 3D reconstructions of a two-view scene. Top two rows: The source and target RGB inputs alongside their corresponding ground-truth (GT) depth maps (from Blender) and scale-aligned DA3 depth predictions, all color-coded by distance. Bottom row (left to right): (1) The reference GT joint point cloud, obtained by unprojecting both GT depths using GT camera poses (PCC = 0.008). (2) A mixed reconstruction utilizing the source GT depth and the target DA3 depth. The target depth is affine-aligned to the GT scale using a foreground/background split (determined via Otsu’s thresholding on the pooled GT depth) to specifically isolate the error introduced by DA3 (PCC = 0.099). (3) The fully estimated point cloud, unprojected using DA3 depths and GT cameras for both views(PCC = 0.203).

Figure 24 Qualitative comparison of ESCvariants on a simulation environment. Panels show the source view (blue border), ground-truth (green border), and three ESCvariant generations (orange border). The bottom row magnifies the yellow dashed region to illustrate 3D geometric consistency using color-matched epipolar lines derived from the source keypoints. While the bottom-right corner of the pink(red) cube nearly touches the red(pink) epipolar line in the ground-truth, it sits nearly flush in ESC-PCC-FT, shows a minor pixel gap in ESC-PCC-BoN, and leaves a small but more prominent gap in ESC-shadow, establishing the order of geometric alignment quality across the variants in this example.
Figure 18 Multi-view geometric inconsistency of a 60-frame accumulated point cloud (DL3DV).
Figure 19 Multi-view geometric inconsistency of a 60-frame accumulated point cloud (DL3DV).

Figure 17 Multi-view geometric inconsistency of a 60-frame accumulated point cloud (DL3DV). Top: 15 of the 60 input frames (stride 4) used to build the cloud. Bottom: the accumulated point cloud, unprojected from the per-frame DA3 depth and DA3-estimated camera poses and shown from two viewpoints (top-down and front, in the reference-camera frame). Each frame’s depth is scored by reprojecting the global cloud into that view (z-buffer) and measuring the relative depth violation rel = (D − D̂)/D̂; points with rel > τ (τ=0.15) are marked red, with opacity proportional to the degree of inconsistency max(rel− τ, 0) (faint = borderline, solid = strongly inconsistent). Geometrically consistent points keep their RGB color.

Figure 7 Sensitivity of the DA3 PCCmetric to controlled scale perturbations. Starting from a clean reference scene, we re-render each object with a random per-object scale jitter of 1–40% and measure (a) PCC, (b) pose AUC@3, 5, 15, 30, (c) relative rotation error (RPE-R), and (d) relative translation error (RPE-T), with depth and cameras predicted by DA3 and FG/BG-split affine alignment (no top-% pruning). With one exception, all evaluated metrics track geometric error monotonically alongside increasing jitter magnitude. Specifically, PCC rises from 0.07 at 0% jitter to 0.62 at 40%, AUC@30 falls from 0.84 to 0.51 (with AUC@3 collapsing from 0.67 to 0 by the 20% mark), and RPE-T increases from 0.77 to 12.35. RPE-R is the only metric that fails to reliably reflect the introduced noise, remaining largely stagnant and breaking monotonicity at 2%, 7%, and 30%.

Each column shows a source–target view pair: the top two rows are the source and target RGB frames, and the bottom two rows show the fused two-view point cloud (top-down and front) built from the GT source depth and DA3-estimated target depth (FG/BG affine-aligned), reprojected under the ground-truth poses. Table 1 Quantitative comparison on novel view synthesis across three datasets. We evaluate perceptual quality using LPIPS, DINO similarity, and DreamSim, and geometric consistency using PCC, on the DL3DV, RE10K, and Tanks & Temples datasets. Oracle indicates the ground-truth label compared against the paired DA3 estimate on the source images. The best, second-best, and third-best results among the ESCvariants in each row are highlighted. Table 5 Mixed training configuration. Values reproduced verbatim from the released config.json (mixed-DA3 run).

papers.title: ESC: Escaping 2D Diffusion Ambiguity with Geometric Constraints for Consistent Novel View Synthesis
papers.tldr: ESC improves 3D-consistent novel-view synthesis by jointly generating target images and depth while enforcing per-pixel geometric consistency.

papers.abstract: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.
authors: Binfei Ji, Zhiwen Cao, Anqi Yang, Prem Seetharaman, Shuo Yang, Ratheesh Kalarot, Yingyan Celine Lin, Mingze Xu
bullets: Addresses the tight coupling between utterance timing and audiovisual diarization in video captioning.
Uses a two-stage approach: synthetic-caption training on 225K clips, followed by reinforcement learning from 2.9K human-corrected clips.
Generates transcripts, utterance timestamps, speaker grouping, and visual descriptions for each utterance.
On DiaDemBench, achieves strong diarization and substantially better timestamp accuracy than Gemini 4 Argon (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME).
Maintains performance on multilingual and minute-long videos and transfers to audiovisual question answering.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison with similar-looking speakers. Each track shows one model’s predicted utterances over time, colored by the ground-truth speaker that its description depicts, with wrong speakers outlined in dark red.

Figure 11. A one-word turn right before another speaker (Mandarin). The young man answers with a single syllable lasting 0.3s (first frame), and the man in the gray suit continues immediately (second frame). DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E keep the short turn as a separate line with the correct speaker. Gemini 4 Argon and DiaDem merge it into the next speaker’s line, so turn A is lost. Gemini’s timestamps also miss every boundary (TIME 0), and DiaDem predicts none. This example shows that accurate timestamps and diarization are tightly coupled, as a model without precise turn boundaries tends to absorb a short turn into a longer neighboring one.

Figure 2. Overview of DiaCap. A speech recognizer Ψ transcribes the audio, and an audiovisual LLM Θ takes the transcript T together with the video and audio to predict the timestamps and speaker of every utterance. DiaCap-E2E predicts Y directly without a recognizer.

Figure 7. Failure case: off-screen speaker merged with the on-screen one. In a handheld phone video, a girl (A) asks her mother where she is going, and the mother (B) answers from off-screen. DiaCap describes a single speaker, gives the mother’s reply (“I’ll go wherever I want”) to the girl, and drops the mother’s cut-off last words. Since only the girl is ever on screen, the model does not infer that a second person is speaking.

Figure 9. Off-screen speakers in a multi-shot scene. The first and last turns are spoken while the camera shows someone else. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute all four turns correctly and describe these speakers as off-screen voices. Gemini 4 Argon gives the woman’s “Uh, Nal-what?” to the man in the blue lab coat and truncates it. DiaDem describes both men only as “man in a lab coat”, so the second man’s two turns go to the first man.

Figure 8. One speaker who goes off-screen. In this typical shot/reverse-shot conversation, a single woman speaks both lines. During the second line, the camera cuts to the listener and the speaker is off-screen. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute both lines to the same speaker. Gemini 4 Argon gives the second line to the visible listener (short reddish-brown hair). DiaDem’s description (“woman with shoulder-length brown hair”) is too generic to identify the speaker, so neither of its lines is credited.

Figure 10. A speaker seen only from behind. The last line is spoken by the man with his back to the camera. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute it to him. Gemini 4 Argon gives it to the man in the gray suit and DiaDem to the man with the mustache, the two people whose faces are visible.

Figure 12. A short interjection from a third speaker. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute all four turns correctly and place every boundary within the collar. Gemini 4 Argon merges the woman’s two turns into one line, so when scoring Gemini, we merge consecutive groundtruth utterances from the same speaker, which leaves three ground-truth turns. Gemini’s timestamps miss most boundaries (TIME 33). DiaDem describes the speaker of the final interjection only as “man’s voice”, which depicts none of the people in the scene.

Figure 13. Four speakers in one room. DiaCap, DiaCap-E2E, and Gemini 4 Argon attribute all five turns correctly. DiaDem gets three of the five turns wrong. It gives “Are you serious?” (C) and “Me too.” (D) to the young woman, and gives her own “I’m okay with that.” to a young man. Gemini’s timestamps drift by about 0.7s on the last three turns (TIME 40), whereas both DiaCap variants place every boundary within the collar (TIME 100).

Figure 3. Training data curation and annotation. (1) Audio, audiovisual, and visual experts tag each clip. We remove clips with unrelated or out-of-sync audio, deduplicate and resample the rest to balance language, speaker count, and visual scenes, and add no-speech clips with empty targets. (2) An audiovisual LLM annotates who says what, and a speech aligner timestamps each utterance. (3) Human annotators correct hard clips mined from the SFT corpus, plus fewer single-speaker clips, to form the RL corpus.
Figure 5. Failure cases. Top: small, distant faces cause segmentation and attribution errors. Bottom: overlapping speech is missed.

Figure 1. Comprehensive dialogue captioning. DiaCap describes who says what, and when, in a single caption. Whereas audio-only diarization assigns each speaker only an anonymous ID, DiaCap identifies each speaker with a detailed description.

papers.abstract: The development of biomedical vision-language models (VLMs) with contrastive image-text pretraining has been driven by scaling to increasingly large and diverse image-text datasets. Beyond scaling, further progress can come from learning richer representations from existing data. We hypothesize that the structure of scientific literature itself provides an additional source of supervision: figures, panels, captions, and accompanying article text encode rich relationships across modalities. Yet, treating these as independent image-text pairs overlooks their relationships. To address this limitation, we incorporate these structural relationships into contrastive image-text supervision. We preserve exact image-text matches while introducing weaker positive supervision for related pairs, such as a panel and the caption of a sibling panel. We upweight cross-article negatives of the same content type to encourage finer discrimination. We also enrich panel descriptions using visual content, original figure captions, and mentioning paragraphs. Pairing panels with these descriptions and whole figures with their original captions yields Loom52M, a dataset of 52.4 million image-text pairs spanning scientific charts and biomedical images. Using Loom52M, BioLoom (DFN-2B) achieves 56.82% domain-balanced mean accuracy across 67 zero-shot classification tasks from 43 datasets in 10 domains, compared with 48.77% for MedPMC-CLIP. On BioLoomBench with concise captions and BioMedFlickr, it achieves bidirectional mean Recall@1 of 63.20% and 10.59%, versus 46.37% and 7.55% for the respective strongest evaluated baselines, BiomedCLIP and MedPMC-CLIP. Code, datasets, benchmarks, and models are available at https://bioloom-clip.github.io/.
authors: Yuwei Yang, Xiaoxiao Sun, Alejandro Lozano, Yuan-Sen Ting, Yuhui Yuan, Liang Zheng, Serena Yeung-Levy
bullets: Scientific articles provide richer supervision than treating each image-text pair independently.

BioLoom reports stronger zero-shot classification and image-text retrieval performance than the evaluated baselines across biomedical benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments.
authors: Zehan Zheng, Yanyuan Chen, Deming Li, Yutao Tang, Jianwen Xie, Alan Yuille, Jieneng Chen, Cheng Peng

Finds outdoor environments are substantially more demanding than indoor settings, with poor performance from existing models.
Highlights multimodal interaction and long-term spatial reasoning as key directions for embodied intelligence.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video question answering enables blind and low-vision (BLV) users to query their immediate surroundings through natural language. However, existing benchmarks and models primarily optimize for semantic agreement with reference answers, reducing visual assistance to a purely factual matching task. In real-world scenarios, a factually correct response remains practically unhelpful if it lacks the spatial orientation, actionable detail, or conciseness required by the immediate task of the user. Drawing upon real BLV egocentric videos and authentic user queries from EgoBlind, we construct the PA-EgoQA, a preference-aligned dataset that reconstructs reference answers according to empirical BLV communication criteria. Based on this dataset, we introduce Preference-Aligned Visual Egocentric Learning (PAVE), a unified learning and inference framework that couples structured answer-policy fine-tuning with deterministic question-conditioned routing to adapt response formulation directly to the surface form of the query at inference time. We further align the model via Filter-GRPO, which pairs a hierarchical correctness-quality reward with contrast-based candidate-group filtering to extract learning signals from both factual accuracy contrasts and fine-grained quality variations among correct answers. Extensive experiments across three vision-language backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in factual accuracy alongside substantial gains in assistive response quality. These results establish a concrete paradigm for translating human-centered response requirements into egocentric supervision, generation policies, and post-training objectives. Code will be provided at https://github.com/shawnliang420/PAVE.

papers.abstract: Structured clinical decisions from volumetric computed tomography (CT) require anatomically grounded predictions and calibrated confidence estimates. However, existing 3D medical multimodal models often suffer from uncalibrated autoregressive decoding and shortcut reliance on irrelevant anatomical regions. We introduce Radev, a decision-native multimodal model that integrates anatomy-guided visual compression, direct candidate prediction, and counterfactual confidence supervision. To bridge global context with fine-grained slice details, a frozen 3D encoder extracts reusable organ-level features, which are dynamically selected by the query to attend to 2D slice features within predicted anatomical bounds. The resulting compact visual tokens enable the language backbone to estimate candidate probabilities in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding. We further propose Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT) to compare predictions under intact and intervened organ representations. CCT encourages confidence to decrease when removing target-organ evidence degrades decision quality, while penalizing excessive confidence drops under unrelated-organ removal. To facilitate rigorous evaluation, we construct CT-Verdict, a comprehensive benchmark spanning binary finding presence, multiple-choice questions, and ordinal severity assessment across both in-distribution and external cohorts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Radev significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both decision accuracy and confidence calibration, while generalizing robustly under distribution shifts. Project page at https://juntaojianggavin.github.io/projects/Radev/
authors: Juntao Jiang, Wenqi Zhong, Guangyu Guo, Dexia Chen, Yilong Hu, Yunhao Bai, Zhenyu Yi, Jianwei Xu, Tony C. W. Mok, Muxuan Gao, Ling Zhang, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang, Zhongwei Qiu

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) used in robot task planning to derive assembly procedures from existing manuals may correctly interpret individual assembly actions yet confuse exact part identities, predict unsupported Part IDs, or produce inconsistent parts across assembly steps. Thus, we propose CAPER (Capacity-Aware Part-grounding and Evidence Refinement), a manual-guided robotic assembly framework that enables VLMs to generate assembly procedures with two modules--PartGround and PlanRefine. PartGround aligns step-level manual evidence with product-specific inventory and part-reference information to identify exact Part IDs and quantities, transforming free-form hardware prediction into evidence-guided assignments represented in a shared Assembly Intermediate Representation (Assembly IR). PlanRefine audits PartGround assignments against finite inventory by removing the lowest-confidence assignments. Uncertain identity cases remain marked for review in the Assembly IR. We evaluate CAPER on the IKEA Assembly in the Wild (IAW) dataset. Experiment results show that CAPER reaches a Finite-inventory Consistency Rate of 83.33% and produces zero observed out-of-inventory Part-ID occurrences. At the plan level, PlanRefine removes all observed inventory-overuse pairs (9 -> 0) and excess units (51 -> 0). Overall, the results indicate that PartGround and PlanRefine improve part reliability, while also enhancing finite-inventory consistency and local prediction accuracy. Project page and video: https://xhzzzz123.github.io/CAPER/

On the IAW dataset, CAPER achieved 83.33% finite-inventory consistency with zero observed out-of-inventory Part-ID occurrences.
It reduced inventory-overuse pairs from 9 to 0 and excess units from 51 to 0.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a vision-language model on its own failures is a direct way to repair it, but accuracy on held-out failures, the obvious measure of success, misleads. Many mined failures are not model errors: a human audit of 100 failures of Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct on questions generated from COCO and GQA found label errors in 37. And mined failures share wording regularities: question-only classifiers get both answers right on 73.2% of held-out failure pairs. We study both traps with verified failure-driven repair (VFR): typed minimal-pair failure mining, verification by three LLM judges that answer without seeing the stored labels, answer-first corrective targets, and LoRA fine-tuning with replay. VFR repairs 82.8% of held-out failures (base model: 10.0%), and on independently labeled, unconditioned pairs it raises overall accuracy from 87.4% to 92.4% through spatial relations, whose accuracy rises from 66.7% to 96.8% even where the wording points to the wrong answer. Yet on negation, of which it repairs 88.9% of held-out failures, its accuracy on unconditioned pairs falls from 88.7% to 79.7%: it breaks negations about absent objects, rare in its training set. Without verification, accuracy on unconditioned pairs falls to 80.8%, below the base model's 87.4%, through a negation shortcut our development benchmarks miss; without failure selection, it stays at 92.0% (one seed) while repair falls to 73.4%. Training also lowers two-image relation accuracy (74.3% to 49.6%; replay data alone: 48.4%); multi-image replay partly and unevenly reverses this. Paraphrasing the spatial questions keeps most of the gain (87.3% vs. the base model's 62.0%), though rewording lowers spatial repair on held-out failures from 92.9% to 76.8%. On What'sUp's independent photos of objects under others, caption choice stays perfect while accuracy on our yes/no pairs falls from 84.5% to 26.4%.
bullets: A human audit found 37% of 100 mined Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct failures had incorrect labels, while question wording alone often predicted answers.
The proposed VFR method uses typed minimal-pair mining, LLM verification, answer-first targets, and LoRA fine-tuning with replay.
VFR raised held-out-failure repair from 10.0% to 82.8% and overall accuracy on independent pairs from 87.4% to 92.4%, especially for spatial relations.
Verification prevented a negation shortcut: removing it reduced independent-pair accuracy to 80.8%; VFR nevertheless hurt negation and two-image relation performance.
Gains were sensitive to wording and distribution: performance dropped on rephrased spatial questions and independent What'sUp photos, where accuracy fell to 26.4%.

papers.abstract: Reliable driving VLMs must do more than answer correctly or localize relevant scene actors: they must determine whether the available visual evidence is sufficient to support an answer. Existing evaluations largely treat grounding and answerability as separate measurements, making it difficult to distinguish well-supported predictions from those localized to relevant but insufficient evidence. We introduce DriveAnswer, a benchmark of 20,151 questions across seven reasoning families, that operationalizes this distinction using matched strong- and weak-evidence configurations. Each pair preserves the underlying scene fact and semantic answer while changing whether the observations support answering, making abstention the appropriate response under weak evidence. On the six-family evaluation, the strongest zero-shot baseline reaches 67.31% strong-evidence accuracy, yet only 21.55% of matched questions satisfy both answer-abstain behavior and complete grounding. With controlled adaptation, Gemma-4-12B reaches 63.29% on this joint capability, nearly tripling its zero-shot performance. Qwen3-VL-8B exhibits the same broad improvement in evidence-sensitive answering and grounding. These results show that semantic correctness, evidence sufficiency, and grounding are distinct capabilities that should be evaluated jointly.
authors: Nhat Ha Nguyen, Sudipta Chowdhury, Lokesh Das
bullets: Introduces 20,151 questions across seven reasoning families with matched strong- and weak-evidence scene configurations.
Tests answer correctness, abstention under weak evidence, and complete grounding jointly rather than separately.
The strongest zero-shot baseline achieves 67.31% strong-evidence accuracy but only 21.55% joint answer-abstain and grounding performance.
Controlled adaptation substantially improves evidence-sensitive answering and grounding, with Gemma-4-12B reaching 63.29% joint capability.
Findings show that semantic correctness, evidence sufficiency, and grounding are distinct capabilities.

papers.abstract: Metacognition includes knowing one's own strengths and weaknesses across kinds of tasks, not only judging whether a single answer is correct. We test whether vision-language models (VLMs) know in advance which kinds of visual tasks and image conditions are hard for them, across a wide range of open and proprietary models. Because some tasks are hard for every model, we separate what a model knows about this shared difficulty from what it knows about itself. We find that VLMs know little in advance about their visual weaknesses. They misjudge their overall accuracy and do not even know which kinds of tasks are hard for every model, and most misjudge how degraded images affect them. We further train VLMs to predict their own accuracy, which teaches them their own level of accuracy on kinds unseen in training but not which kinds are hard for them. However, information about these weaknesses appears once a model starts solving. On a few unlabeled questions of a kind, the probability a model assigns to its own answers follows weaknesses particular to the model, across kinds of tasks and image conditions. VLMs thus hold information about their own weaknesses that their stated predictions do not yet reflect. By separating what is particular to a model from what holds for every model, our evaluation offers a test for methods that aim to teach VLMs their own weaknesses, and the answer probability offers them a signal to start from.
bullets: Evaluates metacognition across visual task types and image conditions in open and proprietary VLMs.
Separates model-specific weaknesses from difficulties shared by all models.
Finds VLMs misjudge both their overall accuracy and the effects of degraded images.
Training models to predict accuracy transfers across unseen task kinds but does not reveal which kinds are personally difficult.
After solving a few unlabeled examples, answer probabilities reflect model-specific weaknesses and provide a signal for improving self-awareness.

papers.title: Do Vision-Language Models Know Their Own Visual Weaknesses? Probing Capability-Level Metacognition
papers.tldr: Vision-language models generally fail to anticipate their own visual weaknesses, but their answer probabilities reveal these weaknesses after seeing a few examples.

papers.abstract: Independently pretrained vision and language models may learn shared structures of the same underlying world, providing a foundation for combining them to build multimodal capabilities. However, a key challenge remains in aligning cross-modal feature representations while preserving access to visual information before and after language adaptation. To this end, we propose sparse alignment with visual evidence-guided residual adaptation (SAVERA), a framework that combines frozen vision and language models through bidirectional alignment in a shared sparse space and prompt-guided residual fusion. Specifically, we first present shared-space projection, activation reconstruction and encoding (SPARE), which represents original visual, adapted visual, and textual features through shared soft-gated sparse encoding, with branch-specific reconstruction to preserve their respective information. Second, we devise bridge--text embedding and activation matching (BEAM), a bidirectional cross-modal alignment module that aligns adapted visual and textual features at both the sample and neuron levels, establishing fine-grained cross-modal correspondence. Finally, we introduce prompt-conditioned residual integration of vision and adapted features (PRIVA), a prompt-guided residual fusion module that models vision--language interactions through gating and attention and integrates complementary information from original and adapted representations through residual fusion. Extensive experiments show that SAVERA achieves competitive performance on image captioning and visual question answering while reducing object hallucination.
authors: Jiajun Shen, Chuancheng Shi, Jiayi Lyu, Yanpeng Sun, Fei Shen, Tat-Seng Chua
bullets: Addresses cross-modal alignment while preserving visual information before and after language adaptation.
Uses SPARE for shared soft-gated sparse representations with branch-specific reconstruction.
Uses BEAM to align adapted visual and textual features at sample and neuron levels.
Uses PRIVA for prompt-conditioned gating, attention, and residual fusion of original and adapted visual features.
Reports competitive image-captioning and visual-question-answering performance with reduced object hallucination.

papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems for computed tomography (CT) remain largely restricted to specific anatomical regions, examination types or predefined abnormalities, limiting their ability to provide comprehensive and spatially grounded interpretations. Here we present FORA, a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts and generates reports across the 28 CT protocols represented in our cohort. Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations supervised by their accompanying reports, FORA learns to localize abnormalities without manually annotated lesions. Its architecture combines multiple-instance learning with an interpretable concept bottleneck that connects spatial evidence, radiological findings and report generation. We first developed and benchmarked the architecture on chest radiographs, achieving state-of-the-art performance, before training a separate model on three-dimensional CT examinations. On 36,619 held-out CT examinations, FORA achieved a macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918 for radiological concept recognition, exceeding the strongest of 18 existing CT models by 0.21. FORA also ranked first on three public benchmarks, outperforming Merlin on its own test set without training on that institution's data (AUROC 0.907 versus 0.826). On independent localization benchmarks for pulmonary emboli, renal masses and rib fractures, FORA's strongest spatial evidence fell within annotated lesions at rates up to 348 times greater than chance. FORA achieved more than threefold higher macro-averaged finding recall than the strongest existing report generator. These results show that a single model can combine broad abnormality recognition, spatial localization and report generation across 12 CT examination types, using routine reports without lesion-level supervision.
authors: Sezgin Er, Utku Turkbey, Alperen Gur, Omer Faruk Durugol, Suprosanna Shit, Murong Xu, Julia Wolleb, Jiayi Wang, Xiaoliang Wang, Hadrien Reynaud, Teodora Spasojevic, Dong Yang, Andriy Myronenko, Pengfei Guo, Yufan He, Can Zhao, Marc Edgar, Andreas Maier, Michael Moor, Mehmet Kemal Ozdemir, Daguang Xu, Bernhard Kainz, Bjoern Menze, Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci

papers.abstract: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict geometry. However, their progress cannot be measured reliably. Published numbers are not comparable, because every paper samples frames, sets resolutions, and selects test splits differently. They are not robust because the alignment required for every up-to-scale prediction can outweigh the gap between models: fitting depth in the wrong space nearly triples its error, and standard trajectory alignment understates the error of failing methods by up to $2.6\times$. And they rarely cover long recordings, dynamic scenes, or aerial views. We present SpatialArena, an open arena that scores geometric models with the same metrics and rules, with robust and deterministic alignment. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular depth to SLAM. It covers 23 public datasets with 418,929 images across indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes, together with Spatial Arena, our own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, we find that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, and that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and overtake video depth models. The benchmark, toolbox, and leaderboard will be publicly released.
authors: Yu Chen, Haosen Yang, Su Ee Tan, Zhensong Zhang, Jifei Song, Jiankang Deng
bullets: Existing results are difficult to compare because papers use different sampling, resolutions, test splits, and alignment procedures.
The arena evaluates five tasks—including monocular depth, 3D/4D reconstruction, and SLAM—on 23 public datasets plus new captures spanning indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes.
Its deterministic alignment and common metrics address evaluation failures that can substantially distort reported errors.
Across 52 models, single-image depth is near saturation on public benchmarks but remains challenging in large, uncontrolled scenes.
Progress increasingly depends on cross-frame and cross-view consistency: feed-forward 3D/4D models match or exceed monocular specialists and outperform video depth models.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are transforming recommender systems into content-aware decision systems. In these systems, multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion are often viewed as robustness-enhancing mechanisms against content manipulation, as compression can filter noisy signals and cross-modal consensus can suppress inconsistent anomalies. We challenge this assumption by showing that the same process can expose a compression-to-consensus (C2C) bias in ranking decisions. Signals that remain salient after compression and receive consistent support across modalities can gain disproportionate influence in candidate comparison, offering an exploitable direction for content manipulation. In this paper, we introduce C3H, a novel inference-time attack that exploits this vulnerability. Rather than relying on noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, C3H promotes a target item by tailoring its multimodal content to align with the decision criteria implicitly expressed by the recommender. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. Code is available at https://github.com/GuoweiGuan666/C3H.
authors: Guowei Guan, Yurong Hao, Jiaming Zhang, Fuyao Zhang, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
bullets: Multimodal compression and cross-modal agreement can unintentionally amplify salient, consistently supported signals.
This creates a vulnerability in ranking decisions that content manipulation can exploit.
C3H is an inference-time attack that aligns a target item’s multimodal content with implicit recommendation criteria.
Unlike noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, it manipulates content without changing model training.
Experiments show increased target-item exposure while preserving overall recommendation utility.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The schematic overview of C3H. Under a strict zero-query setting, the framework operates in two stages: (1) Cue Scoring (Stage I) ranks candidate cues from (t0, v0) by compressionsurvivability κ̂ and cross-modal consensus χ̂, selecting a hero cue fh and a secondary cue fs by joint score S = κ̃ · χ̃. (2) Stealthy Editing (Stage II) amplifies fh, fs via text shaping and a low-distortion image transform, gated against the stealthiness set B.

papers.tldr: C3H exploits compression-to-consensus bias in multimodal LLM recommenders to increase a target item’s exposure through tailored multimodal content.

papers.abstract: In object pose estimation methods, predicted poses are expressed with respect to a canonical frame, defined by a reference model of that object. In learning-based methods, an arbitrarily chosen modeling convention defines this canonical frame, which is then used to generate the ground-truth pose-annotations for training. Object pose estimation methods are therefore bound to such arbitrary conventions, restricting generalization. In this work, we propose that such a canonical frame can instead be derived for any object, and present RestPose, an approach towards open object pose estimation that does not require reference models or canonical frame conventions during training. From a single input image, we generate an object mesh and canonicalize it through a geometric and physical analysis of the object, then use foundation model-based dense matching to estimate the pose. We choose category-level benchmarks for our experiments, which contain instances across various object categories and enable us to measure the effectiveness of our canonicalization. Across HouseCat6D, NOCS, and Omni6DPose datasets, we improve on the supervised state-of-the-art methods by 18.3 points in absolute metrics and 13.8 points in scale-agnostic metrics, without requiring task-specific training. Code will be published.
authors: Sandeep Inuganti, Weihang Li, Benjamin Busam, Didier Stricker, Jason Rambach
bullets: Addresses the dependence of pose estimation on arbitrary, object-specific canonical frames and reference models.
Generates an object mesh from one image, then canonicalizes it using geometric and physical analysis.
Uses foundation-model-based dense matching to estimate the object pose.
Evaluated on HouseCat6D, NOCS, and Omni6DPose, improving over supervised state-of-the-art methods by 18.3 absolute and 13.8 scale-agnostic metric points.
Scope: experiments focus on category-level benchmarks; code is planned for release.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview. RestPose computes a canonical frame from generated geometry. A masked reference view yields a generated mesh of a remote. Figure 3. RestPose pipeline. Onboarding runs once per object. A mesh is generated from one masked view, with its depth in the RGB-D setting, in the generator’s native frame. one unique canonical frame is selected, and the azimuth is read from the radial profile, giving the canonical rotation. Inference runs per detection. Templates are rendered from cameras placed around the RestPose mesh, and reciprocal matches against each are counted. The template with most inliers wins, and its matches are lifted to a Sim(3) fit inside RANSAC. In case of insufficient inliers, the detection takes the boxed ICP branch instead. In the RGB-only setting onboarding uses no metric-scale sensor depth and the query’s predicted depth has arbitrary scale. Multi-view labelling runs post hoc on the per-frame outputs. Each frame’s estimate is first labelled jointly among the four flips, and the labelled poses then vote for a consensus.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted to enhance the multimodal reasoning of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods share a common limitation of Module-Level Credit Entanglement, in which the vision encoder, projector, and LLM modules are jointly optimized using the same advantage signals even when perceptual correctness and final-answer correctness differ. To address this limitation, we propose Module-Specific Policy Optimization (MSPO), a framework that separates perceptual and outcome-based learning signals across model modules. Specifically, MSPO uses responses to perception checklists comprising auxiliary questions about visual information to derive an advantage for training the vision encoder. From these responses, MSPO computes the Confidence-aware Perception Reward (CaPR), using a perception sign obtained by thresholding checklist accuracy to determine reward direction and posterior confidence from a Beta distribution over latent perception accuracy to scale reward magnitude. We then derive the vision advantage through group-relative normalization of CaPR and scale it using main-task success rates. This advantage guides updates to the vision encoder, while the projector and LLM retain outcome-based GRPO updates. Extensive experiments on seven mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that MSPO outperforms existing RL-tuned models on average at both the 3B and 7B scales.
authors: HuiSeong Cho, Jun Yeong Park, Yu Rang Park
bullets: Addresses module-level credit entanglement when visual perception and final-answer correctness diverge.
Uses auxiliary visual perception checklists to generate vision-training signals.
Computes confidence-aware perception rewards from checklist accuracy and Beta-distribution-based confidence.
Applies group-relative normalization and task-success scaling to form the vision advantage; projector and LLM use GRPO advantages.
Outperforms existing RL-tuned models on average across seven mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks at 3B and 7B scales.

papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation of vision-language models has produced increasingly elaborate methods built on CLIP and on one shared principle: the zero-shot text classifier is the anchor, and labeled images only correct it. We argue that this principle reflects CLIP's visual features rather than a property of the task. We provide a simple Bayesian interpretation, in which a class name is worth exactly kappa = sigma^2 / tau^2 labeled images, the ratio between the visual spread of a class and the misalignment of its name. The Bayes classifier of this model counts text as kappa more samples. With modern frozen encoders, few-shot adaptation then reduces to a well-regularised convex probe. Specifically, we introduce TASP, a simple convex logistic regression on frozen features that incorporates class-name embeddings as weighted training examples and as a regularization prior. On the standard 11-dataset benchmark, TASP with frozen PE-Core-L features achieves 87.1% accuracy at 1 shot and 91.4% at 16 shots, outperforming state-of-the-art few-shot vision-language adaptation methods by 4.6 to 11.0 percentage points. While stronger representations explain much of this improvement, controlled comparisons on matched features show that existing frozen-encoder adaptation methods do not materially improve on this probe. We further find that the weight assigned to text matters more than how it is incorporated, and that combining self-supervised visual features with vision-language representations is most beneficial for weaker visual encoders. Together, these findings suggest that progress in few-shot vision-language adaptation depends more on representation quality and the appropriate use of text supervision than on increasingly complex adaptation mechanisms.
authors: Reda Bensaid, Ismail Ben Ayed, Fran\c{c}ois Leduc-Primeau, Vincent Gripon
bullets: Challenges the assumption that zero-shot text classifiers should always anchor adaptation; this may reflect CLIP’s visual features rather than the task itself.
Introduces a Bayesian view where text contributes an equivalent of κ = σ²/τ² labeled images, based on class variability and name misalignment.
Uses TASP: logistic regression on frozen visual features, incorporating class-name embeddings as weighted training examples and a regularization prior.
On an 11-dataset benchmark with frozen PE-Core-L features, TASP reaches 87.1% at 1 shot and 91.4% at 16 shots, outperforming prior methods by 4.6–11.0 percentage points.
Finds that text weighting matters more than its integration mechanism; gains rely substantially on representation quality, especially for weaker visual encoders.
