papers.selection_reason: Presents a simple yet effective few-shot adaptation method for vision-language models, relevant to Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: Text Is Just Another Shot in Vision-Language Models: Simple Probes on Frozen Encoders Do It

papers.abstract: Surgical resection planning centers on generating executable resection surfaces from anatomical evidence and operative constraints. Medical multimodal foundation models enable anatomical understanding, and segmentation models predict resection regions, but neither translates these capabilities into explicitly constrained, executable resection surfaces. We present GeoSurge, an anatomy-grounded framework that combines mask-derived metrics with structure-aware point-cloud tokens to generate executable, editable resection surfaces. To make resection geometry learnable and editable, GeoSurge maps actions to parametric geometry through a surface-action grammar. Using this grammar, anatomy-oriented and tumor-centered templates generate candidates, which are filtered by hard constraints and semantic deduplication. Training supervision is then derived from candidate-expert geometric agreement and independently recomputed feasibility metrics. At inference, the reasoner uses patient evidence and surgical requirements to select or revise an action, which an independent geometry engine subsequently materializes and verifies. GeoSurge achieves the best overall scores on DeepTumour Liver and CRLM-QA, improving the constraint satisfaction rate from 73% to 100% on CRLM and from 56% to 99% on GeoSurge-Bench.

papers.abstract: We present VenusOCR2.0, a compact 1B-parameter vision-language recognizer designed for both high-accuracy and high-throughput document parsing across text, tables, and formulas. To continuously improve recognition quality without self-training collapse, we build a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) data engine where the model acts strictly as a weakness probe, while external multi-expert medoid consensus, VLM visual verification, and factorized synthesis supply reliable supervision across pretraining, curated SFT, and RLVR. VenusOCR2.0 couples a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder and 2x2 spatial token merging with a Qwen3-0.6B decoder, adopting compact atomic OTSL tokens to shorten table sequences and reduce structural errors. To further eliminate the autoregressive decoding bottleneck, we introduce PTPv2, a lightweight ($\sim$67M) decoupled parallel draft module that combines frozen multi-layer verifier conditioning, a standalone learned mask, and block-causal all-position next-token prediction. On OmniDocBenchv1.6, VenusOCR2.0 achieves an overall score of 96.45 and a state-of-the-art 98.57 formula CDM, substantially outperforming massive general-purpose VLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro (92.91) and Qwen3-VL-235B (89.78). Deployed in vLLM on a single H20 GPU, PTPv2 delivers a 2.96x single-request speedup and up to 2.36x higher batched throughput while guaranteeing lossless, token-for-token equivalence with standard autoregressive decoding.

bullets: Targets unified parsing of text, tables, and formulas with high accuracy and throughput.

Introduces PTPv2, a ~67M-parameter parallel draft module that preserves token-for-token equivalence with autoregressive decoding.
On OmniDocBenchv1.6, reports 96.45 overall and 98.57 formula CDM; PTPv2 provides up to 2.96× single-request speedup and 2.36× batched throughput on one H20 GPU.

papers.abstract: Changes in image viewpoint and question formulation can alter latent knowledge representations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, output correctness and overall representational drift provide limited insight into how these changes affect model decisions. We therefore evaluate latent knowledge stability across visual and linguistic elicitation conditions from two complementary perspectives: answer preference and internal support. Specifically, we devise the margin retention score (MRS), which measures the first-order projected degradation of the initial answer's logit margin over competing options across conditions and assesses how changes in latent knowledge representations affect this margin. We also present latent knowledge support-structure stability (KSS), which evaluates reference-correct items by comparing internal support profiles constructed using the margin gradient under the reference condition, which jointly reflects changes in how internal support is distributed and changes in total support magnitude. We further construct MMStableBench, comprising 19,452 knowledge items (facts), each probing the same latent knowledge across varied image viewpoints, semantically equivalent question formulations, and answer-option permutations. Experiments across 15 MLLMs show that MRS and KSS reveal latent knowledge instability not captured by accuracy, while an MRS-inspired regularizer further improves the generalization of edited latent knowledge.
authors: Chuancheng Shi, Shangze Li, Wenhua Wu, Zifeng Cheng, Pengyang Shao, Fei Shen, Tat-Seng Chua
bullets: Evaluates latent knowledge stability from answer preference and internal support perspectives.
Introduces Margin Retention Score (MRS) to measure degradation in the original answer’s logit margin across conditions.
Introduces Knowledge Support-Structure Stability (KSS) to compare changes in internal support profiles for correct answers.
Presents MMStableBench with 19,452 knowledge items spanning viewpoint, question-formulation, and answer-option variations.
Across 15 MLLMs, MRS and KSS expose instability missed by accuracy; an MRS-inspired regularizer improves generalization of edited knowledge.

papers.abstract: Vision foundation backbones are often treated as drop-in upgrades for improving region proposals in open-vocabulary panoptic segmentation (OVPS). Yet, improvements in backbones often fail to translate well into downstream cross-domain performance. Using ODISE, a diffusion-based OVPS model with a CLIP-based recognition branch, as a testbed, we replace its diffusion visual extractor with DINOv2, ConvNeXt, or DINOv3, and find that backbone upgrades can introduce a grouping-recognition mismatch: an alignment gap between dense-region features and CLIP text embeddings. Across source and near-domain, the newer DINOv3 variant improves source-domain performance but collapses on several cross-domain targets, whereas other baselines, interestingly, show the opposite. Stage-wise diagnostics, linear probes, and region-text alignment analyses indicate that DINOv3 embeddings retain semantic information but are geometrically incompatible with CLIP. We test adaptations, including text-side adapters, conformal mask retention (CMR), and a lean 2.7M-parameter visual-side LoRA, and find that text-side adaptation is more sensitive to vocabulary overlap. CMR provides only limited and target-specific gains, indicating that retention alone cannot resolve the full cross-domain failure. To understand why ADE20K resists improvement across all interventions, we evaluate OVSeg, CAT-Seg, and MaskCLIP. This separates two failure axes: a recoverable visual-to-CLIP interface gap that visual-side LoRA largely repairs, and a vocabulary-boundary limitation shared by the evaluated CLIP-based recognition systems that requires different remedies.
authors: Huy Hoang Nguyen, Oliver Zendel, Tobias Glueck, Minh Nhat Vu, Andreas Kugi
bullets: The study identifies a grouping–recognition mismatch between region features and CLIP text embeddings as a hidden cross-domain failure mode.
Replacing ODISE’s diffusion extractor with DINOv2, ConvNeXt, or DINOv3 produces divergent domain-transfer behavior; DINOv3 improves source results but collapses on several targets.
Diagnostics show DINOv3 preserves semantic information, but its embedding geometry is incompatible with CLIP.

A 2.7M-parameter visual-side LoRA largely repairs the visual-to-CLIP interface gap; text adapters are more sensitive to vocabulary overlap, while conformal mask retention offers limited, target-specific gains.
ADE20K failures persist across OVSeg, CAT-Seg, and MaskCLIP, revealing a separate vocabulary-boundary limitation in CLIP-based recognition systems.

papers.abstract: Geospatial reasoning segmentation aims to localize geographic targets from language requiring semantic inference beyond direct visual perception. However, existing benchmarks often operationalize reasoning as category omission while overlooking attribute mixing, which neglects explicit-category reasoning, introduces perceptual shortcuts, and fails to precisely evaluate reasoning capability. To diagnose and address these limitations, we first reformulate geospatial reasoning segmentation along category expression (explicit vs. implicit) and attribute nature (perceptual vs. inferential), and audit 90,708 queries across existing benchmarks to reveal that pure explicit-inferential queries account for only 0.61% whereas 31.98% mix both attribute types. We then develop a three-stage pipeline that harnesses OpenStreetMap attributes while mitigating geometric and semantic noise to construct RSReasoner, a large-scale dataset of 106,610 images with 213,220 reasoning queries, and RSReasoner-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 75,400 queries across four canonical types and controlled variants. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RSReasoner-Bench precisely evaluates model capability across multiple dimensions while exposing shortcut behaviors, and fine-tuning on RSReasoner boosts both reasoning and cross-type generalization. Our findings offer key insights for future geospatial reasoning research and benchmark design. Datasets and code will be released at https://github.com/Ricardo-XZ/RSReasoner.
authors: Xu Zhang, Xinpeng Zhang, Yunrui Zou, Hongliang Chen, Xiaotian Jiang, Yang Zheng, Kaitai Guo, Jimin Liang

papers.abstract: Specialists post-trained from a shared checkpoint acquire complementary capabilities, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) can consolidate them into a single model. However, we find that existing consolidation methods, from weight merging to MOPD, fall short when specialists diverge substantially from the shared checkpoint, whereas prior studies mostly examine specialists that remain close to it. We present a unified recipe for multimodal MOPD that consolidates such specialists back into the single student they branched from. The recipe specifies initialization, data selection, balanced supervision across teachers, and preservation of existing capabilities for consolidation, together with a targeted refinement stage for capabilities that still lag behind their specialists. In an industrial setting with six specialists, the student closely approaches each specialist in its own domain and surpasses the perception specialist. It recovers 97.0% of their average gain, compared with 79.8% for IM-MOPD. In the fully open five-domain setting with Qwen3-4B, our method recovers 95.7% of the specialists' average gain after consolidation and 97.5% after refinement, compared with 94.1% for IM-MOPD. We further analyze the full pipeline through mechanism ablations and training dynamics, providing practical guidance for diagnosing incomplete consolidation. Code will be released.
authors: Zihan Liang, Zikun Qu, Ben Chen, Fan Yang, Wenwu Ou, Min Zhang, Zhongxiang Dai, Xinchao Wang
bullets: Addresses the failure of existing weight-merging and MOPD methods when specialists diverge far from their shared starting checkpoint.
Combines careful initialization, data selection, balanced multi-teacher supervision, and capability preservation.
Adds targeted refinement for capabilities that remain weaker than those of the specialists.
With six industrial specialists, the student closely matches each domain specialist and surpasses the perception specialist.

Recovers 97.0% of specialists’ average gain in the industrial setting and 95.7% after consolidation—or 97.5% after refinement—in the open five-domain setting, compared with 79.8% and 94.1% for IM-MOPD, respectively.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) planners inherit semantic knowledge from pretrained vision-language models, but their reasoning is rarely grounded in 3D scene structure and its evolution over time. We introduce GeoVLDrive, a geometry-grounded VLA framework for 3D spatiotemporal reasoning and planning. Multi-layer features from a 3D foundation model augment the vision-language backbone through gated cross-attention. A structured latent chain of thought (CoT) organizes future scene geometry, key-agent motion, and meta-actions into ordered, separately supervised latent states. An action expert generates trajectory proposals from these states and multi-layer scene features, and ranks them using scene-grounded, interacting score tokens. We also introduce NAVSIM 3DQA to train and evaluate metric 3D spatial and motion understanding. GeoVLDrive achieves 91.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2. On NAVSIM 3DQA, the geometry-grounded backbone scores 89.2% overall, 4.6 percentage points above the fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-2B baseline. On LingoQA, the backbone achieves 68.6% Lingo-Judge accuracy.
authors: JiaHui Huang, Songyan Zhang, Hanbing Li, Hanchao Leng, Kuiyuan Yang, Guang Chen, Hangjun Ye, Chen Lv

Generates and ranks trajectory proposals with an action expert and scene-grounded interacting score tokens.
Reports 91.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and 89.2% on the proposed NAVSIM 3DQA benchmark.

papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) delivery is an important application of the low-altitude economy, enhancing the flexibility and accessibility of last-mile logistics. Existing UAV delivery methods generally rely on precise terminal coordinates, predefined terminal specifications, or task-specific localization procedures, limiting the scope and flexibility of delivery. As UAV logistics becomes more intelligent, open-ended semantic descriptions offer a new paradigm for specifying terminal destinations. However, conventional aerial navigation methods have limited ability to generalize to delivery scenarios that require open-vocabulary terminal navigation. To enable this broader delivery paradigm, we propose CoFiNav, a VLM-guided coarse-to-fine UAV semantic navigation framework that progressively grounds relation-defined terminal destinations through hierarchical semantic search and active 3D observation. Given a task description, a coarse prior map from OpenStreetMap (OSM), and accumulated observations, CoFiNav uses a vision-language model (VLM) to determine which unresolved entity or spatial relation should be verified next. A geometry-aware module converts the semantic observation request into feasible viewpoints using RGB images and LiDAR, while conventional motion planning handles safe execution. Experiments across multiple urban environments show that CoFiNav outperforms representative adapted baselines in success rate while requiring shorter flight paths and fewer observations.
authors: Xuanpu Wang, Shun Hu, Bing Li, Rongqing Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of delivery systems requiring precise coordinates, fixed terminal specifications, or task-specific localization.

Converts semantic observation requests into feasible viewpoints using RGB imagery and LiDAR, then executes them with conventional motion planning.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models often rely on global context and language priors while overlooking answer-determining local details. Privileged visual on-policy self-distillation supervises full-image student rollouts using a frozen teacher that views high-resolution evidence crops. Yet our cross-scale diagnostics show that models retain over half of their full-image accuracy when local evidence is completely masked, indicating that single-image correctness does not guarantee reliance on local evidence, while the need for visual correction also varies across tokens with their spatial attention states. We propose STAR, a visual on-policy self-distillation framework combining independent counterfactual dual-world rollouts with spatial-attention-guided target reconstruction. Local image editing constructs paired worlds with identical questions and backgrounds but distinct answer-determining facts, where a shared student samples trajectories independently to expose contextual shortcuts under image-consistent prefixes. Within each world, the teacher contrasts real and mean-color crops to determine the visual correction direction, while the divergence between student image attention and a teacher-centroid spatial reference adaptively controls token-wise target log-probability reconstruction. Without auxiliary attention losses or test-time tool overhead, STAR improves Qwen3.5 across scales by up to 8.04 percentage points in average accuracy over initialization across six fine-grained benchmarks, reaches OPSD's final accuracy $4.7\times$ faster, and generalizes to out-of-domain reasoning tasks.
authors: Yi Zou, Zhuang Yan, Yudong Zhang, Xu Wang, Yang Wang
bullets: Models can preserve over half their full-image accuracy even when local evidence is masked, revealing shortcut reliance.
STAR creates counterfactual image worlds with identical questions and backgrounds but different answer-relevant facts.
A teacher compares real and mean-color crops to identify visual corrections, while spatial-attention divergence guides token-level target reconstruction.
STAR improves Qwen3.5 by up to 8.04 percentage points across six fine-grained benchmarks, reaches OPSD’s final accuracy 4.7× faster, and generalizes to out-of-domain reasoning tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often recognize fine-grained details more accurately in a relevant crop than in the full image. Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) methods exploit this by transferring the advantage of a crop-view teacher to a full-image student. However, their supervision relies on region-specific questions curated through an elaborate synthesis pipeline, which brings three weaknesses: (1) every region needs a question--answer pair written exclusively for it, locking training into costly QA curation that is hard to scale to unlabeled images; (2) all rollouts of a region answer the same question, so the teacher supervises only the details it asks about, leaving other visual elements in the region unsupervised; and (3) every question presupposes that its target exists, so the student becomes prone to answering even when the target is absent. In this paper, we study how to turn unlabeled images into broad visual supervision through multi-aspect self-description and privileged-view distillation, and propose CaptionOPD, which replaces tailored questions with a fixed set of image-agnostic caption prompts, ranging from general descriptions to focused captions of parts, colors, counts, text, and layout. The rollouts of a region receive different prompts, so the teacher supervises various aspects of the region. Moreover, because caption prompts mask the model to describe what is visible instead of querying a specific target, they avoid presupposing what the region contains. Using the model itself as the crop-view teacher, CaptionOPD requires no questions, no answers, and no larger model annotations: only images and region boxes. Experiments show that, trained on the same images and regions, CaptionOPD outperforms prior OPD methods across multiple fine-grained and general perception benchmarks.
authors: Haozhan Shen, Liangbo He, Jun Lan, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Tiancheng Zhao, Jianwei Yin
bullets: Addresses costly, narrow, and target-presupposing QA supervision in multimodal on-policy distillation.
Uses fixed, image-agnostic caption prompts covering descriptions, parts, colors, counts, text, and layout.
Distills a model’s crop-view outputs into a full-image student using varied prompts across region rollouts.
Requires only images and region boxes—no questions, answers, or larger teacher model annotations.
Outperforms prior OPD methods across multiple fine-grained and general perception benchmarks when trained on the same images and regions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Caption Handoff. (a) Given a boxed full image, the student generates a general caption whose first sentence typically identifies the target object. (b) Standard distillation retains the box cues during training and supervises the entire caption, causing the student’s perception to rely on oracle boxes. (c) The proposed caption handoff removes the box cues from both the student’s image and prompt, while keeping the teacher’s cropped view unchanged. The first sentence serves purely as a textual anchor (masked from the loss), and only the remaining detailed description is supervised on the clean full image.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on questions with false premises. Each question presupposes an absent target: (a) a scooter rather than a bicycle, (b) a dog figurine rather than a real dog, and (c) a bowl of strawberries rather than oranges. QA-trained baselines (Vision-OPD, S2VOPD, and VAD) blindly follow the question’s premise and hallucinate the queried object, whereas CaptionOPD faithfully identifies what is actually present and rejects the false premise. All models are based on Qwen3.5-9B. More examples are shown in Appendix E.

Figure 1: Comparison of prompt construction and rollout allocation between previous fine-grained OPD and CaptionOPD. (a) Previous fine-grained OPD relies on a large VLM to synthesize a tailored question qi for every image–region pair and spends all K rollouts answering that same question qi, tying training to costly QA curation while supervising only a single queried detail per region. (b) Our CaptionOPD eliminates per-region QA generation by reusing a fixed, image-agnostic pool of caption templates (detailed in Section 3.1) across all images, assigning diverse prompts across the K rollouts to supervise multiple visual aspects of each region.

papers.abstract: Visual decision-making demands accurate judgments and timely responses. Yet for multiple questions sharing the same visual input, autoregressive multimodal large language models generate answers token by token, accumulating sequential decoding costs as question count grows and delaying completion of the decision set. Their predictions can also vary with question order. We introduce ViDM, which transforms multi-question visual inference into parallel decisions in a single forward pass, improving both accuracy and inference efficiency. ViDM organizes shared visual context, multiple questions, and question-specific decision slots into one sequence, reusing the native language-model head to produce all answer distributions simultaneously. A Decision-Query Mask aligns each decision query's direct attention with shared context and its corresponding question, while case-balanced multi-order training strengthens robustness to question reordering. Across nine benchmarks spanning image, multi-image, and video tasks, ViDM improves Qwen3.5-4B's average accuracy from 73.49% to 77.55% while achieving 8.4x the baseline's average end-to-end throughput. On GQA, where each evaluated image has 11.4 questions on average, the end-to-end speedup reaches 20.3x. ViDM also improves mean and worst-order accuracy while reducing order-induced variation across multiple benchmarks, with further validation on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and InternVL3.5-4B.
authors: Xudong Tan, Peng Ye, Chenyu Huang, Yaoxin Yang, Huafeng Qin, Tao Chen
bullets: Addresses sequential decoding costs and sensitivity to question ordering in multi-question visual inference.
Organizes shared visual context, questions, and decision slots into one sequence for simultaneous answer prediction.
Uses a Decision-Query Mask to connect each decision with the shared context and its corresponding question.
Case-balanced multi-order training improves robustness to reordered questions and reduces order-induced variation.
Across nine benchmarks, ViDM raises average accuracy and achieves substantial throughput gains, including up to 20.3× speedup on GQA.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Architecture and training pipeline of ViDM. A shared decision head reuses native LM-head rows to map decision states to K answer distributions in parallel, without autoregressive answer decoding. (Right) During training, the same question set is presented in M distinct orders, with predictions aligned to their question-specific labels. Case-balanced Multi-order CE averages cross-entropy over questions and orders within each case, then weights cases equally, encouraging order-robust decisions.

papers.abstract: Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.

papers.abstract: Universal Multimodal Embedding (UME) models map heterogeneous multimodal inputs into a shared embedding space, where pairwise similarity supports diverse downstream tasks. Recent reasoning-driven UME approaches use intermediate reasoning to generate additional context for embedding, but often incur extra computation at inference. In this paper, we explore the matched candidate (i.e., the paired target) as an alternative source of context, asking whether a model can "see the answer" during training and "learn to embed" without it at inference. However, direct conditioning on this privileged context can introduce candidate-specific information unavailable from the query alone or cause the candidate-conditioned query representation to collapse toward the candidate embedding. To address this, we introduce Hindsight-Enhanced Multimodal Embeddings (HEME), which learns query-grounded hindsight representations from such candidate context. HEME first trains a hindsight teacher with a hindsight attention mask, mismatched-candidate conditioning, and query-token alignment to limit excessive reliance on the candidate. It then freezes the teacher and distills its hindsight representation and similarity distribution into a standalone student embedder. At inference, the student independently encodes queries and candidates without candidate conditioning or the hindsight teacher. Experiments on MMEB-V2 and the agent and text tasks of MMEB-V3 demonstrate the effectiveness of HEME and show that it enables more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-driven methods.
authors: Yoonki Cho, Youngju Na, Taegeun Yang, Jinhwan Seo, Sung-Eui Yoon
bullets: UME models embed heterogeneous multimodal inputs in a shared space for similarity-based tasks.
HEME addresses the risk that candidate-conditioned representations overfit to or collapse toward the candidate.
A hindsight teacher uses masked, mismatched-candidate conditioning and query-token alignment to learn query-grounded representations.
A standalone student distills the teacher’s representations and similarity distributions, requiring no candidate conditioning or teacher at inference.
Experiments on MMEB-V2 and selected MMEB-V3 tasks demonstrate effectiveness and more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-based methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of HEME. (a) Hindsight teacher training. The candidate and query passes encode their inputs independently, while the hindsight pass conditions the query on its matched candidate by reusing the candidate KV cache. The hindsight mask allows candidate context to influence the embedding only through query content tokens. Together with mismatched-candidate conditioning and query-token alignment, this encourages the hindsight representation to remain grounded in the query. The mismatched-candidate hindsight pass is omitted for clarity. (b) Learning from hindsight. The frozen hindsight teacher supervises a standalone student through embedding and similarity-distribution matching, while the student is also trained with standard InfoNCE. Distribution matching aligns the teacher and student similarity distributions over the same in-batch candidates, using their respective candidate embeddings (c̄ and c). At inference, only the standalone student embedder is used.

Figure 3. Query-grounded hindsight and its transfer to inference. (a) For a target C+ and a challenging near-miss C−, the hindsight pass shows larger query-token shifts on words that distinguish the two candidates; at inference, HEME exhibits stronger target–near-miss separation in the illustrated examples. (b) For a single page C+ answering two different questions, conditioning on the same answer produces question-specific hindsight rankings; from the question alone, HEME exhibits corresponding retrieval behavior.

Figure 1. Reasoning at test time vs. hindsight during training. (a) Reasoning-driven UME approaches generate additional context through intermediate reasoning at test time. (b) HEME instead uses the matched candidate as privileged context during training: a hindsight teacher produces a candidate-conditioned hindsight representation, which is distilled into a standalone embedder. At test time, HEME encodes queries and candidates independently without the hindsight teacher or additional reasoning steps.

papers.abstract: We address the problem of learning audio-visual representations from co-occurring modalities. Multimodal contrastive learning typically assumes that paired observations provide shared views of the same underlying information. While this may be true for datasets collected in constrained environments, it does not always hold. For instance, co-occurring audio and visual signals can differ substantially in their content due to off-screen sounds. Nevertheless, standard contrastive objectives treat all paired samples as equally aligned. In this work, we propose Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (CGAAL), a model-agnostic objective that leverages modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between audio and video. CGAAL uses these agreement scores to weight the contribution of each positive pair. A warm-up period and gradual thresholding strategy progressively introduce this alignment-aware training signal. We demonstrate the generality of CGAAL by applying it to three contrastive baselines, consistently improving their performance on audio-visual retrieval.
authors: Omar Emara, Nan Lu, Dima Damen, Hazel Doughty
bullets: Standard contrastive learning assumes co-occurring audio and video are equally aligned, but off-screen sounds can violate this assumption.
CGAAL uses modality-specific captions to estimate audio-video semantic agreement.
Agreement scores weight positive pairs, with warm-up and gradual thresholding to introduce alignment-aware training progressively.
Applied to three contrastive baselines, CGAAL consistently improves audio-visual retrieval performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our caption-guided alignment-aware learning (CGAAL). As in standard contrastive learning, we (a) learn a shared space for audio-visual retrieval where audio and video encoders project each modality into a shared embedding space where we measure their similarity. Rather than treating all co-occurring pairs as equally positive, we instead use (b) modality specific captions to estimate the alignment of each positive pair. After first warming up the representation with all positive pairs, CGAAL uses the estimated alignment scores to weight positive pairs in a contrastive loss (c). A gradually increasing threshold introduces the alignment scores gradually so that the weakest correspondences are down-weighted first. This produces a shared embedding space in which proximity better reflects audio–visual correspondence, rather than co-occurrence alone.

Figure 1: Alignment in audio-video contrastive learning. Standard contrastive methods assume strong semantic correspondence between modalities of a given sample, encouraging alignment even when the modalities share little semantic content. This can encourage the model to associate audio and visual content that does not correspond. We thus propose CGAAL which determines how strongly to pull the modalities’ embeddings of a sample according to a pair’s semantic agreement.
Figure 7: Performance vs. alignment score. The relative improvement of our method compared to CLIP and CoMM increases with alignment score.

Figure 3: Alignment score estimation. We prompt the LLM to predict the alignment score by: (1) setting the criteria for measuring the semantic alignment with clear inputs (modality captions) and the output (alignment score); (2) providing examples with different alignment strength alongside an explanation to calibrate the scores across various examples; and (3) providing the vision and audio caption pair for which a score needs to be predicted.

Figure 4: Examples of modality-specific captions with varying semantic alignment. We show high (top), moderate (middle) and weak (bottom) alignment examples. High (row1,col1): vision shows cooking on stove while audio has distinct sizzling sound. Moderate (row2,col3): walking is not evident from the audio. Weak (Row3 col 3): no evidence of golfing in the audio.
Figure 8: Qualitative Results for A2V over different alignment levels. Our retrieved videos show better fine-grained semantic correspondence with the audio query.

Figure 5: Impact of Synthetic Misalignment on Training Set. We show the distributions of caption-based alignment scores for the full pretraining set (left) and the 15% of the samples selected for audio shuffling (right). The original pretraining set (blue) already contains many low-scoring pairs, suggesting substantial natural variation in audio–visual correspondence. Adding synthetic misalignment (orange) shows a clear shift towards lower scores.
Figure 6: Reliability of Alignment Scores. Captionbased LLM scores closely agree with human ratings of audio–visual correspondence.
Table 2: Zero-Shot Retrieval. Adding CGAAL improves a model’s ability to generalise to unseen datasets, particularly with increased misalignment in training.

Table 3: Model Ablation. Alignment weighting contributes most to our performance. Gradual thresholding gives a further gain with synthetic misalignment, while warm-up improves without it.

Table 1: Comparative Results. Combining our approach with standard contrastive baselines (SLIP, CMC and CLIP) improves retrieval performance both with and without synthetic misalignment.

papers.abstract: Human gaze provides a rich window into attention and intent, making its understanding essential for applications ranging from social signal analysis to human-robot interaction. Existing methods typically employ highly customized architectures relying on auxiliary inputs like head crops or depth maps, causing cascading errors and inference overhead. Trained on single domains and confined to isolated gaze following with heatmap outputs, they lack flexibility and generalization for diverse interactive scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present LookAnything, a foundation model that unifies diverse gaze-centric tasks for holistic gaze following. Benefiting from large-scale multi-task and cross-domain training, LookAnything flexibly adapts to various settings, generating diverse outputs (points, boxes, heatmaps, and language) and supporting broad gaze-centric localization, description, and reasoning. At its core, we introduce learnable gaze-prior queries to promote gaze-aware representation learning, eliminating the need for auxiliary external inputs. To facilitate this paradigm, we construct HoliGaze, a comprehensive corpus and benchmark comprising 311K question-answer pairs across 5 capability dimensions and 9 distinct tasks. Experiments demonstrate that LookAnything consistently outperforms 33 leading vision-language models on holistic gaze following, while remaining highly competitive with dedicated specialists across 5 conventional target detection benchmarks. Evaluation on unseen datasets and deployment on a real robot further validate its strong out-of-domain generalization and flexible adaptation in real-world scenarios.
authors: Jiayu Tang, Yuchen Zhou, Hongsheng Wu, Hanjing Ye, Ke Huang, Cheng Wang, Yuqin Dai, Yufei Huang, Yonggen Ling, Chao Gou
bullets: Addresses the limited flexibility, domain generalization, and inference overhead of specialized gaze-following systems.
Uses learnable gaze-prior queries to develop gaze-aware representations without head crops or depth maps.
Supports diverse outputs, including points, boxes, heatmaps, and language, across broad gaze-centric tasks.
Introduces HoliGaze, a benchmark with 311K question-answer pairs spanning 5 capability dimensions and 9 tasks.
Outperforms 33 leading vision-language models and generalizes to unseen datasets and real-robot deployment; scope centers on gaze-centric interaction scenarios.

figures.caption: Figure 4 Model architecture overview. LookAnything appends learnable gaze-prior queries to the multimodal input sequence to learn gaze-aware representations via auxiliary geometric supervision (scene depth, source head grounding, and gaze target heatmap). The language head then autoregressively decodes the answer in a unified output space. The auxiliary branches can be selectively skipped during inference. Top-left: The structurally disentangled block-wise attention mechanism isolates functional specialization by preventing heterogeneous query groups from attending to one another.

Figure 1 Overview. (a) Left: Sourced from diverse scenarios, we design a scalable data engine to transform heterogeneous annotations into a unified Q&A format. The resulting large-scale HoliGaze dataset provides the essential data foundation for holistic gaze following. (b) Down: LookAnything is a generalist foundation model that unifies diverse gaze-centric tasks. By introducing learnable gaze-prior queries, it eliminates the need for computationally expensive external inputs and flexibly generates versatile outputs (points, boxes, heatmaps, and language) for broad localization, description, and reasoning. (c) Right: We establish HoliGaze-Bench across 9 distinct gaze-centric tasks to systematically evaluate 33 leading VLMs. LookAnything demonstrates superior performance over other VLMs on this comprehensive benchmark, while achieving highly competitive results against dedicated specialists on 5 conventional gaze following datasets.

Figure 3 Data engine and dataset statistics of HoliGaze. The data engine converts 8 source datasets into unified Q&A samples via four stages: (1) unifying heterogeneous records into a shared schema, (2) completing missing annotations using off-the-shelf models, (3) generating openQA and MCQ pairs via task-specific templates, and (4) conducting human verification. papers.abstract: Diagnosing with X-rays often requires reasoning about the 3D locations of abnormalities and their spatial relationships to surrounding anatomical structures, yet such reasoning remains challenging due to the loss of spatial information in 2D projections. To address this challenge, we propose Dreaming in CT (DiCT), a three-stage progressive CT-to-X-ray reasoning transfer framework that leverages a CT vision-language model (VLM) to guide an X-ray VLM. Through this CT-guided transfer, the student acquires CT-informed 3D reasoning capabilities, enabling it to reason directly from 2D X-rays without explicit CT reconstruction at inference time. The framework begins with instruct the dreamer, which equips the X-ray student with initial CT-oriented reasoning capabilities and establishes a structured interface that distinguishes X-ray observations from CT imagination. Building on this structure, visualize the dream introduces CT-guided on-policy distillation (OPD), where the CT teacher selectively guides the X-ray student's reasoning trajectories to transfer 3D anatomical knowledge. Finally, manifest the dream adapts the acquired reasoning capabilities from digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) to real clinical X-rays. Experiments across two VLM backbones on 3D-RAD and ReXVQA demonstrate DiCT's effectiveness across radiological reasoning tasks, achieving a 1.66 percentage point improvement over a CT reconstruction-based baseline on 3D-RAD Abnormality Identification with 12.77$\times$ lower inference computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongYep/DiCT.
authors: Zhenghao Lu, Xiaotian Zhang, Songtao Jiang, Yiqun Lin, Siming Fu, Hualiang Wang, Zuozhu Liu
bullets: Addresses the loss of 3D spatial information in X-ray projections, which complicates reasoning about abnormalities and anatomy.
Uses a three-stage CT-to-X-ray transfer process: initial CT-oriented reasoning, CT-guided on-policy distillation, and adaptation from synthetic DRRs to clinical X-rays.
Separates observed X-ray evidence from imagined CT information to structure the student’s reasoning.
Evaluated with two VLM backbones on 3D-RAD and ReXVQA across radiological reasoning tasks.
On 3D-RAD Abnormality Identification, improves 1.66 percentage points over a CT-reconstruction baseline with 12.77× lower inference computation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview and performance comparison of DiCT. Figure 2. Method overview. DiCT comprises three complementary stages: (1) instruct the dreamer initializes X-ray and CT-oriented reasoning through structured SFT. (2) visualize the dream applies masked CT-guided OPD from the CT teacher to the X-ray student’s own responses. (3) manifest the dream adapts the distilled policy to real clinical X-rays through clinical GRPO with task rewards and a KL anchor. DiCT enables X-ray-only inference without CT reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Multi-image benchmarks aim to test whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) combines evidence across images, but many of their items can be answered from a single image. Across about 33k items from 19 public benchmarks, our audit and a two-stage single-image filter find that one image or the question alone settles 24.2% of them. On these items, MLLMs recover from one image a median 78% of the accuracy that all images add over the text alone, so these items reward answering from one image, which we call the single-image shortcut. MLLMs take this shortcut even on items where one image is not enough. On such items, most of their wrong answers repeat an answer they give from one image, at a rate well above chance. We build ASTERISM, to our knowledge the largest audited multi-image benchmark, from these 19 benchmarks by keeping their items that need more than one image. Its 18.7k items, 2.0k of them corrected or rewritten, share one format, one scorer and seven task categories. We also release ASTERISM-Train with 49k training items and ASTERISM-Lite, a hard subset whose items we manually verify one by one. On ASTERISM-Lite, the strongest proprietary MLLM scores 68%. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), now common in MLLM post-training, rewards the shortcut as well, because a correct answer read off one image earns as much reward as one that combines images. In line with this, existing RLVR objectives add little to the ASTERISM score. To stop rewarding the shortcut in training as ASTERISM does in evaluation, we propose cross-image credit assignment (CICA), an extension of RLVR that moves the credit toward the tokens that need more than one image. On three open-source MLLMs, CICA raises the ASTERISM score by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than twice the gain of each general and vision-specific RL objective trained on the same data.
authors: Chanseul Cho, Dongwoo Kim, Noori Bae, Seungjae Moon, Seongsu Lee, Youngmin Ro
bullets: Across ~33k items from 19 benchmarks, 24.2% can be solved from one image or the question alone.
On shortcut-prone items, one-image answers recover a median 78% of the accuracy gained by using all images.
MLLM errors on items requiring multiple images often repeat their single-image answers, indicating shortcut use beyond solvable cases.
ASTERISM retains 18.7k multi-image-dependent items, with corrected or rewritten examples, unified formatting, scoring, and seven task categories.
CICA improves ASTERISM scores by 2.6–6.0 points across three open-source MLLMs, outperforming tested general and vision-specific RL objectives.

papers.abstract: Reference-guided photographic color grading helps users realize their aesthetic intent by selectively drawing on the color and tonal characteristics of a reference photograph. Doing so requires understanding which characteristics users wish to adopt and translating these preferences into controllable edits. However, image-only reference methods align overall appearance without instruction-grounded selection, while pixel-space generative editors typically produce flattened images without editable parameters, limiting subsequent refinement. To address these challenges, we introduce JarvisAura, a multimodal aesthetic agent that formulates photographic color grading as structured decision-making in an editable parameter space. JarvisAura offers three key advantages: (1) an aesthetic agent paradigm that integrates visual attribute perception, strategy-level reasoning, and parameterized execution for interpretable and controllable photographic color grading; (2) a unified reasoning-to-execution pipeline that connects aesthetic planning with backend rendering and editable parameter refinement; and (3) a three-stage training strategy comprising Parameter-Grounded Continual Pre-Training for parameter-appearance grounding, Reference-Grounded Supervised Fine-Tuning for reference-guided reasoning and parameter decisions, and Reference-Aligned Group Relative Policy Optimization for rendered-outcome refinement with multidimensional rewards and dynamic data derivation. On Ref-Bench, JarvisAura achieves the best scores among methods with results across reported automatic metrics and a 74% human-rated task-success rate, exceeding GPT-Image-2.5 by 9 percentage points.
authors: Kunjie Lin, Haitao Zhang, Bosheng Chen, Lanhui Xu, Gaofeng Pan, Yuxin Lin, Tianjiao Liu, Yi Yang, Yue Huang, Xinghao Ding, Zixu Lin, Yunlong Lin
bullets: Addresses the lack of instruction-grounded reference selection and editable controls in existing photographic grading methods.

Uses three training stages to ground parameters in appearance, learn reference-guided decisions, and refine rendered outcomes with multidimensional rewards.
On Ref-Bench, it reports the best results among evaluated methods across automatic metrics and achieves 74% human-rated task success, 9 percentage points above GPT-Image-2.5.

papers.abstract: Visual On-Policy Distillation (OPD) commonly uses cropped or zoomed-in image regions as teacher-side privileged information to improve fine-grained perception in small Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). However, local pixel-level cues are insufficient for complex visual reasoning that requires global structure, spatial relationships, and high-level semantics. We propose Visual Cue On-Policy Self-Distillation (VC-OPD), which extends teacher-side privileged information beyond local image regions to question-conditioned visual cues. Advanced MLLMs generate cues capturing key visual details, structural relationships, and semantic evidence needed to answer each question. A multi-stage quality filtering process selects reliable cues, which are provided only to the teacher during training. This enables informative token-level supervision along student-generated trajectories, helping the student learn to identify and reason over critical evidence directly from the original image. No additional information is required at inference time. Since advanced MLLMs are used only for visual cue generation, VC-OPD is compatible with both open-weight and proprietary black-box models. Experiments on STEM and general visual reasoning benchmarks show consistent improvements across model scales over reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation baselines. Notably, a 4B model trained with VC-OPD outperforms many baselines with 8B or more parameters, demonstrating effective capability transfer through question-conditioned visual cues.
authors: Qinxuan Wang, Zheyu Zhang, Yijing Yang, Han Shu, Chuang Wang, Peipei Yang, Shuo Tang, Jie Hu, Shiming Xiang
bullets: Addresses the limits of cropped or zoomed image regions for reasoning involving global structure, spatial relations, and semantics.
Uses advanced MLLMs to generate question-specific cues containing relevant visual details, relationships, and evidence.
Applies multi-stage quality filtering before providing cues exclusively to the teacher for token-level on-policy supervision.
Works with open-weight and proprietary black-box models because advanced MLLMs are used only during cue generation.
Improves performance across STEM and general visual reasoning benchmarks; a 4B model surpasses many larger baselines, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: A rigid body can fit at its start and goal yet collide with a wall as it moves between them. Inspired by the moving sofa problem, we introduce SofaSpace, a benchmark for visual spatial reasoning through continuous planar rigid-body transport and environment construction. SofaSpace contains 3,000 scenes organized around three challenges: geometric compatibility, nonlocal maneuver planning, and interactive and temporal coordination. Four task views ask models to plan a motion, reconstruct a layout, design an environment that meets transport requirements, or jointly generate a layout and a motion. A separate set of 534 SofaSpace-Hard tasks tests planning and judgment. A geometric verifier checks the entire body throughout each submitted motion. On static planning tasks, endpoint agreement and continuous validity differ substantially within the same submitted plans: Claude drops from 97.2% to 52.8%, DeepSeek from 100.0% to 30.6%, and Kimi from 97.2% to 29.4%, while the strongest configuration retains 98.3% full validity. Environment construction reveals a further gap. Of 295 feasible layouts generated by the strongest configuration, 181 satisfy all evaluated functional requirements; for Kimi, one of 172 does. These results show how executable checks distinguish endpoint agreement from valid motion and geometric feasibility from functional compliance.
authors: Ze Rong, Kun Shi, Zhedong Zheng
bullets: Introduces 3,000 visual-spatial reasoning scenes covering geometric compatibility, nonlocal maneuver planning, and interactive temporal coordination.

A geometric verifier evaluates the entire moving body throughout each submitted trajectory, not just its start and goal positions.
Static-plan endpoint agreement can substantially exceed full continuous validity; environment generation also shows poor functional compliance despite feasible layouts.
Results highlight the need to distinguish endpoint agreement from executable motion and geometric feasibility from satisfying all environment requirements.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are advancing in physical reasoning, but whether they can understand external physical drivers from internal observations remains an open question. Existing benchmarks have not specifically targeted this setting. To this end, we introduce CaveBench, a benchmark for abductive physical reasoning from internal observations. Models receive apparatus descriptions and internal images while the external controls remain hidden, and must infer the operations responsible for the observed responses. CaveBench spans 20 apparatus scenes in five physical domains and contains 10,200 simulated episodes, split into 9,000 training, 1,000 validation, and 200 test episodes. Questions span one to six events and require the complete control set at every event, testing whether an explanation accounts for the entire process. Synchronized observations and control records provide the inputs and reference answers. Evaluating 27 VLM configurations yields six-event exact-match accuracies of 68.0% for the strongest closed-source model and 12.5% for the strongest open-weight model. Seven adaptation baselines show that single-event gains need not improve complete sequences. Error analysis identifies failures in visual identification, physical inference, evidence integration, and action composition, specifying where current models struggle to connect internal phenomena with their external causes.

papers.abstract: Achieving both interpretable and high-performance inference is a key challenge in deep learning. While Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) provide inherent interpretability, they are constrained by task-specific training and rely on isolated visual concepts that fail to capture higher-order visual semantic relationships. Conversely, Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate zero-shot capabilities through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, standard CoT lacks a strict causal dependency between the generated rationale and the final output, compromising faithfulness. To bridge this gap, we propose Relational Bottleneck Models (RBMs), a novel training-free framework that transforms any off-the-shelf LVLMs into inherently interpretable models in a plug-and-play manner. RBMs consist of two stages: (i) Structured Rationale Generation (SRG), which explicitly models semantic interactions between visual concepts as subject-predicate-object triplets, and (ii) Rationale-Grounded Decoding (RGD), which enforces a strict causal dependency between the rationales and the final output. RGD aggregates rationale-conditional next-token distributions via an importance-weighted product-of-experts strategy, strictly excluding the image inputs from the decoding context. Extensive zero-shot evaluations across diverse benchmarks and LVLM backbones demonstrate that RBMs achieve superior interpretability while improving task performance over CBM baselines, entirely without task-specific fine-tuning.
bullets: Addresses the limited relationships captured by Concept Bottleneck Models and the weak causal faithfulness of standard Chain-of-Thought reasoning.
Uses Structured Rationale Generation to represent visual semantics as subject–predicate–object triplets.
Applies Rationale-Grounded Decoding to make final predictions depend strictly on generated rationales, excluding direct image input during decoding.
Works as a training-free, plug-and-play framework for off-the-shelf Large Vision Language Models.
Zero-shot evaluations across diverse benchmarks and backbones report improved interpretability and task performance over CBM baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Proposed Method. Relational Bottleneck Models (RBMs) consisting of (i) Structured Rationale Generation (SRG) and (ii) Rationale-Grounded Decoding (RGD). (i) SRG produces rationales for the final output by a set of semantic relation triplets of visual concepts in an input image. Each rationale is defined by a semantic relational triplet (subject, predicate, object) and an importance score. This structured rationale representation enables rich interpretability of high-level visual semantic relationships between concepts beyond the independent visual concept rationales often used in CBMs. (ii) Given rationales from an input image and a query, RGD constructs a composite next-token distribution by ensembling conditional distributions for each semantic relation triplet via importance-weighted product-of-experts. By decoding output tokens with this composite distribution, RBMs ensure the interpretability of the final outputs.

Figure 1. Overview. We propose an interpretable model, Relational Bottleneck Models (RBMs), based on large vision language models (LVLMs) in a plug-and-play manner. Previous Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) offer limited interpretability through their isolated concepts and are often limited in their applicability to the fixed task during training. In contrast, our RBMs can provide informative rationales, formed by visual semantic relation triplets with selfverbalized importance scores, and can be flexibly applied to various tasks that backbone LVLMs can solve without additional training.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to relate past experience, current spatial state, and future motion while following natural-language instructions. Recent approaches improve these capabilities through long-horizon memory, state-aware reasoning, and future prediction, yet these components are often modeled separately, leaving navigation state evolution insufficiently connected across time. We argue that camera pose provides a natural geometric representation for bridging past, present, and future states. Based on this insight, we propose PoseVLN, a pose-aware VLN framework that jointly learns navigation decisions and geometric state evolution. PoseVLN organizes visual memory and the current observation in an episode-relative coordinate frame, and jointly predicts the next K navigation actions together with a local $\Delta$Pose over the same horizon. The predicted $\Delta$Pose is composed with the current trajectory-level pose to obtain the future pose state, which is recursively propagated throughout navigation, forming a continuous geometric state evolution from past memory to future motion. Experiments on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val-Unseen splits demonstrate the effectiveness of explicitly modeling geometric state evolution, with PoseVLN outperforming the strongest compared baselines by 2.6 and 2.9 percentage points in success rate, respectively, using only single RGB observations.
authors: Pengyu Hou, Mingfei Han, Haihong Hao, Xiaolong Wu, Bo Dong, Xiaojun Chang, Salman Khan, Bin Shi
bullets: Addresses the weak connection between navigation memory, current state, and future motion in existing VLN systems.
Represents visual memory and observations in an episode-relative coordinate frame.
Jointly predicts the next K actions and local pose changes, recursively propagating future pose states during navigation.
Achieves gains of 2.6 and 2.9 success-rate points over the strongest compared baselines on R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val-Unseen, using single RGB observations.

papers.abstract: People reason with pictures as well as words. Interleaved multimodal reasoning gives models a similar way to solve problems by creating intermediate images and using them to guide further reasoning. Training models with this ability usually relies on task-specific demonstrations, which are difficult to collect. We introduce ThinkMorph-SSL, a two-stage training recipe that uses images themselves as a source of supervision. The first stage, pretext reasoning, converts visual pretext tasks, such as image colorization and denoising, into instruction-free interleaved traces. Models describe a corrupted or transformed image, generate a restored or canonical image, and interpret the result. The second stage uses automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning. At the same instruction-tuning budget, models trained with pretext reasoning outperform those trained with instruction tuning alone. The full recipe improves over the base model by an average of 11.33 accuracy points across twelve benchmarks. These results show that supervision derived from images can build the visual skills needed for interleaved reasoning and improve learning from task-specific demonstrations.
authors: Jiawei Gu, Linjie Li, Yiming Liu, Yunzhuo Hao, Huichen Wang, Guanzheng Chen, Zhichao Peng, Luxin Xu, Xinyu Zhang, Li Luo, Disen Lan, Zican Hu, Mingyang Song, David Valente, Alex Jinpeng Wang, Yafu Li, Ganqu Cui, Zhengyuan Yang, Qizhe Xie, Yejin Choi, Ranjay Krishna, Yu Cheng
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of collecting task-specific demonstrations for interleaved multimodal reasoning.
Converts image colorization, denoising, and similar pretext tasks into instruction-free reasoning traces.
Uses restored or canonical images within traces, followed by interpretation, to develop visual reasoning skills.
Adds automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning.
Improves over the base model by an average of 11.33 accuracy points across twelve benchmarks; pretext reasoning also outperforms instruction tuning alone at the same budget.

papers.abstract: Geometric rotary position encodings (RoPE) incorporate 3D camera geometry into multi-view attention by rotating token features according to viewing rays, depths, and reprojected image coordinates. Each coordinate is rotated across a progression of frequencies--its frequency band--yet existing implementations leave this band to inherited defaults, either retaining standard 2D RoPE's top frequency or letting the frequency span grow exponentially with the attention head dimension. We show that this unstandardized setting can reverse benchmark rankings. In novel view synthesis on RealEstate10K, RayRoPE matches the strongest baseline in the 47M model (144-channel heads), yet trails by 1.2 dB in the 25M model (48-channel heads), and exhibits the same reversal when varying head size alone at fixed model width. Populating a 243x range with four frequencies instead of the 3x default at 48 channels recovers 0.9 dB of that gap. Across view synthesis and two-view depth estimation, overly narrow bands consistently blur correspondence, whereas all three projection-based encodings perform reliably when their top frequency lies within 0.3--3 rotations per 8-pixel patch (10--90 rotations across 256x256 RealEstate10K). At the opposite extreme, overly wide bands degrade RayRoPE through a forward-backward asymmetry: averaging rotations over a predicted depth interval damps high frequencies in the forward pass, yet leaves their gradients with respect to predicted depth undamped. Blocking only those high-frequency depth gradients recovers 90--93% of the lost PSNR, showing that forward smoothing does not guarantee backward stability. Guided by this analysis, we distill practical guidelines--setting bands in image coordinates, populating spans in small heads, and avoiding unconditional same-view damping--and advocate reporting and matching frequency bands in future multi-view benchmarks.
authors: Seonghyun Jin, Youngmin Kim, Jong Chul Ye
bullets: Unstandardized frequency bands can reverse benchmark rankings across model head sizes.
Narrow bands blur correspondences; reliable performance occurs when top frequencies span roughly 0.3–3 rotations per 8-pixel patch.
Very wide bands destabilize RayRoPE because high-frequency depth gradients remain undamped despite forward-pass smoothing.
Expanding a 48-channel band from a 3× to 243× span recovers 0.9 dB of a reported performance gap.
The study recommends image-coordinate band selection, denser frequency population in small heads, and avoiding unconditional same-view damping.

papers.abstract: First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. However, it incurs heavy memory and system overhead from backpropagation, optimizer states, and a reference model. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. We find that directly applying standard ES or vanilla ARS to VLMs suffers from two fundamental failure modes: (i) patch-grid overfitting, fitting fragile grid-specific visual token artifacts while ignoring spatial invariants, and (ii) catastrophic forgetting, degrading general perception and out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks due to unbounded high-rank parameter and policy drift. We propose ARS-VLM, a visually aligned Augmented Random Search framework for forward-only VLM post-training. First, ARS-VLM extracts a contrastive visual basis from bilinearly paired cross-grid views, concentrating perturbations on shared visual signals while suppressing patch-shift artifacts. Second, ARS-VLM anchors shallow visual-fusion layers with a soft subspace prior while freeing deep reasoning layers, restraining policy drift without a reference model. Third, ARS-VLM scores perturbations on paired views to discard view-fragile directions during top-k selection. We evaluate ARS-VLM on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B on multimodal reasoning tasks. On 8B, ARS-VLM reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO (7.5x fewer optimization steps) and avoids the late OOD collapse of vanilla ARS and ES. Moreover, ARS-VLM achieves 75.41% single-view micro accuracy across seven OOD vision reasoning benchmarks, compared with 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO, using forward-only post-training.
authors: Xiangwei Wang, Jianyuan Lin, Peng Wang, Saman Halgamuge
bullets: Standard ES/ARS for VLMs can overfit patch-grid artifacts and catastrophically forget general or OOD capabilities.
It extracts a contrastive visual basis from paired cross-grid views to focus perturbations on shared spatial signals.
A soft subspace prior anchors shallow visual-fusion layers while allowing deeper reasoning layers to adapt.
Paired-view scoring filters view-fragile perturbations during top-k ARS selection.

On Qwen3-VL-8B, it reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO and maintains OOD performance, achieving 75.41% average single-view micro accuracy across seven benchmarks versus 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO.

papers.abstract: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar enables privacy-preserving, all-weather physical scene understanding across darkness, smoke, and walls. However, standard instruction tuning treats continuous radar streams as static text-like tokens, causing near-random global radar-to-text retrieval and severe physical drift under sensor blackouts. Conversely, coupling pairwise contrastive losses (e.g., SigLIP) directly into the shared backbone improves retrieval but injects $O(B^2)$ repulsive gradients that fracture continuous coordinate manifolds ($R^2 Rollout) and sample-axis Batch-VICReg to predict +3.0 s physical states; a stop-gradient alignment head then maps frozen prompt states onto the text hypersphere with false-negative masking. On a 4,541-window tri-domain suite (77/60.25/60 GHz) against 10 baselines, freezing the physical backbone and training only the decoupled head lifts R->T R@10 from 5.95% to 15.01% and improves MedRank from 107.0 to 60.0 while preserving identical physical readout: 3.37 deg ($R^2=+0.961$) blackout +3.0 s torso tilt, 1.89 m ($R^2=+0.679$; 1.19 m/+0.863 at the RF front-end) cluttered UAV altitude, 2.04 m ($R^2=+0.461$) behind-wall NLOS range, 0.9976 virtual-RIS invariance, and 100% fall recall. Across five 0.5B-1.8B LLM families (15 zero-overhead models), World-JEPA improves retrieval and 75%-drop completion in 10/10 runs and blackout tilt in 4/5 (Span-Euc), 2/5 (Scatter), and 5/5 (per-family best) over SFT.
authors: Yicheng Huang, Feng Ke, Linhan Chen, Ziyi Jiang, Xiu Yin Zhang
bullets: Addresses static text-like tokenization and backbone damage from direct contrastive alignment of continuous radar streams.
Uses a frozen physical world model with Batch-VICReg temporal prediction and a stop-gradient alignment head with false-negative masking.
On a 4,541-window, tri-domain suite, R→T R@10 increases from 5.95% to 15.01% and MedRank improves from 107.0 to 60.0.
Preserves physical readouts for blackout tilt, cluttered UAV altitude, behind-wall range, virtual-RIS invariance, and fall detection.
Across five LLM families, improves retrieval and 75%-drop completion in all 10 runs, with blackout-tilt gains varying by model family.

papers.tldr: PhysRF-WorldJEPA adapts heterogeneous LLMs to mmWave radar by decoupling language alignment from physical representation learning, improving radar–text retrieval while preserving robust physical-world predictions under difficult sensing conditions.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses large vision-language models (LVLMs) by calibrating quantization parameters on a small dataset without retraining. However, despite increasingly sophisticated calibration strategies, prior methods suffer substantial performance degradation under low-bit weight--activation quantization. To understand this degradation, we locate where quantization error is concentrated and examine the corresponding weight and activation distributions. We observe that a few outliers dominate the ranges shared by per-channel (PC) weights and per-token (PT) activations, leaving insufficient resolution for most values and mapping many of them to zero. These findings motivate a shift in focus from calibration refinement to the underlying quantization representation. We therefore present Rotate-and-Refine Quantization (RRQ) as a simple, effective baseline for LVLM PTQ, combining local Hadamard transforms with group quantization and efficient group-aware execution. Across 8 multimodal tasks and diverse quantization settings, RRQ substantially outperforms baselines while reducing inference time and memory usage. At W4A4, it retains over 96\% of full-precision performance on 8B models and over 99\% on a 32B model, compared with less than 8\% for these baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/kmc3661/RRQ
authors: Minchan Kang, Kyeonghye Park, Seoyoung Cho, Junhee Lee, Daeshik Kim, Yucheol Cho
bullets: PTQ degradation is traced to outliers that dominate shared quantization ranges, causing many typical values to collapse to zero.
The work shifts attention from increasingly complex calibration strategies to the underlying quantization representation.
RRQ combines local Hadamard transforms, group quantization, and group-aware execution.
Across 8 multimodal tasks, RRQ improves performance over prior baselines while reducing inference time and memory use.
At W4A4, it retains over 96% of full-precision performance for 8B models and over 99% for a 32B model; baselines retain less than 8%.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these abilities. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated benchmark with 3,368 questions of eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts. Layouts follow hospital design guidelines, answers are computed from the 3D scenes, and paired scene states test whether models change their answers when relevant evidence changes. Videos are photorealistic, and ten physicians screened the layouts. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K, our 44,750-question training set, lifts two MLLMs 16-20 points above the best proprietary model. 3D maps given to the fine-tuned MLLM as input go largely unused: replacing them with another video's, even when they are ground truth, barely changes its accuracy. The proposed GeoJeV instead lets the MLLM compute with 3D: it reconstructs a scene memory from each video, selects 3D operations and their arguments from the MLLM's question state, and adds their evidence to its option scores. It achieves the highest accuracy of all evaluated models, narrowing the gap to physicians.
authors: Yang Bai, Yingzhi Xia, Ling Lin, Jun Cheng, Lin Fu, Huazhu Fu
bullets: Introduces 3,368 questions across eight spatial-reasoning types, based on 373 photorealistic hospital-room walkthroughs and paired scene changes.
Across 35 MLLMs, the best models score 45.7% (open) and 53.6% (proprietary) macro accuracy, below physicians’ 79.0% on a subset.
Patient-relative direction reasoning is especially difficult: 27 of 32 open models score below 40%.
Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K improves two MLLMs by 16–20 points, while supplied 3D maps are largely ignored.
GeoJeV enables explicit 3D scene reconstruction and operations, achieving the highest accuracy among evaluated models and narrowing the physician gap.

papers.abstract: The widespread deployment of latent generative models (LGMs) makes generated image source attribution essential for copyright auditing and data governance, yet practical attribution should remain reliable under common post-processing and platform-induced processing. Existing reconstruction-based attribution methods summarize an image's reconstruction response to a single global scalar, such as the reconstruction error or the ratio of two consecutive errors. These summaries discard channel-frequency structure, allowing image content and post-processing variation to obscure source evidence and making attribution after spreading difficult. We instead uncover a more stable source-discriminative cue under post-processing: the frequency-resolved evolution of residual energy across repeated applications of the same reconstruction operator. Motivated by this insight, we characterize a phenomenon we term Spectral Contraction and use it to build SpCon, a source-attribution framework that accesses only the target model's VAE. SpCon obtains adjacent residuals through two deterministic reconstructions, builds a spectral-contraction representation from their frequency-resolved relative energy change, and aggregates Student-t response densities for each source-condition pair over a finite set of fitted reference components. The same representation supports three settings according to non-belonging reference availability: none (Target-Only, TO; belonging references only), external out-of-domain sources (External-Reference, ER), or known in-domain competitors (Known-Reference, KR). Across seven LGMs, TO, ER, and KR attain average AUROC/AP of 0.8786/0.6344, 0.9404/0.7886, and 0.9652/0.8626 over the 35 conditions, all outperforming the strongest baseline (0.8154/0.5277), and achieve 0.8581/0.5507, 0.9369/0.7549, and 0.9734/0.8773 on the three social platforms.
authors: Chao Wang, Zijin Yang, Yaofei Wang, Yuang Qi, Weiming Zhang, Kejiang Chen
bullets: Existing methods reduce reconstruction behavior to a single scalar, losing frequency-specific source evidence.
SpCon uses two deterministic VAE reconstructions to measure frequency-resolved relative changes in residual energy, termed Spectral Contraction.
The framework supports target-only, external-reference, and known-reference attribution settings.
Across seven latent generative models and 35 conditions, all settings outperform the strongest baseline; performance remains strong on three social platforms.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on source attribution for generated images using spectral contraction. While a forensic task, it deals with the properties of generative models (Latent Generative Models) and their outputs.
papers.title: Not the Scalar, but Its Evolution: Robust Source Attribution for Generated Images
papers.tldr: SpCon improves generated-image source attribution by modeling how reconstruction residual energy evolves across frequencies, making attribution more robust to post-processing and platform processing.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) strengthens model capabilities through feedback from humans and environments. However, emerging evidence suggests that reward optimization can produce outputs whose errors are harder for humans to detect. To address this issue, we construct ITHV (the Image-Text Hallucination Verifiability Dataset), comprising 2,728 visually grounded instances that distinguish between obvious hallucinations, which humans readily detect, and elusive hallucinations, which humans struggle to identify. We then propose DAPO-V, an extension of DAPO that maximizes correctness subject to a budget on verifiability-aware risk. Specifically, DAPO-V combines a verifiability-aware reward with adaptive dual control, where larger penalties are assigned to incorrect responses on questions with lower human verification accuracy. An adaptive multiplier further adjusts the penalty strength according to risk-budget violations. Across three MLLM base models, DAPO-V improves overall accuracy while substantially improving accuracy on elusive hallucination questions by 5.78--9.72 percentage points over accuracy-only DAPO. We further test DAPO-V with a blinded human study, which shows that hallucinations are more readily detected in DAPO-V than those of the base model.
authors: Jianhong Pang, Ziyi Ye, Qiuxia Hou, Yanhao Zhang, Zuxuan Wu
bullets: RL can increase capability while making errors harder for humans to recognize.
ITHV contains 2,728 visually grounded instances distinguishing obvious from elusive hallucinations.
DAPO-V combines verifiability-aware rewards with adaptive dual control under a risk budget.
Across three MLLM base models, it improves elusive-hallucination accuracy by 5.78–9.72 percentage points over accuracy-only DAPO.
A blinded human study found DAPO-V hallucinations easier to detect than those from the base model.

papers.title: More Powerful, Less Verifiable? Mitigating Hard-to-Verify Hallucinations in MLLM's Reinforcement Learning
