papers.abstract: In-context segmentation (ICS) uses one or a few annotated reference images to specify what to segment in a target image. Existing training-free ICS approaches typically rely on manually designed inference procedures, which may limit how flexibly reference information is combined. Learned in-context inference offers an adaptive alternative, but acquiring this capability through segmentation-specific training can compromise generalization to unseen domains. We therefore ask: can a pretrained in-context learner infer what to segment from annotated references without segmentation-specific training? We introduce SegPFN, a training-free framework that reformulates ICS as tabular classification over frozen visual features. A frozen tabular prior-data fitted network (PFN) uses labeled reference patches as context to classify patches in the target image. We comprehensively benchmark SegPFN against major existing ICS methods across 11 datasets spanning semantic, part, and personalized segmentation. SegPFN improves overall mean intersection-over-union (mIoU) by 4.7 points over the strongest overall baseline and achieves the highest average mIoU in four of five task-shot settings. Further analyses show that hard-negative reference patches improve fine-grained target discrimination, while joint conditioning enables SegPFN to use multiple references effectively. These results show that SegPFN offers a simple and effective paradigm for training-free in-context segmentation.
authors: Jiajian Ma, Yihao Qiao, Ke Chen, Kaiyue Feng, Wushuang Rui, Abhishek Jha, Aarti Darji, Yiqiu Shen
bullets: Reformulates in-context segmentation as tabular classification over frozen visual features.
Uses labeled reference patches as context for classifying patches in a target image, avoiding segmentation-specific training.
Benchmarked across 11 datasets covering semantic, part, and personalized segmentation tasks.
Improves overall mIoU by 4.7 points over the strongest overall baseline and leads in four of five task-shot settings.
Hard-negative references aid fine-grained discrimination, while joint conditioning supports multiple references.

papers.abstract: Specialist medical vision-language models (VLMs) are strong within their specialties but hard to unify: their training data are often private, and independently developed specialists cannot be assumed to share an architecture. Deploying these large models separately is costly. We present HuluOPD, an on-policy distillation recipe that unifies heterogeneous specialists into one lightweight VLM using only unlabeled prompts, without requiring reference answers or the specialists' training data. The lightweight model answers each prompt, and the specialist of the prompt's modality supervises its response; a continuation-aligned cross-tokenizer loss makes this possible even when they differ in architecture and tokenizer. We apply HuluOPD to five specialists, for ultrasound, pathology, optical coherence tomography, fundus photography, and dental imaging. To distill and evaluate them, we build HuluOPDCorpus, 914k unlabeled prompts, and HuluOPDBench, 47k held-out test items, from over 90 public datasets, and score all models under one protocol on 132k test items, including third-party benchmarks. A single model with 10% of the five specialists' combined parameters retains 94% of their question-answering performance, and one with 2% retains 89%. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of unifying heterogeneous medical specialist VLMs without requiring their training data or a shared architecture.
authors: Yuncheng Zhang, Songtao Jiang, Yitian Tang, Zijie Meng, Zihan Xu, Xuxiang Ren, Jian Wu, Hualiang Wang, Zuozhu Liu
bullets: Addresses the cost and incompatibility of deploying independently developed specialist medical VLMs.
Uses on-policy distillation: the lightweight model answers unlabeled prompts, while the relevant specialist supervises each response.
A continuation-aligned cross-tokenizer loss enables distillation across different architectures and tokenizers without reference answers or specialist training data.
Introduces HuluOPDCorpus (914k prompts) and HuluOPDBench (47k test items), with evaluation on 132k items across five imaging specialties.
Models using 10% and 2% of the specialists’ combined parameters retain 94% and 89% of their question-answering performance, respectively.

papers.abstract: Comparing two entities in an image, multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) often answer wrongly. We find that the answer bias enters not when the model sees, but when it decides with the image in view: the model's own descriptions of the two entities often already hold the right answer. We therefore propose D$^3$ (Describe, Don't Decide): the model describes each entity alone, decides from these descriptions without the image, and merges this decision with its direct answer. Without any training, D$^3$ improves all 79 model-benchmark pairs across ten benchmarks and eight 7-9B MLLMs. On held-out GQA comparison questions, the mean accuracy of these models rises from 72.4% to 83.2% (up to +21.5% per model), higher than that of Qwen2.5-VL-32B answering directly (82.8%). Code will be available at https://github.com/paul-swu/describe-dont-decide.
bullets: MLLMs often identify the correct comparison evidence in their descriptions but make errors when deciding with the image visible.
D³ has the model describe each entity independently, compare the descriptions without the image, and combine that decision with its direct answer.
The training-free method improves all 79 model–benchmark pairs tested across ten benchmarks and eight 7–9B MLLMs.
On held-out GQA comparison questions, mean accuracy increases from 72.4% to 83.2%, with gains up to 21.5% per model.
The approach is evaluated for image-based comparison questions; the abstract does not establish broader task coverage beyond these settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2. D3 describes with the image in view and decides without it. Left: the direct answer. Given the image and the original question, the MLLM answers wrongly; pimg (orange) is its probability for each option. Right: the three steps of D3; in the first two, the MLLM takes the box on its left and returns the one on its right. Describe Each Entity Alone: the two entities and the aspect (yellow) are read from the question, and each entity is described in its own call, with the image but not the original question, giving d1 and d2 (green). Decide Without the Image: given only d1, d2, and the original question (the text-only call), the MLLM gives the description-based decision pdesc (purple). Merge at Equal Weight: the output is the option y with the larger (1 − λ) pimg(y) + λ pdesc(y), where λ = 1 2 (Eq. 1). The snowflake marks the frozen MLLM, the same in every call. Example: Qwen2.5-VL on one GQA question.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a training-free inference strategy to correct answer bias in multimodal LLMs, directly relevant to multimodal foundation model behavior.
papers.title: Describe, Don't Decide: Correcting Answer Bias in Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: D³ reduces answer bias in multimodal LLMs by making them describe image entities separately before deciding between them.

papers.abstract: Even when multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer incorrectly, their internal cues often point to the relevant region. A widely used remedy re-presents the cue-selected region as an enlarged crop to supply finer detail. However, we find that much of its gain requires no new detail: it largely survives when the crop comes from the already-seen low-resolution input, and partly even when the region's cached tokens are merely copied. Part of re-presentation's gain thus comes from drawing attention to evidence the model already holds. We propose InCue, a test-time framework that makes better use of this evidence without additional visual input. InCue treats visual attention and predictive-entropy gradients as Internal Cues, couples them into a spatial target, and optimizes only an offset on the existing visual tokens to steer attention toward it. Under matched visual-token budgets, InCue achieves state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming recent test-time methods and improving four MLLMs by up to 8.9% on V$^*$ and 23.4% on its hard samples. Its gains carry over to eight general benchmarks. Code will be available at https://github.com/paul-swu/InCue.
authors: Shuwei Wu, Siyue Yu, Longin Jan Latecki
bullets: Re-presenting cropped regions helps partly by highlighting evidence the model has already seen, not only by supplying finer detail.
InCue combines visual-attention and predictive-entropy gradients to identify a spatial target.
It optimizes an offset over existing visual tokens, avoiding additional visual input while preserving matched token budgets.
The method reportedly achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving four MLLMs by up to 8.9% on V* and 23.4% on hard samples, with gains across eight general benchmarks.
Scope: InCue is a test-time framework and relies on internal cues available from the MLLM.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of InCue. The MLLM stays frozen, and the only free variable is an additive offset ∆U on the cached visual tokens U0. SCC couples the read-out attention cue A with the sensitivity cue S, obtained by backpropagating the predictive entropy H(p), into the joint response J . RCR amplifies J inside the best-scoring window W ⋆ to form the spatial target T . Test-time optimization then updates ∆U to increase the overlap between the current attention A(k) and T (k). The cues and the target are refreshed at every step k, and the answer is read out after K steps (Output): here it changes from (C) pink to the correct (D) black.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a test-time optimization framework that steers MLLM visual tokens using internal cues, fitting both test-time learning and multimodal LLM research.

papers.abstract: A driving planner needs both scene semantics, which vision-language models (VLMs) provide, and spatial structure, which geometric foundation models recover from visual history. We present VLG-Drive, which keeps both models frozen and trains only a fusion interface and a planner from trajectory labels. At each camera-grid cell, the interface fuses the paired VLM and geometry features into one joint token through a geometry-anchored residual, and a command-conditioned planner reads these tokens to predict the ego trajectory. VLG-Drive achieves 31.78 EPDMS on NavHard under perturbed initial states, the highest among the compared methods, and 88.27 PDMS on NavTest from cameras alone. Pointwise fusion outperforms independent VLM and geometry streams on both benchmarks. In closed-loop driving on 420 HUGSIM scenarios, VLG-Drive outperforms all compared planners. These results indicate that a lightweight planner trained on fused features of frozen vision-language and geometric foundation models is an effective alternative to adapting either model for planning.
authors: Junge Zhang, Jie Zhu, Yanqi Jia, Xiangyu Xu, Zixun Huang, Wenbin He, Xin Li, Jiachen Li, Liu Ren
bullets: Combines scene semantics from a VLM with spatial structure from a geometric foundation model.
Fuses paired features at each camera-grid cell using a geometry-anchored residual interface.
Trains only the fusion interface and command-conditioned planner from trajectory labels.
Reports 31.78 EPDMS on NavHard, 88.27 PDMS on NavTest, and strong closed-loop performance across 420 HUGSIM scenarios.
Pointwise fusion outperforms using independent VLM and geometry streams; the approach avoids adapting either foundation model.

papers.abstract: Shape decomposition represents 3D objects as a compact set of geometric primitives for interpretable modeling and simulation. However, existing decomposition methods are trained primarily for geometric fidelity, without explicit constraints on physical plausibility, and can therefore produce disconnected parts or physically unstable reconstructions. We present PhysDec, an agentic framework that draws on a pretrained vision-language model's semantic understanding and commonsense reasoning to predict material-aware primitive decompositions from a few images. Within this framework, PhysDec-Loop is an agentic pipeline that reasons about part structure and materials, using a reference 3D point cloud for geometric feedback and physical verifiers to guide iterative refinement. Through self-evolution, we further develop another agentic pipeline, PhysDec-Evolved, which learns from prior corrections to predict primitive decompositions from images without point-cloud feedback or a correction loop at inference. Experiments show that PhysDec-Loop improves geometric fidelity, physical plausibility and visual quality over geometry-focused baselines, while PhysDec-Evolved approaches its performance at substantially lower inference cost.
authors: Wenchao Ma, Rui Yu, Fan Zhu, Jiachen Liu, Sharon X. Huang
bullets: Targets failures of geometry-only decomposition, such as disconnected or physically unstable parts.
PhysDec-Loop combines semantic and material reasoning with point-cloud feedback and physical verifiers for iterative refinement.
PhysDec-Evolved learns from prior corrections to work without point-cloud feedback or an inference-time correction loop.
Experiments report improved geometric fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality over geometry-focused baselines, with PhysDec-Evolved achieving similar performance at lower inference cost.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding requires resolving fine visual details within the context that gives them meaning. Additional views can improve localization, but their value depends on what evidence they expose and how much context they preserve. We explore a capability of vision-language models (VLMs): even when their coordinate predictions are incorrect, they can describe visual evidence worth inspecting. We introduce \textbf{SPARK}, \textit{\textbf{S}emantic \textbf{P}robe-guided \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{R}egion see\textbf{K}ing}, a training-free framework that turns this semantic guidance into targeted visual observations. Exploration probes describe relevant context and distinguishing target details, while verification probes identify evidence needed to assess emerging hypotheses. Their spatial attention guides view placement, contextual responses determine crop extent, and observation history encourages complementary inspection. The resulting predictions are combined through uncertainty-weighted voting. On ScreenSpot-Pro, SPARK improves grounding accuracy over single-view inference by 13.9, 25.2, and 16.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, and UI-TARS, outperforming all compared test-time methods for each backbone. Consistent gains across four additional benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse interfaces and grounding tasks. These results establish semantic probing as an effective mechanism for turning a frozen VLM's understanding of what to inspect into more accurate GUI grounding.
authors: Ruixiao Shi, Fu Feng, Yucheng Xie, Jing Wang, Xin Geng
bullets: GUI grounding benefits from additional views, but effective inspection must balance fine detail with contextual meaning.
SPARK uses exploration probes to identify relevant context and target details, then verification probes to test emerging localization hypotheses.
Spatial attention guides where to look, probe responses determine crop extent, and observation history promotes complementary views.
Uncertainty-weighted voting combines observations into final predictions.
On ScreenSpot-Pro, SPARK improves single-view accuracy by 13.9–25.2 percentage points across three VLM backbones and also gains on four additional benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Subliminal learning refers to a surprising phenomenon in language models wherein a prompt given to one model (e.g., preference for cats) can be subliminally distilled to another model via training on data that is ostensibly meaningless (e.g., number sequences). This paper shows that text-based subliminal learning transfers cross-modally, in particular, a topic/preference (e.g., animals) transferred through number sequences across vision-language models also changes how images are generated and represented. First, we show that a diffusion model using the student as its text encoder generates the student's animal more often than with the original model as its text encoder, but not its color or style. We then investigate the mechanism behind this phenomenon and which concepts transfer across modalities. A constant component of the student's change accounts for much of the shift of image representations toward the trait. Adding this component uniformly can change the generated animal, which depends on the whole prompt, but not concepts such as color or style, which are encoded in a single token. Finally, we introduce weight lens as an approach to identify a subliminal trait from the weights of a single trained model, and show that it identifies the trait of nearly every student, including traits that do not surface in generated images.
authors: Saraswathy Amjith, Kimia Hamidieh, Antonio Torralba, Yoon Kim
bullets: A topic or animal preference can be distilled between vision-language models via number sequences.
The transferred animal preference affects image generation and representations, but color and style preferences do not.
A constant component of the student’s parameter change explains much of the shift toward the transferred trait.
The effect depends on how concepts are distributed across prompt tokens: whole-prompt traits transfer more readily than single-token attributes.
The proposed weight lens detects subliminal traits in nearly every trained student, including traits absent from generated images.

papers.abstract: Scientific measurements reported in scholarly articles are often embedded in compound figures rather than available as machine-readable data. Recovering these measurements at literature scale requires an integrated workflow for figure localization, panel decomposition, chart identification, numerical reconstruction, and experimental context association. We present \textit{SciFig2Data}, an automated, high-throughput workflow for harvesting structured experimental data from scientific PDF repositories. The system integrates multi-scale document element detection, adaptive compound figure decomposition, two-stage OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided multimodal large language model (MLLM) reconstruction. It further incorporates directory-level batch execution, caching, and structured logging to support large-scale processing. We demonstrate the workflow on two biomedical literature corpora comprising 605 toxicology and pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle (LNP) articles. The pipeline successfully reconstructed 468 and 242 tabular outputs from the respective corpora, illustrating its practical applicability to literature-scale scientific data harvesting. By associating reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata, SciFig2Data provides a workflow for transforming graphical evidence in scholarly publications into structured, context-enriched data records for downstream AI4Science applications.
authors: Xinhe Wu, Yicheng Ye, Yadong Jin
bullets: Addresses the challenge of recovering machine-readable measurements embedded in compound scientific figures.
Combines figure localization, panel decomposition, OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided MLLM reconstruction.
Adds batch processing, caching, and structured logging for high-throughput repository-scale extraction.
Applied to 605 toxicology/pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle articles, producing 468 and 242 tabular outputs, respectively.
Links reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata for downstream AI4Science applications.

papers.abstract: Harnesses for vision-language models (VLMs) have grown with the models' capabilities, notably for images far larger than those seen in training, where downscaling loses small details. Most of them wrap the VLM in a fixed procedure, such as a zoom tree, that decides in advance where it looks and how the evidence is combined. These procedures make up for the weaknesses of older models by keeping them on a task-specific path, but with frontier models that reliably plan and use tools, they can lower accuracy. We propose RVLM-X, a task-generalizable recursive VLM harness that runs unchanged across photographs, charts and maps. Following the recursive inference of Recursive Language Models, the VLM programmatically controls its own visual context in a code REPL that holds the full-resolution image and calls itself recursively on regions that it chooses. With a cost-efficient frontier model as the base of every method, RVLM-X is more accurate than a single call on all 7 public benchmarks and has the highest pooled accuracy. Because existing benchmarks mostly test whether a model finds one small detail, we also introduce MapGenBench, procedurally generated maps whose questions combine fine-detail perception with multi-step reasoning. There, RVLM-X answers 71.4% of held-out questions against 55.5% for the strongest baseline. Overall, our findings suggest that as VLMs plan and use tools more reliably, letting the model write its own visual search works better than fixing one in advance.
authors: Aadi Palnitkar, Dmytro Kurdydyk, Xiaomin Lin
bullets: Fixed zoom procedures can constrain frontier VLMs that are capable of planning and tool use.
RVLM-X uses a code REPL containing the full-resolution image, enabling recursive self-selection of regions and context.
The same harness operates across photographs, charts, and maps without task-specific changes.
It outperforms a single full-image call on all seven public benchmarks and achieves the highest pooled accuracy.
On the introduced MapGenBench, RVLM-X reaches 71.4% accuracy versus 55.5% for the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Understanding a group conversation means deciding, from video and audio, who is speaking and to whom. Leading systems treat these tasks offline on single-channel clips and align models with a self-evaluation reward. We propose BEARING, a geometry-first alternative built on one measured signal: the direction from which a microphone array beside the camera hears a sound. A label-free calibration learned from the stream registers this direction into the camera image, and an online registry of faces, voices and directions needs no enrollment. The registered direction serves as (i) a visual prompt for a vision-language model, a marker on the speaker or an arrow toward an off-screen source; (ii) one input of a reliability-weighted fusion with visual active-speaker detection, for speakers in the same direction from the array; and (iii) a verifiable reward for alignment: the named speaker must sit where the sound comes from, the confidence must match that check, and always answering "group" earns nothing. Every decision is online, with the lookahead as an explicit parameter. On 9,498 addressee-labelled utterances from three AMI sites and egocentric EasyCom, the direction prompt raises speaker accuracy from 54% to 74%; addressee accuracy moves by about two points, because telling one addressee from the group depends on the words more than on where people are. For co-located speakers on AVDIAR, visual active-speaker detection holds 95% where direction alone falls to 59%. The verifiable reward beats self-evaluation under GRPO, reward-ranked fine-tuning and DPO; shrinking the lookahead from 5 s to 0.5 s costs 4.5 DER points on AMI, and learning the registration online costs a dip in the first two minutes before the system overtakes vision alone. Code and evaluation protocols will be released.
authors: Nader Lobandi, Lombe Chileshe, Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini, Mohammad H. Mahoor
bullets: Calibrates microphone-array sound direction to the camera image without labels, while tracking faces, voices, and directions online without enrollment.
Uses the registered direction as a visual prompt, fuses it with visual active-speaker detection, and provides a verifiable alignment reward for model training.
Raises speaker accuracy from 54% to 74% on AMI and EasyCom; addressee accuracy improves by only about two points because addressee identification depends more on language.
For co-located speakers, visual active-speaker detection reaches 95% accuracy versus 59% for audio direction alone on AVDIAR.
Performance depends on temporal lookahead and online calibration: reducing lookahead to 0.5 seconds costs 4.5 DER points, with an initial calibration dip.

papers.title: BEARING: Who Is Talking to Whom? Grounding Acoustic Direction in Vision for Online Multi-Party Conversation

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed how humans interact with information, enabling natural-language interfaces across various domains. They are increasingly deployed for geospatial applications including map-based question answering, location-based services, and natural-language interfaces to spatial databases. But are LLMs truly location-aware, able to reliably interpret and precisely answer location queries involving real-world coordinates, points of interest (POIs), and geospatial distances? To answer this concretely, we present LimoBench, a street-level benchmark of 82 natural-language location queries over seven canonical spatial operations: geocoding, reverse geocoding, routing, directionality, range search, $k$-nearest-neighbor search, and spatial join. The queries are grounded in real map data of West Lafayette, Indiana, and are graded by location and semantic complexity. They are designed to probe LLMs' street-level spatial awareness, from simple lookups to multi-step spatial reasoning. We also present Limo, an approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enhances the location awareness of LLMs. Limo grounds LLMs in PostGIS-backed spatial data through a compact set of tools. We find that ungrounded models mostly achieve single-digit accuracy (3.1% for GPT-6 Luna) across different spatial operations. In contrast, the same models achieve near-perfect accuracy (99.3% for GPT-6 Luna) when given access to Limo's spatial tools through MCP. Current LLMs thus have limited and unreliable street-level spatial knowledge, while grounding provides accurate answers at modest overhead (+0.2 s latency, 7.7$\times$ tokens, and 2.2$\times$ cost for GPT-6 Luna). We release the benchmark, Limo toolset, and evaluation code to encourage the community to evaluate their own location-aware LLM approaches.
authors: Gautam Choudhary, Jack Peng, Udesh Kumarasinghe, Rachel Rafik, Yousef Hammad, Ahmed Samy, Walid G. Aref
bullets: Benchmarks 82 natural-language queries across seven spatial operations, including geocoding, routing, range search, and spatial joins.
Uses real map data from West Lafayette, Indiana, with queries spanning simple lookups to multi-step spatial reasoning.
Ungrounded models mostly reach single-digit accuracy, while MCP-based grounding raises GPT-6 Luna accuracy from 3.1% to 99.3%.
Grounding incurs modest reported overhead in latency, token use, and cost.
Releases the benchmark, Limo toolset, and evaluation code for further research.

papers.abstract: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. We perform paired forward ablation and find that nearly nine out of ten high-confidence commits are insensitive to the image, while degenerate and hallucination samples exhibit significant increases in the entropy of deep-layer attention organization. Based on this diagnosis, we propose CD-APC, a training-free decoding method. CD-APC performs evidence-adjusted scoring within a base-supported pool and uses dual gating based on model acceptability and contrastive concentration to decide whether to commit, together with an inverse-window mechanism that adapts to inter-step difficulty. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, CD-APC consistently improves performance, indicating that stable visual evidence improves model outputs.
authors: Tongxiao Hu, Yikai Zhao, Qiyan Zhao, Xiaosong Yuan, Xuhang Chen, Pengzhou Cheng, Xiaofeng Zhang
bullets: High-confidence token commitments are often insensitive to image evidence, limiting confidence-based decoding.
Degenerate and hallucinated outputs show increased entropy in deep-layer attention organization.
CD-APC adjusts candidate scores using visual evidence within a base-supported pool.
Dual gating and an inverse-window mechanism adapt commitment decisions to acceptability and decoding difficulty.
The method consistently improves results across two backbones and five benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Learning spatial representations often relies on explicitly predicting geometric quantities, but how physical geometry is organized within learned representations remains less understood. We ask whether 3D structure can emerge from learning relations across 2D observations, without 3D prediction targets. We introduce RePT, which learns compact relations between distinct physical points through cross-view 2D point prediction. The learned relation space develops a geometric organization in which magnitudes, angles, and neighborhoods reflect physical 3D displacement. A single linear readout fitted on 16 scenes recovers displacement length and angle on 39 held-out scenes without refitting (Pearson r = 0.72 and 0.78). The ARKitScenes-trained checkpoint also retains strong geometric organization on ScanNet++, showcasing generalizability. In controlled comparisons, distinct-point relational prediction consistently yields stronger geometric organization than matched same-point correspondence learning. This organization depends on additive relations and adaptive scene context, and higher point-transfer accuracy does not by itself produce stronger organization. More broadly, our results suggest that 3D geometry need not be an explicit prediction target and can instead emerge as a structural property of representations trained to relate 2D observations, pointing to relational prediction as a complementary route to learning the representations that spatial intelligence builds on.

Organization depends on additive relations and adaptive scene context; point-transfer accuracy alone is insufficient.

papers.abstract: Cognitive neuroscience learned that an activation map is not a map of necessity. Regions that light up during a task are not always needed for it, and only lesions reveal which ones are. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) vision-language models come with an activation map for free, since the router records which experts respond to image and text tokens, and recent work reads modality-specialized experts off this map. We bring the lesion. In Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B, Kimi-VL-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, 3 to 12% of the experts are vision-exclusive: image tokens route to them at up to five times the uniform rate and text tokens almost never. In Qwen3-VL they receive a quarter of all image-token routing, and lesioning all of them costs less than one percentage point on average over eight perception benchmarks and free-form OCR, no more than lesioning a random set of the same size. In Kimi-VL and Gemma-4 the lesion also costs no more than a random set. Scoped lesions, which remove an expert set only at image positions or only at text positions, then show where the models do depend on their experts. In Qwen3-VL, silencing every expert at every image position costs 3 points, against 45 at text positions, where the dependence sits in dual-use experts that text-only tasks need as well. Across models the image-side dependence is 2 to 3 points in Qwen3-VL and Kimi-VL and 26 in Gemma-4. Reading text in images is the one ability that needs image-position experts in every model. The exclusive experts receive informative patches, produce outputs of ordinary size, and stay inert under sensory deprivation: text-only training recruits them only when load balancing forces it. In Kimi-VL the balancing bias itself manufactures most of them. Load balancing draws the modality map in the part of the computation the models depend on least. Expert selection, pruning and skipping should follow the lesion, not the map.
authors: Zhixuan Ge, Anqi Li, Kexin Geng, Wei Qiu
bullets: Across Qwen3-VL, Kimi-VL and Gemma-4, 3–12% of experts are vision-exclusive and can receive substantial image-token routing.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning agents increasingly rely on external tools, such as 3D reconstruction, segmentation, and geometric computation, to answer questions that a multimodal large language model (MLLM) cannot resolve from pixels alone. Tool access, however, shifts the bottleneck to orchestration: the agent must decide which tools to call, in what order, and how to interpret their outputs, yet a stateless agent repeats the same mistakes across tasks. We ask whether a frozen tool-using agent can improve its orchestration from its own interaction history, without parameter updates. We present SpatialCraft, a self-evolving framework that maintains two forms of external knowledge: Experiences, condition-action tactics distilled by contrasting rollouts of the same task, and Skills, multi-step procedures with explicit activation and termination conditions. Three designs couple the two streams. Experiences can be anchored to a Skill, appearing only while it is active rather than once per task. A Contrastive Utility Score estimates each Experience's effect by randomly withholding it across rollouts of the same task, separating its contribution from task difficulty, and Experiences with consistently positive utility are consolidated into the Skills they support. Across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones, SpatialCraft achieves the best accuracy in all 20 settings, showing that a frozen agent can learn to orchestrate spatial tools from its own experience.
authors: Xiwei Liu, Yulong Li, Xuhui Li, Zhixiang Lu, Haolin Yang, Jianxu Chen, Yifan Lu, Di Fan, Yutong Xie
bullets: Addresses repeated orchestration errors when agents choose and sequence spatial tools.
Stores condition–action Experiences and procedures with activation and termination conditions as Skills.
Uses contrastive rollouts to estimate an Experience’s utility and consolidates consistently useful ones into Skills.
Combines Experiences and Skills through three designs, including skill-activated experiences.
Achieves the best accuracy across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones, covering 20 settings.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models effectively learn action policies from robot demonstrations, but struggle to generalize to changes in object positions and task goals. General multimodal foundation models (MFMs) offer complementary scene understanding and spatial reasoning, but remain slow and unreliable for direct fine-grained control. To understand how MFMs can improve VLA spatial generalization, we conduct a systematic capability analysis across multiple VLA architectures using atomic-stage interventions, revealing that many failures stem from poor target grounding and global spatial routing, while local manipulation skills remain largely usable. Based on these findings, we propose MFM-VLA, a selective collaboration framework in which an MFM provides target grounding and spatial guidance, controllers execute free-space motion, and the VLA retains control over fine-grained manipulation. We fine-tune the VLA with action-chunk-level dense geometric captions and perturbed-state recovery data to improve local guidance following and recovery from unfamiliar handoff states. A development-calibrated capability router selects between direct VLA execution and MFM-assisted execution to avoid unnecessary intervention. Across LIBERO-PRO, ALOHA-Sim-PRO, RoboCasa365, and real-world chemistry tasks, MFM-VLA improves success rates by 14.9, 74.0, 3.6, and 30.9 percentage points, respectively, over the corresponding base VLA. The project page is available at https://tom-zgt.github.io/MFM-VLA
authors: Guangting Zheng, Shaoxuan Wang, Yu Yuan, Zhipeng Tang, Jiajun Deng, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: VLA failures often arise from inaccurate target grounding and global spatial routing, while local manipulation skills remain usable.
The framework selectively combines MFM guidance, controller-based free-space motion, and VLA fine-grained control.
Dense geometric captions and perturbed-state recovery data strengthen local guidance and recovery from unfamiliar handoff states.
A calibrated router invokes MFM assistance only when needed.
Success rates improve over base VLAs across simulated and real-world chemistry tasks, with gains ranging from 3.6 to 74.0 percentage points.

The adapted VLA performs contact execution, while a separate grasp monitor triggers bounded controller-assisted local recovery.

papers.abstract: We introduce CoRe, in which understanding and generation jointly shape one contextual representation for images and one for text, trained from scratch. Each representation is read for understanding, conditions the other modality, and is the space in which that modality is generated by a continuous flow from Gaussian noise. With 383M parameters trained on CC12M and no pretrained language model, text encoder, or VAE at inference, CoRe matches a same-data contrastive-only baseline in global understanding and reaches COCO-30K FID 10.10, comparable to much larger generators built on pretrained components. In controlled comparisons at equal data and architecture, CoRe generates better in both directions (text to image and image to text) than a representation shaped by understanding alone and then frozen, and follows prompts better than generating in a space that understanding does not shape. In the other direction, with an attentive segmentation probe, on monocular depth, and when read by a frozen language model, CoRe surpasses the contrastive-only baseline: generation adds information that stronger readouts reach. Because generation runs inside the understanding representation, frozen real-image probes read and steer intermediate states and the model ranks its own samples without extra training. Because both modalities use continuous flows, both also distill to a few steps. Our controls indicate why one representation suffices: understanding organizes the representation semantically, while generation makes it retain more information.
authors: Hangke Sui, Chang Li, Yuyan Li, Mohammad Haris Baig, Daniel Ulbricht
bullets: Addresses the tension between representations optimized for understanding and those optimized for generation.
Uses one contextual representation per modality: each supports understanding, conditions the other modality, and is generated via a continuous flow from Gaussian noise.
Trained from scratch with 383M parameters on CC12M, without pretrained language models, text encoders, or inference-time VAEs.
Matches a contrastive-only baseline on global understanding and achieves COCO-30K FID 10.10, while outperforming controlled understanding-only representations in both generation directions.
Generation enriches representations for segmentation, monocular depth, frozen-language-model readouts, probing, steering, self-ranking, and few-step distillation.

papers.abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/
authors: Shaina Raza, Mohamed Hafez, Ahmed Y. Radwan, Khalid Elgazzar, Kathryn Hume
bullets: Provides four matched real/fake audio-video combinations per source clip, enabling direct measurement of modality reliance.
Covers face swaps, whole-frame video diffusion, and voice conversion across four tasks: authenticity, manipulation type, identity verification, and explanation.
Evaluates multimodal LLMs, trained detectors, and LoRA-fine-tuned MLLMs.
MLLMs perform poorly on four-way authenticity and detect video-only fakes much more reliably than voice-only fakes; trained detectors perform strongly in-distribution.
Held-out-generator testing shows reduced detector performance, while LoRA improves explanation scores; generalization and explanation remain open challenges.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for audio-video deepfake detection with a recognition objective and systematic evaluation of multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
papers.tldr: MOZAIC is a paired audio-video deepfake benchmark that disentangles whether models detect fake visuals, fake audio, or both, revealing strong performance gaps and weak generalization and explanation.

papers.abstract: Recent work on Large Language Models (LLMs) suggests that reasoning capabilities can be enhanced at test time not only through longer token-level reasoning traces, but also through additional computation in latent space. This raises a natural question for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs): can additional computation in latent space improve visual perception at test time? In this work, we first verify that MLLMs contain stable reusable layers that can be re-forwarded at inference time without disrupting normal generation. Based on this observation, we propose \textbf{Lo}ok \textbf{Ba}ck in the \textbf{L}atent \textbf{S}pace (\textbf{Lobals}), a training-free decoding method that identifies the contiguous layer window with the strongest visual-token attention and re-forwards through it, allowing the model to revisit visual evidence in latent space. We demonstrate that this latent-space revisit strategy can improve MLLMs' performance across diverse multimodal settings, including general vision-language tasks, visual hallucination tasks, and vision-centric tasks.
bullets: MLLMs contain stable layers that can be re-forwarded at inference time without disrupting generation.
LoBaLS identifies a contiguous layer window receiving the strongest attention from visual tokens.
The method re-forwards this window to let the model revisit visual evidence in latent space.
It improves performance across general vision-language, visual hallucination, and vision-centric tasks.
The approach is training-free and operates at test time.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) has increasingly benefited from tool-integrated pipelines that ground computation in explicit geometry. However, existing systems often compile queries into relatively open-ended artifacts, such as code, task constraints, tool plans, or gathered evidence, leaving what must be resolved before execution under-specified. This can lead to unnecessary tool acquisition and iterative refinement, while still producing plausible reasoning traces from incomplete spatial commitments. We identify this failure mode as under-committed query compilation. To address it, we propose PEPS, a training-free agent Parsing Executable Primitives for Spatial reasoning under a typed FESM schema over Frame, Entity, State, and Metric. PEPS follows a parse-before-execute principle: the Parser commits each query to a compact set of executable requirements; the Executor selectively grounds the required primitives through fixed geometric APIs and deterministic computation; and the Verifier checks whether these requirements are fulfilled, enabling early termination or targeted repair. Experiments on three spatial reasoning benchmarks and four VLM backbones show that PEPS improves reasoning accuracy while substantially reducing refinement rounds, API cost, and end-to-end latency over strong tool-integrated baselines. These results demonstrate that knowing what a query requires before execution makes tool-integrated spatial reasoning not only more reliable, but also more efficient.
bullets: Addresses under-committed query compilation, where systems execute before fully specifying what must be resolved.
Uses a typed FESM schema covering Frame, Entity, State, and Metric.
A Parser defines executable requirements; an Executor grounds only needed primitives via fixed geometric APIs; a Verifier enables early termination or targeted repair.
Across three benchmarks and four VLM backbones, PEPS improves accuracy while reducing refinement rounds, API cost, and latency.
The approach is training-free and focused on spatial reasoning with explicit geometric computation.

papers.abstract: Speech and audio language models connect continuous acoustic representations to decoders pretrained primarily on text data. Most such models use MLP or Q-Former interfaces to map acoustic features into the decoder's input space, requiring the decoder to learn how to interpret the resulting representations. We investigate whether grounding these representations in the decoder's existing text embeddings can help it use acoustic information while better preserving its pretrained text capabilities. We present ConvexLLM, a general-purpose speech and audio language model whose C-Gate interface represents audio as continuous convex combinations of frozen text embeddings. ConvexLLM achieves an eleven-task VoiceBench aggregate of 75.36, the highest among the open-weight models we compare, and an MMAU Test-mini accuracy of 62.50%. Its largest margins over the baselines are on spoken knowledge and reasoning tasks, while the strongest baselines are more accurate on audio understanding and transcription. In a comparison with a 2B-parameter decoder, C-Gate achieves higher aggregate spoken-language performance than MLP and Q-Former interfaces, with text-task performance close to MLP and task-dependent tradeoffs in transcription and audio understanding. These results support convex combinations of text embeddings as a viable interface for general-purpose speech and audio language models.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of making text-pretrained decoders effectively interpret continuous audio representations without degrading text performance.
Introduces C-Gate, an interface that represents audio as continuous convex combinations of the decoder’s frozen text embeddings.
Achieves a VoiceBench aggregate score of 75.36 and 62.50% accuracy on MMAU Test-mini.
Outperforms compared interfaces on aggregate spoken-language performance, especially on spoken knowledge and reasoning.
Shows trade-offs: stronger baselines perform better on some audio-understanding and transcription tasks.

papers.abstract: Contrastive objectives power state-of-the-art multimodal models, but their training remains slow, relying on long stochastic optimization. We propose a Unified Framework for Efficient Contrastive Alignment via Kernels (UniCon), which spans linear and nonlinear encoders as well as one-to-one and many-to-many alignments. At its core, UniCon introduces the contrastive similarity weight matrix $S(\gamma)$, which enables closed-form global solutions that provably replace minibatch back-propagation with exact updates. Through the lens of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS), UniCon provides a kernelized perspective that unifies contrastive alignment and reveals its connection to spectral methods. To validate the theory, we conduct experiments on synthetic, unimodal, multimodal, and zero-shot tasks, demonstrating that UniCon achieves substantial efficiency gains while preserving generality and strong empirical performance.
authors: Hangke Sui, Yuqing Wang, Minh N Do
bullets: Targets the training inefficiency of contrastive objectives in multimodal and related models.
Supports linear and nonlinear encoders, plus one-to-one and many-to-many alignment settings.
Introduces a contrastive similarity weight matrix, S(γ), for closed-form global solutions.
Uses a reproducing kernel Hilbert space view to connect contrastive alignment with spectral methods.
Experiments across synthetic, unimodal, multimodal, and zero-shot tasks show efficiency gains with strong empirical performance.

The near-identity structure and visual similarity of both matrices indicate that UniCon and SGD-CLIP achieve comparable discriminative performance in unimodal contrastive alignment.

papers.abstract: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.
authors: JB Kim, Byungwoo Jeon, Kyungmin Lee, Hyeonmo Kang, Cheonbok Park, Shinyoung Joo, Jinwoo Shin, Jeonghoon Kim
bullets: Problem: Visual understanding and generation use heterogeneous representations, making them difficult to integrate in one model.
Method: Abstraction Fusion builds shared visual tokens from hierarchical frozen-encoder features.
Method: Block-wise MoT adds a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model at block boundaries.
Result: Shared representations improve generative learning while preserving pretrained understanding and maintaining comparable reconstruction fidelity.
Implication: Pretrained vision-language representations can serve as an effective foundation for visual generation.

papers.abstract: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.
authors: Xiwei Liu, Yulong Li, Xuhui Li, Xinlin Zhuang, Zhixiang Lu, Haolin Yang, Jianxu Chen, Yifan Lu, Zhiran Zhang, Yutong Xie
bullets: Introduces 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, starting from a single view.
Compares each model’s exploration with same-budget random walks and oracle routes to separate purposeful seeking from spatial reasoning.
Uses 3D-verified questions, masked-evidence abstention tests, and human verification of over 95% of sampled questions.
Across 23 VLMs, the strongest models seek evidence purposefully but lose useful information through limited memory.
Weaker and specialized models perform near random exploration or fail to reason from gathered evidence.

papers.abstract: Preference tuning of text-to-image diffusion models spends most of its compute generating candidate images, yet training prompts are typically sampled uniformly at random, wasting compute generating images that provide too little signal for model alignment. To best utilize the available compute, we study prompt selection, where at each iteration we identify the most useful prompts for preference tuning. We separate prompt selection into a utility score, an estimator of that utility score, and batch selection. Within this framework, we propose Selection by PRedicting Objective-grounded UTility (SPROUT). The utility score is predicted on every prompt in the pool, including unseen prompts, by a text-only model, refit after every iteration on all utilities observed so far. A randomized acceptance rule then turns these predictions into a batch, so no images are generated beyond those used for training. For direct group preference optimization (DGPO), the objective-grounded utility is the norm of the gradient that the objective produces from a prompt's group of images. Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion 1.5 with DGPO on GenEval, SPROUT matches the final score of uniform sampling in about 44% of the iterations and improves the area under the learning curve with respect to both uniform sampling and CGPO, a recent variance-based prompt sampler. The efficiency gains hold under four held-out reward models never used in training, and the ranking of methods carries over to DPG-Bench and T2I-CompBench++. Our code is available at https://github.com/ADDAPT-ML/SPROUT.
authors: Kangping Hu, Akshay Mehra, Stephen Mussmann
bullets: Uniformly sampled prompts can waste compute on examples with little training value.
SPROUT uses a text-only model to predict each prompt’s objective-grounded utility, refitting after every iteration.
For DGPO, utility is defined as the norm of the objective gradient from a prompt’s image group.
A randomized acceptance rule forms training batches without generating images beyond those used for training.
On Stable Diffusion 1.5, SPROUT reaches uniform sampling’s final GenEval score in about 44% of the iterations and improves learning-curve area across multiple reward models and benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SPROUT at iteration t, with stages 1 and 2 as in Algorithm 2. (1) Generalizable utility model: a text-only utility model ft is fit on the train set of prompt–utility pairs from earlier iterations (circled prompts) and predicts the utility ŷt(p) of every prompt in D, including prompts never generated from; its predictions are scaled into acceptance probabilities at(p). (2) Diversitypreserving batch selection: the pool D is visited in a random order and each prompt is accepted with probability at(p) until B prompts pt,1, . . . , pt,B are accepted; the inset contrasts this with top-B selection (Appendix F). (3) Focused data generation: πt−1 generates G images for each accepted prompt only, the reward model scores them, and preference tuning updates the model to πt; each accepted prompt pt,i is then labeled with its utility yt,i, computed from its rewards or from the update (dashed arrows), and (pt,i, yt,i) joins the train set of the next iteration.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for instruction-conditioned robot control, yet their understanding of task-relevant 3D relations and how these relations evolve during manipulation remains largely implicit. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{WeaveVLA}, a framework that enhances VLA action generation by explicitly modeling task-relevant relative 3D relations and maintaining relational context across observations. WeaveVLA employs a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to encode relative 3D relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references. Pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate geometric evidence across observations to maintain evolving spatial context. A learned-query readout summarizes the updated graph representations into compact relational tokens, which condition the action expert alongside the original vision-language context. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages spatial structure preservation. We instantiate WeaveVLA on StarVLA-GR00T and $\pi_{0.5}$, achieving over 98\% average success on LIBERO with both backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, WeaveVLA improves success from 74.9\% to 82.0\% and from 85.7\% to 87.8\%, respectively, with additional improvements on CALVIN D$\rightarrow$D. On three real-world tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T-based variant improves average success from 55.6\% to 70.0\% under standard conditions and from 33.3\% to 53.3\% under OOD perturbations, surpassing the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline in both settings.
authors: Zien Wang, Yuhao Pan, Yunfeng Fan, Nan Cheng, Xin Xia, Wenchao Xu
bullets: Addresses the implicit modeling of evolving 3D relations during manipulation.
Uses a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to represent objects, the gripper, and reference points.
Maintains temporal spatial context with pair-specific recurrent edge states and summarizes it into relational tokens for action generation.
Adds an auxiliary geometry-reconstruction objective to preserve spatial structure.
Achieves over 98% average success on LIBERO and improves performance on LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and real-world tasks, including under OOD perturbations.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image models can learn from their own mistakes by distilling a self-teacher conditioned on a vision-language critic's revised prompt. However, such self-teachers barely improve alignment, and both they and their hindsight-contrast variants absorb the critic's unintended additions to the scene, such as lighting or scenery. We attribute this to two factors: (1) the prompt already specifies the desired fix, so a useful revision must go beyond the failed span, often rewriting the entire scene and adding details that overshadow the fix; (2) although the critic localizes the error to a single span, self-teachers condition on the rewrite, entangling the intended fix with unintended additions. Motivated by these insights, we propose Hindsight Twins (HinT), which fills the critic's revision template once with the intended fix and once with the observed error and distills only their velocity difference, anchored at the user's prompt. Because text encoders spread the edit of a single slot to all other tokens, HinT further aligns the twins' token states outside the slot. Across Qwen-Image-2512, SD3.5-M, and FLUX.2-klein, HinT keeps the rate of critic-induced bias at the base-model level while matching or exceeding the alignment gains of prior self-distillation, and it keeps improving over twelve rounds of self-training where contrastive baselines decay.
authors: Jiaze Li, Jingyang Chen, Wenhao Zhao, Haoran Xu, Zhenlong Yuan, Dianmo Sheng, Yuanxing Zhang
bullets: Self-distillation from revised prompts often absorbs unintended additions such as lighting and scenery.
HinT creates paired revisions containing the intended fix and the observed error, then distills their velocity difference from the original prompt.
It also aligns token states outside the edited slot to prevent text-encoder spillover.
Across Qwen-Image-2512, SD3.5-M, and FLUX.2-klein, HinT maintains base-level critic bias while matching or exceeding prior alignment gains.
HinT continues improving through twelve self-training rounds, unlike contrastive baselines that decay.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning across multiple views requires inferring the 3D relations between objects and the camera from 2D observations, which depends on cross-view correspondence and scene geometry that vision-language models (VLMs) do not reliably extract. Pretrained vision encoders already capture this information in their latent features, with CLIP linking objects to image regions, DINOv3 matching semantics across views, and VGGT encoding multi-view geometry. However, VLMs do not benefit from these features when we present them directly in context as grayscale feature images. We therefore propose LatentParse, a training-free framework that parses latent features into explicit spatial evidence for VLMs. In LatentParse, an analyst VLM probes the features of all three encoders with predefined tools that locate objects, track them across views, and measure motion between views. It then distills the results into a concise text report, which is provided together with the images to the VLM to answer the question. We evaluate LatentParse on MMSI-Bench, MV-RoboBench and SPAR-Bench, where it improves all five VLMs over the photo-only baseline by 0.7-2.4 percentage points on average. On MMSI-Bench, it raises Qwen3.8-27B from 34.4% to 39.5%, with the largest improvements of 19.2 percentage points on the camera-related questions. These results suggest that latent features become useful for spatial reasoning once they are parsed into relation evidence, without training. Code is available at https://github.com/Harvard-AI-and-Robotics-Lab/LatentParse.
authors: Zhuoying Yang, Yichen Guo, Kathy Jia, Zichang Su, Ayesha Kashif, Nange Hai, Jeffrey Ming Han Li, Zhewen He, Silvio Kempf, Ni Jiachen, Junjie Yang, Muhammad Hamza, Zakaria El Ouahidi, Gabriel Azpitarte, Manling Li, Yi Fang, Shuhong Liu, Mengyu Wang
bullets: Problem: VLMs struggle to extract cross-view correspondences, 3D object relations, and camera geometry from 2D images.
Method: An analyst VLM uses predefined tools to parse CLIP, DINOv3, and VGGT features for object localization, cross-view tracking, and motion measurement.
The parsed evidence is distilled into a concise text report and supplied with the images to a target VLM.
Across three benchmarks and five VLMs, LatentParse improves average performance by 0.7–2.4 percentage points over photo-only inputs.
On MMSI-Bench, Qwen3.8-27B improves from 34.4% to 39.5%, with the largest gain on camera-related questions.

papers.title: Parsing Visual Latents for Multimodal Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: LatentParse converts pretrained vision features into textual spatial evidence, improving multimodal VLM reasoning across multiple views without training.

papers.abstract: Solving multimodal tasks requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to form a unified understanding of the image and the question text. However, under causal attention in current VLMs, a token can attend only to what precedes it. Whichever modality comes first is therefore encoded under partial observation of the input, uninformed by the rest of the multimodal context. We introduce Second-Look Prompting (SLP), a training-free method that repeats the image-question pair in the input. In the repeated copy, every visual and textual token can attend to the complete input, yielding a unified multimodal encoding of the pair. Moreover, the added visual tokens contribute computation beyond re-exposing the image: even a blank image in their place can improve reasoning. Across 12 benchmarks, SLP improves the overall average score of every evaluated model, spanning nine open-source models (3B-72B) and three proprietary frontier models, with gains reaching 5.6 points for Gemini 3 Flash on MATH-Vision. Our analysis reveals two complementary mechanisms: the question guides where the second image attends, and the added visual tokens act as a prefill scratchpad whose hidden states retain answer-relevant information from the image and question. These findings highlight input presentation as a simple yet effective way to improve VLM performance.
authors: Yicheng Zhang, Xun Zhang, Jingyuan Ma, Tianyu Yu, Yuan Yao
bullets: Addresses causal-attention limitations, where the first modality is encoded without seeing the rest of the input.
Uses a training-free repeated image-question input to create a unified multimodal encoding.
Added visual tokens also serve as a computation scratchpad; even blank replacements can help reasoning.
Improves average performance for all evaluated models across 12 benchmarks, including gains up to 5.6 points on Gemini 3 Flash for MATH-Vision.
Analysis identifies question-guided visual attention and answer-relevant hidden-state retention as complementary mechanisms.

papers.abstract: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.

Evaluated on 28 e-commerce benchmarks across eight business scenarios and 64 public general-purpose benchmarks.
The largest model outperforms substantially larger open-source models on e-commerce tasks; all models outperform similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterparts on general-purpose evaluations.

papers.abstract: Geometry Problem Solving (GPS) serves as a rigorous test of the complex reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), particularly when solutions require auxiliary constructions absent from the input diagram. However, explicit diagramming methods suffer from unstable image generation quality and cascading errors, while existing implicit attention mechanisms primarily focus on visible elements, limiting their ability to support reasoning that requires additional geometric constructions. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{AuxCA} (Auxiliary-Clues-Aware GRPO), a reinforcement learning framework that helps models learn transferable auxiliary-construction strategies that can be applied beyond the training domain without explicit diagram generation at inference time. Specifically, we introduce Auxiliary Clues Dependency (\textbf{ACD}) to quantify the influence of auxiliary visual clues on token generation and integrate it into GRPO through fine-grained advantage weighting. Furthermore, we incorporate an auxiliary incentive reward to encourage the effective use of auxiliary geometric clues in correct solutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AuxCA-8B outperforms the explicit-plotting baseline Bagel-Canvas and achieves competitive performance with leading proprietary models on auxiliary-dependent plane geometry problems. Improvements on analytic geometry, solid geometry, and external benchmarks further suggest that the learned strategies can transfer beyond the training domain. Code is available at https://github.com/fukua23/AuxCA
authors: Qigong Lei, Qingsong Wang, Wang Lin, Qianyi Yang, Chang Yao, Jingyuan Chen
bullets: Targets geometry problems whose solutions require constructions missing from the input diagram.
Introduces Auxiliary Clues Dependency to weight token-level advantages within GRPO reinforcement learning.
Adds an auxiliary incentive reward to encourage effective use of auxiliary geometric clues.

Reported gains on analytic geometry, solid geometry, and external benchmarks indicate transfer beyond the training domain.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The overall framework of AuxCA. Following GRPO, the policy model first samples a group of outputs {y1, · · · , yG} conditioned on the auxiliary-enhanced input Iaux. We then calculate the token-level Auxiliary Clues Dependency di by measuring the probability shift between predictions conditioned on Iaux and those conditioned on Iorg without auxiliary visual clues. The sampled sequences are then scored by the reward model to derive the sequence-level advantages Ai. Finally, the model parameters are optimized by adjusting the advantage Ai based on the dependency di via the function ψ, thereby helping the model learn transferable auxiliary-construction strategies.

papers.abstract: Modeling multimodal data from partially paired samples is critical for advancing domains like biomedicine, where vast unimodal datasets and foundation models exist but paired data remains scarce. Existing fusion methods rely on large-scale paired datasets, limiting their use in scenarios with incomplete pairing. We introduce CAMEO, an adversarial learning-based modality fusion framework that integrates modalities from small, partially paired datasets. Combining any pre-trained unimodal encoder with a cross-modal latent alignment mechanism, CAMEO learns shared representations requiring only minimal paired samples. Evaluated on computational pathology tasks such as niche classification and cell type composition prediction, CAMEO achieves superior data efficiency, outperforming contrastive approaches like CLIP in low paired-data regimes, and highlighting the benefits of adversarial alignment when paired annotations are scarce. To facilitate further research, we additionally release a fully annotated HuggingFace dataset comprising three organs and paired image and gene expression modalities. By extending fusion methods to address limited pairing and small-scale datasets, we provide a framework that advances multimodal learning and broadens its applicability to real-world biomedical problems.
authors: Merel Kuijs, Till Richter, Rushin H. Gindra, Korbinian Traeuble, Christian Matek, Rebeka Lukn\'arov\'a, Tingying Peng, Fabian J. Theis
bullets: Addresses multimodal fusion when large paired datasets are unavailable.
Combines pretrained unimodal encoders with adversarial cross-modal latent alignment.
Requires only minimal paired samples to integrate image and gene-expression modalities.
Outperforms contrastive methods such as CLIP in low-paired-data regimes on computational pathology tasks.
Releases a fully annotated dataset covering three organs with paired imaging and gene-expression data.

papers.abstract: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world locations. However, it remains unclear whether they can leverage spatial context and whether their predictions are geographically biased. We introduce GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. GeoDecisions comprises two tasks: (1) geo-aware image classification, and (2) location rating on objective and subjective topics. Evaluating six decision models against supervised task-specific models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision: textual coordinates alone provide insufficient context for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. We also find substantial geographic bias. On everyday photos, despite achieving higher accuracy, open-weight decision models exhibit more spatially clustered errors than supervised models. Moreover, across all five subjective topics, every decision model gives lower ratings to locations with lower socioeconomic conditions. Finally, we propose a training-free method that combines decision models with a location prior to improve their spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/GeoDecisions.
authors: Wilson Wongso, Hada Melino Muhammad, Xiachong Lin, Hao Xue, Flora D. Salim
bullets: Introduces GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for spatial awareness and geographic bias.
Evaluates geo-aware image classification and location ratings on objective and subjective topics.
Textual coordinates alone are insufficient for classifying everyday and satellite imagery; vision is necessary.
Decision models show geographically clustered errors and consistently lower subjective ratings for lower-socioeconomic locations.
A training-free location prior improves spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias.

papers.abstract: Paired compositional benchmarks such as Winoground ask each image to prefer its matching caption and each caption to prefer its matching image. A failed Group decision can come from a wrong caption preference or from the cross-image comparison alone, and Group Score merges the two. Choosing between retraining the encoder and changing the scoring rule therefore requires separating them. We study mean-erasure, which projects each frozen image embedding away from the mean of the two normalized candidate captions. We prove that the projection preserves every within-image caption ranking and makes Group Score equal baseline Text Score. On Winoground, mean-erasure raises CLIP ViT-B/32 Group Score from 9% to 31%, and five CLIP and SigLIP checkpoints gain 21 to 27 percentage points. ColorSwap shows a similar gain for color-object binding. A score decomposition shows that about 60% of Image failures already score the correct joint assignment above the swapped one and fail only on an offset between the two images. Fixed corrections and a learned bilinear scorer gain under one point. A direction estimated from retrieved captions gains about five points with two captions and falls below baseline with sixteen. Before retraining an encoder for paired retrieval, measure the Group loss that mean-erasure recovers: gains beyond baseline Text Score require changing the caption decisions themselves.
bullets: Winoground Group Score combines caption-ranking errors with cross-image comparison errors, making failure sources hard to separate.
Mean-erasure projects each image embedding away from the mean of its two candidate caption embeddings while preserving within-image caption rankings.
It raises CLIP ViT-B/32 Group Score from 9% to 31%, with 21–27 point gains across five CLIP and SigLIP checkpoints; ColorSwap shows a similar pattern.
About 60% of Image failures already rank the correct joint assignment above the swapped one, indicating an offset between images as the remaining failure.
Fixed corrections and a learned bilinear scorer provide under-one-point gains; caption-retrieval directions help with two captions but fall below baseline with sixteen.
