papers.title: Where Compositionality Hides: Shared-Content Interference in Vision-Language Retrieval
papers.tldr: Mean-erasure reveals that much of CLIP’s compositional retrieval failure comes from cross-image scoring offsets rather than incorrect image–caption decisions.

papers.abstract: Language often refers to an object by its parts, as in asking to point to a part or to turn an arbitrarily posed object so that two named parts lie in given directions. Both tasks need the direction from the object's center to the part's center, not the part's own orientation. A natural approach segments the part and takes the centroid of its mask. However, high mask overlap predicts the pointing direction poorly when a part is spread out relative to its distance from the object center. Language-guided part segmentation is trained and evaluated by mask overlap, which leaves a gap between the masks it produces and the part geometry that these tasks use. We close this gap by learning point evidence, weights over the observed points whose weighted centroid gives the part's location. Geometric Readout Supervision (GRS) trains these weights through the centroid's position and adds direction supervision on the parts used in reorientation commands. GRS improves both tasks even with a single frozen encoder and a single input pose. We implement this supervision in GeoRead3D, a system for pointing and reorientation from part descriptions. A language model maps each description to a known part name. Dual-Route Part Evidence combines refined segmentation evidence with directly predicted point evidence to locate each part. On PartNeXt and Artiverse, GeoRead3D points within $22.5^\circ$ for 74.1% and 60.0% of queries, 5.8 and 7.3 percentage points above the strongest baselines. Its reorientation success exceeds the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 7.8 points.
authors: Zhangcheng Hou, Kevin Tonkich, Tomoaki Ohtsuki
bullets: Part-mask overlap can poorly reflect the direction from an object’s center to a spatially extended part.
Geometric Readout Supervision trains point evidence through centroid position and adds direction supervision for reorientation.
Dual-Route Part Evidence combines refined segmentation with directly predicted point evidence.
On PartNeXt and Artiverse, it reaches 74.1% and 60.0% pointing accuracy within 22.5°, outperforming the strongest baselines by 5.8 and 7.3 points.
Reorientation success exceeds the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 7.8 points, using a frozen encoder and a single input pose.

papers.abstract: A generator can follow a spatial plan, but the benefit of supplying that plan depends on what the model can already do from text. In a controlled study with 18 paired training seeds, correcting predicted positions and sizes improves spatial intersection-over-union by 0.030, yet direct text is non-inferior at matched training compute. In a pretrained generator, a fixed rule layout improves two-object task success over the same text-only adapter by 12.50 percentage points, mostly by separating objects that already appear in the correct order. We then ask whether a more precise instruction can achieve the same separation across conditioning paths. On 288 new task families, adding a minimum-gap instruction improves success by 37.15 points with the text-only adapter, by at most 0.69 points with widely spaced regions, and by 6.94 points with tightly spaced regions. Under tight regions, 230 of 288 baseline images have the correct objects and direction yet miss the required gap, ruling out a high baseline success rate as the sole explanation for the weak text response.
bullets: Correcting predicted positions and sizes raises spatial IoU by 0.030, while direct text is non-inferior at matched training compute.
In a pretrained generator, a fixed rule layout improves two-object task success by 12.50 percentage points over a text-only adapter, largely by separating correctly ordered objects.
A minimum-gap instruction improves success by 37.15 points with the text-only adapter, but by at most 0.69 points with widely spaced regions and 6.94 points with tightly spaced regions.
Under tight regions, most baseline images contain the correct objects and direction but fail the required gap, indicating weak text responsiveness rather than simply low baseline success.

papers.title: When Do Spatial Plans Help Text-to-Image Generation? Causal Control, System Utility, and Text Responsiveness

papers.abstract: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.
authors: Ting Chen, Geng Li, Guohao Chen, Hanjia Lyu
bullets: Existing CD evaluations can be confounded by candidate filtering, generation trajectories, and response biases.
CONCOR uses controlled comparisons between ground-truth and hallucinated candidates.
Its Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM) measures correction direction, composition, and reliability.
Different CD methods trade off consistent grounding against stronger but more error-prone corrections.
Contrast strength can help or hurt methods depending on their correction behavior, motivating direct evaluation of contrastive corrections.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces CONCOR, a controlled benchmark for evaluating contrastive decoding methods in MLLMs to mitigate hallucinations, focusing on the correction mechanism itself rather than just final output.
papers.title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Contrastive Decoding for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Large Language Models

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires a vision-language model~(VLM) to understand metric distances, three-dimensional relationships, and viewpoint-dependent geometry. Learning these capabilities typically requires externally curated training data. This paper introduces Spatial-Zero, a VLMs' training framework that can self-evolve through autonomous spatial exploration with zero data. Spatial-Zero addresses two key challenges in autonomous spatial exploration: reliably generating valid spatial interaction tasks and providing accurate supervision for learning from these tasks. Specifically, a proposer specifies object configurations and questions, and a Coder turns them into executable scene programs that produce multi-view images and explicit scene geometry. A Geometric Oracle checks spatial constraints, visibility, and answer uniqueness and derives ground-truth labels from executed geometry; these labels supervise the Solver and ground difficulty feedback, while validation outcomes guide subsequent task generation. Across six spatial reasoning benchmarks and three VLM backbones, Spatial-Zero yields consistent gains through iterative self-evolution. After three iterations, Qwen3.5-9B improves average accuracy by 3.23 percentage points; with Qwen3.5-4B, Spatial-Zero also outperforms existing VLM self-evolution methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/YutongLi2024/Spatial-Zero
authors: Yutong Li, Haoyu Zhao, Daoguo Dong, Ziyi Ye, Yugang Jiang
bullets: Targets metric distance, 3D relationships, and viewpoint-dependent geometry in VLMs.
A proposer and Coder create object configurations, questions, executable scene programs, and multi-view images.
A Geometric Oracle verifies spatial constraints, visibility, and answer uniqueness while deriving ground-truth labels.
Validation and difficulty feedback guide iterative task generation and Solver training.
Across six benchmarks and three backbones, it produces consistent gains; Qwen3.5-9B improves average accuracy by 3.23 percentage points after three iterations.

papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving spatial reasoning training for VLMs with geometric supervision directly fits spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Spatial-Zero: Self-Evolving Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models from Zero Data
papers.tldr: Spatial-Zero enables VLMs to improve spatial reasoning without external training data by autonomously generating, validating, and learning from executable 3D spatial tasks.

papers.abstract: In video temporal grounding, a correct interval can come from finding the event, answering blind or fitting one annotation style, and Recall at IoU scores them alike. We measure evidence dependence, how much the answer rests on the event's frames. Our fixed-answer audit edits either the frames inside the annotated interval or, as a placebo, as many frames elsewhere in the same video, and compares the two drops in the annotated answer's likelihood. Supervised fine-tuning and three public checkpoints trained with IoU-reward reinforcement learning raise the accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-7B by 9 to 20 points, partly by answering blind and by fitting one annotation. Yet their answers rest on the event no more than the base model's, and the same holds for IoU-reward training on our data at the audit's frame rate. This comparison is a difference of the model's own likelihoods, so we can train on it. A placebo contrast and a bound on the placebo drop rule out learning to react to any edit. With them, evidence dependence rises in all five base models we train, and the weight on clean supervision controls how much. Added to IoU-reward training, the objective raises evidence dependence while keeping the accuracy gain. Masking the event's frames makes the trained models decline or miss the event more often than their base; masking as many other frames does not. The dependence moves to another event when the query names it, and holds on a second dataset and under patch scrambling, an edit never used in training.
authors: Zijie Jin, Shuai Zhao, Haoran Tao, Chaomin Huang, Liwen Luo
bullets: Introduces an evidence-dependence audit comparing likelihood drops after editing frames inside the annotated interval versus an equal number of frames elsewhere.
Finds that supervised fine-tuning and IoU-reward reinforcement learning improve accuracy but do not increase reliance on event frames.
Uses a placebo contrast and a bound on placebo effects to train models against generic edit sensitivity.
Evidence-dependence training increases reliance on relevant frames across five base models, while preserving IoU-reward accuracy gains.
The effect transfers to other queried events, a second dataset, and patch scrambling not seen during training.

figures.caption: Figure 5: The placebo-controlled models respond to the query and to the evidence. (a) Each point gives a model’s change from its base (mask, nats per token) in the partner contrast, the drop when the event’s frames are masked minus the drop when a partner event’s frames are, with the event’s own query (horizontal) and with the partner’s (vertical). Figure 1: Accuracy and evidence dependence are separate axes. Left: the audit scores the same correct answer, the annotated interval y⋆, with the event’s frames masked (xE) and with as many frames masked elsewhere, the placebo (xO). The schematic bars show the two drops in the answer’s log-likelihood, dE and dO , and their difference ψ for three kinds of model. Right: each point places one post-trained model by its change from its own base (the origin) in R@0.5 (horizontal) and in evidence dependence Γ, the change in ψ (vertical), with R@0.5 on the full test split and Γ on the first 200 test questions; lines are 95% intervals. The grey band is the audit’s resolution, the farthest from zero that the 95% interval of Γ reaches between two seeds of one recipe (Section 2). Accuracy-oriented training (dark grey) moves models right but not out of the band; SFT, IoU-GRPO and mDPO-style are trained from Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and the public checkpoints (open diamonds) are compared with it. The placebo-controlled objective (green) moves them up. Marker shape gives the base model, its several points differ in α or β, and light-filled points use the smaller β=0.03 (Section 4).

Figure 2: Part of the added accuracy comes from answering blind or fitting one annotation; Γ keeps its sign under both label sets. (a) shows, for all-black videos under Time-R1’s prompt template, the fraction of questions still given an interval (open circles) and answered correctly (dots); the dashed line is a fixed (0, 10) s window on the real videos, and green rows are our placebo-controlled Qwen models at weight α. (b) scores each model on the questions annotated in both Charades-STA and TimeLens against each label set; the two rankings of the nine 7B configurations barely agree (Spearman 0.15). Open diamonds are public checkpoints; open grey circles are the Qwen2.5-VL-7B base (Qwen-7B); thin lines are our 7B models (green) and SFT (dark grey); thick lines are TimeLens-8B (dark) and our adapter of it trained on the original labels (green). (c) gives Γ (mask, nats per token, first 200 test questions) with 95% intervals for each label set as the fixed answer (filled: Charades-STA; open: TimeLens), with the audit’s resolution as a grey band; the TimeLens-8B SFT row has only the TimeLens value.

Figure 6: On each question, the audit scores one fixed answer while editing either the evidence frames or as many other frames. The annotated answer y⋆ and the query q are held fixed and scored by teacher forcing. Editing the frames inside the annotated interval gives xE ; editing as many frames outside it with the same operator gives the placebo xO . The drops of the answer’s log-likelihood under the two edits are dE and dO , and ψ = dE − dO . The figure shows one mask draw; the audit averages dO over three draws. The right panel shows how a trained model is compared with its base: Γ is the mean trained-minus-base change in ψ over H∩, the questions both models localise on the clean video (IoU ≥ 0.5), and the trained model’s placebo drop dO is reported next to it, under the mask and the swap operator.

Figure 7: Two models give the same correct interval for different reasons. Panels (a) and (b) each show a test question on which the Qwen2.5-VL-7B base and its placebo-controlled model (α=0.5) predict the same interval, with IoU above 0.7. The top rows show the native frames with the annotated ones outlined, followed by the annotated interval and both predictions. The bars below give the drop in the answer’s log-likelihood (nats per token) when the evidence frames are swapped out and when as many frames outside the interval are swapped the same way. In (a), for the same correct interval, the base loses 0.06 nats per token under the evidence swap and its trained model 3.81, with placebo drops of 0.11 and 0.00.

Figure 8: The placebo-controlled objective scores each training pair on the clean video and on both edits. The trainable model and the frozen base score the fixed annotated answer on the clean video x, the evidence edit xE and the placebo edit xO . Their log-likelihood differences rθ enter the evidence margin and the placebo contrast, the placebo drops of both models enter the placebo bound, and the total loss adds clean supervision to the operator losses (Equations 3–4).

Figure 10: The query-crossed design scores the same answer under the question’s own query and under a partner event’s query. Both conditions score the annotated interval of event A and use the same two edits: masking A’s frames, or masking the frames of a partner event B of the same video. Only the query changes, from A’s own to B’s. A model that reads the query shows a contrast that reverses under B’s query; a model that responds to edits at the answer’s timestamps shows the same contrast under both queries. The bars are schematic; Figure 5a and Table 16 give the measurements.

Figure 11: On QVHighlights, the placebo-controlled models keep a positive Γ (mask) while SFT stays at zero, and the placebo-controlled TimeZero model answers far fewer black videos than its base. (a) Each Charades-trained model is placed by its paired change in R@0.5 on QVHighlights (horizontal) and its Γ (mask) (vertical), with 95% intervals; the grey band marks the out-of-domain accuracy resolution (Appendix A.1). Qwen-7B is Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Green points are placebo-controlled models, trained at β=0.1 unless the label gives β; the β=0.03 model uses α=0.5. (b) For each base model on Charades-STA (STA) and QVHighlights (QVH), the black-video answer rate of the base (open) is set against that of its placebo-controlled model at α=0.5 (filled); squares are TimeZero and circles Qwen-7B.

Figure 9: Evidence dependence grows throughout training; SFT’s stays within the audit’s resolution from the start. Checkpoints are taken every 50 steps (400 pairs) of one placebo-controlled run (α=0.5, β=0.1) and of two SFT runs from Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and each checkpoint is audited against the base. (a) The curves give Γ (mask) with 95% intervals, and the grey band marks the audit’s resolution. (b) The curves give the trained model’s placebo drop on the same questions, and the dashed line marks the base’s.

Figure 3: The placebo contrast, and then the bound, bring the trained model’s own placebo drop back to the base’s. The left panel plots, for objectives trained from Qwen2.5-VL-7B on the same pairs and audited on the same questions, the trained model’s evidence drop dE and own placebo drop dO under masking (nats per token), from the base (top) to the full objective at α=0.5 (bottom); the dashed line is the base’s placebo drop.

Figure 4: Evidence dependence falls with the weight on clean supervision; the accuracy change depends on the base. The top row shows Γ (mask, nats per token, first 200 test questions) and the bottom row the change in R@0.5 from the model’s own base (points, full test split), with 95% intervals. (a) Each column plots one base against α at β=0.1; TimeLens-8B is built on Qwen3-VL, and the grey band is the audit’s resolution. (b) plots Qwen2.5-VL-7B at α=0.5 against β, with SFT at β → 0.

Table 1: Training for accuracy adds correct answers but not evidence dependence; the placebo-controlled objective adds both. All models start from Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. The base row gives levels. Every other entry is a change from the base on the same questions under the same template, except each model’s own placebo drop dO . Accuracy is measured on all 3,720 Charades-STA test questions, the likelihood audit (Γ and dO , in nats per token) on the first 200 test questions, the evidence share on the first 1,000, and follows onH∩ of the first 200. Accuracy changes are in points, and brackets give 95% intervals. Bold marks a change in points whose interval excludes zero or a Γ beyond the audit’s resolution, and grey a Γ within it.

Table 6: Γ does not follow the change in clean-video NLL. Each row pairs a model with its base: our trained models, the three public checkpoints against the Qwen2.5-VL-7B base (the pairs of Table 1), and TimeLens-8B against Qwen3-VL-8B. All values use the mask operator on H∩, the n∩ questions both models localise. The columns give the clean-video negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the annotated answer in nats per token for the base and the trained model, then Γ (mask), its sign fraction (the fraction of H∩ on which ψ rises) and Γc, the change in the bounded index c = (dE − dO)/(|dE |+ |dO|+ 0.05), with its 95% interval. papers.title: Accuracy Is Not Evidence: Measuring and Training Evidence Dependence in Video Temporal Grounding

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception and language understanding from vision-language models (VLMs) with action prediction for robotic manipulation. Although multi-view observations provide complementary scene information, VLMs model cross-view interactions based on 2D feature similarity, which can lead to physical inconsistency in the form of cross-view incorrect association between distinct entities and cross-view information fragmentation about the same entity. To address these challenges, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D for physically consistent robotic manipulation. Specifically, Cross-View Association Modeling (CAM) is proposed to introduce cross-view spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space to reduce cross-view incorrect association. Entity Coherence Organization (ECO) is designed to organize cross-view local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, thereby addressing cross-view information fragmentation. Consistent Action Conditioning (CAC) is introduced to condition action prediction on task-relevant 3D entity evidence for cross-view consistent action execution. Experiments on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks establish ConsisX as an effective and competitive framework for robotic manipulation.
authors: Yunhe Zhang, Long Gao, Yuedong Fu, Gang He, Li Xu, Chang Wu, Pengyu Li
bullets: Addresses incorrect cross-view associations and fragmented information about the same entity caused by 2D feature-based interactions.
Uses Cross-View Association Modeling to impose spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space.
Uses Entity Coherence Organization to combine local observations into coherent 3D entity evidence.
Uses Consistent Action Conditioning to guide actions with task-relevant, cross-view-consistent 3D evidence.
Evaluated on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks, where it is reported as effective and competitive.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can localize through their text interface, grounding open-vocabulary objects, complex referring expressions, text lines and layout regions with strong semantic understanding. They write the boxes one after another as a single sequence, although the instances of a query, unlike the words of a sentence, form an unordered set with no sequential dependence. The number of decoding steps therefore grows with the number of instances, which makes dense scenes the most expensive. Decoding the instances in parallel avoids this growth, but streams that cannot see each other duplicate some instances and miss others. We propose \method, which writes a single point into each query as a spatial anchor and asks for the matching instance nearest to that point within a local radius, or \none. Given the image, the anchored queries are independent, so they are decoded in parallel as leaves of a prefix tree that shares the image and the query, and the model is trained on the same tree. Coarse-to-fine anchors refine only the regions where instances are found, duplicate suppression keeps one box per instance, and set-level reinforcement learning optimizes the set F1. Only the prompt and the attention mask change, not the architecture. On three different VLMs and 12 benchmarks covering detection, OCR, layout and referring, \method is at most 5.5 F1 below sequential decoding trained on the same data, while its speedup grows with instance density and reaches 21.9$\times$ on dense scenes.
authors: Shuxuan Li, Jialiang Kang, Yanghao Zhou, Ziye Zhu, Zhilin Zhao, Xiao Yang
bullets: Sequentially grounding unordered object instances is inefficient because decoding steps grow with scene density.
Each query receives a spatial anchor; the model finds the nearest matching instance within a local radius or returns none.
Anchored queries are decoded independently in a shared prefix tree, with coarse-to-fine refinement and duplicate suppression.
Set-level reinforcement learning optimizes set F1 without changing the model architecture.
Across three VLMs and 12 detection, OCR, layout, and referring benchmarks, performance is at most 5.5 F1 below matched sequential decoding.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically rely on vision-language model (VLM) features as the primary perceptual source for action prediction, showing strong generalization across diverse robotic manipulation tasks. Although VLM features can identify which entities are relevant to action prediction, precise manipulation also requires understanding where task-relevant entities are located within the spatial layout, how their geometric structure constrains physical interaction, and when spatial or geometric information should make a greater contribution to action prediction. To this end, we introduce {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA to organize VLA perception and action prediction around which, where, how, and when. Specifically, {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA retains VLM-based semantic entity perception which and further introduces spatial distance perception where and geometric structure perception how with adaptive spatial-geometric guidance when to enrich the perceptual information available for action prediction. Experiments across real-world settings and simulation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and superior performance of {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA.
authors: Yunhe Zhang, Long Gao, Yuedong Fu, Gang He, Li Xu, Chang Wu, Songyuheng Gao
bullets: VLM features identify which entities matter, but may lack information about their location and physical structure.
The framework organizes perception around which, where, how, and when.
It adds spatial distance perception and geometric structure perception to semantic entity understanding.
An adaptive spatial-geometric guidance mechanism determines when these cues should influence action prediction.
Experiments in real-world and simulated settings demonstrate its effectiveness and superior performance.

papers.abstract: Recent work has sought to localize the internal mechanisms underlying visual reasoning skills in vision-language models. These methods largely overlook separability and composability in both mechanism identification and evaluation. We propose separability and composability as two important desiderata for skill localization. Separability requires identified mechanisms to contribute primarily to their target skills while having limited effects on other skills, enabling precise diagnosis and targeted intervention. Composability requires skill mechanisms to be combinable to support complex tasks, allowing a small set of mechanisms to account for broader capabilities. In this work, we propose a multi-skill interpretability framework DISCO, built around these two properties. For identification, we propose Separable Head Selection, which selects skill-specific attention heads based on their contributions across skills. For evaluation, we are the first to design metrics for measuring separability and composability of identified heads. Extensive experiments on three VLMs and four fundamental visual reasoning skills demonstrate the effectiveness of DISCO. It achieves the highest separability, outperforming the strongest baseline by 24.80, 18.38, and 13.75 points across the three models, respectively, while also achieving the highest composability on all three models.
bullets: Existing skill-localization methods largely overlook whether mechanisms are separable across skills and composable for complex tasks.
DISCO introduces a multi-skill interpretability framework centered on separability and composability.
Separable Head Selection identifies attention heads that contribute primarily to their target skills.
New metrics quantify the separability and composability of identified heads.

Experiments across three VLMs and four visual reasoning skills show the highest separability and composability, with separability gains of 24.80, 18.38, and 13.75 points over the strongest baseline across the models.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) is a fundamental task in multimedia understanding, where state-of-the-art methods have achieved prominent success relying on the assumption of complete, well-aligned multimodal inputs. However, real-world unconstrained scenarios often suffer from unpredictable modality degradation and information loss, leading to catastrophic performance collapse of existing MER models that heavily depend on facial cues as the core inference anchor. However, few systematic works evaluate model robustness under diverse, fine-grained incomplete settings, as prior works are limited to coarse-grained full-modality removal and neglect interpretable analysis of emotional reasoning. To bridge this gap, we formally define the Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Recognition (IMER) task, which benchmarks model generalization and robustness under multi-grained modality and emotional information loss. We further construct MIME, a dedicated IMER benchmark with 2,000 video segments covering realistic fine-grained facial-detail degradation, severe facial degradation, and extreme full-modality loss, surpassing the limited coarse-grained settings of prior works. We also propose the Chain of Emotion (CoE) analysis paradigm with tailored metrics to dissect the fine-grained emotional cue perception and reasoning process of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Extensive experiments on seven mainstream MLLMs reveal that body language and scene context act as critical compensatory mechanisms under facial degradation, while a pronounced gap exists between models' basic visual perception ability and high-level cognitive reasoning. Our work provides a focused evaluation platform and actionable insights for advancing robust multimodal emotion recognition. Our dataset and code are public at https://yuxinokk.github.io/MIME.
authors: Yuxin Jia, Xing Lan, Wensong Wang, Jian Xue, Feiliang Ren, Ke Lu
bullets: Introduces the Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Recognition (IMER) task for evaluating robustness under varied emotional and modality degradation.
Provides MIME, a benchmark of 2,000 video segments spanning facial-detail degradation, severe facial degradation, and complete modality loss.
Proposes Chain of Emotion (CoE) analysis and tailored metrics to examine emotional-cue perception and reasoning in MLLMs.
Experiments with seven mainstream MLLMs show that body language and scene context can compensate for degraded facial information.
Finds a gap between basic visual perception and higher-level emotional reasoning; dataset and code are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Interactive segmentation models turn a few clicks into a segmentation prediction across domains, so annotators only decide where the prediction still needs correction. Annotation thus becomes a loop of inspecting the prediction and clicking again. Each step of this loop is a visual judgment, which suits general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents. In this work, we focus on letting these agents run this loop on 3D volumes. However, the MLLM in such an agent takes only 2D images as input, so the agent must observe the 3D volume in 2D. Since the loop calls the MLLM many times, this observation must be token-compact enough to keep every call cheap, yet informative enough to show error regions in the 3D prediction. We meet both needs with tri-planes, the three orthogonal planes that cross at one point in the volume. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that tri-planes are context-efficient yet keep sufficient detail to show error regions in the 3D prediction. Building on tri-planes, we introduce TriSegAgent, an MLLM agent that refines the 3D prediction iteratively. Within the agent, the MLLM only judges the prediction on tri-planes, while a visual harness turns each judgment into a 3D action in code. To make the loop reliable, the harness places each click at an exact voxel in the volume and checks whether to accept the 3D prediction. To evaluate the agent, we build a diverse benchmark of 690 regions of interest (ROIs) from 35 public medical datasets across three imaging modalities. With frontier MLLMs, TriSegAgent reaches an overall Dice about 10 points above the strongest baseline, and its lead is even larger on targets below 3 cm. With flash-level MLLMs, it outperforms a recent 3D segmentation agent built on a frontier MLLM.
authors: Qingqiao Hu, Jialin Li, Meilong Xu, Kehan Qi, Yipeng Zhang, Lin Tian, Hongwei Bran Li, Klaus Mueller, Xiaoling Hu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of giving 2D-input MLLMs informative, token-efficient views of 3D prediction errors.
Represents each volume with three orthogonal planes intersecting at a point, preserving detail around error regions.
An MLLM judges tri-plane predictions while a visual harness converts judgments into precise voxel-level 3D clicks and validates predictions.
Evaluated on 690 ROIs from 35 public medical datasets across three imaging modalities.
Achieves about 10 Dice points over the strongest baseline with frontier MLLMs, with larger gains for targets smaller than 3 cm; also outperforms a recent 3D agent using flash-level MLLMs.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding requires precise clicks at low latency. Recent models such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement. However, screenshot downsampling removes detail needed to locate small controls, while fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. We introduce PixelOne, which transfers spatial knowledge from a search teacher to a student that predicts clicks directly from screenshots at native resolution. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions. The student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, the same decision head selects a visual token, and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, all in one forward pass. A click-aligned loss encourages pixels inside the target box to score above those outside. Across four benchmarks, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy, the highest among the evaluated single-forward grounders, with a mean latency of 0.43 s per target.
authors: Kanghui Tian, Shuai Dong, Yuhan Zhu, Congcong Wang, Ji Zhao, Tianxiang Jiang, Zhixiong Zhang, Shengyuan Ding, Yi Wang, Jiaqi Wang, Yu Qiao
bullets: Addresses detail loss from screenshot downsampling and coarse fixed bins when locating small GUI controls.
Uses a search teacher to select and zoom into candidate rows, columns, and regions.
Distills the teacher’s spatial distributions into a student with box supervision and a click-aligned loss.
At inference, a decision head selects a visual token and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it.
PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B reaches 83.8% mean accuracy across four benchmarks with 0.43 s mean latency per target.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have emerged as a promising approach for scaling deep learning models while maintaining computational efficiency. However, existing MoE adaptations for Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models suffer from significant computational overhead during sequential training and degradation of zero-shot capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose CLIP-FMoE, a novel approach that integrates MoE architecture into CLIP fine-tuning. Our method uses Isolated Constrained Contrastive Learning, a pipeline that trains specialized experts on cluster-based data partitions to accelerate expert specialization. Additionally, we introduce a Fusion Gate mechanism to mitigate catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves consistent improvements on downstream tasks while preserving zero-shot capabilities. Furthermore, our method demonstrates robust performance across varying context lengths, making it particularly suitable for diverse real-world applications.
authors: Luong Tran, Lan-Cuong Nguyen, Huynh Dang Nguyen, Dat Nguyen Cong, Dung D. Le, Van Nguyen

Uses Isolated Constrained Contrastive Learning to train experts on cluster-based data partitions.
Introduces a Fusion Gate to reduce catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks show consistent downstream improvements while retaining zero-shot performance.
Demonstrates robust performance across varying context lengths; specific datasets and numerical gains are not reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for spatial tasks such as navigation and manipulation, where they must infer geometry and object relationships from visual input in order to act correctly. Existing benchmarks usually test perception and reasoning in isolation, making it hard to tell whether failures come from visual understanding, downstream reasoning, or the bridge between them. We introduce VeriWorld, a benchmark for spatial reasoning in interactive 3D environments with executable actions and deterministic verification. For task families where all three channels are well-defined, we evaluate matched visual, structured, and combined input conditions on the same instance, environment, and verifier; families without a clean visual/structured/combined split are reported separately. This design supports controlled comparisons of perception, reasoning, and their interaction. Using this setup, we uncover two diagnostic findings. First, models often perform much better when task-relevant information, such as object identity, current state, or target location, is given explicitly than when it must be read from the rendered scene, revealing a recurring visual-to-structure gap. Second, action-space and harness design can change outcomes even under the same task and information condition, showing that interaction protocol is itself a confounding variable. VeriWorld is open-sourced to support reproducible and fine-grained evaluation of spatial reasoning in VLMs.
authors: Yan Zheng, ShengYun Peng, Xuyao Liang, Xiaoyan Cong, Nuo Chen, Bangya Liu, Zihan Wang, Wenyan Cong, Zhiwen Fan, Zhangyang Wang
bullets: Targets failures in navigation and manipulation where models must infer geometry and object relationships from visual input.
Compares matched visual, structured, and combined inputs on identical instances, environments, and verifiers when possible.
Finds a recurring gap: models perform better when object identity, state, or target location is provided explicitly than when inferred from rendered scenes.
Shows that action-space and interaction-harness design can alter results, making protocol a confounding factor.
Open-sourced for reproducible, fine-grained evaluation of spatial reasoning in VLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the 11 tasks in VERIWORLD, spanning four families. Interactive Control (closedloop, multi-round): MazeNavFPS (first-person grid maze navigation), Billiards (2D pool trajectory planning), TunnelNav3D (curved-tunnel flythrough), PlaceOnBottom (object stacking). Trial-and-Error Prediction (submit-and-check): BoxFold (predict the folded shape), MovingShooter (aim at a moving target), LightWar (aim and launch a projectile at a distant beacon across a large outdoor terrain). Photoreal Grounding (photorealistic 3D scenes): SceneGrounding (recover the camera pose of a given screenshot in two photoreal interior levels), ObjectGrounding (localize named kitchen objects with 3D markers in a photoreal apartment scene). Computational Physics (Slang/CUDA simulation): CurvyBilliards (ball dynamics on a parametric surface), DropToTarget (surface design for target landing). Family colours match the row banners in Table 2; Sec. 5 reports these tasks using separate core, specialized, and harness-diagnostic tracks.

Figure 1: Batch control improves performance under both evaluated information channels at an equal move budget. Same task (MazeNavFPS, 30 mazes), same model (Gemini-3.1-Pro), and the same budget of primitive moves for both protocols (125/170/210 moves for 3×3/4×4/5×5 grids): switching the action interface from Single (one move per call) to Batch (3–6 moves per call) lifts Pass@1 from 0.57 to 0.93 under VP (vision + position log) and from 0.57 to 0.97 under VRP (VP + raycast), while Batch uses fewer moves on average. Under an equal budget of 50 model calls, Batch also outperforms Single for every evaluated model (Sec. 5.3 and Table 10). This motivates VERIWORLD’s three-axis design — task, information channel, and action harness — in which the harness is treated as a first-class experimental variable rather than a fixed implementation detail.

Figure 2: VERIWORLD evaluation pipeline. A Python generator maps a seed to task parameters and instantiates the scene in Unreal Engine 5 (rendering + game-runtime bridge for in-process code execution). A VLM agent runs a closed step loop: screenshot + action log → thoughts / actions / updated knowledge → execute in UE5; the new screenshot and log feed back for up to T rounds. A deterministic Python verifier checks pass / fail at runtime for every task; some families additionally have a solvability certificate (Lean 4 or deterministic simulation, depending on the task; §3.3).

Figure 4: LightWar successful arc, V+Telemetry condition. A 2×3 stack of arc replay frames sampled at t = 0.51, 1.53, 2.54, 3.56, 4.58, 5.59 s after launch, taken from a Gemini 3.1 Pro Pass@1 episode on seed=0 (hit_forest_hilltop_beacon). The agent fires a glowing projectile from a low-elevation forest clearing (frame 1) and tracks the ballistic arc until it intersects a hilltop beacon (frame 6, bright impact flare). Each frame is the harness’s per-tick render passed back to the agent at the next round; together they form the visual evidence the agent uses to plan the next shot. Per-round screenshots like these are part of the V condition; V+Telemetry additionally reports the scalar miss distance of each shot. Without the miss distance (V-only), the mid-tier panel models (Sonnet, Opus, Kimi, Qwen3-VL-30B) drop from 0.33 to 0.00 Pass@1.

Figure 5: Six rendering variants of the ObjectGrounding harness. The main-table V/C contrast (grid-marker family, fourth column) compares 9 bboxes with small index labels inside the boxes vs. the same bboxes with enlarged, camera-facing labels under an offcenter camera; the harness-diagnostic V/C contrast (single-marker family, second column) repeats the same label-rendering ablation under a sparser, single-bbox scaffold. Auxiliary numbered-ball variants (first and third columns) are the original baselines from which the bbox variants were derived; they are not used for the V/C tables but are the scene context the seed sampler draws from. Within each family, V and C differ only in how the index labels are rendered; both include the marker-to-world-coordinate table.

Table 1: VERIWORLD is the first benchmark to jointly support interactive 3D environments, executable code-as-action, deterministic verification, scalable parametric generation, and diagnostic evaluation through controlled input conditions. Prior benchmarks typically capture only subsets of these capabilities—focusing on perception, interaction, or evaluation in isolation—while VERIWORLD integrates all components within a unified and verifiable framework. ✓ = supported, ✗ = not supported, ∼ = partial.
Table 2: Task families in VERIWORLD. We organize 11 tasks into four families by interaction paradigm and the type of spatial reasoning required. Family colours match the row banners of Table 3.

Table 4: Grid mazes under an equal primitive-move budget: batch outperforms single-step control under both information variants. Pass@1 over 30 mazes per cell (grids 3, 4, 5 × 10 seeds). Batch and single share a budget of 125, 170 and 210 primitive moves for 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5 grids; the batch prompt asks for 3–6 commands per model call and single sends one. B-only:S-only counts the mazes solved only by batch and only by single, which shows whether batch wins on the same mazes or the two protocols simply solve different ones. VP = rendered observation + position history; VRP = VP + a 4-direction raycast scan. These are auxiliary harness variants, not core V/S/C conditions.

Table 8: MazeNavFPS auxiliary information-channel sweep, 5×5 grids, 9-seed extension. Maze navigation does not cleanly fit the core V/S/C taxonomy: a closed-loop ReAct agent inevitably accumulates an action-history memory across rounds, so even the rendered-observation-only condition retains an implicit structured channel. We sweep four auxiliary information channels (all under batched action control, Bf ), holding the model lineup fixed at four frontier VLMs: V – rendered observation only; no harness-tracked position log; RP – 4-direction raycast wall distances + harness-tracked position log; no rendered observation; VP – rendered observation + position log; VRP – rendered observation + raycast + position log. We restrict to the hardest 5×5 grid for an apples-to-apples shape comparison and use nine seeds {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 42} that produce different maze topologies. Each per-model cell reports Pass@1 over valid episodes; Avg pools them across the four models. Each cell has n = 9 except RP (Gemini 7, Opus 4, GPT-5.2 5), VP (Opus 7) and VRP (Opus 4, GPT-5.2 8).

Table 10: Grid mazes under an equal budget of 50 model calls. Each cell shows Pass@1, with average rounds (model calls) in parentheses. The batch prompt asks for 3–6 commands per call and single executes one, so batch can execute more primitive moves. VP = rendered observation + position history; VRP = VP + a 4-direction raycast scan.

Table 3: Core V/S/C information-condition results. We include tasks for which visual (V), structured-only (S), and combined (C) conditions are defined on seed-generated task instances with the same action interface and verifier; ObjectGrounding has no structured-only condition and is reported with V and C. V provides rendered observations and task-specific metadata describing the scene setup and action interface, while retaining task-specific demands for visual identification or state estimation. S provides explicit information such as object attributes, current or target coordinates, and physical parameters without images. The S−V gap measures the resulting change in task performance (Appendix A.1). The C−max(V,S) column measures whether simply combining rendered and structured inputs improves over the better single channel. Positive S−V indicates a benefit from explicit task information, which can reduce demands on visual identification and state estimation; negative C−max(V,S) means that the combined condition, including its task-specific instructions, underperforms the better single channel, and does not by itself isolate a fusion deficit.

Table 14: ObjectGrounding core V/C panel (grid-marker family, 12 models). C − V positive means making the nine candidate bboxes’ index labels readable helps performance: the agent can now reference a specific bbox by index instead of describing it visually. 9 of 12 models gain; macro-average C − V = +0.10. papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for spatial reasoning in interactive 3D environments with VLMs; fits spatial intelligence and embodied AI.
papers.title: VeriWorld: A Verifiable Visual SWE-Bench for Spatial Reasoning in 3D Environments
papers.tldr: VeriWorld benchmarks VLM spatial reasoning in interactive 3D environments by separating visual perception, structured reasoning, and interaction effects with executable, deterministically verified actions.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) has recently become a central paradigm for advancing Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), as demonstrated by systems such as OpenAI's o3 and the R1 series. Despite significant progress in LLMs, how to leverage RFT to unify visual perception, step-by-step reasoning, and agentic tool use into one coherent training paradigm remains an open challenge. In this work, we present Visual Reinforcement Fine-Tuning++ (Visual-RFT++), a unified framework that extends RFT to both visual perception tasks and multimodal agentic workflows, enabling LVLMs to reason with images, act upon images, and evaluate their own outputs using verifiable reward. With Visual-RFT++, open-source LVLMs not only show significant gains on diverse visual perception tasks, but also acquire agentic abilities such as web searching for real-time information and code-based image manipulation (e.g., cropping, rotation, and analysis). Across visual perception tasks, including fine-grained classification, few-shot detection, reasoning grounding, and open-vocabulary detection, Visual-RFT++ delivers strong gains over SFT, including a +24.3 percentage points improvement in one-shot fine-grained classification and +21.0 percentage points on COCO's 4-shot setting and +15.4 percentage points on LVIS with around several hundred samples. To evaluate agentic behaviors, we introduce the Multimodal Agentic Tool Bench (MAT) with MAT-Search and MAT-Coding. Visual-RFT++ surpasses its baseline by +18.6 F1 / +13.0 EM percentage points on MAT-Coding and +10.3 F1 / +8.7 EM percentage points on MAT-Search. It also shows gains of 29.3 F1 and 25.9 EM percentage points on multi-hop QA benchmarks such as 2Wiki and HotpotQA, demonstrating strong cross-modal generalization. Visual-RFT++ introduces a data-efficient and reward-driven framework that strengthens both visual reasoning and agentic adaptability.
authors: Ziyu Liu, Zeyi Sun, Xiaoyi Dong, Yuhang Cao, Haodong Duan, Dahua Lin, Jiaqi Wang, Yuhang Zang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying visual perception, step-by-step reasoning, and agentic workflows in LVLMs.
Enables models to reason about and manipulate images, search the web, and evaluate outputs through reward signals.
Improves diverse visual tasks over supervised fine-tuning, including fine-grained classification, few-shot detection, and grounding.
Introduces the Multimodal Agentic Tool Bench (MAT) for evaluating search and code-based image manipulation.
Reports gains on MAT tasks and multi-hop QA, indicating cross-modal generalization with relatively few training samples.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Framework of Visual-RFT++ for Visual Perceptions. Given the question and visual image inputs, the policy model generates multiple responses containing reasoning steps. Then the verifiable reward such as IoU reward and CLS reward is used with the policy gradient optimization algorithm to update the policy model.

Fig. 2: Overview of Visual-RFT++. Compared to the (a) Visual Instruction Tuning that is data-hungry, (b) our Visual Reinforcement Fine-Tuning++ (Visual-RFT++) is more data efficient with limited data. (c) We successfully empower Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) with RFT on a series of multimodal tasks, and present examples of the model’s reasoning process at the bottom.

Fig. 5: Data Annotation Pipeline of our proposed Multimodal Agentic Tool Bench (MAT): (a) MAT-Search, a manually annotated and verified dataset for agentic search, and (b) MAT-Coding, an automatically generated dataset for agentic coding with a structured pipeline. papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) estimate, understand, and predict human motion, but mainly from RGB cameras. Depth, LiDAR, mmWave, and WiFi complement RGB under poor lighting, through occlusions, and in privacy-sensitive applications, but existing multisensory models cover only some of these sensing tasks. Covering all of them from any sensor subset is challenging, since the tokens of heterogeneous sensors are semantically inconsistent and spatially misaligned, paired multisensory data are scarce, and the tasks need different temporal granularities. We present OmniSenMo, a multisensory language model that takes the human skeleton as a common reference for all sensors. Its skeleton-grounded motion representation turns each sensor into joint tokens, one per body joint, so that any sensor subset is fused joint by joint and expressed in the motion vocabulary that the language model learned from motion capture and text. We pretrain it on all five sensors generated by our multisensory simulator, and Multi-Granularity Observation gives each task the frames it needs. On a cross-action split of MM-Fi, the same model with all five sensors outperforms the models compared on each task, including LEO-Fuse in pose estimation (84.1 vs. 89.0 mm MPJPE) and HoloLLM in unseen-action recognition (69.2% vs. 42.8%). Even without RGB, it outperforms both methods that use RGB, and in a cross-dataset validation on XRF55, it recognizes unseen actions far better than HoloLLM.
authors: Cheng Guo, Qiming Cao, Pu Perry Wang, Pu Wang, Hongfei Xue
bullets: Addresses heterogeneous, spatially misaligned sensors, scarce paired data, and task-specific temporal requirements.
Represents each sensor as joint-level tokens using the human skeleton as a common reference for fusion.
Pretrains on simulated multisensory data and uses Multi-Granularity Observation to match task-specific frame needs.
On MM-Fi, achieves 84.1 mm MPJPE for pose estimation versus 89.0 for LEO-Fuse, and 69.2% unseen-action recognition versus 42.8% for HoloLLM.
Maintains strong recognition without RGB and generalizes to unseen actions on XRF55; evaluation focuses on the reported datasets and simulated pretraining setup.

Learned recovery seeds take the place of a missing sensor (here depth). One context of the language model (Qwen2.5-VL with LoRA) contains the prompt, the joint, fused, holistic, and visual tokens, and the human queries under role-masked attention. In training, the frozen vision encoder also serves as the VLM teacher (dashed). Multi-Granularity Observation (MGO) sets the frames that each task uses. Only non-RGB encoders have the holistic path, distilled from the frozen vision encoder on synchronized RGB. (b) Fusion queries attend to each available sensor through its own cross-attention (CA), a router over the available sensors S mixes them, and the averaged per-sensor pose is added to the fused tokens.

papers.abstract: We introduce Audio-Visual Rearrangement (AVR), a novel task in which an agent hears a spoken request, retrieves a suitable object, and delivers it to the requesting user or an instruction-specified destination. AVR requires the agent to understand the spoken request and acoustically localize the speaker for delivery. To support this task, we construct a dataset covering three query types: explicit target specification, speaker-relative spatial references, and implicit user intent, spanning eight subtypes with diverse object selection and delivery requirements. Moreover, we propose a framework that integrates a motion-aware spatial audio module into an audio-visual large language model to encode spatial cues from the spoken request and update them as the agent moves. We further incorporate auxiliary supervision for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding through multitask instruction tuning to improve action prediction. Experiments establish baseline performance in both seen and unseen environments, laying the groundwork for future research on embodied intelligence and human-robot interaction. The code will be publicly available soon.
authors: Ruohao Guo, Jiatong Ye, Chenwei Dong, Jinxing Zhou, Dantong Niu, Guangyao Li, Zhenbo Li
bullets: Defines a task combining speech understanding, object retrieval, speaker localization, and delivery.
Provides a dataset with three query types, eight subtypes, and varied object-selection and delivery requirements.
Integrates motion-aware spatial audio into an audio-visual large language model to track spatial cues during movement.
Uses multitask instruction tuning for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding.
Reports baseline results in seen and unseen environments; code is planned for public release.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our baseline framework. Details of the Motion-Aware Spatial (MAS) Audio Encoder are shown in the left panel. The original audio encoder preserves speech understanding, while the parallel MAS Audio Encoder extracts binaural spatial cues and updates them according to the agent’s motion. A lightweight projector maps these features into the language model’s token space, where they are combined with speech, visual, and textual tokens to predict executable skills. The action executor interacts with the environment and returns execution feedback for closed-loop decision making.

Figure 1. Overview of Audio-Visual Rearrangement. Given a spoken request, an agent must (1) search for and pick up a suitable object and (2) navigate to the requesting speaker and hand it over. This requires understanding what to retrieve from speech, visually grounding the target object, and acoustically localizing the speaker among multiple people, as well as navigation and manipulation.

Figure 4. AVR trajectories in unseen environments. The top and bottom examples correspond to explicit and implicit requests. Each example shows a top-down scene view, an occupancy map, and egocentric observations during exploration (1), target acquisition (2), and approach to the speaker (3). Blue and orange paths indicate object search and sound-source search. Paths connect recorded decision locations along the navigation mesh. Selected views include a simulator-rendered snapshot for illustration.

Figure 3. Distributions of initial speaker azimuths and sourceagent Euclidean distances across AVR episodes. Left: Polar histogram showing the spatial distribution of initial speaker azimuths relative to the agent. Right: Histogram illustrating the distribution of source-agent distances, spanning from 2 to 12 meters.

Figure 5. Cumulative success across initial Geodesic distances. (a) Complete AVR task success. (b) Handover to the correct recipient. Blue and orange denote seen and unseen episodes. Distances are computed on the static-scene navigation mesh.
Table 2. Success rates (%) of our method across eight AVR query subtypes on the seen and unseen splits.
Table 1. Evaluation on the audio-visual rearrangement benchmark across seen and unseen environments.
Table 3. Ablation study on the unseen split. Components are added cumulatively to the monaural baseline. Ours further incorporates multitask supervision and response-loss weighting.
Table 4. Robustness to spatial distractors on the unseen split.

papers.abstract: Pathologists reach a diagnosis by integrating morphological evidence across regions and magnifications along viewing trajectories. Existing pathology AI rarely reflects this process: models predict from selected image regions, answer questions within fixed visual contexts, or navigate slides autonomously. We formalize pathologist-led streaming diagnosis, in which the pathologist controls navigation while a copilot selectively describes incoming views and synthesizes accumulated evidence into a final diagnosis. We record five pathologists' viewing trajectories on 1,791 TCGA whole-slide images (WSIs) spanning ten organs, with response labels, morphological descriptions, and session-level findings and diagnoses. We construct PathStreamBench to assess response timing, morphological description, and session-level diagnosis, alongside auxiliary video understanding. We introduce PathStream, which jointly learns streaming responses and diagnosis through two-stage training, with a diagnosis-attention loss guiding attention during diagnosis to relevant visual and textual evidence accumulated as the examination unfolds. PathStream outperforms 14 vision-language models and three domain-fine-tuned baselines on the core tasks, achieving a trajectory WSI Relevance score of 77.87, surpassing the strongest domain-fine-tuned baseline's 62.76. Without additional training, its diagnostic capabilities generalize to new educational pathology videos, three external centers, and an unseen organ.
authors: Dankai Liao, YuFeng Wu, Ziyue Wang, Guanxi Liu, Tianyi Zhang, Zeyu Liu, Linghan Cai, Yueming Jin
bullets: The work addresses the gap between pathology AI and pathologists’ trajectory-based, multi-region, multi-magnification diagnostic workflow.
Five pathologists’ viewing trajectories across 1,791 TCGA whole-slide images and ten organs support PathStreamBench, covering response timing, morphology, session-level findings, and diagnosis.
PathStream jointly learns streaming responses and diagnosis, using a diagnosis-attention loss to focus on relevant accumulated visual and textual evidence.
It outperforms 14 vision-language models and three domain-fine-tuned baselines; its trajectory WSI Relevance score is 77.87 versus 62.76 for the strongest domain-fine-tuned baseline.
Without additional training, the model generalizes to educational pathology videos, three external centers, and an unseen organ.

figures.caption: Figure 3. PathStream overview. PathStream jointly learns response timing, morphological description, and final diagnosis from a causal sequence of frames and responses, with diagnostic attention supervision guiding evidence integration.

Figure 2. Data curation and PathStreamBench construction. (a) Organ distribution across the TCGA, private, and PEAN cohorts, followed by pathologist-guided slide review, trajectory replay, and expert annotation of response points and morphology. (b) The benchmark evaluates response timing, streaming morphological description, session-level diagnosis, and auxiliary pathology video understanding along the viewing sequence. (c) Distribution of PathStreamBench samples across the four tasks and their categories.

Figure 7. Streaming responses and final diagnoses. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and PathStream outputs alongside pathologist annotations for the same WSI. Red text marks errors in descriptions, response timing, or diagnosis. Ellipses mark omitted frames or text.

Figure 1. Motivation of streaming diagnostic copilots. Static models such as multiple instance learning (MIL) and pathology vision-language models (VLMs) aggregate patches or answer questions about a given visual context, while pathology agents select their own viewing trajectories. The proposed PathStream follows the pathologist’s navigation, describes the evolving morphology, and integrates accumulated evidence into a final diagnosis.
Figure 6. Organ-wise comparison. Four-task performance across ten TCGA organs.

Figure 8. External diagnostic generalization. PathStream and domain-fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B on the TCGA test set, the private three-center cohort, and the PEAN skin cohort. Left to right: diagnosis ROUGE-L F1, WSI Precision, and WSI Relevance.
Figure 4. Diagnostic evidence attention alignment. Matching descriptions to microscopic findings guides attention to supporting evidence during diagnosis generation.

Table 1. Trajectory and video benchmark results. Tasks 1, 2, and 4 use trajectory inputs. All scores are multiplied by 100; higher is better. Bold and underlined scores indicate the best and second-best reported results in each column.

papers.abstract: Can a language model learn more from the same information simply by encountering it in different forms? We answer this in the affirmative by introducing Multimodal View Training (MVT), a simple training approach that presents identical information through text, speech, and images, without requiring new facts or supervision. Starting from a text sample, MVT generates corresponding audio and rendered-text image views, and trains a multimodal language model to produce the same target output across all three views. To further bring these benefits to text-only large language models (LLMs), we train lightweight connector modules to pretrained audio and vision encoders, allowing the LLM to learn from multimodal inputs while retaining its text-only architecture at inference. Across question answering, machine unlearning, and knowledge editing, adaptive MVT improves QA recall by +15.2 percentage points, forget quality by +40.7 points, and editing generality by +25.2 points over text-only training. Combining MVT with standard augmentation further improves QA and editing generality. Our theoretical analysis illustrates how training across modalities can shift weight updates toward shared factual content and reduce their reliance on features specific to each view.
authors: Devang Kulshreshtha, Priyanka Kaswan, Minh Pham, Chinmay Hegde, Niv Cohen
bullets: Uses identical content in text, audio, and rendered-text image views, training the model to produce the same output from each.
Connects pretrained audio and vision encoders to text-only LLMs through lightweight modules, preserving text-only inference.
Improves question-answering recall, machine unlearning, and knowledge-editing generality over text-only training.
Combining MVT with standard augmentation further benefits QA and editing generality.
Theory suggests multimodal training emphasizes shared factual content over view-specific features.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Testing the theoretical assumptions on TOFU QA. (a) Cosine between the gradient of each view of a question and that of a reworded version of the same or a random question (mid-training adaptive MVT checkpoint; dashed lines: mean). (b) Cross-view disagreement over training. (c) Activation agreement per layer: cosine between views of the same question minus that between different questions, for text-only training vs adaptive MVT.

Figure 1. MVT: same supervision, different views. Text, speech, and printed-text views share target y. Their losses are combined before one LoRA update to the shared LLM. Connectors are pretrained or learned via text reconstruction, then frozen during MVT.

Figure 2. Performance across text, speech, and image queries. Grey bars average the four baselines (text-only, paraphrasing, NEFTune, SymNoise); purple bars average their combinations with adaptive MVT. Appendix C.1 reports all values.

Table 1. MVT improves learning, unlearning, and editing. Each baseline is compared with its MVT-augmented version. Scores are percentages; bold marks the best mean in each three-row group. The final three rows report averages of the four method means; the last column averages the six metric means.

Table 3. MVT on text-only LLMs. Alignment reports held-out NLL (nats) and character error rate (CER, %) on 1,000 WikiText sentences before MVT training (lower is better). Task scores compare text-only training with adaptive MVT. Task scores are percentages; bold marks the better mean for each model. The final two rows average task-score means across all five models.
Table 2. Qualitative comparison of training methods on QA, unlearning, and editing. Red : wrong answer; green : correct answer.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a multimodal training approach that augments LLMs with audio and vision views via lightweight connectors; directly fits multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Multimodal View Training: Learning More Through Different Modalities
papers.tldr: Multimodal View Training helps language models learn more effectively by presenting the same information as text, speech, and images, improving factual learning and editing without adding new facts or supervision.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models can extract structured fields from scanned financial documents, yet they provide no indication of when a field might be wrong. We derive per-field confidence estimates from the token log-probabilities the model already produces, via a token-to-span alignment procedure that maps logprobs onto each extracted value within the structured JSON output. Evaluated on two benchmarks (CORD v2 receipts, Kleister NDA legal contracts) with three VLM families, the minimum token probability per field achieves Area Under the ROC Curve (AUROC) 0.74-0.91 for error detection, far exceeding verbalized confidence (0.53-0.56). The uncertain fields form a natural training curriculum: fine-tuning via Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) improves accuracy from 78.5% to 87.5% on CORD (67 examples) and from 70.7% to 75.1% on multi-page NDA contracts (259 examples), while substantially improving error detection on Kleister NDA (AUROC 0.70 to 0.85, Area Under the Accuracy-Rejection Curve (AUARC) 0.78 to 0.92). The loop requires no annotation beyond the training-split ground truth, demonstrating that confidence-guided curriculum selection transfers to complex multi-page documents when combined with native multi-image training. A frontier model (Claude Sonnet 4) used as a pseudo-label judge achieves ~92% reward agreement with ground truth on both benchmarks, suggesting this loop can operate without human annotation.
bullets: Addresses the lack of trustworthy uncertainty estimates when VLMs extract structured fields from scanned financial documents.
Aligns token log-probabilities with extracted JSON spans; the minimum token probability per field is a strong error signal.
Across CORD v2 and Kleister NDA with three VLM families, token confidence reaches AUROC 0.74–0.91, outperforming verbalized confidence.
Using uncertain fields as a GRPO training curriculum improves extraction accuracy and, on Kleister NDA, error-detection AUROC from 0.70 to 0.85.
A frontier model can serve as a pseudo-label judge with about 92% reward agreement, suggesting reduced reliance on human annotation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Pipeline overview. Top: A single greedy VLM call produces structured JSON with token logprobs; the confidence stage aligns logprobs to field spans and routes each field to GREEN (auto-accept) or AMBER/RED (human review). Bottom: The uncertain fields form a training curriculum for GRPO fine-tuning, closing a self-improvement loop. Dashed arrow indicates an optional next iteration.

Figure 6: Selective prediction curves on Kleister NDA before and after GRPO fine-tuning. The baseline model’s confidence signal is noisy and barely exceeds overall accuracy at intermediate coverage; after GRPO, the curve is smooth and maintains near-perfect accuracy up to 20% coverage, enabling practical selective-prediction workflows on multi-page legal documents.

Figure 5: Selective prediction curves on CORD before and after GRPO fine-tuning. The post-GRPO curve is uniformly higher, reflecting both improved accuracy (87.5% vs. 78.5% on the expanded scoreable set) and better calibration (the model’s confidence ranking aligns more closely with actual correctness).

Figure 3: Reliability diagram (Qwen3-VL-8B, CORD, greedy). ECE= 0.165. Bars show observed accuracy per confidence bin; the gap below the diagonal indicates systematic overconfidence. Bottom: sample counts per bin.

Figure 2: Example documents with per-field confidence routing. Coloured bounding boxes on the images correspond to table rows. GREEN fields are auto-accepted; AMBER/RED fields are routed to human review at the field level, not the document level.
Figure 4: Selective prediction curve (Qwen3-VL-8B, CORD). AUARC=0.942. Reviewing in confidence order catches errors rapidly.

Table 2: min_prob AUROC (with 95% bootstrap CI half-width) across three model families and two datasets. All CIs exclude 0.5; the signal is statistically discriminative in every condition. Verbalized and Random baselines produce only a confidence score, not extractions, so accuracy is not applicable (—).
Table 4: Qwen3-VL-8B performance on CORD vs. Kleister NDA. GREEN accuracy exceeds 90% on both; the fixed thresholds transfer without recalibration.

Table 8: GRPO self-improvement on Kleister NDA (Qwen3VL-8B, 259 training examples, rank-16 QLoRA, 3 epochs, native multi-image input). All calibration metrics improve substantially; RED fields collapse from 45 to 15 (−67%). Both avg_prob and min_prob AUROC are reported; they are nearly identical on NDA, unlike CORD where min_prob leads by 1.6 points (Table 3).

Table 10: Curriculum error rate by selection signal. On CORD (short fields), all signals are equivalent. On NDA (long fields), avg_prob identifies genuinely wrong fields while min_prob selects uncertain-but-correct ones. Higher curriculum error rate provides stronger learning signal, though training format fidelity and data volume are equally important (see text).

Table 5: Greedy vs. sampling on CORD (Qwen3-VL-8B). Sampling producesmore aligned fields but degrades every calibration metric. The temperature-scaled distribution no longer reflects true uncertainty.
Table 3: Error detection AUROC for individual signals and combinations (Qwen3-VL-8B, CORD, greedy). The composite uses domain-calibrated weights; the rank-average ensemble is parameter-free.

Table 9: Per-field accuracy on NDA before and after GRPO (8-page evaluation). Δ: percentage-point change. +/−: fields that switched from incorrect to correct or vice versa. GRPO sharply improves the hardest field (jurisdiction) while slightly degrading effective_date; the net accuracy gain of 4.4pp masks this asymmetry.

Table 1: Extraction accuracy by confidence routing bin (Qwen3-VL-8B, CORD v2, greedy decoding). Only the 285 fields with successful logprob-to-span alignment are included; a later experiment (Section 6.1) evaluates the full JSON-parseable set. AMBER accuracy is based on only 12 fields and should be interpreted cautiously.
Table 6: Platt scaling on min_prob (CORD, 500 random splits per size). GREEN accuracy rises substantially; AUROC is unchanged (monotone transform).

Table 7: Self-improvement on CORD (67 training examples, rank-16 QLoRA). papers.selection_reason: VLM confidence estimation and GRPO fine-tuning for document extraction; fits multimodal LLM topic.
papers.title: Could This BE Any More Wrong? Teaching VLMs to Know What They Don't Know in Document Extraction
papers.tldr: Token-level confidence from VLM outputs reliably identifies erroneous document fields and can guide training to improve both extraction accuracy and error detection.

papers.abstract: Multimodal embedding models map heterogeneous inputs into a shared representation space, yet text-only, image-only, and composed inputs are still presented in distinct formats and follow different routes through the model. This fragmentation prevents heterogeneous tasks from jointly optimizing the same end-to-end encoding process, limiting supervision transfer across input configurations. To address this issue, we propose unification before encoding and instantiate this paradigm in RenderEmbed. The framework uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert heterogeneous inputs into a common visual substrate for encoding with a VLM. From the resulting visual tokens, Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding produces compact retrieval representations by interleaving learnable anchors and fusing their states across layers, retaining broad context and fine-grained cues. Interventional Rendering Learning trains these representations to remain sensitive to content changes and stable across rendering variations through complementary semantic and rendering interventions. Extensive experiments on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, spanning diverse retrieval tasks, show that RenderEmbed outperforms prior state-of-the-art models at the same scale and exhibits strong out-of-domain generalization. Compared with MetaEmbed, RenderEmbed improves MMEB Overall Precision@1 by 1.7 points, with a larger 2.1-point gain on out-of-domain tasks. Transfer and scaling analyses further show that a shared visual pathway enables more effective learning from heterogeneous supervision.
authors: Xu Yuan, Pangjing Wu, Wenqi Fan, Qing Li
bullets: Addresses fragmented encoding pathways that limit shared supervision across heterogeneous inputs.

papers.abstract: Confidence estimation for large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) aims to assess how likely a particular generated response is to be correct. We investigate how learning this assessment can benefit from the model's predictive reliability on the underlying query. Binary correctness supervision, however, assigns identical labels to occasional errors and frequent failures, as well as isolated successes and consistent success. These outcomes can arise from substantially different predictive behavior under stochastic decoding. We propose a confidence-learning framework that supplements realized response correctness with query-level predictive reliability. We estimate reliability through repeated generations under a fixed model and decoding configuration, then combine the empirical success rate with individual correctness to construct a graded confidence surrogate. The surrogate differentiates responses sharing the same correctness label while preserving the average predictive reliability of the sampled response pool. To learn this target, we condition an independent confidence estimator on the query and its full generated response, and optimize backbone LoRA adapters together with a projection and scalar confidence head using mean squared error. Repeated sampling is required only for supervision construction; inference scores an individual response without additional generations. We establish ordering and mean preservation properties of the surrogate and derive a selective-risk bound connecting population surrogate prediction error to the error rate among accepted responses. We evaluate the framework across language and vision-language models, examining confidence calibration and selective prediction.
authors: Chen Li, Xiaoling Hu, Chao Chen
bullets: Binary correctness labels miss differences between occasional errors, frequent failures, isolated successes, and consistently correct behavior.
The method combines an individual response’s correctness with query-level empirical success rates from repeated generations.
An independent confidence estimator uses the query and full response, trained with LoRA adapters and a confidence head via mean squared error.
Repeated generations are needed only to construct supervision; inference evaluates each response in a single pass.
The paper proves ordering and mean-preservation properties and derives a selective-risk bound, then evaluates calibration and selective prediction in language and vision-language models.
