papers.abstract: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.
authors: Ce Zhang, Jianshu Zhang, Jinxi He, Xiyuan Yang, Pan Wang, Han Liu, Katia Sycara, Yaqi Xie
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining useful evidence in a single pass under bounded frame storage and unknown future questions.
Groups recurring failures by cause and searches papers, model cards, and code for adaptable methods or pretrained perception models.
Can jointly add perceptual capabilities and revise how their evidence is stored and retrieved.
Selects accuracy-improving revisions on validation streams, then optimizes for faster revisions within a quality tolerance.
Across three benchmarks, it achieves the best accuracy within frozen-backbone comparisons; on OVO-Bench, it reaches 75.1% accuracy with 0.30-second average response time using Qwen3-VL-8B.

(c) MORSE makes online research part of this loop. papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces MORSE, a framework for optimizing the memory harness of a frozen video-language model (Qwen3-VL-8B). It addresses the problem of selecting evidence to retain in a streaming video system, which aligns with both Multimodal Foundation Models (VLMs) and Efficient AI (token eviction/pruning). The use of open-world auto-research to adapt the system is a novel approach to memory optimization.
papers.title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
papers.tldr: MORSE improves streaming video memory by using recurring failures to search for and integrate external research, achieving strong accuracy and efficient querying with frozen video-language backbones.

papers.abstract: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.
authors: Zehao Liu, Huashuo Lei, Xi Lin, Haoang Li, Yuliang Chen, Huarui Zhang, Yifan Wang
bullets: Problem: Embodied agents may be vulnerable to environment-only attacks even when models and instructions are unchanged.
Method: EnvTrap creates paired safe, trap, and benign null-trap scenarios to test action safety and consequence prediction.
Finding: Environment rearrangements produced hazardous actions at an average rate of 83.4% across five evaluated action policies.
Finding: Models performed near chance at predicting consequences, whereas human evaluators achieved high accuracy; similar vulnerabilities appeared in world models.

Defense and scope: A consequence-aware defense reduced trap triggers by 76.3 percentage points in simulation and 62.9 points across physical backends, while targeting a broader physical-reasoning deficit.

Through Semantic-Spatial Alignment, Spatial Constraint Sampling, and rigorous Plausibility Verification, it reveals how subtle physical layout changes cause consequence-blind embodied agents to execute hazardous actions in both simulation and real-world deployments.

Figure 3: The consequence-aware defense framework. A VLM is fine-tuned on the EnvTrap dataset to predict physical action outcomes. papers.abstract: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D}{CARE-3D}.
authors: Xiaoqian Hu, Ruihong Qiu, Yanran Tang, Sen Wang
bullets: Addresses the limits of supervised imitation and outcome-only rewards for embodied 3D reasoning.
Uses SFT to establish valid tool interactions, then applies GRPO while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen.
Introduces Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence-sensitive credit assignment.
Uses Group Coverage Sampling to maintain exploration across grounding tools.
On MSQA and Beacon3D, improves over SFT and answer/format-reward-only GRPO, particularly in spatial reasoning and grounding-answer coherence.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of CARE-3D. At inference, the agent selects a grounding tool and reasons over its returned evidence. GRPO updates the agent using the resulting rewards.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation enables the recognition of arbitrary categories through natural language descriptions and has recently been extended from natural images to remote sensing. However, existing approaches primarily focus on three-channel optical imagery or limited-band multispectral data, while pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to directly exploit the rich spectral information of hyperspectral imagery (HSI) without additional adaptation. More importantly, different land-cover categories rely on distinct spectral cues, which may be weakened by uniform fusion. To address these challenges, we propose SpectralRoute, a training-free framework for open-vocabulary hyperspectral segmentation. Specifically, we construct complementary spectral views from HSI and enrich category descriptions with external spectral knowledge, enabling frozen vision-language models to extract diverse spectral-semantic responses. We then introduce a class-adaptive spectral routing mechanism that selectively amplifies discriminative spectral responses for each category, overcoming the limitations of uniform fusion. Furthermore, physical spectral priors are incorporated to refine predictions for visually similar land-cover categories. Experiments on three hyperspectral benchmarks demonstrate that SpectralRoute consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods without additional training.
authors: Qingmei Li, Xiaoya Fan, Juepeng Zheng, Jianxi Huang, Haohuan Fu
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of applying vision-language models to hyperspectral imagery with rich, category-dependent spectral information.
Constructs complementary spectral views and enriches text descriptions with external spectral knowledge.
Uses class-adaptive spectral routing to amplify discriminative spectral responses instead of uniformly fusing them.
Incorporates physical spectral priors to refine predictions for visually similar land-cover categories.
Outperforms existing methods across three hyperspectral benchmarks without additional training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SpectralRoute. The framework starts with knowledge-enhanced text representation and multiview spectral construction, followed by vision-language feature extraction using frozen CLIP to compute cross-modal similarities. Spatial pooling and softmax transform the similarities into routing weights. Class-adaptive spectral routing inputs both the routing weights and visual features to perform weighted summation and amplification. Physics-guided refinement integrates spectral prototypes, semantic gating, and initial scores to generate the final prediction.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of segmentation maps on the Pavia University dataset. Previous methods suffer from severe category confusion and fragmented boundaries, whereas SpectralRoute achieves sharper boundaries and finer category separation.

Figure 4. Parameter sensitivity analysis of temperature τ and scaling factor γ. While simpler scenes favor smaller values, highly complex scenes rely more on strong spectral amplification. Our method adaptively scales with scene complexity and maintains robust performance.

Figure 1. Motivation of SpectralRoute. The task requires pixelwise prediction from HSIs and open vocabularies. However, RGBpretrained VLMs miss continuous spectra, causing visual ambiguity among certain categories. In contrast, hyperspectral signatures provide distinct physical evidence. SpectralRoute exploits this through multi-view routing, semantic enrichment, and physical priors to achieve fine-grained separation. in hyperspectral classification and semantic segmentation, existing methods predominantly operate under a closed-set assumption [35], where models are trained to recognize a predefined set of categories using annotated samples. Such dependence limits their flexibility in handling previously unseen categories [9, 18] and adapting to diverse Earth observation scenarios [28]. In practical applications, land cover categories may vary across regions, sensors, and requirements, making repeated data annotation and model retraining impractical [49]. Therefore, enabling flexible, textdriven recognition of land cover categories without additional training represents an important direction for hyperspectral image interpretation [15, 41].

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of segmentation maps on the Washington DC Mall dataset. Previous methods exhibit category confusion in heterogeneous urban regions, whereas SpectralRoute better preserves the spatial organization of major land-cover categories and captures fine-grained structures.

papers.abstract: Video corpus moment retrieval (VCMR) requires finding the video and time interval that match a text query in a corpus of videos. We present RELAY, a training-free framework for VCMR that shares memory across queries. RELAY processes a batch of queries in three stages: search with a query bank, ranking with video notes, and localization with video prompt caching. In the search stage, an embedding model scores each video by its best-matching frame. The query bank penalizes videos that score highly for many other queries in the batch. In the ranking stage, a vision-language model (VLM) writes notes on each candidate video's scenes, people, objects, and actions once. Then, a large language model (LLM) reranks the candidates from these notes. In the localization stage, a VLM predicts the time interval of the moment in the top-ranked video. When multiple queries select the same video, prompt caching lets the VLM reuse its frames. On the three VERIFIED benchmarks, RELAY outperforms the trained baselines in video retrieval R@1 without training. Without any labeled moment, its predicted intervals are shorter than the annotated ones. In VCMR, it achieves similar performance to VideoSearch-R1 on one benchmark and trails it at IoU 0.5 on the other two. Human annotators also mark shorter moments than the original annotations of the benchmarks. A single margin, calibrated on a few labeled queries, widens the predicted interval to the annotation convention of the benchmarks. With it, RELAY outperforms the trained baselines in VCMR at IoU 0.5.
authors: Chenwei Xu, Shang Wu, Zhenyu Pan, Jianshu Zhang, Pranav Maneriker, Lie Lu, Fan Du, Manling Li, Han Liu
bullets: Processes query batches through search, candidate ranking, and temporal localization.
Uses a query bank to reduce cross-query confusion and video notes for LLM-based reranking.
Caches video prompts and frames when multiple queries target the same video.
Outperforms trained baselines in video retrieval R@1 on three VERIFIED benchmarks.
Predicted intervals are initially shorter than annotations; a single calibrated margin improves VCMR at IoU 0.5.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline of RELAY. The top row follows one query of a batch through the three stages. The bottom row is the memory that the queries of the batch share. 1⃝ Search: the embedding model scores each video by its best-matching frame. The query bank subtracts a bias from each score. The bias is larger for a video that matches more queries. 2⃝ Ranking: a VLM writes notes on each candidate video once. An LLM orders the candidates from their notes. Reciprocal rank fusion merges this order with the embedding-based ranking. 3⃝ Localization: the VLM predicts the start and end of the moment in the top-ranked video. Queries for the same video share a prompt prefix containing its timestamped frames. Each request adds the current query.

papers.abstract: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.
bullets: The benchmark evaluates transcription fidelity beyond CER, including invented errors, edit-markup precision/recall, and line structure on 1,000 Brazilian Portuguese essays.

The model recovers 67% of insertions, 77% of illegible deletions, and preserves line structure on 97% of pages.
It still changes 60% of likely misspellings, and unseen words remain a challenge on another corpus.
The 4-bit model runs on ordinary CPUs at about one minute per page; released resources include the model, benchmark code, and review data.

papers.selection_reason: Fine-tuned vision-language model for error-preserving handwriting transcription; relevant to multimodal LLM development and evaluation.
papers.title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays
papers.tldr: Escriba-OCR-1B is an open, 1B-parameter model that transcribes handwritten Portuguese essays with low character error while preserving many edits and layout features, though it still normalises most likely misspellings.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in open-world manipulation, yet their performance often saturates when training data are naively pooled across heterogeneous robots, tasks, and environments. Distributionally robust data mixture optimization, exemplified by Re-Mix, can recover much of this performance, but its weight search requires training full-scale policies twice on the entire corpus, placing it out of reach for most laboratories. We present ProMix, a compute-efficient instantiation of the proxy-reference DRO recipe for robotic imitation learning: a 15M-parameter proxy learns per-domain sampling weights by minimizing worst-case excess loss against a frozen reference model, and the learned weights transfer, without re-tuning, to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters. We further provide, to our knowledge, the first controlled analysis of the reference model's role in robotic DRO, showing that removing it induces over-pessimism toward noisy, low-quality domains (-3.8% average and -14.3% worst-domain success rate), and that entropy regularization is needed to prevent weight collapse. Evaluated on 9500 real-world episodes from the Open-X Embodiment dataset, ProMix improves the average success rate over uniform mixing from 68.4% to 76.2%, matching Re-Mix within evaluation noise while reducing mixture-optimization cost to a backbone-independent 11 GPU-hours - versus 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B for full-scale searches - with a +17.1% absolute gain on the worst-case domain.
authors: Qie Sima, Wei Xue, Yike Guo
bullets: Targets performance saturation caused by naively mixing heterogeneous robot, task, and environment data.
Uses a 15M-parameter proxy and frozen reference model to learn domain sampling weights via proxy-reference DRO.
Transfers learned weights without retuning to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters.
On 9,500 real-world Open-X Embodiment episodes, improves average success from 68.4% to 76.2% over uniform mixing and matches Re-Mix within evaluation noise.
Reference removal causes over-pessimistic weighting, while entropy regularization prevents weight collapse; optimization costs 11 GPU-hours and is backbone-independent.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The ProMix Framework Architecture. The pipeline consists of two stages: (Stage 1) a proxy-reference optimization loop that learns optimal domain weights p∗ by minimizing the worst-case excess loss of a 15M trainable proxy against a frozen reference model; (Stage 2) single-pass training of the final VLA model using the transferred weights p∗. The entire mixture search costs 11 GPU-hours,whereas a full-scale Re-Mix search costs 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B.

Fig. 2: Evolution of the domain weights during the proxy search. Each panel traces the seven domain weights pi from uniform initialization (top to bottom: full method, without the reference model, without entropy regularization); the shaded band marks the final 10k-step window averaged into p∗.

Fig. 3: Summary of the main empirical effects. (a) Mixture-search cost: a full-scale search costs 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B, whereas the ProMix search is fixed at 11 GPU-hours regardless of backbone. (b) Per-domain improvement over uniform mixing at the 50M scale. (c) Transfer of the 15M-learned mixture to final models at three scales without re-tuning (95% CIs over 5 seeds).

TABLE II: Ablation Study: Role of the Reference Model and Entropy Regularization. Variant weights are evaluated by training the 50M final model as in Table I; compute follows the accounting conventions described in Section V-A. “Weight Entropy” is H(p∗) = − ∑ i p ∗ i log p ∗ i (lower values indicate more concentrated weights).

TABLE III: Domain statistics for the Open-X subset used in our experiments. Episode counts are the number of trajectories whose language annotation matches the task domain in the source Open-X dataset. “Split” reports the native train/test division of each source dataset.
TABLE I: Success Rate (%) Comparison across Data Mixture Strategies on Open-X Embodiment at the 50M scale.

papers.selection_reason: Optimizes data mixtures for VLA imitation learning, directly fitting robot learning and multimodal LLM training.
papers.title: ProMix: Efficient Data Mixture Optimization for Robotic Imitation via Proxy-Reference DRO
papers.tldr: ProMix efficiently learns robust data-mixture weights with a small proxy model, improving robotic imitation performance while avoiding full-scale mixture searches.

papers.abstract: Accurate chest X-ray radiology report generation (RRG) requires recognizing clinically relevant abnormalities and accurately describing them. Although Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves the clinical accuracy of generated reports, our analyses suggest limited improvements in visual representations for abnormality recognition. To address this limitation, we propose a selective regional visual distillation framework that enhances visual representations of challenging abnormalities while preserving existing visual capabilities. Specifically, we train a region-aware teacher with targeted supervision on challenging anatomical regions to acquire complementary visual knowledge. Rather than transferring all teacher features, we verify their utility through regional feature replacement and select only those that improve the original student's performance. We further introduce a Spatially Gated Residual Adapter (SGRA) to distill these verified features while minimizing interference with the student's existing visual representations. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray demonstrate improved clinical report accuracy and region-level abnormality recognition across different multimodal large language model backbones, while largely preserving performance on non-target findings.
authors: Rui Zuo, Qinyue Tong, Ziqian Lu, Zheming Lu
bullets: Targets the limited visual-representation gains of language-focused GRPO for radiology report generation.
Trains a region-aware teacher with targeted supervision on difficult anatomical regions.
Uses regional feature replacement to identify only teacher features that benefit the student.
Applies a Spatially Gated Residual Adapter to distill selected features while reducing interference.
Improves report accuracy and region-level abnormality recognition on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, while largely preserving non-target findings.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the proposed selective regional visual distillation framework. Region-Aware Teacher Training: A region-aware teacher is trained with region-specific questions and anatomical annotations to enhance visual representations of disease-associated regions in challenging cases. Regional Feature Utility Verification: Teacher features are substituted into the corresponding student regions, and the resulting changes in the student’s correct-answer scores are used to identify beneficial regional features for distillation. Selective Regional Distillation with SGRA: A Spatially Gated Residual Adapter (SGRA) learns from the selected teacher features through regional feature distillation, while a feature preservation loss constrains changes to non-target regions.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison of visual attribution before and after regional distillation. Representative error-correction cases from MedGemma 1 4B (top) and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (bottom), showing changes in generated reports and visual attribution to the corresponding abnormality regions. Attribution maps are computed using gradient × activation. For Qwen3-VL, attributions are aggregated from the final visual embeddings and DeepStack features, whereas for MedGemma, they are computed at an intermediate visual encoder layer. Due to differences in model architecture, feature resolution, and visualization settings, the attribution maps are computed differently and may exhibit distinct appearances. Therefore, we focus on before-and-after comparisons within each model rather than directly comparing attribution intensities across models.

Figure 1. Clinical performance and visual attribution before and after GRPO. We focus on Qwen3-VL, as its larger clinical gains from GRPO compared with MedGemma make the effects of GRPO more evident. (a) Representative CXR cases show similar disease-region attribution patterns despite corrected clinical predictions after GRPO. (b) Exchanging visual encoders between SFT and GRPO models has little effect on CheXbert F1 and RadGraph F1. The multimodal projector remains frozen in both stages. Parentheses indicate the source of the substituted visual encoder (VE), while the leading model name indicates the source of the remaining components. GT denotes ground truth.

Figure 2. The region-aware teacher, trained with region-level supervision, provides targeted guidance for enha cing the student’s visual representations in challenging regions. When the student incorrectly predicts a disease while the teacher correctly identifies it in the corresponding image region, that region is selected for distillation after passing regional feature utility verification. The visual tokens corresponding to the selected region are then extracted from both models, and the student’s tokens are aligned with their teacher counterparts to improve the visual representations associated with the student’s prediction errors.

Table 1. Comparison with state-of-the-art methods on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray. All methods are trained on MIMIC-CXR for RRG and directly evaluated on IU-Xray without any further fine-tuning. Our method uses only MIMIC-CXR for task-specific training, while some baselines may include IU-Xray in their pretraining. Micro-F1 and Macro-F1 are computed using CheXbert, while RG-F1 denotes RadGraph Partial F1. BLEU-1/2/3/4 and METEOR are computed at the corpus level, whereas ROUGE-L and RadGraph Partial F1 are averaged over individual reports. Best and second-best results are highlighted in bold and underlined, respectively.
Table 3. Generalization of our method across different MLLM backbones on MIMIC-CXR. Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct follows the same training and distillation pipeline described in our method.

Table 5. Report-level clinical performance on MIMIC-CXR. Disease labels are extracted from generated and reference reports using CheXbert. Count denotes the number of positive reference cases for each finding in the MIMIC-CXR test set. Other 10 Findings denotes the remaining ten categories not targeted by regional distillation, with their results micro-averaged and reported.

Table 4. Region-level abnormality recognition on challenging and randomly sampled cases from MIMIC-CXR. Each subset contains 300 samples: the challenging subset consists of 150 positive and 150 negative cases, while the random subset is randomly sampled. P, R, and F1 denote precision, recall, and F1 score, respectively.

Table 2. Ablation study on MIMIC-CXR using MedGemma 1 4B. SFT + GRPO denotes the original model without distillation. Vanilla Distillation uses a standard residual adapter to distill regional features from samples where the student is incorrect but the teacher is correct. Utility Verification follows the same setting but further filters samples based on their verified utility.

papers.selection_reason: Enhances visual representations in MLLMs for radiology report generation, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Beyond Language Optimization: Enhancing Visual Representations for Radiology Report Generation
papers.tldr: A selective regional visual distillation framework improves chest X-ray report generation by strengthening recognition of challenging abnormalities without disrupting existing visual capabilities.

papers.abstract: Perception systems often make discrete decisions: flag a hateful meme, predict whether a pedestrian will cross, detect a spoofed voice, or select the next move in a game. System-1 models, such as OneJev and Jev-Omni, read the media and return probabilities over the options in a single forward pass, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate text. Which multimodal decisions can System-1 models handle, and where do MLLMs perform better? We introduce S1Arena-MM, a benchmark that gives every model the same decision requests and scores the probabilities it returns. It contains 51,060 questions across 94 tasks with image, video, and audio input, drawn from 94 public datasets and three program-generated ones. It also includes 102 closed-loop game environments that a model plays from screenshots; in real-time mode, the game continues while the model decides. We evaluate 33 open models: 12 System-1 models and 21 MLLMs read at the answer token. On static decisions, the best System-1 model leads the best MLLM by 4.9 percentage points on images and is within one point of it on video and audio. Post-training for decisions mainly improves the probabilities: on video, a System-1 model has a lower Brier score than the MLLM that it is post-trained from in 10 of 12 pairs. With up to 2,048 thought tokens per question, the most accurate MLLMs pass the best System-1 models only slightly, and thinking raises the Brier score of most MLLMs. Closed loops separate the models: three System-1 models built on a 27B MLLM reach 22.0-33.3% progression in BALROG, and no other model exceeds 9.7% with thinking off. In real-time GameWorld, latencies of up to 1.1 s per decision cause no measurable loss of progress for System-1 models. Code and data: https://github.com/zhaoyang02/S1Arena-MM.
authors: Lang Lin, Tianyu Chen, Yi Gu, Yang Zhao, Xinran Song, Xinyang Liu, Jianpeng Cheng, Mingyuan Zhou
bullets: Evaluates 33 open models—12 System-1 models and 21 MLLMs—on 51,060 questions across 94 image, video, and audio tasks plus 102 closed-loop games.
On static decisions, the best System-1 model leads the best MLLM on images and is nearly tied on video and audio.
Decision-focused post-training mainly improves probability calibration; on video, System-1 models generally achieve lower Brier scores than their MLLM counterparts.
Extended MLLM reasoning provides only slight accuracy gains and often worsens Brier scores.
In closed-loop games, System-1 models achieve markedly higher progression and tolerate up to 1.1-second decision latency without measurable loss in real-time play.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Static accuracy does not predict closed-loop progress, and post-training for decisions mainly improves the probabilities. One point per model; a gray arrow goes from each base MLLM to the System-1 model post-trained from it. Static: the 32 video tasks that every model takes. (a) The four models with the highest static accuracy (65.8–66.9%) reach 7.0–33.3% progression in BALROG. (b) In 10 of 12 pairs, the System-1 model has a lower Brier score than its base, while its accuracy changes by −6.9 to +5.6 points.

Figure 2. A decision request and the answers of a System-1 model and its base MLLM. The request is from the pedestriancrossing task, the System-1 model is d3, and its base MLLM is Qwen3.8-27B. The request names the video and the window that the model may see, 0–2.5 s of a 13-s clip, and adds a mark that outlines the target pedestrian in red. We show four frames spread evenly over the window, draw the outline thicker than in the input so that it stays visible at this size, and shorten the state text. An open MLLM gets the same request as a prompt (Appendix A).

Figure 3. Thinking can raise accuracy but worsen Brier scores. Accuracy and Brier score of four MLLMs on the image tasks and the 32 static video tasks against the mean number of thought tokens per question. At zero tokens, thinking is off, as in Tables 3 and 4. The other points cut one thought per question at 128 to 2,048 tokens. The star and the dashed line mark d3, which writes no tokens.
Figure 4. The prompt of an open MLLM for one request (Kinetics-700, action candidates).

Table 3. Video and closed-loop results of 33 models. Accuracy (%) and Brier score average the tasks of each input kind, each task with equal weight: 20 short-video, 7 long-video and 3 audio-visual tasks, and the 5 public benchmark subsets (accuracy only). Static averages the 32 video tasks that every model takes (short video, long video, and public subsets) and leaves out the audio-visual tasks. Rank is by static accuracy, and within a family the rows follow it. The grey columns are the static scores, and a lower Brier score is better. Blue rows are the three most accurate models (darker is better), and bold is the best per column. –: the model does not take audio. Closed loop: GameWorld progress and BALROG progression (%), mean over 97 playable environments; VS-Bench return, min-max normalized per game over the models with results (%).

Table 5. System-1 models minus the MLLMs they are posttrained from. Each System-1 model is followed by its base MLLM in gray. Differences in percentage points (Brier: absolute). Positive differences in accuracy and in closed-loop scores, and negative differences in Brier score, favor the System-1 model. Video static: the 32 video tasks that every model takes. AV: audiovisual tasks. Image and audio: the tasks of Table 4. Agentic: the paused closed-loop scores of Table 3. Green: the System-1 model is better by at least 1 point (0.01 in Brier score), orange: worse by at least as much. –: one of the two models has no result.

Table 8. Accuracy (%) per video task: System-1 models. Src.: sources; Q.: questions; –: the model does not take audio. A task with several sources averages their accuracies. Bold: the best model of the row in this table.

Table 6. Latency per decision at batch size 1. Median wall time from a request to its probabilities on NVIDIA H100 80 GB SXM GPUs, one request at a time after a warm-up, including media decoding and every question of the request; loading is not included. Every model gets the same requests: 10 per short-video, longvideo and public-subset task, 20 per audio-visual (AV) task, and 100 closed-loop decisions (Loop). –: the model does not take audio. Bold: the lowest latency of a column.

Table 7. The 13 MLLMs with a thinking mode, with thinking on. Each model’s row gives its scores with one thought of at most 2,048 tokens per question (per decision in closed loops), and the gray row under it its scores with thinking off, from Tables 3 and 4. Green: thinking on is better by at least 1 point (0.01 in Brier score), orange: worse by at least as much. The columns are those of Table 5. VS-Bench is normalized per game with the range of Table 3, which holds the models with thinking off. Thought tokens: the mean per question, and per decision in closed loops (video: the static and audio-visual questions). –: the model does not take audio.

Table 15. Spoken conversations. Counts over the 631 episodes. Turn-taking (117 episodes): Spoke counts the episodes in which the model speaks after the moment at which the other speaker took the turn in the recording, Time is the median time from that moment to its first audible speech (0 if it is already speaking then), and Early counts the episodes in which it speaks before that moment. Pauses: the marked pauses, of 277, during which it speaks. Stops after: cancelled responses out of the episodes in which the interruption (of 200) or the backchannel (of 98) was played. Stopping is expected after an interruption and unwanted after a backchannel. Cens.: right-censored episodes. With the shared voice, Qwen3Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct speaks for every model, and Time includes the 500 ms of silence that the voice activity detector waits for. Own speech: the system speaks with its own voice and turn policy, so these rows do not compare decisions, and MiniCPM-o 4.5 in its own mode reports no cancellation, so its stops are not counted.

Table 9. Accuracy (%) per video task: Open MLLMs, read at the answer token. Src.: sources; Q.: questions; –: the model does not take audio. A task with several sources averages their accuracies. Bold: the best model of the row in this table.

Table 1. Domains of the non-agentic decisions. A task is one type of decision, and it draws on one or more sources, most of them public. Video counts short videos, long videos, and audiovisual input together. The public benchmark subsets keep their original questions and are reported apart from the other domains. –: no task.

Table 2. Closed-loop game suites. Playable: environments whose actions a choice question can express and that run on the pinned harness. Episodes: per model, over all environments. All episodes are in paused mode.
Table 11. Sources of the video tasks. License and tier as in Table 10. 7 sources whose annotations we do not redistribute are rebuilt from them by a loader. –: built for this benchmark.
Table 12. Sources of the audio tasks. License and tier as in Table 10.

Table 14. GameWorld in real-time mode. Progress over the games that a model plays in both modes, 33 games with five tasks each (32 for Clef and Clef-Flash). Latency: the game time that real-time mode charges per decision, the model’s median latency on the closed-loop decisions of Table 6 in a separate run on H100 PCIe GPUs, rounded to 10 ms. ∆: real-time minus paused progress (points). SE: the standard error of ∆ over the games.

Table 10. Sources of the image tasks. License as the source states it. Tier of the instructions: A, the source’s instructions verbatim; B, adapted from the source; C, newly written from the source’s labeling criteria. 3 sources whose annotations we do not redistribute are rebuilt from them by a loader. –: built for this benchmark.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark comparing System-1 models and MLLMs on multimodal decisions, including video and closed-loop game environments, relevant to MLLM evaluation and video understanding.
papers.title: S1Arena-MM: Which Multimodal Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
papers.tldr: S1Arena-MM benchmarks System-1 models and MLLMs on multimodal decisions, finding System-1 models highly competitive on static tasks and substantially better in latency-sensitive game loops.

papers.abstract: A zero-shot vision-language classifier is highly sensitive to the class names it receives. Even when images remain unchanged, replacing familiar labels with synonyms, abbreviations, or ontology terms can significantly alter predictions. We investigate this \emph{vocabulary shift} using a leakage-free evaluation protocol across Tiny ImageNet, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, and ImageNetV2. With CLIP ViT-B/16, alternative class names reduce top-1 accuracy by $14.8$--$17.6$ percentage points. To address this issue, we propose \emph{image-grounded concept linking}, a training-free method that maps class names to visual concepts and uses a reliability gate to improve predictions. The method outperforms a template ensemble across all four datasets, achieving a pooled gain of $1.8$ points. We further evaluate five vision-language backbones across four datasets. Our method improves performance in $16$ of $20$ backbone--dataset combinations, with no significantly negative results. It also reduces pooled negative log-likelihood across all five backbones. Stronger text linking and transductive refinement provide no consistent improvements, suggesting that accurate visual class-name linking remains the main challenge. A second CLIP ViT-B/16 seed confirms the improvement on ImageNetV2, but not on ImageNet-A.
authors: Behraj Khan, Shabir Ahmad, Tahir Qasim Syed, Syed Ahmad Chan Bukhari
bullets: Vocabulary shifts—such as synonyms, abbreviations, and ontology terms—reduce CLIP ViT-B/16 top-1 accuracy by 14.8–17.6 percentage points across four datasets.
The proposed training-free method maps class names to visual concepts and applies a reliability gate to improve predictions.
It outperforms a template ensemble on all four datasets, with a pooled gain of 1.8 points.
Across five backbones and four datasets, it improves 16 of 20 combinations and reduces pooled negative log-likelihood for every backbone.
Results suggest accurate visual class-name linking is the central challenge; gains were not consistently replicated for ImageNet-A with a second seed.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Vocabulary shift and image-grounded concept linking. (a) A deployment string is encoded once and linked to a soft distribution over the top-M concepts of a lexicon memory. For each test image, the class score is a von Mises–Fisher mixture over those candidates; a reliability gate adds the raw string as one more component when the link is weak, and the prediction is the highest gated score. Both encoders are frozen (snowflakes) and nothing is trained. The example string is illustrative. (b) CLIP ViT-B/16, seed 0, test classes of four datasets. Calling the classes by held-out WordNet lemmas instead of their development names costs 14.8–17.6 points, and a perfect linker would recover most of it. Ours closes part of the gap on every dataset (point estimates); Tab. 2 gives paired intervals against the template ensemble.

Figure 4: Ours − CLIP ensemble for every backbone and test set. Top: top-1 accuracy (points, higher is better). Bottom: NLL (nats, lower is better). Points are paired differences with 95% class-level bootstrap intervals (seed 0); diamonds are the approximate inverse-variance pool over the four sets. Filled markers: the interval excludes zero. Dashed line: no difference.

Figure 5: Sensitivity to M of the fused gated variant on each test set (diagnostic, test data, not used for selection; circles mark the selected M). Accuracy varies by at most 1.5 points over M ∈ [3, 320] once the link temperature and the gate are calibrated on text strings.

Figure 2: Paired differences per test set (coloured; 95% class-level bootstrap intervals) and pooled (black diamond; approximate). Dashed line: no difference. Ours beats the CLIP ensemble on every set, and the gate is positive on every set. Fused linking never helps, and transductive link resolution changes sign across domains.

Table 5: Five dual-encoder backbones, four test sets (top-1 points, seed 0, inductive). Every cell is a paired difference with a 95% class-level bootstrap interval; bold: the interval excludes zero. The pipeline, splits and vocabulary draws are the same in every row, and all hyper-parameters are re-selected per backbone with the rules of Sec. 3. ‡Inverse-variance pooling over the four sets, as in Tab. 2; approximate, because the sets share ImageNet classes. The CLIP B/16 rows reproduce Tab. 2 exactly.

Table 10: Backbone study: top-1 accuracy (%) on the held-out names (seed 0, inductive). Dev. name: raw CLIP with development names (grey, reference). Gap: dev. name − CLIP raw. Bold: best non-oracle method. Link acc.: fraction of test-class names whose top-1 link is the true concept, with the CLIP memory and with the fused linker, averaged over the three draws (OOL classes count as wrong).

Table 1: Top-1 accuracy (%) under held-out names, inductive setting (one test image at a time). All methods use frozen CLIP ViT-B/16 and one seed. The first row (grey) uses each class’s development name and is shown only as the unshifted reference. Bold: best non-oracle method per column. “Fused” rows are the text-linking extension of Sec. 3.

Table 11: Extensions across backbones (top-1 points, seed 0; bold: interval excludes zero; I2: heterogeneity across the four sets). Fused hard linking is below CLIP-memory hard linking in every pair. The fused gated variant is mostly below Ours and beats it significantly only once (CLIP L/14, Tiny-IN). Transduction alone helps in 19 of 20 pairs, while transductive link re-estimation on top of it changes sign across sets and is never significant after pooling.

Table 4: Transductive setting (the whole unlabeled test pool is available). Accuracy and ECE in %. Both CLIP baselines use the same EM code and centroid refinement as our variant, with one slot per class, so the second difference row isolates the effect of the lexicon links. Pooled over the four sets: transduction alone ≈ +2.5 [+1.7, +3.3]; link EM + centroids − CLIP ens. + transd. ≈ 0.0 [−1.6, +1.7] (heterogeneity I2 = 0.80).

Table 6: All metrics for the main arms on every test set (one seed). Acc: mean top-1 over three vocabulary draws. Worst: worst draw. All: images correct under all draws. Cons: pairwise prediction consistency. ECE in %, 15 bins. NLL in nats. “+ T”: transductive.

Table 7: Robustness and calibration differences with 95% class-level bootstrap intervals (1000 resamples; ECE on draws pooled over vocabularies). All/Cons/ECE in points, NLL in nats. Bold: interval excludes zero.
Table 9: Learned text adaptor (ablation, Tiny-IN only), top-1 %. Limg adds an image cross-entropy through Eq. (4) on seen classes.

Table 12: Second seed (CLIP B/16). The seed changes the class split, the held-out names and the vocabulary draws, so the two rows of a set are different test problems, not repeated measurements of one. n: test classes; Gap: renaming cost (points). Paired top-1 differences with 95% class-level intervals; bold excludes zero.

Table 2: Paired accuracy differences with 95% class-level bootstrap intervals (2000 resamples). Bold: interval excludes zero. ‡Inverse-variance pooling over the four test sets with SE ≈ (hi−lo)/3.92. The test sets share ImageNet classes, so they are not independent, and the pooled intervals are approximate and likely too narrow.

papers.selection_reason: Robust vision-language recognition under vocabulary shift; fits multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Seeing Beyond Names: Image-Grounded Concept Linking for Robust Vision-Language Recognition
papers.tldr: Image-grounded concept linking makes zero-shot vision-language classifiers more robust to changes in class names without additional training.

papers.abstract: Reasoning distillation offers a promising approach to transfer temporal reasoning capabilities of powerful Video-LLMs to open-source student models. However, teacher and student Video-LLMs may construct different temporal observations from the same video due to the adoption of distinct video sampling pipelines. A reasoning trajectory valid under the teacher's observations may rely on evidence inaccessible to the student and thus cannot be directly executed based on the student's observations. We formalize this as a conditional target mismatch, thereby revealing the Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap. To bridge this gap, we propose an acquisition-to-execution framework that first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior and then further optimizes the execution capability of this prior across multiple observations. We further introduce Execution-Aware Reference Regularization, which retains the existing prior when it is executable under current observations, while allowing a greater degree of adaptive adjustment when it is not. Experiments across multiple Video-LLM backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks show that explicitly optimizing observation-conditioned execution consistently outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, with gains extending to held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.
authors: Junzhou Chen, Jindong Wang, Gang Zhou
bullets: Different sampling pipelines can make teacher reasoning depend on evidence unavailable to the student, creating a Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap.
The framework first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior, then optimizes its execution across multiple observations.
Execution-Aware Reference Regularization preserves the prior when executable and permits adaptive changes when observations differ.
Across multiple backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks, the approach outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, including on held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Automated electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has advanced substantially with deep learning, yet many methods remain task-specific and label-dependent. Large language models (LLMs) and time-series foundation models (TSFMs) offer complementary pretrained representations, but integrating them is challenging because of mismatched feature spaces and the lead- and scale-dependent structure of ECG signals. We propose LAF-ECG (Lead-Aware Foundation Fusion for ECG), a dual-foundation framework that extends MedTsLLM with a lead-aware interface to a frozen TSFM backbone while retaining its reprogramming pathway. The proposed framework captures multi-resolution temporal context, fuses temporal and language-aligned ECG representations through adaptive residual integration, and employs branch-specific supervision with cross-branch alignment. LAF-ECG achieves 71.10% accuracy and 62.43% macro-F1 on PTB-XL, and 89.73% accuracy and 65.94% macro-F1 on Chapman-Shaoxing, outperforming MedTsLLM on both datasets. These results highlight the value of preserving lead-specific temporal structure when combining temporal and language foundation representations for ECG classification. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/kkianamm/LAF-ECG.
authors: Kiana Taktehrani, Maryam Hosseini, Amir Keynia, Aram Montazami, Arash Mohammadi
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining time-series and language foundation models for lead- and scale-dependent ECG signals.
Uses a lead-aware interface to a frozen time-series foundation model while retaining MedTsLLM’s reprogramming pathway.
Fuses temporal and language-aligned representations with adaptive residual integration, branch-specific supervision, and cross-branch alignment.
Reports 71.10% accuracy/62.43% macro-F1 on PTB-XL and 89.73% accuracy/65.94% macro-F1 on Chapman-Shaoxing.
Outperforms MedTsLLM on both datasets; the approach is focused on ECG classification and preserves lead-specific temporal structure.

papers.abstract: Successful manipulation requires a policy to understand where things are and how they will move, yet action demonstrations leave this spatiotemporal structure implicit. While explicit 4D supervision has proven effective, reducing the cost of dense 4D prediction remains challenging. This paper introduces \method, a lightweight yet expressive decoder that efficiently injects holistic 4D scene understanding into policies and improves success rates. At its core is a query-based decoder attached to a pretrained policy, which casts many spatialtemporal tasks into one unified interface (e.g. depth, 2D/3D point motion, multi-view correspondence, and hand-eye relations). This design enables efficient training and inference without sacrificing expressivity: the policy learns rich 4D structure from a small number of sampled queries during training, while the decoder can be removed at inference with zero additional overhead. Across multiple backbones, simulated environments, and real-world settings, \method achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance, outperforming competing methods while training up to $5\times$ faster. Probing analyses further reveal that this 4D structure is recoverable from the policy.
authors: Siyuan Xie, Jinxi Xiao, Ran Ji, Yikai Liu, Mingxi Li, Xuebing Li, Ye Shi, Yuxiang Gao, Jiayuan Gu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning where objects are and how they move from action demonstrations without costly dense 4D supervision.
Attaches a query-based decoder to a pretrained policy and unifies tasks such as depth, point motion, correspondence, and hand–eye relations.
Learns rich spatiotemporal structure from a small number of sampled queries during training.
The decoder can be removed at inference, adding zero runtime overhead.
Achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance across simulated and real-world settings, with training up to 5× faster; probing shows the policy retains recoverable 4D structure.

papers.abstract: Audio description (AD) makes visual media, such as video, accessible to blind or low-vision (BLV) audiences, but the high cost of professional production limits coverage. Due to recent advances in AI, numerous approaches to automatically generate intermediate AD scripts and/or final AD audios have been proposed. We present an expert evaluation of AI-generated AD scripts for movies in Italian and German that compares two AI systems, a GPT-4o- and a Qwen-based pipeline, against human-authored descriptions. Professional audio describers rated description quality and annotated errors using a detailed error taxonomy that includes content, character, fluency and coherence errors. The results show that while GPT-4o outperforms the Qwen models, both AI systems still fall short of human professional quality: the generated descriptions show substantially higher error rates and lower quality ratings. Based on the error annotations, we identify two key areas that require improvement: 1) character references, which includes both issues with identification and coherent naming, and 2) content errors and hallucinations, where the AD misrepresents or invents events. These error types are particularly critical, as they directly affect the viewer's ability to follow the narrative.
authors: Annette Rios, Lukas Fischer, Sarah Ebling
bullets: Professional audio describers evaluated movie AD scripts from two AI pipelines against human-authored descriptions.
Evaluation covered description quality and errors in content, character references, fluency, and coherence.
GPT-4o performed better than the Qwen-based systems, but both produced more errors and received lower quality ratings than human work.
The most critical issues were incorrect or inconsistent character references and content errors or hallucinations.
The study focuses on Italian- and German-language movie descriptions and does not establish human-level quality.

papers.abstract: As medical VLMs are increasingly evaluated for clinical decision-support scenarios, knowing when to trust their predictions is critical. Closed-ended medical VQA has become a common benchmark format because it enables automated scoring. Yet, systematic investigation into whether this format changes the reliability problem remains scarce. We identify a failure mode that we call stable wrongness: models can produce incorrect yes/no answers that remain confident and repeatable even when patient-specific visual evidence is removed or mismatched. This failure violates the premise behind sampling-stability uncertainty methods, including recent hallucination-aware calibration (HAC) variants: disagreement is informative only when errors are unstable. When shortcut-driven errors are themselves stable, sampling agreement can remain deceptively high. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity (CAS), which shifts reliability estimation from answer stability to evidence sensitivity. CAS uses cross-modal counterfactual interventions, such as text-only, black, and corrupted images, to audit whether a committed yes/no answer remains supported when visual evidence is invalidated. Across 7 VLMs and 3 benchmarks, CAS outperforms the best HAC-family scores across all evaluated settings, achieving a macro-averaged AUROC gain of +0.150 for error detection. Mechanistic analysis further shows that CAS recovers hidden errors in the HAC-confident region and that its strongest standalone signal is counterfactual decision-boundary shift rather than hard prediction stability. Our findings suggest that closed-ended evaluation should test visual dependence, not only answer stability, in safety-critical medical contexts.
authors: Qi Wu, Xiaoyu Liu, Ao Wang, Rongsheng Wang, Wenting Chen, Wenxuan Wang, Qingsong Yao
bullets: Identifies “stable wrongness”: incorrect yes/no predictions may remain confident and repeatable even when images are removed or corrupted.
Argues that sampling-stability uncertainty methods can miss shortcut-driven errors because agreement does not guarantee evidence-based reasoning.
Introduces Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity (CAS), which tests whether answers change appropriately under text-only, black, or corrupted-image interventions.
Across 7 VLMs and 3 benchmarks, CAS improved error-detection macro-AUROC by 0.150 over the best HAC-family scores.
Finds that counterfactual decision-boundary shifts are more informative than prediction stability and recover errors missed by HAC.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential for industrial anomaly detection and understanding. However, reliably identifying subtle anomalies remains challenging, as existing approaches often struggle to acquire and verify fine-grained visual evidence beyond global observations. To address this challenge, we propose EVAD, an evidence-guided visual search framework that enables MLLMs to actively seek and examine diagnostically informative visual evidence for reliable anomaly reasoning. Specifically, EVAD begins with a global visual assessment to identify potentially anomalous regions for further inspection. Building upon this observation, we introduce a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-guided exploration strategy that progressively acquires visual evidence through two complementary operations: semantic refinement for fine-grained inspection and spatial expansion for contextual verification. The acquired evidence is subsequently evaluated and integrated to support more informed and reliable anomaly decisions. Extensive experiments across multiple industrial anomaly detection tasks demonstrate that EVAD achieves state-of-the-art performance in most evaluated settings, highlighting the effectiveness of active evidence exploration for fine-grained anomaly understanding and reasoning. The code will be publicly available upon publication.
authors: Peng Chen, Chao Huang, Yangyang Liu, Maodong Wu, Jinyi Xu, Mingbo Yang, Yunkang Cao, Fangjun Huang
bullets: Targets the difficulty of detecting subtle anomalies that global visual observations may miss.
Starts with a global assessment to identify regions requiring closer inspection.
Uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to guide semantic refinement and spatial expansion of visual evidence.
Evaluates and integrates the acquired evidence for more reliable anomaly reasoning.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance in most evaluated settings across multiple industrial anomaly detection tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed EVAD framework. papers.abstract: Rotating, translating, or rescaling an object in a photograph requires revealing unseen surfaces, preserving visible appearance, and updating shadows and reflections. Reconstructed 3D assets, rendered at the target pose as a 3D state, provide explicit geometric guidance, but their imperfect textures may conflict with the photograph, while standard paired training does not explicitly teach the editor which source to trust. To address this, we propose counterfactual state supervision, which constructs controlled photo--state conflicts through hidden-surface repainting, hidden geometry with re-rendered shadows and reflections, and visible-surface texture replacement. This teaches the editor to follow the 3D state for unseen content while preserving photograph-visible appearance. However, learning this distinction does not ensure that it is maintained during sampling. We therefore introduce symmetric counterfactual correction, which uses state-side and photo-side twins, which share the photograph and the state respectively, to construct directed latent perturbations toward condition-inconsistent targets and train recovery toward the target specified by the current condition. Both strategies operate only during training, requiring no architectural changes or additional inference steps. Experiments on OBJect and SpatialEdit-Bench demonstrate strong spatial editing performance and content preservation, while controlled ablations show improved source selection and sustained responsiveness to conditioning during sampling.
bullets: Addresses object rotation, translation, and rescaling when unseen surfaces, shadows, and reflections must be generated consistently.
Introduces counterfactual state supervision with controlled conflicts between photographs and 3D states to teach source selection.
Adds symmetric counterfactual correction using photo-side and state-side twins to preserve conditioning responsiveness during sampling.
Training-only strategies require no architectural changes or extra inference steps.
Experiments on OBJect and SpatialEdit-Bench report strong spatial editing and content preservation, with ablations showing improved source selection.

papers.selection_reason: 3D-aware object editing with explicit geometric state guidance and spatial transformations, matching spatial reasoning and 3D-aware multimodal modeling.
papers.title: Seeing vs. Knowing: Counterfactual Supervision and Correction for 3D-Aware Object Editing
papers.tldr: A 3D-aware editing framework trains models to trust reconstructed 3D states for unseen content while preserving photograph-visible appearance and conditioning this behavior during sampling.

papers.abstract: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning is an effective way to accelerate multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods degrade substantially under aggressive pruning, especially on visual grounding (VG). We analyze the sources of this degradation from the perspective of the output shift that pruning causes in decoder layers, and decompose this shift in closed form into two terms, an image summary error and an attention allocation error. The summary error stems from the loss of visual information, and the allocation error from the drop in the share of attention assigned to visual tokens. To reduce both errors, we propose CAR (Coverage selection and Attention Reallocation), a token pruning framework that restores attention share while maintaining information. Specifically, to minimize the summary error, whose upper bound tightens as the retained tokens better cover all visual tokens, our coverage selection retains tokens that are both salient and non-redundant, with saliency from encoder heads chosen by a label-free probe. To minimize the allocation error, our attention reallocation reassigns the attention of the discarded tokens to the retained ones through a closed-form logit bias. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B with $90\%$ of the visual tokens pruned, CAR retains $93.0\%$ of the unpruned accuracy on visual question answering (VQA) and $77.9\%$ on VG, against $26.5\%$ for the best existing method on VG; the logit bias alone raises the VG accuracy of existing methods by up to $24$ points. Experiments on multiple MLLMs across VQA, VG and video understanding show that CAR generalizes well and consistently outperforms existing methods.
authors: Xixi Jiang, Pingcheng Dong, Chen Yang, Xin Yang, Kwang-Ting Cheng
bullets: Visual token pruning accelerates MLLMs but can sharply hurt performance, especially visual grounding, due to decoder output shift.
The shift is decomposed into image summary error from lost information and attention allocation error from reduced visual-token attention.
Coverage selection keeps salient, non-redundant tokens using a label-free encoder-head probe.
Attention reallocation transfers discarded-token attention to retained tokens via a closed-form logit bias.
With 90% pruning on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, CAR retains 93.0% of unpruned VQA accuracy and 77.9% of visual-grounding accuracy; results generalize across MLLMs and tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses visual token pruning in MLLMs with a novel coverage-selection and attention-reallocation framework.
papers.title: CAR: Reducing Decoder Output Shift in Visual Token Pruning via Coverage Selection and Attention Reallocation
papers.tldr: CAR makes aggressive visual token pruning more reliable by preserving broad visual coverage and reallocating attention from discarded tokens to retained ones.

papers.abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) store entities with photos and names and link them by facts. MMKG methods predict links between known entity IDs, and image retrievers, from CLIP to MLLM embedders, return entities that look like a query photo or match its description. Neither answers a common question about a new photo: which graph entity is related to the one shown, such as the team of a pictured player or the city of a landmark. We call this knowledge graph relational image retrieval (KRIR): given a photo and a natural-language relation, retrieve the related MMKG entity, which rarely resembles the photo, whether the depicted entity is in the graph (known) or not (unseen). We build three benchmarks from YAGO, Wikidata and in-the-wild OVEN photos. The task hides two hops: recognising which graph entity is shown, and recalling what it is connected to. GraphSeer bridges them inside one multimodal LLM: it links the photo to the graph, reads the facts of the best match, and retrieves with the hidden state at which the model is about to say the answer. An unseen entity has no facts of its own, but every candidate answer does, so a listwise verifier reads the other end of the graph: it re-ranks the top candidates by their facts and photos in one forward pass, and the facts matter far more than the photos. With Qwen3.5-27B, GraphSeer improves MRR on known entities by 24.2-70.0% over an MLLM embedder fine-tuned on the same data with the same budget. When it also fuses and verifies the embedder's candidates, it improves MRR on unseen entities by 12.5-25.6%, and on known entities it beats KG-completion models given the ground-truth entity ID.
authors: Linyu Li, Zhi Jin, Yuanpeng He, Haoran Duan, Dongming Jin, Wenchun Jing, Xuan Zhang, Gadeng Luosang, Nyima Tashi
bullets: Introduces knowledge graph relational image retrieval (KRIR), where the target entity may look unrelated to the query image.
Builds benchmarks from YAGO, Wikidata, and in-the-wild OVEN photos, covering known and unseen entities.
Uses an MLLM to link the image to the graph, read relational facts, and retrieve candidates from the answer-generation hidden state.
For unseen entities, a listwise verifier re-ranks candidates using their graph facts and photos; graph facts are substantially more useful than photos.

With Qwen3.5-27B, improves MRR over comparable MLLM embedding retrieval by 24.2–70.0% on known entities and 12.5–25.6% on unseen entities; it also surpasses KG-completion models when given the true entity ID.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) extract structured data from documents by generating the requested JSON one token at a time, so their sequential steps grow with the length of the answer. Yet in key information extraction (KIE) the schema already fixes the answer's structure: keys, nesting and lists are known before decoding, and only the values are unknown. We exploit this with a non-autoregressive extractor that writes the structure from the schema, sizes every list with a count pass, and predicts all values in parallel, in a fixed number of passes that does not grow with the document. Each value is decoded with connectionist temporal classification (CTC) in its own block of slots, so its length never has to be predicted, and a value that is still open after its block gets a larger token budget. Zero-shot on VAREX, CORD and FUNSD, our 4B extractor is 3.5$\times$ faster than the diffusion-VLM competition on average (up to 5.6$\times$) and more accurate, with 4--6 forward passes per document where block diffusion needs 12--74. The same extractor also drafts for speculative decoding with its own autoregressive base: it runs 8.3$\times$ faster than autoregressive decoding (up to 10.4$\times$) within 0.4 points of its accuracy, and 3.3$\times$ faster than speculative diffusion decoding while 13.0 points more accurate. We release the model and code.
authors: Shaked Perek, Avihu Dekel, Ben Wiesel, Sivan Harary, Eli Schwartz
bullets: Problem: Autoregressive VLMs decode JSON sequentially even though KIE schemas already specify the output structure, causing latency to grow with answer length.
Method: Fill the schema directly, use a count pass to size lists, and decode each value in parallel with CTC slot blocks and adaptive token budgets.
Results: Zero-shot on VAREX, CORD, and FUNSD, the 4B model is 3.5× faster than diffusion-VLM competitors on average and uses 4–6 forward passes per document.
It also serves as a speculative-decoding draft model, running 8.3× faster than autoregressive decoding with accuracy within 0.4 points.
The model and code are released.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Decoding trace on a VAREX test form, coloured by the forward that wrote each token. The first bidirectional pass commits most of every value (blue) and the later confidence passes fill what it was unsure of (orange). The extended budget (green) writes the end of the longest value, the physician’s details, and all eleven values are exact. In the speculative mode the verifier accepts all eleven unchanged.

Figure 2. Schema-parallel CTC decoding. (a) A count pass reads the image and the schema and sizes every list. (b) The schema is written out as a skeleton in which every value gets a block of n [M] slots. (c) A bidirectional forward predicts all slots of all values at once; this is repeated for T passes, each but the last revealing the slots predicted with probability above τ and re-predicting the rest (blanks are never revealed; the last pass takes the argmax of every slot), with the image–prompt key/values computed once. (d) CTC collapse first merges repeats, then drops blanks (∅); a value still open after its block gets n more slots (budget +n).

Figure 4. Sequential cost vs. document size. Forward passes (left, log scale) and latency (right) per document against the number of keys in its schema, pooled over VAREX, CORD and FUNSD (1,924 documents; median and interquartile range per bin). Our forward count stays at 4–6 for every document, while block diffusion’s grows with the size of the JSON it generates. Masked diffusion on our own skeleton (value-decoder ablation, 8 steps) is also flat but needs more forwards than CTC and is slower.

Table 1. Accuracy and latency on three zero-shot benchmarks. Every method gets only the image and the benchmark’s schema. VAREX: VAREX-Bench score (official scorer); CORD: field F1; FUNSD: pair F1. Latency: mean ms per document over all documents, one document at a time (Sec. 4.1). NAR: token budget up to 3n per value; NAR-SD: a two-pass draft and up to three verification rounds, values still open at the cap fall back to their first draft. Averages in the text are geometric means of the per-benchmark speedups. Ours, masked diff. is our model with its CTC slots replaced by masked diffusion with 8 steps (Tab. 2).

(b) Speculative mode by the cap on verification rounds, predicted list counts, drafts with T=2; values still open at the cap fall back to their first draft. papers.selection_reason: Non-autoregressive schema-parallel decoding for VLMs directly reduces inference latency and is a transferable efficiency idea.
papers.title: Fill in the Blanks: Non-Autoregressive Schema-Parallel Key Information Extraction with CTC Decoding
papers.tldr: A schema-aware, non-autoregressive KIE model uses CTC to decode all values in parallel, substantially reducing document-extraction latency while maintaining or improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Answering questions over long multimodal documents requires locating relevant evidence across pages containing text, tables, and figures. When the document exceeds the model's context window, selective retrieval becomes necessary. We introduce VistaTree, a document question-answering agent that builds a summary tree directly from rendered page images. VistaTree segments documents into contiguous page spans, recursively groups them into a topic hierarchy, and refines sibling summaries to distinguish neighboring sections. At query time, the agent uses node summaries to select relevant nodes and reads the corresponding pages, using hierarchical navigation when the full outline exceeds the context budget. Experiments on MMLongBench-Doc and LongDocURL evaluate answer quality and retrieval cost using a locally hosted vision-language model, and quantify the performance gap between global and hierarchical access to the index.
authors: Yexiang Cheng, Xiaochen Zheng, David Tokar, Tatyana Y. Doktorova

papers.abstract: When two musicians in an ensemble play the same instrument, they sound alike and their instruments look alike. Audio-only separators, and audio-visual separators that rely on appearance, cannot tell them apart. What still differs is how each player moves, and when. We study same-instrument per-player separation: a user clicks one musician in a video and receives that musician's sound alone, even when other players in the video play the same instrument. Our model follows the clicked player and describes them with high level video features and the velocities of body and hand keypoints. A pretrained music separator attends to these tokens through cross-attention. Earlier motion-based separators were scored only on synthetic mixtures of solo videos. We give the first per-player evaluation of same-instrument separation on real ensemble recordings. On 58 players in URMP, each sharing an instrument with at least one other player in the piece, our model reaches a median SDR of 5.3 dB, while four released separators, audio-only and audio-visual, stay at or below 0.3 dB. The gap is wider on same-instrument duets, and our model also beats the audio-visual baselines on their own MUSIC benchmark. Tests show that the gain comes from movement: replacing the video with a still frame removes it, and so does shifting the video by a fraction of a second against the audio.
authors: Abhinaba Roy, Ambuj Mehrish, Sebastiano Vascon, Dorien Herremans
bullets: Targets per-player separation when appearance and audio cues cannot distinguish musicians playing the same instrument.
Uses high-level visual features and body/hand keypoint velocities from the clicked player.
Feeds these motion-aware tokens via cross-attention into a pretrained music separator.
On 58 same-instrument players in URMP, it achieves a median SDR of 5.3 dB versus at most 0.3 dB for four released baselines.
Ablations show the improvement depends on synchronized movement, not static appearance; it also outperforms audio-visual baselines on MUSIC.
