(b) Tool-augmented inference: Tool-use models depend on external execution and observation feedback. (c) Scaffolded reinforcement learning: T2S progressively replaces executed tool observations with self-simulated ones, using hidden reference observations for consistency rewards and privileged on-policy self-distillation. (d) Tool-free inference: The resulting model performs perception and reasoning without external tool execution.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly use external visual tools to acquire evidence during reasoning, yet learning when to invoke these tools remains challenging. Existing tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) methods often rely on call-contingent rewards to encourage beneficial tool use, but such reward engineering can distort the task objective and lead to degenerate calling behaviors. We argue that effective tool-use learning requires identifying not merely which questions are difficult, but which failures are attributable to missing visual evidence and can therefore be corrected through tool observations. We propose AOVO, a data-centric framework that enables MLLMs to learn effective tool use through perception attribution and policy-adaptive data sampling (PADS), without introducing tool-specific rewards. It counterfactually probes the model's reasoning states to identify observation-sensitive questions, distinguishing them from reasoning-dominated ones. PADS then periodically estimates category-level observation effects from recent policy rollouts and dynamically reallocates the training distribution toward questions where visual observations provide informative learning signals, while optimizing solely for final-answer correctness. Experiments across diverse visual perception and multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over competitive tool-use MLLMs, with causal analysis further validating the data-centric perspective for learning effective visual tool use.
authors: Jin Cui, Xinyue Long, Jiepeng Zhou, Boran Zhao, Pengju Ren, Hao Dong
bullets: Tool-use RL rewards tied to tool calls can distort objectives and encourage degenerate calling behavior.
AOVO uses perception attribution to distinguish failures caused by missing visual evidence from reasoning-dominated failures.
Policy-adaptive data sampling reallocates training toward questions where visual observations provide informative learning signals.
The framework optimizes final-answer correctness without introducing tool-specific rewards.
Experiments across visual perception and multimodal reasoning benchmarks show consistent improvements, with causal analysis supporting the data-centric approach.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of AOVO. (a) Student rollout.(b) Counterfactual probe: from the same reasoning state, the student continues both without and with each expert’s observation. (d) Training: after SFT, the model is trained with outcome-only GRPO, and PADS periodically adjusts how often each category is sampled.

papers.abstract: Action Quality Assessment (AQA) aims to evaluate the quality of human actions, yet existing methods are predominantly developed and evaluated on individual datasets with different task formulations and assessment criteria. We introduce X-AQA, the first unified training and evaluation framework for general-purpose AQA with multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We construct X-AQA-40K, a training corpus comprising 40,163 samples from 22 data sources across four domains: competitive sports, fitness exercises, rehabilitation, and general skills. We convert heterogeneous annotations into a unified question-answering format, incorporating dataset-specific annotation guidelines and official scoring rules when available. Using this corpus, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B to develop a single MLLM capable of handling diverse AQA tasks. We further establish X-AQA-Bench, which evaluates both in-distribution (ID) performance on datasets represented during training and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on four held-out datasets. The resulting model outperforms all evaluated open-source MLLMs on X-AQA-Bench and achieves competitive performance relative to proprietary MLLMs. Ablation studies further demonstrate that multi-domain joint training and explicitly providing assessment criteria in prompts both improve OOD generalization. X-AQA establishes a unified foundation for advancing general-purpose AQA across diverse real-world domains. Data and models are released at \hyperlink{https://huggingface.co/collections/Kelly0510/x-aqa}{here}.
authors: Kaili Zheng, Wei Ding, Yuchen Ding, Kaiwen Wang, Xun Zhu, Chenyi Guo, Yudong Zhang, Ji Wu
bullets: Addresses fragmented AQA methods that use dataset-specific task formulations and scoring criteria.

Converts heterogeneous annotations into a unified question-answering format while preserving assessment guidelines and scoring rules.
Fine-tunes Qwen3.5-9B and evaluates it with X-AQA-Bench on in-distribution and four held-out out-of-distribution datasets.
Reports stronger performance than evaluated open-source MLLMs, competitive performance with proprietary MLLMs, and improved OOD generalization from joint training and explicit criteria prompts.

papers.abstract: Vision Banana showed that a closed image generator, instruction-tuned to paint perception outputs as RGB images, becomes a generalist vision model. Does this carry over to \emph{open} generators, and if not, what fails? We answer with \textbf{Open Vision Banana (OVB)}, an open framework that adapts the 7B diffusion generator of Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, using a single shared low-rank adapter and public data. Each task is a \emph{task contract} whose RGB encoder, instruction, and decoder share one specification and are checked before training. Studying 42 externally evaluated checkpoints from two 100k-update runs, six exact weight-space merges, and eight controlled shorter runs, we find that the gap to the closed system is specific and measurable. Geometry is learned early while absolute scale is not: median-aligned NYUv2 $\delta_1$ stays at 0.89--0.93 throughout training as unaligned $\delta_1$ wanders between 0.11 and 0.50. The scale is not committed by a single sample: a ten-seed ensemble lifts unaligned $\delta_1$ from 0.348 to 0.516 without retraining. Depth and 2D segmentation compete for the shared adapter, and weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it. Finally, lower validation flow loss comes with lower Cityscapes accuracy (Spearman $\rho\approx-0.9$ between loss reduction and mIoU), so the loss cannot select checkpoints. We release code, contracts, training data, and all evaluation outputs.
authors: Xu Lin, Ruilin Yao, Haoran Xu, Zixiang Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Zhao, Pu Miao, Chonghan Liu
bullets: Adapts Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and referring segmentation.
Uses a shared low-rank adapter, public data, and task contracts that align each task’s encoder, instruction, and decoder before training.
Geometry is learned early, but absolute depth scale remains unstable; ensembling predictions improves unaligned depth accuracy without retraining.
Depth and 2D segmentation compete for adapter capacity, and weight merging does not remove this trade-off.
Lower validation flow loss correlates with worse Cityscapes mIoU, making the loss unreliable for checkpoint selection; code, data, contracts, and evaluations are released.

The source enters as visual tokens and reference latents, the instruction as the text condition, and the target latent is generated from noise in 50 flow steps. The generated RGB image r̂q is converted by a parameter-free decoder Dq into a structured prediction ŷq: metric depth, a class-ID map, instance masks, or a binary mask. papers.abstract: Social simulations often use language model agents to represent people who differ on several measurable traits. However, describing a trait profile in a prompt does not guarantee the agent will express each trait at its intended level. We propose a method that calibrates agents to multidimensional profiles using activation steering: (i) extract steering directions for each trait, (ii) learn a shared mapping from steering strengths to measured trait scores, and (iii) search for a steering intervention for each target. We use Bayesian optimization for this search and evaluate the method on the Big Five personality scores of 500 OpenPsychometrics respondents. In each of five rounds, the assigned interventions yield lower mean absolute error across respondents than the prompting and steering baselines. Further, the model's responses to a given intervention yield the same trait profile regardless of whose target motivated it, so a poor match for one respondent can be the best match for another. When we match each respondent to the closest profile found across all tested interventions, Bayesian optimization yields 16.6% lower mean absolute error than uniform random search at the same evaluation budget. Our method thus offers a way to build social agents whose measured traits dovetail with those of the people they seek to represent. Whether this closer fit translates to improved predictions of downstream behavior remains an open question.
bullets: Prompted trait descriptions may not reliably produce the intended personality levels.

A limitation is that improved personality-profile matching has not yet been shown to improve downstream behavior prediction.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent videos as thousands of visual tokens, creating a large key-value cache whose memory grows with video length. At the same time, small VLMs that fit on limited hardware understand video far worse than large models. Existing compression methods shorten visual tokens into a brief prompt to save memory, yet the small model still processes them through fixed weights and cannot close this capability gap. To address both challenges, we introduce Video-as-Weights (VaW), which compiles a video once without seeing any question into the parametric and token memory of a frozen interpreter VLM. Specifically, a compiler VLM watches the video, and a single weight decoder jointly generates the interpreter's LoRA weights and optional prefix tokens from every compiler layer, enabling both same-model compilation and strong-to-weak transfer across model sizes and depths. Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter beats full in-context reading by 1.7 points when compiled by itself and by 4.3 points with a 9B compiler, reducing context from up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens while using 5.5x less memory than the video's key-value cache. Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone, and all-layer decoding outperforms layer-wise generation by 2.9 points. Mechanistic analysis shows that with prefix tokens, the weights mainly alter attention queries and MLP down projections to guide retrieval and store a baseline summary, whereas without tokens, they shift to attention output projections to write video content directly into the residual stream.
authors: Wentao Zhang, Ian Miao, Chen Qu, Bill Bi, Donna Schut, Yuntian Deng, Yale Song
bullets: Addresses video VLMs’ growing key-value memory and the capability gap of small models.
A compiler VLM processes the video once and a decoder generates interpreter LoRA weights plus optional prefix tokens, without seeing questions.
Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter improved over full in-context reading by 1.7 points alone and 4.3 points with a 9B compiler.
Compression reduces up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens and uses 5.5× less memory than the video’s key-value cache.
Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone; their roles differ depending on whether prefix tokens are used.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in expert domains face a trade-off between agentic tool use, which externalizes expertise behind brittle multi-turn runtimes, and end-to-end specialization, which internalizes expertise only implicitly at task-level granularity. We propose internalized meta-capabilities: atomic, parametrically internalized, and composable reasoning units that an LLM can select and combine within a single chain-of-thought (CoT). We instantiate this idea as Med-Agentic for medical visual diagnosis, where the model emits a capability-tagged structured CoT in one forward pass, turning capability invocation into tagged token generation rather than external tool calls. For training, Med-OPD performs multi-teacher on-policy distillation with token-level dual-factor teacher routing conditioned on both the image and the active capability tag, strictly generalizing per-prompt teacher routing. We show that this routing gives an unbiased estimator of the same expected teacher-KL gradient. Across public medical imaging datasets spanning nine anatomies and eight modalities, Med-Agentic consistently improves in-distribution and out-of-distribution diagnostic accuracy over the strong competitors.
authors: Yucheng Zhou, Junwei Sheng, Jianbing Shen
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between brittle external tool use and implicit end-to-end specialization in medical LLMs.
Represents atomic, composable reasoning capabilities that the model selects through tagged token generation.
Uses Med-OPD, a multi-teacher on-policy distillation method with image- and capability-conditioned token-level teacher routing.
Evaluated across public datasets covering nine anatomies and eight imaging modalities.
Reports consistent in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy gains over strong competitors.

papers.abstract: Cities are sensed by many platforms at once: on-board cameras, LiDAR and radar on autonomous vehicles, roadside units at intersections, drones and satellites overhead, and the GNSS traces of millions of trips. Yet most learned representations are built for one platform, one city, and one task. We survey this fragmented landscape through a single lens, the Urban State Representation (USR): a georeferenced, layered, time-varying, uncertainty-aware state that any sensing platform can write to and any downstream task can read from. We (i) formalize USR and five desiderata for it, and relate it to bird's-eye-view (BEV) features, occupancy, vectorized maps, neural fields and 3D Gaussians, scene graphs, road-network graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents; (ii) organize sensing platforms, cross-view (ground-aerial) matching, fusion operators, 3D geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models and data engines in one taxonomy that spans sensors to decisions; (iii) compile 26 urban datasets and simulators across ego, cooperative (V2X), aerial, trajectory, and language settings, with a metric glossary, a cross-benchmark results snapshot, a trend analysis, and a platform-coverage gap analysis; and (iv) review applications and propose, as an outlook, USR-5, a five-test protocol with explicit references and one aggregate score for measuring whether a state is shared, together with a research agenda of six open problems covering cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance. This survey is an entry point for computer vision, autonomous driving, transportation, and urban computing researchers; the paper list, datasets, and USR-5 code are at https://github.com/binayksingh/Awesome-Urban-State-Representation.
authors: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
bullets: Formalizes USR and five desiderata, relating it to representations including BEV features, occupancy, maps, neural fields, scene graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents.
Provides a sensor-to-decision taxonomy covering sensing platforms, cross-view matching, fusion, geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models.
Compiles 26 urban datasets and simulators spanning ego, V2X, aerial, trajectory, and language settings, alongside metrics, benchmark results, trends, and coverage gaps.
Introduces USR-5, a proposed five-test protocol and aggregate score for evaluating whether representations are genuinely shared across platforms and tasks.
Highlights open problems in cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance.

papers.abstract: 3D vision-language models (3D VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. However, their reliance on multi-view inputs produces long visual token sequences, imposing substantial computational overhead during inference. Existing pruning methods often rely on token salience or feature diversity as proxies for representativeness, without explicitly modeling the representation gap between the original token set and the retained subset, thereby leading to suboptimal representation of the original scene. In this paper, we propose ReMiC, a training-free, representation-driven token pruning framework based on minimax hierarchical clustering. ReMiC treats retained tokens as prototypes for the original observations, formulating pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget. Local prototype initialization allocates tokens according to regional representation needs, while global prototype refinement updates the selected prototypes using cross-region information to further reduce the maximum representation error. Extensive experiments conducted on three representative 3D VLMs across five 3D scene understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of our method. Notably, by retaining only 10% of visual tokens, ReMiC preserves 93.2% of the performance of Video-3D LLM and achieves a $2.04\times$ faster inference speed.
authors: Bangfeng Yan, Chaoning Zhang, Yuanhao Liu, Pengcheng Zheng, Mengyuan Li, Wei Dong, Sheng Zheng, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets the long visual token sequences created by multi-view 3D inputs.
Formulates pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget.
Uses local prototype initialization followed by global cross-region refinement via minimax hierarchical clustering.
Evaluated across three 3D VLMs and five 3D scene-understanding benchmarks.
With 10% of visual tokens retained, preserves 93.2% of Video-3D LLM performance and delivers 2.04× faster inference.

papers.abstract: Operating in the physical world requires reasoning beyond what cameras directly capture. In a city, radio signals are invisible to the lens, yet their strength is governed by the buildings and streets an image does show. Given only these visible structures, can vision-language models (VLMs) infer the invisible radio field they shape? Probing true physical reasoning requires exact fields in real cities, alongside controlled interventions where a single physical factor changes. We build a label-free engine that turns any coordinate on Earth into a ray-traceable city, simulates matched single-factor counterfactuals, and computes every answer exactly. This yields RadioVISTA, a benchmark and training dataset for visual reasoning about invisible fields. Physically, a radio field is the sum of its propagation paths, yet across six continents we uncover a striking field-path dissociation: frontier VLMs accurately judge where a field is strong, but fail to tell whether a single direct or one-wall path exists. Open models fail even earlier at reading the field itself, and are systematically wrong, scoring below random guessing even when credited for any of four attempts. On unseen cities, fine-tuning brings a 9B open model close to frontier proprietary models on fields, yet neither supervised nor reinforcement fine-tuning improves path tracing. Supervising only final answers teaches models to approximate the field, yet leaves single-path geometry out of reach.
authors: Yiyang Zhu, Xin Li, Guangyuan Liu, Ziheng Liu, Jiayi Zhang, Chau Yuen
bullets: Creates a label-free benchmark and training dataset using ray-traced cities, exact fields, and matched single-factor counterfactuals.
Evaluates both field-level prediction and fine-grained reasoning about direct or one-wall paths across six continents.
Frontier VLMs judge field strength well but fail at identifying whether individual paths exist; open models often fail at field prediction itself.
Fine-tuning a 9B open model improves field inference on unseen cities but does not improve path tracing.
Results suggest that learning final field answers does not produce the underlying single-path geometric reasoning.

We investigate this with RadioVISTA, which converts any coordinate into a ray-traceable city (1), perturbs one physical factor at a time (2), compiles the resulting fields into a physics exam with simulated ground truth (3) and probes what VLMs perceive and learn (bottom).

papers.selection_reason: Probes VLMs' physical/spatial reasoning about invisible fields from visible city structure, fitting spatial intelligence and embodied spatial reasoning.
papers.title: Seeing the Invisible: How Vision-Language Models Read, Predict and Trace Radio Fields
papers.tldr: RadioVISTA shows that vision-language models can often infer radio-field strength from visible urban structures but struggle to trace the underlying propagation paths.

papers.abstract: Reliable vision systems should connect numerical claims to visible evidence. In visual measurement, this requires mapping candidate values to image-specific physical states. StateBind-200 augments 200 real images with human-refined local geometry and matched Numeric, Calibrated, and Physicalized interfaces. Across a 128-image held-out evaluation and 6,696 controlled calls, physicalizing identical candidates raises three-model majority accuracy from 75.54% to 91.13%, a source-image-balanced gain of +15.30 points. Calibration and additional reasoning leave most of the gap intact; target localization can succeed despite incorrect value-lattice binding, with a larger burden for two-endpoint ruler spans. An independent 40-image geometry audit yields a 0.08-tick median target discrepancy and preserves the main effect under disagreement sensitivity. We further propose Factorial StateBind, a training-free selective verifier. Two VLMs propose target and lattice components, an independent VLM validates their evidence, and valid combinations are resolved deterministically. A precision mode selected on 69 development images combines component validity, four-way agreement, and state separation. Applied unchanged to held-out evaluation, this high-precision evidence gate reaches 91.67% candidate precision across 36/128 images (28.12%) and 9.68% of ordered cells. The results identify instance-specific symbol-to-state binding as a distinct reliability bottleneck and provide an interpretable evidence gate for numerical visual claims.
bullets: Introduces StateBind-200: 200 real images with refined local geometry and matched Numeric, Calibrated, and Physicalized interfaces.
Physicalizing identical candidates raises three-model majority accuracy from 75.54% to 91.13%, a +15.30-point source-image-balanced gain.
Calibration and extra reasoning do not close the remaining gap; localization can succeed while value-lattice binding fails, especially for two-endpoint ruler spans.
Proposes Factorial StateBind, a training-free verifier that independently checks target and lattice evidence before deterministic resolution.
Its high-precision mode achieves 91.67% candidate precision on 36/128 held-out images, covering 28.12% of images and 9.68% of ordered cells.

papers.selection_reason: Exposes symbol-to-state binding gaps in visual measurement with geometry-aware evaluation and a verifier; directly fits spatial intelligence and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: StateBind: Exposing the Symbol-to-State Binding Gap in Visual Measurement
papers.tldr: StateBind shows that reliable visual measurement depends on binding numerical candidates to image-specific physical states, and that explicit physicalization plus evidence verification substantially improves accuracy.

papers.abstract: As vision-language models enter remote smartphone trade-in, sellers already upload six views and a diagnostic screen, which makes it easy to treat the human quote as a step a model can take over. A model may mark a crack or read the screen, yet the quote is a staff form: appearance fill stays near 0.25, and the closed models that score a little higher do so only on the orders they answer, so human appraisal remains necessary. Two obstacles stand in the way. (1) Single-view defect sets and attribute benchmarks do not score an order-level form under a fixed input contract, so a box or a leaked field can be mistaken for a finished quote. (2) The unread half of the form is the staff fields, and a model left to emit boxes or captions does not learn them. We present PhoneQC, a 335-order iPhone-heavy cut that ranks systems by a 0 to 100 form score (Score100) only inside matched protocols (images alone; images plus a detector sidecar), with a declared upper bound that is not ranked as a peer. As a case study on that board, field-only LoRA freezes the backbone, adapts attention projections, and supervises staff fields while leaving the defect list empty; the adapter sees the same images as the zero-shot model. On image-only T1 the 3B model rises from 26.6 to 33.3 at coverage 0.928; without the empty-blocker item the open ranking still favors the adapter, while the remaining gap to a person stays large on this cut.
authors: Zihan Deng, Xinpei Lin, Du Tiantian, Lequan Yu
bullets: Evaluates order-level quotes from six phone views plus a diagnostic screen, rather than isolated defects or attributes.
Uses Score100 from 0–100 within matched protocols: images only or images with detector sidecar; a declared upper bound is not ranked as a peer.
Introduces field-only LoRA, which adapts attention projections to predict staff fields while leaving the defect list empty.
On image-only T1, the 3B model improves from 26.6 to 33.3 at 0.928 coverage; the remaining gap to human performance is large.
Scope: results are reported on a 335-order, iPhone-heavy cut, and model answering coverage affects comparisons.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks and adapts multimodal LLMs for order-level visual inspection; directly relevant to multimodal large language model evaluation and fine-tuning.
papers.title: PhoneQC: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Order-Level Smartphone Trade-in Inspection
papers.tldr: PhoneQC benchmarks multimodal LLMs on complete smartphone trade-in forms and finds that field-focused adaptation improves open-model scoring, but human appraisal remains substantially ahead.

papers.abstract: Agentic text-to-image systems wrap generators in loops of planning, routing, verification and refinement, and report large gains on compositional benchmarks, almost always relative to a single sample. We ask how much of the gain survives against Single-tool Rejection Retry (\ours): the strongest generator already in the system's pool, an off-the-shelf verifier, and retries that stop at the first accepted image under the system's own budget. Auditing four recent systems with official evaluators, we find that on GenEval SRR matches the accuracy of OctoT2I (0.962 vs.\ 0.96), recovers 63 to 90% of the gain of GEMS depending on the verifier, and exceeds GenPilot by 12 points with 2.3 generations per image; the effect persists with generators not tuned to the benchmark and on T2I-CompBench++. A closed-form analysis predicts the accuracy of SRR at every budget and shows that its gain is capped by the verifier's likelihood ratio. The same analysis also exposes genuine agentic gains: on GenEval 2, even the best of five samples chosen by the evaluator stays 15 points below the score GEMS reports (12 at the upper end of its 95% interval). We prove a ceiling on the accuracy that routing across generators can add, bracket it between one and three points on OctoT2I's own pool, and show that what OctoT2I's routing buys is compute (about 2.5 less than SRR at equal accuracy), not accuracy. In our offline distillation experiments selected samples teach the generator no more than random ones, which a short information argument explains. We end with a reporting checklist for agentic generation papers.
authors: Jian Xu, Delu Zeng, Qibin Zhao
bullets: Single-tool Rejection Retry (SRR) repeatedly samples the strongest available generator and stops when an evaluator accepts an image.
SRR matches OctoT2I on GenEval and recovers 63–90% of GEMS’s gain, depending on the verifier; it also outperforms GenPilot and generalizes to other generators and T2I-CompBench++.
The analysis predicts SRR’s accuracy across budgets and shows its improvement is limited by the verifier’s likelihood ratio.
Some agency remains: on GenEval 2, GEMS exceeds the best-of-five evaluator-selected samples by 12–15 points.
Routing mainly reduces compute rather than improving accuracy for OctoT2I; selected samples also provide no more distillation benefit than random samples.

figures.caption: Figure 4. SRR on Z-Image-Turbo, GenEval prompts. Each row shows the attempts of one slot with the NVILA score v and the official verdict; the blue frame marks the returned image. Retrying fixes counts and spatial relations that the first sample gets wrong (rows 1–2), even though the strict verifier rejects some correct images (row 1, third attempt). The verifier occasionally accepts a wrong image (row 3). When the generator essentially never produces a correct image (row 4, q ≈ 0), no amount of selection helps; this is where changing the generator or the prompt can pay off.

Figure 3. GenEval against the generations actually spent, for SRR with each tool and three verifiers (R = 1, . . . , 5; log scale). Dashed gray lines mark the scores reported by the audited systems that use each tool. The dotted line is the prediction of Proposition 1 from per-prompt single-attempt statistics, which overlaps the measured NVILA curve. At equal generations, stopping at the first accepted image (solid) dominates best-of-R without early stopping (dashed blue).

Left: on GenEval, singletool rejection retry (SRR) with the strongest tool of each audited system, compared with the gain that system reports over its own single-sample baseline (hatched). Dark blue: NVILA verifier (95% bootstrap intervals); light blue: generic Qwen2.5-VL7B verifier with a threshold calibrated on disjoint prompts. Right: on GenEval 2 the picture reverses. Even the best of five samples chosen by the evaluator itself (green) stays 14.8 GM points below GEMS, a lower bound, up to cross-paper protocol differences, on the gain due to planning and prompt rewriting. The dotted line is our single-sample score.

Figure 5. Routing on GenEval, one generation per prompt, official evaluator as oracle verifier. Gain of per-prompt routing over the best single model of each pool, chosen in-sample (dotted) or on two seeds and evaluated on the other two (blue; dots are the two folds). The in-sample advantage largely disappears out of sample, as Theorem 1 predicts. Full results in Supp. Tab. S1.

Figure 6. Accuracy against compute on OctoT2I’s tool pool (GenEval, official evaluator, NVILA at θ = 0.8, at most four generations). Compute is measured latency on one A6000 in units of one Flow-GRPO generation, including verifier calls. OctoT2I’s point converts its reported time per image (10.02 s vs. 19.07 s for Flow-GRPO alone) by the same unit. It reaches the accuracy of SRR at about 40% of the compute, which none of the trainingfree cascades we tested matches.

Figure 2. GenEval 2 (Soft-TIFA GM, official code) for Z-ImageTurbo. SRR saturates near 35 because the verifier rarely accepts long prompts. No rule that selects among R samples can exceed the green ceiling; GEMS (reported) exceeds it by 14.8 points at R=5. Full numbers, including AM and D-OPCD, are in Supp. Tab. S2.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes agentic text-to-image systems and separates retry/selection gains from genuine agency; transferable to evaluation of multimodal generation systems.
papers.title: Is It the Agent or the Retry? Separating Selection from Agency in Text-to-Image Generation
papers.tldr: Much of the reported advantage of agentic text-to-image systems can be reproduced by retrying a strong generator with a verifier, though some genuine gains remain.

papers.abstract: In open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) of remote-sensing imagery, class-name prompts can miss objects with varied appearances, while richer descriptions can activate competing classes. We propose Response-Oriented Prompt Selection for SAM 3 (ROSE-SAM3), a training-free framework that selects descriptions using frozen SAM 3 responses on unlabeled target-domain images. We screen candidate descriptions for coverage beyond the native prompts while protecting reliable native class responses, retaining candidates that pass these checks on at least four of five image folds. An offline directed acyclic graph (DAG) search then evaluates candidate combinations and builds a compact PromptBank for each class. Each bank retains the native prompts and adds selected descriptions, which we call residual prompts. At inference, the bank is fixed, and Semantic-Instance Cooperative Head (SICH) uses instance evidence to refine semantic responses before assigning pixel labels. We also introduce RS-OVSS-C to evaluate robustness under six image corruption families across eight remote-sensing datasets, preserving their class vocabularies and reference labels. ROSE-SAM3 achieves 57.3% mean mIoU across eight clean benchmarks and 54.7% on RS-OVSS-C, achieving state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/YanghuiSong/ROSE-SAM3.
authors: Yanghui Song, Chengfu Yang, Yongpeng Wen, Zhanxuan Hu, Wei Lu, Qi Ming, Nanqing Liu, Heng-Chao Li
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fixed class-name prompts and varied object appearances, while avoiding descriptions that trigger competing classes.
Uses frozen SAM 3 responses on unlabeled target-domain images to screen candidate descriptions, then applies offline DAG search to build compact per-class PromptBanks.
Retains native prompts and adds selected residual prompts; SICH further refines semantic responses using instance evidence at inference.
Introduces RS-OVSS-C, a corruption-robustness benchmark spanning six corruption families and eight remote-sensing datasets.
Reports 57.3% mean mIoU on eight clean benchmarks and 54.7% on RS-OVSS-C, with state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free response-driven prompt selection for open-vocabulary segmentation with a frozen multimodal foundation model; transferable to multimodal prompt optimization.
papers.title: ROSE-SAM3: Response-Oriented Prompt Selection for Open-Vocabulary Remote Sensing Segmentation

papers.abstract: Thinking at length before answering is expected to strengthen the visual reasoning of vision-language models (VLMs), yet hybrid VLMs often get lost in thought: their thoughts loop or exhaust the budget without an answer, so thinking can score below answering directly. Existing early-exit methods watch a thought for the moment its answer is ready and force the answer out of it, but in a hybrid VLM that moment often never comes. We find that the remedy is not to stop a failing thought earlier, but to stop taking its answer: once a thought is given up, the model's own direct answers decide. Based on this, we propose **YOTO (You Only Think Once)**, a method that answers first and thinks at most once. YOTO draws direct answers until a probe-weighted vote settles; only an unsettled problem receives a single thought, which a failure head on the hidden state monitors and stops as soon as it predicts failure, handing the problem back to direct answers. At a matched 20k-token budget, YOTO is up to 5.9 points more accurate than the strongest early-exit baseline, using one failure-head threshold across model sizes. Keeping the released weights frozen, it adds only two linear probes. On the full MathVision benchmark, YOTO improves Qwen3.5-2B from 40.1% to 57.3% and Qwen3.5-4B from 68.3% to 73.7%, above the 72.8% that Qwen3.5-9B, a model more than twice its size, reaches with thinking. Its gains carry over to five further benchmarks and a second model family. These results suggest that hybrid VLMs reason better by answering first and thinking once than by thinking longer.
authors: Tianyi Tan, Wentao Wang, Xiaohan Li, Zining Ren, Siyuan Li, Xutao Mao, Rui Qian, Luoxi Zhang, Shiwen Ni
bullets: Hybrid VLMs can loop or exhaust their thinking budget, making extended reasoning worse than direct answering.
YOTO uses probe-weighted voting among direct answers and invokes one thought only when answers remain unsettled.
A failure head monitors the thought and returns to direct answers when failure is predicted.
With frozen model weights and two linear probes, YOTO gains up to 5.9 accuracy points over the strongest early-exit baseline at a matched 20k-token budget.
On MathVision, it raises Qwen3.5-2B from 40.1% to 57.3% and Qwen3.5-4B from 68.3% to 73.7%, with gains transferring across additional benchmarks and a second model family.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The failure head at work on two MathVision problems with Qwen3.5-2B. Dots are the head’s score at each check of the thought. Top: the thought falls into a loop; the score sinks below θ at the fourth check, YOTO stops the thought there, and four more direct answers settle the problem, while the released thinking mode returns no answer. Bottom: the direct answers disagree, two wrong ones with high probe scores; the head keeps the thought, which finishes and decides the vote.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (video LLMs) answer a wide range of questions about real videos, yet they remain weak at fine-grained motion such as whether an object speeds up or slows down. Existing methods train these models on synthetic motion clips, on order pretext tasks such as reordering shuffled clips, or with rewards that compare ordered and perturbed frames. None of them requires that the label be unrecoverable from the frames once their order is discarded, so a model can fit such data from static cues without learning to use frame order. We propose ORDO, a framework that builds this requirement into the training data. We define order-necessary supervision as data in which the unordered set of frames has the same distribution under competing labels, and we realise it for motion attributes with three constructions, time-reversal pairing, matched spatial extent and uniform interval coverage. A procedural curriculum of six motion primitives instantiates these constructions, and low-rank adapters of the language model are trained on it with an answer-level objective and self-distillation replay on real videos. With 4,000 synthetic clips, ORDO raises the mean accuracy over four motion benchmarks by +7.6, +4.9 and +5.1 points on Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3-VL-8B and Molmo2-8B, while the same training with shuffled frames changes it by less than one point. Code and generator will be made publicly available.
authors: Jiaye Luan, Chaoning Zhang, Pengcheng Zheng, Dongshen Han, Sheng Zheng, Ping Guo, Caiyan Qin, Yang Du, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets failures on motion attributes such as speeding up or slowing down, which models may otherwise solve using static visual cues.
Constructs order-necessary supervision through time-reversal pairs, matched spatial extent, and uniform interval coverage.
Uses six procedural motion primitives, low-rank adaptation, answer-level training, and self-distillation replay on real videos.
Training on 4,000 synthetic clips improves mean accuracy across four motion benchmarks by 7.6, 4.9, and 5.1 points for three video LLMs.
Shuffled-frame training yields less than one point of change, supporting the importance of order-dependent supervision.

papers.abstract: The usefulness of an in-context demonstration for a vision-language model (VLM) depends on both the query image and the task posed about it. We study whether the frozen target VLM's own decoder states, read before answer generation, can select such demonstrations. BehaviorICL represents each image and task by a task-conditioned processing signature, the hidden states at the final input position across all decoder layers. Its training-free variant, BehaviorICL-Raw, averages cosine similarities between corresponding layer states and passes the retrieved examples with their reference answers to the same VLM. When the same NICO++ images are asked about their object or their context, Raw retrieves largely different demonstrations for the two questions and outperforms an image retriever given task-matched demonstrations on both VLMs. Across two VLMs and eight classification and visual question answering datasets, Raw gives the highest average accuracy among training-free retrievers on both VLMs and exceeds RICES with a CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder by 3.83 points on Qwen and 1.85 on InternVL. A lightweight shared projection, BehaviorICL-Proj, brings further gains on classification. Analyses of extraction text, decoder depth and bank answers help explain these gains, and attention analysis describes how the task text shifts attention at the extraction position toward the classified object. These results support the target VLM's internal states as a practical basis for visual in-context learning.
authors: Chenyang Wang, Jiamo Hu, Chengrui Wu, Lingyue Chen, Jianguo Chen, Xun Xu, Xulei Yang
bullets: Demonstration usefulness depends on both the query image and the task, so retrieval should be task-aware.

Across two VLMs and eight classification/VQA datasets, Raw achieved the best average accuracy among training-free retrievers, outperforming CLIP-based RICES by 3.83 points on Qwen and 1.85 on InternVL.
A lightweight projection variant further improved classification; analyses link gains to task text, decoder depth, bank answers, and attention shifts.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($\delta_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.
authors: Chi Yan, Guoyang Zhao, Wentao Yuan, Yixiao Ge, Yanning Zhou, Dan Xu
bullets: Existing VLMs struggle with metric 3D inference because uncalibrated views leave geometry ambiguous.
StereoVLM learns from binocular observations through correspondence, disparity, calibration-conditioned depth, and semantic spatial reasoning.

Disparity supervision generalizes better to unseen environments than direct binocular depth supervision.
Interventions show performance relies on cross-view geometry, while hierarchical supervision improves broader spatial and manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Nautical charts encode safety-critical maritime information through standardized symbols, attributes, text, and heterogeneous geometries. Interpreting these charts and assessing the navigational significance of successive chart updates requires recognizing nautical features, determining their spatial relationships, and applying navigational knowledge. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising approach to nautical-chart interpretation, yet systematic evaluation of their fine-grained nautical feature recognition, chart-based spatial reasoning, and application of navigational knowledge to assessing chart changes remains limited. We introduce ENC-QA, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 77,312 questions derived from 6,612 National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Electronic Navigational Charts (ENCs). The benchmark evaluates four complementary capabilities: ENC Perception, Spatial Reasoning, Joint Perception and Spatial Reasoning, and Application. Of these, 8,227 questions form a progressive subset that decomposes selected chart-change cases into linked questions progressing from change detection to criticality assessment, enabling case-level analysis of how models use perceptual and spatial evidence to determine the navigational significance of chart changes. Evaluations of 10 open-weight VLMs reveal substantial limitations in fine-grained nautical feature recognition and feature-grounded spatial reasoning. Controlled evidence interventions show that relevant perceptual and spatial information improves change-criticality accuracy. Our findings establish ENC-QA as a diagnostic resource for nautical-chart understanding and safety-critical navigational decisions. We will release the benchmark and evaluation code upon publication.

papers.abstract: Audio language models (ALMs) can answer clinical questions from speech, outperforming baselines built on handcrafted acoustic features. Reasoning ALMs generate a chain of thought that refers to properties of the speaker's voice before predicting. Each statement the model makes about the voice needs to be checked against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. On clinical speech, existing evaluations score only the final answer. We introduce Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark grading each acoustic claim in the chain of thought against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. It covers five clinician-rated datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, and assesses claims for factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency across reworded and different questions. Across ten open-weight reasoning ALMs evaluated zero-shot, claim balanced accuracy ranges from 0.52 to 0.58, claims change under resampling and rewording, and the most consistent models are not the most factual. Fine-tuning a 7B ALM with GRPO on a reward for claims that agree with clinicians raises its claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and its mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61, while preserving answer accuracy on per-dimension questions. SLP-Bench is available upon request, subject to approval by the providers of each dataset.

papers.abstract: Frontier models have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose reasoning capabilities, opening new possibilities for intelligent decision making in the physical world. In autonomous driving, many recent approaches seek to leverage these capabilities through additional adaptation for action output, particularly in scenarios where existing models underperform. We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a zero-shot framework that combines frontier models' general-purpose reasoning with the planning competence of specialized driving models through an inference-time harness. In GAC, specialized planners generate multiple candidate trajectories and make an initial selection, while a frozen frontier model serves as an action critic that assesses the selected trajectory against scene evidence and either retains it or reselects from the available candidates. The harness combines camera images with spatial overlays, provides driving context and reasoning principles through textual instructions, and regulates the information available at each stage to support trajectory assessment and reselection. On HUGSIM, GAC raises DrivoR's HD-Score to 43.2, achieving state-of-the-art performance among methods trained without additional simulation data. GAC also consistently improves closed-loop driving safety across three planners, with relative HD-Score gains of up to 32.1%. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 further reveal how GAC improves planning performance by correcting up to 52.13% of eligible unsafe trajectory selections while introducing new failures in only 0.67% of originally high-quality selections. These results demonstrate the potential of harnessing frontier models to improve driving safety through inference-time cooperation with specialized planners.
authors: Yun Yan, Shizhi Hu, Zhichao Li, Yang Guan, Shiqi Liu, Jiaxin Gao, Xiangteng Zhang, Wenbo Ding, Jiuhua Zhao, Hui Guo, Xintao Yan, Keqiang Li, Shengbo Eben Li

papers.abstract: Text labels provide descriptive information about elements in visual scenes. In 3D visualization, the arrangement of these labels and their connections to target locations forms an annotation layout. Assessing layout quality supports comparisons between alternative layouts. However, existing quality measures often focus on specific layout properties and may not fully reflect human judgments of overall quality. Moreover, a layout may appear clear from one viewpoint but suffer from occlusion or clutter from another. To address these issues, we propose a multi-view quality assessment method based on a multimodal large language model (MLLM). We fine-tune a compact MLLM using structured supervision from human ratings to predict a rating for each quality dimension in each view. These ratings are aggregated into view-level and sample-level quality scores. To support training and evaluation, we construct the Annotation Layouts with Quality Assessment (ALQA) dataset, containing 3,216 layout samples from 1,072 3D objects across 13 categories. Each layout is rendered from 5 predefined viewpoints, and each view is independently rated by 3 human raters across 5 quality dimensions. On ALQA, our method agrees more closely with human reference scores than the evaluated MLLM baselines, and a user study demonstrates strong agreement with human preferences in layout ranking.

Reports closer agreement with human reference scores than evaluated MLLM baselines and strong agreement with human layout preferences in a user study.

papers.abstract: Automatic digitization of hand-drawn sketches into editable formats is crucial for modern document workflows and LaTeX integration. Converting sketches into executable TikZ code provides a structured representation of diagrams, but remains challenging due to noisy and ambiguous inputs, which hinder reliable interpretation and limit the effectiveness of token-level supervision for ensuring global diagram validity. To address these challenges, we propose Sketch2TikZ, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes sketch-to-code generation via a sequential multi-reward strategy, combining Code-Structure ($\mathcal{R}_{cs}$), OCR ($\mathcal{R}_{ocr}$), CleanDIFT ($\mathcal{R}_{cd}$), and Self-Similarity ($\mathcal{R}_{ss}$) rewards to enforce textual, visual and structural correctness. We evaluate Sketch2TikZ on the SkeTikZ and FlowChart-3B benchmarks using metrics including compilation success rate (CSR), image similarity, code similarity, and character similarity. Our method achieves near-perfect compilation success and improves visual and textual alignment over strong open-source baselines, while remaining competitive with proprietary GPT-based vision-language models. Extensive ablations demonstrate that curriculum-based reward scheduling is critical for reducing reward interference, stabilizing training and mitigating proxy over-optimization. Overall, our results highlight the effectiveness of reference-aware, multi-objective reinforcement learning for structured diagram generation from noisy sketches.
authors: Shubham Paliwal, Arushi Jain, Monika Sharma, Manasi Patwardhan
bullets: Targets reliable sketch digitization for editable LaTeX diagrams despite noisy and ambiguous inputs.
Combines code-structure, OCR, visual, and self-similarity rewards in a sequential optimization strategy.
Evaluated on SkeTikZ and FlowChart-3B using compilation, image, code, and character similarity metrics.
Reports near-perfect compilation success and stronger visual/textual alignment than open-source baselines, while remaining competitive with GPT-based vision-language models.
Curriculum-based reward scheduling reduces reward interference, stabilizes training, and limits proxy over-optimization.

papers.abstract: Visually rich documents (VRDs) convey knowledge through textual, visual, and layout information that text-centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Text-RAG) struggles to fully exploit. Recent Vision-RAG approaches enable retrieval and generation directly from document images, retaining this multimodal information. However, earlier Vision-RAG methods commonly adopt coarse retrieval representations and full-page visual contexts, which can obscure local evidence and introduce substantial redundancy and computational overhead. To address these challenges, we propose MV-VisRAG, a region-level Vision-RAG framework that uses semantically complete regions for both document representation and visual augmentation. Specifically, MV-VisRAG first constructs these regions through a ContentAdaptive Regionalization module. It then encodes them into local region vectors and a page-level global vector using a VLM-based retriever trained through multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning. With this compact multi-vector representation, MV-VisRAG performs late-interaction retrieval and estimates region contributions from the resulting matching scores. These contributions guide the selection of relevant regions, which are then rearranged into a compact visual context for generation. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate retrieval and generation gains over corresponding baselines, while region-level augmentation substantially reduces visual tokens and computational cost. Our code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xandery-geek/MV-VisRAG.
authors: Xu Yuan, Liangbo Ning, Yujuan Ding, Qing Li, Wenqi Fan
bullets: Targets the loss of local multimodal evidence and high overhead in text-centric and earlier Vision-RAG systems.

papers.abstract: Echocardiography assesses the structure and function of the heart. Cardiologists read each study across several standard views and report the findings visible in those views by cardiac structure. AI foundation models can learn to analyze these studies from clinical reports, reducing annotation burden and supporting clinical interpretation. However, existing models are trained by pairing each video with the full clinical report, including structures and findings its view does not show. This mismatch lets a model associate a finding with incidental or spurious signals rather than its visual evidence, which limits accuracy, anatomical grounding and clinical trust. Here we introduce EchoAlign, a vision-language foundation model developed on 2.87 million echocardiographic videos and images from 159 clinical centers. EchoAlign aligns each cardiac structure, video and study with its report text, and a visibility matrix restricts supervision to the views that actually depict each structure. We compare it with five public foundation models on 0.47 million test videos across ten unseen external datasets from more than 25 clinical centers. EchoAlign achieves the highest mean AUROC of 0.890 (95% CI, 0.881 to 0.897) for classification and the highest mean quadratic weighted kappa of 0.530 (95% CI, 0.511 to 0.544) for severity grading. Across 62 clinical findings, EchoAlign provides one model that detects findings, grades their severity, estimates measurements and segments cardiac structures.

Achieves mean AUROC 0.890 for classification and mean quadratic weighted kappa 0.530 for severity grading across 10 unseen external datasets.

papers.abstract: PathOPEN is a histopathology dataset for visual question answering. Two clinical pathologists selected 157 cases with 229 available original images and wrote open-ended, five-option multiple-choice and close-ended (yes/no) questions. They supplied both a correct and a wrong answer for 201 of the 309 open-ended questions. Each case records the organ, pathology category and regional anatomy, and each image records its magnification. The dataset includes 6,870 augmented images and four manifests that select subsets to improve balance by individual metadata field. Five additional pathologists and two vision-language model judges rated items with scoring rubrics, and six models answered questions zero-shot across the three formats. The metadata support subgroup evaluation, and the paired answers can be used to construct preference examples.
authors: Awais Naeem, Zhongling Xu, George Huang, Amy Coffey, Nkechi Okonkwo, Mario Saab-Chalhoub, John Lee Sang, Dina Kokh, Muhammad Zulfiqar, Ankita Shukla, Hairong Wang, Chandra Krishnan, Ying Ding
bullets: Includes 157 cases, 229 original images, and 6,870 augmented images spanning organ, pathology, anatomy, and magnification metadata.
Provides open-ended, five-option multiple-choice, and yes/no questions, with paired correct and incorrect answers for many open-ended items.
Uses ratings from five additional pathologists and two vision-language-model judges to assess item quality.
Offers balanced metadata-based manifests for subgroup evaluation and paired answers for constructing preference examples.

papers.abstract: Multimodal fact verification faces a fundamental accessibility bottleneck: while large proprietary models exhibit cross-lingual robustness, small vision-language models suffer a severe, disproportionate accuracy collapse on low-resource languages. Closing this gap traditionally requires prohibitive scale or extensive language-specific fine-tuning. In this work, we propose Offset Recovery via Bilingual Inference-time Technique (ORBIT), an algorithmic intervention that mitigates this collapse at inference time. ORBIT estimates span-specific offset vectors from parallel claim-evidence instances and applies them to claim and evidence representations, targeting the cross-lingual degradation induced by low-resource evidence. Experiments across 81 configurations reveal that ORBIT substantially recovers both accuracy and F1-score in low-resource settings, exposes calibration offset norms as a diagnostic proxy, and outperforms translation-based and steering baselines.
authors: Huy Trieu, Duy-Minh Nguyen-Tran, Thanh-Dat Nguyen, Huy Tien Nguyen, Tung Le
bullets: Addresses the disproportionate cross-lingual accuracy collapse of small vision-language models on low-resource evidence.
Estimates offset vectors from parallel claim–evidence instances and applies them to claim and evidence representations.
Evaluated across 81 configurations, ORBIT substantially improves low-resource accuracy and F1-score.
Calibration offset norms provide a diagnostic proxy for cross-lingual degradation.
Outperforms translation-based and other activation-steering baselines.

papers.title: ORBIT: Offset-based Activation Steering for Cross-lingual Multimodal Fact Verification

papers.abstract: Model merging combines experts fine-tuned from a shared backbone, such as LoRA adapters of a large language model, into one multi-task model without further training. Existing methods apply one rule to every task, yet the accuracy they lose is uneven across tasks. We show that the lost accuracy remains recoverable from each task's residual, its task vector minus the merged update, and that a task's validation headroom, the share of its expert validation accuracy the merge loses, indicates where recovery pays off. Residuals from different tasks interfere, so they must be merged rather than summed. We propose HR-Merge, a training-free wrapper around any merging method. It weights each residual by its task's headroom, re-merges the weighted residuals with the base operator, and adds the result back at a strength selected on validation, falling back to the base merge when no strength helps. On six NLI adapters of LLaMA-3 8B, HR-Merge lifts TIES from 93.29 to 94.29 normalized accuracy, above all tested bases, mainly by recovering its weakest task. In vision, on three CLIP backbones, up to 20 tasks, and LoRA merging, it generally improves or preserves base accuracy and yields the best model in every setting.
authors: Jiakang Huang, Xueyan Zhang, Renyi Cai, Jingcheng Niu, Jiaru Li, Yining Wang, Josh Zhang, Jiahe Jiang, Jinman Zhao, Gerald Penn, Baharan Mirzasoleiman
bullets: Existing merging rules lose accuracy unevenly across tasks, with recoverable information remaining in each task’s residual.
HR-Merge weights residuals by each task’s validation headroom, re-merges them with the base operator, and adds the result back at a validation-selected strength.
It is a wrapper around any model-merging method and falls back to the base merge when refinement does not help.
On six LLaMA-3 8B NLI adapters, it improved TIES normalized accuracy from 93.29 to 94.29, mainly helping the weakest task.
Across CLIP backbones, up to 20 tasks, and LoRA merging, it generally improved or preserved accuracy and achieved the best model in every reported setting.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free model merging method (HR-Merge) that weights residuals by validation headroom to recover lost accuracy, applicable to both LLMs and vision models.
papers.title: HR-Merge: Model Merging with Headroom-Weighted Residual Refinement
papers.tldr: HR-Merge improves training-free model merging by using validation headroom to selectively re-merge task residuals, recovering accuracy lost by the base merge.

papers.abstract: Bringing multimodal intelligence from the cloud to users' devices keeps sensitive data local and reduces inference cost, but deploying a specialized model per capability duplicates vision-language capacity under tight memory and compute budgets. We formalize heterogeneous capability density (HCD), measuring how broadly and effectively a model serves heterogeneous task families per unit of resident inference memory. High HCD across representation, generation, and decision raises two challenges: these capabilities need visual evidence at different spatial granularities under a fixed token budget, and separately collected task corpora yield conflicting updates to shared parameters, while cross-task paired supervision is costly and ambiguous for open-ended inputs. We present WePM, a family of pocket models unifying representation, generation, and decision within one vision-language backbone. Multi-Granularity Visual Budgeting (MGVB) allocates a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained banks; Unified Listwise Knowledge Distillation (ULKD) enriches separately collected data with soft teacher guidance, avoiding cross-task paired annotation; Stable and Efficient Multitask Optimization (SEMO) regulates each task's contribution through explicit loss weights and exposure schedules, with sequential gradient accumulation under memory constraints. In the joint representation-generation setting, WePM outperforms all baselines across five evaluation groups, raising the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74. In single-task evaluation, WePM-4B attains the best average score over 30 embedding, 39 generation, and seven typed-decision benchmarks (72.86, 62.41, 61.11). Against the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less resident weight memory, a 2.64-fold higher HCD.
authors: Zhiqiang Yuan, Qiwei Yan, Liwei Yang, Jinzhe Liu, Yang Liu, Zhongyan Hou, Liyan Xu, Peixiang Luo, Jiapei Zhang, Ying Deng, Jie Zhou, Jinchao Zhang
bullets: Targets on-device deployment, where separate specialized models duplicate capacity under tight memory and compute budgets.
Introduces MGVB to allocate a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained visual information.
Uses ULKD for soft teacher guidance and SEMO for loss/exposure regulation and memory-constrained optimization.
Improves joint representation-generation performance, raising the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74 across five evaluation groups.
Achieves slightly higher balanced performance than the strongest separate-model stack with 61.9% less resident weight memory and 2.64× higher HCD.
papers.selection_reason: Unified on-device multimodal LLM with visual token budgeting and multitask optimization; directly fits multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs
papers.tldr: WePM unifies vision-language representation, generation, and decision capabilities in one memory-efficient pocket model by reconciling visual-scale and multitask training conflicts.

papers.abstract: Transportation models, whether they simulate traffic or support planning, are only as reliable as the road networks they run on, down to the lanes and turns at each intersection. Practitioners still take such a network from GIS files and supply its junction and movement data by hand, a task that recurs with each new base year and design alternative, or they generate it from open map data. OpenStreetMap's lane tags give the correct layout for only 13 of the 44 approaches we test; open map data are often incomplete or inaccurate. Satellite and street-level imagery, in contrast, cover all 44 and show their lanes as painted. Vision-language models (VLMs) can read such imagery, but asked directly they lose geometric consistency when the same lane must be matched across a satellite crop, street-level photos taken from different poses and an ID-labelled network. We therefore present PAVE (Perceive, Anchor, Verify, Edit), a harness in which code measures what can be measured, traffic engineering knowledge enters as general rules and checks, and the model makes only the open judgements, each anchored to network IDs so that checks catch answers that contradict a measurement, a second reading or a traffic rule. Scored against human labels at signalised intersections, PAVE raises the share of exactly correct lane layouts from 49-64% with a single request to 86-91% for two VLMs, with most of the gain coming from reading one approach at a time on traced lanes. The same division of work edits a real network to a planning brief: the model names the links and nodes of each part of a facility, and code builds the edit from a design template. Of 18 edits, 16 pass every network check, against none when the model writes its own code, and 2 contain a design or coding error, against 7. An analysis shows where VLMs lose geometric consistency and which check catches each failure.
authors: Yajun Liu, Jinxi Wu, Juan Pablo Mill\'an Raya, Xuesong Zhou
bullets: Addresses manual or unreliable open-map extraction of lane and junction data for transportation models.
Uses a Perceive–Anchor–Verify–Edit workflow: VLMs make limited judgments while code measures, links observations to IDs, and checks consistency.
At signalised intersections, exact lane-layout accuracy improves from 49–64% with a single request to 86–91% for two VLMs.
For planning-driven network edits, 16 of 18 edits pass all network checks; model-written code produces none that pass every check.
Scope: evaluated on 44 approaches and 18 edits, with remaining errors involving design or coding mistakes.

papers.abstract: The safety of a request to a vision-language model often depends on the image: asking how to serve a dish is harmless for fresh food and harmful for spoiled food. High accuracy on situational safety benchmarks does not tell us whether a model's safety representation encodes both the scene and the user's intent, because a benchmark can often be solved from one modality alone. Studying frozen vision-language safety representations, we audit five public situational benchmarks and find that each admits a unimodal shortcut: images alone predict the labels, and on same-image prompt pairs a probe that never sees the photograph reaches 0.9645 AUROC. We therefore build a controlled evaluation that crosses safe and hazardous scenes with observation and action requests, so that no single-modality rule can exceed 0.500 group-ranking accuracy. On this control, linear probes on intermediate states of Qwen3-VL-8B and SmolVLM2-2.2B reach 0.958 and 0.930, showing that the scene-intent conjunction is linearly decodable; concatenating separately encoded image and text states already recovers most of this signal, so decodability is not evidence of a fusion mechanism. The same probes screen cheaply but generalize poorly to unseen images and other benchmarks. Reliable multimodal safety evaluation therefore needs controls that rule out unimodal shortcuts before accuracy is read as evidence of joint understanding.
authors: Guijia Zhang, Hongbo Qiu, Guohao Cai, Hao Zheng, Jiajun Zha, Hanqing Wang, Zhenhao Zhang, Huihao Jing, Shing-Chi Cheung, Haoxuan Che, Harry Yang
bullets: Auditing five public benchmarks reveals image-only label predictability; same-image prompt probes achieve 0.9645 AUROC without seeing images.
A controlled evaluation crosses safe and hazardous scenes with observation and action requests, preventing any single-modality rule from exceeding 0.500 group-ranking accuracy.
Linear probes on intermediate states reach 0.958 for Qwen3-VL-8B and 0.930 for SmolVLM2-2.2B, indicating scene-intent conjunctions are decodable.
Concatenated image and text representations recover most of the signal, so decodability alone does not prove a fusion mechanism.
Probe-based screening is cheap but generalizes poorly to unseen images and other benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Image-first causal masking makes the final prompt token the earliest state that sees both modalities, and controlled modality ablations expose which modality each evaluation suite rewards. Panel a plots measured Qwen3-VL-8B attention weights over token blocks [v1, . . . ,v4,r1, . . . ,r3,e]: visualto-text attention v → r,e is identically 0.0, while the final prompt token e attends across visual and textual keys. Panel b confirms bit-exact visual invariance max |∆hI|= 0.0 under matched-length prompt swaps in image-first prefill versus 155.7 in a prompt-first control. Panels c and d show fixed-probe prompt interventions shifting scores by 0.26–1.86 SD and flipping 6.3%–32.2% of predictions on public benchmarks alongside 65.7%–93.4% on same-image intent pairs. Panel e contrasts retrained modality ablations: on same-image pairs the blind text probe matches the joint probe, whereas on symmetric four-way scene-action groups the joint probe far exceeds the 50.0% unimodal ceiling.

Figure 1. Safety benchmarks can be solved from one modality, and a symmetric control is needed to test joint scene-intent information. Panel a, top: on identical MOSSBench photographs paired with benign and harmful prompts, a probe that sees a blind gray canvas reaches 0.9645 to 0.9846 AUROC, so the text alone decides the label. Panel a, bottom: our four-way MSSBench control crosses a safe and a hazardous scene with an observation and an action request, so that risk requires both modalities; an intermediate joint probe ranks the unsafe case first in 0.958 of groups, against a 50.0% bound for any single-modality rule. Panel b, a secondary result: on Qwen3-VL-8B a cached probe costs 0.234 ms per request at batch size 1, against 95.82 ms for an independent safety pass, and in a separate end-to-end run it adds 0.36% to the 68.0 ms prefill.

Figure 3. Cross-benchmark transfer fails through ranking collapse, which threshold recalibration cannot repair. In panels a and b, applying a source-calibrated 5%-FPR threshold across VSCBench and MSSBench over L1–L4 inflates hollow-circle FPR up to 79.5% on MSSBench→VSCBench. Recalibrating at the 95th percentile of labeled benign target scores with fixed probe weights places all 16 solid-circle points at 4.2%–5.1% FPR, shown with 95% Wilson intervals; because the same benign rows set and evaluate the threshold, this FPR is in-sample by construction. In panel c, transferred AUROC drops to 0.48–0.67, well below the 0.80–0.98 target ceiling. In panel d, percentile-calibrated recall at 5% FPR reaches 6.4%–14.4% TPR, and oracle-threshold recall shown as diamonds reaches 6.9%–14.8% TPR, far below the 34.4%–88.9% target ceiling bars.

Figure 4. Image-disjoint splits remove shared-image leakage, and cached probing anchors the lowlatency deployment frontier. Realized test TPR in panel a and realized test FPR in panel b show 95% Wilson intervals under a 5% calibration FPR target on image-disjoint splits: cached probes lead on both SmolVLM2 suites, within-benchmark safety passes lead on both Qwen3-VL suites, and the hollow circle marks the inflated 88.0% recall produced by request-grouped leakage on Qwen3-VL with MSSBench. papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on general visual tasks, yet their ability to understand mathematical images remains limited. This paper investigates whether explicit reasoning and textual image descriptions can enhance VLMs' performance on binary yes/no visual mathematical questions. To achieve this, we curated a paired evaluation set to benchmark prominent open-source VLMs under varying prompt and input conditions. In particular, we leverage Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and use textual descriptions, either replacing or augmenting visual inputs, to isolate and evaluate mathematical comprehension. Our results show that explicit reasoning improves performance, especially in paired consistency accuracy, while textual image descriptions do not consistently help and may degrade performance. These findings suggest that reasoning is important for stable visual mathematical judgement, whereas description-based intermediates require more careful design.
authors: Guangcheng Song, Weichuan Wang, Linqi Song
bullets: Evaluates open-source VLMs on binary visual mathematical questions using a paired benchmark.
Compares visual inputs with Chain-of-Thought prompting and textual descriptions that replace or supplement images.
Finds that explicit reasoning particularly improves paired consistency accuracy.
Textual descriptions do not consistently help and can reduce performance.
Suggests description-based intermediate representations need better design.

papers.abstract: Initial public offering (IPO) filings describe what a company does and what it intends to become. Yet whether individual forward-looking claims are subsequently realized is difficult to assess. We introduce Vision Follow-Through (VFT), a benchmark and agentic pipeline that separates claim extraction, category assignment, verifiability, and evidence-grounded follow-through assessment. \vftclaims{} contains 5,066 human-annotated claim spans from 50 IPO filings, while \vftverify{} adds verifiability tiers, follow-through outcomes, and cited later evidence for 1,000 claims. Across language models, classifying human-annotated claims is substantially easier than extracting claims from full filings. Extraction coverage also varies sharply by category, with Organizational/Culture claims recovered far less often than Market Opportunity claims. Follow-through assessment poses a separate challenge: model judgments diverge from human assessments in different ways rather than exhibiting a single consistent bias. These results show that reliable assessment of corporate follow-through requires both finding the relevant claims and grounding subsequent judgments in later evidence.
authors: Vidhyakshaya Kannan, Shiv Banafar, Michael Galarnyk, Sagnik Nandi, Soumeya Kannan, Shauray Arora, Abanoub Abdelmalak, Sudheer Chava
bullets: Introduces an agentic pipeline that separates claim extraction, category assignment, verifiability, and follow-through evaluation.

Language models classify annotated claims more reliably than they extract claims from complete filings.
Extraction varies by claim type, with Organizational/Culture claims recovered less often than Market Opportunity claims.
Follow-through judgments differ from human assessments in varied ways, underscoring the need for evidence grounding.
