papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) still struggle with fine-grained understanding of high-resolution images: attention heads vary in their reliability for grounding target entities and their attributes, while localized details are often disconnected from the broader scene context. We propose EAGLE (Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding), a plug-in framework that jointly selects grounding signals and organizes hierarchical visual evidence. EAGLE employs a fine-grained dataset to screen visually-grounded attention heads, followed by entity-aware grounding to extract target-specific regions. It then integrates hierarchical evidence construction and question-guided routing to select optimal view combinations, feeding them into the frozen MLLM to enhance fine-grained visual understanding. Experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B demonstrate that EAGLE consistently improves performance across both backbones and achieves SOTA results on V*, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K compared with existing methods using the same backbone.
bullets: Addresses unreliable attention-head grounding and weak connections between local details and global scene context.
Screens visually grounded attention heads using a fine-grained dataset, then extracts entity-specific regions.
Builds hierarchical evidence and uses question-guided routing to select complementary image views.
Improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B across evaluations, achieving reported SOTA results on V*, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K with matched backbones.

figures.caption: Figure 1. EAGLE overview. (a) Offline voting builds a 128-head pool; the dynamic ranker selects Top-K heads per entity word, with K = 16 chosen on the validation set. (b) Question-guided word weights combine their heatmaps into an entity-phrase grounding map. (c) Two localization rounds construct intermediate and detail images from original pixels. Question-guided routing selects the final views for the frozen MLLM.

Figure 2. Head selection and entity grounding on the soda-can example. (a) Attention maps for “soda” from all 28 heads of the displayed HiDe layer and EAGLE’s selected Top-16 heads. (b) HiDe’s token-wise crops lead to “silver”, whereas EAGLE combines “soda” and “can”, refines the region, and answers “green”.

Figure 4. View-combination examples. O, I, and D denote the original, intermediate, and detail views. Only I + D correctly identifies the blue backpack in (a); O + I + D recovers the car–lion relation in (b); and O + I preserves the context needed for the hall–bus relation in (c). Green marks the correct prediction for each case.

papers.title: EAGLE: Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding
papers.tldr: EAGLE improves fine-grained high-resolution image understanding by grounding target entities and routing hierarchical visual evidence into frozen MLLMs.

papers.abstract: Handwritten mathematical expression recognition (HMER) requires joint recovery of symbol identity and two-dimensional syntax, so a locally plausible transcription may still be structurally wrong. We study whether a compact vision-language model can be adapted to generate linearized Symbol Label Graphs (SLGs) under limited computing resources. Starting from a 4-bit Qwen3-VL-4B checkpoint, we apply rank-16 Low-Rank Adaptation to the vision, language, attention, and MLP modules and train with instruction-formatted CROHME 2019 examples. We compare this model with an internally implemented ViT-Transformer baseline, a zero-shot Qwen3-VL configuration, and additional internally evaluated alternatives. On the 1,198 valid CROHME test examples, the CROHME-only model obtains 524 exact matches (43.74%) and a corpus BLEU-4 score of 77.67, compared with 4.92% and 43.26 for the task-specific ViT baseline. An ablation that adds 2,000 manually written, formula-guided samples decreases exact match to 42.32%, exposing a domain-alignment issue rather than an automatic benefit from more data. The principal contribution is therefore an evidence-backed, resource-efficient formulation of HMER as multimodal structural generation, together with a controlled data-composition ablation and an analysis of the remaining gap between local token overlap and globally correct structure.
authors: Manh Tuan Ha, Xuan Bao Viet Tran, Vo Minh Dat Nguyen, Minh Nhat Vo, Quoc Trung Nguyen, Van Bay Nguyen
bullets: HMER must recover both symbol identities and two-dimensional mathematical structure, not just locally plausible tokens.
The approach fine-tunes Qwen3-VL-4B with rank-16 LoRA across vision, language, attention, and MLP modules using instruction-formatted CROHME 2019 data.
On 1,198 valid test examples, the model achieves 43.74% exact match and 77.67 corpus BLEU-4, versus 4.92% and 43.26 for an internally implemented ViT-Transformer baseline.
Adding 2,000 manually written, formula-guided samples reduces exact match to 42.32%, indicating a domain-alignment problem rather than an automatic benefit from more data.
The study highlights a remaining gap between local token overlap and globally correct mathematical structure.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we analyze multi-layer visual representations in large vision-language models (LVLMs) and examine the effectiveness of layer-wise features and multi-layer fusion for anomaly detection. Representative LVLMs connect visual encoder features to a language model through a projector. In this design, deep visual encoder features carry high-level semantics and alignment with text representations, whereas shallow and intermediate layers retain information relevant to vision-centric tasks, such as local appearance and fine-grained shape. It is therefore important to choose layer representations and fusion methods according to the nature of the downstream task. Focusing on anomaly detection, we compare layer-wise features and multi-layer fusion across multiple supervision levels and a variety of classifiers, and examine from several perspectives how multi-layer visual representations affect downstream performance. By analyzing the resulting performance differences, we further discuss the contribution of each layer representation to anomaly detection and provide empirical insights into representation selection for vision-centric tasks.
authors: Satoshi Hashimoto, Hitoshi Nishimura, Mori Kurokawa
bullets: Deep layers provide semantic, text-aligned features, while shallow and intermediate layers preserve local appearance and fine-grained shape information.
The study compares individual layer features with multi-layer fusion for anomaly detection.
Experiments cover multiple supervision levels and a variety of classifiers.
Layer contributions are analyzed to provide guidance for selecting representations in vision-centric tasks.
The abstract reports empirical comparisons but does not specify datasets or numerical results.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming lets a language model inspect and edit another model's weights, offering an alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We evaluated both approaches using Qwen3.5-0.8B on a fixed reference-frame task (128 items), StepGame (200 items), and two untrained distance-comparison tasks. With thinking enabled, the public patch (p50c) raised mean accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% on the reference-frame task and from 19.2% to 33.7% on StepGame across three sampling seeds. Randomly permuting its weight change removed the gain. Further closed-form edits did not improve on p50c, whereas a rank-1 LoRA adapter trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8%, respectively, with 0.09% trainable parameters. Removing the worked solutions from supervision prevented the adapter from passing the learning gate. The trained adapters reached 82% accuracy on unseen StepGame sentence templates, 42% on held-out difficulty levels 6-10 after training on levels 1-5, and 33-50% on unseen heading-answer combinations. Their target gains coincided with a sharp decline on the distance tasks: accuracy fell from 94% and 92% under p50c to 0-2%, and their outputs applied the StepGame solution template to distance questions. With thinking disabled and reasoning requested in the visible answer, the base model also solved the distance tasks while remaining weak on the target tasks. The comparison reveals a trade-off between improving spatial task performance and preserving neighbouring skills: the public edit restored completion while preserving distance performance, whereas supervised adaptation produced much larger target gains together with interference across tasks.
authors: Yalin Yang, Xiao Huang, Yanan Wu, Hao Yang, Ryan Zhenqi Zhou
bullets: Weight-space programming improved reference-frame accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% and StepGame accuracy from 19.2% to 33.7%; permuting the edit removed the gain.
A rank-1 LoRA trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8% on the two target tasks using 0.09% trainable parameters.
Without worked-solution supervision, the adapter failed the learning gate; generalization was partial across templates, difficulty levels, and heading-answer combinations.
Adaptation reduced distance-task accuracy from 94% and 92% to 0–2% and caused outputs to apply the StepGame solution pattern to distance questions.
The comparison exposes a trade-off between larger target-task gains and preservation of neighboring skills.

Randomly permuting the elements of p50c’s weight change within each tensor returns accuracy to the base level, prompting does not improve on p50c, and LoRA adapters trained on worked solutions approach ceiling on both tasks even at rank 1, provided the supervision includes the intermediate steps.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that visual tools can improve multimodal reasoning. However, the effects of tools vary substantially across samples, and benchmark accuracy alone does not reveal whether tool interactions are beneficial or redundant. We present $R^2$, a framework that recognizes and reduces redundant visual tool use in vision-language models. We first introduce a sample-level Category Analysis of Tool Utility (CAT), which categorizes samples according to whether a model can benefit from tools. This analysis reveals that benchmark scores may obscure a model's tool-use ability. Across seven benchmarks, samples benefiting from tools account for at most 12.44% of each benchmark, while the majority gain little from tool interaction or are even harmed by it. To assess individual calls, we propose the Visual Feedback Dependency (VFD) metric, which compares the likelihood of the same subsequent reasoning under actual and alternative visual feedback without an external evaluator or trajectory regeneration. Redundancy-Aware GRPO (RA-GRPO) combines this dependency signal with a category-conditioned base call cost to assign relative efficiency advantages among correct trajectories, supplementing outcome-based supervision. Across the seven benchmarks, RA-GRPO reduces the mean number of tool calls by 12.39% relative to Vanilla GRPO at comparable benchmark accuracy. Evaluated by tool-utility category, RA-GRPO improves category macro-average accuracy over Vanilla GRPO by 3.35 percentage points.
authors: Yilin Zhao, Jinyu Wang, Wenming Yang
bullets: CAT classifies samples by whether visual tools help, revealing that tool-benefiting samples comprise at most 12.44% of each of seven benchmarks.
VFD measures whether a tool call affects subsequent reasoning by comparing actual versus alternative visual feedback, without external evaluation or trajectory regeneration.
RA-GRPO uses VFD and category-conditioned call costs to reward efficient, nonredundant tool use alongside outcome correctness.
RA-GRPO reduces mean tool calls by 12.39% at comparable accuracy and raises category macro-average accuracy by 3.35 percentage points over Vanilla GRPO.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models for medical image segmentation often produce masks that conflict with the accompanying text, especially under multi-site/multi-lesion descriptions. We trace this failure to two factors: (i) highly templated and repetitive clinical language causes one-to-one hard contrastive learning to yield numerous false negatives, weakening cross-modal alignment; and (ii) predominantly vision-driven, one-way cross-attention lacks a language-dominant, spatially aware pathway, hindering effective injection of textual semantics into the spatial visual domain. To this end, we propose Consistency-enhanced Two-stage Segmentation (C2Seg). In the pretraining stage, Cluster-aware Contrastive Learning uses a frozen strong baseline to construct an intra-batch text similarity matrix as soft labels, thereby alleviating false negative conflicts and producing more discriminative visual representations. In the fusion stage, we introduce a Bidirectional Complementary Attention Module, where each modality dominates attention along its own path, fostering deep interaction and structural consistency between visual and textual representations. In order to enhance the expressive power of multimodal features, we further adopt KAN-based Attention Gating. Without updating the language encoder, our approach significantly improves text-mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/C2Seg.
authors: Jie Gui, Hang Tu, Wen Sha, Xiuquan Du
bullets: Addresses text-mask conflicts caused by repetitive clinical language and vision-dominated cross-attention, especially for multi-site or multi-lesion descriptions.

Adds KAN-based Attention Gating to strengthen multimodal feature representations without updating the language encoder.
Reports improved text-mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets.

papers.abstract: Many questions about videos ask for a number, such as how tall a person is, how far a cart travels, or how fast a ball leaves a ramp. We study this task, quantitative physical reasoning from video, where the inputs are a video, a question, and a prior of known facts such as object sizes, speeds, and distances from the camera to named objects. End-to-end video-language models lack an explicit metric scale and physical consistency, and their errors cannot be inspected. We present SceneRuler, which instead recovers a measurable physical scene and answers with that scene as evidence. Its central principle, Minimal Sufficient Reconstruction, builds, for each question, only the smallest scene that suffices to measure the asked quantity, and tests sufficiency on measurements rather than assuming it. The scene is written as a program whose structure a vision-language model writes and whose magnitudes are left to measurement. Physics-guided Fitting measures them through physical motion laws, so that gravity itself can anchor the metric scale, and marks every parameter, and the read-out of the asked quantity, as determined or undetermined. Each question receives a read-out and an answer. The read-out is the asked quantity evaluated on the scene, and it is empty when the scene does not fix that quantity. The answer is always given by a model that takes the scene as evidence. We evaluate on QuantiPhy and also apply the method to 27 in-the-wild videos that we collected, which have no ground-truth answers. On its validation split, the final answer reaches a mean relative accuracy of 0.709 against 0.624 for the strongest baseline, and the reconstruction determines the asked quantity on 47 of 158 questions, where the final answer reaches 0.781. Because every intermediate quantity is explicit, each answer can be traced to the objects, scale, and motion behind it.
authors: Yumeng He, Gezheng Kang, Fanlian Zeng, Yin Yang, Chenfanfu Jiang
bullets: Targets questions requiring physical quantities such as height, distance, and speed from video plus known prior facts.

Represents scene structure as a program, estimates magnitudes with physics-guided fitting, and can use gravity to establish metric scale.
Marks parameters and outputs as determined or undetermined; answers are generated with the reconstructed scene as evidence.
On QuantiPhy validation, achieves 0.709 mean relative accuracy versus 0.624 for the strongest baseline; fully determined cases reach 0.781 on 47 of 158 questions.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models can infer sensitive geographic information from ordinary images by combining visual, textual, architectural, and environmental cues. This capability creates a privacy risk: users may reveal fine-grained location information even when explicit metadata such as GPS tags has been removed. We study this problem as geolocation inference in multimodal language models and present GeoCloak, a cue-aware perceptual editing framework for reducing location leakage from shared images. GeoCloak uses an accessible multimodal model as a proxy to identify geolocation-relevant cues, localizes high-impact regions through object grounding, and applies localized semantic edits designed to disrupt downstream geolocation predictions while preserving the overall scene content. Experiments on street-level image datasets show that GeoCloak substantially reduces administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models, while maintaining automatic perceptual-quality scores closer to those of the original images than pixel-level perturbation baselines. These results suggest that cue-level semantic editing is a promising direction for reasoning-based visual privacy, while also highlighting open challenges in deployment cost, semantic plausibility, and adaptive evaluation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language agents can reconstruct rooms from video as editable 3D scenes, but convincing renders do not establish geometric accuracy. We introduce a scan-referenced evaluation and use controlled experiments to study reconstruction accuracy, the role of geometric inputs, and agents' ability to verify and correct their scenes. Our geometric score measures surface, depth, and furniture placement agreement with laser scans of 30 real rooms on a 0-100 scale. The strongest tested agent, GPT-6 Astra, scores 51.4 from video alone, while a dense reconstruction from the same video scores 75.9. Given the point cloud used for that reconstruction, Astra produces an editable scene that scores within three points of it. Agents also inherit input errors: rescaling the supplied geometry changes scene scale almost proportionally. During revision, viewing renders improves appearance more consistently than geometry. Logs of their tool calls show that agents repeatedly measure their inputs but rarely compare them with the scenes they build. To provide this missing check, we introduce a geometric error report that compares each saved scene with the agent's input points and lists the largest discrepancies. Without new geometric evidence, the report raises the revision gains of GPT-6.1 Terra and Sol by 3.9 and 5.5 points over concurrent controls.
authors: Ziyang Long, Yen-Liang Lin, Shifan Zhu, Allen Tu, Meher Gitika Karumuri, Chenqi Li, Srikumar Sastry, Sarosij Bose, Mellon M. Zhang, Hsin-Jung Yang

Agents inherit geometric input errors, while render-based revision improves appearance more reliably than geometry.
A geometric error report improves revision gains by 3.9 and 5.5 points for two tested agents without adding geometric evidence.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer private information from shared images, including locations, personally identifiable information (PII), and personal attributes such as age and sex, even from medical images. Adversarial perturbations can protect such information against black-box VLMs, but existing methods overlook image quality and introduce visible artifacts into the images they protect. We present SecretAgent, the first general multi-agent framework that protects image privacy against VLMs while preserving visual fidelity. LLM agents iteratively locate the visual evidence that reveals private information and adapt an invisible perturbation to the target VLM's answers and to an appearance reviewer agent, which rejects any candidate with visible artifacts. We instantiate SecretAgent with two complementary variants: SecretAgent-Gradient optimizes the perturbation through six surrogate encoders for cross-model transferability, and the gradient-free SecretAgent-Tool composes procedural noise and achieves the best perceptual fidelity on three of the five datasets. Experiments on four privacy applications (geolocation, PII, facial, and medical) across five datasets and six VLMs show that SecretAgent preserves image quality substantially better than existing methods while achieving state-of-the-art privacy protection in every application, and that its protection transfers to other VLMs.
authors: Minda Zhao, Yue Zhang, Mengyu Wang
bullets: Targets privacy leakage from images, including geolocation, PII, facial attributes, and medical information.
Agents identify visual evidence exposing sensitive content and iteratively adapt invisible perturbations based on VLM responses and an appearance reviewer.
SecretAgent-Gradient uses six surrogate encoders for cross-model transfer; SecretAgent-Tool is gradient-free and uses procedural noise.
Evaluated across four applications, five datasets, and six VLMs, it improves perceptual quality over prior methods while providing state-of-the-art privacy protection.
Protection transfers across different VLMs, though the abstract does not specify detailed quantitative results or limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of SecretAgent. (a) Given an image x and its private queries Q, the Privacy Assessor (A1) first queries the target VLM on x (t = 0). The tabs mark the four privacy tasks across five datasets, with a street-view image as the running example. The history Ht records the outcomes of every round and the latest and best candidates. In round t, the Planner (A2) reads Ht−1 and outputs a plan pt of where and how to perturb, including the regions Rt; the Configurator (A3) sets its numerical parameters θt; and noise injection produces the candidate x̃t = x+ δt with ∥δt∥∞ ≤ ϵ. The Appearance Reviewer (A4) rejects candidates with visible artifacts and returns their appearance reports to Ht, and passes the others to A1. After T rounds, SecretAgent outputs the most protective passing candidate. (b) In SecretAgent-Gradient, A3 weights six frozen surrogate encoders by at,k, and each round takes a sign-gradient step inside the mask Mt that pushes the features of x̃t away from those of x on the full image and the planned regions. In SecretAgent-Tool, A2 assigns noise families to the regions as components, A3 sets their parameters, and the masked components are summed and clipped to ϵ.

papers.selection_reason: A multi-agent framework for privacy protection against VLMs using invisible perturbations. While relevant to VLMs, it focuses on security rather than the core embodied or generative research interests.
papers.title: SecretAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Privacy Protection against Vision Language Models
papers.tldr: SecretAgent uses collaborating LLM agents to hide private information from vision-language models while keeping protected images visually natural.

papers.abstract: Recent scaling studies ask whether vision-language models still need a visual encoder by comparing encoder-free and encoder-based models on the next-token loss of the text in image-text data. This loss can fall without any use of the image, and two runs with the same loss can differ in what they take from it. Visual information gain (VIG) is the loss increase when the image is replaced by a uniform one. It splits exactly into global information, carried by image statistics, and layout information, which shuffling the patches within the image destroys. We apply it to decoders with 158M to 1.04B parameters that read pixel patches through a linear embedding, evaluated every billion tokens up to 40B, and to 19 public checkpoints. In our decoders the image lowers the loss by 3% to 46%, depending on the image type. Global information is present after the first billion tokens. Layout information starts near zero, grows slowly with training and does not grow with model size on five of six image types, and a larger batch reaches the same loss with less of it. With a frozen SigLIP 2 encoder in front of the same decoder the loss is lower only when the arrangement of the image is intact. On shuffled images the losses with and without the encoder agree to within 0.04 nats on five of six image types, so the net advantage of the encoder in the loss is layout information, above all the ability to read text in images. Public encoder-free models at production scale (Gemma 4 12B, NEO, Mono-InternVL) do acquire layout information. On the same documents they have 0.53 to 0.76 nats of it, against 0.65 to 0.82 for recent encoder-based models and 0.04 to 0.07 for our decoders, and their released training stages show it rising. These results agree with the reported parity of the two families when both are trained from scratch and place the reported advantage of a pretrained encoder in layout information.
authors: Zhixuan Ge, Anqi Li, Wei Qiu
bullets: Visual information gain (VIG) measures how much an image reduces loss versus a uniform replacement and separates global statistics from spatial layout.
In 158M–1.04B encoder-free decoders, global information appears early, while layout information grows slowly and is largely insensitive to model size.
A frozen SigLIP 2 encoder helps only when image arrangement is preserved; on shuffled images, its loss is nearly identical to the encoder-free setup.
Production-scale encoder-free models acquire substantial layout information, approaching recent encoder-based models on documents.
The findings support parity between model families trained from scratch and attribute pretrained-encoder benefits primarily to layout information.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces visual information gain to analyze encoder-free vs encoder-based multimodal pretraining.
papers.title: What Does the Visual Encoder Buy? Visual Information Gain in Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining
papers.tldr: Visual encoders mainly improve multimodal pretraining by providing layout-sensitive information—especially text-reading ability—rather than simply lowering text loss.

papers.abstract: Zooming into a region often turns a wrong answer from a vision-language model (VLM) into a right one, and a growing literature takes this as evidence that the model lacked the pixels. But a zoom changes several things at once. It removes the surrounding context, re-tokenizes, at a higher density, pixels the model has already seen, and, if the first pass was downsampled, exposes detail the model never received. We separate these factors for each failure. Holding the first pass fixed, we vary only the second look and assign every failure to the cheapest one that fixes it: reusing cached tokens, isolating the region, re-tokenizing the seen pixels, or acquiring new ones. The study covers 2,753 zoom-rescued failures of Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL and InternVL3 on V*, ZoomBench and TextVQA, at first-pass budgets from 17x fewer pixels than the source to native resolution. First, most rescued failures did not lack the pixels: upsampling the pixels the model had already seen fixes 47-73% of them even at 17x downsampling, against 1-3% for a random region. Second, the first-pass budget decides how often new pixels are needed: depending on the benchmark, new pixels are required for 23-50% of the rescues at 17x and for 12-23% at 4x. The missing-pixel reading and the accounts that dispute it thus hold at different budgets. Third, the useful magnification is large and differs between objects and text: seen pixels fix more failures up to 6-12x their first-pass size per side on objects and saturate by 4x on text, and even native pixels gain from being rendered beyond native resolution. Allowing any magnification, 68-94% of the failures at 17x need no new pixels. These models more often need a better rendering of evidence they already have than new pixels, which motivates re-tokenizing a region before acquiring it.
authors: Zhixuan Ge, Anqi Li, Kexin Geng, Wei Qiu
bullets: The study decomposes zoom benefits into cached-token reuse, region isolation, re-tokenization of seen pixels, and acquisition of new pixels.
Across 2,753 zoom-rescued failures in three VLMs and three benchmarks, upsampling previously seen pixels fixed 47–73% of failures, versus 1–3% for random regions, even under heavy downsampling.
New pixels were needed for 23–50% of rescues at 17× downsampling and 12–23% at 4×, showing that the initial pixel budget changes the interpretation of zoom success.
Useful magnification differs by content: seen pixels help up to 6–12× per side for objects and saturate around 4× for text; even native pixels can benefit from further enlargement.
With unrestricted magnification, 68–94% of failures at 17× downsampling required no new pixels, motivating re-tokenization before acquiring additional image content.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Strict regime partition of zoom-rescued failures. Panel rows are benchmarks and panel columns are models. Within a panel, rows are regimes and columns first-pass budgets (coarse to fine), and the area of each dot is the share of that budget’s rescued failures assigned to the regime (number in %, n under each column). This is the strict partition: a condition counts only if it fixes the sample while its sham does not. Reading down a column gives the partition at one budget, and reading along a row shows how a regime grows or shrinks as the first pass gets finer: R4 empties, down to zero for InternVL3 on V∗ at 2.8×, and R1/ R2 fill. The dotted line marks the native crop’s own magnification (≈ 4× at a 17× first pass), and the dashed marker the magnification at which the seen-pixel curve reaches 90% of its plateau. papers.selection_reason: Decomposes zoom-rescue failures in VLMs, clarifying when re-tokenization vs new pixels are needed.
papers.title: What Does a Zoom Actually Add? Decomposing Fine-Grained Perception Failures in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Zooming often fixes VLM errors by rendering already-seen pixels better—not by revealing new visual information—and the balance depends on the initial image resolution.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for embodied perception and reasoning, yet their physical understanding is largely evaluated on questions answerable from images. Many properties critical to manipulation, such as an opaque bottle's fill level or an object's compliance, may only be revealed through touch. We introduce TouchBench, an egocentric vision-language-tactile benchmark that distinguishes visually answerable questions (Tier A) from those involving properties hidden from the camera (Tier B). It pairs head-mounted video with synchronized 137-channel whole-hand tactile sensing, comprising 900 clips from five participants across 11 tasks, with 900 absolute and 4,102 relative questions. Four state-of-the-art VLMs average 66.4% accuracy on Tier A relative questions but only 49.8% on Tier B, near chance (50%). To bridge this gap, we propose Tactile-as-Prompt (TaP), which presents 34 interpretable tactile statistics as text, enabling VLMs to reason with touch without a learned tactile encoder. TaP raises zero-shot Tier B relative accuracy to 62.9% and reaches 73.1% after leave-one-user-out fine-tuning, outperforming video alone (67.4%) and a learned tactile-token encoder (67.3%). The gains extend to unseen objects and users. On a separate 20-hour in-the-wild corpus, tactile text improves fine-tuned contact-question accuracy from 67.1% to 75.5%. These results highlight the limits of vision-only physical reasoning and establish language as an effective interface for tactile perception.
authors: Ziyao Zeng, Ziyi Kou, Chuan Qin, Mia Huang, Roger Boldu, Zhiwen Fan, Daniel Rakita, Eric Whitmire, Li Guan
bullets: Introduces an egocentric vision-language-tactile benchmark separating visually answerable questions from camera-hidden physical properties.
Combines head-mounted video with synchronized 137-channel whole-hand tactile sensing across 900 clips, 11 tasks, and five participants.
Four VLMs achieve 66.4% on visually answerable relative questions but only 49.8% on touch-dependent questions, near chance.
Tactile-as-Prompt (TaP) represents 34 tactile statistics as text, raising Tier B zero-shot accuracy to 62.9% and leave-one-user-out accuracy to 73.1%.
Tactile text also improves contact-question accuracy on a separate in-the-wild corpus from 67.1% to 75.5%.

papers.abstract: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. Same-section H&E and mIF provide what both gaps lack: mIF measures every cell without manual annotation, which gives cell-level ground truth for each step that clinical guidelines prescribe, from delineating a tissue compartment to counting and normalizing the marker-positive cells within it. We therefore present HERMES (H&E-mIF Reasoning with Multimodal Evidence Supervision), an R1-style MLLM that reasons jointly over paired H&E and mIF in guideline steps and is trained with a process reward that checks every stated quantity against this truth. Across four field-level TIME tasks in colorectal cancer, HERMES (4B) reaches an average accuracy of 84.5%, compared with 74.7% for the strongest of twelve proprietary, general, medical and pathology MLLMs, and a higher share of its intermediate quantities is correct than for the strongest open-weight baseline. Without the process reward, reinforcement learning barely improves on supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%) and fewer stated quantities are correct; editing a decisive stated quantity changes the answer as implied in all 885 test questions. Without retraining, it keeps the highest average accuracy on an external cohort imaged with CODEX (76.4% vs. 67.3%) and on head and neck cancer, a cancer type absent from training (76.7% vs. 72.5%).

bullets: Addresses two gaps: H&E-only pathology models lack mIF-derived cell phenotypes, and final-answer rewards do not verify intermediate reasoning.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) remain unreliable on spatial reasoning problems that require composing grounded relations across multiple objects. Yet, scaling reasoning supervision is challenging since human-annotated visual datasets often rely on fixed relational annotations and coarse object localization, making it difficult to obtain precise intermediate reasoning states across diverse spatial configurations and complexities. We introduce FARON (Fully Automated Reasoning Over spatial relatioNs), a framework that executes spatial queries to provide both execution-grounded reasoning supervision and verifiable outcome rewards. Rather than relying on existing annotated data, FARON constructs synthetic 2D and 3D scenes with explicit geometries, enabling configurable object arrangements, spatial relations, and multi-step compositions. Deterministic query execution yields intermediate sets and final answers, providing precise supervision without manual relation annotation. Our pipeline converts intermediate states into natural-language reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while the execution-derived answers provide verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Controlled experiments show that trace-based SFT improves multi-step spatial reasoning over final-answer supervision and that subsequent group relative policy optimization (GRPO) provides further gains. The resulting models also demonstrate transfer across external spatial reasoning benchmarks and multiple LVLM backbones without benchmark-specific fine-tuning. These results show the potential of using spatial query execution as a unified, flexible source of reasoning supervision and verifiable outcome rewards for multimodal spatial reasoning.
authors: Jiyoon Pyo, Dongwon Jung, Zekun Li, Nayeon Kim, Muhao Chen, Yao-Yi Chiang
bullets: Targets LVLM unreliability when composing grounded spatial relations across multiple objects.
Builds configurable 2D and 3D scenes with explicit geometries and executes spatial queries deterministically.
Provides intermediate execution states for supervised fine-tuning and final answers as rewards for reinforcement learning.
Controlled experiments find trace-based SFT improves over final-answer supervision, with GRPO providing further gains.
Shows transfer to external spatial reasoning benchmarks and multiple LVLM backbones without benchmark-specific fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient prompt learning has become a cornerstone for adapting pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), yet it remains highly vulnerable to label noise in few-shot Web and retrieval scenarios. Existing noise robust methods typically rely on hard sample selection or deterministic label correction, which discard valuable semantic ambiguity and overlook how observed annotations are actually generated. To bridge this gap, we reformulate noisy prompt learning through the perspective of data generation, proposing SACP, a Semantic-aware Annotation Channel-based Prompt learning framework. Instead of suppressing noise heuristically, SACP decouples latent clean-label prediction from instance-dependent annotation generation. By integrating frozen VLM semantic priors with lightweight visual residuals, SACP constructs a structured annotation channel optimized via generalized expectation-maximization with soft posteriors. Furthermore, a posterior-aware memory is introduced to preserve label uncertainty during test-time inference. Extensive experiments across different synthetic benchmarks and the real-world noisy Food101N dataset demonstrate that SACP achieves state-of-the-art performance against its counterparts in different label noise patterns, especially under severe asymmetric noise.
authors: Zibin Geng, Yitong Bao, Jia Li, Xuefeng Jiang, Sheng Sun, Yuwei Wang, Min Liu
bullets: Targets label noise in few-shot vision-language prompt learning for Web and retrieval settings.

Combines frozen VLM semantic priors with lightweight visual residuals in a structured annotation channel.
Uses generalized expectation-maximization with soft posteriors and a posterior-aware memory for test-time uncertainty.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on diverse vision-language tasks, but their computational demands limit deployment under constrained budgets, particularly on edge devices. Many works focus on Knowledge Distillation (KD) and try to transfer knowledge from powerful teacher models to students. In addition to reducing model size, visual token compression provides a complementary route to efficiency, but introduces mismatched visual token counts that complicate direct token-wise knowledge transfer. To mitigate this, we propose DVTR-KD, a knowledge distillation framework based on \textbf{D}ense \textbf{V}isual \textbf{T}oken \textbf{R}econstruction, which reconstructs the teacher's dense visual tokens from the student's compressed tokens. We reconstruct visual states after the final LLM layer and at the input to an intermediate layer identified as important for visual-information readout. At the intermediate layer, reconstruction is supervised through the teacher's response predictions rather than by direct token-wise KL or MSE matching. An auxiliary attention-readout loss complements this response-level supervision by aligning how the student and the original teacher integrate contextual information when predicting responses. Evaluations on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DVTR-KD improves the performance of token-compressed students while retaining the inference efficiency afforded by visual token compression.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of knowledge transfer when visual token compression creates mismatched teacher and student token counts.
Reconstructs teacher visual states after the final LLM layer and before an important intermediate layer.
Uses response-level supervision at the intermediate layer instead of direct token-wise KL or MSE matching.
Adds an attention-readout loss to align contextual information integration during response prediction.
Evaluations across diverse benchmarks show improved performance for token-compressed students while retaining inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding enables web agents to translate natural-language instructions into actionable interface locations. However, dense layouts and small, visually similar controls can lead models toward plausible but incorrect elements, while refinement around a single prediction may leave alternative targets unexplored. We propose the Multi-Hypothesis Verification Framework (MHVF) for training-free GUI grounding. It combines multi-hypothesis exploration with local visual verification using a single pretrained vision-language model. To explore alternative targets, MHVF constructs spatial hypotheses from multiple full-screen predictions and examines the corresponding regions through zoomed re-localization. To resolve ambiguity among the resulting candidates, it verifies their agreement with the instruction in marked local views. Verification scores then guide a second round of local search and rank candidates retained from both search levels for final selection. Experiments with five general-purpose and GUI-specific models across eight benchmark settings demonstrate improvements in grounding accuracy in most settings. MHVF improves UI-Venus-Ground-7B by 4.3 and 2.1 percentage points on Mind2Web and VisualWebBench, respectively, and raises Qwen2.5-VL-7B's accuracy on ScreenSpot-Pro from 23.6% to 53.6%.
bullets: Addresses errors from dense layouts and visually similar controls, where single-prediction refinement can miss the correct target.
Uses one pretrained vision-language model to generate full-screen hypotheses, zoom into candidate regions, and verify instruction–region agreement.
Verification scores guide a second local-search round and rank candidates from both search stages.

Across five models and eight benchmark settings, MHVF improves accuracy in most settings; examples include +4.3 and +2.1 points for UI-Venus-Ground-7B and 23.6% to 53.6% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B on ScreenSpot-Pro.

papers.abstract: Multi-step visual reasoning suffers when early visual misinterpretations persist as incorrect premises in subsequent reasoning. We argue that how visual evidence is represented during reasoning matters as much as how much of it is gathered. Rather than appending observations and inferences to an ever-growing dialogue, we introduce a Visual Board-centered harness that separates visual observations, uncertain interpretations, and derived reasoning within a structured, capacity-bounded, and revisable workspace. This separation makes each premise explicit and auditable, so that conflicts between what is seen and what is derived become detectable even by a text-only critic and can trigger targeted reinspection of the original image. Without task-specific training, our harness consistently outperforms standalone models across 4B, 8B, Qwen3-VL-Flash, and 32B configurations on Euclid30K, SolidGeo, and ChartQA bar charts, with gains of up to 11.68, 18.42, and 24.82 percentage points, respectively. Under identical tools, critic, and interaction limits, the structured Board outperforms shared free-form notes by 6.67 to 13.00 points and no-Board retries by 7.35 to 18.80 points while using 7.9\% to 38.2\% fewer tokens. Supervised fine-tuning on harness trajectories further improves direct answering and critic-free tool use, with positive transfer to chart reasoning.
bullets: Addresses error propagation from treating uncertain visual interpretations as established premises.
Separates observations, uncertain interpretations, and derived reasoning in a capacity-bounded, auditable workspace.
Enables text-only critics to detect conflicts and trigger targeted reinspection of the original image.
Without task-specific training, outperforms standalone models and free-form or no-Board alternatives across geometry and chart tasks.
Supervised fine-tuning on Board trajectories further improves direct answering and critic-free tool use, with transfer to chart reasoning.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the Visual Board-centered harness. The VLM Solver keeps the original image available, maintains a revisable Board, and invokes focused crop or whole-image queries whenever a visual premise requires checking. A text-only Critic reviews the submitted premises and derivation to return structured feedback, without directly inspecting the image. History compression preserves both the current Board and direct image access.

Figure 2. Overview of results. (a) Without task-specific training, the Visual Board harness improves all four backbone configurations on all three benchmarks over their standalone models. (b) On 500 Euclid30K questions with identical tools, Critic, and interaction limits, the structured Board (•) is more accurate than shared free-form notes (▲) and no-Board retries (×) for every backbone, while using fewer tokens than no-Board retries (dashed arrows). (c) Supervised fine-tuning of a Qwen3-VL-4B Solver on geometry harness trajectories helps critic-free tool use far more than direct answering.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.
bullets: Introduces a multimodal Jacobian lens that maps vision and language states into the decoder vocabulary’s shared semantic space.
Uses token sets and internal concept interventions to measure concept accessibility, selective access, and causal effects.
Finds that accessed concepts participate in downstream computation and reasoning through counterfactual tests.
Proposes two J-space metrics for tracking cross-modal concept alignment, which develop before reliable selective access.
Observes similar accessibility, query-dependent selectivity, and intervention patterns across VLM families and sizes, despite differing internal organisation.

papers.abstract: Reliable reasoning for long-horizon embodied tasks requires predictions grounded in the observed execution state. We present ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B vision--language model that combines spatial grounding, task understanding, and progress estimation. To train the model, we curate 3.7 million question--answer pairs, drawing execution supervision from egocentric human videos, robot episodes, and simulation. These questions span different stages of an execution and connect task-level judgments with observed progress and outcomes. We then fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this collection together with additional task, spatial-grounding, and progress-estimation data. Across six public task-reasoning benchmarks, ACE-Brain-0.7 achieves an average score of 76.5, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 72.7 and Claude Opus 5.5 at 73.5. Our model also leads the evaluated models in spatial grounding, averaging 75.90 across seven benchmarks and reaching 91.25 Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg. Controlled evaluations further indicate that our task-only model makes more effective use of visual history and more accurately distinguishes execution states. Together, these results show that ACE-Brain-0.7 effectively combines spatial perception with temporal understanding, delivering strong execution-grounded reasoning and comparing favorably with closed-source models.
authors: Yinhe Wang, Shijun Shi, Feng Pan, Tao Tao, Wei Mao, Jiangning Zhang, Zhiyao Ren, Yihang Jiao, Haoming Gu, Yunpeng Qing, Jiyu Guo, Zhi Hou, Dacheng Tao, Xiaogang Wang

papers.abstract: Frontier text-to-image (T2I) foundation models predominantly rely on multi-billion parameter Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) pretrained across massive compute clusters, creating an accessibility barrier for academic laboratories. When training DiTs from scratch on single consumer GPUs (e.g., an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 24\,GB VRAM), practitioners encounter three primary bottlenecks: quadratic attention sequence costs, Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation graph breaks induced by variable aspect-ratio bucketing, and an autoencoder throughput wall where frozen Variational Autoencoder (VAE) operations dominate step latency. In this work, we introduce \textbf{Asuka-FM}, an end-to-end system and architectural framework demonstrating that competitive dual-stream DiTs ($\sim$206M parameters) can be pretrained from scratch on a single consumer GPU in $\sim$160 GPU hours for under \$55. Asuka-FM integrates four core designs: (i) an AdaLN-free dual-stream DiT backbone reducing parameter count; (ii) structured sequence sparsification via Sparse-Dense Residual Fusion (SPRINT) to cut attention FLOPs by over 50\%; (iii) continuous aspect-normalized Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) coupled with shifted square crop training, guaranteeing static tensor shapes while unlocking zero-shot virtual camera control; and (iv) a pixel adaptation phase utilizing a lightweight (10M parameter) Patch Detailer Head operating under velocity regression ($v$-prediction). Evaluated on open-domain benchmarks without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Asuka-FM achieves GenEval 0.588 / DPG 78.96 scores at 256px and GenEval 0.609 / DPG 78.51 scores at 512px, setting a new Pareto-optimal efficiency standard for democratic foundation modeling.
authors: V\'ictor Rodrigo Gonz\'alez, Pablo M. Olmos, Ignacio Peis, Alejandro Lancho
bullets: Targets quadratic attention, variable-resolution compilation breaks, and VAE throughput bottlenecks in single-GPU DiT pretraining.
Uses an AdaLN-free dual-stream backbone, SPRINT sequence sparsification, continuous aspect-normalized RoPE, and shifted square crops.
Adds a lightweight Patch Detailer Head for pixel adaptation with velocity regression.
Pretrains an approximately 206M-parameter model in about 160 GPU hours for under $55 on consumer hardware.
Reports GenEval scores of 0.588 at 256px and 0.609 at 512px, with DPG scores of 78.96 and 78.51, respectively, without benchmark-specific fine-tuning.

Bottom Row (Stage 2): The 13-layer dual-stream DiT executes SPRINT sequence sparsification: shallow blocks (fθ) supply high-frequency dense skips ft, deep middle blocks (gθ) process macro-semantics over a 75%-sparse grid, and dense decoder blocks (hθ) fuse representations to predict flow trajectories. Finally, the lightweight 10.09M Patch Detailer Head (PDH) transfers representations directly to RGB pixels under native v-prediction.

papers.abstract: Understanding how objects move in dynamic scenes requires recovering their 3D motion from visual observations and predicting their positions at unobserved times. Existing methods either optimize scene-specific velocity fields or impose predefined physical and kinematic assumptions. We instead study learning a continuous-time dynamics operator across scenes, mapping multi-view visual observations to 3D object kinematics. We introduce Adaptive Pixel Flows (\ours{}), which learns this operator from multi-view RGB-D observations without per-scene optimization or predefined motion models. The method fuses observations from all cameras into a shared voxel grid in world coordinates, from which the network predicts a continuous-time velocity field. Because the operator is trained across scenes, it learns motion priors that carry over to unseen scenes. The field can then be integrated from observed states to predict object positions between observations and beyond the observed sequence. On held-out PhysInOne scenes, \ours{} improves F1 over the strongest competing method by 2.5\% for in-between prediction and 15\% for future prediction. Compared with per-scene velocity-field methods, the improvements are 30\% and 85\%, respectively. Applied zero-shot to Spring-Gaus, it improves future-prediction F1 by 12\%.
bullets: Addresses 3D motion recovery and temporal prediction without per-scene optimization or predefined physical assumptions.
Fuses all camera observations into a shared world-coordinate voxel grid and predicts a continuous-time velocity field.
Integrates the learned field from observed states to estimate intermediate and future object positions.
Improves F1 on held-out PhysInOne scenes by 2.5% for in-between and 15% for future prediction over the strongest competitor.
Transfers zero-shot to Spring-Gaus, achieving a 12% future-prediction F1 improvement.

papers.abstract: Video understanding, particularly with accompanying audio, remains a central challenge in multimodal intelligence. In this report, we introduce \textbf{WeMM-Video}, a family of Chinese-English bilingual omni-modal foundation models spanning 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants. Centering on joint audio-visual perception and reasoning, WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video processing within a hybrid-thinking paradigm, seamlessly supporting both a non-thinking instruct mode for fast, direct responses and a thinking mode for explicit step-by-step reasoning. The models are trained on a large-scale multimodal corpus of approximately 1.2 trillion tokens through progressive pre-training and a multi-stage post-training pipeline incorporating multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL. Evaluated across more than 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video demonstrates superior performance in omni-modal video understanding and reasoning, while maintaining highly competitive capabilities across general audio, silent video, image, and text tasks. Specifically, in omni-modal video evaluations, our flagship WeMM-Video-35B-A3B establishes a new open-source state of the art, substantially outperforming proprietary models such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 while narrowing the gap with the strong Gemini-3.0-Flash, and our compact WeMM-Video-9B surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. We publicly release the WeMM-Video family along with our evaluation and reproduction pipeline to foster further research and development in the open-source community.
authors: Changli Tang, Jie Yang, Tianyi Wang, Lei Li, Daoze Zhang, Zijie Xin, Zhan Liu, Li Li, Jinchang Xu, Fengyun Rao, Chao Zhang, Jing Lyu
bullets: Supports unified text, image, audio, and video processing in both fast instruct and explicit reasoning modes.
Offers 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants trained with progressive pre-training and multi-stage post-training.
The flagship 35B-A3B achieves a reported open-source state of the art on omni-modal video evaluations.
The 9B model reportedly surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct on these evaluations.
The model family, evaluation suite, and reproduction pipeline are publicly released for research.

papers.abstract: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp
bullets: Evaluates five LLMs editing convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks.
Covers Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS, and Entity-30, with more than 2,600 edit processes scored for success, side effects, and accuracy loss.
Compares standard training, label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and Edit-Ready Training (ERT).
ERT rehearses the direct closed-form weight edits performed by LLMs and achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across evaluated baselines.
The framework, tasks, editing trajectories, and scores are planned for release.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Edit-Ready Training (ERT) to prepare vision models for LLM-driven weight-space programming. This explores a novel interaction paradigm between LLMs and vision models, relevant to both language and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
papers.tldr: A benchmark shows that training vision models specifically for LLM-driven weight edits—especially with Edit-Ready Training—substantially improves editability and performance.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.
authors: Yuqi Tang, Yang Shi, Yuran Wang, Tengfei Liu, Rundong Wang, Zongyang Qiu, Qixun Wang, Zhuoran Zhang, Xuanyu Zhu, Yifan Xu, Yiyan Ji, Shujie Li, Shixuan Liu, Haotian Wang, Yuanxing Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Chengwei Qin
bullets: Targets missed brief actions, incorrect action order, and confusion about the camera wearer’s motion.
Uses a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline to create structured captions with video overviews, timed steps, adaptive narration, and key moments.
Trains caption refinement with GRPO using rewards for factual accuracy, coverage, temporal alignment, and non-redundancy; pose-derived motion facts strengthen supervision when available.
Built from 50,000 examples across eight egocentric video sources and evaluated on five benchmarks.

Reports leading performance among evaluated open-source models, with additional gains over specified proprietary baselines on PhysCapBench and Minerva-Ego; ablations support the reward design and coarse-to-fine annotation.

papers.title: EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning

papers.abstract: Agentic visual reasoning improves vision-language models by selectively enlarging evidence without adding new scene content, but the benefit depends on whether fine structure remains accessible and whether local observations stay grounded in the full scene. We identify three recurring bottlenecks: high-frequency detail can be attenuated during visual-token formation; spatially distributed evidence can remain encoded yet difficult for the language model to retrieve; and isolated crops can weaken whole-detail correspondence through scale and positional mismatch. ResVision addresses these limitations with two complementary components. Spectrum-Matched Resizing (SMR) estimates image complexity and selects an adaptive global sampling scale, avoiding unnecessary enlargement on simple inputs while allocating more visual tokens to detail-rich images. Context-Preserving Inspection (CPI) returns each inspected crop together with the complete working view, preserving local detail and global context across tool turns. We evaluate Direct and Agentic variants on four frontier VLMs and 29 benchmarks spanning six visual-reasoning families. Complete ResVision (Agentic Base plus SMR plus CPI) is best for every model, improving by 3.36 to 4.94 points over Direct Base and 1.87 to 2.94 points over Agentic Base. These results show that adaptive visual sampling and context-preserving inspection address distinct, complementary constraints in multimodal reasoning.
authors: Guojian Zhan, Jiahao Xu, Yahui Liu, Yao Hu, Chuan Mu
bullets: Targets three bottlenecks: lost high-frequency detail, difficult retrieval of distributed evidence, and weakened crop-to-scene correspondence.
Spectrum-Matched Resizing (SMR) selects a global sampling scale based on image complexity, avoiding unnecessary enlargement while allocating more tokens to detailed images.
Context-Preserving Inspection (CPI) pairs each inspected crop with the complete working view to retain local detail and global grounding.
Evaluated across four frontier VLMs and 29 benchmarks covering six visual-reasoning families.
The full Agentic system improved over Direct Base and Agentic Base for every model, with gains of 3.36–4.94 and 1.87–2.94 points, respectively.

papers.abstract: AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing Skill.png: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We show that Skill.png significantly outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requiring only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensemble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in the ensemble. Skill.png thus presents the first agent skill that can be optimized with gradient descent while retaining transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at: https://github.com/omseeth/skill.png
authors: Maximilian Seeth, Chengzhi Martin Hu, Marie Kempkes, Paul R\"ottger, Leo Schwinn
bullets: Textual skills are easy to transfer but cannot be continuously optimized; model finetuning is optimizable but model-specific.
The method uses gradient descent to optimize skill-like images through a frozen VLM’s vision encoder.
A single image can be jointly optimized for an ensemble of VLMs, enabling transfer across those models.
Across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks, Skill.png outperformed frontier-LLM-optimized textual skills in 9 of 16 settings.
Combining optimized image and text skills further improves agent performance; image skills use 64–256 tokens versus roughly 900–2,000 text tokens.

papers.abstract: Thinking with images (TwI) empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to overcome perceptual bottlenecks by actively cropping and zooming into fine-grained visual details, promising both higher accuracy and interpretable, region-grounded reasoning. However, our analysis shows that the improved accuracy of TwI models does not guarantee faithful tool use; they frequently invoke tools without actually relying on the zoomed region, undermining the reliability of tool-assisted reasoning. We trace this unfaithful behaviour to the training data: when questions are answerable without zooming, the model can answer correctly while ignoring the returned evidence, and this problem is exacerbated during training as the model becomes better at answering without tools. To keep zooming useful throughout training, we adapt the training data to the model's evolving capability and train on questions where correct zoomed evidence can still help the model answer correctly. This selection is supported by a data synthesis pipeline that localises small objects and constructs verifiable questions about their fine details, and complemented by an adaptiveness reward that favours tool-free answers when zooming is unnecessary. The experimental results show that our method substantially improves reasoning faithfulness and achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual search benchmarks (+11.6% on V*, +7.9% on HR-Bench 4K, and +9.4% on HR-Bench 8K). On multimodal hallucination benchmarks, our model also outperforms the compared TwI baselines. These results suggest that improving TwI faithfulness does not sacrifice accuracy and that both can be learnt from the right training data without directly supervising the reasoning process.
authors: Yu Zhao, Jiaxin Zhang, Rohit Saxena, Fazl Barez, Pasquale Minervini, Yiwen Guo
bullets: TwI models often invoke zooming but ignore the returned visual evidence, especially when questions are answerable without tools.
The method dynamically selects questions where zoomed evidence remains necessary and useful as the model improves.
A synthesis pipeline creates fine-detail questions about localized small objects, while an adaptiveness reward discourages unnecessary tool use.
The approach improves visual search performance by 11.6% on V*, 7.9% on HR-Bench 4K, and 9.4% on HR-Bench 8K, and outperforms compared TwI baselines on multimodal hallucination benchmarks.
Results indicate that faithfulness and accuracy can improve together without directly supervising the reasoning process.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can act as closed-loop robot-use agents (RUAs) by writing and executing control code through tool interfaces. However, turning an open-weight VLM into a high-performing embodied agent requires a complete post-training stack: out-of-the-box open VLMs fail completely at interactive tool contracts, strong frontier teachers are accessible only as black-box endpoints without exposed weights or token probabilities, and supervised imitation alone plateaus under rollout distribution shift. We present EmbodyAgent, an end-to-end post-training framework with three tightly coupled pipelines: (1) a black-box data synthesis pipeline that queries a strong teacher under a forced think-then-code contract and filters trajectories by task success; (2) an SFT pipeline that distills the explanation-and-program targets into an open-weight 9B VLM with both vision and language encoders trainable; and (3) an online RL pipeline that optimizes student-generated episodes via group-relative advantage with a runtime-error-penalized outcome reward. All three pipelines share one primitive-free Python execution tool exposing only raw visual observation and seven-dimensional end-effector control, with no action decoder and no interface shift across stages. Under a strictly separated evaluation protocol on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks (disjoint state splits, greedy test-time decoding, training-only safeguards), held-out success on 100 test states rises from 0/100 (base 9B VLM) to 14/100 (after SFT) and 84/100 (after RL), while training rollout success climbs from 8.4% to 87.7% and median model calls per episode drop from 36 to 11. We further identify a self-reinforcing runtime-error mode induced by outcome-based RL on executable code, and establish a failure-category monitoring and sampling-side curation protocol that stabilizes training.
authors: Wei Dai, Jinkun Liu, Jiayi Chen, Han Liu, Wenbo Ding, Shaolun Huang
bullets: Addresses failures in tool-contract following, limited access to frontier teacher internals, and imitation degradation under rollout distribution shift.
Synthesizes and filters teacher trajectories, distills explanation-and-code targets into a trainable 9B VLM, then optimizes student rollouts with runtime-error-penalized rewards.
Uses the same primitive-free Python tool throughout, exposing only visual observations and seven-dimensional end-effector control.
On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks, held-out success improves from 0/100 for the base model to 14/100 after SFT and 84/100 after RL; median calls per episode fall from 36 to 11.
Finds and mitigates a self-reinforcing runtime-error failure mode through failure monitoring and sampling-side curation.

papers.abstract: Images under non-uniform coupled degradations require diverse restoration capabilities for different degraded regions. Existing methods employ globally uniform operations, potentially overlooking regional differences and causing incomplete restoration or even damage to image content. Moreover, a degraded region may require successive restoration actions, and earlier actions may alter residual degradation characteristics or introduce artifacts, potentially hindering subsequent restoration. To address these challenges, we propose RegionAgent, an adaptive restoration framework that trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) through two-stage preference learning to generate a region-specific restoration action at each iteration. Specifically, we first train the VLM to select an action suited to the current region through step-level Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), using preferences derived from immediate restoration feedback to supervise only the differing component in each action pair. To account for the effects of current actions on subsequent restoration, we then apply trajectory-level DPO, using preferences derived from complete trajectory scores to supervise the sole differing action in each trajectory pair. Furthermore, as conventional image-pair datasets do not directly provide preferences over regional restoration decisions, we construct a regional restoration preference dataset comprising 10K action pairs and 20K trajectory pairs for two-stage VLM training. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate strong restoration performance under both mixed and single degradations. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of two-stage preference learning in improving restoration quality.
authors: Weiyu Zhou, Jiacong Tang, Tao Hu, Axi Niu, Jinqiu Sun, Peng Wu, Wei Dong, Qingsen Yan
bullets: Targets mixed or coupled degradations where globally uniform restoration can miss regional needs or damage content.

Uses trajectory-level DPO to account for how earlier actions affect later restoration and artifacts.

Experiments across multiple datasets show strong performance on mixed and single degradations; ablations support both preference-learning stages.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires agents to acquire visual evidence and integrate partial observations into coherent three-dimensional representations. We introduce SpatialScout-V2, which extends SpatialScout's active mapping task from simulation to real residential scenes through three advances: real visual observations, preservation of original scene content, and interactive exploration of recorded views. Built from 100 homes in Realsee3D, the benchmark covers 3,171 target objects across 29 categories. Given a fixed target inventory, agents autonomously select recorded viewpoints and viewing directions, integrate calibrated RGB observations, and iteratively estimate and revise object centers within a fixed interaction budget. We evaluate the localization accuracy and completeness of object-center maps using mean IoU, IoU-threshold hit rates, and target coverage. Evaluating seven frontier vision-language models (VLMs), we find that six achieve an all-target mean IoU below 20\%. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches only 22.52\%, with just 18.36\% of targets exceeding an IoU of 0.5. Further analysis shows that broad submission coverage can coexist with limited localization accuracy, while target omissions further reduce overall scores. These results highlight substantial challenges in constructing accurate and complete object-center maps through active exploration of real scenes.
authors: Zhaoxi Zhang, Hao Liang, Linxuan Wu, Yiming Xu, Yifu Yuan, Kun Liang, Chenming Tang, Meiyi Qiang, Wentao Zhang, Weikang Li, Yunfang Wu

Across seven frontier VLMs, six score below 20% all-target mean IoU; the best model reaches 22.52% mean IoU, with 18.36% of targets above IoU 0.5.

papers.abstract: Multi-view vision-language-action (VLA) models still face challenges in spatial generalization, particularly under changes in camera viewpoints and robot initial states. These models typically receive action supervision only in the robot base frame, requiring them to implicitly learn the spatial correspondence between observations from each view and base-frame actions. We propose One View, One Action (OVOA-VLA), which learns to predict actions in each view's camera frame, allowing the same physical motion to provide diverse, observation-aligned supervision across views. OVOA-VLA jointly trains a base-frame expert and view-specific action experts, whose robot-state inputs and action targets are expressed in their respective camera frames. Two complementary directed attention graphs model both directions of interaction between the base and view-specific experts, jointly leveraging view-specific action supervision to improve base-frame prediction. Cross Graph Consistency further encourages agreement between the two graphs' base-frame predictions for the same sample. With the same multi-view inputs, the model supports both full and base-only inference. Experiments across multiple simulation benchmarks demonstrate improved manipulation performance and robustness to camera-viewpoint and robot-initialization perturbations. Full and base-only inference achieve average success rates of 88.1% and 85.7% on LIBERO-Plus, respectively. In real-world evaluations, base-only inference raises the average success rates from $\pi_{0.5}$'s 28.3% to 58.3% across three tasks under spatial distribution shifts.
authors: Jinxi Liu, Ruifeng Zhai, Hao Liu, Guangrun Wang
bullets: Addresses viewpoint and robot-initialization shifts in multi-view vision-language-action models.
Predicts actions in each camera frame, providing observation-aligned supervision for the same physical motion.
Jointly trains a base-frame expert and view-specific experts with two directed attention graphs.
Uses Cross Graph Consistency to align the graphs’ base-frame predictions.
Achieves 88.1% full-inference and 85.7% base-only success on LIBERO-Plus; real-world base-only success reaches 58.3% under spatial shifts.
