papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single framework. However, prevailing approaches often separate their visual representations or backbone computation to accommodate the different requirements of these two tasks, which limits the degree of unification. In this paper, we present HiUni, which revisits this design choice and explores whether a pretrained vision language model can be directly extended into a unified model with extensive parameter sharing. Specifically, HiUni reuses the same language-aligned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both capabilities, while confining task-specific computation to the output side. Yet such a design introduces two key challenges. Generation in pixel space is difficult to optimize, and semantic abstraction in pretrained ViT discards fine spatial details required for synthesis. To address these challenges, HiUni introduces a \emph{Pixel Diffusion Head} tailored to direct pixel-space optimization and a lightweight \emph{HiGate} pathway that provides fine-grained spatial details near the output stage. Extensive experiments show that HiUni achieves a similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM while attaining competitive performance on image generation and editing. Controlled comparisons and analyses further demonstrate that a single dense backbone can effectively support both capabilities without task-specific backbone computation, highlighting a simpler path toward unified multimodal modeling.
authors: Jiahao Hu, Jingdong Du, Yichen Zhang, Yi Song, Zhenyu Zhang, Jiaxin Niu, Ruihang Li, Xiangzhao Hao, Yiqian Zhang, Yong Huang, Zefeng Zhang, Zheyuan Gu, Shuohuan Wang
bullets: Targets the fragmented architectures commonly used for multimodal understanding and generation.
Reuses the same language-aligned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both tasks, with specialization confined to the output side.
Introduces a Pixel Diffusion Head for direct pixel-space generation and a HiGate pathway to restore fine spatial details lost by semantic visual representations.
Maintains a similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM while achieving competitive image generation and editing performance.
Experiments indicate that one shared dense backbone can support both capabilities without task-specific backbone computation.

papers.abstract: A corridor, its mirror reflection, and its image on a display can look identical, yet their physical surfaces lie at different depths. We test whether bounded camera motions distinguish these explanations. Intervene3D takes an image and an initial geometry estimate, predicts the view under each hypothesis and candidate motion, and selects a motion by maximin separability. It reports the mechanism and first physical surface only if the available motions separate the hypotheses still in contention. Otherwise it abstains. An adequacy test also rejects observations that no hypothesis explains. On a matched synthetic benchmark with exact landmarks, disabling abstention gives confident answers on 76.4% of unresolvable scenes. With abstention, none receives a confident answer under exact or noisy landmarks. At 100% accuracy on answered scenes, maximin selection answers 61.0% of scenes and summed selection 43.1%. The adequacy test lowers wrong answers on strongly curved mirror scenes from 56.8% to 12.4%. Real display experiments compare two hypotheses using one frozen depth-network estimate. The second image supplies photometric evidence and is never passed through the depth network. One executed motion reduces the pooled median surface error of twelve networks by 31.5%. These networks have larger error inside the annotated panel than outside on 33.4% of illusion-benchmark images. They place the first physical surface behind the glass on 36.9% of Mirror3D frames.
authors: Reshad Ul Karim, Abrar Samin, Sammam Mahdi, Syeda Maliha Tabassum, Md Rashad Al Hasan Rony
bullets: Visual observations can be identical for real corridors, mirror reflections, and displays despite different physical surface depths.
The system predicts views under competing hypotheses and candidate motions, choosing the motion that maximizes worst-case separability.
It reports a mechanism and first physical surface only when the available motion distinguishes the remaining hypotheses; an adequacy test rejects unexplained observations.
On synthetic scenes, maximin selection answered 61.0% with 100% accuracy, while disabling abstention produced confident answers for 76.4% of unresolvable scenes.
In real display experiments, one motion reduced pooled median surface error by 31.5% across twelve depth networks; substantial errors remained on illusion images.

papers.selection_reason: Active camera-motion reasoning for disambiguating 3D physical geometry; fits spatial intelligence and 3D vision.
papers.title: Less Than Meets the Eye: Action-Set Identifiability and Principled Abstention for 3D Physical Geometry
papers.tldr: Intervene3D uses targeted camera motion and principled abstention to distinguish ambiguous 3D physical explanations, achieving perfect accuracy on answered synthetic scenes while avoiding confident answers when scenes are unresolvable.

papers.abstract: Audio LLMs can know when a queried sound occurs but fail to say it. We find a few attention heads that track the queried sound: they shift when the query changes, follow the sound when it moves, and removing or blocking them often hurts the model's timestamps. Yet the answer does not express what they track. Intervals read directly from these heads outperform the model's original answer and recover events that its timestamps miss. To bring this timing into the answer, we introduce head-guided decoding, which needs no training. It keeps the model's decision on whether the sound is present and rescores its candidate timestamps with a prior from these heads. Heads selected on development data transfer unchanged to new recordings and free-text queries, where head-guided decoding improves the timestamps of three audio LLMs, scores above their head readout on every benchmark, and, in most settings, outperforms random-head guidance. On recordings released after the models were trained, head-guided decoding raises mIoU from 0.07-0.36 to 0.48-0.56. These results suggest that poor temporal answers in audio LLMs partly reflect a failure to say rather than to hear, and that the model's own attention can close part of this gap.
authors: Jongbhin Woo, Jaewook Jeong, Joon Son Chung
bullets: The identified attention heads shift with the queried sound and follow it as it moves, while disrupting them often harms timestamp accuracy.
Intervals read directly from these heads recover events missed by the model’s original timestamps and outperform its answer.
Head-guided decoding preserves the model’s sound-presence decision and rescores candidate timestamps using attention-derived priors.
Heads selected on development data transfer to new recordings and free-text queries, improving timestamps across three audio LLMs.
On post-training recordings, mIoU increases from 0.07–0.36 to 0.48–0.56.

papers.selection_reason: Audio LLM attention-head analysis and head-guided decoding for temporal event timing; relevant to multimodal LLM behavior and decoding.
papers.title: When Sounds Turn Heads: Recovering Event Timing That Audio LLMs Fail to Say
papers.tldr: Audio LLMs may detect when a sound occurs but fail to verbalize its timing; using a few sound-tracking attention heads enables training-free timestamp correction.

papers.abstract: Flat color-block drafts specify layout and regional color while leaving interior detail unspecified, yet pretrained flow-based generators can preserve their flat appearance even under photorealistic prompts. We trace this behavior to a cross-scale mechanism linking fine pixel variation to regional means in variational autoencoder (VAE) latent space. Flattening photo regions systematically shifts their latent means, with offsets concentrated along a shared channel direction within each backbone. Controlled field exchanges in FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image establish the effect of this displacement on texture generation: adding the photo-derived regional mean field to a flat latent restores texture, whereas adding its complementary field alone largely preserves flatness. A second-order encoding expansion explains how encoder curvature can convert zero-mean perturbations into mean shifts. An analytically solvable conditional Gaussian flow shows how regional noise averaging enables near-unit endpoint sensitivity at high signal-to-noise ratios. This mechanism motivates training-free rendering through pixel dither before encoding, mean-field scaling, and early boundary holding. Paired low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with draft conditioning improves content recovery and produces photo-like regional means under the standard velocity objective. Explicit regional mean guidance remains effective after adaptation, continuously controlling texture and improving color fidelity. These findings connect encoding shifts to persistent generation behavior and support interventions evaluated for texture, spatial fidelity, and semantic recovery.
authors: Zihan Gu, Jiangcan Jia, Hua Zhang, Lulu Zhao
bullets: Flattening image regions changes their latent means along backbone-specific channel directions, linking fine detail to regional statistics.
Controlled latent-field swaps in FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image show that restoring photo-derived regional means restores texture, while complementary fields mostly preserve flatness.
A second-order encoder analysis and a conditional Gaussian-flow model explain how zero-mean detail and regional averaging can produce persistent mean shifts and high endpoint sensitivity.
Training-free interventions—pixel dithering, mean-field scaling, and early boundary holding—enable texture control without retraining.
Draft-conditioned LoRA improves content recovery and photo-like regional means; explicit regional mean guidance remains effective and improves texture and color fidelity.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Regional means connect encoding, trajectory retention, and rendering control. papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the mechanism of texture generation in flow-based models, revealing how regional mean latents govern spatial fidelity, which is relevant to geometry-aware generation.
papers.title: Why Flat Drafts Stay Flat: Region-Mean Latents Govern Texture in Flow-Based Image Generation
papers.tldr: Regional mean shifts in VAE latents largely determine whether flat drafts remain textureless or recover photorealistic detail in flow-based image generators.

papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in qualitative spatial reasoning, but remain limited in quantitative spatial reasoning. Current work leverages the VLM agent to invoke external vision tools to perform computation. However, these methods usually bind each functional requirement to a single predefined vision specialist, implicitly resulting in fixed and rigid tool pipelines. In practice, addressing diverse spatial scenarios and tasks demands a broader diversity in pipeline orchestration and vision specialist selection to achieve robust spatial reasoning. However, such diversity leads to a combinatorial execution space, making it challenging for the agent to orchestrate the optimal pipelines and specialists for different scenarios. In this work, we propose SpatialMem, a memory framework that enables a VLM agent to accumulate tool-use experience and leverage that memory to orchestrate vision specialists to solve the spatial reasoning problem. SpatialMem builds a two-level memory structure, with task memory capturing tool orchestration and scene memory capturing tool selection. It further introduces a dual-state trajectory optimization process to preserve successful tool experiences and refine suboptimal ones. Moreover, existing spatial reasoning benchmarks suffer from quality issues and limited coverage of scene types and tasks. To address these gap, we propose MetricBench, a benchmark covering both indoor and outdoor scenes and three quantitative spatial reasoning tasks. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on MetricBench, Q-Spatial, and SpatilRGPT-Bench, outperforming best VLM baselines by 32% on MetricBench. Additionally, the memory design yields a 9.1% absolute gain over a memory-free agent on MetricBench.
authors: Zinan Zheng, Nuo Chen, Jia Li
bullets: Targets VLMs’ limitations in quantitative, rather than qualitative, spatial reasoning.
Uses task memory for tool orchestration and scene memory for selecting vision specialists.
Applies dual-state trajectory optimization to retain successful tool-use experiences and refine weaker ones.
Introduces MetricBench, covering indoor and outdoor scenes across three quantitative spatial reasoning tasks.
Reports state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks, with a 32% improvement over the best VLM baseline on MetricBench and a 9.1-point gain over a memory-free agent.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes SpatialMem, a hierarchical memory framework for VLMs to perform quantitative spatial reasoning by accumulating tool-use experience and orchestrating vision specialists.
papers.title: SpatialMem: Building Quantitative Spatial Reasoning Agents with Hierarchical Memory
papers.tldr: SpatialMem equips VLM agents with hierarchical memory to learn tool orchestration and selection for more robust quantitative spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised foundation models are often said to need fewer labels than supervised training. We test this on a forestry task: classifying 20 tree species classes in 0.2 m aerial images from the TreeSatAI dataset. We compare a frozen DINOv3 model pretrained on 493 million satellite images, with only a linear classifier trained on top, against an ImageNet ResNet-50 that is fine-tuned end to end. On the official split, fine-tuning wins clearly (macro F1 0.764 vs. 0.685). However, 28.8% of the official test patches overlap a training or validation patch, and copying the label of the nearest such patch is correct for 83.6% of them. We therefore build a spatial split that holds out whole 2 km squares with a 200 m buffer. On this split the comparison becomes inconclusive (0.648 vs. 0.640, paired 95% CI of the difference [-0.054, 0.016]), and the learning curves of the two models overlap at every label budget from 343 to 33,126 training patches. On the five rarest classes, the frozen model achieves a higher mean F1 (0.566 vs. 0.445), although the confidence interval for this difference includes zero ([-0.05, 0.23]). Diagnostics show that the frozen features mainly miss differences between closely related species, such as the two native oaks. Choosing the input size and layer on validation data (224 px, block 16) raises the frozen model to 0.662 on the spatial split. A comparison that looks decisive on the official split is thus inconclusive under geographically separated evaluation. We release the spatial split and our code.
bullets: Studies 20-class tree-species mapping in 0.2 m aerial imagery from TreeSatAI.
Compares a frozen DINOv3 encoder with a linear classifier against end-to-end fine-tuned ImageNet ResNet-50s.
On the official split, fine-tuning scores higher, but substantial patch overlap may inflate performance.
On a spatial split with held-out 2 km squares and buffers, performance is statistically inconclusive and learning curves overlap across label budgets.
Frozen features perform better on the rarest classes but mainly confuse closely related species; validation-based input/layer selection improves them.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Official vs. spatial evaluation on TreeSatAI. (a) In the official split, test patches lie between training patches, and many overlap one (filled squares). The same 2.4 km window is shown in both maps; each square is one 60.8 m patch. (b) Our split assigns whole 2 km squares to training, validation or test, and drops patches within 200 m of a square with another role. (c) Over all 20 classes, the clear lead of the fine-tuned ResNet-50 on the official split becomes inconclusive on the spatial split. (d) On the five rarest classes, the fine-tuned model loses much more than the frozen DINOv3 model; the remaining difference on the spatial split has a confidence interval that includes zero. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals from resampling whole 2 km squares.

papers.selection_reason: Empirically compares frozen foundation model features against fine-tuned CNNs for tree species mapping, highlighting the efficiency and data leakage issues in current evaluation splits.
papers.title: Does It Depend on the Split? Frozen Satellite Features vs. Fine-Tuned CNNs for Tree Species Mapping
papers.tldr: Fine-tuned CNNs outperform frozen satellite features on the official split, but geographically separated evaluation makes the difference inconclusive and favors frozen features for rare species.

papers.abstract: Although memory-augmented architectures have expanded the ability of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to process long videos, existing retrieval processes still largely rely on global semantic matching and lack state-driven temporal control, often returning fragmented or redundant evidence and failing to maintain a coherent evidence chain. To address this challenge, we propose EvoMem, a time-aware long-video memory agent guided by self-evolving retrieval skills. EvoMem constructs a hierarchical time-indexed memory, where different types of evidence are aligned onto a unified video timeline; during retrieval, temporal cues from acquired evidence are further converted into explicit signals that constrain subsequent memory access. To address recurring procedural errors in long-video question answering, such as unclear retrieval targets, improper memory access paths, or premature stopping, EvoMem introduces retrieval skills to provide process-level guidance, enabling the agent to dynamically adjust retrieval content, memory operations, and target temporal ranges according to the current evidence state, while deciding when to stop. Furthermore, inspired by reinforcement learning, we formulate skill evolution as a reward-guided policy improvement process. Each candidate skill is treated as an external policy patch, and rewards are assigned according to answer-correctness state transitions on the validation set. In this way, effective skills are accepted and low-quality skills are rejected without updating model parameters. Experiments on four long-video question answering benchmarks show that EvoMem significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average accuracy of 60.1% and an average improvement of 8.6 percentage points over the previous best methods, demonstrating its effectiveness for long-video reasoning.
authors: Yutong Guan, Meixing Shi, Haoran Sun, Bing Sun, Yuxiang Cai, Yankai Jiang
bullets: Builds a hierarchical, time-indexed memory that aligns diverse evidence along a unified video timeline.
Uses temporal cues from retrieved evidence to constrain and guide subsequent memory access.
Introduces retrieval skills that adapt search targets, memory operations, temporal ranges, and stopping decisions based on the current evidence state.
Evolves skills through reward-guided policy improvement, accepting useful policy patches without updating model parameters.
Across four benchmarks, achieves 60.1% average accuracy and an 8.6-point average gain over prior best methods.

Figure 1: Motivating example of EvoMem. (a) Base VLMs suffer from redundant frames and limited context. (b) HippoMM’s textcentric semantic memory may miss fine-grained visual evidence. (c) WorldMM lacks explicit temporal control for maintaining evidence chains. (d) Skill-free retrieval lacks guidance on what to seek, where to search, and when to stop. (e) EvoMem uses self-evolving skills for time-aware memory retrieval and coherent long-video reasoning.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces EvoMem, a memory agent for long-video reasoning that uses self-evolving retrieval skills guided by RL, addressing procedural errors in long-context video understanding.
papers.title: EvoMem: Self-Evolving Skills for Time-Aware Long Video Memory Agents
papers.tldr: EvoMem improves long-video question answering by using time-aware memory retrieval and self-evolving skills to maintain coherent evidence chains.

papers.abstract: Micro-Doppler radar enables contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR), but deployment robustness remains underexplored. We compared full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using subject-disjoint in-distribution cross-validation and few-shot cross-age, cross-orientation, and cross-dataset transfer. Full fine-tuning suffered negative cross-dataset transfer, while frozen features under-adapted on cross-orientation. Only PEFT avoided both failures. We paired DINOv3 with all-layer principal-singular-direction adaptation (PiSSA), to our knowledge the first application of a self-supervised image foundation backbone to radar micro-Doppler HAR. DINOv3-PiSSA ranked first among PEFT methods in every evaluated setting. Under our protocol, its Small variant matched the in-distribution accuracy of the prior Base-size PEFT state of the art using 4.5x fewer total parameters, with only 3% trainable. It surpassed a size-matched variant of that baseline in every evaluated setting, with transfer gains increasing with shift severity: 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Ablations attributed improvements to both pretraining and adapter recipe, with the pretraining contributing most under compound shift. Code and protocol are available at https://github.com/KeryanChelouche/udoppler-ssl.
authors: Keryan Chelouche (ETIS UMR 8051, CY Cergy Paris Universit\'e, ENSEA, CNRS, Cergy, France, Fondation L\'eonie Chaptal, Sarcelles, France), Petr Dobias (ETIS UMR 8051, CY Cergy Paris Universit\'e, ENSEA, CNRS, Cergy, France), Nistor Grozavu (ETIS UMR 8051, CY Cergy Paris Universit\'e, ENSEA, CNRS, Cergy, France), Olivier Romain (ETIS UMR 8051, CY Cergy Paris Universit\'e, ENSEA, CNRS, Cergy, France)
bullets: The study evaluates full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and PEFT under in-distribution and few-shot distribution-shift settings.
Full fine-tuning fails under cross-dataset transfer, while frozen features under-adapt to cross-orientation shifts; PEFT avoids both issues.
DINOv3-PiSSA is presented as the first use of a self-supervised image foundation backbone for radar micro-Doppler HAR.
Its Small variant matches prior Base-size PEFT in-distribution accuracy with 4.5× fewer total parameters and only 3% trainable.
It ranks first among evaluated PEFT methods, with transfer gains of 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points as shift severity increases.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that parameter-efficient fine-tuning of self-supervised vision backbones (DINOv3) effectively handles distribution shifts in radar micro-Doppler human activity recognition, contributing to test-time adaptation and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Self-supervised Vision Backbones Survives Distribution Shift in Radar Micro-Doppler HAR
papers.tldr: Parameter-efficient adaptation with DINOv3-PiSSA improves robustness of radar micro-Doppler HAR under age, orientation, and dataset shifts while using far fewer trainable parameters.

papers.abstract: Traffic scenario understanding requires combining fine-grained visual evidence with spatial and temporal reasoning. Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can use specialized perception tools, but effective collaboration faces two challenges: terminal rewards provide limited guidance for intermediate decisions and error recovery, while repeated planning adds unnecessary cost across similar tasks. Echoing the fast-slow dichotomy of human cognition, we propose StarTV-Agent, which combines policy learning with experience evolution to support adaptive reasoning when needed and efficient reuse of prior experience when possible. During training, Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) combines process advantages with terminal advantages, while Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL) provides validated teacher demonstrations targeting the student's weak questions. During inference, Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR) enables a fast path by selecting suitable workflows and binding task-specific arguments and resource references, while a slow ReAct-based path handles tasks without suitable workflows. We further design label-free feedback based on execution completion, workflow adoption, and cost savings to guide workflow reuse and memory updates. Across three challenging benchmarks, StarTV-Agent achieves up to 8.0% relative performance improvement, while reducing token consumption by up to 52.1%.
authors: Linjia Kang, Binhan Jiang, Juan Yang, Zhiqin Song, Xiangsen Wu, Qionglin Ren, Jiang Liu, Zhongjiang He, Hao Sun
bullets: Addresses limited guidance for intermediate decisions and the cost of repeated planning in tool-augmented VLMs.
Uses policy learning and experience evolution, including RSPO for process-aware training and WDL for weakness-targeted demonstrations.
At inference, LAWR reuses suitable workflows for a fast path, while a ReAct-based path handles novel tasks.
Label-free feedback from execution, workflow adoption, and cost savings updates workflow memory.
Across three benchmarks, reports up to 8.0% relative improvement and up to 52.1% lower token consumption.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of StarTV-Agent. (B) Policy Learning: RSPO combines role-sensitive process and terminal advantages, while WDL provides targeted teacher demonstrations for weak tasks. (C) Inference with Experience Evolution: The agent follows a fast path by reusing suitable parameterized workflows or a slow ReAct-based path for adaptive reasoning. Label-free execution feedback guides workflow reuse and memory updates.

papers.selection_reason: Tool-augmented VLM agent for traffic scenario understanding with spatial and temporal reasoning and workflow reuse, relevant to multimodal foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Generalist Meets Specialists: An Evolving Multimodal Agent with Persistent Tool Orchestration for Traffic Scenario Understanding
papers.tldr: StarTV-Agent improves traffic scenario understanding by combining adaptive tool-based reasoning with persistent workflow reuse, boosting performance while reducing token usage.

papers.abstract: Recognizing when a requested spatial condition holds in streaming video can require maintaining and updating spatial knowledge across changing viewpoints. We study this capability through proactive spatial reasoning, where a model receives a query in advance and determines whether and when to respond as the stream unfolds. We introduce ProSpace-Bench, comprising nine tasks across object, camera, and scene reasoning, and ProSpace-Train for supervised training. To support spatial decisions, we propose ProSpace-VLM, which injects explicit geometric encodings estimated causally from incoming frames into intermediate VLM layers, using the existing KV cache as spatial memory and spatial token selection for efficient streaming. Experiments reveal a substantial gap between VLMs and humans, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines. Analyses examine how ProSpace-VLM represents previously observed spatial information across changing viewpoints.
authors: Junyoung Hong, Minsu Kim, Jaehyun Kim, Jeonghwan Cho, Jiwoo Lee, Seon Joo Kim
bullets: Studies proactive spatial reasoning: answering whether and when a queried spatial condition becomes true as video unfolds.
Introduces ProSpace-Bench with nine object-, camera-, and scene-level reasoning tasks, plus ProSpace-Train for supervised learning.
Injects causal geometric encodings into intermediate VLM layers, uses the KV cache as spatial memory, and selects spatial tokens for efficient streaming.
Experiments show a substantial VLM–human gap, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines.
Analyzes how the model retains previously observed spatial information across viewpoint changes.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Task overview of ProSpace-Bench. Bounding boxes mark target objects in object-level tasks. The blue needle in Ego Rotation indicates the camera’s viewing direction; the star in Origin Return and the cylinder in Visual Homing mark the starting position.

Figure 3. Architecture of ProSpace-VLM. A causal geometry encoder estimates 3D point maps and camera poses from incoming frames. The resulting geometric encodings are injected into visual tokens. papers.abstract: Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off. Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough. An agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUNE improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks and achieves competitive results against existing medical VLMs and agents.
authors: Qiming Huang, Hanze Dong, Jipeng Zhang, Mike Zheng Shou, Xinxing Xu, Furu Wei
bullets: Introduces Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four medical image types with answer-relevant masks and multiple renderings.
Shows that different presentations of the same mask can substantially alter model behavior.
Finds that masks can reveal missed diagnostic evidence but also induce incorrect associations, even when the mask is correct.
Introduces TUNE, which manages evidence acquisition, presentation, and answer updates.
TUNE improves mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points for a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone across three public medical VQA benchmarks, and by 9.1 points over direct tool use across seven benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Spurious correlations can give image predictors high in-distribution accuracy but poor generalization under distribution shift. We introduce $\textbf{Rank2Replace}$, which transfers knowledge of task-relevant evidence from pretrained vision--language models (VLMs) to small predictors through training-time augmentation for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. The VLM ranks object-centric slots by task relevance and guides rank-dependent replacement with same-rank slot embeddings from another image. This augmentation retains the original image's label, encouraging reliance on preserved task evidence as incidental cues change, and supports combination with existing OOD methods. Across four datasets and six splits under shared frozen slot embeddings, the default cross-entropy configuration reaches macro-averaged average-group and worst-group accuracies of $80.43\%$ and $65.28\%$ without environment labels or dataset-specific replacement tuning. Slot corruption improves both macro-averaged metrics for all fourteen OOD training methods. Combining it with slot ranking and IRM reaches $81.96\%$ and $72.68\%$. Controlled ablations support the ranking and replacement design, with gains across five ranking VLMs and six extractor--predictor combinations. Permutation-invariant predictors further improve both macro-averaged metrics over their unaugmented counterparts while using VLM guidance only during training for efficient inference.
authors: Bo-Han Feng, Keng-Te Liao, Shou-De Lin
bullets: A VLM ranks object-centric slots by task relevance, then replaces slots with same-rank slots from another image.
The method preserves the source label while changing incidental visual cues, encouraging predictors to use task-relevant evidence.
It works without environment labels or dataset-specific replacement tuning and can combine with existing OOD methods.
Across four datasets and six splits, the default setup achieves 80.43% macro average-group and 65.28% macro worst-group accuracy; combining ranking with IRM reaches 81.96% and 72.68%.
Benefits are observed across 14 OOD methods, five ranking VLMs, and six extractor–predictor combinations; VLM guidance is needed only during training.

papers.abstract: Preference training is the standard recipe for reducing object hallucination in vision-language models, and each new method reports a lower CHAIR score. We ask what that reduction consists of. Every trained system is compared with its base model's caption truncated to the same object recall, which removes the part of the gain that comes from saying less; the remainder is compared with what a deliberately weak, frozen, eleven-feature post-hoc probe fitted on 500 annotated images can reproduce. All criteria were specified in the analysis code and frozen before the outputs they judge existed. For eight public methods on LLaVA-1.5-7B, the probe reproduces at least two thirds of what training removes beyond saying less for 7 of 8 methods on COCO, 8 of 8 on AMBER and 6 of 8 on Object HalBench, with RLAIF-V the consistent exception; a later public method released for both LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL (SENTINEL) meets the same bar on both. On our own DPO checkpoints the accounting holds on Qwen2.5-VL but fails on InternVL2.5 on COCO (2 of 4 training designs). At matched recall, the base model plus the probe beats truncation for 8 of 9 LLaVA-1.5 systems on COCO and 9 of 9 on AMBER, on the two newer backbones, and when realized as actual sentence deletion. The same measure prices training signals: DPO on the model's own samples labelled by the probe or by an object-level CLIP score recovers 0.70 and 0.87 of the beyond-brevity gain of ground-truth-labelled DPO on Qwen2.5-VL (the probe 0.73 on InternVL2.5), both beat length-matched random labels, and CLIP labels buy more than probe labels on COCO. Human judgements show that the sentences the probe deletes are wrong more often than those truncation would delete; a human check of the CHAIR evaluator's precision falls below our pre-set bar, which we report as a limitation.
bullets: The study separates CHAIR improvements into reduced verbosity versus genuine hallucination reduction by matching object recall with truncated base-model captions.
A frozen, 11-feature probe trained on 500 annotated images reproduces at least two thirds of beyond-brevity gains for most evaluated methods, with RLAIF-V as the main exception.
At matched recall, the base model plus probe generally outperforms truncation across LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2.5, COCO, and AMBER evaluations.
Probe- or CLIP-based preference labels recover substantial portions of ground-truth-labelled DPO gains, while outperforming random labels; CLIP labels perform better on COCO.
Human checks support the probe’s deletions, but also identify insufficient precision in the CHAIR evaluator as a limitation.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates 'cheap pruning' techniques in vision-language models (VLMs) to reduce object hallucinations, directly addressing efficiency (token pruning) and VLM robustness.
papers.title: What Does Anti-Hallucination Training Buy? Saying Less, Cheap Pruning, and the Rest
papers.tldr: Much of anti-hallucination training’s apparent benefit comes from shorter captions and can be replicated by a cheap post-hoc probe, though some methods and backbones retain gains beyond brevity.

papers.abstract: Multimodal safety guards increasingly generate rationales alongside safety predictions, yet whether these rationales are reliable remains largely unexplored. We systematically study *rationale hallucination* from two perspectives: visual rationale hallucination, where rationales contain unsupported visual facts, and safety attribution hallucination, where grounded content is assigned an incorrect safety interpretation. Across rationale-generation methods, multiple vision-language backbones, and safety datasets, we find that rationale hallucination is widespread and does not consistently diminish with higher classification accuracy or increased model scale. Further analysis of the Think-with-Image paradigm shows that hallucination is concentrated in fine-grained attributes and relations, while visual tools are often invoked infrequently or without sufficient spatial focus. Based on these findings, we propose *Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning* (TCG-RL), which rewards tool use only when it improves rationale grounding over a tool-free reference. TCG-RL substantially reduces rationale hallucination while maintaining competitive safety prediction performance. By revealing the gap between prediction correctness and rationale reliability, our study motivates a shift in multimodal safety guarding from outcome-only evaluation toward safety decisions that are both accurate and verifiably grounded.
authors: Yingshuo Wang, Weixiang Zhao, Guancheng Li, Jiahe Guo, Yu Zhang, Yanyan Zhao
bullets: Rationale hallucination includes unsupported visual facts and incorrect safety interpretations of grounded content.
Hallucination remains common across generation methods, vision-language backbones, and safety datasets, even with higher classification accuracy or model scale.
Fine-grained attributes and relations are especially problematic; visual tools are often underused or lack sufficient spatial focus.
Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning (TCG-RL) rewards tool use only when it improves grounding over a tool-free reference.
The findings support evaluating safety guards for both prediction accuracy and verifiable rationale grounding.

papers.title: When Safety Rationales Hallucinate: Diagnosing and Grounding Multimodal Safety Guards
papers.tldr: Multimodal safety guards can produce accurate predictions with hallucinated rationales, but contrastive reinforcement learning that rewards useful tool grounding substantially improves rationale reliability without sacrificing safety performance.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the stage in which Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) advance their capability to reason over video. However, the VideoLLM also learns to answer from textual regularities of its training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. The regularities behind the shortcut are hard to define at the data level, and the shortcut forms regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. The shortcut is hidden behind a rise in accuracy within the training distribution, yet it is not required for the rise and even costs SFT the gain the video offers under distribution shift. We therefore propose Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which intervenes on the fine-tuning update where the shortcut is written rather than on the data. VETO calibrates the subspace that the text alone occupies in the activations of the base model and projects the update onto its orthogonal complement. The VideoLLM is thus left to ground its answer in the full input, with the shortcut suppressed as it forms and never defined. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves the gain of SFT on the training distribution and suppresses the shortcut. On six benchmarks under shift it gains more than SFT and answers from the full input rather than the shortcut. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/VETO.
authors: Youngwoo Shin, Jongsuk Kim, Junmo Kim
bullets: SFT can make VideoLLMs rely on textual regularities instead of video evidence, even when in-distribution accuracy improves.
VETO intervenes in the fine-tuning update rather than defining or filtering shortcut-related data.
It identifies the subspace occupied by text-only inputs and projects updates onto its orthogonal complement.
Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves in-distribution SFT gains and improves performance on six shifted-distribution benchmarks.
The method is designed to ground answers in the full video-text input, though its scope is evaluated on the reported models and benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Pipeline of VETO. Calibration, once per VideoLLM, collects the activations of the textonly input at every layer and takes the leading directions of their spectrum as the shortcut subspace. papers.abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.
authors: Yajie Qi, Wei Wei, Lin Li, Lijun Zhang, Jianye Hao
bullets: Addresses sparse rewards, long horizons, and inconsistent goals from prompt-only language-model guidance.
Introduces CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset built from Craftax-Classic interaction trajectories.
Uses offline KLTDPO fine-tuning to align the VLM with goal preferences, followed by online goal-guided RL.
The method collects diamonds earlier and achieves the highest score and reward in experiments.
It attains the highest success rates on most achievements; results are scoped to Craftax-Classic.

papers.abstract: 3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6\% on ScanRefer and 70.4\% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. The code and models are available at https://github.com/liujia99/DACA
authors: Jiaming Liu, Linghe Kong, Guixu Zhang, Huaxi Huang
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and poor failure recovery in pipeline-style 3D visual grounding agents.
Uses a semantic anchor for optical-flow tracking and VLM-based local verification.
Uses a geometric anchor for voxelization and multi-keypoint projection to reason over 3D space.
The two anchors exchange information in a closed-loop tool-calling process to select subsequent perception-action steps.
Achieves 73.6% Acc@0.25 on ScanRefer and 70.4% overall accuracy on Nr3D in zero-shot evaluation.

papers.abstract: DeepStack-style vision-language models feed visual tokens to the language model at its input, and again at deeper layers. We call these the main entry and the later entries. What do the later entries add when the model already has the image? We give the entries versions that differ in one object's color and see which one the answer follows. On photographs, the original DeepStack follows the later entries, while Qwen3-VL-8B/32B follow the main entry. Does weakening the main entry give the later features more influence? On synthetic images, we keep this conflict and reduce color saturation at the main entry only. The unchanged later features gain a stronger effect on the relative scores of the two colors, in all four models, including Granite Vision. This holds even under mild desaturation, when accuracy without the conflict stays at 100%. To test whether later features can also correct errors, we degrade both entries and restore only the later ones. The same blur costs both Qwen models 50 percentage points of accuracy on stripe orientation. The 32B model recovers 48 points and the 8B model only 8. Accuracy with one clean entry predicted which entry each model can lose, and five of six tested predictions held on new GQA attribute questions. With the other entry zeroed, Qwen3-VL-8B loses only 0.3 points on its main entry alone, and DeepStack at most 3.45 points on either entry alone. In split inference on these questions, DeepStack can then send only its main-entry features at higher precision. This takes 49% fewer bytes than all entries at a shared precision, at similar accuracy.
authors: Yucheng Du, Yi Nian, Ruixue Lian, Yue Zhao, Xiyang Hu
bullets: The study compares conflicting object-color information placed in the main input entry versus later-layer entries.
On photographs, DeepStack follows later entries, whereas Qwen3-VL-8B/32B follows the main entry.
Reducing saturation only at the main entry increases the influence of unchanged later features across four models, even when normal accuracy remains 100%.
When both entries are blurred and only later features are restored, Qwen3-VL-32B recovers 48 of 50 accuracy points, while the 8B model recovers 8.
Entry-specific influence predictions generalize to most tested GQA attribute questions, enabling DeepStack split inference with 49% fewer bytes at similar accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Interprets visual token entry roles in DeepStack-style VLMs and proposes efficient split inference; fits MLLM analysis.
papers.title: Interpreting DeepStack-Style Vision-Language Models: Do Input or Deeper-Layer Visual Tokens Drive Answers?
papers.tldr: DeepStack-style models do not consistently rely on deeper visual tokens: their influence depends on the model and the quality of the main visual entry.

papers.abstract: Multimodal image fusion traditionally generates a single fused image from paired observations at a specific viewpoint, limiting comprehensive scene perception and adaptability to diverse perceptual objectives. To overcome these limitations, we present LIFT, a novel framework for our proposed language-controlled 3D image fusion (L3D-IF) paradigm that extends multimodal image fusion from 2D images to free-viewpoint 3D scenes, enabling language-guided fusion tailored to diverse perceptual objectives. First, LIFT formulates Semantic Modality Binding (SMB), which interprets language instructions to identify semantic targets and their associated modality preferences and grounds these targets in corresponding regions of a shared Gaussian scene, establishing persistent semantic-to-spatial correspondences for consistent fusion control across viewpoints. Second, Language-Conditioned Gaussian Appearance (LCGA) is developed to achieve scene-wide multimodal appearance modeling by combining adaptive multimodal blending with language- and viewpoint-conditioned appearance refinement, enabling spatially adaptive realization of diverse fusion appearances while preserving source fidelity at pure-modality endpoints. Finally, we construct a Multi-View Language-Supervision (MVLS) dataset that associates language instructions and calibrated viewpoints with modulated fused images, providing effective supervision for learning instruction-dependent fusion from finite multi-view observations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LIFT achieves coherent multimodal fusion across continuous viewpoints, accurate semantic target localization, and consistent regional fusion control under diverse language instructions.

papers.abstract: We propose VC-VQA, a large-scale benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning, aiming to systematically evaluate the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition and complex multi-stage reasoning. Unlike existing benchmarks that primarily treat visual information as entity recognition and rely on text-based external knowledge, VC-VQA explicitly models the role of visual information by considering both its source (internal vs. external images) and stage of involvement (pre-retrieval vs. post-retrieval). Specifically, VC-VQA requires models to retrieve external visual evidence, identify visual clues before retrieval, and localize, verify, or match retrieved knowledge against the internal image. We further construct a controlled multimodal knowledge base with traceable textual and visual evidence for each sample. We evaluate 21 representative MLLMs under four settings: no external knowledge, with provided evidence, knowledge base retrieval, and open-web search. Experimental results lead to three key findings: current models still struggle with vision-centric knowledge reasoning; fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition remains the primary bottleneck; and agentic retrieval highlights the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration. Overall, VC-VQA provides a more challenging benchmark for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in MLLMs. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/CASIA-IVA-Lab/VC-VQA.
authors: Jiatong Ma, Yuchen Liu, Longteng Guo, Yichen Yuan, Yuze Wu, Dongze Hao, Ru Zhen, Yanhao Zhang, Haonan Lu, Jing Liu
bullets: Models must use visual evidence both before and after knowledge retrieval, including identifying clues, retrieving images, and localizing or verifying matched knowledge.
The benchmark distinguishes internal versus external images and provides traceable textual and visual evidence in a controlled multimodal knowledge base.
Twenty-one MLLMs are evaluated across no-knowledge, provided-evidence, knowledge-base retrieval, and open-web search settings.
Results show that vision-centric reasoning remains difficult, with fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition as the main bottleneck.
Agentic retrieval suggests benefits from multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration.

papers.abstract: Efficient chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) requires reducing both intermediate reasoning steps and their execution cost. Latent CoT methods compress textual rationales into continuous thoughts, yet their full-precision (FP) models retain substantial storage and computation costs. Lowering numerical precision could reduce these remaining costs, yet direct quantization severely degrades reasoning accuracy, particularly with 4-bit weights and activations. Operator and perturbation analyses reveal key sensitivity and direction-dependent predictive effects of continuous-thought errors, motivating preservation of information retrieval and subsequent reasoning beyond reconstruction accuracy. We therefore introduce QL-VLM, a dynamics-aware Quantization framework for efficient Latent reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). First, Dynamics-Guided Quantization (DGQ) uses nonuniform codebooks that preserve rotary-key structure, mitigating quantization-induced distortion in vision-language information retrieval. Second, Dynamics-Preserving Distillation (DPD) aligns continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher, maintaining predictive consistency through subsequent low-precision reasoning. On ScienceQA-IMG with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM achieves 90.43% accuracy and improves baseline by 40.33%, with 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit CoT.
authors: Yanjing Li, Sheng Xu, Baochang Zhang, Xianbin Cao, Yawei Li
bullets: Targets the storage and computation costs of full-precision latent reasoning in VLMs.
Dynamics-Guided Quantization preserves rotary-key structure to reduce distortions in vision-language information retrieval.
Dynamics-Preserving Distillation aligns latent thoughts, readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher.
On ScienceQA-IMG using Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM reaches 90.43% accuracy.
Reports 16.64× fewer bit-operations and 6.40× lower measured latency than explicit chain-of-thought.

papers.abstract: An age prompt can change how a vision-language model (VLM) rates the emotion evoked by an image. Does the change predict how people of different ages rate that same image? We evaluate 17 VLMs on 900 OASIS images using young-, middle-, and older-adult prompts and estimate image-specific age differences from ratings by 822 participants. Without an age cue, models closely track average human valence (median Pearson $r=0.891$). Under an older-adult prompt, 16 of 17 models assign lower valence on average than under a young-adult prompt. Yet after adjusting for image pleasantness, correlations between model and human age effects range from $-0.030$ to $0.093$, against an estimated ceiling of $0.595$. The discrepancy is clearest on 54 sensitive images rated as pleasant. Across models, the older prompt reduces valence by $0.845$ points on average, while older participants rate these images $0.443$ points higher than younger participants. Providing human ratings from other images improves agreement on the direction of age differences, although image-specific fidelity remains modest on 600 held-out images ($r_{\mathrm{part}}=0.105$). These results show why evaluations of demographic personalization in foundation models need human comparisons at the level of individual stimuli. Project page available at https://shahriyar-zaman.github.io/age-conditioned-emotion-reasoning/
authors: Shahriyar Zaman Ridoy, Azmine Toushik Wasi, Lin Gu, Ruogu Fang
bullets: Evaluates 17 VLMs on 900 OASIS images with young-, middle-, and older-adult prompts, comparing them with ratings from 822 participants.
Without age cues, models closely match average human valence, but age-conditioned effects show near-zero agreement with human age effects.
Older-adult prompts lower model valence for 16 of 17 models, whereas older participants often rate sensitive pleasant images more positively than younger participants.
Human ratings from other images improve prediction of the direction of age differences, though image-specific agreement remains modest.
Findings emphasize evaluating demographic personalization against human judgments for individual stimuli, not only aggregate behavior.

papers.abstract: Extending multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from images to videos faces substantial memory and latency challenges due to the massive number of visual tokens. These challenges have driven the development of numerous visual token compression methods and more efficient LLM architectures. However, existing compression methods are often evaluated with different training setups, tasks, and models, making fair comparison difficult. Meanwhile, the growing use of hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures raises questions about whether compression strategies transfer across backbones. We present VidToC, a controlled evaluation framework for representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time encoding strategies, covering training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary video understanding tasks. Our results reveal task-dependent compression behavior and characterize the effects of compression placement, time encoding, and backbone choice. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing and selecting video token compression strategies across tasks and training settings.
authors: Zihan Xiao (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China), Boshen Xu (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China), Pei Fu (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Jianzhong Ju (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Zhenbo Luo (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Jian Luan (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Qin Jin (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China)
bullets: Video MLLMs face major memory and latency costs from large numbers of visual tokens.
Existing compression methods are difficult to compare fairly because evaluations use different setups, tasks, and models.
VidToC provides a controlled framework spanning representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time-encoding strategies.
Experiments across three video-understanding tasks show that compression behavior depends on the task, compression placement, time encoding, and backbone.
The study offers empirical guidance for selecting compression strategies, including across hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures.

papers.abstract: In multimodal multi-turn dialogue, dialogue history plays a dual role: reliable responses provide useful context for subsequent turns, whereas hallucinated responses can propagate errors across turns. Existing training-free methods globally adjust the effect of dialogue history on generation, making it difficult to suppress misleading information without weakening useful context. To address this trade-off, we introduce Support-Guided Triadic Decoding (SGTD), a training-free framework that selectively controls the influence of unreliable history and fuses complementary predictions during decoding. Specifically, Historical Answer Support Estimation measures the visual support of historical responses against type-matched alternatives and identifies low-support content that may mislead later generation. Support-Targeted Attention Intervention then weakens the influence of this content while preserving the surrounding dialogue, producing a support-refined prediction. Triadic Decoding combines this prediction with the full-history prediction and answer-free visual evidence, while the Support-Adaptive Plausibility Constraint filters implausible tokens using visual agreement and historical support. Experiments on MMHalSnowball and VisDiaHalBench across representative LVLMs show that SGTD consistently achieves the highest accuracy under hallucinated histories while preserving the benefits of factual context.
authors: Yiheng Li, Wenhao Wang, Xingyi Li, Zhilin Tang, Zichang Tan, Zhen Lei, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets error propagation from hallucinated responses in multi-turn multimodal dialogue.
Uses historical answer support estimation to identify responses with weak visual grounding.
Applies targeted attention intervention to suppress misleading history while retaining useful context.
Fuses full-history, support-refined, and answer-free visual predictions with plausibility filtering.
Evaluated across representative LVLMs on MMHalSnowball and VisDiaHalBench, achieving the highest reported accuracy under hallucinated histories while preserving factual-context benefits.

papers.title: Support-Guided Triadic Decoding for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Dialogue with LVLMs
papers.tldr: SGTD reduces multimodal dialogue hallucinations by selectively downweighting unsupported historical answers and combining history-aware and visual-only decoding signals.

papers.abstract: Despite strong multimodal capabilities, large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate when linguistic priors outweigh visual evidence or when predictions are grounded in irrelevant or misleading image regions. Training-free contrastive decoding mitigates hallucinations by contrasting the original prediction with an auxiliary one that exposes linguistic priors. Yet existing methods focus on altering the auxiliary input or computation and do not ensure that either branch uses query-relevant visual evidence during decoding. We propose Visual Evidence-Guided Decoding (VEGD), a training-free framework that identifies query-relevant visual evidence and guides its use throughout contrastive decoding. VEGD locates this evidence by aggregating localization heads with strong visual responses and coherent spatial structure, then selectively weakens it in the auxiliary image. During generation, VEGD directs visual-carrier heads in both branches toward the same evidence location, strengthening access to intact evidence in the main branch while anchoring the auxiliary branch to its weakened counterpart. An adaptive distribution fusion strategy then combines or contrasts their predictions according to distribution divergence. Experiments across diverse LVLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that VEGD consistently reduces hallucinations.
authors: Yiheng Li, Wenhao Wang, Xingyi Li, Mingda Jia, Zichang Tan, Yinhang Tang, Zhen Lei, Yang Yang
bullets: Addresses hallucinations caused by linguistic priors and irrelevant or misleading image regions.
Uses localization heads to identify query-relevant evidence with strong visual responses and coherent spatial structure.
Selectively weakens the identified evidence in the auxiliary image and guides visual-carrier heads in both decoding branches to the same location.
Adaptively fuses or contrasts branch predictions based on their distribution divergence.
Experiments across diverse LVLMs and benchmarks show consistent hallucination reduction.

papers.title: Contrast Where It Matters: Visual Evidence-Guided Decoding for Mitigating Hallucinations in LVLMs
papers.tldr: VEGD reduces LVLM hallucinations by steering contrastive decoding toward query-relevant visual evidence while weakening that evidence in an auxiliary branch.

papers.abstract: We present DRVEXO-4B-Unified, a modular multimodal assistant built around a 4B language backbone. A self-contained checkpoint combines text, image, and speech inputs with reference-conditioned speech output and structured interaction. A temporal residual connector adapts acoustic sequences to the language interface; explicit text boundaries support incremental speech synthesis; and three task-conditioned scoring heads rank supplied action candidates alongside generative tool calls. These interfaces connect conversation to application-defined choices while leaving action authorization to the application. The system obtains 74.22% on all 900 MMMU validation questions, exceeding the published validation scores of Gemma 3 4B IT and InternVL3.5-4B without test-time scaling. Strict prompt-level IFEval accuracy is 82.26% and MATH-500 accuracy is 89.40%, above the original Qwen3-4B non-thinking report's 81.2% and 84.8%, respectively. On NVIDIA GB10, the model achieves a speech-synthesis first-chunk latency of 390 ms. For concurrent text generation, a growth-aware admission policy completes a 128-answer batch at 594.41 output tokens/s, including filling and draining, without preemptions. We plan to release the model weights and accompanying code under Apache License 2.0, retaining applicable third-party terms.

papers.abstract: Physical AI requires models that understand spatial relationships and dynamic environments and translate observations into actions under limited onboard compute. We present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI comprising TuringPAI-VL for shared vision-language understanding, TuringPAI-Drive for autonomous driving, and TuringPAI-Embodied for robotic manipulation. TuringPAI-VL is a 0.65B model built on HybridViT-MLQ, which combines convolutional local aggregation with Transformer-based global modeling. Multi-scale Latent Queries integrate spatial features and observation history within the same visual Transformer, providing a compact, structured interface to the language model. Training combines general vision-language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision. TuringPAI-VL supports general multimodal understanding and improves quantitative geometric perception over Qwen2-VL-2B, while providing a shared initialization for the two downstream VLA models. For autonomous driving, TuringPAI-Drive maintains all evaluated ADE/FDE metrics within 1.2\% of a full-token HybridViT baseline using the MLQ interface and achieves comparable aggregate scores in an in-house simulation evaluation. Using XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT) on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC, TuringPAI-Drive generates trajectories at 12\,Hz in on-vehicle operation. For robotic manipulation, TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8\% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites. These results demonstrate a shared vision-language foundation for driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.

papers.abstract: We study how to obtain a task-specific Vision-Language Model (VLM) for language-guided path generation between start and end points on remote sensing images. We explore this question from three aspects. First, we implement three widely used architectural approaches and compare their performance. Second, we design a scalable method for constructing pre-training data and build an effective pre-training dataset with a degree of diversity. Methods trained on this dataset achieve promising zero-shot performance. Third, we construct three benchmarks that support stratified evaluation and design three metrics for path generation. We investigate this problem through extensive experiments. The results show that the zero-shot performance of methods trained on the constructed pre-training dataset can exceed that of some advanced commercial VLMs. Code and Dataset can be available at https://github.com/jzdang/RemoteVLPG
authors: Junzhe Dang, Mengmeng Zhang, Yuxiang Zhang, Wei Li

Reports that trained methods can outperform some advanced commercial VLMs in zero-shot evaluation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have greatly improved input understanding in universal multimodal embedding models. However, this understanding does not ensure that their embeddings preserve the evidence needed to distinguish relevant items from confusable alternatives. To preserve essential discriminative evidence in embeddings, this paper proposes DiLE, a discrimination-aware latent-space learning framework that combines task guidance with on-policy retrieval feedback. Specifically, a few learnable queries are used to encode task-relevant information in a compact latent space. Reasoning instructions and auxiliary answer-generation supervision shape these representations to support both task understanding and retrieval discrimination. To address task-specific discriminative needs, we design shared-private expert adaptation that integrates cross-task knowledge sharing with task-specific representation learning. Building on this, the on-policy hard-negative distillation is introduced: the student retrieves confusable candidates, and a reverse KL divergence objective aligns its embedding-based similarity distribution with the teacher's fine-grained relevance distribution over these candidates. Candidates are periodically refreshed using updated student snapshots, tying teacher supervision to the student's evolving retrieval behavior and confusions. Across four model configurations that span two backbone generations, DiLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMEB-v2, UVRB, and MRMR, demonstrating its effectiveness across modalities and tasks.
authors: Ben Kang, Junda Wang, Yuxuan Yuan, Hang Li, Yuhan Liu, Xin Chen, Wanting Geng, Tong Lin, Pei Fu, Dong Wang, Jian Luan, Huchuan Lu

papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.
authors: Zhengbo Zhou, Dooman Arefan, Shandong Wu

Experiments on datasets built from CBIS-DDSM and VinDr-Mammo report better evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained token budgets.
Inference benchmarking shows reduced prefill latency.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential in parameterized layout generation via tool-augmented code synthesis. However, LLMs lack spatial awareness, making one-shot generation unreliable. While layout quality can be evaluated with established techniques, a critical gap remains: geometric-domain evaluation outcomes cannot be directly translated into actionable code-level fixes, trapping iterative refinement in blind refactoring. We propose SGLayout, a self-refining framework that closes this gap via a schema-guided mechanism. Upon code execution, a structured schema captures the correspondence between each code-level instance and its geometric attributes, establishing a bidirectional link between code space and geometry space. Emulating engineer review practices, SGLayout evaluates layouts along two complementary dimensions: intent compliance through quantitative structural checking and qualitative vision-language assessment, and rule compliance through DRC. All identified violations are then back-projected through the schema onto precise code targets, enabling surgical repair. This closed-loop process iterates until layout convergence. On a curated benchmark of 112 parameterized layout generation tasks using GDSFactory, SGLayout achieves a 76.79% pass rate, compared with 50.89% for the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to recognize small visual entities and understand their relationships. Scene graphs offer a natural way to represent this information, organizing visual entities as nodes and their relationships as edges. However, we identify two challenges: existing scene graph benchmarks provide insufficient coverage of fine-grained entities and the relationships among them, and existing methods for fine-grained visual understanding have yet to effectively leverage such graph-structured information in MLLMs. To address these challenges, we introduce Fine-Grained Multimodal Scene Graph Benchmark (FG-GraphBench) and FiGRA. FG-GraphBench is a benchmark comprising three complementary tasks: fine-grained visual question answering (FG-QA), image captioning (FG-Caption), and image description generation (FG-Description). We develop a two-stage construction pipeline that discovers and grounds fine-grained entities and establishes their relations to construct the fine-grained multimodal scene graphs (MSGs) in FG-GraphBench. Building on these MSGs, we propose FiGRA, a Fine-grained Graph Representation Augmentation method for MLLMs. FiGRA adopts a two-stage training strategy. It encodes multimodal entity and relation features as continuous graph tokens, and integrates them into the MLLM. Experiments show that FiGRA significantly outperforms strong baselines across three tasks of FG-GraphBench. Further analyses confirm the effectiveness of FG-GraphBench and highlight the importance of preserving fine-grained entity and relation information for visual understanding.
authors: Sicheng Liu, Xunkai Li, Ziyu Han, Xingnan Zhang, Ru Zhang, Rong-Hua Li
bullets: Targets limited coverage of fine-grained entities and relationships in existing scene-graph benchmarks and methods.
Introduces three tasks: fine-grained visual question answering, captioning, and description generation.
Builds fine-grained multimodal scene graphs using a two-stage entity discovery, grounding, and relation-construction pipeline.
FiGRA encodes multimodal entities and relations as continuous graph tokens and integrates them into MLLMs through two-stage training.
Experiments report significant improvements over strong baselines across all three benchmark tasks; analyses emphasize preserving fine-grained information.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a fine-grained multimodal scene graph benchmark and graph-token augmentation for MLLMs, directly relevant to multimodal large language model understanding.
papers.title: FG-GraphBench: Benchmarking and Enhancing Fine-Grained Visual Understanding with Multimodal Scene Graphs

papers.abstract: Panoramas can serve as shared scene backgrounds for multi-shot video generation, but most existing panorama generators take text alone or a single input image. We present a single model that generates a full equirectangular panorama from a text caption and K in {0,...,4} perspective conditioning views taken by a four-camera rig at one viewpoint. We fine-tune a pretrained text-to-image rectified-flow transformer in two stages. In the first stage, each conditioning view is appended to the token sequence together with the ID of its camera slot, and the number of views varies during training, so one set of weights serves every input setting. In the second stage, we improve the region not covered by any conditioning view. Supervised training computes its loss on noisy latents of the ground truth and never scores a panorama the model has generated and decoded, so we propose Uncovered-Region GRPO (UR-GRPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that rewards the candidates a vision-language model prefers in pairwise comparisons on crops around this region. Because the slot ID alone does not tell the model which way the rig points, we also offer an optional variant that writes each view's camera direction into its position encoding, which lets the user decide where each view appears in the output. With one conditioning view, our model outperforms the previous state of the art, 360Anything, trained on the same data and evaluated with the same code, on Laval Indoor and gives mixed results on an indoor subset of SUN360; the second stage improves the results for every number of conditioning views.
authors: Rui Hong, Xugang Ye, Jana Ko\v{s}eck\'a, Kai Fan
bullets: Addresses panorama generation for multi-shot video by combining captions with up to four views from a four-camera rig.
Fine-tunes a pretrained text-to-image rectified-flow transformer with camera-slot-aware view tokens and variable numbers of inputs.
Introduces Uncovered-Region GRPO, using vision-language-model preferences on crops of regions not covered by conditioning views.
An optional direction-aware positional encoding lets users control where each view appears in the panorama.
With one view, it outperforms 360Anything on Laval Indoor, shows mixed results on SUN360, and the second stage improves results for all view counts.
