papers.selection_reason: Generates panoramas from text and perspective views using a unified transformer, a spatial generation task.
papers.title: Zero to Four Views: Unified Panorama Generation and Preference RL for Unobserved Regions
papers.tldr: A unified model generates full panoramas from text plus 0–4 perspective views, using variable-view conditioning and preference-based reinforcement learning to improve unseen regions.

papers.abstract: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.
authors: Xuwei Ding, Skylar Zhai, Linxin Song, Jiarui Feng, Dongqi Fu, Huajun Xi, Junnan Li, Jingcheng Liang, Jieyu Zhao, Yinglong Xia, Hong Li, Jian Kang
bullets: Introduces 125 procedurally generated interactive CAPTCHAs covering five spatial abilities, solved via clicks and drags.
Humans solve 94.1% of tasks, while GPT-6 Astra fails 25.9% and Kimi K3 fails 68.0%.
Most model errors stem from misreading screenshots; reasoning often reinforces incorrect beliefs instead of correcting them.
Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B raises success from 1.6% to 33.1% and improves performance across seven out-of-distribution benchmarks.
The benchmark and training gym are designed to scale spatial-action learning and support transfer to real-world scenes.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers (DiTs) now render long, legible text in images, and feature caching is a standard way to accelerate them. Caches are judged by image-level metrics, which do not check whether the rendered text is still correct. We find that caching silently rewrites this text. On Z-Image, TaylorSeer at 2.9x fewer FLOPs lowers word accuracy from 62% to 46%, while ImageReward and CLIP Score barely change. Sampling with fewer steps at the same compute keeps almost all of this text, so the loss comes from how the cache predicts the skipped steps. Decomposing the cache error along classifier-free guidance (CFG), we trace this loss mainly to the guidance term, the difference between the conditional and unconditional predictions, which caches extrapolate worst on text. Correcting the guidance inside the text alone recovers most of the lost text. We therefore propose GuideCache, which recomputes both CFG branches only on the tokens with the largest predicted guidance error, using the guidance terms that the cache already stores. At 2.4x fewer FLOPs, GuideCache restores full-compute prompt fidelity on Z-Image and Qwen-Image, and on Z-Image it renders text as well as or better than ToCa, TeaCache, and FasterCache while staying much closer to the full model's output. GuideCache works with caches of any order, and on top of fewer sampling steps it keeps more text than step reduction at a higher speedup. These results suggest that acceleration methods for text-rendering models should be evaluated on the text they render.
authors: Kun Zhou, Wenmian Yang, Zhensheng Wang, Weijia Jia
bullets: Feature caching can silently rewrite image text even when image-level metrics such as CLIP Score and ImageReward barely change.
The text loss primarily comes from caching errors in classifier-free guidance, especially the difference between conditional and unconditional predictions.
GuideCache recomputes both guidance branches only for tokens with the largest predicted guidance errors, using cached guidance information.
At 2.4× fewer FLOPs, it restores full-compute prompt fidelity on Z-Image and Qwen-Image and outperforms or matches prior caches on Z-Image text rendering.
The work argues that acceleration methods for text-rendering models should be evaluated directly on rendered-text accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses text rendering artifacts in cached diffusion transformers (DiTs), a key issue for text generation in multimodal models.
papers.title: Text Lives in the Guidance: Preventing Silent Text Rewriting in Cached Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: GuideCache preserves rendered text during diffusion-transformer caching by selectively recomputing guidance for tokens most likely to suffer text corruption.

papers.abstract: Existing weakly supervised image manipulation localization (IML) methods typically rely on annotation-specific training strategies, hindering the joint use of diverse annotations within a single model. This limits the scale of usable training data and constrains further progress. We propose UniIML, a teacher-student framework that maps diverse weak annotations into a unified representation to guide the Segment Anything Model (SAM) in generating multiple candidate masks. However, SAM is designed for general-purpose segmentation and has limited sensitivity to manipulation traces; its predicted quality scores alone may therefore fail to reliably identify the candidate that best delineates the manipulated region. We introduce Ordinal Safe Consensus (OSC), which first filters candidates using trusted weak-annotation constraints encoded in the unified representation. It then ranks the remaining candidates separately by consistency with weak annotations, SAM-predicted quality scores, and cross-view stability, aggregating these rankings for an initial selection. To assess how changes in the evaluation criteria affect candidate selection, OSC repeats ranking and selection while omitting one criterion at a time. The most frequently selected candidate is adopted as the final mask, and its relative selection frequency quantifies selection stability. We construct soft pseudo-labels from the selected candidate's predicted probabilities and estimate pixel-level supervision weights based on selection stability, pixel-level agreement among candidates, and predictive certainty. The student receives direct supervision in regions defined by weak annotations and learns from soft pseudo-labels elsewhere through reliability-weighted distillation, enabling unified training across weak annotation types. Experiments show that UniIML achieves superior average performance compared with state-of-the-art IML methods.
authors: Songlin Li, Hui Ma, Zhiqing Guo, Dan Ma, Gaobo Yang, Xin Liao
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing weakly supervised IML methods use annotation-specific training strategies.
Uses a teacher–student framework to convert diverse weak annotations into a shared representation that guides SAM to generate candidate masks.
Introduces Ordinal Safe Consensus (OSC), which filters and ranks candidates using annotation consistency, SAM quality, and cross-view stability.
Builds soft pseudo-labels and pixel-level supervision weights from selection stability, candidate agreement, and predictive certainty.
Experiments report superior average performance over state-of-the-art IML methods, without specifying numerical results in the abstract.

papers.title: A Unified Framework for Image Manipulation Localization Under Multi-Type Weak Supervision

papers.abstract: Looped vision-language models (VLMs) deepen visual reasoning by repeatedly applying weight-tied modules. However, their decoding memory grows with recurrent depth and limits the image size and batch size that fit in a fixed memory budget. Each recurrent step produces its own key-value (KV) states, so the cache holds several copies of the same image. We find that, after an exact prefill, earlier steps still need access to visual information but can reuse the final visual KV within the same module. We propose FoldCache, which compresses visual KV along the recurrent axis while preserving the full prefill computation. FoldCache partitions recurrent steps within each module into groups and retains the final visual KV of each group for its members to share during decoding. Sharing stays within module boundaries, while question and answer KV remain separate for each step. The grouping granularity controls the degree of compression, and folding can be combined with token eviction and quantization to further reduce memory use. On LoopVL, FoldCache approximately halves prefix KV memory while matching full-cache accuracy on five open-ended benchmarks. These memory savings support batch sizes up to 1.7 times those of a full cache under the same GPU memory budget, and up to 2.6 times with the more aggressive FoldCache-Lite.
authors: Kun Zhou, Wenmian Yang, Zhensheng Wang, Yanzeng Li, Weijia Jia
bullets: Looped VLMs store separate visual KV states for each recurrent step, limiting image and batch sizes under fixed memory.
FoldCache preserves exact prefill computation, then groups recurrent steps within each module to share the final visual KV during decoding.
Question and answer KV states remain separate, and grouping granularity controls the memory–compression trade-off.
On LoopVL, it approximately halves prefix KV memory while matching full-cache accuracy across five open-ended benchmarks.
The method enables up to 1.7× larger batches, or up to 2.6× with the more aggressive FoldCache-Lite; it can also combine with token eviction and quantization.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of FoldCache on LoopVL. (a) During prefill, the invocations of a group write their visual KV into one shared buffer in turn, so it ends with the last invocation. (b) Cycle-wise folding (default) keeps r2, r3, r6, r7, and module-wise folding (FoldCache-Lite) keeps r6, r7. Groups never cross module boundaries. (c) At decoding, each invocation of a sample attends to its group’s visual segment, stored once per group and sample, and to its own question and answer KV, and the two results are merged by log-sum-exp.

Figure 1. Folding the visual KV of a looped VLM. LoopVL runs its two modules eight times, (LLLH)× 2, and each invocation stores its own visual KV. After an exact prefill, FoldCache keeps only the visual KV of the last invocation of each module in each cycle. papers.abstract: GUI grounding maps a screenshot and a natural language instruction to the coordinates of the intended interface element. Existing approaches improve grounding through visual scaling, instruction scaling, and sampling scaling, yet it remains unclear which grounding bottlenecks these strategies address and where their gains saturate. To address this gap, we introduce ScaleDiag, a controlled diagnostic framework that isolates the effects of visual input, instruction information, and prediction sampling on GUI grounding by independently varying target scale and surrounding context, target-specific information and auxiliary descriptions, and candidate coverage and selection, respectively. We evaluate ScaleDiag across five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models and find that each scaling strategy operates within a much narrower regime than commonly assumed. (1) Visual scaling is governed by target occupancy rather than a fixed crop ratio, with full-screen errors typically rescued once the target occupies only 0.32% of the cropped view, while further zooming eventually becomes harmful. (2) Instruction scaling is driven by information that identifies the target rather than description richness itself, as even ground-truth-derived attributes such as color, size, and shape are often neutral or harmful, while appearance and spatial descriptions account for over 90% of the achievable gain. (3) Repeated sampling exposes a different limitation, as correct coordinates are frequently generated but remain difficult to select, leaving 5.1--11.0 points of oracle headroom while geometric consensus provides almost no improvement. Together, these results show that test-time scaling is constrained by distinct operating regimes rather than benefiting monotonically from more visual focus, richer instructions, or additional samples. Our code is available at https://github.com/YenanLiu/ScaleDiag.
authors: Chen Liu, Zhen Fang, Xin Yu, Dadong Wang, Ling Chen
bullets: Visual scaling depends on target occupancy, not a fixed crop ratio; zooming too far can hurt.
Instruction scaling benefits mainly from appearance and spatial cues, while added attributes such as color, size, and shape are often neutral or harmful.
Repeated sampling often generates correct coordinates but fails to select them, leaving 5.1–11.0 points of oracle headroom.
Geometric consensus provides almost no improvement, indicating that sampling and selection have distinct bottlenecks.
Findings are based on five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our controlled diagnostic framework for GUI grounding. (a) Controlled visual interventions vary the visual evidence while keeping the instruction fixed. We construct target-centered, aspect-ratio-preserving crops at different area ratios, and separately add resized distractor screenshots while preserving the target screenshot at its native resolution. (b) Controlled instruction interventions keep the screenshot and target fixed while modifying the instruction. Rule-based attribute injection appends ground-truth-derived position, color, size, or shape cues, whereas an LLM generates natural descriptions from appearance, spatial, functional, and goal-oriented views. (c) Repeated sampling keeps both the screenshot and instruction fixed and generates multiple coordinate predictions, allowing us to compare greedy decoding, coordinate-medoid consensus, and oracle candidate coverage. Together, these interventions isolate the effects of visual evidence, instruction information, and candidate selection.

papers.abstract: Can a frontier model repair a vision-language model (VLM) by rewriting its weights? Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 need such a repair: in thinking mode they fall into loops on many image questions, repeating themselves until the token limit, spending the whole budget and losing the answer. The usual remedies act on the decoding, leaving the looping model as it was, or must be told what to change. Yet the cause is written in the weights. Keel, the first agentic weight-editing method for VLMs on image tasks, finds and removes it there. Told only the symptom, an editor, a frontier multimodal LLM acting as an agent, locates the cause, edits the weights and tests them, with a failure census and instruments showing it the failing images and where the VLM attends; among several editors, the harness keeps only edits that clearly reduce the failure without lowering accuracy on questions no editor saw. The repair needs no training, keeps the model's size and per-token cost, and applies to already-edited weights. The editors expose where the loops live: from the original weights, independent editors on both models trace them to the attention outputs of the middle layers, and the smaller VLM stops consulting the image inside a loop. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, across six image benchmarks from visual mathematics to GUI grounding, the edit removes most loops on every benchmark and shortens answers, and the edited models are significantly more accurate than the thinking models on average; the larger one gains most on GUI grounding, a task absent from the practice questions. Because the repair lives in the weights, it combines with budget forcing where held-out questions favor it: on the best available weights, Keel has the best average accuracy on both models, significantly above every training-free baseline we compare on the larger one.
authors: Jiajun Fan, Neil He, Bangji Yang, Qinglong Zheng, Ziwen Wang, Chaoran Cheng, Changyi Yang, Hanqi Mao, Ge Liu
bullets: Targets repetitive thinking loops in small vision-language models that waste the token budget and lose answers.

Edits are retained only when they reduce looping without harming accuracy on unseen questions.
Independent editors locate the issue in middle-layer attention outputs, where the smaller VLM stops consulting the image during loops.
Across six image benchmarks on Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2B, Keel removes most loops, shortens answers, and improves average accuracy; it also combines well with budget forcing.

papers.abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as GDP.pdf and GDP.xlsx do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.

Uses expert-weighted rubrics and a sandboxed agentic autorater, which matched human expert judgments on 96.2% of criteria (κ = 0.91).
Claude Fable 5.2 achieved the highest Climb-WSR (56.6%) and overall WSR (73.3%), followed by Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% and 71.9%); Carbon used 5.7× fewer tokens.
Even the strongest evaluated models scored below 57% on frontier criteria, indicating substantial room for improvement.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.
authors: Takahiro Miki, Robin Schmid, Manthan Patel, Turcan Tuna, Julia Richter, Julian Nubert, Joonho Lee, Matthias M\"uller, Marco Hutter
bullets: Targets robust autonomous navigation in diverse, unstructured real-world terrain.
Uses a VLM to interpret scenes, assess risks, understand signs, and assign navigation costs.
Converts semantic outputs into a real-time dense risk map through open-vocabulary segmentation.
Conditions pre-trained RL policies for agile locomotion and local navigation.
Real-world trials achieved kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, while exposing limits in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the ROAM pipeline. The proposed system bridges high-level reasoning from vision-language models (VLMs) with low-level actuator commands for autonomous robot control. It processes RGB images and robot descriptions through a VLM to generate object labels enriched with risk, preferred area, and steppable values. These labels are converted into semantic images using open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, which operates at a higher frequency than the VLM analysis. The semantic images are then fused with elevation maps to create an environmental representation that reinforcement learning (RL) policies utilize for fast and robust robot control.

Fig. 2. Deployment of ROAM across diverse environments. These include natural outdoor settings such as mountain trails (A to E), forests (F), and grassy areas (G), as well as urban environments such as university campuses (H) and roads (I). The system was also tested in indoor settings (J to L). Additionally, we evaluated its performance in the presence of various challenges, such as smoke (M), train tracks (N), and signage (O).

Fig. 4. Comparison of ROAM with baselines on a course with semantic and contextual challenges. The experiment covered a 1.2 km path with challenges such as an inaccurate global path deviating into bushes or grass, a mannequin lying on the path as an obstacle, and a construction zone with warning signs. (A) Robust pathfinding. The global path was offset into bushes [(i) and (ii)] and into grass [(iii) and (iv)]; (i) and (iii) show ROAM, and (ii) and (iv) show the geometry-only baseline. The map shows the paths of the three methods and the global path. The remaining panels show the robot views, the risk and preferred-area images, and the VLM responses before and after ROAM read the “ROAD WORK AHEAD” sign (r1) and the “END ROAD WORK” sign (r2), followed by snapshots of the geometry-only baseline (g1 to g3) and ViNT (v1 to v3). Information icons mark the ViNT interventions.

Fig. 5. ROAM brings world knowledge to locomotion, local navigation, and exploration. (A) ROAM reads signs and uses this information in locomotion: (i) metal cans with a “WARNING: EXPLOSIVE CANS” sign and (ii) wooden pallets on grass without a sign, with a sign on the pallet, and with signs on the grass. The table in (i) lists the VLM labels and their values, the boxes in (ii) show the VLM responses, and the map in (ii) shows the wooden pallet (orange outline) and the foot trajectories for the three sign conditions. (B) Comparison of ROAM with a geometry-only baseline on (i) a campus route, (ii) a route next to a railroad, and (iii) a snow-covered path. In (i), images 1 to 4 correspond to the numbered points along the paths taken by the two methods, highlighting the different terrains encountered, such as paved areas, gravel, and grass. (C) Exploration behavior in the presence of an obstacle blocking the path: (i) the blocked path, (ii) the alternative route along the path, (iii) the shortcut through the grass, and (iv) the return to the global path. The robot explored along the path after encountering the obstacle and took a shortcut through the grass to merge back to the global path.

Fig. 6. Comparison of VLM output abstractions for navigation. (A) Comparison of VLM-based navigation methods by output type. ROAM outputs semantic labels and values, avoiding the need for spatial understanding. Methods outputting directions or coordinates require spatial reasoning; those generating direct commands (such as velocity) additionally require embodiment understanding. (B) Example trajectories from different methods, including three “select label” variants. ROAM information can augment label placement on ground regions. (C) Quantitative evaluation of the safety and preferred ratios, defined as the fraction of all trajectory pixels, pooled over the scenes (N = 27 scenes; see Statistical analysis), that lie within the hand-labeled “safe” and “preferred” regions. Error bars, 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

The route encompassed diverse terrains, including gravel paths, rocky sections, grassy areas, and segments near a lake and train tracks. The steepest segment of the hike had a gradient of approximately 30%, posing a substantial challenge for locomotion. (B) Seealpsee experiment. papers.abstract: Tracking a hidden object through a video is effortless for humans, yet it remains a bottleneck for vision language models (VLMs). In the shell game, where a ball is hidden under one of several identical cups that are then swapped, VLMs that answer directly stay near chance, thinking models fail on long games, and fine-tuning learns only the lengths it has seen. We argue that the limit is serial computation: each swap must be composed with the last result, and a VLM of fixed depth has only a fixed number of state transitions for it. To address this, we propose RecurrentVLM, which makes every attention layer of a pretrained VLM recur over time by computing the keys and values of finished frame groups from the layer's own output. With a single answer token, RecurrentVLM reaches 100% on VET-Bench and 99.6% on MET-Bench, and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps. We also observe several interesting phenomena: length generalization emerges suddenly at an aha moment; without recurrence, each swap costs an attention layer; the ball's state forms in the first four attention layers; and recurrence keeps the latest state at the cost of details of earlier moments. These results suggest that recurrent VLMs are a potential solution for tracking the states of unobserved objects in video. Code will be released.
authors: Dingqiang Ye, Jiacong Xu, Wen Zhang, Yiqun Mei, Vishal M. Patel
bullets: VLMs struggle with shell-game tracking because each swap requires composing a new state with the previous one.
RecurrentVLM applies every attention layer recurrently, recomputing keys and values from completed frame groups while using a single answer token.
It achieves 100% on VET-Bench, 99.6% on MET-Bench, and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps.
Length generalization appears abruptly, while recurrence preserves the latest state but loses details from earlier moments.
The findings suggest recurrence can support tracking unobserved object states in video.

(b) We cache keys and values of the layer’s own output, once per frame group, so every attention layer becomes a recurrence over time. (c) Each query reads keys and values of earlier tokens’ inputs in (a), but of earlier frame groups’ outputs in (b).

(a) Over training: share of swaps on which the frame-wise answer equals the model’s own last answer updated by the current swap (black), and per-swap accuracy on swaps 31–50 (red). (b) Accuracy on 50-swap games with one head of attention layer 4 switched off; any single head of attention layer 3 or 5 keeps at least 60%. papers.abstract: Adapting robot policies to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with limited real-world data remains a key bottleneck to generalist robots. The multimodality and scarcity of robotics data lead end-to-end approaches to overfit and break under small distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation can alleviate this by correcting frozen policies at inference, but most methods ground their correction in a signal learned implicitly from robotic datasets, making it susceptible to the same shifts as the policy it corrects. Recent methods that instead exploit explicit spatial information are typically limited to coarse corrections, missing the nuanced, task-relevant motion most manipulation tasks require. We propose VG-Steer, which corrects existing policies by transferring the nuanced motion of successful in-distribution rollouts, captured along meaningful geometric axes, known here as object-relational distance pairs. VG-Steer leverages the semantic understanding of Large Vision Models (LVMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reasoning, which combines the task-relevant entity pairs and their object-relational distance projections into a single tailored visual-geometric guidance signal. In a simulation benchmark, it efficiently corrects flow-matching policies under pose and task-goal shifts; on a real robot experiment, it widens the region of the workspace the frozen policy covers, more than doubling its success rate on cable placements one grid step outside the training positions, and steers a single-task policy toward objects it was never trained on while nearly eliminating object confusion. Project website: https://arthurfenderbucker.github.io/VG-Steer/
authors: Arthur Bucker, Pramod Anantharam, Jonathan Francis, Jean Oh
bullets: Addresses OOD failures caused by scarce, multimodal robotics data and policy overfitting to small distribution shifts.
Combines LVM/VLM semantic reasoning with object-relational distance pairs along meaningful geometric axes to form task-specific guidance.
Transfers motion patterns from successful in-distribution rollouts without retraining the policy.
Works in simulation for pose and task-goal shifts and on a real robot for cable placement and unseen-object steering.
In reported experiments, it more than doubled success one grid step outside training positions and nearly eliminated object confusion when steering toward unseen objects.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of our visual-geometric policy steering framework. Offline analysis (at task initialization, once per episode): (1) we retrieve the most relevant successful in-distribution rollout τ∗ by weighted image (DINOv2) and text (CLIP) similarity; (2) a VLM selects the task-relevant object-relational distance pairs per motion phase (e.g., gripper–cube distance d1, cube–table distance d2, gripper orientation θ), evaluated per timestep into the reference trends Φ; (3) a VLM with SAM2 matches the demonstration objects to the live OOD scene (e.g., the cylinder takes the cube’s role), re-targeting each pair. Online steering (every action chunk): (4) perception projects the live scene into the same distance space and aligns each pair to Φ within a window, giving the reference d∗. At every denoising step, a differentiable dynamics model F forecasts the features d(A) of a candidate chunk A, and a line-searched gradient step on the trajectory loss corrects the frozen policy’s velocity field, yielding the steered chunk A′.

Fig. 5. Positional generalization. Every rollout is plotted at the Mahalanobis distance of its measured cable position (dots near 100 are successes, near 0 failures), with per-zone success rates and 95% Wilson intervals (squares) and a per-method logistic fit, crossing 50% at 2.8σ (base) and 3.4σ (VG-Steer).

Fig. 9. Visual-geometric guidance via VLM-selected distance pairs. Offline (a–c): the demonstration is segmented (Gemini 3 Flash + SAM2) and split into sub-trajectory phases (STRAP); the VLM selects each phase’s entity pairs, projections, and sub-goal constraints. Online (d–e): the live scene is matched to the demonstration, and the guidance steers the frozen policy so the selected projected distances track the reference.

Fig. 4. Positional sweep on cable bagging, in the camera view. (a) Training distribution of the 110 cable grasps in the demonstrations. (b) The single reference rollout, with its end-effector path split into sub-trajectories. (c, d) Per-cell outcomes: dots mark the measured cable position of every trial, filled green for success, red rings for failure.

Fig. 2. Differentiable guidance injection. At each denoising step, the candidate chunk is rolled out by forward kinematics, and the guidance loss (position, orientation, gripper) is differentiated; a golden-section line search sets the step size, and the correction is applied to the policy’s velocity field, steering the trajectory without modifying weights.
Fig. 8. Real-world outcome breakdown (share of rollouts, counts on bars). Residual failures concentrate in grasp and transport, which the guidance does not address.

Fig. 7. Task variation on cable bagging. Left: the single reference rollout above the new setting in which cable, banana and spoon share the workspace. Center, right: confusion matrices (instructed object in rows, reached object in columns) for the base and the guided policy.
Fig. 6. Disambiguating the target object in a cluttered scene. In red and blue, the distance pairs used per sub-trajectory (ST0 approach, ST1 transport).

Fig. 3. Per-action-chunk inference overhead on π0.5 (mean over the four suites, CUDA-synchronized). With VG-Steer a chunk takes ∼73 ms in total (1.2× the base’s ∼61 ms), comparable to gradient-only VLS (∼70 ms total); full VLS costs ∼20× more, scaling with its particle count (20 here).

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising approach to improving visual reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, not all samples benefit equally from privileged visual guidance, and uniform token supervision can dilute visually grounded signals. We propose VisAlloc, a dual-level framework combining sample-level visual filtering with token-level counterfactual reweighting. A fixed paired-teacher filter retains samples answered correctly from an evidence-centered positive crop but incorrectly from a spatially displaced negative crop. At the token level, both EMA teachers score the same student-generated response, and their absolute log-probability differences measure view sensitivity. Additional supervision targets tokens admitted by sensitivity or teacher-distribution disagreement, with shared frozen-prior, template-bigram, and student--teacher divergence gates. Inverse-frequency redistribution preserves the total additional weight within each micro-batch, while the positive teacher remains the sole distillation target. Inference requires only the full-image student. Across eight benchmarks, our 4B and 9B models achieve macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, outperforming Vision-OPD reproductions by 0.97 and 0.52 points, respectively. Code on GitHub: https://github.com/Kaelyn01/VisAlloc
authors: Haoran Xu, Tian Chen, Yuhe Wu, Yanbo Zhao, Junchi Liao, Hongyu Wang, Jiaze Li, Wentao Wang, Yanfeng Li, Rui Qian
bullets: Filters training samples using positive evidence-centered crops versus spatially displaced negative crops.
Reweights tokens based on view sensitivity and disagreement between positive and negative visual teachers.
Uses multiple gates and inverse-frequency redistribution while keeping the positive teacher as the only distillation target.
Inference requires only the full-image student, avoiding teacher or crop-based overhead.
Across eight benchmarks, the 4B and 9B models reach macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, respectively, exceeding Vision-OPD reproductions by 0.97 and 0.52 points.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of VisAlloc. (A) Paired-view construction produces an evidence-centered positive crop and a spatially displaced negative crop. A fixed paired-teacher filter then retains samples that the positive teacher answers correctly and the negative teacher answers incorrectly, after annotation-quality checks. Each retained sample keeps its full image and paired teacher views. (B) Both teachers score the same student-generated response under aligned prefixes. (C) Realized-token sensitivity supplies the continuous base; sensitivity or teacher-distribution disagreement admits a bonus under shared context gates, and inverse-frequency redistribution preserves its total before mean normalization. (D) Only the positive teacher supplies the weighted JSD target, and EMA updates once after the actor update. The displayed redistribution is for E > 0, and zero-budget batches retain zero bonus. The views and bonuses are schematic (λ = 4, 4B).

The first three runs extend to step 65; orange/purple end at step 60. (a) Mean response length decreases from ≈80–95 to 66–77 tokens; no collapse is observed over the recorded steps. papers.abstract: Existing activation steering methods for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) use the global activation mean as the steering vector, which tends to cause cross-task interference and unstable performance. We trace this failure to the multi-centered geometry of task activations. The global mean lands in the empty region between clusters and is faithful to no single task. Moreover, the steering signal in each task-pure local cluster is low-rank, and different query tasks benefit from emphasizing different families of local-basis directions under the shared routing protocol. To address this, we propose MAST (Medoid-Anchored Subspace Steering), a training-free, input-adaptive activation steering framework. MAST groups samples by task, performs multi-center clustering within each group, and selects one representative medoid per cluster. At inference time, each query is routed to multiple representative medoids. For each matched cluster, a low-rank local steering direction is extracted and aggregated across clusters to produce the final steering vector. Building on MAST, MAST-PR (Probe-Reweighted) uses a lightweight task-aware probe to reweight task-specialized local-direction families, yielding a further average improvement of +8.09 points over MAST.
bullets: Global-mean steering can fall between task-activation clusters, causing cross-task interference and instability.
MAST clusters task activations, selects representative medoids, and routes each query to multiple relevant clusters.
It extracts low-rank local steering directions and aggregates them into a query-specific steering vector without training.
MAST-PR adds a lightweight task-aware probe to reweight specialized direction families, improving average performance by 8.09 points over MAST.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of MAST. Step 1 (offline). Within each task, K-medoids clustering (K=5) builds the prototype bank B of 20 medoids, whose directions are largely misaligned with the task global mean. Step 2 (online). Adaptive routing by sq,c selects the top-k medoids (k=3). Step 3 (online). Each selected cluster is blended into vc and summed into the steering vector v. Contrastive directions are extracted from teacher-forced support completions, whereas routing uses separately extracted answer-free prompt contexts (Section 4.1). The extension MAST-PR reweights the taskspecialized directions βτ via a lightweight probe.

papers.title: MAST: Medoid-Anchored Subspace Steering for Visual Grounding in Multimodal LLMs

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with accurately capturing camera-object relations, especially for object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera shots. This stems from the fact that existing MLLMs are trained on images with limited diverse camera-object relations and corresponding textual descriptions. To address this, we propose a synthetic generation pipeline to create large-scale 3D visual instruction datasets. Our framework takes 3D assets as input and uses rendering and diffusion-based image generation models to create photorealistic images preserving precise camera-object relations. Additionally, large language models (LLMs) are used to generate text prompts for guiding visual instruction tuning and controlling image generation. We create Ultimate3D, a large-scale 3D-grounded 2D visual instruction dataset. Ultimate3D consists of 240K VQAs with precise camera-object annotations, and corresponding benchmark. MLLMs fine-tuned on our proposed dataset outperform commercial models by a large margin, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 29.7% on camera-object relation recognition tasks. Our code, dataset, and benchmark will contribute to broad MLLM applications.
authors: Liu He, Yizhi Song, Ruiqi Xu, Baris Sarper Tezcan, Xiao Zeng, Albert Y. C. Chen, Lu Xia, Shashwat Verma, Sankalp Dayal, Min Sun, Cheng-Hao Kuo, Daniel Aliaga
bullets: Targets weaknesses in recognizing object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera shots.
Uses 3D assets, rendering, diffusion-based image generation, and LLM-generated prompts to produce photorealistic training images with precise relations.
Provides 240K visual question-answer pairs with camera-object annotations and a corresponding benchmark.
MLLMs fine-tuned on Ultimate3D achieve a reported 29.7% average accuracy improvement over commercial models on camera-object relation tasks.
Scope is focused on 3D-grounded camera-object relation recognition.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Generating Synthetic Visual Instruction Dataset. Our framework uses open-sourced 3D assets to generate photo-realistic images with precisely controlled camera-object relation. Corresponding text instructions are also generated by Large Language Model (LLM). The generated Ultimate3D dataset (240K) and benchmark (8K) advance baseline MLLM models (Gemma-4, Qwen3-VL, etc.) to outperform commercial MLLMs (GPT-5.5, Gemini-3.5, etc.) on camera-object relation recognition tasks. The left panel illustrates representative MLLM failures, while the right panel provides a direct same-image comparison between base and Ultimate3D-fine-tuned models.

Fig. 5: Ablations on Image Generation Pipeline. Our framework shows superior performance by using multi-ControlNet with SDXL backbones, and introducing both Canny edges and depth maps as visual priors. It consistently delivers better robustness and quality compared to text-only SDXL and [80]. When these visual priors are removed (top-right: removing all visual priors; bottom-right: removing depth prior), the generator often fails to produce good results and brings lower generation success rate (see Sec 4.6, [80] only achieves 55.11% success rate v.s. ours 93.07%)

Fig. 2: Our Framework. Each shade box corresponds to a section in Sec. 3. Given open-sourced 3D assets, our approach leverages a 3D Renderer to generate 3D visual priors (Iβ) preserving ground truth camera-object relation (β). Meanwhile, LLMs take 3D asset category to generate diverse image descriptions (Timg) as conditional guidance. Both the 3D visual priors and diverse text prompts are used to generate synthetic images (Isyn) by multiple ControlNet-based networks. Corresponding text QA instructions (Tqa) are generated by LLMs given the ground truth camera-object relation. Our Ultimate3D dataset and benchmark (i.e. pairs of Tqa and Isyn) contribute to fine-tuning and evaluation of MLLMs.

Fig. 3: 3D Visual Prior Rendering. With a general camera model, our method utilizes a 3D Renderer (e.g., Blender) to render multiple 3D visual priors given arbitrary camera-object relations. O: camera center; A: object center; D: camera-object distance.

Fig. 4: Qualitative Results. We show responses by GPT-5.5, Gemini-3.5-Flash with high thinking, Gemma-4-31B-it, and finetuned Gemma-4-31B-it on the Ultimate3D benchmark. Each model is asked questions (in gray boxes) regarding object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera-shot type, together with the input images on the left. The model responses illustrate that the Gemma-4-31B-it model finetuned on Ultimate3D can precisely recognize camera-object relations on synthetic images. GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.5-Flash with high thinking sometimes provide correct answers, but also exhibit inconsistent predictions across relation types. The original Gemma-4-31B-it frequently fails to produce the correct camera-object relation labels, while the finetuned model provides substantially more accurate and taskrelevant answers.

Table 1: Quantitative Comparisons. We evaluate open-source and closed-source MLLMs on the Ultimate3D and MMVP benchmarks. LLaVA and Llama models are fine-tuned using their original full fine-tuning recipes, while Gemma-4 and Qwen models are fine-tuned with LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning (for Qwen, the vision-language merger is also fully trained). Results report MLLM response accuracy (%) for object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera-shot recognition. Superscripts indicate the fine-tuning setup: F full fine-tuning and L LoRA fine-tuning.

Table 2: Generalization. We finetune LLaVA1.6-13B model using a mixture of both general VQA and camera-object relation VQA datasets. Without degradation on general VQA tasks, finetuned model improves its ability on camera-object relation recognition and beats SOTA (i.e. GPT4o) by 28.42% accuracy on Ultimate3D benchmark. ∗ denotes the average accuracy (%) across all 3 types of camera-object relation VQAs in Tab. 1.

papers.abstract: Visualizing intermediate representations could help us inspect the reasoning steps underlying a model output. Unified multimodal models offer this opportunity by combining understanding and generation in one architecture. Their image generators can access representations formed while processing text. We introduce the V-lens, which uses this connection to visualize a chosen token's hidden state without training a decoder. Across four diffusion-based and two purely autoregressive unified models, the resulting images reveal key intermediate concepts that connect a question to its answer even when the concepts are never named explicitly. Controlled tests show how this content changes with context, token position, and depth. We then introduce lens tuning, which supervises selected hidden states with pictures through the V-lens. Across BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and HunyuanImage-3.0, the rate of correct visualizations of pronoun referents rises from 2-11% to 86-94%. Surprisingly, such visual supervision also improves text answers without supervising the answer tokens directly. Code is available at https://github.com/multimodal-ai-lab/V-lens.
authors: Tobias Braun, Marcus Rohrbach, Lorenzo Cavallaro
bullets: Unified models can expose intermediate reasoning concepts through their text-conditioned image-generation pathways.
V-lens visualizes a selected token’s hidden state without training a separate decoder.
Across six models, visualizations reveal implicit concepts linking questions to answers.
Concepts vary with context, token position, and network depth.
Lens tuning raises correct pronoun-referent visualizations from 2–11% to 86–94% and improves text answers indirectly.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are often asked several questions about the same image in a single prompt (co-asking), yet existing evaluations report conflicting accuracy gains and hallucinations at the prompt level without tracking how individual answers change. By pairing each question's single-question and co-asked answers across 22 open-weight VLMs (1B-35B), we find that erratic net shifts reflect two opposing effects: on Densely Captioned Images (DCI), every model repairs 15.4%-29.8% of its single-question errors under co-asking, while the share of correct answers turned wrong falls from 30.8% on weaker models to 4.7% on stronger ones. Across all 14 models supporting custom attention masks, we show through attention readouts and layer-window interventions that earlier same-image questions read visual information into their question tokens in the early-to-middle layers during prefill, helping later questions concentrate image attention onto their queried targets. This visual help accumulates across the scene even across non-overlapping regions, whereas blocking earlier questions from attending to the image lowers both target localization and accuracy in all 14 models. While cross-question help is established during shared question reading, part of the co-asking damage enters later during answer decoding when the decoder attends to other question stems. We therefore introduce Read Together, Answer Apart, a training-free decoding mask that keeps shared prefill intact and isolates each answer from other stems, improving co-asking accuracy on 12 of 14 models on DCI (up to +4.71 percentage points, closing 70% of the pooled gap to asking alone) and on 10, 8, and 5 of the 14 models on WebUI, FinTabNet, and GQA (up to +11.4, +5.3, and +1.1 points).
authors: Xinyi Guo, Kaile Huang, Xitong Ling, Mingyi He, Chende Zheng, Jianyu Xu, Chao He, Dongqing Song
bullets: Co-asking produces mixed effects because it both repairs single-question errors and creates new errors.

Earlier questions transfer visual information across the image during early-to-middle prefill layers, improving later-question target localization.
Some damage arises during answer decoding when answers attend to other question stems.
The training-free Read Together, Answer Apart mask improves accuracy on most tested models across DCI, WebUI, FinTabNet, and GQA.

papers.abstract: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on general video understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to reason about participant roles in aggressive interactions remains largely unexplored. Existing violence and crime datasets primarily evaluate whether aggression occurs, without testing whether models can identify who performed the action, who received it, and how participants are related within the scene. To address this gap, we introduce A$^3$Bench, a benchmark to study aggressive action and association in videos. The benchmark evaluates whether models can jointly recognize aggressive actions, distinguish aggressors from victims and bystanders, and correctly bind actions to participants under challenging distractor settings. We benchmark 17 multimodal models and find that they struggle substantially on fine-grained aggressive-scene understanding. Performance degrades consistently as reasoning complexity increases, with models frequently confusing aggressors with victims or bystanders, revealing a systematic failure in role-action association rather than coarse aggression recognition alone. We further observe that increasing model scale or generic reasoning models experience limited improvement. Finally, we explore a simple role-graph prompting strategy that encourages structured reasoning over participant interactions, leading to improvements in compositional reasoning. Our findings highlight that reliable aggressive-scene understanding remains a major challenge for current MLLMs and motivate future research on role-aware video reasoning beyond coarse violence detection. Code and dataset: https://github.com/austincbaker/A3Bench.
authors: Austin C Baker, Raiyaan Abdullah, Daniel Zeev Yoffe, Shruti Vyas, Yogesh S Rawat

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (omni-modal LLMs) can respond to spoken requests directly through voice and video calls. Such requests rely on the scene shared by the user and the assistant, so the same utterance may call for different help or for no response. Most audio-visual benchmarks provide questions as separate text input, and interactive benchmarks mostly score a response as a whole. It thus remains unclear whether a model recognizes when the user is asking for help, and whether its reply meets the user's need once the request is recognized. We propose O-IN-Bench to evaluate how well omni-modal LLMs understand spoken intentions. A model watches a complete video with native speech and outputs one text response, or [SILENCE] when no response is needed. O-IN-Bench contains 1,000 Chinese and English samples in five categories and 16 subcategories. Contrastive pairs combine the same request with different scene conditions to test whether the response changes with the context. A sample-specific rubric judges language, intent, and content separately, and O-IN-Engine verifies each rubric against the video. Across 30 omni-modal model configurations, the best overall score is 59.6, achieved by Gemini3.7-Flash. Gemini3.7-Flash passes 74.4% of the intent judgments but only 42.6% of the content judgments. When the speech is a conversation between peers rather than a request to the assistant, even strong models often keep responding. When a reply must satisfy several people, the best score is only 25.9. These results indicate that recognizing a request and meeting its requirements are separate abilities, and O-IN-Bench measures each of them.
authors: Zijie Xin, Tianyi Wang, Daoze Zhang, Jie Yang, Changli Tang, Qijie Wei, Fengyun Rao, Xirong Li
bullets: Tests complete videos with native speech, requiring a text reply or [SILENCE] when no response is needed.
Includes 1,000 Chinese and English samples across five categories and 16 subcategories, with contrastive scene-based pairs.
Uses separate rubric scores for language, intent recognition, and content fulfillment, verified against each video.
Across 30 model configurations, the best overall score was 59.6; intent recognition outperformed content fulfillment.
Models often respond to peer conversations and struggle when a reply must satisfy multiple people.

papers.abstract: Semantic 3D mapping is a powerful representation that enables platform agnostic mobile robot navigation in challenging offroad conditions. Current vision foundation models can accurately predict semantics zero-shot on structured scenes but performance is compromised in natural environments. On the other hand, 3D point clouds encode valuable information for discriminating semantics in scenarios where vision foundation models fail. In this work, we propose fitting a sphericity-elevation distribution for each semantic class to act as geometric anchor. Only the points with the most confident vision foundation model predictions are considered when fitting to produce high quality geometric prior distributions. The geometric prior is fused with the vision foundation model prediction to produce the final semantic mapping. The proposed prior improves SAM3 baseline by +6.3 in mIoU and +8.9 in accuracy on the RELLIS-3D dataset, and by +1.7 in mIoU and +2.1 in accuracy on the WildScenes dataset. The source code will be made public upon paper acceptance.
bullets: Vision foundation models struggle with semantic prediction in natural, unstructured offroad scenes.
The method fits a sphericity–elevation distribution for each semantic class using only high-confidence vision predictions.
These class-specific geometric priors are fused with vision foundation model outputs to produce the final 3D semantic map.
The approach improves the SAM3 baseline on RELLIS-3D by 6.3 mIoU points and 8.9 accuracy points, and on WildScenes by 1.7 and 2.1 points, respectively.
The work focuses on offroad semantic mapping and plans to release its source code upon acceptance.

papers.tldr: Geometric priors based on point-cloud sphericity and elevation substantially improve zero-shot 3D semantic mapping in offroad environments.

papers.abstract: Zero-Shot Multimodal Anomaly Detection (ZSMAD) aims to identify both appearance and geometric defects in novel categories without relying on target-specific training data, making it especially valuable in real-world scenarios constrained by data scarcity, privacy concerns, or high annotation costs. While recent approaches successfully adapt vision-language models like CLIP to achieve this open-vocabulary generalization, they still face significant challenges: (i) severe geometric information loss during 3D-to-2D point cloud rendering; (ii) spatially noisy 2D feature maps produced by raw CLIP patch embeddings, compounded by shallow late-stage modality fusion; and (iii) severe cross-modal semantic misalignment due to decoupled processing streams. To address these limitations, we propose AggCLIP, a novel framework that adapts frozen CLIP representations for ZSMAD by explicitly incorporating local geometric structure and visual spatial context. Specifically, to accurately localize fine-grained defects, we design a Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation (GSA) module that refines back-projected 3D point features via density-adaptive neighborhood weighting, alongside a Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CSA) module that smooths multi-scale 2D patch embeddings using a lightweight trainable adapter. Furthermore, to prevent semantic drift between modalities, we introduce a Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive (DSPC) loss, which aligns the abstract concepts of normality and abnormality across the point cloud and RGB streams. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed AggCLIP framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies benchmarks under both one-vs-rest and cross-dataset zero-shot settings, notably surpassing the strongest competitive methods by up to 2.9% in pixel-level AUPRO.
authors: Zhi Li, Hanyu Wang, Fei Shen, Zhengtao Zhang
bullets: Targets appearance and geometric defects in unseen categories without target-specific training data.
Uses Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation to refine 3D point features with density-adaptive neighborhoods.
Uses Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation to smooth multi-scale CLIP patch embeddings with a trainable adapter.
Introduces Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive loss to align normality and abnormality concepts across modalities.
Reports state-of-the-art results on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies, with up to 2.9% higher pixel-level AUPRO than competing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Paradigm comparison for zero-shot multimodal anomaly detection. (a) Existing ZSMAD pipelines typically suffer from three fundamental limitations: Geometric Loss during 3D-to-2D rendering, Spatial Noise and Weak Integration due to raw CLIP embeddings and simplistic late-fusion, and Semantic Misalignment between prompts and multimodal features. (b) The proposed AggCLIP framework effectively addresses these gaps. It refines noisy back-projected point features via the Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation (GSA) module, suppresses 2D spatial noise using Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CSA) paired with a learnable Adapter, and directly enforces deep cross-modal semantic interaction via the Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive (DSPC) loss.

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models for materials science rely on effective mechanisms for incorporating three-dimensional structural representations. MatterChat addresses this challenge using a large bridge module between a pretrained structural encoder and the LLM, together with a separate contrastive alignment stage. We instead ask whether this bridge can adaptively select and combine representations from multiple structural encoders according to the target property. We find that supervised and generative material encoders provide complementary information for property prediction. We found that, for Zatom-1, this information is not concentrated in the final layer. Instead, the most informative representations occur at different depths depending on the target property. This motivates Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF), a lightweight attention-based bridge that uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations. The bridge is trained directly on downstream prediction tasks, allowing representation selection and material-language alignment to be learned jointly without separate contrastive pretraining. Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, with up to 47.8% lower RMSE, while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and halving the overall training time. Further experiments incorporating UMA-S demonstrate TCAF's flexibility across encoder combinations, with the three-encoder configuration achieving the highest macro-average classification accuracy of 89.61%.
authors: Huu Binh Ta, Alex Morehead, N. Benjamin Erichson, Ferdinando Fioretto, Sandeep Madireddy
bullets: MatterChat uses a large bridge and separate contrastive alignment; this work instead learns representation selection jointly on downstream tasks.
Different target properties benefit from representations at different depths of Zatom-1, while CHGNet and Zatom-1 provide complementary information.
Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations.
Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, including up to 47.8% lower RMSE, with fewer trainable parameters and half the training time.
Adding UMA-S shows flexibility across encoder combinations; the three-encoder setup reaches 89.61% macro-average classification accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our proposed Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF) methodology. (a) Frozen domain encoders (Zatom-1 and CHGNet) extract complementary atom-level representations from a crystal structure. Here, features from all 16 Zatom-1 layers are retained, and CHGNet features are projected from 64 to 512 dimensions. (b) The property requested by the prompt selects a learned task residual, which is added to 32 latent queries. Two Perceiver blocks apply cross-attention to the structural features, followed by latent self-attention and a feed-forward network. These taskconditioned queries allow the bridge to weight encoder sources and layer depths differently for each property. (c) The fused latents are projected into the language-model embedding space and combined with prompt embeddings. A frozen language model then generates the response. The trainable components are optimized jointly using a downstream language-modeling objective.

papers.title: Choosing the Right Representations: Task-Aware Fusion for Multimodal Materials Language Models
papers.tldr: TCAF adaptively fuses task-relevant representations from multiple materials structure encoders, improving multimodal property prediction with fewer parameters and shorter training.

papers.abstract: Questions about long egocentric video often depend on one brief moment, such as the second a hand puts an object down. A vision-language model (VLM) that sees a few evenly spaced frames usually misses it. Training-free methods rank frames with a separate image-text model or ask the VLM to write a time. In a controlled test, the VLM itself locates the moment better when it chooses among labeled frames, and we read this choice from its output distribution. With the same candidates, this choice lands on the evidence more often than image-text scores or a written time span, and it compares all candidates in one decision. Based on this finding, we propose EgoJev, a training-free frame selector for wearable assistants. EgoJev reads where the evidence is from labeled thumbnails and looks again at the windows it points to. It places its few answer frames at the quantiles of the resulting distribution. One frozen VLM selects, answers and returns the evidence time, with no second model. A wearable device can encode its coarse thumbnails while it records. With Qwen3.5-4B and 8 answer frames, EgoJev raises QAEgo4D accuracy from 51.2% with uniform sampling to 62.0%, and it outperforms recent training-free frame selectors on QAEgo4D and MyEgo. A single-level version runs on a Mac and an iPhone.
bullets: Uniformly sampled frames often miss the short moments needed to answer egocentric-video questions.
The method reads the VLM’s output distribution when it chooses among labeled candidate frames, rather than asking for a written timestamp.
EgoJev revisits the selected temporal windows and places a small number of answer frames at distribution quantiles.
With Qwen3.5-4B and 8 answer frames, accuracy on QAEgo4D improves from 51.2% with uniform sampling to 62.0%.
The approach is training-free, runs with one frozen VLM, and has a single-level version for Mac and iPhone deployment.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses egocentric video understanding by reading VLM decisions, directly relevant to embodied AI and learning from human/egocentric video.
papers.title: EgoJev: Finding Evidence in Egocentric Video by Reading VLM Decisions
papers.tldr: EgoJev uses a frozen VLM’s labeled-frame choices to locate brief evidence in long egocentric videos, improving question-answering accuracy without training or a second model.

papers.abstract: Visual foundation models provide powerful representations for diverse tasks, but their features become stale as visual content changes between image observations. Refreshing them requires new frames and repeated runs of a computationally expensive image encoder. We introduce ALIVE, an event-based method that incrementally updates native foundation model features between image observations. Given an anchor image, ALIVE uses subsequent events to transport and correct existing multi-layer features extracted by a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Its lightweight updater is trained end-to-end using only synthetic data, without downstream task supervision, and transfers directly to real-world event streams without any adaptation. Across three real-world datasets and five task-dataset settings spanning object detection, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation, ALIVE outperforms all evaluated event-based methods in every metric. On DSEC, when the anchor frame is 200,ms old, ALIVE improves over anchor-image predictions by 30.9,mAP in detection, 11.6,mIoU in segmentation, and 15.9% in depth AbsRel. Compared with image re-encoding, ALIVE reduces FLOPs by 82.4% and latency by a factor of 2.5.
authors: Rong Zou, Haiqing Hao, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses feature staleness when visual content changes between image observations.
Uses events to incrementally transport and correct multi-layer DINOv3 features from an anchor image.
Trains a lightweight updater end-to-end on synthetic data without downstream-task supervision and transfers to real event streams without adaptation.
Across three real-world datasets and five task settings, it outperforms evaluated event-based methods for detection, segmentation, and depth estimation.
On DSEC with a 200 ms-old anchor, it improves anchor predictions by 30.9 mAP, 11.6 mIoU, and 15.9% AbsRel, while reducing FLOPs by 82.4% and latency 2.5× versus image re-encoding.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ALIVE. (a) Training uses synthetic RGB–event sequences. A frozen DINOv3 encodes every RGB frame: F0 initializes the feature state (with memory h0 = 0), and later frames provide teacher features Ft. For each event packet E(t−,t], the ALIVE updater Uθ predicts a displacement dt that transports both the features and the memory, a residual correction ∆t that yields Ut, and a signed, zero-sum 3× 3 kernel kt per token that refines Ut into F̂t. The ConvGRU memory ht conditions the residual and the refinement. All modules are trained jointly with feature-level losses only, without task labels or task heads. (b) The trained updater is applied without adaptation to real event streams. Moment matching aligns the per-channel statistics of F̂t with the anchor moments to produce the updated features F̄t, and frozen task heads trained on DINOv3 features of real RGB images read F̄t directly. Predictions are shown 200 ms after the anchor on DSEC, and detections are drawn on the RGB frame at that time for visualization only (C: car, P: person).

The top four rows show the anchor frame, the events between the anchor and the target time (red: positive, blue: negative), the target frame, and the ground truth. papers.selection_reason: Introduces an event-based method to incrementally update foundation model features (DINOv3) at inference time, addressing feature staleness and efficiency.
papers.title: ALIVE: Bring Foundation Features to Life with Events
papers.tldr: ALIVE efficiently keeps frozen visual foundation-model features current between image frames by using event streams, improving downstream vision tasks while avoiding repeated image encoding.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is moving from the harness of prompts and tools around a base model toward the model itself. However, existing RSI still faces key challenges, including harness-bound gains that stay outside the base model, black-box supervision that reads only the model's outputs, and imprecise edits whose site and strength are fixed in advance. To address these challenges, we propose BaseRSI, a new paradigm of Recursive Harness Internalization: the base model improves its harness, then writes what the harness adds into its own weights through training-free edits, round after round on its own responses. To support this paradigm, we introduce ReGap, a mechanism that supervises every transformer block with the high-dimensional activation difference that the harness makes at that block alone, and updates the block's weights along this signal in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this mechanism, we further propose ReKey, an algorithm that writes this signal by regression into a few key-value neurons of every block, and measures the site and strength of each edit on the model's own responses. Moreover, the base model fills every role of this recursion with forward passes alone, and its edits, written at different sites, compose in one checkpoint without refitting. Experimental results on ten visual reasoning benchmarks show that BaseRSI consistently improves a base vision-language model both in distribution and on held-out benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/BaseRSI.
authors: Mingda Zhang, Yuanhao Dong, Qiang Huang, Rui Qian, Yanjin Li, Zhenyu Liu, Xiao Huang, Zihao Yang, Jian Wang, Pinjia He, Xiaoying Tang
bullets: Addresses harness-bound gains, output-only supervision, and fixed edit locations or strengths in recursive self-improvement.
ReGap supervises each transformer block using the harness-induced activation difference and updates it in a low-dimensional subspace.
ReKey regresses these signals into a few key-value neurons per block while measuring edit site and strength from the model’s own responses.
The model performs all recursive roles using forward passes, and edits from different sites compose within one checkpoint.
Across ten visual reasoning benchmarks, BaseRSI improves the base model both in-distribution and on held-out benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of BaseRSI. Top: Recursive Harness Internalization runs an outer loop that evolves the harness and an inner loop in which the model with its harness teaches the model alone, round after round. Left: ReGap supervises every block with the teacher–student gap and keeps it as a low-dimensional update. Right: ReKey writes the gap into key–value neurons at a measured site and strength.

papers.abstract: Image-to-code methods for 3D scene reconstruction produce executable code that generates editable digital content and supports visual simulation. However, existing methods primarily rely on appearance similarity, which provides limited guidance for distinguishing errors in geometry, materials, and illumination. Light shapes scene appearance through its interactions with geometry and materials, influencing shading, cast shadows, and reflections. We therefore present LightHarness, a VLM-based agentic framework that incorporates explicit lighting reasoning into iterative scene reconstruction. To be specific, we leverage complementary geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues to jointly refine scene structure and appearance, and propose Lighting Reasoning Memory to maintain light-source hypotheses, which supports evidence, and revision history throughout iterations. Together, they support reasoning about partially visible and unseen sources, with evidence-guided verification directing subsequent revisions. Our framework reconstructs explicit scenes through coherent reasoning about geometry, materials, and illumination without additional training or differentiable rendering. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior image-to-code reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, further supporting downstream scene editing, object insertion, and versatile relighting.
authors: Zeting Luo, Yifan Li, Shuai Yang
bullets: Addresses the limits of appearance-only guidance for diagnosing geometry, material, and illumination errors.
Combines geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues during iterative scene refinement.
Uses Lighting Reasoning Memory to track light-source hypotheses, evidence, and revision history, including partially visible or unseen sources.
Requires no additional training or differentiable rendering.
Reports improved reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, with benefits for editing, object insertion, and relighting.

papers.abstract: Multimodal knowledge graph reasoning (MKGR) aims to infer missing facts by jointly exploiting relational structures, textual descriptions, and visual evidence. Existing embedding-based methods effectively capture graph topology, but their fixed multimodal representations are less effective for query-specific fine-grained semantic reasoning, while generation-based methods are vulnerable to noisy retrieval and may produce invalid entities. To address these challenges, we propose NaviGATE, a noise-aware generative framework for MKGR. NaviGATE first aligns graph-derived structural representations with textual semantics, then performs structure-aware internal knowledge activation by fine-tuning the multimodal language model with multimodal entity summaries and injected structural tokens. In the noise-aware dual-view instruction tuning stage, NaviGATE jointly optimizes retrieval-free and retrieval-aware views: reliable retrieved candidates are reinforced through contrastive logit sharpening, while misleading candidates are suppressed through parametric consistency distillation. In inference, structure-constrained decoding restricts generation to valid entities in the target knowledge graph. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that NaviGATE consistently outperforms strong unimodal, multimodal, and generation-based baselines, and remains robust under noisy retrieval scenarios.
authors: Jie Peng, Yongxue Shan, Yongfu Zha, Cui Miao, Xiaodong Wang
bullets: Addresses the limits of fixed multimodal embeddings and noisy, invalid outputs from generative MKGR methods.
Aligns graph structure with text and activates internal knowledge using multimodal entity summaries and structural tokens.
Jointly trains retrieval-free and retrieval-aware views, reinforcing reliable candidates and suppressing misleading ones.
Uses structure-constrained decoding to restrict predictions to entities valid in the target knowledge graph.
Outperforms strong unimodal, multimodal, and generative baselines and remains robust under noisy retrieval.

papers.abstract: Industrial anomaly detection plays a pivotal role in precision manufacturing, where joint analysis of multimodal data emerges as a critical approach to enhance detection accuracy. Feature reconstruction, a dominant paradigm for such joint analysis, is primarily implemented through intra-modal and cross-modal methods, both of which are plagued by significant limitations. Intra-modal reconstruction neglects complementary cross-modal information, while its cross-modal counterpart is prone to projection errors and ambiguous one-to-many mappings (e.g., same textures mapping to multiple geometries), leading to detection failures. To address these limitations, we propose a novel feature reconstruction paradigm, Fuse Before Reconstruct (FBR), which first fuses multimodal features and then performs reconstruction for anomaly detection. Firstly, we propose a bidirectional cross-modal attention mechanism to achieve deep feature complementarity between image and point cloud features, mitigating projection bias through channel alignment and dynamic spatial prior integration. Besides, a learnable pixel-wise gated fusion strategy is adopted to preserve multi-modal structural consistency while optimizing local feature combination. Finally, dual-path collaborative reconstruction is implemented to recover original modal features from the fused representations, where cross-modal consistency constraints effectively eliminate mapping ambiguities. Extensive experiments show that FBR achieves 98.3% I-AUROC on MVTec 3D-AD and 92.6% I-AUROC on Eyecandies, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods by +2.9% and +4.1%, respectively.
authors: Zhi Li, Hanyu Wang, Qiyu Chen, Fei Shen, Zhengtao Zhang
bullets: Addresses weaknesses of intra-modal reconstruction and cross-modal reconstruction, including missed complementary information, projection bias, and ambiguous mappings.
Uses bidirectional cross-modal attention with channel alignment and dynamic spatial priors to combine image and point-cloud features.
Applies learnable pixel-wise gated fusion to preserve structural consistency and optimize local multimodal feature combinations.
Uses dual-path collaborative reconstruction with cross-modal consistency constraints to recover the original modalities.
Reports 98.3% I-AUROC on MVTec 3D-AD and 92.6% on Eyecandies, improvements of 2.9 and 4.1 percentage points over prior state-of-the-art methods, respectively.

These features undergo initial fusion through the BiCMA, followed by gated fusion refinement via the SGAF to produce the final fused representation Ffinal.
