papers.abstract: Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) aims to disambiguate mentions in multimodal contexts by grounding them to specific entities in a knowledge base. A pivotal challenge in MEL is capturing multi-level correspondences: the semantic consistency between mention-entity pairs and the complementary correlations across modalities. However, existing methods often suffer from element dominance due to their reliance on coupled interactions or coarse global aggregations. In response, we propose the Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction (MECI) framework. First, to capture multi-element mention-entity correspondences, we develop a Multi-view Experts Network that leverages a "divide-and-conquer" strategy for decoupled feature learning to mitigate element dominance, supported by a KL-guided routing mechanism that governs expert specialization and collaboration. Furthermore, to model cross-modal complementary correlations, we propose a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module, where a dynamic modality-aware weighting network refines interactions across hierarchical semantic levels, thereby integrating multi-granular evidence to counteract element dominance. Finally, we incorporate a generative semantic refinement stage that utilizes large language models for zero-shot re-ranking. Extensive experiments on WikiDiverse, RichpediaMEL, and WikiMEL show that MECI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving Hits@1 by 1.95%, 7.30%, and 2.31%, respectively.
authors: Jie Peng, Yongxue Shan, Yongfu Zha, Xiaodong Wang
bullets: Addresses element dominance caused by coupled interactions and coarse multimodal aggregation.
Uses a Multi-view Experts Network with decoupled feature learning and KL-guided expert routing.
Introduces hierarchical multimodal interactions with dynamic modality-aware weighting.
Adds zero-shot generative semantic refinement for final re-ranking.
Improves Hits@1 by 1.95%, 7.30%, and 2.31% on WikiDiverse, RichpediaMEL, and WikiMEL, respectively.

papers.abstract: Text prompted 3D computed tomography (CT) segmentation requires both full slice context and fine boundary precision across volumes where over $80\%$ of organ prompted slices lack the queried target. Existing medical vision language models (VLMs) are largely non native segmenters: they delegate pixel delineation outside the VLM by compressing reasoning into a 1D [SEG] vector for an external Segment Anything Model (SAM) decoder, quantizing masks into lossy discrete codebooks, or issuing box prompts to stateless external SAM tools without empty slice screening or spatial state memory. We introduce NativeSeg, a native vision language segmentation framework on Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapted Qwen3.8-27B that performs dense mask decoding, volumetric triage, spatial error self diagnosis, and multiround local zoom directly over the VLM's 2D spatial visual tokens without external SAM decoders. NativeSeg decodes confidence maps from upper layer 2D spatial tokens fused with a five slice U-Net pathway, halts at zero zooms on $>91\%$ of standalone evaluations via a native presence gate ( ), localizes uncertain boundaries via a 20 cell multiscale error gate ( ), and accepts zoomed updates only when predicted error decreases. Trained solely on adult CT, NativeSeg improves Round $0$ DSC by $+19.81$ and $+7.04$ points over discrete codebook and 1D [SEG] readouts on the identical backbone, reaches $86.81\%$ adult and $87.04\%$ zero shot pediatric DSC, and safely refines 2D nnU-Net ($89.52\%$ adult; $86.86\%$ pediatric), 3D SegVol ($86.81\%$), and 3D VoxTell ($89.85\%$).
authors: Chengqian Ma, Gaole Dai, Zijie Meng, Weixuan Jin, Yijie Du, Yuexiao Ma, Xiawu Zheng, Fei Chao
bullets: Addresses missing-target slices and boundary imprecision in text-prompted 3D CT segmentation.
Uses a LoRA-adapted Qwen3.8-27B with dense mask decoding from 2D spatial visual tokens plus a five-slice U-Net pathway.
Performs volumetric triage, spatial error diagnosis, and multiround zooming, accepting refinements only when predicted error decreases.
On adult CT, achieves 86.81% DSC and 87.04% zero-shot pediatric DSC; it also safely refines several existing segmentation systems.
Scope is limited by training solely on adult CT, despite the reported pediatric zero-shot evaluation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about long interleaved inputs, such as documents of many pages and collections of hundreds of images, but they are slow to start: on inputs of about 100K tokens, the prefill takes most of the wait for the first output token. A common approach prunes the input by scoring its tokens with the target model itself or with a small model of the same family that first writes an answer. However, this scoring takes much of the time that pruning saves. We find that the evidence for a question lies in a few whole units (images or paragraphs), and that a small hybrid model finds them with one attention head of an early layer, even at half image resolution. Based on these findings, we propose SkimPrefill, which lets the small hybrid model read the whole input first, up to that early layer, with images at half resolution. Most layers of the small hybrid model (Qwen3.5-0.8B) run in linear time, so this pass is short. SkimPrefill then ranks every unit with that head and gives the target the top units as an ordinary shorter prompt. One untrained selector serves targets of different model families. Extensive experiments on MMLongBench at 128K tokens, with 19 datasets of five task types, show the effectiveness of SkimPrefill. With 10% of the input tokens kept, SkimPrefill speeds up the prefill of Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3-VL-32B by 3.7 times, 11.6 time and 8.2 times while maintaining their average accuracy.
authors: Xiaolin Lin, Kai-Chiang Wu, Bing Li, Grace Li Zhang
bullets: Targets the high first-token latency caused by prefill on roughly 100K-token interleaved image-text inputs.
Uses an early attention head in a small hybrid model, with images at half resolution, to rank whole input units.
Keeps the top 10% of tokens/units and feeds them to the target VLM as a shorter ordinary prompt.
A single untrained selector transfers across different target model families.
On MMLongBench at 128K tokens, it maintains average accuracy while reporting 3.7×, 11.6×, and 8.2× prefill speedups for three target models.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems have been shown to suffer from shortcut learning and causal confusion, limiting their ability to generalize robustly under distribution shift. To mitigate these limitations, recent works based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have explored incorporating linguistic reasoning capabilities into driving decision-making, reporting improvements in driving performance. In particular, counterfactual (CF) reasoning has been proposed to enable self-reflective, high-level causal understanding. However, it remains unclear whether the language-based reasoning mitigates shortcut learning or merely shifts it from visual representations to linguistic patterns, creating an illusion of causal understanding. Moreover, existing approaches often conflate intervention-based reasoning with CF reasoning, leaving the effects of genuine CF reasoning unexplored. In this work, we examine what CF reasoning actually induces in VLM-based autonomous driving and observe that it shifts the action distribution toward more conservative behaviors while increasing uncertainty in reasoning and decision-making. This effect persists under reinforcement fine-tuning, suggesting that it is not merely a transient artifact. Furthermore, visual attention analysis shows that CF reasoning does not alter visual grounding, while causal intervention experiments reveal that masking causally relevant and non-causal factors in accident scenarios results in comparable decision change rates. Overall, these results suggest that CF reasoning does not induce genuine causal reasoning grounded in visual evidence. Instead, it acts as a linguistic shortcut that reshapes the action distribution, teaching models what to say but not how to reason, highlighting a gap between language-based reasoning and causal understanding in autonomous driving.
bullets: VLM-based driving systems may shift shortcut learning from visual features to linguistic reasoning patterns.
CF reasoning makes actions more conservative and increases reasoning and decision-making uncertainty.
The effect persists after reinforcement fine-tuning, indicating it is not merely transient.
Visual attention is largely unchanged, and masking causal versus non-causal factors produces comparable decision changes.
The study highlights a gap between language-based reasoning and true causal understanding in driving.

papers.abstract: Active visual reasoning enables multimodal models to answer challenging visual questions by gathering fine-grained evidence through iterative image inspection and tool use. However, accumulating crops and reasoning tokens expands the key-value (KV) cache, making compression important for reducing memory and inference costs. Existing KV compression methods typically select historical tokens based on attention, recency, or redundancy. These criteria do not explicitly distinguish locally replaced evidence from complementary information needed for future exploration: each crop refreshes a local region, while earlier views may still support subsequent decisions. Discarding such evidence can impair accuracy or require additional search, while scoring and cache reorganization can offset the computational savings from compression. We introduce CanopyKV, a training-free KV compression framework that uses parent-child crop relationships to retain complementary evidence, keeps retained history stable, and protects the state needed for ongoing reasoning. Tool metadata provides retention signals without additional attention scoring, while compact KV storage reduces subsequent attention costs. Across VisualProbe, V*, HR-Bench, and MME-Lite, CanopyKV achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and end-to-end efficiency among the evaluated KV compression methods. On MME-Lite, it retains approximately one-quarter of Dense's total KV while improving accuracy by 10.5 percentage points and accelerating complete reasoning by $1.64\times$.
authors: Lei Yang, Dayan Wu, Yiliang Zhu, Xinze Liu, Hengjie Zhu, Zihao Zhang, Ding Wang, Peng Fu, Zheng Lin
bullets: Active visual reasoning accumulates crop and reasoning tokens, causing KV-cache growth and higher memory and inference costs.
Existing compression criteria may discard earlier views that remain useful for future exploration, especially when crops replace only local evidence.
CanopyKV uses parent–child crop relationships and tool metadata to retain complementary history, stabilize retained tokens, and protect ongoing reasoning state.
It avoids additional attention-based scoring and reduces subsequent attention costs through compact KV storage.

Across four evaluated benchmarks, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and end-to-end efficiency among the compared KV-compression methods; on MME-Lite, it retains about one-quarter of Dense’s KV, improves accuracy by 10.5 percentage points, and speeds reasoning by 1.64×.

papers.abstract: Scientific figures carry evidence for the claims that cite them, so reviewing a paper means checking that a figure agrees with the text, and not only describing what the figure shows. Benchmarks of figure-text verification typically hand the model the figure, the claim, or the knowledge that an inconsistency exists, which leaves untested whether a model can find the figure worth checking in a complete paper, relate a visual element to the claim it conflicts with, and recognize the conflict. We study this autonomous setting on 31 full manuscripts, each carrying a reviewer-documented figure-text inconsistency from PRISMM-Bench that is hidden from the model. Six multimodal models review each PDF under a neutral prompt, and we then add one input at a time to the same manuscripts. Of 1,445 open-ended reviews, 60.6% mention the flawed figure, yet a grading rubric accepts only 3.3% as diagnosing its contradiction; a blind audit finds the rubric lenient, so we read these as rubric-accepted rates and compare conditions rather than absolute values. In a separate controlled run, naming the figure, without stating that it is flawed, raises rubric-accepted diagnosis from 4.3% to 20.4%, while a consistency instruction and coarse visual cues do not. When the contradiction is visible only in the rendered figure, text-only review yields no accepted diagnosis, while review of the rendered pages with the figure named reaches 15.8%. A baseline that lets the model choose which figures to check, ranked by centrality, stays at 4.8%. Deciding what to verify is thus a large part of the difficulty, and the selection rule we tested does not resolve it. Multimodal document understanding should be evaluated on whether a model can propose what to verify, not only answer questions about a figure it is handed.
authors: Guijia Zhang, Hongbo Qiu, Jiajun Zha, Guohao Cai, Hao Zheng, Huihao Jing, Kexu Cheng, Shipeng Luo, JinYang Huang, Shing-Chi Cheung, Changsheng Lu, Haoxuan Che, Harry Yang
bullets: The study evaluates six multimodal models reviewing 31 full scientific manuscripts with hidden, reviewer-documented inconsistencies.

Contradictions visible only in rendered figures receive no accepted diagnoses from text-only review, versus 15.8% when the figure is named and pages are rendered.
A centrality-based figure-selection baseline reaches only 4.8%, highlighting the difficulty of autonomously selecting evidence to verify.

papers.abstract: Embodied AI systems, such as drones and autonomous vehicles, improve navigation by enhancing perception in environments containing unseen objects. While Visual Language Models (VLMs) offer strong image understanding, their real-world application is underexplored. For effective deployment, open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) models, leveraging models like CLIP to assign pixel-level labels from text, must be robust to outdoor conditions, adverse weather, and varying viewpoints. Despite their potential, these models encounter significant challenges in cross-domain generalization, hindering their practical use in embodied AI applications. In this work, we present Pixel2Perspective, a benchmark for multi-angle object localization and open-vocabulary segmentation across both aerial and ground perspectives. This benchmark supports thorough evaluation across different viewpoints and sensor modalities. We assess foundational models like CLIP and advanced OVSS models using a curated dataset that spans varied outdoor conditions, sim-to-real scenarios, and multiple sensors, including infrared, to support the development of robust and generalizable perception systems. We also present a novel framework, Multi-Source RGB-IR Uncertainty Quantification (MSRIQ), which jointly models aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties across RGB and infrared imagery. This approach supports robust evaluation of open-vocabulary segmentation models across diverse environmental conditions. Our work sets a robustness-driven benchmark, providing key insights and laying the foundation for future research in open-world embodied AI perception. The benchmark and project page are available at https://aniruddhsikdar1.github.io/publications/pixel2perspective/
authors: Aditya Gandhamal, Aniruddh Sikdar, Arya Kishor, Suresh Sundaram
bullets: Targets robust perception for embodied AI in unseen objects, adverse weather, cross-domain settings, and changing viewpoints.

Introduces Multi-Source RGB-IR Uncertainty Quantification (MSRIQ) to model aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty jointly.
Provides a robustness-focused foundation for evaluating and improving open-world embodied-AI perception.

papers.abstract: Domain adaptation for semantic segmentation is challenging when target-domain images are unavailable during training. Zero-shot domain adaptation addresses this by adapting models using only textual descriptions of the target domain. However, existing prompt-learning methods are not well suited for ResNet-based CLIP vision backbones or pixel-level cross-modal feature alignment. We propose CROMPT, a prompt-learning framework for zero-shot domain adaptation in semantic segmentation. CROMPT introduces Cross-Modal Feature Augmentation (CROMA), combining Random Visual Prompting with Hybrid Textual Prompting (HTP) to jointly adapt visual and textual representations. We further propose CROMA-VL, which leverages vision-language models to generate domain-conditioned prompts, and a progressive easy-to-hard adaptation strategy for improved domain invariance. Experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods, achieving 1.63-2.63% mIoU gains while maintaining inference-time complexity. These results establish CROMPT as an effective and efficient framework for zero-shot multi-domain semantic segmentation. OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=FxqFsIL685
authors: Aniruddh Sikdar, Arya Kishor, Snehashis Dhibar, Suresh Sundaram
bullets: Addresses zero-shot domain adaptation when target-domain images are unavailable during training.

Adds CROMA-VL for vision-language-model-generated, domain-conditioned prompts and a progressive easy-to-hard adaptation strategy.
Improves mIoU by 1.63–2.63% over strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods on two benchmark datasets.
Maintains inference-time complexity, supporting efficient zero-shot multi-domain segmentation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) reason about long videos over hundreds to thousands of tokens. Every decoding step re-reads the key-value (KV) cache of the entire video. Must the model keep looking while it reasons? In LookAway, the model first writes timestamped notes on what the question needs and then puts the video away. Once the notes close, the inference engine hides the video's KV cache for the rest of the response. Across both hybrid and pure-attention VLMs, dependence on the video is concentrated early in the response. On Qwen3.6-27B, writing notes preserves accuracy better than free reasoning at the same withdrawal step. Replacing them with another video's notes harms accuracy, whereas keeping the video visible alongside the model's own notes adds no significant benefit. Without additional training, LookAway nearly matches full-video thinking accuracy at 0.12-0.13 times its modeled decode cost. To shorten this initial look, we fine-tune the model on its own correct LookAway responses. Reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers while penalizing KV reads. The trained model puts the video away after a median of 66-68 tokens. Across three held-out benchmarks, it writes more tokens than an identically trained full-video model yet reads only 27-35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy.

Without extra training, LookAway nearly matches full-video accuracy at 0.12–0.13× the modeled decode cost.
With fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, the model withdraws after a median of 66–68 tokens and reads 27–35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy across three held-out benchmarks.

papers.title: Do Thinking VLMs Need to Keep Looking at Long Videos? Write It Down, Then Look Away

papers.abstract: Vision-language generation has predominantly relied on autoregressive and discrete diffusion models. Autoregressive models generate tokens sequentially, while discrete diffusion models typically predict tokens independently within each denoising step. We propose ViLFlow (Vision-Language Flow), a continuous-flow vision-language model that combines joint modeling of output embeddings with parallel token decoding. ViLFlow adapts pretrained continuous language generation to visual question answering and image captioning through learned image guidance and prediction-aware token decoding. A visually adapted teacher provides image-guided predictions as additional denoising supervision. The denoiser learns to reproduce these predictions directly, retaining one image-conditioned prediction per generation step. We train the token decoder on denoiser predictions and paired reference text to improve the conversion of continuous outputs into words. The decoder can be adapted independently, improving answering and captioning without further denoiser training. For captioning, it also supplies text feedback during late denoising, allowing decoded words to inform subsequent refinement. ViLFlow outperforms autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines by up to 8.46 percentage points on VQAv2 and 4.50 points on GQA without GQA training. On COCO Karpathy test, it improves CIDEr by 16.25 over masked diffusion and 17.81 over sampled autoregression.
authors: Kevin Zhai, Bian Sun, Zhenyi Wang, Song Wang
bullets: Addresses the sequential decoding of autoregressive models and independent per-step prediction in discrete diffusion models.
Jointly models output embeddings with parallel token decoding using learned image guidance and prediction-aware decoding.
Uses a visually adapted teacher for image-guided denoising supervision and trains a decoder to convert continuous predictions into words.
The decoder can be adapted independently; for captioning, decoded text also provides feedback during late denoising.
Reports gains of up to 8.46 points on VQAv2, 4.50 points on GQA, and 16.25 CIDEr over masked diffusion on COCO Karpathy test.

papers.abstract: Video world models keep the world in the context of a generator, so a revisit is synthesized again and earlier edits can drift or disappear. We present WM^MLLM, the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), for persistent, editable world generation from a single image. WM^MLLM keeps the world state outside every generator, as a panorama with a revision history, and lets the MLLMs write it: they turn each request into operations on this state, select where a local edit is written, and check every candidate before it becomes the next state. Image generators only propose views, and video only presents them. Users can walk to new places and return, edit objects through text or a box, place subjects, and change lighting, weather or season. By construction, a revisit at the same revision reproduces the earlier view exactly, a local edit leaves every panorama pixel outside its region unchanged, and each request starts from the result of the previous one. Against six world model baselines on MBench-A, WM^MLLM has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics (Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0) and completes the most camera round trips (85.3% versus at most 50.9%). It has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns against 15 baselines. On 112 local edits judged blind, selecting the region to write after generation raises completion from 34.8% to 83.0%. On 258 WBench and MBench-A items, all 46 revisits recover their earlier views, and all 97 local edits that pass the check leave panorama pixels outside their region unchanged.
authors: Baiang Li, Enze Xie, Jincheng Yu, Jin Wang, Haozhe Liu, Yitong Li, Juanxi Tian, Felix Heide
bullets: Maintains world state outside the generator as a panorama with revision history, preventing revisit drift and preserving prior edits.
Uses MLLMs to translate requests into state operations, select edit regions, and validate generated candidates before updating the world.
Supports navigation, text- or box-based object edits, subject placement, and changes to lighting, weather, and season.
Reports the strongest results across stated environment-recovery and editing benchmarks, including consistent revisits and region-preserving edits.
Scope is single-image initialization with generated views serving presentation rather than state storage.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models increasingly rely on textual reasoning to solve advanced multimodal tasks. Despite its effectiveness, this paradigm faces two fundamental limitations. First, relying on textual reasoning alone can limit perceptual ability in vision-centric questions, where accurate answers depend on interpreting task-relevant visual evidence. Second, applying textual reasoning uniformly across inputs overlooks question-dependent variation in both reasoning modality and depth, often producing verbose and unnecessary traces when little logical inference is required. To this end, we propose Adaptive Visual-Textual Reasoning (AVTR), which introduces visual imagination as a complementary reasoning modality to textual thinking, enabling the model to revisit its visual observations and distill the salient evidence through generative visual reflection. Furthermore, we formulate reasoning-modality selection as a learned routing problem, allowing a single policy to adaptively harness the complementary strengths of visual reflection and textual reasoning in response to the perceptual and inferential demands of the input. Across 16 benchmarks, AVTR improves the average score by 4.5 points over Qwen3.5 baseline, while reducing inference latency by 33\%. It also scales effectively into a smaller size backbone, outperforming the evaluated 2B-scale baselines.
authors: Xiaoqian Shen, Yunyang Xiong, Changsheng Zhao, Saksham Suri, Chong Zhou, Zechun Liu, Zhipeng Cai, Zhuang Liu, Qi Qian, Wei Wen, Hongyu Xu, Hanxian Huang, Ernie Chang, Yanbei Chen, Vikas Chandra, Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi, Mohamed Elhoseiny, Lemeng Wu

Uses generative visual imagination to revisit observations and distill task-relevant visual evidence.
Learns to route each input between visual and textual reasoning based on its perceptual and inferential demands.
Across 16 benchmarks, improves the average score by 4.5 points over the Qwen3.5 baseline and reduces inference latency by 33%.
Also scales effectively to a smaller backbone, outperforming the evaluated 2B-scale baselines.

The connector and generator provide training-only supervision and are removed at inference. papers.abstract: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game environments and players to collect diverse and verifiable gameplay experience at scale. In the Game2Player loop, a Builder agent adapts existing web games, exposes their internal state, and defines tasks with state-based progress measures and success checks. A Coding Player and a VLM Player then attempt the tasks and report problems to the Builder for repair, so that play serves as both environment validation and training data collection. With Game2Player, we build 568 verified web games with 3,436 tasks, collect 15.7K trajectories (307 hours of gameplay), and hold out 50 games as the benchmark PlayerBench. To evaluate the collected experience as training data, we train VLM agents with progress-weighted SFT, assigning greater weight to steps that advance task progress. Game2Player-9B improves progress from 14.3% to 31.2% on PlayerBench and from 30.0% to 53.1% on the external GameWorld benchmark. More broadly, our work suggests a path for visual agents to scale their gameplay experience by building, verifying, and learning from existing game worlds.
authors: Xirui Jiang, Yuxi Chen, Rui Yang, Feng Luo, Pengcheng Wang, Bingxuan Li, Zihao Zhao, Yushan Li, Han Wang, Manling Li, Yang Zhang, Shiyu Chang, Tong Zhang, Huan Zhang

Produces 568 verified games, 3,436 tasks, 15.7K trajectories, and the 50-game PlayerBench benchmark.

papers.abstract: Training-free open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) has made strong progress by adapting CLIP-like representations to dense prediction, but its remaining errors are often local, structured, and tied to the active label space. A successful correction must be visually plausible, legal under the target vocabulary, and executable in the segmentation score field. We propose SEER, a training-free test-time repair layer for Semantic Evidence and Executable Region propagation. SEER casts post-prediction OVSS repair as evidence-conditioned label propagation. The OVSS score space proposes compact candidate labels, a frozen VLM verifies closed-set regional evidence, and an execution gate certifies whether the evidence is legally and semantically actionable. The accepted label is then propagated by an OVSS-side policy: coherent high-confidence regions allow broad propagation, while object- or boundary-risk cases use conservative score-grounded propagation. Across eight standard OVSS benchmarks, SEER reaches 58.0 average mIoU without updating OVSS weights. Matched-input controls isolate the repair mechanism, while resource measurements report the cost of the complete frozen system.
authors: Junyang Chen, Xiao Li, Yiguo Qiao, Wenbin Li
bullets: Targets local, structured OVSS errors that depend on the active label vocabulary.
Uses OVSS scores to propose candidate labels and a frozen vision-language model to verify regional semantic evidence.
An execution gate accepts only evidence that is both vocabulary-legal and actionable in the segmentation score field.
Applies broad propagation to coherent high-confidence regions and conservative score-grounded propagation near objects or boundaries.
Achieves 58.0 average mIoU across eight standard OVSS benchmarks without updating OVSS weights; controls and resource measurements assess the repair mechanism and full-system cost.

papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly deploy downloaded open-weight GUI agents. A backdoored agent passes acceptance tests on clean data and misbehaves only when a visual trigger appears on screen, turning an unvetted checkpoint into a supply-chain risk. However, existing sample-level detectors target image classifiers and CLIP-style encoders, leaving step-level backdoor detection for GUI agents unaddressed. On clean steps, the instruction drives the action; when an unreferenced screen region hijacks the step, the instruction loses control over the decision state or that region dictates it instead. We term this signature intent--evidence dominance inversion and propose IDEA (Intent-Dominance Evidence Audit) to detect backdoor activation at inference time for each step without trigger knowledge or attack data. Specifically, Intent Counterfactual Probing (ICP) measures how far redirected instructions move the decision state, and Region Causal Audit (RCA) quantifies how far ablating a candidate region moves it. A gated conformal score compares both displacements against clean steps at the same distance from the clean manifold, providing a finite-sample false-positive guarantee. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B across five attack families show that IDEA consistently detects backdoor activation under a controlled false-positive rate and outperforms state-of-the-art detection methods, while localizing the trigger region for every alarm and adding only modest inference overhead.
authors: Zhizhuo Kou, Sizai Hou, Jian Yang, Ge Sun, Junyu Luo, Wenkai Zhang, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Addresses step-level backdoor detection for open-weight GUI agents, which existing image- and CLIP-focused detectors do not cover.
Uses Intent Counterfactual Probing to measure instruction influence and Region Causal Audit to measure candidate-region influence.
A gated conformal score compares these effects with clean steps at comparable manifold distances, providing a finite-sample false-positive guarantee.
Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B across five attack families report consistent detection at controlled false-positive rates, trigger localization, and modest overhead.
Scope: detection is performed per step without trigger knowledge or attack data; the abstract does not specify detailed quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Reliable lithology interpretation requires accurate geological recognition and reasoning grounded in visual evidence. Although Multimodal Large Language Models show promise in remote sensing, their reliability in geological interpretation remains unclear. We introduce HyGeoBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 10,000 questions based on hyperspectral imagery across three dimensions: reasoning reliability, prior_evidence contrast, and spectral discrimination. It covers ten task types, with both multiple-choice and open-ended response formats. Integrating hyperspectral satellite imagery with geological annotations and verified evidence, HyGeoBench examines reasoning errors, conflicts between geological priors and visual evidence, and cross-band inconsistencies. Evaluations reveal limitations in fine-grained recognition and evidence-grounded interpretation. To address these challenges, we propose HyGeoAgent, a tool-augmented framework integrating region observation, text knowledge retrieval, same-band image retrieval, and native PCA analysis through adaptive tool use. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over the corresponding base models, improving geological image interpretation across diagnostic dimensions.
authors: Jun Wang, Fengpeng Li, Wei Han, Yuxuan Li, Tianjin Huang, Jining Yan, Sheng Wang, Kan Sun, Lizhe Wang
bullets: Introduces a 10,000-question hyperspectral benchmark spanning reasoning reliability, prior–evidence contrast, and spectral discrimination.
Covers ten task types with multiple-choice and open-ended formats, using geological annotations and verified evidence.
Finds limitations in fine-grained lithology recognition, evidence grounding, and consistency across spectral bands.
Proposes HyGeoAgent, combining region observation, text retrieval, same-band image retrieval, and native PCA analysis.
Reports consistent improvements over corresponding base models across the benchmark’s diagnostic dimensions.

papers.abstract: High-resolution visual question answering (VQA) requires models to identify question-relevant small objects in high-resolution images and select the correct answer based on what they recognize, demanding fine-grained perception. Previous methods focus on obtaining better visual evidence (image crops), but obtaining it alone is insufficient, using it effectively is equally crucial. Visual evidence should therefore be utilized as effectively as possible throughout inference. We argue that small-target evidence is obscured by unconditional information that remains observable in subsequent processing even after the condition on which it should depend is removed. Such information hinders the effective use of small-target evidence. We propose R$^{3}$Sieve (Residual-Region-Response Sieve), a training-free framework. We divide inference into three stages---localization, cropping, and answering---and introduce distinct counterfactual references to suppress interference at each stage. During localization, the Shared-Subspace Canceller (SSC) uses a generic image description to construct a counterfactual reference and obtain question-relevant attention maps. During cropping, the Unique-Contribution Spotter (UCS) constructs counterfactual references from visual and non-visual features to identify distinctive, complementary crop regions. During answering, the Content-Aligned Voter (CAV) constructs an image-free branch to calibrate answer responses. Experiments on three high-resolution VQA benchmarks show that R$^{3}$Sieve achieves the highest overall accuracy among compared methods across diverse settings, improving base models by up to 21.5 percentage points.
authors: Yifan Cao, Yawen Zhang, Xiaocui Yang, Faxian Wan, Shi Feng, Daling Wang, Yifei Zhang, Shangshu Yu, Xianbing Zhao
bullets: Targets the problem that small-object evidence can be obscured by unconditional information during inference.
Uses counterfactual references across three stages: SSC for question-relevant localization, UCS for complementary crop selection, and CAV for answer calibration.
Evaluated on three high-resolution VQA benchmarks across diverse settings.
Reports the highest overall accuracy among compared methods, improving base models by up to 21.5 percentage points.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Overview of R3Sieve. Each module removes the unconditional information of one stage with a counterfactual reference. Figure 2. Comparison of high-resolution VQA approaches. (a) Training-based methods acquire visual evidence. (b) Search-based methods locate relevant regions iteratively. (c) Attention-based methods guide cropping with attention signals. (d) Our R3Sieve uses all-stage counterfactual filtering to suppress unconditional information during localization, cropping, and answering, improving evidence utilization.
Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of BVS and our contribution scoring. BVS often highlights irrelevant regions, while our method better focuses on the queried targets.

R3Sieve suppresses interference during localization (SSC), cropping (UCS), and answering (CAV), progressively reducing distractor responses and strengthening target responses (bottom), yielding the correct answer.

papers.abstract: CLIP-style contrastive image-text pretraining is widely used in radiology data, where each image is paired with one report and every other report in the batch is treated as a negative. Under this recipe, two failures appear, neither of which is systematically addressed by existing contrastive learning theory: zero-shot evaluation peaks then degrades while training loss keeps decreasing, and training fails to learn from large batches. We hypothesize the cause is structural rather than radiology-specific: many unpaired reports share clinical findings with a given image, so CLIP's paired-identity target is systematically biased, not merely noisy. To test this, we construct CLEVR-Radiology, a synthetic testbed that preserves only this overlapping-fact structure and reproduces both failures. With evidence that the structure is sufficient to reproduce the failures, we develop a target-misspecification theory that explains both failures from a single deterministic gradient bias amplified by batch size, and use it to motivate a minimal compatibility-based correction, CorLIP: text is treated as positive whenever its clinical assertions agree with the image, with no architecture changes. Beyond benchmark improvements, CorLIP largely removes the post-peak degradation, makes large-batch training succeed where it previously collapsed, substantially amplifies the gains from more data, and is the only configuration that remains stable up to B=2048. The correction transfers from chest X-ray to 3D CT modalities.
authors: Yunhe Gao, Ashwin Kumar, Jiaming Liu, Chong Wang, Maya Varma, Fuying Wang, Stefania L. Moroianu, Louisa Fay, Sergios Gatidis, Akshay S. Chaudhari, Curtis Langlotz
bullets: The paired-identity contrastive target causes zero-shot performance to decline despite decreasing training loss and prevents effective learning from large batches.
A synthetic CLEVR-Radiology testbed shows that overlapping clinical facts alone reproduce both failures, indicating a structural rather than radiology-specific issue.
The authors explain the failures through a deterministic, batch-size-amplified gradient bias from target misspecification.
CorLIP treats reports whose clinical assertions agree with an image as positives without changing the model architecture.
CorLIP reduces post-peak degradation, enables stable large-batch training, improves data scaling, remains stable up to B=2048, and transfers from chest X-rays to 3D CT.

papers.selection_reason: Contrastive vision-language pretraining with a theoretical correction to CLIP-style targets; transferable to multimodal foundation model training.
papers.title: Rethinking Contrastive Targets in Radiology Language-Image Pretraining
papers.tldr: CLIP-style radiology pretraining fails because reports with matching clinical findings are mislabeled as negatives, and CorLIP corrects this with compatibility-based targets.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning connects visual observations, geometric estimates, and linguistic decisions into a coherent derivation. Yet tool-augmented agents often acquire evidence without clear targets, combine outputs under inconsistent object or reference-frame semantics, and misjudge evidence sufficiency. Thus, more tools or calls do not reliably improve reasoning. We introduce Space-X, a spatial-reasoning framework that self-evolves toward complete, continuous evidence-chain construction. An Execution Agent acquires, associates, and judges evidence per problem using role-specific memory. A Control Agent diagnoses evidence-chain breaks from execution traces and jointly revises tools, interfaces, skills, memory organization, and decision rules. This loop co-evolves capability and evidence use: evidence needs guide capability development; usable results guide actions. Across multiple benchmarks, Space-X yields gains with four base models. Relative to baselines, GPT-6-sol improves answer accuracy on ViewSpatial and MMSI by 50.39% and 23.07%, respectively; Gemini-3.8-Flash gains 47.50% and 25.22% on these benchmarks. This provides a unified route from fragmented spatial clues to traceable, derivable answers.
authors: Zijian Zhang, Wenqing Tian, Qiang Liu, Liang Wang
bullets: Addresses tool-augmented agents’ inconsistent object/reference-frame semantics and poor judgment of evidence sufficiency.
Uses an Execution Agent to acquire, associate, and assess evidence with role-specific memory.
Uses a Control Agent to diagnose evidence-chain failures and revise tools, interfaces, skills, memory, and decision rules.
Across multiple benchmarks and four base models, it reports substantial accuracy gains on ViewSpatial and MMSI.
Provides a unified approach for deriving answers from spatial evidence rather than simply increasing tool calls.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a self-evolving spatial-reasoning agent framework that chains visual, geometric, and linguistic evidence, directly fitting spatial intelligence in multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Space-X: Self-Evolving Spatial Agents Weaving Clues into Evidence Chains
papers.tldr: Space-X is a self-evolving framework that helps spatial agents turn fragmented visual and geometric clues into coherent, traceable evidence chains.

papers.abstract: People often understand the world by comparing different views of it. Vision-language models (VLMs), however, receive these views as separate images and still struggle to relate them. One problem is data. Training on these tasks requires groups of images with a known relationship: the same object from different viewpoints, or the same scene before and after a change. Such examples are hard to collect at scale from existing photo collections. We introduce ReSynth, which turns single-image perception and controllable image generation into cross-image relational supervision. Localized editing produces before-and-after pairs, viewpoint generation produces multiple views of the same instance, and verified scene contents support comparisons of counts and attributes. ReSynth combines Qwen3-VL-8B's captioning, grounding, and counting capabilities with Qwen-Image-2.1's generation and editing capabilities. It verifies single-image facts such as object counts and attributes, then combines these facts to construct multi-image QA. Using GRPO on approximately 440K ReSynth questions, with no real images during training, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B improve by 17.73 and 6.10 average points on BLINK, MUIRBench, and VLM2-Bench, while single-image performance is broadly preserved on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and improves across all four evaluated benchmarks on Qwen3-VL-8B. Notably, this supervision enables the 8B perception model itself to outperform Qwen3-VL-235B on BLINK and MUIRBench.
authors: Yilin Wang, Xin Yu, Xinyi Guo, Xiangxi Zheng, Dongxing Mao, Linjie Li, Zhengyuan Yang, Alex Jinpeng Wang
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of scalable training data for cross-image relationships such as viewpoint changes and before/after differences.
Uses localized editing, viewpoint generation, and verified scene content to construct multi-image question-answer pairs.
Combines Qwen3-VL-8B for captioning, grounding, and counting with Qwen-Image-2.1 for image generation and editing.
GRPO training on approximately 440K synthetic questions improves evaluated multi-image understanding while broadly preserving single-image performance.
The resulting Qwen3-VL-8B surpasses Qwen3-VL-235B on BLINK and MUIRBench, according to the abstract.

papers.selection_reason: Synthetic supervision for multi-image understanding, improves VLMs and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: ReSynth: Constructing Synthetic Supervision for Multi-Image Understanding
papers.tldr: ReSynth creates synthetic multi-image relational supervision from single images, improving VLMs’ ability to compare views, changes, counts, and attributes without using real images during training.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) grasp the overall content of an image but often miss the fine details a question hinges on, such as a small object in a large photo or a number in a dense infographic. Yet even when their answer is wrong, the region they point to often contains the evidence. We introduce Self-Elicited Evidence (SEE), a training-free method that lets a frozen VLM look again where it points. When the initial answer has low confidence, SEE prompts the model to propose regions where the details may appear, answers the question on these enlarged crops, and aggregates the answers with the original prediction through confidence-weighted voting. The model also answers with its own transcript, which helps on text-rich images. SEE needs no detector or OCR engine. Across five backbones, SEE improves every small-object benchmark by 2.3-13.1 points and outperforms five training-free baselines on small objects. With SEE, Qwen3.5-4B surpasses the direct answer of Qwen3.5-9B and matches the 6 times larger Qwen3.5-27B.
authors: Alin-Ionut Popa, Tuo Zhang, Dimitrios Dimitriadis
bullets: Addresses VLMs missing small objects, numbers, and other details despite often localizing relevant evidence.
Uses a training-free, detector- and OCR-free pipeline triggered by low-confidence answers.
The VLM proposes likely evidence regions, answers from enlarged crops and its own transcript, then performs confidence-weighted voting.
Improves small-object benchmarks by 2.3–13.1 points across five backbones and beats five training-free baselines.
Enables Qwen3.5-4B to surpass Qwen3.5-9B’s direct answers and match the 6× larger Qwen3.5-27B.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SEE. Step 1: the frozen model M answers the whole-image view vI ; if its confidence pvI reaches τ , SEE returns this direct answer. Step 2: otherwise SEE elicits evidence with two operations: Zoom enlarges the K regions rk that the model proposes when asked where to look, giving the zoomed views vk, and Read has the model transcribe the image, giving the reading view vR. Step 3: the model answers every view, and each view votes for its answer yv with its confidence pv (Eq. 5). One frozen model, no training.

Figure 6. How SEE decides, on real questions (Qwen3.5-4B unless marked 0.8B). Each cell shows the image with the model’s own regions (yellow), the evidence that decided (the winning zoom or the transcript), and every view’s confidence (green: right; red: the direct answer’s wrong answer; grey: another wrong answer; dotted: the gate τ ); above the bars, direct answer → SEE’s answer. The model’s regions find the target (a, d), the transcript settles text (b), and agreeing zooms outvote the most confident view (c). Failures: two confident zooms on the wrong logo (e), or a crop that keeps only one of the two objects being compared (f). Cases were mined automatically by category; more in App. C.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free method to improve frozen VLM fine-grained perception via self-elicited evidence and confidence-weighted voting.
papers.title: SEE: Unlocking the Hidden Perception of Frozen VLMs
papers.tldr: SEE improves frozen VLMs’ fine-detail perception by having them revisit self-identified image regions and combine crop-based answers with the original prediction.

papers.abstract: Proactive video understanding requires vision-language models (VLMs) to decide not only what to answer as a video unfolds, but also when newly arrived evidence warrants a response and when to remain silent. Although modern VLMs excel at offline long-video understanding, they struggle in proactive streaming settings, leading prior work to introduce task-specific reinforcement learning or auxiliary triggering modules. We find that explicit reporting rules and structured streaming context substantially improve a frozen VLM's proactive response performance. We exploit this observation to build SIMPLEPRO, a training-free baseline for proactive video understanding. At each decision step, the model combines recent high-resolution frames, bounded historical observations, and prior answer records to determine whether new information warrants a response and, when needed, generate a concise answer. The system then filters consecutive duplicate answers while retaining the raw outputs as context for subsequent decisions. Without any parameter updates or auxiliary triggers, SIMPLEPRO with a 4B backbone consistently outperforms specialized proactive systems across OVO-Bench, StreamingBench-PO, and ProactiveVideoQA. SIMPLEPRO shows overall performance gains as backbone size increases from 2B to 32B. We hope this simple yet effective method will serve as a strong baseline for proactive video understanding, and we will release our code and inference pipeline to support future research.
authors: Yilin Wang, Xiangxi Zheng, Dongxing Mao, Linjie Li, Zhengyuan Yang, Alex Jinpeng Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deciding both what to answer and when to respond in streaming videos.
Uses recent high-resolution frames, bounded history, and prior answer records as context for a frozen VLM.
Applies explicit reporting rules and filters consecutive duplicate answers while preserving raw outputs for future decisions.
A 4B-backbone version outperforms specialized proactive systems across three benchmarks, with gains increasing from 2B to 32B backbones.
Designed as a simple baseline; it uses no parameter updates or auxiliary trigger modules.

papers.abstract: Inferring the unseen side of a 3D assembly requires reasoning about part placement and occlusion. Different assemblies can match the observed views while producing different hidden views, leaving the target ambiguous. We introduce SixthView, a benchmark in which models predict a sixth orthographic view from five observed views and information about the component shapes. The benchmark contains 602 synthetic polycube assemblies with 2--10 parts and requires a dense grid of part labels for the missing view, allowing both exact-view and cell-level evaluation. For each item, we exhaustively verify that all legal assemblies consistent with the exact component geometry and observed label grids yield the same target view. With these inputs, the task tests symbolic assembly and coordinate reasoning. The image-only variants additionally require shape recovery from rendered views, where occlusion can make different 3D shapes look identical. We evaluate three vision-language models under four input conditions. Across 552 items with complete evaluations, exact-grid accuracy with images plus exact text ranges from 33.2% to 85.4%. Adding exact text to separate images improves accuracy by 19.7--63.0 percentage points, whereas adding images to exact text changes it by only $-0.5$ to $+2.1$ points. Separate image panels outperform a merged sheet by 6.7--11.1 points. The results show that performance depends strongly on access to exact symbolic information, with little further improvement from images once the geometry is specified. bullets: The task predicts a sixth view from five observed views plus component-shape information, requiring part-placement, occlusion, and coordinate reasoning.
It includes 602 synthetic polycube assemblies with 2–10 parts and evaluates dense part-label grids using exact-view and cell-level metrics.
The benchmark verifies that every legal assembly consistent with the inputs has the same hidden target view, removing inherent ambiguity.
Across three vision-language models, exact-grid accuracy ranges from 33.2% to 85.4% across evaluated conditions.
Adding exact text geometry substantially improves image-based performance, while adding images to exact text provides little benefit; separate image panels also outperform merged sheets.

papers.abstract: Children's book illustrations carry developmental, pedagogical, and cultural responsibilities that are often formally codified in guidelines. As AI systems begin entering children's publishing pipelines, both as evaluators and as generators, a natural question arises: can they reliably meet the structural, safety, and cultural standards required? We investigate this across three criteria: guideline compliance, safety, and cultural alignment, using Indonesia's Book Leveling Guideline as a government-issued evaluation framework with explicit visual criteria for four reading levels. To understand how well VLMs can identify and apply these guideline criteria, we first evaluate them on real published children's book pages and compare their assessments against a human baseline. To then examine whether AI-generated illustrations meet the same standards, we apply the VLM judge to images produced by two generation models and cross-check them against a subset of human illustrator raters. We find that VLMs are reliable on explicit criteria such as compliance and safety, but fall short on cultural alignment, systematically missing content that human raters flag as culturally inappropriate. AI-generated illustrations show the same blind spot: they satisfy structural and safety criteria but fail to capture implicit cultural details that human raters consistently identify.
authors: Rian Adam Rajagede, Rochana Prih Hastuti, Fitri Hasanah Amhar
bullets: Evaluates AI understanding across guideline compliance, safety, and cultural alignment.
Uses Indonesia's Book Leveling Guideline across four reading levels as the evaluation framework.
Compares VLM judgments on published book pages with human assessments.
Applies VLM evaluation and human cross-checks to illustrations generated by two models.
Finds a cultural alignment gap in both VLM evaluation and AI-generated illustrations.

papers.abstract: A deployed multimodal predictor may face missing modalities after its weights can no longer be changed. This raises a question that training-time repair does not answer: what part of the resulting error is still correctable from the information that remains? We show that this part is characterized by the Bayes gap, the difference between the model's prediction and the Bayes prediction given the observed modalities. For cross-entropy and squared error, excess risk measures this gap in the geometry of the loss; ambiguity in the observed modalities cannot be removed. Thus, a badly degraded prediction is not necessarily a correctable one. Estimating the Bayes prediction normally requires labels. However, when a model observing more modalities is conditionally correct, averaging its outputs conditional on the remaining modalities recovers this target without retrieval labels; with the same fixed blend and neighbors, it is no worse in expected cross-entropy or Brier risk than averaging hard labels. Some such assumption is unavoidable: otherwise the target is not identifiable from unlabeled data alone. GUARD (Gated Utility-Aware Recalibration for Deployment) leaves the deployed predictor unchanged. It estimates a candidate correction by retrieval, learns from deployment-matched labeled data when correction is likely to help, and calibrates a threshold on a held-out split by conformal risk control. Under exchangeability, the marginal probability that GUARD applies a correction whose loss increase exceeds a prescribed tolerance is bounded by a preset level, regardless of the learned score. In controlled experiments, correction gain follows headroom rather than raw error; across nine frozen model-dataset pairs spanning six domains, GUARD retains most of blanket correction's gain within harm budgets that blanket correction often exceeds.
authors: Hoang Pham Cong, Long D. Nguyen, Ho Viet Duc Luong, Nguyen Tran Minh Nhat, Binh P. Nguyen, Huynh Thi Thanh Binh
bullets: The correctable error is the Bayes gap between the deployed prediction and the Bayes prediction given the modalities that remain; ambiguity itself cannot be removed.
When a more-complete model is conditionally correct, averaging its outputs can estimate the missing-modality Bayes target without retrieval labels.

GUARD leaves the deployed model unchanged, learns when candidate retrieval corrections are useful from deployment-matched labeled data, and calibrates an application threshold with conformal risk control.
Under exchangeability, the probability that an applied correction exceeds a specified loss-increase tolerance is bounded by a preset level.

Across nine frozen model–dataset pairs spanning six domains, correction gains track headroom rather than raw error, and GUARD retains most blanket-correction gains within harm budgets that blanket correction often exceeds.

papers.abstract: Segmenting each reported finding in a radiology scan would allow findings to be measured and tracked over time and let AI systems generate reports that are verifiable, but so far AI models have performed poorly at this task. To advance this task, we organized the ReXGrounding Challenge at MICCAI 2026, the first challenge dedicated to it. Given a non-contrast chest CT scan and the set of findings from its report, participants trained models to produce the corresponding set of 3D segmentations. The challenge used 2,992 training and 200 validation scans from the ReXGroundingCT dataset, and evaluated methods on a held-out test set of 300 scans with 582 findings, exhaustively annotated by board-certified radiologists. In total, 48 teams from 15 countries made 760 submissions, and the best method reached a Dice of 0.375 and a hit rate of 0.77, matching agreement between two independent radiologist groups (Dice 0.32, hit rate 0.76, on a 50-scan subset). On the 100 scans of the pre-challenge benchmark, the winner reached a Dice of 0.390, against 0.285 for VoxTell, the best model before the challenge, which five of the six best teams fine-tuned. Non-focal findings remained far harder to segment than focal ones, instance F1 stayed below inter-reader agreement (0.34 vs. 0.47), and models sometimes segmented the right abnormality in the wrong location. Top methods thus match radiologist agreement in Dice, but non-focal findings, findings with multiple instances, and adherence to the anatomical location described in the text remain open problems.

papers.abstract: Text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation requires layouts satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints. However, existing diffusion methods rely primarily on static textual conditions, limiting their ability to assess evolving scenes and translate semantic discrepancies into executable object-level corrections. MLLM-based post-hoc refinement provides semantic feedback but remains decoupled from denoising, potentially disrupting scene coherence.We propose ReflectScene, an MLLM-guided closed-loop diffusion framework. First, we introduce Hierarchical Prior-Grounded Scene Understanding that aligns structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence, to interpret object-specific context and scene global semantics via a frozen multi-modal large language model (MLLM). Second, we propose MLLM-Guided Semantic Reward Evaluation to distill MLLM's diagnoses and assessments on possible candidate corrections into a lightweight Reward Predictor, enabling correction decision making with reduced computation burden. Finally, Decision-Conditioned Trajectory-Consistent Diffusion is proposed to integrate selected corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection, correcting object layout in the generated scene while preserving non-target arrangements throughout denoising.Experiments on 3D-FRONT demonstrate improved functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive generation quality and diversity.
authors: Jiawei Shen, Jie Feng, Junpeng Zhang, Guanbin Li, Wanyi Chen, Weisheng Dong, Guangming Shi
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints with static text-conditioned diffusion.
Uses hierarchical scene understanding to align structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence and interpret both object context and global semantics.
Distills MLLM feedback about candidate corrections into a lightweight reward predictor for efficient correction decisions.
Integrates selected object-level corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection during denoising.
On 3D-FRONT, improves functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive quality and diversity.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ReflectScene. ReflectScene integrates hierarchical scene understanding and MLLM-guided decisions into objectcentric diffusion. At each denoising step, intermediate clean estimates are assessed to select object-level actions, providing transient conditioning, while buffered non-STOP actions are executed every 50 steps to update a persistent correction state. This state is projected onto subsequent clean estimates before DDPM posterior sampling, with decision-effect consistency learning promoting target recovery and non-target preservation.

papers.abstract: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.
authors: Yeongtak Oh, Donghyeok Lee, Joonhee Oh, Jaewon Jeong, Sungroh Yoon
bullets: PReMind-Bench evaluates memory access, visual grounding, abstention, hazard response, and their joint success across hazards and personal contexts.

Existing models often handle personalization or safety in isolation but fail when both are required together.
At 4B, PReMind improves interdependency joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base and also improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention.
Gains persist under forced-call evaluation, a second LLM judge, multiple training seeds, and unseen hazard groups.

papers.abstract: Accurately matching human intentions in 3D space is an important goal of artificial intelligence. Recently, 3D Intention Grounding (3D-IG) has emerged, aiming to localize target 3D objects given a natural-language intent. Unlike conventional visual grounding with descriptive referring expressions, 3D-IG intents are abstract and non-descriptive, making object localization substantially more challenging. This requires inferring latent functional requirements from non-descriptive intents and aligning them with object-level 3D representations. However, existing methods largely rely on implicit intent-object matching, leading to logical gaps and limited interpretability, robustness, and generalization. To address these challenges, we propose Chain-of-Causal Reasoning (CoCR), a causality-inspired functional dependency reasoning framework that explicitly bridges abstract intentions and candidate objects through intermediate functional requirements. Specifically, CoCR progressively decomposes complex intents into ordered functional requirements, thereby forming an explicit intent-function-object reasoning chain that links abstract intentions to object suitability. Building on this chain, we construct a causality-inspired functional dependency graph to model requirement-attribute relationships and introduce a causal-visual alignment module that aligns function-aware representations with the geometric-semantic features of 3D point clouds, enabling bidirectional verification between structured functional reasoning and visual evidence. Extensive experiments on 3D Intention Grounding and 3D Visual Grounding demonstrate that our method enhances intent-aware object localization. Our code is available at https://2490o.github.io/CoCR.
authors: Zihao Zhang, Aming Wu, Yang Li, Yahong Han
bullets: 3D intent grounding must localize objects from abstract, non-descriptive language, which is harder than conventional visual grounding.
CoCR decomposes complex intents into ordered functional requirements, forming an intent–function–object reasoning chain.
A functional dependency graph models requirement–attribute relationships, while causal-visual alignment connects functional reasoning with 3D geometric and semantic features.
Bidirectional verification links structured functional reasoning with visual evidence for more interpretable and robust localization.
Experiments on 3D intention and visual grounding show improved intent-aware object localization; the abstract gives no specific numerical results.

Subsequently, Intent Causal Grounding is performed through the construction of a causal graph, defining the causal relationships between functional requirements and object attributes. The graph is iteratively updated via causal–visual feature alignment and causal pruning. Finally, causal reasoning is conducted based on the updated graph to achieve object selection and localization.

papers.abstract: In weight-space programming, a language model edits a network's weights directly, without gradients. We ask what a successful repair of this kind relies on. We plant faults in the weights of two vision-language models, SmolVLM-256M and LFM2-VL-450M, and check each edit made by a coding agent against the original weights. Without being told where to look, the agent finds rescaled rows in the projector and noise in the vision encoder of both models, infers the unknown scale factors, restores most or all of the rescaled weights to their exact original values, and returns accuracy to near its original level; programs that it writes from such weights repair unseen checkpoints of the same model without feedback. These repairs depend on a trace of how the faults were computed. The original weights have 16-bit precision, and faults computed in 32-bit arithmetic leave low bits that only the damaged weights carry. Rounding those bits away leaves each model's answers to our test questions unchanged, and the agent, unaided, then restores no weight exactly: on SmolVLM it no longer finds the damage, and in a single session on LFM2-VL its only gain comes from rescaling answer-token embeddings, which changes how often the model answers yes. Marking the damaged weights again in their low bits brings the edits back to them. Rounded weights still hold statistical evidence of the rescaling, in the distribution of stored values and in row norms, and one sentence in the prompt that names such a statistic directs the agent's edits to the damaged rows on both models. Swapped rows or columns, which leave the set of stored values unchanged, are not found unaided on either model within our session budgets. We recommend that studies of weight repair report the number format of the weights and include a rounded control.
bullets: A coding agent repaired rescaled projector rows and noisy vision-encoder weights in SmolVLM-256M and LFM2-VL-450M without being told where the faults were.
It inferred scale factors, restored many or all affected weights exactly, and recovered accuracy near the original level; generated programs also repaired unseen checkpoints of the same model.
Repair relied on low-order bits preserved by 32-bit fault computation against 16-bit original weights, rather than solely on unchanged model behavior.
Rounding away those bits prevented exact repair, although value distributions and row norms still enabled repair when explicitly mentioned in the prompt.
Swapped rows or columns were not found unaided; the authors recommend reporting weight format and using rounded controls in repair studies.

The model gives the same answers to all test questions in both copies, but the agent repairs only the unrounded one (checkpoints A–C; clean accuracy 83.3%).

papers.abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in 3D computed tomography (CT) classification, but high accuracy does not reflect whether their predictions rely on the correct anatomical evidence. We introduce ORGANIC3D, a framework for evaluating and improving organ level image text alignment through controlled anatomical interventions. Our benchmark assesses 12 vision encoder checkpoints and 7 generative VLMs using matched patient comparisons, organ erasure, lesion replacement, and laterality perturbations, revealing substantial alignment failures even among top performing models. To learn organ level image text correspondence, ORGANIC3D aligns each finding sentence with the anatomy aware image features and trains on edited scans to anchor this alignment in the organ's image evidence. We further extend this framework to generative VLMs, promoting evidence dependent question answering and report generation. Trained exclusively on public data, ORGANIC3D achieves SOTA classification AUROC on CTRATE, Merlin, and the heldout RADChestCT dataset and reaches 77% laterality accuracy, compared with at most 66% for prior models. Its generative VLM matches or exceeds all evaluated publicly released VLMs on visual question answering, achieves the highest report accuracy, and retracts 96 to 99% of target organ findings after organ removal, versus a maximum of 69% for other models. Together, these results establish ORGANIC3D as a framework for testing whether 3D CT vision language models ground their predictions in anatomical evidence and for improving organ level alignment alongside predictive accuracy.

Achieves strong classification, laterality, visual question answering, and report-generation performance using only public data.
After organ removal, its generative VLM retracts 96–99% of target-organ findings, indicating improved evidence-dependent reporting.

papers.abstract: In vision-language models (VLMs), a few sink tokens attract a disproportionate share of attention. While previous studies have examined why these tokens attract attention, we investigate how the sink-key direction affects attention to image and question tokens. Across four probed VLMs, boosting the magnitude of positive sink-aligned components increases attention on average, whereas boosting negative components decreases it; these responses persist through later layers. This identifies the native sink key as a reference for controlling attention beyond its own position. Motivated by this finding, we propose SHRINK, a training-free method that partially reduces sink-aligned components across visible keys during generation. On nine benchmarks under sampled reasoning, it improves mean accuracy by 5.1 and 2.7 percentage points on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-3B, with smaller gains on the other two main models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Gemma-3-4B. Beyond SHRINK, rescaling sink-aligned key components can replace the attention operations of two existing attention-steering methods, GIFT and ACG, with comparable accuracy on hallucination benchmarks.
authors: Hui Zhu, Saleh Zare Zade, Rafi Ibn Sultan, Xiangyu Zhou, Dongxiao Zhu
bullets: Positive sink-aligned components increase attention to image and question tokens, while negative components decrease it; effects persist in later layers.

Across nine benchmarks, SHRINK raises mean accuracy by 5.1 points on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and 2.7 points on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, with smaller gains on two other models.
Rescaling sink-aligned key components can substitute for the attention operations in GIFT and ACG with comparable hallucination-benchmark accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.
authors: Hui Zhu, Saleh Zare Zade, Rafi Ibn Sultan, Deng Pan, Arun Ross, Dongxiao Zhu
bullets: Targets the informationless BOS representation created by causal masking, which later tokens repeatedly attend to.
At one prefill layer, allows only the BOS query to attend to all visual and textual input tokens; all other causal attention remains unchanged.
Requires no training, added parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead.
Improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and recent sink-intervention methods across eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks.
Mechanistic analysis finds reduced BOS sink dominance and more attention allocated to content-bearing prompt tokens.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) encode images with 2D encoders that capture little 3D structure. A common approach is to feed the policy estimated depth, but a UAV chooses its own altitude, must judge distances tens of meters away, where monocular depth is less reliable, and must relate its forward and downward views. On long aerial routes, adding depth features directly brings no significant gain (42.5% vs. 42.6% success), so we study how 3D information should be given to the policy. Analyzing flight failures, we find that two forms of 3D grounding fail in opposite ways: explicit 3D lifting of depth collides less on the way but more often fails to finish at the target, while implicit alignment with a 3D geometry model finishes more often but collides more. We propose GRID, which combines both: (1) it lifts monocular depth into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV's frame for both cameras, and (2) during training only, it aligns its visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model, at no inference cost. GRID adding explicit lifting to implicit alignment significantly increases how often the policy reaches the target ($61.5\% \rightarrow 69.5\%$, $p<0.001$), and adding implicit alignment to explicit lifting significantly increases how often it completes the task once there ($57.7\% \rightarrow 61.4\%$, $p<0.05$). On TravelUAV (3,005 test episodes), GRID achieves the best success rate on every split, with relative gains over the state of the art of 9.5% (seen), 17.1% (unseen objects) and 25.4% (unseen map).
authors: Anas Anwarul Haq Khan, Amrin Kareem, Muhammad Umer Sheikh, Biplab Banerjee, Muhammad Haris Khan
bullets: Problem: 2D visual encoders and unreliable monocular depth struggle with long-range distances, altitude selection, and coordinating forward/downward views.
Method: Lift depth from both cameras into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV frame, while aligning visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model during training.
The two components address complementary failure modes: explicit 3D lifting reduces collisions, while implicit geometry alignment improves target completion.
GRID raises target-reaching from 61.5% to 69.5% and task completion after reaching the target from 57.7% to 61.4%, with reported statistical significance.
On TravelUAV, GRID achieves the best success rate across all splits, with relative gains of 9.5%–25.4% over the prior state of the art.
