papers.abstract: Omni Models process audio, vision, and text within a unified language backbone, yet often produce different answers for semantically equivalent inputs across modalities. Existing representation-level analyses do not distinguish between information that predicts whether disagreement will occur and the representation whose perturbation affects the model's answer. In this paper, we estimate a low-dimensional Answer Subspace from answer-position representations and use it to separate answer-related components from the remaining representation. Across three Omni Models and two multimodal reasoning tasks, information predictive of cross-modal inconsistency lies mainly outside the Answer Subspace, concentrating in a reproducible two-dimensional representation that is not explained by a fixed modality offset. Matched interventions reveal distinct behavioral roles: perturbing the Answer Subspace substantially changes the model's predictions, whereas perturbing the disagreement representation, like a random subspace of the same dimensionality, leaves them almost unchanged. Our key finding is that cross-modal disagreement can be induced by misaligning modality-specific answer representations: perturbing the Answer Subspace for only one modality induces disagreement, whereas applying the same perturbation to both largely preserves agreement. Thus, the representation that predicts disagreement is distinct from the answer-level representation through which disagreement can be induced, showing that linear decodability does not imply behavioral efficacy.
bullets: Omni Models can answer differently to semantically equivalent audio, visual, and textual inputs.
The study separates an Answer Subspace from a representation that predicts whether cross-modal disagreement will occur.
Across three Omni Models and two multimodal reasoning tasks, disagreement-predictive information concentrates in a reproducible two-dimensional representation outside the Answer Subspace.
Perturbing the Answer Subspace changes predictions, while perturbing the disagreement representation has little effect, similar to a matched random subspace.
Applying Answer Subspace perturbations to one modality induces disagreement; applying the same perturbation to both modalities largely preserves agreement.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Paired audio and image representations in the Answer Subspace across six model–task conditions. Gray lines connect the two modality conditions of each item. Agreement pairs remain within the same answer region, whereas disagreement pairs separate across answer regions.

Figure 1: Layer-wise probe performance over normalized backbone depth. (a) Answer-probe accuracy shows that the model’s prediction becomes linearly decodable from the answer-position representation in the middle layers. (b) Disagreement-probe accuracy shows that disagreement-predictive information lies primarily outside the answer-related representation, with its orthogonal complement outperforming both the answer-related representation and matched random subspaces.

Figure 7: Prediction changes under matched interventions across shift magnitudes. Left and right panels show the external and spatial task families, respectively. Lines denote the mean across three models and shaded regions the range across models. Perturbations of the Answer Subspace produce a strong dose-dependent effect, whereas perturbations of the Disagreement-Predictive Subspace remain comparable to a random two-dimensional subspace drawn from the Answer Subspace complement.

Figure 3: Answer decoding under option permutation. Despite substantial variation in model behavior, the decoded answer consistently matches the model’s updated prediction. Squares, diamonds, and circles denote content following, letter retention, and decoded-answer agreement, respectively.

Figure 2: Disagreement-probe accuracy using the leading one, two, or three right singular vectors of the reshaped disagreement-probe coefficient matrix, selected within each training fold. Performance increases substantially from one to two directions, with little additional improvement from the third. Dashed and dotted lines denote the full hidden-state and Answer Subspace probes, respectively. Appendix B.3 reports percondition results and bootstrap stability.

Figure 4: Alignment of the recovered subspaces with the modality-discriminating axis. Despite near-perfect modality separability, both subspaces are nearly orthogonal to this axis. Removing the mean modality offset has negligible effect on disagreement-probe accuracy. Appendix B.6 reports the per-condition values.

Figure 8: Disagreement induced by symmetric and asymmetric Answer Subspace interventions. Applying the perturbation to one modality produces substantially more disagreement than applying it to both under the same layer, magnitude, and operation.

Figure 5: Disagreement-probe accuracy after controlling for the audio-condition prediction. Filled and open circles denote answer-controlled and unrestricted accuracy, respectively, and dashed ticks mark the labelpermutation null. Appendix B.7 reports the strata and sample sizes.

Table 5: Agreement between the answer decoded from the final-layer Answer Subspace and the model’s actual prediction, reported separately for each modality condition and for items where the two conditions agree or disagree. Agreement exceeds 0.93 throughout, including items where the two conditions produced different letters.

Table 10: Fraction of predictions changed across intervention magnitudes α, measured in target-subspace standard deviations, over 100 items per condition. Answer Subspace interventions increase monotonically and exceed both controls from α = 2 onward.

Table 1: Effect of removing the difference block. The first two columns are balanced accuracy of the disagreement probe on the full complement; Overlap is the mean principal-angle cosine between the two-dimensional subspaces recovered under the two parameterizations.

Table 6: Option permutation, decomposed. N is the number of (item, modality) pairs. Model behavior is how the model’s own prediction moved: to the letter now holding the original content, staying on the original letter, or to a third letter. The remaining columns are the fraction of pairs on which the answer decoded from the Answer Subspace agrees with the model’s new prediction, overall and restricted to the two behavior groups. The readout follows the model in every group, including when the model stays on the original letter.

Table 12: Answer Subspace intervention split by cohort, at the smaller magnitude. Disagreement items change more often in four of the six conditions, and the sign of that difference agrees with the difference in settling depth — the normalized depth from which the decoded answer stops changing — in every condition (ρ = 0.94, p = 0.005). At α = 40 both cohorts are near ceiling and the difference disappears. Cohort sizes are unequal because the split follows the model’s own behavior, so these comparisons are the least powered in the paper and we do not build any claim in the body on them.

Table 2: Conditions used throughout. Used is the number of items on which the answer letter could be resolved in both conditions; Agree and Disagree split those items by whether the two modality conditions produced the same letter. Half-dec. layer is the layer at which answer-probe accuracy first reaches the midpoint between chance and its final-layer value, and Half-dec. depth the corresponding normalized depth. Interv. depth is the normalized depth of the layer at which interventions are applied.

Table 3: Balanced accuracy of the disagreement probe at the final layer under five feature sets: coordinates inside the Answer Subspace, inside its orthogonal complement, a rank-matched random readout of that complement (mean of five draws), a rank-matched PCA readout of the complement, and the full hidden state. Chance is 0.5. The complement matches the full state to within 0.014 in every condition, while the two rank-matched readouts of the same complement fall well short of it, so the result does not follow from the complement’s dimensionality alone.

Table 4: Number of retained directions and stability of the recovered plane. The first four columns are balanced accuracy of the disagreement probe on k directions of the complement, and on a random two-dimensional subspace of the same complement. Bootstrap align. is the mean principal-angle cosine between the plane recovered from an item-level bootstrap resample (30 resamples) and the plane recovered from the full sample; Min is the smallest such value and Null the 95th percentile obtained when the resampled directions are replaced by random ones.

Table 7: Geometry at the intervention depth. Pair distance is the mean distance between the two modality conditions of the same item inside the Answer Subspace, split by cohort, with their ratio. Excess/dim is how much more the excess separation of disagreeing pairs concentrates inside the Answer Subspace than in its complement, per dimension. Separability is the balanced accuracy of a probe predicting which modality the input arrived in from the answer-position state; the two cos columns are the cosine of the principal angle between the single axis that probe defines and each subspace. Removing the mean modality offset changes disagreement accuracy by at most 0.0031.

Table 9: Median distance between the two modality conditions of the same item, computed in the full threedimensional Answer Subspace rather than in the two-dimensional projection shown in Figure 6, in units of the coordinate standard deviation. Disagree is the number of disagreement items among N ; Dist. disagree and Dist. agree are the median pair distances within each cohort and Ratio their quotient.

Table 8: Holding the audio-condition prediction fixed. A fully answer-pair-matched comparison is impossible because a fixed pair of predictions determines the disagreement label, so we stratify on the audio-condition prediction alone and pool the within-stratum results. Strata is the number of audio-condition answers that contain both cohorts, N the number of items retained, and Null the 95th percentile of a label-permutation null computed under the same stratification. The matched values exceed that null in every condition and are no lower than the unrestricted ones; the unrestricted value for Qwen2.5-Omni on spatial falls below the null, which is why the body claim rests on the matched series.

Table 11: Number of predictions changed out of 100 items. All arms use the same layer, operation and magnitude within a depth group. Perturbing the Answer Subspace at the intervention depth changes 89–100 predictions, and the same perturbation applied before the answer becomes decodable changes 0–3. The Disagreement-Predictive Subspace and the random control are both near zero and show no consistent ordering: the random control exceeds the disagreement subspace in three of the six conditions, most visibly for Gemma-4-E4B on spatial, where a random two-dimensional subspace changes 18 predictions. In that condition the two arms are therefore not distinguishable and the claim rests on the gap against the Answer Subspace rather than on an ordering between the controls.

Table 13: Change in the top-two answer margin after removing each subspace, over 240 (item, modality) pairs. Values in bold differ from zero at the 95% level under a paired bootstrap. Two independent random draws at k = 2 are shown to indicate the spread of the control itself.

Table 14: Fraction of originally agreeing items on which disagreement appears, by intervention magnitude α in units of the coordinate standard deviation. Asymmetric perturbs the Answer Subspace under one modality only; the symmetric control applies the identical shift to both. N is the number of originally agreeing items evaluated. The asymmetric arm exceeds the control in all six conditions at α = 40 (by at least a factor of 3.07), in five of six at α = 20, and in none at α ≤ 5.

papers.selection_reason: Representation-subspace analysis of cross-modal inconsistency in omni models, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Understanding Cross-Modal Inconsistency through Representation Subspaces in Omni Models
papers.tldr: Cross-modal inconsistency is predicted by a distinct low-dimensional representation, but disagreement is behaviorally induced by misaligning modality-specific answer representations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide a unified interface for language-conditioned visual perception. In pixel-to-sequence grounding, autoregressive coordinate generation requires multiple sequential decoding steps per box, increasing inference cost with the number of instances. Pixel-to-embedding methods reduce this overhead but lack explicit spatial encoding when using a shared special token. We introduce SemGeo, a token-efficient visual grounding framework that represents each instance with a single grid token for coarse localization. A geometric decoder reuses visual features and hidden states to recover precise discrete box coordinates in parallel. To train proposal generation and box localization together, we introduce Gaussian soft labels that encode coordinate distances during supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Reinforcement post-training further combines box-set rewards with coordinate supervision on model-generated proposals. This stage trains the language model and geometric decoder on their own predictions to mitigate the mismatch between teacher-forced training and inference. Across eight benchmarks spanning object detection, referring object detection, and document layout grounding, SemGeo achieves the highest F1@mIou among compared MLLMs on six benchmarks. It also delivers $2.07\times$ and $1.25\times$ the mean box-generation throughput of representative grounding baselines under vLLM and Transformers, respectively, while achieving higher accuracy in both comparisons.
authors: Zhaojie Chen, Junyan Yang, Le Yang, Qi Dang, Yucheng Huang, Qianyi Che, Zhaoqiang Chen, Xinqi Zhu, Qiang Zhao
bullets: Autoregressive coordinate generation is costly because each box requires multiple sequential decoding steps.
SemGeo uses a single grid token for coarse instance localization, then a geometric decoder recovers precise discrete box coordinates in parallel.
Gaussian soft labels encode coordinate distances to jointly train proposal generation and localization.
Reinforcement post-training uses model-generated proposals with box-set rewards and coordinate supervision to reduce the teacher-forcing mismatch.
Across eight benchmarks, SemGeo leads in F1@mIoU on six and achieves higher accuracy with 2.07× and 1.25× the mean throughput of representative baselines under vLLM and Transformers.

Highlighted cells and boxes illustrate coarse proposals and decoded geometry. Fig. 4. Qualitative comparison of SemGeo-SFT and SemGeo on two LVIS examples. All geometrically valid predictions are drawn without deduplication; exact repetitions overlap. Colors follow the queries. Pred counts all outputs, including invalid boxes; GT counts queried instances.

papers.selection_reason: Token-efficient MLLM visual grounding with geometric decoding and explicit spatial coordinate recovery.
papers.title: Semantic-Guided Geometric Decoding for Token-Efficient Visual Grounding
papers.tldr: SemGeo makes visual grounding more efficient by generating one token per object and decoding precise box coordinates in parallel, achieving strong accuracy with higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are widely used as zero-shot image quality assessors, yet their good-vs-poor answers agree only moderately with human opinion. We ask whether these models fail to see quality or fail to say it. Layer-wise probes on five VLMs point to the second: quality is linearly decodable from the vision encoder and still from the last language layer, far better than the answer reveals, and about a hundred labels recover most of it. The loss lies mainly in the final read-out, which partly reads something else: relative to human opinion, it over-rewards colorfulness and under-rewards sharpness on all five models. We test this by intervention: if the read-out is at fault, a closed-form edit of a single last-layer neuron, fitted to many prompts at once, should close the gap and no more. Both hold. Under prompts never used for fitting, the edit recovers 86--100\% of what a ridge head on the last-layer state, fitted under the same prompts, finds beyond the answer on KonIQ. Where that gap is small, it gains little, too little for our transfer criterion on the two largest models; where the head itself is below the answer, it lowers the score; and it works only when written from the middle of the language model on. Unlike unconstrained fine-tuning, the edit leaves perception question answering intact. It does not carry over to yes-or-no or rating questions, and it reverses the good--poor contrast after sentiment-laden sentences. Code will be made available.
authors: Zhuangzi Li, Shilv Cai, Jian Jin, Zhiyi Pan, Haihong Xiao, Weisi Lin
bullets: VLMs encode image quality well internally, yet their good-vs-poor answers align only moderately with human opinion.
Layer-wise probes across five VLMs indicate the main failure is the final read-out, which overweights colorfulness and underweights sharpness.
The method edits a single last-layer neuron using multiple prompts, without unconstrained fine-tuning.
On unseen prompts for KonIQ, the edit recovers 86–100% of the improvement available from a ridge head on the last-layer state.
The edit is prompt- and layer-sensitive: it does not transfer to yes/no or rating questions and can reverse judgments after sentiment-laden sentences.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and edits VLM read-out for image quality assessment; relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Lost in Read-out: Locating the Image Quality Gap in Vision-Language Models with a Closed-Form Edit
papers.tldr: A closed-form edit to the final language read-out substantially recovers VLM image-quality judgments hidden in their representations, but only under specific prompts and layers.

papers.abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon
authors: Oleg Pavlov, Nikita Gavrilov, Soslan Kabisov, Gennadii Savrasov, Andrey Kuznetsov, Anton Konushin, Dmitrii Zhemchuzhnikov
bullets: Targets privacy and affordability challenges for practitioners handling proprietary CAD parts.
Decomposes reconstruction into sequential visual decisions about what to build and correct.
Uses geometric tools for precise construction while focusing the agent on visual reasoning.
Runs on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops and integrates with FreeCAD.
The authors report higher reconstruction quality than prior approaches across the main benchmarks, including frontier-model-based systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The CADMAGEDDON agent loop, shown on one real turn of a Fusion 360 run (state 2 to state 3). Qwen3.8-27B issues one command per turn and refers to geometry mainly by name. The driver returns the saved state with the smallest residual. Highlighted options are those used in this turn. The residual render was made afterwards for illustration (the agent read it as text), and –split F4 replaces the equivalent value Y=1.4894 that the agent copied from the faces output. papers.abstract: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.
authors: Tian Lyu, Yichen Jiang, Ziyuan Cheng, Yunda Yan, Xiangyu Pan, Junjie Jiang, Jialin Yu, Boyu Ning, Pietro Li\`o, Fan Mo
bullets: Addresses recursive drift in entity poses and spatial relations during long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control.
Rolls out a scene graph alongside the visual model, couples graph and visual changes, and applies a bounded residual using graph-motion context and node positions.
Acts as a plug-in for DINO-WM and DreamerV3 without backpropagating graph-learning or correction gradients into the original visual dynamics.
Across 32-step rollouts, reduces joint-position error by 11–28%; on real inverted-pendulum sequences, lowers DINO-WM pole-angle error from 12.56° to 6.69°.
In simulated inverted-pendulum control, JointGV-corrected rollouts enable 46/50 successful episodes versus none with original rollouts.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of JointGV. Given the current RGB observation and action, the original visual world model (yellow) predicts the uncorrected next visual state Zt+1 and its change ∆Zt. In parallel, JointGV (blue) uses Relation Transformer (RelTR) features to construct a task-conditioned scene graph and predicts the node-feature change ∆N̂t. For the spatial-token case shown here, learned projections map the visual-token and graph-node changes into a shared space, where a change-alignment adapter produces the graph-motion context. The predicted node positions provide a complementary position context. A bounded, gated correction combines these contexts with the original visual prediction to produce Ẑt+1 = Zt+1 + Ct. papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.
authors: Jiachun Li, Zhuoran Jin, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Introduces MentalGrid, a benchmark for spatial reasoning without intermediate visual feedback.
Finds that simple simulations are limited by perception, while complex ones suffer from weak multi-step reasoning.
Proposes a three-stage curriculum trained on 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples.
SpatialWalker achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model and outperforms Gemini-3-Flash on spatial simulation.
Generalizes to out-of-domain benchmarks with a 4.9% average gain.

papers.abstract: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. We address these limitations with MM-ReportBench, a multimodal report evaluation benchmark covering 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables. Each task is paired with an expert-curated reference report featuring standardized chapter structures and verifiable key insight points, constructed through a hybrid pipeline of multimodal reports generation based on Monte Carlo Tree Search and rigorous human quality control. For robust evaluation, we design a dual-judge evaluation framework: Text Judge Model assesses textual quality along structural completeness, grounded insight verification with numerical fact-checking against source tables, and novelty analysis that distinguishes genuine analytical discovery from trivial paraphrasing; Visualization Judge Model evaluates generated visualizations across data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. They also evaluate cross-modal consistency. Extensive experiments on 20 state-of-the-art models reveal critical weaknesses: even the strongest model achieves only 68.9 overall score, with numerical hallucination affecting 38.5% of reports and genuinely novel insights remaining rare. Our ablation studies further demonstrate that single-judge evaluation consistently inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment, confirming that rigorous and reliable benchmarking demands multi-faceted, complementary evaluation probes.
bullets: Covers 386 tasks drawn from 185 real-world tables, with expert-curated reports, standardized structures, and verifiable key insights.
Uses dual judges: a text evaluator checks structure, numerical grounding, and novelty, while a visualization evaluator assesses fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and correctness.
Also measures consistency between generated narratives and visualizations.
Evaluation of 20 state-of-the-art models finds persistent weaknesses, including numerical hallucinations and few genuinely novel insights.
Single-judge evaluation overestimates performance by 8–12 points, supporting complementary multi-faceted evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and dual-judge evaluation for multimodal report generation from tables, directly relevant to multimodal LLM capabilities.
papers.title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables
papers.tldr: MM-ReportBench is a 386-task benchmark for evaluating whether models can generate faithful, insightful text-and-visualization reports from tables.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) capture cross-modal relationships between image and text, yet their adaptation to institution-specific clinical tasks remains underexplored. In this study, we fine-tuned a pretrained 3D medical VLM for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) classification using paired abdominal CT scans and radiology reports from a different institution with acquisition characteristics that differ from the model's original pretraining corpus. We compared two adaptation strategies: full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), motivated by the common use of PEFT to reduce computational cost and enable adaptation under limited-data constraints. Both approaches achieve strong downstream HCC classification performance despite the cross-institutional domain shift, with PEFT reaching an AUC of 0.79 and F1 of 0.70, and full fine-tuning achieving an AUC of 0.82 and F1 of 0.71. Although these results remain below the performance reported by supervised HCC classification approaches, our method achieves improvements over the pretrained model through CT-report contrastive learning without requiring lesion-level annotations or HCC classification labels as training targets. Full fine-tuning converges rapidly but overfits within a few epochs, whereas PEFT (ConvLoRA for the image encoder and LoRA for the text encoder) attains comparable performance while updating approximately 1% of the model parameters, although requiring more training steps. We also examine the role of contrastive temperature, observing that temperature initialization significantly affects classification performance. This study demonstrates that a 3D medical VLM can be efficiently adapted to institution-specific HCC classification using self-supervised CT-report contrastive learning, while highlighting the practical trade-offs between full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
authors: Febryan Putra Kartika, Cheng-Yu Ma, Ying-Jia Lin, Chi-Tung Cheng, Kuan-Fu Chen

Both methods improve over the pretrained model without lesion-level annotations or HCC labels as training targets.

papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.
authors: Chang Sun, Yijun Tian, Zhenwei Tang, Yuchen Deng, Yifan Simon Liu, Chenxu Wang, Wei Wang
bullets: Targets hallucinations caused when irrelevant or misleading audio, video, or text cues distort another modality’s prediction.
Uses Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration when unimodal branches disagree, selecting task-relevant evidence and alternative answers.
Uses Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery when branches agree, checking layer-wise evidence consistency and strength to detect false consensus.
Evaluated on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across hallucination mitigation and audio-visual reasoning tasks.
Reports up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding and 7.7% average improvement over the best baseline, as stated in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation. In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.
authors: Zane Fu, Yanzhao Zheng, Jinze Liu, Ziting Qin, Qianshan Wei, Jihuai Zhu, Yipeng Yu, Baohua Dong, Hangcheng Zhu, Ruohui Huang
bullets: OPD’s apparent resistance to backdoors is challenged because teacher probability distributions can still transmit malicious behavior.
Unlike offline distillation, propagation is rare at low poisoning ratios but rapidly approaches full attack success beyond a critical threshold.
The mechanism is continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass from the teacher, rather than explicit malicious target responses.
Experiments across multiple model families and datasets, supported by theoretical analysis, identify this overlooked security risk.
A trigger design is proposed that enables propagation with zero explicit trigger injection.

papers.title: As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing

papers.abstract: Multimodal post-training has moved from broad instruction tuning toward reinforcement learning for image and video reasoning, where outcome rewards can improve final-answer accuracy. Yet these rewards are assigned to complete generated trajectories, while visual evidence is used only at sparse and uneven positions inside the response. Recent work has begun to make multimodal RL more token-sensitive through grounding signals or external token-level weighting. We ask a more specific question: can the allocation of the same trajectory-level reward be inferred from the model's own multimodal computation, rather than from an auxiliary annotator, perception module, or process label? We propose Gaze-RL, a representation-driven policy optimization method that redistributes completion-level advantage through a latent reward landing field. The field is computed from internal cross-modal geometry and local predictive uncertainty, assigning larger update weight to positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing while remaining mean-one, so the total credit of each rollout is preserved and only its positionwise allocation changes. Gaze-RL requires no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural modification, and improves both Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 across a broad range of image and video benchmarks.
authors: Lixuan He, Tianzhe Chu, Shulin Tian, Shikang Zheng, Feng Chen, Yi Ma
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between sequence-level rewards and sparse visual evidence in multimodal reasoning.
Infers a latent reward landing field from cross-modal representations and local predictive uncertainty.
Reweights token-level updates toward positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing, while preserving total rollout credit.
Requires no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural changes.
Improves Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 across a broad range of image and video benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding, yet remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning. Recent studies explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. However, these approaches either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme, regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. Through systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion, we find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels (e.g., distance estimation vs. route planning) require geometric representations of different granularities, revealing that fixed fusion cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements. To bridge this gap, we propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations. SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics, and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. Furthermore, we introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse. Gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. Experiments demonstrate that SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaosb-star/SpatialMind.
authors: Shibin Zhao, Hao Tan, Fan Yang, Haixin Wang, Feilong Chen, Yidong Ma, Chaoyang Zhao, Ming Tang, Jinqiao Wang
bullets: Fixed or single-level geometric fusion cannot meet the differing representation needs of tasks such as distance estimation and route planning.
GeoFus uses a gating network conditioned on text, visual semantics, and geometry to combine shallow, intermediate, and deep features across LLM decoder layers.
Negative-entropy regularization helps prevent gate collapse during adaptive fusion.
Gate visualizations suggest that the framework adjusts geometric granularity according to task requirements.
SpatialMind achieves competitive spatial-benchmark performance, including a 72.3 score on VSI-Bench.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks. However, it remains unclear whether their predictions are grounded in the visual content itself or are largely driven by statistical co-occurrence patterns and commonsense correlations learned from large-scale image-text corpora. Existing vision-language benchmarks predominantly consist of samples that conform to human commonsense, allowing models to achieve strong performance by exploiting dataset priors rather than genuinely understanding image content. To address this limitation, we present ContraSense, a systematically constructed benchmark for evaluating faithful vision-language understanding. ContraSense consists of carefully curated counter-intuitive image-text pairs that deliberately violate common expectations, substantially reducing the effectiveness of statistical biases and requiring models to rely on visual evidence for reasoning. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on a diverse set of representative open- and closed-source MLLMs. The results reveal a substantial performance gap between current MLLMs and humans: even the strongest closed-source model achieves only about 60\% accuracy, compared with 96.04\% for human participants. These findings demonstrate that current MLLMs still struggle with faithful visual understanding and highlight the need for more robust multimodal reasoning grounded in image content. The ContraSense benchmark is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/LingLin00/ContraSense.
authors: Ling Lin, Heng Su, Xiangzeng Liu, Yang Bai, Congcong Zhu, Jingrun Chen
bullets: Existing vision-language benchmarks may reward statistical co-occurrences because their examples usually match human expectations.
ContraSense uses carefully curated counter-intuitive image–text pairs that require reasoning from visual evidence.
Evaluations cover diverse open- and closed-source multimodal large language models.
The strongest closed-source model reaches about 60% accuracy, versus 96.04% for humans.
The benchmark highlights the need for more visually grounded multimodal reasoning and is publicly available.

Each image contains at least one counterintuitive scenario designed to assess whether visual-language models can provide accurate responses based on the image content itself without relying on common-sense prior knowledge from the training data. This benchmark provides a unique and powerful tool for studying the robustness and real-world visual understanding capabilities of VLMs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as central foundation models combining multimodal perception with text comprehension. While VLMs are traditionally built via late fusion by continued pre-training an off-the-shelf language model on multimodal (image-text) data, mixing modalities from the start of pre-training (early fusion) has recently gained traction. However, the fundamental trade-offs between these paradigms remain poorly understood, resulting in expensive and heuristic-driven training recipes. In this paper, we systematically analyze the learning dynamics of these multimodal pre-training processes, showing that validation losses during vision-language fusion can be modeled by separating the base learning trajectory, where different data types contribute at distinct rates, from a distribution shift driven by the competition between modalities. We derive a scaling law that unifiedly describes these dynamics, enabling accurate loss predictions across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes. Crucially, our law characterizes the trade-off between early and late fusion: under a fixed data budget, early fusion preserves text performance while late fusion favors vision performance, yielding a trade-off that increasingly tilts toward early fusion as model size scales. Extensive experiments confirm that our scaling law reliably captures multimodal learning dynamics and governs fusion decisions.
authors: Seng Pei Liew, Teppei Suzuki, Seiya Tokui
bullets: Analyzes the trade-offs between early fusion, which mixes modalities from the start, and late fusion, which adapts a pre-trained language model.
Separates learning trajectories by data type from modality competition-induced distribution shifts.
Predicts validation losses across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes.
Finds that early fusion better preserves text performance, while late fusion favors vision performance under a fixed data budget.
The trade-off increasingly favors early fusion as model size grows, with experiments supporting the law’s predictive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Identity matching asks whether two records denote the same identity, yet the answer depends on the target granularity. Two records may match at the base level but not at the variant level: they share an underlying design while differing in attributes such as color or size. Final matching accuracy does not separately characterize the capabilities involved. To study this problem, we use e-commerce as a challenging real-world domain. We introduce PURE, a diagnostic benchmark for multi-granularity multimodal identity matching covering four capability dimensions: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Evidence-grounded Judgment. The benchmark comprises 1,457 multiple-choice questions across 14 tasks, derived from real-world matching pairs and verified by two domain experts. Across ten recent MLLMs, overall scores range from 47.1% to 86.0%. Understanding receives the highest mean score and Judgment the lowest, with weaknesses in visual difference localization and variant-level rule judgment. Modality ablations show that models benefit from multimodal evidence but can incorrectly identify conflicts between matching records. In direct matching, most models recognize matching pairs more reliably than non-matching pairs at the base level, whereas the reverse holds at the variant level. PURE therefore reveals what aggregate matching accuracy hides: not only whether models judge a pair correctly, but where they struggle to interpret evidence and apply matching criteria.

papers.abstract: A visual question answering (VQA) model can pass every image-only and question-only test yet fail when the same changes occur together. Standard robustness reports average over conditions and therefore cannot say which accepted requests remain vulnerable. We introduce M3-Test, a coverage audit that aligns each clean input with its single-modality variants and a complete 5x5 family, 4x4 strength joint library, so that any reduced test suite can be replayed on the same requests. Across 2.6 million responses from four vision-language models, joint failures affect 26-29% of the Qwen questions that pass all 40 single-modality tests, although fewer than 0.6% of their joint records fail. Passing the 25 maximum-strength corners does not close this gap: 11-14% of the accepted questions still fail elsewhere in the library. Re-executing the archived failures reproduces about 90% of them, against a 0.3-0.6% flip rate among matched passing controls, and re-checking the most fragile failure records supports 80-89% of them. On the evidence examined, neither execution noise nor grading error can fully account for the gap. The same aligned grids make previous evaluations reusable. On held-out images, a risk order learned from other models discovers about 80% of affected Qwen questions within 25 additional queries, compared with 65-68% for maximum-first and 53-57% for pairwise covering arrays. M3-Test thus turns a passing robustness suite into a request-level account of what remains untested, supporting acceptance, regression review and test allocation.
bullets: VQA models can pass all image-only and question-only tests yet fail when both modalities are perturbed together.

Archived failures were reproduced at about 90%, while matched passing controls flipped only 0.3–0.6%, suggesting noise and grading errors do not explain the gap.
A cross-model risk order found about 80% of affected Qwen questions within 25 extra queries, outperforming maximum-first and pairwise covering-array strategies.

papers.abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) foundation models provide transferable representations for diverse perception tasks in all-weather Earth observation. However, their development often relies on costly large-scale SAR pretraining, raising the question of whether such extensive domain-specific pretraining is necessary. We find that modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs) already provide visual encoders that can outperform dedicated SAR foundation models as downstream initializations. This motivates a new paradigm: reuse general visual capabilities and devote domain training to brief specialization. We therefore introduce SARVIA, an adaptive post-pretraining method that specializes modern MLLMs using self-supervised visual questions with computable answers. These questions are constructed from unlabeled observations through general image tasks that capture spatial relations and SAR-specific tasks that exploit native measurements and SAR--optical correspondence. A shared answer-prediction objective jointly trains low-rank adapters across visual and language components, with loss-driven task sampling. We then export the adapted visual encoder as a standalone backbone. With 600 adaptation steps and 2 GPU-hours, SARVIA outperforms the compared foundation models on all six SAR detection and segmentation benchmarks. Compared with dedicated SAR pretraining, SARVIA reduces domain-training costs by orders of magnitude while improving visual transfer across architectures and scales. This new paradigm shifts the emphasis from repeated, costly pretraining to a reusable specialization process that can benefit from advances in open MLLMs. Dataset and code: https://github.com/zcablii/SARVIA.
authors: Yuxuan Li, Zichen Tian, Qianru Sun
bullets: Motivation: Large-scale SAR-specific pretraining is costly, and modern MLLM visual encoders can provide strong downstream initializations.
Method: Adapt MLLMs with self-supervised visual questions derived from unlabeled imagery, combining general spatial tasks with SAR-specific measurements and SAR–optical correspondence.
Optimization: Jointly train low-rank adapters across visual and language components using a shared answer-prediction objective and loss-driven task sampling.
Result: Using 600 adaptation steps and 2 GPU-hours, SARVIA outperforms the compared foundation models across six SAR detection and segmentation benchmarks.
Scope: The adapted visual encoder is exported as a standalone backbone, emphasizing reusable specialization rather than repeated SAR pretraining.

papers.abstract: A vision-language model (VLM) can judge 3-D relations from the picture or from the ground layout. In photographs the two usually agree. We separate them with CueClash, rendered scenes in which the 2-D cue for each of five relations is right on exactly half the statements. The shortcut gap is accuracy when the cue is right minus accuracy when it is wrong. For Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.6 Flash at low reasoning effort it is +18 to +37 percentage points. It is +7 to +29 without two relations whose cue-wrong items are confounded with borderline cases or occlusion. Given ground coordinates and each relation's definition, they answer 99 to 100% correctly. Pixel measurements with camera depths remove most of the gap for objects fitting through openings. The failure lies in the step from the picture to the layout. The maps that the models draw of the scene from above mostly keep the depth order but, like the picture, shorten depth. GPT-5.5's maps stay close to a copy of the picture. Opus 5.5's and Gemini's maps undo about 0.6 of this shortening. Gemini's then shrink all depths by a further uniform factor. Opus 5.5 follows the picture mainly on fits, and its maps correct depth about as much as human observers of real scenes do. The three models also lose accuracy on CV-Bench photographs where a reliable 2-D cue misleads. In two open models the layout information reaches the language model, but their maps lose much of it.
bullets: Rendered scenes isolate five 3-D relations, with the image cue correct for half of the statements and wrong for the other half.
At low reasoning effort, three frontier models show shortcut gaps of +18 to +37 percentage points, or +7 to +29 when confounded relations are excluded.
When given ground coordinates and relation definitions, the models reach 99–100% accuracy, locating the main failure in image-to-layout reasoning.
Top-down scene maps usually preserve depth order but compress depth; GPT-5.5 largely copies the image, while Opus 5.5 and Gemini partially undo the compression.
The models also lose accuracy on photographs when reliable 2-D cues conflict with the true relation; pixel measurements with camera depths reduce the gap for objects fitting through openings.

papers.title: CueClash: Frontier Vision-Language Models Judge 3-D Relations Close to the Picture Plane
papers.tldr: CueClash shows that frontier vision-language models often judge 3-D relations from misleading 2-D picture cues rather than accurately recovering scene layout.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) is essential for detecting objects beyond the categories seen during training. Establishing vision-language associations is crucial for recognizing unseen categories, while integrating complementary visual features across levels supports detection at different scales. However, existing methods often provide insufficient textual guidance for object regions, rely on limited cross-modal alignment strategies, and underuse complementary features across levels, limiting their ability to detect unseen categories and objects of varying scales. To address these limitations, we propose a Text-Guided Modality Correction Network (TMCNet) that incorporates textual guidance into region feature extraction, cross-modal alignment, and multi-scale decoding to strengthen region-category semantic correspondence and promote complementary feature fusion across levels. First, a text-guided modality encoder incorporates textual semantics into queries to guide regional feature aggregation, reducing semantic ambiguity in object representations. Second, a cross-modal alignment module strengthens the correspondence between region representations and category semantics through interactions between visual and textual features. Finally, a progressive text correction decoder combines a top-down pathway with lateral connections to progressively fuse text-guided deep semantic features with shallow visual features at the corresponding scales, preserving both semantic information and spatial detail for objects of different sizes. Experiments on two public datasets, COCO-OVD and LVIS-OVD, demonstrate that TMCNet achieves strong performance in open-vocabulary object detection using simple text queries as guidance. Extending TMCNet to open-vocabulary segmentation also yields performance gains, demonstrating its cross-task applicability and extensibility.
authors: Yu Quan, Dong Zhang, Ping Gong, Peng Huang, JinHui Tang
bullets: Targets weak textual guidance, limited vision-language alignment, and underused multi-scale features in OVD.
Uses a text-guided modality encoder to incorporate category semantics into regional feature aggregation.
Applies cross-modal alignment to strengthen correspondence between region representations and category meanings.
Employs progressive text correction decoding to fuse deep semantic and shallow spatial features across scales.
Shows strong results on COCO-OVD and LVIS-OVD, with gains also reported for open-vocabulary segmentation.

papers.abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.
authors: Thorben Prein, Elton Pan, Rafael G\'omez-Bombarelli, Santiago Miret
bullets: Motivation: Experiments provide coupled molecular and spectral measurements, but conventional models often use only one conditioning direction.
Method: Randomly masks modalities and trains a transformer on multiple denoising tasks across 3D structures, UV, IR, and Raman spectra.
Contribution: A single model supports flexible any-to-any generation and arbitrary subsets of available measurements.
Result: On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, with reported gains over spectra-to-structure and specialist structure-to-spectra baselines.
Scope: The approach also supports molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references; ablations show benefits over structure-only training across model sizes.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of MOSAIC training and architecture. (a) At each training step, we perform any-to-any training by randomly selecting target modalities T and conditioning (context) modalities C. For example, IR and Raman provide conditioning for generating UV and molecular structure. (b) The pretrained encoder converts the conditioning modalities into context tokens, while each target modality is noised to xm t at timestep tm. We pass both sets of tokens to an MMDiT [7], where each of the D blocks applies joint self-attention across them. The model predicts target velocities vθ, which are used at inference to iteratively generate the target modalities from noise. The same model handles different combinations of conditioning and target modalities.

Figure 5: Model and data scaling. (a–c) Acc@1, H-RMSD and Composition across model scale. (d) The structure-only model overfits, while the multimodal model (gold) remains stable. Adding IR only as a co-target (purple) outperforms struct-only and captures most of the 3-spectra advantage. (e) Spectra generation quality across model scale. (f–h) Data scaling with an M-scale decoder.

Figure 2: MOSAIC: Multimodal any-to-any training unlocks new capabilities in scientific generative models. (a) Joint training over molecular structure, UV, IR, and Raman spectra with sampled conditioning and target modalities. (b) Structure generation accuracy improves with model size and exceeds that of the structure-only variant. (c) Any-to-any training enables structure generation, spectrum generation, missing-view completion, joint generation and spectral retrieval with a single model.

Figure 1: Scientific measurements provide complementary views of the same physical entity. With multimodal any-to-any training, a single model learns to generate any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset.

papers.title: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. The naive aggregation of these objectives via composite loss functions often induces optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference within the shared latent space. To resolve this, we introduce a unified representation-learning paradigm that reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold. Our approach maintains perceptual reconstruction as a supervisory signal and integrates a ranking-based discriminative constraint by systematically ordering matched and mismatched reconstruction outputs. This formulation embeds discriminative information seamlessly into the generative process, alleviating the risk of loss competition. Specifically, we propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by ensuring higher scores for matched pairs than for mismatched pairs, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which addresses supervision bias by focusing on mismatched comparisons within reliable feature subspaces. The proposed objectives are designed to be plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modifications to existing generative reconstruction frameworks. Theoretical analysis establishes rigorous connections to AUC/pAUC optimization and provides generalization guarantees. Extensive experiments validate that our method advances both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.
authors: Boyu Han, Qianqian Xu, Shilong Bao, Zhiyong Yang, Qingming Huang
bullets: Addresses the conflict between contrastive discrimination and generative reconstruction in visual encoders for MLLMs.
Recasts reconstruction as a ranking problem that scores matched outputs above mismatched ones.
Introduces AUCGR for AUC-based ranking and pAUCGR for focusing on reliable mismatched comparisons to reduce supervision bias.
The objectives are plug-and-play and require no architectural changes.
Experiments report improved discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation, supported by theoretical generalization analysis.

papers.abstract: Decision models can answer a typed question about an image with a probability per option, without generating text. In our case study of Clef-flash (post-trained Qwen3.5-9B backbone) on industrial inspection benchmarks, we ask whether it localizes the anomalies it detects. We obtained uneven results with zero-shot detection: per-category image AUROC 0.924 on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2. On the former, the decision head's routing attention produces 0.391 mean per-image pixel AUROC, and hiding the image tokens from it leaves detection unchanged. The multimodal LLM's backbone attention does point at the defect, however it falls below a center prior when we change question. It falls below chance if we remove textual context in the question, partly due to backbone attention leaving the object, while the head's map hardly changes. The backbone's states carry the location when probed with normal images, on the test-split images, however, the decision depends on the defect region. A larger model, Clef, that comes with a post-trained Qwen3.8-27B backbone, gives no useful map in the decision head either. We found that it's possible to recover anomaly location by asking question specifically on an image region, retraining the head or reading the backbone, but none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.
bullets: Zero-shot image-level detection is strong on MVTec AD but weaker on MVTec AD 2.
The decision head’s routing attention provides poor pixel localization, and hiding image tokens does not change detection.
Backbone attention can indicate defects, but localization depends on question wording and textual context and may fall below chance.
Anomaly location can be recovered through region-specific questions, head retraining, or backbone probing, though none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.
A larger Clef model also produces no useful localization map in its decision head.
papers.selection_reason: Case study of a Qwen-based multimodal decision model and its anomaly localization is relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Deciding Without Pointing: A Case Study of Whether a Decision Model Localizes the Anomalies It Detects
papers.tldr: Clef-flash detects industrial image anomalies but its decision head generally does not reliably localize them.

papers.abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) achieves impressive zero-shot image classification performance by comparing image embeddings against class-specific text embeddings. While recent few-shot methods leverage labeled training samples to improve upon this zero-shot baseline, they often predominantly rely on image embeddings and underutilize the semantic structure of the text embeddings. In this paper, we introduce DEFTS, a data-efficient, training-free few-shot classification method strictly in the text subspace. We first demonstrate empirically that while raw text embeddings can be suboptimal as direct classifiers, the linear subspace they span remains highly discriminative. DEFTS therefore proposes to reduce the image-text modality gap by projecting estimated image prototypes directly into this subspace. Importantly, by expressing these prototypes as linear combinations of text embeddings, DEFTS reduces a high-dimensional estimation problem to the derivation of just a few coefficients. These coefficients are then computed via a Bayesian posterior mean, using a prior naturally centered on the original text embedding coordinates. Extensive experiments across 12 image classification benchmarks demonstrate that DEFTS significantly improves upon existing training-free methods.
bullets: Addresses the underuse of CLIP’s semantic text structure in existing few-shot methods.
Projects estimated image prototypes into the text-embedding subspace to reduce the image–text modality gap.
Represents prototypes with a small number of text-embedding coefficients instead of estimating them in the full image space.
Computes coefficients using a Bayesian posterior mean with a prior centered on the original text-embedding coordinates.
Experiments on 12 image-classification benchmarks show significant improvements over existing training-free methods.

papers.abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV)-conditioned large language models (LLMs) enable language-interactive driving, but onboard deployment requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation. We present GridDriver, an efficient BEV-conditioned LLM framework combining trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, natural-language navigation, driving explanations, and scene question answering. Lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens provide scene context to a shared LLM, while frame-wise scheduling interleaves trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation. GridDriver achieves competitive performance on public benchmarks, reaching 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared planning and QA checkpoint. Spatial representation analyses demonstrate improved geometric information retention and trajectory prediction compared with Q-Former compression. The system achieves 32.7 ms standalone planning latency and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline. We further evaluate planning on our own data recordings and demonstrate open-loop onboard operation on a research vehicle. Across public benchmarks and real-world evaluations, we identify strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.
authors: Katharina Winter, William Engel, Zain A. Alishammat, Fabian B. Flohr
bullets: Addresses the challenge of running autoregressive language generation alongside real-time onboard driving planning.
Uses lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception, spatially structured tokens, and frame-wise scheduling to interleave planning with asynchronous language generation.
Supports trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, navigation instructions, driving explanations, and scene question answering.
Reports 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM, 57.6% nuScenes-QA accuracy, 32.7 ms standalone planning latency, and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline.
Evaluations include public benchmarks, proprietary recordings, and open-loop operation on a research vehicle; the abstract notes both strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models(VLMs) while preserving the target model's outputs, but its speedup diminishes under high concurrency serving as the system becomes more compute bounded as the batch size increases. This problem is pronounced for multimodal speculative decoding as the long range of the image tokens in the prompt can significantly increase the computational cost during draft token prediction. The block-diffusion drafters (e.g. DFlash, DSpark) can effectively speed up the draft model efficiency by predicting multiple draft tokens in one forward pass, but their speedup for VLMs under high concurrency is still modest (<9%). In order to understand this gap, we examine the information flow between different modalities from target model to draft model and identify the sparsity pattern of visual attention between the target and draft models: only small set of key-value heads in the draft model need direct visual feature attention in the context and only visual features from top level layers in the target model need to be attended in the context. We therefore propose VisHead-Spec, which selects a small, fixed set of key-value (KV) heads to attend to all image features from top level layers in the target model and restricts the remaining heads to text features. On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, VisHead-Spec-8 lets 8 of the drafter's 40 KV heads read the image while keeping accepted length within 0.3% of the block-diffusion draft model baseline (i.e. DSpark). At batch size 64, its throughput gain over autoregressive decoding increases to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, its speedup remains comparable to DSpark.
authors: Xin Guo, Arushi Rai, Xiang Zhou, Qiang Zhang, Siyu Lin, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
bullets: High-concurrency VLM serving becomes compute-bound, while long image-token contexts make draft prediction expensive.
The method identifies sparse cross-modal information flow: only a few draft KV heads need visual features, primarily from the target model’s top layers.

On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, accepted length stays within 0.3% of the DSpark baseline.
At batch size 64, throughput gain reaches 16.0% versus 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, performance remains comparable.

papers.abstract: Multimodal models increasingly reason by synthesizing pixels, sketching maze paths within interleaved chains of thought or rolling out video solutions frame by frame. Each visual thought runs the full diffusion schedule inherited from photorealistic synthesis, so iterative denoising dominates inference cost. We study how to allocate test-time compute along two axes: when to render visual thoughts rather than thinking in text or answering directly, and how many denoising steps each thought requires. Controlled interventions that vary only how the thought is rendered uncover three regimes. Causal thoughts carry the plan and become legible early: an 8-step sketch nearly matches a 50-step render in accuracy, commits to the same plan as often as two independent full renders agree, and in video models mostly fails by stalling short of the goal, so the rollout abstains. Decorative thoughts can be omitted without loss, whereas harmful thoughts lower accuracy. Because the regime depends on both model and task, always drawing is suboptimal. Across 14 model-benchmark pairs of three interleaved reasoners, answering directly, without any thinking, wins 9 pairs, and choosing among direct, text-only, and visual tiers from ten labeled examples per pair raises mean accuracy from 60.7% (always drawing) to 65.1%. Where drawing pays, we propose sketch-and-vote, which samples 8-step sketches (a step count chosen without labels) from independent noises until one answer reaches three votes. With this one setting, sketch-and-vote beats full rendering with fewer denoising steps on an image reasoner and two video reasoners, by 8.6 points on VSP spatial planning and by 9.6 and 22.1 points on mazes.
authors: Sheng Lu, Guangpin Tao, Tong Lu, Ying Tai
bullets: Full diffusion denoising makes visual thoughts expensive, but causal plans often become clear after only 8 steps.
Visual thoughts vary by role: causal sketches help, decorative thoughts can be omitted, and harmful thoughts may reduce accuracy.
Across 14 model–benchmark pairs, direct answering was best in 9; selecting among direct, text-only, and visual modes improved mean accuracy from 60.7% to 65.1%.
The proposed sketch-and-vote method samples 8-step sketches until one answer gets three votes, outperforming full rendering on selected image and video reasoning tasks.
The best rendering strategy depends on both the model and task; video rollouts may fail by stalling before reaching the goal and should abstain.

papers.selection_reason: Allocates test-time compute in generative visual reasoning by choosing when to render and how many denoising steps; relevant to efficient AI and multimodal interleaved reasoning.
papers.title: Sketch, Don't Paint: Allocating Test-Time Compute in Generative Visual Reasoning
papers.tldr: Visual reasoning need not use full diffusion: selectively render brief sketches—and sometimes skip visual thinking entirely—to reduce test-time compute while preserving or improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in vision-language tasks; yet, whether they maintain consistent understanding of information-rich visuals (InfoVis) when the surface language changes remains unclear. To quantify this capability, we introduce MInfoVisQA, a parallel benchmark with 8,960 QA configurations derived from 128 seed instances across 24 languages. We construct seed-matched, language-parallel visuals and QA pairs by disentangling numerical-structural data from text and programmatically synchronizing translated labels. We evaluate 25 MLLMs under two settings: Language-Aligned QA (LQA, matching visual-text languages) and Cross-Language QA (XQA, fixed QA language with varying visual languages). The results show that aggregate accuracy masks substantial robustness gaps: two models with comparable mean LQA accuracy (80.4\%) exhibit performance spreads of 7.8 and 20.3 percentage points across languages. Moreover, all 25 models score lower with non-English visuals under fixed English QA, underscoring the need for cross-language sensitivity metrics.
authors: Changjiang Jiang, Jiang Zhou, Xinbin Yuan, Fan Zhang, Tao Feng, Zhuohan Xie
bullets: Introduces 8,960 parallel QA configurations from 128 seed instances spanning 24 languages.
Creates language-matched visuals and QA pairs by separating numerical-structural data from text and synchronizing translated labels.
Evaluates 25 MLLMs in language-aligned and cross-language settings.
Models with similar mean aligned accuracy can have markedly different across-language performance spreads.
All evaluated models perform worse with non-English visuals when questions remain in English, motivating cross-language sensitivity metrics.

papers.abstract: Persistent spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents to operate reliably in environments they repeatedly encounter. It requires recognizing revisited places despite viewpoint changes, distinguishing them from similar-looking rooms, and updating memories as environments change. Yet existing evaluations often leave physical place identity across separated visits implicit. We introduce ReSpaceBench, a benchmark comprising 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes, organized into 9 tasks spanning room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream reasoning. Controlled walkthroughs define visits by physical room entry and deliberately include same-type room distractors and cross-session object changes. Our evaluation of 32 models and 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks reveals substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated zero-shot model achieves 50.5% overall accuracy and 52.2% on a 450-question subset, compared with 90.1% for human annotators. The evaluated agentic frameworks offer no overall improvement over direct inference with the same base model. Analysis of agent execution traces reveals evidence omissions and incorrect cross-visit room associations as major failure modes, suggesting that iterative evidence seeking alone does not ensure consistent spatial memory. Further analyses expose a gap between recognizing familiar rooms and identifying the correct visited room, while annotation-guided sampling highlights the importance of preserving intervening visits and transitions. We also provide RS-30K, a separate training dataset from synthetic sources with no template, scene, route, or video overlap with the benchmark. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, with the largest gains in association and improvements extending to real-life scenes.
bullets: Benchmarks persistent spatial memory with 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes and 9 tasks.
Tests room association, state tracking, and downstream reasoning under viewpoint changes, distractor rooms, and changing objects.
The best evaluated zero-shot model reaches 50.5% accuracy versus 90.1% for human annotators; agentic frameworks do not improve overall results.
Key failures include omitted evidence and incorrect associations between rooms visited at different times.
Training on the separate RS-30K dataset improves Qwen3-VL-8B from 35.5% to 60.4%, especially on room association and real-life scenes.
