papers.abstract: Existing Large Vision-Language Model benchmarks primarily evaluate visual understanding in general everyday scenarios, leaving historical consistency with a specified era and country largely underexplored. To address this gap, we propose AnachroBench, a controlled discriminative benchmark for evaluating historical consistency in visual scenes. It contains 1,600 image pairs from eight countries spanning the late 19th to the early 20th century, each pairing an original historical image with an anachronistic version containing a seamlessly inserted modern object. AnachroBench evaluates three aspects: Inserted Object Perception, which tests whether models detect the inserted modern object; Era-Country Consistency, which assesses whether the scene is consistent with the specified era and country; and Conditional Era-Country Consistency, which measures consistency judgments only when the inserted object is correctly perceived. A false consistency judgment occurs when a model perceives the modern object but still judges the scene as historically consistent. Overall, AnachroBench reveals a gap between inserted object perception and era-country consistency judgments, providing a targeted evaluation of this behavior.
bullets: Introduces a controlled benchmark for historical consistency, an underexplored aspect of vision-language evaluation.
Contains 1,600 paired images from eight countries spanning the late 19th to early 20th century.
Measures inserted-object perception, era-country consistency, and conditional consistency given correct object detection.
Finds a gap between recognizing inserted modern objects and judging scenes as historically inconsistent.
Identifies false consistency judgments when models detect the object but still accept the scene as historically consistent.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, often failing to effectively utilize critical evidence already encoded in their visual representations. Existing approaches address this limitation through repeated visual processing or explicit reasoning, introducing substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we propose ReAccess, a lightweight framework that preserves and reuses question-relevant visual evidence through compact associative memory. Constructed during a single visual prefill, the memory supports progressive evidence retrieval that steers both attention queries and hidden representations, enabling effective visual grounding without repeated image encoding or explicit reasoning traces. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both general visual understanding and fine-grained perception, while achieving substantially faster inference than existing reasoning-intensive approaches, demonstrating a promising path to efficient multimodal reasoning.
bullets: Addresses VLMs’ difficulty in exploiting critical evidence already present in visual representations.
Builds a compact associative memory during a single visual prefill, avoiding repeated image encoding.
Progressively retrieves evidence to guide attention queries and hidden representations without explicit reasoning traces.
Experiments report consistent gains in general visual understanding and fine-grained perception.
Achieves faster inference than reasoning-intensive approaches, though specific benchmarks and quantitative results are not given.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving visual agents keep what they learn as skills: key frames with step notes on a task's steps and their order. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is now a popular way to train such skills into a vision-language model that matches, on its own answers, a teacher that also reads the written order. At deployment, frames often go missing or show an unusual order, as when a person or a website reorders the steps. Existing internalization methods keep any order they store in the frame-reading weights: trained on full frames, the model guesses when they are missing, and trained with frames withheld, it stores the order, so memory can override what it sees. We propose PriorSplit, which fills in missing frames from an order kept outside the model, with no training beyond OPSD. It counts which of two neighboring steps comes first in training episodes, and the model checks if both asked steps are in view: if so, it answers from the frames, and otherwise the counts answer. Extensive experiments on synthetic skills with five models and on step-tagged order questions in new episodes of seen web, cooking and egocentric tasks demonstrate that, with frames missing, PriorSplit outperforms every compared method at OPSD's training cost. With Qwen3-VL-4B on synthetic skills, it also stays close to OPSD on unusual orders, where methods that gain most by storing the order fall behind.
bullets: Addresses a key failure mode of OPSD-trained skills: memorized step order can override what the model actually sees.
Stores pairwise step-order counts outside the VLM and uses them only when one or both queried frames are unavailable.
When both relevant steps are visible, the agent answers from the frames; otherwise, it consults the external prior.
Requires no training beyond standard on-policy self-distillation.
Experiments across synthetic skills and web, cooking, and egocentric tasks show the best performance under missing frames, while remaining close to OPSD on unusual orders.

papers.selection_reason: VLM agents with skill memory and handling of missing frames/order; relevant to embodied memory and multimodal LLM agents.
papers.title: Prior-as-Skill: Remember Outside and Read Inside with On-Policy Self-Distillation for Self-Evolving VLM Agents
papers.tldr: PriorSplit separates visual evidence from an externally stored order prior, improving self-evolving VLM agents when frames are missing while remaining robust to reordered steps.

papers.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer others' beliefs, goals, and intentions, is a cornerstone of social intelligence. Multimodal ToM requires inferring an agent's mental state from evidence that is available to that agent, rather than from the complete episode observed by the solver. Existing LLM-based and Bayesian model-based approaches reconstruct global event traces, yet they do not explicitly distinguish objective events from agent-admissible evidence during hypothesis evaluation. Consequently, agent-inaccessible events or semantically misaligned actions and utterances may influence the inferred belief, goal, or social intention, leading to perspective leakage and source or route confusion. We formulate this limitation as an evidence-admissibility problem: evidence should contribute to a mental-state hypothesis only when it is accessible to the relevant agent, preserves its information source, and is diagnostic of the queried mental-state variable. To operationalize this principle, we propose PIP-ToM, an evidence-admissibility interface that constructs agent-specific evidence stores, aligns them with structured mental-state claims, and calibrates model-based hypothesis scores while preserving the underlying Bayesian inference process. PIP-ToM with GPT-4o outperforms existing ToM methods across MuMA-ToM, MMToM-QA, and Hi-ToM, achieving average accuracies of 92.56%, 95.00%, and 95.00%, respectively.
bullets: Frames perspective leakage and source/route confusion as an evidence-admissibility problem.
Builds agent-specific evidence stores and aligns them with structured mental-state claims.
Calibrates model-based hypothesis scores while preserving the underlying Bayesian inference process.
With GPT-4o, reports strong performance across MuMA-ToM, MMToM-QA, and Hi-ToM, with accuracies of 92.56%, 95.00%, and 95.00%.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained vision-language models excel across varied perception tasks, but adapting them to novel downstream settings without sacrificing generalization remains non-trivial. Existing parameter-efficient prompt learning method often yields inconsistent representations and fails to account for semantic distribution shifts. In this work, we present DiscoVL, a disentangled cross-modal representation learning framework that couples orthogonal adversarial regularization with structured cross-modal alignment for vision-language models. To address the insufficient cross-modal interaction, our DiscoVL designs a multi-branch low-rank residual aligner that decomposes representations into subspaces and enables bidirectional cross-modal feedback between visual and textual streams at each layer. Furthermore, while conventional triplet constraints overfit features to class centroids, we design an orthogonal regularization for adversarial triplet loss, which prevents centroid collapse and substantially boosts generalization. Evaluations on 15 benchmarks demonstrate that DiscoVL delivers consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods for base-to-novel generalization, cross-dataset evaluation, and few-shot learning
bullets: Targets inconsistent representations and semantic distribution shifts in parameter-efficient prompt learning.
Uses a multi-branch low-rank residual aligner to decompose representations and provide bidirectional visual-textual feedback at each layer.
Introduces orthogonal regularization for adversarial triplet loss to avoid centroid collapse and improve generalization.
Evaluated across 15 benchmarks, with consistent improvements reported for base-to-novel generalization, cross-dataset evaluation, and few-shot learning.

papers.abstract: When a vision-language model describes an image, it names one object at a time and it rarely repeats itself, yet how the model plans this order is far from obvious. We characterize the mechanism a VLM uses to decide where to look before it looks. The mechanism has four main parts. First, binding heads match the relevant text tokens against the image and resolve them into pointers to the matched image region. Second, the same binding heads bind each written answer to the region it came from, and the model turns it into a progress signal: a cursor, the position in the image up to which the list has been written. Third, a select step chooses the nearest unwritten region after the cursor, or stops. Finally, gaze heads execute the chosen pointer and return a concept of what is drawn there, which language heads and the late MLPs turn into a word in the language of the question. We validate each part of this mechanism through causal patching in Qwen3-VL models on a synthetic visual retrieval task, and test our mechanisms against alternative hypotheses. We further show that the mechanism holds across input formats, natural photographs, and languages, and that its binding, relay, and gaze heads appear at every model size from 2B to 32B. This work allows us to investigate how a VLM turns a question and an image into a sequence of answers, layer by layer and token by token. More broadly, it opens a way to study how models plan over complex multi-step tasks with long rollouts. Our project is available at https://plan.baulab.info/
authors: Rohit Gandikota, Arnab Sen Sharma, Adam Belfki, David Bau
bullets: Binding heads link text tokens and previous answers to their corresponding image regions.
A progress signal acts as a cursor marking how far through the image’s regions the model has written.
A selection step chooses the nearest unwritten region or stops generation.
Gaze heads execute the selected pointer, while language components convert the retrieved visual concept into an answer word.
Causal patching in Qwen3-VL models supports the mechanism across formats, photographs, languages, and model sizes from 2B to 32B parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Task setup: We provide an image strip with each panel containing a shape and a letter. We ask the model to retrieve the label of the panel that contains the queried shape. (b) The mechanism, with tokens across and layers down. The model solves the task early, at the shape token star, well before it answers: (1) binding heads match the request against the image and resolve a pointer to the matching panel. (2) Relay heads carry that pointer to the “:” token, where the answer has to be produced, and (3) gaze heads execute it to retrieve the letter from that panel. (4) Once T is written, binding heads bind it to its panel, and the model calculates its progress and (5) selects what answer to mention next (by repeating steps 3-5) or to stop if none is left.

Figure 3: (a) Relay heads transfer the pointer from the shape token to the colon. When each relay head may read only one token at a time, the pointer is transferred mostly when the relay heads at the colon token read the shape token. Each cell is the mean gain of K over T on 500 heldout pairs. (b) A copied comma state skips a written panel at layers 20-21. When patching the source’s comma-token residual into the target’s colon-token residual, one layer at a time: at layer 20 the target skips to its next candidate, T, in 91.0± 2.4% of pairs, and in 70.0± 3.9% at layer 21. From layers 22-28 it takes the source’s next panel pointer, W, and from layer 30 the source’s letter, A. (c) A copied comma state says where the list goes on. With a more targeted setup, we find at layers 20 and 21 the model answers with the first candidate “after panel 4”, W, in 98.4± 1.1% and 97.6± 1.3% of pairs. The shaded band marks layers 20-21.

papers.abstract: Structure-level wildfire vulnerability assessment is critical for reducing losses in wildland-urban interface communities, yet existing methods often fail to combine parcel-scale ignition pathways with community-scale geographic coverage. This study introduces Wildfire-SSR (Satellite and Street-view for wildfire Risk), a geolocation-aware multimodal framework that integrates macro-scale satellite context with micro-scale street-view evidence. A Vision-Language Model extracts wildfire-relevant building and site attributes from pre-event street-view panoramas and converts them into structured semantic text. These features are spatially aligned with satellite imagery through a decoupled cross-attention fusion decoder, while a frozen satellite-pretrained DINOv3 encoder captures overhead visual context. Alternative geolocation embedding strategies are evaluated to anchor text-derived features within each satellite patch. The framework is tested on approximately 37,000 structures affected by the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires in Los Angeles, using wildfire risk labels derived from relative post-event damage patterns to better represent inherent structural vulnerability. Rotary Positional Embedding provides the strongest spatial grounding, achieving a building localization F1 score of 0.6735 and a harmonic mean F1 score of 0.2476 for five-class pixel-level risk classification, outperforming unimodal baselines and an unanchored multimodal configuration. The model also shows a conservative bias in higher-risk classes, reducing severe-risk underestimation, and completes end-to-end assessment of the study area in 37 minutes on a single GPU. Wildfire-SSR reframes cross-view fusion as localized semantic alignment and provides a scalable tool for mitigation prioritization, resilience planning, and insurance-oriented wildfire risk assessment.
authors: Yu-Hsuan Ho, Yiming Xiao, Hao-En Lai, Ali Mostafavi, Samuel D. Brody
bullets: Addresses the gap between parcel-scale ignition pathways and community-scale geographic coverage in wildfire vulnerability assessment.
A Vision-Language Model extracts building and site attributes from pre-event street-view panoramas and aligns them with satellite context using cross-attention and geolocation embeddings.
Evaluated on approximately 37,000 structures affected by the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires in Los Angeles, with labels based on relative post-fire damage patterns.
Rotary Positional Embedding performed best, reaching a building-localization F1 of 0.6735 and a five-class pixel-level risk harmonic mean F1 of 0.2476.
The model reduced severe-risk underestimation and assessed the study area in 37 minutes on a single GPU, supporting mitigation and resilience planning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed geolocation-aware multimodal framework for structure-level wildfire risk assessment. The pipeline addresses the limitations of isolated unimodal approaches by integrating macro-scale satellite imagery with micro-scale street-view data. A Vision-Language Model first extracts semantic building vulnerabilities from street-level images into structured text descriptions. To bridge the spatial disconnect between modalities, the geographical coordinates of the street-view captures are mapped to local relative coordinates and injected into CLIPencoded text embeddings. A decoupled cross-attention multimodal fusion decoder then aligns these geolocation-aware text features with overhead visual features extracted via DINOv3. The proposed model processes these fused representations into pixel-wise risk labels, which are then transformed into a detailed, actionable community-scale wildfire risk map.

Figure 2: Overview of the model architecture. Ground-level street-view images are first processed by a Vision-Language Model to extract structured semantic attributes, which are combined with their geographic coordinates to form spatially anchored text embeddings. A multimodal fusion decoder then integrates these location-aware micro-level features with macro-level visual features extracted from pre-event satellite imagery via a frozen satellite-pretrained vision encoder to generate precise, structure-level wildfire risk maps.

Figure 6: Pixel-level wildfire vulnerability predictions from the proposed RoPE-based multimodal framework (right) compared against the ground-truth building-level risk labels (left) for representative tiles in the Eaton and Palisades study areas. Colors denote the five ordinal risk classes from minimal to extreme; the comparison illustrates the model’s capacity to capture broad spatial patterns of structural vulnerability while highlighting residual confusion between adjacent low and moderate tiers.

Figure 5: Study area: final perimeters of the 2025 Eaton and Palisades wildfires in the Los Angeles region, showing the wildland-urban interface neighborhoods used for structure-level vulnerability evaluation. Perimeter data are sourced from the City of Los Angeles GeoHub (City of Los Angeles, 2025c).

Figure 4: Schematic representation of the geometric localization algorithm. To preserve view-angle perspective, orthogonal normal vectors (ns) are cast from the street-view camera’s heading direction. The intersection of these street vectors with the heading vectors (nb) originating from adjacent building centroids determines the precise spatial anchor point on the observed facade.

Figure 3: Structure of the two-way cross-attention block utilizing a decoupled attention mechanism. Geolocation embeddings (GEs) are injected specifically into the queries (Q) and keys (K) to facilitate spatial routing, while values (V ) remain purely semantic to preserve micro-level building attributes. The block consists of three sequential steps: sparse text self-attention to capture geometric dependencies between structural, sparse-to-dense cross-attention to update textual context with overhead visual data, and dense-to-sparse cross-attention to infuse the macro-level visual map with ground-sourced semantic details.
Table 3: Ablation study results on input modalities and geolocation embeddings. Best results are bolded, second-best are underlined.
Table 4: Results of the label reconstruction diagnostic experiment utilizing explicit risk levels as text input. Best results are bolded, second-best are underlined.
Table 1: Performance comparison of geolocation embedding strategies. Best results are bolded, second-best are underlined.
Table 2: Quantitative evaluation of building wildfire risk classification across pixel-level and building-level aggregated metrics. Best results are bolded, second-best are underlined.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the answer can be decoded from their own hidden states. We trace this failure from the visual tokens to the answer letter, in Qwen3-VL (2B-32B), InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B, on synthetic shape matching, same-instance point correspondence (HPatches), and semantic correspondence (SPair-71k), and find two distinct failure points, a small set of attention heads that carries the comparison, and a repair that touches 0.02% of the parameters. Two failure points: exact copies are compared but not read out. An answer-position probe exceeds the calibrated output by 15 to 25 points in every family, for nameable and unnameable shapes alike, and steering along the probe's direction moves no more answers than random directions. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but never reach the answer. One pathway: redistributing the cross-image attention of 16-32 heads, with its mass preserved, removes 17-22 points of synthetic and 15-32 points of HPatches accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads. A lever that training finds on its own: training only these heads' query and key projections raises SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 25.1 points (InternVL3.5-8B), beats both layer-matched and attention-matched heads, and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. An unconstrained all-layer adapter routes 21-51% of its gain through the attention of the same heads, against at most 7% for random heads, and does so by changing what they read (83-86% of the effect) rather than their weights. Every decision rule was frozen before its run, and every reported number is recomputed by independent verification scripts.
bullets: The failure occurs at two stages: correspondence is present in visual tokens but is not reliably read out, and cross-image attention in a small set of heads is misrouted.
Across Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, and Gemma-3, answer-position probes outperform calibrated outputs by 15–25 points, while steering does not reliably change answers.
Redistributing attention in 16–32 identified heads causes 15–32-point accuracy drops, far larger than changes from random or attention-matched heads.
Training only the query and key projections of these heads improves SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points for Qwen3-VL-8B and 25.1 points for InternVL3.5-8B, with transfer to HPatches and BLINK.

papers.abstract: Question answering over ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing scenes poses a tension for multimodal large language models: global overviews obscure small objects and local attributes, whereas detailed crops consume substantial context. Compressing inspected crops into short sequences of continuous visual latents offers a compact memory once crop tokens are discarded, yet diagnostic studies on natural images find that models often ignore latent content, leaving unclear whether compact latents can retain fine-grained targets lost in downsampled UHR remote sensing scenes. To isolate evidence retention from region selection, we encode high-resolution crops into latent memory tokens for frozen backbones and evaluate both their predictive utility and content dependence. Across two generations of Qwen-VL on LRS-GRO, a 64-token memory achieves 7.6- to 9.9-fold compression of retained crop tokens and improves accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image alone, recovering most of the high-resolution crop gain with consistent behavior on XLRS-Bench. Substituting memory from another image or another region of the same scene reduces accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points and yields lower accuracy than removing memory altogether, demonstrating that predictions depend on the encoded regional evidence. Restoring the source crop within the same model reduces the accuracy loss caused by zeroing or removing memory. These findings establish that compact visual latents retain useful local evidence in UHR remote sensing and identify evidence availability as a key factor governing their contribution.
authors: Meng Tang, Siyuan Du, Yuxin Liu, Shuaishuai Cao, Di Wang, Haonan Guo
bullets: UHR scenes create a trade-off between global context, which hides small details, and high-resolution crops, which consume substantial context.
The study encodes high-resolution crops into 64 latent memory tokens for frozen multimodal backbones, isolating evidence retention from region selection.
Across two Qwen-VL generations, memory compresses crop tokens by 7.6–9.9× and improves accuracy by 2.5–4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image.
Replacing memory with another image or region lowers accuracy by 5.8–7.4 points, showing predictions depend on the encoded local evidence.
Results are consistent on XLRS-Bench and indicate that evidence availability governs the usefulness of compact visual latents.

papers.abstract: AI systems for creative media generation expand human capabilities yet risk diminishing human agency. A core problem is anchoring, where the user's thinking becomes anchored to a polished, generated artifact, shifting the user's role from active authoring to reactive editing. We propose pre-generation belief controls that can empower creators to inspect, revise, and steer the AI's interpretation before any media is generated, so that the initial anchor is set by the human. We formalize four design principles and instantiate them in the Proactive Co-Creator (PaCC), a system for early-stage conceptual ideation and prototyping that proactively surfaces its assumptions and uncertainty through clarifications, belief graphs, and media attributes, inviting users to shape the AI's beliefs before generating the final outcome. Using PaCC as a design probe in a small-scale, single-arm exploratory user study, we observed that participants reported directionally positive sense of agency and process control relative to their familiar prompt-based AI tools, noting that surfaced assumptions helped them think through details they had overlooked, whereas their feelings about ownership and authorship diverged
bullets: Creative AI can anchor users to generated artifacts, shifting them from active authors to reactive editors.
The proposed approach uses pre-generation belief controls so users can inspect, revise, and steer the AI’s interpretation first.
PaCC surfaces assumptions and uncertainty through clarifications, belief graphs, and media attributes during early ideation and prototyping.
A small exploratory study found directionally positive perceived agency and process control compared with familiar prompt-based tools.
Participants valued surfaced assumptions for revealing overlooked details, but reported divergent feelings about ownership and authorship.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The Proactive Co-Creator (PaCC) interface for shaping AI’s beliefs before generation (§2). (A) Prompt entry with optional reference images. Creators control AI proactiveness (A1) across three tiers: literal extraction (low), reasonable scene inference (medium; e.g., adding a “party table” to the cat party), or creative liberty (high; e.g., a “disco ball”). Modality tabs switch between Image, Story, and Video (A2). (B) Belief Graph: An editable visualization of explicit entities (solid borders), AI-inferred entities (dashed borders), and relationship edges (e.g., “hosting”). (C1–C2) Clarification Questions: Offers 3–5 selectable options per question so creators can resolve ambiguity and guide the AI’s interpretation; clicking “You Decide” delegates a specific choice to the AI. (D1–D2) Entity Attribute Editing: Adjusts properties of individual nodes. (E1–E2) Media Attributes: Controls global scene aesthetics (e.g., lighting, style, pacing). By surfacing and aligning assumptions and possibilities prior to media generation, PaCC establishes the human intent as the anchor.

papers.abstract: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.
authors: Shuyi Ouyang, Xiaojun Tang, Zijian Zou, Xintong Zhang, Mingli Song, Guannan Zhang, Hongwei Xue
bullets: Covers 211 creation and modification tasks across presentations, static graphics, animations/videos, and web interfaces.
Separately measures Task Fulfillment and Artifact Performance across content, organization, visuals, and delivery.
Uses task-specific rating anchors grounded in source materials, intended audiences, purposes, media, and artifact inspection records.
Evaluates nine model-harness configurations, whose overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52.
Artifact Performance explains 73.4% of the score gap between the highest- and lowest-performing configurations.

papers.abstract: Streaming video LLMs can continuously observe the world, yet often handle user requests in isolation. We introduce ALIVE, an interactive streaming video model supporting proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. We construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage training. Contrastive supervised fine-tuning teaches when and how to respond, while reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) combines trajectory-level and local advantages to refine decisions, responses, and silence across multi-turn interactions. We also introduce FSI-Bench to evaluate feedback seeking and subsequent task completion. ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among the compared models on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench, demonstrating strong streaming understanding and interactive capabilities.

papers.abstract: Children using Scratch to learn programming can struggle with text-heavy, lengthy explanations and hints during debugging. Verbal interactions based on screen sharing or camera data may be an interesting alternative for supporting learners. We therefore explore the quality, use, and perceptions of fifth- and sixth-graders' verbal interactions with a GenAI tutor. The goal is to investigate the quality and use of the multimodal GenAI tutor in the given context. First of all, a pilot study of eight tasks conducted without students helped inform the process of the tutor's classroom evaluation. The classroom study was realized after fifth- and sixth-graders had participated in six Scratch classroom lessons. Then 23 students were introduced to the tutor, worked on the eight tasks with the GenAI tutor, and completed a questionnaire. The analysis of the pilot and classroom study shows that the tutor's responses were intelligible and actionable, and no single turn revealed a complete solution. However, the tutor missed existing errors in 61.5% of 603 error-related classroom turns, compared to 15.7% in the pilot study. Children's voice prompts were brief and mostly responded to the tutor. Although a video had explained that responses could be incorrect, 39.1% of the children trusted the tutor's answers to always be correct. These findings have implications for educators and learners using multimodal GenAI tutors, as they need to be aware that an intelligible and human-like voice does not ensure correct support. For developers, our results suggest that screen sharing alone does not ensure responses that match the program state.

papers.abstract: Visual grounding benchmarks usually do not consider the contextual uncertainty of real-world scenarios. In this study, we construct a novel benchmark, the Japanese evaluation for Ambiguous visual Grounding with Dialogue (JAG-D) dataset. It consists of human-robot conversational multimodal interactions covering different types of ambiguity, arising from visual and linguistic categories. We evaluate the capabilities of different state-of-the-art Visual Language Models (VLMs) for ambiguity recognition and resolution. We compare dialogue context grounding performance for visual and linguistic ambiguity resolution. Our experiments show that VLMs can substantially improve the resolution of linguistic ambiguity, especially Japanese zero anaphora, by using dialogue context. We further conduct a comparative analysis to understand whether grounding improvements arise from the semantic content of the dialogue or from its conversational structure.

papers.abstract: Temporal medical image segmentation relies on pixel-wise annotations, which are prohibitively expensive for long image sequences. Existing weakly-supervised methods reduce the annotation burden per frame but still require repeated annotations across the sequence. Furthermore, sparse supervision can result in temporally unstable representations. Addressing both challenges requires a model that can leverage strong spatial priors from large-scale pretraining while minimizing reliance on dense annotations. Frozen 2D vision foundation models provide a promising basis for this by offering transferable spatial representations with low trainable parameters. However, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits their ability to propagate reliable information across anatomical sequences. To address this, we present a weakly-supervised framework for temporal segmentation from a single scribble-annotated frame, with all remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of DINOv3 encoders present in the mean-teacher architecture. Furthermore, a set of complementary losses, including a temporal loss helps generate reliable segmentation priors for the unlabeled frames. This formulation decouples annotation costs from sequence length while retaining the transferable spatial knowledge of the pretrained encoder. Extensive experiments on the publicly available CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms other scribble-supervised methods. These results show that accurate and temporally consistent segmentation can be achieved from extremely sparse supervision, substantially reducing annotation requirements for temporal echocardiographic segmentation and providing a practical framework for scalable clinical deployment.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large audio-language models (LALMs) have broadened audio understanding across speech, sound, and music, with tool-based agents further supporting these tasks by invoking predefined audio tools. However, a persistent gap remains between perceiving acoustic content and using it as evidence for reasoning: recognizing what is audible does not ensure that a model can identify which cues resolve an uncertain decision. To bridge this gap, we propose Think2Listen, an evidence-centric learning framework for agentic audio understanding. Guided by evidence before commitment, Think2Listen couples iterative reasoning with a targeted LALM interaction to actively seek acoustic cues that distinguish competing hypotheses and revise candidate judgments based on the observations returned. It learns what to ask, how to use evidence, and when to stop, using observation-induced changes in candidate-state to inform training credit. Extensive evaluations on two benchmarks spanning seven audio categories demonstrate that Think2Listen achieves (I) enhanced multi-step audio reasoning, with gains in overall accuracy of 5.08%--17.67% over competing audio agents; and (II) improved audio understanding and reasoning across speech, sound, and music, boosting overall accuracy by 2.29%--13.10% over the corresponding baselines. The source code is available at https://github.com/JinWang79/Think2Listen.

papers.abstract: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared backbone, which processes them alongside text and images. To develop the model's agent capabilities, we construct verifiable environments for tool use, search, and coding, as well as specialized workflows involving machine learning experiments and scientific software. Task completion is checked against execution results, changes in environment state, or submitted artifacts. We evaluate Sage S1.5 Flash on 33 benchmarks across seven domains. In the primary comparison against five baselines, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench~2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench~II (54.2). These results show particular strengths in using documentary evidence, producing verifiable workbooks, and carrying out machine learning tasks, alongside competitive performance in desktop and browser workflows that require the model to act on visual feedback.

papers.abstract: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.
authors: Yong Liu, Zhanpeng Shi, Peicong Lin, Zhenyi Zhong, Yizhou Dang, Wendi Wu, Haoling Li, Shuangjia Zheng
bullets: Addresses the separation between biomolecular structure models and language models.
Qwen3.5-9B processes sequences enriched with ESM2 residue features and invokes a pretrained SimpleFold head through a folding request.
The structure head receives protein information only through the LLM’s residue states and achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808, 0.635, and 0.900 on three evaluated sets.
Compared with an ESM2-3B/SimpleFold-3B baseline, differences were inconclusive for 100–299-residue chains and lower for 300–600-residue chains.
Protein training reduced accuracy on the evaluated 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%.

papers.selection_reason: General-purpose LLM that outputs protein structures; fits multimodal LLM and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model
papers.tldr: Calpha shows that a general-purpose LLM can use its own sequence representations to trigger single-chain protein folding, but with weaker long-chain performance and reduced general-language accuracy.

papers.abstract: Furniture assembly planning requires inferring subassembly hierarchies from individual parts and a target illustration. Existing raster-based methods do not explicitly exploit the geometric and structural information in SVG drawings. We introduce VASR, a framework that fuses features from a dedicated SVG encoder with visual representations from a pretrained vision-language model to predict assembly hierarchies. To avoid penalizing valid alternatives to a reference assembly tree, we propose Repair-Aware Hierarchical Policy Optimization (RHPO) with hierarchy-preserving equivalence rewards. RHPO further uses repair-cost feedback to favor decisions with lower downstream correction costs among candidates with comparable equivalence-aware rewards. VASR achieves the highest Equivalent-Hard F1 among the evaluated methods, outperforming GPT6-Astra by 17.69 percentage points on the IKEA-derived test set while maintaining strong performance on an independent furniture dataset.
authors: Ruizhe Wang, Rui Liu, Hongliang Chen, Junyi Guo, Fangyu Wu, Yaran Chen
bullets: Targets assembly hierarchy inference from individual parts and target illustrations.
Fuses a dedicated SVG encoder with representations from a pretrained vision-language model.
Uses RHPO to reward hierarchy-preserving equivalent solutions rather than only matching one reference tree.
Adds repair-cost feedback to prefer decisions requiring fewer downstream corrections.
Achieves the best Equivalent-Hard F1 among evaluated methods, including a 17.69-point gain over GPT6-Astra on an IKEA-derived test set, with strong independent-dataset performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Assembly architecture and RHPO training (a–c) The indexed parts and target drawing illustrate four assembly steps. Each resulting subassembly maps to an internal node of the reference tree, also shown in nested JSON. (d) For a fixed goal or action, unassisted rollouts estimate full success (Q) and tree quality (V). Separate repair rollouts estimate the mean number of subsequent repairs (C). At the first certified downstream error, the verifier rolls back, replaces the erroneous merge using the annotated graph and reference tree, and resumes the frozen policy. GRPO uses Q and V at both decision levels and favors lower repair cost among eligible candidates with near-best quality and a certified paired cost gap. Action-only distillation transfers probability mass from verified invalid actions to verified valid actions while preserving the mass on unknown actions.
Figure 3. Ablation study of VASR. VASR-S is trained only through the supervised stages (T2–T4).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces VASR, a framework for furniture assembly planning using a vision-language model and hierarchical policy optimization, directly addressing robot manipulation and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: VASR: Vector-Aware Assembly Planning with Equivalent Structures and Repair-Cost Feedback
papers.tldr: VASR improves furniture assembly planning by combining SVG geometry with visual-language features and optimizing for valid, low-repair-cost assembly hierarchies.

papers.abstract: Image generators are good at drawing scenes in which things that belong together appear next to each other. In almost every image they generate, and in almost every benchmark used to evaluate these images, "belonging to the same whole" and "adjacent to each other" go together. Therefore, we cannot know whether the model truly grasps the scene as a whole, or simply makes each part connect with its adjacent parts. We propose GJBench to disentangle the two. It requires the model to draw a scene as a scattered jigsaw puzzle: an image is cut into interlocking pieces, then moved apart and rotated. Thus, the spatial plausibility of the scene exists only in how these pieces collectively point to a whole. The model may have a reference image, a target layout, both, or neither. We separately evaluate three requirements: whether the scene is broken down into a specified number of separate pieces, whether the pieces interlock, and whether the pieces can reconstruct the reference scene. While every open and closed model we evaluated could draw these scenes well as a whole, none could keep them together as scattered puzzle pieces, and the three requirements categorized failures into different patterns. The models draw separate pieces but miscount them in different ways, and unless their outlines are provided, the pieces rarely interlock, and their content does not reconstruct the reference image. We also found that the target layout helps the puzzle pieces fit together, while the reference image improves neither their count nor their fit. These findings show that keeping a scene continuous across space that the canvas no longer shows remains an open problem for image generators.
bullets: Tests whether models understand a scene as a whole rather than relying on local adjacency.
Evaluates piece count, interlocking geometry, and reconstruction of the reference scene separately.
All evaluated models produced plausible scenes globally but failed to maintain coherence across scattered pieces.
Models often miscounted pieces; without provided outlines, pieces rarely interlocked or reconstructed the reference.
Target layouts improved piece fitting, while reference images did not improve counting or fitting.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark disentangling scene-wholeness from adjacency in image generators; directly tests spatial reasoning and scene-level spatial understanding.
papers.title: Can Image Generators Hold a Scene Together When Space Is Broken Apart?
papers.tldr: GJBench reveals that image generators struggle to preserve scene coherence when a scene is split into separated, rotated jigsaw pieces.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification. We evaluate 11 representative open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The strongest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves an overall score of only 41.63\%, with cross-modal EEG alignment emerging as a major bottleneck. We further examine model behavior from a neurophysiological perspective and analyze how temporal, spectral, spatial, and physiological EEG structure relates to model successes and failures. Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can reshape model predictions by helping models recognize the neurophysiological patterns present in the input and connect them with relevant neurological knowledge, narrowing the gap between general multimodal competence and EEG understanding. EEGProbe provides a testbed for current VLMs and a basis for developing future multimodal models that can interpret EEG evidence more reliably. The EEGProbe benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/2122ZHU/EEGProbe.
authors: Haozhe Zhu, Dan Yuan, Chenghao Gu, Feike Xu, Yue Wen, Shin'ichi Konomi
bullets: Benchmarks 11 open- and closed-source VLMs using 620 questions across 13 subtasks and three EEG capabilities.
Evaluates signal classification, cross-modal alignment, and neurophysiological reasoning without EEG-specific adaptation or feature engineering.
Preserves EEG temporal structure and uses signal-necessity testing plus expert verification to reduce shortcut-based answers.
The strongest evaluated model scores only 41.63% overall, with cross-modal EEG alignment as a major bottleneck.
Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can improve recognition of EEG patterns and connect them to neurological knowledge.

papers.title: EEGProbe: Do Vision-Language Models Really Understand EEG? A Benchmark for Signal-Grounded EEG Signals Evaluation
papers.tldr: EEGProbe shows that current vision-language models have limited ability to understand minimally processed EEG, especially for cross-modal alignment.

papers.abstract: Embodied capabilities such as visual grounding, spatial reasoning, navigation, and driving understanding are often developed in separate vision-language specialists fine-tuned from a common pretrained model.Deploying the specialists separately multiplies storage, whereas merging them into one dense model forces conflicting task updates to share parameters and loses part of each specialist's expertise.We introduce UNITE, a framework that consolidates such specialists into a compact shared-backbone mixture of experts. UNITE keeps the feed-forward block of each specialist as a routable expert and represents the expert bank through a shared-anchor one-bit factorization: a shared floating-point anchor plus expert-specific, row-scaled binary deviations.The anchor is optimized jointly with the scales and signs through closed-form alternating updates, using only source weights and no calibration data.Router adaptation then adjusts token-level expert selection with the backbone and experts frozen, updating fewer than $0.6$M parameters ($<0.01\%$ of the $8.8$B active parameters). Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, the complete UNITE model occupies $20.3$ GB, $1.16\times$ the storage of one dense specialist and $59.6\%$ below the uncompressed MoE. Across $22$ benchmarks and R2R Val-Unseen, UNITE matches six static merging methods in mean retention of best-specialist performance, leads all of them on Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and all four navigation metrics, and surpasses every source specialist on all five 3D scene understanding benchmarks (up to $+19.1$ on Scan2Cap) and on R2R navigation. Relative to the uncompressed MoE, factorization is nearly lossless on $21$ of $22$ benchmarks; the exception is VSI-Bench, where frame-count experiments suggest impaired use of cross-frame evidence.UNITE thus consolidates complementary embodied capabilities near single-model storage.
authors: Tao Tao, Anke Tang, Enneng Yang, Zhi Hou, Xiaogang Wang, Dacheng Tao
bullets: Targets storage growth from separately deploying specialists and interference from dense weight merging.
Retains each specialist’s feed-forward block as a routable expert and compresses experts with a shared floating-point anchor plus binary, row-scaled deviations.
Uses closed-form alternating factorization from source weights alone, then adapts token-level routing by updating fewer than 0.6M parameters.
Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, it uses 20.3 GB—1.16× one dense specialist and 59.6% less than the uncompressed MoE.
Across 22 benchmarks and R2R, factorization is nearly lossless on 21/22 benchmarks; VSI-Bench is the main exception, likely due to weaker cross-frame evidence use.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Storage versus capability retention for four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists. Keeping them separate (gray) costs 70.1 GB; static merging (violet, Table I) cuts this to 17.5 GB, but every merging method then falls below the navigation specialist’s 57.5% R2R Val-Unseen success rate, reaching at best 55.2% (Table III). UNITE (blue) needs only 20.3 GB, 1.16× the single-specialist footprint, and surpasses the specialist at 59.6% success rate.

Fig. 6. Score change contributed by each consolidation stage (top-1 routing throughout). Left: one-bit factorization of the expert bank, reducing total model weight storage from 50.2 to 20.3 GB. Right: router adaptation at constant storage. Bars beyond ±5 points are truncated and labeled with their value. ShareRobot (Traj., on a different scale) improves from 0.34 to 0.26 and 0.25. Full numbers are in Tables IV and V.

VSI-Bench score as a function of the maximum number of sampled video frames for the uncompressed and the one-bit expert bank (same backbone, top-1 routing, no router adaptation; all 5,130 questions). The two models are within 1.2 points at four frames. The uncompressed MoE gains 17.0 points from 4 to 64 frames, whereas the one-bit MoE stays within a two-point band, indicating limited benefit from additional frames after factorization. papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are often evaluated by converting model outputs into discrete answers. The conversion protocol determines which scores become predictions and can strongly influence the reported results. We introduce RAMP (Readout Aware Multimodal Protocol), a systematic framework that compares direct yes/no token logits, surface-form scores, and typed or reversed A/B interfaces under fixed model checkpoints and paired visual questions. On 500 POPE adversarial questions, typed versus bare readout changes accuracy by $-20.2$ percentage points for SmolVLM-256M, $-16.4$ for TinyLLaVA-1.1B, and $+1.8$ for Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Paired transitions reveal extensive prediction changes even when the net accuracy difference is small: 79 of 104 binary ChartQA items change correctness for SmolVLM-500M, despite a $+1.0$-point net difference. We further analyze prompt wording, candidate forms, option position, cross-task effects, and calibration. An independent offline replay reproduces 16,140 first-token decisions from saved raw scores with exact agreement. Our findings establish answer readout as a measurable component of multimodal evaluation and provide a reproducible protocol for analyzing model comparisons.
authors: Jianye Zeng, Qiao Yikang, Duan Huang, Ziying Song

On 500 POPE questions, typed versus bare readout changes accuracy by −20.2 points for SmolVLM-256M, −16.4 for TinyLLaVA-1.1B, and +1.8 for Qwen2.5-VL-3B.
Paired analyses find extensive prediction changes even when net accuracy shifts are small, including 79 of 104 changed ChartQA correctness outcomes for SmolVLM-500M.
Analyzes prompt wording, candidate formatting, option position, cross-task effects, and calibration.
Offline replay reproduces 16,140 first-token decisions exactly, supporting reproducible readout analysis.

papers.abstract: While text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models achieve remarkable quality, they risk producing harmful content. Existing safety mechanisms often rely on indiscriminate, global interventions that induce unintended semantic drift and degrade image quality. To address this, we propose Adaptive Spatial Classifier Guidance (ASCG), a necessity-driven framework that employs probabilistic monitoring to activate guidance selectively upon harm detection. By leveraging Grad-CAM for localized suppression, ASCG effectively removes harmful concepts while preserving superior semantic fidelity compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we overcome the limitations of traditional metrics like NudeNet---which fails to assess semantic integrity---by introducing a VLM-based evaluation framework to provide a fine-grained, robust analysis of both safety and context preservation. Our results demonstrate that ASCG not only balances safety and fidelity but also exhibits remarkable plug-and-play synergy with existing frameworks to establish state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Younghwan Kil, Joonhyeong Park, Giung Nam, Juho Lee
bullets: Addresses quality and semantic drift caused by indiscriminate global safety interventions in text-to-image diffusion models.
Uses probabilistic monitoring to activate suppression only when harmful content is detected.
Applies Grad-CAM for spatially localized removal of harmful concepts.
Introduces a VLM-based evaluation framework to assess both safety and context preservation beyond NudeNet.
Reports improved safety–fidelity balance and plug-and-play compatibility with existing safety frameworks.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models often synthesize policy-violating content, necessitating robust safeguards and rigorous evaluation frameworks. However, current approaches remain largely monolithic in both execution and evaluation, limited to coarse-grained categorization within broad unsafe concepts. Such approaches fail to account for the specific constituent factors of a violation, resulting in weak learning signals and allowing model collapse to bypass safety checks. To overcome these limitations, we propose Example-Based Spatial Guidance (EBSG), a training-free method that utilizes user-editable exemplar packs to provide granular spatial guidance for precise concept steering. Unlike existing methods that coarsely steer the entire image away from a broad concept, EBSG decomposes these categories into specific sub-concepts via exemplar text-image pairs, providing explicit, localized steering signals for more robust safety control. Furthermore, we introduce a vision language model (VLM)-based evaluation protocol that provides a fine-grained assessment, avoiding the pitfall of conventional binary evaluators that permit model collapse to bypass safety checks. Empirically, EBSG achieves state-of-the-art erasure performance across diverse safety datasets and concept categories, spanning four nudity benchmarks, seven I2P harmful-concept slices, and four MJA metaphor categories, while supporting multi-concept removal and transferring to a modern backbone, SD3.
authors: Younghwan Kil, Giung Nam, Joonhyeong Park, Jinwoo Shin, Juho Lee
bullets: Targets weaknesses in coarse, monolithic safety methods that overlook the constituent factors of unsafe concepts.
Decomposes broad concepts into specific sub-concepts using exemplar text-image pairs, producing localized steering signals.
Introduces a fine-grained VLM-based evaluation protocol designed to reduce loopholes from binary safety evaluators and model collapse.
Reports state-of-the-art erasure performance across multiple nudity, harmful-concept, and metaphor benchmarks.
Supports multi-concept removal and transfer to the SD3 diffusion backbone.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of EBSG. A concept pack groups K paired target/anchor keyword–image exemplars into F disjoint families for a target concept h. papers.title: Example-Based Spatial Guidance for Training-Free Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models

papers.abstract: Semantic visual classification commonly aligns visual embeddings with semantic spaces induced by pretrained text encoders. However, such spaces are typically high-dimensional, weakly aligned with visual feature geometry, and insufficiently discriminative for downstream classification tasks. We propose TaSS, a framework for learning a task-adaptive low-dimensional semantic space that preserves semantic structure while explicitly optimizing class separability. TaSS is constructed through a parameterized geometry transformation of pretrained text embeddings that enlarges inter-class margins via distance reshaping and improves intra-class compactness through prototype-preserving semantic constraints. The resulting semantic space maintains meaningful semantic relationships while producing a discriminative geometry tailored for classification. Frozen visual encoder features are subsequently aligned to TaSS using a lightweight MLP, enabling improved discriminative learning without fine-tuning pretrained backbones. We further provide theoretical analysis showing that TaSS preserves semantic consistency while enforcing enhanced inter-class separation and controlled intra-class variance. Extensive experiments on skeleton-based human action recognition, video classification, and image classification benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing semantic alignment approaches, with gains exceeding 3 percentage points on average and up to 8.5 points on challenging datasets.
authors: Nikalal Kaldera, Wanqing Li, Chris Bunn, Philip O. Ogunbona
bullets: Addresses high-dimensional semantic spaces that are weakly aligned with visual features and insufficiently discriminative.
Transforms pretrained text embeddings to enlarge inter-class margins and compact intra-class representations while preserving semantic structure.
Aligns frozen visual features to the learned space with a lightweight MLP.
Provides theoretical guarantees for semantic consistency, class separation, and controlled intra-class variance.

Reports consistent gains over semantic alignment baselines across action, video, and image classification benchmarks, exceeding 3 percentage points on average and reaching up to 8.5 points on challenging datasets.

papers.abstract: Visual adversarial perturbations can substantially impair large vision-language models (LVLMs) despite introducing only subtle input changes. To understand how these small changes cause substantial errors, we investigate their optimization and propagation through the model, revealing two key findings. First, stronger attacks rely on finer iterative optimization, while subtle input perturbations induce representation discrepancies that are amplified layer by layer through the vision encoder and persist in the language model. Second, disrupting the alignment between within-patch input patterns and the model's computation reduces clean-adversarial representation discrepancies and substantially weakens attacks. Together, these findings suggest that adversarial effectiveness depends on both fine-grained perturbation patterns and their coupling with the model's computation. Motivated by these findings, we propose SmoothShift, a lightweight, training-free defense that combines local smoothing and spatial transformations. Smoothing weakens fine-grained perturbation patterns, while spatial transformations disrupt their alignment with the encoder's patch grid. SmoothShift requires no model updates, auxiliary networks, or additional model inference. Experiments cover three LVLM families on four datasets and robustly fine-tuned Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models on eight classification datasets. Evaluations across eight attack methods and multiple perturbation budgets demonstrate improved robustness while largely preserving clean performance. SmoothShift also provides robustness gains under defense-aware attacks using mixed-gradient BPDA with EOT.
authors: Xiaoqing Chen, Jiayi Ouyang, Dongrui Wu
bullets: Adversarial attacks exploit subtle perturbations whose representation discrepancies are amplified through the vision encoder and persist into the language model.
Attack strength depends on fine-grained iterative optimization and the coupling between perturbation patterns and model computation.
SmoothShift combines local smoothing with spatial transformations to weaken perturbation patterns and disrupt patch-grid alignment.
It requires no model updates, auxiliary networks, or extra model inference.
Across multiple LVLM and CLIP settings, attack methods, and perturbation budgets, it improves robustness while largely preserving clean performance, including against defense-aware attacks.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning improves the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by removing redundant visual tokens, yet the reliability of existing selection signals has not been systematically examined. We analyze token selection under semantics-preserving perturbations and across representative pruning criteria, revealing two limitations. First, attention-based importance shifts non-uniformly under perturbations, so magnitude alone cannot distinguish stable evidence from unstable saliency (local instability). Second, attention- and diversity-based methods select substantially different subsets despite comparable performance, showing that useful evidence is not confined to a unique subset (global inconsistency). These findings motivate reliable token-set construction. We instantiate this perspective in CoRePruner, a training-free framework combining instruction-aware diversity with reliability-aware attention. Across image benchmarks, multiple MLLM architectures, and token budgets, CoRePruner improves performance, especially under aggressive pruning, and remains competitive on video benchmarks. Our results establish reliability as a central consideration in visual token selection.
authors: Chaehee Song, Seokil Ham, KiHyun Seol, Jihyun Lee, Yubin Choi, Changick Kim
bullets: Attention importance can change unevenly under semantics-preserving perturbations, exposing local instability.
Different pruning criteria often select substantially different token subsets despite similar performance, revealing global inconsistency.
CoRePruner is a training-free method using instruction-aware diversity and reliability-aware attention.
It improves performance across image benchmarks, MLLM architectures, and token budgets, particularly under aggressive pruning, while remaining competitive for video.
The study argues that reliability should be a central criterion for visual token selection.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models can produce fluent responses containing objects, attributes, or relations unsupported by the image. We study an implemented alignment pipeline that normalizes released fine-grained hallucination supervision, validates chosen-rejected preference pairs with vision-language judges, repairs rejected chosen responses, and trains LLaVA adapters with standard or severity-aware direct preference optimization. The study uses 16,143 normalized feedback records and 8,386 released preference pairs, comparing direct training with zero-shot and two-shot judged severity-margin variants. The zero-shot variant reduces Object HalBench CHAIRs from 53.00 to 36.00 and CHAIRi from 15.72 to 10.41. Across aligned models, AMBER-Hal decreases from 35.90 to 25.10-26.90, accompanied by reduced visual coverage. In contrast, the base model retains the highest valid POPE adversarial F1, 84.18 versus 83.87-83.91 after alignment. These results support benchmark-dependent reductions in generative hallucination rather than uniform superiority of severity-aware alignment. We distinguish implemented pipeline components from the preference paths used in the reported experiments and discuss the limits of attributing gains to judging, repair, or the training objective individually.

papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models (MFMs) support generalizable inference in distributed mobile sensing applications by integrating heterogeneous data streams. However, existing MFM inference pipelines typically require complete and synchronized multimodal inputs, whereas mobile sensing streams arrive asynchronously due to network variability and heterogeneous data volumes across modalities. Waiting for all modalities increases end-to-end latency, while inference with incomplete inputs can reduce accuracy. We argue that multimodal inference should depend on the utility of available information rather than modality completeness. Based on this principle, we propose AdaModalX, a progressive multimodal inference framework that decouples inference execution from modality synchronization through runtime utility-aware orchestration. At each device, importance-aware data uploading uses a lightweight probe distilled from the edge-side MFM to allow reliable samples to exit locally while uncertain samples continue uploading. At the edge, on-demand MFM activation constructs candidates from fully received samples and, when needed, imputed features derived from partially received delayed inputs. A lightweight contribution assessor built on frozen MFM encoders estimates candidate utility and activates the MFM once the candidate meets its corresponding utility threshold. Experiments on four mobile sensing applications show that AdaModalX improves the accuracy-latency trade-off, achieving up to 26.97% accuracy improvement and up to 64.75% end-to-end latency reduction.
authors: Xiangrui Xu, Sicong Liu, Zhiwen Yu, Zimu Zhou, Bin Guo
bullets: Addresses the latency and accuracy challenges caused by asynchronous, heterogeneous mobile sensing streams.
Uses utility-aware data orchestration: local probes retain reliable samples while uncertain ones continue uploading.
At the edge, constructs inference candidates from complete inputs or imputed features from delayed partial inputs.
A contribution assessor using frozen MFM encoders triggers full MFM inference when candidate utility reaches a threshold.
Across four mobile sensing applications, reports up to 26.97% higher accuracy and 64.75% lower end-to-end latency.

papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) is transforming intelligent transportation systems by connecting roadside cameras, edge computing units, vehicles, and traffic infrastructure into a shared sensing and decision-making ecosystem. However, transmitting raw traffic video over vehicle-to-everything (V2X) links is bandwidth-intensive, while deploying large multimodal models directly on resource-constrained vehicles is often impractical. To address these limitations, this article proposes VISTA (Vision-Informed Semantic Traffic Awareness), a multimodal vision-language edge-intelligence framework that combines predictive video representation learning with lightweight language-based reasoning to provide communication-efficient traffic situational awareness. In the proposed architecture, roadside surveillance units employ the Video Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (V-JEPA) and an attentive-pooler module to convert traffic video clips into compact future-scene embeddings. These embeddings are transmitted through V2X links to vehicle-mounted systems, where a TinyLlama small language model, enhanced with a custom visual adapter, interprets the embeddings alongside natural-language (NL) traffic queries. VISTA enables vehicles to obtain interpretable traffic information, reason about upcoming scene dynamics, and identify potential collision risks without receiving raw video streams. Experimental results in a digital-twin urban traffic environment show that VISTA achieves 97.77% accuracy and an 89% F1 score for future collision prediction while reducing the communication payload by several orders of magnitude compared with raw RGB video transmission. These results demonstrate the feasibility of embedding-based multimodal intelligence for low-latency, communication-efficient, and safety-oriented IoT-enabled transportation systems.
authors: Murat Arda Onsu, Poonam Lohan, Burak Kantarci, Aisha Syed, Matthew Andrews, Sean Kennedy

papers.abstract: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.
bullets: Introduces 854 benchmark items in 427 minimal pairs of 2D rigid-body chain-reaction scenes, with simulator-computed outcomes.

papers.abstract: In visual storytelling, a believable character must not only look consistent across scenes but also \textit{behave} in ways that reflect their personality. Current text-to-image (T2I) models preserve visual appearance effectively, yet consistently fail to maintain personality-relevant behavior---a failure we term \textit{trait collapse}. We show that conventional metrics (CLIP Score, DINO similarity) are blind to this failure, and that abstract personality descriptors and scene-level emotion labels do not produce consistent improvements over neutral prompts across models. To systematically diagnose trait collapse, we introduce \textbf{ViStoryBench-Personality}, a story-level benchmark combining an expert-validated Visual Cues Lexicon (Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.757$) with a six-dimensional metric suite covering personality alignment, cross-scene stability, and behavioral coherence. Evaluating seven T2I systems, we confirm a persistent semantic gap between abstract trait labels and visual evidence, and find that visual identity consistency does not imply personality consistency. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{Trait-Behavior-Visual (TBV)}, a training-free prompting framework that decomposes personality traits into renderable visual constraints. TBV improves Personality Alignment Score by up to $+22.1\%$, with larger gains in models with stronger language-conditioning capacity.

bullets: Conventional CLIP and DINO similarity metrics miss personality inconsistency across story scenes.

TBV translates personality traits into concrete, renderable visual constraints without training.
TBV improves Personality Alignment Score by up to 22.1%, especially in models with stronger language conditioning.

papers.abstract: Is a face or a voice still heard once the words are known? Incomplete multimodal learning increasingly uses large language models (LLMs) as fusion engines: modality features enter as token blocks and missing modalities become placeholders. We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with counterfactual views, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them. Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision-language accuracy by 46.1-53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model's answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR) trains views as unimodal judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree. It achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks without extra inference cost in accuracy mode. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/CoVeR/.
authors: Wenhao Li, Chong Xiao, Xiaokun Bai, Rundong He, Zhuang Qi, Xusheng Liang, Zhibin Wu, Qiangchang Wang
bullets: LLM fusion can override readable visual or audio evidence when transcript information is available.
MR-Bench evaluates language shortcuts using four typed sentiment benchmarks and 900 human-validated clips from seven sources.
Language-shortcut clips expose a measurement issue: text-only answer inversion can reach 94.4%, so accuracy alone does not prove non-verbal reasoning.
CoVeR trains unimodal views as judges and withholds fused supervision when their predictions disagree.
CoVeR achieves 61.7% language-shortcut and 93.6% non-verbal-shortcut accuracy in standard mode; robust mode improves the former to 63.0% but reduces the latter to 84.8%.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Constructing MR-Bench. Candidates are clips whose unimodal judgments disagree with the words (here a CH-SIMS clip with human unimodal labels on [−1, 1]); a panel of four text-only LLMs keeps a language-shortcut (LS) candidate only if the majority misreads its transcript, and three annotators keep a clip only if the majority recovers the label from the full clip and the misleading polarity from the shortcut channel. Models are then asked the same binary question from every input they support.

LLM-Fusion supervises the fused prediction on every sample (left); the test-time override lets confidently disagreeing views of the frozen model replace the fused decision (middle, Eqs. (3) and (4)); CoVeR trains the views as unimodal judges and withholds the fused task loss wherever a judge disagrees with the text judge (right), running the full view alone at test time.
