papers.title: Words Speak Louder? Exploring the Language Shortcut of LLM-Driven Incomplete Multimodal Learning
papers.tldr: LLM-based multimodal fusion often shortcuts through language, and CoVeR improves reliance on non-verbal evidence by training with counterfactual modality views.

papers.abstract: Visual reasoning often requires maintaining intermediate spatial states that are difficult to express in text. Existing approaches either rely on external drawing tools or image generators, or encode these states in latent tokens without explicit spatial correspondence to the input image. We introduce SelfMark, which enables MLLMs to construct and use visual marks directly in their native visual feature space. By treating the visual token grid as a canvas, SelfMark establishes explicit spatial correspondence between marks and images. This is achieved through a locate-mark-read procedure, where the model identifies relevant locations, constructs task-dependent mark features, and reads the resulting visual features to guide its reasoning. We jointly train a single model on spatial planning, dense counting, high-resolution VQA, and line tracing. Across six benchmarks, SelfMark outperforms state-of-the-art MLLM-based methods specialized for individual tasks. These improvements also persist with a stronger backbone, demonstrating the effectiveness of visual marking across different model capabilities. Overall, SelfMark provides a unified approach to visual reasoning by integrating spatially grounded marks directly into the visual feature space of MLLMs.
authors: Jiazhen Liu, Yanghao Wang, Chaolei Tan, Long Chen
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of representing intermediate spatial states in text or latent tokens without explicit image correspondence.
Uses a locate-mark-read procedure over the visual token grid as a task-dependent reasoning canvas.
Trains one model jointly for spatial planning, dense counting, high-resolution VQA, and line tracing.
Outperforms specialized MLLM-based methods across six benchmarks, with gains also holding for a stronger backbone.
Provides a unified framework for integrating explicit visual marks directly into MLLM visual features.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SelfMark. (1) Locate: after reading the image and the question, the MLLM emits a type token, here <PTS>, and fills in mask placeholders, one per patch, in a single forward pass; a lightweight head turns them into the locate conditions. (2) Mark: a lightweight editor, which never sees the image, translates the conditions into mark features on the same grid as the visual tokens. (3) Read: the same MLLM reads the original visual tokens and the question, followed by the mark tokens, and answers. Dashed orange parts are used only in training: Lloc fits the conditions to position labels, Lmark aligns the mark features with the target Z∗, the frozen-ViT features of the marks drawn on a blank canvas, and the answer is trained with CE and RL; no marks are drawn as pixels at inference.

Figure 1. Four ways of thinking with an image. A simple counting task reveals how different approaches handle visual evidence. (a) Think in text translates visual structure into words, risking plausible but ungrounded descriptions such as “rows of five.” (b) Draw in pixels relies on an external vision module to annotate the image, inheriting its missed detections. (c) Latent imagination encodes intermediate visual states in a handful of latent tokens, leaving their spatial grounding implicit. (d) SelfMark takes a different route: the MLLM first locates the targets, a lightweight editor marks them in its visual feature space, and the MLLM reads the resulting marks alongside the original visual tokens. Each dot corresponds to a located object, turning counting into explicit, inspectable visual reasoning. The same locate–mark–read procedure handles the other tasks with other marks (bottom).
Figure 3. Inference cost. (a, b) Performance vs. latency on V* and FSC-147 (upper left is better). (c) Latency vs. object count.

For SelfMark, we report results as mean ± standard deviation over three seeds. Best results are in bold, and second-best results are underlined.

papers.tldr: SelfMark gives multimodal LLMs a native visual workspace for creating spatially grounded marks that support visual reasoning.

papers.abstract: Geometric deep learning has made available a large variety of structurally equivariant neural network architectures, meaning a particular transformation of their input causes a predictable transformation of their output. But structural equivariance is a very strong inductive bias that can limit performance if chosen poorly. In contrast, choosing an architecture with low geometric bias necessitates data augmentation to obtain correct behavior; extending the training process. We propose a novel neural network architecture that is soft equivariant; we select a set of symmetry groups and during training the network will become equivariant only to those symmetry groups that are appropriate given the training data. After training we can inspect the network to obtain a symmetry fingerprint that will tell us exactly which symmetries ended up being relevant and to what degree. We show how our architecture and the fingerprinting process work in the case of an image classification task.
authors: Bart M. N. Smets, Gijs Bellaard, Pieter Wils
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between overly restrictive built-in equivariance and costly data augmentation.
Introduces an architecture that can become equivariant to selected symmetry groups based on the training data.
Provides a post-training fingerprint indicating which symmetries are relevant and to what degree.
Demonstrates the architecture and fingerprinting process on image classification.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: An input image is first converted to a set of geometric tokens through splatting. GLInT processes these tokens to, in this case, classify the image. After training, the model can be inspected to obtain a symmetry fingerprint that tells us which of our candidate symmetry groups are relevant (shown are the subgroups of Aff+(2) that we used, see also Fig. 3).

Fig. 4: MNIST test errors over 20 independent training runs. We train ViT on both the original MNIST and a rasterized version of our splatted MNIST to show the fidelity of our tokenization method. We also train GLInT with and without noise to show that fingerprinting noise does not degrade performance.

Fig. 3: The set of symmetry subgroups of Aff+(2) we are interested in. Green arrows add translations. Red arrows add rotations. Blue arrows add isotropic scaling. Purple arrows add area-preserving maps.

Fig. 2: Top row: a sample from the MNIST dataset [10] (28 × 28 pixel images). Bottom row: splats made with a higher order Gaussian splatter using 16 Aff+(2) × R3 tokens (3 coefficients per splat since we use 3 orders of Gaussians). The splats are rendered at 128×128 with a unique color assigned to each splat/token.

Comparing the columns of this table with those in Table 1 allows us to accurately infer which group was used for the augmentation.

Every column shows the fingerprint IH of the corresponding symmetry group H. Note that all fingerprints are unique.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a soft-equivariant architecture that learns geometric invariance and symmetry groups, providing a mechanism for geometric reasoning and spatial understanding in neural networks.
papers.title: Symmetry Fingerprinting with Geometric Learnable Invariants Transformers
papers.tldr: A soft-equivariant transformer learns which geometric symmetries matter for a task and exposes them through an interpretable symmetry fingerprint.

papers.abstract: Pictograms are a core modality in augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), yet recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot reliably interpret or produce pictogram sequences. Two obstacles explain this gap: the absence of a standardized pictogram grammar and the scarcity of parallel text-pictogram data. We introduce Retrieval-Augmented Pictogram Selection (RAPS), an annotation method that refines a rule-based transcription system's output with LLM-based concept extraction and retrieval over a pictogram vocabulary, handling cases where hand-written rules fail (named entities, numbers, polysemous words) without requiring new rules. Applied to French, RAPS yields a synthetic corpus of 1.4 million parallel pairs, of which 300k are publicly released. In a human ranking study where annotators order four pictogram transcriptions of the same sentence, RAPS outperforms the rule-based state of the art. Moreover, we show that standard reference-based metrics separate systems of clearly different quality but fail to rank strong systems against each other. Finally, we build an instruction-tuned model that supports interaction in several AAC modalities: it accepts pictogram or text input and answers in pictograms, speech, or text.
authors: Alexandre Audibert, Fran\c{c}ois Portet, Benoit Favre, Maja Jonck Hjuler
bullets: Addresses the lack of standardized pictogram grammar and parallel text–pictogram data for training MLLMs.
RAPS combines rule-based transcription with LLM concept extraction and pictogram-vocabulary retrieval, covering entities, numbers, and polysemous words without adding new rules.
Produces 1.4 million French parallel pairs, with 300,000 released publicly.
Human evaluators rank RAPS transcriptions above the rule-based state of the art.

Reference-based metrics distinguish clearly different systems but struggle to rank strong systems reliably; an instruction-tuned model supports text or pictogram input and pictogram, speech, or text output.

papers.abstract: Background: Before laryngoscopy, clinicians assess the likely cause of hoarseness and whether to suspect a precancerous or malignant lesion. Whether voice-based artificial intelligence (AI) supports pre-laryngoscopic categorization is unknown. Methods: We developed an auditory large language model that generates a patient-level assessment card (provisional category, voice-quality ratings, and rationale) and a prespecified malignancy alert from voice recordings, patient information, and acoustic measures obtained before laryngoscopy at one center. We evaluated both in a held-out test set and a later cohort. In a sequential reader study, 32 otolaryngology clinicians categorized held-out cases without AI and, 1 to 2 weeks later, reviewed their initial categories with the card (without the alert). Results: Across 800 paired assessments, reader accuracy was 49.8% before and 56.8% after review (difference, 7.0 percentage points; 95% CI, 1.7 to 13.5; P < 0.001); 99 categories changed from incorrect to correct and 43 from correct to incorrect (ratio, 2.30; 95% CI, 1.22 to 5.31). Accuracy rose 14.7 points when the model was correct and fell 8.7 when incorrect. Provisional-category accuracy was 72% in held-out testing and 67% in temporal validation. The malignancy alert flagged 85.7% and 86.8% of precancerous or malignant lesions. Sensitivity for precancerous or malignant lesions increased from 53.9% to 75.0% after AI-assisted review (difference, 21.1 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.3 to 42.0). Conclusions: In this single-center study, clinicians' pre-laryngoscopic categorization accuracy was higher after reviewing the AI assessment card, although the sequential design cannot fully separate AI assistance from reassessment; gains depended on model correctness without clearly selective adoption. Randomized and external evaluations, including of the malignancy alert, are needed.
authors: Siyuan Hou, Shuting Yang, Zengrui Jin, Liyu Cheng, Siyin Wang, Yunhan Shi, Xueyan Li, Rong Hu, Yuhong Lin, Qiyu Chen, Yanru Li, Ji Wu, Bowen Zhou, Mangsuo Zhao, Wen Xu, Chao Zhang
bullets: 32 otolaryngology clinicians assessed 800 cases before and after reviewing AI-generated assessment cards.
Reader accuracy increased from 49.8% to 56.8%, with more incorrect-to-correct than correct-to-incorrect category changes.
Sensitivity for precancerous or malignant lesions rose from 53.9% to 75.0% after AI-assisted review.
The model’s provisional-category accuracy was 72% in held-out testing and 67% in temporal validation; its malignancy alert flagged about 86% of relevant lesions.
The sequential, single-center design limits causal interpretation, and the malignancy alert was not evaluated in the reader study.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are routinely aligned with offline pairwise RLHF objectives, but multimodal preference data is scarce and treats every response token as equally informative. Under a small preference budget, pair construction becomes nearly irrelevant: standard DPO-style, image-conditional, and self-improvement objectives all perform within 1.1 points on MM-RLHF metrics and 0.5 points on hallucination rates, matching the SFT baseline. We call this entropy-blind preference optimization: the learning signal ignores policy uncertainty, which in chain-of-thought VLMs concentrates on specific fork tokens where visual claims are made. We introduce GEM-MM, extending entropy-guided preference modeling to VLMs. It samples on-policy candidates, rewards high-entropy reasoning forks, penalizes uncertain final answers, and updates the model via group-normalized policy gradients. On a 3000-prompt MM-RLHF budget with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, GEM-MM achieves the best entropy-depth preference score (61.7% vs. 57.3-58.4% baselines) and implicit-reward accuracy (41.4%). Crucially, it reduces AMBER hallucination from 23.4-24.0 to 20.6 and CHAIR from 5.0-5.1 to 4.6 at matched caption coverage. It also ranks best on all three HallusionBench granularities, with a conservative operating point raising the near-chosen rate to 62.4%. An off-the-shelf multimodal reward model ranks GEM-MM first, and two such models independently confirm our main ablations (p < 0.001). We report confidence intervals, paired significance tests, metric-reward functional overlaps, and document a collapse mode when exceeding the fair budget. Code and evaluation harness: https://github.com/SNOWTEAM2023/GEM-MM
bullets: Standard preference objectives perform similarly under small multimodal preference budgets, suggesting they are largely entropy-blind.
GEM-MM samples on-policy candidates, targets high-entropy reasoning decisions, penalizes uncertain answers, and uses group-normalized policy gradients.
With a 3,000-prompt budget, it improves entropy-depth preference and implicit-reward accuracy over baselines.
Hallucination rates decrease on AMBER and CHAIR, while performance also leads across HallusionBench granularities.
The method can collapse when exceeding the fair preference budget, defining an important scope limitation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the GEM pipeline instantiated by GEM-MM for vision-language models (adapted from Zhao et al. [2026a]). Given a multimodal query x = (xI , xQ) (text-only q in the original figure) drawn from a preference pool {a−, a+}, the Reflective Inference Engine πθ elaborates k chain-of-thought candidates; Cognitive Filtering computes per-token entropy and an entropy-guided score that rewards fork tokens while penalizing uncertain final answers; SEGA forms a contextual group advantage and applies a full-parameter gradient update. The cognitive feedback loop returns only to the inference engine (updated policy), which then re-samples candidates on the next cycle and does not re-enter the entropy-scoring block directly.

papers.tldr: GEM-MM reduces VLM hallucinations by allocating preference-learning signals to uncertain reasoning forks while penalizing uncertain final answers.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) encode a high-resolution image into thousands of visual tokens, which dominate the cost of the prefill stage. Visual token reduction removes most of these tokens, but two problems remain at extreme budgets. The vision encoder still processes every patch of the image, and the few surviving tokens often miss the small regions that hold the answer. In this paper, we propose Glance-ETD, a two-stage token reduction framework guided by a lightweight question-conditioned scorer. In the first stage, a glance encoder views the image at low resolution and re-encodes only the question-relevant regions at native resolution. In the second stage, Evidence-Tempered Diversity (ETD) selects the final tokens by combining diversity with the evidence predicted by the scorer, so that the kept tokens cover the scene and retain the answer. A single-rollout self-distillation recipe trains the MLLM with the glance encoder. With only 5% of the visual tokens, Glance-ETD retains 91.6% of the full-token performance of Qwen3.5-4B across fourteen benchmarks and outperforms the strongest prior method, LT-OPD, by 17.3 points and the same training recipe with DivPrune by 6.0. It also speeds up the time to first token on 4K images by 3.1x and generalizes to three other MLLMs and to high-resolution document benchmarks, with the largest gains on text-rich tasks.
authors: Yuxuan Wang, Guangxiang Zhao, Yuxuan Tian, Yahui Han, Xinyu Tan, Feiyu Wang, Zongwei Lv, Xiangzheng Zhang, Lin Sun, Tong Yang
bullets: Addresses the cost of processing thousands of image tokens and the risk of missing small, answer-relevant regions.
Uses a two-stage, question-conditioned process: low-resolution region glancing followed by native-resolution re-encoding of relevant areas.
Selects final tokens with Evidence-Tempered Diversity, balancing scene coverage with predicted answer evidence.
At 5% of visual tokens, retains 91.6% of Qwen3.5-4B’s full-token performance across 14 benchmarks and improves over prior baselines.
Provides 3.1× faster time to first token on 4K images, with especially strong gains on text-rich tasks and transfer to other MLLMs.

papers.abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that models trained on different modalities converge toward a shared representation. Related work aligns frozen image and text encoders on natural images without paired data. We test zero-pair alignment on five datasets across four modalities: natural images, environmental audio, chest radiographs, and 3D computed tomography (CT). It succeeds only on COCO and fails on the other four. We analyze the failures and find that alignment must first locate the subspace where the modalities co-vary and then orient the mapping within it. Consistent with previous studies, medical imaging is the hardest case: its shared subspace carries the smallest fraction of the variance. When this fraction is small, alignment needs image-text pairs, and random-matrix theory predicts how many pairs are needed. These findings motivate LightAlign: a few pairs let a ridge regression between two frozen encoders locate and orient the mapping simultaneously, and a classifier fitted only on report text then predicts findings from the mapped images. On 3D CT, LightAlign surpasses models trained end to end on image-report pairs without finding-level labels: with only 200 pairs, LightAlign outperforms CT-CLIP on CT-RATE (0.754 vs. 0.733 AUROC), and with only 100 CT-RATE pairs, it does so on RAD-ChestCT, an out-of-distribution dataset from a different hospital. On CheXpert, it reaches 0.862 mean AUROC with only about 5% as many pairs as models trained on MIMIC-CXR.
authors: Yipeng Sun, Jiajun Wang, Siyuan Mei, Yan Xia, Siming Bayer, Vincent Christlein, Andreas Maier
bullets: Zero-pair alignment succeeds on natural images (COCO) but fails on environmental audio, chest radiographs, and 3D CT.
Successful alignment must identify the shared cross-modal subspace and orient the mapping within it; medical imaging is hardest because this subspace explains little variance.
LightAlign uses a few image-text pairs and ridge regression to jointly locate and orient a mapping between frozen encoders.
A text-only classifier can then predict findings from mapped medical images without finding-level labels.
On CT and chest X-ray benchmarks, LightAlign achieves strong results with substantially fewer pairs and generalizes to an out-of-distribution hospital dataset.

papers.title: What Matters for Cross-Modal Alignment
papers.tldr: Cross-modal alignment often fails without paired data, but a small number of pairs can make frozen-encoder alignment effective—especially for medical imaging—via LightAlign.

papers.abstract: The emergence of foundation models has marked a transformative shift in AI, enabling robust generalization across diverse downstream tasks through putative zero-shot learning. Large Language Models and Vision Language Models have demonstrated strong capabilities in tasks such as image interpretation, report generation, and question answering by effectively learning from multimodal data-images paired with associated text often with minimal supervision. In the healthcare domain, this ability to align visual and textual information reduces the reliance on extensive manual annotations, as models can leverage existing clinical reports and imaging data to learn meaningful representations. This integration holds promise for improving diagnostic support, treatment planning, and overall patient care, even in data constrained settings. In this review, we provide a definitive taxonomy of the medical VLM landscape, tracing the evolution from early Contrastive Alignment and Generative MLLMs to the cutting edge frontiers of Dense Pixel Grounding, Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), and Reasoning Incentivized (RL) architectures. We critically examine the "medical bottleneck" identifying the persistent challenges of data scarcity, the "hallucination" risks in generative diagnostics, the computational strain of 3D volumetric processing, and the lack of standardized, clinically grounded evaluation metrics.
authors: Taha Razzaq, Murtaza Taj, Asim Iqbal
bullets: Medical VLMs align clinical images with associated text to support image interpretation, report generation, and medical question answering.
The review presents a taxonomy spanning contrastive alignment, generative multimodal LLMs, dense pixel grounding, sparse mixture-of-experts, and reasoning-incentivized architectures.
Potential applications include diagnostic support, treatment planning, and improved patient care in data-constrained settings.
Key challenges include limited medical data, hallucinations in generative diagnosis, computational demands of 3D imaging, and insufficient standardized clinical evaluation.
The scope is a review of the field rather than a report of new experimental results.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks introduced through data poisoning, making effective backdoor detection a critical security challenge. In this paper, we uncover a novel connection between VLM hallucinations and backdoor behaviors and exploit this connection for backdoor detection. Our key insight is that poisoned training data induces strong language priors toward the backdoor target token, while such priors are also a major source of hallucinations. This suggests that enhancing hallucinations can expose hidden backdoor-related priors. Specifically, backdoored VLMs tend to hallucinate backdoor target tokens more frequently across diverse inputs, while the hallucinated tokens of clean VLMs are largely random and exhibit no stable target-specific bias. Based on this observation, we propose HalluProbe, which enhances hallucinations during output decoding and measures the distributional consistency of hallucinated tokens to identify backdoored VLMs. We evaluate HalluProbe against six representative VLM backdoor attacks across three models. Experimental results demonstrate that HalluProbe can effectively detect backdoored VLMs with an accuracy exceeding 90%, outperforming existing backdoor detection methods.
authors: Ji Guo, Xiaolong Qin, Jin Jiang, Yijing Liu, Pei Ke, Aiguo Chen, Wenbo Jiang
bullets: Backdoor poisoning creates strong language priors for target tokens, which also drive hallucinations.
Backdoored VLMs hallucinate target tokens frequently across varied inputs, unlike clean models’ largely random hallucinations.
HalluProbe enhances hallucinations during decoding and analyzes the consistency of hallucinated-token distributions.
Evaluated across six attacks and three models, it achieves over 90% detection accuracy and outperforms existing methods.

Finally, it calculates the frequency gap between the top two tokens and compares it against a predefined threshold to determine whether the examined VLM is backdoored.

papers.abstract: We ask whether a compact universal multimodal embedding models can produce better search embeddings by running the same layers again. Looped transformers add computation with nearly unchanged model size, making them an appealing alternative to a larger encoder. Their success in language-model reasoning and recent use for retrieval motivate the idea, but higher retrieval scores alone do not reveal what an extra pass contributes. We study eleven loop designs and training variants on three checkpoints of one vision-language architecture. Our protocol distinguishes whether a model uses its extra pass, whether its image states respond to the query, and whether those updates improve retrieval. We prove that an image placed before the query remains query-independent through repeated layers when information only travels forward. We then open a query-to-image path in three ways, including order-alternating recurrence, which places the query first on the next pass. Each path produces query-sensitive image states. For bidirectional attention and order alternation, freezing later visual updates does not lower accuracy. On all 78 datasets of the Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark version 2 (MMEB-V2), a standard added loop loses 0.46 points against its trained control; an intermediate generative stage changes the effect to +0.36. A model pretrained with recurrence gains +4.23 points over its own loop-removed control and benefits from query-conditioned image updates when answering visual questions or locating objects from text.
bullets: The study evaluates 11 loop designs and training variants across three checkpoints of one vision-language architecture.
A standard added loop slightly hurts performance: −0.46 points versus its trained control on all 78 MMEB-V2 datasets.
An intermediate generative stage changes the effect to +0.36 points, while recurrence pretraining yields a +4.23-point gain over its loop-removed control.
Order-alternating recurrence and bidirectional attention create query-sensitive image states; freezing later visual updates does not reduce accuracy in these designs.
Query-conditioned updates are especially useful for visual question answering and text-based object localization.

Scores use top-1 hit rate for images and videos and nDCG@5 for documents, on a 0–100 scale. The retrofit uses order-alternating recurrence. The native control uses the same pretrained weights without repetition and trains longer. The zero ring separates gains from losses.

Right: changes in the eight-image-task score under visual freeze; circles show seed-matched changes and bars their means. Opening a query path produces sensitivity without an accuracy cost under freeze for the measured added loops. The native loop is strongly affected; Figure 4 tests whether its dependence is query-specific.

In the native LoopVL embedder, second-cycle visual states are replaced by states computed from the same image under another instance text; actual text states are retained. Dots show two seeds and short bars their means. Scores use MMEB’s diagnostic candidate pools. Question answering and grounding are more affected than composed retrieval. A separately trained single-pass control still scores higher. The middle and right points use exactly the same loop checkpoint. Opening a path permits dependence but does not guarantee that training will exploit it.

papers.selection_reason: Studies layer reuse and query-conditioned updates in multimodal embedding models; relevant to multimodal foundation model design.
papers.title: When Does Reusing Layers Help Multimodal Embeddings?
papers.tldr: Reusing transformer layers helps multimodal retrieval only when recurrence enables useful query-conditioned image updates and is supported by training.

papers.abstract: Open-weight model hubs now ship not only chat checkpoints but a long tail of derivatives---fine-tunes, safety guards, vision--language models (VLMs), audio wrappers, and generative heads---yet residual-stream safety audits still often intervene at a single site, usually the text decoder $T$. We ask a localization question under one shared mean / rank-1 difference-in-means (DiM) extract$=$intervene protocol, with matched-norm random and empty-rate controls: does causal chat attack lift concentrate at $T$, or do perceptual encoders, projectors, and fusion paths ($E$/$P$/$F$) supply a comparable bypass? On the mixed-input settings we stress-test---HADES adversarial images paired with harmful text prompts, and spoken AdvBench via text-to-speech (TTS) or silence---text DiM at $T$ raises attack success rate (ASR) while the same mean DiM at $E$/$P$/$F$ does not; attacks track harmful text rather than image or audio content. Margin-rank and leverage probes on a Vision leaf show that this recipe is extremal at $T$ and near chance at $P$/$E$, which pressures a weak-extractor reading of those flat cells for the DiM family we study. Catalog breadth and mapper-free base$\to$derivative transfer when residual widths match provide supporting coverage under the same gates; generative U-Nets are a separate band under generation judges. The primary claim is this recipe-scoped $T$ vs.\ non-text intervenability asymmetry---intervention accessibility under mean / rank-1 DiM, not a claim that refusal is absent or fully represented outside $T$ (text vs.\ perceptual contrasts and pooling differ by site). On VLGuard Unsafe prompts ($n{=}200$; Llama-Guard), the same $T$ vs.\ $P$/$E$ directionality holds at modest absolute ASR ($0.030{\to}0.150$ at $T$). An intervention-oriented Class$\times$site ledger records where this protocol still hooks as supporting coverage, not as a universal multimodal bypass.
authors: Chansu Han, Seok-Hwan Choi, Takeshi Takahashi
bullets: Text-site ($T$) DiM interventions increase attack success on mixed image-text and audio-text inputs.
Equivalent interventions at perceptual encoders, projectors, and fusion paths ($E/P/F$) show no comparable lift.
Probes suggest the method is informative at $T$ but weak or near chance at $E/P$ for the studied DiM family.

papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial reasoning from monocular video enables vision-language models (VLMs) to understand how 3D environments evolve over time, supporting physical world understanding and embodied intelligence. Existing efforts primarily address observed-dynamics understanding, whereas agents in dynamic environments also require future-dynamics prediction beyond the observation boundary. Moreover, external geometric processing and textual descriptions can increase inference complexity or lose information when representing continuous dynamics. These limitations motivate a shared internal state that preserves observed dynamics and remains predictive beyond the input video. Accordingly, we present Pros4D, a framework for modeling evolving 4D worlds in latent space that unifies retrospective understanding of observed-dynamics with prospective reasoning for future-dynamics prediction. Specifically, Pros4D-Engine derives geometry-grounded supervision and constructs paired examples for both tasks, while Pros4D-Bench evaluates them across eight spatial task categories spanning dynamic cameras, objects, and scenes. At the model level, Pros4D compresses observed dynamics into latent observed states and autoregressively rolls them forward into latent future states. 4D Latent Alignment (4DLA) grounds these states through complementary visual-semantic and geometric supervision, while joint language supervision connects them to task reasoning. Experiments across benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines in both capabilities.
authors: Rongxin Gao, Dongxuan Liu, Chu Li, Chengyang Ji, Jialing Huang, Runyu Chen, Kairun Wen, Chenxin Li, Jingrui Ye, Haosong Zhen, Xinghao Ding, Yue Huang, Yuzhi Huang, Xiaodong Tu, Jingyan Jiang
bullets: Addresses the gap between recognizing observed dynamics and forecasting dynamics beyond a video’s observation window.
Encodes video dynamics into latent observed states and autoregressively rolls them forward into latent future states.
Uses 4D Latent Alignment to combine visual-semantic and geometric grounding with joint language supervision.
Pros4D-Engine creates geometry-grounded training examples, while Pros4D-Bench evaluates eight dynamic spatial reasoning categories.
Experiments report consistent improvements over strong baselines on both observed-dynamics understanding and future-dynamics prediction.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal safety alignment heavily relies on a text-centric paradigm, assuming risks are explicit in language or globally prominent in images. However, real-world hazards are often visually subtle or peripheral, causing existing models to fail due to their reliance on coarse, global visual representations. In this work, we study fine-grained visual safety alignment and introduce a challenging 1,200-sample benchmark across four domains, where hazards necessitate localized inspection. To address this, we propose Fine-Grained RLAIF (FGR), a reinforcement learning framework that casts image zoom-in as a learnable perception policy. FGR employs a decomposed reward design to jointly align three core safety behaviors: (i) where to look via a visual evidence reward, (ii) when to act via a tool-formatting constraint, and (iii) how to reason via visually grounded safety explanations. FGR achieves accuracy ranging from 86.71% to 93.00%, consistently outperforming strong multimodal and agent-based baselines.
authors: Chunxue Xu, Yiwei Wang, Yujun Cai, Songze Li
bullets: Introduces a 1,200-sample benchmark spanning four domains, focused on hazards requiring localized visual inspection.
Frames image zoom-in as a learnable perception policy through reinforcement learning.
Uses decomposed rewards to guide where to look, when to use the tool, and how to produce visually grounded safety explanations.
Reports accuracy of 86.71%–93.00%, outperforming the evaluated multimodal and agent-based baselines.

papers.abstract: Recent efforts to improve the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have explored visual token pruning, quantization, and feature compression. However, the properties that determine whether transformed visual tokens remain usable by a frozen decoder are not well characterized. We introduce \textbf{TIVS (Token Identity Versus Statistics)}, a training-free intervention framework that separately studies sequence permutation, token retention, numerical precision, and statistical replacement under controlled conditions. On 192 POPE questions, three token permutations change TinyLLaVA accuracy by only $-0.17$ percentage points on average, while changing 4.69\% of individual predictions. Diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements decrease accuracy by 25.0 and 28.1 points on the same subset. Further experiments with exact moment constraints, quantization error, token retention, and additional visual tasks reveal how strongly the effects depend on the original feature values and the evaluation setting. These findings provide an empirical basis for assessing visual token transformations in frozen MLLMs and designing more reliable multimodal interfaces.
authors: Yikang Qiao, Jianye Zeng, Duan Huang, Ziying Song
bullets: Introduces a training-free framework separating permutation, retention, precision, and statistical replacement effects.
On 192 POPE questions, three token permutations changed TinyLLaVA accuracy by only −0.17 points on average, despite altering 4.69% of predictions.
Diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements reduced accuracy by 25.0 and 28.1 points, respectively.
Additional experiments show that transformation effects depend on original feature values and evaluation setting.
Provides empirical guidance for evaluating visual-token transformations and designing multimodal interfaces.

papers.abstract: Vision models are trained on 2D images of a 3D world. Do their hidden features encode the direction from which the camera views a scene, and if so, in what form? We study the relative viewing direction $\alpha$ of two objects in rendered scenes where both object centres stay at fixed pixels while the camera moves, so that perspective, shading and shadows change but the projected layout does not. In eight pretrained models, from diffusion models to self-supervised and image-text encoders, $\alpha$ is encoded in a strikingly simple form: a single two-dimensional plane in the hidden space, shared across scenes, in which the difference between the two objects' features traces $(\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$. The plane keeps its orientation when lighting, colours, floors and object shapes change. This encoding is more than a summary of a few visible measurements: readouts fitted on one set of camera paths stay accurate at camera positions outside their range in seven of the eight models, whereas decoders of the measured object and shadow geometry, equally accurate within that range, fail there. In the diffusion transformer PixArt-$\alpha$, the plane forms abruptly at a single block and carries direction information to later blocks, yet editing it changes the objects rather than the generated viewpoint. We also examine how this encoding carries over to scanned real objects.
bullets: Tests viewing direction while keeping object centers fixed, isolating changes in perspective, shading, and shadows.
Across eight pretrained models, feature differences trace $(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ in a scene-shared 2D plane.
The plane remains stable across lighting, colors, floors, and object shapes.
Readouts generalize to camera positions outside their training paths in seven of eight models, unlike geometry-based decoders.
In PixArt-$\alpha$, the representation appears abruptly in one block and persists later, but editing it changes objects rather than viewpoint; transfer to scanned objects is also examined.

papers.abstract: Comprehensive audio-visual perception requires both semantic and spatial reasoning. Existing spatial models suffer from poor generalization due to data scarcity, while semantic-only models fail to capture spatial characteristics completely. We introduce a model capable of jointly reasoning over binaural audio and vision on semantic and spatial tasks with improved generalization. To overcome the shortage in real-world data, we develop an automatic pipeline that localizes the sound source in a video, estimates its relative 3D trajectory, and renders binaural audio. We then use this to spatialize VGGSound, allowing us to train at a much larger scale. We demonstrate improved performance and generalization on spatial reasoning tasks while still remaining competitive on semantic tasks compared to semantic-only models.
authors: Mengyu Yang, You Zhang, Vishnu Raj, Olha Townsend, James Hays, Andrea Fanelli, Gautam Bhattacharya
bullets: Addresses poor spatial generalization caused by limited real-world audio-visual data.
Automatically localizes sound sources, estimates relative 3D trajectories, and renders binaural audio.
Spatializes VGGSound to provide larger-scale training data.
The resulting model improves spatial reasoning and generalization while remaining competitive on semantic tasks.
Scope: performance depends on automatically estimated source locations and trajectories.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly read a scene and report it to someone who acts on the report, sometimes under objectives that differ from that person's. We ask whether a stated incentive moves what a VLM reports, and whether this changes when the value must be read from pixels rather than given as text. In seeded synthetic scenes, a model reads the position of a target on a labelled axis and reports one integer to a fixed receiver; it is paid, in simulation, for accuracy or for a report a few units to one side, and every scene is also presented with the true value as text. Across a pilot and three follow-up studies with hash-frozen protocols, four small open VLMs from three families, and 15,170 held-out trials, a stated payoff moved reports in both modalities, and exact compliance at three units was significantly lower with the image than with text for three of four models; Qwen2.5-VL 7B showed no reliable difference. Adding the true value as text to the image prompt removed the gap in every model. For InternVL3 the gap vanished on scenes it read correctly when it wrote its reading first; for Gemma 3 it persisted. For Qwen2.5-VL 3B, which read every scene correctly, the gap held in four of five payoff paraphrases, nearly vanished when the model wrote its reading before its report or when the prompt stated that the client wants the truth, vanished with an unpaid goal, and persisted when the model reported before stating its reading; how often it shaded at all, even with text, depended strongly on the wording. When told that the client wants the true value, three of four models still shaded every text report. Visual input did not make these advisors reliably more truthful; it made compliance with a stated incentive depend on whether the read value is made explicit and on output order, a dependence that text-only evaluations and mean-shift metrics do not reveal.
bullets: Across 15,170 held-out trials, stated payoffs shifted reports in both image and text conditions.
Exact compliance with a three-unit reporting incentive was lower from images than text for three of four small open VLMs; one model showed no reliable gap.
Adding the true value as text to image prompts eliminated the image–text gap across models.
Writing the visual reading before the final report sometimes removed the gap, but effects varied by model and prompt wording.
Visual input did not reliably increase truthfulness: several models still shaded reports even when told the client wanted the truth.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of incentive-driven misreporting in vision-language models; fits MLLM behavior and evaluation.
papers.title: Read, Then Shade? How Visual Evidence Changes Incentive-Driven Misreporting in Vision-Language Advisors
papers.tldr: Visual input makes incentive-driven misreporting less consistently compliant than text-based reporting, with the effect depending on explicit value reading, prompt wording, and output order.

papers.abstract: RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) sensors provide complementary observations, yet their distinct sensing characteristics make effective cross-modal coordination challenging. Although existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process paired RGB-T inputs, they often fail to translate cross-modal relations into effective task-specific decisions, leaving the potential of these relations to improve task performance and robustness largely untapped. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RelMLLM, an RGB-T MLLM that explicitly learns to exploit cross-modal relations in task-specific decision making. It represents modality reliability, the cross-modal relation, and the dominant modality as a verifiable decision state. We derive task-grounded supervision for this state by comparing RGB-only, TIR-only, and paired RGB-T task outcomes. A hierarchical relation-guided reward supervises modality-specific evidence, relation-state prediction, and the final task output, while encouraging consistency across evidence, relation, and decision. We evaluate RelMLLM on natural RGB-T grounding, RGB-T visual question answering, and held-out sensor degradation. RelMLLM improves grounding accuracy and degradation robustness over its Qwen3-VL baselines while preserving performance on general RGB-T reasoning benchmarks. These results demonstrate that effectively exploiting cross-modal relations leads to more accurate and robust RGB-T decisions. Code and model weights are publicly available.
authors: Tianyi Zhao, Qihao Xu, Jiawen Xi, Duanni Meng, Bo Zhao, Maoxun Yuan, Xingxing Wei, Bo Li
bullets: Targets the difficulty of turning complementary RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) information into effective, task-specific decisions.

Applies hierarchical relation-guided rewards to align modality evidence, relation-state prediction, and final outputs.
Improves RGB-T grounding and robustness to sensor degradation over Qwen3-VL baselines while preserving general RGB-T reasoning performance.

papers.abstract: Automatic evaluation of artistic style transfer remains an open problem: existing metrics score an image pair in isolation, without seeing an example of the intended style transformation, and correlate poorly with human judgment. We introduce StyleJudge, a compact vision-language evaluator conditioned on a small set of reference source-to-stylized pairs before scoring a query pair, mirroring how a human rater calibrates to a style before judging a candidate. On a human-annotated benchmark of 878 rated pairs across 12 artistic styles (728 from 10 training/validation styles, 150 from 2 unseen styles), our efficient 0.8B-parameter StyleJudge reaches a Pearson correlation of 0.291 (Spearman 0.325) with human ratings on seen styles and 0.381 on unseen ones. On seen styles, it achieves the highest positive correlation among tested metrics: Gram-matrix style loss and CLIP similarity correlate weakly ($r=0.041$, $r=0.168$), while LPIPS (scored higher when closer to the source) correlates negatively ($r=-0.404$). We achieve this by distilling evaluation knowledge from a 72B-parameter vision-language teacher used only during training, which reaches $r=0.327$, confirming that most of its human alignment survives compact distillation. For training, we build a dataset of source-to-stylized pairs across the 12 styles via LoRA-adapted diffusion, densified with graded intermediate examples from a high-resolution image-morphing pipeline so the evaluator recognizes partial and complete stylization. On two held-out validation styles, StyleJudge reaches 28.2% exact-match agreement with its teacher's structured scores versus 1.1% for the untuned base model, with 67.8% shorter reasoning traces, and scores a pair in 39 s (median) using 2.5 GB of GPU memory on one NVIDIA T4. We release the human-rating benchmark, annotation guideline, SDXL-adapted FreeMorph code, and model weights.
authors: Lokesh, Pramukto Mandal, Somanshu Juneja, Jashnoor Singh, Amit Kumar, Pranav Adlinge, Richa Thakur, Kunal Swami, Aditya Nigam

papers.title: StyleJudge: A Human-Validated, In-Context-Learning Vision-Language Evaluator for Artistic Style Transfer

papers.abstract: Image steering aims to provide fine-grained control over concepts in generated images, enabling targeted and continuous manipulation without broadly altering the generation process. Recent steering methods for diffusion models primarily focus on the text-conditioning space or rely on costly auxiliary training. Deviating from that, we here propose a novel steering approach that extracts visual concept directions directly from the image-side activations of Diffusion Transformers. Specifically, we showcase few-shot concept extraction in the activation space using a simple difference-of-means estimator over intermediate residuals. We observe (a) scene-level concepts such as lighting, weather, and style are distributed across image tokens, as well as (b) local concepts such as object colors, textures, materials, and facial attributes are concentrated in specific regions. Towards controlling both concepts, we introduce a new unified training-free framework that uses global difference-of-means for (a) distributed concepts and masked difference-of-means for (b) local concepts, preventing local signals from being diluted by global averaging. Notably, using only a handful of positive and negative prompt pairs, our method identifies and extracts reusable concept directions that can be injected at inference for continuous steering. Quantitatively, our method outperforms text-encoder steering and training-free activation-editing baselines, as well as is competitive with specialized editing models. Our results suggest that as concept directions can be applied at patch level, our method enables precise targeted and compositional steering, manipulating multiple concepts in the same image.
bullets: Uses difference-of-means over intermediate image-side residual activations to extract reusable concept directions from a handful of positive and negative prompt pairs.
Applies global averaging for distributed scene concepts such as lighting, weather, and style.
Uses masked, region-specific averaging for local concepts including colors, textures, materials, and facial attributes.
Injects extracted directions at inference for continuous, targeted, and multi-concept steering without auxiliary training.
Outperforms text-encoder steering and training-free activation-editing baselines, while remaining competitive with specialized editing models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our few-shot concept extraction and steering pipeline. (1) We start from a small set of negative and positive prompt pairs, optionally with masks for localized concepts extraction. (2) We extract residual activations from a selected Diffusion Transformer block and estimate a concept direction using difference-of-means between positive and negative residuals. For global concepts, this is computed over all image tokens and for local concepts, it is restricted to the masked region patches. (3) At inference time, the resulting concept vector is injected into transformer blocks to steer generation, either globally or within a selected region.

Figure 2: Qualitative examples of concept steering. We show representative examples of our method across different concept families. Each row corresponds to a held-out prompt and visualizes the effect of increasing the steering strength α. The examples illustrate that extracted concept directions can produce smooth steering while preserving the main content of the image.

Figure 3: Compositional and targeted steering. Examples of different concept directions being applied to different regions in the same image. By selecting the spatial area to steer, our method enables targeted steering such as changing two different objects with two different colors or textures, as well as modifying different attributes of two persons. Notably, global concepts can be combined, as shown with snowy + anime in a single inference steering pass.

Figure 4: Edit success versus content preservation. We compare methods using ∆VQA to measure whether the requested edit is achieved and LPIPS to measure visual drift from the original image. Better methods appear toward the upper-left, indicating stronger edit success with less content drift. We note that ∆VQA slightly decreases at steering level 5, as some concepts appear at lower strengths and stronger interventions can lead to oversteering.

Figure 5: Extraction layer ablation. We sweep the layer used to extract the concept direction while keeping the injection range fixed. Layer 18 provides the strongest trade-off between edit success and content preservation.
Figure 6: Extraction timestep ablation. We compare concept directions extracted from individual denoising timesteps. The first denoising step provides the strongest edits.

Figure 8: Qualitative ablation samples – object concept: blue. Top row of each panel: extractiontimestep ablation. Bottom row: extraction-layer ablation.

For each example, increasing the steering strength α progressively increases the presence of the target concept while preserving the reference image. In contrast to FLUX.2 direct prompt editing, which produces a single edit for a given instruction, our approach provides continuous and progressive control over edit strength.
Figure 9: Qualitative ablation samples – global concept: snowy. Top row of each panel: extractiontimestep ablation. Bottom row: extraction-layer ablation.
Figure 12: Qualitative examples of concept steering. We present more qualitative samples across concepts.

Figure 10: Representative failure cases. We show examples of semantic mismatch, spatial drift, and concept entanglement. papers.selection_reason: Training-free concept steering in Diffusion Transformers; transferable to multimodal generative model control.
papers.title: Few-Shot Visual Concept Extraction for Steering Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: A training-free, few-shot method extracts global and local visual concept directions from Diffusion Transformer activations for precise, compositional image steering.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D understanding aims to localize and segment arbitrary objects beyond predefined categories. However, existing approaches based on Gaussian Splatting often rely on expensive preprocessing and lengthy training, limiting their applicability when fast and lightweight solutions are desired. We propose a lightweight, training-free framework for query-driven 3D instance segmentation on Gaussian Splatting. Instead of conventional mask-wise CLIP embeddings, we use dense pixel-level CLIP features to preserve fine-grained semantic information and enable flexible text-driven localization without relying on predefined instance proposals. Given a text query, we identify a high-quality target region in a carefully selected pivot view and propagate it across views using a video segmentor, providing consistent and comprehensive coverage of the target instance. We then lift the resulting 2D tracklets to 3D Gaussians through a novel visibility voting strategy, yielding accurate 3D segmentation masks with clean object boundaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups over existing open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods. These results highlight the effectiveness of our framework for efficient open-vocabulary 3D understanding without per-scene training.
authors: Nhat-Quynh Le-Pham, Khoi Nguyen, Binh-Son Hua
bullets: Uses dense pixel-level CLIP features instead of mask-wise embeddings for fine-grained, proposal-free localization.
Selects a target region in a pivot view and propagates it across views with a video segmentor.
Lifts 2D tracks into 3D Gaussians using visibility voting to produce consistent segmentation masks.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups.
Supports efficient open-vocabulary 3D understanding without per-scene training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our approach. We present a novel query-based framework for open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation. Given multi-view images and a text query, we extract pixel-level CLIP features to produce similarity maps and identify a 2D pivot instance region. The pivot is refined and propagated across views within a fixed frame budget using a Tracking Segmentor with our Mask Refinement module to ensure geometric consistency and coverage. The resulting masks are lifted to 3D Gaussians via visibility voting, forming an occlusion-aware 3D instance mask, which is rendered at novel views to obtain high-quality 2D instance segmentation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models can memorize and reproduce training samples during inference, raising serious privacy and copyright concerns. Existing inference-time mitigation methods often suppress conditional information globally, which may reduce memorization but can also harm semantic alignment and image quality. In this paper, we revisit memorization from the perspective of cross-attention heads. Through systematic analysis and targeted ablation, we find that memorization is mainly driven by a small subset of shallow-layer attention heads with abnormally strong semantic control, rather than by the entire cross-attention mechanism. Motivated by this finding, we propose Projection-based Top-k Attention Head Suppression, a targeted inference-time mitigation method. Our method first identifies the top-k attention heads most related to memorization using a semantic-control score, and then removes their condition-specific components through directional projection between conditional and unconditional representations. This design selectively weakens memorization-related features while preserving useful semantic information. Extensive experiments on different diffusion models and datasets show that our method effectively reduces memorization and achieves a better trade-off between memorization mitigation and image quality than existing approaches.
authors: Puwei Lian, Yujun Cai, Songze Li, Yuezu Lv, Guanghui Wen
bullets: Memorization is concentrated in a few shallow-layer attention heads with unusually strong semantic control.
The method identifies the top-k memorization-related heads using a semantic-control score.
It removes condition-specific components via projection between conditional and unconditional representations.
Experiments across diffusion models and datasets show reduced memorization with a better quality–mitigation trade-off than existing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our framework. The left panel illustrates the computation of multi-head attention. Based on this process, we introduce two modifications on the right panel: (1) Identifying attention heads with strong semantic control through attention map analysis. (2) Applying projection-based suppression to mitigate memorization-related components in the selected heads.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison with baselines. The first column shows the memorized training images, while the remaining seven columns present the results of baselines and our method. papers.title: Memorization Lives in a Few Attention Heads: Mitigating Memorization in Diffusion Models via Projection-Based Suppression
papers.tldr: A small number of shallow cross-attention heads drive diffusion-model memorization, and selectively suppressing them can reduce memorization while better preserving image quality and semantic alignment.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models remain susceptible to visual hallucinations, often mixing grounded information with unsupported claims in the same response. Response-level reinforcement learning assigns a shared advantage to all tokens in a response, causing negative updates to suppress correct information alongside unsupported claims. To reduce hallucination while preserving useful visual information, we introduce SARGO (Self-guided Advantage-Routed Grounding Optimization), a post-training framework for selective reinforcement and suppression through on-policy self-guidance. Direct and reciprocal weighting gives better-supported tokens stronger reinforcement on positive updates and weaker penalties on negative updates. Agreement between overall and hallucination-specific advantages selects when to apply this guidance. At the response level, a reference-calibrated reward couples factuality with the retention and expansion of grounded information, discouraging lower hallucination scores obtained through omission. Experiments on Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, and Gemma3-4B demonstrate that SARGO outperforms the evaluated mitigation baselines across Obj-Hal, AMBER, THRONE, and SHR evaluations. SARGO achieves these gains while preserving useful visual information and general multimodal capabilities.
authors: Jinyu Li, Zhiming Zhang, Hao Fang, Hongyao Yu, Bin Chen, Albert Ma, Shu-Tao Xia
bullets: Addresses response-level reinforcement learning, which can penalize correct content alongside hallucinated claims.
Uses on-policy self-guidance with direct and reciprocal token weighting based on grounding support.
Applies guidance only when overall and hallucination-specific advantages agree.
Employs a reference-calibrated reward to improve factuality without encouraging information omission.
Outperforms evaluated mitigation baselines across Obj-Hal, AMBER, THRONE, and SHR while retaining multimodal capabilities.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SARGO. The frozen initial policy supplies reference responses for reward calibration, while the current policy scores its own rollouts under ordinary and privileged contexts to obtain token-level grounding support. Agreement between overall and hallucination-specific advantages selects when self-guidance applies. Direct and reciprocal weighting modulate the relative strength of token-level reinforcement and suppression, illustrated by bar magnitude. Neutral routes retain uniform token weights.

Figure 3. Effects of token weighting and advantage routing on Qwen3-VL-4B. All variants share the same response reward. No weighting uses uniform token weights. Positive only and Negative only apply teacher weighting in one branch, retaining uniform weights in the other. RL-only routing uses the overall advantage alone to select the weighting branch. Figure 1. Object hallucination and information retention on Obj-Hal. Comparison of SARGO and baselines on (a) Qwen3-VL-4B, (b) Qwen3-VL-8B, and (c) Gemma3-4B. Lower CHAIRi and higher object recall (ObjRec) indicate better performance. SARGO achieves the lowest CHAIRi across all three backbones while retaining high object recall.
Figure 4. General multimodal performance on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B. Comparison on (a) MME total score and (b) MMStar accuracy (%). SARGO improves both metrics over Vanilla at both scales.
Figure 6. Visualization results comparing OPSD, GRPO, SymMPO, and SARGO. Hallucinations are marked in red.

papers.abstract: The rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has highlighted the need for comprehensive benchmarks to assess their capabilities and limitations in remote sensing (RS). However, evaluating MLLMs in large-size synthetic aperture radar (SAR) scenarios remains challenging, as understanding complete scenes requires both global semantic interpretation and fine-grained target perception. Existing SAR benchmarks predominantly rely on small image patches, limiting their ability to assess these capabilities jointly. To address these limitations, we present XLSAR-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the perception and reasoning capabilities of MLLMs in large-scene SAR imagery. XLSAR-Bench comprises 405 images with an average size of 7153$\times$7153 pixels, ten tasks spanning visual question answering, visual grounding, and detailed image captioning, with all evaluation samples meticulously annotated manually, assisted by a semi-automatic captioner. Experimental results from general-purpose and domain-specific MLLMs reveal persistent challenges in understanding large SAR scenes and accurately perceiving small targets. We have open-sourced XLSAR-Bench to support further research in developing more powerful MLLMs for complete large SAR scenes.
authors: La Jiang, Lingfeng Chen, Jiaqi Zhu, Fengrong Guo, Jiehua Zhang, Panhe Hu, Li Liu, Zhen Liu
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 405 large SAR images averaging 7153×7153 pixels.
Covers 10 tasks, including visual question answering, visual grounding, and detailed image captioning.
Uses manually annotated evaluation samples with assistance from a semi-automatic captioner.
Tests both general-purpose and domain-specific MLLMs.
Finds persistent difficulties in interpreting large scenes and accurately perceiving small targets; the benchmark is open-sourced.

papers.abstract: Generative models increasingly write a chain of thought before drawing, and report large gains from doing so. We ask what that text contributes, by substitution rather than ablation: holding the generator, sampler and seeds fixed, we replace the think block with controlled alternatives and measure the image. Across a unified model with a think mode, a reinforcement-learned reasoning generator, and a planner driving a frozen diffusion model, the same picture emerges. Content-free prose of matched length is worth nothing or less ($-0.05$ to $-0.15$). One sentence from an unrelated 8B model, naming the subject and a few identifying details, matches the generator's own plan in three to six times fewer conditioning tokens. The value sits where the referent is in doubt: writing down a name is worth $+0.33$ when it is right and $+0.05$ when it is wrong, and where the generator already succeeds the whole effect is $-0.07 \pm 0.07$. Cutting a plan at the text encoder's window leaves 272 of 286 images byte-identical, and a plan rewritten to fit that window ties a bare identification ($+0.003 \pm 0.044$), so a plan contains nothing the identification does not already supply. Field-level interventions find only colour executed reliably, and a control writing the same sentences into the user prompt shows that limit belongs to the generator rather than to the planning channel. Two judges and two annotators replicate the central contrasts. A think block earns its keep as a specification of what to draw, not as a plan that is carried out.
authors: Jian Xu, Delu Zeng, Qibin Zhao
bullets: Controlled substitutions show that matched-length, content-free prose provides no benefit and may hurt performance.
A short external sentence naming the subject and key details matches the model’s longer plan using 3–6× fewer conditioning tokens.
The benefit is concentrated in ambiguous cases where correctly identifying the referent matters; otherwise the effect is negligible or slightly negative.
Truncation and rewriting experiments show that the plan’s useful information is already captured by a compact identification.
Only colour is reliably executed among tested field-level interventions, and the same limitation appears when text is placed directly in the user prompt.

papers.abstract: Recent pre-trained vision-language models often encounter a Multi-Domain Task-Incremental Learning (MTIL) scenario in practice, where a set of classes of multi-modal tasks arrive incrementally. Due to privacy concerns and memory constraints, MTIL with pre-trained models encounters forgetting of knowledge from old tasks, degradation of zero-shot transfer capability, and underfitting of new-task knowledge. To overcome these challenges, previous MTIL methods attempt to learn a discriminative cross-task identification (CTI) module and an effective new-task adaptation (NTA) module. However, current CTI modules suffer from severe task confusion between seen and unseen tasks, and NTA modules cannot adaptively balance the performance and parameter cost while incorporating task-specific knowledge. To alleviate the above dilemmas, we propose an effective and efficient TSP-DLoRA method for MTIL, which consists of Task Subspace Projection (TSP) and Dynamic Low Rank Adapter (DLoRA) modules. Specifically, our TSP module includes a task identifier classifier based on task-specific subspaces and a feature projection strategy that can determine the identifier associated with samples from both seen and unseen tasks. Our DLoRA improves the knowledge adaptation from new tasks by dynamically assigning Low Rank Adapter (LoRA) across transformer layers based on the task distributions. Experimental evaluations across 11 datasets, using three performance metrics, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. Code is available at https://github.com/FerdinandZJU/TSP-DLoRA.
authors: Hao Fu, Qian Feng, Hanbin Zhao, Jiahua Dong, Xu Tan, Lina Wei, Chao Zhang, Hui Qian
bullets: Addresses forgetting of old-task knowledge, reduced zero-shot transfer, and underfitting of new tasks under privacy and memory constraints.
Uses Task Subspace Projection to identify seen and unseen tasks through task-specific subspaces and feature projection.
Uses Dynamic LoRA to allocate low-rank adapters across transformer layers according to task distributions.
Evaluated on 11 datasets with three metrics, showing the method’s effectiveness.
The abstract does not report specific numerical results or limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The training process of the DLoRA module in our method. The DLoRA module integrates LoRA into the first Lt transformer layers of both the image and text encoders. The gating mechanism before the LoRA modules in the image encoder determines whether to activate the LoRA based on the feature F ′ v(x) derived from the original CLIP. Only the LoRA and the gating mechanisms are trained, while the remaining parts are kept frozen.

Figure 1: (a) Comparison with existing methods. Unlike ZSCL, our method eliminates the need for additional storage and improves parameter efficiency. Compared to MoE-Adapter, our approach incurs significantly lower computational overhead with fewer trainable parameters. In contrast to DIKI, ours not only achieves higher accuracy but also precisely distinguishes whether samples belong to previously seen tasks (Precise Task ID). (b) Mechanism comparison. Existing training-free CTI applies the same NTA operation to both seen and unseen tasks, restricted by a weight “W ”. Conversely, our TSP module explicitly identifies the boundary between tasks, directing unseen samples to the original CLIP while processing seen samples with DLoRA. (c) Performance trade-off. Our method achieves a superior trade-off between average accuracy (both seen and unseen tasks) and parameter efficiency compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Figure 3: The workflow of the TSP module of our method in training and inference processes. During training phase, for image dataset of every task, the TSP module decomposes the image features via SVD and selects top r singular vectors from the right singular vector matrix to be the corresponding task subspace. During inference phase, for every test sample, the TSP module computes the cosine similarity between the raw feature extracted from original CLIP and the subspaces associated with each seen task. The result is compared against a threshold, denoted as “thres.”. The sample is classified using the corresponding DLoRA module if the cosine similarity exceeds the “thres.”. Otherwise, the original CLIP model is utilized to classify the sample.

Figure 6: Visualization of six task-specific distributions generated by the TSP module. We randomly selected 1,000 samples from each dataset. The majority of samples are correctly classified, as shown by their corresponding colors. A small number of samples are misclassified as unseen tasks, while an even smaller number are incorrectly assigned to other seen tasks. Overall, the TSP module achieves an accuracy exceeding 90% for each task.

Figure 4: The distribution of similarity scores for the TSP module across different tasks. The red line denotes a threshold set at 0.96. The majority of samples exhibit similarity scores above this threshold. The dense distribution of similarity scores also indicates the TSP module’s capability to effectively capture and extract critical information from each task.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal agents are expected to move beyond multimodal understanding toward completing complex tasks in realistic multimodal environments. In these settings, information is distributed across heterogeneous files and modalities, with cross-file and cross-modal dependencies requiring agents to continually coordinate perception, reasoning, and tool use as newly gathered evidence informs subsequent actions. However, existing omni-modal benchmarks primarily focus on multimodal perception and understanding, leaving complex task completion through sustained interaction with multimodal workspaces underexplored. We introduce Omni-Workspace, a benchmark comprising 380 deep-research-style tasks across four multimodal workspace types and two difficulty levels. These tasks require agents to inspect and process workspace files, retrieve external information when needed, integrate evidence across files and modalities, and produce artifacts satisfying explicit requirements. Evaluating 18 representative models reveals limitations in long-horizon multimodal workspace execution, with the best model scoring only 65.93 on average. Further analysis identifies multimodal context inflation and task-state drift as recurring challenges. Motivated by these findings, we further propose OmniFocus, a lightweight approach combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking to improve performance and efficiency. Omni-Workspace advances the evaluation and development of omni-modal agents toward autonomous completion of complex tasks in multimodal workspaces.
authors: Yuhao Wang, Yucheng Zhao, Yiran Zhong, Feida Zhu, Hongcheng Liu, Qichao Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Wang
bullets: Introduces 380 deep-research-style tasks spanning four multimodal workspace types and two difficulty levels.
Tasks require file inspection, external information retrieval, cross-file and cross-modal evidence integration, and artifact creation.
Evaluation of 18 representative models shows persistent limitations in long-horizon workspace execution; the best average score is 65.93.
Analysis identifies multimodal context inflation and task-state drift as recurring failure modes.
Proposes OmniFocus, combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking to improve performance and efficiency.
