papers.abstract: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, where open video LLMs use several stages, 9M to 172M samples and 64 to 256 tokens per frame on average, the resulting V-JEPA-LM models (1B to 8B, Qwen3 and Llama) lead every size class in average score across eleven video benchmarks; our 4B model scores 72.1, against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model. A controlled encoder x supervision study shows that the encoder decides what can be read and the supervision what is read: at a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on the speed questions of natural benchmarks. Code and models: https://github.com/kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM.
authors: Keuntae Kim, Dongjun Kim, Yong Suk Choi
bullets: V-JEPA retains shared representations of dynamics such as direction, speed, order, and state, but standard caption-based training largely leaves them unused.
Counterfactual pixel transformations create answer-balanced video variants whose answers depend specifically on the visual change.
Models are trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples using 32 visual tokens per frame.
V-JEPA-LM models from 1B to 8B lead their size classes across eleven video benchmarks; the 4B model scores 72.1.

papers.abstract: Multimodal agentic coding requires robust visual reasoning to analyze observations and evaluate generated artifacts. Current frameworks largely rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, where agents depend on their intrinsic vision to execute visually grounded tasks. However, this architectural coupling introduces a fundamental bottleneck. Agent performance remains strictly bounded by internal perceptual limitations. Furthermore, text-only agents lack native perception. Without specialized tools, they cannot perform visual reasoning. To overcome these constraints, we introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) paradigm. Prior visual tool-use merely manipulates images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read. In contrast, VaaT reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as callable external utilities. As a result, text-only agents can completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Meanwhile, vision-capable agents can dynamically augment their native perception on demand. We instantiate this paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. We comprehensively evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that VHarness consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy across both text-only and multimodal coding agents. These findings highlight that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities provides a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems.
authors: Haolin Yang, Wenshan Wu, Jin Jiang, Yu Cheng, Yan Xia, Ting Song, Yangyu Huang, Zhiliang Peng, Wenhui Wang, Hangbo Bao, Yuzhe Zhang, Wen-Da Wei, Tengchao Lv, Li Dong, Lei Cui, Furu Wei

VHarness implements VaaT through five atomic actions in a unified framework.
Across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D tasks, VHarness improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy for text-only and multimodal agents.
The approach provides a modular, flexible foundation for visual reasoning in agentic coding systems.

papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems increasingly combine sensed time series with external text such as expert reports and news, yet how reliably models use text that agrees or conflicts with the sensed history remains unclear. We introduce the first real-world diagnostic benchmark organized by text-history relationship: 1,762 text-window pairs across sensor telemetry (Weather), web-service traffic (Wikipedia), and market data streams (Finance), each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified by whether the text's direction agrees with the historical trend, opposes it, or is not stated. Across ten pretrained models evaluated zero-shot, we investigate text selection and combination under text-history relationships (RQ1) and error diagnosis and horizon-scaled revision control (RQ2). For RQ1, we compare two types of text on paired Weather windows: one directly forecasts temperature changes, while the other describes related weather conditions, such as winds and fronts. Under Aligned, the first type yields the lowest error for most models. Under Conflicting, it increases most models' error above the no-text baseline; we therefore add only its stated magnitude and timing to the second type. Compared with either type alone, this combination lowers mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for six models and raises directional accuracy (DA) for seven. For RQ2, an error decomposition attributes the error increase to oversized revisions, and a training-free rule that limits them outperforms forecasts both with and without text for the four models with this trade-off, lowering MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raising DA by 2.99%-9.71%. Our dataset is available at https://github.com/Shelton1202/ACU-Bench.
authors: Xintong Wang, Haihan Nan, Ruidong Li
bullets: Introduces a real-world benchmark of 1,762 text–time-series pairs from Weather, Wikipedia traffic, and Finance, labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified.
Evaluates ten pretrained models zero-shot on text selection, combination, error diagnosis, and forecast revision control.
Aligned, directly predictive text generally performs best; conflicting text often worsens forecasts relative to using no text.
Combining forecast-oriented text with related-condition text improves MASE for six models and directional accuracy for seven.
A training-free rule limiting oversized revisions improves both metrics for four models, with gains reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP are trained to align images and text, not to represent taxonomies. Yet empirical studies show that CLIP embeddings exhibit hierarchical structure aligned with the hierarchy of semantic concepts. A theoretical characterization of why such hierarchy emerges from a non-hierarchical objective remains open. In this paper, we formalize this phenomenon as Hierarchical Angular Separation (HAS), a geometric property whereby each non-leaf concept embedding is more similar to its descendants than to off-branch concepts. Empirically, we show that HAS holds approximately in raw images and randomly initialized CLIP image embeddings, while in text embeddings it holds approximately only after contrastive learning. To theoretically explain this asymmetry, we analyze an unconstrained features model in which the image embeddings are fixed and only the text embeddings are trained. At the global minimizer, the text-side HAS violation percentage at each node is at most the image-side HAS violation and near-violation percentage. The key mechanism is the hierarchical co-occurrence structure of image-text pairs, which biases text embeddings toward root-centered image prototypes. For a linear contrastive loss, we derive a closed-form solution that makes this mechanism explicit. We extend the analysis to the InfoNCE loss and establish analogous guarantees under sufficient regularization. Synthetic experiments validate the theory and show that HAS is transferred even beyond the regimes covered by our analysis.
authors: Nghia Nguyen, Tianjiao Ding, Lachlan Ewen MacDonald, Ren\'e Vidal
bullets: Defines Hierarchical Angular Separation (HAS), where concepts are closer to descendants than to off-branch concepts.
Finds that HAS approximately exists in raw images and randomly initialized image embeddings, but emerges in text embeddings after contrastive learning.
Analyzes a model with fixed image features and trained text features, proving that text-side HAS violations are bounded by image-side violations and near-violations.
Attributes transfer to hierarchical co-occurrence patterns in image–text pairs, which pull text embeddings toward root-centered image prototypes.
Derives a closed-form result for linear contrastive loss, extends guarantees to InfoNCE with sufficient regularization, and validates them on synthetic experiments.

papers.abstract: Reward models are a core component of modern text-to-image systems, serving as the objective for inference-time selection and RL-based post-training. A key prerequisite is visual understanding: to judge prompt adherence and ground aesthetic preferences, a reward model must bind attributes, resolve relations, and count reliably. We find that widely-used reward models perform poorly on targeted visual reasoning evaluations. Even when starting from strong vision-language backbones, preference fine-tuning erodes these capabilities, and continual-learning baselines fail to mitigate a steep tradeoff between visual reasoning and preference accuracy. We propose a data-centric intervention that injects visual reasoning supervision into preference learning by flipping the pairing axis. To complement conventional human preference data (paired images under a shared prompt), we convert existing visual reasoning datasets into preference pairs that share the same image but differ in prompt, and train on the mixture. This yields a Pareto improvement in both visual understanding and preference prediction. Across inference-time best-of-n selection and RL post-training, the resulting reward model improves text-to-image generation on challenging compositional prompts (GenEval) by an average of 4.0% and 5.5% respectively, outperforming HPSv3 which was trained on 6x more preference pairs.
authors: Shiye Su, Xiaohan Wang, Ludwig Schmidt, Serena Yeung-Levy
bullets: Existing text-to-image reward models struggle with attribute binding, relational reasoning, and counting.
Preference fine-tuning weakens the reasoning abilities of strong vision-language backbones, creating a tradeoff with preference accuracy.
The method converts visual-reasoning data into prompt-based preference pairs sharing the same image, then mixes them with human preference data.
This produces a Pareto improvement in visual reasoning and preference prediction.
Generation improves on compositional GenEval prompts by 4.0% with best-of-n selection and 5.5% with RL post-training, outperforming HPSv3 despite using fewer preference pairs.

papers.abstract: Safety in robotics does not solely depend on geometric constraints, but also on semantics: the given task, environment properties, and interactions between objects in the scene. We present a framework based on vision-language models (VLMs) to infer task- and scene-dependent safety constraints for robot manipulation. We provide the VLM a structured safety tool based on an RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction that first decides whether the task should be rejected since its execution may result in a non-recoverable hazardous outcome. Otherwise, it identifies preventable object-pair hazards and specifies the spatial relations that must be avoided. Open-vocabulary segmentation and depth information are then used to ground the detected objects in 3D and construct continuous risk fields that represent the corresponding hazardous regions. These fields are integrated with an obstacle avoidance module that corrects nominal robot motions during execution while accounting for the risk field. We evaluate the framework on preventable hazards, tasks requiring rejection, and safe variants in simulation and the real-world. Project website: https://vlm-hazard-riskfield.github.io
authors: Mariana Sosa Guzm\'an, Yide Song, Amin Abyaneh, Gregory Dudek, Hsiu-Chin Lin

Rejects tasks likely to cause non-recoverable harm; otherwise identifies preventable object-pair hazards and unsafe spatial relations.
Grounds hazards in 3D using open-vocabulary segmentation and depth, producing continuous risk fields.
Integrates risk fields into obstacle avoidance to modify nominal robot motions during execution.
Evaluated in simulation and the real world on preventable hazards, rejection-required tasks, and safe task variants.

papers.abstract: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of assistants that respond only after user prompts.
Introduces Model-Initiated Conversation, Stream-Aware Tool Calling, and Interactive Visual Grounding.
Adds Long-Horizon Interaction Memory for continuity across extended video streams.
Uses a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and three-stage training scheme to integrate these behaviors.
Reports leading performance among open-source streaming models on public benchmarks and releases model weights and inference code.

papers.abstract: Federated vision-language models (FedVLMs) represent one of the emerging frontiers of machine learning, aiming to integrate federated learning within the fine-tuning pipelines of vision-language models (VLMs). In this work, we introduce BLEND, a new framework designed to jointly enhance the personalization and generalization capabilities of FedVLMs. BLEND proposes a selective VLM parameter fine-tuning and aggregation strategy that consists of (i) global vision and text adapters shared across clients, and (ii) a personalized vision projection adapter tailored to each client. BLEND further introduces a novel loss function that blends the outputs of the global and personalized adapters to achieve personalization, while simultaneously promoting generalization through a principled anchor design implemented via the projection heads of the zero-shot VLM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BLEND consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting its ability to effectively balance personalization and generalization across diverse system settings. (Code is available at: https://github.com/payamsiabd/BLEND.git)
bullets: Addresses the challenge of improving both client personalization and cross-client generalization in FedVLMs.
Fine-tunes and aggregates global vision and text adapters shared across clients.
Uses a personalized vision projection adapter for each client.
Blends global and personalized adapter outputs, with zero-shot VLM projection heads providing generalization anchors.

papers.abstract: We study the implicit bias of Riemannian gradient flow for hyperbolic multiclass classification with fixed class prototypes in hyperbolic space $\mathbb H^n$. Our framework accommodates general permutation invariant relative margin (PERM) losses, a class that includes cross entropy and other standard multiclass losses. Our analysis is based on a decomposition: at large radius, the distance to each prototype splits into a radial term and a direction dependent term described by the Busemann function. This yields two main results. First, we prove a radial dichotomy: the sign of a drift coefficient $μ$ determines whether the radius is pushed toward the ideal boundary or back toward the interior; if the positive drift persists, then $r(t)=\tfrac12\log t+O(1)$, while persistent negative drift returns the trajectory to the large radius threshold in finite time. Second, we show that large-radius directions can approach critical points of the Busemann risk on $\partial\mathbb H^n$, even during radial return. These results provide a rigorous large-radius perspective on two phenomena we refer to as boundary saturation and near-boundary clustering in hyperbolic representation learning.
bullets: Studies Riemannian gradient flow with fixed hyperbolic class prototypes under general permutation-invariant relative-margin losses, including cross entropy.
Decomposes prototype distances at large radius into radial and direction-dependent Busemann terms.
Shows the drift coefficient’s sign determines whether trajectories move toward the ideal boundary or return toward the interior.
Under persistent positive drift, the radius grows as one-half log time plus a bounded term; persistent negative drift causes finite-time return to a large-radius threshold.
Shows directions can approach critical points of the boundary Busemann risk, including during radial return.

papers.abstract: Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to localize human-object pairs and recognize their interactions. Traditional supervised methods perform strongly but rely on task-specific training. Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer a promising route to training-free HOI detection through their broad visual-semantic knowledge and versatile perceptual and reasoning capabilities. However, existing approaches largely invoke these capabilities through loosely coordinated inference stages. This fragmented execution restricts the role of interaction hypotheses in guiding visual exploration, leaving key participants overlooked and local ambiguities unresolved. Furthermore, propagating early semantic assumptions through subsequent visual grounding and relation prediction induces self-reinforcing semantic circularity. To resolve these challenges, we propose HarnessHOI, a training-free framework that transforms passive MLLM inference into an active interaction-centric harness. Specifically, we introduce an interaction-guided perception mechanism that projects emerging interaction hypotheses back into the visual space to discover missing participants and refine ambiguous evidence through targeted observation. Furthermore, a relation-agnostic geometric adjudication module reconciles multi-source evidence to establish a unified spatial basis for grounded interaction reasoning across multiple actions and semantic roles. Extensive experiments on HICO-DET and V-COCO demonstrate that HarnessHOI achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed harness for complex interaction understanding. Code will be released upon publication.
bullets: Targets fragmented MLLM inference, overlooked participants, unresolved visual ambiguities, and semantic circularity in training-free HOI detection.
Uses emerging interaction hypotheses to guide targeted visual exploration and discover missing human-object participants.
Applies relation-agnostic geometric adjudication to reconcile evidence across actions and semantic roles.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods on HICO-DET and V-COCO.
Code is planned for release upon publication.

papers.abstract: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.
authors: Ellis Brown, Chris Hoang, Shengyi Qian, Shang-Wen Li, Mike Lewis, Marjan Ghazvininejad, Luke Zettlemoyer, Lucas Beyer, Mengye Ren, Jakob Verbeek, Saining Xie, Hu Xu
bullets: The study disentangles visual pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement under controlled compute and data.
A vision encoder trained jointly from scratch performs on par with a pretrained encoder, making a separate visual-pretraining stage unnecessary.
Removing dedicated vision capacity harms visual understanding, even when the backbone is enlarged by an equivalent parameter count.
Vision-only modules integrated into early backbone layers perform comparably to pre-fusion encoders and may reduce time to first token.
Findings persist across backbone sizes, free encoder-pretraining assumptions, and pretrained language-model initialization.

papers.title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
papers.tldr: Dedicated vision capacity matters more than a pretrained visual encoder, and it can be integrated early within the multimodal backbone rather than placed before fusion.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires connecting visual observations to the geometry, objects, and persistent state of an environment. Images alone leave these relationships implicit, while disconnected annotations make it difficult to study appearance, camera motion, and scene changes under a common reference. We introduce Spatial Foundry, a collection of 5,280 furnished residential 3D scene configurations with editable assets and aligned visual, geometric, and temporal data. Its modalities include floor plans, perspective and panoramic RGB, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, instance-level 3D bounding boxes, and camera trajectories paired with video. Shared scene coordinates link observations across views and time; editable source scenes enable additional camera paths and controlled object changes. We describe the data representation and construction workflow, and discuss applications in floor-plan-conditioned 3D generation, geometric reconstruction, instance-level perception, camera-conditioned video generation, shared world modeling, and scene editing. Controlled camera and scene variations support spatial perception and world-model research. The public project page provides videos and an interactive colored point-cloud preview.
bullets: Combines floor plans, RGB images and panoramas, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, 3D instance boxes, and camera-trajectory video.
Uses shared scene coordinates to align visual, geometric, and temporal observations.
Editable source scenes enable new camera paths and controlled object changes.
Supports applications including 3D generation, geometric reconstruction, instance perception, video generation, world modeling, and scene editing.
Scope is focused on furnished residential 3D scene configurations and controlled spatial variations.

papers.abstract: Humans naturally parse visual scenes into coherent individual objects rather than scattered features, a capability cognitive science calls object binding. While recent work shows that pretrained Vision Transformers (ViTs) intrinsically acquire this ability, how native self-attention computations mechanistically keep object instances separate remains unresolved. By studying this across eight pretrained ViTs, we found that instance separation is expressed more strongly in attention routing than in token content: selected query-key relations distinguish individual objects more reliably than value similarity or residual representations. Inside heads, patches belonging to one individual tend to read from a common image region, which we term their attention address. Visually distinct parts of one person share an address, whereas identical duplicated instances receive separate, movable addresses. These shared destinations arise in part because query interactions with the spatial structure of keys direct attention toward consistent regions for one object and elsewhere for another. In DINOv2 and most other backbones we tested, editing this query component at the selected head redirects its attention address toward another individual. Grouping patches by this query component separates same-category instances, reaching .615 FG-ARI versus .289 for the same clustering of final-layer features, which tend to merge them.
authors: Khalil Sabri, Guillaume-Alexandre Bilodeau, Nicolas Saunier, Wassim Bouachir
bullets: Instance separation is stronger in selected query–key attention relations than in value similarity or residual representations.
Patches from the same object tend to attend to a common image region, while visually identical instances receive distinct, movable addresses.
Query interactions with the spatial structure of keys help establish these object-specific attention destinations.
Editing the query component in selected heads can redirect an attention address from one individual to another.
Clustering by the query component separates same-category instances better than clustering final-layer features (FG-ARI .615 vs. .289).

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how pretrained Vision Transformers (ViTs) perform instance binding via 'attention addresses', providing mechanistic insights into the internal representations of foundation models.
papers.title: Objects as Addresses: Instance Binding in Vision Transformer Attention
papers.tldr: Vision Transformer attention binds object instances by routing their patches to shared, instance-specific spatial “addresses,” rather than primarily through token content.

papers.abstract: Differential morphing attack detection (D-MAD) compares a trusted live capture with a document image that may contain a facial morph. We investigate whether labelled validation data can improve a frozen-parameter vision-language evaluator through prompt selection rather than model fine-tuning. Version~1 generates 50 candidate prompts and selects the top-ranked instruction using a security-oriented loss that prioritises missed morph attacks (MACER) while accounting for bona fide classification errors (BSCER), response failures, parse failures, and decision inconsistency. Version~2 recursively revises prompts using aggregate validation feedback. On a subject-disjoint test set of 160 pairs spanning LMA, MIPGAN-2, and PIPE, the selected Version~1 prompt achieves a (19.17\%) morph attack classification error rate (MACER), with (0.00\%) observed bona fide sample classification error rate (BSCER), compared with (70.00\%) MACER for a controlled manual prompt. The paired (50.83) percentage-point difference has a (95\%) subject-bootstrap interval of ([43.33,58.33]). Recursive revision does not surpass the best Generation~0 validation loss; the reported revised descendant obtains (31.67\%) test MACER. All 23 attacks missed by Version~1 are landmark-based (LMA) morphs. Overall, the results show that prompt formulation can substantially influence frozen-parameter VLM-based D-MAD performance, while also highlighting the challenge of recursive prompt refinement under a compact 10-subject validation setting.
bullets: The approach selects or revises prompts using labelled validation feedback and a security-oriented loss emphasizing missed morph attacks.
The best Version 1 prompt achieved 19.17% MACER and 0.00% BSCER on a subject-disjoint test set of 160 pairs.
It outperformed a controlled manual prompt by 50.83 percentage points in MACER, with a 95% subject-bootstrap interval of [43.33%, 58.33%].

papers.abstract: Remote sensing change detection usually relies on large collections of temporally aligned, pixel-level annotations, which limits its scalability across regions, imaging platforms and application domains. Recent zero-shot approaches reduce the need for supervision, but they often localize fine-grained changes poorly because their features are coarse or inconsistent across time. We present SpotDiff, a training-free, plug-and-play framework for zero-shot change detection built by composing complementary vision foundation models. SpotDiff uses DINOv3 for semantically robust features, AnyUp to reconstruct them at pixel resolution, and SAM 3 for text-guided region-of-interest proposals, which an inference-time multi-scale strategy (SWIMS) makes reliable on small objects. Change is then measured by comparing the reconstructed features of the two dates inside the proposed regions, with no learnable components, fine-tuning or change labels. To our knowledge, SpotDiff is the first change detection method to use a universal feature upsampler, which alone adds 13.8 F1 over bilinear upsampling of the same features. On LEVIR-CD, SpotDiff reaches 82.46 F1, 2.06 points above the strongest prior training-free method, and on the multi-class SECOND benchmark it improves building change detection by 10.3 IoU and the six-class average by 2.2 IoU. Qualitative results on PlanetScope (3 m) and Sentinel-2 (10 m) imagery show that the same pipeline transfers across resolutions without modification. Our results indicate that composing modern foundation models is an effective route to scalable, label-free change detection.
authors: Anit Upadhyaya, Ata Akbari Asanjan, Chaitanya Jalluri, Subash Yeggina, Jeremy Kravitz
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable change detection without temporally aligned pixel-level labels.
Combines DINOv3 features, AnyUp pixel-resolution reconstruction, SAM 3 region proposals, and the SWIMS multi-scale inference strategy.
Measures feature differences within proposed regions with no learnable components, fine-tuning, or change labels.
Improves over bilinear upsampling by 13.8 F1; achieves 82.46 F1 on LEVIR-CD and gains on SECOND building and multi-class detection.
Transfers across PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 resolutions without pipeline changes.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of SpotDiff. The Similarity Module encodes both images with a frozen vision foundation model, reconstructs pixelresolution features with a universal upsampler and computes their per-pixel cosine similarity. The Region of Interest Proposal Module segments instances of the prompted category in each image with multi-scale inference (SWIMS) and fuses them across time. The Change Detection Module marks a candidate instance as changed when its mean similarity falls below a threshold. No component is trained.

papers.selection_reason: A zero-shot change detection framework that composes modern foundation models (DINOv3, SAM) without learnable components, demonstrating scalable label-free detection.
papers.title: SpotDiff: A Plug-and-Play Framework for Zero-Shot Change Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery

papers.abstract: Embodied interaction requires an agent to integrate multimodal perception with verbal and nonverbal behaviors to effectively communicate its intentions, including speech, body motion, and facial expressions. We present XBot-Omni, a Thinker--Talker--Actor architecture that extends the Omni paradigm to robotic modalities, including body motion and facial expressions, with ``X'' representing the extensibility to robotic-specific modalities. The Thinker processes text, images, audio, and video to formulate contextually appropriate responses, which are then realized by the Talker and Actor through speech and coordinated bodily expressions, respectively. In this report, we innovatively introduce the concept of ``Actor'' as a dedicated component for embodied agents: a coordinated, streaming module that leverages the native representations of the Thinker and Talker within an end-to-end pipeline, introducing only modest latency overhead. This unified architecture enables multimodal generation conditioned on omni-modal inputs directly to prevent information loss in staged designs. We comprehensively evaluate XBot-Omni across seven benchmarks, demonstrating strong multimodal understanding capabilities on both general-domain and robot-centric videos, as well as high-quality, natural, and well-coordinated motion generation. Furthermore, our results validate its capability to generate embodied multimodal responses directly from omni inputs, meeting the diverse requirements of embodied interaction. XBot-Omni enables robots not only to perceive the omni world but also to express themselves through speech and bodily behaviors, extending Omni models from conversational interaction to embodied communication in physical environments.
authors: Kerui Gu, Xing Fu, Shuoyang Sun, Cheng Peng, Jingru Duan, Huayu Gu, Zhenyu Chen, Jiaxin Huang, Cheng Wen, Rui Zhen, Kairui Chen, Zhihui Peng, Shaoli Huang
bullets: Addresses embodied interaction by jointly integrating multimodal perception with verbal and nonverbal behaviors.
Uses a Thinker–Talker–Actor pipeline: the Thinker understands omni-modal inputs, while the Talker and Actor produce speech and coordinated bodily expressions.
Introduces the Actor as a dedicated, streaming embodied-output module that reuses native Thinker and Talker representations with modest latency overhead.
Directly conditions multimodal generation on omni-modal inputs to reduce information loss from staged designs.
Evaluation across seven benchmarks reports strong multimodal understanding and high-quality, natural, coordinated motion generation for embodied responses.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Thinker–Talker–Actor architecture of XBot-Omni. Thinker representations provide response semantics and scene context, while native Talker states provide speech-generation conditions. For motion generation, semantic control translates interaction context into gesture requirements, including spatial pointing targets. These requirements and speech–action alignment guide an autoregressive generator whose tokens are decoded into body motion. The facial expression pathway combines a chunk transformer with a flow-matching generator. Output illustrations are schematic.

Checks: reported support; crosses: outside the described design; dashes: unreported or inapplicable, including motion-related features without motion output.

papers.selection_reason: Extends the Omni paradigm to robotic modalities (body motion, facial expressions) with a Thinker-Talker-Actor architecture for embodied multimodal interaction.
papers.title: XBot-Omni: An Omni-Modal Model for Embodied Understanding and Interaction
papers.tldr: XBot-Omni is an extensible omni-modal architecture that lets robots understand text, images, audio, and video and respond through coordinated speech, body motion, and facial expressions.

papers.abstract: The proliferation of user-generated video content has made accurate and robust no-reference video quality assessment (NR-VQA) a highly important challenge. Existing research increasingly relies on architecturally complex multi-branch pipelines or computationally intensive fine-tuning of single-branch backbones. In this paper, we investigate whether a single frozen video foundation model can serve as an effective NR-VQA backbone, and propose HiVE-VQA, the first framework (to our knowledge) to apply a JEPA-based video encoder to this task. HiVE-VQA extracts token grids from multiple depths of a pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder and stacks them into a hierarchical spatio-temporal volume, which a compact 3D convolutional head fuses across its layer, spatial, and temporal axes, combining low-level distortion cues from shallow layers with the semantic and temporal context captured at greater depths. The encoder remains frozen throughout, so only the head is trained: 5.2M parameters (5.7\% of the total), with no auxiliary multi-modal models and an inference cost that is invariant to video resolution. Trained solely on LSVQ and evaluated without any fine-tuning, HiVE-VQA outperforms 17 state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in SROCC and PLCC on both intra-dataset (LSVQ-test, LSVQ-1080p) and cross-dataset (KoNViD-1k, LIVE-VQC) benchmarks. These results indicate that hierarchical, depth-wise fusion of features from a single frozen video foundation model provides a more effective and efficient basis for NR-VQA than task-specific multi-network fusion. Code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/RobHam99/HiVE-VQA.
authors: Robbie Hamilton, Fan Zhang, David Bull
bullets: Targets robust NR-VQA without complex multi-branch pipelines or backbone fine-tuning.
Stacks token grids from multiple encoder depths into a hierarchical spatio-temporal volume.
A 3D convolutional head fuses layer, spatial, and temporal information while the encoder remains frozen.
Trains only 5.2M head parameters, with inference cost invariant to video resolution.
Trained on LSVQ and outperforms 17 SOTA methods across intra- and cross-dataset SROCC and PLCC benchmarks.

The results shown here are based on frozen model parameters, without performing any fine-tuning on these datasets.

papers.title: HiVE-VQA: Hierarchical Interaction via Volumetric Embedding for Video Quality Assessment
papers.tldr: HiVE-VQA uses hierarchical features from a single frozen V-JEPA video encoder with a compact 3D head to achieve efficient, strong no-reference video quality assessment.

papers.abstract: Quantifying disease-associated renal tubular remodeling is challenging because tubular appearances are heterogeneous. We introduce TuMAP (Tubular Morphotype-Aware Pathomics), a pipeline combining (1) dual-view foundation-model representations and provisional morphotype annotation, (2) compositional and within-morphotype pathomics, and (3) patient-level statistical inference. From 456,158 tubules in 358 PAS-stained kidney biopsy slides, TuMAP identified eight image-based morphotypes, seven of which showed stable subsampling assignments. Across 219 patients in six diagnostic groups, diabetic nephropathy (DN) and tubulointerstitial nephritis/acute tubular injury (TIN/ATI) each differed from minimal change disease in seven morphotype proportions, while IgA nephropathy differed in six. DN showed reduced nuclear solidity and increased eccentricity across all eight morphotypes. Area-normalized nuclear density exposed additional within-morphotype differences. TuMAP provides a framework for separating changes in tubular morphotype composition from phenotypic differences within morphotypes.
authors: Ruijie Wu, Yuechen Yang, Yanfan Zhu, Yu Wang, Shilin Zhao, Ming-Tsun Tsai, Szu-Yuan Li, Shuo-Ming Ou, Tz-Heng Chen, Haichun Yang, Yuankai Huo
bullets: Addresses heterogeneity in disease-associated renal tubular remodeling.
Uses foundation-model representations, provisional morphotype annotation, compositional and within-morphotype pathomics, and patient-level inference.
Identified eight image-based tubular morphotypes, with seven showing stable subsampling assignments.
Analyzed 456,158 tubules from 358 PAS-stained kidney biopsy slides across 219 patients and six diagnostic groups.
Distinguished disease groups through morphotype proportions and nuclear features, including reduced solidity and increased eccentricity in diabetic nephropathy.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the TuMAP pipeline. (1) Dual-view tubular representation: Texture and shape views encoded with frozen UNI2-h are harmonized and clustered into provisional M1–M8 morphotypes. (2) Dual-level morphotype-aware pathomics: Composition and within-morphotype phenotypes are quantified. (3) Patient-level statistical inference: Measurements are aggregated per patient and morphotype (red circle: M1 median solidity in one DN biopsy; note different y-axis scales), followed by regression with HC3 robust standard errors and FDR control.

Fig. 3. Patient-level comparisons vs. MCD (n = 219). (a) Mean morphotype shares (%) with adjusted logit-share effects (SD). (b,c) Tubular/nuclear effects (SD), labeled by M number; dots mark FDR q< 0.05. (d–f) M1 tubular solidity, nuclear minor axis, and assigned nuclei per 10,000 µm2 of contour area (including lumen). Points represent patients; asterisks mark FDR q < 0.05.

Fig. 2. Eight provisional morphotypes (456,158 tubules; 358 slides). Left: UMAP (200,000 points). Right: M1–M8 counts, median area/circularity, and representative tubules (20-µm bars). Segment-like names are not immunohistochemically confirmed.
Table 1. Comparison cohort (219 patients). Tubules: total on analyzed sections; tubules/patient: median [IQR]. GS: globally sclerosed glomeruli (%), median [IQR] (190 patients with available GS%).

papers.selection_reason: Applies dual-view foundation model representations for medical pathology analysis, demonstrating a pipeline for morphotype-aware quantification.
papers.title: TuMAP: A Dual-View, Morphotype-Aware Pathomics Pipeline for Quantifying Renal Tubular Remodeling
papers.tldr: TuMAP combines dual-view morphotype analysis with pathomics and patient-level statistics to quantify both the composition and within-morphotype phenotypes of remodeled renal tubules.

papers.abstract: Merging independently fine-tuned checkpoints into a single multi-task model requires no data, no labels, and no gradient steps. In practice the task vectors of different tasks interfere, and the standard remedies--averaging, magnitude pruning, sign election--operate entry by entry, ignoring that each delta induces a low-dimensional update on the hidden features it acts upon. We recast merging as a subspace interference problem. For every two-dimensional weight tensor we take the top-r right-singular subspace of each task's delta--the input directions along which that task moves the representation most--and remove from each task vector the component lying in the union of the other tasks' subspaces. The resulting Joint Null-Space Projection (JNSP) is closed-form and order-independent, needs no forward pass, and is defined entirely by the checkpoint set. On eight CLIP image-classification tasks JNSP merges ViT-B/16 experts to 89.45% average accuracy without using a single image, 11.88 points above the strongest parameter-wise training-free baseline (TIES-Merging, 77.57%), 14.22 above Task Arithmetic, and 0.98 above WUDI's data-free consensus merge (88.47%). The gain holds across three backbones on the independently trained TALL release (+10.8, +12.6, +9.1 over TIES for ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14) and replicates there at 89.20%; controls confirm the source--a single shared subspace instead of per-task ones loses 2.9 points, and a sequential variant collapses to 69.6%. On RoBERTa-large the same projection underperforms plain task arithmetic, which we report rather than hide. Code is available at https://github.com.
bullets: Addresses interference between task vectors during data-free, training-free checkpoint merging.
Uses top-r right-singular subspaces of each weight-delta tensor and projects each task update into the joint null space of the others.
The closed-form, order-independent method requires neither forward passes nor data, labels, or gradient steps.
Achieves 89.45% average accuracy on eight CLIP image-classification tasks, outperforming reported training-free baselines; results also replicate across multiple ViT backbones.
Performance is not universal: JNSP underperforms plain task arithmetic on RoBERTa-large.

figures.caption: Figure 2. One merged prediction, traced through the operator. Image 5721 of the Stanford Cars test split, predicted by the same merged checkpoints as the Cars column of Table 1. Left: the test image, and the same input drawn as a cell grid. Middle: the three steps of JNSP for this task, with schematic graphics for the delta and the basis (no checkpoint is stored for rendering them). The two retention figures are averages over tensors and come from our r=16 run: Cars keeps 83.7% of its own delta norm, and the merged model keeps 30.4% of the aggregate norm. Right: predictions of JNSP, TIES-Merging and Task Arithmetic on this image, with each method’s Cars accuracy. JNSP is correct; both entrywise baselines predict the same wrong class. The sample is one of 962 Cars test images on which JNSP is correct and both baselines err (of 8,040). WUDI is not shown because its per-sample predictions were not saved.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on held-out test images. Each column is one image; rows give the ground-truth label and the predictions of JNSP, TIES-Merging, and Task Arithmetic (blue: correct, red: incorrect). Samples are drawn at random from cases where JNSP is correct and both baselines err. The merge is entirely data-free in all three methods; only the merge rule differs. Per-image agreement counts are in Appendix L.

Figure 3. How JNSP merges one tensor. (1) The top-r right singular vectors Si of ∆i are the input directions task i moves most. (2) The other tasks’ bases are stacked and orthonormalized to U∪; the orange wedges are directions task i must give up; Si itself is not added to U∪, but any part of it inside the peer union is removed. (3) ∆i is projected onto Ni, keeping ∆̃i and removing the rest; the kept parts are summed into θmerge. The construction never depends on task order.

Figure 6. Order dependence at matched rank r=8. (a) Per task, the sequential score (red) against the joint score (blue), in merge-list order. Early tasks survive sequential merging nearly intact; later ones are progressively gutted, while the joint score does not depend on list position. (b) The same sequential accuracies as a function of list position (solid red), with the joint scores as a reference (blue dashed) and each task’s retained delta norm (grey, ∥τ̃i∥F /∥τi∥F , computed as one pooled ratio over all 53 tensors). Sequential retention stays between 81.7% and 100% at every position and shows no downward trend across the list (the last task retains 90.9%, above the 81.7% minimum), so the collapse cannot be read as “later tasks lose their norm”. Joint projection retains less on average (77.7–91.2%) and scores 18.4 points higher, so the amount removed does not explain the collapse.

Figure 11. Where the margin comes from. Per-task difference between JNSP (r=16) and a competing method, on our ViT-B/16 checkpoints (Table 1). Left: against TIES-Merging, the strongest entrywise baseline on average; the gain is small only on the two tasks the entrywise rule already handles well (MNIST, SVHN). Right: against the best of TSV-M, Iso-C, Iso-CTS and AlphaMerging on each task, a much tighter comparison; JNSP leads on five of eight tasks and trails on three, by at most 1.77 points, and the mean per-task advantage is 0.47 points. The right-panel opponent differs from task to task, so its mean is not a difference of two table averages.

Figure 7. Cross-task subspace overlap on ViT-B/16, Eq. (9) averaged over the 53 merged tensors (r=16). The diagonal is 1 by construction. Independent random subspaces at these widths would sit at 0.018 on average; every off-diagonal cell is at least seven times that, and the mean is 0.179, or 9.9 times chance. The darkest pairs share an input modality or a visual statistic.

Figure 8. Where the removal lands. (a) Retained fraction per transformer block under the aggregate definition of Table 14 (r=16, %); no block stands apart. (b) Fraction of each task’s delta energy captured by its own top-16 right-singular directions. Datasets whose updates concentrate in few directions score higher; the two are correlated at r=0.85 across the eight tasks.

Figure 9. Where the error lives. (a) Per-class recall for each task: box spans the interquartile range, thick bar the median, whiskers the 5th/95th percentiles, and the red dot the worst class. (b) The standard deviation of per-class recall against the concentration ϕ of the task’s update (the top-16 energy share of Figure 8b). Spread falls almost linearly in ϕ (r=− 0.89, eight tasks).

Figure 10. Bootstrap intervals, both checkpoint releases. Point estimates and 95% percentile intervals over the evaluation set (2,000 resamples) for the eight tasks, our ViT-B/16 checkpoints and the independently trained TALL release. Intervals are narrow where the test set is large and the task is saturated, and widest on DTD—the smallest test set (1,880 images) at a mid-range accuracy.

Figure 5. Rank and mechanism. (a) Joint projection has a broad optimum around r=16 (shaded), leading the shared-basis control by 2.1–3.2 points at every rank; the sequential variant at matched rank collapses to 69.64. (b) The same runs on the same accuracy axis, placed against the fraction of aggregate delta norm they retain; the path runs r=32 → 20 → 16 → 12 → 8 left to right: accuracy peaks at intermediate retention, and the shared basis retains more norm at every rank while scoring lower, so the score is not a function of how much is deleted.

papers.title: Joint Null-Space Projection for Data-Free Model Merging

papers.abstract: Change detection in remote sensing conventionally relies on spatially aligned bi-temporal imagery, which may be unavailable or unreliable in practical scenarios. Recent single-temporal approaches address this limitation by learning structural evidence, such as building regions, from a labeled source dataset and transferring it to unseen target imagery using only the current image. However, adaptation to the source dataset can over-specialize pretrained features and reduce their cross-dataset generalization, a risk that this paper argues is higher when the feature adaptation is parameterized independently of the states used for prediction. To address this issue, the current study introduces SALT, a State-Aligned Low-Rank Transfer framework. SALT keeps a DINOv3 backbone frozen and learns negative and positive structural states that both score each patch and, through State-Aligned Low-Rank Adaptation (SALA), span the rank-2 subspace in which patch features are corrected. Directional State Alignment supervises these corrections to raise the evidence of positive patches and lower that of negative ones, while Geometry Preservation limits changes to the pairwise relations among pretrained patch features. Experiments on LEVIR-CD and the WHU aerial building dataset show that, at the pixel level and in both transfer directions, SALT outperforms four baselines reproduced under a common source-only protocol, improving over the strongest reproduced baselines by 9.45 and 5.79 points in pixel-level AP and by 27.69 and 14.25 points in IoU (LEVIR-CD to WHU and WHU to LEVIR-CD, respectively), with only 0.068M trainable parameters and 40.2 ms per image. In order to facilitate reproducibility and further research, the source code of SALT is available at https://github.com/gthpapadopoulos/SALT
authors: Aggelos Psiris, Georgios Angelidis, Giorgos Sfikas, Maria Vakalopoulou, Thomas Lagkas, Panagiotis Sarigiannidis, Georgios Th. Papadopoulos
bullets: Addresses single-temporal cross-dataset structural localization when aligned bi-temporal imagery is unavailable or unreliable.
Freezes a DINOv3 backbone and learns positive/negative structural states that score patches and define a rank-2 correction subspace.
Uses directional state alignment to separate positive and negative evidence, with geometry preservation limiting distortion of pretrained patch relationships.
On LEVIR-CD and WHU, outperforms four reproduced source-only baselines in both transfer directions at pixel-level AP and IoU.
Uses 0.068M trainable parameters and 40.2 ms per image; code is publicly available.

papers.abstract: This report summarizes the Mobile Unified Multimodal Understanding (MUMU) track of the 8th Large-scale Video Object Segmentation (LSVOS) Challenge, held in conjunction with ECCV 2026. MUMU asks for a single unified model that jointly performs multi-concept image tagging over quality, scene, and event vocabularies, open-vocabulary object detection, and concise image captioning, within a budget of 0.5B parameters and 8 GB of peak inference memory. Submissions are ranked by a weighted task score scaled by an efficiency factor. We describe the tasks, rules, and evaluation protocol, report the final results, and review the methods of the top three teams. All three leading solutions build on the compact Florence-2-base model, but extend it in different ways: lightweight tagging heads with cross-task inference refinement, a shared low-rank adapter trained on coverage-aware multi-source data with task-dependent decoding, and a training-free pipeline that maps captions to tags and applies detection test-time augmentation. The results show that a compact prompt-based vision-language model can serve all three outputs when supervision, decoding, and cross-task cues are designed for each task, while open-vocabulary detection on novel categories remains the main bottleneck.
authors: Chang Liu, Henghui Ding, Tong Yang, Dayoung Kil, Seong-heum Kim, Qilin Xiang, Ronghao Zheng, Ziyang Zhang, Shanlin Jiang, Ruohan Shi, Qilin Fan, Chengfeng Qiu, Kaifeng Wei
bullets: Requires one model to perform multi-concept image tagging, open-vocabulary object detection, and concise captioning.
Models are constrained to 0.5B parameters and 8 GB peak inference memory, with rankings combining task performance and efficiency.

The top three solutions extend Florence-2-base using lightweight heads and refinement, shared low-rank adaptation with task-specific decoding, or a training-free caption-to-tag and detection-augmentation pipeline.
Results indicate that supervision, decoding strategies, and cross-task signals are important for compact unified multimodal models.
Open-vocabulary detection on unseen categories remains the main limitation.

papers.abstract: Natural language explanations promised by modern Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) offer autonomous driving systems a path toward detailed scene description and interpretable decision making on the road. While recent benchmarks have begun assessing these models on driving scenes, they mainly target routine traffic conditions and general comprehension tasks based on existing driving datasets and therefore fail to evaluate model performance on the rarest and most safety-critical driving events, also known as "corner cases". To provide a comprehensive evaluation of Video LLMs on precisely these scenarios, we introduce DashBench, a benchmark testing 25 Video LLMs on 1,709 carefully curated driving videos spanning not only collision-related corner cases but also rare non-collision ones. Through extensive prompts and open-ended question answering, we expose a critical capability gap: all evaluated models perform substantially below the threshold required for safety-critical driving applications, frequently misjudging or missing dangerous events on the road ahead and hallucinating non-existent agents or actions in their explanations. We believe DashBench, combining an extensive dataset with a rigorous evaluation toolkit and a detailed diagnosis of current model limitations, drives progress toward safer, more explainable autonomous driving systems. The code and data will be shared at: cornercase-dashbench.github.io
authors: Gabriel Manalu, Minh Son Hoang, Hyeontaek Hwang, Jaesung Lee, Hyojin Choi, Tran Tuan Phong, Seon Kwon Kim, Saad Wazir, Daeyoung Kim

All evaluated models fall substantially short of safety-critical requirements.
Models often miss or misjudge dangerous events and hallucinate agents or actions in their explanations.
The benchmark includes an evaluation toolkit and diagnosis of model limitations; code and data will be released.

papers.abstract: Adapting general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to Autonomous Driving (AD) is thought to require heavy 3D spatial priors or intrusive architectural overhauls to compensate for a lack of spatial grounding. In this work, we present a counterintuitive pilot study: off-the-shelf general VLMs already exhibit remarkable adaptability across diverse driving tasks, while precise metric depth remains the primary missing link, a bottleneck readily addressable via onboard sensors and depth foundation models. To this end, we introduce the Triplet Incremental Training Framework, a non-intrusive paradigm that seamlessly instills 3D geometric awareness into a general VLM backbone while fully preserving its open-world capabilities. Driven by automatically constructed (image, depth, QA pair) triplets, our framework operates via a unified tri-stream training pipeline: an unfrozen primary VLM stream to adapt to driving tasks, an auxiliary depth stream that guides the visual backbone to implicitly imagine 3D scene geometry via explicit geometric constraints, and a frozen twin VLM stream employing logit-level KL distillation to prevent semantic drift. Crucially, the auxiliary depth branch is discarded during deployment, ensuring the enhanced geometric awareness comes with zero inference overhead. We evaluate our framework across four major benchmarks targeting four diverse capabilities spanning 3D spatial perception, driving-oriented language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art driving VLMs, rivals domain-specific expert models in 3D perception, and successfully retains its original general reasoning capabilities. This demonstrates that Triplet Incremental Training offers a unified, deployment-ready paradigm for transforming general foundation models into robust driving intelligences.
authors: Shengtao Wu, Zichao Dong, Weixuan Qiao, Xiaolu Liu, Xin Zhan, Junbo Chen, Jianke Zhu
bullets: General VLMs transfer well to diverse driving tasks, but precise metric depth is the main limitation.
The framework trains on automatically constructed image–depth–QA triplets using three streams: task adaptation, depth-guided geometry learning, and frozen-model KL distillation.
The auxiliary depth branch is removed at deployment, preserving the original model’s open-world reasoning capabilities.
Evaluation covers 3D perception, driving language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding.
The method reportedly surpasses existing driving VLMs, approaches expert models in 3D perception, and retains general reasoning ability.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal alignment is the standard objective for building multimodal representations. We show that alignment as a \emph{sole} objective is lossy wherever modalities are informationally asymmetric---where neither can express what the other carries. Visual question answering is an obvious case: a question is a selective relational operator probing a dense visual field whose fine-grained features no query recovers, so what alignment preserves is not what the task requires. We prove an \textbf{Alignment Redundancy Bound}: alignment-only Dirichlet energy minimization retains at most the redundant information atom $\Red(Z; X_1, X_2)$, annihilating private modality-specific structure $\Unq(Z; X_m)$ and cross-modal synergy $\Syn(Z; X_1, X_2)$. We introduce \textbf{Decomposed JEPA (D-JEPA)}, which factorizes latents into an aligned shared core and private modality-specific fibers. The shared core retains most of the structure alignment targets; the private fibers recover what alignment discards, via contextual masked prediction and asymmetric cross-subspace independence. Under information asymmetry, alignment-only training undergoes catastrophic semantic collapse on compositional reasoning benchmarks, surviving only on binary queries. D-JEPA averts this collapse, substantially improving downstream accuracy over both alignment-only and alignment-with-reconstruction baselines, and restoring a positive multimodal synergy gap in place of the baseline's inverted gap. Information-theoretic audits confirm that D-JEPA recovers most of the mutual information available from a frozen backbone, and causal fiber-swap interventions demonstrate that the recovered information is causally localized in the private fibers.
bullets: Alignment alone preserves redundant cross-modal information but can discard private and synergistic information under modality asymmetry.
The method decomposes each latent into an aligned shared core and private modality-specific fibers.
Contextual masked prediction and asymmetric cross-subspace independence train the private fibers to recover discarded structure.
On compositional reasoning benchmarks, D-JEPA avoids alignment-only semantic collapse and improves downstream accuracy over alignment-only and reconstruction baselines.
Information audits and fiber-swap interventions indicate that recovered information is substantial and causally localized in the private fibers.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning can teach vision-language models (VLMs) to decline harmful image-text requests, but how safe the result becomes is set indirectly, through reward weights found by trial runs. Stating safety as budgets on the rate of harmful assistance and the rate of over-refusal, enforced by Lagrange multipliers inside GRPO with an off-the-shelf scorer as the cost, is the natural fix, and it fails twice. The multiplier compares the scorer's mean with the budget, and scorers built for ranking get the mean wrong: a fixed-point analysis shows that the mean bias, not the budget, then decides whether the multiplier settles, saturates or switches off. And standard GRPO standardizes the penalized reward within each group, which cancels the multiplier before it reaches the gradient. Two-channel constrained GRPO repairs both: the base reward keeps the raw score for the within-group comparison, the penalty and the constraint estimate pass through a monotone map fitted on judge-labeled training responses, and the advantage keeps the multiplier. On a Qwen3-VL-2B policy with a training-free readout of an open 4B model as the scorer, held-out harm on 1,037 adversarial prompts falls from 8.9% under standard GRPO to 4.8%, lower in every seed, where the uncalibrated budget gives 7.6%; over-refusal stays at most 2% on 400 benign queries and MMBench is unchanged. The gain is largest where the intent sits in the image (10.1% -> 5.1%) and grows on the unseen HADES benchmark (28.9% -> 12.8%). Order-preserving distortions of the scores reproduce each predicted controller state in every seed, and the results hold under a map fitted on another judge's labels, an image-reading judge and a human audit.
bullets: Safety budgets fail with ranking-based scorers because mean-score bias miscalibrates Lagrange multipliers, while standard GRPO normalization can cancel their effect.
The method keeps raw rewards for within-group comparisons, maps scorer outputs monotonically for constraint estimation, and preserves the multiplier in the advantage.
On adversarial prompts, harm fell from 8.9% with standard GRPO to 4.8%, versus 7.6% for an uncalibrated budget.
Over-refusal remained at most 2%, MMBench performance was unchanged, and harm reductions extended to image-dependent intents and unseen HADES data.
Results were consistent across seeds and robust to alternative judges and human auditing.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires both spatial scene understanding and task history. However, many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely primarily on current observations, without explicitly integrating spatial structure and task history. Appearance-based memories can be sensitive to occlusion and viewpoint changes, while spatial representations of the current scene alone do not preserve how the scene has changed during task execution. We introduce STVLA, a framework that incorporates features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal memory alongside visual representations. This allows the policy to recall past scene structure as context for current action decisions. To select informative history, STVLA uses a mathematically grounded scoring rule that balances relevance to the current observation with complementary evidence from memory. Across evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge, STVLA achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods on each benchmark. On real-world block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, it improves success over $\pi_{0.5}$ by $58.33$, $30.00$, and $35.00$ percentage points, respectively. These results support integrating scene geometry into temporal memory to improve manipulation requiring both spatial precision and task history. Project website: \href{https://stvla.github.io/}{https://stvla.github.io/}

papers.abstract: We present UniSpark-9B, a unified multimodal model that investigates hybrid attention for visual understanding and generation. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts backbone with approximately 9B parameters in each branch, UniSpark combines full attention for explicit token interactions with GatedDeltaNet linear attention for compact context propagation. Autoregressive text prediction and visual flow matching jointly support visual question answering, text-to-image generation, instruction-guided editing, and interleaved text-image prediction. In interleaved generation, noisy visual targets are isolated from subsequent predictions, while clean visual representations provide context for later outputs. A blockwise protocol enforces this distinction through attention masks in full-attention layers and recurrent-state retention rules in linear-attention layers. The selected training sources contain 159.7M generation samples, 213.4M understanding samples, and 624.8K interleaved sequences. A four-stage curriculum jointly trains multimodal understanding and visual generation, refining answer accuracy and instruction following while extending image synthesis to 2K. UniSpark scores 2470.3 on MME-S and 0.83 on GenEval. Qualitative examples further illustrate its capabilities in interleaved image generation, video synthesis, and video editing. Together, these results demonstrate that hybrid attention provides an effective backbone for unified multimodal understanding and generation.

papers.abstract: We present EvenVLM, the first text and multimodal (VQA) dataset for Even (Lamut), an endangered Northern Tungusic language spoken by approximately 6,800 people in Siberia. Our dataset comprises 50,521 structured Even-Russian entries extracted from dictionary and phrasebook sources via GPT-4o Mini-based parsing, from which we synthetically generate 107,543 training examples spanning translation, grammar, reading comprehension, and semantic classification. To address tokenization inefficiency on Even's agglutinative morphology, we propose a three-step tokenizer expansion algorithm that adds Even-specific graphemes (eng, oe, o-umlaut), whitelisted vocabulary, and BPE merges, reducing average tokens per word by 27% (4.99 to 3.64). Using LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-4B, we adapt the model for text tasks (0.53% trainable parameters, rank 32) and separately for visual question answering (rank 64, frozen vision encoder). Our best configuration achieves 11.4% exact match and a 13.6 weighted score on text benchmarks, 0.1283 chrF for sentence translation, and 65% accuracy on VQA (up from 0% for the base model and text-only fine-tuning). We release our datasets, evaluation benchmarks, and training pipeline to support further research on Even and other low-resource languages.

papers.abstract: Multimodal dataset distillation (MDD) aims to reduce the cost of vision-language pre-training by synthesizing compact image-text datasets. Although recent feature-matching methods have improved distillation efficiency, synthetic data may become specialized to the model representations encountered during optimization, limiting generalization to unseen model states. We propose Model Distribution-Aware Multimodal Dataset Distillation (MDA-DD), which leverages supervision from a dynamic staggered queue of models at different training stages. We further introduce asymmetric dual projection for complementary alignment in visual and linguistic spaces and an uncentered second-order moment objective that retains mean-related cross-modal information. Experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO demonstrate consistent retrieval improvements over existing methods across synthetic-data budgets. With only 100 synthetic pairs, MDA-DD improves IR@1 and TR@1 on Flickr30K by 12.9 and 18.2 percentage points, respectively, over the strongest baseline at the same budget, outperforming all compared methods using 500 pairs on both datasets across all six retrieval metrics.

papers.abstract: Advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have improved remote sensing image analysis and supported geospatial decision-making. However, fine-grained understanding of remote sensing imagery remains challenging for VLMs. Large variations in object scale, complex geospatial relations among instances, and limited visual detail hinder precise instance localization, visible attribute identification, and spatial relation understanding, potentially leading to descriptions that lack visual grounding. Existing datasets and benchmarks insufficiently assess end-to-end instance localization and captioning without target-specific textual cues. To support this evaluation, we introduce RICapBench, a dataset and benchmark that unifies instance localization and fine-grained captioning in remote sensing. RICapBench contains 245,466 instance-level annotations and 498,005 spatial relation tuples spanning general remote sensing, UAV remote sensing, and dense small-object scenarios. Each annotation pairs an object's oriented bounding box with a natural language description of its visible attributes and spatial relations to surrounding instances and environmental elements. To evaluate the accuracy and completeness of spatial relation captioning, we propose a remote sensing spatial relation parser and the RelCap-F1 metric. We combine RelCap-F1 with instance localization and attribute captioning metrics into a composite metric, RICScore. Our evaluation of 15 advanced open-source and closed-source VLMs identifies instance localization as a major bottleneck for these models. LocateAnything achieves the highest RICScore of 31.68, but scores lower on spatial relation captioning than other task-fine-tuned open-source VLMs. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Xldln/RICapBench.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly capable, yet their reasoning in complex remote sensing scenes can remain coarse-grained and insufficiently grounded in task-relevant visual evidence. We propose Gravity and Flight (G&F), a framework for scene specialization with limited supervision that separates visual and reasoning verification while coupling policy updates. It combines Evidence-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning (EoT-SFT) and Relational Transfer Policy Optimization (RTPO). EoT-SFT teaches fine-grained observation and faithful reasoning through description, analysis, and supported conclusions. RTPO independently samples responses to scene-matched image pairs with fine-grained visual differences under a shared task. Its rubric-based verification combines Gravity, which checks visual fidelity and description coverage, and Flight, which takes descriptions as premises to assess evidence use and relations between paired judgments. Their scores and task correctness yield a shared pair-level advantage that couples policy updates from both responses. Using 1,008 demonstrations and 500 training pairs for harbor specialization, G&F achieves a mean score of 69.12 across six evaluation sets, exceeding the backbone and supervised initialization by 9.76 and 4.56 points. Matched controls show gains over single-image and joint-input RL, and removing either verification view reduces performance. Applying G&F to urban specialization also improves on the base model and supervised initialization across three evaluation subsets. Project details and updates are available at https://github.com/Z0ngL1ng/Gravity-and-Flight.
authors: Yuheng Zong, Minghua Wang, Xin Zhao, Xiaobin Liu, Yongjian Dong, Chanho Eom

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective post-training approach to improving fine-grained perception in multimodal large language models by amortizing costly inference-time zooming operations into a single-pass recipe. However, vanilla OPD is inherently susceptible to linguistic momentum: the teacher can follow the student's erroneous prefixes, thus weakening corrective supervision. To address this, we propose Blink On-Policy Distillation (BlinkOPD), in which the teacher "blinks" at every token: it reads the same prefix once with its eyes open and once with its eyes closed. A first-glance gain further strengthens the correction on rollouts that conflict with the teacher. By extracting more effective supervision from each on-policy trajectory, BlinkOPD achieves state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks using only 500 training images (12x less data) than existing OPD methods. Beyond fine-grained perception, BlinkOPD also demonstrates strong zero-shot improvements across ten held-out benchmarks spanning general visual perception, visual hallucination, and multimodal reasoning abilities. Code: https://github.com/Supltz/BlinkOPD
authors: Tangzheng Lian, Hang Zhang, Guanyu Hu, Renjiu Hu, Zhensong Zhang, Jiankang Deng, Jifei Song
bullets: Vanilla OPD can exhibit linguistic momentum, where the teacher follows the student's mistakes instead of correcting them.
BlinkOPD has the teacher read each prefix twice: with visual input (“eyes open”) and without it (“eyes closed”).
A first-glance gain amplifies corrective supervision on rollouts that disagree with the teacher.
It achieves state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks using 500 training images, 12× less data than existing OPD methods.
It also improves zero-shot performance across ten held-out benchmarks covering visual perception, hallucination, and multimodal reasoning.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Overview of BlinkOPD. The student generates rollouts from the full image I and question q, together denoted by xs. The frozen privileged teacher θ0 reads each student prefix twice: once with its eyes open on the zoomed crop (p+t ), and once with its eyes closed (p∅t , Sec. 3.1). Their log-ratio rt keeps the privileged visual evidence, while the prefix-induced linguistic drift shared by both cancels. A prefix-free first glance of the same teacher flags rollouts whose answer conflicts with it, and the gain is raised by a factor γ on these rollouts (Sec. 3.2). The student is trained toward the resulting distillation target (Sec. 3.3). At test time, the student runs alone in a single pass.

papers.abstract: Universal multi-modal fusion often fails not because modalities are insufficiently aligned, but because the fusion process allocates information poorly: redundant evidence is repeatedly amplified, modality-unique evidence is over-smoothed during alignment, and task-dependent synergistic evidence is insufficiently activated. We present RADIANT (Redundancy-Aware Dynamic Information Allocation Network), a task-general framework that organizes fusion around three complementary roles: suppressing redundant cross-modal overlap, preserving modality-unique evidence, and composing task-conditioned synergy through cross-modal interaction. Specifically, stable matrix-exponential projections are used to reduce interference among shared and modality-unique streams, while task memory with hard positive updates selects which synergistic interactions should be activated for the current fusion regime. Extensive experiments across six heterogeneous fusion tasks show consistent improvements over the compared methods. On FLIR, RADIANT improves downstream detection mAP@0.5 from 91.2% to 96.8%, a gain of 5.6 percentage points (6.1% relative) over GIF. RADIANT also exhibits strong direct cross-dataset transfer, with further gains from inference-time task-memory adaptation while keeping all network weights frozen. Additional ablations and sensitivity studies support the robustness of the allocation mechanism.
bullets: Targets redundancy amplification, over-smoothed unique modality cues, and underused task-dependent interactions.
Uses stable matrix-exponential projections to reduce interference between shared and modality-unique streams.
Employs task memory with hard positive updates to activate relevant cross-modal synergies.
Across six heterogeneous fusion tasks, it consistently improves over compared methods.
On FLIR, detection mAP@0.5 rises from 91.2% to 96.8% over GIF; task-memory adaptation also improves cross-dataset transfer with frozen weights.
