papers.abstract: Accurate plant disease recognition is essential for intelligent agriculture, but few-shot settings provide limited labeled samples that may not capture diagnostic symptoms and intra-class variations. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, offer transferable visual-semantic knowledge. However, existing CLIP-based methods often rely on coarse class semantics and global visual representations, overlooking disease-specific diagnostic information and fine-grained local cues. Excessive few-shot adaptation may also cause over-specialization and weaken the generalization ability of large-scale pre-training. We propose a description-guided, two-stage CLIP adaptation method to address these issues. Symptom and comparative descriptions enrich class semantics with typical visual symptoms and discriminative cues between similar diseases. The enhanced semantics guide the aggregation of class-relevant patch evidence to calibrate global image-text matching with fine-grained cues. For adaptation, we first update the vision-language encoders with lightweight parameters, then freeze them and train a linear classifier. At inference, the classifier is used for in-domain prediction, while class prototypes from the adapted text encoder support cross-domain prediction and retain vision-language transferability. Experiments with two backbones show that our method achieves the highest mean accuracy in most few-shot settings on PlantVillage, Cassava, and Pear, reaching 93.16%, 79.30%, and 96.56%, respectively, with ViT-L/14 under 16-shot. On class-aligned cross-domain evaluation across 21 shared PlantDoc classes, it achieves 56.96% accuracy, outperforming all compared methods. These results demonstrate its effectiveness in fine-grained few-shot plant disease recognition and cross-domain generalization.
authors: Zhenkun Ye, Qian Zhou, Hua Zou
bullets: Addresses limited labeled data, coarse class semantics, and overlooked fine-grained disease cues in few-shot recognition.
Enriches class descriptions with symptoms and comparisons between similar diseases, then aggregates class-relevant patch evidence to calibrate image-text matching.
Adapts CLIP with lightweight encoder updates followed by linear-classifier training; adapted text prototypes support cross-domain prediction.
Under 16-shot evaluation with ViT-L/14, reaches 93.16% on PlantVillage, 79.30% on Cassava, and 96.56% on Pear.
Achieves 56.96% accuracy on 21 shared PlantDoc classes in cross-domain evaluation, outperforming compared methods.

papers.abstract: Distinguishing different heat sources in low-resolution infrared (IR) images is inherently difficult, as multiple thermal emitters often collapse into ambiguous and overlapping responses. Existing super-resolution methods hallucinate structures from such ambiguous 2D evidence, leading to thermal drift, boundary merging, and unreliable restoration under infrared degradations. We propose FlowIR, a depth-driven rectified flow framework that resolves thermal ambiguity by injecting 3D geometric cues into the generation process. Pseudo-3D depth lifting and depth-guided 3D convolutions disentangle overlapping foreground objects, while cluster-wise inter-attention suppresses cross-source feature contamination. A Thermal-Geometry Consistency Loss further enforces geometric alignment during refinement. Built upon a lightweight rectified flow backbone, FlowIR restores IR images in only a few steps, producing sharply separated, degradation-robust, and geometrically faithful high-resolution results.
authors: Xingyue Zhu, Qinyun Mei, Zhexi Min, Yang Zou, Xingyuan Li, Zhiying Jiang, Jinyuan Liu
bullets: Addresses thermal ambiguity in low-resolution IR images, where overlapping emitters cause boundary merging and unreliable restoration.
Injects pseudo-3D depth cues through depth-guided 3D convolutions to disentangle overlapping foreground objects.
Uses cluster-wise inter-attention to reduce feature contamination between distinct thermal sources.
Applies a Thermal-Geometry Consistency Loss to preserve geometric alignment during refinement.
Its lightweight rectified-flow backbone enables restoration in only a few steps and improves robustness to IR degradations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of $432$ strictly paired test cases across $48$ executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a $3 \times 3$ factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across $12$ representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to $64\%$), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.
authors: Zhiyu Hou, Wen-Jie Shu, Harold Haodong Chen, Weilin Ruan, Chenfei Liao, Liuzhou Zhang, Disen Lan, Xiaogang Xu, Qi Chen, Ser-Nam Lim
bullets: Introduces 432 paired test cases across 48 executable 4D world families and six dynamic challenge categories.
Evaluates 12 models across draft granularity and appearance-alignment conditions.
Finds a strong tension between preserving world dynamics and realizing requested appearance.
Richer visual drafts improve structural anchoring but can reduce appearance fidelity; conflicting cues cause source leakage of up to 64%.
WorldDraft-Primer improves both preservation and visual realization for frozen video renderers.

papers.abstract: Potholes impose billions of dollars in annual vehicle damage, yet detectors report only where potholes are, not how severe they are or what to do. Judging severity from a single RGB image is ill-posed, and ungrounded vision-language model (VLM) assessments tend to be over-conservative. We present a five-stage modular framework for the offline assessment of already-detected potholes that combines geometric measurements with VLM reasoning: perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro severity classification with composite risk scoring, and natural-language warning generation. We evaluate it on 3,092 potholes in 1,119 dashcam scenes against independent references. Severity agreement with a prediction-free three-annotator panel is weak (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.139$, 95% CI [0.00, 0.28]; $n = 101$) and far below the annotators' agreement with one another ($\kappa = 0.605$); against physically measured depth on an independent RGB-D dataset, it is also weak ($\kappa = 0.098$), although the predicted classes preserve the order of measured depths. The severity classes are therefore perceived visual categories, not depth measurements. Geometric grounding does change the warnings: relative to an image-only baseline, it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier and raises critical-tier assignments by 109% (Stuart-Maxwell $p < 10^{-15}$), and in a blind study, three raters preferred the grounded warnings 3.5:1. A six-arm prompt ablation attributes the hybrid prompt's rule adherence to the per-pothole measurements rather than to the rubric or worked examples. At USD 0.105 per scene, it suits large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; its maneuver suggestions are advisory research outputs, not validated vehicle guidance.
authors: Abdalmalek Aburaddaha, Zaid A. El Shair, Ali Al-Bustami, Samir A. Rawashdeh
bullets: Pothole detectors locate defects but generally do not assess severity or recommend actions; single-image severity estimation is inherently ambiguous.

The five-stage offline pipeline applies perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro classification with composite risk scoring, and warning generation.

Geometric grounding substantially changes warnings: it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier, increases critical-tier assignments by 109%, and is preferred 3.5:1 over image-only warnings in a blind study.

Severity agreement is weak with both human references and measured depth, although predictions preserve the ordering of measured depths; the categories should be interpreted as visual perceptions, not depth estimates.
The system costs USD 0.105 per scene and is intended for large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; maneuver suggestions are advisory and not validated vehicle guidance.

papers.abstract: Our objective is to enhance VLMs ability to distinguish the roles of the left and right hands in egocentric actions. We introduce sub-action detection, a task that requires models to explicitly recognise the left- and right-hand roles and their manipulated objects within an ongoing high-level action. To address this challenge, we propose BiScopeNet, a framework that augments existing video-LLMs without modifying their vision encoders or language models. BiScopeNet incorporates two components: FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention-based module that selectively aligns video features with textual context to emphasise action-relevant cues, and MetaLoss, a masked, object-weighted loss that prioritises visually grounded terms. To supervise sub-action detection, we introduce BiScopeCap-100K, a large-scale video-level dataset curated from existing egocentric datasets, providing dense captions that jointly describe high-level actions, left/right-hand roles, and manipulated objects, enriched with spatial metadata for grounding. Across the evaluated Video-LLM backbones, BiScopeNet improves action, hand-role, and object recognition over the corresponding supervised baselines, achieving the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated configurations on BiScopeCap.
authors: Sadegh Rahmaniboldaji, Filip Rybansky, Quoc Vuong, Frank Guerin, Andrew Gilbert
bullets: Introduces sub-action detection, requiring explicit recognition of hand roles and manipulated objects during high-level actions.
Adds FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention module that emphasizes action-relevant visual cues without changing the underlying vision or language encoders.
Uses MetaLoss, a masked object-weighted loss that prioritizes visually grounded terms.
Introduces BiScopeCap-100K, a densely captioned egocentric video dataset with hand-role, object, action, and spatial metadata.
Improves action, hand-role, and object recognition across evaluated Video-LLM backbones, with the strongest aggregate performance among tested configurations on BiScopeCap.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a framework for pothole risk assessment that combines geometric measurements with VLM reasoning, demonstrating the utility of geometrically grounded vision-language models for driving safety and spatial understanding.
papers.title: Sub-actions in Action: Text-Guided Hand-Role Alignment for Sub-Action Recognition
papers.tldr: BiScopeNet improves egocentric video models’ ability to identify left- and right-hand roles and their manipulated objects within ongoing actions using text-guided feature alignment and targeted supervision.

papers.abstract: Satellite constellations now image the Earth daily, capturing the lifecycle of events from deforestation to urban construction. Anticipating these events before completion enables timely intervention, yet existing systems cannot jointly identify where a change occurs, what it will become, and when it will finish across an open vocabulary. Building such a model requires diverse event data, but events are like needles in a haystack, making manual annotation at global scale infeasible. We address this problem by representing change as the vector difference between vision-language model embeddings at distinct time points. This arithmetic approach allows us to search for semantic transformations directly in the latent space, enabling (1) an automated data engine for global event discovery without manual annotation and (2) the largest global satellite event dataset to our knowledge, comprising 21,000+ locations across 64+ event types with ~2M images from PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 spanning six continents, to train (3) a novel global-scale event anticipation model. Our model detects change with a 93.5% max F1 score, outperforms baselines 3.6x on predicted event retrieval, and forecasts completion dates with a 3-day median error, even nine months before completion. Code: https://github.com/ShreelekhaR/predicting-the-needle
authors: Shreelekha Revankar, Mikhail Klassen, Creon Levit, Ash Hoover, Kavita Bala, Bharath Hariharan
bullets: Targets the challenge of identifying where change occurs, what it becomes, and when it finishes across diverse event types.
Represents temporal change as vector differences between vision-language model embeddings to search for semantic transformations.
Uses this approach to automate global event discovery without manual annotation.
Introduces a dataset with 21,000+ locations, 64+ event types, and approximately 2 million satellite images across six continents.
The resulting model achieves 93.5% maximum F1, 3.6× stronger predicted-event retrieval than baselines, and 3-day median completion-date error up to nine months ahead.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel method for open-vocabulary event anticipation in satellite imagery using vision-language model embeddings, creating a large-scale dataset and demonstrating strong performance in predicting future events and completion dates.
papers.title: Predicting the Needle in a Petabyte Scale Haystack: Open-Vocabulary Event Anticipation in Satellite Imagery
papers.tldr: A vision-language embedding approach enables open-vocabulary satellite event discovery and anticipation at global scale, detecting and forecasting events months before completion.

papers.abstract: Learning from paired modalities is commonly equated with aligning them: two encoders are trained until the embeddings of a pair coincide in a shared space. We study whether cross-modal retrieval and classification can instead be obtained while the two encoders' own embedding spaces remain directly unaligned. DuoJEPA trains one encoder per modality with the self-supervised LeJEPA objective and appends to each encoder a single transformer layer that translates its embedding into the other encoder's space, supervised by a contrastive objective computed entirely within that target space. No loss term compares the two own spaces directly, although the encoders are optimised jointly through the translation objective. In our experiments, the translator's residual connections determine where the cross-modal pressure is absorbed: with a residual translator the two encoders become directly aligned, whereas with a skipless (residual-free) translator a paired-cosine test detects no alignment in the final models, and at most a weak one in the ablations, at comparable cross-modal performance. The learned class-token translation is well approximated by a single scaled rotation of the source space. We evaluate DuoJEPA on two modality pairs that differ in nearly every respect. On chest radiographs and reports from CheXpert Plus, it attains a zero-shot AUC of 86.6 and a cross-modal retrieval score of 78.5, compared with 60.0 and 64.2 for our reimplementation of LeVLJEPA with the same encoders and data. On Sentinel-2 optical and Sentinel-1 radar imagery, the frozen encoders fall within the range of published Sentinel foundation models under our reproduction of the Copernicus-Bench linear-probe protocol, the translator retrieves the paired image of the other sensor among 4,000 candidates in 77-79% of cases, and a patch-level extension transfers the within-image similarity structure of the scene.
authors: Mahmut S. Gokmen, Mitchell A. Klusty, Evan W. Damron, Caroline N. Leach, Samuel E. Armstrong, V. K. Cody Bumgardner
bullets: Uses LeJEPA self-supervised encoders with a single transformer translator per modality, trained by contrastive loss in the target space.
Residual translators induce direct encoder alignment, while skipless translators preserve largely unaligned native spaces with comparable cross-modal performance.
The class-token translation is well approximated by a single scaled rotation.
On CheXpert Plus, it achieves 86.6 zero-shot AUC and 78.5 retrieval, versus 60.0 and 64.2 for the compared LeVLJEPA reimplementation.
On Sentinel-1/2 imagery, it achieves 77–79% retrieval among 4,000 candidates and transfers within-image similarity structure at patch level.

papers.title: DuoJEPA: Cross-Modal Translation Between Unaligned Self-Supervised Embedding Spaces

papers.abstract: This work addresses the problem of finding a concealed object in an environment by unifying formalisms for partially observable environments with multi-modal priors drawn from a mix of ontologies, semantic networks, LLMs, and VLMs. We propose a concealment-adaptive mixed-observability MDP (CA-MOMDP), a Bayes-adaptive setting where uncertainty is over both object locations and which nodes can conceal them, held as a hypothesis with a bounded ontology prior and resolved only by interaction. We define a hierarchical transition system (HTS) to abstract the environment into room and object nodes that can be planned over via our CA-MOMDP. We further propose a COMBS-score: a multi-modal fusion of a human informed semantic network, LLM, and VLM, to initialize the belief over object locations, which grounds our abstractions and reduces reliance on a single model. Belief is maintained via Bayes' rule, which never lets a look rule out a closed container. We prove a present target is found in a bounded number of searches under exact perception and that its location is never ruled out given missed detection under noisy perception. We ablate each component to demonstrate their significance. Across five simulator configurations, from a gridworld to Matterport3D with a real detector, COMBS finds 92-100% of in-distribution and 92-100% of out-of-distribution targets, matches or beats the baselines in processing speed, significantly outperforms a per-step LLM policy at lower cost on the larger scenes, recovers more out-of-distribution placements than a TidyBot ranking, and matches an LLM-only prior at a fraction of its per-decision latency. COMBS is the only standalone method that can declare a target absent at a stated error level, and the per-step LLM policy offered a termination action abandons 12-22% of targets that were present, against 1.6-3.2% for COMBS on the same episodes.
bullets: Models uncertainty over both object locations and which environmental nodes may conceal them using a concealment-adaptive mixed-observability MDP.
Plans over room and object nodes through a hierarchical transition system.
Fuses human-informed semantic networks, LLMs, and VLMs to initialize location beliefs, then updates them with Bayes’ rule.
Across five simulated settings, finds 92–100% of in- and out-of-distribution targets and generally matches or outperforms comparison methods.
Can declare a target absent at a stated error level; it abandons fewer present targets than a per-step LLM policy.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes COMBS, a multi-modal Bayesian search method that unifies ontologies, LLMs, and VLMs to locate concealed objects in partially observable environments.
papers.title: COMBS: Concealed Object Multi-modal Bayesian Search
papers.tldr: COMBS combines Bayesian search, hierarchical environment abstractions, and multimodal priors to efficiently find concealed objects while avoiding false conclusions that objects are absent.

papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that pretrained image generators encode real-world understanding beyond image synthesis. Vision Banana exploits this by framing vision tasks as conditional image editing. However, its data, weights, code, and implementation details are not public. We present Open Vision Banana (OVB), a fully open and reproducible recipe for converting pretrained generators into unified multi-task perception systems. Our analyses identify the design choices that matter most for generalization, including color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing. These choices interact, so individually helpful choices can hurt when combined with others. Starting from 4B and 9B parameter open-weight base models and using 2.1M-3.8M training pairs from public datasets, OVB surpasses Vision Banana's reported Cityscapes zero-shot performance (73.9 vs. 69.9 mIoU) and rivals state-of-the-art affine-invariant depth estimators. Its non-zero-shot variants come within five points of Vision Banana on referring and reasoning segmentation but remain further behind on instance segmentation. All models largely retain the base model's image-editing abilities. With legend ensembling, we introduce a test-time scaling method for generator-based perception. It segments an image under several class-color legends and fuses the results by majority vote, correcting unstable color-class bindings and improving mIoU by up to 8.7 points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining. We release the dataset construction and processing pipeline, the training and evaluation code, as well as the final, intermediate, and ablation checkpoints. Project website: https://openvisionbanana.github.io
authors: Arpit Jadon, Valentinos Pariza, Jona Ruthardt, Ryousuke Yamada, A. Sophia Koepke, Andrei Bursuc, Yuki M. Asano
bullets: Identifies interacting design factors for generalization, including color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing.
Trains 4B- and 9B-parameter open-weight models on 2.1M–3.8M public-dataset training pairs.
Surpasses reported Vision Banana Cityscapes zero-shot segmentation performance and approaches state-of-the-art affine-invariant depth estimation.
Legend ensembling improves segmentation by up to 8.7 mIoU points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining.
Releases data-processing, training, evaluation, and checkpoint resources for reproducibility; instance segmentation remains a weaker area.

papers.selection_reason: Unified recipe for converting generative models into multi-task perception, including depth estimation, relevant to spatial understanding.
papers.title: Open Vision Banana: A Fully Open Recipe for Generative Visual Perception
papers.tldr: Open Vision Banana provides a fully open recipe for adapting image generators into unified multi-task vision systems, achieving strong segmentation and depth results with reproducible resources and test-time legend ensembling.

papers.abstract: Aerial imagery captured by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) plays a vital role in applications such as surveillance, disaster response, and large-scale environmental monitoring. Automatic generation of textual descriptions for such imagery is essential for reducing manual inspection overhead and enabling better downstream decision-making. However, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), despite their impressive captioning capabilities, are prone to hallucination, producing descriptions that are inconsistent with the visual input. This problem is significantly amplified in aerial imagery due to its unique challenges such as extreme viewpoint variation, small objects, class imbalance, and ambiguous visual entities. Existing hallucination detection approaches either rely on computationally expensive large external models such as GPT-4, which perform poorly on aerial domains, or treat the problem as a rigid binary classification task, ignoring the inherent uncertainty in ambiguous cases. To address these limitations, we propose a lightweight, reference-free framework for hallucination detection and correction in free-form aerial image captioning. Our method leverages state-of-the-art MLLMs, specifically InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL, to detect hallucinated content in generated captions with minimal computational overhead. Detected hallucinations are corrected through a dedicated refinement module that improves the factual consistency of the original captions. Extensive experiments on the Labelled Illusion Dataset (LID) demonstrate that our framework significantly reduces hallucination rates while remaining practical for real-time deployment in resource-constrained environments. Code is available at: https://github.com/Debolena7/Hal_Detect.
authors: Debolena Basak, Somsubhra De, Maunendra Sankar Desarkar
bullets: Targets aerial-captioning hallucinations worsened by viewpoint variation, small objects, class imbalance, and visual ambiguity.
Uses InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL to detect hallucinated content without external references or expensive models.
Applies a dedicated refinement module to correct detected hallucinations in free-form captions.
Experiments on the Labelled Illusion Dataset show reduced hallucination rates and support real-time use in resource-constrained settings.

papers.abstract: We present a training-free system for the EBMV @ ECCV 2026 challenge "Event Stream Understanding with EventBench" (General Understanding track), which evaluates vision-language models on five event-camera understanding tasks. We use none of the challenge's training data: our goal is to measure how far off-the-shelf, RGB-pretrained models can go on event data through representation and prompting alone. For four of the five categories (gesture recognition, detailed understanding, causal reasoning, and event OCR) we render event bins as red/ON, blue/OFF frames, select a category-specific subset of bins, stitch them into a single grid image, and query the same frozen Qwen3.5 9B vision-language model with a category-specific prompt for all four tasks. The fifth category, action recognition, feeds every bin directly into the organizers' EventGPT-Plus-2B. The system reaches 62.28% overall accuracy across 2,084 test questions (rank 9/27), led by action recognition and causal reasoning (80.27%, 77.22%) and limited most by gesture recognition and event OCR (54.70%, 34.57%). We visualize test samples from every category together with the exact images the model receives, score six alternative representations against the evaluation server, and analyze the full test set post hoc. That analysis shows that our bounding-box crop almost never tightened around content, so event OCR text reached the model at roughly one fifth of its horizontal resolution, and that detailed-understanding predictions are skewed toward the first two answer options.
authors: Md Kamrujjaman Mobin, Md Salman Shamil, Md Adnan Arefeen
bullets: Evaluates five EventBench event-camera understanding tasks without using challenge training data.
Renders event bins as red/blue ON/OFF frames, selects and grids bins, then prompts a frozen Qwen3.5 9B model for four tasks; action recognition uses EventGPT-Plus-2B directly.
Achieves 62.28% overall accuracy on 2,084 test questions, ranking 9th of 27.
Performance is strongest on action recognition (80.27%) and causal reasoning (77.22%), and weakest on gesture recognition (54.70%) and event OCR (34.57%).
Post-hoc analysis identifies poorly tightened crops that reduce OCR resolution and a bias toward the first two answer choices in detailed understanding.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free evaluation of frozen VLMs on event-camera understanding tasks spanning VLM and video-like temporal reasoning.
papers.title: How Far Can Frozen Vision-Language Models Go on Event Data? A Training-Free Study on EventBench
papers.tldr: A fully frozen, training-free pipeline shows that RGB-pretrained vision-language models can achieve moderate performance on event-camera tasks through event-to-image rendering and task-specific prompting, but struggle with OCR and gesture recognition.

papers.abstract: Despite impressive advances in large language models (LLM), vision-language models (VLM) still exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities. Recent progress in feed-forward 3D reconstruction has enabled precise, real-time geometric understanding from visual inputs. In this work, we propose SpaceMCP, a framework that leverages these advances to introduce an MCP-style paradigm for spatial reasoning. Our approach augments a VLM with structured function calls, allowing it to query a scene graph for spatial information such as distances, object positioning, and camera properties. The scene graph is constructed in real time using feed-forward 3D reconstruction to recover metric geometry, combined with open-vocabulary segmentation to identify and localize relevant objects within the scene. Paired with the VLM's strong reasoning capabilities, the VLM is able to combine this primitive information to solve more complex spatial tasks. Without any training, SpaceMCP achieves state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, outperforming recent spatially post-trained VLMs and improving its base VLM by 15-22 points per benchmark. We argue that, given the contrast between the relatively slow progress in native VLM spatial reasoning and the rapid advances in feed-forward 3D computer vision, this paradigm offers a promising path forward for enabling robust spatial reasoning.
authors: Ameen Izhac, Nobuko Yoshida, Ronald Clark
bullets: Addresses the limited native spatial reasoning abilities of current vision-language models.
Builds a metric scene graph using feed-forward 3D reconstruction and open-vocabulary segmentation.
Lets the VLM query distances, object positions, and camera properties, then combine them for complex spatial tasks.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench, and VSTI-Bench, improving its base VLM by 15–22 points per benchmark.
Scope: relies on the quality and availability of real-time 3D reconstruction and object segmentation.

papers.tldr: SpaceMCP enables VLMs to perform stronger spatial reasoning by querying a real-time 3D scene graph through structured function calls, without additional training.

papers.abstract: This paper focuses on improving the behavioral diversity and effectiveness of language-conditioned manipulation policies trained through imitation learning. Recently, continuous-action policies have become mainstream in robotic manipulation, but the lack of diverse demonstrations tends to restrict their behavioral diversity. For grasping, a fundamental subtask of manipulation, 6-DoF grasp detection provides diverse grasp hypotheses, but open-loop execution constrains responsiveness in dynamic environments. This motivates us to combine the diversity of grasp hypotheses with the adaptability of continuous-action policies. To this end, we propose GraSLA, a lightweight and effective spatial-language-action model with grasp hypotheses as geometric priors. In particular, we employ spatial and language foundation models to encode scene geometry and task semantics, and integrate them with grasp hypotheses through bidirectional cross-attention for continuous action prediction. On LIBERO, GraSLA achieves an average success rate of 99.30%.
authors: Jibao Yuan, Zixiang Zhao, Wensong Xu, Siqi Lu, Shaofei Chen
bullets: Addresses limited behavioral diversity in imitation-learned, language-conditioned manipulation policies.
Uses spatial and language foundation models to encode scene geometry and task semantics.
Integrates grasp hypotheses as geometric priors through bidirectional cross-attention for continuous action prediction.
Achieves a 99.30% average success rate on LIBERO.
Targets more responsive behavior than open-loop grasp execution in dynamic environments.

(b) Bidirectional attention first updates the spatial and language tokens, then jointly updates them and the grasp tokens. Finally, the language tokens are further refined through self-attention.

papers.title: GraSLA: A Lightweight Spatial-Language-Action Model with Grasp Hypotheses as Geometric Priors
papers.tldr: GraSLA combines diverse 6-DoF grasp hypotheses with spatial-language-action modeling to produce adaptive, continuous manipulation policies.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used across the sciences, but whether their internal computations correspond to known scientific operations or proceed through different mechanisms remains unclear. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for assessing reliability, identifying failure modes, and learning new science from the models. We present, to our knowledge, the first causal mechanistic interpretability study of an astronomy foundation model, AION-1, focusing on its multimodal advantage in redshift prediction, where combining imaging with photometry outperforms photometry alone. We find that this advantage is largest for spatially extended and dust-attenuated galaxies, and that most of it is localized to the first of the encoder's twelve blocks. Within that block, how well a property is linearly decodable does not predict whether it can be localized. Spatial extent is causally used, and one attention head dominates linear probing for it, yet ablating that head has negligible effect on redshift prediction: the information is distributed across heads and is decodable again one layer after we erase it. Dust attenuation shows the opposite pattern: it is only weakly decodable anywhere in the encoder, yet a single head is necessary for most of the multimodal advantage, particularly for the most dust-attenuated galaxies, and keeping that head as the only active head in its block preserves nearly all of the advantage. None of the astrophysically motivated operations we tested explains what this head computes. Whether this reflects a limitation of current interpretability methods or a computation that does not correspond to any known astrophysical operation remains open, and resolving it is a prerequisite for using interpretability as a tool for scientific discovery.
authors: Rachel C. Zhang, Alberto Bietti, Wes Gurnee, Alessandro Favero, Miles Cranmer
bullets: The study examines why multimodal inputs outperform photometry alone, especially for extended and dust-attenuated galaxies.
Most of the multimodal benefit is concentrated in the encoder’s first block.
Spatial extent is causally used but distributed across attention heads, so ablating the most linearly decodable head has little effect.
Dust attenuation is weakly decodable yet depends strongly on a single attention head that preserves most of the multimodal advantage.
The identified dust-related computation does not match tested astrophysical operations, leaving its mechanism unresolved.

papers.selection_reason: Causal mechanistic interpretability of a multimodal astronomy foundation model; directly relevant to understanding multimodal foundation-model computations.
papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of an Astronomy Foundation Model
papers.tldr: A causal analysis of AION-1 shows that its imaging–photometry advantage in redshift prediction relies on distinct, partly opaque mechanisms for galaxy extent and dust attenuation.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in medical large multimodal models (LMMs) have brought promising progress to clinical decision support, yet hallucination, the generation of confident but clinically unverifiable outputs, poses a critical threat to the reliability demanded in high-stakes medical settings. Existing hallucination detection methods, predominantly designed for unimodal settings, fail to capture the visual-linguistic dynamics inherent to medical imaging. We formulate the problem of hallucination detection in LMMs as disproportionate distribution of attention weights across the modalities during answer token generation. We quantify modality-specific attention concentration across layers and heads using the Gini coefficient and demonstrate statistically significant redistribution of attention mass between visual and textual tokens in hallucinated responses. We leverage these features to train a logistic regression-based classifier and evaluate it on two medical LMMs across three medical imaging modalities, demonstrating that our method achieves competitive or superior performance against contemporary hallucination detection baselines.
authors: Sachin Acharya, Niyoj Oli, Shishir Adhikari, Aminu Lawal, Yash Raj Shrestha, Prashnna K Gyawali, Binod Bhattarai
bullets: Targets hallucination detection in high-stakes medical imaging applications.
Uses Gini coefficients to quantify modality-specific attention concentration across layers and heads.
Trains a logistic-regression classifier on attention-based features.
Evaluated on two medical LMMs across three imaging modalities.
Reports competitive or superior performance against existing hallucination-detection baselines.

(b) Each matrix is decomposed into text and visual components, isolating response-token attention to prompt and image tokens. (c) Modality-specific Gini coefficients (Gt, Gv) quantify attention concentration. (d) The coefficients are aggregated into a 2 × L ×H feature tensor. (e) A lightweight logistic regression probe σ predicts hallucination.

Fig. 1. Image, visual attention heatmap, and response attention graph (left to right). (a) Hallucinated: diffuse visual attention (low visual Gini) and concentrated text attention (high text Gini). (b) Non-hallucinated: focused visual attention (high visual Gini) and diffuse text attention (low text Gini).

Table 1. Mean Gini coefficients for hallucinated (H) and nonhallucinated (NH) responses, their difference (Diff. = H − NH), and Cohen’s d for the five most statistically significant attention heads in each modality. Heads are selected based on p-values comparing the two response groups.
Table 2. Hallucination detection performance.
Table 3. Significance of attention decomposition.

papers.selection_reason: Detects hallucination in medical large multimodal models via modality-specific attention concentration, directly relevant to multimodal LLM reliability.
papers.title: MAGIC: Modality-Aware Gini Inspection for Clinical Hallucination Detection in LMMs
papers.tldr: MAGIC detects clinical hallucinations in medical LMMs by measuring imbalanced attention between visual and textual tokens during answer generation.

papers.abstract: A large audio-language model (LALM) can answer "is a cat present?" about a mixture correctly, and its confidence can drop when the cat is removed, yet this does not show that it can tell the cat's presence from its absence. We introduce TRACE. It deletes the queried source and each rival in turn and asks whether every view still containing that sound outscores the view with it removed. Across 8 LALMs and 3,456 controlled mixtures, 6.3% of correct answers fail this ordering: the target-absent view scores at or above some target-present view, a conflict no shared threshold repairs. A target-only score check misses 42.5% of them. The share rises from 4.9% to 8.4% as target SNR falls from +5 to -5 dB, even on units correct at every level, and survives loudness and re-pairing controls. Accuracy certifies the answer; TRACE audits whether it orders presence above absence. Code and data: https://github.com/yikise/TRACE.
authors: Yi Zhang, Yi Li, Hongwei Du
bullets: Correct answers and confidence drops after source removal do not guarantee source-sensitive reasoning.
TRACE removes the queried sound and each rival, then checks whether all target-present views outrank the target-absent view.
Across 8 models and 3,456 controlled mixtures, 6.3% of correct answers showed contradictory source ordering.
A target-only score check missed 42.5% of these conflicts, which increased as target SNR decreased.
The conflicts persisted under loudness and re-pairing controls, including for units correct at every tested SNR.

papers.abstract: In computer vision, vision-language and self-supervised encoders are two unique paradigms characterized by global language alignment and high-quality vision-only patch representations, respectively. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often use the former because of language alignment, despite the recent rise in vision-centric tasks resembling traditional dense vision tasks that would likely benefit from the high-quality patch representations, raising the question whether self-supervised models could aid MLLMs in vision-centric tasks. To investigate this, we define semantic (in)consistency of patch tokens from language-aligned encoders and identify two sets of tokens, semantically consistent (SCTs) and semantically inconsistent (SITs). Through systematic probing via the removal of SCTs or SITs from the input of modern MLLMs, we show higher reliance on SCTs than SITs, as removal of the former induces larger performance drops. This demonstrates that MLLMs benefit from semantic consistency of vision tokens. With this in mind, we devise a simple yet effective extension of the MLLM training objective that combines traditional language modeling with semantic guidance via minimization of semantic inconsistency. This strategy, named Semantically-Guided Training (SGT), combines the signals of both loss terms to push the vision encoder towards providing semantically consistent tokens, while preserving language alignment. Extensive evaluation shows that SGT outperforms all baselines and MLLMs with specialized vision encoders on vision-centric benchmarks while keeping strong scores on text-centric benchmarks, thus setting state of the art on average across all tasks. Our results highlight the importance of combining language alignment and semantic consistency through the lens of MLLMs rather than independently from them and pave the way towards the design of better MLLM vision encoders.
bullets: Problem: Language-aligned vision encoders may provide weaker patch representations for vision-centric, dense-vision tasks.
Method: The study identifies semantically consistent and inconsistent patch tokens and probes their importance by selectively removing them.
Contribution: It introduces Semantically-Guided Training (SGT), which augments language modeling with a semantic-inconsistency minimization objective.
Result: Removing consistent tokens causes larger performance drops, and SGT outperforms the evaluated baselines and specialized vision-encoder MLLMs on vision-centric benchmarks.
Scope: SGT maintains strong performance on text-centric benchmarks and achieves the best average results across the evaluated tasks.

papers.abstract: Automatic evaluation is now central to text-to-image benchmarking, but the verifier that converts generated images into scores is often treated as an implementation detail. We argue that this is unsafe: an automatic benchmark score is a property of the image generator, prompt distribution, verifier, verifier-use protocol, and scoring rule, not of the generator alone. We study this issue in structural counting, a controlled setting where human-visible counts can be audited. We construct a verifier-centric audit suite over seven counting objects: cell phones, chairs, and traffic lights for object counting, and clover leaflets, dresser drawer fronts, power-strip sockets, and turbine blades for substructure counting. Across 6,240 generated images from Qwen-Image-2512 and FLUX.2-dev, we compare open MLLM verifiers under count-only, reject-aware, zero-shot and few-shot protocols, plus TIFA-like target queries, a detector baseline, and frontier closed-model checks on two hard objects. On a balanced 2,280-image evaluation split, aggregate score matching can coexist with image-level disagreement, and verifier-use protocols and generator distributions change the measured reliability. Every verifier-protocol configuration also shrinks the human score difference between the two generators, by 7.5-25.0 pp, and with a third generator, Z-Image, all four tested protocols reverse the human ordering of Z-Image and FLUX.2-dev on our fixed prompt suite. GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 checks do not remove the failure modes: GPT-5.5 still has only 59.92% clover valid-count fidelity, while Claude Opus 4.7 has lower same-slice agreement ($\kappa=0.432$). We propose reporting automatic benchmark scores with a factorized verifier reliability profile: aggregate score gap, image-level agreement, generator-comparison distortion, valid-image count fidelity, rejection behavior, output compliance, and directional bias.
authors: Shurun Li, Michael Hua Wang, Haibo Zeng, Long Wang
bullets: Automatic scores depend on the generator, prompts, verifier, verifier-use protocol, and scoring rule—not the generator alone.
A verifier-centric audit covers object and substructure counting across multiple models, protocols, and verifier types.
Aggregate score agreement can hide image-level disagreements, while protocol and generator distributions alter measured reliability.
All tested configurations narrowed human performance gaps, and some reversed the human ranking of generators.
Frontier closed models also showed counting and agreement failures, motivating factorized reliability reporting.

papers.title: Verifier Choice is a Benchmark Design Variable: Auditing Structural Counting Evaluation in Text-to-Image Models

papers.abstract: Infographic charts communicate data through cohesive compositions of visual elements such as charts, text, and images. Existing infographic chart datasets primarily annotate individual elements with bounding boxes and category labels. Such element-level annotations do not capture hierarchical and spatial relationships, limiting their use for understanding how elements are organized and related within an infographic and for generating well-organized designs. To address this limitation, we introduce ChartGalaxy++, a richly annotated dataset of 217,195 infographic charts. At the core of this dataset is a scene graph representation, in which nodes represent visual elements and semantic groups, and edges encode their hierarchical and spatial relationships. For real infographics, we construct scene graphs by detecting and progressively grouping visual elements; for synthetic ones, we derive them directly from the generation process. We demonstrate the utility of ChartGalaxy++ through three applications: 1) image-to-scene-graph prediction, 2) scene-graph-augmented infographic question answering, and 3) evaluation of scene graph preservation in image generation. Together, these applications highlight the value of ChartGalaxy++ for advancing chart understanding and generation.
authors: Duan Li, Zheng Wang, Jiangning Zhu, Yuhui Yuan, Shixia Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitations of datasets with only element-level bounding boxes and category labels.

papers.abstract: Radiotherapy contour ranking can support quality assurance, but vision-language model (VLM) gains may reflect supervision, score construction, available inputs, or representation access. We evaluated frozen MedGemma 1.5 in a single-institution study, a 12-patient held-out HaN-Seg test, five-fold cross-fitting on 30 non-test HaN-Seg patients, and transfer without refitting to 120 SegRap2023 patients. On held-out HaN-Seg, a supervised readout of the final prompt state exceeded a supervised readout of the model's yes/no output probabilities by +0.3047 pooled average precision (AP; 95% patient-bootstrap interval [+0.2822, +0.3269]); the advantage persisted against a parameter-count-matched nonlinear control. A readout of projected visual tokens exceeded the final-state readout in cross-fitting and transfer (+0.0706 AP averaged equally across patients on SegRap; 95% interval [+0.0607, +0.0804]), while a structured panel-feature readout remained competitive with visual tokens. The anatomy-conditioned readout did not demonstrate an advantage over the native-feature comparator. These results motivate visual-token and structured-feature controls in medical-imaging VLM evaluations; outcomes were computational or synthetic, not clinical acceptability.

An anatomy-conditioned readout showed no advantage over the native-feature comparator.

papers.abstract: Multilingual Text-Based Person Retrieval (TBPR) aims to retrieve individuals with texts in multiple languages. Despite its practical importance, it has been overlooked by existing research, which mainly focuses on English-only retrieval. The only prior attempt at multilingual TBPR suffers from (1) the absence of a large-scale, multilingual pretraining dataset and (2) a suboptimal model architecture for multilingual text encoding and cross-modal alignment, which employs a shared encoder that overlooks linguistic heterogeneity and relies on English as a pivot for cross-modal alignment, introducing English-centric bias. For this, we contribute MultiPedes, the first large-scale, pedestrian-centric multilingual pretraining dataset. It contains 10 million image-text pairs across four languages, constructed by a multilingual quality-aware data construction pipeline. We also propose ViSeLA (Vision-grounded Semantic Learning and Alignment), a novel framework featuring: (1) a semantic-aware multilingual learning module that extends the mixture-of-experts architecture by routing language-invariant semantics to specialized experts for improved multilingual feature learning; and (2) a vision-grounded cross-modal alignment module that employs a semantic probe to capture fine-grained semantics across modalities, enabling direct cross-modal alignment without relying on a pivot language. Extensive experiments on both multilingual and English-only TBPR datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ViSeLA. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/Flame-Chasers/ViSeLA
authors: Xinyu Zhou, Fan Li, Shasha Chen, Min Cao, Ahtamjan Ahmat, Qiaoming Zhu, Mang Ye
bullets: Addresses English-centric limitations in multilingual TBPR, including scarce large-scale pretraining data and pivot-language alignment bias.
Introduces MultiPedes, a pedestrian-centric dataset with 10 million image-text pairs across four languages.
Uses semantic-aware multilingual learning with mixture-of-experts routing for language-invariant semantics.
Employs a semantic probe for direct, fine-grained vision–text alignment without relying on English.
Experiments on multilingual and English-only TBPR datasets demonstrate ViSeLA’s effectiveness; code and data are publicly available.

In the first stage, consensus-guided filtering leverages both domain-specific and domain-agnostic evaluators to identify and remove noisy samples from large-scale image–text pairs collected from public datasets, resulting in higher-quality data. In the second stage, large language models are employed to perform machine translation at scale, generating multilingual descriptions and constructing the MultiPedes dataset.

papers.abstract: Pathologists rarely diagnose from a single image: they scan a section at low power for architecture, zoom into selected fields for cytology, and integrate the evidence across views and scales. Pathology benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), however, mostly ask about one image or require whole-slide pipelines, and the few that show several fields draw nested regions from cancer slides of one public cohort. We introduce CaseScope, a benchmark of diagnosis from several curated fields of one lesion: CaseScope-Teaching, 436 cases from a residency-training image library, reconstructed, de-identified, harmonised against a WHO-based ontology and re-examined by a pathologist wherever an automated pre-review raised a doubt, and CaseScope-Atlas, 800 cases from 88 published atlases (387 of them figure series of one disease), labelled from the captions by two LLMs that must agree. They cover 843 entities across 18 organ systems and pose 4,679 items in six tasks, from open-ended and ten-way diagnosis with ontology-guided hard negatives under circular evaluation to the verification and location of morphological findings. Across twenty-eight open and four proprietary MLLMs, diagnoses are unstable -- the best open and proprietary models are correct under all ten option rotations on 17.9% and 61.7% of the teaching cases -- and wrong answers favour the classic look-alike; open models make little use of the additional fields on teaching cases, where the one-line specimen site matters more, although on atlas cases with three or more fields the fields count about as much as the site; and most open models verify findings barely above chance (median 62.0% vs. 50%, best 81.5%), gaining a median +3.4 points from images; proprietary models reach 83.2-93.2%. Rankings broadly replicate between the sources. The evaluation code is available at https://github.com/Wenchuan-Zhang/CaseScope.

papers.abstract: Language-guided place recognition requires recovering geographic identity across visual observations beyond the image from which a description originates. However, aggregate retrieval scores often entangle observation transfer, gallery competition, and linguistic evidence, obscuring the underlying recognition capability. We introduce AcrossPlace, a provenance-aware benchmark establishing a systematic evaluation standard for bidirectional language--vision place recognition. Built upon GSV-Cities, AcrossPlace comprises 56,726 places across 23 cities, 156,800 automatically generated, rule-filtered descriptions, and 113,404 target images. Each description retains its source-image provenance, while retrieval operates on disjoint target observations. Text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) retrieval share a unified place-identity relevance criterion supporting multiple valid matches. Two geographic protocols evaluate unseen places within represented cities (P0) and generalization to held-out cities (P1). Paired observation comparisons, gallery-controlled evaluations, fixed-query scaling, and blinded annotation auditing systematically characterize retrieval performance. Across three training seeds, place-supervised SigLIP2 T2I Recall@1 decreases from 19.69% on source images to 12.31% on independent targets under P0. For fixed P1 queries, expanding the gallery from 500 to 8,425 places reduces Recall@1 from 14.67% to 2.87%. A 240-description audit further reveals discrepancies between automated acceptance and factual evidence. These findings establish AcrossPlace as a reproducible evaluation standard for assessing transferable place identity across visual observations and geographic environments.

bullets: Introduces a provenance-aware benchmark for bidirectional text-to-image and image-to-text place recognition with multiple valid place matches.

Evaluates unseen places within known cities (P0) and generalization to held-out cities (P1), with gallery-controlled and observation-transfer tests.
Place-supervised SigLIP2 T2I Recall@1 falls from 19.69% on source images to 12.31% on independent targets under P0.

papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion generation is emerging as a competitive alternative to autoregressive generation by denoising the entire token sequence through iterative refinement. Its global planning and progressive correction capabilities are particularly well suited to autonomous driving. However, transferring this generation paradigm from general-purpose settings to driving introduces substantial domain gaps in both training and inference. To unlock its potential, we propose a multi-stage optimization pipeline for standard vision-language model architectures, without auxiliary action experts or specialized mixture-of-experts Transformer, spanning post-training and inference. During supervised fine-tuning, we optimize the representation of planning inputs to suppress hallucinations in task responses. During reinforcement learning, we introduce metric-guided diversity filtering to identify stronger learning starting points and improve policy exploration. At inference time, we propose Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding (DAD), which adaptively adjusts decoding modes according to scene complexity. Based on this pipeline, we develop Masked Diffusion Drive (MD-Drive), improving its performance by 29.7\% over the unoptimized model. Experiments on the NAVSIM closed loop benchmark and the nuScenes and DriveCoT open loop datasets show that MD-Drive outperforms autoregressive VLM baselines with the same architecture, while achieving a more favorable balance between performance and computational cost than systems with different architectures through discrete diffusion training and inference.
authors: Shunming Liu, Pei Huang, Yajing Sun, Huaxiao Liu
bullets: Addresses domain gaps when transferring discrete diffusion generation to autonomous driving.

Reinforcement Learning: Checkpoints of varying maturity levels are screened based on diversity and accuracy metrics, after which they are fed into the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training process. Inference: dVLM exhibits distinct confidence trends across different driving scenarios. DAD mechanism transforms these trends into specialized inference sequences to optimize output quality.

papers.abstract: Surround-view video understanding in autonomous driving is a crucial capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve reliable driving reasoning. Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera. Existing MLLMs primarily focus on front-view information, while their spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning abilities remain unknown. To address this gap, we propose MVDriveBench, a high-information-density video QA benchmark for autonomous driving, characterized by synchronized surround-view inputs, spatio-temporal understanding, and reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. We design 12 categories of QA tasks that cover the complete reasoning pipeline from low-level visual perception to high-level driving decision-making, enabling a systematic evaluation of MLLMs surround-view spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities in complex driving environments. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on MVDriveBench. The results show that current MLLMs still exhibit insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning ability. Meanwhile, closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim reveal a correlation between surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities and closed-loop driving performance, highlighting the importance of comprehensive multi-view understanding for reliable vehicle control.

papers.abstract: Long-context multimodal intelligence requires revisiting earlier images as conversations and documents accumulate, yet retaining an image does not guarantee reliable access to its details. By varying context length, redistributing a fixed text passage around the image, and changing positions without adding text, we identify the positional relation between images and questions as a direct influence on visual access. To address this gap, we propose Visual Position Re-Anchoring (VPR), a training-free method that shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing. It operates directly on the existing KV cache, preserving standard attention computation without extracting attention maps or adding model forward passes. We develop static and continuous compensation schedules, using the static schedule by default. Across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks, static VPR improves 97 of 100 model--task scores. Further analysis shows greater attention to regions containing answer evidence across six checkpoints, with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies. These findings demonstrate an efficient way to sustain visual access through positional adjustment within the cache.
authors: Juntao Xu, Qichai Zhao, Rui Sun, Zhouyang Jiang, Shiwei Wu, Zhi Li, Kaisheng Ma, Yu Liu
bullets: Image–question positional relationships can impair visual access even when the image remains in context.

papers.abstract: Medical imaging is essential for diagnosing disease, guiding treatment and monitoring patients over time. Although artificial intelligence has advanced image interpretation, existing medical models often address restricted tasks, while general-purpose proprietary models lack access to private clinical imaging required to achieve medical expertise. Developing models that can interpret complex examinations and communicate their findings in the context of clinical decisions remains a major challenge. Here, we show that Neuro-VL, a vision-language model trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care, can interpret complete imaging examinations and engage in natural language conversations about their findings. Across internal and international datasets, Neuro-VL outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models in diagnosing, localizing, and describing abnormalities, as well as generating comprehensive radiology reports. The model also compared serial examinations to assess disease progression and more reliably resisted misleading clinical assumptions than leading frontier models from OpenAI and Google. These results extend health system learning beyond individual predictions to interactive image interpretation and longitudinal disease monitoring. They demonstrate how the collective clinical experience of health systems can be used to develop medical AI with specialized expertise and broad clinical capabilities.

Interprets complex neuroimaging examinations and communicates findings through natural-language conversation.
Diagnoses, localizes, and describes abnormalities; generates comprehensive radiology reports and assesses disease progression across serial exams.
Outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models across internal and international datasets, including resistance to misleading clinical assumptions.
Scope: focused on neuroimaging and trained on routine clinical-care data; the abstract does not specify detailed evaluation metrics or limitations.

The dataset captures the full spectrum of neurological pathology, including neoplastic, vascular, infectious, degenerative, traumatic, and other conditions. b, Neuro-VL was trained to generate robust radiological interpretations of neuroimaging accompanied by an auditable reasoning trace. To reason over image and language input, Neuro-VL integrates a visual encoder with an LLM through a vision-language connector (not shown). The visual encoder incorporates a hierarchical attention mechanism inspired by the inherent structure of neuroimaging data and is pretrained using radiology reports, enabling it to extract semantically rich visual features from complex neuroimaging studies. c, We evaluated Neuro-VL across internal health-system cohorts and 24 international public datasets spanning 21 countries. This evaluation covered diverse tasks, including localization, feature description, diagnosis, report generation, and longitudinal disease monitoring, as well as a comprehensive red-teaming evaluation.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models, but answer accuracy only partly reflects its effect. Pruning can change the probabilities of alternative response tokens even when greedy answers remain correct and unchanged. We compare full and pruned response distributions under shared reference prefixes. Average predictive drift grows with compression on fixed correctly answered samples. Separate analyses associate larger drift with more confidence-decision disagreements and sampling failures. We propose DiFiT (Distribution-Fidelity-guided Token pruning) to learn discrete selection from reference answers and full-token response distributions. Dual-View Distillation matches probabilities across the vocabulary, while answer supervision supports task quality. A learned scorer and differentiable Top-$K$ learn which visual evidence to retain. A multi-budget mask objective supports different retention ratios through one shared ranking over a frozen model. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, DiFiT reduces sampling-induced negative flips by 30.3% relative to FastV at 10% retention on four-task greedy-correct controls. It preserves 98.74% of baseline performance on MME at 30% retention.
authors: Jingyuan Zhang, Nihao Niu, Xinyang Lv, Beibei Han, Xiaoyun Wang, Yanning Hou, Ke Xu
bullets: Visual token pruning can alter alternative-token probabilities even when greedy answers stay unchanged.
DiFiT learns which visual tokens to retain using full-model response distributions and reference-answer supervision.
Dual-View Distillation aligns vocabulary-level probabilities, while differentiable Top-K selection supports discrete pruning.
A shared ranking supports multiple retention budgets with one frozen model.
On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it reduces sampling-induced negative flips by 30.3% versus FastV at 10% retention and preserves 98.74% of baseline MME performance at 30% retention.

papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models for global weather forecasting achieve remarkable predictive accuracy, yet they frequently produce states that violate fundamental physical laws, including conservation of mass, hydrostatic balance, or spectral energy scaling. We term these outputs physical hallucinations and propose PhysXAI, a rigorous diagnostic framework that detects, localises, and attributes such inconsistencies. Unlike existing post-hoc metric suites, PhysXAI is a learnable system that explicitly decouples forecast error from physical plausibility. We formalise the problem through a novel joint condition on numerical and physical residuals, and introduce a multi-branch encoder that extracts representations from conservation, dynamical, spectral, cross-variable, and spatiotemporal residuals. A key innovation is a physics-consistency contrastive learning objective, which we theoretically show the latent representation to be approximately isometric to the physical residual space, ensuring that diagnostic decisions remain grounded in physically meaningful deviations. We further derive an adaptive multi-objective loss with gradient-based weighting to balance competing diagnostic objectives. The framework produces spatially resolved hallucination maps, violation-type classifications, and calibrated Bayesian uncertainty, enabling both detection and interpretable attribution of physical inconsistencies. We conduct a comprehensive comparative evaluation of PhysXAI across ERA5, WeatherBench 2, and MERRA-2, using forecasts from GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and NeuralGCM, with Python-written code and a fully reproducible experimental protocol. Our theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation establish PhysXAI as a principled framework for diagnosing physical hallucinations and advancing trustworthy AI for weather forecasting.
bullets: Targets violations of mass conservation, hydrostatic balance, spectral energy scaling, and other physical constraints.
Decouples forecast-error assessment from physical plausibility using joint numerical–physical residual conditions.
Combines residual representations across conservation, dynamics, spectra, variables, and space–time with contrastive learning and adaptive multi-objective weighting.
Produces spatial hallucination maps, violation-type classifications, and calibrated Bayesian uncertainty for attribution.
Evaluated across ERA5, WeatherBench 2, and MERRA-2 forecasts from GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and NeuralGCM; the abstract reports theoretical and empirical validation but no specific numerical results.

papers.abstract: Intelligent fault diagnosis models are typically developed for a single machine under a specific set of operating conditions, such that each new machine or condition requires retraining from scratch. This one-machine-one-model paradigm scales poorly. Although transfer learning and domain generalization can reduce the labeling burden, they primarily seek domain-invariant commonality, potentially discarding machine-specific characteristics that are critical for diagnosis. This paper proposes TFC-MMFD, a time-frequency-condition multimodal fusion foundation model for rotating-machinery fault diagnosis under multi-element heterogeneous scenarios. Statistical indicators, time-frequency images, vibration sequences, and textual machine and condition descriptions are tokenized into a unified language-like space, allowing inputs of different physical origin to be represented as a single sequence. A LLaMA backbone, together with cross-modal bidirectional attention and a Q-Former, then distills this sequence into fault-mode queries. Diagnosis is performed by matching these queries against natural-language fault-mode anchors rather than fixed class indices, while regression-adversarial condition disentanglement and condition-conditioned masked pre-training improve robustness to changing conditions. Across four progressive tasks on ten public bearing datasets spanning diverse bearing types, speeds, and loads, TFC-MMFD attains 99.40% accuracy and 99.16% macro-F1, maintains over 80% accuracy on most interpolated unseen conditions without adaptation, and improves from 20.26% to 95.63% accuracy on an unseen machine with only five labeled samples per class. It outperforms the strongest of eight domain-generalization baselines by 10.57 percentage points and compares favorably with a recent bearing foundation model while using less than half of its fine-tuning data.
authors: Xinyu Zou, Jian Ma, Liang Ma, Chen Lu, Tao Peng, Yingjie Li

papers.abstract: Frozen vision-language models often match concepts mentioned in a caption without respecting their negation: a query "a kitchen with no toaster" favors an image containing a toaster. Yet these models are substantially stronger at matching affirmative descriptions. We exploit this asymmetry with Negation-Aware Evidence Scoring (NAES), which reformulates negated descriptions into affirmative queries and combines their evidence by caption structure. A lightweight text decomposer, NegSplit, identifies this structure by extracting negated spans and the remaining affirmative context. For captions with an affirmative remainder, NAES matches that content and applies a presence-based correction for the denial. When no affirmative content remains, it queries the denied object's presence and reflects the evidence around a reference to score the negated description. With LAION-2B CLIP, NAES achieves 82.4% accuracy on COCO-MCQ and 93.0% on VOC2007-MCQ, surpassing KTN by 2.9 and 0.9 percentage points; with OpenAI CLIP, it exceeds PeakPatch accuracy by 4.4 and 26.0 points, respectively. NAES also improves negated-description retrieval on COCO and MSR-VTT, with gains extending to SigLIP, SigLIP 2, and larger CLIP encoders. The strongest multiple-choice results use competing descriptions to center and align evidence; retrieval improvements persist without this conditioning. These findings show that explicitly separating affirmative matching from denied-object evidence can substantially improve negation-aware ranking.
authors: Aashish Pokhrel, Tejas Anvekar, Shivanand Venkanna Sheshappanavar
bullets: Addresses CLIP’s tendency to favor images containing objects described as absent.
NegSplit extracts negated spans and remaining affirmative context from captions.

Multiple-choice scoring benefits from competing descriptions for evidence alignment, while retrieval gains persist without this conditioning.

papers.title: Saying No by Asking Yes: Affirmative Decomposition and Evidence Reflection for Frozen CLIP

papers.abstract: The visual world is cluttered: robust vision-language reasoning requires ignoring irrelevant information. Yet vision-language models (VLMs) can suffer substantial accuracy losses when answering questions about a target image with distractors present. Existing mitigations focus on selecting relevant images or limiting information exchange between images. Through a systematic analysis of three open 7-8B VLMs on five perception benchmarks adapted to include distractor images, we show that distractors reduce accuracy even when models correctly identify the relevant image, suggesting that selection alone is not enough. To understand the mechanism behind this interference, we combine attention analysis with targeted knockouts in Qwen2.5-VL and identify middle-layer distractor-to-text connections as a pathway through which irrelevant visual information affects reasoning. We introduce answer consistency regularization, which encourages consistent answer distributions with and without distractors. Without directly constraining attention, this objective reduces middle-layer attention from question tokens to distractor images, consistent with the pathway our analysis implicates. With five distractors, our approach improves circular accuracy by an average of 16 percentage points over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline across the five benchmarks while preserving single-image performance.
authors: Marie Amale Huynh, Regev Cohen, Serena Yeung-Levy, Sivan Doveh
bullets: Distractors lower accuracy even when the model correctly selects the relevant image, so image selection alone is insufficient.

Targeted knockouts in Qwen2.5-VL support these connections as a pathway for irrelevant visual information to affect reasoning.

With five distractors, the method improves circular accuracy by an average of 16 percentage points over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline while preserving single-image performance.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) are compared mainly by accuracy averaged across findings, a summary that can hide complete failure on a single diagnosis. We audit five open medical VLMs (MedGemma-4B, Lingshu-7B, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and MedVLM-R1) on 6,048 ChestX-ray14 questions balanced by sex, age, finding, and label. On the 432 pneumothorax-positive X-rays, HuatuoGPT-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL detect zero cases while MedGemma and Lingshu detect 38% and 67% of the same images. The two failing models answer "no" to all 864 pneumothorax cases (balanced accuracy 0.500, chance), yet produce fluent, anatomically specific explanations that name the signs of a collapsed lung and then deny them, with no hedge or abstention. This failure is not an artifact of prompting, image resolution, label ambiguity, or model scale. It persists across four prompt formats, at native resolution, and on single-label cases. A within-model control shows the same forced prompt gives HuatuoGPT 79% recall on nodule but only 6% on pneumothorax. It survives a tenfold scale increase (Qwen2.5-VL-72B detects 4%) and replicates on SIIM-ACR, an independent dataset with radiologist-drawn masks, where the failing models detect 0 of 432 confirmed pneumothoraces, including 0 of the 144 largest lesions. Reading the models' logits and internal states shows this is not blindness. The two failing models are highly confident yet no better than chance and a linear probe recovers pneumothorax from their hidden representations even where recall is zero, so the finding is represented internally but suppressed at the output. Aggregate accuracy therefore cannot establish that a medical VLM can see a given finding, because a model that misses one can still describe it convincingly. Reporting per-finding recall and specificity on balanced cases is needed to tell the difference.

bullets: Five open medical VLMs were audited on balanced ChestX-ray14 questions across findings and patient attributes.

The failing models consistently denied pneumothorax with fluent, specific explanations and no abstention, despite chance-level balanced accuracy.
The failure persisted across prompts, resolutions, single-label cases, model scale, and an independent SIIM-ACR dataset.
Hidden-state probes recovered pneumothorax information, suggesting output suppression rather than visual blindness; per-finding recall and specificity are therefore necessary.

papers.abstract: Aerial spatial intelligence (ASI) requires models to understand objects and spatial relationships across changing viewpoints and scales. Evaluating these abilities as models evolve calls for fresh physical observations, yet producing new aerial spatial questions requires repeatedly establishing entity identities, geometric references, and cross-view correspondences. We introduce \textbf{RSLiveBench-UAV}, a continually evolving vision-language benchmark driven by recurring acquisition of real UAV imagery. Its update protocol admits images captured after the preceding release and delays answer disclosure. An entity-centered production workflow uses geometry-assisted association to link repeated observations of physical vehicles, reuse human-verified attributes, and combine them with view-specific annotations and spatial references for traceable question generation. All tasks use deterministic scoring without model judges. We evaluate 30 general-purpose, remote-sensing, and embodied models on 35,491 question records from ten scenes, covering 17 tasks across 2D perception, 3D perception, cross-view perception, and reasoning. All 18 tested embodied models outperform the three selected remote-sensing comparators in Overall, although the strongest embodied model scores 43.29 versus 59.88 for GPT-6-Astra. Fine-grained vehicle recognition remains challenging, and performance varies across heights and camera pitches. Retrospective scene-group comparisons and rolling-window replay characterize score-pattern consistency under scene renewal. RSLiveBench-UAV connects fresh physical observations, entity-centered answer production, and systematic model evaluation to support continual assessment of ASI. Benchmark will release at https://rslivebench.space
