papers.abstract: Does multimodal training shape how a language model thinks, even when the input is text only? We test this with targeted causal ablations across 10 multimodal configurations from 6 model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. We contrast spatial-imagery tasks that invite mental scene construction with symbol-manipulation tasks solvable by symbolic rules alone. We identify a vision-language axis in hidden-state space and ablate its projection at inference. In Chameleon-7B, this ablation drops accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) navigate by 27.6 pp while leaving boolean expressions intact (+5.6 pp), a 33.2 pp double dissociation. The effect is direction-specific and layer-localized, extends to mental-simulation tasks such as mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective taking, and is not explained by task difficulty, reasoning depth, or sequential update load. Together, these results reveal emergent vision-shaped thinking (EVT): text-only reasoning that causally recruits representations introduced or strengthened by vision-language training, without assuming an image-like internal format. The measured effect is spatially concentrated at 7-8B and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in the tested 32B configuration. In dual-path unified models (BAGEL, Janus-Pro), the causal handle localizes to the generation pathway as a compact one-dimensional carrier. The understanding pathway also encodes spatial information in a higher-rank, probe-decodable form, but is not the causal handle. To separate decodability from causal use, we analyze concentration, alignment, and semantic location. These diagnostics explain why behavior, probing, and intervention can diverge. Multimodal training thus reshapes the geometry of text-only reasoning, not just how visual input is processed.
authors: Qi Zhang, Bohan Wang, Qianru Sun, Hanwang Zhang
bullets: Across 10 multimodal configurations and 6 model families, the study contrasts spatial-imagery tasks with symbol-manipulation tasks.
Ablating a vision-language direction in hidden states sharply harms spatial navigation while preserving—and slightly improving—boolean reasoning in Chameleon-7B.
The effect is direction-specific, layer-localized, and extends to mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective-taking.
Vision-shaped thinking is concentrated at 7–8B in the tested models and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in a tested 32B model.
In dual-path models, the causal signal lies in the generation pathway; probe-decodable information in the understanding pathway is not necessarily causally used.

papers.abstract: We present Hy ASR 3.0, a large language model (LLM)-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) system that delivers strong recognition accuracy, supports flexible contextual conditioning, and maintains robust recognition performance across diverse speech conditions. Hy ASR 3.0 supports Mandarin Chinese, English and 13 Chinese dialect groups, including Cantonese. Among the evaluated systems, it achieves the lowest aggregate error rates on public Mandarin Chinese, English, and Cantonese benchmarks and the lowest error rates on the corresponding internal test sets, alongside first-tier dialect recognition performance. Beyond audio-only transcription, Hy ASR 3.0 supports multiple forms of external context, including hotword lists, question--answer dialogues, and summaries, enabling the use of task-relevant information during recognition. The model also leverages intra-utterance context to disambiguate homophonic and phonetically similar keywords using information from other parts of the same utterance, without requiring a separate contextual input. Evaluations demonstrate strong contextual recognition in both external-context and intra-utterance settings, as well as robust recognition of long-form speech, children's and older adults' speech, low-volume speech, and speech in noisy environments. This report describes the model architecture and training methodology and presents evaluations across recognition accuracy, context utilization, and robustness.

papers.abstract: AI-generated content (AIGC) has substantially narrowed the visual gap between natural and synthetic images, while existing detectors often rely on generator-specific artifacts and exhibit limited generalization to unseen models. This motivates a fundamental question: which intrinsic physical image characteristics provide stable, discriminative cues for distinguishing natural from AI-generated images? We investigate this by systematically identifying robust physical features and incorporating them into a vision-language representation without external textual prompts at inference. We first analyze 15 handcrafted physical descriptors across images from over 20 generative models. Based on cross-generator stability and real-fake discriminability, we propose a Feature Stability-Discriminability Validation Assessment (FSDVA) to select a compact set of reliable features. Five core features, including Laplacian variance, Sobel statistics, and residual-noise variance, are then used to construct structured textual descriptions encoding physical evidence for CLIP-based learning. We integrate these physics-enriched descriptions with image representations via a native physics-guided multimodal framework, adapting CLIP ViT-L 14 with LoRA. At inference, the model requires only the input image, with no external captions or manual prompts. On GenImage, our method achieves 99.0 percent accuracy on SDv1.4 and 96.7 percent on Wukong, with a mean of 97.23 percent across eight generative models versus 95.8 percent for C2pCLIP under the same setting. On UniversalFakeDetect, it maintains strong, stable generalization across diverse and unseen generation settings. These results show that carefully selected physical image statistics provide complementary forensic evidence to pretrained vision-language representations, enabling interpretable, more generator-agnostic AIGC detection.
bullets: Existing detectors often depend on generator-specific artifacts and generalize poorly to unseen models.
The proposed FSDVA selects five robust, discriminative physical features from 15 handcrafted descriptors analyzed across 20+ generators.
These features are converted into structured textual descriptions and integrated with image representations through a CLIP-based multimodal framework with LoRA adaptation.
On GenImage, the method reaches 99.0% accuracy on SDv1.4, 96.7% on Wukong, and 97.23% mean accuracy across eight generators, exceeding the cited baseline.
The approach maintains stable generalization on diverse and unseen settings and requires only the input image at inference.

papers.title: From Pixels to Prompts: Physics-Guided Language Enhancement for AI-Generated Image Detection

papers.abstract: Open-weight Vision-Language Models (VLMs) score 85-94% on spatial benchmarks (BLINK Spatial, What's Up CLEVR) yet collapse to chance on simple geometric questions when object, scene, and texture priors are stripped away. We introduce and open-source Sophon, a procedurally generated diagnostic of paired colored point-cloud stimuli across three coordinate systems (1D linear, 2D Cartesian, 2D polar) and four question types (binary, categorical, comparative, quantitative). Across four open architectures (LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen2.5-VL, Idefics3), accuracy clusters at 47-52% while frontier models (Opus 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.4) clear 77-83% and humans reach 84-94%. We use linear probes and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to trace the open-weight failures. Probes of the vision encoder (ViT) and language decoder (LLM) recover Sophon spatial information at 83-85% and 80-86% accuracy, respectively, and the language tower's reasoning circuit answers text-only controls (point clouds as sets of coordinates) at +40 pp over visual stimuli. Language tower per-layer attention attribution localizes visual integration to mid-stack layers. At readout, models elevate the correct answer-set tokens but select among them randomly. We localize the mechanism by tuning individual and grouped components across every architecture's stack, including the vision tower (ViT workspace and reader), the projector, and the language tower (LLM workspace and reader). These experiments demonstrate that this mid-stack workspace holds circuitry capable of organizing the spatial signal so that the frozen reader can decode it. LoRA fine-tuning adjusts that circuitry such that 7B-class VLMs answer Sophon spatial reasoning questions at frontier aggregate accuracy. This work suggests that these models do not have a capability gap for spatial reasoning but suffer from a routing bottleneck that targeted fine-tuning repairs.
authors: J. Zach Gazak, Ryan Swindle, Justin Fletcher
bullets: Introduces an open, procedural diagnostic using colored point clouds across 1D and 2D coordinate systems and four question types.
Open-weight VLMs perform near chance (47–52%), despite much higher scores on conventional spatial benchmarks.
Probes show spatial information is recoverable in both vision and language components, while text-only controls substantially outperform visual inputs.
Attention and component-tuning analyses localize the failure to mid-stack visual-integration and reasoning workspaces, where models identify answer sets but choose randomly.
LoRA fine-tuning brings 7B-class VLMs to frontier-level aggregate accuracy on Sophon, supporting a routing-bottleneck explanation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Sample Sophon stimuli, one per (question type, coordinate system) cell: 1D linear / categorical (left), Cartesian / binary (center), polar / quantitative (right). Each panel shows its coordinate system and ground truth transform parameter. No objects, scenes, or textures appear in any stimulus (Appendix B).

Figure 5: Per-layer GT vs competitor logit gap, five LoRA conditions, four architectures. Each panel projects the answer position hidden state through the unembedding WU at every decoder layer and reports the mean gap between the ground truth direction token and its same axis competitor (e.g. “left” vs “right”). The shaded region marks the reader band. In every architecture BASE and READER sit at or below zero throughout, so reader-band training installs no contrast. The three trained conditions rise late in the stack and largely coincide, and WORKSPACE’s contrast appears despite the reader band and WU being frozen. The reader band’s contrast emerges when the workspace is reorganized to feed it (§5.3).

Figure 4: Quantitative answer distribution taxonomy. Bar height is Pearson r between parsed answer and GT magnitude (n=200). Filled = stimulus engaged: Perceiver (r≥0.5, top-1<50%), Direction perceiver (r≥0.5, top-1≥50%). Hatched/outline = engagement failure: Noisy (r<0.5), Few anchor (top-3≥50%), Constant (top-1≥85%). Labels above bars are answer uniqueness (nunique/n). Human scale r reflects rater unit ambiguity. See all models version in Appendix U.

Grok 4.20 collapses to a near constant token output under greedy decode (Appendix I).

(a) Linear probe accuracy on Sophon direction classification at each encoder layer. Five frozen encoders cluster at 83−85% in mid-to-late layers regardless of pretraining objective (Appendix C). Figure 14: Decoding temperature partially releases Grok-4.20’s constant token attractor on categorical cells but not on binary cells, and does not improve the per-model mean accuracy of any frontier VLM. Top panel: constant token rate (fraction of samples assigned the most common parsed answer) versus decode temperature for the 15 (model, cell) combinations that collapse at temp=0 (const ≥ 85%). Lines staying above the 85% threshold indicate a persistent attractor, and lines dropping below indicate a decode induced artifact. All three GPT-4o (purple) cells release, as does the single Sonnet 4.6 (orange) cell. Of Grok-4.20’s 11 collapsed cells, 4 release (the categorical cells on Cartesian trans x, Cartesian trans y, Cartesian rotation, plus the rotation quantitative cell) while the 7 binary and comparative cells stay ≥ 88% at every temperature. Figure 22: Opus 4.6. Quantitative answer distribution vs. ground truth on the four (coordinate system, transform) cells. Each panel overlays the ground truth histogram (gray fill) with no hint predictions (red, solid edge) and range hint predictions (blue, hatched). The two horizontal range bars at the top show the no hint stimulus support (red dashed) and the explicit range supplied by the hint (blue solid), and mode of response annotations point at the dominant text anchor in each condition. The polar scale panel is the only cell where Opus 4.6 tracks the stimulus continuously (r=0.80, perceiver class). The other three panels collapse to a single mode near 90◦ or ∼1.0 regardless of GT (canonical few anchor). Range hints shrink the support of the predicted distribution but do not move the mode toward GT, which is the basis for our claim that hints constrain the answer set rather than reveal perception.

Figure 24: GPT-5.4. Same layout as Fig. 22 (no range hint condition was run for GPT-5.4, so the blue series is absent). Rotation values spread but are not strongly correlated with GT.

Figure 23: GPT-4o. Same layout as Fig. 22. Figure 20: Vocabulary distractor effect across five categorical specs. Each dumbbell connects random restricted accuracy (open marker, 2 transform appropriate direction words offered) to random full accuracy (filled marker, all 6 direction words offered, order randomized in both conditions). The translation (Cartesian Translation X / Translation Y) and polar Radial (radial translation, answer choices inward / outward) cells plunge toward the 6-way chance floor under the full vocabulary across both open (Qwen-7B, NeXT-7B) and frontier (GPT-4o, Opus 4.6) tiers. The extra rotation tokens (clockwise, counterclockwise) draw probability mass away from the correct translation answer even though the underlying transform is not rotational. The Cartesian Rotation control stays flat because rotation vocabulary is already among the choices in both conditions, so widening the option set adds no novel distractors. The pattern is consistent across capability tiers, supporting the claim that the failure is at the answer set interface rather than at perception.

papers.selection_reason: Procedural diagnostic for spatial reasoning in VLMs, identifies routing bottleneck and shows fine-tuning improves spatial intelligence, directly relevant to spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: Sophon: A Procedural Diagnostic for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Sophon reveals that open-weight VLMs often contain spatial information but fail to route it through their reasoning circuitry, a bottleneck that targeted LoRA fine-tuning can repair.

papers.abstract: BEST-RQ, based on random projection and quantization, has been a well-established self-supervised learning approach to learn speech representations from large-scale unlabeled audio due to its high performance and efficiency. However, in BEST-RQ representations learned by random quantization can be sensitive to the choice of quantization targets. To address this issue, we propose a distributionally robust extension of BEST-RQ that seeks representations robust across multiple quantization configurations. Specifically, we define groups by codebooks and formulate the training as a group Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) problem. Rather than optimizing solely for the average loss across groups, our approach adaptively reweights groups to emphasize those performing poorly. Additionally, we regularize DRO with a Kullback-Leibler divergence to prevent excessive distribution deviation. We evaluate our approach on the Multilingual LibriSpeech dataset and show that the distributionally robust BEST-RQ achieves superior performance over the conventional uniform average across multiple codebooks.
authors: Muhammad Khan, Xiaodong Cui, Brian Kingsbury, George Saon
bullets: BEST-RQ can be sensitive to the choice of random quantization targets.
The method groups training examples by codebook and formulates learning as group Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO).
It adaptively upweights groups with higher loss and uses KL-divergence regularization to limit excessive reweighting.
Experiments on Multilingual LibriSpeech show improved performance over uniform averaging across codebooks.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed DRO-BEST-RQ with KL regularization. For an utterance i, the acoustic features xi are first projected into a lower-dimensional space using a shared projection matrix P . The resulting representations are then quantized using multiple fixed random codebooks Cg to generate group-specific pseudo-labels yi g . The input acoustic features are processed by a shared encoder and group-specific prediction heads. The cross-entropy loss is computed for each codebook on those masked frames which are then combined through the KL-regularized DRO objective.
Table 2: Illustration of the Group DRO weighting mechanism across four BEST-RQ codebooks at an arbitrarily selected iteration.
Table 3: WER (%) on the MLS test sets

papers.selection_reason: Improves speech representation learning (BEST-RQ) for multimodal models using distributionally robust optimization.
papers.title: Distributionally Robust BEST-RQ For Speech Representation Learning
papers.tldr: A distributionally robust version of BEST-RQ improves speech representations by emphasizing poorly performing quantization configurations instead of treating all codebooks equally.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) perform strongly on multimodal tasks, Document Understanding (DU) among them, but the benchmarks that measure them mostly cover English documents and narrow problems. How well current VLMs generalize across languages, tasks, styles and layouts therefore remains unclear. We introduce MDU, a multilingual DU benchmark of 23146 examples spanning 13 tasks and five languages: English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish. The tasks isolate complementary capabilities, from surface-level text and Markdown extraction through summarization, classification and named-entity recognition to layout-sensitive passage and layout extraction. We evaluate 45 state-of-the-art open-weight VLMs from 1.7B to 235B parameters, plus one commercial system under the same protocol. The benchmark is far from saturated: the best average is 69.0, only eight of the 45 evaluated systems reach 65, and the two best results come from 27B models rather than from the largest systems we evaluate. Performance is uneven in ways that scale does not fix. The gap between the strongest and weakest language does not close as models grow, and it survives controlling for the domain composition of each language. Capabilities also do not improve together: once we partial out overall model quality, per-task scores are largely uncorrelated, and transcription ability in particular trades off against semantic extraction.
authors: Matteo Gabburo, Daniela Baiamonte, Stefano Simonazzi, Silvia Gardini, Sean Cesare Lazzeri, Andrea Zugarini
bullets: Introduces MDU, a benchmark with 23,146 examples across 13 document-understanding tasks and five languages: English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish.
Covers capabilities from text and Markdown extraction to summarization, classification, named-entity recognition, and layout-sensitive extraction.
Evaluates 45 open-weight VLMs ranging from 1.7B to 235B parameters, plus one commercial system, under a shared protocol.
The benchmark is not saturated: the best average score is 69.0, only eight open-weight systems reach 65, and the top two results come from 27B models.
Language and task performance remain uneven as models scale; transcription ability can trade off against semantic extraction.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks multilingual document understanding in vision-language models, fitting multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: Benchmarking Multilingual Document Understanding in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: MDU shows that current vision-language models remain far from robust multilingual document understanding, with performance varying substantially by language and task rather than simply improving with scale.

papers.abstract: Prompt-tuning has emerged as a parameter-efficient technique for adapting large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) to downstream tasks while keeping the pre-trained weights frozen. However, prompt-tuned VLMs often suffer from a base-to-novel dual miscalibration problem, where models typically show underconfidence on base classes and overconfidence on novel classes. Current VLM calibration approaches address this dual miscalibration either separately or jointly, but lack a geometric understanding of the hyperspherical embedding space and thus fail to exploit angular discriminative properties to adjust distorted decision boundaries. To address this, we propose M-PFT, a novel angular-margin approach for prompt tuning that introduces two complementary objectives to promote class discriminability and semantic anchoring. This enlarges the angular margin by 1) minimizing the maximum cosine similarity between tunable class embeddings to reduce embedding collapse and 2) minimizing the angular distance between each tunable embedding and its corresponding zero-shot embedding to preserve semantic geometry. Extensive experiments across 9 prompt-tuning methods with various backbones on 15 diverse datasets show that our approach reduces the average calibration error on novel classes, while remaining competitive on base classes and maintaining comparable accuracy. Further analyses reveal that M-PFT effectively adjusts distorted decision boundaries induced by prompt tuning while preserving the pre-trained embedding space, improving calibration with negligible computational overhead.
authors: Udaya Sampath K. Perera Miriya Thanthrige
bullets: Addresses dual miscalibration: underconfidence on base classes and overconfidence on novel classes.
Uses two objectives: separates tunable class embeddings and anchors them to corresponding zero-shot embeddings.

papers.abstract: Radar systems can recover scene geometry and recognize predefined categories, but these outputs do not provide a persistent spatial representation for open-ended language queries. Such queries require linking observations from different viewpoints to the same physical locations. We present TextRadar, a framework that constructs a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field from panoramic radar observations. The field combines occupancy with scale-dependent language features at surface locations, allowing the reconstructed scene to be queried with new descriptions. A single-frame radar distillation model predicts aligned ranges and language features from each radar observation. Using radar-estimated poses, we register these predictions to reconstruct the field from radar alone in a new scene. Experiments on approximately 20k synchronized observations across seven buildings demonstrate scene-level natural-language querying and prompt-free semantic visualization. Analysis of camera-to-radar concept transferability shows stronger agreement for structures, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.
bullets: Addresses the lack of spatially persistent, language-queryable representations in radar-based scene understanding.
Distills each radar observation into aligned geometry and language features, then registers them using radar-estimated poses.
Constructs a scene-level field combining occupancy with scale-dependent language features at surface locations.
Demonstrates natural-language querying and prompt-free semantic visualization across seven buildings and about 20k synchronized observations.
Concept transfer is stronger for structures, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.

figures.caption: Fig. 13 Overview of the TextRadar framework. A rotating mmWave radar provides high-resolution panoramic RF measurements, while a front-facing camera supplies multiscale language supervision during data collection. Building on these inputs, TextRadar jointly learns geometry and language-aligned embedding from RF measurements and builds a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field, which supports several tasks.

Fig. 3 Scene-level natural-language querying of small structures and objects. The field localizes architectural structures, including (a) “Stairs” and (b) “Windows,” as well as compact objects, including (c) “Trash bin” and (d) “Human.” The RGB images provide representative observations of the queried regions, with dashed boxes indicating the corresponding targets. For categories with multiple instances, such as stairs and windows, the system simultaneously highlights geometrically separated regions throughout the scene.

Fig. 2 Scene-level natural-language querying of large building structures. The reconstructed geometry is colored according to the cosine similarity between the scene-level feature at each surface point and the CLIP text embedding of the query. Warmer colors indicate higher semantic relevance. The queries (a) “Ceiling” and (b) “Floor” activate complementary upper and lower surfaces across multiple corridors and room regions. The spatially coherent responses over distant parts of the environment show how the persistent occupancy-language field associates related structures across a common 3D coordinate system.

Fig. 5 Natural-language querying of high-level concepts. The prompts describe human configuration, affordances, and functional regions: (a) “Standing” localizes a standing person, (b) “Going down” highlights a descending staircase, (c) “Things to sit” retrieves a bench and other seating, (d) “Taking a rest” identifies a shared seating area, (e) “Entrance to other places” highlights doorways and passages, and (f) “Working region” identifies the occupied workspace in a laboratory office. These examples show responses to contextual prompts beyond direct object and material names.

Fig. 9 Radar-camera feature disagreement. The top row highlights concepts dominated by visual content: (a) televisions and monitors, (b) information signs, and (c) exhibition boards. The bottom row highlights appearance-dependent concepts: (d) ribbed texture, (e) yellow color, and (f) roughness and grid patterns. Dashed boxes mark the relevant regions in the RGB observations. While the camera-derived features clearly distinguish these regions by displayed content, color, or fine surface appearance, the radar-predicted features often assign them similar embeddings and thus fail to distinguish them.

Fig. 1 TextRadar constructs a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field from radar observations. A robot collects panoramic mmWave measurements along a trajectory (left). Surface geometry and language features predicted from these measurements are integrated in shared 3D coordinates (center). The right panels illustrate natural-language querying, prompt-free semantic visualization, and camera-to-radar concept transferability. The query “Things to sit” highlights a bench, while the feature visualization reveals semantic organization without specifying a prompt. Comparisons of radarpredicted and camera-derived features show stronger agreement for structures, objects, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.

Fig. 8 Prompt-free semantic visualization of material-related regions. The examples show (a) wood doors, (b) a glass window, and (c) a metal cabinet. The highlighted material regions occupy distinct portions of the projected feature space and therefore appear with colors different from their surrounding walls and structures. The agreement between the radar-predicted and camera-derived PCA images indicates material-related information being retained beyond range geometry alone.

Fig. 6 Prompt-free semantic visualization of general indoor structures. For each example, the rows from top to bottom present the rendered panoramic RGB image, the predicted range image, the three-component PCA projection of the radar-predicted CLIP features, and the corresponding camera-derived reference projection. The predicted and reference features are projected using a shared PCA basis, and the three principal components are mapped to RGB channels. Similar colors therefore indicate nearby positions in the projected semantic feature space, rather than predefined semantic classes. Large structural regions, including ceilings, floors, walls, corridor openings, and wall-mounted structures, form spatially coherent groups in the radar-predicted visualization and broadly agree with the camera-derived reference.

Fig. 4 Geometry and natural-language queries. Each example shows, from top to bottom, the rendered panoramic RGB reference, the range image predicted from the radar measurement, the query-relevancy map obtained from the radarpredicted CLIP-aligned features, and the corresponding map obtained from the camera-derived reference features. Warmer colors indicate higher cosine similarity to the text query. The queries cover materials, including (a) “Glass,” (b) “Metal,” and (c) “Marble”; objects, including (d) “Trash bin,” (e) “Chairs,” and (f) “Human”; and structures, including (g) “Stairs,” (h) “Floor,” and (i) “Ceiling.” The radar-predicted maps localize both compact objects and extended structural regions, remain spatially consistent with the recovered geometry, and broadly agree with the camera-derived reference maps.

Fig. 7 Prompt-free semantic visualization of structures and objects. The examples examine (a) stairs, (b) humans, and (c) chairs, with two scenes shown for each concept. The dashed boxes in the rendered RGB image indicate the structures or objects of interest. A shared PCA projection is used for each prediction-reference comparison, allowing their color organization to be compared directly. Stairs, human silhouettes, and individual chairs emerge as coherent regions whose boundaries follow the corresponding geometry, despite some differences in their sizes, shapes, and spatial extents.

Fig. 11 Example scenarios in our dataset. The dataset spans common indoor environments, including hallways, lounges, offices, classrooms, and open floor areas. These examples are captured by the front-facing camera on the robot and illustrate the visual context used to generate language supervision.

Fig. 12 Radar-camera feature disagreement around glass. Each column presents one example, and the rows show the rendered panoramic RGB reference, the radar-predicted range image, and the pixelwise cosine similarity between radarpredicted and camera-derived CLIP features. Dashed orange boxes indicate glass windows. Warmer colors represent stronger feature agreement, and cooler colors represent weaker agreement. Similarity decreases around the indicated glass regions, where the two sensors observe different scene content.

Fig. 10 Hardware platform for data collection. The mobile robot carries a rotating mmWave MIMO radar, a 3D LiDAR, and a front-facing camera. A stepper motor rotates the radar, while the battery and WiFi router rotate with the radar to prevent cable twisting and are placed behind it for weight balancing. Radar commands are sent through the wireless router. (a) Front view. (b) Rear view.
Table 2 Per-building radar-camera concept agreement. Each building is the held-out test split in the leave-one-building-out protocol.

papers.abstract: We propose a multimodal transformer framework for efficiently modeling long1 financial documents that combine structured tabular data with noisy, unstructured2 textual disclosures. The framework represents financial tables as semantically3 enriched token sequences and integrates them with long-form text through a cross-4 attention mechanism that explicitly captures cross-modal dependencies. In par-5 ticular, we augment each numerical variable with a semantic embedding derived6 from its textual definition, enabling the model to encode both numerical magnitude7 and economic meaning. This design yields a more expressive and parameter-8 efficient representation of tabular data compared to value-only embeddings. Using9 a large-scale dataset of financial statements and MD&A disclosures, we show that10 structured numerical features remain the dominant source of predictive signal;11 however, textual information provides consistent incremental gains when incor-12 porated via cross-attention rather than simple concatenation. Our results further13 demonstrate that noisy textual disclosures are most useful when conditioned on a14 stable, semantically structured tabular representation. In particular, using frozen15 variable-level tabular representations as cross-attention queries enables the model16 to weight MD&A chunks differently for each financial variable and observation.17 These findings suggest that cross-attention provides an efficient mechanism for18 table-conditioned aggregation of long-form narrative evidence.
bullets: Financial documents combine structured numerical tables with long, noisy textual disclosures.
Each numerical variable is enriched with an embedding derived from its textual definition, capturing both value and economic meaning.
Cross-attention links table variables to relevant text more effectively than simple concatenation.
Tables provide the dominant predictive signal, while text adds consistent gains when conditioned on structured representations.
Frozen variable-level table representations let the model weight narrative chunks differently for each variable and observation.

papers.abstract: Embodied systems need geometric perception that exploits available observations beyond images alone. Recent feed-forward 3D models incorporate geometric priors, including camera poses, intrinsics, and depth. However, handling noisy poses, preserving accurate priors, and recovering physical scale require more than simply accepting these inputs. We introduce \emph{Vision-Prior Geometry Grounded Transformer} (VPGGT), a VGGT-based framework that extends OmniVGGT for prior-aware embodied perception. We formulate sensor-motivated pose corruptions from ground-truth trajectories for training and introduce a parameter-free \emph{prior residual connection} (PRC) to mitigate \emph{prior dilution}, where predictions are less accurate than their supplied pose priors. Our noise formulation targets camera poses; supplied intrinsics and depth receive no additional corruption. We further introduce \emph{Metric Global Attention}, which conditions a global scale token on available pose and depth scales and predicts a shared metric scaling factor for the geometric outputs. Experiments across four datasets show that \emph{PRC} improves translation-direction accuracy and joint pose AUC over a matched training baseline when camera priors are provided for all views, under both exact and corrupted poses. These results support explicit prior access during refinement as a useful addition to feature-level conditioning.
bullets: Addresses noisy camera poses, prior dilution, and missing physical scale in prior-aware geometric perception.
Introduces sensor-motivated camera-pose corruption for training while leaving supplied intrinsics and depth uncorrupted.
Adds a parameter-free Prior Residual Connection to retain and refine pose priors explicitly.
Uses Metric Global Attention to predict a shared scale factor from available pose and depth scales.
Across four datasets, PRC improves translation-direction accuracy and joint pose AUC with exact or corrupted pose priors.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of VPGGT. Images and optional camera or depth priors are encoded and processed by a shared alternating-attention backbone. PRC places available camera priors in the camera head’s refinement state after its initial prediction. A Scale Encoder conditions a global token on available metric-scale statistics, using learned placeholders when they are absent. The camera, depth, and pointmap heads predict geometry, and a scale head supplies a shared factor that converts translations, depths, and points to metric units.

Figure 5: Pose-prior corruption in the training data. Two examples are shown for each dataset. Within each panel, the left plot displays the complete trajectory, while the right plot displays a selected segment of the same ground-truth and corrupted trajectories. Colors identify the ground truth and corruption realizations, as indicated by the plot legends. Ground-truth and corrupted poses share a coordinate system, without independently fitted trajectory or scale alignment. Spatial units and segment information are provided in the plots.

Figure 2: Prior dilution during camera refinement. A0 is released OmniVGGT; A1 uses the same checkpoint with PRC enabled, without additional training. All views receive camera priors; no depth is supplied. Colors distinguish methods and markers distinguish datasets. Dashed lines show input-prior scores. Reset is a state intervention, not a learned iteration.
Figure 4: Prior Residual Connection. PRC retains feature-level conditioning and supplies aligned camera priors as the state from which subsequent residual updates are predicted.

papers.selection_reason: Explicitly targets prior-aware geometric perception for embodied systems, with direct relevance to spatial intelligence and 3D foundation models.
papers.title: Deep Prior Learning for Embodied Perception
papers.tldr: VPGGT improves embodied 3D perception by explicitly preserving camera-pose priors and recovering metric scale under noisy pose inputs.

papers.abstract: Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. We propose five principles and organize them into a recursive logic for a more rigorous procedure of mechanistic inference. These principles provide a framework that supports scientific discovery in two senses: it helps turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge of mechanisms within models, and it makes those mechanisms sufficiently precise to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.
authors: Zhimin Hu, Chen Jiang, Hanbo Xie, N. Apurva Ratan Murty, Sashank Varma
bullets: MI increasingly studies internal computations, not just predictive behavior.
The paper identifies recurring inferential bottlenecks shared by neuroscience and MI.
It proposes five principles organized into a recursive framework for mechanistic inference.
The framework aims to make findings cumulative within models and precise enough to generate external, testable hypotheses.
Claims about what model mechanisms reveal about the broader world require evidence beyond MI.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A recursive logic for mechanistic inference. For a given neural system with behavior of interest, it can be investigated by different candidate objects of study: neurons, features, circuits, population geometry, and dynamics. We propose five principles to organize mechanistic research as a recursive process in which evidence informs further questions and revisions to earlier claims. An individual study may address a subset of these questions and revisit them as needed. Red arrows connect these five inferential questions: which object explains the phenomenon (P1), whether represented information is used in computation (P2), what computational role it plays (P3), how roles are organized (P4), and what remains invariant across conditions or implementations (P5; illustrated here across random seeds). Measurement choices constrain every inference (P0). A, B, and C denote computational roles. This process supports the discovery of candidate model mechanisms (within-model discovery), which can generate domain hypotheses and establish their plausibility beyond the model requires independent evidence (beyond-model discovery).

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a logic of inference for mechanistic interpretability, providing a framework for rigorous scientific discovery within neural network models.
papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
papers.tldr: Mechanistic interpretability needs a rigorous logic of inference to turn internal model observations into reliable, testable mechanistic explanations.

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors are commonly evaluated on real/fake classification alone, but real-world applications require explanations of the visual evidence behind each prediction. Joint vision-language models struggle with authenticity assessment, producing "real" narratives for manipulated images. To address this, we propose a decoupled predict-then-explain pipeline as our submission to the ACM Multimedia 2026 Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge, with methods trained and evaluated on the XPlainVerse benchmark. A vision-foundation-model ensemble first classifies the image, then a Qwen3-VL-8B model generates a decision-conditioned explanation of the visual evidence. For fake images, a second Qwen3-VL-8B compresses that text into a short non-expert summary without using the image. We further apply metric-aligned Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to optimize both explainers against the challenge criteria. Under matched conditions, GRPO raises complex BERTScore-F1 from 0.686 to 0.712 and also improves grounding (entity and evidence F1); our submission ranked first on complex BERTScore-F1 and seventh overall.
authors: Luka Dragar, Peter Peer, Vitomir \v{S}truc, Borut Batagelj
bullets: Addresses the gap between real/fake classification and explaining the visual evidence behind predictions.
Uses a vision-foundation-model ensemble for authenticity prediction, followed by a decision-conditioned Qwen3-VL-8B explainer.
Adds a second Qwen3-VL-8B to compress fake-image explanations into short, non-expert summaries without image access.
Metric-aligned GRPO improves complex BERTScore-F1 from 0.686 to 0.712 and also improves entity and evidence grounding F1.
Ranked first on complex BERTScore-F1 and seventh overall in the Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge.

papers.abstract: Video world models promise general-purpose interactive simulators, but their training is limited by action supervision: action labels are scarce, fragmented across incompatible specifications, and do not scale with the unlabeled video pretraining corpus. A common workaround jointly trains an action encoder to compress consecutive frames into a latent action and a decoder to reconstruct the next frame from the previous frame and that latent, forcing the latent to capture only new information. This has two limitations: learning the action space from scratch can limit generalization to unseen domains, and the bottleneck trades expressiveness for separation, with tighter settings losing nuance and looser ones risking scene leakage under domain shifts. We argue for a different starting point: rather than learning actions from scratch, we start from a pretrained foundation model (V-JEPA 2), whose embeddings of a frame pair already carry substantial action information after large-scale, diverse video pretraining. The remaining challenge is to extract the action while discarding the scene. We propose a label-free contrastive adaptation framework that pulls together frame pairs sharing the same motion under a different scene and pushes apart pairs from the same scene with different motion, reshaping the geometry of the pretrained space without imposing a reconstruction bottleneck. We introduce a unified evaluation protocol along three axes (action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned video generation quality) across robot manipulation, camera navigation, game, and driving benchmarks, most of which are unseen during adaptation. Compared with annotation-free latent-action methods, our representations are substantially more expressive while matching their scene invariance, and they yield world models that transfer demonstrated actions to new scenes more faithfully.
authors: Runjia Li, Minghao Chen, Junyu Xie, Philip Torr, Andrea Vedaldi, Tomas Jakab
bullets: Addresses scarce, fragmented action supervision in video world-model training.
Starts from V-JEPA 2 frame-pair embeddings instead of learning an action space from scratch.
Uses label-free contrastive adaptation: matches similar motion across scenes and separates different motion within a scene.
Evaluates action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned generation across robotics, navigation, games, and driving.
Reports more expressive representations with comparable scene invariance and better transfer of actions to new scenes than annotation-free latent-action methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed learning pipeline. Left: Contrastive action adaptation. An anchor frame pair (ot, ot+k) is encoded as a two-frame clip by the OnlyAct encoder ϕθ, a pretrained foundation model with low-rank adapters whose weights are shared across all branches. The positive keeps the action but changes the scene: the moving region of the anchor, found by optical flow, is cut out and pasted at a shifted location onto the background of a different scene (for moving cameras, a different photometric augmentation of the anchor is used instead). The hard negative is drawn from a non-overlapping window (ot′ , ot′+k) of the same video, sharing the scene but corresponding to a different action. In the action space, the anchor is pulled towards its positive and pushed away from its hard negative. Right: Action-conditioned video world model. The frozen OnlyAct encoder ϕθ maps consecutive frame pairs into the learned action space, yielding an action stream α1:t that conditions an autoregressive video world model Gψ. Given past frames o1:t and the action stream, Gψ predicts the next frame ot+1, and is rolled out autoregressively to generate subsequent frames.

papers.abstract: Adding abstention to a task-adapted multimodal model can discard correct answers, including capabilities acquired during adaptation. We formulate abstention repair as maximizing correct abstention on unanswerable questions under a budget on newly lost correct answers. We propose ReFrain (Regression-Free Abstention), which combines a linear probe on first-token logits, threshold calibration on held-out image clusters, and a deterministic veto that replaces rejected outputs with the displayed "none of the above" option while preserving all other responses. "Regression-free" denotes zero loss on the calibration set at the zero-budget target. All abstention methods in our main comparison start from the same answering-SFT checkpoint; we separately track lost correct answers, repaired errors, and retained SFT gains. On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, ReFrain at zero budget retains all 57 SFT-gained answers with no losses and improves correct abstention by 7.30 percentage points. At a 0.5% calibration budget, it reaches 74.05% correct abstention with 8 losses and retains 55 gains; CLIP-UP EmbLoRA reaches 64.65% with 62 losses, 41 repairs, and 40 retained gains. The same probe at its default threshold loses 298 correct answers. With models and thresholds frozen, confirmation on 228 independent question clusters yields 66.05% correct abstention and no losses at the 0.5% point, exceeding EmbLoRA by 32.72 percentage points. Ordinary refusal SFT achieves higher correct abstention at greater regression cost. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/ModeLiberaL/ReFrain.
bullets: Targets correct abstention on unanswerable questions under a budget for newly lost correct answers.
Combines a linear probe on first-token logits, image-cluster threshold calibration, and a deterministic “none of the above” veto.
At zero calibration budget on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, it retains all 57 SFT-gained answers with no losses and improves correct abstention by 7.30 percentage points.
At a 0.5% budget, it achieves 74.05% correct abstention with 8 losses and retains 55 SFT gains; independent confirmation gives 66.05% with no losses.
Ordinary refusal SFT attains higher abstention but with greater regression cost; results are reported under frozen models and thresholds.

papers.abstract: Remote-sensing foundation models increasingly unify representations across sensing modalities and downstream tasks, yet their prediction mechanisms remain largely task-specific. Separate decoders, prediction heads, and objectives leave prediction fragmented across tasks. This naturally raises a question: can heterogeneous remote-sensing tasks share the prediction process? UniFlow-RS answers this question with a single latent flow-matching predictor shared across tasks. This requires addressing two key challenges: unifying heterogeneous prediction spaces and harmonizing joint optimization across tasks. First, we cast heterogeneous task outputs into structured visual targets in a common latent space, allowing them to be modeled by the same pretrained flow predictor. Task-dependent conditioning further accommodates differences in input configurations. Second, we optimize all tasks with a common Flow Matching objective, eliminating task-specific prediction losses. To mitigate optimization mismatch across tasks and modalities, we introduce Task-Modality Adaptive Timestep Sampling (TMAS), which dynamically allocates training timesteps according to the online learning state of each task-modality group. Using a single shared model, UniFlow-RS handles six tasks and thirteen datasets, surpassing recent task-specific state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks while remaining competitive on the others. Beyond these benchmarks, the same checkpoint demonstrates strong zero-shot transfer across unseen datasets, task settings, occlusion conditions, and near-infrared false-color imagery, without target-specific adaptation.
authors: Jianlong He, Liang Liao, Jing Xiao, Chaofeng Chen, Gui-Song Xia
bullets: Addresses fragmented prediction caused by separate decoders, heads, and objectives across remote-sensing tasks.
Represents diverse outputs as structured visual targets in a shared latent space with task-dependent conditioning.
Trains all tasks using a common Flow Matching objective and introduces TMAS to balance task–modality optimization.
A single checkpoint supports six tasks and thirteen datasets, outperforming task-specific methods on several benchmarks and remaining competitive on others.
Shows zero-shot transfer to unseen datasets, task settings, occlusions, and near-infrared false-color imagery without target-specific adaptation.

papers.title: UniFlow-RS: Unified Generative Prediction for Heterogeneous Remote-Sensing Tasks

papers.abstract: Multimodal contrastive learning models such as CLIP are vulnerable to backdoor attacks with diverse trigger structures, ranging from localized patches to globally distributed perturbations, with recent attacks increasingly optimizing these triggers in the representation space. Existing post-hoc defenses based on clean fine-tuning may leave backdoors active, while trigger-inversion methods depend on accurately estimating the attack target and trigger. We observe that backdoored encoders exhibit structure-dependent representation sensitivity: global perturbations preferentially expose distributed backdoors, whereas local patch perturbations are more effective for localized backdoors. Based on this observation, we propose Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense (GARD), a target- and trigger-agnostic post-hoc defense. GARD optimizes complementary global and local adversarial probes to maximally displace clean-image representations, and then realigns the perturbed representations with detached clean anchors while preserving image-text alignment. The resulting model requires no additional computation at inference time. Across six visual backdoor attacks and two CLIP visual backbones, GARD reduces the attack success rate below 1% in all 12 evaluated attack-backbone combinations while maintaining competitive clean accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of adversarial representation probing for repairing backdoored multimodal contrastive encoders.
authors: Yuhong Wang, Yujun Cai, Lei Feng, Songze Li
bullets: Backdoors may use localized patches, global perturbations, or representation-space triggers, limiting conventional post-hoc defenses.
GARD exploits structure-dependent sensitivity: global probes target distributed backdoors, while local probes target localized ones.
The method realigns adversarially perturbed representations with detached clean anchors while preserving image–text alignment.
Across six attacks and two visual backbones, it reduced attack success below 1% in all 12 combinations while maintaining competitive clean accuracy.
GARD is target- and trigger-agnostic and adds no inference-time computation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of GARD. (c) GARD jointly performs complementary global and local adversarial probing and realigns perturbed representations with clean semantic anchors while preserving clean image–text alignment. (d) A single GARD framework effectively defends against both localized and distributed backdoor triggers without target estimation or trigger reconstruction.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses security vulnerabilities in multimodal contrastive learning models (CLIP) using a target- and trigger-agnostic adversarial representation defense.
papers.title: GARD: Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense against Backdoors in Multimodal Contrastive Learning Models

papers.abstract: Personalizing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) as intelligent assistants has recently emerged as an active research topic, where an MLLM is expected to go beyond generic, one-size-fits-all replies, and instead generate responses grounded in user-specific objects, entities, and concepts encountered during interactions. Nevertheless, existing studies mainly focus on personalizing MLLMs on a static, predefined set of personalized concepts and require users to manually and frequently extend this set to accommodate newly emerging concepts, which is infeasible in dynamic-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we recast conventional MLLM personalization as an Open-Set problem, and propose TAME-O, the first long-context open-set personalized MLLM assistant. Specifically, TAME-O introduces a training-free, plug-and-play Concept Reconciliation Skill (CR Skill). It enables the assistant to automatically unlock novel concepts during prolonged human-MLLM interactions while preventing confusion with previously unlocked ones, allowing the MLLM to continually grasp more and more concepts and progressively refine the modeling of known ones. Extensive experiments under the open-set personalization setting underscore the efficacy of our method.
authors: Rongpei Hong, Jian Lang, Ting Zhong, Fan Zhou
bullets: Existing personalization methods rely on a static concept set that users must manually update, limiting use in dynamic environments.
TAME-O is a long-context, open-set personalized MLLM assistant.
Its plug-and-play Concept Reconciliation Skill automatically unlocks novel concepts during extended interactions.
The method helps distinguish new concepts from previously learned ones while progressively refining known concepts.
Experiments in open-set personalization support the effectiveness of the approach.

papers.abstract: Understanding the progress of an activity requires tracking how the objects involved change over time. Object state readout provides this information by describing a target object's states and transitions across video frames. Although multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate detailed visual descriptions, these descriptions may leave the attributes needed to distinguish successive states insufficiently specified. In this paper, we propose look-ahead state readout (LASER), an anticipation-guided agent for object state readout that uses possible next-step changes to determine which attributes to inspect in the present. Given temporally ordered frames and a target object, LASER converts anticipated changes into targeted visual questions and inspects the current frame to establish attribute values. It then checks state readouts and forecasts against independent observations of subsequent frames, refining a state record used to generate the final description. Reusable textual observation skills guide this process and are refined by tracing discrepancies with reference captions to the responsible instructions. Candidate revisions are selected on separate videos based on improved caption quality without increased contradictions with reference facts. Model parameters remain frozen throughout adaptation and inference, and the revised skills remain fixed during evaluation. Experiment results and further analysis on OSCaR and PLM RCap show consistent improvements of LASER over strong baselines and existing approaches, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach.
bullets: Addresses underspecified attributes in multimodal language-model descriptions of changing object states.
Uses anticipated changes to generate targeted visual questions about the current frame.
Validates readouts and forecasts against later frames, then refines a state record for final descriptions.
Adapts reusable textual observation skills by tracing caption discrepancies, without updating model parameters.
Shows consistent improvements over strong baselines on OSCaR and PLM RCap, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual perception requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to locate and interpret subtle evidence within complex scenes. Constructing supervision for this ability is challenging: questions must have correct, unambiguous answers that depend on actual fine-grained visual details rather than coarse cues or language priors. Verifying these properties makes manual annotation labor-intensive and automatic generation difficult for models that themselves struggle with fine-grained perception. Yet the same models can often recognize such details once the region is zoomed in. We exploit this global-to-zoom perception gap and introduce ZoomGain, a data construction pipeline that constructs questions about the full image from visual information gained only by zooming in. It verifies each answer on the zoomed view with multiple models, ensures that each question remains unambiguous in the full image and cannot be answered from language priors, and specifically generates high-quality distractors for multiple-choice questions. With this pipeline and human-only screening (no manual QA editing), we build ZoomGainBench, a 1,000-question bilingual benchmark on which the best of 28 VLMs achieves only 61.08. Failure analysis reveals that models favor a particular type of distractor when answering multiple-choice questions incorrectly. Beyond evaluation, training on just 9K ZoomGain samples substantially improves the visual perception capabilities of our 4B/9B models, enabling them to outperform several hundred-billion-parameter models across various perception benchmarks. The trained 9B model achieves SoTA performance on several benchmarks, such as 90.25 on HR-Bench 4K. These results establish global-to-zoom perception gaps as a practical basis for scaling fine-grained visual supervision for both evaluation and training. Our code is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/ZoomGain.
authors: Haozhan Shen, Liangbo He, Jun Lan, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Tiancheng Zhao, Jianwei Yin
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of creating unambiguous questions that require genuine fine-grained visual evidence rather than coarse cues or language priors.
Uses a global-to-zoom pipeline to generate full-image questions, verify answers with multiple models, test ambiguity, and create challenging distractors.
Builds ZoomGainBench, a 1,000-question bilingual benchmark; the best of 28 evaluated VLMs scores 61.08.

Training on 9K ZoomGain samples substantially improves the authors’ 4B/9B models, with the 9B model reaching 90.25 on HR-Bench 4K and outperforming much larger models on reported perception benchmarks.
Human involvement is limited to screening without manual question-answer editing; remaining errors include models’ preference for a particular distractor type.

papers.selection_reason: Constructs fine-grained visual supervision for VLMs using global-to-zoom perception gaps, improving multimodal perception and training.
papers.title: ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision
papers.tldr: ZoomGain turns details visible only after zooming into high-quality supervision for training and evaluating fine-grained vision-language models.

papers.abstract: A vision-language model may take left-right direction from the orientation of image content within patches, its vision transformer's (ViT) position code, or token positions and order in its language model (LLM). Ablations show the ViT code is necessary; we test sufficiency by mirroring only a position code. In Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-4B and InternVL3-2B, mirroring ViT width positions reproduces the flipped-image answer on 84.3-93.2% of CV-Bench left-right questions (Qwen2.5-VL-3B: 87.5%, partly a left fallback). With two options, this also counts disruption; a half-grid shift flips most answers too. With the ViT code intact, LLM-side id and token-order mirrors change few left-right answers in all three series (a weak id test in Qwen2.5-VL). In Qwen2.5-VL-7B the effect sits in the global-attention ViT blocks, mostly the last. On What'sUp, flipping content and token order, not the position code, keeps more on/under than left-right answers at the flipped-image answer. Post hoc analyses qualify these results. On CV-Bench items with located objects, random permutations flip 18.9-31.0 points more answers when reversing the objects' order than when keeping it. On What'sUp, in Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL, the share of the left-right changes made by random permutations that land on the mirror relation is mostly below chance. Counted as returns to the original answer, the What'sUp contrast of support with left-right relations is clear only in InternVL3-2B. Most remaining errors give the same relation whichever object is asked about, suggesting that repair may target relation binding, object localization or use of the reference object.
authors: Enhao Cui, Junzhi Yang, Yaoshun Lin, Yuhan Feng, Zijian Chen
bullets: The study tests whether left/right judgments come from image content, ViT position codes, or language-model token positions.
Mirroring ViT width positions reproduces flipped-image answers on 84.3–93.2% of CV-Bench left/right questions across several Qwen and InternVL models.
The effect is concentrated in global-attention ViT blocks, especially the final block in Qwen2.5-VL-7B; shifting the position grid also changes many answers.
Mirroring LLM-side token IDs or order produces few left/right changes, whereas reversing object order substantially affects some CV-Bench answers.
What'sUp results qualify the finding: many errors appear tied to relation binding, object localization, or use of the reference object.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes spatial reasoning in VLMs via position-code counterfactuals, directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Where Do Vision-Language Models Get Left and Right? Position-Code Counterfactuals in Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL and InternVL3
papers.tldr: Mirroring a ViT’s horizontal position code often flips vision-language models’ left/right answers, while language-side position changes have little effect, though object order and relation binding also influence errors.

papers.abstract: Text-guided segmentation models receive an image and a short caption about the lesion, and on public benchmarks the caption improves accuracy considerably. On colonoscopy and breast ultrasound, however, the size, count and location words of each caption were computed from the mask that later scores the prediction, and the chest X-ray captions were written by benchmark annotators. We tested what two published models take from them. On colonoscopy and chest X-ray, it is mostly the lesion's extent. Keeping only the size word or the lung-zone phrase recovers 84 to 98 percent of the improvement over an empty caption, and removing it loses 52 to 77 percent. The rest matters little, and a polyp called a rock is segmented just as well. We call this extent leakage. On breast ultrasound, nearly half the captions also name the diagnosis, which carries part of the benefit. Retraining on three datasets shows that models pick up this habit from their training captions, though only partly on breast ultrasound, and that it weakens their segmentation from the image alone. The leak can be measured without training a model, since caption words alone predict lesion area (coefficient of determination 0.54 to 0.77 on six of seven test sets). Without the test mask, the best method we tested, which estimates extent from the image, reaches 74.59 Dice on colonoscopy against the published 77.23. We propose an evaluation protocol that keeps what a caption says about the image apart from what it copies from the label.
authors: Niran Nataraj, Ankita Das, C. Krishna Mohan, Kenji Kawashima
bullets: On colonoscopy and chest X-ray, size or lung-location words recover 84–98% of the gain over empty captions, while removing them loses 52–77%.
Semantic content contributes little in these settings; even replacing a polyp description with “rock” yields similar segmentation.
Breast ultrasound captions partly benefit from diagnosis terms, but extent leakage remains present.
Models learn this shortcut from training captions, which can weaken their image-only segmentation ability.
Caption words alone predict lesion area, and an image-based extent estimate reaches 74.59 Dice on colonoscopy versus 77.23 for the published method.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes extent leakage from annotation-derived prompts in vision-language medical image segmentation, directly relevant to multimodal foundation-model behavior and evaluation.
papers.title: Counterfactual Analysis of Extent Leakage from Annotation-Derived Prompts in Vision-Language Medical Image Segmentation
papers.tldr: Caption-based gains in medical image segmentation are often driven by leaked lesion-extent information copied from annotation masks rather than by meaningful visual descriptions.

papers.abstract: Under a fixed frame budget, video understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) depends on whether the sampled frames provide sufficient evidence for the question. Sufficient frame evidence supports direct answering, whereas less informative observations may benefit from reasoning that connects the available cues. We introduce EVAThink, which enhances video understanding through evidence sufficiency-guided training for adaptive thinking. First, Recoverable Evidence Gap Mining constructs evidence-dense and evidence-sparse video views that share the same question and answer under an identical frame budget. It retains pairs where sparse views yield lower direct-answer accuracy than dense views but benefit from explicit reasoning, providing supervision for response-mode selection. Second, Evidence-Guided Two-Stage Reinforcement Learning uses stage-specific rewards to guide training with evidence-based mode preferences and then refine response efficiency, while first-token advantage regularization mitigates mode collapse. Trained on only 6.7K curated samples, EVAThink consistently improves upon the base model across video understanding benchmarks under both 32- and 64-frame budgets, while outperforming strong baselines on average. The code, model, and datasets are available at \href{https://github.com/ChangtiWu/EVAThink}{EVAThink}.
authors: Changti Wu, Ruizhe Fan, Bin Wang, Lei Zhang, Yuxiang Zhang
bullets: Addresses fixed-frame video understanding when sampled views may contain sparse or insufficient evidence.
Mines paired dense and sparse video views with the same question and answer to supervise response-mode selection.
Uses two-stage, evidence-guided reinforcement learning to first encourage appropriate thinking modes and then improve response efficiency.
First-token advantage regularization helps prevent collapse to a single response mode.
Trained on 6.7K curated samples, it consistently improves the base model across benchmarks at 32- and 64-frame budgets and outperforms strong baselines on average.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of EVAThink. Recoverable Evidence Gap Mining constructs the evidence-contrastive pairs through video cropping or concatenation, retaining pairs with a direct-answer accuracy gap and a reasoning gain on the sparse view. Evidence-Guided TwoStage Reinforcement Learning first trains response-mode selection using preferences derived from evidence-contrastive pairs, then refines response efficiency on the remaining pairs, using stage-specific rewards and first-token advantage regularization.

Figure 5. Case studies of adaptive thinking: EVAThink avoids unnecessary reasoning (left), prevents reasoning-induced errors through direct answering (middle), and resolves errors through evidence-grounded reasoning (right).

Figure 1. Motivation for evidence sufficiency-guided training for adaptive thinking. For the same question and frame budget, sufficient frame evidence supports direct answering, while thinking can help make better use of limited frame evidence.

papers.abstract: Three-dimensional scene graphs (3DSGs) can provide robots with persistent metric-semantic representations for spatial reasoning, but the existing methods have primarily been developed for indoor and terrestrial environments. In this paper we investigate how a representative outdoor open-vocabulary method transfers to maritime environments and which adaptations are needed. Our experiments show that zero-shot representative outdoor 3DSG descriptions agree with our labeled ground truth for a majority of geometry-supported objects on our data, but the resulting map exhibits considerable physical-entity fragmentation, and its terrestrial higher-level assumptions don't capture maritime spatial organization needs. We therefore keep the underlying mapping method and post-process its accumulated evidence. We show a metric-semantic consolidation method followed by geometry-grounded multi-view vision-language model (VLM) reasoning that reconciles remaining fragments into physical entities and groups entities through observations into local places. In parallel, we construct maritime macro regions using map priors and onboard water and structure observations, and associate them with the local places. The resulting representation reduces physical-entity fragmentation beyond both the baseline and our geometry-semantic consolidation component alone, supports correspondence of fixed local places across repeated maritime traversals, and improves contextual retrieval on our reviewed queries over tested baselines. These results show how an outdoor open-vocabulary map can be adapted into persistent maritime scene memory with our methods for object/place identity and spatial abstractions.
authors: Kim Alexander Christensen, Dina Zimmermann, Martin Steinert, Eleni Kelasidi
bullets: A representative outdoor 3D scene-graph method transfers reasonably to maritime environments for many geometry-supported objects, but produces substantial physical-entity fragmentation.
The method preserves the underlying mapper and post-processes accumulated evidence to consolidate fragments using metric-semantic cues and geometry-grounded multi-view VLM reasoning.
Consolidated entities are grouped into local places, while maritime macro regions are built from map priors and onboard water and structure observations.
The resulting representation reduces fragmentation, supports matching fixed local places across repeated traversals, and improves contextual retrieval on reviewed queries over tested baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the maritime scene-memory pipeline. It first accumulates persistent map fragments and their observation histories, followed by a conservative geometricsemantic consolidation. Selected geometrically grounded multi-view observations are then processed by a visionlanguage model (VLM) at two abstraction levels: physicalentity reconciliation decides which fragments belong to the same object, while place formation groups persistent entities and observations into meaningful local places. In parallel, coarse maritime regions are derived from geographic topology and onboard water/structure evidence. Local places are associated with these regions and corresponding places are related across repeated traversals, forming a persistent scene memory for contextual retrieval.
Fig. 3: Macro regions compared. The first is defined by [39] while P00 and P03 are from our method. The regions are largely consistent, with one small extra region in P03.

Fig. 4: Place persistence and retrieval at the Northern port quay. The same fixed setting is matched despite different vessel occupancy and reconstructed geometry. Place relations retrieve 6/6 reviewed vessel records across P00 and P03, compared with 3/6 for the 50m radius baseline centered at the P00 anchor location in both surveys.

papers.tldr: Adapting open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs with geometry-semantic consolidation and maritime spatial abstractions enables more persistent, coherent scene memory for robots operating across repeated maritime traversals.

papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that pretrained image generators can support diverse visual tasks. Yet directly applying them to language-guided unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) segmentation exposes a key limitation: a plausible mask may correspond to the wrong instance among small and repeated objects. We call this mismatch between mask rendering and expression-level target selection the Grounding-Rendering Gap. We present DroneSegEdit, which combines RGB proposal rendering with language-grounded, proposal-constrained verification to select supported foreground while retaining rendered geometry. DroneSegEdit adapts the open-weight LongCat-Image-Edit model using task-specific LoRA and fixed color-to-label decoding. For referring segmentation, a Language-Grounded Spatial Verifier (LGSV) reads hierarchical states from the frozen multimodal large language model backbone to derive expression-conditioned spatial evidence, which is mapped back to the rendered proposal without introducing foreground outside it. On RIS-LAD, DroneSegEdit reaches a new state of the art at 52.78 mIoU, 7.16 points above the previous best. It remains competitive overall on UAVid-RIS and VDD-RIS, with its clearest class-wise gains on compact, application-relevant categories, notably vehicles and humans. A separate verifier-free experiment extends the RGB interface to full-scene parsing: a task-specific adapter jointly renders all classes from one task-level instruction without enumerating class names or palette colors.
authors: Dehua Chen, Long Xin, Jiangtao Wei
bullets: Addresses the Grounding-Rendering Gap: visually plausible masks can target the wrong small or repeated object.
Uses RGB proposal rendering plus proposal-constrained language verification, preserving rendered geometry while filtering unsupported foreground.
Adapts LongCat-Image-Edit with task-specific LoRA and fixed color-to-label decoding.
Achieves 52.78 mIoU on RIS-LAD, 7.16 points above the previous best, and shows notable gains for vehicles and humans.
Also demonstrates verifier-free full-scene parsing from a single task-level instruction.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks underpin fundamental tasks in a wide range of signal domains, such as image, audio, and language processing. However, their internal mechanisms are notably difficult to interpret. Internal activations are structured signals transformed across layers that may encode a multitude of interdependent relationships, as individual neurons frequently represent multiple underlying concepts. Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover the internal mechanisms of neural networks by identifying components whose activations are causally responsible for specific behaviors. In such a context, this article provides an overview of advances in mechanistic interpretability for the analysis of causal inference in deep neural networks.
authors: Lorenzo Cirillo, Irene Amerini, Andrea Cavallaro
bullets: Deep neural networks are difficult to interpret because their layered activations encode complex, interdependent relationships.
Individual neurons may represent multiple concepts, complicating direct interpretation.
Mechanistic interpretability analyzes components whose activations are causally responsible for model behaviors.
The article reviews advances, methods, and frameworks for causal analysis across image, audio, and language-processing systems.

Fig. 6.
