papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models are pretrained on satellite and aerial imagery, but whether such an encoder beats a strong generic one for few-label land-use/land-cover mapping remains unclear, as prior comparisons rarely isolate the pretraining data. We study five matched pairs of Earth-observation (EO) and generic encoders sharing objective and architecture (DINO/SatDINO, DINOv3/DINOv3-SAT, MAE/SatMAE, MAE/Scale-MAE, CLIP/RemoteCLIP) within a benchmark of 14 frozen encoders on five RGB scene-classification datasets (0.06-30 m GSD). With native preprocessing, we evaluate k-NN, linear and attentive probes and image retrieval over six low-label splits, using paired per-image significance tests. EO pretraining is not uniformly helpful: on most datasets and metrics, it significantly improves three pairs (SatDINO, Scale-MAE, RemoteCLIP, the latter evaluated only on unseen datasets) and significantly hurts two (linear probe: DINOv3-SAT by up to 22.5 points, SatMAE by up to 8.8), with opposite outcomes even for two MAEs pretrained on the same fMoW-RGB imagery. These effects are robust to patch-token pooling and attentive probing, concentrate on small man-made objects, and are largest with 1-5% labels. Across encoders, the silhouette score of frozen embeddings predicts k-NN accuracy and retrieval mAP almost perfectly (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.96$ on four of five datasets). Pretraining on satellite imagery is thus not a reliable selection criterion; candidate checkpoints must be validated on target data.
authors: Sandarbh Agrawal, Rakshith Sathish, Ashwathi Nambiar
bullets: Compares five architecture- and objective-matched EO/generic encoder pairs among 14 frozen encoders across five RGB scene-classification datasets and six low-label splits.
Tests k-NN, linear and attentive probes, and image retrieval using native preprocessing and paired per-image significance tests.
EO pretraining significantly helps some pairs but hurts others—even for MAEs pretrained on the same fMoW-RGB imagery.
Effects are strongest with 1–5% labels, concentrate on small man-made objects, and persist across token pooling and attentive probing.
Frozen-embedding silhouette score strongly predicts k-NN accuracy and retrieval performance on four of five datasets.

papers.title: Satellite Pretraining Is Not One Thing: A Matched-Pair Study of Generic and Earth-Observation Foundation Models for Scene Classification

papers.abstract: Multimodal remote sensing pretraining commonly relies on exact instance-level correspondence across modalities, implicitly treating strictly paired observations as a prerequisite for learning transferable representations. In this work, we revisit this assumption by relaxing cross-modal correspondence from the instance level to the semantic level. We introduce Semantic Pairing (SemPair), a pairing-relaxed pretraining strategy that replaces exact instance pairs with class-consistent cross-instance pairs. To characterize the effect of correspondence relaxation, we formulate a latent-factor model that separates cross-modal dependence into shared semantic structure and instance-specific correlation, showing that SemPair preserves the former while marginalizing instance-specific cross-modal correlations in expectation. We further introduce Mixed Pairing (MixPair) as a controlled interpolation between semantic and exact pairing to study correspondence granularity along a continuous spectrum. Extensive experiments consistently show that SemPair achieves transfer performance comparable to exact pairing (ExaPair), while MixPair reveals a non-monotonic relationship between downstream transfer and the instance-pairing ratio. These results demonstrate that exact instance correspondence is not a prerequisite for effective multimodal remote sensing pretraining and establish cross-modal correspondence granularity as an important design dimension for transferable multimodal representation learning. More broadly, this finding suggests a practical route toward scaling multimodal pretraining with reduced dependence on costly instance-aligned data.
authors: Xianping Ma, Yu Zhang, Mingzhe Jiang, Wanxin Xie, Qing Zhu, Nan Xu, Xiaokang Zhang, Yuanxin Ye
bullets: Reframes cross-modal pairing from exact instance alignment to class-consistent semantic alignment.
Uses a latent-factor analysis to show semantic structure is preserved while instance-specific correlations are averaged out.
Introduces MixPair to continuously control the degree of exact versus semantic pairing.
Experiments find SemPair performs comparably to exact pairing, while transfer varies non-monotonically with the exact-pair ratio.
Suggests reducing reliance on costly instance-aligned multimodal data for scalable pretraining.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents offer strong multimodal reasoning and perception, but they struggle to provide the evidence required for high-stakes verification. To address these limitations, we propose DisasterAgent, an evidence-driven agent that uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow to generate verifiable disaster reports from bitemporal optical imagery. DisasterAgent first invokes a specialized vision expert toolkit in the perception phase to build a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (STPG), serving as a structured memory to store and organize disaster-induced changes across space and time. Evidence-based Augmentation (EA) then extracts evidence from the STPG, attaching inline citations that form a closed evidence loop from each statement to the supporting visual evidence. Extensive experiments on the DisasterM3 and RSCC benchmarks demonstrate that DisasterAgent consistently outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents. Notably, compared with the original model, it improves the average score for disaster report generation on DisasterM3 by 13.5\% and ST5-SCS on RSCC by 15.34\%, providing a more accurate and verifiable solution for disaster emergency response. The code will be available at https://github.com/ZhijianLi2003/DisasterAgent.
authors: Zhijian Li, Jiawei Song, Chao Ren, Yidan Zhang, Peijin Wang, Xian Sun, Kun Fu
bullets: Addresses the lack of verifiable evidence in report-level disaster assessment using vision-language models and agents.
Uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow over bitemporal optical imagery.
Builds a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph to organize disaster-related changes across space and time.
Extracts graph evidence and attaches inline citations, creating a link from each report statement to supporting imagery.
Outperforms compared baselines on DisasterM3 and RSCC, with reported gains of 13.5% and 15.34% on the respective metrics.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The overall architecture of DisasterAgent. The framework processes multimodal inputs through two primary stages. (1) Skill Routing: Driven by the VLM’s interpretation of the query, the system dynamically routes to appropriate skills within a pre-defined repository and seamlessly registers the required functional tools. (2) Skill-Guided Workflow: Guided by the registered skills, the framework sequentially executes a three-step pipeline comprising Perception, Evidence-based Augmentation, and Generation.

Fig. 4. Illustration of the SCE extraction pipeline. The VLM first reasons over the STPG to generate atomic factual claims. Each claim is then independently verified against the raw bitemporal images to obtain a confidence score. Finally, claims with scores above the threshold are filtered to form the robust SCE set.

papers.abstract: We present Walrus, a unified 8B speech-and-audio foundation model handling speech recognition (including code-switching and multi-talker speech), speech-to-text and speech-to-speech translation, text-to-speech, emotion recognition, audio captioning, and general audio understanding. Our main contribution is not a new architecture but a data-centric training recipe; we use a standard decoder-only backbone initialized from Gemma 4, so that gains can be traced to the data. For speech generation, Walrus predicts low-bitrate discrete speech tokens, and a lightweight token-to-waveform decoder converts them into high-fidelity audio. The recipe is a three-stage data curriculum that moves from broad multilingual data to multi-talker, code-switching, and domain-specific data. At each stage, task-aware and dataset-aware weighting balances tasks with very different token budgets and protects core skills from forgetting. Trained on over 600M samples covering more than 20 tasks and 100 languages, Walrus leads on most multilingual, multi-talker, and code-switching ASR, speech translation, and audio understanding benchmarks, outperforming both open speech language models of comparable size and dedicated task-specific models. On most benchmarks, it even matches or surpasses the $4\times$ larger Qwen3-Omni's performance. Results suggest that data engineering is a primary driver of quality in multi-task speech and audio modeling.
authors: Alkis Koudounas, Osamu Take, Hayato Futami, Quentin Jodelet, Emiru Tsunoo
bullets: Handles ASR, code-switching and multi-talker speech, speech translation, TTS, emotion recognition, audio captioning, and general audio understanding.
Uses a standard Gemma 4-initialized decoder-only backbone; the main innovation is training data and curriculum design rather than architecture.
Trains on over 600M samples spanning 20+ tasks and 100 languages, with staged data expansion and task- and dataset-aware weighting.
Reports leading performance on most multilingual, multi-talker, and code-switching benchmarks, often matching or exceeding the much larger Qwen3-Omni.
Scope: results emphasize the importance of data engineering for multi-task speech and audio modeling; the abstract does not specify individual benchmark scores.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Walrus, our most capable SpeechLLM yet. Input speech is encoded by the USM encoder into continuous representations, which are passed to the decoder-only Gemma 4 backbone together with a natural-language task prompt. For recognition, translation, and understanding tasks, the backbone generates text. For TTS and S2ST, it generates discrete speech tokens at 25 Hz (325 bits per second), which a VQ decoder and a Vocos-based vocoder convert into a waveform. The vocoder is also conditioned on the source speech to transfer speaker identity and prosody.

Figure 3: Training data composition of Walrus. Recognition dominates the mix (45%), followed by translation (27%) and understanding (21%), while generation is deliberately kept small (7%). The detailed breakdown shows that standard ASR and instruction-following data anchor the recognition and understanding families. This distribution reflects our data-centric design: core recognition is heavily represented to protect it from forgetting, while token-heavy generative tasks are downweighted.

Figure 2: Walrus against the best previous system (among AF3, Gemma4, Qwen2.5-Omni7B, Phi4-MM) across recognition, translation, and understanding benchmarks. Scores are normalized so that higher is better (ASR and CS-ASR shown as word/character accuracy, translation as BLEU or ASR-BLEU, understanding as accuracy, captioning as CLAP-Sim×100). Both Walrus variants advance the frontier on most axes, and the Research variant extends it further, most notably on code-switching, internal entertainment ASR, and audio understanding.

papers.abstract: Answering spatial questions about multi-source scenes requires a model both to identify each sound and to locate it. Existing spatial audio-language models obtain spatial information from a dedicated encoder, which separates spatial and semantic processing into distinct feature spaces. We study whether a general-audio codec trained without spatial supervision can serve both purposes. A controlled layer-wise analysis shows that the frozen codec retains spatial information, with lateral cues carried by the difference between the two ear channels. This information, however, is not readily accessible: in dual-source scenes, a model trained on these features predicts left/right at chance and, on the remaining axes, assigns the detected direction to the queried and the non-queried source equally often. We attribute this failure to an audio--text information asymmetry, in which the audio contains both sources while the answer describes only the queried one. A controlled $2\times2$ experiment shows that either completing the scene description or exposing the inter-channel difference lifts left/right accuracy above chance, whereas binding directions to the queried source requires both. Building on these findings, AURA keeps the codec and the language model frozen and exceeds the strongest dedicated system on SpatialSoundQA by 10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy, with about 40\% of its trainable parameters.
authors: Boyan Han, Xiaoyan Wang, Zhe Sun, Ziqi Wang, Yujun Cai, Hongli Cao, Yiwei Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Liang An
bullets: A general-audio codec retains spatial information despite being trained without spatial supervision, with lateral cues encoded in the left–right channel difference.
Naively using these features fails in dual-source scenes because audio describes both sources while the answer refers to only the queried one.
A controlled 2×2 study finds that complete scene descriptions or exposing inter-channel differences improves left/right accuracy; both are needed for source-direction binding.

AURA freezes both the codec and language model, yet surpasses the strongest dedicated system on SpatialSoundQA by 10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy with about 40% of its trainable parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 5: AURA architecture. (a) Existing dedicated spatial pathways and general-audio pathways are separate and rely on different feature spaces, so features cannot be shared for unified perception. (b) AURA provides a shared, frozen general-audio codec representation that unifies perception in a single audio feature space. (c) Details of the AURA pipeline: for each ear, RVQ layers L0–L2 and L3–L7 are summed into content-oriented (S) and acoustic-oriented (A) bands, and adding the band-wise interaural difference yields six slots. A shared projector maps these slots to audio tokens for the language model, which generates a scene description and, for relation questions, a geometric analysis before the final answer.

Each map is normalized to its own maximum.

These comparisons reveal that the increasing sensitivity to interaural and room changes in deeper RVQ layers is not specific to X-Codec.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for multimodal and embodied tasks, yet aggregate accuracy or consistency alone does not reveal whether a judge changes its verdict for the right reason. We propose State-Conditional Invariance (SCI), a reliability principle requiring a judge to remain stable under semantics-preserving changes in presentation while responding to causal interventions that change the task outcome. We instantiate SCI in GridWM-Judge, a simulator-grounded diagnostic benchmark built from deterministic MiniGrid trajectories with aligned Full, evidence-removal, and counterfactual variants, plus presentation and representation probes. Across five diagnostic tasks, GridWM-Judge tests local perception, action-conditioned transitions, presentation stability, representation exchangeability, and Full-CF causal discrimination. Our diagnostic evaluations reveal heterogeneous failure modes, including sensitivity to evidence presentation and encoding, low activation on successful trajectories, and weak paired counterfactual discrimination. Perception-controlled analyses further indicate that visual grounding and objective recovery are substantial, model-dependent bottlenecks. These results motivate jointly reporting correctness, presentation stability, and causal sensitivity instead of relying on a single score.
authors: Qinan Zhang, Xinyu Wang, Qihang Jin, Tianyuan Wang, Hongbing Luo, Pengfei Li, Wenjun Lv, Yu Kang, Jian Di
bullets: Aggregate accuracy and consistency can miss whether a VLM judge changes its verdict for the correct reason.
State-Conditional Invariance (SCI) requires presentation stability under semantics-preserving changes and causal sensitivity to outcome-changing interventions.
GridWM-Judge uses deterministic MiniGrid trajectories with full, evidence-removal, counterfactual, presentation, and representation variants.
Five diagnostic tasks expose failures in evidence presentation, encoding, successful-trajectory activation, and paired counterfactual discrimination.
Results support jointly reporting correctness, presentation stability, and causal sensitivity.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of GridWM-Judge. The framework integrates simulator-based exam generation, VLM judging, and automatic scoring to assess four SCI diagnostic conditions (C1–C4). Ground-truth metadata are hidden from judges and used for scoring. The example illustrates that presentation consistency alone does not guarantee causal discrimination or reliable judging.

Figure 7: Dataset generation pipeline from environment seed to validated exam item. Each seed first produces a successful Full rollout; the aligned NoCue and CF variants are then constructed, validated, and converted into task-specific exam items. papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) have opened up new possibilities for generating rich interleaved text-image content. However, they generally lack native support for coordinating the two modalities, and translating coarse user requests into coherent multimodal compositions also requires explicit planning. We propose UniWeaver, a structured, model-agnostic harness framework that integrates multimodal planning, generation, and visual feedback to produce coherent interleaved outputs. To train UMMs for this task, we construct UniWeaver-10K, a dataset of 10,000 tasks across 20 task families, paired with execution trajectories guided by UniWeaver. We also introduce UniWeaver-Bench, a task-oriented benchmark systematically assessing text coverage, writing quality, visual coverage, and image-text alignment. Experiments show that UniWeaver achieves state-of-the-art performance and improves interleaved text-image generation across multiple UMM backbones.
authors: Hongxu Chen, Zixuan Zhong, Donghao Zhou, Haodong Li, Xiaomin Yu, Tianhao Li, Shiyao Yu, Zhongwei Wan, Pheng-Ann Heng
bullets: Addresses UMMs’ limited native coordination between text and image modalities and their difficulty translating coarse requests into coherent compositions.

papers.abstract: Open-Vocabulary Scene Graph Generation (OV-SGG) requires models to recognize visual relationships beyond the training vocabulary, yet existing methods often rely on dataset-specific object--predicate co-occurrence patterns. Under long-tailed distributions and noisy object localization, such reliance leads to biased, entangled relation representations, limiting both rare-relation recognition and generalization to unseen predicates. To address these challenges, we propose RaRe, a reasoning-aware relational representation learning framework that transforms MLLM-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales into structured relation embeddings. Rather than using CoT only as an intermediate reasoning trace for final prediction, RaRe directly optimizes the rationale-derived representation space to improve inter-relation discriminability. Specifically, RaRe first aligns rationale embeddings with textualized relation descriptions through self-supervised contrastive learning, and then refines rationale generation with a specificity-oriented reinforcement learning objective that encourages semantically object-pair-specific relational evidence. Experiments on VG150 and PSG demonstrate improved category-balanced recognition over existing baselines, while the additional gains from learning vary across datasets and proposal settings. Code available at: https://artanic30.github.io/project_pages/RaRe.
authors: Jiawei Xiao, Boya Wang, Longtian Qiu, Shan Ning, Xuming He

Experiments on VG150 and PSG show improved category-balanced recognition over existing baselines.
Additional gains vary across datasets and proposal settings.

papers.abstract: Event cameras record asynchronous changes in brightness. To use a general visual model as a recording trigger, a system must represent these measurements in a form the model can interpret. We compare direct grayscale accumulation, two temporal encodings, and two intensity reconstructors on paired real event data. On 192 windows from four held-out DSEC recordings, thresholds calibrated only on development data yielded 40 of 52 person detections and 12 of 140 background positives with E2VID. The strongest direct temporal encoding at an admissible fixed cutoff yielded 14 detections and seven background positives. A retrospective comparison at a common 10% background-positive cap yielded 40 detections for E2VID and at most 19 for any direct encoding. FireNet+ had lower preparation cost and produced 21 detections with zero observed background positives at its frozen cutoff. On the same 192 windows, Qwen3-VL-4B yielded 33/52, 2/140 with E2VID and 9/52, 9/140 with the highest-recall direct rendering, the three-bin image (person detections, background positives). A 96-second exploratory replay illustrates the sensitivity of episode capture and recording starts to cutoff selection. The experiments identify a detection benefit from reconstruction under controlled input history and distinguish it from the cost and false starts of continuous triggering.

With Qwen3-VL-4B, E2VID achieved 33/52 person detections and 2/140 background positives; the best direct rendering achieved 9/52 and 9/140.

A replay study shows that cutoff selection strongly influences episode capture and recording starts.

papers.abstract: Automated segmentation in multi-view echocardiography is essential for comprehensive cardiac assessment, yet remains challenging due to substantial anatomical and appearance variability across standard acoustic windows. In this paper, we present P2Echo, a unified framework capable of segmenting diverse cardiac structures across multiple standard echocardiographic views using a single model controlled by structured view-aware text prompts. Unlike recent foundation model adaptations that rely on implicit latent priors, P2Echo explicitly conditions the segmentation process via a novel Dynamic Image-Text Alignment (DyITA) module. DyITA integrates a differentiable routing mechanism and token differential operators to dynamically modulate decoder features according to the requested view and target structure. This allows the network to adaptively switch its processing pathways for different views without architectural changes. Extensive experiments on a large-scale internal dataset (seen during training) and held-out evaluation on three external datasets demonstrate that P2Echo matches or exceeds both view-specific specialists and state-of-the-art universal models at a fraction of their computational cost, offering an efficient, controllable solution for multi-plane cardiac analysis. Code is available at: https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/P2Echo.

papers.abstract: Hyperbolic vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as a rapidly growing area of research, reporting strong zero-shot performance alongside an interpretable embedding space in which radius orders representations by generality. But how hyperbolic are hyperbolic VLMs in practice? We investigate this at the exponential map, the single operation through which curvature enters an otherwise Euclidean network. We show that across MERU, HyCoCLIP, ARGENT, and PHyCLIP, the exponential map is well approximated by the identity function, i.e., pairwise distances and angles in the pre-map Euclidean space barely change under projection, and removing the map at inference leaves evaluation scores unchanged. Motivated by this observation, we train Euclidean VLMs on CC3M from scratch under the same hierarchy losses. Over roughly the final 90% of the training steps, the training statistics are nearly indistinguishable from those of their hyperbolic counterparts, and the resulting models match the evaluation scores and recover the same radial distributions. Our findings establish Euclidean space as a sufficient substrate for hierarchical vision-language learning as it is currently practiced, and motivate new paradigms in which hyperbolic geometry can deliver on its theoretical promise. Code is available at https://github.com/fbyrman/hyperbolic-vlms.
authors: Freek Byrman, Partha Das, Stijn Verdenius, Pascal Mettes
bullets: Analyzes the exponential map, the main point where curvature enters hyperbolic VLMs.

Euclidean VLMs trained with the same hierarchy losses match hyperbolic models’ training behavior, scores, and radial distributions.
The results suggest current hierarchical VLMs do not yet exploit hyperbolic geometry’s theoretical advantages.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models widely adopt Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (MRoPE), an extension of Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) that incorporates temporal, height, and width axes to encode the spatial structure of visual tokens. However, MRoPE also assigns height and width coordinates to text tokens that lack inherent spatial structure, introducing spatial positional effects into text-vision attention. Existing MRoPE variants explore different frequency allocations and coordinate layouts, with their designs suggesting different intuitions about these cross-modal effects: they may provide useful spatial references for associating language with visual regions, or introduce unnecessary positional preferences that hinder text-vision interactions. In this work, we disentangle intra-visual spatial structure from cross-modal spatial effects to investigate this question. We identify a constraint of shared coordinate layouts that prevents eliminating cross-modal spatial effects while preserving intra-visual spatial encoding, and develop controlled experiments to isolate their respective contributions. Our results across multiple model scales, MRoPE variants, and benchmarks show that cross-modal spatial effects provide little additional benefit as spatial references and can even impair model performance, while intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained grounding.
authors: Zhaoyi Liu, Haichuan Zhang, Xiaochuan Gong, Yancheng Zhu, Bowei Tian, Wanghao Ye, Yufan Zhang, Ang Li
bullets: MRoPE assigns spatial coordinates to both visual and text tokens, potentially affecting text–vision attention.
The work separates intra-visual spatial structure from cross-modal spatial effects to study their distinct roles.
It identifies a limitation of shared coordinate layouts that prevents removing cross-modal effects without also losing visual spatial encoding.
Controlled experiments across model scales, MRoPE variants, and benchmarks find that spatial references for text tokens provide little benefit and can impair performance.
Intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained visual grounding.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of attention-specific coordinate assignments for disentangling cross-modal and intra-visual spatial effects. (a) Two coordinate assignments for visual patches. The original coordinates pa = (timg, ha, wa) preserve each patch’s spatial location, while the neutral coordinates p̃a = (timg, h̃, w̃) assign identical height and width coordinates to all patches within an image. Here, h̃ = w̃ = timg for the diagonal text layout. (b) Attention-specific coordinate assignments. Independently selecting original or neutral coordinates for text-vision (T-V) and vision-vision (V-V) attention yields four controlled configurations, while text coordinates and text-text (T-T) attention remain unchanged. (c) Geometric view on the (h,w) plane. In the w/o T-V Spatial configuration, original coordinates preserve spatial relationships among visual patches in V-V attention, while neutral coordinates yield identical relative rotations between any text token and all visual patches in T-V attention. This enables independent evaluation of the two spatial effects.

papers.abstract: Accurate localization of abnormalities in three-dimensional (3D) CT scans is essential for linking automated predictions with clinically relevant pathological findings. We propose Uni-Loc, a vision-language framework that unifies pathology classification and 3D localization using scan-level supervision. Uni-Loc derives both predictions and localization maps from spatial similarities between pathology-conditioned queries and image features. A token-to-voxel upsampling module enables high-resolution localization, while gradient-guided thresholding identifies pathology regions without additional learned parameters. Evaluated on five localization tasks comprising 355 annotated CT scans, Uni-Loc achieves macro-averaged voxel-level AUROC/AUPR of 96.1\%/34.5\%, outperforming relevance propagation (80.7%/13.9%) and gradient saliency (88.7%/8.1%). Uni-Loc also achieves classification AUROC of 88.39% on CT-RATE and 78.03% on RAD-ChestCT, improving over a matched baseline. These results demonstrate effective 3D pathology localization without requiring pathology-specific voxel-level supervision.
authors: Hao-Chih Lee, Zahi A. Fayad, Xueyan Mei
bullets: Addresses the challenge of clinically meaningful 3D pathology localization from weak, scan-level supervision.
Generates pathology predictions and localization maps from pathology-conditioned query–image feature similarities.
Uses token-to-voxel upsampling for high-resolution maps and gradient-guided thresholding without extra learned parameters.
Across five tasks and 355 annotated CT scans, achieves 96.1% voxel-level AUROC and 34.5% AUPR, outperforming the compared saliency methods.
Reports classification AUROCs of 88.39% on CT-RATE and 78.03% on RAD-ChestCT, improving over a matched baseline.

papers.abstract: In remote inference, edge devices transmit high-resolution images over wireless links to a receiver, where an artificial intelligence (AI) model answers task-specific questions about these images to enable reliable decisions. These answers are often determined by a small set of task-causal pixels, such as those of text, whose corruption changes the answer, so these pixels must be delivered with high fidelity. Conventional transmission protects every pixel equally, so it either consumes many resource elements (REs) or corrupts these regions at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). To overcome these limitations, in this paper, a zero-shot, domain-agnostic framework, termed semantic-criticality tiered allocation of resources (STAR), is proposed. In particular, a per-pixel semantic-criticality indicator (SCI) is derived from the attention of a frozen vision-language model, so new tasks and domains are handled by changing only the prompt, without retraining. The resulting task causality-aware resource allocation problem over protection tiers is solved exactly by a threshold rule on the SCI, realized by a coded tier for the task-causal pixels and an uncoded, downsampled base layer for the full image. Simulations over a 5G New Radio link demonstrate that STAR attains a semantic accuracy of at least 0.98 for $E_s/N_0 \geq -4$ dB and, at comparable semantic reliability, reduces the REs of robust coded transmission by 59.5% and 91.5% on factory- and vehicle-monitoring datasets, respectively, the latter without any change to the models. Although a deep joint source-channel coding baseline uses fewer REs at comparable semantic accuracy, it must be retrained with labeled data for every new task or domain.
authors: Albert Shaju, Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas, Mingzhe Chen
bullets: Targets remote image inference where only a small set of task-causal pixels determines the AI answer.
Derives a per-pixel semantic-criticality indicator from a frozen vision-language model, adapting to new tasks or domains through prompts rather than retraining.
Solves tiered resource allocation with an SCI threshold: coded transmission protects critical pixels, while an uncoded downsampled layer carries the full image.
Over a 5G New Radio link, STAR reaches at least 0.98 semantic accuracy for $E_s/N_0 \geq -4$ dB.

At comparable reliability, it reduces resource elements by 59.5% and 91.5% on factory- and vehicle-monitoring datasets, respectively; unlike the joint source-channel baseline, it requires no per-task labeled retraining.

The technical idea of using VLM attention to guide communication or decision-making is transferable to Embodied AI and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: STAR: Semantic-Criticality Tiered Allocation of Radio Resources via Zero-Shot Learning
papers.tldr: STAR uses zero-shot vision-language attention to identify task-critical pixels and allocate stronger wireless protection to them, achieving high semantic accuracy with substantially fewer radio resources.

papers.abstract: Accurate and timely identification of road closures is critical for large-scale navigation and logistics systems, yet remains challenging due to the need to jointly reason over visual evidence, spatial context, and road network topology. Existing approaches either rely on manual map updates or focus on detecting closure-related objects without resolving which road segment is affected. In this work, we introduce a unified multimodal and multitask framework that jointly performs road closure classification (no, partial, complete) and road segment association within a single learning architecture. Our model integrates graph-structured map data, satellite imagery augmented with projected street-level detections, and street-view images using modality-specific encoders and cross-modal transformer attention, enabling explicit reasoning over visual cues and network topology. Evaluated on nearly 20K real-world scenarios collected from a large-scale commercial vehicle fleet, our approach achieves 72.7% closure classification accuracy and 60% road segment association accuracy, outperforming frontier vision-language models by over 28 percentage points on closure classification while being over 4,000x smaller and 100x faster at inference. Extensive ablations demonstrate the importance of cross-modal attention, edge-aware pooling, and graph message passing for accurate geospatial reasoning. This work establishes the first benchmark for joint road closure classification and segment-level attribution, and shows that task-specific architectural inductive biases substantially outperform general-purpose multimodal models for structured geospatial understanding.
authors: Izzeddin Teeti, Vaibhav Kango, Nidhi Sridhar, Mohamed Moustafa
bullets: Targets timely, segment-level road-closure mapping for navigation and logistics.
Fuses map graphs, satellite imagery with projected street-level detections, and street-view images using modality-specific encoders and cross-modal transformer attention.
Performs joint classification of no, partial, or complete closure and road-segment association.
Evaluated on nearly 20K fleet-collected real-world scenarios, achieving 72.7% classification accuracy and 60% segment-association accuracy.

Outperforms frontier vision-language models on classification while using substantially fewer parameters and faster inference; results highlight the value of graph reasoning and cross-modal attention.

papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) grounding maps a screenshot and a natural-language instruction to the screen location where an agent should act. Zoomed views can reveal small targets but may lose the context needed to identify them. We introduce GroundCascade, a training-free controller that uses agreement between a grounder's full-screen and zoomed predictions to decide when to consult a complementary model. It selects between zoomed predictions while preserving corroborated full-screen locations. An optional Finalizer predicts from an unmarked joint crop when disagreement remains (Full); omitting it yields the two-stage Selective variant. GroundCascade reaches 85.33% on ScreenSpot-Pro with Indeed-UI-32B/8B/32B and 88.43% on the visible-target OSWorld-G-Refined subset with Qwen3.6-27B/3.8-27B/3.8-27B, gains of 2.66 and 2.35 percentage points over the stronger standalone two-pass grounder. On UI-Vision, GroundCascade reaches 72.20% category-balanced accuracy, with Selective slightly higher at 72.28%. Across these three evaluations, GroundCascade in Full mode uses 2.42-2.73 calls per request, 31-39% fewer than unconditionally acquiring both models' two-pass predictions. At matched second-model call budgets, selective acquisition gains 1.52-2.56 points over standalone Two-pass, compared with 0.22-0.69 points from stratified random acquisition. GroundCascade leads the official ScreenSpot-Pro leaderboard and exceeds reported GUI-specialist comparisons on OSWorld-G-Refined and UI-Vision, subject to differences in external evaluation protocols.
bullets: GUI grounding must balance zoomed detail against full-screen context, which can cause incorrect target selection.
The training-free controller compares full-screen and zoomed predictions, preserving corroborated locations and consulting a complementary model selectively.
An optional Finalizer resolves remaining disagreements from an unmarked joint crop; the Selective variant omits it.
It achieves 85.33% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 88.43% on visible-target OSWorld-G-Refined, and 72.20–72.28% on UI-Vision.
Full mode uses 31–39% fewer model calls than unconditional two-model, two-pass acquisition; results depend on external evaluation protocols.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can render a photorealistic analog clock but cannot control the time it displays. Across four pretrained models, fewer than 1% of generated clocks place both hands within 6 degrees of the requested time; the models instead collapse onto visually dominant configurations such as the canonical 10:10 pose. The same failure appears when a specific fraction of a circular object is requested, where models return complete or conventionally sliced objects. We observe that these two failures share a geometric structure: both target quantities can be parameterized by angular variables. We introduce a geometric token encoding framework that conditions generation directly on these angles. Each angular component is encoded as a periodic sine-cosine feature and projected into a role-specific token embedding that is injected into the prompt before a frozen text encoder. To spatially ground these tokens without requiring localization input at inference, we introduce Stochastic Localization Relaxation (SLR), which stochastically relaxes attention supervision from component-level to object-level to unconstrained localization during training. For clocks, we additionally introduce a hand-swap preference objective that discourages assigning the correct angles to the wrong hand roles. On analog clocks our method reaches 63-78% Acc@6 degrees across evaluation methods, compared with below 1% for the baselines. On circular-fraction generation, it achieves 89.5% Acc@0.10, while maintaining 88.8% on unseen object categories and 84.9% on unseen target values, compared with roughly 20% for pretrained baselines.
authors: Furkan G\"uzelant, Basavaraj Sunagad, Aysegul Dundar, Adam Kortylewski
bullets: Problem: Text-to-image models struggle to generate objects with precisely requested angular configurations, often defaulting to common visual patterns.
Method: Encode target angles with periodic sine-cosine features as role-specific prompt tokens, using Stochastic Localization Relaxation to ground them spatially.
Clock generation adds a hand-swap preference objective to preserve the roles of the hour and minute hands.
The method achieves 63–78% clock accuracy within 6° versus below 1% for baselines, and 89.5% accuracy for circular fractions versus roughly 20%.
It generalizes to unseen object categories and target values, reaching 88.8% and 84.9% accuracy, respectively.

Both tasks share the same MLP architecture and condition a LoRA-adapted SD 2.1 denoising U-Net. Right: Stochastic Localization Relaxation (SLR). Training samples one of three localization regimes (55/30/15%): component-level CALL using component boxes, object-level CALL using a shared object box, and unconstrained standard cross-attention. No localization input is required at inference.

papers.selection_reason: Geometric token encoding for angular control in text-to-image generation; directly relevant to spatial/geometric grounding in multimodal generation.

papers.tldr: Geometric angle tokens enable pretrained text-to-image diffusion models to control clock times and circular fractions far more accurately than standard prompting.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are typically evaluated by whether they produce correct answers, but correctness alone does not reveal whether their outputs are supported by the right visual evidence. We introduce VIGOR, a benchmark for evaluating VIsually GrOunded Rationales in MLLMs. VIGOR represents visual rationales as explicit concepts paired with pixel-level groundings, covering multiple abstraction levels including low-level visual properties, intermediate structures, objects, parts and high-level motion, relations. To construct VIGOR at scale, we develop an automatic annotation framework that reuses existing dense supervision when available and generates missing concept groundings through proposal-based annotation followed by conservative multimodal verification. Using VIGOR, we evaluate whether MLLMs "look at what they say" by comparing model-derived visual evidence for each expressed concept against annotated ground-truth rationales. Our results show that current MLLMs exhibit limited visual rationale correctness and reveal distinct grounding failures across concept levels. VIGOR provides a benchmark and scalable data construction pipeline for studying whether MLLM outputs are supported by appropriate visual evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/deep-real/VIGOR
authors: Yanlin Chen, Tang Li, Xi Peng
bullets: Represents visual rationales as concepts paired with pixel-level groundings across multiple abstraction levels.
Uses scalable annotation that combines existing dense supervision with proposal-based grounding and conservative multimodal verification.
Evaluates whether models “look at what they say” by comparing expressed concepts with their grounded visual evidence.
Finds that current MLLMs have limited visual rationale correctness and exhibit different grounding failures across concept levels.
Provides a benchmark and data-construction pipeline for studying visually supported MLLM outputs.

papers.title: VIGOR: Benchmarking Visual Rationale Correctness in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: VIGOR benchmarks whether multimodal language models justify their answers with the correct visual evidence, not merely whether the answers are correct.

papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly receive UI screenshots as part of bug reports, yet degraded image quality - caused by low resolution, compression artifacts, or small rendered text - can prevent them from identifying the relevant UI elements and source files. Vision-language models become less reliable as image quality deteriorates, while OCR-assisted approaches may propagate recognition errors from degraded inputs. Both approaches are limited when the visual evidence required for localization is no longer clearly observable in the query screenshot. We propose augmenting coding agents with repository-rendered reference images: crisp screenshots generated from the same codebase that the agent is tasked with modifying. These references provide readable visual evidence of the application's UI while preserving the current, potentially bug-containing implementation state. Because they are generated from the available repository rather than requiring a known bug-free version, they can be produced automatically for reproducible application states without manual image annotation. We evaluate the approach on a controlled benchmark derived from SWE-bench Multimodal by injecting visual UI bugs into a real web application. We vary screenshot degradation and reference-image provision and measure whether the coding agent identifies the correct source file. The results show that reference images improve file localization especially for degraded image quality, increasing the gold file match rate under fourfold downsampling with JPEG compression. We confirmed with further analysis that the proposed approach recognizes text approximately 12 percentage points better than language biased OCR under the same degradation.
authors: Fumiki Yohena, Toshiaki Sota, Shota Suzuki, Tomoko Okamoto, Michiaki Tatsubori
bullets: Problem: Low-resolution, compressed, or text-heavy UI screenshots can prevent agents from identifying relevant interface elements and code files.
Method: Generate crisp UI reference images directly from the target repository, preserving its current implementation state and avoiding manual annotation or a known bug-free version.
Evaluation: A controlled benchmark based on SWE-bench Multimodal injects visual UI bugs and varies screenshot degradation and reference-image availability.

Results: Reference images improve source-file localization, particularly under fourfold downsampling with JPEG compression; text recognition improves by approximately 12 percentage points over language-biased OCR under the same degradation.
Scope: The approach is evaluated on controlled web-application UI bugs and focuses on identifying the correct source file.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) often report a finding because the question names it; standard benchmarks miss this. From public segmentation datasets we build counterfactual views without manual annotation: the lesion erased by inpainting, a same-shape control edit elsewhere, and unedited lesion-free images. The evidence sensitivity gap (ESG) is the rate of absent-or-refer answers after erasure minus the rate after the control edit; it is zero for a model that ignores the image or reacts to both edits alike. MedScope-4B (Qwen3.5-4B, LoRA, image tools) was trained on label-derived trajectories, selected by a pre-registered rule and tested once against nine frontier and six open VLMs; four pre-registered checks then probed the mechanism. On 507 internal cases across five imaging types, MedScope-4B reached ESG 0.758 and claimed an erased lesion in 9.6% of cases, against 0.27-0.47 and 41-62% for the frontier models (all p<0.001), without significant loss of accuracy on real lesions. Without counterfactual views ESG fell to 0.279+-0.107 (three seeds); the effect replicated on MedGemma 1.5 4B and two unseen inpainting tools. At four external centres the advantage held but frontier models detected more real lesions; on a fresh external test MedScope-4B detected 0 of 48 pneumothorax films, with net utility below gemini-4-argon's (-0.36 [-0.50, -0.23]). Matching the control edit was not shown to matter; over three seeds no fresh-external ESG advantage over removal-based DPO was established; a paired-view consistency objective did not beat a matched-compute control, while that continuation alone cut erased-lesion claims on unseen tools at every seed, at a cost in sensitivity at one. Training on erased and edited images gives a small model an evidence-gated disposition that prompting does not give frontier models; it does not improve perception, and rare critical findings need coverage.
bullets: Standard VLM benchmarks may reward models for repeating findings named in questions rather than verifying image evidence.
MedScope-4B was trained with lesion-erased views, control edits, and label-derived trajectories to promote evidence-sensitive reporting.
On 507 internal cases, it achieved an evidence sensitivity gap of 0.758 and claimed erased lesions in 9.6% of cases, with no significant loss of real-lesion accuracy.
The effect replicated across another model and unseen inpainting tools, while prompting alone was insufficient.
External testing revealed scope limits: frontier models detected more real lesions, and MedScope-4B detected 0 of 48 pneumothorax films on a fresh test.

papers.title: Seeing Is Not Believing: Counterfactual Lesion Erasure Teaches a Small Medical Vision-Language Agent to Report Only What the Image Shows
papers.tldr: Training on counterfactual lesion-erased images helps a small medical VLM report findings only when they remain visible, but it does not improve perception and can miss rare critical findings.

papers.abstract: Multimodal (e.g. vision-language, in this work) attribution aims to interpret the models without access to ground-truth explanatory supervision. Existing multimodal attribution methods typically rely on paired modalities as proxy supervision, implicitly assuming that image-text pairs are semantically aligned. Information bottleneck (IB)-based attribution methods follow this general paradigm and instantiate it through a global sufficiency-compression objective. In realistic multimodal datasets, however, this assumption is frequently violated due to partial semantic misalignment and unreliable cross-modal correspondences. Through theoretical analysis, we show that, under such misalignment, information-bottleneck-based attribution objectives exhibit a structural limitation: by assuming equal reliability across all proxy supervision signals, they induce posterior over-contraction and forced explanations. To address this issue, we propose TIB, a sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck framework that adaptively modulates attribution strength according to cross-modal reliability, without assuming semantic alignment. Extensive experiments on controlled benchmarks and large-scale datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed approach, while also validating the identified failure mode.
authors: Qiming Huang, Peixi Liu, Jianbo Jiao
bullets: Existing information-bottleneck attribution methods can produce forced explanations when paired modalities are partially misaligned.
Theoretical analysis identifies posterior over-contraction as a structural failure caused by treating all proxy supervision signals as equally reliable.
TIB uses a sample-wise tempered information bottleneck to modulate attribution strength based on cross-modal reliability.
Experiments on controlled benchmarks and large-scale datasets demonstrate TIB’s effectiveness and validate the identified failure mode.

papers.title: TIB: Sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck for Multimodal Attribution beyond Alignment Assumption

papers.abstract: Multimodal attributed graphs (MAGs), in which nodes carry text, images, and other modalities while edges encode relations among entities, underlie e-commerce, social media, content platforms, and creative applications. Learning on MAGs has developed along two complementary lines: graph-centric methods redesign how modalities are fused, propagated, and connected within message passing, while foundation-model-centric methods pretrain transferable multimodal graph encoders or bring graph context into multimodal large language models for prediction and generation. In parallel, several benchmarks have appeared with different datasets and evaluation protocols. This survey takes an algorithm-centric and evaluation-grounded view of the field and makes three contributions. Modeling: we introduce a unified message-passing formulation and organize methods into five integration levels (feature, propagation, topology, learning, and foundation model), covering discriminative and graph-conditioned generative models; within this formulation we derive representative methods as special cases, compare their assumptions, expressiveness, and cost, and identify cross-modal sensitivity as a property that separates otherwise similar architectures. Datasets and evaluation: we review recent benchmarks, summarize their datasets and metrics, define model-independent descriptors (label homophily, average degree, clustering, and edge provenance), and map each evaluation protocol to the baselines it uses. Frontiers: we connect multimodal graph learning to AI agents, covering the multimodal graphs that agents perceive and remember and graph engineering, the practice of organizing agent workflows as explicit graphs; we then discuss open problems, concrete efforts for the community, and research directions, including when graph structure helps in the presence of strong multimodal foundation models.
bullets: MAGs combine multimodal node attributes with relational edges and support applications such as e-commerce, social media, and content platforms.
Methods are organized into five integration levels: feature, propagation, topology, learning, and foundation-model integration.
The survey covers both discriminative and graph-conditioned generative models using a unified message-passing formulation.
It reviews datasets and evaluation protocols, introducing model-independent descriptors including label homophily, degree, clustering, and edge provenance.
It connects multimodal graph learning with AI agents and identifies open questions about when graph structure benefits strong multimodal foundation models.

papers.selection_reason: Survey of multimodal graph learning including graph-conditioned multimodal LLMs and agent memory; relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Multimodal Graph Learning: A Survey of Models, Benchmarks, and Frontiers

papers.abstract: We study when and how multimodal input improves knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) in large vision--language models. Using a controlled evaluation over 1,500 WebQSP and CWQ questions and six VLMs within a fixed KGQA pipeline, we compare text-only prompting against text-plus-graph visualization at the per-question level and analyze performance changes as a function of reasoning complexity, model size, and image layout. Adding a graph image yields an average gain of 1.85 F1 points, driven by strong precision improvements on low-complexity questions (+4.65 F1). Mixed-effects and regression analyses show that these multimodal gains do not depend strongly on model scale, but are highly sensitive to graph layout: image-only settings sharply degrade performance, hierarchical Graphviz layouts outperform less organized renderings, and decomposing large subgraphs into separated paths yields the largest improvements. Taken together, the results indicate that visual prompting primarily aids KGQA by enhancing prediction precision in low-complexity contexts, provided that visual design respects cognitive and perceptual constraints. To optimize both accuracy and inference efficiency, we argue for adaptive visual prompting policies that selectively append diagrams to small, visually sparse subgraphs with well-structured layouts, avoiding unnecessary visual clutter and token overhead on complex queries. We conclude by relating these findings to a visual notation design theory, outlining how principled diagram encoding can guide future multimodal VLM prompting.
authors: Luiz do Valle Miranda, Andreas L. Opdahl, Grzegorz J. Nalepa
bullets: Evaluates text-only versus text-plus-graph prompts across 1,500 WebQSP/CWQ questions and six VLMs.
Graph images improve average F1 by 1.85 points, mainly through a +4.65 F1 precision gain on low-complexity questions.
Benefits are largely independent of model scale but highly dependent on visualization layout.
Hierarchical Graphviz layouts and separated paths perform best; image-only prompts and cluttered graphs can hurt performance.
The findings support adaptive prompting that adds diagrams selectively to small, visually sparse subgraphs to limit clutter and token overhead.

papers.abstract: Intelligent landslide detection is essential for disaster prevention. However, existing models primarily focus on isolated visual tasks, require extensive labeled data, and lack deep analytical and scene-understanding capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LandslideFM, the first unified foundation model that connects visual perception tasks with contextual interpretation of landslides. Specifically, LandslideFM adapts to multiple visual tasks via a Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning framework that leverages limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data. Furthermore, predicted landslide regions provide explicit spatial guidance to a Vision-Language Model adapted through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, enabling comprehensive landslide reasoning. To support training and evaluation in this domain, we also present LandslideVL, the first benchmark for intelligent landslide analysis, combining visual imagery and newly introduced textual prompts. Comprehensive experiments across public datasets and LandslideVL demonstrate that LandslideFM achieves superior quantitative and qualitative performance. Most importantly, LandslideFM surpasses general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide reasoning and scene analysis. Our code is released at https://github.com/wangshanwen001/LandslideFM.
authors: Shanwen Wang, Sirui Wang, Xin Sun, Jungong Han
bullets: Addresses the limited labeled data and weak scene-understanding capabilities of existing landslide detection models.
Uses Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning to support multiple visual tasks with labeled and unlabeled data.
Feeds predicted landslide regions as explicit spatial guidance to a parameter-efficiently adapted vision-language model for reasoning and analysis.
Introduces LandslideVL, a benchmark combining landslide imagery with textual prompts for intelligent landslide analysis.
Experiments on public datasets and LandslideVL report strong quantitative and qualitative performance, including better specialized reasoning than general-purpose VLMs.

papers.abstract: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.
authors: Haoran Zhang, Huizhen Sun, Hanbin Wen, Jie Leng, Jiaxin Zhu, Zhaohua Sun
bullets: Introduces a benchmark covering 56 sites, four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 imagery, and 238 questions across ten land-change tasks.
Agents must perform preprocessing such as cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization rather than relying on curated inputs.

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) have exhibited strong global modeling capabilities through iterative refinement. We observe that mask uncertainty follows an overall downward trend during iterative denoising, while a few denoising steps exhibit localized entropy spikes closely associated with hallucinations. We argue that anomalous steps can be identified by measuring the entropy deviation of each denoising step from its neighboring temporal window. We hypothesize that discrete token commitment discards the distributional information at masked positions, limiting the continued interaction between candidate semantics and the context during entropy spikes. With this goal, we present StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding strategy that leverages semantic context to achieve reliable denoising. The core of our method lies in a step-aware switch between discrete denoising and latent refinement. The model employs probability-weighted embeddings at entropy spike steps to preserve diverse reasoning hypotheses and performs multiple rounds of continuous refinement. Meanwhile, a refinement controller monitors distributional stability to reduce unnecessary loops and switch the model back to standard discrete denoising. Through extensive experiments, StepRefine demonstrates significant hallucination mitigation across different MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.
authors: Zhongxing Xu, Zhonghua Wang, Zhe Qian, Shiyan Su, Ming Hu, Xiaocheng Zou, Wei Feng, Mingquan Lin, Yuyin Zhou, Yifan Peng, Hamid Rezatofighi, Zongyuan Ge
bullets: MDLM denoising uncertainty generally decreases, but localized entropy spikes are linked to hallucinations.
The method identifies anomalous steps by comparing step entropy with that of a neighboring temporal window.
At spike steps, probability-weighted embeddings preserve multiple semantic hypotheses instead of committing to discrete tokens.
A stability-aware controller performs repeated latent refinement only when needed, then returns to discrete denoising.
Experiments report significant hallucination mitigation across multiple MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Entropy spikes characterization across decoding steps. (a) Token-level scatter of stepwise entropy change on LLaDA-V (top) and Dream-VL (bottom). On both models, entropy spikes mostly occur in the early-to-middle decoding stage, when few tokens have been committed and the available context is still limited. (c) Effect of random remasking on performance using LLaDA-V. Top: replacing low-confidence remasking with random remasking at 10% of randomly selected steps causes a substantial drop on three datasets. Bottom: applying the same random remasking only at entropy spike steps yields negligible change. At entropy spike steps, confidence signals may become less discriminative, making discrete commitment decisions less reliably grounded in the current contextual information.

(c) A step is flagged as an entropy spike when its stepwise entropy change exceeds the µ+ σ bound from the calibration window.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes step-aware decoding to mitigate hallucinations in multimodal diffusion language models.
papers.title: Rethinking in Spikes: Mitigating Hallucinations in MDLMs with Step-Aware Decoding
papers.tldr: StepRefine reduces hallucinations in multimodal diffusion language models by detecting entropy-spike denoising steps and temporarily refining token distributions in a continuous embedding space.

papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) offer complementary routes to post-training. For visual agents, however, tool use presents two related challenges. Models may overlook useful tool-returned observations, while poorly grounded actions can limit the evidence available for subsequent distillation. We introduce Reframe, a post-training framework that treats the observation state, rather than only the output distribution, as an object of alignment. First, Ground-Drop-GRPO (GD-GRPO) trains spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and stochastic removal of the original visual input, encouraging them to acquire grounded evidence and use the returned observations. Second, Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) replaces deficient tool actions with canonical ones mid-rollout and resumes distillation from the repaired observation. The two stages complement each other, as learning to rely on tool-returned observations can help the policy benefit from observation repair. Neither stage requires a task-specific SFT cold start. Extensive experiments over 14 image and video benchmarks demonstrate that Reframe outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD. Ablation results show that GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain compared with outcome-based GRPO.
bullets: Addresses agents overlooking useful tool-returned observations and taking poorly grounded actions that limit later evidence.
Uses Ground-Drop-GRPO to train spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and randomly removed original visual input.
Uses Observation-Gated-MOPD to replace deficient tool actions with canonical actions and continue distillation from the repaired observation.
Evaluated on 14 image and video benchmarks, Reframe outperforms Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD.
Ablations show GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain over outcome-based GRPO.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of GD-GRPO. The policy samples multi-turn tool-use rollouts. After the first successful tool call, the original input o0 is dropped with probability 0.5 while tool-returned observations ot remain visible, so the answer must rely on what the tools have retrieved. Rollouts are grouped by their pre-sampled drop flag di, and advantages are normalized within each subgroup so that dropout does not confound the comparison.

Figure 4. Overview of OG-MOPD. Tool actions of the student policy are checked against annotated evidence using an IoU threshold. Missing, invalid, or poorly grounded actions are replaced with annotation-derived actions to obtain query-relevant observations. Injected action tokens receive NLL supervision, while retained student-generated tokens are trained with MOPD.

Figure 1. Overview of Reframe: visual agents should produce reliable intermediate results and truly look at them. (a) Outcome-based RL without explicit grounding rewards can permit observation neglect. (b) Vanilla MOPD may supervise trajectories conditioned on a poorly grounded observation state. (c) Our GD-GRPO rewards grounded actions and encourages reliance on tool-returned observations. (d) Our OG-MOPD repairs deficient tool actions before continuing distillation.

Figure 2. Construction pipeline of Reframe-100K. We first collect public data sources and preprocess them into a raw data pool. We then drop samples answerable from text alone, and audit the rest with 8 rollouts on the full input (F ) and on the annotated evidence alone (E), discarding samples that are (1) too easy or too hard; (2) insufficiently supported by their evidence. Remaining suspicious samples are diagnosed by Qwen and removed only when a final reviewer confirms an answer or evidence error.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) integrate information across modalities, but become unreliable when those modalities disagree. Under conflicting inputs, MLLMs may favor modalities that are not the most reliable for the task, thus motivating inference-time control of modality arbitration. We identify a small set of attention heads, termed arbitration heads, that causally influence whether predictions follow visual or textual evidence. Building on this, we introduce a lightweight, training-free intervention that biases these heads toward a designated trusted modality at inference time. The identified heads are stable across calibration set sizes and generalize across settings, and steering them enables effective bidirectional control of modality reliance across diverse benchmarks. Our findings identify an effective control mechanism to align MLLM predictions with task-specified modality priorities. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/modality-arbitration.
bullets: MLLMs can make unreliable predictions when modalities disagree, sometimes favoring the less reliable source.
The work identifies a small set of causally influential attention heads, called arbitration heads, that control visual-versus-textual reliance.
Biasing these heads at inference time enables bidirectional control over modality preference across diverse benchmarks.
Arbitration heads remain stable across calibration-set sizes and generalize across settings.
Code is publicly available at github.com/zhaoyingpan/modality-arbitration.

papers.abstract: As multimodal agents accumulate increasingly long interaction histories, effectively retrieving and utilizing past information becomes critical for long-term interaction. Existing memory systems typically rely on semantic retrieval over compressed memories and expose predefined representations, which may miss relevant memories and overlook heterogeneous evidence needs across queries. We introduce \textbf{\hivemem}, a multimodal memory framework that interleaves \textbf{\textsc{H}}or\textbf{\textsc{i}}zontal Memory Expansion with \textbf{\textsc{Ve}}rtical Evidence Composition. For horizontal memory expansion, \hivemem organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors, expanding semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors to recover complementary information. For vertical evidence composition, each retrieved memory retains multiple evidence forms, including compact summaries, captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and interaction history. A lightweight trainable selector independently composes an evidence subset for each retrieved memory, enabling query-adaptive utilization of heterogeneous multimodal information. This two-dimensional design jointly broadens memory coverage and adapts the evidence contributed by individual memories. Experiments across three multimodal memory benchmarks show that \hivemem consistently improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90\% compared with the most efficient competing multimodal baselines.
bullets: Addresses missed relevant memories and fixed representations in semantic-retrieval memory systems.
Builds a relational graph of memory episodes using textual and visual anchors, then expands retrieved seeds with neighbors.
For each memory, selects among summaries, captions, grounded views, raw images, and interaction history based on the query.
Across three multimodal memory benchmarks, improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90% versus efficient multimodal baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of HIVE-MEM. papers.abstract: In ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing images, the objects that questions count in a region or relate by direction often span only a few pixels. Existing methods mainly decide where a vision-language model (VLM) should look and trust its answer in the chosen view. We show that this assumption fails for counting, and measure VLMs as one calibrates a sensor. All eight open VLMs tested fall increasingly short once a view holds more than a certain number of objects, about five for most on DOTA aerial images. This counting horizon narrows as views grow and objects appear smaller. An empirical power-law response model predicts the undercount a split recovers and the spurious counts it adds, and supports the rule of splitting only views beyond the horizon. In GeoScope, a text-only language model parses the question into a typed spatial program that fixes the region and its resolution. The VLM only grounds and counts within its operating range, and directions are computed explicitly from the grounded boxes. To our knowledge, it is the first UHR method to split views by a measured limit of the VLM. Without training, it improves Qwen3-VL-8B by 16.3 points on regional counting and 10.5 on spatial relations in XLRS-Bench, and has the highest reported accuracy, trained methods included, on regional counting and on the whole benchmark by question. On UHR-Micro it improves global and regional counting by 16.8 and 36.2 points, 15.6 of the former from splitting. On MME-RealWorld counting it gains 11.4 points, and we show that an option that is almost never correct yet often chosen distorts comparisons there. Project page: https://avalon-s.github.io/GeoScope/
bullets: VLM counting accuracy degrades sharply beyond a view-dependent horizon of roughly five objects, especially as objects become smaller.
A text-only language model converts questions into typed spatial programs that specify regions and resolution.
GeoScope splits only views exceeding the measured counting horizon, while the VLM grounds and counts within its reliable range.
It computes directional relations explicitly from grounded object boxes rather than relying solely on VLM judgments.
Without training, it reports substantial gains across XLRS-Bench, UHR-Micro, and MME-RealWorld counting tasks.

papers.abstract: Urban traffic flow prediction is a cornerstone of intelligent transportation systems, yet accurate forecasting under adverse weather conditions remains a significant challenge. Existing data-driven models, while effective for routine patterns, often struggle with the sparse data and complex non-linear shifts associated with rare meteorological events. These methods typically treat environmental contexts as shallow numerical features, failing to capture the underlying semantic reasoning-why and how specific adverse conditions alter mobility behaviors across regions with different functional compositions. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-STG, a unified framework that integrates Large Language Model (LLM)-derived semantic priors with graph-based spatiotemporal learning. Multi-STG introduces an LLM-empowered semantic enhancement module that transforms comprehensive context descriptions such as weather, POIs, and holidays into high-level semantic embeddings, effectively providing a knowledge-driven complement to data scarcity. Furthermore, we design a multimodal attentional fusion mechanism to dynamically weigh heterogeneous inputs and a semantic-enhanced prediction head with gated residual calibration to robustly adjust forecasts based on semantic guidance. Extensive experiments on real-world multi-city private car datasets demonstrate that Multi-STG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing MAE by 11.82\% on average relative to the strongest baseline across three cities, while maintaining stable performance under sparse and non-stationary conditions.
bullets: Targets sparse data and nonlinear traffic shifts during rare adverse weather events.
Converts weather, points of interest, and holiday descriptions into semantic embeddings using an LLM.
Fuses heterogeneous inputs with multimodal attention and calibrates predictions through a gated residual head.
Outperforms the strongest baseline by an average 11.82% MAE across three cities, with stable performance under sparse, non-stationary conditions.

papers.abstract: As vision-language models (VLMs) move toward interpreting medical images directly, their outputs increasingly include not just a label but a stated confidence and a written justification. Yet the field still predominantly evaluates VLMs using just accuracy. We evaluate the coherence between answer, confidence, and explanation across four VLMs on breast density and BI-RADS categorization, using two mammography datasets. We perform controlled perturbations of the question, multiple choice option orders, and the images and assess changes in the three outputs. Our results suggest confidence does not decrease even as the mammography image is changed. Shuffling the options also changes most VLMs' answers. Notably, there are cases where a model's own stated reasoning contradicts its final answer, a distinction accuracy alone cannot capture but one that governs whether an AI-generated answer can be trusted.

Tests robustness with controlled changes to questions, answer-option order, and images.

papers.abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) encode substantial expert knowledge within their weights, yet their direct application to specialised classification domains such as benthic imagery remains limited. Meanwhile, vision transformers trained on these tasks rely predominantly on low-level visual latents (colours, textures, and shapes) that lack the higher-level reasoning humans employ for identification. We propose Guided Hierarchical Multi-Label (GHiML) learning, a pipeline that extracts conceptual latent variables from a VLM conditioned on training data, generates sample-relevant captions grounded in those variables, and fuses the resulting textual embeddings with image embeddings via cross-attention and a per-node gated router. We also introduce the inverted HML score ($d_{\mathrm{inv}}$), a similarity score that evaluates hierarchical multi-label predictions through graph traversal distance and a cardinality penalty, providing an interpretable alternative to existing measures, which are insensitive to realistic degradations in sparse, deep hierarchies. Experiments on BenthicNet, FathomNet and iNaturalist show that the router improves macro $F_1$ over the vision-only baseline by up to 6.7 pp and $d_{\mathrm{inv}}$ by up to 21.1 pp on in-domain benthic data, with gains persisting under distribution shift. Ablations locate the contribution of the text itself: on the multi-label biotic hierarchies, removing the per-sample text signal degrades $d_{\mathrm{inv}}$ while leaving macro $F_1$ unchanged, consistent with text acting through prediction cardinality rather than node discrimination, whereas iNaturalist, whose annotations are single-label, loses 18.7% of macro $F_1$. Our results support the hypothesis that VLMs contain exploitable specialised knowledge that, when appropriately elicited, can augment classification in domains where direct visual learning is insufficient.
bullets: Extracts conceptual latent variables from a VLM and generates captions grounded in each image’s relevant concepts.
Fuses text and image embeddings using cross-attention and a per-node gated router for hierarchical multi-label prediction.
Introduces the interpretable inverted HML score (d_inv), combining graph-traversal distance with a cardinality penalty.
On benthic datasets, improves macro F1 by up to 6.7 percentage points and d_inv by up to 21.1 points over vision-only models, with gains under distribution shift.
Ablations suggest text mainly improves prediction cardinality in multi-label hierarchies, while single-label iNaturalist loses 18.7% macro F1 without it.
