papers.abstract: Answer accuracy alone does not distinguish failures in acoustic perception, rule knowledge, and rule application. AuDiR (Audio Diagnostic Reasoning) examines these distinctions through controlled input interventions. Each item contains an audio clip, a multiple-choice question, a task-general rule, and a textual description of the acoustic observations needed to answer. Three conditions progressively supply the rule and observations; a fourth removes the audio while retaining the question and rule. The first correct diagnostic condition assigns an operational response label, without identifying a unique internal cause. The current benchmark contains 201 items in 18 families drawn from 9 sources, with answer references documented separately from percept extraction. In a preliminary evaluation of Gemini-3.8-flash, accuracy is 29.3% without supplied information, 31.3% with the rule, and 98.5% with the observations also supplied. No-audio accuracy is 23.9%, with a confidence interval containing the 25.0% chance rate. A family-level knowledge probe associates incomplete rule recall with larger gains from rule provision. These results show the benefit of supplying acoustic observations as text, while incomplete validation, possible recognition shortcuts, and non-monotonic responses limit stronger failure-attribution claims.
bullets: Targets three stages of audio reasoning: acoustic perception, rule knowledge, and rule application.
Uses four controlled conditions that progressively provide rules, textual acoustic observations, or no audio.
The benchmark has 201 items across 18 families from 9 sources, with answers separated from percept extraction.
In a preliminary Gemini-3.8-flash evaluation, accuracy rose from 29.3% unaided to 98.5% when observations were supplied; no-audio accuracy was near chance at 23.9%.
Incomplete validation, recognition shortcuts, and non-monotonic responses limit definitive attribution of internal failure causes.

papers.abstract: To address unreliable cross-view association in long-sequence feed-forward dense SLAM, this letter presents V3DSAM, an open-vocabulary semantic dense SLAM system that establishes physical correspondences at both the scene and object levels. The system combines feed-forward geometric estimates from VGGT-SLAM 2.0 with open-vocabulary semantic observations from SAM3. We introduce semantic-geometric dual-scale loop verification, which identifies false loop closures using pixel-level bidirectional reprojection and object-level 3D spatial correspondences, without accessing backbone-internal features. We further propose geometry-anchored persistent instance mapping, which defines physical instances through class-constrained 3D connectivity in an optimized global coordinate system and assigns global IDs without inter-frame identity propagation. The proposed verifier rejects all four false loop candidates in our TUM RGB-D evaluation, while long-sequence ScanNet experiments show improved instance identity consistency. Thus, V3DSAM reduces dependence on internal backbone features and temporal ID propagation for robust long-term cross-view association.
bullets: Targets unreliable cross-view association in long-sequence dense SLAM.
Combines VGGT-SLAM 2.0 geometric estimates with SAM3 open-vocabulary semantic observations.
Uses pixel-level bidirectional reprojection and object-level 3D correspondences to reject false loop closures.
Maps persistent instances via class-constrained 3D connectivity in a globally optimized coordinate system, avoiding temporal ID propagation.
Rejected all four false loop candidates in TUM RGB-D evaluation and improved instance identity consistency on long-sequence ScanNet experiments.

papers.abstract: Discrete autoregressive modeling, notably through next-token prediction, has become a cornerstone of modern language models. Extending this paradigm to vision allows visual and language models to converge on a unified framework, thereby fostering shared methodology and infrastructure. This work investigates a central question: how far can a finite discrete vocabulary go in representing the richness of the visual world? We present dNaViT, a Discrete Native-resolution Vision Transformer that produces discrete visual primitives analogous to language tokens. Built upon a frozen pretrained encoder, dNaViT applies lightweight residual modulation with a dual-branch objective to inject reconstruction-aware cues into semantic features. By leveraging grouped product quantization, it scales discrete capacity without inflating spatial sequence lengths, while a balanced training recipe maintains both semantic and pixel-level information. Consequently, dNaViT functions as a versatile discrete visual tokenizer, enabling unified encoding across downstream tasks alongside high-fidelity image decoding. Extensive evaluations show that dNaViT matches or exceeds task-specific baselines across 12 visual understanding benchmarks, 4 generation benchmarks, and an image editing benchmark. These findings demonstrate that a compact discrete vocabulary can serve as a universal visual currency and unlock the full potential of fully unified, native multimodal methodology.
bullets: Addresses whether a finite discrete vocabulary can represent the richness of visual content.
Uses a frozen pretrained encoder with lightweight residual modulation and a dual-branch reconstruction-aware objective.
Applies grouped product quantization to expand discrete capacity without increasing spatial sequence length.
Provides unified visual encoding and high-fidelity image decoding across downstream tasks.
Matches or exceeds task-specific baselines across 12 understanding, 4 generation, and 1 image-editing benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 6 Overview of the code-conditioned Refiner. Code embeddings condition a flow decoder through global context tokens and time-conditioned spatial residuals. A multi-step teacher is distilled into an efficient one-step student with adversarial supervision. The timestep t in the diagram corresponds to τ in the equations. Increasing the quantization group count (G64) improves reconstruction fidelity, whereas combining fewer groups (G16) with the one-step Refiner preserves fidelity while enhancing perceptual quality.

Figure 3 Overview of dNaViT. (a) A frozen representation encoder handles arbitrary resolutions, with ResMod injecting multi-level information before group-wise product quantization. The shared discrete codes are decoded by individual ViT decoders into pixel and semantic reconstructions. (b) ResMod fuses intermediate features and predicts a zeroinitialized scale-and-shift residual. (c) Pixel and semantic branches are optimized with image and feature reconstruction losses, respectively.

Figure 4 Tokenization and Unified Codes for Downstream Tasks. (a) At spatial position t, the modulated feature zt is split into G channel groups and quantized with group-specific codebooks E(g), yielding indices (k (1) t , . . . , k (G) t ) and their embeddings. (b) Understanding supplies only code indices to the language model (LM) through newly initialized group-wise embedding tables {W(g)}Gg=1, trained jointly with the LM. (c) Reconstruction concatenates the indexed embeddings from the frozen tokenizer codebooks and feeds them to the pixel decoder Dpix. (d) Generation and editing use a multi-sub-token head atop the LM to predict each position’s multi-level indices, optionally conditioned on a reference image, then decode through the same frozen codebooks and pixel decoder.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP achieve strong performance across computer vision tasks, yet their image-text alignment is less reliable for infrared (IR) imagery because large-scale pre-training is dominated by visible-spectrum data. Due to the high cost of the infrared-text labeling, we investigate adapting CLIP to IR through only paired infrared-visible images, which requires considering modality-specific knowledge while preserving scene content and CLIP's image-text alignment. To achieve this, we propose TMT (Text-Derived Modality Knowledge Transfer), which adapts CLIP's image encoder through a text-defined infrared-to-visible direction and supervision from paired IR-visible images. First, we found that modality discrepancy can be described by corresponding text embeddings, thus using the direction of text embedding differences to guide the knowledge transfer between visible and infrared modalities without erasing infrared-specific information. To enhance the representation of semantics and details of infrared images, we introduce Generative-Perceptual Co-Supervision that combines semantic alignment from CLIP visible image encoder with diffusion noise-prediction feedbacks. On four source-disjoint IR classification benchmarks, TMT achieves the highest mean zero-shot accuracy among the compared methods (48.92%). It also achieves the best IR-text retrieval results among the compared methods without infrared-text supervision during adaptation and the highest open-vocabulary segmentation mIoU on both CART and SemanticRT among the CLIP-like methods.
bullets: Addresses CLIP’s weaker infrared image-text alignment caused by visible-spectrum-dominated pretraining.
Uses text-embedding differences to guide infrared-to-visible knowledge transfer while preserving infrared-specific information.
Introduces Generative-Perceptual Co-Supervision, combining CLIP semantic alignment with diffusion noise-prediction feedback.
Reports the highest mean zero-shot accuracy among compared methods on four source-disjoint IR classification benchmarks (48.92%).
Also achieves the best IR-text retrieval and strongest open-vocabulary segmentation among compared CLIP-like methods on the reported benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Speech comprehension in the human brain is an incremental process that begins with acoustic processing and advances to linguistic processing. While recent studies have revealed that the hierarchy of deep neural networks (DNNs) correlates with the ascending auditory pathway, the exact nature of this DNN-brain alignment remains underexplored. In this study, we investigate how DNN representations align with the brain's acoustic-to-linguistic processing. Specifically, we employed neural encoding models to simulate neural responses to acoustic (i.e., speech and noise envelope) and linguistic features (i.e., word onset and surprisal). By applying representational similarity analysis (RSA), we quantified the similarity between these neural responses and the DNN embeddings generated by a pre-trained automatic speech recognition (ASR) model, both before and after fine-tuning on audiovisual noisy data. Our results demonstrate significant DNN-brain alignment: embeddings from shallow layers exhibit higher similarity to neural responses associated with acoustic features, while those from deeper layers align more closely with neural responses related to linguistic features. Importantly, the fine-tuning process enhances this alignment by improving noise processing in shallower layers and refining linguistic representations in deeper layers. These results suggest that fine-tuned DNN models can naturally develop human-like processing patterns in noisy environments, highlighting a functional alignment between the human brain and DNNs in speech representation.
bullets: The study examines how DNN representations align with the brain’s acoustic-to-linguistic speech-processing hierarchy under audiovisual noise.
Neural encoding models represent acoustic features (speech/noise envelopes) and linguistic features (word onset and surprisal).
Representational similarity analysis compares these neural responses with embeddings from a pre-trained ASR model before and after fine-tuning.
Shallow DNN layers align more with acoustic neural responses, while deeper layers align more with linguistic responses.
Fine-tuning improves noise processing in shallow layers and linguistic representations in deeper layers.ﬁ

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic of analysis framework for computing representational similarity between DNNs embeddings and neural responses. For transformer-based DNNs (top panel), the model is fine-tuned on speech data with congruent audiovisual noise, starting from a pre-trained initialization. Then, embedding vectors of stimulus input are extracted from 12 transformer hidden layers, and utilized to calculate representational dissimilarity matrixs (RDMs). For neural encoding model (bottom panel), the EEG data in each EEG channel is predicted based on a linear combination of time-shifted stimulus features (speech envelope, noise envelope, word onset, and word surprisal). The encoder weights (temporal response functions) are estimated by maximizing the correlation between the actual neural responses and simulated neural responses. The simulated neural responses to stimulus features are utilized to calculate RDMs. Representational similarity is index through Spearman correlation between the RDMs of model embeddings and simulated neural responses.

Figure 3: Topographic maps of representational similarity between DNN embeddings and simulated neural responses to speech envelope, noise envelope, word onset, and word surprisal in speech processing with audiovisual-congruent noise. Results for pre-trained model (A), and fine-tuned model (B). Black dots denote the significant channels.

Figure 4: (A-C) Representational similarity of speech envelope, noise envelope, word onset, and word surprisal for the pre-trained, fine-tuned models, as well as their differences. The representational similarity was averaged across channels and participants. (D-E) Representational similarity for acoustic and linguistic features in the pre-trained, and fine-tuned models. papers.abstract: Foundation models increasingly combine geometry, semantics, and spatial context for three-dimensional scene understanding, but their suitability for forensic crime scene reconstruction remains unclear. This study presents a structured forensic evaluation framework for egocentric foundation models and demonstrates it using the Egocentric Foundation Model for 3D (EFM3D). Four simulated indoor crime scenes were recorded with Meta Project Aria Gen~1 at Robert Gordon University's East Lodge House forensic training facility. The framework evaluates room-scale reconstruction, semantic scene understanding, computational performance, and forensic suitability. Across the four scenes, EFM3D generated meshes averaging $12{,}668\pm2{,}430$ vertices and $24{,}838\pm4{,}903$ faces, with 39,529 recorded semantic predictions spanning 21--24 categories at a mean confidence of 0.40. Because reference meshes and expert-labelled 3D ground truth were unavailable, these statistics are treated as descriptive outputs rather than measures of geometric or detection accuracy. Final inference runs processed $1{,}388\pm203$ snippets per scene at $0.69\pm0.01$ samples/s and required $50.77\pm6.12$ minutes per recording. A seven-criterion capability profile indicated stronger support for room geometry, furniture localisation, scene context, and spatial relationships than for fine-scale forensic evidence. The results position EFM3D as a complementary tool for contextual documentation and scene review rather than a replacement for high-fidelity forensic capture. The framework provides a reproducible basis for evaluating future egocentric foundation models in specialised forensic settings.
bullets: Addresses the unclear suitability of egocentric foundation models for crime scene reconstruction.
Evaluates room-scale geometry, semantic understanding, computational performance, and forensic suitability across four simulated indoor scenes.
EFM3D produced descriptive meshes and semantic predictions, but unavailable reference meshes and expert 3D labels prevented accuracy measurement.
The model showed stronger support for room geometry, furniture localisation, scene context, and spatial relationships than for fine forensic evidence.
Inference required substantial processing time, supporting use as a complementary review tool rather than a replacement for high-fidelity forensic capture.

papers.abstract: Transformers are built with continuous symmetries in the attention mechanism. We derive $ρ$, a scalar invariant that measures each head's capacity to couple to rotary positional encodings. This framework allows us to analyze heads without forward passes, opening a new research direction into data-independent analysis of modern LLMs. Empirically, we find that $ρ$ predicts induction heads, the most-studied circuit type in mechanistic interpretability, with Spearman correlation between $-0.55$ and $-0.74$ across four bias-free RoPE models spanning $135$M to $7$B parameters. As a preliminary proof of concept, we use $ρ$ to apply YaRN to only the top-50% positional heads, which degrades perplexity less than uniform application. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/rho-invariant.
bullets: ρ measures each attention head’s capacity to couple with rotary positional encodings.
Across four bias-free RoPE models (135M–7B parameters), ρ predicts induction heads with Spearman correlations from −0.55 to −0.74.
Applying YaRN only to the top 50% of positional heads causes less perplexity degradation than applying it uniformly.
The study focuses on bias-free RoPE models and presents targeted YaRN application as a preliminary proof of concept.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions. However, reliable manipulation in open-world environments requires robust spatial understanding: the ability to identify targets in complex layouts (spatial reasoning) and adapt to scenes that continuously evolve through interaction (spatial memory). Yet existing embodied benchmarks fall short in evaluating spatial understanding: they often introduce strong visual cues that bypass spatial reasoning, and focus on static scenes that offer little insight into an agent's capacity for spatial memory. To address this gap, we introduce GeoMind, a systematic benchmark for structured spatial understanding through tabletop manipulation. GeoMind comprises 54 evaluated task variants organized around spatial reasoning and spatial memory. It also incorporates a scalable pipeline that automates the generation and annotation of task instances with verified targets and executable interactions. Extensive evaluations across diverse embodied agents reveal their consistent weaknesses in spatial understanding. Our findings highlight that these agents struggle to track identities after spatial changes and convert relational or geometric constraints into executable actions. We release the GeoMind benchmark at https://github.com/Notfound-JH/GEOMIND-benchmark.git.
bullets: Targets gaps in existing benchmarks, including shortcut visual cues and predominantly static scenes.
Covers 54 task variants spanning spatial reasoning and spatial memory.
Uses an automated pipeline to generate and annotate tasks with verified targets and executable interactions.
Evaluations show consistent weaknesses in tracking object identities after spatial changes and translating relational or geometric constraints into actions.
The benchmark is publicly released on GitHub.

papers.abstract: General-purpose vision-language models struggle with crisis imagery due to its inherent noise, ambiguity, and high variability across disaster events - yet timely, accurate scene understanding is critical for humanitarian response. To address this, we introduce DisasterVLG, a large-scale multi-task dataset containing 1.24 million disaster images from 142 countries paired with 33 million structured annotations spanning dense captioning with localization, incident assessment, relational scene descriptions, and crisis-grounded visual question answering (VQA) across diverse hazard types and scene contexts worldwide. Unlike prior disaster benchmarks that focus narrowly on classification, DisasterVLG unifies recognition, grounded reasoning, and uncertainty-aware interpretation. A distinguishing feature is its evidence-grounded annotation design: each VQA instance includes supporting evidence text that links visual observations to answers, alongside positive and negative question pairs, multiple answer formats, and difficulty labels. Visual grounding layer links caption phrases to image regions and relationship statements to subject-object boxes, with explicit labels for visual supports and clues. To support rigorous evaluation, we construct a human-verified test set of 38K images (1.15M annotations) spanning broad geographic regions and disaster types. Experiments with domain-adapted vision-language models demonstrate strong performance across disaster captioning, incident recognition, and grounded VQA, while also exposing the limitations of general-purpose models in crisis-specific reasoning. DisasterVLG establishes a scalable, reproducible benchmark for vision-language models that must reason reliably under real-world uncertainty. We will publicly release the dataset, trained models, and code.
bullets: Introduces 1.24M disaster images from 142 countries with 33M structured annotations.
Covers localized dense captioning, incident assessment, relational scene descriptions, and crisis-grounded VQA.
Links answers and descriptions to visual regions, supporting evidence, clues, negative pairs, answer formats, and difficulty labels.
Provides a human-verified test set spanning diverse geographic regions and disaster types.
Experiments show domain-adapted models perform strongly but reveal persistent limitations of general-purpose models in crisis reasoning.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose CM3AE 2.0, a unified RGB Frame and Event-Voxel/-Frame pre-training framework. By jointly learning multimodal spatiotemporal representations and exploiting latent cross-modal dependencies through cross-modal generation, the framework enhances multimodal information interaction and collaborative modeling capabilities. Specifically, we first propose an Event-aware Spatiotemporal Masked Reconstruction (ESMR) strategy to learn unified multimodal spatiotemporal representations. It leverages event responses to guide masking toward dynamically salient regions. Through spatiotemporal masked reconstruction, it learns spatial structures and their temporal variations from continuous RGB-Event observations. In addition, it incorporates multimodal fusion reconstruction and cross-modal contrastive learning to facilitate the modeling of cross-modal complementary information and the learning of shared representations. Building upon this, we further propose a Hierarchical Cross-modal Generation (HCG) strategy to learn latent cross-modal dependencies through visual and language generation. At the visual level, Event-conditioned RGB generation is performed using a pre-trained diffusion model to capture visual associations between the two modalities. At the language level, video-level text description generation based on joint RGB-Event representations establishes connections between multimodal visual features and linguistic semantics, further enriching the learning of cross-modal dependencies. Extensive experiments on four diverse downstream tasks demonstrate that CM3AE 2.0 consistently improves performance, validating the effectiveness and generalization capability of the proposed pre-training framework.
bullets: Uses event responses to mask dynamically salient regions for spatiotemporal masked reconstruction of RGB–event observations.
Combines multimodal fusion reconstruction and cross-modal contrastive learning to capture complementary and shared information.
Learns latent cross-modal dependencies through event-conditioned RGB generation and video-level text description generation.
Experiments across four diverse downstream tasks show consistent performance improvements and support the framework’s generalization.
Scope: the abstract does not specify datasets, quantitative gains, or task-specific limitations.

papers.abstract: Small multimodal models can misjudge emotion when words, voice, and visual cues conflict. We present EmoHarness, which runs such a model, the frozen student, inside a harness: the prompts, settings, and verification code around its calls. A human-written starting harness, the scaffold, numbers the student's visual observations, transcript, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence and has the student weigh candidate emotions against it. In Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), a stronger LLM, the Builder, reads the student's errors and execution traces offline and edits the harness; static checks and validation gates decide which edits are kept, and the Builder never sees evaluation items. On 5,507 MME-Emotion items, EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6-13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders. Transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of this boost (+5.38 to +10.71); the scaffold changes the audio-augmented call by -0.79 to +2.54, partly through extra multi-label predictions, and evolved edits add at most +0.95, although no evolved increment survives Holm correction. The harness's emotion context also transfers to IntentQA, with small gains for three of four students, none of which survives correction. EmoHarness thus boosts small multimodal students chiefly by supplying and organizing audio-derived evidence.
bullets: Addresses emotion errors when verbal, vocal, and visual cues conflict.
Runs a frozen student model inside a harness that structures observations, transcript, and prosody as citable evidence.
Meta-Harness Evolving uses a stronger Builder to edit and validate the harness offline without seeing evaluation items.
Across 5,507 MME-Emotion items, Recognition improves by 7.6–13.4 points over video-only calls for four students and two Builders.
Most gains come from transcripts and prosody; scaffold and evolved-harness effects are smaller, and evolved gains do not survive Holm correction.

papers.selection_reason: Uses a meta-learning approach (evolving a harness) to improve a multimodal model's emotion understanding at inference time, relevant to Test-Time Learning, Multimodal LLMs, and LLMs.
papers.title: EmoHarness: Boosting Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Meta-Harness Evolving
papers.tldr: EmoHarness improves small multimodal models’ emotion understanding mainly by organizing transcript and prosody evidence through a structured prompt-and-verification harness.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversation (MERC) combines lexical, acoustic, visual and conversational cues, but accepting audio and video does not establish their effective or robust use. We audit off-the-shelf Omni models while holding the target transcript and prior textual context fixed and adding, removing or replacing target audio and video. In the primary evaluation of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Baichuan-Omni-1.5 and MiniCPM-o 2.6 on MELD and the full five-session six-class IEMOCAP set, T+A improves Accuracy in all six model-dataset pairs, with four gains significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Across three source mappings, unrelated A/V (RandA/V) lowers Accuracy relative to Full in all 18 comparisons; all 18 remain significant under dialogue-cluster inference and BH-FDR correction, both on common-valid pairs and when invalid/OOM outcomes are treated as incorrect. Comparisons with modality-omission baselines further distinguish replacement penalties from mismatch-specific harm. A Qwen/MELD case study finds significantly greater gold-vs-best-candidate margin recovery in Late than Early or Middle under decision-query audio knockout, relative to an edge-count-matched Video-Sham control, using Holm-corrected tests. These results distinguish genuine-modality benefit from sensitivity and vulnerability to misleading input.
bullets: Evaluates Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Baichuan-Omni-1.5, and MiniCPM-o 2.6 on MELD and IEMOCAP with transcripts and textual context held fixed.
Adding target audio and text improves accuracy across all six model–dataset evaluations, with four gains remaining significant after FDR correction.
Replacing target audio/video with unrelated inputs reduces accuracy in all 18 comparisons, with significance robust to dialogue-cluster and BH-FDR correction.
Omission baselines separate general modality sensitivity from harm caused specifically by mismatched inputs.
A Qwen/MELD case study suggests later-stage audio processing better recovers correct decisions after audio removal than earlier or middle-stage processing.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates multimodal LLMs (Omni models) for conversational emotion recognition, relevant to Multimodal Large Language Models.
papers.title: When Audio and Video Mislead: Evaluating Multimodal AI for Conversational Emotion Recognition
papers.tldr: An audit of multimodal conversational emotion models shows that audio can improve predictions, while mismatched audio/video consistently harms performance, revealing vulnerability to misleading inputs.

papers.abstract: An open-vocabulary segmentation readout silently loses a class deployed beyond its training categories. It still emits masks with high confidence, but the class never wins a single pixel. The training loss falls anyway, and mIoU can even rise while classes die. We show that which classes collapse is written in the class-name list alone. Before any image is seen, we rank each class's collapse risk from its text similarity to the training vocabulary alone. The ranking holds at AUROC 0.69-0.96 across nine model families, twelve backbones and eight pretraining recipes. Two further families, measured only after the predictions were written down, land in the same band. What the list writes, it can rewrite. With identical images and a class's counterpart moved in or out of the training list, retraining flips that class's gain over the frozen baseline by 21 IoU points; swapping in unrelated names changes nothing. We find a vocabulary-distance mechanism behind the collapse. Collapsed classes lose every vote to near-name neighbors, but in the frozen features they survive. Turning down the readout's amplitude, or stopping training early, brings them back, up to +16 points, without retraining; trained with its amplitude held down, the readout never collapses.
bullets: Some classes receive no winning pixels despite high-confidence masks, while training loss and mIoU may improve.
Text similarity to the training vocabulary predicts collapse risk before seeing images, with AUROC 0.69–0.96 across 9 model families, 12 backbones, and 8 pretraining recipes.
Changing whether a class’s near-name counterpart is in the training list can shift its IoU by 21 points, while unrelated names have no effect.
Collapse arises when near-name neighbors take every readout vote; the class remains represented in frozen features.
Reducing readout amplitude or stopping training early can recover collapsed classes by up to 16 IoU points; amplitude-constrained training avoids collapse.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes class collapse in open-vocabulary segmentation readouts via text-vocabulary similarity, relevant to multimodal model behavior.
papers.title: Text Alone Predicts Which Classes a Segmentation Readout Keeps
papers.tldr: Class-name vocabulary alone can predict and even prevent which open-vocabulary segmentation classes will collapse during readout training.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Reasoning (MER) requires perceiving and integrating emotion cues from multiple modalities. Recent advances increasingly leverage Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to enhance reasoning capacity. However, due to the inherent heterogeneity in conveying emotions across modalities, these models often suffer from modality imbalance and confront flawed emotion understanding. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis on MER models and uncover two key empirical insights. (i) In MER, modality imbalance manifests two distinct failure modes: unimodal over-reliance and insufficient cross-modal utilization, which call for different intervention strategies. (ii) MLLM layers exhibit implicit functional hierarchies in multimodal emotion processing, playing separable roles in stabilizing unimodal representations and integrating cross-modal information. Motivated by these observations, we propose a Layer-Aware Modality Rebalancing (LAMR) framework by explicitly aligning intervention strategies with layer roles. Specifically, we first introduce two quantized metrics for adaptive layer role profiling. In each layer, Modality Entropy (ME) measures the dispersion of modality contributions, and Cross-modal Intensity (CMI) captures the strength of cross-modal interactions. Then, we respectively enhance modality equilibrium in stabilization layers and cross-modal propagation in integration layers. Extensive experiments on two comprehensive MER benchmarks demonstrate that LAMR effectively mitigates modality imbalance and improves emotion reasoning across diverse MLLM backbones, without additional training.
bullets: MER imbalance has two failure modes: over-reliance on one modality and inadequate cross-modal use.
MLLM layers serve distinct roles in stabilizing unimodal representations and integrating modalities.
LAMR profiles layers with Modality Entropy and Cross-modal Intensity.
It balances modality contributions in stabilization layers and strengthens cross-modal propagation in integration layers.
Experiments on two MER benchmarks show improved emotion reasoning across diverse MLLM backbones.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed LAMR framework. Adaptive Layer Role Profiling automatically partitions Transformer layers into stabilization layers and integration layers. papers.selection_reason: Adaptive layer profiling mitigates modality imbalance in multimodal emotion reasoning with MLLMs.
papers.title: Layer Roles Matter: Mitigating Modality Imbalance in Multimodal Emotion Reasoning via Adaptive Layer Profiling

papers.abstract: In modular grounding a frozen detector proposes regions and a vision-language model (VLM) selects one, at lower cost than letting the VLM decode a box, but it is unclear where such systems fail. We hold perception fixed---every trained selector chooses among the same frozen proposals, which contain the referent for at least $99.8\%$ of RefCOCO/+/g queries---and vary the selection interface one factor at a time for two VLMs of one family (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B). On RefCOCOg, what the selector reads matters more than how it is built: the VLM's image-conditioned query encodes the referent's location and beats a text-only query by $0.15$--$0.18$ with every head tested (by less for InternVL3-8B, whose vision encoder differs; one head tested). The remaining errors are rankings among a few top candidates; a cross-attention selector supervised with every valid box reaches the VLM's coordinate decoding on RefCOCOg, and with Qwen2.5-VL on RefCOCO/+ when also trained on their data. Beyond that distribution it does not: on Ref-L4's Objects365 images, mostly of categories outside training, every trained head falls to $0.19$--$0.28$ while Qwen decoding keeps about $0.8$ (InternVL3's drops too), neither a wider detector prompt nor a class-agnostic proposer closes the gap, and on public reasoning benchmarks Ref-Adv-s and RefBench-PRO full-budget heads trail decoding by $0.19$--$0.37$ although proposals cover most referents. A trained verifier reduces to an existence probe on the VLM's query state and does not beat the VLM's yes/no answer on public no-target benchmarks.
bullets: Frozen detector proposals contain the referent for at least 99.8% of RefCOCO/+/g queries, isolating proposal selection as the main bottleneck.
Image-conditioned VLM queries encode location and outperform text-only queries by 0.15–0.18 on RefCOCOg across tested selection heads.
Cross-attention selection can match coordinate decoding in-distribution, especially with supervision on the target data.
Out of distribution, selection accuracy drops to 0.19–0.28 on Ref-L4, while coordinate decoding remains about 0.8; broader proposals and prompts do not fix the gap.
Verifier training mainly probes whether a target exists and does not outperform the VLM’s direct yes/no answers on no-target benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses VLM proposal selection in grounded referring tasks; relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial understanding.
papers.title: Where Does Proposal Selection Fail? Diagnosing Frozen Vision-Language Queries over Detector Proposals
papers.tldr: Frozen-proposal grounding usually fails at selecting among candidate regions—not at detecting the referent—and selection generalizes poorly beyond training distributions.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation has advanced through large-scale pretraining and strong visual backbones, yet metric depth remains sensitive to scene-level scale. Indoor rooms and outdoor driving scenes occupy very different depth ranges, but most depth decoders infer this global structure implicitly from visual features. We ask whether scene-level semantic structure can instead act as an upstream prior that shapes the metric output space before dense prediction. We present LangDepth (SemanticBins), a monocular depth architecture that couples strong visual features with a scene-conditioned output space. A frozen CLIP encoder and a learnable bank of scene- and geometry-oriented concept keys convert image features into a compact scene descriptor, without requiring per-image text or an external captioner. A Scene Prior Module (SPM) maps this descriptor to a scene-conditioned metric depth interval, providing a global range anchor before dense decoding. In parallel, a DINOv2-L backbone with a lightweight FPN extracts dense visual features, and a Per-Pixel Assignment Network (PPAN) assigns pixels to the scene-prescribed bin structure. A confidence gate fuses the dense visual estimate with the SPM prior. We train LangDepth jointly on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI under a modest supervised depth budget, without web-scale depth supervision or pseudo-labelled depth data. A single model achieves delta_1 = 0.960 on NYU, 0.960 on KITTI, 0.887 on DIODE indoor, 0.946 on iBims-1, and 0.861 on SUN RGB-D. Beyond aggregate accuracy, the SPM predicts compact indoor ranges and much wider outdoor KITTI ranges, the gate becomes SPM-dominant on outdoor scenes, and perturbing the routed scene context causes large drops on KITTI and iBims-1. These results support scene-conditioned output spaces as a practical and interpretable mechanism for cross-domain monocular depth estimation.
bullets: Addresses scene-scale variation between indoor and outdoor environments, which can make metric depth estimation sensitive to global range.
Uses a frozen CLIP encoder and learned scene/geometry concept keys to form a compact scene descriptor without per-image text or captioning.
A Scene Prior Module predicts a scene-conditioned depth interval, while DINOv2-L, an FPN, and PPAN perform dense depth decoding with confidence-gated fusion.
Trained jointly on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI with modest supervised depth data, the single model reports strong results across NYU, KITTI, DIODE, iBims-1, and SUN RGB-D.
Scene priors adapt to compact indoor versus wider outdoor ranges; disrupting routed scene context substantially harms performance on KITTI and iBims-1.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: LangDepth (SemanticBins) pipeline. The input image is encoded by a frozen CLIP ViT-B/32, whose image features are routed through learnable scene and geometry concept keys to produce a compact scene descriptor z. The Scene Prior Module (SPM) uses only z to predict a scene-conditioned range (dmin, dmax), ordered bin centres {ck}Kk=1, and a global prior over those centres. In parallel, DINOv2-L with a lightweight FPN extracts dense visual features. PPAN conditions these features on z and predicts per-pixel bin weights {Wk}Kk=1 and a gate map g. Depth fusion forms the visual estimate dvis = ∑ k Wkck and the SPM prior dSPM = ∑ k πkck, then outputs d̂ = g ⊙ dvis + (1− g)⊙ dSPM.

Table 3: SPM range statistics. The SPM predicts compact indoor ranges and a much wider outdoor range for KITTI. The learned prior over bin centres is highly concentrated across datasets, indicating that the SPM primarily acts as a sceneconditioned range predictor and global scale anchor.
Table 4: Confidence gate statistics. KITTI is strongly SPM-dominant, while indoor datasets are more balanced or slightly vision-dominant.

Table 2: Component ablation study. All variants use the same matched ablation protocol and are intended for relative component comparison. w/o gate fusion bypasses the confidence-gated SPM blend but still uses CLIP concept routing and the SPMdefined bin structure; it is not a no-text baseline. The ablation protocol applies perimage median scaling uniformly on all benchmarks, including KITTI, which accounts for the difference in KITTI AbsRel relative to Tab. 1 (0.054 vs. 0.064); the latter follows the benchmark-standard direct metric evaluation for KITTI.

Table 5: Eval-time scene-context perturbation. Perturbing the routed scene descriptor at evaluation time causes large accuracy drops on KITTI and iBims-1. ∆ denotes the change in δ1 relative to the original prediction.

papers.selection_reason: Vision-language scene priors for monocular depth estimation; combines multimodal and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: LangDepth: Vision-Language Scene Priors for Semantic Binning and Cross-Domain Monocular Depth Estimation
papers.tldr: LangDepth improves cross-domain monocular depth estimation by using vision-language scene priors to set a global metric depth range before dense pixel-level prediction.

papers.abstract: Textured 3D meshes specify object geometry and appearance, making them a natural query for finding a particular asset in an image. We introduce LocateAnyMesh, a vision-language model that uses the mesh itself as part of its prompt. A frozen 3D encoder maps colored surface points to a compact token sequence, which a learned connector places alongside image and instruction tokens. We evaluate two grounding models with PPAT mesh tokens: LAM-Select selects image-region proposals, while LAM-Direct predicts coordinates directly. Neither requires rendered query views or view-template matching. New objects require a single encoder pass and no object-specific fine-tuning. LAM-Select improves localization on the reported real-image suites and the official BOP YCB-V evaluation. Secondary experiments compare mesh encoders, and a LAM-Direct study isolates surface color. A single-seed LAM-Select continuation supplies pointing and mesh-only description evidence without replacing the reported localization model. The results support mesh tokens as a query representation, with remaining limitations in presence decisions, identity binding, proposal coverage, and descriptive fidelity.
bullets: Uses a frozen 3D encoder and learned connector to combine colored mesh tokens with image and instruction tokens.
Introduces LAM-Select for selecting image-region proposals and LAM-Direct for directly predicting coordinates.
Avoids rendered query views and view-template matching; new objects need only one encoder pass without object-specific fine-tuning.
LAM-Select improves localization on reported real-image suites and the official BOP YCB-V evaluation.
Limitations include presence decisions, identity binding, proposal coverage, and descriptive fidelity.

figures.caption: Figure 5: YCB-V accuracy and runtime context with Blackwell timings for our models. Seen- and unseenobject leaderboard points have separate external-only Pareto frontiers. Our PPAT models use official 900-image BOP AP on the vertical axis and reported GB200 batch-21 time from the eight-image pilot on the horizontal axis (21/median queries/s). These coordinates come from different cohorts; LAM-Direct also uses different checkpoints for accuracy (45,823 updates) and timing (10,000). LAM-Select uses 31,434 updates for both, with cached proposals in the timed pilot. External methods retain their reported hardware and timer boundaries. Our models saw YCB-V objects during training and are excluded from both frontiers. This is reference context, not a controlled speed–accuracy comparison. Table 14 reports Uni3D-S accuracy and timing.

Figure 6: Two grounding systems on matched held-out HB queries. LAM-Direct and LAM-Select both use PPAT. Every column uses the same RGB image and mesh query. Blue boxes are predictions; dashed green boxes are visible targets. All predicted boxes are shown, and hits require IoU ≥ 0.5. Rows illustrate shared success, LAM-Select-only success, LAM-Direct-only success, a LAM-Select wrong-object selection, and absent-query disagreement. They were chosen by a fixed median rule within these outcome strata, not sampled to estimate success rates. Selection used all three systems; this view shows only the PPAT columns. Mesh previews are reader aids, not image inputs. Matched test inputs do not make this a controlled backbone ablation. More examples: Section C, including the same cases with Uni3D-S in Fig. 10.

Figure 7: Mesh-only descriptions from R and M10k@10k. Fixed before output inspection: zero-based positions 0, 37, 75, 112, 150, 187, 225, 262 in the evaluation-ID sort of all 300 identities, without quality ranking. Each row shows view_0 for the reader and the literal correct-mesh responses; only terminal EOS is omitted. The models receive mesh tokens and the instruction, but no image or render.

Figure 8: M10k@10k native pointing on real BOP images. The fixed gallery takes the first two present query IDs in each suite after sorting, without using outcomes: three are hits and five are misses. Text is the literal model response with only terminal EOS omitted. Coordinates use the size-minus-one pixel convention. Orange points and green visible-mask outlines determine the displayed hit/miss labels; the crops, masks, and labels are evaluation-only reader aids and were not model inputs.

Figure 4: Training examples and mesh categories. Examples and the asset inventory come from the earlier LAM-Direct data analysis. Blue boxes mark training targets; GSO meshes are scanned. The histogram counts each eligible mesh ID once across all sources, including YCB-V. Native labels are supplemented by categories inferred from descriptions; smaller groups form “Other categories” (Section A.4).

Figure 3: LAM-Select, initialized from VLX-Seek-1.5-10B. A frozen 3D encoder and a trainable connector place mesh features alongside image, region, and instruction tokens. An image-only detector supplies candidate boxes. The Qwen3.5 decoder generates region IDs or an explicit refusal; selected IDs map back to the candidate boxes. Gray modules are frozen; orange modules are trained.

Figure 2: Same CAD input, different network representations. Model-based detection and LocateAnyMesh ground a supplied CAD asset in a scene image using rendered views and native 3D tokens, respectively.

Figure 21: R descriptions: supported, generic, and unsupported responses. Each panel shows the complete input image and a positive-reference crop of the queried identity for the reader only; the crop is neither a mesh render nor a model input. Panels (a,b) hold the image and instruction fixed while substituting another present mesh: a supported label becomes a generic answer, whose identity is uncertain rather than demonstrably wrong. Panels (c,d) show an appropriate refusal and an unsupported description under same-suite absent-image controls. Text is the verbatim content of <ground>, with grounding/object wrappers and the end-of-sequence marker omitted. Examples were selected after review by the lowest review ID within these outcome strata, pairing (a) with its mesh substitution; they illustrate behavior, not its frequency.

Figure 20: R native point-prompt failures. These are the only two answers containing complete pointcoordinate tags among 32 fixed present-target queries to the localization checkpoint. The displayed points come directly from the generated coordinates, scaled from [0, 1000] to the original image dimensions. Both miss the target’s visible box and mask. Point markers, target-box overlays, and enlarged detail crops are reader aids; the model receives only the unannotated image, mesh features, and instruction. Responses are literal, including the incomplete grounding wrapper; only the end-of-sequence marker is omitted. No answer meets the exact requested format. This one-prompt transfer test does not establish general pointing performance.

Figure 10:Matched HB detections with the full encoder comparison. LAM-Direct with PPAT and LAM-Select with PPAT or Uni3D-S receive identical image/query inputs. Blue boxes are predictions; dashed green boxes are visible targets. Hits require IoU ≥ 0.5. All predictions are shown. These are the same five selected cases as Fig. 6; selection used all three systems, including the Uni3D-S control. Mesh previews are reader aids, not image inputs.

Figure 9: LAM-Direct multiple-instance localization on real HOPE images. Every-instance prompt, four-box limit. Three selected examples find both targets with extra boxes; the fourth misses one target. Blue boxes show every prediction, dashed green boxes show all targets, and insets show the queried mesh. Display crops retain all boxes.

Figure 14: Mesh-only description. Each row shows three correct excerpts and one incorrect excerpt from the LAM-Direct multitask checkpoint. Mesh renders are for the reader; the model receives no image input. Full responses: Figs. 15 and 16.

Figure 11: Localization across datasets. Solid orange boxes show predictions; dashed green boxes show ground truth. Insets show query meshes, and text below each image gives the model output. Hits have IoU≥ 0.5.

Figure 17: Mesh-only descriptions: ABO and GSO. Multitask checkpoint, correct mesh (left) and random swap (right), with full literal responses. Renders illustrate the inputs; the model receives only mesh tokens. These are two cases from the fixed audit.
Figure 16: Full mesh descriptions (e–h). The second description row of Fig. 14, in the same order. These selected examples do not replace the fixed visual audit.

Figure 12: Query color separates similar statues. (a–f) Two mesh queries in one HB image; the gray twin gives identical outputs in (c,f). Only the ISO-1 twins isolate query color; arm A is shown for context. (g) A refusal in another frame. (h) All 23 frames containing both statues.

Figure 18: Mesh-only descriptions: GSO and Objaverse. Multitask checkpoint, correct mesh (left) and random swap (right), with full literal responses. Renders are for the reader only. Together with Fig. 17, these panels show four cases from the fixed audit.

Figure 15: Full mesh descriptions (a–d). The first description row of Fig. 14, with three views per mesh and complete literal responses. Correctness labels in the compact gallery assess only the shown excerpts.

Figure 19: Pointing: a hit and a miss. Multitask checkpoint, ABO cases 18 and 22 from the fixed print set. Each scene and instruction is held fixed while the mesh is swapped. The original-query point lies inside the target box in case 18 and outside it in case 22. Literal outputs include the swapped-query responses. These selected cases do not estimate accuracy.

Figure 13: Pointing in synthetic ABO scenes. The LAM-Direct multitask checkpoint’s blue points hit three target boxes and miss one. Dashed green boxes mark the targets; insets show the query meshes. These selected cases do not estimate accuracy.

Table 7: Training settings of the two headline PPAT systems. LAM-Select is evaluated at an intermediate checkpoint; LAM-Direct uses the completed 100K arm A. “100K” denotes identity scale, not update count. A query and a packed training sequence are different exposure units; these are not compute-matched runs. For LAM-Direct, decoder LoRA and the connector train 124,982,272 of 3,668.3M parameters (3.4%).

Table 6: Token contracts for the two PPAT systems. Both use 65 frozen PPAT features, projected into their decoder width. Added vocabulary embeddings are frozen; projected features replace the mesh placeholders. LAM-Select selects proposed regions; LAM-Direct predicts coordinates. Point and selection templates listed below are LAM-Direct interfaces, not measured LAM-Select capabilities.

Table 9: Evaluation cohorts and coverage of the two PPAT systems. A check marks a measured result; n/e means not evaluated in the accepted record. Shared cohort counts alone do not establish parity; saved image/query inputs and the scorer have been matched for HOPE, LM-O, and HB. Absent queries use up to eight sampled classes per image; YCB-V queries all 21 models under official BOP amodal scoring; the other rows use the internal visible-box protocol. HB and HOPE use validation splits with public ground truth. Simulated rows retain the original splits and the contamination limitation in Section 4.
Table 1: The two LocateAnyMesh variants, named by output mechanism. Parameters are released fullsystem size classes, not adapter-inclusive audits. Both variants use frozen PPAT mesh tokens.

Table 3: Official BOP YCB-V detection with PPAT. Both systems use the same 900 target images across 12 scenes and query all 21 objects per image (18,900 queries). Ground truth uses mask-derived amodal boxes and BOP low-visibility ignore handling. AP is COCO AP@[.50:.05:.95]. LAM-Select uses its 31,434-update checkpoint; LAM-Direct uses arm A at 45,823 updates. These complete-system comparisons are not compute-matched. Timing is the reported GB200 batch-21 pilot on eight images: approximate seconds/image is 21/median queries/s, the median of three repeat-level cohort means; the range spans those repeats. Timing and AP use different cohorts; LAM-Direct timing uses 10,000 updates, and LAM-Select timing uses cached proposals. The full encoder comparison is in Table 14; timer boundaries and malformed-answer accounting are in Section B.6.

Table 8: LAM-Direct ablation-anchor training sources. Rows count annotations; effective rows apply the repeat factor. Objects are pool / usable after excluding 97 GSO and 405 ABO evaluation identities (502 total). YCB-V supplies 21 models in real photos and BlenderProc PBR renders; the other four sources use Isaac Sim or tabletop renders. Unqueryable assets in these frames serve as distractors. These inventory counts are not verified LAM-Select pool counts; LAM-Select’s prepared query-row composition is reported separately in Table 5.

Table 4: LAM-Select with PPAT on non-development HB. Native visible-box outputs at IoU ≥ 0.5, with maximum one-to-one matching. The first four rows partition 1,481 target instances; absent false positives use a separate denominator of 2,208 queries. This run has zero invalid outputs and no multi-box answers on this cohort. Lower counts are better for errors, higher for matched instances.

Table 5: LAM-Select prepared training manifest. Weighted query rows sampled with replacement. LAM-Select’s PPAT reference and Uni3D control consume the same order; the reference checkpoint consumes only part of the manifest. These counts are not unique-image or unique-mesh counts and do not describe LAM-Direct’s separately sampled training recipe.

Table 14: Official BOP YCB-V encoder accuracy and reported Blackwell time. All 900 target images, 12 scenes and 18,900 image–object queries; mask-amodal COCO AP@[.50:.05:.95] with BOP low-visibility ignore handling. LAM-Select checkpoints have 31,434 updates; LAM-Direct arm A has 45,823. All systems use the same official target list and scoring protocol for AP. Times are approximate median cohort-mean seconds/image from three repeats of the separate eight-image GB200 batch-21 pilot; ranges span those repeats. The LAM-Direct timing checkpoint has 10,000 updates rather than 45,823; LAM-Select timing uses cached proposals and excludes live detection. These are assembled accuracy/runtime summaries; see Section B.6.

Table 15: Secondary mesh-encoder comparison within LAM-Select. Native house visible-box mAP at 31,434 updates on 50 HOPE images and 300 images each for LM-O and HB. Both encoders share queries and detector proposals. HB’s development-excluded column uses 276 images; the full HB column includes all 13 scenes. Official YCB-V scores and the separate Blackwell timings are in Table 14. These are encoder-plus-connector comparisons, separate from the two-system comparison in Table 2.

Table 20: LAM-Direct frozen encoder comparison. House visible-box mAP. The historical Uni3D variants have no official YCB-V evaluation; headline-system scores appear in Table 14. All arms use 10,000 updates, seed 42, and LoRA 𝑟=64. The first two change only the encoder package; Uni3D-G also changes canonical axis, dtype, and topology. HB commit, FP, and Discrim use scenes 2–13; HB mAP uses all 13. LAM-Select’s separate encoder experiment uses a different schedule (Table 15).

Table 11: LAM-Select instance and absence errors on HOPE and LM-O. Native visible-box outputs on 50 and 300 images, respectively, at IoU 0.5. Matched, uncovered, covered/refused and covered/missed counts sum to the number of target instances (920 on HOPE; 2,319 on LM-O). The final column counts absent queries emitting a box, not the number of false-positive boxes. These single-threshold counts do not decompose AP.

Table 10: Full mesh-encoder comparison of LAM-Select HB errors. Native visible-box outputs on 276 nondevelopment images at IoU ≥ 0.5, with maximum one-to-one matching. The first four rows partition 1,481 target instances; absent false positives use 2,208 queries. Both runs have zero invalid outputs and no multi-box answers on this cohort. Higher is better for matched instances; lower is better for errors.

Table 2: Two grounding systems with PPAT mesh tokens. House visible-box COCO mAP on 50 HOPE and 300 images per other suite; HB includes all 13 scenes. LAM-Select uses optimized autoregressive inference and retains all selected boxes; its top-one HOPE mAP is 0.319. Other LAM-Select cells are unchanged by top-one filtering on this cohort. LAM-Direct uses one-box decoding; image/query inputs and the scorer are matched on all three suites. These are internal-protocol results; Table 3 reports official BOP YCB-V separately.

Table 16: LAM-Direct prompt and box-limit comparison on selected HOPE queries. On 48 two-instance queries, recall (%) uses 96 targets and precision (%) uses all valid predicted boxes. Both-found counts require well-formed answers but allow extras. Single exact means one matched box with no extras; absent FP counts queries emitting a box (eight controls each). LAM-Select’s native multi-box benchmark results use a different query population and cannot fill this pilot.

Table 21: Mesh-only reference agreement under correct and swapped inputs. Blinded Astra judgments against Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct captions, with the target reference and instruction held fixed. Measured rows use the LAM-Direct multitask checkpoint; no LAM-Select result in this table uses this caption-agreement rubric. The newer LAM-Select study uses blinded visual review (Section C.3.1). This is not a comparison between the two headline localization checkpoints.

Table 12: Paired target following under mesh substitution. Success counts out of 18 pairs in each donor group, at IoU 0.5. Co-visible success requires a source hit without a donor hit before substitution, and a donor hit without a source hit afterward. Absent-pair success requires a source hit followed by a valid empty answer. Primary success allows unrelated extra boxes; exact-set success requires a one-to-one match for every target instance and no extras in both conditions. Failed source controls and invalid answers remain in the denominators.

Table 17: Reported Blackwell GB200 timing. Eight images, 21 queries per image, three repeats. Throughput is the median across repeats. Approximate batch-21 seconds/image is 21 divided by the reported throughput, the median of the repeat-level cohort means, not the median of individual-image latencies. Peak allocated memory covers the reported batch sweep, including loading and warmup. Baseline timings retain malformed answers: 2/168 queries for PPAT and 1/168 for Uni3D-S per repeat. Full batch results and timer boundaries are in Section B.6.

Table 19: LAM-Direct ISO-1 color and gray twins. Identical configuration, LoRA 𝑟=64, and 10,000 updates; token stores differ only in –force-gray. HB mAP uses strided-300 over 13 scenes; Discrim uses scenes 2–13. Both arms re-score bit-identically; training-run uncertainty remains (Section 4.2). Both checkpoints use the retired in-graph stack and are compared with each other. Neither headline checkpoint has a matched color/gray training pair under this protocol.

Table 22: Exploratory LAM-Select image-plus-mesh description controls. Counts use all 𝑛 attempts in each condition. Assistant identity judgments are supported (S), uncertain (U), or contradicted (C); the four remaining present-mesh substitutions are refusal-like outputs with identity rated not applicable. Appropriate abstention counts only affirmative assistant judgments, retaining negative, uncertain, and not-applicable cases in 𝑛. Refusal-like text includes bare no/None, but excludes <objects>None</objects>: no proposals were supplied, so this field is not evidence of abstention. – denotes a measure not reported for that condition. These are review counts, not calibrated human accuracy.

Table 13: Synthetic-suite transfer of the selected LAM-Direct checkpoint. Arm A at 45,823 updates, with PPAT and one-box decoding. House visible-box mAP on 300 strided images per held-out suite, with max_neg_per_image=8. These use the original held-out splits before duplicate removal (Section A.4). This single configuration does not measure the effect of training-set scale.

papers.title: LocateAnyMesh: Grounding 3D Mesh Queries in 2D Images with Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: LocateAnyMesh grounds textured 3D mesh queries in 2D images by encoding the mesh directly as tokens for a vision-language model.

papers.abstract: Recent progress on contrastive audio-language models can be attributed mainly to the scale and quality of their training data. Larger training datasets expose models to a broader range of sounds and corresponding audio captions. To exploit this, we collect 1.48 billion audio samples from academic datasets, internet datasets, web collections, Common Crawl, and YouTube, and process them with a multi-stage curation pipeline. Furthermore, we generate short and long captions for samples in our corpus that lack them. We use our dataset to study the scaling behavior of contrastive audio-language models based on the NaFlex architecture for the audio encoder. Our experiments identify trade-offs between model size and training data for a given compute budget. Moreover, our resulting models, CLAP2, outperform prior audio-text models of comparable size on the MAEB and HEAR benchmarks. We release our dataset, captions, model checkpoints, and code.
bullets: Addresses the need for larger, broader, and higher-quality audio-caption training data.
Aggregates audio from academic, internet, web, Common Crawl, and YouTube sources using multi-stage curation.
Generates short and long captions for samples without existing captions.
Studies model-size versus training-data trade-offs for NaFlex-based contrastive audio-language models.
Releases the corpus, captions, CLAP2 checkpoints, and code; CLAP2 outperforms similarly sized prior models on MAEB and HEAR.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the LAION-Audio-XL dataset curation pipeline. We collected 1.48B audio samples from online platforms, of which 1.47B entered deduplication. Removing silent audio, duplicates (including SemDeDup [59]), and evaluation data leaves 1.28B audio samples. We then selected 500M audio samples based on categorical taxonomy annotations. The same annotations were used to prompt Qwen3-Omni [61] and MOSS-Audio [42] to generate short and long captions for 471M audio samples without textual descriptions, resulting in 500M captioned audio samples in total (the 500M selection). The 365M audio samples that are up to 30 seconds long form LAIONAudio-XL.

Figure 6: Embedding model performance by size. Average score across the individual tasks of MAEB (all 30 tasks) and HEAR (17 tasks). Blue squares are our own runs. Filled circles are audiotext models, and unfilled circles are audio-only models with no text component. Model sizes count only the audio and text parts of each model.

Figure 3: Scaling behavior on our LAION-Audio-XL dataset. MAEB-30 error rate (1 − mean score) per compute C (GFLOPs). Left: the compute-Pareto-optimal runs (solid points) of all warmup-stable-decay and cosine learning-rate-scheduled runs, with our fitted scaling function and its 95% bootstrap CI (1000 resamples). With α = 0.0574, the error reduces by 3.9% for each doubling of compute (≈ +1.8 mean MAEB-30 points at the largest budget). Right: each model size, from two WSD runs per size with individual cooldown phases, and the compute-Pareto envelope.

Figure 5: Compute-optimal allocation between model size and samples seen. For each compute budget C (GFLOPs), the long WSD run with the lowest MAEB-30 error gives the model size Nopt (blue circles, left axis) and samples seen Dopt (red squares, right axis). Circled points mark interior minima. Power-law fits give Nopt ∝ C0.405 and Dopt ∝ C0.583: the optimal number of samples grows faster than the optimal model size.

Figure 4: Domain-specific scaling on our 365M dataset. MAEB-30 error rate (1 − mean score) per compute C (GFLOPs) per model size and domain. Solid points are the compute-Pareto-optimal WSD and cosine LR runs used for the fit, the band the 95% bootstrap CI (1000 resamples). Speech and music scale well, sound saturates around C = 1.5× 1010.

Figure 9: Audio:text capacity choice does not significantly affect performance up to 64M samples. Left: parameter composition of the four capacity splits for model sizes XS and M. Within a tier, the non-embedding total is held constant. The 50k-vocab token embedding is adapted to the individual layer dimensions and is a fixed lookup cost, not encoder capacity. Right: Mean MAEB percentage scores over 30 tasks per training sample seen D show that the audio-to-text tower ratio does not have a significant effect up to 64M samples.

Figure 10: Scaling behavior on the full MAEB benchmark and per task type. Error rate (1 − mean score) of the full MAEB-30 and of each task-type subset per compute C (GFLOPs). The band marks the 95% bootstrap CI with 1000 resamples. It shows clear trends in compute scaling for zero-shot (ZS) classification, pair classification, and retrieval. In contrast, it isolates the saturating classification task.

Figure 11: Scaling predictions We are able to accurately predict our best performing frontier models with more than 1011 GFLOPs of compute. We can do this with a mean squared error of 7.35× 10−5 on the 0–1 error scale or a mean absolute error of 6.4× 10−3.

Figure 12: Validation loss per compute C. We plot our models based on compute and data scale against their validation loss with batch size B = 256. We can see clear valleys in the loss at smaller compute scales, indicating the optimal compute for a given data scale (warmup-stabledecay only).

Figure 8: Visualization of the sound taxonomy. The five levels contain 11, 837, 3,150, 393, and 25 nodes, respectively, for a total of 4,416 nodes, including 4,085 leaves. Coloured inner arcs denote the 11 top-level groups, ordered clockwise from speech at the top. Branches show 77 of the 837 secondlevel categories, selected by descendant leaf count and audio sample count in the deduplicated pool of 1.28B audio samples (grey numbers, respectively). Italic rows summarize omitted categories and their leaves.

Figure 7: Segmentation comparison after 8M samples per run. Diamonds and whiskers show the MAEB-30 mean and standard deviation over three seeds. Open circles show individual runs. Time: seconds from reading the source audio to written FLAC clips, per hour of written clips, on the same 227 hours of YouTube audio using 72 CPU cores.

Table 2: MAEB benchmark results. Parameter counts (Params) include only the audio and text parts of each model. Results for our models use the last checkpoint of each size’s WSD run: 1024M samples for XXS, XS, S, M, L, evaluated with un-normalised audio embeddings and with all-caps text inputs lowercased. We report the mean performance over 30 tasks, domain-specific (18 speech, 6 music, 6 sound tasks), and task-specific results: classification (12, including one multilabel), zeroshot classification (2), pair classification (3), clustering (3), and retrieval (10, including one reranking task). All scores are in %. Models are grouped by size, the best value in each column within a group is bolded.

Table 1: LAION-Audio-XL compared to existing audio-text datasets, including standalone dataset releases and the training data of audio encoders and audio-language models. Our LAIONAudio-XL dataset is sourced from a range of online platforms and websites, and from existing data collections, and datasets (details are provided in Appendix H). †Dasheng trains on audio only. ‡Not publicly released. Captions counts the text entries each source reports (captions, ASR transcripts, QA pairs); – under Audio means not reported; ∗ marks values derived from clip counts and clip lengths.
Table 7: Architecture settings shared by all tiers in the scaling study. For details on architecture shape refer to Table 6 & 8.

Table 13: HEAR benchmark results for the models of Table 2 and the audio-only encoders of Figure 6, with the same embeddings as there. We report the mean over 17 tasks (all HEAR tasks except Beehive and Maestro 5h), domain-specific means and the three HEAR task types: clip classification, multi-label tagging (FSD50K) and timestamp event detection (DCASE 2016). Audio-only models are evaluated by the models’ authors or the official HEAR 2021 leaderboard. Audio-text models are evaluated by us. Within each group models are sorted by the mean, and only models with every value available are listed. For audio-only models, we retain the best one or two variants of each method by mean score All scores are in %. The best listed value in each column is bolded, separately for the audio-only models and for the audio-text models together with ours.

Table 3: Model tiers for scaling study: Hidden dimension d, parameter counts, and forward-pass compute per encoder. Audio parameters include the MAP pool and projection layers. Text parameters include the pool and output projection but exclude the 50,260 × dt token-embedding table. Total parameters refer to the full model size, including embeddings. GFLOPs are forward-pass FLOPs per clip at the training length distribution.

Table 14: MSEB benchmark results on the English tasks, for most models of Table 2 (same parameter counts and checkpoints). We report the mean over 62 higher-is-better scores from 52 tasks (speaker clustering scores age, gender and speaker identity separately), domain-specific means (40 speech, 2 environmental sound, 20 bird sound scores) and task-specific means: classification (16), clustering (26), reranking (5), reasoning (5), and retrieval (10). Stability (Stab., 5 tasks) is the continuous edit distance between the embeddings of clean and noise-augmented speech; it is lower-isbetter and not part of the mean. Speech transcription and salient-term segmentation are not reported, since they score text output that an embedding model does not produce. Multilingual tasks, the image–speech retrieval tasks, and the full-index document retrieval (we use the small index) are not run. All scores are in %. The best value in each column is bolded.

Table 5: Attaching raw metadata strings leads to the highest accuracy. Overall ranking of two captioning models with three prompt types across the same 976 audio samples, evaluated with Gemini 3.6 Flash (thinking: low). Mean rank ranges from 1 (best) to 6 (worst). Win rate refers to being the best caption for a clip (higher-is-better). The ± values give 95% percentile confidence intervals over B = 20,000 resamples of the 976 audio samples.

papers.abstract: Audio language model benchmarks provide comprehensive evaluation across diverse tasks. However, some tasks can be answered from the transcript or even the question alone, and benchmark scores can therefore confound acoustic understanding with language modeling ability. We distinguish lexical tasks, for which the transcript usually suffices, from global-attribute and within-recording-structure tasks, which require the model to analyse the recording beyond its words, either as a whole, for properties such as the speaker and emotion, or within it, for patterns such as stress and intonation. We evaluated 19 open models and Gemini 3.1 Pro on 92 tasks from 6 benchmarks and estimated the recording gain, the accuracy advantage of the original recording over references that retain its words, by comparing the recording with synthetic readings of its transcript and by adding it to the transcript. On attribute and structure tasks, the open models fall behind Gemini by 28.6 and 41.9 percentage points, and about half or more of each deficit lies in the recording gain. Nevertheless, linear probes in Gemma-4 12B and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B show that the acoustic information needed for answering is already readable in early language-model layers, while the readout of many cues declines in the layers that follow. We therefore constructed training data and trained LoRA adapters in these layers, with a content anchor, which raises attribute and structure accuracy by 12.8 to 44.4 points in the two models and keeps mean lexical accuracy within 1 point of the base model. Most of the improvement appears as larger recording gains. These results suggest that training improves the use of acoustic information that the models already encode.
bullets: Benchmarks can overestimate acoustic understanding because many tasks are answerable from the transcript or question alone.
The study separates lexical tasks from global-attribute tasks (e.g., speaker, emotion) and within-recording structure tasks (e.g., stress, intonation).
Across 19 open models and Gemini 3.1 Pro, open-model deficits are especially large on attribute and structure tasks, with much of the gap tied to recording-specific information.
Linear probes show relevant acoustic information is often readable in early layers but becomes less accessible in later layers.
LoRA adapters trained in these layers, using a content anchor, improve attribute and structure accuracy while keeping lexical accuracy nearly unchanged.

papers.abstract: Evaluating general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for surgical scene understanding remains limited due to scarce surgical data and fragmented evaluation protocols. We address these challenges through a two-stage evaluation framework for surgical scene understanding. In Stage I, we introduce SurgKnowBench, a diagnostic benchmark that harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks and evaluates proprietary and open-source MLLMs to map the boundary of pretrained surgical competence. SurgKnowBench reveals that current models retain partial visual priors but remain weak on relational and procedural understanding and workflow assessment. Building on this failure frontier and motivated by the scaffolded nature of surgical training, we introduce SurgAgentGym, an agentic environment where general-purpose MLLM agents can use bounded knowledge search over SurgWiki and general-purpose visual grounding for surgical tasks. SurgAgentGym evaluates whether generalist agents can improve surgical understanding at inference time through tool-mediated evidence use, without additional surgical training. Our results show that agentic inference narrows the gap mainly for perception-heavy tasks, while fine-grained localization and expert-style assessment remain persistent bottlenecks. This opens a path toward future studies of agentic surgical understanding.
bullets: SurgKnowBench harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks to evaluate proprietary and open-source multimodal models.
Current models show partial visual knowledge but weak relational, procedural, and workflow understanding.
SurgAgentGym enables agents to use bounded SurgWiki searches and general-purpose visual grounding without additional surgical training.
Tool-mediated inference mainly improves perception-heavy tasks; fine-grained localization and expert assessment remain bottlenecks.
The framework supports future research on agentic approaches to surgical understanding.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires understanding how objects and observers are arranged in a scene and how their relations change with viewpoint or movement. Vision-language models (VLMs) typically perform both steps through model-internal reasoning, forming an implicit scene interpretation from partial views and imagining the consequences of spatial transformations. A misread scene can lead to a wrong answer, while even a correct interpretation does not ensure that imagined transformations satisfy spatial constraints. We introduce Spatial Harness, which represents scenes as explicit and executable world states to ground spatial reasoning in physics-engine feedback. A Perceiver integrates scene constraints extracted from the question with specialized visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame. The resulting state is instantiated in a physics engine, where a Reasoner executes viewpoint changes and uses computed measurements and rendered views to guide reasoning. We evaluate on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs. On MindCube, Spatial Harness improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%, surpassing pySpatial by 7.52 percentage points. Given identical annotated object and camera poses, it reaches 98.25% versus 71.81% for model-internal reasoning. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/Spatial-Harness
bullets: VLMs can fail when they misinterpret scenes or mentally simulate transformations that violate spatial constraints.
A Perceiver combines question-derived constraints with visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame.
A physics engine executes viewpoint changes and provides measurements and rendered views to guide a Reasoner.
Evaluated on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs.
On MindCube, it improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%; with identical annotated poses, it achieves 98.25% versus 71.81% for internal reasoning.
