papers.abstract: 3D visual grounding (3DVG) localizes language-referred objects in 3D scenes, with broad applicability in both indoor and outdoor environments. However, existing 3DVG research focuses on static indoor objects, limiting its use in dynamic outdoor autonomous driving. Motion descriptions, which capture the temporal dynamics of moving objects, offer a promising way to address this challenge. We therefore introduce MoT3DVG, a large-scale dataset for dynamic-aware outdoor 3DVG with temporally evolving motion descriptions. It contains 850 scenarios with 31,128 frames from nuScenes dataset, and provides 144,568 language prompts with motion-aware descriptions for dynamic objects across time. We further propose DynaVG, a novel framework that effectively leverages temporal cues for outdoor 3DVG. In addition to the standard modality-specific encoders, DynaVG introduces a Short-Long Integrated Dynamic Encoding (SLIDE) module before the language-point cloud alignment. SLIDE models both local motion cues and global temporal context via short-term window encoding and long-term window shifting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG, validating the effectiveness of motion-aware encoding. Our work reveals open challenges and promising directions for future research in outdoor 3DVG.
bullets: Targets the gap between static indoor 3D visual grounding and dynamic outdoor autonomous-driving scenarios.
Provides 850 nuScenes scenarios, 31,128 frames, and 144,568 temporally evolving motion-aware prompts.
DynaVG uses the SLIDE module to capture both short-term local motion and long-term temporal context before language–point cloud alignment.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG and support the value of motion-aware encoding.
The benchmark also highlights open challenges for future outdoor 3D visual grounding research.

papers.abstract: Visual chain-of-thought (visual-CoT), also known as "thinking with images", equips LVLMs with the ability to locate and use key visual evidence for reasoning. However, acquiring such visual-CoT capabilities requires costly post-training and tightly couples them to a specific backbone, making transfer to other LVLMs difficult. Existing cross-model transfer methods typically treat visual-CoT as a monolithic capability, using a unified representation that ignores the functional distinction between grounding and reasoning and introduces stage-irrelevant interventions. To address this problem, we propose Viscot-steer, a training-free activation steering framework for transferring visual-CoT capabilities across heterogeneous LVLMs. Specifically, Viscot-steer first disentangles visual-CoT into grounding and reasoning vectors and extracts them from the source-model layers associated with the corresponding capabilities. It then aligns the vectors with the activation space of the target model and steers the grounding and reasoning layers during bounding-box prediction and reasoning-trace generation, respectively. Across benchmarks covering high-resolution visual understanding, general visual perception and reasoning, and mathematical visual reasoning, Viscot-steer transfers capabilities from different visual-CoT models to architecturally diverse LVLMs and outperforms the strongest capability-transfer baseline by an average of 1.86 percentage points on the primary evaluation metrics.
bullets: Addresses costly, backbone-specific post-training for visual-CoT capabilities.
Disentangles visual-CoT into grounding and reasoning components rather than treating it as one capability.
Extracts source-model capability vectors, aligns them to the target activation space, and steers relevant layers at different stages.
Works across heterogeneous LVLMs and benchmarks spanning high-resolution understanding, perception/reasoning, and mathematical visual reasoning.
Outperforms the strongest capability-transfer baseline by an average of 1.86 percentage points on primary metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our Viscot-steer framework. (a) Disentangled vector extraction. papers.abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning have made verifiable rewards a central post-training paradigm for improving multimodal reasoning. However, methods such as GRPO remain data- and compute-inefficient, spending rollout and annotation budget on prompts that provide little learning signal. We propose DISCOVER, an online data-discovery framework for budgeted multimodal GRPO that enables vision-language models to dynamically identify prompts that are most useful for the current policy. DISCOVER first organizes the multimodal sample pool into semantic clusters and queries a small set of density-diverse representative samples to obtain initial reward observations. During training, it estimates the utility of unannotated samples by transferring sparse reward feedback from queried samples. Since sample utility changes as the policy evolves, DISCOVER dynamically updates these estimates with recency-weighted rollout observations. It then selects only high-utility prompts for annotation using a policy-conditioned score that accounts for reward variance and difficulty. Once the discovery budget is exhausted, DISCOVER continues with utility-based replay. Experiments on ViRL39K and VLAA-Thinking with Qwen3-VL-2B show that DISCOVER substantially improves multimodal mathematical reasoning under a strict 10% unique-sample budget, outperforming budget-matched random selection, hard-example sampling, full-pool GRPO under the same training-step budget, and online selection baselines. Ablations further validate the importance of semantic coverage, online reward transfer, and stable discovery cadence, establishing DISCOVER as a practical framework for data-efficient multimodal RL post-training.
bullets: Targets wasted rollout and annotation costs from low-signal prompts in verifiable-reward multimodal RL.
Clusters samples semantically, queries diverse representatives, and transfers sparse reward feedback to estimate unannotated-sample utility.
Continuously updates utility using recency-weighted rollouts and selects prompts based on reward variance and difficulty.
Uses utility-based replay after the discovery budget is exhausted.
On ViRL39K and VLAA-Thinking with Qwen3-VL-2B, improves mathematical reasoning under a 10% unique-sample budget; ablations support its key design components.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Cluster-balanced online discovery and frozen-pool reweighting. During discovery, observed easy/hard prompts (green/red) are admitted across clusters while cosine-KNN transfers sparse feedback to unobserved candidates (yellow). Once the unique-prompt budget is exhausted, the pool is frozen and subsequent GRPO steps reweight replay from the buffer; intensity encodes recency.

Figure 1: DISCOVER pipeline. Offline (green, left): prompts are embedded, clustered via spherical k-means, and seeded with REPR samples. Online (blue, right): GRPO rollouts from πθt feed a recency-weighted buffer; cosine-KNN transfers sparse statistics to unobserved prompts; utility scoring (Eq. 7) ranks all candidates. The budget switch routes scores to cluster-balanced discovery (Eq. 8), which admits new prompts until budget B is exhausted, after which frozen-pool replay (Eq. 9) reweights the existing pool. Both modes return prompts to the policy.

papers.abstract: Describing hours of audio requires accurate event timing and sustained descriptive detail throughout the recording. We present LongCap, a framework for timestamped audio captioning (TAC), with the human-annotated LongCapBench and three diarization-inspired metrics: Timeline Error Rate (TER), Granularity Error Rate (GER), and Caption Similarity (tcpCapSim). LongCap interleaves audio chunks with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and retained context to support length extrapolation within a 1M-token inference context window. Event-level reannotation restores caption detail, while systematic studies examine model scaling, dependency supervision, and self-distillation. LongCap-Diar achieves strong benchmark results and extrapolates to 16 hours of concatenated audio despite training on recordings no longer than 40 minutes. Our TAC models are competitive with Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus on short clips, outperform evaluated baselines in caption similarity and timeline accuracy in segment-level comparisons on LongCapBench-TAC-Long, and caption full recordings approaching two hours. On LongCapBench-TAC, 9B and 35B-A3B offer favorable size-performance tradeoffs, while 122B-A10B substantially improves event-dependency recovery. These findings support long-horizon general audio understanding and provide a foundation for always-on voice agents.
bullets: Introduces LongCapBench and three metrics for timeline accuracy, granularity, and caption similarity.
Interleaves audio chunks with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and context retention for length extrapolation.
Event-level reannotation restores descriptive detail, while studies examine scaling, dependency supervision, and self-distillation.
LongCap-Diar extrapolates to 16 hours despite training on recordings up to 40 minutes and can caption recordings approaching two hours.
Models are competitive on short clips and outperform evaluated baselines in segment-level caption similarity and timeline accuracy.

papers.abstract: We present SoftPAT3D, a physics-augmented framework for text-to-3D scene generation in which deformable objects, such as cloth, stuffed toys and ropes, are generated as physically valid, simulation-ready bodies and placed in intersection-free contact with the furniture that supports them, with one another and with themselves. Existing physics-augmented pipelines simulate rigid bodies only and cannot accommodate a generated deformable object, which text-to-3D generation returns as a geometrically invalid mesh, sometimes self-intersecting, that has no rest shape, no material model and no admissible initial state. These are the inputs a deformable simulation requires, and we construct each from information already in the pipeline. The rest shape comes from how the object is manufactured rather than from the generated physically inconsistent deformed configuration, and a material library assigns each deformable object its initial elastic parameters, which can then be optimized. The occluded support is regenerated and converted into a watertight collision mesh, each object is released from an optimizable placement above the supporting part that the prompt specifies, and the complete scene is driven to static equilibrium under one unified contact model, with completion verified by geometric checks and a vision-language model. When a scene fails the prompt, a grid search over placements corrects it, and the adjoint of a differentiable simulation of the same contact energy reaches the targets the grid does not, places several bodies jointly and recovers and optimizes material parameters. Multi-body scenes equilibrate in a single simulation, and the pipeline also runs from the text prompt alone. On all sixty-five prompts, SoftPAT3D produces no undesired interpenetration of any kind, whereas every other system does, and its scenes directly support scene editing and robotic manipulation.
bullets: Addresses the inability of existing physics-augmented text-to-3D systems to handle deformable objects with invalid meshes, missing rest shapes, and absent material models.
Constructs rest shapes, collision meshes, material parameters, and admissible placements from information available in the generation pipeline.
Uses unified differentiable contact simulation to bring multi-body scenes to static equilibrium, with grid search and adjoint optimization for placement and material refinement.
Verifies prompt compliance and geometric validity using checks and a vision-language model.
Across 65 prompts, reports no undesired interpenetration, while every compared system exhibits some; the approach also supports prompt-only scene generation.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SoftPAT3D. Each card shows the state of one prompt at that point of the pipeline, and its label names the step that produced it. (a) The prompt is expanded into a reference image, segmented and lifted as in PAT3D, and the support hidden under each deformable object is inpainted, regenerated and converted into a collision mesh (Sec. 3.4). (b) Each deformable object receives a rest shape from its manufacturing process under a size prior (Sec. 3.2), a material from the material library and a placement above the part the prompt names (Sec. 3.4). (c) One simulation brings the scene to equilibrium under a single contact barrier (Sec. 3.3), and the result passes the geometric checks and the prompt check (Sec. 3.5); a scene that fails enters placement optimization (Sec. 3.6).

papers.selection_reason: Physics-augmented text-to-3D scene generation with spatial/physical reasoning and support for robotic manipulation.
papers.title: SoftPAT3D: Physics-Augmented Text-to-3D Scene Generation with Deformables

papers.abstract: Multi-task scene understanding models typically rely on modified vision encoders or complex decoders for cross-task interaction, which limits their flexibility and compatibility with off-the-shelf vision foundation models (VFMs). We introduce Virtual Task Prompting (VTP), which frames multi-task prompting as retrieving task-adaptive compositions from a shared virtual state, where both the state and routing process are optimized in an end-to-end manner. Concretely, VTP maintains an expanded set of virtual tasks alongside the backbone. At each layer, learnable routing matrices read task-specific compositions as input to interact with image tokens and write the processed results back, forming explicit pathways that capture the intricacies among tasks outside the encoder. Since VTP keeps the backbone clean, it integrates seamlessly with pretrained VFMs, advancing the state of the art on Pascal-Context and NYUD-v2. Stress test on Taskonomy with 13 heterogeneous tasks further shows VTP's robustness in extreme settings. Ablations and analysis indicate that VTP's gains stem from adaptive routing rather than increased capacity. The project page is available at https://jacky1128.github.io/VTP/.
bullets: Addresses the rigidity and incompatibility of conventional modified encoders or complex decoders for multi-task interaction.
Maintains shared virtual tasks and uses learnable routing matrices to compose task-specific prompts at each layer.
Keeps the vision backbone unchanged, allowing seamless integration with pretrained vision foundation models.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on Pascal-Context and NYUD-v2, with robustness across 13 heterogeneous Taskonomy tasks.
Ablations suggest improvements come from adaptive routing rather than simply increasing model capacity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Qualitative results on Pascal-Context [9]. VTPtimm produces precise fine-grained object segmentation (bags), body-part parsing (human arms) with tighter saliency (suppress the spurious background). Key regions are with red circles. VTPvit-5 and VTPdinov3 and more results on Figure 5.
Figure 3: Qualitative results on Taskonomy [77] with 9 dense tasks. VTPtimm produces apparently more accurate predictions than the baseline. VTPvit-5 and VTPdinov3 and more results on Figure 8.

Figure 5: Qualitative results on Pascal-Context [9]. VTPtimm produces precise fine-grained object segmentation (bags), body-part parsing (human arms) with tighter saliency (suppress the spurious background). VTPvit-5 and VTPdinov3 further sharpen the details. Key regions are with red circles.

Figure 6: Additional qualitative results on Pascal-Context (Set 1). Two multi-person outdoor scenes that stress-test inter-individual disambiguation. Left: a man holding an infant against a cluttered natural background. TaskPrompter [71] (red circles) lets semantic labels bleed across the person with background contour in segmentation, fragments body-part assignments at the overlapping arms in parsing, and over-highlights background clutter in boundary. Right: a crowded group where closely spaced individuals share similar appearance. TaskPrompter’s parsing labels entangle across adjacent persons, with leg assignments bleeding from one individual into the next. In both scenes, VTPtimm recovers coherent per-person segmentation masks, disentangled body-part labels, and tighter saliency focus. VTPvit-5 and VTPdinov3 [57, 52] further resolve fine-grained inter-person boundaries, saliency, and produce geometrically smoother surface normals, approaching the ground-truth.

Figure 7: Additional qualitative results (Set 2). A challenging street scene that stress-tests two orthogonal challenges simultaneously: extremely small and thin semantic objects (distant poles, a tiny person occupying only a handful of pixels) and dense edge structures from road markings, building contours, and lampposts. TaskPrompter [71] (red circles) drops these tiny objects entirely from its segmentation and parsing maps, and produces a large spurious saliency blob on the background sky. VTPtimm begins to recover the thin structures in segmentation and parsing while suppressing the false saliency response. VTPvit-5 and VTPdinov3 further sharpen the objects (the blue and green masks in Semseg) and produce boundaries that capture both macro building contours and micro pole edges.

Figure 8: Qualitative results on Taskonomy [77]. An indoor scene with 9 dense prediction tasks under the extreme 13-task joint training regime. From top to bottom, predictions become progressively finer and more accurate. TaskPrompter [71] produces over-smoothed depth maps, flat curvature, and imprecise edges, while VTPtimm through VTPdinov3 successively recover depth discontinuities, surface details, and region coherence, converging toward the ground truth. This progressive improvement requires no additional computational cost. Only the backbone weights are swapped among VFMs.

Table 5: Comparisons to further ablating VTP’s effectiveness and contribution on PascalContext [9]. We compare VTP against (1) standard PEFT (LoRA) on a frozen ViT, (2) HPS with DINOv3 and task-specific heads, (3) TaskPrompter forcibly adapted to DINOv3, (4) multi-task PEFT methods (Polyhistor, VMT-Adapter, MTLoRA) with their original frozen-backbone setting, (5) the same multi-task PEFT methods extended with a fully tunable ViT-L backbone, and (6) our VTPtimm. ∆p is computed relative to TaskPrompter [71]. The results demonstrate that the effectiveness of VTP is attributed more to its prompting design, rather than the VFMs or the added capacity. Although it shares similar technical formation with those PEFT methods, their goals are different. VTP as a multi-task model architecture jointly trains the base model and the VTP modules, surpassing PEFT methods on both fully and partially fine-tune scenarios.

VTPtimm is with ImageNet-pretrained weights, while VTPdinov3 and VTPvit-5 employ DINOv3 [52] and ViT-5 [57] without any modification. ∆p (%) denotes the average MTL gains relative to TaskPrompter [71] (∆p=0). ↑ (↓) indicates higher (lower) values are better. papers.abstract: Despite world-class snow monitoring by the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute (SMHI) and Finnish Meteorological Institute (FMI), no station-anchored, multi-parameter snow benchmark dataset exists for the Nordic boreal domain. We present Hydro-Dataset v1.1, a reproducible open-source pipeline that harmonizes 582 SMHI meteorological observation stations across nine hydrological winters (2015/16-2023/24) into a CF-1.9 NetCDF product with 1.8~million annotated station-days. Six derived snow parameters, such as Snow Water Equivalent (SWE), snow phenology, melt rates, degree-day melt factor, rain-on-snow flags, and freeze-thaw cycles, supply benchmark-ready labels for hydrological foundation model training. ERA5-Land cross-validation (Pearson R=0.78, bias=-262mm) confirms observation-anchored SWE provides a more reliable benchmark than reanalysis for machine learning training.
bullets: Harmonizes 582 SMHI stations across nine hydrological winters (2015/16–2023/24).
Produces a CF-1.9 NetCDF dataset with 1.8 million annotated station-days.
Includes six derived snow labels, including SWE, snow phenology, melt rates, rain-on-snow events, and freeze-thaw cycles.
ERA5-Land cross-validation supports observation-anchored SWE as a more reliable ML benchmark than reanalysis.
Scope is the Nordic boreal domain and the dataset version is Hydro-Dataset v1.1.

papers.abstract: Medical Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) leverages the semantic richness of radiology reports to learn 3D representations, yet current architectures remain fundamentally anatomy-agnostic. While clinical diagnostics rely on organ-specific context, standard encoders apply a uniform, dense parameterization to all volumetric patches, and existing Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers gate on isolated local features without explicit access to the organ composition of the scan or crop. We propose Anatomy-Activated Mixture-of-Experts (A$^{2}$MoE), a framework that incorporates anatomical inductive biases within the model's computational path. A$^{2}$MoE introduces two key components: (1) a Histogram Representation Router (HRR) that conditions expert selection on global visual context and a predicted anatomical composition histogram, encouraging anatomy-dependent expert weighting; and (2) an Organ-Query Multi-Scale Projector (OQMSP) that utilizes learnable queries to extract organ-level embeddings for fine-grained alignment without requiring manual annotations at inference. By routing at the patch level rather than the token level, A$^{2}$MoE reduces routing complexity by orders of magnitude while satisfying load balancing by construction. Pre-trained on over 60,000 multi-phase CT scans, A$^{2}$MoE achieves state-of-the-art performance across segmentation, classification, and detection benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our anatomically grounded inductive biases support robust generalization to MRI and ultrasound, establishing a scalable foundation for medical representation learning. The code is available at https://github.com/gmum/A2MoE.
bullets: Addresses anatomy-agnostic encoders and local-only MoE routing in 3D medical VLP.
Uses a Histogram Representation Router to select experts based on global context and predicted anatomical composition.
Introduces an Organ-Query Multi-Scale Projector for fine-grained organ-level alignment without manual inference-time annotations.
Patch-level routing lowers routing complexity and enforces load balancing by construction.
Pre-trained on over 60,000 multi-phase CT scans, it reports state-of-the-art results across segmentation, classification, and detection, with generalization to MRI and ultrasound.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the A2MoE architecture. Given a 3D CT input XI n, the Histogram Representation Router (HRR) combines visual context and anatomical composition to predict stagespecific expert weights shared across spatial positions. These weights combine the outputs of all experts {E(s) k }Ks k=1. OQMSP uses shared organ queries Q to aggregate multi-scale encoder features Xs into organ-level visual embeddings Zvis. These are aligned with corresponding text embeddings ztxt, obtained through a frozen text encoder and a trainable linear projection, using Lalign. A parallel decoder combines encoder features with spatial skip connections and is supervised by Lseg. At inference, anatomical composition is predicted from image features.

The full model (#3 +OQMSP) achieves the best average rank on both metrics (DSC: 1.00, HD95: 2.25) and is statistically distinguishable from the majority of competing methods (p = 4.51 · 10−8 and p = 1.88 · 10−6, respectively).

Figure 1: Comparison of MoE routing strategies. (a) MoE routing: The input feature map x is pooled to form a global visual context, which is passed through an MLP router to produce logits over K experts. Softmax-normalized weights are then used to compute a convex combination of expert outputs Ek(x). Routing depends solely on visual features. (b) In addition to visual context, a foreground-normalized organ-composition histogram h̃ is embedded and fused with visual features to jointly condition the router. Each foreground entry represents the corresponding organ’s share of the total foreground voxel mass in the input crop. A learnable class-to-expert affinity matrix A(s) introduces a structural prior via a log-probability term log(h̃Ã(s) + ϵ), biasing expert selection toward anatomically consistent assignments. The resulting logits are softmax-normalized to obtain routing weights, and the final output is computed as a weighted sum of expert responses.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in vision foundation models (VFMs) has made automated open-vocabulary 3D bounding box annotation increasingly feasible by jointly leveraging LiDAR point clouds and images. However, partial observations remain a major challenge in sparse driving scenes, where visible LiDAR points often cover only a small fraction of the object's surface and provide insufficient cues for estimating its full spatial extent. As a result, existing methods often produce mislocalized boxes or leave objects unlabeled. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{\Ours{}}, an automated annotation framework that leverages image-generated 3D assets as amodal geometric priors for partially observed objects. By establishing correspondences between input images and rendered views of 3D assets, \Ours{} robustly aligns canonical amodal geometry with partially observed world-space LiDAR point clouds. To improve temporal consistency and reduce computational cost, \Ours{} generates a single asset per instance, estimates its metric scale once at a single frame and propagates it across frames for dynamic instances, and aggregates multi-frame observations for static instances. 3D object detectors trained on annotations from \Ours{} improve performance over strong baselines by 14.1 mAP on the nuScenes dataset and by 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for the vehicle class on the Waymo Open Dataset (WOD). Our project page is available at: \href{https://oliver0922.github.io/AmodalBox/}{https://oliver0922.github.io/AmodalBox/}
bullets: Addresses box mislocalization and missed objects caused by sparse, partial LiDAR observations in driving scenes.
Aligns canonical amodal 3D asset geometry with partially observed world-space LiDAR using image-to-rendered-view correspondences.
Improves consistency and efficiency by estimating each instance’s scale once, propagating it across dynamic-object frames, and aggregating observations for static objects.
Detectors trained on AmodalBox annotations improve by 14.1 mAP on nuScenes and 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for vehicles on Waymo Open Dataset.

We then align the amodal 3D prior [23] with the partial LiDAR point cloud across their coordinate spaces using correspondences obtained from image-level matching. Finally, we generate a 3D bounding box annotation from the aligned amodal asset.

(9)), propagate it across frames, and align each frame (Eq. (10)).

papers.abstract: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.
bullets: Targets the scalability and resource costs of continuous cooperative perception in multi-agent traffic.
Combines conventional object detection, VLM-based occlusion reasoning, physics-based visibility constraints, and Chain-of-Thought prompting.

Achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind-spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing.
Designed as an interpretable, bandwidth-efficient approach for connected traffic systems.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown promise as interactive agents, yet precise, programmatic 3D graphics editing remains difficult to train because existing systems largely rely on closed-source model APIs and lack deterministic, state-verifiable execution environments. We present BlenderFORGE, a trainable data-environment-optimization framework for open-weight MLLM agents that edit explicit Blender scenes through Blender Python (bpy) code generation. BlenderFORGE targets four fundamental state-verifiable editing task families: object placement, shape-key editing, lighting adjustment, and material modification. It integrates three components: (1) a scalable perturbation-based data generation pipeline built from curated assets and large-scale 3D scene repositories; (2) an isolated Blender Sandbox for deterministic code execution, structured state export, and closed-loop reward computation; and (3) a two-stage training pipeline that uses offline teacher trajectories for cold-start Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and sandbox-computed rewards for multi-turn tool-agentic Reinforcement Learning (AgentLoop-RL). Experiments across the four task families show that the resulting open-weight Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B BlenderFORGE agents substantially improve over their base models and achieve competitive performance with several zero-shot proprietary MLLM baselines on selected metrics. Additional cross-benchmark evaluations and camera-reframing experiments provide evidence of transfer beyond the original training setting.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of training precise 3D-editing agents without closed-source APIs or deterministic execution environments.
Supports object placement, shape-key editing, lighting adjustment, and material modification tasks.
Combines perturbation-based data generation, an isolated Blender Sandbox, offline SFT, and sandbox-rewarded AgentLoop-RL.
Trained Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B agents improve over their base models and are competitive with selected zero-shot proprietary baselines.
Cross-benchmark and camera-reframing evaluations suggest transfer beyond the original training setting.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The BlenderFORGE architecture. BlenderFORGE is a unified framework that integrates a scalable 3D asset-based data generation pipeline with an interactive Blender sandbox to enable training MLLM agents in 3D graphics editing. (Left) Data Generation Pipeline: 3D assets are perturbed and filtered through a visibility check to ensure that the changes are observable. (Right) Training Loop: The validated data flows into training with an interactive Blender sandbox, enabling SFT and RL for MLLM agents.
Figure 1: Overview of the learning process under the BlenderFORGE framework. MLLMs learn the correspondence between visual changes and 3D-graphics edits from scene perturbations.

Figure 3: Perturbation-based data generation pipeline. We illustrate the pipeline using object placement as an example. Starting from a base Blender scene, the pipeline removes redundant scene elements, selects editable objects or attributes, applies rule-based perturbations, and places aligned cameras so that the start–goal change remains observable. The resulting start and goal renderings are passed through a visibility check before the final (ss, sg) task pair is exported.

papers.abstract: Lane-level map updating requires temporally consistent, physically valid, and auditable road-scene semantics despite occlusions, ambiguous lane markings, temporary obstacles, and viewpoint changes. We present RoadState, a production-deployed vision-language system that transforms sequential road-scene observations into structured lane-level semantics for Baidu Maps' map-updating pipeline. Its core model, RoadState-VLM, formulates road-scene understanding as autoregressive state estimation, predicting the current structured road state from the previous observation and symbolic state together with the current observation. We introduce Geometric Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT), which uses a directed acyclic graph of semantic dependencies as a domain prior to improve semantic consistency and reasoning fidelity across interdependent road-state dimensions. Extensive experiments on a real-world dataset show that RoadState-VLM achieves 94.33% mean accuracy across six road-state dimensions, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned VLM baseline. Ablation studies further demonstrate the complementary effectiveness of Geo-CoT and temporal transition context. A cascaded routing pipeline directs routine cases to lightweight models while reserving complex cases for RoadState-VLM. Since its deployment in March 2025, RoadState has supported lane-level map updating across more than 360 cities and reduced overall production costs by 30%. Together with human-in-the-loop auditing, the system maintains robust performance under stress-test conditions. These results demonstrate how domain-prior-enhanced reasoning, structured state interfaces, selective routing, and human quality control can bridge the gap between VLM-based road-scene understanding and large-scale lane-level map updating.
bullets: Addresses inconsistent and physically invalid road semantics caused by occlusions, ambiguous markings, obstacles, and viewpoint changes.
RoadState-VLM predicts the current structured road state from prior observations, symbolic state, and the current image.
Geo-CoT uses a dependency graph as a domain prior to improve consistency across interdependent road-state dimensions.
Reports 94.33% mean accuracy across six dimensions and complementary benefits from Geo-CoT and temporal context.
Deployed across 360+ cities, the cascaded system reduced production costs by 30% while retaining human-in-the-loop quality control.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can generate procedures that look convincing on paper, but do they work in practice? In this paper, we propose crochet as an ideal testbed for physically grounded procedural reasoning in VLMs. Crochet cannot be reliably simulated or automated: the only way to know what a pattern produces is to make it by hand, yet verification is tangible and cheap, requiring nothing but a hook and a ball of yarn. We introduce FoundationChain, a deceptively simple test of procedural reasoning: given an image of a basic crochet object, can VLMs infer how it was made and generate a pattern that produces the same result? We crochet 40 patterns generated by four VLMs by hand. Even at this scale, physical execution not only reveals failures that automated proxies cannot detect, but also enables a more precise diagnosis of their causes and consequences: while models write fluent, convincing patterns, only four are free of errors, and our analysis exposes deficiencies in visual, geometric and procedural reasoning.
bullets: Introduces FoundationChain, which asks VLMs to infer a crochet pattern from an object image.
Uses hand-crocheting as a tangible, low-cost way to verify whether generated procedures work.
Evaluates 40 patterns from four VLMs through physical execution.
Only four generated patterns are error-free.
Failures reveal weaknesses in visual, geometric, and procedural reasoning that automated checks may miss.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have made progress in general visual tasks. However, limitations remain in fine-grained visual tasks requiring evidence from minute image regions. Existing methods primarily train models using evidence-related regions while overlooking the influence of extensive background regions, resulting in a limited ability to resist interference from irrelevant regions. We propose selective positive-negative on-policy self-distillation (SPN-OPSD), which considers both evidence and background regions. Supervision from both views improves the model's ability to resist interference from irrelevant regions. Furthermore, selective token-level distillation provides more informative supervision, improving the model's ability to attend to evidence regions in Fine-Grained Visual Tasks. On Qwen3.5-2B, SPN-OPSD improves accuracy on V* Bench, ZoomBench, and MME-RealWorld-Lite from 76.44%, 45.92%, and 57.43% to 84.82%, 54.56%, and 59.56%, respectively. Similar gains are also observed on Qwen3.5-0.8B.
bullets: Fine-grained visual tasks require extracting evidence from minute image regions, where background content can distract models.
The method uses selective positive-negative on-policy self-distillation with both evidence and background views.
Selective token-level distillation provides targeted supervision for attending to relevant regions.
On Qwen3.5-2B, accuracy improves across V* Bench, ZoomBench, and MME-RealWorld-Lite; similar gains appear on Qwen3.5-0.8B.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly adopted as end-to-end driving planners, yet they suffer from cross-city domain shift. Existing methods treat this shift as a single quantity addressed by uniform alignment or single-site editing. We challenge this view on two counts: (i) domain shift in VLM trajectory planners is inherently structured across modality and layer, and (ii) a locate-then-repair recipe matched to this structure outperforms every uniform-objective baseline. We analyse domain shift via activation patching and uncover two regularities. (F1) Modality axis. Image and text tokens exhibit distinct shift patterns in each VLM. (F2) Layer axis. The layer-wise shift partition is architecture-dependent and dataset-stable. These findings recast domain shift as a two-dimensional tensor indexed by modality (image vs. text tokens) and layer, motivating a simple principle: locate where shift occurs, and repair only there. We instantiate this principle in MoLaRx (Modality-Layer Repair), a locate-then-repair framework. The Causal Importance Score (CIS) estimates the domain shift as a modality-layer tensor and partitions the layers into functional zones. CIS-Guided Selective Repair (CISR) then applies a matched operator (Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) / low-rank adaptation (LoRA) / freezing) to repair each zone, with the composition adapting automatically to each architecture. We evaluate MoLaRx on three architecturally distinct VLMs (LFM2-VL-1.6B, Qwen2-VL-2B, and PaliGemma2-3B) across two cross-city benchmarks (nuScenes and Argoverse 2). MoLaRx attains the lowest cross-city trajectory-error gap among adaptation methods in all six main-table settings, while using 50-60% fewer trainable parameters and 8.4-10.9 ms lower inference latency. In contrast, uniform MMD-only adaptation collapses in all six settings, highlighting the importance of structure-guided repair.
bullets: Domain shift is structured across image versus text tokens and across model layers, rather than being a single uniform discrepancy.
Activation patching reveals architecture-dependent but dataset-stable layer-wise shift patterns.
MoLaRx estimates a modality-layer shift tensor with the Causal Importance Score and partitions layers into functional zones.
CISR applies zone-specific MMD, LoRA, or freezing operations to match each region’s needs.

Across three VLMs and two cross-city benchmarks, MoLaRx achieves the lowest trajectory-error gap in all six settings, with fewer trainable parameters and lower inference latency; uniform MMD-only adaptation collapses.

papers.abstract: Image-text alignment models such as CLIP are typically trained with contrastive learning, where unpaired examples are treated as strict negatives. While this assumption introduces noise by penalising semantically related pairs, existing solutions often rely on heuristic similarity thresholds that lack statistical grounding and sensitivity to dataset-specific noise distributions. In this paper, we propose Permute-then-Adapt (PTA), a framework that leverages efficient weak models to identify missed positives while controlling Type-I error relative to a conditional permutation reference, up to calibration approximation error. Unlike standard distillation or arbitrary thresholding, PTA estimates a random-pairing reference distribution from the weak teacher's similarity scores and uses its upper tail, determined by $α$, to select auxiliary positives. The calibrated positive set is then trained against by a single multi-positive contrastive objective: each anchor maximises the total probability mass it assigns to its positive set. Offline calibration with the weak model adds negligible training overhead. Experiments show gains over heuristic soft-label approaches in object recognition, cross-modal retrieval, and data efficiency. Project repository: https://github.com/JinhaoLee/Permute-then-Adapt.
bullets: Addresses false negatives in contrastive image-text training, where semantically related pairs may be penalized.
Builds a random-pairing reference distribution from weak-teacher scores and selects auxiliary positives from its upper tail using α-controlled Type-I error.
Trains with a multi-positive contrastive objective that aggregates probability mass over each anchor’s calibrated positive set.
Offline calibration adds negligible training overhead.
Reports improvements over heuristic soft-label methods in object recognition, cross-modal retrieval, and data efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Permute-then-Adapt (PTA). The student is optimized with a positive-set marginal likelihood objective.

In contrast, PTA (green solid) estimates a dataset-specific permutation null and adapts its cutoff to control Type-I error relative to that reference at level α, up to calibration approximation error.

papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs have made remarkable progress in perceiving the physical world, while their perceptual scope remains largely human-centric, focusing on what humans can directly see or hear. This progress raises the prospect of perception beyond human limits, such as extending hearing to sounds that are inaudible to humans. More broadly, the physical world is full of waves, vibrations, and oscillations, only a small fraction of which are directly audible to humans. This invites the extension of multimodal LLMs toward a broader form of machine hearing, which remains largely underexplored. To investigate this direction, we introduce the Machine Hearing Benchmark (MHB), comprising 6,128 instances across 13 tasks and seven domains. MHB spans highly heterogeneous input regimes, with sampling rates from approximately $10^{-5}$ to $10^6$ Hz, sequence lengths from $10^1$ to $10^6$ samples, and both single- and multi-channel inputs. Evaluations of current open-source and proprietary Audio LLMs (ALLMs) reveal limited zero-shot transfer to machine hearing. Supervised adaptation on machine-hearing data alone does not close this gap, suggesting that the challenge extends beyond data exposure to a systematic mismatch between existing audio front ends and machine-hearing inputs. To address this mismatch, we introduce MachEar, a lightweight encoder extension that complements the pretrained Audio LLM for machine-hearing inputs. The results show that MachEar equips a pretrained Audio LLM with stronger machine-hearing capabilities while largely preserving its existing audio understanding performance.
bullets: Introduces MHB, a benchmark with 6,128 instances across 13 tasks and seven domains covering highly varied signals and input regimes.
Current open-source and proprietary Audio LLMs show limited zero-shot transfer to machine-hearing tasks.

MachEar is a lightweight encoder extension designed to adapt pretrained Audio LLMs to these inputs.
MachEar improves machine-hearing capabilities while largely preserving existing audio understanding.

papers.abstract: Visual citations show where an answer is supported, but not how the cited content contributes to it. In scientific document question answering, a model may read a value directly, compress several observations, or combine evidence to infer a conclusion. We study typed visual provenance, where a system generates an answer together with source regions and explicit support relations. We introduce ReViE, a dataset of 3,941 questions over complete scientific documents, with page, section, and region annotations labeled as Quotation, Compression, or Inference. We further propose VisProve, which augments joint answer and provenance generation with differentiable Spatial Evidence Reading and Evidence-Answer Relation Feedback. VisProve conditions next-token prediction on localized visual evidence and its estimated support relation through a gated norm-bounded residual. On the document-disjoint ReViE test set, VisProve improves Typed-F1 from 3.52 to 5.48 and Section-F1 from 45.99 to 53.24 over joint supervised fine-tuning with the same backbone, while Page-F1 changes only marginally. These results suggest that coupling visual grounding with support relation modeling mainly improves fine-grained provenance, while the low absolute Typed-F1 reveals a substantial gap between answer generation and precise visual evidence attribution.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can recognize events in images and parse sentences, but it remains unclear when they bind visual Agent-Patient structure to linguistic semantic roles across languages whose role cues depend on morphology, word order or construction. We introduce ROLECUE, a controlled diagnostic that pairs 192 validated two-person action images with German, Turkish, Japanese, English, Korean and Bangla sentences in canonical and patient-first orders. The evaluation separates image-only role recognition, text-only role parsing, direct image-sentence matching, response-compliance behavior and an external modular composition of the model's own component predictions. Across eight recent open-weight VLMs, ROLECUE reveals a structured spectrum: some models fail visual or linguistic component tests, some largely solve the diagnostic, some collapse to constant semantic assent and several show component-joint gaps in which reliable image-only and text-only role predictions do not survive direct joint inference. The largest non-degenerate gaps reach 44.9 percentage points, with final bootstrap intervals confirming that the effect is not a point-estimate artifact. These results reveal multilingual component-joint performance gaps and acceptance biases hidden by aggregate VLM benchmarks and show why component diagnostics are necessary before interpreting joint multimodal errors.
bullets: Evaluates Agent–Patient role binding using 192 two-person action images and sentences in six languages.
Separates visual role recognition, text parsing, image–sentence matching, response compliance, and modular composition.
Across eight open-weight VLMs, identifies visual, linguistic, joint-inference, and constant-assent failure patterns.
Finds non-degenerate component–joint gaps as large as 44.9 percentage points, with bootstrap intervals supporting their robustness.
Shows that aggregate benchmarks can hide multilingual role-binding failures and motivates component-level diagnostics.

papers.abstract: Cinematic composition questions depend on in-frame geometry that vision-language models (VLMs) use inconsistently. External perception tools can expose this geometry, but naive prompt injection can overwrite useful visual predictions. On ShotBench composition, pre-question geometry reduces Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 49.5% to 46.3%; corrupted measurements lower it to 33.6%. CompositionEvidence derives nine reproducible features from frozen detection, depth, and line experts and supplies their shared 24-dimensional representation through two interfaces. A training-free channel appends gated neutral evidence after the question, reaching 56.2% (+6.7, exact McNemar p=0.0018) and 48.4% under corrupted evidence. A minimal-training channel maps the same representation to four soft tokens with a 7.37M-parameter projector while leaving the VLM frozen; it reaches 61.0% (+11.5). Across nine VLMs, including five commercial models queried through official provider APIs, zero-shot accuracy ranges from 43.8% to 63.0%, and the text channel changes it by +6.7 to -6.9 points; the highest baseline is among the regressions. The effect of explicit geometry depends on measurement reliability and on how the receiving model integrates it.
bullets: Composition questions rely on in-frame geometry that VLMs use inconsistently, while naive geometry prompting can hurt performance.
It derives nine features from frozen detection, depth, and line experts into a shared 24-dimensional representation.
A training-free gated text interface reaches 56.2% accuracy and remains more robust to corrupted evidence than pre-question prompting.
A minimally trained four-token projector reaches 61.0% while keeping the VLM frozen.
Across nine VLMs, geometry changes performance from −6.9 to +6.7 points, showing that reliability and model integration are critical.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) inherit strong textual reasoning capabilities from their language backbones and text pretraining, but often fail to apply the same level of competency to visual inputs. We show that this degradation cannot be attributed to only perception failures, by evaluating models on semantically-equivalent text and rendered-text image inputs: models can accurately read text in the images and recover near-text performance when provided their own transcriptions, but just cannot reason well on the images directly. We characterize this discrepancy as a modality reasoning-access gap, where models fail to route perceived visual content into existing reasoning machinery accessible with text. To bridge this, we propose TIGER (Text-to-Image Gap-targeted training for Enhanced Reasoning), which first mines synthetic modality counterfactuals where a model succeeds on a text problem but fails when provided the corresponding rendered image, and post-trains the model on the image input via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), along with SFT and DPO variants. Importantly, although trained exclusively on synthetic rendered-text images with no multimodal annotations, TIGER results in model performance improvements across diverse real-world visual benchmarks including geometric diagrams (MathVerse), multi-disciplinary sciences (EMMA, MMMU), complex charts (ChartQAPro), and embodied spatial reasoning (RoboSpatial-Home). TIGER also complements existing state-of-the-art RLVR visual reasoning methods, yielding further performance gains. Analysis involving reasoning-subspace activation and activation patching provide support indicating that TIGER helps to align visual-to-reasoning pathways toward text reasoning states. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/minhngh/Tiger.
bullets: Identifies a modality reasoning-access gap: models can read rendered text in images but struggle to reason over the images directly.
Mines synthetic cases where a model succeeds on text but fails on the equivalent rendered image.
Post-trains on these image inputs using GRPO, with SFT and DPO variants also explored.
Training only on synthetic rendered-text images improves performance across diagrams, science, charts, and embodied spatial reasoning benchmarks.
Activation analyses suggest TIGER aligns visual-to-reasoning pathways with text-reasoning states and complements existing visual RLVR methods.

papers.abstract: The task of visual reasoning relative pose identification (VRRPI) has exposed critical weaknesses in the multi-view 3D spatial reasoning capabilities of modern vision-language models (VLMs). We present a systematic analysis of VLMs' behavior in VRRPI, uncovering stable output biases where VLMs disproportionately predict specific motion patterns regardless of visual evidence. To mitigate these inherent biases, we propose self knowledge re-expression with iterative debiasing (SKR-ID), an annotation-free pipeline that adapts VLMs for VRRPI using only randomly extracted unannotated image pairs. SKR-ID transitions VLMs' output mechanism from generic next-token prediction to task-optimized classification heads. The pipeline proceeds in two stages: (1) a cold-start initialization using debiasing object-centric prompts to anchor motion inference in 2D visual evidence; and (2) a recursive logit-ranking mechanism that enforces statistical parity by using the median logit value as a dynamic threshold. Experimental evaluation across frontier VLMs on standard benchmarks demonstrates that SKR-ID significantly mitigates systematic biases. Our method improves open-source VLMs' Macro-F1 scores from 35.0-45.4% to 53.7-58.0%, without using any annotated data. These results show that SKR-ID can effectively improve 3D reasoning performance from a severely collapsed baseline. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/astudentuser/Codes_of_SKR-ID.

Across frontier VLMs and standard benchmarks, open-source models’ Macro-F1 improves from 35.0–45.4% to 53.7–58.0%.
The approach targets severely collapsed baselines and does not require annotated data.

papers.abstract: Visual data are often expressed through multiple complementary modalities (e.g., images and segmentation masks), each capturing different aspects of the same underlying structure. Most existing multimodal methods adopt a top-down paradigm, learning a shared latent variable through joint training from scratch, which limits scalability. We propose Split and Bridge (SnB), a bottom-up framework for multimodal generation that couples pretrained unimodal diffusion models at sampling time. Rather than learning a unified latent space, SnB generates coherent multimodal samples by following a shared diffusion trajectory up to a split point and then branching into modality-specific trajectories guided by a bridge module. This design enables plug-and-play reuse of powerful pretrained models without joint training, making it scalable and easily adaptable. Across standard benchmarks (PolyMNIST, CelebAMask-HQ) and more complex settings (PIE-Bench++, ROCO), SnB achieves a strong balance between sample quality and coherence. We show that SnB naturally extends to downstream zero-shot tasks such as interleaved co-generation, image editing, and style coupling/decoupling. Our results demonstrate that bottom-up generation provides a practical framework that complements existing top-down multimodal approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/AhmadArrabi/SnB
bullets: Addresses the scalability limits of jointly trained shared-latent multimodal models.
Shares a diffusion trajectory until a split point, then uses a bridge module to guide modality-specific generation.
Supports plug-and-play reuse of pretrained unimodal diffusion models.
Achieves a strong balance of sample quality and cross-modal coherence across several benchmarks and complex settings.
Extends naturally to zero-shot co-generation, image editing, and style coupling/decoupling.

papers.abstract: Mental simulation, the ability to reason by constructing and updating internal visual states, is central to flexible human cognition, but remains elusive in current multimodal large language models. Latent multimodal reasoning offers a promising route toward this capability by interleaving text with continuous visual latent blocks, allowing models to maintain internal visual workspaces without decoding them into pixels. In this paper, we ask whether these latent visual states actually matter. Through a direct perturbation analysis across representative latent-reasoning MLLMs, we find that they often do not: dropping, replacing, or shuffling generated visual latents has only minor effects on the model's own final-answer probability, while equivalent perturbations to the linguistic reasoning trace are substantially more damaging. We call this failure mode Mental Simulation Collapse (MSC): the model appears to perform interleaved visual reasoning, but routes most answer-relevant computation through text. We further diagnose that MSC follows naturally from existing training objectives: visual alignment can make generated latents resemble helper-image embeddings, but it does not require the decoder to rely on them; subsequent text-only supervision further leaves the semantic role of the latent pathway unidentifiable. To address this, we introduce AnchorSim (Anchored Mental Simulation), a contrastive distillation framework that trains models to make their generated visual latents consequential. Across multiple visual reasoning benchmarks, AnchorSim improves performance, while diagnostic re-evaluation shows that visual perturbations now meaningfully affect predictions. Our results expose a fundamental failure mode of latent multimodal reasoning and demonstrate that mental simulation must be anchored to model behavior in order to matter.
bullets: Identifies Mental Simulation Collapse (MSC): perturbing visual latents has little effect, unlike perturbing text reasoning traces.
Attributes MSC to training objectives that align visual latents without requiring downstream reliance on them.
Introduces AnchorSim, a contrastive distillation framework for anchoring generated visual latents to model behavior.
Reports improved performance across multiple visual reasoning benchmarks and stronger sensitivity to visual-latent perturbations.
Shows that effective latent mental simulation requires visual states to be causally relevant to predictions.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of AnchorSim. Given an initial image and query, the model produces an interleaved reasoning trajectory consisting of textual thoughts tk and intermediate visual simulations zk. AnchorSim trains the student policy with two complementary signals. First, a visual-blind branch masks the previous generated visual state zk−1 and is stopped from receiving gradients; the student is encouraged to diverge from this blind prediction, preventing “lazy text” reasoning that ignores visual latents. Second, a simulation-anchored teacher, updated as an EMA of the student and conditioned on the ground-truth answer, provides reliable reasoning targets under the full context. The student is optimized to minimize the JSD to the teacher while maximizing the JSD from its visual-blind counterpart, thereby anchoring textual reasoning to the generated visual simulations.

Figure 1: Vision vs. text perturbation impact across four multimodal latent-reasoning models. Each panel reports the mean log-probability (±1 SEM) of the model’s final-answer span. We compare four conditions applied independently to the vision block (blue) and the reasoning text block (purple): Full (unchanged), Drop (removed), Cross (replaced from another sample), and Shuffle (permuted). Step 2 shows them on the vision block; the charts apply them to both blocks in turn. A larger drop from Full indicates that the perturbed block carries more answer-relevant information. In most conditions, perturbing the text block degrades the answer substantially more than perturbing the visual block, indicating that computation is routed primarily through the linguistic stream.

Figure 5: Perturbation analysis. (a) OLS slope S between perturbed and unperturbed answer logprobabilities for Qwen-interleaved and ANCHORSIM, where S ≈ 1 indicates little effect. (b) Closed-loop analysis, where the model regenerates the rest of the trajectory after the perturbation.

Figure 9: Per-sample vision vs. text perturbation impact for CoVT-7B on V*Bench. CoVT emits a fixed three-encoder visual-block template per trajectory, so all perturbation conditions are evaluated on the full 100-sample set. Vision-side perturbations leave many samples close to the no-impact diagonal, whereas text-side perturbations move a substantial subset below the diagonal. This shows that the model’s final-answer probability is more sensitive to corrupted reasoning text than to corrupted SAM, depth, and DINO pad hidden states.
Figure 4: Qualitative example on SAT-R. ANCHORSIM-7B achieves better visual–text interleaving and correctly predicts the answer. Blue squares denote visual latent tokens.

Figure 2: Per-sample vision vs. text perturbation impact for Mirage-7B. Each panel plots the perturbed final-answer log-probability (y = lpperturbed) against the unperturbed baseline (x = lpfull) for the vision block (blue) and reasoning text block (purple). Points further below the y=x diagonal (dashed) and lower ordinary-least-squares fit slopes (solid lines) indicate a larger performance drop. Across all conditions, the text fit has a lower slope than the vision fit, demonstrating that perturbing the linguistic chain degrades the answer more than perturbing the visual latents.

Figure 11: Qualitative example on EMMA. The model solves a diagram-grounded STEM problem by combining textual reasoning with visual grounding. AnchorSim encourages the reasoning chain to revisit visual latents when deriving the final answer, rather than relying only on language priors.

papers.abstract: Recommender systems are transitioning from static retrieval engines into interactive assistants grounded in physical environments. However, current studies largely neglect the combined complexities of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark for evaluating frontier vision-language models (VLMs) as situated recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. We reformulate recommendation as a situated assistance process in which an assistant interacts with a user while sharing the user's egocentric view. Our benchmark simulates real-world shopping environments (e.g., supermarkets and home furnishings stores), requiring assistants to elicit preferences, ground recommendations in the environment, and guide the user to relevant locations through dialogue. The benchmark evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified interactive protocol. Extensive experiments reveal persistent challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in their ability to integrate global contextual information with local observations. SituRecBench provides a rigorous foundation for advancing the development of situated assistants in the real world.

papers.abstract: Pose awareness characterizes the extent to which a learned feature space aligns with the underlying object-pose manifold, such that observations with similar poses exhibit greater feature similarity than those with increasingly different poses. While such structure is desirable for pose-sensitive 3D vision tasks, visual foundation models pre-trained on individual 2D images typically lack explicit 3D or pose supervision. This raises a fundamental question: Do 2D visual foundation models exhibit pose awareness after large-scale pretraining? To answer this question, we introduce PoseBench, a systematic benchmark to probe pose awareness in pretrained visual features. Our evaluation follows a progressive design: held-out rendered views probe intrinsic pose-aware structure under controlled conditions, while real-image queries evaluate how robustly this structure remains accessible under real-world variations. We further introduce pose-graph-based refinement as a complementary probe of compatibility between feature neighborhoods and the underlying pose manifold. Across 31 publicly available checkpoints from 10 pretraining families, PoseBench reveals that pose awareness is an implicit but non-uniform property of 2D visual foundation models, and consistent gains from pose-graph refinement suggest that feature spaces retain structure compatible with the underlying pose manifold. PoseBench therefore provides a systematic basis for understanding and selecting pretrained features for pose-sensitive 3D vision tasks.
bullets: Benchmarks pose awareness through progressively harder probes, from controlled rendered views to real-image queries.
Introduces pose-graph refinement to test compatibility between feature neighborhoods and the underlying pose manifold.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show strong visual perception capabilities, but existing evaluations largely focus on single-view or multi-view settings with shared camera parameters, leaving the challenge of multi-agent collaborative scenarios underexplored. In such settings, multiple agents observe a shared environment from independent viewpoints, and reliable decisions require reasoning across these independent observations of the same environment. To study this problem, we introduce MaRiO, a benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaborative reasoning, and evaluate 23 state-of-the-art MLLMs on it. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (1) tasks governed by static perception are generally easier than tasks that require transformational event sequences; (2) most models struggle to resolve cross-agent correspondences, with errors increasing with scene complexity; and (3) models show limited ability to leverage geometric cues present in the scene. As an initial step toward addressing these challenges, we explore geometry-guided synthetic view augmentation that generates intermediate transition frames between agent observations, providing auxiliary spatial context that improves performance in certain categories. Overall, our results highlight that multi-agent collaborative reasoning remains an open challenge and an important direction for multimodal embodied systems. The code is available on the project page: https://omarftt.github.io/MaRiO-page/.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) in medical retrieval-augmented generation must be able to say when a retrieved report contradicts the X-ray, so understanding whether they can detect such conflicts is important for safe deployment. The sycophancy mask hypothesis holds that these models internally detect conflicts but refuse to report them, concealing a detected contradiction. We introduce a three-part diagnostic that separates concealment from uncertainty: representation probing, activation steering, and two-way forced choice. Across four instruction-tuned VLMs on chest X-rays, we confirm behavioral suppression of contradiction and find that a linear probe separates matched from mismatched inputs, beyond what a simple CLIP model achieves. Steering the learned conflict direction never elicits contradiction, and forcing a binary choice does not recover one; instead, cross-modal attention to the image drops on mismatched pairs. We conclude that these models fail to contradict because the mismatch registers as hedged, gated uncertainty rather than concealed knowledge, calling for re-grounding and uncertainty surfacing. Code is available at https://github.com/mohamed-eldagla/Uncertainty-Not-Concealment/.

papers.abstract: While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have improved automated radiology report generation, they remain prone to hallucinations, necessitating clinically meaningful risk-control methods. Conformal prediction (CP) provides statistical guarantees, yet existing CP approaches rely on uncalibrated automated extractors and fail to account for the clinical relevance of errors. We introduce clinical admissibility criteria (CLARITY), a framework for evaluating radiology reports that explicitly distinguishes clinically consequential errors from minor deviations. To eliminate reliance on automatic judges, we collected radiologist annotations of MLLM-generated reports using CLARITY. By benchmarking CP strategies and automatic evaluation metrics against these expert annotations, we demonstrate that commonly used admissibility proxies systematically fail to detect clinically relevant errors. Our findings reveal that automated admissibility judgments are largely decoupled from true clinical admissibility.
bullets: MLLM-generated radiology reports can hallucinate, creating a need for clinically meaningful risk control.
The framework distinguishes clinically consequential errors from minor report deviations.

papers.abstract: A phone screen can be wrong in ways that need no reference: a label that runs off the screen, letters that touch, a line that breaks one character before its end, one button with sharp corners among round ones. We ask whether a model can box every such fault on a screenshot, given no target design and no reference image. Such a critic could serve as a cheap first pass over generated pages before a designer reviews them, but only if it stays silent on clean pages. ScreenProof poses this target-free critique over three families of faults: general faults, local style faults (one element breaks the style its page sets) and text layout faults (letter spacing, line height, line breaks). A data engine makes each fault in page code and records the changed element's box, and hard negatives change every sibling alike. No frontier judge is reliable: frontier models flag 18-62% of clean real screenshots and 18-82% of clean generated pages, find 47-72% of text layout faults, and rarely find a foreign icon (5-19%). Our small critic ProofJudge (Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA), trained on code-made pages with one to four faults each and keeping a finding only when it is confident, reaches F1 0.48, the highest of all judges (Gemini 4 Argon 0.37; open models at most 0.15; 0.46 even without the confidence cut), and is the only fault-finding judge within 15% false alarms on clean pages (2% real, 9% generated), the property such a first pass needs, at about a hundredth of Argon's cost. It finds the most general faults (59%) but fewer local style faults than Argon (25% against 41%) and fewer text layout faults than the API judges (43%; Gemini 4 Argon 47%). Against a named brand the task is harder still: models know a design language about as well as its public documentation states it.
bullets: Targets three fault families: general UI errors, local style inconsistencies, and text-layout problems.
Generates faults directly in page code, records the altered element’s box, and uses hard negatives where all siblings change consistently.
ProofJudge, a Qwen3.5-9B model with LoRA, reaches F1 0.48 and limits false alarms to 2% on real clean pages and 9% on generated ones.
It detects general faults best (59%), but is weaker on local style faults (25%) and text-layout faults (43%).
Named-brand critique remains difficult; models largely know a design language only as well as its public documentation describes it.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving fundamentally demands dense understanding of visual, semantic, and geometric information, yet existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained with sparse supervision such as language instructions or trajectory signals. This direct mapping from dense visual observations to sparse representations forces the model to compress or even discard critical scene information essential for safe driving. We argue that this limitation does not stem from insufficient model capacity, but from the lack of explicit mechanisms that encourage the formation of dense world representations in the latent space. In this spirit, we propose a novel paradigm for driving intelligence, Think Densely, Act Sparsely, and instantiate it with an efficient and interpretable framework, LECDrive (Latent Expert Cognitive Chains for Vision-Language-Action autonomous Driving). The core idea is to mimic the hierarchical perception process of humans by embedding a progressive chain of latent expert cognition within the VLA model. Concretely, we inject a compact set of task-specific latent tokens as carriers, enabling the model to internalize dense knowledge from foundational vision models, including visual representations (DINOv3), semantic structures (SAM3), and spatial geometry (DepthAnything3), while maintaining efficient inference. This interdependent cognitive chain follows a curriculum learning principle, where supervision is progressively structured from representation to semantics and geometry. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LECDrive consistently improves the performance of base VLMs across multiple autonomous driving benchmarks, covering key tasks such as object perception, state prediction, and trajectory planning. These findings suggest that constructing dense world models through structured latent expert chains is a promising direction for VLA-based autonomous driving.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between dense visual driving information and sparse language or trajectory supervision in VLA models.
Introduces a progressive chain of task-specific latent expert tokens within the VLA model.
Distills visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from DINOv3, SAM3, and DepthAnything3.
Uses curriculum-style supervision that progresses from representation to semantics and geometry while targeting efficient inference.
Experiments across multiple autonomous-driving benchmarks report consistent improvements in object perception, state prediction, and trajectory planning.

For trajectory planning, LECDrive combines discrete motion primitives with continuous offset refinement to improve robustness and precision.

papers.abstract: Financial candlestick understanding requires locating visual elements, aligning them across trading dates and panels, and combining observations through numerical and financial reasoning. Answer accuracy alone does not reveal whether predictions are supported by chart evidence. We introduce Code-Interactive Financial Candlestick Reasoning and present Fin-Thinker, a model based on Qwen3.5-9B that generates and executes code to acquire evidence and perform computations. The model uses the returned observations to guide subsequent reasoning. To train these capabilities, we construct FinKLine-32K with 32,184 replay-verified code-observation trajectories collected through teacher-guided student exploration. These include successful solutions with and without error recovery. Our three-stage training framework combines foundational visual-code fine-tuning, financial process supervision of successful reasoning and corrective continuations, and execution-feedback reinforcement learning. For evaluation, we introduce FinKLineBench with 1,200 questions across 138 financial task types to assess answer correctness, code execution, and evidence grounding separately. On FinKLineBench, Fin-Thinker improves strict accuracy by 13.1 and 33.2 percentage points over the best-performing direct-answer baseline among those evaluated and its base model with sandbox access, respectively. Training-stage ablations further show that financial process supervision and execution-feedback reinforcement learning yield successive improvements in both answer accuracy and GPT-5.6-judged grounded accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the need to locate and align chart elements across dates and panels while combining visual, numerical, and financial reasoning.
Uses a Qwen3.5-9B-based model with code generation, execution, observation feedback, and a three-stage training framework.
Introduces FinKLine-32K, a dataset of 32,184 replay-verified code-observation reasoning trajectories.
Introduces FinKLineBench, covering 1,200 questions across 138 financial task types with separate measures for correctness, execution, and evidence grounding.

Fin-Thinker improves strict accuracy by 13.1 and 33.2 percentage points over the evaluated direct-answer baseline and its sandbox-enabled base model; ablations support the value of process supervision and execution-feedback reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: 3D spatial reasoning from video remains challenging for VLMs because videos provide sequential, view-local observations rather than persistent metric scene records. Many questions must be answered in a query-specified perspective rather than the observed camera viewpoint, and prompting with a fixed set of RGB views may miss sparse or occluded visual cues. To address these gaps, we introduce BEV3SR, a training-free and backbone-agnostic framework for RGB-D videos with camera parameters. BEV3SR turns video observations into queryable metric bird's-eye-view (BEV) scene memory and formalizes each query into an evidence-aware spatial task. The Spatial Task Formalizer specifies the query's reference frame, spatial constraints, objective, and evidence requirement. The evidence requirement determines the appropriate reasoning pathway. A query treated as requiring geometric evidence is handled by the Geometric Reasoner, which deterministically computes the answer using the metric BEV records in the query-specified reference frame. Otherwise, a query treated as requiring visual evidence is passed to the Visual Evidence Aligner, which uses BEV-indexed object records and their associated supporting views to retrieve object-consistent and scene-context RGB frames for VLM grounding. Within a standard 16-frame budget, BEV3SR consistently improves different VLM backbones across multiple 3D scene QA benchmarks, delivering large gains on spatially intensive questions and significant improvements on open-ended scene QA. These results demonstrate that BEV3SR offers an effective, efficient, and interpretable framework for explicit 3D spatial reasoning from video.
bullets: Addresses view-local, sequential video observations, query-specific viewpoints, and sparse or occluded evidence.
Formalizes each query’s reference frame, spatial constraints, objective, and required evidence.
Computes geometry-based answers deterministically from metric BEV records in the requested reference frame.
Retrieves object-consistent and contextual RGB frames for VLM grounding when visual evidence is needed.
Improves multiple VLM backbones across 3D scene QA benchmarks, especially spatially intensive and open-ended questions, within a 16-frame budget.
