papers.abstract: When should a robot look at the cup, and when at the portafilter? Spatial-reasoning benchmarks evaluate whether a model can describe a scene, but manipulation needs something more specific: the ability to acquire the particular evidence that makes the current command executable. A view that is informative for one task can be useless for another, even at the same workstation. We introduce Seeing What Matters, a benchmark for task-conditioned actionable spatial belief in simulated tabletop manipulation. Across three domains--coffee workstation, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance--the benchmark provides 860 frozen evaluation cases; expanding across methods, budgets, and inference repeats yields more than 115,000 evaluator episodes under two protocols: closed-loop actionability and same-object functional out-of-distribution generalization. Each case pairs a set of candidate RGB views with a manipulation command, shared scripted skills, and hidden postconditions, so the benchmark directly measures whether a view-selection policy acquires the observations its command actually needs. We also provide a diagnostic reference pipeline that maintains a spatial-functional belief state and ranks views by missing evidence. At primary budget settings, this pipeline reaches 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success; ablating the functional or command-binding components collapses performance to near zero. Seven vision-language models, evaluated on the same cases, reach only 26-43%. Replacing the reference pipeline's coverage metadata with frozen RGB-derived scores preserves 98.5%/98.9% success; shuffling the visual scores collapses it to 15%/11%, confirming that the result depends on image content. These gaps suggest that spatial belief for manipulation should be evaluated not by scene-level completeness, but by whether it acquires the evidence the current command requires.
bullets: Evaluates task-conditioned actionable spatial belief across coffee, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance domains.
Includes 860 frozen cases and over 115,000 evaluator episodes using closed-loop actionability and functional-OOD protocols.
A diagnostic belief-state pipeline ranks views by missing functional evidence and achieves 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success.
Seven vision-language models achieve only 26–43% on the same cases.
Ablations show that command binding, functional reasoning, and image content are essential to performance.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.
authors: Lingyun Song, Ziyao Chen, Kang Pan, Xiaolin Han, Yifei Zhang, Xiaoqi Wang, Yudai Pan, Xuequn Shang
bullets: Targets locality erosion and catastrophic forgetting during sequential factual updates.
Restricts updates toward the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces.
Uses a dynamically computed risk mask to protect stability-critical factual parameter regions.
Integrates edited knowledge at inference with prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion.
Experiments on two multimodal benchmarks show competitive performance across five metrics and stability over 1,000 sequential updates.

papers.abstract: Animation is pervasive on the Web, the CSS animation property alone appears on over three-quarters of webpages. Yet existing webpage code generation benchmarks target static screenshots, user-triggered interactions, or isolated motion graphics, leaving the ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and coding agents to reconstruct complete animated webpages largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce AnimWeb-Bench, the first benchmark for animated webpage code generation from videos. It comprises 124 real-world webpages spanning 7 application domains and 33 animation types, with 91.9% of pages combining multiple types, each paired with a reference video and the static assets of the original webpage. We further propose a human-aligned, two-dimensional evaluation protocol: Static Appearance Fidelity measures structure, text, color, and visual similarity on aligned keyframes, while Animation Fidelity tracks UI components across frames and compares their position, size, velocity, and appearance with those in the reference video. Evaluating 14 MLLMs and three coding agents reveals: (1) reproducing webpage animations is substantially more difficult than reproducing static appearance; (2) explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve the reconstruction quality of coding agents; and (3) rapid, continuous changes are harder to reproduce than discrete state transitions. Our code and dataset are available at https://starry1001.github.io/AnimWeb-Bench-website/ .
authors: Zhongyi Zhang, Jingyu Xiao, Shuqing Li, Michael R. Lyu
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 124 real-world webpages across 7 domains and 33 animation types, paired with reference videos and original static assets.
Provides a two-dimensional evaluation protocol measuring static appearance fidelity and animation fidelity across aligned frames.
Finds that webpage animation reconstruction is harder than reproducing static visual appearance.
Shows that explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve coding-agent reconstruction quality.
Reports that rapid, continuous motion is more difficult to reproduce than discrete state transitions.

papers.abstract: Shallow-water UAV imagery provides centimeter-scale observations of benthic environments, but water-induced distortions complicate interpretation. To our knowledge, we present the first systematic zero-shot benchmark of unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for both assessing water-induced distortions and restoring shallow-water imagery within the same model framework. We evaluate five open-weight unified MLLMs with frozen pretrained weights and without access to paired reference images or descriptions of the true seabed. The benchmark contains 1,000 image pairs: 600 semi-synthetic UAV scenes created by applying synthetic water distortions to real shallow-water imagery and 400 fully synthetic through-water scenes. Three independent human annotations cover five distortion types. We evaluate four assessment prompts (P0-P3), from direct instruction to structured task decomposition, on all 1,000 images and four diagnosis-guided restoration prompts (R0-R3) on a common 100-image subset. Assessment varies substantially by model and prompt, with systematic prediction biases and a best pooled balanced accuracy of 0.654 for distortion presence. The best pooled PSNR gain is +0.255 dB, no unified MLLM improves pooled LPIPS, and some outputs alter scene structure or hallucinate content. Two restoration-only baselines also show limited transfer: InstructIR achieves a pooled PSNR gain of +0.040 dB, while PromptFix degrades all four pooled metrics under every prompt. These results show that recognizing shallow-water degradation does not imply reliable physical restoration and provide a reproducible baseline for future work.
authors: Dario Scilla, Omar A. Lopez, Mattia Rosso, Kasper Johansen, Matthew F. McCabe
bullets: Evaluates five frozen, open-weight unified MLLMs on distortion assessment and restoration without paired references or true-seabed descriptions.
Uses 1,000 image pairs spanning semi-synthetic UAV scenes and fully synthetic through-water scenes, with human annotations covering five distortion types.
Assessment performance varies by model and prompt; the best pooled balanced accuracy for detecting distortion presence is 0.654.
Restoration gains are minimal: the best pooled PSNR improvement is +0.255 dB, while no unified MLLM improves pooled LPIPS.
Some restorations alter scene structure or hallucinate content, showing that degradation recognition does not ensure physically reliable restoration.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Benchmarking of Unified Multimodal Models for Shallow-Water UAV Image Distortion Assessment and Restoration
papers.tldr: A zero-shot benchmark finds that unified multimodal models can inconsistently detect shallow-water image distortion but generally fail to restore imagery reliably without reference information.

papers.abstract: Prompt learning adapts vision-language models such as CLIP by optimizing a short learnable prompt. The cross-entropy objective pulls this prompt toward base-class specialization, whereas generalization to unseen classes benefits from staying close to CLIP's zero-shot feature space. Because both objectives act on the same prompt, their gradients conflict at convergence, and in our experiments no single-prompt loss design clearly improves on the cosine baseline. We propose Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC), which gives each objective its own prompt. Starting from a base-trained prompt, DMC trains a specialization prompt and a generalization prompt, and merges their text features with a fixed coefficient at test time, at the inference cost of a single prompt. A linear mode connectivity (LMC) corridor in text-feature space keeps the classification loss low for every classifier interpolated between the two endpoints, and a Visual Anchor KL term preserves CLIP's zero-shot class-similarity distribution of each image during specialization. We further argue that such regularizers should satisfy class-permutation invariance (CPI), and show via Fano's inequality, in an idealized model, that violating CPI lower-bounds the drop in novel accuracy by a term proportional to the mutual information between the prompt and the base-class labels. Across 11 datasets, DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, and its interpolation curves pass beyond the single-prompt operating point, shifting the base-novel frontier rather than trading along it. Code is available at https://github.com/IemProg/DMC.
authors: Imad Eddine Marouf, Khalid Oublal, Enzo Tartaglione, St\'ephane Lathuili\`ere
bullets: Problem: A single prompt must balance base-class specialization with preservation of CLIP’s zero-shot behavior, causing conflicting objectives and limited generalization.

Method: Train separate specialization and generalization prompts from a base-trained prompt, connect them through a low-loss text-feature interpolation corridor, and merge their features using a fixed coefficient.
Regularization: Use a Visual Anchor KL term to preserve CLIP’s image-level class-similarity distribution, while enforcing class-permutation invariance.
Theory: Fano’s inequality links violations of class-permutation invariance to reduced novel-class accuracy through prompt–base-label mutual information.

Results: Across 11 datasets, DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, with interpolation curves extending beyond the single-prompt trade-off point.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Decoupled Mode Connectivity on Flowers102 (joint CE loss landscape). The 2D plane in CLIP text-feature space is anchored at fw1 (zero-shot CLIP); the x-axis spans toward fŵ2 (fine-tuned CoOp checkpoint) and the y-axis is the Gram–Schmidt orthogonal component of fgen (text features of DMC’s converged generalization prompt) relative to fw1 . Each grid point is re-normalized per class before the joint base+novel CE loss is evaluated; construction details in Appendix G. Before DMC (left): the single-prompt baseline traces the linear path; the inset shows the base–novel trade-off, with base and novel accuracies crossing over as α varies. During DMC (middle): the two prompts start collapsed at fŵ2 (epoch 0) and separate during training. After DMC (right): the converged DMC corridor lies inside the low-loss valley, with the operating point at α = 0.20 marked by the star; the inset confirms base and novel accuracies are both high and stable along the corridor.

Figure 2: Empirical interpolation curves on Caltech101, SUN397, UCF101, and EuroSAT (CoOp base, 3-seed mean). Each curve traces the family of classifiers from fgen (α=0, near zero-shot) to fspec (α=1, fully specialized). Solid: DMC (full method); dashed: DMC w/o VA. Gray dots mark the MERGETUNE baseline; blue stars mark the operating point; the green arrow shows the shift from baseline to operating point. The boxed ∆HM value reports the gap (operating point vs. baseline), read off the seed-averaged curves; it can differ from Table 1 by up to 0.23 HM.

Figure 8: Food101 and DTD. Food101 has a flat frontier; DMC shifts the operating point slightly (+0.08 HM). DTD is the only dataset in these figures where DMC is slightly below the baseline (−0.77 HM).
Figure 9: EuroSAT and UCF101. EuroSAT shows the largest improvement among these datasets (+2.43 HM). UCF101 achieves +1.80 HM. (Both datasets are also shown in the main paper, Figure 2.)
Figure 7: StanfordCars and FGVCAircraft. Both fine-grained datasets show clear operating-point shifts: +1.96 HM on StanfordCars and +1.89 on FGVCAircraft.

Figure 11: HM landscape on Flowers102. Same 2D plane and overlays as the main-paper Figure 1, with the heatmap recolored by harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy (high HM in blue). The DMC corridor lies on the high-HM peak; the operating point at α = 0.20 sits near the corridor’s HM maximum ≈ 84. The single-prompt linear path along the bottom of the plane traverses an HM ridge that peaks below ≈ 80 at every mixing weight, consistent with the single-prompt ceiling of Lemma 1 along this path.

Figure 12: HM landscape on Caltech101. Caltech101 is a near-ceiling task (zero-shot CLIP attains HM ≈ 95), so the landscape varies over a much narrower range, [92.8, 96.9], than Flowers102 ([64.9, 84.6]). Despite the compressed dynamic range, the same geometry is visible: the DMC corridor lies on a high-HM ridge offset from the linear single-prompt path, and the operating point at α = 0.20 sits near the ridge maximum. Flat-but-shifted performance is the expected near-ceiling behavior of decoupling: when single-prompt HM is already close to the achievable upper bound, DMC’s gain shrinks (CoOp+DMC gains +0.14 HM over MERGETUNE on Caltech101, Table 1).
Figure 13: Pareto fronts for α selection on four datasets. Stars mark Pareto knee points. As α increases, features move right (better base fit) and down (more drift from fw1 ).

Figure 4: Gradient conflict at convergence. ρ = cos(∇cLCE, ∇cR) at the converged single-prompt checkpoint, averaged over the full training set. ρ < 0 on every dataset-baseline pair; Flowers102 shows the strongest conflict (ρ ≈ −0.95 for CoOp).

Figure 5: DMC decoupling dynamics during training. Both prompts are initialized from ŵ2. Blue: cos(fgen, fw1 ) rises sharply within 10 epochs and saturates near 0.97–0.99, confirming rapid convergence toward zero-shot geometry. Orange: cos(fspec, fw1) decreases overall under CE supervision, with oscillations from the LMC coupling. Final values range from ∼0.45 (Flowers102, strongest separation) to ∼0.65 (OxfordPets, weakest). Purple dashed: cos(fgen, fspec) reflects the feature separation, decreasing from ∼1.0 to 0.50–0.67. The shaded region visualizes the decoupling gap. Single seed, with VA; Table 10 reports the 3-seed endpoint cosines (without VA; with-VA averages in its caption).

Figure 3: Ablation: learned fgen vs. fixed fw1 . Both variants retrain cspec with the same loss (CE + VA + LMC), differing only in the generalization endpoint. At small α, including α = 0.20, the learned fgen (solid) gives a higher HM than the fixed fw1 (dashed).

Figure 14: HM, Base accuracy, and Novel accuracy vs α on four datasets. Each row is one dataset; columns show HM, Base, and Novel accuracy. The dashed red line marks α = 0.20. Base accuracy increases monotonically with α (the specialization prompt dominates), while Novel accuracy decreases (generalization degrades). The HM peak reflects the trade-off between these opposing trends and lies in α ∈ [0.10, 0.35] across all datasets.

Figure 10: ImageNet — CoOp+DMC, KgCoOp+DMC, MMA+DMC. Interpolation curves on ImageNet (seed mean of the 21-point α sweep). The blue star marks the operating point at the fixed α = 0.20 (the same value used for all held-out datasets, selected on Flowers102+Caltech101). At the operating point, DMC yields +0.01 HM on CoOp+DMC (72.89 → 72.90), +0.27 HM on KgCoOp+DMC (72.82 → 73.09), and −0.25 HM on MMA+DMC (73.15 → 72.90; the MMA panel shows an earlier single run, whose boxed value differs) over MergeTune. The operating-point shift on ImageNet is small relative to the specialized datasets (Figure 2); this is consistent with ImageNet’s high-diversity 1000-class set, where the single-prompt envelope already covers most of the achievable operating points and decoupling has less headroom than on specialized tasks like EuroSAT or StanfordCars. Unlike the other interpolation-curve figures in this appendix, only the DMC (with VA) curve is shown: a DMC-without-VA ablation was not run on ImageNet.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC) for prompt learning in vision-language models to improve generalization to novel classes, addressing a key LLM/MLM challenge.
papers.title: Decoupled Mode Connectivity for Base-to-Novel Generalization in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: DMC improves base-to-novel generalization in vision-language prompt learning by separately optimizing specialization and generalization prompts, then merging their text features at inference.

papers.abstract: Dense video object captioning (DVOC) localizes, tracks, and describes object trajectories within a video. Existing methods process each camera view independently, producing separate camera-local tracklets and captions for the same person across cameras. These outputs lack a unified description and leave complementary appearance evidence across views unused. We therefore formulate cross-view DVOC (CVDVOC), which associates these tracklets into scene-level global trajectories and generates one caption for each trajectory from synchronized views. To support this task, we construct CRTrack-Cap from CRTrack by auditing text-identity links and converting usable referring expressions into canonical captions. It retains 425 global trajectories and 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, with canonical captions for 335 identities. We adapt CHOTA to the cross-view setting as CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate tracking and caption quality. Our reference framework combines View-Exclusive Cross-Camera Association (VECA) for grouping tracklets with Conflict-Evidence Gating (CEG) for integrating caption evidence using its reliability and disagreement across views. Against three single-view methods adapted with MvMHAT for cross-view association, our framework achieves CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 and 33.48 on the scene-disjoint in-domain and cross-domain tests, respectively. Together, CRTrack-Cap and our framework provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for describing the same person consistently across camera views.
authors: Xiangqun Zhang, Likai Wang, Zekun Qian, Rui Zhou, Ruize Han, Wei Feng
bullets: Formulates cross-view dense video object captioning (CVDVOC), combining synchronized multi-camera evidence instead of processing views independently.
Constructs CRTrack-Cap with 425 global trajectories, 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, and canonical captions for 335 identities.
Introduces CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate cross-view tracking and caption quality.
The reference framework uses VECA for cross-camera association and CEG to integrate reliable, non-conflicting caption evidence.
It reports CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 in-domain and 33.48 cross-domain on scene-disjoint tests.

papers.abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common kidney cancer in adults. We present a region-aware architecture for CT-based ccRCC classification. Tumor and 0--10 mm peritumoral context are pooled separately from shared frozen DINOv3 feature maps. A shared position-aware slice aggregator precedes fixed training-only principal component analysis (PCA). The resulting representations are fused with radiomics using two scalar feature gates. Evaluation on KiTS23 and 111 external cases yields internal test and external AUCs of 0.8078\pm0.0154 and 0.9094\pm0.0015. Compared with matched single-tumor readout, mean AUC increases by 1.50 and 2.34 percentage points, respectively. Early-PCA and reconstruction controls yield lower internal mean AUCs, while external AUC is similar for early and late PCA. These findings highlight the joint role of regional readout and slice aggregation in adapting frozen visual features to renal CT.
authors: Yuan Liang, Sourav Bhattacharjee, Abraham Campbell
bullets: Separately pools tumor and 0–10 mm peritumoral regions from shared frozen DINOv3 features.
Uses position-aware slice aggregation, training-only PCA, and gated fusion with radiomics.
Achieves internal and external AUCs of 0.8078±0.0154 and 0.9094±0.0015 on KiTS23 and 111 external cases.
Outperforms matched single-tumor readout by 1.50 and 2.34 percentage points in mean AUC.
Results support combining regional readout with slice aggregation; external performance is similar for early versus late PCA.

The encoder receives unmasked CT slices. T and C pass separately through the same trainable position-aware slice aggregator (PSA), followed by fixed PCA32. Two scalar gates fuse the concatenated image vector with radiomics. CT is displayed at [−200, 300] HU.

papers.selection_reason: Adapts frozen DINOv3 features for renal tumor classification using region-aware slice aggregation, demonstrating spatial reasoning in 3D medical data.
papers.title: Dual-Region Slice Aggregation for CT-Based Renal Tumor Classification
papers.tldr: A region-aware model improves CT-based ccRCC classification by separately aggregating tumor and peritumoral context before fusing features with radiomics.

papers.abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) classification from computed tomography (CT) may benefit from representations that capture different aspects of tumour phenotype. However, simply concatenating reconstruction-derived features, image--text embeddings, and radiomic descriptors may not fully exploit their complementary information. We propose MSR-ABC, a global--local framework integrating MedVAE, MedSigLIP, and radiomics. Spatially matched local image descriptors interact through cross-representation attention, while radiomic auxiliary supervision encourages the pooled local representation to retain quantitative tumour attributes. A gated residual mechanism integrates local information with global summaries. Area-aware pooling and visual and soft-text prompting complete the framework. We evaluate discrimination using a patient-level split of 396 KiTS23 cases and an external cohort of 111 TCGA/TCIA cases, reporting mean AUROC over three training seeds with 95% patient-bootstrap confidence intervals. MSR-ABC achieves mean AUROCs of 0.806 internally and 0.879 externally. Internally, it exceeds global MedVAE--radiomics and three-source concatenation by 3.35 and 3.61 AUROC percentage points, respectively. Removing any source lowers mean AUROC in both cohorts, with the largest decreases following radiomics removal. Individual removal of cross-representation attention, auxiliary supervision, or gated fusion also lowers internal mean AUROC. These findings are consistent with complementary contributions within the integrated architecture and support further investigation of structured representation fusion for non-invasive renal tumour characterisation.
authors: Yuan Liang, Sourav Bhattacharjee, Abraham Campbell
bullets: Addresses the limited benefit of simply concatenating reconstruction, image–text, and radiomic features.
Uses MedVAE, MedSigLIP, and radiomics in a global–local framework with cross-representation attention, radiomic auxiliary supervision, gated residual fusion, area-aware pooling, and prompting.
Evaluated on patient-level splits of 396 KiTS23 cases and an external cohort of 111 TCGA/TCIA cases.
Achieves mean AUROCs of 0.806 internally and 0.879 externally, outperforming specified internal baselines by 3.35–3.61 percentage points.
Ablations indicate that all feature sources and key fusion components contribute, with radiomics removal causing the largest drop.

The circled plus adds fusion and image–text logits. Solid and dashed arrows denote inference and training-only paths. Dots mark branches. Crossings without dots are unconnected. papers.selection_reason: Fuses MedVAE, MedSigLIP, and radiomics for medical image classification, focusing on spatial reasoning and feature fusion.
papers.title: MSR-ABC: Complementary Feature Fusion for Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma Classification
papers.tldr: MSR-ABC improves ccRCC classification from CT by fusing complementary global, local, image–text, and radiomic representations.

papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar offers a privacy-preserving and illumination-robust alternative for human mesh reconstruction (HMR). However, high-fidelity radar HMR remains challenging. Sparse point cloud-based methods suffer from information loss and missed detections, while raw radar tensor methods like RT-Mesh lack fine-grained semantics and explicit local body modeling. In this paper, we propose RadarDINO, a radar HMR framework that distills visual semantics from a DINOv3 teacher into 3D radar representations and introduces explicit geometric supervision. DINOv3 descriptors are transferred to radar voxels via calibrated RGB-radar geometry, providing voxel- and body-part-level supervision for part-aware radar representations. We further incorporate vertex- and joint-losses to directly constrain reconstructed geometry. On the M4Human dataset, our method outperforms the SOTA baseline across all three evaluation splits.
authors: Furkan Mert Algan, Zhifan Ni, Eckehard Steinbach
bullets: Addresses information loss in sparse radar point clouds and weak semantics in raw radar tensor methods.
Distills DINOv3 visual descriptors into 3D radar voxels using calibrated RGB–radar geometry.
Provides voxel- and body-part-level supervision for part-aware radar representations.
Uses vertex and joint losses to directly constrain reconstructed human geometry.
Outperforms the prior state-of-the-art baseline on all three M4Human evaluation splits.

papers.title: RadarDINO: Distilling a Visual Foundation Model into mmWave Radar for Human Mesh Reconstruction
papers.tldr: RadarDINO improves privacy-preserving human mesh reconstruction from mmWave radar by transferring visual semantics and applying explicit geometric supervision.

papers.abstract: While MLLMs can often identify what happens in a video, they still struggle with fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning, which requires precise grounding when and where the supporting evidence appears and composing such evidence into a coherent reasoning chain. This challenge is exacerbated by the lack of scalable data construction and evaluation pipelines that provide granular, verifiable supervision linking reasoning steps to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.To address this gap, we present V-STORM, a structure-aware framework that transforms videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs (STSGs) and derives Grounded Chain of Thought (GCoT) from validated evidence paths, making each reasoning step traceable to structured and verifiable spatio-temporal evidence.Under this framework, we construct a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark, both featuring GCoT annotations that link reasoning to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.Experiments reveal a clear separation between evidence localization and evidence composition: current MLLMs can often identify relevant spatio-temporal cues, yet still fail to integrate them into correct multi-step reasoning, exposing a bottleneck that answer-only evaluation largely obscures. Moreover, fine-tuning with V-STORM substantially improves both answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness, validating its effectiveness as supervision for faithful and evidence-grounded video reasoning. Our dataset, benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.
authors: Dian Jiao, Yuqian Yuan, Jiaqi Zhu, Mingjian Gao, Siwen Tan, Yunqi Cao, Jinhui Li, Sijing Li, Zhenxuan Fan, Haoyang Wang, Wenqiao Zhang, Siliang Tang
bullets: Addresses MLLMs’ difficulty composing precise temporal and spatial evidence into coherent multi-step reasoning.
Represents videos as Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs and derives grounded reasoning chains from validated evidence paths.
Introduces a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark with grounded chain-of-thought annotations.
Finds that MLLMs often localize relevant evidence but struggle to compose it correctly, a weakness hidden by answer-only evaluation.
Fine-tuning with V-STORM improves answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness.

papers.abstract: Large language models have expanded beyond text to vision, audio, and other modalities, but understanding raw electromagnetic (EM) signals remains challenging. Wideband recordings can contain millions of samples, whereas existing waveform-based EM models are primarily evaluated on short in-phase and quadrature (IQ) segments, leaving long-recording understanding and detailed description insufficiently explored. We introduce LEMMO, a large EM model for instruction-driven recognition and description of long raw IQ recordings. LEMMO combines a linear-attention EM encoder with anti-aliased temporal resampling to process up to eight million complex samples. Its EM-text interaction module conditions learnable queries on instructions before retrieving signal evidence. Compact queries support recognition, while structured queries with auxiliary factual supervision organize scene-level properties, signal attributes, and cross-signal relationships for detailed description. We also construct and release a unified 1.38-TB corpus of real-world and synthetic EM signals, including LEMMO-ShortQA and LEMMO-LongDesc. Compared with MERLIN-LoRA, LEMMO improves mean EM-Bench perception accuracy by 15.77 %, mean strategy-generation ROUGE-L F1 by 4.38 points, and mean LEMMO-ShortQA accuracy by 14.31 %. It also improves categorical and numerical fact F1 on both LEMMO-LongDesc tasks while preserving its language backbone's MMLU performance. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/N1rv4n4/LEMMO and https://huggingface.co/datasets/DaftJun/RFLAS, respectively.
authors: Mingkai Li, Jiajun Wu, Yihan Mao, Zilin Sang, Taosong Yu, Yuan Ma, Minghe Liu, Qianqian Yang, Zhiguo Shi
bullets: Addresses the limited long-recording and detailed-description capabilities of existing waveform-based EM models.
Combines a linear-attention EM encoder, anti-aliased temporal resampling, and instruction-conditioned EM–text interaction.

Introduces a unified 1.38-TB corpus with LEMMO-ShortQA and LEMMO-LongDesc datasets.
Outperforms MERLIN-LoRA across reported perception, strategy-generation, QA, and factual-description metrics while preserving language-backbone MMLU performance.

papers.abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pulse sequences organize radiofrequency excitation, gradient encoding, and signal acquisition, determining magnetization evolution and image formation. Sequence research requires translating imaging objectives into executable protocols meeting physical and acquisition constraints, refined via physical simulation, signal reconstruction, and scientific evaluation. Sequence construction, physical verification, parameter search, and assessment involve many tools and manual decisions, limiting automation from objective to verifiable sequence. We develop SmartBloch-Agent, an integrated framework for automated MRI sequence design and optimization. Given objectives and scientific constraints in natural language, an AI agent interprets goals, plans tasks, orchestrates tools, and makes feedback-informed decisions, drawing on a construction module and optimizers for structural design and parameter search. Our GPU-accelerated SmartBloch engine supplies physical computation for both stages, so the framework configures, per sequence and objective, event validation, Full-Bloch magnetization evolution, signal acquisition, image reconstruction, and scientific evaluation, and closes the loop without external MRI simulators. Results return to the agent to guide sequence revision, parameter optimization, and candidate selection, and the design files carry simulation, reconstruction, and evaluation evidence, forming an output package for a real-scanner workflow. Experiments show the framework automatically designs and optimizes MRI sequences for varied objectives and constraints, refines candidates with physical feedback, and improves several parameter-estimation metrics and downstream quantitative reconstruction. SmartBloch-Agent unifies objectives, design, physical execution, and evaluation into a continuous workflow for end-to-end automation of MRI sequence research.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language models and diffusion generators have driven rapid progress in brain-to-image generation, while EEG-based reconstruction is still constrained by low signal-to-noise ratio and cross-subject semantic shifts. Zero-shot cross-subject reconstruction poses even greater challenges: EEG semantic embeddings learned from source subjects deviate from the manifold of image embeddings of the unseen target subject, particularly when neither target labels nor target image embeddings are available. To address this issue, we introduce the Semantic Preservation and Subspace Calibration (SPSC) framework, which first uses Object Mask Contrastive Regularization (OMCR) with object identity for backend training, and then constructs Subspace Candidate Gate (SCG) to achieve label-free semantic correction for target subjects during inference. Specifically, OMCR regularizes the conditioning space with object-level positive samples to preserve object-level feature neighborhoods within the reconstruction prior and low-level branch, while SCG exploits training image prototypes and batch statistics of unlabeled target EEG to select candidates for each task within subspaces of image prototypes. Under the leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) setting across ten subjects on the THINGS-EEG dataset, SPSC improves the cross-subject reconstruction from 0.552 to 0.713 on CLIP and from 0.612 to 0.745 on Alex.5. These significant gains indicate that the semantically calibrated conditions can better support generation for the target subjects under label-free inference.
authors: Yutang Lu, Shuai Jiang, Fei Su, Zhicheng Zhao
bullets: Addresses semantic shifts and low signal-to-noise ratio in unseen-subject EEG reconstruction without target labels or image embeddings.

In leave-one-subject-out evaluation across ten THINGS-EEG subjects, CLIP improved from 0.552 to 0.713 and Alex.5 from 0.612 to 0.745.
Scope: evaluation is reported on the THINGS-EEG dataset under label-free target-subject inference.

papers.abstract: The main challenge of multi-modal image registration is shared structural feature extraction with higher accuracy and lower computational complexity. Compared with a State Space Model (SSM), the State Space Principles (SSP) formulation of Mamba-3 uses a more accurate discretization with lower truncation error while maintaining linear complexity. However, vanilla SSP is designed for natural language processing (NLP) and is not directly suitable for images. To address this issue, we propose a novel non-causal SSP (NC-SSP) with shared structure awareness and develop a coarse-to-fine registration method named RegNC-Mamba3. First, NC-SSP is designed to eliminate the dependence of the integral computation on the scanning path. By combining relative-weight normalization with aggregation over all circular scan paths, NC-SSP constructs a globally hidden state without long-range decay, which provides a wider receptive field and higher efficiency than the original Mamba-3. Second, NC-SSP is modified to strengthen the extraction of cross-modal structural features. When computing hidden states and feature interactions, we construct complex-valued sequences in NC-SSP by applying learnable Log-Gabor kernels, with different orientations to each head for frequency-domain modulation. This improves the perception of shared structural information across modalities and increases both registration accuracy and quality. Experiments on VIS-SAR and VIS-IR demonstrate that RegNC-Mamba3 outperforms the compared detector-based and semi-dense multi-modal registration methods.
authors: Zhikang Li, Yan Wu, Xin Hu, Yi Dai, Ming Li
bullets: Addresses accurate, efficient shared-structure extraction for multi-modal image registration.
Introduces non-causal SSP (NC-SSP), which removes scan-path dependence and aggregates circular paths for a global hidden state without long-range decay.
Uses relative-weight normalization to provide a wider receptive field while retaining linear-complexity processing.
Applies learnable, orientation-specific Log-Gabor kernels to construct complex-valued sequences for stronger cross-modal structural perception.
A coarse-to-fine RegNC-Mamba3 method outperforms compared detector-based and semi-dense methods on VIS-SAR and VIS-IR registration tasks.

papers.abstract: Reasoning traces improve vision-language models on complex multimodal tasks, but forcing every input to follow a long reasoning process leads to overthinking and unnecessary inference cost. We study adaptive fast/slow thinking for VLMs, where one model answers directly for simple inputs and reasons step by step when needed. Fast answers and slow traces often come from distinct behavior policies, making a single-reference offline objective misweight one mode. We propose DUAL-REFERENCE BOLT (DR-BOLT), which distinguishes the desired fast/slow mixture reference from the sampling distribution and corrects their mismatch in reward-weighted training. Fast/slow partition competition explains routing in the optimal target; an efficient source-wise correction approximates the exact objective when response formats are well separated. Matched Qwen3-VL comparisons use identical candidate banks to isolate the objective from slow-teacher quality. DR-BOLT improves score-length trade-offs over the evaluated offline and online baselines on ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, with a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and a 2.90-fold end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO. These results support adaptive reasoning in the studied two-reference setting, while broader robustness remains open. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongbinLin3589/DR-BOLT.
authors: Hongbin Lin, Sizhe Zou, Juangui Xu, Xinyue Xu, Zhuoli Ouyang, Stanislav Kolchin, Chengwei Qin, Zhongxiang Dai, Yao Shu

On ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, improves score–length trade-offs over evaluated offline and online baselines.
Reports a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and 2.90× end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO; broader robustness remains open.

papers.title: Learning When to Think: Dual-Reference Offline Optimization for Adaptive VLM Reasoning

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering forces multimodal large language models to reason under strict visual-token budgets, creating a tradeoff between broad temporal coverage and fine-grained spatial detail. Uniform sampling preserves coverage but often obscures decisive local cues, while caption-based or frame-similarity retrieval operates over lossy proxies that can miss motion, state changes, and before-after relations. We recast long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem: given a fixed budget, decide how much to spend on global context versus high-resolution local evidence, and where in the video to draw that local evidence from. We introduce AdaAlloc, a training-free inference framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between a global video overview and localized visual detail. AdaAlloc first plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to locate candidate evidence segments and refines them into a compact temporal memory. The selected policy controls both frame sampling density and resolution, combining sparse, lower-resolution global frames with denser, higher-resolution local frames drawn from the refined memory. The final answerer reasons over the allocated global context and refined local evidence. Across LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench, AdaAlloc improves over budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points and outperforms the compared frame-selection and agentic methods on their reported benchmarks.
bullets: Recasts long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem under a fixed budget.
Plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to refine candidate evidence segments into compact memory.
Combines sparse low-resolution global frames with dense high-resolution local frames from refined memory.
Outperforms budget-matched uniform sampling and frame-selection/agentic methods on LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench.

papers.title: AdaAlloc: Adaptive Visual Token Allocation for Long-Video Question Answering

papers.abstract: Recent work tests whether language models can introspect by injecting a concept direction into their activations and asking whether they notice it and can name it. These studies are text-only. Vision-language models (VLMs) face an additional problem, known in cognitive psychology as reality monitoring: they must keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see. We therefore ask: can VLMs distinguish injected concepts from image content? We introduce a paradigm that varies the image and the injected concept independently. On each trial, the model reports what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. This design scores both whether the model identifies the concept and which source it assigns to it. Across six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably identifies injected concepts (35% vs. 3% for steering alone), with almost no false alarms. Even then, the source it reports is fragile. Strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen, and a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports. The same failure appears in ordinary captioning, where injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs. Evaluating multimodal self-reports therefore requires checking both their content and their reported source.
authors: Tina Khezresmaeilzadeh, Seyedarmin Azizi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
bullets: Introduces a reality-monitoring paradigm that independently varies image content and injected concepts.
Models report what they see, whether a thought was injected, and the thought’s identity, enabling separate content and source evaluation.
Among six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably detected injected concepts, with few false alarms.
Source attribution remained fragile: strong or visual-pathway injections were often reported as seen, while visible objects suppressed correct thought reports.
The same issue affects ordinary captioning, where injected objects appeared in captions of real photographs.

Thought injections use layer 37 and α=0.2, except for the stronger thought (α=0.4) and the laptop example (layer 33). The sight injection uses a visual concept direction at image tokens in layer 21. The model can name an injected thought while correctly naming a visible object (green). A stronger thought is instead reported as visible, and a sight injection makes the model describe pizzas in a zebra photograph (orange). Photographs: COCO [13].

papers.selection_reason: Investigates source attribution and introspection in VLMs, relevant to multimodal foundation model understanding.
papers.title: Did I See It or Think It? Probing Reality Monitoring in Vision-Language Models with Concept Injection
papers.tldr: A new test shows that vision-language models rarely distinguish injected thoughts from visual content, and even when they detect them, they often misattribute their source.

papers.abstract: When a multimodal LLM miscounts in a diagram, does it fail at seeing or at counting? Existing visual graph and puzzle benchmarks vary visual density and algorithmic hardness together, confounding the two. We pair counting questions about the same drawing that sit in different counting-complexity classes, such as its spanning trees (a determinant) and its simple paths (#P-complete), and use a transcription probe and a text-only control to separate reading from computing. We test Gemini, Gemma and Qwen3-VL models; for the Gemini models, the answer depends on how the model computes. In chain of thought, most of them read small drawings correctly and then fail at counting, at a rate set far more by the size of the answer than by its complexity class (for the primary model, the odds of an exact answer fall 2.38-fold per decade of the answer). Given code and an exact transcription, the primary model counts correctly even on 10x10 grids, and reading becomes the bottleneck: a single view misses horizontal edges, and a second reading of a rotated copy with crop checks reads 86/96 large grids exactly, against 57/96 when the upright reading is simply repeated.
bullets: The study separates visual reading from algorithmic counting using paired questions on the same drawings with different complexity classes.
Transcription probes and text-only controls distinguish perception errors from computational failures.
In chain-of-thought, Gemini models usually read small diagrams correctly but struggle as answer size grows more than as complexity class changes.
With exact transcriptions and code, the primary model counts correctly even on 10×10 grids, shifting the bottleneck to visual reading.
A rotated second view with crop checks reads 86/96 large grids exactly, versus 57/96 when repeating the upright view.

papers.title: Seeing vs. Counting: Complexity Twins Show Where Multimodal LLMs Fail on Diagrams
papers.tldr: Multimodal LLMs often see diagrams correctly but fail when counting large answers, while better transcription and code can largely resolve the problem.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models combine image understanding and generation within one system, creating an opportunity to improve both capabilities through paired image--text supervision. We examine the outputs of a pretrained unified model in both directions and observe a loss of specificity: generated images can contain the requested objects with incorrect attributes, while captions identify a scene without expressing its distinguishing details. These failures call for supervision that specifies both the visual content to realize and the descriptive differences to distinguish. We propose UniMore, a post-training method that derives these complementary learning tasks from the fine-grained content of image--text pairs. The generation route predicts grounded crops from their corresponding phrases, matching the scope of the condition and visual target while using the native visual objective. The understanding route combines positive-caption fitting with ranking against captions that omit or alter details, conditioned on the full image. The two routes are optimized independently, and their learned updates are combined into a single unified model without changing its inference procedure. Experiments show gains across multiple understanding and generation benchmarks.
authors: Haoyue Bai, Yinyi Luo, Yicheng He, Qingsong Wen, Sharon Li, Jindong Wang
bullets: Targets attribute errors in generated images and overly generic captions.
Uses phrase-grounded crops for generation to align visual targets with textual conditions.
Trains understanding with positive captions plus negatives that omit or alter image details.
Combines independently learned generation and understanding updates without changing inference.
Reports gains across multiple understanding and generation benchmarks.

papers.title: UniMore: Fine-Grained Supervision for Unified Understanding and Generation
papers.tldr: UniMore improves a unified multimodal model’s specificity in both image generation and understanding through fine-grained, paired image–text supervision.

papers.abstract: Referring multi-object tracking enables users to specify targets through natural language, but existing Refer-MOT benchmarks primarily focus on single-camera settings. We formalize Referring Multi-Target Multi-Camera Tracking (Refer-MTMCT), where free-form queries specify identity-consistent trajectories to be recovered across a network of sequential, sparse-overlap cameras. We introduce Refer-CityFlow, a benchmark built on CityFlow's global cross-camera identity annotations and augmented with language queries requiring joint language grounding, cross-camera association, and spatio-temporal reasoning. Refer-CityFlow covers 96 videos from 40 roadside cameras with 660+ identity-consistent cross-camera trajectories, 4,362 trajectory-level descriptions, and 7,699 queries, including 1,699 real-user queries collected from 50 participants. Reference experiments on the four-camera Scenario 02 show that single-camera referring trackers reach 14.95-18.28 HOTA on real-user queries, while the evaluated cross-view method achieves about 0.05 HOTA in direct transfer. To establish reference performance, we provide M3Track, a modular multimodal reference framework in which a large language model (LLM)-based agent orchestrates interchangeable detection, tracking, and cross-camera association modules. M3Track reaches 44.10 HOTA and 65.40 IDF1 on the same real-user query set. The project repository is available at https://github.com/phuongnguyen194/Refer-CityFlow-and--M3Track.
authors: Phuong T. Nguyen, Hao Vo, Tam Bang, Hoang K. Tran, Hoang-Minh Dau, Mahshid Malazizi, Tuan-Anh Hoang, Mina Sartipi, Thanh-Nam Doan, Ngan Le, Hoang H. Nguyen
bullets: Formalizes Referring Multi-Target Multi-Camera Tracking (Refer-MTMCT), combining language grounding, cross-camera identity association, and spatio-temporal reasoning.
Presents Refer-CityFlow: 96 videos from 40 cameras, 660+ cross-camera trajectories, 4,362 descriptions, and 7,699 queries, including 1,699 real-user queries.
Single-camera trackers transfer poorly, achieving 14.95–18.28 HOTA on real-user queries, while an evaluated cross-view method reaches about 0.05 HOTA.
Introduces M3Track, a modular multimodal framework coordinated by an LLM-based agent across detection, tracking, and camera-association modules.
M3Track achieves 44.10 HOTA and 65.40 IDF1 on the reported real-user query set.

papers.title: Refer-CityFlow and M3Track: A Benchmark Dataset and Reference Framework for Language-Driven Multi-Target Multi-Camera Tracking

papers.abstract: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing imagery provides rich spatial details but poses challenges for accurate and efficient multimodal understanding. Existing evidence acquisition methods selectively explore relevant image regions, yet largely rely on generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for intermediate search control. However, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) primarily aligns these models with human-preferred responses rather than explicitly optimizing region-level relevance judgments, while repeated autoregressive decoding introduces additional computational overhead. To address these limitations, we propose GeoJeV, a training-free method that formulates evidence acquisition as spatial probability-driven decision making. At each evaluated region, a frozen JeV model produces a probability distribution over candidate regions. Specifically, Region Rank prioritizes candidate regions, Sparse Branch adaptively determines branching width through sparse probability support, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth based on branch sparsity and distribution concentration. By coordinating search priority, branching width, and refinement depth through a shared distribution, GeoJeV reduces reliance on RLHF-aligned generation and eliminates intermediate decoding. Experiments on LRS-GRO, MME-RealWorld-RS, and LRS-VQA achieve accuracies of 60.59%, 52.79%, and 34.32%, respectively. Across the three benchmarks, GeoJeV improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B by +5.32pp with only 1.12 additional seconds per question, while achieving a 7.8-fold inference speedup over the recent method.
authors: Xinyi Niu, Lingfeng Chen, Jiehua Zhang, Panhe Hu, Li Liu, Zhen Liu, Yongxiang Liu
bullets: Addresses inefficient and poorly targeted region exploration in multimodal understanding of ultra-high-resolution imagery.
Uses a frozen JeV model to score candidate regions and coordinate search decisions.
Region Rank selects priorities, Sparse Branch adapts branching width, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth.
Achieves 60.59%, 52.79%, and 34.32% accuracy on LRS-GRO, MME-RealWorld-RS, and LRS-VQA, respectively.
Improves Qwen3-VL-8B’s average accuracy by 5.32 percentage points with 1.12 seconds of added latency, and is 7.8× faster than a recent method.

GeoJeV with Qwen3-VL-8B achieves the highest accuracy among the plotted methods, exceeding WeaveEarth by +5.58 pp.

Fig. 2: Overview of GeoJeV. (Left) JeV estimates a spatial probability distribution over candidate regions. (Middle) Region Rank sets search priority, Sparse Branch adapts branching width, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth through early stopping. (Right) The acquired regions are consolidated and assembled into a spatial evidence canvas for final answering.
Fig. 3: Overview of the three benchmarks. Headings report image counts and average resolutions, while bars show question counts and percentages.
Fig. 5: Qualitative example of GeoJeV inference, showing spatial probability-driven evidence acquisition, spatial evidence canvas construction, and final answering by a frozen MLLM.
Fig. 4: Accuracy–latency trade-off with Qwen3-VL-8B. Each point shows mean accuracy and end-to-end latency across three benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Spatial probability-driven evidence acquisition for MLLMs in remote sensing, with region-level spatial reasoning.
papers.title: GeoJeV: Unified Spatial Probability for Training-Free Efficient Evidence Acquisition in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
papers.tldr: GeoJeV enables efficient, training-free evidence acquisition in ultra-high-resolution remote sensing by using a shared spatial probability distribution to guide region search without intermediate autoregressive decoding.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.
authors: Mingjia Huo, Yao Fu, Bo Chang, Yaqing Wang, Dawei Zhu, Dylan Zhang, Xinyang Yi, Lichan Hong, Ed H. Chi, Hao Zhang, Jiaxi Tang
bullets: Benchmarks VLMs on 20 Atari 2600 games using high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams.
Separates in-game dynamics from inference speed to test spatiotemporal perception, reasoning, and action grounding.
Finds failures in tracking object motion and direction, brittle sequential decisions, and over-reliance on textual history over new visual feedback.
Analyzes which game scores reliably reflect competence and examines the effects of memory design and prompting.
Highlights a persistent gap between passive visual understanding and active decision-making in dynamic environments.

papers.title: AtariBench: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in Atari Gameplay

papers.abstract: No-reference image quality assessment (IQA) of low-dose CT predicts the score that radiologists would assign to a slice without a full-dose reference, as needed to compare dose protocols and denoisers. Trained CT IQA networks agree well with radiologists but output only a score, whereas multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can explain a score but perform poorly on CT when only prompted. We propose a measurement-aware MLLM, built on Qwen3.8-27B, that rates a slice from its image together with six image-domain measurements of noise, sharpness, high-frequency content and streaks, given to the language model as percentiles in text. On the LDCT-IQA 2023 test set, it reaches an Overall score of 2.735, on par with the retrained challenge winner (2.735) and MedSigLIP-FiLM (2.713), and substantially above its base MLLM used as a zero-shot agent. Shuffling the measurements at test time reduces the score by 0.048, mostly through noise, but the same measurements also lead the model to assign higher scores to over-smoothed denoised images.
authors: Kerem Basim, Tolga Demiroglu, Mehmet Ozan Unal, Metin Ertas, Isa Yildirim
bullets: Addresses the need to assess low-dose CT quality without full-dose reference images.

papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models can interpret volumetric images, but processing full volumes is costly because hundreds of slices produce long, redundant visual-token sequences. Existing compression methods often couple content selection with budget determination. We observe that neighboring slices share visual features and that attention concentration varies across visual encoders. We propose VoluCompose, a training-free, model-agnostic framework that separates what visual content to retain from how many tokens to allocate. Its hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units and uses the Lorentz distance to account for feature magnitude and direction during token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement. Its capacity control module uses visual-encoder attention entropy to allocate more tokens when attention is more dispersed. We evaluate VoluCompose on two tasks across three datasets and four backbones. Across nine calibrated settings, VoluCompose attains the highest mean quality--retention hypervolume among the compared methods. It achieves a mean relative quality of 121.68\% against the uncompressed references while retaining 22.78% of visual tokens on average. Compression remains robust even at a 10% token budget. Across settings, the lowest ROUGE-L ratio to the uncompressed reference is 96.4\% for VoluCompose. The corresponding minima for the compression baselines range from 15.0% to 70.5%. Code is available at https://github.com/yezanting/VoluCompose.
authors: Zanting Ye, Yunrui Lin, Shengyuan Liu, Jing Hao, Chen Hu, Yefeng Zheng, Lijun Lu
bullets: Addresses the high cost and redundancy of processing hundreds of volume slices in medical vision–language models.
Separates visual-content selection from token-budget allocation instead of coupling them.
Groups contiguous slices into ordered units and uses Lorentz distance for token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement.
Uses visual-encoder attention entropy to assign more tokens where attention is more dispersed.
Across nine settings, retains 22.78% of tokens on average while achieving 121.68% mean relative quality and robust performance at a 10% budget.

papers.abstract: We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand-object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations. While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are reshaping remote sensing by shifting the field from task-specific modeling toward general-purpose geospatial intelligence. Mapping the damage to buildings stands to benefit substantially from this shift, as GFMs pretrained on large-scale Earth observation data provide generalizable geospatial representations that can facilitate effective responses to sudden-onset disasters. Although parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) facilitates GFM adaptation, parameter efficiency does not necessarily translate into label efficiency. Building damage mapping remains challenging due to scarce pre-existing labeled data or limited time for annotation. When weak supervision is introduced to alleviate the labeling bottleneck, we identify the difficulty of learning sufficiently discriminative representations as a key challenge for label-efficient GFM adaptation. To address this challenge, we propose a Positive-Unlabeled GFM Adaptation (PUMA) framework that requires annotations for only a small number of damaged buildings. More specifically, PUMA integrates non-contrastive weakly supervised representation refinement to mitigate the impact of noisy supervision on representation learning from a gradient perspective, and latent-state-based label disambiguation to enable reversible supervision refinement without requiring class prior estimation. Extensive experiments on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world demonstrated the effectiveness and robustness of PUMA. A real-world application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires further highlighted its potential to accurately map damage under highly limited supervision. More broadly, these findings suggest that weakly supervised PEFT offers a label-efficient pathway from GFMs to real-world applications.

papers.abstract: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon in large language models (LLMs) where a teacher passes a hidden preference to a student through training data unrelated to that preference. We study whether subliminal learning also occurs in vision-language models (VLMs). We finetune a teacher VLM to prefer a specific animal or facial attribute and use a control teacher from the same base model. Both teachers generate numbers for an unrelated visual task involving geometric shapes. Two students initialized from the same base VLM are finetuned on the same images, using numbers generated by either the biased or control teacher. Across VLMs ranging from 2B to 7B parameters, we find that both animal and facial preferences can transfer through this unrelated task. Students trained on biased-teacher outputs select the target more often than control students, with a difference of up to $\sim$10 percentage points in the animal preference task. Transfer can become stronger with more training data and varies with the target preference, model, and how the numbers are generated. Beyond preferences, we show that the biased student's explanations use more of the same words and phrases as the biased teacher's explanations than those of the control student, even when all three models select the same image. These results matter for training VLMs and show that training on unrelated data may change both a VLM's image preferences and how it explains its choices, and that transfer can become stronger with more training samples.
authors: Arman Hatami, Romina Aalishah, Ilya E. Monosov

papers.abstract: Instruction tuning of large language models and large vision language models relies on massive training data, which incurs substantial computational and storage costs. Meanwhile, training data often contains redundancy, noise, and low quality samples. Existing data selection methods mostly rely on diversity, importance, or a combination of both, without explicitly constraining the distributional consistency between the selected subset and the full data in the embedding space. We propose QMAC, a quality aware multiband characteristic function matching method that formulates data selection as a joint optimization problem of distribution matching and quality filtering. QMAC matches the empirical characteristic functions of the selected subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, capturing both global semantic coverage and local perturbations, while using task related quality scores to filter noisy and low quality samples. We systematically evaluate QMAC on 4 data types, 8 target models, and 44 benchmarks. Experimental results show that QMAC outperforms existing data selection baselines on standard image-text instruction data, substantially surpasses random selection on standard text instruction, image-text reasoning, and text reasoning data, and exceeds full data training in multiple model and budget combinations. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.
authors: Peng Sun, Yi Yang, Mingshuo Chen, Chunxiao Li, Yao Zhu, Huawen Shen, Tianfan Fu

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling often seeks better answers by sampling multiple responses from a frozen model, yet conventional temperature sampling generates every candidate along the same fixed computation path. We introduce architectural sampling, a training-free method that generates candidates through distinct forward computations by reusing selected blocks of decoder layers. Varying the block location and repetition count introduces computational diversity without updating model weights or adding auxiliary parameters. Across five Qwen checkpoints and twelve multimodal benchmarks, architectural sampling improves pass@9 over standard-path temperature sampling by 6.58 percentage points on average at the same nine-candidate budget. Reusing early layers yields the strongest gains, and the improvement in candidate coverage persists even under greedy decoding. The resulting candidates show lower lexical overlap and improve accuracy when used as rollouts for label-free test-time reinforcement learning. These findings extend the benefits of our architectural sampling beyond candidate coverage, demonstrating more effective learning from a model's own outputs.
bullets: Motivation: Standard temperature sampling explores candidates along the same computation path, limiting diversity.
Method: Reuse selected decoder-layer blocks with different locations and repetition counts to create training-free computational diversity without changing model weights.
Result: Across five Qwen checkpoints and twelve multimodal benchmarks, it raises pass@9 by 6.58 percentage points on average at the same nine-candidate budget.
Early-layer reuse performs best, and improved candidate coverage persists even with greedy decoding.
The more diverse, less lexically overlapping candidates also improve rollouts for label-free test-time reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Data-driven Riemannian geometry provides nonlinear interpolation and geometric representations of high-dimensional data. For these operations to be statistically meaningful, paths between observations should preferentially traverse high-likelihood regions. Existing scalable pullback constructions typically use a unimodal Gaussian latent distribution, assuming that the data reside close to a single manifold. For multimodal data, mapping separated modes or local structures into one Gaussian region can require substantial transport deformation and compromise the resulting geometry. We introduce a pullback geometry for data supported on mixtures of manifolds. Using a latent Gaussian mixture, we define its Riemannian metric as the matrix square of the responsibility-weighted expected component precision. The metric is smooth and positive definite and recovers the existing Gaussian construction in the single-component limit. For structured overlapping mixtures, we establish conditions under which the log-density is concave along geodesics, providing a formal connection between the proposed geometry and paths through high-likelihood regions, and derive the corresponding local curvature relations. We instantiate this geometry in a normalizing flow with adaptive mixture learning, allowing the number of active components to emerge from the data and supporting component-wise reconstruction and local effective-dimension estimation. Experiments on synthetic geometric data, a controlled multi-view image setting with a known reference trajectory, and MNIST show reduced transport distortion, competitive path support, close reference-trajectory recovery, and improved interpolation realism. These results extend scalable pullback geometry beyond datasets that reside close to a single manifold while retaining tractable and interpretable local structure.
bullets: Addresses distortion caused by forcing separated modes or local structures into a single Gaussian latent space.
Defines a smooth positive-definite metric from responsibility-weighted component precisions, recovering the Gaussian case with one component.
Provides conditions linking geodesics to high-likelihood paths and derives associated local curvature relations.
Implements the geometry in a normalizing flow with adaptive mixture learning, enabling component-wise reconstruction and local effective-dimension estimation.
Experiments on synthetic data, multi-view images, and MNIST report reduced transport distortion, strong trajectory recovery, and more realistic interpolations.

papers.abstract: As Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) transition toward natively unified architectures, evaluating their safety in synergistic harmful image-text generation tasks becomes a critical challenge. Unlike unimodal threats, synergistic risks emerge when text and image modalities are coordinated to produce harm that significantly exceeds their individual components. We introduce UnifiedAttack, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate LMM safety in collaborative scenarios by focusing on the harmfulness gain achieved through cross-modal synergy. The benchmark incorporates samples filtered for their multimodal potential alongside a novel subset of synthesized disinformation queries. To verify identified vulnerabilities, we propose a synergistic hijacking framework featuring In-Context Reskinning (ICR) and Cognitive Planning Injection (CPI). ICR utilizes few-shot learning to wrap adversarial intent in benign virtual shells to desensitize safety filters, while CPI hijacks the reasoning path by enforcing a plan-then-execute paradigm. By compelling the system to commit to a neutral logical plan, we exploit its internal drive for consistency to induce the synchronized generation of harmful multimodal content. Extensive evaluations on state-of-the-art architectures demonstrate that UnifiedAttack consistently bypasses modern alignment. Our findings reveal that the structural helpfulness and logical coherence of unified models can be systematically weaponized, highlighting the urgent need for logic-aware defenses in synergistic generation tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/UnifiedAttack .
bullets: Targets synergistic harms whose combined image-text effect exceeds the risks of either modality alone.
Introduces a benchmark with multimodally promising harmful samples and synthesized disinformation queries.
Uses Synergistic Hijacking with In-Context Reskinning and Cognitive Planning Injection to evade safety filters and steer harmful generation.
Evaluations across state-of-the-art architectures find consistent alignment bypasses.
Highlights the need for logic-aware defenses against weaponized helpfulness and coherence.

papers.abstract: Grounded reasoning, where a model outputs text coordinates of relevant locations in chain-of-thought reasoning, is a common strategy for solving complex visual reasoning problems. However, the benefits and limitations of grounded reasoning are understudied. We study where and why grounded reasoning is most useful. To do so, we introduce a chain-of-thought analysis method to measure how much a model uses its outputted grounding in its thinking trace and perform a detailed ablation study of a grounded reasoning training recipe. We find that grounded reasoning improves counting but shows no significant gain over baselines without coordinate grounding across a wide range of spatial reasoning and perception benchmarks. Using several synthetic tasks, we show that grounded reasoning is most useful when a task requires undescribable references, which are visual concepts that are difficult to describe in language. However, we observe that many existing visual reasoning benchmarks are solvable with only describable text references. To close this gap, we introduce BrickVision, a new benchmark that requires undescribable visual references to solve.
bullets: Studies when and why models benefit from outputting coordinate-based visual grounding in chain-of-thought reasoning.
Introduces an analysis method to measure whether models actually use their predicted grounding in reasoning traces, plus an ablation of the training recipe.
Finds improvements for counting but no significant gains over non-grounded baselines across broad spatial reasoning and perception benchmarks.
Synthetic tasks show grounding is most useful for undescribable visual references that are difficult to express in language.
Introduces BrickVision, a benchmark designed to require such undescribable visual references.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.
bullets: Addresses the gap between 2D vision-language pre-training and reliable 3D robotic manipulation.
Jointly trains action prediction with alignment between VLA visual features and a frozen 3D perception model.
Unifies heterogeneous robot datasets across embodiments, tasks, scenes, and geometric annotations.
Uses feature-dependent layer aggregation, partial depth/calibration, and probabilistic state dropout to improve spatial supervision and visual reliance.
Training-only auxiliary components enable direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights without changing inference.
