papers.abstract: Reward machines (RMs) have been proposed as a reward formulation in reinforcement learning (RL) to capture non-Markovian tasks where credit assignment depends on history. By representing reward functions as automata, RMs expose the task's temporal structure and allow such rewards to be handled within a Markovian framework. However, they assume a labelling function, a proposition-grounding oracle for observations, which must be manually engineered for each environment, limiting their wider applicability. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing RM-VLM, a novel approach in which a large language model (LLM) generates an RM from a natural-language task description, and a vision-language model (VLM) acts as the labelling function, grounding the RM's propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning. A VLM-based value function estimator is used to assess the agent's progress towards each RM transition and derive a dense reward signal. We evaluate RM-VLM on three domains covering non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection. Our experimental results show that RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.
bullets: Addresses the need to manually engineer proposition-grounding functions for reward machines.
An LLM generates the reward machine from a natural-language task description.
A VLM grounds reward-machine propositions in image observations during policy learning.
A VLM-based value estimator provides dense rewards based on progress toward reward-machine transitions.
Across grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection, it achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods.

papers.abstract: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, completes only 53.5% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline replay benchmarks and real-world interaction, where assistant responses affect user behavior and task outcomes.
Provides simulators for cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface tasks, plus persona-conditioned users with execution errors and out-of-plan behavior.
Introduces IVG-Bench with 315 interaction scenarios for evaluating visual grounding, actionable guidance, latency, and task completion.
The best evaluated model completed 53.5% of tasks within the time limit; the interaction-quality metric achieved 78.5% agreement with human preferences.
A proof-of-concept GRPO experiment improved task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B in the cooking environment.

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models can simulate different observers, yet it remains unclear how assigned perspectives reshape their internal representations and whether these changes govern their judgements. Here, we investigate the representational geometry of persona-conditioned visual interestingness in Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. Across 100 images and 53 prompting conditions, we systematically vary persona content and the linguistic framing used to introduce it, while recording behavioural ratings and layer-wise hidden states. We observe a systematic reorganisation of representational geometry across processing depth: early layers primarily encode image identity, whereas persona-specific structures emerge in later layers. Strikingly, prompt framing reshapes internal representations more strongly than persona identity, whereas persona content has a greater impact on behavioural judgements. This dissociation is further illustrated by minimal identity statements that alter representations even without changing responses. These findings demonstrate that representational distance does not necessarily reflect behavioural relevance. More broadly, they reveal how simulated perspectives emerge as distinct structures within the representational space of artificial cognitive systems, highlighting a fundamental distinction between the geometry of internal representations and their functional consequences.
bullets: Early layers mainly encode image identity, while persona-related structure emerges in later layers.
Prompt framing changes representations more strongly than persona identity.
Persona content has a greater effect on interestingness judgements than on representational geometry.
Minimal identity statements can alter representations without changing responses.
The findings caution that representational distance alone does not indicate behavioural relevance.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with impressive perception and understanding capabilities will enable a range of downstream applications. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements hinder the real-world implementation, particularly for resource-constrained edge devices. Quantization has emerged as an effective solution for deploying large models. While post-training quantization (PTQ) successfully retains the performance at moderate bit-width (e.g., W8A8), it suffers from severe performance degradation under low-bit quantization (e.g., W4A8), especially for small-scale models that are more suitable for edge deployment. In this paper, we propose ProQuant, a novel weight-activation quantization-aware training (QAT) framework tailored for low-bit MLLMs. First, to align the limited finetuning dataset distribution with the pretrained dataset distribution, we propose a self-relabeling (SRL) scheme to resample the responses of the open-source multimodal dataset. Second, we are the first to take a decoupled view of multi-modal (MM) understanding and language modeling abilities. We propose a progressive block activation (PBA) mechanism to prioritize the MM understanding recovery. We also introduce a vision-sensitive factor $\vecτ$ that effectively identifies the MM-critical layers. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks, covering models with 2B-8B parameters, show that ProQuant significantly outperforms existing methods. For example, our W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct improves average accuracy by impressively 6.6% and achieves performance comparable to full precision counterparts with only approximately 1% performance drop. Code is available at https://github.com/yufeixue-ai/ProQuant/.
bullets: Targets severe accuracy degradation from low-bit quantization in resource-constrained edge MLLMs, especially small models.
Uses self-relabeling to better align limited fine-tuning data with the pretrained data distribution.
Introduces progressive block activation to recover multimodal understanding before language-modeling capabilities.
Employs a vision-sensitive factor to identify layers critical to multimodal understanding.
Across 2B–8B models and multiple benchmarks, W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct gains 6.6% average accuracy and remains about 1% below full precision.

papers.abstract: Medical 3D scans and reports are inherently hierarchical, with diagnostic cues concentrated in specific anatomical regions across multiple levels of organization. Yet, most medical vision-language models ignore this structure and fail to focus on clinically relevant anatomy. We introduce MedHiVE, which combines hierarchical vision-language Soft Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) with contrastive learning to jointly model fine-grained anatomy and global scan context. To our knowledge, MedHiVE is the first framework to route both vision and text tokens through a two-level SMoE hierarchy organized by anatomical scale, coupling this with report-derived anatomy-level contrastive alignment for 3D medical imaging. This replaces the direct region-text alignment of statically pooled features and vision-only hierarchical routing of prior work with dynamic, slot-based cross-modal information flow across anatomical scales. MedHiVE operates via a two-level, learnable token-routing mechanism, where local image and text features are first routed through a local SMoE and then fused by a global SMoE into unified multimodal representations. Contrastive learning aligns both anatomy-level and global vision-language representations in a unified space. Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision, MedHiVE consistently surpasses 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets on 3 tasks: segmentation, classification, and detection, demonstrating the importance of hierarchical modeling. The code for MedHiVE is at github.com/szczurek-lab/MedHiVE.
bullets: Addresses the failure of existing models to capture clinically relevant anatomy across hierarchical scales in 3D scans and reports.
Routes both image and text tokens through local and global anatomy-organized Soft Mixture-of-Experts layers.
Uses anatomy-level and global contrastive alignment to learn unified vision-language representations.
Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision and evaluated on segmentation, classification, and detection across 6 datasets.
Reports consistent improvements over 11 state-of-the-art methods; the approach is scoped to 3D medical imaging and the evaluated tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the MedHiVE framework. A hierarchical encoder processes a 3D CT scan and anatomy masks alongside a full report representation zTi and anatomy-specific snippet representations zTi,a, extracted through a frozen text encoder. The global vision representation zIi is contrasted with zTi , while local vision representations zIi,a are aligned with zTi,a for each anatomical structure a. This yields anatomy-aware vision-language representations that enhance downstream segmentation, classification, and detection.

Figure 4. An overview of the 2D projections of anatomical segmentation masks from the Merlin dataset [6]. We consider 14 abdominal anatomical groups to facilitate analysis and model training (see Table 3). These projections illustrate the spatial distribution of the anatomies across representative slices.

Figure 2. Overview of the HiVEL layer. Global and anatomylevel vision tokens and text tokens are routed to E global experts FFNG and F local experts FFNL via first-level routers. The resulting slots are concatenated and processed by a second-level router. Global vision and text tokens are fused with H shared experts FFNS outputs via residual connection, yielding enhanced vision tokens x̂ and text tokens t̂. Vision tokens are used at all stages s ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}, while text tokens are enabled at s ∈ {3, 4}.
Figure 6. Text preprocessing pipeline.

Figure 10. Qualitative evaluation of tooth segmentation on the GEPAR3D test set. We benchmark MedHiVE against ground truth labels and four state-of-the-art baselines. MedHiVE exhibits superior spatial and semantic consistency, leveraging its ability to capture long-range dependencies for large-scale dental arches while preserving high-fidelity boundaries in smaller, individual tooth structures. While competing methods frequently suffer from topological discontinuities (e.g., fragmented roots) or oversegmentation in high-density regions, our approach maintains global structural integrity and local connectivity. The zoomed-in regions (red boxes) highlight MedHiVE’s robustness in resolving ambiguous inter-proximal boundaries where baseline models typically fail to maintain clear separation.

Figure 9. Qualitative multi-class segmentation results on the KiTS 2023 internal test set. We evaluate the proposed MedHiVE against ground truth annotations and four state-of-the-art baselines for the joint segmentation of the kidney parenchyma, cysts, and tumor masses. MedHiVE demonstrates superior spatial and semantic consistency by effectively modeling the hierarchical dependencies between nested structures; it captures the global morphology of the kidney while maintaining high-fidelity boundaries for small, low-contrast cysts and heterogeneous tumor regions. Unlike competing methods, which frequently exhibit topological fragmentation or semantic leakage (e.g., misclassifying tumor voxels as healthy tissue), our approach preserves structural integrity across varying object scales. The zoomed-in insets highlight MedHiVE’s ability to resolve ambiguous boundaries in complex cases of multi-focal cystic disease, where baseline models suffer from oversegmentation and loss of connectivity.

Figure 8. Qualitative multi-organ segmentation performance on the AMOS-CT validation set. We compare the proposed MedHiVE against ground truth labels and four state-of-the-art baselines across 15 abdominal organs. MedHiVE demonstrates superior spatial and semantic consistency, leveraging long-range dependency modeling to maintain the global anatomical context of large-scale organs (e.g., liver, stomach) while ensuring high-fidelity boundary localization for small, low-contrast structures (e.g., adrenal glands, gallbladder). While competing methods frequently suffer from inter-class leakage and topological discontinuities in anatomically crowded regions, our approach preserves structural integrity and inter-organ spatial relationships. The highlighted regions (red boxes) illustrate MedHiVE’s robustness against oversegmentation at organ interfaces, where baseline models often fail to resolve clear semantic boundaries due to similar intensity profiles in non-contrast CT.

Figure 7. Qualitative segmentation results on the PANORAMA test sets. We compare the proposed MedHiVE against the ground truth and four state-of-the-art baselines. MedHiVE demonstrates superior spatial and semantic consistency, accurately capturing long-range dependencies in large-scale structures (e.g., the pancreas parenchyma) while maintaining high-fidelity boundaries for fine-grained objects like PDAC lesions and pancreatic ducts. Unlike competing methods that suffer from topological discontinuities or oversegmentation, our approach consistently preserves structural integrity across varying object scales.

Figure 3. Qualitative segmentation results on four datasets, from top to bottom: PANORAMA, AMOS, KiTS and GEPAR3D. Comparison of MedHiVE with the top five baselines. Red boxes highlight significant artifacts or missing components in baseline predictions. MedHiVE shows superior consistency with the ground truth in these challenging regions.

Figure 11. Qualitative comparison of visual grounding performance on external in-house abdominal CT scans with kidney lesions. Each row displays a representative abdominal CT slice paired with its corresponding part of radiology report describing kidney tumors or cysts; in the absence of voxel-wise annotations, the report serves as the reference. Grounding predictions are shown for MedHiVE (left), Merlin (center), and fVLM (right). All models are fine-tuned on KiTS 2023. MedHiVE segments lesions consistent with the radiology reports, whereas Merlin and fVLM overshoot the lesion extent or place predictions in a kidney the report leaves unremarkable (red boxes).

Figure 5. Visualization of the 3D projections of anatomical segmentation masks from the Merlin dataset [6], shown from the front, left, right, and back views. These projections highlight the global structural consistency and anatomical coherence of the segmented structures. Consistent with the 2D setting, we consider 14 abdominal anatomical groups for clarity and downstream processing (see Table 3). The multi-view renderings provide a qualitative assessment of segmentation quality across the full 3D volume.

Table 4. Quantitative segmentation and detection performance on the PANORAMA test sets (NIH, MSD, and In-house). Evaluation metrics include mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm), while PDAC detection efficacy is measured via Sensitivity and Specificity (%). The best results are highlighted in bold. MedHiVE demonstrates state-of-the-art performance, particularly in the challenging task of PDAC segmentation, where it significantly outperforms existing Transformer and Mamba-based architectures. Notably, our method achieves a substantial boost in mDSC for the In-house PDAC dataset (65.8%) and the Overall PDAC average (54.2%), representing a major improvement over the second-best performing models. Additionally, MedHiVE exhibits the lowest mHD95 and the highest sensitivity for patient-level detection, underscoring its clinical utility in identifying low-contrast ductal adenocarcinomas across diverse multi-center cohorts.

Table 5. Quantitative segmentation results on the KiTS dataset. Performance is evaluated across three distinct labels: Kidneys, Tumor, and Cyst. Results are reported in DSC (%) for individual classes, with mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm) representing the overall average performance. MedHiVE achieves the highest performance in mDSC and mHD95, consistently outperforming both CNN-based and advanced sequence-modeling baselines. Specifically, the model shows a marked improvement in the segmentation of small, irregular structures compared to pure Mamba or Transformer architectures. The achievement of the lowest mHD95 further validates our method’s precision in boundary localization, demonstrating its robustness in handling the high anatomical variability and complex pathologies inherent in kidney tumor imaging. The best results are bolded.

Table 6. Quantitative multi-organ segmentation performance on the AMOS-CT dataset. The evaluation encompasses 15 distinct anatomical structures across a wide range of scales and morphologies. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results per category indicated in bold. MedHiVE achieves superior overall performance, demonstrating a high degree of robustness across both large, high-contrast organs (e.g., Liver, Spleen) and smaller, more complex structures (e.g., Adrenal Glands, Duodenum). Notably, our method establishes a new state-of-the-art for the Pancreas and Duodenum, which are traditionally challenging due to their low-contrast boundaries and proximity to the gastrointestinal tract. Furthermore, the significant reduction in mHD95 compared to both Transformer-based and pure Mamba-based baselines indicates a superior ability to preserve global topological consistency while maintaining fine-grained local details. MedHiVE exhibits competitive or superior Dice scores across the majority of classes, underscoring the generalizability of our proposed architecture.

Table 7. Detailed quantitative evaluation of tooth segmentation on the GEPAR3D test set. Results are categorized by individual teeth following the FDI World Dental Federation notation across all four quadrants. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results per category indicated in bold. MedHiVE achieves the highest overall segmentation accuracy and the lowest mHD95 among all compared methods. The performance is notably consistent across different tooth types, effectively bridging the gap between large molars and smaller incisors. In particular, our model demonstrates superior precision in the upper and lower left quadrants, where it maintains high fidelity for complex occlusal surfaces and inter-proximal spaces. The significant reduction in the average Hausdorff distance suggests that MedHiVE is less prone to the isolated voxel noise and topological errors that often degrade the clinical utility of baseline segmentation outputs.

Table 1. Comprehensive performance comparison across segmentation, classification, and detection tasks. Segmentation performance is reported in mDSC (%), while PDAC classification and detection are reported via Sensitivity (%), Specificity (%), and mAP (%). VRAM is measured in gigabytes (GB) (↓), and speed in million voxels per second (MV/s) (↑). The best results are bolded.

Table 8. Quantitative segmentation performance on the ToothFairy2 dataset subset. Evaluation follows the FDI World Dental Federation notation across the upper and lower dental arches. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results highlighted in bold. MedHiVE demonstrates a clear state-of-the-art advantage, particularly in maintaining structural continuity across the most challenging anatomical sites. Our method significantly outperforms all baselines in the posterior extremities, specifically the third molars (FDI 18, 28, 38, 48), where standard models typically struggle with severe under-segmentation or total loss of connectivity. Furthermore, MedHiVE attains the second-best mHD95 among all methods. These results validate the robustness of our approach in handling the high morphological variability and lower image quality characteristic of the ToothFairy2 benchmarks, ensuring precise tooth-by-tooth delineation across the entire oral cavity.

Table 12. Ablation study on the AMOS-CT validation set across 15 organ classes. We evaluate the impact of the Text (T) supervision and Contrastive Loss (CL) components on segmentation accuracy (mDSC) and boundary precision (mHD95). The results demonstrate that incorporating textual representations (Config #2) consistently improves performance for anatomically complex organs, while the full MedHiVE framework (Config #3) achieves the highest overall accuracy and a significant reduction in Hausdorff Distance (mHD95 from 5.0 to 3.6 mm). This suggests that the joint contrastive objective effectively regularizes the latent space, particularly benefiting small-scale structures such as the adrenal glands and duodenum. B, T, and CL indicate baseline, text-conditioned representations, and contrastive loss, respectively. The best results are bolded.

Table 10. Ablation study on the PANORAMA and in-house datasets demonstrating the impact of multi-modal supervision. We evaluate our proposed method across three diverse test sets: NIH (public), MSD (public), and a multi-institutional In-house dataset. Segmentation quality is measured through mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm). Additionally, we report patient-level PDAC detection performance using Sensitivity/Specificity (%). The results indicate that while text guidance (T) significantly improves tumor localization, the addition of contrastive learning (CL) is crucial for refining boundary transitions, as evidenced by the reduction in mHD95. The best results are bolded.

Table 11. Ablation study on the KiTS dataset demonstrating the impact of multi-modal supervision. We evaluate the incremental contribution of text-based prompts (T) and contrastive learning (CL) over the baseline (B) architecture. Segmentation performance is reported via class-specific DSC (%) for Kidneys, Tumors, and Cysts, alongside aggregate mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm) metrics. The results indicate that text guidance (T) primarily benefits cyst segmentation, while the addition of contrastive learning (CL) yields the largest gain for tumors and further reduces mHD95. The best results are bolded.

Table 14. Ablation study on the GEPAR3D dataset, including ToothFairy2 subset across 32 individual tooth classes (FDI notation). We evaluate the contribution of Text (T) conditioning and Contrastive Loss (CL) on fine-grained dental segmentation. While the baseline (Config #1) performs adequately on centralized teeth, the integration of textual representations (Config #2) provides a significant performance boost in boundary precision, reducing mHD95 from 6.5 to 2.0 mm. Notably, the full MedHiVE framework (Config #3) demonstrates superior robustness in segmenting distal molars (e.g., FDI 18, 28, 38), which are typically prone to severe imaging artifacts and morphological variation. This confirms that the contrastive objective effectively regularizes the feature space for anatomically rare or obscured structures. This indicates that the benefit of the anatomy-level contrastive objective can depend on overlap between the pre-training anatomy inventory and the target structures. B, T, and CL denote baseline, text-conditioned representations, and contrastive loss, respectively. The best results are bolded.

Table 13. Ablation study on the GEPAR3D test set, excluding ToothFairy2 subset across 32 dental classes (FDI notation). We quantify the influence of Textual Supervision (T) and Contrastive Loss (CL) on fine-grained segmentation. The inclusion of text-conditioned representations (Config #2) yields substantial gains in semantic recognition across the dental arch. Crucially, the full MedHiVE framework (Config #3) achieves the highest boundary fidelity, reaching sub-millimeter precision (mHD95: 0.5 mm). This indicates that the contrastive objective mitigates surface errors effectively in anatomically complex regions, such as the lingual surfaces of incisors (FDI 11, 21) and the occlusal pits of molars (FDI 36, 46), where baselines exhibit higher spatial variance. As this dataset covers dental anatomy absent from our pre-training inventory, the anatomy-level contrastive objective is expected to contribute less here. B, T, and CL denote baseline, text-conditioned representations, and contrastive loss, respectively. The best results are bolded.
Table 3. List of selected anatomies.

Table 9. Comparative quantitative analysis of tooth segmentation on the full dataset, including GEPAR3D [42] and ToothFairy2 [8, 9, 31] subsets. Evaluation is conducted for individual teeth using FDI World Dental Federation notation across all four quadrants. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results bolded. MedHiVE achieves the highest overall mDSC, particularly in the segmentation of molars and premolars. MedHiVE achieves the second-best mHD95, indicating precise boundary localization. Notably, the performance gap is most pronounced in the posterior regions, where complex root morphologies and proximity to distal anatomical landmarks typically challenge standard segmentation models. These results underscore the effectiveness of our architectural design in maintaining local precision while capturing the global context of the complete dental arch.

papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical multimodal MoE for 3D medical vision-language; fits multimodal LLM and 3D pretrained modeling.
papers.title: Multimodal Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Modeling
papers.tldr: MedHiVE uses hierarchical multimodal mixture-of-experts and contrastive learning to align anatomy-level and global information in 3D medical vision-language modeling.

papers.abstract: Automating printed circuit board (PCB) routing requires coordinating board-level connectivity decisions with geometric execution under strict design rules. Although recent agents can interact with native routing tools, reliable routing on complex boards remains challenging. We present PCBRouteAgent, a multimodal PCB routing agent inspired by how human engineers coordinate global strategy with local execution. A Global Routing Planner combines board images and structured electrical and geometric information to specify connection topology, routing order, corridors, and layer transitions. A Detailed Routing Executor realizes these guides through KiCad's native routing engine and performs bounded local recovery. Unresolved failures are returned as structured feedback, enabling targeted guide revisions while preserving accepted routes. We evaluate PCBRouteAgent on 247 synthetic and real-world boards from four PCBWorld-Bench test splits. It achieves clean-pass rates of 100%, 94.9%, 100%, and 40% on D2, D3-A, D3-B, and D3-C, respectively. On the three real-world subsets, PCBRouteAgent outperforms the best evaluated baseline in clean-pass rate by 13.9, 36, and 10 percentage points, respectively.
bullets: Targets PCB routing, which requires coordinating connectivity strategy, geometry, and strict design rules.
Uses board images plus electrical and geometric data to plan topology, routing order, corridors, and layer transitions.
Executes plans through KiCad’s native router with bounded local recovery and structured feedback for guide revision.
Achieves clean-pass rates of 100%, 94.9%, 100%, and 40% across four PCBWorld-Bench splits.
Outperforms the evaluated baseline on three real-world subsets, while performance drops substantially on D3-C.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel task of describing human facial expressions of a facial image in natural language, which captures the nuances of facial actions and emotional states beyond traditional emotion categories or facial action units (AUs). To achieve the facial expression captioning model, we propose a three-stage training framework that trains a vision-to-language model using synthesized image-text pairs and the BLIP-2 pre-training techniques. To overcome the challenge of missing training image-text pairs for facial expression captioning, we propose a strategy that involves synthesizing and combining captions using GPT-3.5 and existing annotations on either emotion categories or AUs. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in generating captions that describe details of facial actions and emotions, as well as the inferential relationship between them, even when those emotions are not present in the training data. It is also demonstrated that the vision-to-language task enhances the performance of the intermediate visual features on both AU detection and emotion classification tasks.
bullets: Addresses the lack of image-caption pairs for detailed facial expression description.
Synthesizes image-text training pairs by combining GPT-3.5 captions with emotion-category and facial-action-unit annotations.
Uses BLIP-2 pre-training techniques to link image encoders with large language models.
Generates descriptions capturing facial actions, emotional states, and their inferred relationships, including unseen emotions.
The learned visual features also improve facial action-unit detection and emotion classification.

papers.selection_reason: Vision-to-language model for facial expression captioning; fits multimodal LLM training and alignment.
papers.title: Describe Your Facial Expressions by Linking Image Encoders and Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A three-stage vision-language framework generates nuanced natural-language descriptions of facial actions and emotions from face images while improving related AU detection and emotion classification.

papers.abstract: Diet is a major determinant of health, yet accurate dietary assessment from free-living meal images remains challenging. Existing retrieval-based Vision-Language Model (VLM) approaches to nutrient estimation typically rely on textual food representations, while, to our knowledge, direct grounding on visually similar annotated meals has not been investigated. We present NutriVisRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework that uses a vision encoder to retrieve similar meals with known nutritional annotations and provide them as multimodal in-context exemplars for VLM nutrient estimation at inference time, without task-specific fine-tuning. We evaluate NutriVisRAG across four datasets, four VLMs, three retrieval encoders, and two prompting strategies, including free-living meals from adults with insulin-treated diabetes, where carbohydrate estimates are compared against two dietitians' annotations. Across all 96 configurations (4 datasets x 4 VLMs x 3 retrieval encoders x 2 prompting strategies), NutriVisRAG reduced the primary estimation error in 56, with improvements more frequent under whole-meal (35/48) than per-item prompting (21/48). Across the evaluated configurations, the lowest NutriVisRAG error was below the best Vanilla error in 13 of 16 VLM--dataset pairs. For GPT-5.4-mini, under whole-meal prompting, the best-performing retrieval encoder for each dataset reduced the primary error on all four datasets relative to Vanilla, with reductions of 1.7--35.7%. Overall, our results show that grounding in multimodal exemplars comprising images and respective annotations can improve nutrient estimation at inference time without task-specific fine-tuning, although the benefits remain configuration-dependent.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of estimating nutrients from free-living meal images, where textual retrieval may not capture visual similarity.
Uses a vision encoder to retrieve annotated meals and supplies their images and nutritional labels as inference-time exemplars.
Evaluated 96 configurations spanning four datasets, four VLMs, three retrieval encoders, and two prompting strategies.
Reduced primary estimation error in 56/96 configurations, with more frequent gains for whole-meal prompting than per-item prompting.
Benefits were configuration-dependent, though the best retrieval setup improved GPT-5.4-mini results on all four datasets under whole-meal prompting.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models are a widely adopted starting point for remote sensing tasks. Most are pretrained on Sentinel-1/2 and Landsat imagery at a ground sampling distance (GSD) of 10m or coarser. Many applications instead rely on very high resolution (VHR) imagery, where individual buildings, roads, and amenities are resolved. We study which pretraining regimes transfer well to this scale. We introduce VHR-Bench, a benchmark suite of ten datasets at 1.5m GSD or finer spanning five task families, eight application domains, and both satellite and aerial platforms. We evaluate twelve encoders in three pretraining tiers with frozen backbones at two training-data fractions. We find that both pretraining on large natural-image collections and VHR-specific pretraining transfer effectively to VHR tasks, with complementary strengths. SkySense leads when labels are scarce; at the full label fraction the web-pretrained DINOv3 ViT-L edges ahead, with the two close together there. Encoders pretrained only on Sentinel-scale imagery transfer least well under RGB input. Guided by these complementary results, we continue the self-supervised pretraining of DINOv3 ViT-L on 1.02 million held-out VHR tiles and evaluate the resulting encoder without changing the downstream protocol. The continued model gives a clear improvement over the released backbone when labels are scarce and a modest one at the full fraction, at no increase in inference parameters or compute. These findings support a generalize-then-specialize strategy: already strong, broad natural-image pretraining can be further improved by a short VHR continuation stage while preserving its general visual features.
bullets: Introduces VHR-Bench: ten datasets at 1.5m GSD or finer, covering five task families, eight domains, and satellite and aerial imagery.
Evaluates twelve frozen encoders across three pretraining tiers and two labeled-data fractions.
SkySense performs best with scarce labels; at the full label fraction, DINOv3 ViT-L is slightly ahead, with both closely matched.
Continuing DINOv3 ViT-L pretraining on 1.02 million VHR tiles improves performance, especially when labels are scarce, without increasing inference parameters or compute.
Findings support a generalize-then-specialize strategy: broad natural-image pretraining followed by VHR adaptation.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates and benchmarks foundation models (GeoFMs) on Very High Resolution (VHR) Earth Observation imagery, focusing on spatial reasoning and geometric features, which aligns with Spatial Intelligence.
papers.title: When GeoFMs Meet VHR: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Very High Resolution Earth Observation Imagery
papers.tldr: VHR-Bench shows that broad natural-image and VHR-specific pretraining transfer best to very high resolution Earth observation tasks, while Sentinel-scale pretraining transfers least effectively from RGB inputs.

papers.abstract: Text-guided image editing with diffusion models struggles with spatial edits (e.g. manipulating objects, changing viewpoints, manipulating occlusions) that depend on the 3D structure understanding of a scene. Marigold and follow-up work demonstrate that a pretrained diffusion backbone already harbors strong geometric priors that can be activated for depth estimation, yet how to redirect these priors toward editing remains unresolved. Through per-layer gradient probing, we discover that the editing and depth objectives are compatible in early transformer layers but actively conflict in late layers, explaining why naive depth-conditioned editing either ignores geometry or degrades visual quality. We present StitchEdit, which first activates the backbone's geometric capability via a lightweight depth-denoising adapter, then selectively fine-tunes this adapter for editing using a probe-guided per-layer learning rate schedule that preserves depth knowledge where it helps and prunes it where it conflicts. On the proposed StitchEditBench, a benchmark of 150 geometry-dependent edits spanning spatial transformation, occlusion manipulation, and viewpoint change, StitchEdit consistently surpasses both instruction-based and depth-conditioned baselines on perceptual quality and geometric fidelity.
bullets: Geometry-dependent edits such as viewpoint changes, spatial transformations, and occlusion manipulation remain challenging for text-guided diffusion editors.
Per-layer gradient probing finds that editing and depth objectives align in early layers but conflict in late layers.
A lightweight depth-denoising adapter activates geometric knowledge before probe-guided, layer-specific fine-tuning for editing.
On StitchEditBench, StitchEdit consistently outperforms instruction-based and depth-conditioned baselines in perceptual quality and geometric fidelity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of STITCHEDIT. Stage 1: Depth activation via a frozen-backbone LoRA adapter. Per-layer gradient probing reveals the layer-wise compatibility between the depth and editing objectives. Stage 2: The probing profile fundamentally determines both the LoRA pruning boundary and the per-layer learning rate schedule for the editing fine-tuning.

Figure 1: Top: Challenging 3D-aware edits generated by STITCHEDIT conditioned on text instructions. The model accurately handles complex object repositions and occlusions while strictly preserving visual quality. Bottom: Qualitative comparison against baselines. Nano-Banana [4] manipulates 2D appearance without explicit scene geometry, while uniformly fine-tuning the depth adapter (Depth-Init) leads to catastrophic forgetting, causing structural failures.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. STITCHEDIT maintains strict geometric consistency while preserving exceptional visual quality. Instruction-based editors frequently fail to respect 3D spatial structures, and Uniform FT suffers from depth degradation.

Figure 3: Per-layer gradient probing profile ρ(l). The probe value saturates near 1 in early layers, decays through the intermediate layers, and drops below zero in late layers, indicating that the editing gradient actively interferes with depth knowledge. The shaded band denotes ±1 standard deviation across the calibration set. This empirical profile directly dictates the pruning boundary le and explicitly guides the per-layer learning rate schedule in Stage 2.

papers.title: StitchEdit: Stitching Depth Priors into Image Editors via Per-Layer Gradient Probing
papers.tldr: StitchEdit improves geometry-dependent diffusion image editing by selectively integrating depth priors into compatible transformer layers.

papers.abstract: Multimodal self-supervised learning is challenged by heterogeneity, unequal informativeness, and complex information interactions across multimodal data sources such as images, text, audio, and tabular data. While contrastive methods effectively align shared semantics, they typically rely on strong multi-view redundancy assumptions, overlooking modality-specific and synergistic information, thus leading to suboptimal representations. We propose the Multimodal Information Interactions Bottleneck (MIIB), a principled framework grounded in Partial Information Decomposition that explicitly encodes redundant, unique, and synergistic information within multimodal interactions. MIIB employs a dual-path model architecture for modality-specific encoding and multimodal fusion, optimized using surrogate tractable entropy-based objectives that enforce minimal sufficient representations without requiring explicit mutual information estimation. By leveraging variational bounds and score-based entropy estimation, MIIB efficiently captures complex cross-modal interactions while suppressing superfluous information. Experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multimodal self-supervised methods. Code is available at https://github.com/wanglingzaishi/MIIB.
bullets: Addresses heterogeneity, unequal informativeness, and complex interactions among multimodal data.
Uses Partial Information Decomposition to represent redundant, modality-specific, and synergistic information.
Employs dual-path modality-specific encoding and multimodal fusion with entropy-based surrogate objectives.
Uses variational bounds and score-based entropy estimation without explicit mutual-information estimation.
Experiments on diverse benchmarks report consistent improvements over existing multimodal self-supervised methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The overall architecture of MIIB. Given n input modalities X = (X1, . . . , Xn), we first augment them to generate two views, X′ and X′′. These views are encoded independently by modality-specific encoders and latent converters to extract latent features e′1 . . . e ′ n and e′′1 . . . e′′n, which provide unified embeddings for subsequent multimodal interaction. These features are then processed by two parallel Transformer streams. The Fusion Transformer processes concatenated multimodal features to produce fused representations Z′, Z′′ while processing individual modality features to yield modality-specific representations Z′ 1 . . . Z ′ n and Z′′ 1 . . . Z′′ n . The Synergy Transformer operates on the concatenated multimodal features to model cross-modal interactions, producing synergistic representations Z′ s and Z′′ s . Finally, these representations are used to compute the modality-specific loss (LMS), modality fusion loss (LMF), and synergistic loss (LSynergy).
Fig. 1. The process framework for multimodal representation learning organizes modality-specific learning and fusion as a sequential yet interdependent process.

Fig. 5. t-SNE visualization of unimodal and synergy representations on the MOSI (left) and MM-IMDb (right) datasets. The figure illustrates the distribution of unimodal representations (Modality 0, Modality 1) and the corresponding synergy representations in the learned embedding space.
Fig. 3. Parameter sensitivity analysis on the UR-FUNNY dataset with respect to the fusion penalty (λfusion), unimodality penalty (λsingle), and the synergy penalty (λsynergy).
Fig. 4. Parameter sensitivity analysis of the hyperparameter γ on the URFUNNY and MOSI datasets.

papers.title: Multimodal Information Interactions Bottleneck for Multimodal Self-Supervised Learning
papers.tldr: MIIB improves multimodal self-supervised representations by explicitly modeling redundant, unique, and synergistic information across modalities.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become the leading approach for photorealistic novel view synthesis, yet its geometric accuracy lags behind its visual quality. Existing depth-guided methods attempt to resolve this by regularizing the optimization with monocular depth priors, typically using a single global scale-and-shift alignment. Crucially, we discover a fundamental flaw in this assumption: modern monocular depth networks systematically exhibit region-dependent, piecewise-linear distortions. This discovery invalidates standard global alignment strategies, which warp scene geometry by enforcing a single transform. To address this, we introduce a spatially varying affine rectification model that corrects monocular disparity into consistent metric depth using regionally smooth, edge-aware fields. We further derive a normal-aware regularizer that uses spatial gradients to couple the rectified disparity with 3DGS depth and normals. Across diverse experimental settings, our sensor-free method shows strong photometric quality of Gaussian Splatting while substantially improving geometric accuracy and outperforming state-of-the art geometry-focused methods.
bullets: Addresses the gap between 3DGS’s strong visual quality and weaker geometric accuracy.
Identifies that monocular depth errors are piecewise-linear and vary across regions, making global scale-and-shift alignment inadequate.
Models depth correction with regionally smooth, edge-aware affine fields.
Uses spatial gradients in a normal-aware regularizer to align rectified disparity with 3DGS depth and normals.
Reports strong photometric quality alongside substantially improved geometry across diverse settings, without sensor data.

figures.caption: Figure 8: We compare the raw disparity predictions of (a) Metric3D-V2 and (b) MoGe against groundtruth sensor depth on the exact same scene. While the distinct network architectures allocate their local scale-and-shift parameters differently, both fundamentally exhibit the same region-dependent, piecewise-linear fragmentation. This confirms that spatial affine distortion is a systemic property of modern foundation depth models.

Figure 2: Method overview. (a) 3DGS renders depth D and normals n, and Depth-Anything-V2 predicts the disparity d. (b) The affine fields α and β are estimated from disparity and depth gradients and smoothed by a guided filter (Sec. 3.1). (c) They supervise the losses of Secs. 3.2 and 3.3. All fields are re-estimated at every iteration.

Figure 1: Robust 3DGS geometry via spatially varying affine rectification. (a-c) Standard 3DGS overfits appearance, producing noisy underlying geometry. In contrast, our method extracts clean, highly accurate meshes while maintaining photorealism. (d) Monocular disparity exhibits piecewise-linear distortions, proving that a single global scale-and-shift alignment is fundamentally insufficient (scatter plot). (e) We overcome this by estimating an edge-aware spatial scale field (αsmooth) to rectify the monocular depth prior, yielding geometrically consistent 3D representations.

Figure 9: Additional qualitative comparison on NeRF-LLFF dataset. Visualized across the Flower, Fern, and Horns scenes under extreme view sparsity (rendered RGB, depth, and surface normal maps). (a) Unconstrained 3DGS severely overfits to the limited training views, resulting in massive floating artifacts and chaotic underlying geometry. (b) DRGS mitigates some artifacts via global depth alignment, but still suffers from noisy surface normals and blurred geometric details. (c) DropGaussian struggles to properly initialize in this sparse setting, leading to heavily corrupted backgrounds and incomplete structures. (d) In contrast, our proposed method leverages spatially rectified monocular priors to extract clean, highly accurate geometry with sharp object boundaries, smooth backgrounds, and highly consistent surface normals, all while preserving photorealistic appearance.

Figure 11: Additional qualitative mesh comparison on ScanNet++ dataset. (a) The DN-Splatter baseline exhibits high-frequency noise and artifacts across large planar surfaces like walls and ceilings. (b) Our proposed method successfully suppresses this noise to reconstruct much smoother, flatter surfaces that better approximate (c) the ground-truth geometry.

Figure 7: Piecewise-linear disparity fragmentation across diverse indoor topologies. Across various scenes, the monocular depth prior consistently fractures into distinct, spatially coherent affine regimes (visualized in red, orange, and grey). The accompanying scatter plots demonstrate that fitting a single global scale-and-shift transform (K = 1) is mathematically ill-posed, as the optimizer would be forced to average errors across fundamentally incompatible linear clusters.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on Mushroom dataset (more in Appendix Sec. E.2). (a) The globally aligned DN-Splatter (Monodepth) baseline suffers from degraded geometries due to structural warping. (c) By rectifying the exact same monocular prior, our method better recovers crisp planar surfaces and sharp complex object boundaries than (b) the sensor-supervised DN-Splatter.

Figure 12: Qualitative comparisons of our proposed geometric regularization on MuSHRoom dataset. Visualized via rendered normals (top row) and depth maps (bottom row). (a) The unconstrained baseline (All off) exhibits severe geometric drift, yielding highly chaotic and noisy surface normals. papers.abstract: Multimodal models are expected to exploit synergistic information, that is, information available only when multiple modalities are observed together. In practice, however, a fusion module can fit the training objective by relying on a dominant modality or on information that modalities share, and the synergy between modalities is often left unused. We propose InfMasking, a unified multimodal learning framework based on Infinite Masking. Before fusion, InfMasking randomly masks the features of each modality; each sampled mask produces a different partial combination of cross-modal evidence and a fused representation of the corresponding modality interactions. All masked fused representations are required to remain consistent with a reference target: the unmasked fused view when training is unsupervised, and the class proxy of the task label when labels are available. Maintaining this consistency across diverse partial combinations discourages reliance on a dominant modality or on shared information alone, and drives the fusion module to learn cross-modal interaction patterns that remain meaningful under partial observations. Since the objective is an expectation over infinitely many masks, we model the masked fused representations as Gaussian and optimize closed-form variational bounds, whose population-moment gaps are controlled by the masking-induced covariance under this model. On the evaluated benchmarks, InfMasking improves predictive performance and yields higher mean PID estimates of task-label synergy in learned modality-specific representations, alongside higher InterSHAP interaction attribution in the trained predictors. Code is available at https://github.com/brightest66/InfMasking.
bullets: Addresses the underuse of information available only from joint modality observations.
Randomly masks modality features before fusion to generate diverse partial combinations of cross-modal evidence.
Enforces consistency with an unmasked fused target or labeled class proxy across all masked views.
Uses Gaussian modeling and closed-form variational bounds to optimize the infinite-mask objective.
On evaluated benchmarks, improves predictive performance and synergy-related PID and InterSHAP measures.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed InfMasking framework. Given n multimodal inputs X = {X1, X2, . . . , Xn}, InfMasking uses label-proxy supervision in the supervised setting (upper) and augmented-view alignment in the unsupervised setting (lower). Both settings share the same backbone architecture. Modality-specific encoders fm, m = 1, . . . , n, extract latent features, and the infinite masking operator samples subsets of their tokens before fusion. The fusion module gϕ then produces the complete multimodal representation Z from unmasked modality features and masked fused representations Z1 mask, Z 2 mask, . . . , Z k mask from sampled combinations of retained tokens across modalities. In the unsupervised setting, the fusion module gϕ additionally produces unimodal representations Z1, Z2, . . . , Zn from individual modalities, whereas in the supervised setting the corresponding unimodal branches are obtained by projecting modality-specific latent features.

papers.abstract: Users of egocentric AI assistants often ask short, ambiguous questions whose intended referents cannot be uniquely resolved from video and dialogue history. For example, "Where did I leave it?" may refer to several previously handled objects. Existing VideoQA systems typically commit to a single interpretation, risking plausible but intention-misaligned answers. We introduce ReferClaw, an agentic framework that formulates egocentric streaming QA as an interactive process: the assistant asks clarifying questions to resolve user intent before answering. Three cooperating agents identify candidate interpretations, request clarification, and generate answers grounded in the resolved intent and visual evidence. A bounded, cost-aware policy balances expected information gain against user effort while limiting clarification turns and question complexity. Referclaw learns from interaction through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization with agent-level credit assignment. Evaluations on augmented egocentric QA benchmarks demonstrate improved answer accuracy and joint answer-and-grounding performance over existing baselines, alongside zero-shot transfer across datasets. These findings support interactive clarification as a practical approach to resolving online user intent in egocentric streaming assistance.

Uses three cooperating agents to propose interpretations, ask clarifying questions, and answer using resolved intent and visual evidence.
Applies a bounded, cost-aware policy to trade off information gain against user effort and limit clarification complexity.
Learns from interactions through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization.
Evaluations report better answer accuracy and joint answer-grounding performance, plus zero-shot transfer across datasets.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing benchmarks mainly focus on static scene understanding. When objects are moved or swapped, models must infer not only spatial relations but also how interventions change the scene state. To address this problem, we introduce CST-Bench, a benchmark for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CST-Bench contains 7,082 examples covering 6 intervention types and 12 transformation operators, with dense causal annotations including intervention sources, affected relations, expected effects, invariant relations, and metric changes. We benchmark general-purpose MLLMs on CST-Bench and further compare post-training strategies on CST-Bench and standard spatial benchmarks. Results show that methods effective for ordinary spatial reasoning can still fail under counterfactual interventions. We further formulate counterfactual spatial reasoning as causal state-transition modeling and propose CT-OPSD, which uses CST-Bench annotations to guide a teacher model in learning counterfactual state transitions and causal reasoning chains. These chains are then distilled into a student model that reasons only from real observations. Overall, experiment results establish CST-Bench as a challenging benchmark and reusable supervision resource for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CT-OPSD further provides an initial demonstration of how its annotations can support model improvement.
bullets: Targets a gap in static spatial benchmarks: reasoning about object moves, swaps, and resulting scene-state changes.
Provides 7,082 examples spanning 6 intervention types and 12 transformation operators.
Includes dense causal annotations covering intervention sources, affected and invariant relations, expected effects, and metric changes.
Introduces CT-OPSD, which teaches a teacher model causal state-transition chains and distills them into a student using real observations.
Experiments show standard spatial-reasoning methods can fail under counterfactual interventions, while CT-OPSD offers initial model improvements.

papers.abstract: We study action-conditioned monitoring of autonomous-vehicle behavior in semantically unusual driving scenes. The target is whether the executed ego action is appropriate for the scene: the same scene can admit both normal and anomalous behavior, so visual unusualness alone does not determine the monitoring label. A Vision-Language Model (VLM) first predicts the scene-required action from an outcome-hidden video window; the monitor then compares that expectation with the realized ego-motion trajectory under an explicit compatibility rule. To study this monitoring task, we contribute a six-field taxonomy of 112 paired scenarios spanning both failure polarities (42 derived from documented incidents), a generated video corpus with estimated trajectories, and an exploratory two-stage monitor on that corpus. On 235 clips from 15 scenario families, the two-stage protocol with a fixed T-2.5 s window obtains 83.0% accuracy and anomaly recall 0.773, versus 74.5% and 0.536 for a single-stage video-only baseline; specificity is 0.880 versus 0.928.
bullets: Targets whether the ego action is appropriate for the scene, not merely whether the scene looks unusual.

On 235 clips from 15 scenario families, achieves 83.0% accuracy and 0.773 anomaly recall, compared with 74.5% and 0.536 for a single-stage baseline.
Specificity is lower than the baseline: 0.880 versus 0.928; evaluation uses a fixed 2.5-second observation window.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires precise control under complex contact dynamics while remaining robust to diverse visual conditions. However, real-world reinforcement learning often overfits to the visual appearance of training scenes. We propose Semantics-to-Contact (S2C), a stagewise framework for visually robust contact-rich manipulation. The insight is to decompose the problem into two stages: semantic focusing and contact refinement. In the first stage, a vision-language model localizes task-relevant regions across visually diverse scenes, providing coarse spatial guidance and reducing the burden of exploration. In the second stage, a real-world human-in-the-loop residual reinforcement learning policy learns fine-grained contact behaviors within the localized region using force feedback. To further improve visual robustness, we introduce an object-centric visual augmentation strategy that randomizes background appearance while preserving the robot and task-relevant objects. Experiments on six contact-rich real-world manipulation tasks exhibit that S2C consistently improves success rates over strong baselines and maintains reliable performance under significant visual and positional variations. These results demonstrate that stagewise semantic focusing and contact refinement provide a practical path toward visually robust real-world contact-rich manipulation. Our demos can be seen in https://edem-ai.github.io/S2C/.
bullets: Addresses the tendency of real-world reinforcement learning to overfit to training-scene appearances.
Stage 1 uses a vision-language model to identify task-relevant regions and guide exploration.
Stage 2 refines contact behavior through human-in-the-loop residual reinforcement learning with force feedback.
Object-centric augmentation randomizes backgrounds while preserving the robot and relevant objects.
Across six real-world tasks, S2C improves success over strong baselines and remains reliable under visual and positional variation.

papers.abstract: To serve a request in a human environment, a robot system must find an object that satisfies a functional requirement and a robot that can feasibly reach it. Scene graphs record which objects exist and where, but they often omit capabilities documented only in product manuals. Retrieval-augmented generation methods can read such manuals, yet they rarely reason jointly over object capabilities, physical instances, robot states, and dynamic connectivity. We introduce E2W-Bench, the Exists-to-Works Benchmark, which links dynamic hybrid scene graphs with real product manuals to evaluate capability-grounded robot--object assignment under availability, mobility, vertical-reach, and connector constraints. We also present Embodied RAG++, a spatially grounded retrieval framework that scopes retrieval to the manuals linked to candidate objects, caches extracted capabilities per product model, and resolves robot--object feasibility through deterministic spatial reasoning. On E2W-Bench, Embodied RAG++ reaches a pair accuracy of 0.90 with Qwen2.5-32B and 1.00 with Llama3.3-70B, compared with at most 0.30 and 0.55 for the baselines, while requiring the shortest preprocessing time among the retrieval-based methods and tying for the lowest total token count.
bullets: Addresses the gap between knowing which objects exist and determining which can fulfill a requested function.
Introduces E2W-Bench, linking dynamic hybrid scene graphs with real product manuals under availability, mobility, reach, and connector constraints.
Scopes retrieval to candidate-object manuals, caches product capabilities, and uses deterministic spatial feasibility checks.
Achieves pair accuracy of 0.90 with Qwen2.5-32B and 1.00 with Llama3.3-70B, outperforming reported baselines.
Uses the shortest preprocessing time among retrieval-based methods and ties for the lowest total token count.

papers.abstract: Panoptic Scene Graph generation (PSG) requires holistic yet fine-grained reasoning over complex relations among objects. However, current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) applied to PSG suffer from a perception bottleneck: they function as static observers limited by fixed-resolution views. As a result, models often overlook critical relations involving small or peripheral objects and struggle to differentiate ambiguous predicates in complex scenes. To address these limitations, we propose PSGAgent, an agentic framework that enhances visual perception for PSG through a think-act-observe loop. PSGAgent allows MLLMs to dynamically refine their visual perception using two tools: a Region Zoom-In Tool for local exploration of small or boundary relations and a Visual Highlight Tool for relation-focused segmentation that filters out irrelevant contextual noise. To optimize decision-making, we construct a two-stage training pipeline. First, we create a high-quality, error-aware Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (M-CoT) dataset that provides robust supervision for cold-start learning. Then, we design a novel hierarchical reward mechanism integrated with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) to enable strategic and adaptive tool usage. Extensive experiments on the PSG benchmark show that PSGAgent achieves SOTA performance, demonstrating strong capability in both holistic and fine-grained scene understanding.
bullets: Addresses the fixed-resolution perception bottleneck that causes MLLMs to miss small, peripheral, or ambiguous object relations.
Uses a think–act–observe loop with Region Zoom-In and Visual Highlight tools for adaptive visual inspection.
Trains the agent with an error-aware multimodal chain-of-thought dataset and hierarchical rewards using GSPO.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on the PSG benchmark, with improved holistic and fine-grained scene understanding.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PSGAgent.We reformulate PSG as amulti-turn, tool-augmented decision-making process. (Left) Trajectory Construction. We perform error-aware data mining to identify challenging cases caused by saliency bias (relations occupying small regions or located near image boundaries) and semantic ambiguity (long-range contextual interference, high predicate confusion, or tail relations). These identified cases are used to synthesize error-aware Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (M-CoT) trajectories through a structured generation pipeline. (Right) Cold-start SFT and RL-based Enhancement. The agent is first initialized via SFT to learn basic tool usage, and then optimized with GSPO for strategic reasoning. Through a think–act–observe interaction loop guided by a hybrid reward function (𝑅outcome, 𝑅causal, 𝑅highlight, and 𝑅format), the agent learns to autonomously invoke tools (Region Zoom-In Tool and Visual Highlight Tool) to achieve holistic and fine-grained scene understanding.

papers.abstract: Solving visual puzzles requires both accurate interpretation of visual evidence and reliable computation under task-specific rules. Embedding visual assumptions and task constraints directly in solving code makes the represented problem difficult to inspect and revise independently. We introduce Vis2State, a training-free agentic framework that abstracts visual puzzles into explicit, revisable problem states linking visual inspection and execution. Visual inspection guides state construction and refinement, while generated programs solve the represented problem. The model constructs both the state and the program without predefined puzzle schemas or solving procedures. Inspection and execution feedback allow it to revise the problem representation and solving procedure independently. Vis2State achieves the state-of-the-art performance on four benchmarks. Cross-model evaluation further demonstrates consistent gains. Ablations, error analyses, and fixed-program state interventions further support the effectiveness of the state-centered design. The code will be made publicly available to facilitate future research.
bullets: Targets the challenge of jointly interpreting visual evidence and applying task-specific rules.
Builds explicit problem states and programs without predefined puzzle schemas or solving procedures.
Uses inspection and execution feedback to revise the representation and solving process independently.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on four benchmarks, with consistent gains across models.
Ablations, error analyses, and fixed-program interventions support the state-centered design.

papers.abstract: We present \textbf{WeLM-Image}, a unified image foundation model that integrates multimodal understanding into text-to-image generation, instruction-guided editing, and multi-reference synthesis. Designed for single-GPU deployment in WeChat's large-scale consumer applications, the model processes text, reference images, and target latents as one interleaved sequence. A Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone combines shared attention with independent understanding and generation parameters to limit optimization interference. Equipping each path with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) modules provides sparse capacity, with 31.7B stored parameters and approximately 5.4B generation parameters activated per target latent token. A generation-oriented data engine combines a knowledge-grounded visual vocabulary with large-scale visual clustering to balance semantic coverage and editing tasks, while training-time evaluation guides iterative data refinement. Bilingual annotations and verified editing supervision support progressive training up to native 1.5K resolution. We optimize generation and editing separately with rubric- and checklist-based rewards, then consolidate the specialized policies through noise-aware on-policy distillation. In the reported overall comparisons, the 1536-resolution model ranks first among the evaluated open-source models on PRISM-Bench, Qwen-Image-Bench, and UnicBench. MeanFlow-based few-step distillation yields WeLM-Image-Turbo, which generates a $1024\times1024$ image in 4.98\,s on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU using eight guidance-free steps.
bullets: Processes text, reference images, and target latents as one interleaved sequence for multiple visual tasks.
Uses a Mixture-of-Transformers backbone with Mixture-of-Experts modules to separate understanding and generation while enabling sparse capacity.
Builds training data with knowledge-grounded visual concepts, clustering, bilingual annotations, and verified editing supervision, scaling to native 1.5K resolution.
Separately optimizes generation and editing, then merges the resulting policies through noise-aware on-policy distillation.

The reported 1536-resolution model ranks first among evaluated open-source models on PRISM-Bench, Qwen-Image-Bench, and UnicBench; its Turbo variant generates 1024×1024 images in 4.98 seconds using eight guidance-free steps on one NVIDIA H20 GPU.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is usually studied as frame selection: which few frames should a vision-language model see? We introduce VideoRouteAudit, a controlled audit that separates this choice from two alternatives, injecting non-visual evidence and routing to another answering model. It holds the backbone, frame budget, decoding, prompt and grader fixed while varying one decision at a time. On the full Video-MME long bucket (n=900, K=8), no tested selector significantly improves over uniform sampling. The largest selection-only estimate is +1.9 pt (95% CI [-1.2,+5.0]) and our cascade is +1.2 pt [-1.7,+4.1]; all are equivalent to uniform within +/-5 pt. The same contrasts are unstable at the n=200 subset scale commonly used: three of four are up to 3.8x larger, one reverses sign, and resampled 200-item subsets reverse the full-bucket effect's sign in 35.8% of draws. The audit also corrects our own first results. The anomaly-domain "+ASR" arms injected no text, so the pooled +4.7 pt gain was selection plus a development prefix. With transcripts, ASR lowers XD-Violence accuracy by 10.0 pt when appended after the question and not at all when placed before it, and lowers UCF-Crime by 13.0 pt either way; on Video-MME, placing it first adds about 4 pt (7 on Qwen2-VL) to uniform sampling and to the cascade alike (post hoc, unadjusted). Swapping the answering model gives the largest contrast (+15.1 pt on MUSIC-AVQA, +33.3 pt on its worst type), but the same audio-visual expert with its soundtrack silenced keeps 92% of the gain (69% with a mismatched soundtrack), so the contrast is mostly a model swap. Code, per-item predictions and scripts that recompute every statistic are available at https://github.com/mikeslin-ir/long-video-qa-audit.
bullets: On all 900 long-bucket Video-MME items, no tested frame selector significantly beats uniform sampling; estimated gains remain within ±5 points.
Results from 200-item subsets are unstable: effects can grow by up to 3.8×, reverse sign, and disagree with the full-bucket effect in 35.8% of resamples.
A claimed anomaly-domain “+ASR” gain was partly caused by a development prefix; transcript placement also changes performance substantially and inconsistently across datasets.
Routing to another answering model produces the largest contrast, but most of its gain persists when the soundtrack is silenced, indicating a model-swap effect rather than selection.
The audit releases code, per-item predictions, and scripts for reproducing all statistics.

papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation of vision-language models must balance two competing goals: learning fine-grained visual distinctions from very limited supervision and preserving the efficiency that makes frozen CLIP-like models attractive for deployment. Existing lightweight adaptation methods, including prompt tuning, LoRA, and cache-based adapters, typically supervise global image embeddings and therefore underuse token-level structure. Conversely, structure-aware methods exploit local evidence but often introduce additional inference-time computation. We propose SD-LoRA, a structural distillation framework that uses token-level graph reasoning only during training and transfers its effects into a lightweight LoRA-adapted CLIP model. During training, a heterogeneous graph teacher models patch-patch, global-local, and visual-text relations over high-resolution ViT tokens. Rather than retaining this graph at test time, SD-LoRA transfers its structural bias into the shared CLIP-LoRA backbone through implicit distillation and Prototype Predictive Alignment, which aligns graph-conditioned representations with support-derived class prototypes. At inference, the graph teacher is discarded; prediction requires only a single CLIP-LoRA forward pass and a cache-based classifier. Across 11 few-shot benchmarks, SD-LoRA improves over a strong CLIP-LoRA baseline by 2.4/1.8/3.0/2.4/2.0 percentage points in the 1/2/4/8/16-shot settings, respectively, without additional graph computation at test time. Results on base-to-novel generalization, cross-dataset transfer, out-of-distribution robustness, and calibration further show that training-time structural supervision improves both accuracy and transfer reliability. Code is available at https://github.com/MR-Sherif/SD-LoRA.git.
bullets: Addresses the tension between fine-grained few-shot visual learning and efficient frozen-CLIP deployment.
Uses a heterogeneous graph teacher during training to model patch-patch, global-local, and visual-text relationships.
Transfers the teacher’s structural bias into CLIP-LoRA through implicit distillation and Prototype Predictive Alignment.
At inference, discards the graph and uses one CLIP-LoRA pass with a cache-based classifier.

Across 11 benchmarks, improves over CLIP-LoRA by 2.4, 1.8, 3.0, 2.4, and 2.0 percentage points for 1-, 2-, 4-, 8-, and 16-shot settings, respectively; also improves transfer, robustness, and calibration.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Few-shot accuracy trends across 11 benchmarks. Each panel shows top-1 accuracy for K ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} shots on one dataset; the first panel reports the macro-average over all 11 benchmarks. SD-LoRA is compared to recent CLIP adaptation methods. Positive values mean structural distillation improves the deployed LoRA+cache model, with especially strong gains in low-shot and fine-grained scenarios.

Figure 2: SD-LoRA framework. It trains a deployable CLIP-LoRA+cache student sθ,η using an auxiliary structural teacher gθ,ψ present only during adaptation. Teacher and student share the LoRA backbone, but the teacher reasons over high-resolution ViT tokens and class-text embeddings with a relation-aware graph transformer. Structural supervision from the graph branch plus Prototype Predictive Alignment updates the shared LoRA parameters θ. At inference, the teacher parameters ψ and graph computation are discarded, and only the lightweight student sθ,η makes predictions.

Figure 1: Structural distillation sharpens token-level evidence. We visualize patch-level attention maps for frozen CLIP and SD-LoRA using cosine similarity between the final [CLS] token and patch tokens. Frozen CLIP attends strongly to background foliage and misclassifies the image as clematis, while SD-LoRA shifts focus toward discriminative flower regions and correctly predicts balloon flower. The graph teacher is used only during training; the visualization is produced from the deployed LoRA backbone without test-time graph computation.

Figure 4: Effect of LoRA placement. We compare fixed LoRA placement and adaptive layer selection under 1/4/16-shot settings. SD-LoRA outperforms both fixed CLIP-LoRA and adaptive CLIP-AST, indicating that adaptive placement complements SD-LoRA: layer selection optimizes where LoRA is inserted, while structural distillation improves how its parameters are trained.

Figure 6: Computational and deployment analysis of our method. A shows the one-time wallclock overhead associated with the additional high-resolution training and re-encoding passes. B reports the computational overhead relative to the CLIP-LoRA training system, showing that the added graph branch increases computation by only 0.61 GFLOPs (+1.31%) while keeping parameter growth modest (+8.0%). C summarizes practical deployment-time metrics on ViT-B/16, including training time, memory footprint, and inference latency. D shows that the method remains well behaved across backbone choices: ViT-B/32 retains competitive average few-shot accuracy, while the higher cost of ViT-L/14 is primarily attributable to the larger backbone rather than to additional method-specific steps.

Figure 5: Effect of cross-modal interaction frequency. We ablate where semantic text–visual interaction is applied across graph layers on Aircraft under 1/4/16-shot settings. Each marker reports the peak accuracy, while the text label indicates the number of epochs required to reach 95% of the peak. Applying interaction in all layers consistently achieves the best peak accuracy across shot regimes and also converges efficiently in the 16-shot setting, reaching 95% of peak in 13 epochs compared with 18 epochs for last only and 22 epochs for none. This suggests that frequent crossmodal interaction improves both final adaptation quality and optimization efficiency.

Table 7: Full 8- and 16-shot comparison on 11 benchmarks. We report top-1 accuracy (%) against representative adapter- and prompt-based CLIP adaptation methods. The best result in each shot group is shown in bold. SD-LoRA is reported in the final row of each shot group. Dataset abbreviations follow Table 6.

Table 17: Full matched comparison of training resolution, cache, and structural supervision. Top-1 accuracy (%) is averaged over four datasets. The graph teacher and PPA head are absent from every deployed SD-LoRA model.
