papers.abstract: Humans can easily recognize the same objects across different viewpoints of a 3D scene, whereas teaching models such multi-view-consistent perception typically requires videos or calibrated multi-view captures, which are considerably more expensive and less diverse than large-scale monocular data.~In this paper, we introduce Feature Puzzles, a novel framework for learning multi-view-consistent segmentation using only single-image semantic segmentation supervision. Specifically, we propose a simple yet effective pipeline that constructs multi-view-consistent segmentation pseudo-labels through image cropping and geometric transformations. We further introduce a lightweight, plug-and-play network that leverages the multi-view-consistent image features learned by existing pretrained 3D foundation models and the generated pseudo-labels to perform multi-view-consistent segmentation. Importantly, our flexible framework supports various types of prompts provided from one or multiple views and can be readily extended to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation. Under this single-image supervision, our feed-forward model achieves the best mIoU on NVOS, remains competitive on SPIn-NeRF and ScanNet++ against baselines using per-scene optimization or in-domain multi-view training, and demonstrates zero-shot transfer to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation. Visual comparisons are available on our project page: https://featurepuzzles.github.io/
authors: Jiahao Ma, Qiang Zhang, Miaomiao Liu, David Ahmedt-Aristizabal, Chuong Nguyen
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited diversity of video or calibrated multi-view supervision.
Builds multi-view-consistent segmentation pseudo-labels through image cropping and geometric transformations.
Adds a lightweight, plug-and-play feed-forward network using pretrained 3D foundation-model features.
Supports prompts from one or multiple views and can extend to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation.
Achieves the best mIoU on NVOS, remains competitive on SPIn-NeRF and ScanNet++, and transfers zero-shot to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation.

papers.abstract: Recent LLM-centric advances can generate attractive furnished rooms by selecting and arranging assets. Yet evaluation remains limited to specific perspectives or predefined questions, failing to reflect overall scene quality. To address this pressing need, we introduce GREP. Its core is a focus shift from defining specific questions to establishing a three-tier evaluation philosophy: basic physical validity checks whether a scene obeys physical constraints; visual coherence concerns compatibility in object scale, style, and composition; and, at the highest level, human-use logic requires object arrangements to align with everyday human habits. Guided by these principles, an evaluation agent autonomously and adaptively identifies issues from scene context, gathers evidence, and produces scores and reports. This supports scene-specific issue discovery and reliable judgments. Experiments show that (1) GREP achieves 87% agreement with human majority preferences, substantially outperforming baseline evaluators. (2) GREP reports improve scene quality through refinement, whereas score-only and no-feedback baselines show slight declines. (3) GREP suggests that as planning ability improves, recent models such as GPT-5.6 Sol can move from relying on pipelines and harnesses to challenging their guidance and constraints, but still lack the ability to resolve the resulting conflicts. Stronger models are therefore expected not only to plan well, but also to adapt to external guidance and constraints more flexibly. Project page: https://han-808.github.io/GREP/
authors: Mohan Cao, Yongsen Mao, Chucheng Xiang, Zhongyuan Liu, Zhihang Zhong, Haiping Wang, Yuan Liu
bullets: Addresses the limits of viewpoint- or question-specific room evaluation by assessing overall scene quality.
Uses a three-tier philosophy: physical constraints, object scale/style/composition compatibility, and everyday usability.
An evaluation agent discovers scene-specific issues, gathers evidence, and produces scores plus refinement reports.
Achieves 87% agreement with human majority preferences and outperforms baseline evaluators.
Feedback from GREP improves scene quality, while score-only and no-feedback approaches slightly reduce it; evaluation remains focused on generated room scenes.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated significant advances in reasoning with visual data, which is particularly important given that much of human knowledge is encoded visually in scientific articles and other sources. However, a gap remains in understanding how artificial agents, powered by VLMs, perceive and navigate decision-making under uncertainty in the presence of visual data. This study explores this gap by evaluating and analyzing autonomous decision-making processes. Building upon prior work in visualization literacy and decision theory, we conducted two complementary studies: one examining how agents perceive and quantify uncertainty encoded in visualizations, and another investigating how artificial agents make decisions based on visual data in the form of images. We analyzed perception accuracy and decision performance across models and visualization types. Our results show that GPT-4o demonstrates the highest accuracy in perceiving uncertainty in pie and bar charts among the tested models. For decision-making, autonomous agents showed the best alignment with rational decision theory when uncertainty was represented through circle charts, icon arrays, or text.
bullets: Investigates artificial agents’ decision-making under uncertainty using visual information.
Conducts two studies: uncertainty perception in visualizations and decisions based on images.
Analyzes perception accuracy and decision performance across models and visualization formats.
GPT-4o achieved the highest uncertainty-perception accuracy for tested pie and bar charts.
Agents aligned most closely with rational decision theory when uncertainty was shown through circle charts, icon arrays, or text.

papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language models score left/right relations near chance, but the symptom has two causes that call for opposite repairs: the relation may survive in the pooled embedding yet be unreachable by native image-text similarity, or pooling may discard it while the dense features retain it. On clean two object photographs, across ten encoders, the lateral polarity is linearly decodable from the flip odd component of the pooled vector at 0.77-0.99, yet a search over a million captions leaves nine of the ten at chance under native scoring: an access failure. On controlled C4 orbits, where the relation is the only thing that varies, pooling keeps the arrangement axis at 0.998-1.000 and loses its polarity, which the patch grid retains: a pooling failure. Both sit downstream of the dense features, so one readout covers both. Our zero parameter, query conditioned spatial moment recomputes the geometry from the patch grid and stores it as a vector beside the native embedding. On a 118,287 image index it raises left/right pairwise accuracy against reversed geometry negatives from 0.51-0.53 to 0.81-0.96 and conditional R@1 among 21 category matched candidates from 0.05 to 0.37-0.75, at under a millisecond per batched query, while reproducing the native ranking exactly for queries that name no relation.
bullets: Across ten encoders, left/right polarity is often linearly decodable from pooled embeddings (0.77–0.99) but remains inaccessible to native image–text scoring.
Controlled experiments show pooling can preserve arrangement while discarding polarity, which remains available in patch-grid features.
A query-conditioned spatial moment recomputes geometry from patch features and stores it alongside the native embedding.
On a 118,287-image index, pairwise accuracy improves from 0.51–0.53 to 0.81–0.96, and conditional R@1 from 0.05 to 0.37–0.75.
The method adds under 1 ms per batched query and exactly preserves native rankings for queries without spatial relations.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and repairs spatial relation failure in VLMs, directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Discarded or Unreachable? Diagnosing and Repairing Spatial Relation Failure in Vision--Language Similarity
papers.tldr: A zero-parameter spatial readout diagnoses whether vision–language models fail on left/right relations because similarity cannot access the information or pooling discarded it, and repairs both cases.

papers.abstract: In biodiversity monitoring, a single image raises several questions: which taxon, how many, which trait, and whether the individual has been seen before. Vision-language models (VLMs) could answer all of these from the image, but their ability is largely untested in biology, as existing benchmarks focus mostly on species identification within a few taxonomic groups. We present Bio-VQA, the largest biological visual question answering (VQA) benchmark and the only one to span four aspects of biological visual understanding: hierarchical taxonomic reasoning, fine-grained attribute grounding, quantitative spatial reasoning, and individual re-identification. Bio-VQA contains 1.86M questions over 217K images from 11 public datasets, and extends right-or-wrong scoring to graded scoring, so a near-miss counts for more than a distant one. Evaluating 18 open-weight models from 3.75B to 38.4B parameters, we find that general visual capabilities do not transfer to biological organisms: the best model counts animals exactly on 41.7% of images with 2 to 10 individuals, less than half its accuracy on everyday objects at the same counts. Taxonomic accuracy falls to one sixth, from 0.72 at phylum to 0.12 at scientific name, and scaling helps mostly at coarse ranks. The gap to a domain specialist widens accordingly, from 0.731 against BioCLIP-2's 0.874 at class (1.2x) to 0.269 against 0.544 at scientific name (2x). On trait size measurement, 15 of the 18 models do no better than an image-blind baseline that predicts one fixed number for every specimen, and on re-identification, 17 of the 18 models fall below chance under adversarial conditions. These failures persist across a tenfold range of model size. We hope Bio-VQA becomes a standard test of how well VLM capabilities transfer to the biological domain.
authors: S M Rayeed, Qian Ma, Charles V. Stewart, Yao Ma
bullets: Introduces a benchmark spanning four biological reasoning tasks: hierarchical taxonomy, attribute grounding, quantitative spatial reasoning, and re-identification.
Covers 1.86M questions over 217K images from 11 public datasets, with graded scoring for near-miss answers.

Scaling improves mainly coarse taxonomic reasoning; many failures persist across a tenfold range of model sizes.
Shows substantial gaps versus domain-specialist models, with performance deteriorating as biological reasoning becomes more fine-grained.

papers.abstract: While discrete tokenization in Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) establishes strong semantic reasoning, it introduces a strict quantization bottleneck that degrades fine-grained visual details, often resulting in structurally accurate but artifact-heavy images. We introduce FlowShift, a parameter-efficient post-training framework that bypasses this bottleneck by converting pre-trained discrete UMMs into continuous rectified-flow generators. Instead of discarding the backbone's semantic priors, FlowShift replaces discrete visual interfaces with continuous latent projections and applies LoRA to the attention layers. To efficiently boost visual quality without semantic drift, we propose Dual-Objective Velocity Vector Distillation (DOVD), which aligns the model with a high-fidelity continuous teacher and ground-truth continuous trajectories. This approach drastically improves perceptual quality while preserving prompt adherence and reasoning. When applied to leading discrete UMMs, FlowShift significantly improves COCO-30K FID and aesthetic scores, while retaining over 99.5% of multimodal understanding capabilities. Ablations confirm DOVD drives generation quality. Ultimately, FlowShift achieves high-fidelity continuous generation without sacrificing pre-trained semantic grounding.
authors: Gayatri Deshmukh, Onkar Susladkar, Adheesh Juvekar, Halil Kilicoglu, Ismini Lourentzou
bullets: Addresses quantization bottlenecks that cause fine-detail loss and visual artifacts in discrete UMM image generation.

Improves COCO-30K FID and aesthetic scores while retaining over 99.5% of multimodal understanding capabilities.
Ablations identify DOVD as the main driver of generation-quality improvements.

papers.abstract: Contrastive pretraining has advanced image-text understanding, yet image, video, and audio encoders are still trained independently, with cross-modal alignment realized mainly through post-hoc binding to a frozen anchor space. We present Omni-Encoder, a general multimodal encoder that processes image, video, audio, and audio-visual inputs within a single SigLIP-2 Vision Transformer with fully shared parameters. Unlike anchor-centric binding or per-modality adapters, all modalities are optimized jointly end-to-end, and the framework is organized from input to training. A modality-native input stage first maps each signal into the shared embedding space, including a 1D-convolutional audio tokenizer that converts mel-spectrograms into tokens aligned with visual patches. A multimodal rotary position embedding parameterized by absolute timestamps then places visual frames and audio segments in a unified spatiotemporal coordinate system. Finally, alternating-modality training interleaves image, video, audio, and temporally aligned audio-visual batches and accumulates their gradients into one update, which we find central to stable joint optimization. Omni-Encoder achieves competitive results on 16 benchmarks across all four modalities with one shared parameter set, and joint training improves each modality over its separately trained counterpart. Code and models will be publicly released.
authors: Xiaofei Sun, Peng Wang, Huayao Liu, Xiaoxiao Xu, Jun Song, Deqing Li, Lin Qu
bullets: Addresses independently trained modality encoders and post-hoc alignment to a frozen anchor space.
Maps each modality into a shared embedding space using modality-native input layers, including an audio tokenizer aligned with visual patches.
Uses timestamp-based multimodal rotary embeddings to unify visual and audio signals in a shared spatiotemporal coordinate system.
Alternates image, video, audio, and aligned audio-visual batches, with joint gradient accumulation for stable optimization.
Joint training improves each modality over its separately trained counterpart while using one shared parameter set.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Omni-Encoder. One SigLIP-2 ViT backbone is shared across image, video, audio, and audio-visual inputs. The framework is organized along the path from input to training: modality-native input tokenization (so heterogeneous signals enter the shared space without distortion), absolute-timestamp multimodal positional alignment (so visual frames and audio segments live on the same temporal axis), and alternating-modality training with cross-modality gradient accumulation (so every update is balanced across modalities).

Figure 3: Multimodal 3D RoPE with absolute timestamps. (a) Video frames and audio tokens share one physical time axis: each token’s temporal coordinate is its absolute timestamp in seconds, so different sampling rates become commensurable and co-occurring content is aligned. (b) Modality-specific position assignment: images use t=0 over the full (h,w) grid; video frames use per-frame timestamps (τk, hi, wj); audio replicates its timestamp into all three sub-spaces (τ, τ, τ). (c) The attention head dimension is split into decoupled T/H/W frequency sub-spaces (33/33/33%, θt=104, θh=θw=103); audio fills all three with τ so the full rotary bandwidth encodes time.

papers.abstract: Connecting a DNA foundation model to a large language model (LLM) usually requires training a connector, and often the LLM too. We show that a closed-form map is enough for gene-level questions. Our method, the socket, fits one ridge regression (the plug) from frozen Evo 2 features to the host LLM's own representation of the gene's symbol, name, and description at an early layer. The plug's output replaces the hidden state at placeholder positions, and no gradient passes through the host. We test it on GeneHop, a five-way multiple-choice benchmark split by homology. In a single run on the held-out test set, under a frozen analysis plan, real DNA beats shuffled DNA on all four hosts: by +22.2 points [19.8, 25.0] on Qwen3.5-4B, +26.1 [24.3, 27.9] on Qwen3.6-27B, +16.7 [14.2, 19.7] on Mistral-7B, and +18.4 [16.2, 21.0] on OLMo-2-7B. All four survive Holm correction, every null control stays within two points of the sham level, and the development results agree within 2.3 points. A layer rule that uses no task items was selected on three hosts; it predicted the working layer of the fourth before any DNA-plug scoring on it. A text-only linear map lets one plug feed any other host, at a cost of at most 0.9 points on test. The socket conveys gene identity: nearest-neighbour retrieval recovers 72-84% of the effect, but the plug beats it on every host by 3.0-5.2 points and keeps most of its effect without training homologs.
bullets: Maps frozen Evo 2 gene features to early-layer LLM representations of gene symbols, names, and descriptions.
Uses one closed-form ridge fit; the host LLM receives the mapped output at placeholder positions without gradient-based training.
On GeneHop, real DNA improved five-way accuracy over shuffled DNA by 16.7–26.1 points across four LLMs, with all effects surviving correction.
Null controls stayed near sham levels, development results matched test results closely, and a task-independent layer rule generalized across hosts.
The socket primarily conveys gene identity, but outperformed nearest-neighbour retrieval by 3.0–5.2 points and transferred across hosts with at most a 0.9-point test cost.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly support construction hazard monitoring, yet their frequent false alarms remain poorly understood. This study investigates whether false struck-by hazard warnings arise from failures in object recognition, spatial relation encoding, or hazard decisions dominated by learned co-occurrence priors. We evaluated Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B using 355 counterfactual worker-excavator scene pairs with controlled spatial proximity and worker-removal variants, combining behavioral analysis, internal representation probing, causal interventions, and decision correction. Both models recognized the entities and encoded their spatial relations (out-of-fold AUROC: 0.82 and 0.91), assigning higher hazard scores to near than far scenes in 79% and 73% of pairs. Nevertheless, 74% and 100% of far scenes were falsely classified as hazardous. Removing the worker reduced Qwen's hazard rate to 11%, while worker presence exerted 2.4- and 3.2-times greater influence on hazard scores than spatial proximity in the respective models. Attention-head interventions, neuron-level interventions, and activation steering failed to eliminate this co-occurrence bias. However, conditioning hazard decisions on the model's own spatial-relation representation improved Qwen's specificity from 0.36 to 0.58 at matched sensitivity, outperforming threshold recalibration. These findings reveal that VLM struck-by false alarms stem primarily from decision-making failures rather than deficiencies in object recognition or spatial encoding, suggesting that future efforts should prioritize conditioning hazard decisions on encoded spatial evidence rather than further improving visual recognition alone.
bullets: Evaluated Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B on 355 counterfactual worker–excavator scene pairs.
Both models encoded spatial relations, but falsely classified 74% and 100% of far scenes as hazardous.
Worker presence influenced hazard scores 2.4× and 3.2× more than spatial proximity, indicating co-occurrence bias.
Attention, neuron, and activation interventions did not eliminate the bias.
Conditioning decisions on encoded spatial relations improved Qwen’s specificity from 0.36 to 0.58 at matched sensitivity.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes spatial-relation encoding and co-occurrence bias in vision-language models for hazard detection; relevant to spatial intelligence in multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Co-Occurrence Priors Override Visual Spatial Evidence: Understanding False Alarms in Vision-Language Models for Construction Struck-By Hazard Detection
papers.tldr: VLMs can recognize workers, excavators, and their spatial relations yet still issue false struck-by alarms because hazard decisions are dominated by worker–excavator co-occurrence priors.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for AI-generated image (AIGI) detection, providing natural-language explanations for authenticity judgments. However, their ability to interpret text within images may also expose these judgments to misleading semantic cues. We systematically evaluate typographic attack strategies across detection-oriented, open-weight, and commercial VLMs, considering both real-to-fake and fake-to-real attacks. Our results show that reasoning modes generally exhibit greater vulnerability than direct modes and that attack effectiveness exhibits pronounced directional asymmetry. Moreover, larger models tend to exhibit higher clean detection accuracy but also higher attack success rates. We further examine attack robustness under image and text transformations and investigate whether overlays indicating the correct class can aid error correction. Together, these analyses characterize how typographic attacks influence authenticity judgments and expose limitations of current VLM-based AIGI detection systems.
bullets: Evaluates typographic attacks against detection-oriented, open-weight, and commercial VLMs.
Studies attacks that flip judgments from real to fake and from fake to real, revealing strong directional asymmetry.
Finds reasoning modes are generally more vulnerable than direct modes.
Larger models tend to achieve higher clean accuracy but also higher attack success rates.
Examines robustness to image/text transformations and whether correct-class overlays help correct errors.

papers.abstract: Effective human-AI collaboration requires partners to establish references through interaction, which becomes fragile when descriptions are ambiguous, similar referents compete, or partners see different things. We study referential uncertainty - uncertainty over which candidate object a description refers to - in a collaborative puzzle task where a human Helper instructs an AI Worker to place pieces. The Worker must identify and communicate its uncertainty, and the Helper must recognize and act on it. We show that a separately elicited belief distribution over candidate pieces is better calibrated (ECE 0.15) and better discriminates correct from incorrect placements (AUROC 0.65) than raw action-token probabilities, which are severely overconfident (0.97 mean confidence, ECE 0.44). Across three frontier vision-language models (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.5), this elicited uncertainty rises predictably with instruction vagueness, but not with competing referents in context, even when those increase errors. The models seldom externalize it, asking for clarification on only 3.5-16.7% of turns. In a controlled human study (N=210), participants given only the Worker's default message accept 78% of wrong placements and cannot tell right from wrong (AUC 0.50). Precise descriptions and, especially, well-targeted hedges cut wrong-move acceptance to 36% while largely preserving correct-move acceptance, compensating for missing shared awareness such as not seeing the Worker's action. But this benefit depends on targeting: a deployable hedge derived from the model's own belief entropy inherits that signal's weakness and can do more harm than good. Externalized uncertainty helps a human partner only when it is accurately targeted.
bullets: Studies referential uncertainty in a collaborative puzzle task where an AI places pieces based on human instructions.
Elicited belief distributions over candidate pieces are better calibrated and discriminative than raw action-token probabilities, which are overconfident.
Across GPT-4.1, GPT-5, and GPT-5.5, uncertainty increases with vague instructions but often misses competing referents that cause errors.
Models ask for clarification infrequently, and humans given default messages accept many incorrect placements without distinguishing them from correct ones.
Precise descriptions and targeted hedges reduce wrong-move acceptance, but entropy-based hedges can be counterproductive when uncertainty is misaligned.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. The collaborative puzzle task and the human study conditions. The partners hold asymmetric information: the Worker (AI) sees the current board and all 24 available pieces but not the target, whereas theHelper (human) sees the target pattern but neither the pieces nor—by default—the Worker’s board. The Helper gives a referring instruction and the Worker selects, places a piece, and replies with a message (here, a blue spiral placed in the target slot). Each condition changes exactly one element of this same turn. Four vary only the Worker’s message while the board stays hidden: Generic (A) is the original message; Described (C) appends a precise description of the placed piece; and Hedged (D) and Self-hedged (E) additionally append an expression of uncertainty—inserted by an oracle on the objectively wrong turns (D) or, in the deployable variant, from the Worker’s own belief entropy (E). The fifth condition, Visible board, keeps the Generic message but reveals the Worker’s board to the Helper—the shared-view control (A/shared). Holding the turn fixed and varying only the message or the board’s visibility isolates how each externalized signal shapes the Helper’s perceived confidence, error detection, and willingness to act.
Fig. 5. Clarification rates on turns with incorrect piece selected (could benefit from clarification) and correct select piece (would not benefit from clarification) across models model.

Fig. 6. Elicited uncertainty as an externalization signal (image modality). (Left) the no-action (question) rate rises with the model’s own elicited belief entropy for all three models—they question more when their belief is more spread out. (Right) ROC of the rule “hedge if belief entropy ≥ 𝜏” for predicting the model’s own wrong placements (scored vs. ground truth piece); all three curves sit close to the diagonal (AUROC 0.55–0.66), so belief entropy is only a weak error predictor. Models externalize uncertainty in proportion to a signal that is itself too weak to cleanly trigger a hedge.

Fig. 3. Instruction specificity (image modality) results per model. (left) stacked outcome composition of Worker response (correct piece / wrong piece / no-action) at each specificity level from overspecified (L1) to vague (L4), with the original utterance (L0) placed between L2 and L3 as the baseline (dashed); the right panel shows mean belief entropy. Accuracy falls and belief entropy rises with vagueness for all models.

Fig. 4. Board confusability (image modality) results per model. (left) stacked outcome composition of Worker responses (correct piece / wrong piece / no-action) and (right) mean belief entropy on a distinct board (B1), the original board (B0), and a confusable board (B2), in order of increasing confusability. Accuracy falls sharply while no-action and belief entropy barely move.

Fig. 2. Reliability curves for the uncertainty signals: (Right) Raw action-token probabilities are over-confident; temperature scaling reduces the gap. (Left) The separately elicited belief provides the strongest combined discrimination and calibration. (Bottom) Distribution of confidence on the placed piece, split by whether the placement was correct or wrong.

Fig. 14. The grading interface (one trial, Generic condition). In this between-subjects study, each participant reviews the flattened interaction up to the current turn and judges the AI Worker’s placement. (a) The dialogue—the Worker’s opening status, the Helper’s instruction (here “bold diagonal lines on a white background”), and the Worker’s placement message. For that message the participant reports two 0–100 judgements, (b) apparent confidence (how confident the Worker sounds) and (c) correctness likelihood (how likely the intended piece was placed), and (d) chooses a single action: proceed, ask the Worker to change/undo, ask it to explain/verify, or give a more specific instruction. (e) As the Helper, the participant sees the target pattern but not the Worker’s board; the board is revealed only in the Visible-board condition. Across conditions we vary only the Worker’s message and board visibility (Table 1), holding the task turns fixed. The available pieces are not shown in any condition as they are also not available to see for the Helper.

Fig. 13. Board confusability (text modality) results per model. (left) stacked outcome composition of Worker responses (correct piece / wrong piece / no-action) and (right) mean belief entropy on a distinct board (B1), the original board (B0), and a confusable board (B2), in order of increasing confusability. Accuracy falls sharply while no-action and belief entropy barely move.

Fig. 11. Instruction specificity (text modality) results per model. (left) stacked outcome composition of Worker response (correct piece / wrong piece / no-action) at each specificity level from overspecified (L1) to vague (L4), with the original utterance (L0) placed between L2 and L3 as the baseline (dashed); the right panel shows mean belief entropy. Accuracy falls and belief entropy rises with vagueness for all models.

Fig. 12. Board (environmental) confusability. The same fixed referring instruction (“place the spiral piece”) is shown against three boards along a confusability axis; the instruction is held constant so that only the competing referents change. Distinct (B1): the target is the only piece of its shape family and thus the sole plausible referent. Baseline (B0): the real board seen in the dialogue, where a couple of incidental look-alikes occur naturally. Confusable (B2): five same-family, same-thickness look-alikes are inserted, burying the target among near-identical distractors. The red ring marks the intended target; the blue ring marks a confusable same-family look-alike. Moving from distinct to confusable makes it increasingly likely that the Worker commits to a look-alike—the environmental (referent-side) axis of referential uncertainty, complementary to instruction vagueness (Fig. 3).

papers.selection_reason: Studies uncertainty calibration and referential communication in vision-language models; relevant to multimodal foundation model behavior.
papers.title: Referential Uncertainty in Human--AI Collaboration
papers.tldr: Human–AI collaboration improves when AI uncertainty about ambiguous references is accurately identified and communicated, but current models rarely externalize it and poorly targeted hedges can hurt.

papers.abstract: Satellite-ground localization estimates the planar position and yaw orientation of a ground camera within a geo-referenced satellite image. Most recent methods map ground and satellite features into a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) space and establish spatial correspondences. However, insufficient depth constraints can assign one ground feature to different distances along a viewing direction, creating geometric ambiguity in BEV feature placement. Similar appearances at different locations can also create descriptor matching ambiguity, while existing descriptor learning lacks explicit semantic supervision to distinguish them. We propose GeoSem-BEV, a geometry-semantic constrained BEV representation learning method. Radial depth supervision constrains distance assignment, and vertical height supervision constrains height aggregation. Shared explicit semantic supervision promotes consistent semantic predictions across views and helps distinguish locations with similar semantics. These constraints improve feature placement and descriptor discriminability, enhancing state-of-the-art BEV localization models. On VIGOR with unknown orientation, GeoSem-BEV reduces mean orientation error by 37.2% and 38.1% in the cross-area and same-area settings, respectively. The corresponding errors are reduced by 10.8% and 15.6% on DReSS-D. On KITTI-CVL, it reduces same-area mean orientation error by 26.8% under 10 degree orientation noise.
bullets: Addresses geometric ambiguity in BEV feature placement and descriptor ambiguity between visually similar locations.
Uses radial depth supervision for distance assignment and vertical height supervision for height aggregation.
Applies shared explicit semantic supervision to produce consistent predictions across satellite and ground views.
Improves orientation localization errors across VIGOR, DReSS-D, and KITTI-CVL, including a 37.2% reduction on VIGOR cross-area evaluation.
Focuses on planar position and yaw localization, with reported evaluations under unknown or noisy orientation settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2: GeoSem-BEV with FG2 as the base model. Geometric supervision constrains radial assignment and height aggregation of ground-view features. A shared semantic head supervises both descriptor fields, and same-class hard negatives penalize spatially incorrect matches.

(a) Upper right: Similar appearances at different locations can produce ambiguous descriptors without explicit semantic supervision. (b) Lower right: Explicit semantic supervision helps distinguish them.

The cyan + and arrow mark the ground-truth camera position and orientation used for alignment. In the right block, each heatmap shows the normalized descriptor-matching response for one ground-view BEV query over satellite locations: warmer colors indicate higher matching scores. The green triangle marks the ground-truth satellite location corresponding to the query cell, and the white star marks the highestscoring predicted location; the reported peak error is the distance between these two markers.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves reasoning by providing token-level supervision from a teacher on a student's own trajectories. Existing methods primarily focus on enhancing this teacher-side guidance (e.g., by enriching teacher inputs and refining teacher feedback), yet we find that limited student perception is another critical bottleneck in multimodal OPD. By providing oracle visual facts, the performance of OPD-trained students can still be substantially improved for both weak and strong teachers. To address this bottleneck, we propose S-OPD, a simple multimodal on-policy distillation framework that explicitly strengthens student perceptual learning through two objectives. Specifically, Teacher-calibrated Policy Contrast separates student policies under original and masked images with teacher-based token-level gating, strengthening the student's reliance on visual evidence during reasoning. Policy Agreement aligns student policies under original and noise-perturbed images, further improving perceptual robustness to visual noise. Notably, our method can be seamlessly plugged into existing OPD frameworks, requiring no additional data annotations, model parameters or inference operations. Extensive experiments on eight benchmarks across student scales and distillation paradigms demonstrate consistent performance improvements, with gains of up to 4.25 points on LogicVista. When combined with existing teacher-side supervision methods, our method can yield further gains. Code is available at https://github.com/Sirilaw/S-OPD.

Experiments across student scales and distillation settings show consistent improvements, reaching up to 4.25 points on LogicVista.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly pair a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) with a flow-matching expert that conditions its action predictions on the VLM's key-value representations. Those representations must carry information useful for control, yet the VLM was never trained for the action expert's flow-matching objective. Two signals can address this: gradients backpropagated from the expert's loss (coupling), or VLM supervision to predict discrete tokens encoding the same target actions. Prominent training recipes forgo the first, blocking expert-to-VLM gradients (insulation) to protect the VLM's existing capabilities, while also supervising it on vision-language data and action tokens. Because vision-language co-training also aims to preserve those capabilities, the additional protection provided by insulation is unclear. At the same time, insulation removes a direct signal about which features continuous action prediction requires. On the other hand, action-token supervision offers an alternative way to learn action-relevant representations, which may explain why insulation succeeds in practice. We disentangle these factors in autonomous driving and manipulation by independently varying action-token supervision and whether the expert's loss updates the VLM. In open-loop driving, insulation is competitive with coupling when action tokens are supervised; without them, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. When both components are trained jointly from the outset, coupling increases closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and 40% without it, and similarly improves robot manipulation performance under both settings. These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM's action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe.
authors: Asher James Hancock, Boyi Li, Yuxiao Chen, Shuhan Tan, Wenhao Ding, Thomas Tian, Yan Wang, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone

The benefit of insulation depends on supervision and evaluation setting rather than being universally protective of VLM capabilities.

papers.abstract: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve a target image given a reference image and a modification text. Although recent approaches leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown significant progress, we argue that the MLLM's compositional understanding remains underutilized. This stems from directly mapping composed queries into a retrieval embedding via contrastive supervision alone, without explicitly resolving the intended visual modifications. In this work, we introduce Factorized MLLM Embeddings (FactEmbed), which decouples compositional query comprehension from building discriminative embeddings. Rather than directly projecting the composed query into a single embedding without internal reasoning, FactEmbed employs a set of factorized latents that simulate the intended visual modifications via an intermediate target imagination objective. This process encourages the latents to ground into target semantics before forming discriminative representations for retrieval. Subsequently, to propagate these factorized representations throughout the model for retrieval, we optimize a factor-level contrastive loss while distilling the decomposed representations into a deeper attention layer of the MLLM. Finally, for efficient inference, we retain the [EOS] token to establish a global-level embedding on top of these factorized latents, while we exploit the mean-pooled factorized latents to rerank a short candidate list at negligible cost, as both are produced by the same forward pass. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FactEmbed outperforms prior works across CIR benchmarks.
authors: WonJun Moon, Seongchan Kim, Dahun Kim, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses the underuse of MLLM compositional understanding when queries are trained only with direct contrastive supervision.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) allow social scientists to analyze video at scale, but researchers must decide which parts of a video to provide as input. We use the term representation validity to examine how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement and subsequent analysis. We compare input representations across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets. No representation consistently performs best. On seven news-related constructs, native-video performance varies little across models (macro-F1 = .70-.77), while extracted-text performance ranges from .52 to .80. Three models perform better with text and three with video. Combining inputs rarely improves performance. Higher classification accuracy also does not reliably produce estimates closer to those based on human codes. The highest-F1 representation best reproduces human-coded regression coefficients in 17 of 42 comparisons. Even when each model uses its highest-F1 deployable representation, 45% of sample-prevalence estimates differ from the human-coded benchmark by more than ten percentage points. Input representation therefore requires validation for both the construct being measured and the quantity estimated from the resulting labels.

papers.abstract: Vision-language verifiers judge whether an image faithfully matches a textual description, yet existing training pipelines typically rely on static supervision from stronger external judges or curated hard-negative data. Such supervision requires external generation or annotation, is teacher-bounded, and is difficult to adapt as model failures evolve. We introduce PROVE (Perturb-and-Repair Optimization for Vision-Language Evaluation), a self-play framework that trains verifiers through a closed perturb-verify-repair-verify loop. Starting from a known-correct image-caption pair, a Mutator introduces a typed perturbation over objects, attributes, counts, or relations. The verifier then judges the perturbed caption and provides textual feedback, which a Repairer uses to recover a faithful caption for re-verification. These two verification rounds produce structured rewards for informative mismatches and visually grounded repairs. Since perturbation, verification, and repair are role-conditioned behaviors of the same evolving multimodal backbone, updating the shared parameters also improves the verifier itself. Experiments show that PROVE improves fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families and strengthens visual-detail robustness on the reference backbone, with limited, benchmark-dependent changes on broader multimodal tasks.
authors: Zijun Huang, Yingjun Du, Cees G. M. Snoek
bullets: Targets compositional image-caption verification involving objects, attributes, counts, and relations.
Uses a shared multimodal backbone as Mutator, Verifier, and Repairer in a closed-loop training process.
Derives rewards from detecting informative mismatches and producing visually grounded repairs.
Improves fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families.
Enhances visual-detail robustness, while broader multimodal-task gains are limited and benchmark-dependent.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PROVE. A single Qwen backbone is reused under three role prompts: Mutator, Verifier, and Repairer. Given a clean image-caption pair, the Mutator produces a localized caption perturbation, e.g., changing an attribute from “red” to “blue”, to create a hard image-text mismatch. The Verifier first judges the perturbed caption and returns a decision-feedback pair (y1, r1) that diagnoses the mismatch. Conditioned on this feedback, the Repairer generates a revised caption, which is then checked by the same Verifier to obtain (y2, r2). Rewards from the two verification rounds train the shared model with DrGRPO, so perturbation, verification, and repair co-evolve within one multimodal backbone.

papers.abstract: Multimodal discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate responses through iterative mask prediction and offer a promising alternative to autoregressive large vision-language models. However, they still suffer from hallucination, producing outputs that are plausible under language priors but insufficiently grounded in the image. We argue that hallucination in multimodal dLLMs is not only a token prediction problem, but also a premature commitment problem: during iterative denoising, some masked positions are unmasked too early because their confidence is driven more by language priors than by visual evidence, and these early commitments can bias later generation. To address this issue, we propose Visual Gain Ordering (VIGOR), a training-free and plug-and-play inference strategy that reorders masked positions according to counterfactual visual evidence. At each denoising step, VIGOR compares the confidence of each candidate token under the original image-conditioned pass and an additional visual-ablation pass, and prioritizes positions whose predictions are more strongly supported by the image. Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO show that VIGOR consistently reduces hallucination and improves multimodal reasoning performance across benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-BPM/Vigor.
authors: Junzhe Chen, Tian Qin, Eugenie Shi, Tianshu Zhang, Qiang Ju, Lijie Wen
bullets: Targets premature token commitments during iterative denoising, which can amplify image-ungrounded predictions.
Uses a training-free, plug-and-play inference strategy requiring no model retraining.
Compares token confidence with and without visual input to estimate counterfactual visual support.
Prioritizes masked positions whose predictions gain more from the image.
Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO report consistent hallucination reduction and improved multimodal reasoning across benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they need to repeatedly reinterpret raw visual observations at every step of an interaction. We propose shifting routine spatial reasoning from images to text and symbols through a 3D geometric abstraction that is refreshed locally from observations and read directly by the language models. Specifically, our interface represents scene geometry via typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounds them from calibrated RGB-D, and returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after each action. Symbolic task structure can thus be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene, with direct visual reasoning invoked only on demand. Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries, positioning explicit geometric state as an effective substrate for agentic robot policies.
authors: Yihang Liu, Yiming Chen, Mingzhe Zheng
bullets: Addresses whether multimodal robot agents must repeatedly reinterpret visual observations during interaction.
Represents object-part geometry with typed, evidence-aware symbolic references grounded in calibrated RGB-D.

Supports offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution with visual reasoning invoked on demand.
The abstract reports improved multi-step manipulation completion and substantially fewer repeated multimodal queries.

papers.abstract: Complex visual question answering often requires vision-language models to think with images, i.e., actively acquire local visual evidence by zooming into informative regions of high-resolution images. Our error analysis shows that many failures in this setting originate from incorrect observation actions, where the model fails to localize key regions or obtain crops that contain sufficient evidence for answering. We further observe that bounding-box tokens exhibit substantially higher generation entropy than ordinary language tokens, indicating high uncertainty when the model decides where to look. However, existing reinforcement learning methods based on final-answer rewards provide only trajectory-level feedback, making it difficult to assign precise credit to the observation actions. We propose Observation Policy Optimization (OPO), an RL algorithm for optimizing observation actions in tool-augmented thinking with images. OPO consists of two core modules. First, Uncertainty-Guided Observation Branching (UOB) treats each image zoom-in tool call as an observation event and selectively branches at high-uncertainty, low-redundancy events during rollout, enabling efficient exploration of alternative cropping decisions and their resulting visual evidence. Second, Evidence-Localized Advantage Attribution (ELAA) compares sibling branches using local evidence-sufficiency rewards and assigns credit only to the corresponding observation-action tokens. By decoupling observation-action optimization from trajectory-level outcome supervision, OPO improves visual evidence acquisition and further enhances visual reasoning performance. Experiments show that OPO consistently improves Qwen3-VL models across scales and achieves competitive performance against larger models and tool-augmented baselines. Code is publicly available.
authors: Junfeng Wang, Jiawei Liu, Yongchao Xu, Tao Jiang, Jiangbo Ai, Jin Zhang, Chong Wang, Qixing Zhang

OPO uses Uncertainty-Guided Observation Branching to explore alternative crops at uncertain, nonredundant observation events.

Experiments show consistent improvements across Qwen3-VL model scales, with competitive performance versus larger and tool-augmented models.

papers.abstract: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module. Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because a DiT is trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treat captioning as a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it to reference-grounded captioning that makes reference bindings explicit. Prompt enhancement translates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training rather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training. Reward modeling pairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specific automatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) can process interleaved text and multiple images in a single context, but how they internally identify the image relevant to a question remains poorly understood. We study this grounding step as in-context image retrieval and introduce ICIR-MCQ, a controlled probe for head-level analysis of image retrieval. Using each head's attention mass over image-token spans, we first identify sparse pointer heads that reliably point to the target image. These heads transfer beyond the probe: a single pointer head is competitive with external vision-language retrievers on a naturalistic multi-image retrieval benchmark, showing that LVLMs contain a strong internal image retrieval signal. Attention alone, however, shows where a head reads from, not what its output passes on to later layers, so we introduce a complementary output-side analysis. For each head, we train a lightweight image retriever on its value-weighted output and use it to identify writer heads, whose outputs contain enough information to identify the target image. Surprisingly, the pointer and writer criteria select substantially different head sets, with only 35 to 47 heads overlapping among the top-100 heads under each criterion. Targeted set-partition ablations show that the heads most important for standard multi-image inference are concentrated in this pointer-writer intersection, while heads selected by only one criterion show less consistent separation from random-head controls. The most consistent causal effects arise from heads selected by both the attention-based pointer and output-side writer criteria. Code and data: https://github.com/parkquasar/Image-Retrieval-Heads.

papers.abstract: Multimodal agents use web and image tools to answer questions beyond their internal knowledge. Some search tasks use images mainly to identify an initial entity, then rely on text retrieval. These tasks offer limited insight into how agents connect information across images, objects, and search steps. We therefore focus on visual context management. This involves organizing and using visual information and linking it to other findings during search. Visually intensive tasks require agents to combine object appearance, local details, or spatial relations with external information. We introduce VisSearch-Bench, with 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. It covers Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide-Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task provides a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete task success, while Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, even with search tools. These results highlight the challenge of linking visual evidence with search results to produce complete answers.

bullets: Introduces 204 human-written tasks spanning 7 domains and 25 subdomains.

Each task includes a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules for overall success and intermediate results.
Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solved 26.47% of tasks.
Findings highlight challenges in linking visual evidence with retrieved information to produce complete answers.

papers.abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is among the oldest and most widely deployed applications of artificial intelligence. This survey reviews its development, focusing on the Foundation Model Era. We define OCR through faithful transcription: within a specified visual scope, OCR should completely reconstruct the text, notation, and document structure observable in the source image, and every textual, notational, or structural element in the output must be verifiable from visual evidence in that image. We trace the development from specialist OCR models toward unified models, examining joint text detection and recognition, structured sequence generation, and the use of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs). We organize contemporary OCR systems into five coexisting families: modular toolkits and task-specific models, specialized document VLMs, hybrid workflows, general-purpose VLMs, and commercial products and managed services. We compare their architectures, data, and training, examining hallucination and omission, insufficient spatial grounding, and inference cost in generative OCR. We review evaluation from character and scene text recognition to parsing individual structural elements and full-page transcription, highlighting gaps in consistent output definitions, attribution of performance to individual components, and coverage of real capture conditions and visible content and structure. Finally, we summarize the challenges facing OCR and discuss directions for future research. We continuously track related work at https://github.com/zhihengli-casia/Awesome-OCR-in-the-Foundation-Model-Era.
authors: Zhiheng Li, Zongyang Ma, Jiaxian Chen, Cheng Cui, Yi Liu, Ziqi Zhang, Chunfeng Yuan, Bing Li, Xiang Bai, Weiming Hu
bullets: Defines OCR as complete reconstruction of all visually observable text, notation, and document structure without unsupported output.
Organizes current systems into five families: modular/task-specific models, document VLMs, hybrid workflows, general-purpose VLMs, and commercial services.
Reviews joint detection-recognition, structured generation, and pretrained vision-language model approaches.
Highlights generative OCR challenges including hallucinations, omissions, weak spatial grounding, and inference cost.
Identifies evaluation gaps involving output definitions, component attribution, real-world capture conditions, and visible structural content.

papers.abstract: Nighttime images are inherently susceptible to complex, compound degradations, making accurate quality assessment exceptionally challenging. Score-based IQA methods condense quality into a single number, lacking the multi-dimensional, language-grounded reasoning required for nighttime evaluation. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a more comprehensive alternative, yet remain constrained by a critical data gap: existing real-world IQA datasets are overwhelmingly daytime-centric and often built from outdated captures, while synthetic alternatives lack nighttime-specific degradation modeling, yielding artifacts far removed from authentic nighttime conditions. To bridge this gap, we present NightIQA, a dataset and benchmark suite purpose-built for MLLM-based nighttime IQA. It comprises three core components: NightIQA-Real, a real-world dataset of 1,769 high-resolution images that we captured ourselves with modern equipment, encompassing six canonical distortion types and structured multi-dimensional annotations; NightIQA-Bench, a benchmark of 1,078 visually grounded multiple-choice questions tailored to MLLM-based nighttime IQA, organized around a four-level evaluation hierarchy spanning Perception, Technical Assessment, Localization, and Reasoning; and NightIQA-Syn, an inherently scalable, scene-aware synthesis pipeline that jointly models global-level and instance-level degradations, with an initial release of 80k high-fidelity images alongside the full generation code. Fine-tuned on NightIQA with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Qwen3-VL-8B outperforms open-source IQA methods and achieves higher overall accuracy than leading closed-source models, highlighting the value of domain-specific data and structured supervision.
authors: Yiding Tian, Jiaojiao Yi, Jiayuan Lu, Pufan Xu, Jinlin Wu, Changyuan Wen, Hongyuan Yu

NightIQA-Syn offers a scene-aware pipeline modeling global and instance-level degradations, with an initial release of 80k images and generation code.
Qwen3-VL-8B fine-tuned with SFT and GRPO outperforms open-source IQA methods and achieves higher overall accuracy than leading closed-source models.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained cross-view localization aims to precisely localize a ground camera against geo-referenced aerial imagery, but current methods typically assume a narrow geographic prior, substantially limiting their applicability when upstream localization remains coarse. To bridge this gap, we study this task over much larger aerial regions. However, this seemingly simple extension fundamentally changes the localization problem: the growing disparity in spatial extent between ground and aerial views makes reliable cross-view matching difficult to establish directly, while the increasing number of look-alike locations in larger regions introduces substantial visual ambiguity. To address these challenges, we propose RingMatch, a search-and-verification framework for wide-area cross-view localization. RingMatch first leverages predictive uncertainty to uncover plausible locations and progressively zooms into their surroundings to obtain increasingly fine-grained evidence, yielding a compact set of promising candidates. We then introduce the depth ring, a novel geometric representation that reveals subtle variations in the spatial layout around a location and serves as a view-shared spatial signature for an LVLM verifier to resolve residual ambiguity. To benchmark this setting, we construct VIGOR-Pro by composing VIGOR aerial tiles into contiguous regions with spatial extents of up to 400 m. Experiments show that RingMatch maintains strong localization performance as the aerial region expands, consistently outperforming representative end-to-end and retrieval-based methods.
authors: Qingguo Hu, Xinyu Ma, Yujie Lin, Yaoxiang Wang, Qi Shi, Zonghao Guo, Chi Chen, Jinsong Su
bullets: Addresses the limited geographic priors and visual ambiguity that hinder fine-grained cross-view localization over large aerial areas.

Introduces depth ring, a view-shared spatial representation used by an LVLM verifier to distinguish look-alike candidates.
Constructs VIGOR-Pro with contiguous aerial regions spanning up to 400 m to benchmark wide-area localization.
Experiments show strong performance as region size grows, outperforming representative end-to-end and retrieval-based methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of RingMatch. RingMatch first performs multi-hypothesis branch-and-zoom search over the aerial region, using predictive uncertainty to expose plausible hypotheses and recursively zoom into them to produce a compact candidate shortlist. It then resolves the remaining ambiguity with depth-ring-grounded verification. Ground observations and candidate aerial patches are mapped to depth rings that capture subtle details of the surrounding spatial layout. The correct candidate exhibits strong consistency with the ground observation, whereas a look-alike candidate does not. An LVLM verifier leverages this evidence to select the final location.

Figure 1: (a) Existing fine-grained cross-view localization methods incur substantially larger errors as the aerial region expands from 35 × 35m to 400 × 400m. (b) A large aerial region can contain multiple look-alike locations compatible with the same ground observation (inset). In this example, locations • A and • B share similar appearance with the true location (⋆). The main differences lie in subtle spatial details, such as building outlines and the arrangement of surrounding vegetation.

Figure 7: Architecture of the aerial-to-ring predictor. DINOv2 and DPT encode the local aerial patch into a dense feature map. The candidate location p conditions the A azimuth queries through FiLM modulation. For each azimuth, a directional beam is sampled from p, and the corresponding query attends only to features along that beam. Each updated query predicts a metric-depth class, producing the aerial depth ring over all azimuths. During training, the predictor is supervised by the ground depth ring extracted from the corresponding panorama.

papers.abstract: Multimodal perception is central to many computer vision applications, including robotics and autonomous driving, where different sensing modalities provide complementary cues. Self-supervised learning offers a scalable solution for exploiting large amounts of unlabeled multimodal data. However, existing methods either neglect modality-specific information by enforcing feature-space alignment between modalities or learn only global representations without preserving spatial structure. We propose DenseTwins, a multimodal self-supervised framework that learns dense representations by explicitly decoupling the dense feature space into shared and modality-specific components. The proposed approach combines dense cross-modal correspondences with redundancy-reduction objectives, enabling the model to capture both shared semantics and modality-specific cues within a structured dense embedding space. DenseTwins jointly optimizes an intra-modal objective across augmented views and a cross-modal objective that aligns shared features while decorrelating modality-specific information. We evaluate DenseTwins across multiple multimodal benchmarks and sensing setups, achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance across multimodal self-supervised baselines. Code available at: https://github.com/CarloSgaravatti/DenseTwins.
authors: Carlo Sgaravatti, Daniele Kopyshevskiy, Davide Secco, Giacomo Boracchi
bullets: Addresses the loss of modality-specific cues and spatial structure in existing multimodal self-supervised learning methods.
Decouples dense features into shared and modality-specific components.
Combines dense cross-modal correspondences with redundancy-reduction objectives.
Jointly trains intra-modal learning across augmented views and cross-modal alignment/decorrelation.
Achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results across multiple multimodal benchmarks and sensing setups.

figures.caption: Figure 2. DenseTwins architecture. For each modality m ∈ {1, 2}, two augmented views are processed by a modality-specific backbone Fm, followed by a projection head Pm that produces both global and dense embeddings. The embedding space is explicitly partitioned into a shared subspace (red) and a modality-specific subspace (blue). Training is based on dense correspondences between feature vectors within each modality and across modalities computed using cosine similarities. The shared components are aligned through redundancy reduction and invariance objectives, while modality-specific components are decorrelated across modalities to preserve complementary information. Intra-modal learning, instead, applies a redundancy-reduction objective, encouraging invariance between augmented views. The final objective combines intra-modal and cross-modal losses applied to both global and dense representations.

Figure 6. Qualitative Results on SUN-RGBD. From left to right we show the RGB image, the depth modality encoded as HHA, the ground-truth semantic segmentation, and the predictions obtained using DeCUR and DenseTwins pretraining. While both methods correctly segment the main scene structures, DenseTwins produces sharper object boundaries and more consistent predictions.

Figure 1. The structure of the dense embeddings of DenseTwins. Two separate encoders F1, F2 process the two input modalities X1,X2 separately, producing two feature maps F1,F2. Finally, two projection heads project F1,F2 into a common latent space Z1,Z2, each divided into modality-shared S1,S2 and modality-specific U1,U2 components.

papers.tldr: DenseTwins learns spatially dense multimodal representations that preserve both shared semantics and modality-specific information through explicit feature decoupling.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often process hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, resulting in substantial computational and memory overhead during inference. Existing training-free pruning methods typically estimate token importance using language-model attention, visual attention, or feature similarity. However, these methods treat visual tokens with uniform criteria and overlook that tokens may serve different roles during visual encoding. In this work, we investigate the evolution of visual token roles in LVLMs and observe that tokens progressively transition from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives as encoding proceeds. Based on this observation, we propose BtsPruner, a training-free role-aware visual token pruning framework that preserves complementary token roles under a fixed budget. Specifically, BtsPruner first identifies the token-role transition point based on the evolution of attention concentration. It then discovers globally referenced representatives from later encoding stages and recursively retrieves local detail tokens from earlier stages to recover complementary fine-grained evidence. Extensive experiments across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen-VL, InternVL, and CogVLM demonstrate that BtsPruner achieves superior performance retention under aggressive token reduction. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, BtsPruner preserves 91.6% of the dense model's performance using only 32 of 576 visual tokens (5.6%). In the high-resolution LLaVA-NeXT-7B setting, it achieves up to a 5.95x CUDA-latency speedup.
authors: Zihao Qi, Zhibo Zhang, Miaoxin Zhang, Jincheng Cai, Zengqiang Yan
bullets: LVLM inference is costly because it processes hundreds or thousands of visual tokens.
The method observes that tokens evolve from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives during encoding.
It identifies this role-transition point, selects global representatives from later stages, and recursively retrieves complementary local tokens from earlier stages.
Across multiple LVLMs, it retains strong performance under substantial token reduction.
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, it retains 91.6% of dense-model performance with 32/576 tokens; on LLaVA-NeXT-7B, it provides up to 5.95× CUDA-latency speedup.

papers.selection_reason: Role-aware visual token pruning for LVLMs; directly addresses token pruning and eviction in efficient multimodal inference.
papers.title: BtsPruner: Role-Aware Visual Token Pruning for Large Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: BtsPruner is a training-free, role-aware method that aggressively reduces visual tokens while preserving both global context and local details in LVLMs.

papers.abstract: We present a spatial-memory system that enables optical see-through AR glasses to recall earlier physical encounters. The dual-camera prototype combines hierarchical visual acquisition with source-linked storage and staged retrieval. Quality screen-ing, global and regional appearance novelty, and temporal support select monochrome observations for detailed RGB cap-ture. Semantic observations retain links to their source images, allowing retrieval to answer indexed historical questions direct-ly or inspect visual details omitted from scene descriptions. The architecture separates capture acceptance, interpretation out-come, and support for a particular question. This distinction motivates two core control mechanisms: bounded reassessment of familiar views when earlier processing leaves an evidence gap, and retention guided by source dependencies. In a 131.35 s egocentric replay, the implemented acquisition policy selected six RGB views from 648 monitoring observations, while feature extraction ran on 97.7% of observations. These results demon-strate selective RGB acquisition and identify frequent local inference as a remaining cost. Exposure duration and cross-view timing further constrain the evidence preserved from se-lected encounters. The system provides a practical acquisition-to-recall architecture for persistent AR assistance, with explicit boundaries between captured evidence, indexed interpretations, and supported historical claims.
bullets: Addresses persistent AR assistance when historical questions require visual evidence from earlier encounters.
Uses hierarchical acquisition: quality, novelty, and temporal cues select monochrome observations for detailed RGB capture.
Links semantic observations to source images and separates capture acceptance, interpretation, and question-specific support.
Introduces bounded reassessment of familiar views and source-dependency-guided retention.
In replay, six RGB views were selected from 648 observations, while feature extraction covered 97.7%; frequent local inference remains costly.

papers.selection_reason: The paper presents a spatial-memory system for AR glasses that uses hierarchical visual acquisition and source-linked recall, directly fitting the 'Embodied Memory' subtopic regarding spatial and temporal memory for agents. papers.title: Spatial Memory for AR Glasses: Hierarchical Visual Acquisition and Source-Linked Recall
papers.tldr: A spatial-memory architecture for AR glasses selectively captures detailed views and links interpretations to source images to support grounded recall of past encounters.

papers.abstract: Time-series interpretation often requires both numerical observations and textual context. Integrating these inputs into a pretrained language model raises a representation question: how should a signal enter the model's token sequence? We present TEMPO, which extends an LLM's vocabulary with discrete codes from a context-aware Transformer tokenizer using finite scalar quantization. A frozen tokenizer maps four-step patches to a 625-code vocabulary; signal tokens, scale statistics, and text are then processed by the LLM's existing self-attention layers. Adaptation updates the new token embeddings and DoRA adapters. With a Qwen3-4B backbone and task-specific fine-tuning, TEMPO achieves macro-F1 scores of 89.0% on activity recognition, 85.0% on sleep staging, and 86.0% on bearing-fault diagnosis. Time-series question answering and qualitative bearing-diagnosis examples further illustrate how this interface combines signal representations with textual context. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of discrete vocabulary extension for time-series understanding.
bullets: Addresses how numerical signals can be integrated into pretrained language-model token sequences.
Uses a context-aware Transformer tokenizer with finite scalar quantization to encode four-step patches into 625 discrete codes.
Combines signal tokens, scale statistics, and text through the LLM’s existing self-attention layers.
Adapts the model by training new token embeddings and DoRA adapters while keeping the tokenizer frozen.
Reports macro-F1 scores of 89.0% for activity recognition, 85.0% for sleep staging, and 86.0% for bearing-fault diagnosis; also demonstrates time-series question answering.

papers.title: TEMPO: Time Series Understanding via Discrete Tokenization
papers.tldr: TEMPO enables LLMs to understand time series alongside text by representing signals as discrete tokens added to the model vocabulary.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) routinely name objects that are absent from the image. Latent steering can reduce this failure in one model forward pass, but a fixed gate treats early and late decoding steps by the same criterion. We observe that predictive entropy varies sharply within free-running generation, while states that commit to short answers occupy a narrow, confident band. We exploit this temporal mismatch by using uncertainty as a causally available, token-local control signal for an existing steering gate. We propose Entropy-Gated Dynamic Rectification (EGDR), which lowers the intervention threshold when entropy derived from the preceding step's already available logits is high and retains the calibrated operating point when it is low. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, the underlying static gate lowers CHAIR CS/CI from 53.00/15.30 to 32.00/14.30; replacing only its constant threshold with EGDR further lowers them to 29.00/13.60. At a matched 58% intervention rate, the corresponding static control obtains 30.50/14.00. The gain over the static gate holds on LLaVA-NeXT-7B and grows with the generation budget, while POPE scores and general multimodal capability remain effectively unchanged. EGDR requires no additional model forward pass and adds roughly 2% measured latency. Our code is available at https://github.com/alvi-uiu/EGDR.
authors: Riasad Alvi, Md. Asaduzzaman Shuvo, Md. Ahashan Habib, Md. Faiyaz Abdullah Sayeedi
bullets: Targets object hallucination caused by LVLMs naming objects absent from images.
Adjusts an existing steering gate using entropy from the preceding step’s available logits: higher uncertainty triggers stronger intervention.
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, reduces CHAIR CS/CI from 32.00/14.30 with a static gate to 29.00/13.60 with EGDR.
The improvement also holds on LLaVA-NeXT-7B and increases with the generation budget.
Maintains POPE and general multimodal performance, adding roughly 2% measured latency.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline of EGDR. (a) Held-out calibration selects the steering depth ℓ∗, estimates the prior-removed direction v(ℓ∗), threshold τ , and entropy band [Hlo, Hhi], and tunes α and wτ . (b) At each decoding step, the current hidden state yields risk Rt, while preceding-step entropy lowers τ to τeff. If Rt > τeff, EGDR injects αv(ℓ∗). This requires no additional forward pass or trained parameter. (c) The adaptive threshold admits states missed by the static gate; at the first token, ê = 0 and τeff = τ .

Figure 1. Overview of EGDR. Both gates share v, ℓ∗ and α; only the threshold differs. (a) A static gate applies one threshold τ at every step. (b) EGDR lowers it to τeff(t) using the entropy of the preceding step’s logits, rescaled to the calibrated band, and so corrects states the static gate misses; at t=1, ê=0 and τeff=τ . Gate strips are schematic; bubbles quote the second paragraph of real LLaVA-1.5-7B captions verbatim (CHAIR: hallucinated objects in red, grounded in green).

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of object hallucination mitigation. LLaVA-1.5-7B captions of a COCO val2014 image under unsteered decoding (Regular), the calibrated static gate, and EGDR at the locked operating point of Sec. 5.1 (greedy, 512 tokens). Objects that the CHAIR evaluator flags as hallucinated against the COCO annotations are in red. Image cropped for display.
