papers.selection_reason: Reduces object hallucination in large vision-language models via entropy-gated steering; directly relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Entropy-Gated Dynamic Rectification for Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: EGDR uses token-level predictive entropy to dynamically control latent steering, reducing object hallucinations in LVLMs without extra forward passes or meaningful capability loss.

papers.abstract: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.
bullets: Addresses the lack of guarantees for language-model arithmetic and the externalization of tool-based computation.
Uses Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter; each pass reads three cells and emits a digit, carry/borrow, and next operation, while fixed runtime controls the sheet.
A Lean proof reduces correctness for all input lengths to checking the finite set of views presented by the runtime; this does not hold when steps access earlier outputs.
All 2,446 deployment views passed, and the model handled signed arithmetic, multiplication, division, square roots, and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length.
The system solved all reported browser test problems and supports symbolic polynomial operations, while a multiplicative adapter gate preserves the base model when arithmetic is unused.

The view (three cells, 32 × 96 pixels) enters Qwen3.5-0.8B as three image tokens after the operation token MUL; the outputs, read at = and two placeholder positions, are the digit, the carry and the next operation. Right: the operation sequence of the same division (Knuth’s Algorithm D) and of the square root of 2,000,000 (56 forward passes). c, Batching four independent procedures: 32 forward passes instead of 73. Fig. 6 | Mechanism. Arithmetic adapter. a, Logit lens: fraction of views whose top token at each depth equals the final output, by operation; ticks mark the median decision depth, triangles the ends of full-attention layers. b, Final-layer states projected onto three discriminant directions, coloured by output, for addition (0–19) and multiplication digits; nearest-centre shares are measured in this projection (Methods). c, Fraction of 80 steps whose output a class-mean intervention changes to its target, against the depth at which it is applied, for addition and multiplication; the shaded band is the fifth full-attention layer.

papers.selection_reason: Small vision-language model with certified exact arithmetic on rendered working memory; fits multimodal LLM/VLM research.
papers.title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model
papers.tldr: Sketchpad certifies arbitrary-length exact arithmetic by having a small vision-language model process a bounded local view of a rendered working sheet at each step.

papers.abstract: Natural human-robot interaction requires robots to interpret language and gestures within a 3D environment to support tasks such as pick-and-place and object retrieval. 3D Embodied Reference Understanding (3D-ERU) supports this by identifying the 3D location of a target object from a scene (point-cloud) containing a human pointing gesture and an accompanying language description. However, current 3D-ERU models lack alignment of cross-modal representations and incur high processing costs that increase with the point-cloud's size. To address this, we propose GVT3D, which employs an Embodied Fusion module that jointly models language, gesture, and vision inputs within a shared embedding space, promoting cross-modal alignment. We additionally introduce a foveation approach that selectively processes the point cloud within a coarse region around the estimated pointing direction to reduce computations. GVT3D achieves ~8% higher accuracy and foveation enables 2.95x faster execution while maintaining comparable accuracy, relative to prior 3D-ERU models.
authors: Vimarsh Shah, Dulanga Weerakoon, Ajinkya Deshpande, Saksham Agarwal, Nilesh Bhatia, Neel Kiran Naik, Parth Shah, Sravan Danda, Sanjay E. Sarma, Archan Misra, Vigneshwaran Subbaraju, Sougata Sen
bullets: Targets robot understanding of object references from a 3D scene, pointing gesture, and language description.
Uses an Embodied Fusion module to jointly represent language, gesture, and vision in a shared embedding space.
Applies foveation to focus point-cloud processing on a coarse region near the estimated pointing direction.
Reports approximately 8% higher accuracy and 2.95× faster execution with comparable accuracy when foveation is used, relative to prior models.

papers.title: GVT3D: Gesture-Vision-Text Token Enrichment for 3D Embodied Reference Understanding

papers.abstract: In-image machine translation (IIMT) replaces text in an image with its translation while preserving the surrounding visual context. Existing task-specific models achieve convincing performance but require massive paired training images before and after translation. As advanced text-to-image (T2I) models have reached a practically usable level of multilingual text generation, we argue that this capability can be transferred to IIMT and present FlowTranslator. It is a training-free IIMT framework that first employs an OCR model and an LLM to generate the translation prompt, which is injected into the T2I-based diffusion model. To optimize the accurate and natural generation of translated text, we introduce two trajectory controls: Region Coupling Release (RCR) partially decorrelates target-branch noise inside the text region early in the trajectory, while Coupling Expansion (CE) amplifies the emerging edit displacement mid-trajectory. Under the EasyOCR read-back protocol, FlowTranslator achieves average PRIM BLEU and COMET scores of 20.6 and 57.2, respectively, substantially outperforming the strong training-based baseline UniTranslator. On the more challenging and realistic whole-image ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese, it reaches 40.1\% exact-match accuracy and surpasses existing editing systems, some of which only address the text-rendering stage rather than the complete IIMT task. These results establish flow-based editing as a strong, fully training-free baseline for IIMT.
authors: Zhixian Li, Xingsong Ye, Yongkun Du, Yunyan Xiao, Yanglin Huang, Pinxuan Chen, Jiyu Zhuang, Cong Xu, Zhineng Chen
bullets: Addresses IIMT without requiring paired before-and-after translation images.
Uses OCR to identify text and an LLM to create translation prompts for a text-to-image diffusion model.
Introduces Region Coupling Release and Coupling Expansion to improve translated-text accuracy and naturalness during editing.
Achieves 20.6 PRIM BLEU and 57.2 COMET under EasyOCR read-back, outperforming UniTranslator.
Reaches 40.1% exact-match accuracy on whole-image ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese; results establish a training-free baseline for IIMT.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of the IIMT framework and editor paradigms. (a) The pipeline: OCR extracts text → a translator produces the translation → a scene text editor generates the output image. (b) Rule-based: remove, render, and paste separately. (c) Training-based: a learned GAN or diffusion editor (requires extra training). (d) FlowTranslator (ours): training-free flow editing with trajectory controls (CE and RCR) for text translation with background preservation.

Figure 2 Overview of FlowTranslator. OCR extracts the source text and forms a source caption, while a frozen LLM translates it to obtain the target caption. A frozen VAE encodes the source image into 𝑍src 0 , from which noise initialization produces 𝑍FE 𝑇 . At each editing step, the same frozen DiT predicts source- and target-conditioned velocities. Their difference updates the flow-editing latent. RCR perturbs the target-branch noise within the detected text region, and CE amplifies the accumulated displacement before it is fed back to the target branch. The final latent 𝑍FE 0 is decoded to produce the translated image.

Figure 4 Qualitative comparison on whole-image ScenePair En→Zh translation. For each example, we show the source image (with red boxes marking text to be translated), the requested target text, and outputs of existing open-source methods, followed by FlowTranslator. FlowTranslator renders the requested Chinese text within the original region. It preserves both the surrounding scene and the local text appearance.

Figure 3 Qualitative results on TTV. Each row shows the source image, the benchmark target image, and the FlowTranslator output for one translation direction. The examples cover EN→DE, FR→EN, DE→EN, and RO→EN.

Table 1 TTV benchmark with EasyOCR read-back and lowercased sacreBLEU. “IIMT-tuned” marks systems trained or fine-tuned on IIMT data. GPT-Image-1 and Qwen-Image are zero-shot prompted unified models. “Masked FlowEdit” is our baseline with identical hyperparameters and the trajectory controls disabled. Average columns are unweighted means over the four directions. For each metric, best in bold, second underlined.

Table 3 ScenePair En→Zh whole-image translation on 1,280 real scenes. All methods share the same text boxes and target translations. “STE-tr.” marks scene-text-editing training and “Zh” native Chinese glyph support. Rows without “Zh” are capability diagnostics rather than head-to-head competitors.

Table 4 Component ablations. Control rows are full PRIM runs (340 images per direction, averaged over the five directions) sharing the same hyperparameters (𝛾=1.3, 15% dilation, RCR 𝜅=0.5, CE 𝑐=0.4) and differing only in the mechanism switches.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free in-image machine translation method using flow-based editing, relevant to spatial understanding and multimodal generation.
papers.title: FlowTranslator: Training-Free In-Image Machine Translation with Flow-Based Editing
papers.tldr: FlowTranslator enables training-free in-image machine translation by combining OCR- and LLM-generated prompts with controlled diffusion-based flow editing.

papers.abstract: Promptable perception, from GroundingDINO to Rex-Omni, puts one model behind one prompt interface and returns coordinates for any localisation task. Every model in that line was built for photographs; none has been given a sketch. We present Sketch-Omni, to our knowledge the first perception MLLM built to work on sketches and from them. On a sketch, the sketch is the image, and text prompts detect, point, resolve object and spatial referring expressions, and ground affordances in it. From a sketch, the sketch is the prompt, and a drawing of one object localises that object in a photograph, even among several of the same category, a query that neither a category name nor a photo exemplar can pose. Two obstacles stand in the way. A photo-trained model's attention is tuned to colour and texture, which a sketch does not have, and no dataset pairs a drawing with the one instance it depicts among others of its kind. We build the training data instead of collecting it. An edge detector turns every labelled photograph into a sketch-like drawing that keeps the photograph's labels, and two constructions produce sketch-to-photo instance pairs from existing data. On top of this, photo-guided relation alignment passes each photograph and its edge sketch through the same model and trains the sketch pass to reproduce how the photograph pass relates phrases to patches and patches to each other. Not one training label is drawn by hand. Sketch-Omni reaches 91.4 F1 on sketch-prompted localisation against 81.8 for the strongest general-purpose MLLM, with a lead that doubles when the photograph holds several instances of the queried category, and it is best in 39 of 40 evaluation cells across six tasks. Code, model, and a hand-annotated benchmark of 2754 sketch-to-photo links will be released.
authors: Dongyu Wang, Dar-Yen Chen, Zhiming Hong, Arkaprabha Basu, Yi-Zhe Song

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal agents have shown promising progress in embodied planning and web interaction. However, existing evaluations often rely on simplified tasks with limited combinatorial structure, leaving it unclear whether current agents can robustly integrate perception and reasoning for multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints. We introduce DualWorldBench, a unified benchmark for evaluating agent planning under controlled symbolic--temporal and grounded--topological complexity. Built around a shared pickup--delivery interface, DualWorldBench consists of three complementary components: TextWorld, which isolates symbolic planning under varying task compositions and release dynamics; SimWorld, which evaluates grounded path planning under controlled topological variation with text, image, or multimodal inputs; and DualWorld-VQA, a diagnostic suite spanning perception, scene understanding, and planning. Experiments reveal a common gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning. In TextWorld, agents struggle to derive optimal task sequences under interacting temporal constraints; in SimWorld, grounded observations are not reliably converted into feasible action sequences. DualWorld-VQA further confirms that perception and topology understanding do not necessarily translate into constrained planning. Together, these results identify the central challenge as composing symbolic or grounded evidence into globally feasible and efficient multi-goal plans. These findings establish DualWorldBench as a challenging testbed for agents with tighter perception--reasoning--planning integration. All datasets and code are publicly available at our project website https://dualworld.netlify.app/.

Datasets and code are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery builds on accurate observations interpreted through domain knowledge and reasoning. For scientific 3D data, this requires understanding structures and spatial relationships, from protein contacts to anatomical organization. Existing multimodal benchmarks largely evaluate text and 2D images, while scientific 3D evaluations vary in representations and protocols across disciplines, limiting cross-disciplinary comparison. To assess these foundational capabilities, we introduce ScienceVision, a cross-domain benchmark for scientific 3D understanding and reasoning through expert-level visual question answering (VQA). We construct 250 questions, with 50 each from Biology, Chemistry, Medical Imaging, Mechanical CAD, and Architecture, through a pipeline combining synthetic question generation with domain-expert review and annotation. Each task pairs a native 3D artifact with a scientific question, a specified response format, and a task-specific reference answer, requiring domain knowledge to be applied to geometric or topological evidence. We evaluate 12 models on the same questions in three settings: visual question answering with native 3D artifacts accessed through an agent harness's file and code-execution tools; the same workflow augmented with expert-inspired viewer inspection and measurement tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP); and visual question answering from prescribed rendered 2D images using an agent harness. All settings use the same task-specific deterministic final-answer scoring. The inspection environment supports view changes, target isolation, and slice inspection. In this main comparison, the best mean answer score is 0.53 out of 1. Mean scores in the native-artifact workflow without additional MCP tools exceed those in the rendered-image workflow for every model, by 17.2 percentage points on average.

papers.abstract: Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation (CD-FSS) aims to segment objects from unseen domains using only a few annotated references. Recent Segment Anything Model (SAM)-based methods have advanced CD-FSS, yet their reference-target visual matching is highly sensitive to target appearance variations. SAM3 introduces text-conditioned segmentation, enabling natural-language descriptions to guide segmentation across target images, but directly using the category name as the condition still yields unstable performance under severe domain shifts. We propose Reference Inversion for SAM3 (RI-SAM3) that leverages SAM3's large-scale vision-language pre-training to learn suitable textual tokens for each target category. RI-SAM3 comprises three core designs: (i) Bi-level Reference Inversion that learns complementary tokens before and after the frozen text encoder: the former remain anchored in SAM3's text space while the latter represent the category more flexibly; (ii) Layer-adaptive Textual Conditioning combines these tokens differently as object queries evolve across decoder layers; and (iii) Presence-aware Confidence Supervision that jointly supervises query confidence and target presence for reliable predictions. With SAM3 frozen, RI-SAM3 optimizes around 12K parameters only per category and it efficiently segments each target in a single forward pass with reusable textual conditioning without per-sample reference-target visual matching. Extensive experiments over multiple widely adopted benchmarks show that RI-SAM3 achieves superior performance consistently in CD-FSS tasks, together with strong robustness, efficiency, and generalization.
authors: Jiahao Nie, Yun Xing, Wenbin An, Qixin Zhang, Yap-Peng Tan, Alex C. Kot, Shijian Lu
bullets: Addresses unstable SAM-based segmentation under severe domain shifts and target appearance variation.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks report consistently superior performance, robustness, efficiency, and generalization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our proposed RI-SAM3 framework. Presence-aware Confidence Supervision (PCS) jointly supervises query-level classification and global presence scores. Once learned, T ∗ c is reused for target segmentation without references or visual matching.

papers.abstract: Surgical scene understanding is pivotal for computer-assisted intervention, yet demands compositional reasoning across instruments, anatomy, and workflow. Existing surgical vision-language models rely on instruction tuning with large-scale question-answer pairs, entailing laborious data curation and costly retraining. To bridge this gap, we propose SurgEye, a perception-reasoning framework that grounds reasoning in a vision foundation model without instruction tuning. Specifically, we devise Routed Multi-Task Perception (RMP) that routes the vision foundation model through task-specific pathways learned from public perception labels, producing spatial and temporal evidence. We further introduce Agentic Compositional Reasoning (ACR) that employs a frozen large language model to coordinate RMP specialists and temporal memory as callable tools, composing evidence across tasks and time into grounded answers. Moreover, we construct SurgEye-Bench spanning eight surgical procedures, pairing each question with perception labels for verifiable evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SurgEye outperforms state-of-the-arts in surgical reasoning. The source code will be available.

Introduces SurgEye-Bench covering eight surgical procedures with perception labels for verifiable evaluation.
Reports outperforming state-of-the-art methods on surgical reasoning; implementation is planned for release.

papers.abstract: Humans imagine scene changes under hypothetical motions, an ability central to spatial reasoning and robotic planning. However, this capability remains underexplored in vision-language models and world models. We formalize this capability as Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI) and introduce FlowBench, a resource for training and evaluating both, with 428K training examples spanning simulated and real-world scenes, household environments and tabletop manipulation, and diverse question types. A scalable, fully automatic pipeline pairs each hypothetical motion with spatial questions and, in simulation, exact outcome frames and optical flow. For VLMs, proprietary models exhibit an imagination gap, performing worse when motion outcomes must be inferred than when observed, and open-source models perform near chance; fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B on FlowBench-Sim-Train raises its accuracy by 29.5 percentage points in simulation and 16.9 on real images, a strong sim-to-real transfer. For world models, training on FlowBench-Sim improves text-to-flow prediction for all four model families we test, raising the accuracy of Psi-0.6 from 52.1% to 61.7%. FlowBench thus serves as a training and evaluation resource for both. Code and datasets are released at https://github.com/liuyifan22/FlowBench.
authors: Yifan Liu, Baihan Zhang, Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Daniel L. K. Yamins
bullets: Introduces Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI) as a benchmarkable capability for spatial reasoning and robotic planning.
Provides 428K automatically generated training examples across simulated and real scenes, household environments, tabletop manipulation, and varied question types.
Finds that VLMs struggle to infer motion outcomes without observing them, while open-source models perform near chance.
Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B improves accuracy by 29.5 percentage points in simulation and 16.9 on real images, indicating sim-to-real transfer.
FlowBench training improves text-to-flow prediction across four tested world-model families, including Psi-0.6.

figures.caption: Figure 3. A scalable, fully automatic, and accurate pipeline for counterfactual data that others can adapt to new simulators and tasks. (a) Four stages: find informative views, plan answer-changing motions, execute them in the simulator, and annotate. Answers are computed by rules on simulator metadata, so they are exact; a VLM only adds reasoning and language variation. (b) The pipeline needs no human labeling, scales to 420K questions across 9.7K houses, and records depth, flow, masks, and reasoning for every example. (c) A training example. The model sees only (I0, tm, tq); coloured nouns refer to the marks of the same colour. The outcome image, flow, depth, metadata, and the reasoning chain cgt→c1→c0 (excerpts) are training annotations that supervise both VLMs and world models.

Figure 5. FlowBench-Real. (a) Four-stage curation pipeline; answers come only from the measured 3D geometry, and a VLM only names objects and checks marks. (b) FlowBench-Real test set: 1,083 questions, one per image pair, over seven categories and five robot datasets. (c) A test question. papers.tldr: FlowBench trains and evaluates models on imagining how scenes change under hypothetical motions, improving both vision-language reasoning and world-model flow prediction.

papers.abstract: Large foundation models often answer even when the available visual or textual evidence is insufficient to support a reliable conclusion. This failure to abstain makes them hard to trust in high-stakes or information-seeking settings, where a confident but unsupported answer can be worse than no answer at all. It also raises a natural question: can the internal mechanisms behind this behaviour be identified and controlled at inference time? We present Dr. No, a feature-steering approach that mines sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set of them during the prefill pass, without retraining the base model. Dr. No is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B across multimodal abstention benchmarks, including UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and additionally benchmarked on language reasoning tasks using Qwen3.5-2B on AbstentionBench subsets. Against multiple uncertainty-based abstention baselines, feature steering achieves a more favourable balance between correct answering and appropriate abstention than post-hoc rejection methods. The gains are strongest on UNK-VQA and on MM-UPD cases involving image--question or question--answer incompatibility, and transfer most clearly to mathematical reasoning subsets of AbstentionBench. However, performance is more limited on absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA, such as MuSiQue. These results suggest that sparse internal features provide lightweight control handles for shaping uncertainty-aware behaviour in foundation models, while also showing that abstention control is source-dependent rather than governed by a single universal signal.
authors: Farid Hasanov, Riccardo Renzulli, Bahram Zonooz, Mykola Pechenizkiy, Decebal Constantin Mocanu
bullets: Addresses overconfident answers unsupported by available visual or textual evidence.
Mines sparse autoencoder features linked to abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set during prefill.
Evaluated with LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B and Qwen3.5-2B across multimodal and language abstention benchmarks.
Produces a better balance between correct answers and appropriate abstention than uncertainty-based post-hoc rejection baselines.
Works best for image–question or question–answer incompatibility and mathematical reasoning, but is weaker for absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA.

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models continue to improve on broad music understanding benchmarks, but which musical features can they perceive and reason about? We investigate this question by introducing PianoBench, a benchmark that tasks language models with reasoning about musical performances across congruent acoustic and symbolic input representations. PianoBench is derived from our new multimodal, training-scale dataset comprising more than 20,000 hours of interleaved transcripts of music and spoken musical commentary from instructional piano videos. Open-weight audio-language models achieve at most 52.8% accuracy on PianoBench, and at best only modestly outperform their accuracy on a no-audio control. In contrast, frontier models using chain of thought achieve up to 93.2% accuracy when provided transcripts of music as text, exposing a gap between perceiving musical features from audio and reasoning about musical events when they are given explicitly. We then test whether mid-training on interleaved musical instruction can improve question answering without chain of thought, raising Qwen 3.5 9B Base's zero-shot accuracy on PianoBench with music transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0% after instruction tuning. These experiments suggest that instructional videos may represent an overlooked source of multimodal supervision for music. Available: https://gclef-cmu.org/pianobench.
authors: Louis Bradshaw, Irmak Bukey, Daniel Chenyu Lin, John Thickstun, Chris Donahue
bullets: Introduces PianoBench, a benchmark for musical perception and reasoning across matched acoustic and symbolic inputs.
Built from a multimodal dataset containing over 20,000 hours of piano instruction transcripts and musical commentary.
Open-weight audio-language models reach at most 52.8% accuracy, only modestly above a no-audio control.
Frontier models achieve up to 93.2% with chain-of-thought when musical content is provided as text, revealing an audio-perception gap.
Instruction tuning on interleaved musical instruction improves Qwen 3.5 9B Base’s transcript-based zero-shot accuracy from 42.8% to 56.0%.

Audio from videos with captions is fetched and screened for piano content. papers.abstract: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often introduces early optimization instability, making it difficult to separate architectural gains from transient training dynamics. We introduce Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that preserves pretrained model behavior at initialization while enabling gradual multimodal conditioning. Integrated across six decoder layers of frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b1 backbones (with 40,404,961,288 trainable adapter parameters used during training), IGCA acts as an exact algebraic no-op at initialization with a maximum output discrepancy of 0.00e+00. Over 59,500 training steps on Falcon-40B, the training loss decreases from 3.9403 to 0.0007 (with final ten step losses of [0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0005, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.0011, 0.0005, 0.0006, 0.0005, 0.0007]). On held-out evaluation, the best gate-on checkpoint achieves a loss of 2.2201 compared to 4.3469 for the gate-off baseline -- a 48.9% reduction (2.1268 nats) -- while average held-out loss improves from 4.3423 to 2.2498 (1.9075 nats) with a mean gate magnitude of $\vert{}\tanh(\alpha)\vert{} = 0.0713$.
bullets: Addresses early optimization instability when adding non-text modalities to frozen language models.
Uses zero-initialized, learnable gated cross-attention inserted across six decoder layers.
At initialization, the bridge preserves pretrained behavior exactly, with reported output discrepancy of 0.00e+00.
On Falcon-40B held-out evaluation, gate-on performance improves loss from 4.3469 to 2.2201 versus the gate-off baseline.
The approach is evaluated with frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b backbones; results reported primarily for Falcon-40B.

papers.title: Zero-Gated Cross-Attention

papers.abstract: Inference-time steering in vision-language models often entangles query-relevant reasoning dynamics with low-level perceptual noise, causing collateral degradation on correct predictions. We propose Question-Contrastive Visual Steering (QCVS) to isolate task-specific intervention directions via double-differential activation probing. By contrasting spatial layout perturbations under the target query against a generic description reference, QCVS cancels task-agnostic visual artifacts without ground-truth supervision. A dual-threshold gating mechanism then evaluates relative interaction strength and signal amplitude, selectively applying a single bounded hidden-state update only when necessary. Empirical evaluations across multiple scales of Qwen3.5 (2B to 9B) and DeepSeek-VL2 on DynaMath and We-Math demonstrate that QCVS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy gains under sparse coverage (approximately 22%-30%). Crucially, QCVS yields repair rates up to 13.98% while suppressing collateral damage down to 0.41%, proving high intervention precision and computational efficiency.
bullets: Targets task-relevant reasoning signals while filtering out low-level visual perturbation noise.
Uses double-differential activation probing with spatial-layout contrasts and a generic-description reference, requiring no ground-truth supervision.
Applies a single bounded hidden-state update through dual-threshold gating only when intervention is warranted.
Evaluated on Qwen3.5 and DeepSeek-VL2 across DynaMath and We-Math, with sparse coverage of approximately 22%–30%.
Reports repair rates up to 13.98% and collateral damage as low as 0.41%, alongside state-of-the-art accuracy gains.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Motivation and computation of QCVS. (a) Describing a scene and counting water-filled glasses require different evidence. The BLINK [19] example has dataset label 3; the crops are human-selected illustrations, not model outputs. (b) One visual encoding feeds a frozen Qwen3.5 model: two questions and three visual conditions give six prefix readouts. (c) Paired clean–control differences at each final assistant-prefix token ta yield the interaction µ. Its direction defines a bounded edit; R and A determine selection. A selected input receives one update at (ℓ∗, ta) in a fresh clean-prefix replay; otherwise, decoding uses the retained clean hybrid state.
Fig. 2. Fixed-action coverage sweep on Qwen3.5-4B/DynaMath. Curves show repairs, harm and net change as percentages of all inputs; net change equals accuracy gain (pp).

papers.selection_reason: Inference-time steering of vision-language model reasoning via activation probing; directly relevant to multimodal LLM methods.
papers.title: QCVS: Question-Contrastive Visual Steering for Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: QCVS improves multimodal reasoning at inference time by selectively steering hidden states to correct errors while minimizing harm to correct predictions.

papers.abstract: Foundational vision models have become the de facto standard for many vision tasks due to their strong performance. However, they are notoriously opaque and remain hard to interpret. We present ALOE (ALign Once to Explain), a one-time, label-free feature alignment approach that efficiently converts foundational vision models into inherently interpretable B-cos variants. Once aligned, the B-cos backbone is used as a drop-in replacement across several downstream tasks-amortizing the cost of interpretability. ALOE is robust across pre-training paradigms (supervised, self-supervised, vision-language) and can preserve teacher-level generalization with orders of magnitude less data than training from scratch. On classification, it strongly outperforms vanilla B-cosification (e.g., +10.5 p.p. top-1 on ImageNet for DINOv3 ViT-B/16), retains strong linear probing, k-NN, and zero-shot transfer competitive with foundational backbones (DINOv3, SigLIP2) across diverse downstream datasets. It also preserves spatially structured features useful for dense prediction, while yielding well-localized and highly human-interpretable explanations by design.
bullets: Addresses the opacity of foundational vision models and the high cost of making them interpretable.
Uses a one-time, label-free feature-alignment procedure to convert pretrained models into B-cos variants.
Works across supervised, self-supervised, and vision-language pretraining paradigms, using far less data than training from scratch.
Preserves strong classification, linear-probe, k-NN, zero-shot, and dense-prediction capabilities while producing localized, human-interpretable explanations.
On ImageNet, improves over vanilla B-cosification by 10.5 percentage points in top-1 accuracy for DINOv3 ViT-B/16.

figures.caption: Figure 2. ALOE vs. B-cosification [4]. ALOE consistently outperforms vanilla B-cosification in ImageNet-1k linear-probe accuracy across model scales for both SigLIP2 [76] and DINOv3 [72] (see (a)). It reaches performance close to the original SigLIP2 and DINOv3 baselines while significantly improving localization scores (Grid-PG, see (b))—even compared against different SOTA post-hoc attribution methods.
Figure 6. Explanation quality. Comparison between model inherent (B-cos: W(x) [11]) explanations after ALOE vs a popular strong method for visualizing vision transformers, AttnLRP [1].

Figure 4. Align Once to Explain. (1) Transform to B-cos—convert a Foundation ViT encoder into a bias-free, dynamic-linear backbone (Sec. 4.1). (2) Align once—label-free feature alignment with cosine distance objective between foundational teacher and B-cos student, on unlabeled images (Sec. 4.2). (3) Deploy—freeze the aligned B-cos backbone for linear probing and zero-shot transfer; faithful, welllocalized explanations follow directly from W (x) (i.e., model summary), amortizing interpretability across tasks (Sec. 5.1).

Figure 7. VLM Zero-Shot Explanations. ALOE aligned B-cos models (SigLIP2 teacher) yield zero-shot model-inherent explanations for VLMs, where the input prompt to the text encoder is “this is a photo of {class name}”. The explanations are visually well aligned with class-specific features.

Across these settings, including the full-data distillation, ALOE remains nearly flat (83.09%–83.87%). Already at 1% (150k images), it reaches 83.79%, within 0.42 p.p. of the SigLIP2 teacher (84.21%) and 8.74 p.p. above the B-cosification reference. The 100% setting reaches 83.87%, leaving only a 0.34 p.p. gap to the teacher.

Figure 3. Conventional vs. B-cos ViT. We replace linear/MLP layers with bias-free B-cos transforms and uncentered normalization, keeping self-attention and residuals intact. This yields a dynamic-linear B-cos ViT with inherently faithful explanations via W(x)x (Sec. 3.1).

Figure 5. PCA Visualization. DINOv3 (row 2) vs. ALOE (row 3) last layer features visualized with 3 principal components and mapped to joint RGB space, preserves global feature geometry that indicates aligned semantics while being inherently interpretable.

papers.title: Align Once to Explain: Feature Alignment for Scalable B-cosification of Foundational Vision Transformers
papers.tldr: ALOE aligns pretrained vision features once to turn opaque foundational models into interpretable B-cos backbones that remain broadly useful across downstream tasks.

papers.abstract: Earth observation (EO) workflows require selecting among known outcomes, estimating confidence, and processing large volumes of imagery. Generative vision-language models can address these tasks, but autoregressive decoding is computationally costly and their confidence estimates are unreliable. Decision models offer an alternative, returning probabilities over candidate answers in a single forward pass. However, their accuracy, calibration, and transfer across EO tasks remain insufficiently understood. We investigate these properties through a diagnostic study of d3-flash (8.4B parameters) across 30 settings from 23 public EO benchmarks. We find that compositional reasoning transfers well and calibration improves over its Qwen3.5-9B backbone on 24 settings, while counting, change quantification, damage grading, and absent-object recognition remain challenging. To address these limitations, we adapt d3-flash through low-rank fine-tuning on public EO training splits, producing EO-Jev. EO-Jev improves significantly over d3-flash on 26 of 30 settings and matches or exceeds specialist references on 20 of 28. It also achieves an average gain of 8.0 points across 12 held-out settings and lower expected calibration error than specialists on 21 of 28 settings. These improvements come at a modest cost of 1.8 points in general decision performance. Our results demonstrate the potential of adapting general decision models into competitive EO generalists while highlighting persistent challenges in quantitative perception, option-order consistency, and calibration under distribution shift.
bullets: Decision models provide single-pass probabilities over candidate answers, avoiding the costly decoding and unreliable confidence of generative vision-language models.
A diagnostic study evaluates d3-flash across 30 settings from 23 public EO benchmarks.
Compositional reasoning transfers well, but counting, change quantification, damage grading, and absent-object recognition remain difficult.

papers.abstract: **Purpose:** Ultrasound biometry is widely used across various clinical applications, including prenatal and cardiac examinations, to obtain quantitative measurements by placing calipers at anatomical landmarks. However, these measurements remain subject to interoperator variability as they rely largely on manual caliper placement. Conventional methods often use specialized prediction heads for different ultrasound tasks, whereas vision-language models offer flexibility through text instructions. However, direct coordinate prediction does not explicitly model spatial likelihood distributions, limiting the representation of localization ambiguity. **Methods:** We propose Kev-Bio, a vision-language model that uses clinical measurement questions to guide ultrasound landmark detection. Inspired by System One decision models, Kev-Bio uses decision representations of the language model to generate queries for each caliper endpoint. These queries are matched against shared dense ultrasound features to produce spatial probability maps, from which landmark coordinates and clinical measurements are derived. The model is trained end-to-end using both landmark localization and clinical measurement losses. **Results:** On the nine-view FU/GU Biometry 2026 dataset, Kev-Bio achieves a mean radial error (MRE) of 22.50 pixels and a clinical measurement mean absolute error (MAE) of 15.38, outperforming the compared baselines in overall performance. **Conclusion:** These results demonstrate the effectiveness of Kev-Bio for ultrasound landmark detection and clinical measurement across different anatomical views. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/Kev-Bio.
bullets: Addresses interoperator variability caused by manual caliper placement in ultrasound biometry.
Uses clinical measurement questions and language-model decision representations to query shared dense ultrasound features.
Generates endpoint probability maps rather than directly predicting coordinates, capturing localization uncertainty.
Trains jointly with landmark-localization and clinical-measurement losses.
On the FU/GU Biometry 2026 dataset, reports 22.50-pixel MRE and 15.38 measurement MAE, outperforming compared baselines.

papers.abstract: Geospatial text spotting involves locating and transcribing geographic labels, such as road names, district names, and landmarks, in raster maps. These labels are often small, densely arranged, and arbitrarily oriented. Although Arabic text recognition has been studied extensively in documents and natural scenes, Arabic geospatial text spotting remains underexplored. We introduce ARABGEOTEXT, an Arabic-centric benchmark covering 970 geographic locations in Riyadh and Jeddah, with 17,875 manually annotated text instances per view type. For each location, we pair an OpenStreetMap (OSM) rendering with a composite created by overlaying that rendering on the corresponding remote sensing (RS) imagery. The paired views preserve label content and pixel geometry, allowing evaluation across different backgrounds. Geographic partitions support in-city and city-disjoint evaluation of detection, recognition, and end-to-end spotting. Experiments with direct Qwen3.5-4B spotting show difficulties in recovering all labels within a tile. We therefore propose a tool-augmented vision-language framework that combines YOLO26 localization and crop rectification with Qwen3.5-4B recognition adapted through low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The framework outperforms direct LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B spotting across both image views and test cities. With localization held fixed, reader adaptation further improves recognition over the pretrained zero-shot reader. The dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yakoubbazi/ArabGeoText.
bullets: Addresses the underexplored task of locating and transcribing small, dense, arbitrarily oriented Arabic geographic labels.
Provides 970 locations in Riyadh and Jeddah with 17,875 manually annotated text instances per view type, pairing OpenStreetMap renderings with remote-sensing composites.
Supports in-city and city-disjoint evaluation of detection, recognition, and end-to-end spotting across different visual backgrounds.
Combines YOLO26 localization, crop rectification, and LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B recognition.
The framework outperforms direct LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B spotting, while reader adaptation improves recognition over the pretrained zero-shot reader.

papers.abstract: Previous research shows that vision-language (VL) models struggle to understand fine-grained image details and tend to focus on the overall layout. Moreover, any weakness in English tends to be further amplified in the multilingual setting. To study that, we extend InpaintCOCO, an English dataset focused on fine-grained visual details, to 13 typologically diverse languages across five language families, creating MultiInpaintCOCO - a new multilingual benchmark of 953 minimal-pair examples. We further test several state-of-the-art models in multilingual multimodal retrieval, considering both light VL CLIP-like encoders and large language models. Our results show that performance degrades substantially for lower-resource languages, with the strongest predictor being the data resources available for the languages rather than typological similarity to English. In cross-lingual retrieval, most models exhibit a systematic bias toward English: when given a correct caption in a non-English language and an incorrect one in English, models preferentially select the English caption. This bias varies considerably across architectures. Among the tested models, Gemma 3 shows the strongest English preference while Qwen 3 is the least biased, despite both reaching similar monolingual accuracy across languages. The code is available at https://github.com/ufal/multi-inpaint-coco.
bullets: Extends InpaintCOCO to 13 typologically diverse languages across five language families.
Introduces 953 minimal-pair examples for multilingual fine-grained visual understanding.
Evaluates CLIP-like vision-language encoders and large language models on multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval.
Lower-resource language performance is driven more by available language data than by typological similarity to English.
Models often prefer incorrect English captions over correct non-English captions; English bias varies by architecture, with Gemma 3 strongest and Qwen 3 weakest among tested models.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation goals are easier to visualize than to specify numerically through explicit geometric constraints. We present VerifLM, a framework that converts image-edited goal configurations into physically verified 6-DoF object poses for planning. Using an edited image, VerifLM recovers an initial relative pose between an active object and a passive object, then prompts a vision-language model to generate axis-wise sampling constraints and a task-specific validation program. Candidate poses are evaluated in a physics simulator, and the VLM selects the most task-consistent retained candidate. To operate without predefined object meshes or physical parameters, VerifLM reconstructs metric object geometry from RGB-D observations and constructs multiple hypothetical simulations with varying physics and geometry. Parallel-world validation evaluates candidates across geometry--physics variations and ranks them by the number of worlds in which they satisfy the validation program. We evaluate VerifLM on nine manipulation tasks. VerifLM achieves the highest task success on eight of nine tasks, with the largest performance gain on goals requiring precise orientation and contact relationships.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of specifying manipulation goals with explicit geometric constraints.
Uses a vision-language model to generate axis-wise pose constraints and task-specific validation programs from edited images.
Reconstructs metric object geometry from RGB-D data and tests candidate poses across simulations with varied geometry and physics.
Ranks candidates by how consistently they satisfy the validation program across parallel simulated worlds.
Evaluated on nine tasks, achieving the highest task success on eight, with the largest gains for precise orientation and contact goals.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) typically process large numbers of multimodal tokens from audio-visual inputs, incurring substantial computational costs and a large memory footprint for the key-value (KV) cache. Aggressive token pruning can alleviate this problem while maintaining competitive performance on multiple-choice tasks, which require only a single option as output. However, we observe substantial quality degradation when generating long-form, open-ended responses. We attribute this gap to query-guided selection, which can retain sufficient evidence for answer selection while discarding details needed for comprehensive generation. This motivates reducing overlapping information across tokens, termed structural redundancy, while preserving diverse content. However, the retained representations may still contain precision redundancy due to unnecessarily high numerical precision in their cached values. To address these two levels of redundancy in token representations, we introduce a training-free framework named R$^2$-Omni. First, Structure-Aware Token Consolidation (STC) consolidates redundant representations using spatiotemporal similarity in video and local continuity in audio. Then, Semantic-Sensitivity Guided Precision Allocation (SSPA) allocates value precision to the retained representations according to the estimated reduction in attention-output error under quantized keys, with query attention and audio-visual alignment providing a semantic prior. Extensive experiments on long-form generation benchmarks demonstrate an average 5.0$\times$ reduction in the memory footprint while preserving 97.98% of baseline generation quality and achieving a 1.48$\times$ end-to-end speedup, highlighting the benefits of jointly reducing structural and precision redundancy.
bullets: Targets quality degradation from aggressive token pruning in long-form, open-ended generation.
Uses Structure-Aware Token Consolidation to merge structurally redundant video and audio representations.
Uses Semantic-Sensitivity Guided Precision Allocation to assign lower or higher value precision based on estimated attention-output sensitivity.
Achieves a 5.0× average memory-footprint reduction, 97.98% of baseline generation quality, and a 1.48× end-to-end speedup.
The framework is training-free and evaluated on long-form generation benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multimodal test-time adaptation (TTA) enables pretrained multimodal models to accommodate distribution shifts during inference using only unlabeled test data, without recourse to the original training data. Compared with unimodal adaptation, multimodal adaptation is further complicated by the coexistence and interaction of multiple representation perspectives. This complexity is particularly pronounced under modality reliability shifts, which preserve modality availability but degrade information quality, and modality availability shifts, which render the corresponding modality entirely inaccessible. Category-conditional Gaussian modeling offers a natural starting point for handling such distributional variations, having proven effective in unimodal test-time adaptation for characterizing representation distributions, yet its extension to multimodal settings requires a more elaborate formulation. To this end, we propose Adaptive Probabilistic Gaussian Calibration (AdaPGC), which extends category-conditional Gaussian modeling across modality-specific and multimodal fusion representations for probabilistic calibration under multimodal distribution shifts. AdaPGC continuously updates category-conditional Gaussian models over modality-specific and fusion representations, using the resulting probabilistic predictions to calibrate source model predictions and guide reliability based rectification, while exploiting their joint distributions to recover unavailable fusion representations. Extensive experiments under diverse modality corruption and missingness conditions demonstrate that AdaPGC effectively improves robustness under both modality reliability and availability shifts. Our source code will be released at https://github.com/XuJinglinn/AdaPGC-plus.
bullets: Addresses multimodal distribution shifts caused by reduced modality reliability or complete modality unavailability.
Extends category-conditional Gaussian modeling to modality-specific and multimodal fusion representations.
Continuously updates Gaussian models during inference using unlabeled test data.
Uses probabilistic calibration for prediction correction and joint distributions to recover unavailable fusion representations.
Experiments across diverse corruption and missingness conditions show improved robustness to both shift types.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed multimodal test-time adaptation framework. The input consists of paired video and audio streams affected by reliability shifts (modality corruption) or availability shifts (missing video/audio). For complete instances, the pretrained source model feeds the fused representation zF into the shared classifier to obtain source logits s; for incomplete instances, it instead uses the representation of the available modality, zV or zA. The category-conditional Gaussian means and priors are initialized from the pretrained classifier, while the covariance and cross-covariance matrices are initialized as identity matrices. During adaptation, these parameters are updated using target-stream statistics to define the discriminants gV , gA, and gF and conditional estimators EV →F and EA→F . For incomplete instances, the available modality representation is used to estimate category-conditional fused representations, whose Gaussian predictions are combined with the unimodal predictions to obtain calibration logits r. For complete instances, the fused Gaussian discriminant produces the calibration logits r = gF (zF ), while discrepancies between unimodal and fused Gaussian predictions guide reliability-aware one-sided alignment.

papers.abstract: An image that is hard to classify on its own may have a helpful neighbor in the same unlabeled batch. Zero-shot vision-language models (VLMs) score images independently and leave this evidence unused. We study small unlabeled query batches with no labeled examples. Visual similarity can reflect pose or background, so it may connect images from different classes. Each image's scores over the class vocabulary offer another way to choose neighbors. We introduce Behavioral Affinity Transduction (BAT), which builds a sparse graph from these class-response profiles. The graph supplies neighbor evidence during prediction. For EM-Dirichlet, it also screens candidate classes and initializes assignments. BAT plugs into direct and iterative readouts of a frozen VLM. Across diverse datasets, BAT improves the mean accuracy of every tested readout. In the main RN50 comparison, soft and hard EM-Dirichlet gain $4.22$ and $2.72$ percentage points.
bullets: Addresses the limitation that frozen VLMs classify images independently and ignore batch-level evidence.
Builds a sparse graph from each image’s class-response profile rather than relying only on visual similarity.
Uses graph-based neighbor information with direct and iterative readouts of a frozen VLM.
For EM-Dirichlet, BAT screens candidate classes and initializes assignments.
Improves mean accuracy across all tested readouts; in the main RN50 comparison, gains are 4.22 and 2.72 percentage points for soft and hard EM-Dirichlet.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential in robotic surgery for question answering, scene understanding, and grounded assistance, but their high computational cost limits real clinical deployment. Knowledge distillation provides a practical way to build compact surgical MLLMs, yet direct distillation is not well suited to surgical data because surgical samples vary greatly in difficulty, visual ambiguity, and required clinical context, making uniform teacher-student transfer unstable. In addition, the role of supervision changes during training: early stages require stronger teacher guidance for multimodal alignment, while later stages rely more on task supervision for effective optimization. To address these challenges, we propose SurgPace, a complexity-aware continuous curriculum framework for progressive distillation of surgical vision-language models. SurgPace estimates sample complexity using predictive confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency, and uses the fused score to guide a continuous easy-to-hard training process. We further introduce hierarchical representation alignment, which aligns the student with the teacher at the feature, logit, and probability levels, while gradually shifting the training focus from teacher imitation to task supervision. This design separates sample-level curriculum from objective-level scheduling, leading to more stable and effective distillation. We evaluate SurgPace on Surg-396K, a benchmark built from four public surgical datasets and covering five dialogue paradigms. SurgPace consistently outperforms strong MLLM distillation baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness for building compact, memory-efficient surgical MLLMs with faster decoding under controlled benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/hezhicheng2002/SurgPace.
bullets: Addresses unstable uniform distillation caused by varying surgical sample difficulty, ambiguity, and clinical context.
Uses predictive confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency to create a continuous easy-to-hard curriculum.
Aligns teacher and student at feature, logit, and probability levels while shifting from teacher imitation to task supervision.
Evaluated on Surg-396K across five dialogue paradigms, where it consistently outperforms strong distillation baselines.
Produces memory-efficient models with faster decoding under controlled benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed complexity-aware curriculum framework for progressive distillation. Teacher confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency are fused into a permissive complexity score, which guides continuous curriculum pacing from easy-first sampling to balanced training. This pacing is coupled with progressive objective interpolation and hierarchical representation alignment, jointly establishing a more structured optimization process that enables stable and efficient compression of surgical vision-language models.

Figure 1: Overview of the proposed SurgPace framework. Given surgical multimodal data, a teacher model first estimates sample complexity offline using complementary confidence and geometric consistency signals, which are permissively fused so that lower scores indicate easier samples. The resulting complexity estimates are then used to guide online curriculum training, where easier samples are emphasized earlier and harder samples are gradually incorporated as training progresses. During this process, the student model learns from the teacher through hierarchical representation alignment at the probability, logit, and feature levels, while a progressive objective schedule adjusts the balance of supervision over time. Together, these components enable stable and efficient compression of surgical MLLMs into a lightweight student model with reduced computational demands.

papers.abstract: Complex documents such as scientific papers contain rich information in tables, figures, and equations; however, existing deep research (DR) agents typically reduce papers to OCR-extracted text. We instead ask whether vision-language models (VLMs) can enable page-native deep research: directly retrieving and reasoning over rendered document page images. We introduce DR Pixel, the first open-source end-to-end multimodal DR agent that uses rendered page images as its sole retrieval and reasoning unit, operating over a corpus of 1.06M pages. To evaluate this setting, we construct DRPixelBench, a benchmark on scientific papers requiring reasoning over text, figures, tables, and equations. Surprisingly, page-native DR already works well without training, outperforming OCR-based baselines across state-of-the-art models like GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Qwen3.6-27B, while requiring fewer tool calls. We next turn to DR training. A key challenge is that teacher trajectories for agentic supervised finetuning are noisy, mixing critical reasoning and action steps with redundant or failed attempts. To address this, we introduce counterfactual credit reweighting, a fine-grained credit assignment method that weights individual reasoning and action steps by their counterfactual contribution to the final answer. Our training improves retrieval recall by about 15 points and final accuracy by over 10 points on DRPixelBench, and likewise outperforms the untrained baseline on four existing benchmarks. On out-of-distribution ViDoRe-V3, DR Pixel comes within 1.8 points of an oracle that is given the gold pages directly. Our results suggest that the conventional OCR-then-retrieve pipeline is not only unnecessary but suboptimal: directly retrieving and reasoning over visual document pages makes complex DR both more effective and more efficient.
bullets: Targets the loss of information from OCR-only processing of figures, tables, equations, and layout.
Introduces an open-source multimodal agent that uses rendered page images as its sole retrieval and reasoning unit over 1.06M pages.
Introduces DRPixelBench, a scientific-paper benchmark requiring multimodal document reasoning.
Counterfactual credit reweighting improves retrieval recall by about 15 points and final accuracy by over 10 points.
On out-of-distribution ViDoRe-V3, the system comes within 1.8 points of an oracle with gold pages; scope is centered on complex scientific documents.

papers.abstract: While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has significantly advanced multimodal reasoning, existing frameworks suffer from a critical "perception-reasoning gap." Due to an over-reliance on seemingly relevant visual tokens, even minor perceptual perturbations can propagate through the reasoning process, leading to compounding hallucinations. To address this issue, we propose MIRA, a training framework that improves robustness to erroneous visual contexts while enhancing logical reasoning ability. By injecting filtered, deceptive visual contexts during training, we construct challenging "hard traps" that stress-test the model's robustness to misleading information. Furthermore, we introduce a group-wise reflection-triggering mechanism that enables the model to autonomously detect and rectify inconsistencies between visual cues and logical constraints, which is ultimately internalized as an intrinsic policy behavior. Importantly, MIRA does not rely on human annotations. Experimental results across multiple reasoning and perception benchmarks show that MIRA yields an average 7% improvement on in-domain benchmarks, with consistent improvements on vision-centric benchmarks. These findings highlight that active error recovery is essential for robust multimodal reasoning. Comprehensive ablation studies and analyses further provide insights into why MIRA is effective.
bullets: Addresses the perception–reasoning gap, where small visual errors can trigger compounding hallucinations.
Injects filtered deceptive visual contexts to create challenging “hard traps” during training.
Uses group-wise reflection triggers to help models identify and correct conflicts between visual evidence and logical constraints.
Reports an average 7% improvement across in-domain benchmarks, with consistent gains on vision-centric benchmarks.
Ablations and analyses support the importance of active error recovery for robust multimodal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Complex video editing requires understanding complex instructions while jointly fulfilling multiple editing requests. Meeting these demands through dense model scaling substantially increases computational cost. We introduce VideoEditor-MoE, the first open-source mixture-of-experts framework for video editing. Beyond sparse MLP-MoE layers, MoE-Attention expands attention capacity through routed key--value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens. Initialized from a 5B video editing model, VideoEditor-MoE scales to 14B and 56B parameters, with approximately 8B parameters activated per token in both variants. Comparisons with existing methods and two complementary baselines, Explicit-MoE and MLP-MoE, assess its benefits over explicit expert guidance and MLP-only expert architectures. Further analyses demonstrate that all experts remain active and reveal that learned routing responds more strongly to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories. Spatial analysis further indicates sensitivity to object-level semantic features. We also identify decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of dense scaling for complex, multi-request video editing.
Introduces MoE-Attention, which routes key–value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens.
Scales from a 5B initialization to 14B and 56B parameters, activating approximately 8B parameters per token in both variants.
Analysis finds routing responds more to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories, with sensitivity to object-level semantics.
Identifies decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling; evaluations compare against existing methods and complementary MoE baselines.

papers.abstract: Cloth-changing person re-identification (CC-ReID) is still very challenging, and no method clearly dominates: methods that lead on one benchmark collapse on the others, because they rest on different identity cues. We show that a general-purpose vision-language model (VLM), used zero-shot as a judge for reranking a short candidate list, beats the expert retrieval models it reranks by a wide and consistent margin. On the four scenarios of CHIRLA, a long-term CC-ReID benchmark that no publicly released Re-ID model is trained on, reranking the candidates of two frozen experts raises rank-1 on every scenario, by 12.9 points on average over the best expert and 9.4 over the best naive ensemble of the two, with no component fine-tuned on the target data. Merging both experts' shortlists matches or beats reranking the stronger expert's shortlist alone, at lower cost. Introducing a VLM does, however, come at a cost: almost all of the pipeline's FLOPs are spent on it. We therefore borrow a criterion from ensembling and invoke the VLM judge only where the two experts disagree at rank 1. This threshold-free gate removes 40% of the calls, and a comparable share of total compute, with no significant drop in rank-1, trading 1.8 to 3.8 points of mAP. Judging remains the dominant cost, but on a benchmark where dedicated experts stall, we find a frozen general-purpose model to be the strongest judge of identity. The code is available at https://github.com/bdager/JudgeReID.
bullets: CC-ReID remains difficult because existing methods rely on different identity cues and do not generalize consistently across benchmarks.
The method uses a VLM as a zero-shot judge to rerank short candidate lists from two frozen expert retrieval models.
On all four CHIRLA scenarios, reranking improves rank-1 by an average of 12.9 points over the best expert and 9.4 over their naive ensemble, without target-data fine-tuning.
Merging both experts’ shortlists matches or exceeds reranking the stronger expert alone at lower cost.
Calling the VLM only when experts disagree at rank 1 removes 40% of calls with no significant rank-1 loss, though mAP drops by 1.8–3.8 points; VLM judging remains the main computational cost.

papers.abstract: Misleading charts can lead vision-language models to conclusions that conflict with underlying data. Existing work focuses on inference-time strategies, while training-time supervision remains less explored. We present VizDAGuide, a DAG-structured supervision method for misleading-chart question answering. The method represents intermediate reasoning states and their dependencies as a directed acyclic graph, assigns supervision weights according to their roles, and serializes the graph into a unified training target for open-ended and multiple-choice QA with single-pass inference. Experiments on two benchmarks across Qwen3-VL and InternVL3.5 models show improvements over a content- and weight-matched Linear CoT-SFT baseline on both answer formats. Process-level evaluation shows gains in grounding and operation execution, while ablations indicate that dependency structure and weighted supervision are most effective when combined. These results support DAG-structured weighted supervision for misleading-chart question answering.
bullets: Targets chart questions where visual presentation can conflict with the underlying data.
Represents intermediate reasoning states and dependencies as a directed acyclic graph.
Serializes weighted graph supervision into one training target for open-ended and multiple-choice QA with single-pass inference.
Improves answer performance over a matched Linear CoT-SFT baseline across two benchmarks and Qwen3-VL and InternVL3.5 models.
Process-level gains occur in grounding and operation execution; dependency structure and weighting work best together.

papers.abstract: Two machines can each recognize an object well and still fail together. We study classifiers that see different parts of one object and send short messages to a receiver that identifies its class. Coordination asks how to design messages together; cooperation asks whether the team outperforms one sender given the whole budget. On three digit datasets, messages designed together beat messages designed apart by 18.07 to 22.68 percentage points on average with two-bit messages, with gains in all 24 configurations. A fixed agreement, you report the row and I the column, recovers about half this gain, with only the receiver learned. Senders that draw the same distinctions waste a narrow vocabulary, and senders whose distinctions cross multiply it. A team has no more possible messages than one sender with the same budget, so a partner must bring evidence the first lacks. A solvable model shows individual statistics alone cannot determine whether a partnership helps. On MNIST digits, six shared bits remove 49.54 percent of the strongest tested solo's errors on average. Paired measurements correctly predicted most sensor teams would reduce average accuracy on new participants. Who should speak is a property of the pair, and must be measured in pairs.
bullets: The study examines classifiers that observe different parts of an object and send short messages to a receiver.
Jointly designed messages outperform separately designed ones by 18.07–22.68 percentage points across 24 two-bit configurations on three digit datasets.
A fixed row/column communication scheme recovers about half the coordination gain while learning only the receiver.
Senders should make complementary distinctions: overlapping distinctions waste limited message capacity, while cross-cutting distinctions expand useful information.
Pairwise measurements predicted that most tested sensor teams would improve average accuracy on new participants.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates coordination between classifiers that process different parts of an object, addressing multimodal communication and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: The Tower of Babel in artificial intelligence: who should speak, and when it pays to listen
papers.tldr: Effective AI teams depend on complementary, jointly designed communication between partial observers—not merely on strong individual classifiers.

papers.abstract: With the popularization of livestreaming applications, automatic camera tuning has become indispensable for ordinary users to enjoy high Quality of Experience (QoE). However, the existing Image Quality Assessment (IQA) methods face two challenges in camera tuning. First, they struggle to identify subtle quality difference between images, which is common in camera tuning. Second, the ability to explain fine-grained differences and to provide suggestions for camera tuning are even more lacking. To address these challenges, we first construct FGLive-Comments, an instruction tuning dataset with rich annotations of both preferences for fine-grained image pairs and quality reasoning from global and local visual evidence, which supports selective adjustment recommendations of camera parameters. Based on FGLive-Comments, we develop Q-CamTuning, a multimodal large language model for livestreaming camera tuning. Its progressive perception-evidence-guidance framework learns quality-aware visual representations, enhances fine-grained reasoning with global-local evidence, and maps quality issues to camera-parameter adjustment directions. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Q-CamTuning outperforms existing IQA models in both quality scoring and fine-grained image pair ranking. User study also validates its ability to recommend camera tuning suggestions.
bullets: Addresses IQA limitations in distinguishing fine-grained quality differences and generating actionable tuning guidance.
Introduces FGLive-Comments, an instruction-tuning dataset with pairwise preferences, global-local quality reasoning, and adjustment recommendations.
Uses a progressive perception-evidence-guidance framework to connect visual quality issues with camera-parameter directions.
Outperforms existing IQA models in quality scoring and fine-grained image-pair ranking.
A user study supports its ability to provide useful camera-tuning suggestions.

papers.abstract: Real-time omnimodal assistants are expected to support people in everyday life, but audiovisual understanding alone does not establish whether they can provide timely and appropriate help. We introduce Omni-Life, a benchmark grounded in real-world user needs, deployment scenarios, and device-dependent observations. It combines controlled video synthesis for hazardous situations and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol. The benchmark contains 400 videos: 290 requiring assistance, with 555 required intervention events, and 110 requiring silence throughout to test whether models can withhold unnecessary responses when no assistance is needed. We evaluate twelve configurations featuring mainstream real-time omnimodal models, jointly assessing event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output. At most 4.48% of videos requiring assistance are handled completely correctly. To examine practical deployment strategies, we study task reminders and response-latency tolerance. Reminders can improve recall by 17.12 percentage points but add approximately 4.6 unwanted responses per minute of reference silence. Increasing latency tolerance by 10s improves recall by at most 5.95 percentage points. These results show that existing models remain insufficient to deliver reliable assistance in real-life applications, calling for tailored model optimization in instruction following, timely proactive intervention, and withholding responses when assistance is not needed.
bullets: Evaluates assistance quality across event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output.
Combines controlled videos of hazards and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol.
Includes 400 videos: 290 requiring assistance and 110 requiring silence, covering 555 intervention events.
Across 12 model configurations, at most 4.48% of assistance-needed videos are handled completely correctly.

papers.abstract: Interleaved multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning improves the visual reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models by dynamically incorporating visual evidence during reasoning. However, existing methods primarily select evidence from historical context. When the reasoning focus shifts, history-guided evidence may remain focused on prior regions and fail to cover the visual information required by the next step. We refer to this lag between visual evidence and subsequent reasoning demands as Temporal Evidence Myopia. To address this issue, we propose Lookahead Prediction-guided Adaptive Visual Refocusing (LPAVR), a training-free test-time framework. LPAVR transforms Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) from a decoding acceleration mechanism into a lookahead signal for anticipating upcoming reasoning intent. During MTP decoding, the draft head generates multiple future tokens, while the target model verifies them in parallel and retains the longest prefix consistent with its decoding trajectory. This target-verified prefix contains near-future semantics, which LPAVR uses to construct lookahead-guided visual evidence and assess whether history-guided evidence covers the indicated regions. If the coverage is sufficient, the history-guided evidence is retained; otherwise, LPAVR switches to the lookahead-guided evidence. This better aligns the visual context with upcoming reasoning and improves consistency between draft predictions and target-model decoding. Experiments on multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that LPAVR improves both reasoning accuracy and the acceptance rates of MTP speculative tokens, jointly enhancing visual reasoning and speculative decoding efficiency.
bullets: Addresses Temporal Evidence Myopia, where history-based visual evidence lags behind shifts in reasoning focus.
Uses Multi-Token Prediction as a lookahead signal rather than only for decoding acceleration.
Retains historical visual evidence when coverage is sufficient and switches to lookahead-guided evidence otherwise.
A training-free, test-time framework evaluated across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
Reports improved reasoning accuracy and higher acceptance rates of speculative tokens.‌
