papers.abstract: Understanding how objects and their spatial relationships evolve in 3D space over time remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), particularly under changing viewpoints. Recent approaches incorporate geometric information into reasoning, but explicit supervision for temporally ordered 4D state evolution and its use as intermediate evidence remains limited. We introduce \textbf{Trace4D}, which trains VLMs to predict 4D state sequences and reason over their inter-timestep changes alongside temporal visual observations. Its 4D-grounded chain-of-thought (CoT) explicitly represents 4D states, analyzes temporal visual context, and connects both as evidence for the answer. We construct Trace4D-Train from in-the-wild videos with 600K 4D perception examples and approximately 70K grounded QA examples, and train with joint supervised fine-tuning followed by geometry-aware GRPO. At inference, Trace4D predicts 4D states and reasoning directly from video without reference annotations or an external geometric model. Experiments on Trace4D-Bench and VLM4D show improved QA accuracy over the base VLMs and benefits from reasoning over 4D state changes and temporal visual observations.
bullets: Targets VLM difficulty in tracking object states and spatial relationships over time under changing viewpoints.
Predicts temporally ordered 4D states, analyzes their changes, and combines them with temporal visual observations in grounded chain-of-thought reasoning.
Trains on in-the-wild videos with 4D perception and grounded QA supervision, followed by geometry-aware GRPO.
Performs inference directly from video without reference annotations or an external geometric model.
Shows improved QA accuracy on Trace4D-Bench and VLM4D over the base VLMs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents that act in the open world need two abilities: world knowledge to interpret what they see, and exploration to find what they cannot yet see. We study how agents combine the two through interactive visual geolocation. GeoGuesser Bench contains 282 tasks in an offline Street View environment where agents rotate, zoom, and move between real panoramas. Its three task types shift the balance from knowledge to exploration: agents (1) report the coordinates of their starting location, (2) name the enclosing street, city, state, or country, or (3) find, read, and count nearby objects. The coordinate tasks in (1) also include 42 real GeoGuessr World Championship rounds, whose expert guesses provide a human reference. We evaluate 23 VLMs: the best accuracy is 62.5% on place naming and 35.0% on object finding, and the best agent averages 4352.4 GeoGuessr points on the championship rounds, against 4770.3 for the better expert in each round. Beyond these headline numbers, world knowledge and exploration are only weakly correlated across models: agents that localize well do not necessarily explore well. To understand where agents fail, we categorize their errors into vision, navigation, and tool-use failures. Further ablations show that the strongest agents, such as Claude Opus 4.8, still perform well with limited views, while weaker agents degrade; customizing the environment thus adjusts task difficulty. The environment's verifiable rewards and restorable state also support training, and our Planner-Worker-Compressor harness cuts planner tokens by 57-61% by compacting the interaction history. We hope GeoGuesser Bench and its environment serve as a high-quality foundation for simulating real-world exploration at scale.
bullets: Introduces 282 offline Street View tasks involving panorama rotation, zooming, and movement, plus 42 expert-referenced GeoGuessr championship rounds.
Tests three task types: coordinate localization, place naming, and finding, reading, or counting nearby objects.
Evaluates 23 VLMs; best reported accuracy is 62.5% for place naming and 35.0% for object finding, while the strongest agent approaches expert GeoGuessr performance.

Shows that environment difficulty can be adjusted through view limits and that a Planner-Worker-Compressor harness reduces planner tokens by 57–61%.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate visual assets through text-based formats such as SVG and CAD, but these symbolic representations describe images using high-level primitives rather than explicit raster values. We ask whether LLMs can instead generate pixel images directly through their existing vocabulary, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. We introduce PixelBench, a benchmark for text-to-pixel (T2P) and image-to-pixel (I2P) generation across multiple resolutions, together with a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation. Models generate an RGB color palette followed by a grid of indices specifying the palette color of each output pixel. In T2P, the strongest models produce recognizable images directly from text. In I2P, the strongest models outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization algorithms at low resolutions. Pixel-understanding performance correlates strongly with generation performance. A resolution-scaling study shows that pixel-generation performance often improves initially before declining at high resolutions. Finally, we introduce Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments visual instruction tuning with caption-palette-grid trajectories. We post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint by mixing general instruction data with our curated PRT data, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks, indicating that explicit pixel reconstruction can provide useful auxiliary supervision.
bullets: Benchmarks text-to-pixel, image-to-pixel, and pixel-understanding across multiple resolutions without image tokenizers or decoders.
Models generate an RGB palette followed by grid indices assigning a palette color to each pixel.
Leading models produce recognizable text-generated images and outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization methods for low-resolution image-to-pixel tasks.
Pixel understanding correlates strongly with generation quality, while performance typically improves at first and then declines as resolution increases.
Pixel Reconstruction Tuning improves Molmo2-4B across 16 visual-centric benchmarks by adding caption–palette–grid trajectories to instruction tuning.

papers.abstract: Clinical evidence is inherently relational: medical images are interpreted with prior studies, cross-modal examinations, reports, and localized findings, and retrieving relevant evidence is therefore central to clinical interpretation. Recent foundation models increasingly encode these heterogeneous sources into shared embedding spaces, yet existing embedding evaluation often focuses on isolated matches, leaving unclear whether current models retrieve relevant evidence across changes in modality, appearance, and granularity. We introduce MedHEB, a unified benchmark with 107 retrieval tasks from 54 datasets, including both in-distribution and held-out-source evaluation, across three axes: evidence form (2D images, 3D volumes, text), pairing type (image--image, image--text, text--text, and modality-bridging visual matching), and relevance granularity (global, question-conditioned, region-level). Under a single ranking protocol, MedHEB varies clinically relevant evidence definitions to test whether embedding proximity remains meaningful across heterogeneous evidence, including modality-bridging visual retrieval and region-level text-to-region retrieval. Across representative models, performance is uneven across retrieval families: models strong on conventional image--text or text--text retrieval are less reliable on modality-bridging and region-level tasks. Current embedding spaces capture some clinical relationships well but do not yet provide balanced retrieval across heterogeneous evidence. We further provide MedEmb, an MLLM-based reference embedding model trained on the MedHEB ID split, as a reproducible baseline for unified 2D--3D--text medical retrieval. We release MedHEB with preprocessing scripts, evaluation code, access manifests, and MedEmb to support research on clinically meaningful medical embeddings.

papers.abstract: A GUI command can be correct at the interface level yet still produce an incorrect assembly. An agent must identify the relevant components, respect their structural relationships, and determine which parts should move during recovery. We introduce MAGAR-Bench, a benchmark of 4,000 multimodal samples from 26 assembly families that separates Assembly Decision, Atomic Action, and Minimal Rework. For rework, the objective counts distinct moved parts within the validated recovery candidate set for each state, rather than the number of actions. We also introduce MAGAR, a selective correction framework built on a frozen policy obtained by supervised fine-tuning. Its key design matches correction granularity to output dependencies. Structured candidates revise assembly fields and rework scope, while complete action candidates keep native GUI primitives coupled with their parameters. A learned selector retains the original prediction unless a candidate passes a task-specific intervention threshold. On recorded states from held-out assembly families, MAGAR improves Overall, the task-balanced aggregate, from 37.50 to 41.39, with gains on all three tasks. Across 209 interventions, 70 correct an error and 22 introduce one. These results support task-specific correction while highlighting the remaining tradeoff between fixing errors and preserving reliable predictions.
bullets: MAGAR-Bench contains 4,000 multimodal samples across 26 assembly families and evaluates Assembly Decision, Atomic Action, and Minimal Rework separately.
Minimal Rework measures the distinct parts moved within a validated recovery candidate set, rather than counting actions.
MAGAR uses a frozen supervised-fine-tuned policy, task-specific candidate structures, and a learned selector with intervention thresholds.
On held-out assembly families, Overall task-balanced performance rises from 37.50 to 41.39, with gains on all three tasks.
Among 209 interventions, 70 fix errors and 22 introduce errors, showing a remaining tradeoff between correction and prediction preservation.

papers.abstract: Engineering drawings specify mechanical parts through orthographic projections. Recognizing which part a drawing depicts underlies part search, design reuse, and digitization, yet no public benchmark measures whether vision models can do it. We introduce Blueprint2CAD, a benchmark for drawing-to-render correspondence: given an orthographic line drawing and a shaded render, usually from another viewpoint, decide whether they show the same part. Its data layer, BlueCAD-30K, applies an open drafting pipeline to 29,925 Zero-to-CAD models, adding view-aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings from six viewpoints, and surface-type metadata. Frozen encoders retrieve the matching part from a 10,000-model gallery with up to 65% Recall@1 when viewpoints are known but 43% when they are not, and the four encoders we test lie within six points of each other: viewpoint, not backbone, is the bottleneck. Six zero-shot vision-language models reach only 0.52-0.67 verification accuracy, with model-specific Yes/No biases that chain-of-thought shifts but does not remove; a quick LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain pairs improves verification accuracy by a few points but sharpens these biases and leaves the viewpoint failure intact.
bullets: Introduces drawing-to-render correspondence: deciding whether an orthographic drawing and shaded render depict the same part.
Builds BlueCAD-30K from 29,925 CAD models with aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings across six viewpoints, and surface metadata.
Frozen encoders achieve up to 65% Recall@1 with known viewpoints, falling to 43% when viewpoints are unknown.
Zero-shot vision-language models reach 0.52–0.67 verification accuracy and exhibit model-specific Yes/No biases.
LoRA fine-tuning slightly improves accuracy but does not solve viewpoint failures and intensifies bias.

papers.abstract: Spatial audio conveys not only what sounds are present, but where they originate and how they interact with the environment. Recent audio-language models increasingly understand and reason about such scenes, yet spatial audio understanding, generation, and editing remain largely separate. We present Spatial Transfusion, a unified first-order ambisonics (FOA) framework that extends a pretrained spatial audio understanding model to generation and editing through flow matching over VAE latents. We formulate editing as a structured scene transformation over a taxonomy of atomic edits. Keeping the pretrained backbone frozen, we introduce modality-based LoRA routing and a curriculum that progressively adds generation, editing, and natural-language interaction. Experiments show that Spatial Transfusion largely preserves spatial understanding while outperforming full fine-tuning in generation and editing. The resulting model supports controllable FOA generation and editing through both structured and natural-language interfaces. Audio samples are available at https://microsoft.github.io/spatial-transfusion/
bullets: Addresses the separation between spatial audio scene understanding, generation, and editing.
Extends a pretrained spatial audio understanding model using flow matching over VAE latents.
Models editing as structured scene transformations with atomic edits and supports natural-language control.
Uses frozen-backbone modality-based LoRA routing and a curriculum spanning generation, editing, and interaction.
Experiments indicate preserved spatial understanding and stronger generation/editing than full fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Computed tomography (CT) provides diverse patient information and various clinical tasks, for which numerous deep learning models have been investigated. Recent years have seen the development of vision-language foundation models that can comprehensively extract clinical features, driven by representation learning that combines CT volumes with radiology reports. Existing approaches typically adopt Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)-based representation learning, where pairs from different cases are, in principle, treated as negative pairs such that the volume and report embeddings are pushed apart. In the biomedical imaging, however, treating different cases as negative pairs is not always appropriate, particularly when clinical similarity exists. In this study, we propose a supervised representation learning framework grounded in clinical knowledge from language foundation models, rather than the weak supervision used in CLIP. Specifically, we utilized a large language model to extract abnormal finding phrases from reports. We then explicitly constructed the target features that the image encoder should output, as the semantic representation of the extracted findings using a biomedical text embedding model. Our Findings-aware Language-Image Pre-training (FiLIP) outperformed weakly supervised approaches in multi-label zero-shot finding classification in both in-domain and external-domain evaluations, and also proved effective when fine-tuned for the downstream task of radiology report generation.
bullets: CLIP-style training can incorrectly separate clinically similar CT volumes and reports.
An LLM extracts abnormal finding phrases from radiology reports.
A biomedical text encoder converts findings into target semantic representations for supervised image training.
FiLIP outperformed weakly supervised methods in multi-label zero-shot finding classification across in-domain and external-domain evaluations.
It also supported downstream radiology report generation after fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in 3D scene understanding from multi-view RGB observations. Yet a fixed object and query can elicit inconsistent target-related responses across camera viewpoints, a phenomenon we characterize as viewpoint-induced semantic drift. We introduce LieVLM, a Lie routing framework for view-robust 3D understanding. Motivated by the rotational component of viewpoint change, Lie routing adapts visual representations by applying local $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ transformations to projected features within learned three-dimensional subspaces. Geometry tokens extracted by VGGT predict local rotation parameters and channel-wise routing coefficients. A closed-form Padé--Cayley map transforms projected visual features, whose identity-relative corrections are projected back and gated into the original visual and geometry features. This design retains the pretrained semantic and direct spatial context while learning view-dependent feature adjustments. Experiments on 3D captioning, grounding, detection, and spatial reasoning show consistent improvements over additive fusion across training scales and backbones. Controlled ablations examine the roles of geometric conditioning and transformation structure. Viewpoint analyses further reveal systematic variation in the predicted routing states alongside more localized target responses and stronger task performance across viewpoint changes.
bullets: Addresses inconsistent target-related responses from different camera viewpoints in MLLMs.
Uses geometry tokens to predict local SO(3) rotations and channel-wise routing coefficients in learned feature subspaces.
Applies a closed-form Padé–Cayley transformation and gates identity-relative corrections into visual and geometry features.
Improves 3D captioning, grounding, detection, and spatial reasoning across training scales and backbones compared with additive fusion.
View analyses show changing routing states, more localized target responses, and stronger performance across viewpoints.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation aims to predict depth maps from single RGB images (forgoing the need for stereo camera pairs) and has seen impressive leaps in performance in recent work due to the introduction of affine-invariant losses and the use of foundation model features. These monocular depth models predict affine-invariant depth, which describes the relative positions of objects in the scene instead of absolute depth. While these models demonstrate strong performance on single image benchmarks and qualitatively consistent predictions in video, their effectiveness at preserving consistent spatial structure has been less thoroughly explored. Many potential real-world applications, such as handling video streams as input, rely on coherent three dimensional consistency in scenes. Further, anchoring relative depth predictions to a metric reference for a given scene is a key challenge for applying monocular depth models to real-world situations. We develop a novel evaluation protocol for monocular depth models using video sequences with moving camera positions to test the consistency of prediction across variation in viewpoint. We demonstrate this methodology over diverse, real-world video sequences where we are able to anchor depth model output to metric depth values using structure from motion. Our work demonstrates open challenges in the development of broadly applicable monocular depth foundation models, particularly with their ability to provide temporal consistency over long time frames. We also identify challenges in the straightforward adoption of structure-from-motion as a metric grounding tool for monocular depth estimation models.
bullets: Motivation: Strong single-image benchmark performance does not guarantee coherent 3D structure over video or viewpoint changes.
Method: Evaluate predictions on real-world video sequences with moving cameras and use structure from motion to anchor affine-invariant depth to metric values.
Findings: The evaluation exposes challenges in achieving temporal consistency over long time periods.
Scope: It also reveals limitations in directly using structure from motion for metric grounding of monocular depth.
Contribution: A viewpoint-sequence benchmark methodology for assessing consistency and metric applicability of monocular depth models.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) suffer from visual hallucination, such as saying an object that is not present in an image. We ask a more fundamental question: whether a VLM is even aware of where it is looking before understanding the semantic meaning in the image. We formulate this question as a LOOK task: identifying which parts of its visual input were available to the model. We construct the task in a self-supervised way without manually labeling the available region to the model. Our experiments show that existing VLMs fail to localize the visible region. We further show that fine-tuning VLMs on the proposed LOOK task improves a model's awareness of visual input.
bullets: Targets visual hallucination and the more basic issue of visual-input awareness.
Defines LOOK as identifying the portions of an image available to the model before semantic interpretation.
Constructs the task without manually labeling visible regions.
Finds that existing VLMs struggle to localize their visible input.
Shows that fine-tuning on LOOK improves visual-input awareness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Where does a hallucination originate? In this example, we ask what animal is grazing in a photograph of a dog on grassland, a model answers “a sheep”. The same wrong answer can arise at two levels of the hierarchy. At the Perceive level, the model uses the image but misrecognizes the dog. At the Look level, the model does not rely on the image at all, and “sheep” follows from the textual context.

Figure 1: Hierarchy of visual understanding: LOOK → Perceive → Understand. We introduce a hierarchical visual grounding structure and argue that visual hallucination can arise from any level. This work focuses on the fundamental Look level.

Figure 4: Illustration of VisABench construction. All conditions use the same prompt, “Does this image contain: dog? Answer with Yes or No.”, with the only difference being the visual input. The grounded answer is Yes in (i) and No in (ii) and (iii).

Figure 5: Four ways to probe visual awareness. The green box shows the available visual region while the red dashed box shows the prediction. (i) We input the full image, but the model boxes the dominant person rather than the whole canvas. (ii, iii) When the context pixels are greyed out or its embeddings are zeroed, the model still locates the dominant person, likely using semantic shortcuts. (iv) In LOOK, the model answers with the whole canvas.

papers.title: Learning to Look: A Foundation for Visual Understanding
papers.tldr: The paper introduces LOOK, a self-supervised task for testing and improving whether vision-language models know which image regions they can actually see.

papers.abstract: The spatial intelligence of large vision-language models (LVLMs) requires the ability to combine local visual observations into a geometrically consistent representation of the physical world. Many static benchmarks assess isolated spatial judgments, such as relative direction or distance, while interactive embodied evaluations combine perception with exploration, planning, control, and simulator-specific execution. To bridge this gap, we introduce RECONSPATIAL, a benchmark centered on multi-view 3D scene reconstruction across indoor, tabletop, and outdoor environments. Given real multi-view images and target-object queries, LVLMs are required to jointly predict oriented 3D bounding boxes in a shared, camera-anchored metric coordinate frame. Reconstructions are evaluated along two complementary axes: Structure for relative layout and Metric for physical scale and camera-anchored placement. Nine atomic spatial QA tasks, grouped into Geometric Perception and Spatial Relations, probe spatial capabilities involved in joint reconstruction. Offline navigation extends evaluation to path planning. Evaluation of 18 frontier LVLMs reveals a consistent gap between relative scene structure and metric reconstruction; even GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4% on Structure but only 58.7% on Metric. Tracing this gap, diagnostic analyses link atomic spatial capabilities to reconstruction quality and show that relational consistency alone does not ensure metric accuracy. Experiments with 3D map injection further separate scene construction from path planning, revealing how these geometric errors limit navigation success. Finally, spatial fine-tuning yields broad transfer across both spatial and general vision-language benchmarks.
bullets: Benchmarks joint prediction of oriented 3D bounding boxes in a shared, camera-anchored metric coordinate frame across indoor, tabletop, and outdoor scenes.
Separates evaluation into Structure, measuring relative layout, and Metric, measuring physical scale and camera-anchored placement.
Includes nine atomic spatial QA tasks and offline navigation to connect reconstruction quality with spatial reasoning and path planning.
Evaluation of 18 frontier LVLMs finds a consistent Structure–Metric gap; even GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4% on Structure versus 58.7% on Metric.
Diagnostic studies show relational consistency does not guarantee metric accuracy, while spatial fine-tuning transfers across spatial and general vision-language benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective post-training paradigm for vision-language models (VLMs). Standard RLVR, however, assigns identical outcome-derived credit to all generated tokens regardless of their perceptual relevance. Recent perception-aware methods estimate visual reliance through image perturbation or masking. These indirect proxies require perturbation branches, while corruption sensitivity does not necessarily identify the visual evidence used for reasoning. We instead shape model perception through native attention, an intrinsic model signal. Rather than treating attention as a post-hoc explanation, we formulate it as a reward-anchored, token-aligned routing signal that encourages attention patterns supporting visually grounded reasoning. To this end, we propose NAS-PO, a Native Attention-Strategy Policy Optimization framework. NAS-PO analyzes native attention with a visual mass policy that quantifies visual allocation and a conditional visual policy that captures spatial routing over visual tokens, making the optimization well-posed. Based on this, Native Attention-Strategy Advantage Shaping (NAS-AS) draws on the visual-mass policy to redistribute signed policy-gradient credit for visually engaged rollouts. The Adaptive Attention-Coupled (AAC) loss then aligns the visual-mass policy on all response tokens and the conditional visual policy on visually active ones, consolidating the visual-routing patterns that drive successful trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that NAS-PO substantially surpasses leading RL-tuned VLMs across 7 out-of-domain reasoning and perception benchmarks, with its effectiveness consistently validated across 8B and 32B. Visual-Routing Sensitivity (VRS) analysis further indicates that the optimized attention prioritizes visually load-bearing regions.
bullets: Standard RLVR gives identical outcome-based credit to all generated tokens, ignoring their visual relevance.
NAS-PO models visual allocation with a visual-mass policy and spatial routing with a conditional visual policy.
NAS-AS redistributes signed policy-gradient credit for visually engaged rollouts, while AAC aligns attention patterns with successful trajectories.
It substantially outperforms leading RL-tuned VLMs across 7 out-of-domain benchmarks at both 8B and 32B scales.
VRS analysis suggests optimized attention focuses on visually load-bearing regions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of NAS-PO. Given an image–query pair (I,Q), the standard GRPO pipeline produces G clean rollouts and verifier-derived group-relative advantages Ai. Using the same clean rollouts, NAS-PO reads native attention ai,t(j) and losslessly decomposes its visual component into a visual-mass policy qi,t, which captures whether and how much a response token relies on the image, and a conditional visual policy ρi,t, which captures where attention is routed over visual tokens. The visual-mass policy also provides visually active indicators ci,t shared by NAS-AS and the conditional branch of AAC. At the trajectory level, NAS-AS summarizes visual reliance into a bounded factor αi and forms Ãi = αiAi. At the token level, AAC aligns q on all valid response tokens and ρ on visually active ones under the unshaped positive-advantage gate [Ai]+. The shaped policy-gradient objective and the adaptively weighted AAC loss jointly update the policy.

papers.abstract: Frequent urban floodwater poses a serious threat to the safety and efficiency of intelligent transportation systems. Existing vision-based methods for floodwater level detection face two main limitations. First, the lack of explicit reasoning leads to poor detection performance and little interpretability. Second, these methods struggle to generalize to the complex and varied real-world road scenes seen from different viewpoints. To address this, we reformulate the task as an explicit visual reasoning problem and propose HydroReasoner, a floodwater level reasoning framework designed for cloud-edge collaboration. HydroReasoner builds on Qwen2.5-VL and is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization. To address the scarcity of reasoning process annotations, we build a floodwater domain knowledge graph HydroKG and design a novel KG path reward. Through deterministic graph traversal over HydroKG, this reward supervises the model's reasoning process at a fine granularity, which improves both reasoning and generalization. For edge deployment, we apply 4-bit quantization to the model, cutting GPU memory usage by 57% and inference latency by 43% while out-of-domain accuracy drops by only 0.2 percentage points. We also propose a confidence-based cloud-edge routing mechanism, which improves system safety and eases the computational load on the cloud. In addition, we build HydroLevel, a floodwater benchmark dataset of 3,000 images, for training and evaluating the model. Experimental results show that HydroReasoner achieves detection accuracy 4.0 and 13.6 percentage points higher than conventional vision baselines in the in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations respectively, with performance dropping by only 4.4 percentage points out of domain.
bullets: Reframes floodwater-level detection as an explicit visual reasoning task to address weak interpretability and poor cross-scene generalization.
Uses Qwen2.5-VL with Group Relative Policy Optimization and a HydroKG-based path reward to supervise reasoning without requiring extensive reasoning annotations.
Introduces HydroLevel, a 3,000-image floodwater benchmark for training and evaluation.
Outperforms conventional vision baselines by 4.0 percentage points in-domain and 13.6 percentage points out-of-domain; out-of-domain performance drops 4.4 points.
4-bit quantization reduces GPU memory usage by 57% and latency by 43%, while confidence-based routing improves safety and reduces cloud computation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed collaborative edge-cloud traffic monitoring network. The system leverages 5G technology to aggregate multi-source floodwater imagery from Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), vehicles (dashcams), and Roadside Units (RSUs). These diverse data streams, captured from heterogeneous viewpoints, are transmitted to the cloud server or processed locally, where the proposed HydroReasoner framework performs efficient and interpretable floodwater level reasoning.

Fig. 2. The overall framework of HydroReasoner. The pipeline comprises three stages: (I) Reasoning Path Generation: the policy model performs explicit reasoning on the input floodwater image and outputs a structured reasoning path. (II) HydroKG Path Verification: the reasoning path is parsed into candidate triples and verified against HydroKG for structural completeness and consistency with domain grading rules. (III) Reward Shaping and GRPO Update: the verification result, together with format and accuracy signals, forms a composite reward that drives the policy update.

papers.abstract: Learning semantic representations for 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising direction for 3D scene understanding. However, existing 2D-to-3D semantic lifting approaches rely primarily on 2D segmentation supervision and lack object-level priors, causing the learned representation to be driven by local mask evidence rather than holistic object structure. In this paper, we present VLSplat, a vision-language guided approach for object-centric semantic lifting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our method augments mask-based lifting with object-level semantic priors derived from vision-language models and refines Gaussian representations using an object-group scene graph. The refinement is performed through two language-guided modules: intra-group refinement suppresses semantic noise within object groups, while inter-group acquisition expands object support regions by incorporating structurally relevant candidates from neighboring groups. Extensive experiments on indoor scene datasets demonstrate that VLSplat improves the semantic consistency and structural completeness of object-level categories. Our code and models are available at https://vlsplat.github.io/.
bullets: Targets semantic lifting methods that rely on local 2D mask evidence and lack holistic object-level structure.
Uses vision-language models to provide object-level semantic priors alongside mask-based lifting.
Builds an object-group scene graph with intra-group refinement to reduce semantic noise.
Uses inter-group acquisition to expand object support with structurally relevant neighboring candidates.
Experiments on indoor scene datasets show improved semantic consistency and structural completeness of object categories.

The scene graph further guides language-based intra-group refinement and inter-group acquisition, improving semantic consistency and structural completeness.

papers.abstract: Geometry is the very form that connects space, time, and matter, serving as the fundamental fabric of the physical world, from continuous fields to discrete structures. Despite its importance, deep learning is inherently blind to geometry. Riemannian geometry stands as a well-established mathematical foundation for studying geometry, yet it remains largely incompatible with deep learning architectures. To bridge this gap, we establish a new learning framework--Geometric Morphology Learning--that learns geometric or topological structures, shapes or conformations for representation learning, reasoning and action modeling. Moving beyond early attempts limited to specific geometric priors, this theory centers on modeling the intrinsic geometry of objects and learning from such geometric or topological knowledge. Specifically, we construct a neural bundle, a unified scaffolding linking local and global structures, and formulate differentiable operators, including connection and curvature, thereby enabling the study of geometry with advanced geometric concepts such as holonomy and cohomology. Consequently, Geometric Morphology Learning opens new horizons in foundation models, reasoning and planning, graph modeling, physical simulation, PDE systems, and dynamics, marking a fundamental shift toward instilling systematic geometry in artificial intelligence.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between geometry’s role in physical systems and deep learning’s limited geometric awareness.
Introduces a neural bundle to connect local and global structures in a unified scaffold.
Defines differentiable geometric operators, including connections and curvature, and supports concepts such as holonomy and cohomology.
Targets applications in foundation models, reasoning and planning, graph modeling, physical simulation, PDEs, and dynamical systems.
The abstract presents a broad theoretical framework but reports no specific experiments or quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about surgical video -- which phase is underway, which instruments act, and when events occur -- underpins operative documentation, workflow analysis, and skill assessment. Yet surgical visual question answering is still largely built on single frames and closed labels that cannot express a duration, an ordering, or a count, and the video models that lift the frame limit typically compress every clip the same way regardless of the question, discarding the temporal evidence the answer needs. Worse, the answers are structurally heterogeneous, spanning five incompatible structures -- binary, classification, multi-label, counting, and sentence-temporal -- that no single training signal scores uniformly well. We propose SurgQ-VLM, a two-stage model for surgical video question answering. Stage 1 trains a question-conditioned dual-stream (slow/fast) compressor for a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B: cross-attention conditions both streams on the question, and each clip's visual tokens shrink 49x from the raw ViT patches (11x vs. post-merge backbone tokens). Stage 2 post-trains with GRPO under an answer-type-aware reward that scores each question on the metric matching its answer structure (micro-F1 for label sets, normalised error for counts, a content-timing blend for temporal windows). On a sealed 21,840-question test split over Cholec80 and CholecT50, SurgQ-VLM reaches 0.779 keyword accuracy and a 10x BLEU-4 gain over zero-shot; GRPO adds 2.5 pp K-Acc (2.0 pp attributable to the answer-type-aware reward), concentrated in the structurally hard types, with answer format unchanged (ROUGE-L). Code is available at https://github.com/DhruvMakwana/SurgQ-VLM.
bullets: Targets limitations of frame-based and uniformly compressed video QA, especially for duration, ordering, and counting questions.
Uses a two-stage architecture: question-conditioned slow/fast visual compression followed by GRPO post-training.
Applies answer-type-specific rewards for binary, classification, multi-label, counting, and sentence-temporal answers.
On a sealed 21,840-question test split from Cholec80 and CholecT50, achieves 0.779 keyword accuracy and a 10× BLEU-4 gain over zero-shot.
GRPO improves keyword accuracy by 2.5 percentage points, with gains concentrated in structurally difficult answer types.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based text-to-image models have recently achieved remarkable success in image synthesis. However, when directly applied beyond their training resolution, these models often suffer from severe semantic degradation, where meaningful semantic content disappears. Although existing training-free high-resolution generation methods can mitigate this issue, the inherent semantic degradation at high resolutions remains largely unresolved, leading to degraded fine-grained details. Furthermore, widely used structural guidance methods lack modeling of the structure and details in the intermediate trajectory, which degrades the quality of the generated results. In this paper, we propose a training-free framework for high-resolution image generation to address these challenges. First, we propose a text-visual scale-decoupled attention (TVSDA) module, which restores the model's ability to generate semantically meaningful content at high resolutions by preserving the global receptive field of text tokens while aligning the receptive field of image tokens with the training resolution. Second, we propose a structure-detail guidance (SDG) strategy that explicitly models structural information and fine details through scale-wise and temporal-wise guidance, overcoming the limitations of conventional low-resolution guidance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves both structural coherence and detail fidelity over existing training-free DiT-based high-resolution generation approaches. The code is available at https://github.com/ljjcoder/Restoring-Semantic-Fidelity.
bullets: High-resolution generation beyond the training resolution can cause severe semantic degradation and loss of fine-grained details.
TVSDA preserves the global receptive field of text tokens while matching image-token receptive fields to the training resolution.
SDG models structure and detail explicitly through scale-wise and temporal-wise guidance.
Experiments show improved structural coherence and detail fidelity over existing training-free DiT-based methods.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance in translating WebUI screenshots into HTML/CSS. However, when they faced multiple frameworks (React/Vue/Angular), they often suffer from negative transfer that leads to compilation failures. These failures commonly stem from mixing framework specific syntax and violating framework constraints. This paper studies supervised fine-tuning for multi-framework WebUI code generation and proposes a phase-wise MLLM tuning method driven by compatibility and heterogeneity signals across frameworks. We first apply a normalization mapping that preserves each framework's native syntax while suppressing noise from variable naming and literal content. We then estimate cross framework heterogeneity and compatibility offline, and automatically derive training groups and their ordering by maximizing a phased objective. Finally, we perform phase-wise adapter tuning to reduce cross framework interference. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that our proposed method improves both generation quality and compilation success rate compared with baselines.
bullets: Addresses negative transfer when generating React, Vue, and Angular code from screenshots.
Normalizes examples while preserving native framework syntax and reducing naming/content noise.
Uses offline compatibility and heterogeneity estimates to derive training groups and their order.
Applies phase-wise adapter tuning to mitigate framework-specific syntax mixing and constraint violations.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks report improved generation quality and compilation success over baselines.

papers.abstract: Understanding and reasoning over 3D scenes from point clouds is essential for a broad range of AI applications. Recent 3D large language models have shown promising results, yet they still face two fundamental limitations: (i) insufficient capability for grounded multi-step reasoning in complex 3D scenes, and (ii) a text-centric inference paradigm that lacks effective interaction between textual reasoning and visual evidence. As a result, these models often fail to verify intermediate inferences, disambiguate similar object instances, and avoid hallucinations. To address these limitations, we propose MMCoT$^3$, the first 3D-Text Interleaved Chain-of-Thought (CoT) framework for 3D scene understanding. The core idea is to explicitly interleave textual reasoning with task-relevant 3D evidence, enabling the model to consult scene observations throughout the reasoning process. In addition, since a textual mention in 3D scenes may correspond to multiple candidate objects, naive object-mention alignment can inject incorrect evidence and mislead subsequent reasoning. To mitigate this multi-instance ambiguity, we design an ambiguity-aware evidence aggregation mechanism that uses query-guided cross-attention to fuse candidate object tokens and inject both evidence and ambiguity cues into the reasoning process. To better equip the model with multi-step reasoning capability, we further develop PointCoT, a large-scale 3D-specific CoT instruction tuning dataset with approximately 176.2K instances spanning captioning, question answering, dialogue, and planning tasks. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks show that our method consistently improves performance and achieves state-of-the-art results, validating the effectiveness of our proposed ambiguity-aware 3D-text interleaved reasoning for 3D scene understanding.
bullets: Addresses weak grounded multi-step reasoning and text-centric inference in 3D large language models.
Interleaves task-relevant 3D scene evidence with textual chain-of-thought reasoning.
Uses query-guided cross-attention to aggregate candidate objects while preserving ambiguity cues.
Introduces PointCoT, a 176.2K-instance 3D chain-of-thought instruction-tuning dataset covering captioning, QA, dialogue, and planning.
Experiments on six benchmarks report consistent improvements and state-of-the-art performance.

papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive means for neurological and mental health assessment, yet existing EEG models are typically developed for individual tasks and are difficult to unify across heterogeneous signal configurations and assessment objectives. Large language models (LLMs) offer a common interface for multiple tasks, but adapting heterogeneous EEG signals to a shared LLM raises a key challenge: how to preserve task-specific signal characteristics while enabling effective language-side parameter sharing. To address this problem, we propose EEG-HealthLLM, a unified and parameter-efficient framework for heterogeneous EEG health assessment. We introduce an Asymmetric Hierarchical Adaptation Strategy: task-specific EEG adapters preserve heterogeneous spatio-temporal dynamics, while a unified shared LoRA is injected into the LLM backbone (e.g., Phi-3) to capture shared high-level assessment semantics across tasks. We further establish EEG-HealthBench by reorganizing five existing EEG resources into paradigms covering epileptic seizure detection, major depressive disorder assessment, anxiety risk assessment, depressive symptom risk assessment, and emotional state assessment under a unified subject-independent protocol. Extensive experiments show that EEG-HealthLLM achieves an average balanced accuracy (BAC) of 69.58%, ranking first among the evaluated methods in both average BAC and macro-F1. Compared with independent single-task LoRA adaptation, it improves average BAC from 67.70% to 69.58% while reducing the aggregate language-side adapter footprint by 80.0%. Further analyses reveal task-dependent cross-task interactions and trade-offs, supporting the proposed hierarchical adaptation strategy. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Marui-88/EEG-HealthLLM.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of combining heterogeneous EEG configurations and multiple neurological and mental-health assessment objectives.
Uses asymmetric hierarchical adaptation: task-specific EEG adapters retain spatio-temporal characteristics, while shared LoRA captures common assessment semantics in an LLM backbone.
Introduces EEG-HealthBench, a unified subject-independent benchmark spanning five EEG assessment paradigms.
Achieves 69.58% average balanced accuracy and ranks first among evaluated methods in average BAC and macro-F1.
Compared with independent single-task LoRA, improves average BAC from 67.70% to 69.58% while reducing aggregate language-side adapter footprint by 80.0%.

papers.abstract: Purpose: To compare two multimodal System 1 decision models (Clef 27B, d1 3B) with three generative vision-language models read out zero-shot from a single answer token (Qwen3.8-27B, which is Clef's backbone; Gemma 4 31B; MedGemma 1.5 4B) on seven radiology tasks. Methods: All models ran locally on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The System 1 models returned a probability for each option in one pass; for the generative models, probabilities were read from the log-probabilities of the option letters. Tasks covered chest CT and radiograph reports (CT-RATE, PadChest), device MR safety records (GUDID), tubes and lines on chest radiographs (RANZCR CLiP), chest CT volumes (CT-RATE), brain MRI motion (MR-ART) and MRI sequence (BraTS 2021), 4,435 cases in total. The primary endpoint was AUROC with bootstrap 95% CIs. Results: All five models retrieved report findings well (AUROC 0.93-0.99). Clef ranked higher than its backbone on CT volumes (0.749 vs 0.668) and tube and line radiographs (0.812 vs 0.766) and lower on motion (0.625 vs 0.709), but it changed decisions more than ranking: it identified 90 of 100 FLAIR volumes, a class its backbone never chose, and cut calibration error on CT volumes from 0.436 to 0.072. d1 was within 0.04 of Clef on reports while using 3 to 9 times less energy per request, but was weak on images. Gemma 4 31B ranked device MR safety best (0.854) and MedGemma 1.5 4B ranked motion best (0.821), yet MedGemma was at chance on MRI sequences and answered "severe" for 93% of motion scans. Conclusion: A single-token readout turns open generative models from several families into usable decision models without retraining, but no model was best on every task and each had task-specific answer biases, so models and decision thresholds should be chosen on local cases.
bullets: Compared two multimodal System 1 models with three generative vision-language models across seven radiology tasks and 4,435 cases.
All models performed strongly on report-finding retrieval, with AUROCs of 0.93–0.99.
Clef improved over its backbone on CT volumes and tube/line radiographs, while showing weaker motion performance and improved CT-volume calibration.
The smaller d1 model approached Clef on reports with substantially lower energy use but performed poorly on images.
No model was consistently best; task-specific biases support selecting models and thresholds using local cases.

papers.abstract: Motion language models (MoLMs) encode 3D human motion as discrete tokens for language-based understanding. Deploying them on monocular video raises two problems. Pose detection yields 2D joint sequences, leaving a dimensional gap from the 3D motion used in training. Moreover, the 2D observation changes with the camera viewpoint, while the depth lost in projection makes the 2D pose ambiguous across viewpoints. We propose MoPort, a view-aware 2D interface that enables MoLMs to take 2D observations as input. We introduce Paired View Alignment (PVA), which gives two views of the same motion a shared 3D teacher target and directly constrains the consistency of their latents, so that 2D observations from different viewpoints are mapped to a consistent semantic representation. Camera-Modulated Encoding (CME) estimates the camera extrinsics from the 2D sequence and uses them to modulate encoding, providing the 2D latents with geometric information about the viewpoint. MoPort achieves R@1 of 0.5674 on HumanML3D and 0.3286 on KIT-ML, outperforming all evaluated baselines. On HumanML3D, its R@1 decreases only from 0.5763 on in-distribution viewpoints to 0.5585 on out-of-distribution viewpoints. We validate portability on three downstream MoLMs. Furthermore, on the real-world RGB video dataset Fit3D, MoPort achieves 80.36\% accuracy. Code will be released upon acceptance.
bullets: Addresses the 2D–3D representation gap and viewpoint ambiguity when applying MoLMs to monocular video.
Uses Paired View Alignment to map different-view 2D observations of the same motion to consistent semantic latents.
Uses Camera-Modulated Encoding to estimate camera extrinsics and incorporate viewpoint geometry during encoding.
Reports R@1 of 0.5674 on HumanML3D and 0.3286 on KIT-ML, outperforming evaluated baselines.
Shows robustness across viewpoints, portability to three downstream MoLMs, and 80.36% accuracy on Fit3D.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes MoPort, a view-aware interface for Motion Language Models to handle 2D observations of 3D motion, addressing spatial understanding and geometric consistency.
papers.title: MoPort: A View-Aware 2D Interface for Motion Language Models

papers.abstract: We present See, Think, Use, a protocol that traces each answer of a vision-language model to perception, reasoning or the use of perception. The diagnosis shows a developer which stage to improve and directs test-time compute to the stage that fails. Benchmarks score the final answer, and an answer that rests on the image earns the same credit as a guess or a memorized prior. The protocol asks the model two extra questions per item and needs no access to its weights. A localization probe asks for a box around every instance and measures seeing, and a text-replacement probe answers from a description and measures thinking. Use is the rate at which the answer follows the model's own perception across counterfactual image pairs. The rate needs no answer labels, because the question and its prior are the same on both images. On two model families and six datasets the protocol shows that the knob that helps follows the task family. Answers follow the model's perception except on images that contradict a common prior, and asking the model to localize first repairs this failure when its boxes are right. Allocating compute by the measured stages comes close to the best uniform policy at lower cost and beats a random allocation of the same compute wherever a knob raises the short stage. We will release the code, the prompts and the per-question outputs.
bullets: The protocol separates failures into seeing, thinking, and using visual evidence.
It uses localization and text-replacement probes, plus counterfactual image pairs, without model-weight access or answer labels for the use measure.
Across two model families and six datasets, the most effective intervention depends on the task family.
Models often follow their perception except when images conflict with common priors; localization-first prompting can repair this when localization is correct.
Stage-based compute allocation approaches the best uniform policy at lower cost and outperforms random allocation when a targeted intervention helps.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses perception and reasoning failures in vision-language models and allocates test-time compute, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: See, Think, Use: Diagnosing Perception and Reasoning Failures in VLMs
papers.tldr: See, Think, Use diagnoses whether VLM errors arise from perception, reasoning, or failure to use perception, enabling targeted test-time computation.

papers.abstract: Processing every video frame through Vision-Language Models (VLMs) adds significant inference cost and limits their ability to comprehend real-time video. Existing approaches either sub-sample frames uniformly, ignoring content and missing important events, or prune visual tokens inside the VLM to cut per-call cost while still invoking the model on every sampled frame. We introduce FOCUS, a training-free three-layer framework that reduces the number of invocations and steers each one towards what matters. Temporal gating measures inter-frame dissimilarity in the patch-embedding space of a smaller VLM from the same family, triggering burst captures only when the scene changes in a semantically meaningful way. Patch-level dissimilarity is then accumulated across the burst and fused with a top-down attention prior into a spatial focus map that encodes where motion and semantic relevance coincide. That map calibrates the VLM's value cache during generation, progressively amplifying vision tokens in task-relevant regions and attenuating off-target ones, without removing any token from the context. The loop closes after each response: text-to-vision cross-attention is extracted from the decoder and fed back as the prior for the next burst, letting the system converge on semantically important regions over successive observations. We evaluate FOCUS on the 500-video EgoSchema subset in streaming mode, with a single Qwen3-VL-8B backbone shared by every method. It reaches 74.8% accuracy using 25.4 VLM calls per clip, against 74.6% with 55 calls for uniform sampling and 74.2% with 55 calls for BOLT. On egocentric video captioning across four domains, it matches the best baseline's quality while issuing 57% fewer VLM invocations than uniform sampling.
bullets: Detects meaningful scene changes with patch-embedding dissimilarity and triggers burst captures selectively.
Combines motion-based patch changes with top-down attention to focus on task-relevant regions.
Reweights, rather than removes, visual tokens during generation using a calibrated value cache.
Feeds decoder text-to-vision attention back into the next observation cycle for iterative refinement.
On a 500-video EgoSchema subset, achieves 74.8% accuracy with 25.4 calls per clip; captioning matches the best baseline with 57% fewer calls than uniform sampling.

papers.abstract: Situational-safety benchmarks label each scene SAFE or UNSAFE and score a multimodal large language model (MLLM) against that label, usually by judging its free-form answer, and these scores guide deployment. We ask what such a label measures. A label score can come from the scene, the request or the benchmark's own files. We propose the Benchmark Card, seven measured fields that tell them apart, and fill it for six benchmarks. Only MSSBench chat leaks the label through its image files: image size alone reaches 82.3% accuracy, matching or beating six of seven commercial models. Elsewhere the signal outside the scene comes from design. In MOSSBench the item partition fixes the label, and on HoliSafe the request alone ranks pairs about as well as the scene. On our corrected chat split, the size rule falls to chance. We then introduce the Spot-Stop decomposition, which compares ranking with labelling on pairs of a safe and an unsafe scene. It splits the gap above a label-swap null into three parts: a threshold part, overlap between safe and unsafe scores, and order that holds only within a pair. Most of fourteen open MLLMs rank better than they label, beyond what their AUROC predicts. On chat, one shared threshold repairs a third to a half of the excess, and label-free recentering recovers it on balanced batches. Recentering on unlabelled scenes of the same situation improves ranking on VSCBench for 13 of 14 models.
bullets: Introduces the Benchmark Card, which separates safety signals arising from the scene, request, or benchmark files, and applies it to six benchmarks.
Finds severe leakage in MSSBench chat: image size alone achieves 82.3% accuracy, while other benchmarks contain design-based shortcuts.
Proposes Spot-Stop, decomposing the gap between ranking and binary labelling into threshold, score-overlap, and pair-specific ordering effects.
Most of 14 open MLLMs rank safe versus unsafe scenes better than they label them; shared-threshold calibration and label-free recentering reduce this gap.
Recentring on unlabeled scenes from the same situation improves ranking on VSCBench for 13 of 14 models.

papers.selection_reason: Audits and analyzes the behavior of Multimodal LLMs on situational-safety benchmarks, providing a framework for understanding label reliability.
papers.title: What Does a Safety Label Measure? Auditing Situational-Safety Benchmarks for Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Situational-safety benchmark scores can reflect dataset artifacts and calibration—not just an MLLM’s understanding of scene safety—so the paper proposes tools to audit and improve their interpretation.

papers.abstract: 3D visual grounding localizes objects in 3D scenes from natural language descriptions, requiring reasoning over semantics, spatial relationships, and multi-view observations. Training-free approaches avoid costly annotations but often rely on explicit scene transformation or scene-level frame selection, which may waste limited visual capacity on query-irrelevant regions. We observe that effective grounding should prioritize observations that provide evidence for the query rather than uniformly represent the entire scene. Based on this insight, we introduce QVR3D, a query-guided visual reasoning framework that operates on RGB-D observations using off-the-shelf foundation models. QVR3D combines Query-Guided Maximum Coverage (QGMC) for selecting complementary query-relevant views with Grounding Probability Estimation (GPE) that integrates instance confidence, attribute consistency, and relationship consistency. The framework supports both single- and multi-object grounding without task-specific adaptation. Experiments on ScanRefer and Nr3D achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, while QGMC also improves frame efficiency across multiple 3D vision-language tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/jwliao1209/QVR3D.
bullets: Targets inefficient scene-level view selection that spends visual capacity on query-irrelevant regions.
Uses Query-Guided Maximum Coverage to select complementary views relevant to the language query.
Uses Grounding Probability Estimation to combine instance, attribute, and relationship consistency.
Supports both single-object and multi-object grounding without task-specific adaptation.
Reports state-of-the-art zero-shot results on ScanRefer and Nr3D, with improved frame efficiency across multiple 3D vision-language tasks.

papers.abstract: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to identify a query-view target in a satellite image, yet reliable instance grounding remains challenging under substantial viewpoint discrepancies. Although recent methods incorporate multimodal prompts, they insufficiently address the varying transferability of linguistic and visual evidence across views. Viewpoint-dependent descriptions (e.g., building facades visible in oblique UAV views but not in top-down satellite images) may become unreliable for satellite grounding, while visually similar instances further complicate target identification. To address these challenges, we rethink CVOGL from a visual grounding perspective and propose GAV (Grounding Across Views), a view-aware framework for constructing target-centered evidence and establishing discriminative cross-view correspondence. Specifically, view-aware referring reasoning mitigates viewpoint-dependent ambiguity, multi-token exemplar prompting and contrastive alignment strengthen visual-semantic correspondence, and scene-level supervision with alignment-based verification distinguishes competing satellite instances. We further introduce CVOGL-Text, a street- and drone-to-satellite benchmark with query-derived expressions. GAV achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoP-UAV with 62.55% Acc@0.5 (+18.19 percentage points) and outperforms evaluated click-point baselines on CVOGL-Text.
bullets: CVOGL must transfer target evidence between street/drone views and top-down satellite imagery despite major viewpoint differences.
GAV uses view-aware referring reasoning to reduce ambiguity from descriptions that are unreliable across viewpoints.
Multi-token exemplar prompting and contrastive alignment strengthen cross-view visual-semantic correspondence.
Scene-level supervision and alignment-based verification help separate competing satellite instances.
GAV reports 62.55% Acc@0.5 on MoP-UAV and outperforms evaluated click-point baselines on the introduced CVOGL-Text benchmark.

papers.abstract: Digital image correlation (DIC) is a widely used non-contact technique for full-field displacement measurement. Data-driven deep-learning DIC offers rapid inference but may generalize poorly to unseen speckle patterns, deformation modes, noise levels, and illumination conditions. Classical optimization-based DIC and recent image-constrained neural formulations avoid labeled displacement data, yet their convergence and accuracy remain vulnerable to initialization, large rigid-body motion, fine non-uniform deformation, and gray-value disturbances. This paper presents a global-to-local hybrid neural DIC framework for robust pixelwise measurement. Stage 1 estimates a dominant in-plane rigid transformation through coarse rotation search, phase correlation, and masked refinement, providing a reliable initialization under large translation and rotation. Stage 2 represents the residual displacement with a hybrid Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) and multilayer perceptron (MLP), and optimizes it using a valid-overlap, illumination-robust structural loss. The local gray-value model explicitly accommodates multiplicative and additive intensity changes. Simulated and real experiments demonstrate accurate and stable displacement recovery under noise, non-uniform deformation, large rotation, illumination variation, and degraded imaging conditions.
bullets: Addresses poor generalization of learning-based DIC and optimization failures caused by large motion, fine deformation, noise, and gray-value disturbances.
First estimates dominant rigid motion using coarse rotation search, phase correlation, and masked refinement for reliable initialization.
Then models residual displacement with a hybrid KAN–MLP neural field optimized using a valid-overlap, illumination-robust structural loss.
Explicitly accounts for multiplicative and additive intensity changes through a local gray-value model.
Simulated and real experiments show accurate and stable recovery under rotation, non-uniform deformation, noise, illumination variation, and degraded imaging.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a hybrid neural field for robust pixel-wise displacement measurement, contributing to spatial intelligence and geometric understanding in computer vision.
papers.title: Robust Pixel-wise Digital Image Correlation under Large Motions and Illumination Variations via a Global-to-Local Hybrid Neural Field

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models re-encode the full observation through a multi-billion-parameter vision-language model (VLM) at every control step, even though scene semantics evolve at roughly 1 Hz while reactive control requires 20-50 Hz. We present a VLA that decouples the two: a VLM runs as a low-frequency semantic anchor whose cached context is reused across control steps, while a flow-matching action expert operates at high frequency, consuming the cached semantics with a fresh, low-latency visual stream from a compact encoder pretrained on robot video with masked reconstruction, optical flow, and depth. The measured age $τ$ of the cache conditions the expert through adaptive layer normalization. Reusing the cache makes the policy a function of its age, and training covers that function explicitly: cache ages sampled from real episode history, plus an age-ramped pixel corruption that erases the stale snapshot the way deployed staleness corrupts content. On the asynchronous deployment stack, the recipe closes most of the staleness gap: on LIBERO-Spatial, 61.4% to 95.5% at a 2 s semantic refresh (95.9% at 1 s, within 1.6 points of the frequency-matched anchor); averaged over the four LIBERO suites, the deployed policy holds 95.2% at a 1 s refresh and 94.5% at 2 s against a 96.3% matched anchor. A forward-only chunk-boundary correction (soft-nudge), an autograd-free reformulation of real-time-chunking guidance, carries per-control-step re-planning without loss (97.1%) at zero added latency. The same lens exposes a second defect: under an instruction-scene mismatch the policy keeps manipulating the scene, and a chain-of-thought verdict gate trained on zero-cost negative episodes freezes execution exactly on mismatched instructions without hurting feasible success.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between roughly 1 Hz scene-semantic updates and 20–50 Hz reactive control.
Caches VLM context and combines it with high-frequency visual features from a compact robot-video-pretrained encoder.
Conditions the flow-matching action expert on cache age and trains it with realistic cache-age histories and staleness-mimicking pixel corruption.
On LIBERO, achieves 95.2% success at a 1 s semantic refresh and 94.5% at 2 s, versus 96.3% for a frequency-matched anchor.
Adds zero-latency chunk-boundary correction and a verdict gate that freezes execution under instruction–scene mismatch.],

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Leap-VLA overview. Slow system: the VLM runs at fslow over a token sequence that appends, after the prompt and the observation, the chain-ofthought region; it produces the cached context C and the chain-of-thought-supervised anchor features, and its reasoning region is emitted as the structured output shown. Because attention is causal, the prompt-region features the expert consumes are unchanged by the appended block (Sec. III-B). Fast system: the flow-matching expert runs at ffast, consuming C and fresh fast-stream features through one pluggable token-block interface: image tokens from the frozen motion-aware encoder (dual-frame, robot-pretrained with reconstruction, optical flow, and depth). The measured cache age τ conditions the expert via AdaRMS, proprioception enters as a dedicated input token, and the control rate f is passed to the action head; training samples τ from the physical episode history.

Bottom: only the goal is changed (“Put the wine bottle on the stove”); the scene and objects are identical. Our model still executes the new instruction, whereas VLA baselines score 0.0–6.8% on this perturbation dimension (ours: 20.4% averaged over the four suites, 8.4–49% per suite). Both rows are successful episodes re-recorded with the evaluation protocol of Table IX (asynchronous deployment: semantic anchor refreshed at each 0.5 s re-plan, fast stream and measured cache age updated every control step); frames are keyframes sampled from the 100 ms-interval agentview replay.

Fig. 13. Failure analysis on LIBERO-PRO task perturbations (libero goal). Rows 1–3: under task-perturbed instructions, the characteristic failure is semantic interference—the policy reverts to the behavior of the trained task. Asked to turn the stove off, it turns the burner on (row 1); asked to put the wine bottle on the stove, it carries the bottle back to the trained rack goal (rows 2–3). Row 4: on the unperturbed original task, failures are motor-level instead (the grasp slips and the bottle is dropped). Perturbed-instruction failures therefore reflect instruction generalization rather than manipulation competence. These modes are systematic rather than cherry-picked: 2/2 recorded failures of “turn off the stove” turn it on, and 2/6 recorded failures of the wine-bottle task revert to the rack.

A dual-frame pair (ot−δ, ot) is fused into a 6-channel input at the stem; a ∼49% row/column strip mask is applied jointly to both frames (pair-level tube masking), and the visible patches go through the compact encoder. Three lightweight decoders share the encoded features: the reconstruction decoder fills in both frames’ masked patches, the optical-flow decoder predicts the dense ot−δ→ot motion of masked patches, and the depth decoder predicts per-pixel depth for each frame. Left: false execution under instruction–scene mismatch—each row is one rollout at increasing time fractions, instruction quoted above; the instruction refers to absent objects, yet the policy grasps an unrelated plate (top) or knocks over a bottle (bottom). papers.selection_reason: Proposes Leap-VLA, a VLA model that decouples a low-frequency VLM backbone from a high-frequency action expert, directly addressing the efficiency of vision-language-action models.
papers.title: Leap-VLA: High-Rate Robot Control from a Low-Rate VLM Backbone
papers.tldr: Leap-VLA enables high-rate robot control by reusing low-rate VLM semantics while adapting to cache staleness with fresh visual input and age-aware action prediction.

papers.abstract: Mobile UI understanding and generation require both fine-grained component perception and reliable structured synthesis. Inspired by the unified direction introduced by UI-UG, we present UI-UG 2, a compact 4B-parameter multimodal large language model (MLLM) that advances mobile UI Understanding and Generation with broader task coverage, a front-end-aligned taxonomy, and online render-aware reinforcement learning. UI-UG 2 constructs a multi-source understanding corpus from RICO, VINS, Android in the Wild, and Android Control, annotated with an 80-category two-level UI taxonomy aligned with front-end component semantics, and pairs it with over 5,000 requirement-screenshot-JSON tuples for progressive structured UI generation through a domain-specific language (DSL). For understanding, UI-UG 2 introduces decomposed rewards for category prediction, OCR fidelity, color recognition, dense grounding, and GUI grounding. Unlike the offline Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-style generation optimization in UI-UG, UI-UG 2 optimizes generation through end-to-end online Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO): sampled DSL outputs are rendered with a Playwright-based server-side pipeline and evaluated using LLM-as-a-Judge and contrastive preference ranking. Experiments show that UI-UG 2 achieves the strongest referring and dense-grounding results among the evaluated models on our 80-category benchmark, and achieves the best composite generation score among compared models at a compact scale (4B). More importantly, we observe a consistent understanding-to-generation transfer: adding fine-grained UI perception supervision improves generation quality under a fixed training budget, suggesting that component-level semantics provide a shared representational foundation for both tasks.
bullets: Targets reliable perception of UI components and synthesis of structured, executable interfaces.
Uses an 80-category, two-level taxonomy with supervision for category prediction, OCR, color recognition, and grounding.
Generates UIs progressively as DSL outputs from requirement–screenshot–JSON training tuples.
Applies online GRPO with server-side rendering and LLM-based and contrastive preference evaluation.
Reports strongest referring/dense-grounding results on its benchmark and the best composite generation score among compared compact models; finer perception also improves generation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become an important paradigm for improving multimodal large language models (MLLMs), especially with automatically verifiable rewards. Self-supervised visual pretext tasks provide such rewards without human annotations. However, existing methods mainly exploit within-instance structure, offering limited supervision for cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison. We introduce Group-and-Order Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning (GO-SSL), a cross-instance jigsaw framework for vision-centric MLLM post-training. Given two visual instances, GO-SSL mixes their local elements and trains the model to group them by instance of origin while recovering the order within each group, coupling instance-level comparison with spatial, temporal, or geometric structure recovery. This paired formulation turns the same unlabeled data into richer verifiable supervision through diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum. We instantiate GO-SSL mainly on cross-image jigsaw tasks and further extend it to 3D depth and video temporal ordering. Across diverse benchmarks, GO-SSL consistently improves over the base MLLM and prior self-supervised post-training baselines, with clear gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding. Further evaluations across model scales and families support its generality. These results suggest that cross-instance comparison provides a useful self-supervised RL signal for improving transferable visual understanding in MLLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/SEU-VIPGroup/GO-SSL.
bullets: Addresses the limited cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison learned by prior within-instance self-supervised methods.
Pairs two visual instances, mixes their local elements, and trains the model to separate them by origin while restoring spatial, temporal, or geometric order.
Uses diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum to create richer automatically verifiable rewards from unlabeled data.
Applied to cross-image jigsaws, 3D depth, and video temporal ordering, with reported gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding across benchmarks.
Evaluations across model scales and families indicate broad generality, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results or limitations.

papers.title: Learning to Group and Order: Cross-Instance Self-Supervised RL for Vision-Centric MLLMs
papers.tldr: GO-SSL improves vision-centric MLLMs by using self-supervised RL to group mixed visual elements by source and recover their original order across paired instances.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-enabled model derivatives must turn intermediate deliberation into a usable answer within a deployment budget. We study that transition in an Ornith checkpoint adapted to multi-camera driving question answering with verifiable rewards. Paired archived outputs show that, on a selected 400-question development screen with a 256-token cap, GRPO increases answer extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%. Of 39 wrong-to-correct transitions, 33 begin with an unextractable base response. The base's 87 unextractable responses all reach the token cap. Checkpoint-verified reconstruction on those same questions gives a much smaller first-pass accuracy gain at 512 tokens: +0.75 percentage points, versus +8.25 at 256. A later answer-cued continuation is analyzed separately; it helps the base more and narrows the adapter difference. On the full 2,511-question development set, this recovery-enabled pipeline reduces mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain. We frame these findings as adaptation of answer delivery under finite budgets, with explicit selection and provenance limits. Ornith's self-scaffolding lineage and newer reasoning-enabled derivatives such as Bonsai motivate the problem, but our measured results concern Ornith alone and do not establish a shared architectural mechanism or cross-model transfer.
bullets: On a selected 400-question screen capped at 256 tokens, GRPO raises answer extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%.
Most wrong-to-correct changes involve previously unextractable responses: 33 of 39 transitions; all 87 base unextractable responses hit the token cap.
Checkpoint-verified reconstruction yields only a +0.75-point accuracy gain at 512 tokens, compared with +8.25 points at 256 tokens.
On the full 2,511-question development set, recovery-enabled tuning cuts mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain.
