papers.abstract: Multi-camera driving question answering provides a discrete test of vision-language models, but post-training gains can reflect changed selected answers or improved answer extraction. We investigate this distinction within the Gemma model family using archived, task-linked WaymoQA evaluations. A zero-shot diagnostic on 5,519 test questions spans effective-small, mixture-of-experts, unified, and dense checkpoints, with serving differences disclosed rather than interpreted as architecture effects. The strongest controlled evidence is a matched-harness Gemma-4-12B base/GRPO pair: accuracy rises from 73.78% to 75.43%, a gain of 1.65 percentage points with a scene-cluster bootstrap interval of [+0.84, +2.41]. There are 215 improvements and 124 regressions; 213 improvements start from an extractable but incorrect base answer, and only two recover previously unextractable responses. Crossing correctness with extraction state shows why correct noncompliant outputs cannot be counted as prediction errors. Category counts reveal a critical safety asymmetry: routine perception gains (+5.93 pp) mask a regression in safety-critical hazard prediction (-1.82 pp), demonstrating that unweighted outcome rewards can trade off rare edge cases for aggregate accuracy. Reward saturation describes sampled training dynamics rather than an architectural ceiling. A separate archived Gemma-31B thinking comparison yields no detected average improvement, with uncertainty that does not establish equivalence. These results support a modest answer-selection gain for the recorded tuning configuration and a reproducible diagnostic accounting, without attributing corrected labels to specific grounding mechanisms or claiming superiority over matched supervised tuning.
bullets: Matched-harness accuracy increased from 73.78% to 75.43% (+1.65 percentage points; bootstrap interval [+0.84, +2.41]).
Most improvements corrected extractable but incorrect answers; only two recovered previously unextractable responses.
Routine perception accuracy rose (+5.93 pp), while safety-critical hazard prediction declined (-1.82 pp).
A separate archived Gemma-31B thinking comparison found no detected average improvement, with uncertainty insufficient to establish equivalence.
Findings are limited to the recorded tuning configuration and do not claim superiority over matched supervised tuning or identify specific grounding mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Remote smartphone recommerce is scaling quickly, and locking a repurchase offer from seller photos and diagnostic screens before the handset arrives has become a central operational task. Existing multimodal resources mainly target defect localization, catalog attributes, or screen reading. They overlook payout-facing scorecards with dual cosmetic and operational ground truth under a declared input contract. This gap stems from two challenges: (1) the lack of a large weakly labeled trade-in corpus kept separate from a compact audited ranking cut, and (2) architectures that either flatten unordered photo bags into one prompt or collapse evaluation into a single price scalar. To address these challenges, we propose PhoneValue-Bench, a dual-ground-truth recommerce framework with PhoneValue-Corpus for weak training on 21,550 orders and 278,748 images, and PV-Rank as the only leaderboard on 335 quality-gated orders. Systems are ranked by CardScore under LeadGate, with Cosmetic Fill and Operational Fill as diagnostics, while grade and price stay off the board. Notably, ValueAgent is a six-stage perception-fusion reference that canonicalizes views, detects regional defects, reads screenshots, and fuses evidence under warehouse-style rules, so bag-of-images prompting is not the only evaluation unit. On the same PV-Rank cut and frozen scorer, this full-system and input-contract comparison finds ValueAgent at 84.1 CardScore against the strongest Flat Vision-Language Model at 69.9, with the largest reported gap in CosFill, while OpsFill remains limited under the two declared contracts. CardScore measures field-fill completeness, not quote accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the lack of payout-facing benchmarks combining cosmetic and operational ground truth under a declared input contract.
Includes PhoneValue-Corpus with 21,550 orders and 278,748 images for weak training, plus 335 quality-gated orders in the PV-Rank leaderboard.
Ranks systems with CardScore and reports Cosmetic Fill and Operational Fill diagnostics; grade and price are excluded from ranking.
ValueAgent uses six-stage view canonicalization, defect detection, screenshot reading, and warehouse-rule evidence fusion.
On the PV-Rank cut, ValueAgent scores 84.1 CardScore versus 69.9 for the strongest flat vision-language model; CardScore measures field completeness, not quote accuracy.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promise for chest radiograph report generation, but adoption remains limited because of hallucinated findings that are not grounded in the image. Correcting these hallucinations and improving overall report quality remains a significant challenge. Prior work has addressed this problem by refining models with reinforcement learning, preference optimization, or chain-of-thought supervision, often at substantial compute cost. To address this gap, we introduce CheXPoT, a program-of-thought (PoT) framework that verifies each generated finding against image features and removes those it cannot ground. CheXPoT decomposes generated reports into predicates with RadGraph and an LLM, grounds these predicates against a DenseNet-121 and Grad-CAM visual evidence table, executes PoT verification code, and rewrites reports after removing unsupported predicates. On a 4,145-image held-out split, CheXPoT yields statistically significant precision gains on 8 of 14 CheXpert classes and F1 gains on 5, with no significant decreases in either metric. CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 19.2% (MedGemma-4B) to 46.8% (MedGemma-4B + CheXPoT) and micro-average F1 from 23.0% to 49.4%, absolute gains of 27.6% and 26.4% respectively. We also tested CheXPoT on other VLM report generators. On LLaVA-Med, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 4.5% to 17.7% and micro-average F1 from 6.3% to 19.4%. On MAIRA-2, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 15.6% to 42.1% and micro-average F1 from 21.0% to 45.3%. Our results suggest that inexpensive post-hoc visual verification may improve VLM trustworthiness by correcting unsupported findings from generated reports. CheXPoT lays a foundation for tools that help validate VLM-generated radiology reports and reduce unsupported findings. These innovations may subsequently help increase trust and adoption of VLM tools in Medicine.
bullets: Targets hallucinated or image-ungrounded findings that limit clinical trust in VLM-generated radiology reports.
Decomposes reports into predicates, grounds them using DenseNet-121 and Grad-CAM evidence, verifies them with program-of-thought code, and rewrites reports.
On a 4,145-image held-out split, it significantly improved precision for 8/14 CheXpert classes and F1 for 5, without significant metric decreases.
For MedGemma-4B, micro-precision rose from 19.2% to 46.8% and micro-F1 from 23.0% to 49.4%.
Also improved results for LLaVA-Med and MAIRA-2, suggesting applicability across multiple VLM report generators.

papers.abstract: Local image--text matching can find strong evidence for individual concepts yet favor captions with incorrect attribute--entity bindings. We introduce ConstraintMatch, a training-free inference method that turns entity-level regional consistency into an explicit matching cost. On the same frozen condition--region similarity matrix, it compares independent crop selection for each category and attribute with a shared crop choice within each entity. Their gap quantifies the score advantage obtained by relaxing the shared-region constraint. Spatial references from the same image calibrate this gap by keeping category evidence fixed while jointly shifting an entity's attribute maps. Per-entity clipping prevents cancellation across residuals, and the scaled mean cost is subtracted from global similarity. ConstraintMatch uses pooled embeddings, and spatial calibration requires no additional encoder calls. With parameters fixed per backbone across tasks, ConstraintMatch improves over global matching by 7.70 percentage points on full ARO Attribute and 5.63 points on held-out SugarCrepe++ attribute swaps, averaged across Qwen~2B and CORE~2B. Against SGI adapted to the same 13-crop budget, the respective gains are 4.85 and 3.51 points. Controlled analyses distinguish the effects of shared-region matching and candidate score calibration. The results establish entity-level evidence selection as a practical scoring principle for compositional multimodal retrieval.
bullets: Addresses incorrect attribute–entity bindings that can survive conventional local image–text matching.
Uses a training-free inference cost comparing independent versus shared regional evidence for each entity.
Calibrates the cost with spatial references, clips per-entity residuals, and subtracts the scaled mean from global similarity.
Uses pooled embeddings without extra encoder calls for spatial calibration.
Improves attribute-swap retrieval over global matching and a same-budget SGI baseline across ARO and SugarCrepe++ evaluations.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) show promise for clinical image understanding, but their computational and memory requirements hinder deployment on resource-constrained clinical hardware. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical compression strategy without retraining, yet its effectiveness depends strongly on the calibration data. We propose CoreCalib, a training-free and quantizer-agnostic framework for constructing compact calibration sets that preserve the target medical VQA distribution. CoreCalib stratifies data by clinical question class, identifies representative visual modes using frozen DINOv2 features with UMAP and HDBSCAN, and expands selected images into class-balanced question-answer pairs. On Kvasir-VQA-x1, we evaluate CoreCalib with MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG using a fixed 128-pair budget. CoreCalib achieves the best METEOR with all three quantizers and the best ROUGE-L with MASQuant and GPTQ. With W4A8 MASQuant, it improves METEOR from 0.5672 with COCO calibration to 0.6234, recovering approximately 41% of the degradation relative to BF16. These results support CoreCalib as a data-centric component for resource-efficient medical VLM deployment. Project page: https://magnusdtd.github.io/CoreCalib/ .
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deploying medical VLMs on hardware with limited compute and memory.
Constructs calibration sets by balancing clinical question classes and selecting representative visual modes with frozen DINOv2 features, UMAP, and HDBSCAN.
Is training-free and quantizer-agnostic, evaluated with MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG using 128 question-answer pairs on Kvasir-VQA-x1.
Achieves the best METEOR for all three quantizers and the best ROUGE-L for MASQuant and GPTQ.
With W4A8 MASQuant, raises METEOR from 0.5672 using COCO calibration to 0.6234, recovering about 41% of the degradation relative to BF16.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of CoreCalib and its role in resource-efficient medical VLM deployment. (A) A medical VLM provides strong clinical VQA capability but requires substantial computational resources; PTQ converts it into a low-bit model intended to reduce the resource burden across a spectrum of computing environments. (B) CoreCalib constructs a compact calibration workload by (1) stratifying the medical VQA data by clinical question class, (2) selecting densityaware representative images using frozen DINOv2 features with UMAP and HDBSCAN, (3) expanding representative images into multiple QA pairs and balancing them across question classes, and (4) forming a small calibration set, such as 128 QA pairs from 23 images. (C) The calibration set can be used with different PTQ methods, including MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG, to produce a quantized medical VLM with improved capability retention.

papers.abstract: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. We introduce ElectrochemLLM, a multimodal information extraction pipeline that jointly identifies structured electrochemical records encompassing electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and their measured physicochemical properties from unstructured scientific PDFs at scale. By combining hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration, the pipeline extracts verifiable, structured data across text, tables, and figures. Evaluated on the battery-electrolyte subset of our manually annotated benchmark of 232 papers, ElectrochemLLM achieves an F-1 score of 0.97, and has been applied to curate ElectroChemDB, a structured database spanning 15,000 electrochemical research articles. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by training machine learning models for electrolyte property prediction, illustrating a complete pathway from unstructured literature to predictive materials discovery.
bullets: Addresses text-only extraction, fragmented context, and numerical hallucinations in electrochemical literature curation.
Combines hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration to process text, tables, and figures.
Extracts electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and measured physicochemical properties.
Achieves an F1 score of 0.97 on a manually annotated battery-electrolyte benchmark of 232 papers.
Produces ElectroChemDB from 15,000 research articles and supports electrolyte property prediction models.

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) unlearning is often treated as an objective-design problem: given multimodal forget data, the goal is to optimize a loss that removes undesirable behavior while preserving retained capabilities. We argue that this view overlooks an equally important data-centric question: how should each forget example be represented before optimization? Existing methods typically keep image-conditioned failures in their original image-text form, implicitly assuming that pixels are the right route for unlearning whenever pixels appear in the input. We challenge this assumption by constructing modality-decomposed versions of VLM benchmarks, enabling controlled comparisons among image-only, text-only, and multimodal representations of the same examples. Our modality-mixing experiments show that unsafe instruction-following behavior is more effectively suppressed through textual representations than through images alone, while purely text-only unlearning can still weaken visual grounding when the target behavior depends on visual evidence. Motivated by this trade-off, we introduce ModRoute, a gradient-guided per-sample modality routing strategy that selectively converts high visual-pressure examples to text-only form while keeping the remaining examples multimodal. Notably, on VLGuard with LLaVA-1.5-7B, ModRoute has the strongest composite unlearning-utility score of 0.847 at $γ=0.5$, a 2.5% improvement over the best random-switching score and $\geq$46% better than pure multimodal or text unlearning. Overall, our results show that effective VLM unlearning depends not only on the objective, but also on the composition and per-sample modality routing of the unlearning data.
bullets: The work reframes VLM unlearning as both an objective-design and data-representation problem.
Modality-decomposed benchmarks enable controlled comparison of image-only, text-only, and multimodal unlearning inputs.
Textual representations better suppress unsafe instruction-following, but text-only unlearning can harm visual grounding.
ModRoute uses gradient-guided, per-sample routing to convert high visual-pressure examples to text-only form and retain multimodal inputs for others.
On VLGuard with LLaVA-1.5-7B, it achieves a composite score of 0.847, outperforming random switching by 2.5% and pure routing baselines by at least 46%.

papers.selection_reason: Modality-routing method for vision-language model unlearning; relevant to multimodal foundation model training and behavior control.
papers.title: Words Before Pixels: Selective Modality Routing for Vision-Language Model Unlearning
papers.tldr: ModRoute improves VLM unlearning by routing each forget example through the modality—text-only or multimodal—that best suppresses the target behavior while preserving visual capabilities.

papers.abstract: Answering a complex question about a long video is a grounding problem: the answer turns on a few seconds of evidence, and vision-language models remain well below human accuracy at finding them. The standard way to spend extra test-time compute on this kind of video reasoning is best-of-N selection: sample several chain-of-thought answers from a fixed model, then let a second model re-watch the video and pick one. Such pipelines are reported by a single headline number, their margin over a majority vote. That number conflates two effects with opposite deployment consequences: the benefit the second model adds by selecting among candidates, and the benefit it would have supplied by solving the question itself. We separate them, measuring the Selection Increment (SI) -- selection accuracy minus the same verifier's accuracy with the candidates withheld -- alongside the margin over self-consistency, across five long-video benchmarks. The Selection Increment is largest for the weakest verifiers: a verifier that solves poorly on its own leaves the candidates the most room to help. Beating the majority vote follows the opposite profile: where the vote already sits near its ceiling no verifier we test improves on it; below that ceiling only the strongest do. On Video-Holmes, the two come apart on a single pool of candidates -- a weak verifier gains +19.3 points from the candidates yet lands 7.1 points below the vote, while the frontier verifier gains the least and beats the vote. The weakest verifier also shows a failure mode: on EgoSchema it picks by where an option sits in the list rather than by what the video shows. Read as a merit score, SI puts a verifier that fails to beat a majority vote at the top of its ranking; read as an audit, it says which of the two effects a headline number delivers. Code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/best-n-selection-video-reasoning.
bullets: Introduces Selection Increment (SI): verifier accuracy with candidates minus its accuracy when candidates are withheld.
Across five long-video benchmarks, weaker verifiers gain more from candidate answers, while stronger verifiers are more likely to beat majority vote.
On Video-Holmes, a weak verifier gained 19.3 points from candidates but remained 7.1 points below the vote; the frontier verifier gained less but surpassed it.
The weakest verifier showed positional-choice bias on EgoSchema, selecting based on option order rather than video evidence.
SI is useful as an audit of where gains come from, but is misleading as a standalone merit ranking.

papers.selection_reason: Separates selection versus solving effects in best-of-N video reasoning, directly relevant to video-language understanding and VLM evaluation.
papers.title: Selecting or Solving? What Best-of-N Verification Delivers in Video Reasoning
papers.tldr: Best-of-N video reasoning gains must be split into candidate-selection benefit and the verifier’s own solving ability, because these can point to opposite conclusions.

papers.abstract: When searching for an object, humans naturally combine semantic intuition - reasoning about where the object is likely to be stored - with geometric awareness of what parts of the space are visible, occluded, or unexplored. Effective robot object search requires the same joint reasoning, yet existing methods rely on only one: geometric methods maintain principled spatial beliefs but lack deep semantic understanding, while language-model based methods leverage commonsense knowledge but maintain no explicit belief over space. We argue that jointly reasoning over semantic and geometric evidence in an explicit 3D belief enables human-like interactive object search that outperforms either modality alone. To test this claim, we build a system that accumulates per-object VLM plausibility scores and geometric occupancy evidence via Bayesian log-odds filtering into a unified 3D voxel belief field. High-belief regions in the combined belief field drive action selection at each step: taking a closer look from a different viewpoint, navigating toward an unexplored region of the workspace, or physically interacting with a closed cabinet. We deploy this system end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid and find that it outperforms geometry-only search and LLM-based planning methods. Project website - https://skymanaditya1.github.io/objsearch-website/
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometry-only methods and language-based planners that lack spatial beliefs.
Combines VLM object-likelihood scores with geometric occupancy evidence using Bayesian log-odds filtering.
Uses high-belief voxel regions to choose viewpoints, explore unseen areas, or interact with closed cabinets.
Evaluated end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid, outperforming geometry-only and LLM-based search methods.

papers.abstract: A spectrum can be given to a model as a table in nanometers or as a plot in photon energy, and the decision should not depend on which one it sees. When the data needed for an answer are missing, the model should say so. We test representation invariance and abstention on measured optical spectra of silicon metasurfaces (MOCLIP) and gold nanoparticles, with labels computed from the data. Each spectrum is shown as four tables (nm, $μ$m, scientific notation, eV) and two plots (nm, eV), and partial spectra remove data inside or outside the queried range. We evaluate the decision models d3-nano and Jev 1.13, three GPT-6 Luna configurations and the Qwen3.5-2B base model. Changing only the representation moves accuracy by up to 41 percentage points within one model, mostly on photon-energy tables and plots. With the same evidence, asking in photon energy instead of wavelength helps some model-view pairs by 16-50 points and hurts others by up to 25. When the relevant extremum is removed, unadapted models rarely answer "undetermined". LoRA fine-tuning of d3-nano improves comparisons on the trained table formats, but much of its gain on unanswerable questions comes from a shortcut: it abstains whenever the input is truncated. Training with answerable truncations avoids the shortcut in all six seeds, with a 90-100 point gap between abstention after inside and outside cuts on held-out structures; with the same amount of extra original-task data, five of six seeds keep the shortcut. On gold spectra the two training sets perform similarly. Multimodal language models used for scientific decisions should be tested on equivalent representations and on missing evidence, not only on average accuracy. We release the tasks, per-response results and analysis code.
bullets: Representation changes alone shifted accuracy by up to 41 percentage points within a model, especially for photon-energy tables and plots.
Changing the query from wavelength to photon energy helped some model–view pairs by 16–50 points but hurt others by up to 25.
When relevant extrema were removed, unadapted models rarely responded “undetermined.”
LoRA fine-tuning improved trained formats but could exploit truncation as a shortcut; training on answerable truncations largely prevented this.
The released tasks, per-response results, and code support evaluation of representation invariance and missing-evidence handling.

papers.abstract: Multi-image vision-language models (VLMs) incur substantial computation when processing long visual sequences. Compressing these sequences must preserve complementary evidence across images and keep tokens from different images separate. Global selection can underrepresent question-relevant images, and pruning in early decoder layers risks removing relevant content before sufficient multimodal processing, yet existing methods spend most of the budget on these early layers. We propose SIEVE, a training-free, single-pass framework that jointly allocates visual tokens across images and decoder depth. SIEVE first pools each image into a compact spatial grid to reduce early processing cost. It then progressively selects representatives using prompt attention under equal per-image quotas and aggregates unselected tokens into similar representatives from the same image. These operations keep every image represented and its tokens separate from other images, while refining the retained representations. A closed-form schedule sets retention counts to target a prescribed average token budget across decoder layers. Across four VLM backbones, SIEVE achieves the highest average at a 6.25% budget on five multi-image benchmarks and four single-image benchmarks, and the highest mean on two video benchmarks. On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, it outperforms the strongest baseline by 9.96 and 9.03 points at 6.25% and 12.5% budgets, and at 12.5% it exceeds the uncompressed model by 2.01 points with 6.6x fewer prefill FLOPs.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of compressing long multi-image visual sequences without losing question-relevant or cross-image evidence.
Pools each image into a compact grid, then progressively selects prompt-relevant tokens under equal per-image quotas.
Aggregates discarded tokens only into similar representatives from the same image, keeping image-specific information separate.
Uses a closed-form depth schedule to distribute token retention across decoder layers.

Across multiple VLM backbones and image/video benchmarks, SIEVE achieves leading average performance at low budgets; on LLaVA-OneVision-7B, it delivers 6.6× fewer prefill FLOPs while exceeding the uncompressed model at a 12.5% budget.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes SIEVE, a depth-aware token compression framework for multi-image VLMs that preserves spatial evidence, relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: SIEVE: Preserving Cross-Image Evidence via Depth-Aware Token Compression
papers.tldr: SIEVE is a training-free token-compression method that preserves evidence from every image while allocating computation across decoder layers, achieving strong accuracy with very small visual-token budgets.

papers.abstract: We propose \emph{Déjà Vu}, a test-time decoding module for semantic correspondence. Matching semantically equivalent keypoints across images of the same object category is challenging due to variations in appearance, viewpoint, and scale. While features from large pretrained vision models carry strong zero-shot correspondence ability, existing methods reduce final matching to greedy top-$1$ nearest-neighbor selection. We show that the correct correspondence appears among the top-ranked candidates far more often than top-$1$ matching achieves: with $30$ candidates, zero-shot features exceed the top-$1$ accuracy of a supervised model. This reveals a \textit{decoding bottleneck} rather than a limit of the representation. Motivated by this observation, we formulate semantic correspondence as a \textit{recall-then-rerank} problem. Our method first nominates an adaptive candidate set, larger when the similarity distribution is ambiguous and smaller when it is confident, then re-ranks the candidates with a graded cycle-consistency score: each candidate is matched back to the source image and penalized by how far its reverse match lands from the original keypoint. The module operates entirely on the similarity matrix already computed by the base method. It consistently improves three representative baselines on SPair-71k, its geometric subset, and PF-Pascal under both unsupervised and weakly supervised settings, with gains of up to $+1.8$ PCK@0.10 on SPair-71k and $+3.4$ PCK@0.15 on PF-Pascal, and $+4.9$ under Keypoint Average Precision.
bullets: Addresses a decoding bottleneck: pretrained vision features often contain the correct match among their top candidates, even when top-1 matching fails.
Uses a recall-then-rerank strategy with candidate-set size adapted to similarity ambiguity.
Scores candidates by graded cycle consistency, penalizing reverse matches that return far from the original keypoint.
Operates entirely on the base method’s existing similarity matrix and improves three baselines across SPair-71k and PF-Pascal settings.
Reports gains of up to +1.8 PCK@0.10, +3.4 PCK@0.15, and +4.9 in Keypoint Average Precision.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method overview. Given a query source patch, we apply top-p sampling on the row of the similarity matrix to form a candidate pool (forward pass). For each candidate, we perform a reverse lookup on its column to identify the nearest source patch (backward pass). Each candidate’s final score is its forward similarity minus a penalty that grows with the distance between its reverse match and the original query.

Figure 5: Qualitative examples showing the benefit of cycle-consistent re-ranking on SPair-71k. papers.abstract: Audio-language models (ALMs) are evaluated on their understanding of both speech and environmental sounds. What remains underexplored is how they respond when spoken claims contradict acoustic evidence within the same recording. We introduce SAC-Bench, a benchmark of intra-audio speech--acoustic conflict comprising 616,031 unique clips from 188 sound-event classes across seven semantic, temporal, and spatial tasks. It pairs environmental recordings with compatible or contradictory synthesized spoken claims and includes audio-only controls where applicable. Across five open-weight ALMs evaluated on semantic and temporal tasks, high audio-only accuracy often coexists with large losses under conflicting claims; Event Identity accuracy is 24.8--46.5 percentage points lower in conflict than compatible conditions. Temporal Order failures persist even when speech follows the complete event sequence, so simultaneous speech--event masking cannot fully explain them. A spatial case study with Spatial-Omni finds lower motion accuracy associated with both spoken claims and the speech source's physical trajectory. Prompt interventions sometimes restore acoustic accuracy, but can also reduce claim-aligned answers without improving grounding or worsen performance. SAC-Bench thus separates acoustic competence, conflict robustness, and intervention effects.
bullets: Introduces 616,031 clips covering 188 sound-event classes and seven semantic, temporal, and spatial tasks.
Tests compatible versus contradictory spoken claims paired with environmental recordings, plus audio-only controls.
Across five open-weight models, Event Identity accuracy drops by 24.8–46.5 percentage points under conflict.
Temporal-order errors remain even when speech comes after the full event sequence, suggesting masking is not the sole cause.
Prompt interventions have inconsistent effects and may not improve acoustic grounding.

papers.abstract: A child learns which words name which things from roughly 100 million words of input. Vision-language models trained at a comparable scale bind words to referents far less reliably, and we argue that part of the gap is structural: the usual next-token captioning objective has no variable standing for "this word refers to that region," so training applies no direct pressure to ground words. We add such a variable by treating each scene as a small assignment problem between the content words heard and the regions seen, solved as entropic optimal transport under two constraints. First, a word may be assigned to a special NOTHING column instead of any region, which matters because most content words in caregiver speech do not name anything visible. Second, no region may receive more than a bounded share of the assignment mass, a capacity constraint that encodes mutual exclusivity. The alignment step costs about eight Sinkhorn iterations, small next to the vision encoder. In controlled simulation, the naive version of the idea, a row-wise softmax that forces every word onto some region, collapses to 0.000 word-to-picture accuracy under realistic non-reference rates, below the 0.058 of captioning alone, while our two constraints reach 0.075 in that regime and 0.700 on clean input. A one-parameter version of the model reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy across three ambiguity conditions (RMSE 0.024). On the SAYCam infant video corpus, adding the alignment loss to a next-token captioning model raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38. A contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark, so our claim is that the loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, not that it sets a new best.
bullets: Motivation: Standard next-token captioning lacks an explicit variable linking words to visual regions, weakening referential grounding.
Method: Solve an entropic optimal-transport assignment between content words and regions, with a NOTHING option for non-referential words and capacity limits enforcing mutual exclusivity.
Results: On SAYCam, alignment improves word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38.

Controlled studies show the constrained formulation outperforms a row-wise softmax under realistic non-reference rates and matches adult cross-situational learning patterns across ambiguity conditions.
Scope: The method improves captioning-based grounding but does not outperform a contrastive model on that model’s benchmark.

papers.abstract: Cross-view geolocalization aims to determine the geographic location of a ground-level image by retrieving its corresponding satellite image, offering a promising alternative for localization in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-denied or degraded environments such as urban canyons, dense forests, and disaster scenarios. Despite recent progress, existing approaches remain limited by the lack of globally diverse training datasets and benchmarks that are often geographically restricted. Furthermore, most benchmarks rely on panoramic ground views, which do not reflect the limited field-of-view imagery captured by real world cameras. To address these challenges, we introduce Cross-View World 500k (CVW500k), a large-scale globally distributed dataset containing over 500,000 ground-satellite image pairs collected across diverse geographic regions and environments. Unlike previous datasets, CVW500k uses limited field-of-view ground images, providing a more realistic and challenging setting for cross-view geolocalization. In addition, we propose GeoQueryNet, a query-based cross-view fusion transformer framework designed to bridge the viewpoint gap between ground and satellite images. The model leverages a CLIP-based visual encoder with parameter-efficient LoRA adaptation and introduces a Cross-View Alignment Module that uses learnable query tokens to extract geographically consistent features across viewpoints. Our code can be found here: https://github.com/Fahim17/Cross_View_World_Dataset.git .
bullets: Cross-view geolocalization supports localization when GNSS is unavailable or degraded.
Existing datasets are geographically narrow and commonly use unrealistic panoramic ground imagery.
CVW500k provides over 500,000 globally distributed ground–satellite image pairs with limited-field-of-view observations.
GeoQueryNet combines a CLIP-based encoder, parameter-efficient LoRA adaptation, and learnable query tokens for cross-view feature alignment.
The abstract does not report quantitative results or comparisons.

papers.abstract: Computational brain imaging is constrained by a mismatch between increasingly diverse tasks and scarce, heterogeneous clinical data. Although existing brain foundation models transfer pretrained representations, their knowledge remains entangled within model-specific features and fixed architectures. This paper proposes BrainGFM, a generative foundation model that extends knowledge transfer beyond representation reuse through a reusable and reconfigurable brain-imaging prior. By pretraining on a corpus of about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices, BrainGFM supported task-aligned data synthesis for low-data predictive learning and task-adapted post-training for image reconstruction. Across 48 downstream tasks, BrainGFM improved segmentation and classification under limited supervision and achieved high-fidelity image enhancement across heterogeneous imaging conditions. Multicenter clinical validation involving 4,796 stroke patients across two internal and four external centers demonstrated its applicability to three clinically relevant tasks around stroke cohorts. Blinded reader assessments showed that BrainGFM-generated FLAIR images approached acquired FLAIR in overall diagnostic quality. In a human-AI collaboration study, BrainGFM assistance yielded a 14% relative improvement in mean radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy. These findings support generative priors as a reusable foundation for heterogeneous computational brain-imaging applications.
authors: Multi-Center Cooperative Clinical Study Group for "Lesion-Phenotype Brain Mapping in Acute Stroke"
bullets: Addresses scarce, heterogeneous clinical data and the limitations of fixed, representation-based brain foundation models.
Pretrains a reusable, reconfigurable prior on about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices.
Supports task-aligned synthesis for low-data prediction and post-training for image reconstruction.
Improved segmentation and classification across 48 downstream tasks and enabled high-fidelity enhancement across imaging conditions.
Multicenter stroke validation showed clinical applicability; radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy improved by 14% with AI assistance.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of BrainGFM for Computational brain imaging. a. Heterogeneity in brain diseases, patient populations, clinical status, acquisition protocols, and clinical centers produces heterogeneous brain imaging distributions and limits the generalization of DL models. b. Our BrainGFM-1.3M comprises about 1.3 million axial slices spanning major MRI sequences and CT, providing a large-scale dataset for brain generative pretraining. c. Our BrainGFM learns a reusable brain-imaging prior from generative pretraining on our BrainGFM-1.3M dataset. d. Task-specific conditioning controls the pretrained generator where class labels are used for class-conditioned synthesis, segmentation masks for spatially conditioned synthesis, and source images for brain image reconstruction. These conditions are combined with task-specific adaptation as detailed in Fig. 6b,c. e. Evaluation spans 48 downstream tasks, comprising 20 segmentation, 8 classification, and 20 imageenhancement tasks. f. Clinical validation in a multicenter stroke cohort assesses BrainGFM for TOAST stroke subtyping, lesion segmentation, and MRI sequence transformation, as well as its clinical utility in reader studies and radiologist-AI collaboration.

Fig. 6 BrainGFM architecture, generative pretraining and downstream adaptation. a. BrainGFM pretraining consists of brain-domain adaptation of a multi-scale visual tokenizer and next-scale autoregressive generative pretraining. A shared encoder (E) and vector quantizer (Q) map brain images and segmentation masks into multi-scale discrete tokens using a shared visual codebook. The autoregressive Transformer learns the distribution of tokens through coarse-to-fine next-scale prediction under categorical modality and sequence conditions. The pretrained decoder (D) reconstructs brain images or segmentation masks from generated tokens. b. Task-aligned data synthesis adapts BrainGFM with limited supervision using LoRA. For classification, task-specific class conditioning enables the synthesis of class-labelled images for training ResNet50. For segmentation, BrainGFM generates task-specific masks and synthesizes corresponding images, producing image-mask pairs for training UNet. c. Task-adapted post-training adapts BrainGFM for image enhancement using paired source-target images. Source-image tokens condition autoregressive prediction of target-image tokens, while LoRA is optimized using token-level prediction and image-level reconstruction losses.

Fig. 7 Data flow and study design of BrainGFM. a. Eleven public brain-imaging resources comprising 64,754 3D volumes and 1,295,080 axial slices were collected and partitioned into pretraining and held-out subsets. The pretraining subset was used for two-stage generative pretraining, including visual tokenizer training and autoregressive modeling.Heldout samples from nine shared datasets, together with 15 additional public datasets, supported downstream evaluation across 48 tasks, including segmentation (20 tasks), classification (8 tasks), and image enhancement (20 tasks). Task-specific training data were constructed through labeled image–mask pair generation, class-conditioned image synthesis, and source– target image pairing. b. Six clinical stroke cohorts comprising 4,796 patients and 4,829 cases from two internal centers (JLH and NFH) and four external centers (NJH, WXPH, NJPH, and CZSPH) were collected. Task-eligible cases were selected according to task-specific imaging and annotation criteria for lesion segmentation, TOAST subtyping, and DWI-to-FLAIR transformation. Internal-center data were used for task-specific training, including low-data settings, while separate internal and external test sets were used for clinical validation.

Fig. 13 Representative cases illustrating diagnostic improvement and deterioration following BrainGFM assistance. a. Six ischemic stroke cases in which BrainGFM assistance improved radiologists’ stroke-subtyping accuracy. b. Two cases in which diagnostic accuracy deteriorated following AI assistance. For each case, DWI and ADC maps are shown alongside patient age, sex, large-vessel occlusion status, and atrial fibrillation status. Donut charts show the proportion of the three radiologists who correctly identified the stroke subtype before (experts alone) and after (experts assisted by AI) BrainGFM assistance, with red and blue sectors indicating correct and incorrect diagnoses. These examples illustrate the potential diagnostic benefits of BrainGFM assistance and the risk of deterioration in initially correct clinical judgments.
Fig. 8 Modality- and sequence-conditioned brain image and segmentation mask generation by BrainGFM.

papers.abstract: Converting a raster image into a resolution-independent, stroke-editable vector sketch while faithfully preserving both structural contours and tonal texture remains challenging: raster-space rendering pipelines are difficult to edit at the stroke level, while generation-from-scratch vectorization methods struggle to remain faithful to an arbitrary input image. We present SketchForge, a training-free framework that converts an input raster image into a resolution-independent SVG sketch through per-instance test-time optimization of Bezier curves, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning. Strokes are seeded via a contour and attention-guided initialization, then refined by a vector-native differentiable rendering pipeline that decouples structural contour strokes from free-form texture strokes under dedicated objectives, composited via multiply-blend layering. Extensive experiments show that SketchForge consistently outperforms existing vector-based baselines in structural fidelity and generation quality. Project page: https://khangcntn123.github.io/SketchForge
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving contours and tonal texture while producing resolution-independent, stroke-editable vectors.
Uses per-image test-time optimization of Bezier curves, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning.
Initializes strokes with contour- and attention-guided seeds, then refines them using differentiable vector rendering.
Separately optimizes structural contour strokes and free-form texture strokes, combining them with multiply blending.
Experiments report improved structural fidelity and generation quality over existing vector-based baselines.],

papers.abstract: Dense labels of the aorta in CT are slow to draw, and the public aortic CT datasets that could stand in for them each label different structures under their own conventions. Large language model (LLM) agents can now write code and read images. We asked whether such a model labels these scans better as a free-form agent that writes its own segmentation code, or inside a harness, where an automated pass labels the scan and the model reviews the result. We built a harness, Taurus, and compared it with free-form agents by blind label recovery: we withheld the human labels of six public datasets (939 volumes) and scored every approach against each dataset's own classes. In the first version of Taurus, the model's review raised the primary metric on only two of six datasets, by less than the noise between two reviews of the same case. A free-form agent running Claude Opus 5.5 scored higher on most datasets. Moving what the free-form agents did well into the automated pass then carried most of the gain on 38 held-out cases. The final version smooths the label surfaces with a fixed rule and checks for the large errors the automated pass tends to make, such as an aneurysm drawn to half its size. Each check that fires puts a multiple-choice question to the model, with candidate corrections drawn on the scan. It matched the surface smoothness of the human references, and in the primary metric we found no difference from the free-form Opus agent, at under half its cost, $1.22 against $2.71 per case. Most of what made Taurus competitive came from the harness and its automation rather than from the language model itself. Taurus shows that this kind of annotation can be automated, so that expert time can move from drawing labels to checking them.
bullets: Dense aortic CT labeling is slow, and public datasets use inconsistent structure-labeling conventions.
Taurus combines automated segmentation with LLM review, targeted error checks, candidate corrections, and fixed surface smoothing.
It was evaluated through blind label recovery on six public datasets totaling 939 volumes, plus 38 held-out cases.
The final system matched the free-form Opus agent on the primary metric and matched human-reference surface smoothness.
The reported cost was $1.22 per case versus $2.71 for the free-form agent; most gains came from the harness and automation.

papers.abstract: Outpainting sparse sketches while preserving contour coherence and stroke style remains challenging. We present SketchBloom, a training-free framework that combines pretrained raster outpainting and style-transfer guidance with per-instance vector optimization. Given a sketch, a scene prompt, and an optional reference style, it produces an editable Scalable Vector Graphic (SVG) composed of Bezier strokes. Adaptive latent blending balances content contours and reference texture without model retraining. A reference-derived stroke vocabulary initializes contour- and DINO-attention-guided strokes, which are optimized separately for structure and texture before contour-emphasizing multiply fusion. As in prior optimization-based vector sketching, no task-specific network is trained; our contribution is the synthesis design specialized to sketch outpainting. On LineArtOut-1K, comprising 1,024 input and style combinations, SketchBloom improves perceptual, semantic, and structural fidelity over the evaluated vector baselines when all methods vectorize the same outpainted raster. This protocol evaluates vector synthesis rather than end-to-end outpainting or reference-style superiority. Runtime is approximately six minutes per pair on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. Project page: https://khangcntn123.github.io/SketchBloom/
bullets: Addresses contour coherence and stroke-style preservation in sparse sketch outpainting.
Combines pretrained raster outpainting and style-transfer guidance with per-instance vector optimization.
Initializes and separately optimizes Bezier strokes for structure and texture, then fuses them with contour emphasis.
On 1,024 LineArtOut-1K input/style combinations, it improves perceptual, semantic, and structural fidelity over evaluated vector baselines under a shared-raster protocol.
Runs in approximately six minutes per pair on a single NVIDIA H200; evaluation does not establish end-to-end outpainting or reference-style superiority.

papers.abstract: A deep understanding of scientific literature often relies on interpreting figures that contain key information beyond the main text. Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract insights from these figures can significantly accelerate knowledge discovery. Existing works on Scientific Visual Question Answering rely on resource-intensive training pipelines that are often inaccessible and require large computational resources. Instead of designing complex architectures, we propose RE- SciVQA, which focuses on improving the quality of retrieved context and fine-tuning small LLMs with parameter-efficient LoRA training. Using a simple query expansion step, relevant section headers are appended to the original question to improve the retrieval coverage. In addition, a simple adjustment of similarity scores is applied using figure references and caption alignment. On the SciVQA benchmark, RE-SciVQA achieves a ROUGE-1 F1 score of 73.9%, outperforming chart-focused models such as UniChart (14.7%), ChartGemma (6.9%), and Matcha-ChartQA (6.3%). Our relevance-enhanced RAG setup also improves the exact match by 11.9% and the fuzzy match by 29.5% compared with a standard RAG baseline, resulting in an overall gain of 14.3%. We also examine closed-ended infinite visual questions, a category in which chart-understanding models often struggle. Our experiments show that using plot digitization instead of synthetic captions leads to an 18.5% improvement for this question type.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost and limited accessibility of existing Scientific VQA pipelines.
Expands questions with relevant section headers and adjusts retrieval scores using figure references and caption alignment.
Uses LoRA to fine-tune smaller LLMs rather than relying on complex architectures or resource-intensive training.
On SciVQA, reports a 73.9% ROUGE-1 F1 score and improves exact and fuzzy matching over standard RAG.
For closed-ended infinite visual questions, plot digitization improves performance over synthetic captions by 18.5%.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in audio and video understanding. However, existing models struggle with long-form, multi-speaker videos, especially in understanding the entire video and recognizing who says what and when. To characterize the capability limit of current omni LLMs and guide future model development, we introduce Omnilingual-MsASR, a multilingual, multimodal benchmark for long-form Multi-speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (MsASR) covering six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers. Omnilingual-MsASR provides parallel audio and video inputs to evaluate models' cross-modal consistency and their ability to exploit complementary cues across modalities. Extensive evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs reveal substantial performance bottlenecks, while their tcpWERs frequently exceed 100%. These findings highlight fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key challenges for future omni-modal foundation models. Our work is available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua-Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua-MSpeaker.
bullets: Covers six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers.
Provides parallel audio and video inputs to assess cross-modal consistency and complementary information use.
Evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs show substantial performance bottlenecks, with tcpWER frequently exceeding 100%.
Highlights fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key open challenges.

papers.abstract: Multi-step visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers complex questions by repeatedly retrieving visual evidence, updating an intermediate state, and deciding whether to continue searching or answer. Yet retrieving relevant evidence does not ensure its effective use throughout the reasoning trajectory. As multi-step reasoning progresses, redundant sources occupy context capacity needed for missing evidence, observations tied to resolved requirements or unproductive searches linger in context, and visual sources are revisited with insufficient detail for fine-grained reading. We term this loss of usable evidence over a reasoning trajectory trajectory-level evidence utilization degradation. To address it, we propose Trajectory-Aware Evidence Coordination (TAEC), a training-free framework that coordinates evidence use around unresolved answer requirements. TAEC tracks these requirements in a shared trajectory state to guide which evidence enters the context, how accumulated memory is retained, and at what level of detail visual evidence is examined. Under a unified evaluation protocol on ViDoSeek, SlideVQA, and MMLongBench-Doc, TAEC achieves the best overall performance against leading training-free visual RAG baselines, with the highest average accuracy across multiple proprietary vision-language models. These results demonstrate that aligning evidence with evolving reasoning needs improves evidence use throughout multi-step visual RAG.
bullets: Addresses trajectory-level evidence utilization degradation, where redundant, outdated, or insufficiently detailed evidence hinders ongoing reasoning.
Uses a shared trajectory state to track unresolved answer requirements.
Guides context inclusion, memory retention, and the visual-detail level used for evidence examination.
A training-free framework evaluated on ViDoSeek, SlideVQA, and MMLongBench-Doc.
Reports the best overall performance among leading training-free visual RAG baselines across multiple proprietary vision-language models.

papers.abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) achieve remarkable success on diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks, yet they still struggle to effectively leverage language-based chain-of-thought reasoning for image generation. As a result, existing reasoning-augmented UMMs often fail to inherit the test-time scaling and fine-grained controllability observed in large language models. We attribute this failure to a fundamental modality mismatch: reasoning is performed in a discrete token space, whereas image generation operates in a continuous space. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Latent Reasoning framework in Continuous space (LARC), which alleviates the token-level bottleneck by reasoning over continuous hidden states. Specifically, the training framework consists of two stages: (i) curriculum supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (ii) information-gain reinforcement learning (RL). First, the curriculum SFT stage gradually converts token-level reasoning into latent reasoning. Subsequently, the information-gain RL stage self-evolves latent reasoning without ground truth supervision. Experiments across diverse text-to-image generation benchmarks show that LARC consistently improves generation quality, prompt following, and compositional fidelity. Notably, LARC achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval with a 7%p gain over BAGEL and demonstrates clear test-time scaling behavior, outperforming token-based generation under both parallel and sequential test-time scaling strategies.
authors: Byungwoo Jeon, Yoonwoo Jeong, Hyunseok Lee, Minsu Cho, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between discrete language reasoning and continuous image generation.

papers.abstract: A panoramic video captures all directions around the camera, but relevant evidence can appear in different directions and at different times. Understanding it requires models to connect observations across the viewing sphere and time. We introduce PanoVideoBench, the first manually annotated benchmark for comprehensive panoramic video understanding. Its 1,000 questions span five categories and 15 question types, with diagnostic annotations for target search and panoramic capabilities. Evaluation of 11 proprietary, open-source, and panoramic-specialized models identifies cross-view tracking and sphere-time evidence integration as their weakest capabilities. To strengthen these capabilities, we construct PanoVideoCoT, the first reasoning dataset grounded in real panoramic video, through sphere-time-grounded synthesis that converts verified panoramic observations and successful agentic explorations into 13,465 QA-CoT pairs. Starting from a general video MLLM, PanoVideoReasoner learns from this corpus through Panoramic CoT SFT and Evidence-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation, a panoramic instantiation of Vision-OPD's OPSD in which the teacher uses verified perspective views to guide student-generated trajectories. It reaches 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving the backbone by 12.5 points and the previous SOTA by 2.6. The gains concentrate on the same spatial, cross-view, and temporal capabilities exposed by the benchmark, showing that grounded sphere-time supervision can equip a general video MLLM with panoramic reasoning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available \href{https://github.com/ening-open/cogalign}{here}.
authors: Ning E, Changde Du, Yizhuo Lu, Huiguang He
bullets: Targets the unclear correspondence between MLLM internal criteria and the latent structure of human cognition.

Improves consistency with human similarity judgments while retaining competitive multimodal benchmark performance.
Searchlight RSA on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset shows increased model–human representational alignment.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Cortical projection of representational alignment improvements across subjects. The heatmaps visualize the voxel-wise difference in ∆̃RSA(c) scores between the aligned and baseline Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct model. Darker colors indicate better representational alignment between models and human brain. Consistent positive shifts are observed, demonstrating that our alignment framework robustly shifts the MLLMs internal representational geometry to be more human-like.

Figure 1: Overview of triplet-level semantic dimension attribution. (a) Human similarity judgements are collected via crowdsourcing. Then learning a representational embedding space via SPoSE yields the multidimensional mental representations of natural objects. (b) For one triplet, we compute the original softmax probability based on the entire representational embedding for all pairs. We then iteratively prune each dimension from the representational embedding space and compute the changes in softmax probabilities relative to those obtained with the full embedding as the relevance score for that dimension. By sorting these relevance scores in descending order, we establish a hierarchical ranking of dimensional importance. The top-1 dimension yielding the maximum probability change is regarded as the most salient semantic dimension driving the human decision-making.

Figure 3: (a) Overview of hybrid dataset. The total dataset includes three subsets: Single-image (126K samples), Multi-image (102K samples), and Cognitive-Alignment (80K samples). (b) Examples. The examples include Spot the Difference, Image Edit Instruction, Visual Storytelling, LLaVAR, COCO Caption, and Odd-One-Out tasks.

Figure 2: Pipeline for dimension-grounded reasoning enhancement. This pipeline illustrates the process of reasoning enhancement via LLM. For one triplet with their textual descriptions and the most salient semantic dimension d∗ driving human decision-making, we integrate them into the structured prompt Prompt(T , cap(T ), d∗). LLM is then utilized exclusively to enhance reasoning. By injecting the dimension d∗, we guide the LLM to perform targeted reasoning enhancement. This effectively converts discrete cognitive criteria for decision-making into explicit CoT rationale r(d∗).

Figure 5: Stability of alignment shifts across different extraction depths. The cortical projections display the alignment improvements ∆̃RSA(c) of subject 1 computed using features from the last layer, the second-to-last layer, and the concatenation of the last four layers. Darker regions reflect better alignment improvement. The spatial distribution of these positive shifts remains consistent regardless of the extraction depth, confirming that the achieved representational alignment with human cognition is robust and not a selective layer choice.

papers.abstract: Inserting an unseen part requires sub-millimetre precision and the correct orientation of keyed features. Current zero-shot agentic manipulation methods built on vision-language models (VLMs) produce spatial outputs that are far too coarse for this. We propose to let a VLM build a sketch model of the task, i.e., a few geometric primitives and two mate frames, which a VLM agent measures with geometric tools in multi-view depth and which a standard planner and compliant controller execute. Because a sketch describes the parts independently of their placement, the robot needs to build it only once per task. A sketch memory stores each agent run and transfers the stored sketch to later placements by point-cloud registration, so that the VLM is called only for unfamiliar parts. After grasping the part, the robot inspects both mating faces at close range and corrects the sketch by shape matching. On 69 simulated insertion episodes, our method inserts 88% of the parts at the assembled pose in a strict kinematic test, while ReKep and MOKA with the same VLM insert none. On new placements of eight tasks, reusing one stored run inserts as many parts as calling the agent in each episode, and it produces the sketch in 3.4 s instead of about 90 s.
bullets: Targets sub-millimetre insertion of keyed parts, where existing VLM-based agents produce overly coarse spatial outputs.
A VLM builds a task sketch with geometric primitives and mate frames; geometric tools, a standard planner, and compliant control execute it.
The robot refines the sketch by inspecting mating faces at close range and shape-matching them after grasping.
A sketch memory transfers prior sketches to new placements via point-cloud registration, invoking the VLM only for unfamiliar parts.
In 69 simulated episodes, SketchMate achieved 88% strict-kinematic insertion versus 0% for ReKep and MOKA; reuse matched fresh agent calls while reducing sketch creation from about 90 s to 3.4 s.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly capable of understanding images and performing complex visual reasoning, suggesting the possibility of using them to automate biological image analysis. This need is becoming increasingly urgent as advances in technology continue to generate ever larger and more diverse microscopy datasets, already exceeding the scale at which manual visual analysis is feasible. With the final aim to use MLLMs for visual comparison of complex phenotypes, we investigate a very simple baseline: comparison of the size of body parts in synthetic images of ants. We find that state-of-the-art open-weight MLLMs fail for some body parts, but not for others, even though the comparison itself is visually trivial for all of them. We evaluate different in-context learning strategies and analyze performance on the related object recognition task. Our results suggest a recognition-driven grounding failure: structures that the models cannot recognize are instead associated with a recognizable semantic concept, impairing the grounding and comparison of both. Further analysis of the vision encoder is consistent with the hypothesis that fine-grained visual structure may be less well preserved without semantic support. Together, our results reveal a surprising limitation of current MLLMs: semantic recognition can gate simple visual comparisons that do not intrinsically require semantic understanding. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/kreshuklab/Open-Weight-MLLMs-Cannot-Compare-What-They-Cannot-Name
bullets: The study tests MLLM comparison of ant body-part sizes in synthetic images, motivated by scalable biological image analysis.
Models succeed on some parts but fail on others despite equivalent visual comparison difficulty.
In-context learning strategies and a related object-recognition task are evaluated.

papers.abstract: A central challenge in multimodal in-context learning (MICL) arises from tasks that are ill-defined without context and require uncovering the underlying rules from demonstrations. Existing methods predominantly treat MICL as direct input-output mapping, overlooking the importance of explicitly inducing and reasoning over such rules, limiting both performance and interpretability. We propose ERIM, Explicit Rule-Induction for Multimodal In-Context Learning, a unified framework that enhances MICL by explicitly inducing the latent rules governing demonstration samples. Leveraging the reasoning ability of multi-modal large language model (MLLM), ERIM constructs rule-centric MICL datasets, introduces explicit supervision for rule induction, and fine-tunes MLLM to perform explicit rule-induction via a two-stage training strategy that combines mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments show consistent performance improvements across diverse MICL settings and demonstrate that correctly inducing underlying rules directly leads to stronger and more stable performance.
authors: Yuquan Li, Xinyang Jiang, Yuhao Xue, Cairong Zhao
bullets: Addresses ill-defined MICL tasks whose solutions depend on uncovering rules from examples.
Uses multimodal large language models to construct rule-centric data and provide explicit rule-induction supervision.
Trains models in two stages with mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning.
Experiments across diverse MICL settings show consistent gains and more stable performance.
The approach focuses on settings where latent rules can be inferred from demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Bridging independent vision-language models (VLMs) and small language models (SLMs) in a modular multi-agent system typically forces them to exchange information as discrete text, which creates a lossy bottleneck for spatial and fine-grained details. This constraint is especially acute for SLMs, whose limited capacity makes them more reliant on the quality of the input signal. Recent latent-communication methods exchange states between language models. How a VLM can pass visual information to a separately pretrained text-only SLM though remains unexplored. We propose \textbf{Latent-Lens}, a lightweight codec that bridges the representation gap between a frozen VLM and a frozen SLM directly in latent space, enabling them to communicate purely through hidden states. The codec consists of a domain encoder that projects hidden states from the VLM into the SLM's embedding space, and an attention decoder formalised as a LoRA that teaches the SLM to attend to these visual prefixes, while training only ${\sim}1.6$M parameters (0.2\% of the combined model size). On visual question answering (CLEVR, GQA), Latent-Lens achieves $81.0\pm7.9$\% and $65.4\pm5.4$\%, compared with $58.3\pm5.7$\% and $61.8\pm1.0$\% for text communication with the same LoRA budget (+30.2--69.8pp relative to frozen text communication), while on image captioning (Flickr8k) it improves over the same baseline by +16.5 (+18.8 frozen). We also evaluate Latent-Lens with TinyLlama-1.1B and InternVL2-1B, which use different architectures, vocabularies, and hidden dimensions.
authors: Mo Shahdloo, Faegheh Sardari, Mathew Salvaris
bullets: Addresses the loss of spatial and fine-grained visual information caused by text-only communication between modular VLMs and SLMs.
Uses a lightweight codec with a domain encoder mapping VLM states into the SLM embedding space and a LoRA-based attention decoder for visual prefixes.
Trains only about 1.6M parameters, or 0.2% of the combined model size, while keeping both models frozen.
Reports higher performance than matched text-communication baselines on CLEVR, GQA, and Flickr8k.
Demonstrates compatibility across models with different architectures, vocabularies, and hidden dimensions.

papers.abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of gene expression is key to studying complex diseases like cancer. While Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) and Single-Cell Transcriptomics (scT) provide high-resolution insights, they remain expensive and scarce. In contrast, standard histopathology Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. This work introduces a Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) capable of simultaneously predicting bulk, spatial, and single-cell transcriptomics directly from WSIs. By extracting morphological features using a Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) (UNI2-h) and constructing spatial graphs at both patch and cell levels, the model learns the hierarchical relationships within the tissue. The network is trained on a combined dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA), Visium, and Xenium samples across lung, kidney, and breast tissues. A hybrid training strategy is employed, leveraging direct supervision alongside weakly supervised consistency losses to ensure predictions align across biological scales. Results show the model accurately predicts gene expression at the slide level and moderately at the patch level (strongest on Xenium), and achieves moderate correlation at the challenging single-cell level. Furthermore, downstream tasks explore the clinical relevance of these predictions, demonstrating their utility in survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification via molecular signatures.
authors: Miguel Andrade, Jos\'e Almeida, Carlos Santiago, Catarina Barata
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and cost of high-resolution spatial and single-cell transcriptomics by leveraging widely available WSIs and bulk RNA-seq.
Extracts morphology with the UNI2-h pathology foundation model and builds hierarchical patch- and cell-level spatial graphs.
Trains with direct supervision and weakly supervised consistency losses across bulk, spatial, and single-cell biological scales.
Evaluated on TCGA, Visium, and Xenium samples from lung, kidney, and breast tissues.
Predictions support survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification using molecular signatures.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have made significant progress in spatial reasoning, particularly by integrating RGB images with depth data, which is often assumed to faithfully reflect physical distances. However, mirrors violate this assumption: they distort depth readings while reproducing object appearances, making reflections difficult to distinguish from real objects. As existing benchmarks rarely consider such reflective scenarios, VLM performance in mirror scenes remains largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce a mirror-centric RGB-D dataset from reflective scenes to evaluate the spatial reasoning capabilities of state-of-the-art VLMs in these scenarios. Specifically, we collect 1,011 RGB-D images from 525 real-world scenes, spanning diverse indoor and outdoor environments, six reflective surface types, and both daytime and nighttime conditions. All images are annotated with reflective surface region masks and mask annotations for both directly observed and mirror-reflected objects. Then, we curate a benchmark named MIRA-Bench (Mirror-Induced Reasoning Ambiguity Benchmark), comprising 14,140 QA pairs across eight sub-tasks organized into three cognitive levels: Reflection-aware Perception, Spatial Reasoning, and Scene-level Decision-making. We evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs on MIRA-Bench and find consistent failures across tasks: models misclassify whether objects are directly observed or reflected, fail to match reflected instances to their real-world counterparts, and produce erroneous spatial inferences. Remarkably, providing depth data actually degrades reasoning performance, implying that VLMs cannot identify incorrect depth in mirror scenes. The code and data are available at https://github.com/EvaYin-cloud/MIRA-Bench
authors: Hao Yin, Tianchen Guo, Heming Du, Yan Ke, Yanbin Liu, Xin Yu
bullets: Introduces a mirror-centric RGB-D dataset of 1,011 images from 525 real-world scenes across varied environments, reflective surfaces, and lighting conditions.
Provides annotations for reflective regions, directly observed objects, and mirror-reflected objects.
Builds MIRA-Bench with 14,140 QA pairs spanning eight tasks and three levels: reflection-aware perception, spatial reasoning, and scene-level decision-making.
State-of-the-art VLMs often confuse reflections with real objects, fail to associate reflections with their sources, and make incorrect spatial inferences.
Depth input degrades performance, suggesting models do not recognize unreliable depth measurements in mirror scenes.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently been extended to vision-language models (VLMs), yet its effectiveness remains limited for text-rich reasoning tasks. We highlight a key factor contributing to this limitation: models frequently arrive at correct final answers despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate steps. We define this phenomenon as Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR). Because standard RLVR rewards only final-answer correctness, it fails to differentiate between properly grounded and misgrounded reasoning, reinforcing both equally. Through token-level analysis, we reveal that CVMR tokens exhibit distinct attention patterns that differ systematically from well-grounded ones. Based on this observation, we propose GRIT, a training framework that incorporates visual grounding into RLVR to mitigate the impact of CVMR. Furthermore, to address the lack of text-rich reasoning benchmarks that allow for systematic evaluation across text length and reasoning depth, we introduce GRIT-Bench. Experiments demonstrate that GRIT significantly improves both reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.
authors: Chanseul Cho, Noori Bae, Dongheon Lee, Youngmin Ro
bullets: Identifies Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR), where models answer correctly despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate reasoning.
Shows that CVMR tokens have distinct attention patterns from well-grounded tokens.
Introduces GRIT, which uses gradient masking to incorporate visual grounding into RLVR training.
Introduces GRIT-Bench for evaluating text-rich reasoning across text length and reasoning depth.
Experiments report improved reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.
