papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard reasoning strategy in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), showing strong performance in complex vision-language tasks such as reasoning segmentation. However, our analysis reveals that indiscriminate CoT usage can lead to degraded performance by inducing unnecessary reasoning, a phenomenon we term overthinking. In reasoning segmentation, overthinking often leads to misalignment between the query's intent and visual grounding. To address this, we propose Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT), a training-free adaptive framework that selectively triggers CoT based on the input's intrinsic difficulty. We find that the entropy of the model's attention maps reliably reflects task difficulty: low entropy indicates confident, localized grounding, while high entropy suggests uncertainty and potential benefit from CoT. DA-CoT uses this entropy signal to determine whether to apply CoT prompting. Additionally, we introduce a Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism that enables the model to automatically flip its reasoning decision when the initial output fails, enhancing robustness by recovering from failures induced by overthinking and underthinking. DA-CoT demonstrates its effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Reasoning Segmentation benchmarks while significantly improving inference efficiency.
authors: Chanseul Cho, Jaesung Jun, Dongheon Lee, Youngmin Ro
bullets: Problem: Always-on CoT can cause overthinking, misaligning visual grounding with the query.
Method: Estimate input difficulty from attention-map entropy; high entropy triggers CoT, while low entropy skips it.
Robustness: Bidirectional Rethinking reverses the initial reasoning choice when the output fails.
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on reasoning segmentation benchmarks and improves inference efficiency.
Scope: Training-free adaptive inference for multimodal reasoning segmentation.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of the proposed DA-CoT framework during inference. The aggregated attention entropy Hagg, computed over the pre-identified layers L, is used to adaptively decide whether to trigger CoT reasoning. If Hagg ≥ τ , the model follows the Difficulty-Aware Prompting Path with CoT for structured reasoning; otherwise, it takes the direct path without CoT for efficient inference. When the initial reasoning path fails to produce a valid output, a discrete flipping signal activates the Bidirectional Rethinking Path, enabling re-evaluation and recovery from overthinking or underthinking. The final bounding boxes or point prompts are then passed to the segmentation head to produce the reasoningaware segmentation result.

Figure 2. Qualitative examples illustrating the contrasting effects of CoT prompting in reasoning segmentation. Left: CoT-detrimental cases, where CoT leads to misgrounding by overthinking spatial reasoning; without CoT, the model correctly identifies the target with concentrated attention and low entropy. Right: CoT-beneficial cases, where CoT enhances performance in ambiguous scenarios by guiding reasoning towards the correct region, as reflected in high-entropy attention maps. The visualized attention entropy (bottom right of each map) provides an intrinsic signal that distinguishes when CoT is helpful or harmful.

papers.abstract: Real-world robotic manipulation requires reasoning about cluttered scenes, partially observable or hidden objects, and semantically appropriate actions, in addition to low-level execution within those scenes. However, existing simulation benchmarks primarily test the latter and remain dominated by comparatively clean environments with limited clutter and narrowly scoped task structure, leaving many forms of commonsense reasoning untested. We address this by introducing a taxonomy of reasoning processes for robotic manipulation grounded in developmental cognitive science. We operationalize this taxonomy through a new benchmark of robot tasks, MolmoSpaces-CommonSense, that requires reasoning about occlusion, containment, support relations, semantically correct grasp points, spatial affordances, and hidden objects. These evaluations require policies not only to recognize relevant scene structure but also to execute correct actions in them. We evaluate several zero-shot generalist manipulation policies. Across model types and architectures, we observe consistent failures in commonsense reasoning: success rates in cluttered scenes drop by over 50% as distractors increase, policies act on incorrect objects in cluttered settings 30% of the time, and affordance-sensitive grasping remains unreliable even with highly specific language prompts, with correct object part selection happening only about 50% of the time. Further, VLM-based success estimation struggles to reliably evaluate rollouts in these settings, suggesting that the challenge extends beyond control to the broader perception-reasoning-action stack. Our results suggest that existing benchmarks may substantially overestimate zero-shot real-world readiness. Code and policy leaderboard link at https://github.com/allenai/molmospaces.
authors: Arjun Guru, Max Argus, Jae Sung Park, Jiafei Duan, Ali Farhadi, Ranjay Krishna
bullets: Introduces a developmental-cognitive-science taxonomy for commonsense reasoning in robotic manipulation.

Evaluates several zero-shot generalist policies on tasks requiring both scene reasoning and physical execution.
Policies show substantial failures: cluttered-scene success drops by over 50%, incorrect-object actions occur 30% of the time, and correct grasp-part selection is about 50%.
VLM-based rollout evaluation also struggles, indicating challenges across the perception–reasoning–action stack.

papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial reasoning is essential for connecting visual intelligence to thephysical world, yet remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), which must preserve scene state while tracking how spatial relations evolve over time. Meanwhile, video generation models (VGMs), trained to synthesize temporally coherent world dynamics, offer a rich source of spatiotemporal representations. We present GenDSR, a framework that transfers intermediate representations from VGM into VLM for dynamic spatial reasoning. Rather than treating a VGM feature as a monolithic prior, GenDSR constructs two complementary branches: a raw branch preserving holistic generative context and a delta branch emphasizing temporal variation. Task-conditioned tokenwise gates then fuse both signals and inject the result into the native visual representation. On DSR-Bench, GenDSR achieves 67.2%, surpassing the previous best result and establishing a new state of the art.
authors: Ke Yang, Zhenyu Zhang, Jun Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of tracking evolving spatial relations while preserving scene state over time.
Transfers intermediate video-generation-model representations into a vision-language model.
Uses complementary raw and temporal-delta branches to capture holistic context and changes over time.
Task-conditioned tokenwise gates fuse these signals with the model’s native visual representation.
Achieves 67.2% on DSR-Bench, exceeding the previous best result and setting a new state of the art.

papers.abstract: Multimodal indirect prompt injection embeds malicious instructions in external media that also contains information needed for the user's task. Existing defenses can block the attack yet impair the model's use of that information, leaving a gap between attack defense and task preservation. We propose ERASE, an on-policy self-distillation method that constructs its reference by erasing the injected region in place. Modality-appropriate blank content replaces the injection while the surrounding media is preserved. A student reading attacked media learns from a frozen base model reading the erased view through full-distribution token-level feedback on its own rollouts. Across image, audio, and video on two model sizes, ERASE records near-zero observed attack success on the evaluated benchmark while retaining task utility close to the undefended clean-input level. On 3B audio, ERASE reaches 60.1% attacked-input accuracy compared with ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level. Experiments show that ERASE reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio while staying close to the base model on the erased input. Out-of-domain accuracy also stays near the base level. Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Shuo Hong, Jiaxin Ma, Xidi Cai, Qianli Ma
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between blocking malicious instructions and retaining useful information from attacked media.
Uses on-policy self-distillation: a student processes attacked inputs while learning token-level behavior from a frozen base model viewing the erased version.
Evaluated across image, audio, and video with two model sizes, achieving near-zero observed attack success while maintaining near-clean-input task utility.
On 3B audio, ERASE achieves 60.1% attacked-input accuracy versus ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level.
Reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio, with out-of-domain accuracy near the base model level.

papers.abstract: While modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been remarkably successful in general scene text recognition, they consistently struggle with the long-tail distribution of text that is degraded by motion blur or low resolution. These limitations are particularly apparent in egocentric applications like smart glasses, where text is often captured in noisy environments. In this paper, we introduce the \textbf{BSTRB} (Blurry Scene Text Recognition Benchmark), a novel benchmark of 8,398 noisy image samples with high-fidelity annotations derived from 1,699 real-world video sequences. To support this, we present \textbf{Hawkeye}, a VLM fine-tuned on BSTRB to read and reason about illegible text by leveraging contextual priors and pixel-level alignment. Our results show that \name matches much larger VLMs on BSTRB overall and exceeds them on text at or below 20 pixels, in a single pass suited to real-time deployment. We characterize the resolution at which current VLMs begin to fail.
bullets: Introduces BSTRB, a benchmark of 8,398 noisy text images from 1,699 real-world video sequences with high-fidelity annotations.

Characterizes the resolution threshold where current VLMs begin to fail.

papers.abstract: Real-world image editing requires coordinating multiple visual transformations with content preservation and reference constraints, yet aggregate scores can readily obscure unmet local requirements. Effective evaluation must therefore identify local failures and translate them into priorities for subsequent model improvement. We introduce WeGenEditBench, comprising 2,740 evaluation instances and 148 task types across single-image, text-intensive, and multi-reference editing. Pre-generated checklists shared across models decompose each request into atomic requirements; item-level deductions and visual evidence are established first and then summarized into scores for edit execution, preservation, visual quality, and task-specific correctness. To support the experience-acquisition component of recursive self-improvement (RSI), we develop WeGenEvoStudio, a unified multi-agent harness for RSI-oriented learning that integrates model-conditioned failure diagnosis, retrieval-grounded data construction, supervised adaptation, and re-evaluation. Among 15 evaluated configurations, GPT-Image-2 leads single-image editing with an Overall score of 4.076, while Seedream-5.0-Pro leads text-intensive editing at 4.291. Evolution experiments across four generation and editing benchmarks demonstrate substantial targeted gains: on their report-selected Top-5 single-image targets, FLUX.2 [dev] improves Overall from 1.083 to 3.517, while Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 gains 13.2%. Together, our benchmark and harness provide a foundation for developing more reliable image models through interpretable evaluation and feedback-driven learning.

papers.abstract: Cameras and vision sensors are widely used for product and process inspection in manufacturing environments. Traditionally, this process required thousands of images of both nominal and defective products to train such models. Recent research shows that vision transformer (ViT) models, such as CLIP, can reduce this requirement to 50-100 images per nominal and defective class. However, collecting even 50 defective images can be difficult in high-yield or low-volume manufacturing processes. In this paper, we examine the utility of two recently proposed structured decision models (Jev and Clef-Flash) in applications using as few as k=2 reference images per class at inference. In the process, we provide three main contributions: (a) a framework for k-shot learning of these models for image classification/inspection applications; (b) an agentic approach for automatically refining the text descriptions that guide image classification in these decision models; and (c) an approach to calibrate the resulting defect probabilities to improve their reliability for inspection decisions. We test these contributions in five manufacturing case studies. Using two reference images per class, both Jev and Clef-Flash outperform CLIP's test accuracies with the same references (0.75-1.00 [Jev] and 0.71-0.99 [Clef-Flash] vs 0.67-0.84 [CLIP]). Furthermore, we show that our agentic refinement of text descriptions significantly improves accuracy across 6 of 8 model-application combinations, and our calibration approach reduces the Brier score in 13 of the 15 model-application configurations. To support the reproducibility of our work, we provide our replication code and have created the R "decisions" package for evaluating additional models. We also provide a publicly available web app that allows practitioners to inspect their own images with no code.
bullets: Addresses inspection settings where defective examples are scarce, requiring far fewer references than conventional models.
Introduces a k-shot learning framework for structured decision models in image classification and inspection.
Uses agentic refinement of text descriptions, improving accuracy in 6 of 8 model-application combinations.
Calibrates defect probabilities, reducing Brier score in 13 of 15 configurations.
Provides replication code, an R package, and a no-code web app for practitioner use.

papers.abstract: Stickers are widely used in social media dialogues to express affect, stance, and intent beyond literal text. Their meanings are often non-literal and context-dependent, making them difficult to handle with generic visual fusion or standalone captioning. We propose Sticker-to-Text Dialogue Reconstruction (S2TDR), a structured multimodal reconstruction framework that converts sticker turns into contextually appropriate textual utterances. S2TDR decomposes sticker interpretation into visual cue extraction, affective-intent inference, and context-aware dialogue reconstruction, using OCR text only as an auxiliary cue when available. The reconstructed dialogue can then be consumed by existing text-based dialogue models. Experiments on sentiment analysis, intent recognition, and dialogue summarization show that S2TDR generally improves multiple downstream models over direct sticker integration methods. Further analyses on component ablations, OCR-empty stickers, and reconstruction quality indicate that structured reconstruction provides an interpretable and effective way to integrate sticker semantics into dialogue understanding.
bullets: Addresses the non-literal, context-dependent meanings of stickers in social media dialogues.
Decomposes interpretation into visual cue extraction, affective-intent inference, and context-aware dialogue reconstruction.
Uses OCR text only as an auxiliary signal when available.
Improves downstream sentiment analysis, intent recognition, and dialogue summarization across multiple models compared with direct sticker integration.
Analyses cover component ablations, OCR-empty stickers, and reconstruction quality, supporting interpretability and effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Vision-language compositionality is the ability to identify which properties, relations, quantities, and states bind to which entities in both an image and a caption, and to match those bindings across modalities. Existing benchmarks evaluate this ability through image-text matching: a model ranks candidate image-caption match similarities and succeeds when the correct match comes on top. In such datasets, paired images differ by more than a single binding: scene, layout, and content all differ, with 97% of pixels changing on average. Such pairs do not isolate compositionality: results are confounded by global image differences. We introduce Compositional Single-EdiT (CompoSET), a benchmark dataset in which each base image-caption pair has an edited counterpart, or foil, that preserves the scene but differs by a single controlled edit, such as color, count, spatial relation, or object state. Base and foil images preserve naturalistic scene complexity yet are visually near-identical: only 8% of pixels change on average. Our dataset has many foils per base scene (~22) in order to separate scene difficulty from edit difficulty, a distinction one-foil-per-base benchmarks cannot make. CompoSET contains 1,776 instances across 80 naturalistic scenes, spanning 16 edit types in 4 semantic categories, with captions at 3 verbosity levels. We test 22 dual-encoder VLMs and find that all models perform at or below chance level on CompoSET, despite scoring well on prior benchmarks. This suggests that apparent progress under prior image-text matching protocols may be an artifact arising from confounds in benchmark design, and that compositional understanding in dual-encoder VLMs is far from solved. CompoSET addresses the confounds and offers a better controlled benchmark to measure future progress.
bullets: Existing image-text matching benchmarks confound compositionality with large global image differences.
Each CompoSET foil preserves the scene while changing one property, relation, quantity, or state; only 8% of pixels change on average.
Multiple foils per base scene (~22) separate scene difficulty from edit difficulty.
The benchmark includes 1,776 instances across 80 naturalistic scenes, 16 edit types, 4 semantic categories, and 3 caption verbosity levels.
All 22 evaluated dual-encoder VLMs performed at or below chance, questioning progress measured by prior protocols.

papers.selection_reason: Controlled single-edit benchmark isolating vision-language compositionality and exposing limitations of multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: CompoSET: A Controlled Single-Edit Benchmark for Vision-Language Compositionality
papers.tldr: CompoSET isolates vision-language compositionality with near-identical image-caption pairs differing by one controlled semantic edit, revealing that tested dual-encoder VLMs perform at or below chance despite strong prior benchmark results.

papers.abstract: Single-exposure high dynamic range (HDR) novel view synthesis (NVS) recovers HDR scenes from low dynamic range (LDR) views captured at a single exposure and estimates camera response function (CRF) for LDR re-exposure. Without HDR ground-truth, using single-exposure LDR views as the sole source of direct supervision underconstrains HDR reconstruction and cannot ensure its faithful recovery, motivating the need for learned LDR-to-HDR reconstruction priors. Moreover, single-exposure LDR views supervise CRF only over a limited range, necessitating a learnable prior for reliable re-exposure beyond it. We propose PriorGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that addresses both challenges by (1) guiding HDR recovery with pseudo-HDR supervision from 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction methods while anchoring it to input LDR views through a closed reconstruction loop; and (2) regularizing CRF modeling with a learnable prior that guarantees monotonicity and promotes plausible responses. Yet cross-view inconsistencies in independently generated pseudo-HDR targets impair scene reconstruction when HDR is encoded directly as Gaussian's color attribute. We therefore introduce a 3D base-gain HDR representation that factors HDR radiance into an LDR base and an overlaid 3D gain field, promoting robustness to such inconsistencies and enabling 3D HDR appearance editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate PriorGS's substantial superiority over baselines.
authors: Armin Shafiee Sarvestani, Sheyang Tang, Jialu Xu, Zhou Wang
bullets: Addresses underconstrained HDR recovery and limited camera response function supervision from single-exposure LDR views.
Uses pseudo-HDR reconstructions as guidance while enforcing consistency with input LDR images through a closed reconstruction loop.
Learns a monotonic CRF prior to support plausible LDR re-exposure beyond the observed intensity range.
Factors HDR radiance into an LDR base and 3D gain field, reducing the impact of inconsistent pseudo-HDR targets and enabling HDR appearance editing.
Reports substantial superiority over baselines in extensive experiments.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of PriorGS. Given single-exposure multi-view LDR captures of a scene, we reconstruct the 3D HDR scene as an LDR base extended by a 3D gain field. Input views supervise the LDR base, while pseudo-HDR targets generated by a 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction model impose LDR-to-HDR prior on HDR recovery. We then re-expose the HDR view by a priorconstrained learnable CRF to match the same input view, which closes the reconstruction loop.

Figure 1: Given the same single-exposure inputs, methods lacking learned LDR-to-HDR priors reconstruct the LDR novel view faithfully but fail at HDR radiance recovery. We leverage this prior to recover radiance much closer to the GT. HDR results are tone-mapped identically for visualization.

Figure 8: Representational capacity of our proposed CRF model on the DoRF database. (a) the 201 DoRF response curves. (b) the independently fitted responses of our CRF. All curves are displayed using a logarithmic irradiance axis; the zero-irradiance samples are included during fitting but omitted from the visualization.

papers.abstract: In multi-task settings, combining multiple modalities allows task representations to draw on signals that a single modality alone would not capture. However, individual tasks may depend disproportionately on particular modalities, a structure that conventional fusion-based architectures do not model explicitly, instead enforcing a unified representation space. Consequently, a task's gradients can affect parameters tied to modalities it barely relies on, leaving features that compromise between competing demands. Although prior work has explored task-weighting and loss-balancing strategies, their effectiveness is limited by the absence of explicit modality separation, preventing models from optimising each modality according to its task-specific importance. To address these limitations, we propose MOSAIC (MOdality-Separated Architecture with Inter-modal Cross-attention), which preserves unimodal representations while enabling controlled interaction between them, and uses modality-specific losses to route gradients to their corresponding partitions. On the Corpus of Everyday Japanese Conversation (CEJC), MOSAIC improves average macro-F1 by 7.4 points across four tasks with a 72% reduction in backbone parameters relative to a fusion-based baseline. Our results demonstrate that modality partitioning yields consistent gains across tasks while requiring far fewer backbone parameters than a fusion-based design.
authors: Aryan Chowdhury, Yizheng Sun, Thomas Carroll, Riza Batista-Navarro
bullets: Targets tasks that rely disproportionately on different modalities, which conventional fused representations do not explicitly model.
Preserves unimodal representations, enables controlled inter-modal interaction through cross-attention, and uses modality-specific losses for gradient routing.
On the CEJC benchmark across four tasks, it raises average macro-F1 by 7.4 points over a fusion-based baseline.
Uses 72% fewer backbone parameters than the baseline while achieving consistent gains across tasks.
Scope: results are reported on the Corpus of Everyday Japanese Conversation and four tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent diffusion-based methods have substantially advanced image editing, yet parametric 3D control at the part level remains challenging. Existing approaches either operate on whole objects with manual rigging, or revert to 2D handles at the part level. They also struggle to model appearance and texture under large transformations, leading to unrealistic outputs in geometry-intensive edits. To address these limitations, we introduce RADI3N, a framework for semantically-grounded part-aware object manipulation with parametric 3D control. Our CS-ARAP deformation module suppresses rotation-field discontinuities at part boundaries via neighborhood covariance smoothing, producing structurally consistent deformations under complex part-level edits. We further introduce an inversion-free selective texture transfer mechanism that suppresses high-frequency positional biases and scales up low-frequency semantic cues within cross-image attention. This eliminates strict spatial bias and supports semantic matching, allowing source appearance to follow the edited part onto its new geometry. Experiments demonstrate that RADI3N achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity, viewpoint consistency, and controllability.
authors: Abdul Wasi, Akhil Gorugantu, Mahesh Bhosale, Anjan Dutta, Junsong Yuan, Sauradip Nag, David Doermann
bullets: Addresses limitations of whole-object rigging and 2D part-level handles in geometry-intensive image editing.
Uses CS-ARAP deformation with neighborhood covariance smoothing to reduce rotation discontinuities at part boundaries.
Introduces inversion-free selective texture transfer to move source appearance onto edited geometry through semantic matching.
Experiments report state-of-the-art geometric fidelity, viewpoint consistency, and controllability.

Intermediate renderings and source views condition the diffusion model via IP-Adapter for identity preservation. Stage 2 (Global 3D Refinement): The Stage 1 Jacobian field is refined using Lrefine, combining handle constraints with SDS gradients from the diffusion model, producing a semantically plausible mesh for final rendering.

papers.abstract: Vision-language agents equipped with tools expose intermediate outputs for inspection and comparison with the model's reasoning, which may offer safety benefits over single-shot models. This paper tests that potential benefit when the sensor reading itself is untrusted, so that the tool and reasoning channels share a common visual fault. We consider a dermatology agent based on segmentation, contrastive retrieval, and an iterative vision-language reasoner and define a coupling taxonomy that distinguishes single-channel errors from joint errors that agree or disagree. On PAD-UFES-20, we show that typographic injection produces detectable directional retrieval capture, whereas physical corruption does not. Crop-first retrieval preserves the payload at a readable scale and produces 55% joint wrong agreement across all cases (71% of faulty cases); full-image retrieval produces 35% (43%). Under a binary decision, if both channels are wrong, their predictions must agree, so hard-label channel comparison cannot detect joint failures, limiting disagreement recall to 0.29 (crop-first) versus 0.57 (full-image). The direction of the order effect is reproduced on the independent HIBA test set.
authors: Nishi Kanta Paul, Md Shihabul Islam Shovo, Md Mostafijur Rahman, Jamil Fayyad
bullets: Defines a fault-coupling taxonomy for separating single-channel errors from joint errors that agree or disagree.

Crop-first retrieval yields more joint wrong agreement than full-image retrieval (55% vs. 35% across cases).

papers.abstract: Histopathology foundation models learn rich embedding representations, but their internal structure remains difficult to inspect. Concept-level interpretability is particularly relevant in computational pathology because pathologists reason through recurring morphological and tissue-level patterns, including tissue architecture, cellular morphology, staining variation, and artifacts. In this work, we investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose embeddings from histopathology foundation models into sparse latent features suitable for expert-assisted interpretation. We train vanilla and Batch-TopK SAE variants on NCT-CRC embeddings, using CONCH as the primary foundation model and UNI2-h as an additional robustness evaluation, and characterize the resulting latent features through reconstruction fidelity, sparsity, coherence, label enrichment, and downstream class-signal preservation. The learned sparse representations preserve most downstream tissue-class information, and their latent features retrieve more coherent and label-concentrated patch groups than raw embedding dimensions or PCA components. Discussions with pathology experts further motivated a WSI-level latent visualization workflow that places feature activations into larger tissue context. Overall, the additional UNI2-h evaluation suggests that the observed behavior is not specific to CONCH, supporting the use of sparse autoencoders for expert-assisted analysis of histopathology foundation-model embeddings, while emphasizing that latent features should be treated as candidate concepts requiring pathological assessment rather than automatically validated histopathological concepts.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of interpreting rich but opaque histopathology foundation-model embeddings in terms of tissue and cellular concepts.
Trains vanilla and Batch-TopK sparse autoencoders on NCT-CRC embeddings from CONCH, with UNI2-h used for robustness evaluation.
Evaluates reconstruction fidelity, sparsity, feature coherence, label enrichment, and preservation of downstream tissue-class information.
Sparse representations preserve most tissue-class signal and yield more coherent, label-concentrated patch groups than raw embedding dimensions or PCA components.

Introduces a WSI-level visualization workflow that places latent activations in broader tissue context; findings appear across two foundation models but do not automatically establish histopathological meaning.

papers.abstract: Voice-interactive large language models process both what a speaker says and how they say it, yet the two channels do not always agree. We ask whether that disagreement degrades speech emotion recognition. Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, we convert the distance between them into a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, and validate the score against human judgement. We evaluate three audiocapable models on acted, conversational and spontaneous speech (eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI). With the model held constant across modalities, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus, after controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for distance in the feature space. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way, which suggests that the difficulty lies in how these models combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself. Text-only effects are unreliable: swapping only the model that reads the transcript reverses their sign on one corpus. Rebuilding the score without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result, and among six simpler alternatives it is the only label-free score that predicts error in all three corpora. Code, data tables and prompts are released.
bullets: The study introduces a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score by measuring text–audio distance in valence–arousal–dominance space.
The score is validated against human judgments and tested across acted, conversational, and spontaneous speech using three audio-capable models.
Audio-related incongruence increases prediction errors across all three corpora, even after controlling for ground-truth emotion and feature-space distance.
Supervised classifiers show the opposite pattern, implicating how audio-language models combine evidence rather than the underlying signal.
Text-only effects are inconsistent across models; a lexicon-free version of the score preserves the central finding and outperforms simpler label-free alternatives in consistency.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview. (MELD has no “happiness” class; its positive label is “joy”.)

Fig. 3. Paradigm dissociation on eNTERFACE (test split, T2 text+audio for the LLMs). This is consistent with the harm arising during raw multimodal integration rather than from the VAD features (the baselines are supervised, however, so this is not by itself proof of mechanism).

papers.abstract: The reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) can be limited by incomplete or inaccurate visual observations in the general domain. In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) scenes, small targets, subtle attributes, and changing viewpoints further complicate perception and understanding. Therefore, we introduce Drone-PUR, a dataset and benchmark organized around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration, corresponding to the three capability dimensions of perception, understanding, and reasoning. Reasoning samples are designed to require models to combine multiple visual clues to derive visually grounded conclusions. Its 11 tasks provide 175k training and 20k test samples spanning single images, image sequences, cross-modal images, and multiple viewpoints. All test samples undergo human review. Evaluating 22 general-purpose VLMs reveals persistent limitations in spatial judgment and cross-modal and cross-view reasoning. Across models, stronger perception is associated with better reasoning, while single-task fine-tuning further reveals selective bidirectional transfer between these capabilities. To examine domain adaptation, we develop UAV-PUR from Qwen3-VL through staged fine-tuning with auxiliary supervision. Its 4B and 8B variants improve overall multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points over their pretrained counterparts, respectively. The dataset and project resources are available at https://drone-pur.github.io.
authors: Jiahe Wu, Bing Cao, Xingyue Guo, Ruipu Zhao, Beiming Yu, Jiekang Feng, Qinghua Hu, Pengfei Zhu
bullets: Targets incomplete visual observations involving small objects, subtle attributes, changing viewpoints, and multimodal inputs.

Finds persistent weaknesses in spatial judgment and cross-modal/cross-view reasoning, with stronger perception linked to better reasoning.
UAV-PUR models adapted from Qwen3-VL improve multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points for 4B and 8B variants, respectively.

papers.abstract: A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words; it must understand requests, reason over context, sustain conversations, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these capabilities within a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice directly processes speech and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. We introduce a two-stage training procedure to adapt the model to speech. The first stage establishes the speech interface, while the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone through supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback--Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data, while local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable efficient online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves a score of 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and a task success rate of 65.51% on $\tau$-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. It also achieves 51.27% English EVA accuracy and 74.13% experience pass@1. Finally, we deploy Apriel Voice 27B Preview on a custom serving platform to support interactive voice interactions.

Uses a two-stage speech adaptation process combining supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and distillation-based losses.
Trains on automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues with efficiency optimizations for online teacher–student distillation.
Reports strong performance across Big Bench Audio, Speech-BFCL, τ-Voice, English EVA, and experience pass@1, with 1.91-second mean latency in thinking mode.
Deployed on a custom serving platform for interactive voice conversations.

papers.abstract: Detailed image captioning is usually framed as an amount problem: a model should mention more visual facts while avoiding hallucination. However, autoregressive VLMs generate captions as ordered sequences, and later generations may be produced under weaker or noisier visual grounding. We therefore argue that long-form captioning should be studied not only by what facts are mentioned, but also by where they appear. We introduce a position-aware rubric representation that decomposes dense human references into atomic visual claims, verifies generated captions against those claims, and induces a quartile-wise composition of supported, hallucinated, and generic content. This lens reveals two qualitatively different failures in long captions: models tend to produce unsupported specificity in the middle, while the final portion often escapes into vague, non-evidential language rather than simply accumulating more hallucination. A same-reference human control does not exhibit these patterns; additional human audits examine the visual validity of the induced labels. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose PAGER (Position-Aware Grounded Evidence Reinforcement), a GRPO training objective with separate signals for supported fine-grained middle evidence, evidence-bearing tail continuation, claim coverage, and content-aware length control. The result is a closed loop: the same ordered claim representation identifies where long captions fail and supplies the position-specific reward needed to repair those failures. Experiments on detailed-caption benchmarks show that PAGER improves position-wise grounding and pairwise caption preference while preserving competitive global caption quality.
bullets: Long captions often become unsupportedly specific in the middle and vague or non-evidential near the end.
A position-aware rubric decomposes references into atomic visual claims and evaluates supported, hallucinated, and generic content by caption quartile.
PAGER applies position-specific GRPO rewards for grounded middle evidence, evidential tail continuation, claim coverage, and content-aware length.

papers.abstract: Despite the success of foundation models in image synthesis, achieving fine-grained spatial control remains a significant challenge, typically requiring auxiliary structural adapters or complex inference-time steering. While modern vision-language (VLM) text encoders possess the latent capacity to represent spatial coordinates, generative models often fail to leverage this information. We demonstrate that the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distribution is a critical determinant of spatial grounding in flow-matching models. Using a novel synthetic benchmark of geometric primitives, we isolate structural mechanics from textural complexity inherent in natural imagery and introduce a rigorous color-aware layout metric to quantify spatial fidelity. We show that training on a centered SNR distribution results in poor layout adherence (25.9%). Instead, we identify high-noise regimes as a "critical learning phase" for spatial grounding. Shifting the training focus toward these stages increases layout adherence to 80.8%, effectively reaching the 83.6% reconstruction ceiling of the underlying variational autoencoder. We find that the necessity for this shift scales with resolution and aspect ratio variance, and that the conservative noise schedules employed by models like FLUX.1 are insufficient for precise layout adherence. Finally, we show that these findings translate to real-world imagery via the COCO dataset (1.0 vs. 57.3 Average Precision), where state-of-the-art layout adherence is unlocked through distribution tuning alone, without architectural modifications.
bullets: Problem: Vision-language encoders contain spatial information, but image generators often fail to use it for precise layout control.
Method: Evaluate spatial grounding on synthetic geometric primitives with a color-aware layout metric, then vary the training signal-to-noise-ratio distribution.
Key finding: Centered SNR training yields 25.9% layout adherence, while emphasizing high-noise stages raises it to 80.8%, near the 83.6% VAE reconstruction ceiling.
Scope: The required SNR shift grows with resolution and aspect-ratio variability; conservative schedules such as FLUX.1’s are insufficient for precise layouts.
Transfer: Distribution tuning also improves layout adherence on COCO, increasing Average Precision from 1.0 to 57.3 without architectural modifications.

papers.selection_reason: Shows SNR distribution tuning unlocks spatial grounding and layout adherence in flow-matching models; fits spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Unlocking Spatial Grounding in Flow-Matching Models via SNR Tuning
papers.tldr: Tuning flow-matching training toward high-noise stages substantially improves spatial grounding without architectural changes.

papers.abstract: Chest computed tomography (CT) reports generated by large language models (LLMs) can describe positive findings that lack localized evidence in the scan. We propose EviGround-CT to verify these findings after report generation. A deterministic extractor identifies positive finding sentences, and a 3D grounding model predicts an evidence mask for each sentence. Using the full sentence retains anatomical location, laterality, and descriptive modifiers in the grounding query. We evaluate report generation on CT-RATE, and grounding and verification on a held-out 100-case ReXGroundingCT subset. Using the available annotations, sentence-grounded verification raises evidence-supported precision (ESP) from 0.263 to 0.365 across 137 extracted in-scope positives, compared with category conditioning. The corresponding unsupported positive finding rate falls from 0.737 to 0.635. The paired case-level bootstrap ESP difference is +0.102 (95% confidence interval: [0.028, 0.181]). The predicted masks associate individual report statements with spatial evidence that can be inspected alongside the CT.
bullets: Targets positive report findings that may lack localized support in the CT scan.
Extracts positive finding sentences deterministically and uses each full sentence as the grounding query.
A 3D grounding model predicts an inspectable evidence mask for every statement.
On annotated cases, evidence-supported precision increased from 0.263 to 0.365, while unsupported positives decreased from 0.737 to 0.635.
Evaluated on CT-RATE and a held-out 100-case ReXGroundingCT subset; scope is limited to available annotations and in-scope positives.

papers.selection_reason: Sentence-to-volume 3D grounding in CT with spatial evidence, relevant to spatial multimodal reasoning and 3D perception.
papers.title: EviGround-CT: Sentence-to-Volume Grounding for Verifying LLM-Generated Chest CT Reports
papers.tldr: EviGround-CT verifies LLM-generated chest CT findings by grounding each positive sentence to a 3D evidence mask, improving evidence-supported precision.

papers.abstract: While the Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that vision and language models converge toward compatible latent geometries, recovering class-level correspondences between unpaired modalities without cross-modal supervision remains challenging. Existing relational matching methods compare within-modality similarity kernels directly, although the same semantic structure may be represented through different numerical parameterizations across modalities. We propose RankAlign, a rank-based normalization strategy for class-level unpaired vision-language matching. RankAlign transforms each within-modality similarity kernel into an ordinal relational representation before permutation matching, while leaving the correspondence space and matching solver unchanged. The resulting representation is invariant to strictly increasing reparameterizations of similarity values while preserving the ordinal structure used for matching. We provide exact-recovery and stability guarantees that characterize correspondence recovery under both exact and partial ordinal agreement. Experiments across diverse frozen vision and language encoders and multiple datasets demonstrate improved and more stable class-level correspondence recovery, including under label corruption and domain shift.
bullets: Addresses class-level correspondence recovery between unpaired vision and language modalities without cross-modal supervision.
Transforms within-modality similarity kernels into ordinal representations before permutation matching, without changing the matching space or solver.
Is invariant to strictly increasing reparameterizations while preserving the ordinal structure used for matching.
Provides exact-recovery and stability guarantees under exact or partial ordinal agreement.
Experiments with frozen encoders show more accurate and stable correspondence recovery under label corruption and domain shift.

papers.title: RankAlign: Vision-Language Representation Alignment via Rank Transformation
papers.tldr: RankAlign improves unpaired vision-language class matching by converting similarity kernels into rank-based representations that are robust to differing similarity scales.

papers.abstract: Recommender systems often suffer from over-concentrated results when optimized for accuracy, limiting recommendation diversity. While diversity has become an important objective, existing methods still face fundamental limitations from both semantic and structural perspectives. On the one hand, multimodal recommender systems provide rich semantic signals, yet are often treated as auxiliary to ID embeddings, leading to ineffective semantic utilization for diversity. On the other hand, the accuracy--diversity trade-off persists during training, where accuracy gains often come at the cost of diversity. We show that this phenomenon is fundamentally governed by both the structural properties of learned representations and the dynamics of optimization. To address these challenges, we propose MOSS, a unified framework for multimodal decoupling through semantic and structural shaping. Specifically, we first introduce an MLLM-based Decoupled Feature Extraction module to disentangle multimodal content into informative representations. To enhance semantic utilization, we design a Category-aware Embedding Selection module that extracts compact, category-aware semantic features. To address structural limitations, we propose two complementary modules: Alternating Dual-Graph Propagation, which alleviates representation collapse by integrating collaborative and multimodal propagation, and Entropy-based Diversity Regularization, which mitigates optimization bias by promoting balanced category exposure. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that MOSS consistently achieves a superior accuracy--diversity trade-off over strong baselines.
bullets: Targets over-concentrated recommendations and the persistent accuracy–diversity trade-off.
Uses MLLM-based decoupled feature extraction and category-aware semantic selection to better exploit multimodal content.
Combines alternating dual-graph propagation with entropy-based regularization to reduce representation collapse and balance category exposure.
Experiments on real-world datasets show a consistently better accuracy–diversity trade-off than strong baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 4: An illustration of the proposed MOSS model. TheMLLM-based Decoupled Feature Extraction module disentangles multimodal content into informative representations. The Category-aware Embedding Selection module selects compact, category-aware features to enhance semantic utilization. The Alternating Dual-Graph Propagation module alleviates dimensional collapse via collaborative and multimodal propagation. The Entropy-based Diversity Regularization module promotes balanced category exposure while preserving accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a framework for multimodal decoupling in recommendation systems using MLLMs and graph propagation, relevant to multimodal reasoning and efficiency.
papers.title: Multimodal Decoupling for Diversified Recommendation through Semantic and Structural Shaping
papers.tldr: MOSS improves recommendation diversity while preserving accuracy by decoupling multimodal semantics and reshaping representation structure and optimization.

papers.abstract: Thermal-to-visible (T2V) face translation has important applications in nighttime biometric recognition, low-light surveillance, and human interpretation of thermal observations. The task remains challenging because thermal images do not directly record visible appearance, while the cross-spectral cues useful for reconstruction vary across frequency components and semantic roles. Existing spatially conditioned models tend to process these cues through a homogeneous adaptation path and do not explicitly separate local structure from global identity. We propose FreqID-Control, a parameter-efficient framework that organizes thermal guidance according to spectral reliability and semantic role while preserving the pretrained generative prior. It combines frequency-routed low-rank adaptation, which allocates separate transformation subspaces to low-frequency structure and high-frequency detail, with shared cross-spectral identity conditioning, which supplies compact global identity tokens independently of spatial thermal tokens. A controlled analysis on MCXFace and SpeakingFaces provides the empirical basis for this design, revealing stable low-frequency correspondence and edge-localized detail correspondence. Experiments on both datasets demonstrate strong image fidelity and biometric identity preservation, while controlled ablations on MCXFace confirm the complementary contributions of frequency routing and shared identity conditioning.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reconstructing visible appearance from thermal images, whose useful cues differ by frequency and semantic role.
Uses frequency-routed low-rank adaptation to separately handle low-frequency structure and high-frequency detail while retaining a pretrained generative prior.
Adds shared cross-spectral identity tokens independently from spatial thermal tokens to preserve global facial identity.
Experiments on MCXFace and SpeakingFaces show strong image fidelity and biometric identity preservation.
Ablations on MCXFace support complementary benefits from frequency routing and identity conditioning.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of FreqID-Control. The thermal input provides a spatial condition through the frozen FLUX-based T2V pathway and a global identity condition through the shared cross-spectral encoder and trainable resampler. Spatial, identity, and noisy-latent states remain separate until multimodal attention. Frequency LoRA-MoE decomposes each current hidden state into low- and high-frequency token components, applies specialized low-rank experts, and routes their updates back to the projection. Gray modules are frozen; orange and green modules are trainable.
Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on four MCXFace test samples. DiffV2IR uses its thermal-only setting; the FreqID-Control column is outlined, and Ground Truth is shown last.
Figure 3: Qualitative component ablation on two MCXFace samples. The full model combines Frequency LoRA-MoE and shared identity conditioning.

Figure 1: Frequency-domain motivation. (a) Absolute real– random mean Complex-NCC gaps across FFT bands. B2–B3 show pair-specific correspondence across datasets, whereas finer-frequency behavior varies. (b) HL1 Complex NCC at thermal-edge and non-edge locations, showing edgeconcentrated transferable detail.

Table 3: Cross-spectral face-recognition results on MCXFace and SpeakingFaces. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a parameter-efficient framework for cross-spectral translation that explicitly separates local structure (frequency routing) from global identity, relevant to spatial reasoning and geometric priors.
papers.title: Frequency Routing and Identity Conditioning for Thermal-to-Visible Face Translation
papers.tldr: FreqID-Control improves thermal-to-visible face translation by routing thermal cues by frequency and conditioning generation on shared identity information.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at instruction following, yet most remain feed-forward: they condition actions only on the current observation and discard both long-horizon temporal context and the hierarchical structure of VLM representations. We present PRIME W0, a hierarchical conditional flow-matching framework that closes this gap through three synergistic designs: (1)per-layer KV injection from a pretrained VLM into an Adaptive MoE action expert; (2)dynamics-aware conditioning via asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and a DINOv2 historical-frame semantic bridge; and (3)Action Dynamic Manifold (ADM) flow matching with covariance-structured noise that respects robot kinematic coupling. PRIME W0 is trained in four stages---VLM pre-training, DAT/NTP visuomotor pre-training, DiT flow-matching decoder assembly with WM injection, and end-to-end SFT---and achieves state-of-the-art results on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with systematic ablations validating each architectural component.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of feed-forward VLA models, which ignore long-horizon context and hierarchical visual-language representations.
Injects pretrained VLM key-value features into an adaptive mixture-of-experts action module.
Uses asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and DINOv2 historical-frame features for dynamics-aware temporal conditioning.
Applies covariance-structured flow matching on an Action Dynamic Manifold to model coupled robot actions.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with ablations supporting the proposed components.

figures.caption: Figure 1: PRIME W0 architecture.

Figure 2: Four-stage training pipeline. (1) VLM Pretrain: the vision–language backbone is trained on general multimodal supervision (e.g. captioning / VQA). (2) NTP / task-specific pre-training: with DAT action tokens, the VLM learns visuomotor next-token prediction over instruction–observation–action sequences. (3) DiT Pretrain: the VLM is frozen while the MoT / Adaptive MoE flow-matching action expert is trained with world-model conditioning to denoise continuous actions (and associated state tokens). (4) SFT: both the VLM and the action expert are jointly fine-tuned end-to-end, optionally with action-prefix tokens that shorten the denoising trajectory at inference. Flame / snowflake icons indicate trainable vs. frozen modules.

Figure 5: Scaling with world-model capacity. LIBERO-Long success scales monotonically with WM size; the largest gain is between 5M and 50M parameters (+5.9%). Better subgoal-image prediction directly benefits the asynchronous WM→VLM→ADM pipeline.

Figure 3: Training data mixture. Robot demonstration data used by PRIME W0 totals approximately 10,000 hours, comprising Teleop (60%, ∼6,000 h; laboratory setups, data-collection factories, and public datasets), UMI (30%, ∼3,000 h; portable UMI fisheye egocentric collection), and Simulation (10%, ∼1,000 h; reconstructed scenes with procedural objects and physics randomisation).

Figure 4: ADM cross-attention to WM subgoal-image tokens across manipulation phases. Attention to WMpredicted subgoal tokens peaks at contact-establishment and placement phases, confirming that forward scene predictions actively condition manifold-constrained action generation during critical moments.
Table 2: Real-robot in-house task comparison. All methods are evaluated on the same physical hardware under identical conditions. Numbers = task success rate (%). Best in bold, second underlined.
Table 4: Component ablation. Each row adds one module on top of the previous variant. Metrics: LIBERO-Long success (%) and real-robot average success (%).

papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical VLA with world-model subgoal prediction for manipulation; fits embodied AI, world models, and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: PRIME W0: Physical Priors from World Models for Embodied Manipulation
papers.tldr: PRIME W0 enhances vision-language-action models for embodied manipulation by combining hierarchical VLM features, world-model dynamics, temporal context, and kinematics-aware action generation.

papers.abstract: Human cognition flexibly draws on a shared perceptual foundation to understand environments, attend to referenced entities, reason about spatial relationships, and act. Endowing aerial robots with an analogous functional organization remains challenging, as existing systems are often specialized for individual capabilities, dependent on offboard computation, or unable to sustain closed-loop operation on resource-constrained platforms. We present OpenFlyV2, a unified onboard vision-language-action architecture that uses a shared vision-language representation to support semantic understanding, language-grounded perception, spatial reasoning, and continuous aerial control within a single model. A compact action expert converts the shared multimodal context into short-horizon flight waypoints, while motion-aware temporal memory and action priors reduce the computational cost of closed-loop execution. We construct \dataset{}, a simulation-based dataset comprising approximately 70,000 navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instruction--response pairs. OpenFlyV2 generates action chunks, each comprising 12 waypoints, entirely onboard at 10 Hz using an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. It transfers zero-shot from simulation to physical quadrotor flight, achieving a 48\% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data. Extensive results demonstrate that broad vision-language competence and continuous closed-loop flight can coexist within a single model on a resource-constrained aerial platform. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Ideal-ljl/AeroBrain.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying aerial perception, language grounding, reasoning, and control without offboard computation.
Uses a shared vision-language representation, a compact waypoint-generating action expert, temporal memory, and action priors.
Trains on approximately 70,000 simulated navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instruction–response pairs.
Runs onboard at 10 Hz on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, producing 12-waypoint action chunks.
Transfers zero-shot to physical flight, achieving a 48% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data.

figures.caption: Figure 6. Architecture of OpenFlyV2. (A) A shared vision-language backbone encodes the current image, instruction, and memory tokens to condition action generation. (B) Motion-Adaptive Memory (MAM) compresses historical action segments and their visual anchors into compact event-level tokens. (C) The Motion-Structured Prior (MSP) selects and adjusts a data-derived motion prototype to construct the action source distribution. The action expert transforms a sample from this distribution into the final action chunk through conditional flow matching.

Figure 4. Quantitative evaluation of aerial understanding and navigation. (A) Comparison with general-purpose vision-language models on color recognition, description generation, visual grounding, distance estimation, and spatial relationship reasoning. Visual grounding is reported as accuracy at an IoU threshold of 0.5 (Acc@0.5), and distance estimation is shown as relative error. (B) Navigation performance in seen and unseen simulated environments, measured by success rate (SR), oracle success rate (OSR), success weighted by path length (SPL), and navigation error (NE). The navigation baselines were trained on our aerial navigation dataset and evaluated on the same 800 seen and 300 unseen episodes as OpenFlyV2. Success requires an explicit stop within 25 m of the goal. Blue and orange bars in (B) indicate seen and unseen environments, respectively. Arrows indicate the direction of better performance.

Figure 2. Shared environments and data composition of OpenFlyV2-130K. The Steps column reports the number of flow-integration (denoising) steps; SR, OSR, and SPL are percentages, and NE is in meters. papers.selection_reason: Onboard VLA model for aerial perception and navigation; directly fits embodied AI and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: OpenFlyV2: An onboard vision-language-action model for aerial perception and navigation
papers.tldr: OpenFlyV2 is an onboard vision-language-action model that combines semantic understanding, spatial reasoning, and closed-loop aerial control on a resource-constrained drone.

papers.abstract: Multimodal learning often suffers from modality imbalance, where the joint optimization process is dominated by a single modality. Existing methods typically estimate modality imbalance from score disparities derived from prediction uncertainty or optimization statistics. However, due to distinct prediction uncertainty and learning dynamics across modalities, direct comparison of such scores may misinterpret intrinsic modality differences as progress gaps, leading to biased imbalance estimation. In this paper, we propose Function-Space Guided Multimodal Optimization (FGMO), which leverages a function-space progress signal to assess modality-wise optimization progress and coordinate optimization across modalities to alleviate modality imbalance. Specifically, we introduce Functional Progress Estimation (FPE) to measure each modality's update-induced function-space response and calibrate it against a loss-aligned unimodal reference, producing a comparable progress signal. Based on this signal, Functional Response Control (FRC) redistributes modality-level function-space budgets and realizes the target responses through tensor-wise learning-rate adjustment. Theoretical analysis establishes a one-step target-contraction property of FRC under bounded controller-state mismatch, and extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FGMO across multiple multimodal benchmarks.
bullets: Addresses modality imbalance caused by optimization being dominated by one modality.
Uses Functional Progress Estimation to measure update-induced function changes relative to a loss-aligned unimodal reference.
Applies Functional Response Control to redistribute modality-level function-space budgets through tensor-wise learning-rate adjustment.
Provides a theoretical one-step target-contraction guarantee under bounded controller-state mismatch.
Experiments across multiple multimodal benchmarks demonstrate FGMO’s effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The overall framework of Function-Space Guided Multimodal Optimization (FGMO). FPE estimates Relative Functional Progress (RFP) from update-induced function-space responses and loss-aligned unimodal references, while FRC uses RFP feedback to perform modality-level response allocation and tensor-wise learning-rate adjustment.

Figure 5: (a) Beneficial Rates of different modality signals under controlled interventions. (b) Training-time comparison with representative multimodal learning methods. (c) Tensor-wise learning-rate allocation across the audio and video branches, where each cell reports the geometricmean learning-rate multiplier.

Figure 4: Sensitivity analysis of the controller gain λ on the Sarcasm and CREMA-D datasets. (a) and (b) Evolution of the absolute log RFP ratio | log Qt| under different controller gains on Sarcasm and CREMA-D, respectively. (c) Impact of λ on the multimodal classification accuracy. The dashed line (λ = 2) denotes the boundary of the ideal target-contraction range.

Table 1: Comparison with SOTA multimodal learning methods. The best results are highlighted in bold. The underline denotes the second-best performance. Gray-shaded results indicate that multimodal performance is lower than that of the best unimodal approach.

papers.selection_reason: Function-space method to balance multimodal optimization; transferable to multimodal foundation model training.
papers.title: Balancing Multimodal Learning via Functional Progress
papers.tldr: FGMO balances multimodal optimization by comparing modality progress in function space and adjusting learning rates to coordinate their contributions.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language model (VLM) post-training is commonly evaluated through answer accuracy. We examine how changes in accuracy and training objectives relate to image-conditioned decisions in a controlled Qwen2.5-VL-3B study on PMC-VQA. We compare supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) restricted to the language model, expanded multimodal adaptation scopes, standard answer-only Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and a counterfactual evidence objective. On 2,000 clean-test questions, language model LoRA SFT changes correct-image accuracy by +1.10 percentage points (95% paired bootstrap CI:-0.85 to +3.05), while visual-benefit events decrease by 2.40 points and image sensitivity decreases by 5.60 points. Paired records reveal 155 acquired and 203 lost visual-benefit events. Broader adaptation yields lower correct-image accuracy than language-model LoRA SFT. Standard GRPO produces mixed-reward groups and parameter updates, with an uncertain clean test accuracy change. A generation audit reveals that canonical option scores can follow a different token path from generated answers. With scores taken along the greedy generation path, the evidence target improves on the training set; its gains over standard GRPO remain inconsistent on validation data at matched training doses. Sample-level analyses trace how evidence scores, decision margins, and generated answers change during post-training. This empirical and measurement audit identifies gaps between optimization activity, target acquisition, and useful held-out visual behavior.
bullets: Evaluates SFT, LoRA, broader multimodal adaptation, standard GRPO, and a counterfactual evidence objective in Qwen2.5-VL-3B on PMC-VQA.
Language-model LoRA SFT slightly increases correct-image accuracy, but decreases visual-benefit events and image sensitivity on clean-test questions.
Broader adaptation performs worse on correct-image accuracy than language-model LoRA SFT; standard GRPO yields mixed rewards and uncertain test changes.
Evidence-target gains appear on training data but remain inconsistent on validation data at matched training doses.
Generation audits show that canonical option scores may not reflect the token path used for generated answers, complicating measurement.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Adaptation-scope comparison using VALID-selected checkpoints on a common clean-test cohort. The three configurations vary which components are trained: language attention adapters, the multimodal merger, and vision adapters. papers.selection_reason: Controlled audit of medical VLM post-training objectives and visual utility, directly relevant to multimodal LLM training behavior.
papers.title: From Reward Signal to Visual Utility: A Controlled Audit of Medical VLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: A controlled audit finds that medical VLM post-training can improve answer accuracy without improving—and sometimes reducing—the model’s useful reliance on visual evidence.

papers.abstract: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. papers.abstract: An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.

papers.selection_reason: Probes spatial state representations in visual foundation models, investigating capabilities like object persistence and predictive updates relevant to spatial intelligence and embodied agents.

papers.abstract: Images reveal appearances, but counting often asks about physical objects. A single entity may be visible directly, in several reflections, or through glass, so detecting every visible occurrence does not determine how many entities are present. Existing visual counting benchmarks rarely separate these two operations. We introduce PhysCount, a benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can distinguish what appears in an image from what physically exists in the scene. PhysCount contains 546 real-world images and 4,595 human-written questions organized into 651 target-specific groups. For each group, annotators locate the relevant appearances, label how each is observed, and identify appearances of the same entity. Four complementary question families test the enumeration of appearances, the enumeration of physical entities, image-formation-specific counting, and appearance--entity correspondence. We measure both accuracy on each family and the proportion of groups answered entirely correctly. Across 40 MLLMs, counting visible appearances is substantially easier than recovering the identities that connect them. Even the strongest model answers every question correctly in only 13.36\% of groups. Performance declines when one entity produces many appearances or when its appearances cross observation modes. Higher image resolution improves access to visual evidence but brings limited gains in complete-group accuracy, whereas answering related questions jointly produces a marked improvement. These results expose a gap between recognizing what is visible and correctly recovering the physical entities behind those observations.

papers.abstract: We present PhysInsert, a framework for physically plausible reference-based object insertion that jointly adapts objects and their surrounding scenes. Existing methods often rely on masked inputs, generation-based pairs, or training pairs with limited viewpoint variation, leaving pose and illumination adaptation and bidirectional object-scene interactions insufficiently constrained. We construct the Insert World dataset with strictly aligned Blender-rendered counterfactual pairs and object references across viewpoints and lighting conditions. Building on these data, Geometry-Guided Adaptation couples a VGGT geometry stream with image and text streams under target-scene feature supervision to guide spatially consistent insertion. Complementary 2D Object-Scene Spatial Supervision jointly supervises object occupancy and environmental changes while grounding spatial instructions in object regions through image-text attention. We introduce PhysInsert-Bench with dedicated cross-environment and cross-view cases requiring illumination and pose adaptation beyond appearance copying. Experiments on PhysInsert-Bench and DreamBooth demonstrate improved image fidelity; a user study further shows more accurate placement and improved lighting integration, perspective, and pose plausibility.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong zero-shot generalization but remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing adversarial fine-tuning methods often use pre-trained model guidance to preserve image--text alignment while improving robustness. Our analysis of visual representation drift reveals complementary limitations of two representative forms of guidance. Matching visual features provides broad coverage by constraining all directions equally, but lacks semantic emphasis. Matching prediction distributions prioritizes semantically relevant directions, but remains limited by the candidate texts and prediction probabilities. These limitations can hinder preservation of pre-trained image--text relationships and degrade zero-shot performance. To address these issues, we propose Textual Response-Aware Guidance (TRAG), which constrains visual representation drift using the pre-trained text encoder's responses to local variations in input embeddings. Specifically, TRAG constructs anchor-level constraints from the response directions and magnitudes around semantic anchors, then aggregates them using pre-trained image--anchor relevance, yielding an image-adaptive constraint. Extensive experiments across architectures and tasks demonstrate state-of-the-art clean and robust performance. Further analysis shows that TRAG helps preserve pre-trained image--text relationships.
authors: Yubo Cui, Xianchao Guan, Zheng Zhang
bullets: VLMs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, while robustness fine-tuning can damage pretrained image–text alignment and zero-shot performance.
Feature matching covers visual directions broadly but lacks semantic focus; prediction matching is semantic but limited by candidate texts and probabilities.
TRAG builds anchor-level constraints from the text encoder’s response directions and magnitudes to local embedding variations.
These constraints are aggregated using image–anchor relevance, producing image-adaptive guidance.
Experiments across architectures and tasks report state-of-the-art clean and robust performance, with better preservation of pretrained image–text relationships.

papers.abstract: We revisit advantage estimation in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and observe that any token-level advantage admits a two-stage factorization: a \emph{sample-level baselining} step that converts scalar verifier rewards into a comparable sequence-level signal, and a \emph{token-level credit assignment} step that distributes that signal over the trajectory. Existing estimators typically address only one of these stages: affine baselines preserve the shape of each task's reward law, so heavy tails and binary cliffs propagate into the gradient, while token-level credit rules tie the size of each token's update to raw confidence scales and need not conserve the total credit issued by the verifier. We propose \textbf{TACE} (Two-stage Advantage and Credit Estimation), a two-stage estimator that addresses both stages. At stage~(S1), we replace linear standardization with a one-dimensional optimal-transport map to a standard normal, which gives a common population reward law across tasks and caps finite-sample outliers deterministically. At stage~(S2), we rank-calibrate a stop-gradient evidence contrast within each trajectory and renormalize the clipped token weights to have mean one, so credit is redistributed across tokens while its total mass and sign are conserved. We prove population-level inter-task moment equity, a deterministic tail bound, and mass-conservation, boundedness, and sign-anchoring properties that affine baselines and unnormalized token weights do not satisfy. On a multimodal reasoning suite, TACE obtains the strongest results on a majority of the benchmarks but does not dominate every setting.
authors: Lang Chen, Zongxin Xu, Borui Wang, Anran Liu, Shitong Chen
bullets: Existing GRPO advantage estimators can propagate heavy-tailed or binary reward scales across tasks.
TACE uses optimal transport to map scalar rewards to a standard normal, aligning reward distributions and deterministically capping finite-sample outliers.
It rank-calibrates within-trajectory evidence contrasts and normalizes clipped token weights to conserve total credit.
The method provides inter-task moment equity, tail bounds, mass conservation, boundedness, and sign anchoring.
On a multimodal reasoning suite, TACE performs best on most benchmarks but not in every setting.

Stage (S2), ours (starting from the evidence ratio of Yang et al., 2026): runs πθ under non-privileged (PS) and privileged (PT ) contexts, rank-calibrates the per-token log-evidence within the trajectory, and applies a sign-anchored, mean-one (mass-preserving) magnitude weight wi,t. The composed token advantage Âi,t = Ai · wi,t plugs into the standard GRPO clipped surrogate.
