papers.abstract: Whether models trained on different modalities converge to the same representation of the world is central to AI. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) conjectures that they do as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe. We turn the hypothesis into a theorem. First, we prove a \emph{Platonic Representation Theorem}: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of one scene--\emph{good views}--and their misalignment is bounded otherwise. Second, we show that next-token prediction is a JEPA with \emph{bad views}, parts of a single document, which explains why language models align with vision only through scale. Third, we validate the theory from 145k captions to the texts of 940M web images, and uncover a scaling law of alignment that predicts unseen runs within seed noise. Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment, and a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP's image encoders better than every language model we evaluated, up to 72B parameters, and than CLIP's text encoder: next-token prediction is a remarkably inefficient route to platonic representations. As a showcase, one rotation turns separately trained encoders into an image captioner (CIDEr .838 on COCO). Even that rotation needs no pair: on the latest pair-free benchmark, our text JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy reported with language models up to 8B parameters, e.g., 64\% against at most 56\% top-5 on ImageNet-100. Positive views, and not scale alone, are thus the lever to build platonic representations.
bullets: Proves a Platonic Representation Theorem: separately trained JEPAs align up to a rotation when positive pairs are observations of the same scene and misalignment is bounded.
Frames next-token prediction as using “bad views,” helping explain its weaker vision–language alignment without large scale.
Finds that good-view training needs 42× fewer samples than next-token prediction to reach the same alignment on the studied corpus.
A 109M-parameter text JEPA aligned better with DINOv2 and CLIP image encoders than evaluated language models up to 72B parameters and CLIP’s text encoder.
A single learned rotation enabled image captioning, while the text JEPA also achieved strong pair-free zero-shot ImageNet-100 performance.

figures.caption: Figure 9. Good views scale. Left and middle: text JEPAs trained on the texts of 2.16M to 940M web images (Recap-DataComp), never on a Flickr or COCO caption, against frozen DINOv2 ViT-B on WIT-1024 (PRH-paper protocol) and on Flickr (R@1 through one rotation fitted on 30k pairs). Solid lines and circles: BERT-S (33M); dashed lines and diamonds: BERT-B (109M), trained with next-token prediction and bad views on the texts of 940M images only, hence single diamonds there. Lines are means over seeds and faint dots the seeds (one seed for the bad-view JEPA at 940M). Shaded: the language models we evaluated (Qwen2.5 0.5–72B, Llama-3-8B and -70B, Mistral-7B; left); grey dashed: CLIP’s text encoder and Qwen2.5-0.5B under the same protocol (middle). Right: image JEPAs trained from scratch (ViT-S on 2.16M and ViT-B on 10M Recap images, ViT-S on ImageNet-1k) and frozen DINOv2, each against the good-view, next-token and bad-view text JEPAs trained on the same texts of 50M web images (WIT; means of three seeds, dots: seeds). We clearly observe that good views beat bad views and next-token prediction at every scale and with every image encoder we compared, and that a 109M good-view JEPA on the texts of 940M images surpasses every language model we evaluated.

Figure 5. Good views align, bad views and next-token prediction do not. Alignment between a separately trained image JEPA and three text encoders on Flickr, at matched epochs (mean of three seeds, band: range; dashed: chance). All start at chance. We clearly observe that the good-view JEPA (caption views) aligns markedly better than the bad-view JEPA (masked spans) and next-token prediction, which nearly coincide, as predicted by Theorem 2 and Proposition 4.

Figure 3. What counts as a positive, and which observations it connects. Eight captions of two scenes (dots), joined as each objective’s positives join them. (a)Good views join every description of a scene and never another, so the world kernel they induce is the world’s own (Theorem 4). (b) Weak corruptions mostly pair a caption with itself, keeping its wording, and join other captions only where their corruptions overlap, which takes dense data. (c) Strong corruptions also coincide across scenes, so the induced kernel mixes scenes whatever the amount of data. (d) Next-token prediction pairs a prefix with its own continuation, and implicitly contexts followed by the same token (Proposition 4): narrow links within scenes, plus spill through frequent tokens. That is, good views fix the world kernel by design, while bad views and next-token prediction get it from the data.

Figure 4. Positives that join less of a scene need more data (Theorem 4). A synthetic world of five classes of six states (literal data, as in Figure 12): alignment of a text JEPA with the image side against the samples per state N and the reach ∆ of its bad views (means over three samplings; a state has width 1/6). White: the 0.9 contour, and ∆ ∝ log N/N (dashed, one fitted constant), the scale of the largest gap between a state’s samples. Reach large enough to cross classes caps alignment (.95), and good views (top strip) align exactly at any N. We observe that weaker positives need more data for the same alignment.

Figure 2. Kernel mismatch bounds misalignment (Theorem 2). Each point is one randomly generated finite world (8–39 states, random marginal, embedding dimension k from 1 to 5) with a pair of kernels on it: the world’s kernel, and a second kernel of the same marginal that mixes in an unrelated kernel with weight 10−4 to 1, as if a second modality had partly different positives. For each pair we compute the two spectral embeddings (Proposition 1) and plot their distance after the best rotation (vertical) against the bound of Theorem 2 (horizontal); of the 300 worlds, half are clustered, with small spectral gaps. We clearly observe that the error lies below the bound in every world (dashed: equality), at 18% of it at most.

Figure 7. Trimming is the knob that matters. One change at a time to the good-view text JEPA on Flickr: R@1 with frozen DINOv2 through one rotation, last epoch, three seeds where they exist (faint dots; large dot: mean of the seeds that do not collapse; black: default). Top: the two changes to trimming, with the change of their mean from the default’s; whole captions as views lose a quarter of the alignment. Dashed: the bad-view JEPA and next-token prediction with the default recipe. That is, trimming matters most, and every variant of the good-view JEPA that does not collapse stays far above both baselines; gradient clipping prevents most collapses.

Figure 8. Good views help on both sides. MSR-VTT, 1,000 test clips. Top: image JEPAs trained on different frames of a clip (good) or crops of one frame (bad), against text JEPAs trained on different captions (good) or spans of one caption (bad); dots are the three seeds, dashed is chance. Bottom: alignment of each with frozen DINOv2, whose own positives are crops. This demonstrates that good views on both sides align best in mutual 10-NN, and that DINOv2 prefers the image JEPA whose positives match its own.

Figure 6. Alignment lives in the leading spectral directions. Left: after the best rotation, correlation between image and text embeddings along the text embedding’s principal directions (good-view JEPA, at initialization and at epoch 199). Right: variance of the text embedding along the same directions. This suggests that alignment concentrates where the spectrum is well separated, consistent with Theorem 2, although noise in low-variance directions would produce the same trend.

Figure 11. A scaling law of alignment in good views and samples seen. Flickr test R@1 (DINOv2 ViT-B, 30k-pair rotation) of BERT-S text JEPAs trained on the texts of 10.2M web images, against the samples seen. Each point is a run, colored by its fraction q of training items with good views (black: q = 0, bad views only). Circles: the grid the law is fitted on; diamonds: runs predicted before training. Lines: the law at five values of q, dashed beyond the fitted range. We observe that R@1 grows linearly in the logarithm of the samples seen at every fraction of good views, faster with more of them, and that the law predicts unseen runs within seed noise up to twice its range.

Figure 12. Weak views need many data, the kind of data sets the ceiling, good views need neither (Theorem 4). A synthetic world of five classes of six states; the image side is a good-view JEPA whose world kernel links states of one class. The text side observes each state through samples on a line, one block per class, with gaps between blocks (left, literal data) or without (right, mixed data); its bad views join two samples with weight e−d2/2∆2 (weak ∆ = .005, medium .08, strong 1; a state has width 1/6). Alignment is the mean canonical correlation of the two spectral solutions over paired observations (k = 4; 1: equal up to a rotation); lines are means over five samplings, bands their range.

Figure 14. One rotation superimposes two separately trained encoders. Top: joint t-SNE of test images after the best rotation (blue) and their captions (orange), at initialization and after training (good-view JEPA); grey lines join 60 random true pairs. Bottom: independent t-SNEs of the image and text embeddings, colored by caption keywords used only for coloring. We clearly observe that after training, images and their captions share one geometry.

Figure 15. Retrieval through one rotation. Image→caption retrieval (good-view JEPA, epoch 199) for five Flickr test images, with the rank of the true caption among the 1,000 above each list (✓would mark it among the top three). We observe that misses are mostly semantically close.

Figure 13. The captioner’s noise and pairs are predicted, not tuned. Flickr test images. Top: CIDEr against the noise the decoder is trained with; dashed, the noise matched to the residual of the rotation (rotation from 1,014 pairs). Bottom: CIDEr against the number of pairs that fit the one linear map, with and without unpaired refinement, against retrieving the nearest caption through the same map; dashed, decoding the true caption embedding. We clearly observe that transfer peaks at the matched noise, and that a few pairs refined on unpaired data match caption retrieval from 1,014 pairs.

Table 4. A 109M good-view JEPA beats every pair-free zero-shot accuracy of Schnaus et al. [54]. The protocol and method of Schnaus et al. [54], unchanged: DINOv2 ViT-B/14 and a text encoder aligned with zero pairs on unpaired halves of COCO train2014, scored on the 40,504 val2014 pairs (FOSCTTM, lower is better) and by zero-shot top-1 on CIFAR-10 and top-5 on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-100 (%). Means over training seeds times the method’s five seeds (std in Section C). Their best: the best number of their paper for each metric over its 21 vision–language pairs, on these data and in any of its five settings (paper/data/schnaus2026_reported.csv); our reruns of their MPNet pair (all-mpnet-base-v2) reproduce their reported .04, 70, 46 and 45. Last row: the ceiling of Procrustes on all training pairs, range over all encoders. Our good-view JEPAs are trained on the texts of 940M and 100M web images. We clearly observe that a 109M good-view JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy of Schnaus et al. [54], matches their best FOSCTTM on these data, and matches or significantly beats their 8B language model under identical conditions, while next-token prediction on the same texts fails; only CLIP’s text encoder, trained on 400M image–text pairs, aligns better on FOSCTTM and ImageNet-100.

Table 3. At scale, good views beat language models up to 72B parameters. Text encoders against frozen vision models under the PRH protocol: mutual 10-NN and unbiased linear CKA on WIT-1024 with DINOv2ViT-B,mutual 10-NNonWIT-1024with CLIPViT-H/14 and on the 5,000 COCO test pairs with DINOv2 ViT-B, and Flickr R@1 through one rotation fitted on 30k pairs. Our three encoders are BERT-B models (109M) trained with 900M samples from the texts of 940M web images (one seed for the bad-view JEPA); –: not measured. More models in Tables 16 to 18. We clearly observe that the good-view JEPA agrees with both vision models more than any other text encoder, while next-token prediction on the same texts falls far behind.

Table 2. Good-view JEPAs agree with DINOv2 more than the pretrained models we tested. Same protocol with a frozen DINOv2 ViTB/14. Top two rows and bottom two: pretrained models (last layer); the others are ours (BERT-S unless named). All entries use final checkpoints, except the early-stopped row (selected on a loss over the validation and test captions, which can only favor this baseline), with no selection on test data (mean ± half-range over three seeds where shown, seed 0 elsewhere). The last column fits the single map on all 30k Flickr train and validation pairs instead of 1k (–: we kept no epoch29 checkpoint to embed the training captions with). No network is trained on pairs in either case. For reference, our Flickr image JEPA vs. DINOv2 (image vs. image) reaches mutual 10-NN .101 and R@1 .217. The rows above the first rule are trained on Flickr (and COCO) captions, so this comparison is in-domain for them and out-of-domain for most pretrained models (all-mpnet-base-v2, trained on a billion sentence pairs, saw Flickr and COCO captions); the Recap rows never saw a Flickr or COCO caption. CLIP’s text encoder was trained with 400M images. Bold: best of ours. This demonstrates that good-view JEPAs have the neighborhoods closest to DINOv2’s and, trained on web text alone, match or exceed the retrieval of text encoders trained on pairs.

Table 1. Good views align across modalities. Image JEPA vs. each text encoder (epoch 199) on 1,000 Flickr test pairs (backbone features; mean± half-range over three seeds): good-view JEPA (caption views), bad-view JEPA (masked spans), next-token prediction, and next-token prediction on pairs of captions of one image; R@1 and R@5 use a single rotation fitted on validation pairs. We clearly observe that caption views beat masked spans and next-token prediction on every metric, even when next-token prediction is trained on pairs of captions of the same image.

Table 17. The ranking holds on COCO. PRH protocol on the 5,000 COCO Karpathy test pairs (first caption), seed 0 for our encoders except the 940M row, the mean of three seeds (each at or above all-mpnet-base-v2); chance mutual 10-NN is .002. We clearly observe that the 109M good-view JEPA aligns best on a second, five times larger benchmark, ahead of language models up to 72B parameters and of text encoders trained on pairs.

Table 18. Good views win with every vision family. WIT-1024 (PRH protocol) for frozen vision encoders trained by pixel reconstruction (MAE), latent prediction (I-JEPA), crops (DINOv2) or image–text contrast (CLIP’s image encoders, the vision models with which language models align best in Huh et al. [22]), against our text JEPAs (good / bad / next-token on the texts of 50M images, seed 0; the 109M good-view JEPA on the texts of 940M images, seed 0) and pretrained language models. We clearly observe that good views beat next-token prediction and bad views with every vision encoder, and that the 109M good-view JEPA beats the three language models with each of them. MAE and I-JEPA align alike, both below DINOv2, which saw far more curated images; we draw no conclusion on the vision objective. With CLIP’s image encoders, the 109M good-view JEPA’s three seeds average .215, .219 and .230, against .193, .203 and .210 for the best of all our language models up to 72B (Qwen2.5-72B), and its next-token and bad-view controls on the same texts .137–.146 and .108–.116 (runs/results/wit_clip.txt).

Table 16. No language model up to 72B parameters reaches the 109M good-view JEPA. PRH protocol (per-layer features, maximum over layer pairs) on WIT-1024 and on the 5,000 COCO test pairs, for base language models from 0.5B to 72B parameters and our 109M good-view text JEPA trained on the texts of 940M images (mean of three seeds). We clearly observe that scaling next-token prediction by 660 times in parameters does not reach the alignment that good views give.

Table 10. The captioner improves without pairs. Building the captioner up one change at a time: Flickr test (1,000 images) and COCO Karpathy test (5,000 images), beam 3 unless stated; consensus rows choose among the greedy caption and 32 samples. The text JEPA is BERT-S trained on the texts of 100M web images; the decoders are trained on its embeddings of Flickr and COCO training captions only, with noise matched to the alignment (σ = 1.9); the image encoders are frozen. The first row is the captioner of Table 9: on Flickr, the Flickr text JEPA and decoder (σ = 3); on COCO, the Flickr and COCO ones (σ = 2); it decodes greedily on Flickr and with beam 3 on COCO. Decoding the true caption embedding gives .694 and 1.305 (captions-as-written row), and .743 and 1.369 with the web-pretrained decoder. Only the rotation is fitted on image–caption pairs. Without consensus decoding, the best captioner reaches .496 and .806. This demonstrates that stronger frozen encoders, a pretrained language model and consensus decoding each add to the captioner, from CIDEr .668 to .838 on COCO, while a larger decoder does not.

Table 8. Cropping matters, the rest barely moves the mean, and clipping prevents most collapses. R@1 against frozen DINOv2 on Flickr test pairs with one rotation fitted on validation pairs (chance .001), last epoch, for three seeds where shown (one otherwise); a run collapses (×) when its last-epoch R@1 falls below .05. Default views: 2 global and 6 local spans of 50–100% and 15–50% of a caption. Mean: over the seeds that do not collapse (–: every seed collapses). ∗Best over checkpoints on the test pairs, for reference only; the other columns involve no selection. That is, every run that does not collapse stays far above the bad-view JEPA and next-token prediction, and without gradient clipping 3 of the 36 runs with the default SIGReg weight collapse. In stable-pretraining as we ran it, SIGReg is scaled by the number of embeddings it sees, so the batch and view rows also change its effective weight: ×2 for batch 512, × 1 2 for 2 + 2 views and ×1.5 for 2 + 10 views.

Table 6. Bad views spend their embedding on nuisance. Scene-explained fraction ρ( f ) = tr C1/2 f /k of each text encoder’s top-k whitened embedding (mean ± half-range over three seeds), the lower bound 2k(1− ρ( f )) of Theorem 3 on the best-rotation error against DINOv2 ViT-B, and that error (means over seeds; bounds from the unrounded fractions; uncorrelated embeddings give 2k, i.e., 64 and 256). We clearly observe that the bound holds for every encoder, and the scene-explained fraction ranks the encoders as their alignment does.

Table 7. The views and the data both set the alignment. BERT-S text JEPAs, one recipe per scale, three seeds (mean and range), scored on WIT-1024 with DINOv2 ViT-B and on Flickr through one rotation fitted on 30k pairs; scene-explained: ρ( f ) on Flickr captions (k = 32, seed 0, Table 6). The paraphrase is written from the alt-text alone by a text-only language model, so that row involves no image captioner. We observe that with the same bad views, LLaVA recaptions align far better than alt-texts, and with the same texts, good views double alignment (Theorem 4).

Table 11. Captions and retrieval for video, from photos alone. Top: zero-shot captioning of the MSR-VTT test clips (20 references each; CIDEr on a 0–1 scale) by our captioner, whose networks never saw a video, a video–caption pair or MSR-VTT text, and by captioners built on CLIP’s encoders without MSR-VTT text, with one trained on MSR-VTT captions for reference (–: not reported). Bottom: alignment (mutual 10-NN fits nothing) and retrieval through one map on the 1k-A split, against zero-shot CLIP. We observe that a rotation fitted on photos captions and retrieves videos, above captioners built on CLIP that use no MSR-VTT text, though CLIP’s jointly trained encoders retrieve better.

Table 14. Alignment keeps growing with the texts of 940M images. Checkpoints of our largest good-view JEPAs (seed 0 unless named; †: mean of three seeds at the end of training; ‡: another seed with twice the effective SIGReg weight, see text; next-token: the same encoder trained to predict the next token; bad views: two masked copies of one text, at the effective SIGReg weight of the first 940M run), scored on WIT-1024 with DINOv2 ViT-B and on Flickr through one rotation fitted on 30k pairs. We observe thatWIT alignment jumps between the texts of 200M and 940M images and rises again by 850M samples, while Flickr retrieval rises more slowly. Bold: best per column.

Table 12. Linear-evaluation features and concatenated encoders align best. Flickr test pairs, text JEPAs trained on Recap texts only (seed 0), each against a frozen self-supervised image encoder through one map with orthonormal rows fitted on the 30k Flickr train and validation pairs (chance: mutual 10-NN .01, R@1 .001). Bottom rows: the CLS + mean patch features of two encoders, each rescaled to unit root-mean-square per coordinate, concatenated. No network is trained on pairs. Notably, with DINOv3 ViT-7B, one rotation retrieves the true caption first for more than half of the test images.

Table 15. A 109M text JEPA beats language models on the PRH benchmark. PRH protocol of Huh et al. [22]: WIT-1024 pairs, per-layer features, clipping, normalization, maximum over layer pairs. For reference, DINOv2 ViT-B × BERT-base scores .111, all-mpnet-base-v2 .118 and CLIP’s text encoder .124 (.113–.137 across DINOv2 sizes for these two); our Flickr-trained text encoders (good / bad / next-token) score .029–.036 with every DINOv2 size and .023–.024 with our Flickr image JEPA; and our Flickr image JEPA × DINOv2 ViT-B (image vs. image) .241. nt: next-token prediction. Our 33M text JEPAs’ entries are means of three seeds, which differ by at most ±.009 with DINOv2 ViT-B; the 109M column is the mean of three seeds (each above every language model). At least 43 of the 1,024 WIT captions appear among the Recap-DataComp alt-texts; on the other 981 pairs, none of the nine text models we checked with DINOv2 ViT-B (ours, Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Mistral-7B) changes by more than .002. This demonstrates that the 109M good-view JEPA surpasses every language model we evaluated with every vision encoder it was scored with, including our image JEPAs trained from scratch.

Table 13. Good views help on both sides (numbers behind Figure 8). MSR-VTT, 1,000 test clips, final checkpoints, mean ± half-range over three seeds (chance: mutual 10-NN .01, R@1 .001). R@1 and R@5 use one rotation fitted on the 1,990 validation clips. Every seed ranks the four combinations the same way in mutual 10-NN; the image-side effect is small and reverses on R@5.

Table 9. Captioning from independently trained encoders. BLEU-4 [45], CIDEr [62] on Flickr test images. The decoder never sees an image; the image encoder never sees text; pairs only fit one linear map. BLEU-4 rewards generic n-grams, so the random map’s fluent but generic captions score above 1,014-pair retrieval on BLEU-4, not on CIDEr. We clearly observe that decoding through the rotation beats retrieving captions through it by a wide margin.

Table 5. Good views also make better text encoders. Text encoders alone (caption→caption retrieval among the 5,000 Flickr test captions: is the nearest caption one of the four others describing the same image?) and alignment measured on projector outputs (seed 0; –: no trained projector). We clearly observe that the bad-view JEPA learns little beyond word overlap (below TF-IDF), while the good-view JEPA goes well beyond it. The image JEPA reaches 78.5% 20-NN accuracy on Imagenette [21] (29.1% at initialization).

papers.selection_reason: Theoretically and empirically studies multimodal representation alignment in joint-embedding predictive architectures, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs
papers.tldr: The paper proves that JEPAs trained on well-matched views can converge to shared representations more efficiently than next-token prediction, challenging scale-only routes to multimodal alignment.

papers.abstract: We present Youtu-Parsing-Omni, an omni-modal parser that converts documents, images, audio, and video into structured records grounded in space and time, providing a perception layer for agents that read, locate, and cite evidence across modalities. Its design rests on one encoder for every modality and one schema for every task. Youtu-Omni-Encoder, initialized from a pre-trained language model to strengthen text reading, encodes all modalities with shared weights in a unified space-time coordinate system, and a few fusion layers let video frames attend to concurrent audio, bringing cross-modal fusion and temporal alignment into perception itself. OmniSchema unifies the outputs of all ten parsing tasks, allowing a single self-evolving post-training procedure, OmniSchema-Aware On-Policy Distillation (OSAD), to provide a shared token-role-based objective across tasks. In each round, the model is trained on its own rollouts against token-level targets from a reference-conditioned copy of itself, which is then refreshed with the trained weights, so that the parser and its supervision co-evolve. With a single 5 B-parameter checkpoint, Youtu-Parsing-Omni achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniDocBench v1.6 (96.96 Overall) and leads all open-weight models on OmniParsingBench (75.08 Avg.), with its advantage concentrated on audio and video. It also achieves the best overall chart-parsing score (95.02) and the highest exact chemical-fingerprint agreement among compared systems, and matches a dedicated optical-music model in character-level transcription of typeset sheet music while staying far ahead of general-purpose systems. Code and model weights are publicly available.
authors: Yunhang Shen, Zhangquan Chen, Xiaotian Li, Zhongpeng Cai, Qing Zhou, Zekai Zhang, Kun Zhang, Zezhong Wu, Jian Hu, Haihan Gao, Heting Gao, Xin Li, Yinsong Liu, Deqian Jiang, Di Yin, Haoyu Cao, Xing Sun, Bing Liu, Yanqiu Qu, Yunfei Wu, Kun Yin, Zhixiang Wei, Yongxiang Hua, Qianyu Li, Xiaoxing Hu, Peiyuan Zhang, Lijiang Li, Dong Xu, Zhenchuan Yang, Yiliang Jiang
bullets: Unifies ten parsing tasks through OmniSchema and a shared token-role objective.
Youtu-Omni-Encoder represents all modalities in a common space-time coordinate system, with audio–video fusion layers.
OSAD uses self-generated rollouts and refreshed reference models for self-evolving post-training.
A single 5B-parameter checkpoint reports leading results on OmniDocBench v1.6 and among open-weight models on OmniParsingBench, especially for audio and video.
It also performs strongly on chart parsing, chemical fingerprints, and typeset sheet-music transcription; code and weights are public.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of omni-modal parsing architectures. We compare how visual and audio inputs are encoded before reaching the language model in the conventional design and in Youtu-Parsing-Omni. (a) Existing omni-modal parsers encode pixels and audio with two separately pre-trained towers, whose streams first meet inside the language model. (b) Youtu-Parsing-Omni replaces both towers with a single encoder, Youtu-Omni-Encoder. Thin modality-specific stems map pixels and log-mel frames to tokens; a shared bidirectional block then contextualizes an arbitrary packed mix of images, audio chunks, and videos under one (𝑡 , ℎ, 𝑤) positional encoding; and a few of its layers (red) attend across modalities within short audio-visual windows (Fig. 4). As a result, pixels and sound share weights and positional encoding, and interact already inside the encoder.

Figure 7. Youtu-Parsing-Omni is the only model above 96 on OmniDocBench v1.6 that also parses images, audio, and video, and its gain over Youtu-Parsing comes mostly from tables and formulas. (a) OmniDocBench v1.6 Overall against total parameters (teal: open-weight), with API systems in a strip at the right; the document specialists at our level have 0.8–1.2 B parameters. (b) Per-metric difference to Youtu-Parsing [4], our previous model, and to TeleOCR [47], the next-best system overall; edit distances are shown as 1 − Edit so that a positive difference always favors Youtu-Parsing-Omni.

Figure 4. Concurrent visual and audio content share fusion windows and a common temporal coordinate system. (a) A video with eight frames (I) and four audio chunks (A), packed in temporal order, with each chunk placed after the frames it overlaps. A non-fusion layer gives every frame and every chunk its own window; a fusion layer starts a new window at every audio-to-frame boundary, so the video forms four (I+A∗) windows; red cells mark the cross-modal pairs, and off-diagonal blue cells the frame-to-frame pairs, that only fusion layers admit. (b) Vision tokens take 𝑡 from the frame index and (ℎ, 𝑤) from the patch grid; audio tokens take 𝑡 from their offset and write into the same temporal rotary slots. Inside a fusion window both advance on the common time scale of Equ. 1.

Figure 8. Encoder architecture and initialization studies. (a) General multimodal (Avg-6); (b) OCRBench; (c) BLINK; (d) LibriSpeech test-clean WER. Blue, green, and pink denote the text-initialized unified encoder, randomly initialized unified encoder, and pre-trained SigLIP-2 [80] and SenseVoice-small [81] towers, respectively.
Figure 1. Youtu-Parsing-Omni ranks first on OmniDocBench v1.6 (a), is the strongest open-weight model on OmniParsingBench (b), and also leads on most domain-specific benchmarks (c).

Figure 2. Omni-modal parsing with one encoder and one schema. Youtu-Parsing-Omni parses documents, natural images, audio, and video with Youtu-Omni-Encoder shared across all modalities, and unifies their parsing tasks in OmniSchema.
Figure 6. OSAD combines token-adaptive on-policy supervision with teacher refresh at each round boundary.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful tool for improving multimodal reasoning. However, standard outcome supervision suffers from credit assignment ambiguity, as a model may receive positive rewards by exploiting language priors or dataset shortcuts rather than grounding its reasoning in the requisite visual evidence. This makes high-quality negative responses critical, since effective negatives should remain plausible under the current policy while exposing the shortcut that should be suppressed. In this paper, we propose EVAN, a multimodal reinforcement learning framework utilizing EVidence-Ablated Negatives to train LMMs against their own language-prior failures. EVAN first identifies highly visually dependent examples using a scaled image information gain metric and preserves data diversity with a mixed-ranking strategy. It then constructs evidence-ablated images by masking the most discriminative image patches, eliciting plausible but visually ungrounded responses from the current policy. During policy optimization, these negative responses are incorporated as bounded auxiliary signals under the clean image, penalizing shortcut learning while maintaining RL stability. Experiments across challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that EVAN mitigates modality imbalance and improves over strong RLVR baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/DawnLIU35/EVAN.git.
authors: Chenxi Liu, Tianyi Xiong, Yanshuo Chen, Heng Huang
bullets: RLVR outcome rewards can miss whether reasoning is grounded in images, allowing language-prior shortcuts.
EVAN identifies visually dependent examples and masks discriminative image patches to generate plausible, ungrounded negative responses.
These negatives are used as bounded auxiliary penalties during policy optimization to suppress shortcut learning while preserving stability.
Experiments on challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks show improved modality balance and performance over strong RLVR baselines.
Scope: the approach targets multimodal reasoning settings where visual evidence is necessary.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained audio-visual question answering (AVQA) requires models to resolve complex cross-modal correspondences and temporally grounding from sparsely distributed evidence. Omni-modal agents, which autonomously orchestrate perception tools to actively collect evidence, achieve strong performance, but it remains unclear whether active perception from both audio and visual modalities depends on broad specialized toolsets, especially audio or visual modality-specific tools. Such systems may also introduce long execution trajectories and substantial inference cost. We investigate whether comparable performance can be retained with a compact workflow exposing only essential perceptual capabilities. Starting from the specialized-tool OmniAgent, we conduct staged controlled experiments that prune the toolset and progressively consolidate modality-specific tools into omni-modal tools, motivating a two-tool agent comprising only Omni-modal captioning and Omni-modal QA. Across three widely used AVQA benchmarks, our compact agent achieves comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent while reducing inference cost by around 70%.
authors: Yi Wang, Tianzi Wang, Peter Bell
bullets: Targets the cost and long execution trajectories of broad tool-based audio-visual agents.
Uses staged tool-pruning experiments and progressively consolidates audio- and visual-specific tools.
The resulting workflow retains only omni-modal captioning and omni-modal question answering.
Evaluated on three widely used AVQA benchmarks with comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent.
Scope: focuses on compacting perception workflows while maintaining performance on benchmark AVQA tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have led to significant progress in visual reasoning capabilities. However, existing benchmarks curate image-question pairs pertaining to object categories with few instances, enabling trivial object referencing and limited visual ambiguity. In this work, we introduce MIMO-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs in a Multi-Instance per Multi-Object categories (MIMO) setting. Each image-question pair in our benchmark pertains to instances belonging to object categories with multiple instances. The presence of such similar feature distractors causes hindrance in basic visual reasoning tasks, necessitating the referring expression to be composed of multiple visual subtasks to uniquely and unambiguously identify the target object. MIMO-Bench comprises 3,802 image-question pairs across attribute binding and numerical counting tasks. Despite impressive performances on existing benchmarks, both SOTA open-source (InternVL, QwenVL) and proprietary (Gemini, GPT-5) models exhibit substantially lower performance on MIMO-Bench, highlighting their limitations in the MIMO setting. The benchmark will be made publicly available.
authors: Saumya Mundra, Ajoy Mondal, Vineeth N Balasubramanian, C. V. Jawahar
bullets: Existing visual-reasoning benchmarks often contain few object instances, allowing relatively easy object reference.
MIMO-Bench introduces 3,802 image-question pairs involving multiple instances across multiple object categories.
Tasks cover attribute binding and numerical counting, requiring multi-step referring expressions to disambiguate targets.
Both open-source models such as InternVL and QwenVL and proprietary models such as Gemini and GPT-5 perform substantially worse in this setting.
The benchmark is intended to be publicly available.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly process multiple views of the same scene, but it remains unclear whether they integrate these observations into a coherent scene-level representation. Existing multi-image evaluations do not isolate this capability, as tasks may admit correct solutions through independent per-view processing without requiring cross-view correspondence. We introduce OneScene-Bench, a controlled benchmark designed to explicitly distinguish when cross-view integration is necessary. Our benchmark evaluates three complementary capabilities on real-world multi-view scenes: unique object counting, cross-view consistency, and spatial reasoning. For counting, we control object overlap across views to separate cases solvable by simple per-view aggregation from those requiring instance-level correspondence. For consistency, we introduce localized edits in shared and view-specific regions, testing whether models distinguish genuine scene contradictions from differences caused by viewpoint and visibility. For spatial reasoning, we construct object relations that require combining spatial evidence across viewpoints to compare physical proximity. We evaluate twelve state-of-the-art open-weight and proprietary VLMs and find that counting accuracy drops substantially on complementary views, ranging from 4.5-50.0%, compared with 45.5-81.5% on complete-overlap examples. Moreover, cross-view consistency remains around 50% across models, including recent proprietary VLMs, despite substantially stronger performance on spatial reasoning. Our results reveal a substantial gap between processing multiple images and integrating evidence across them, highlighting the need for evaluations that explicitly test scene-level multi-view understanding. Code and data are available at https://github.com/swathisuhas/OneScene-Bench.
authors: Swathi Suhas, Anurag Das, Bernt Schiele, Jonas Fischer
bullets: Introduces a controlled benchmark for testing cross-view integration in real-world multi-view scenes.
Evaluates unique object counting, cross-view consistency, and spatial reasoning.
Counting accuracy drops substantially on complementary views, reaching 4.5–50.0% versus 45.5–81.5% with complete overlap.
Cross-view consistency remains near 50% across models, including proprietary VLMs, while spatial reasoning is comparatively stronger.
Highlights a major gap between handling multiple images and combining evidence across views.

papers.abstract: Contextual embeddings represent chunks of a document with respect to the document's global context. These models are typically trained and evaluated under the assumption that a relevant document contains only a single relevant chunk. In this work, we argue that in real-world use cases a retriever should not only find answers spread over several chunks but also surface the evidence needed to verify them. To address this, we introduce pplx-embed-v2-context, a family of contextual embedding models trained by distilling graded chunk-level relevance from a query-aware context compression model. This removes the need for gold-chunk labels and makes the training targets independent of the chunking. We utilize a vision-language backbone for training and release pplx-embed-v2-context in 9B and 0.6B sizes with compatible embedding spaces. On the evaluation side, we introduce two benchmarks that label both the chunks that answer a query and the evidence needed to verify the answer. Context-bench is a controlled diagnostic, and Q2D-Chunk is built from real-world search queries. To encourage further research, we also publish Q2D-Chunk as a public leaderboard. Our 9B model sets a new state of the art on both benchmarks and ConTEB. We find that the visual retrieval capabilities of our 9B model transfer from its vision-language base model and propose to extend chunking to image inputs. We demonstrate that our models achieve state-of-the-art performance among dense retrievers on visual ViDoRe-V3 and that performance improves with granular image chunking.
authors: Sedigheh Eslami, Markus Krimmel, William Barber, Antoine Chaffin, Maximilian Schall, Jonas Golde, Louis Milliken, Ekaterina Glazkova, Denis Bykov, Bo Wang

Releases compatible 9B and 0.6B embedding models trained with a vision-language backbone.
Introduces Context-bench and Q2D-Chunk, which evaluate answer and verification evidence retrieval; Q2D-Chunk includes a public leaderboard.
The 9B model achieves state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks, ConTEB, and visual ViDoRe-V3 among dense retrievers.
Visual retrieval transfers from the backbone, and finer-grained image chunking improves performance.

papers.abstract: Gardening in the backyard implies living there, while checking into an Airbnb more likely means staying for a few days. Such duration judgments are important for understanding human mobility, travel behavior, and social context. However, duration is rarely stated explicitly in social media posts and must instead be inferred from noisy textual, visual, and contextual cues. In this paper, we investigate whether vision-language models possess such duration commonsense. We create a new corpus of geotagged tweets co-annotated by humans and LLMs to serve as a testbed for this task. We find that state-of-the-art models struggle with duration inference, even when guided by multi-turn Chain-of-Thought prompting. Error analyses further reveal that models often fail to integrate critical contextual information, or they overly rely on prominent visual details while overlooking subtle hashtags and semantic nuances. These findings underscore the significant challenges remaining in context-aware multimodal understanding.
authors: Chenyang Yu, Zhaomin Xiao, Yan Huang, Eduardo Blanco
bullets: Introduces duration commonsense reasoning as a task for interpreting human mobility and social context.
Builds a geotagged-tweet corpus co-annotated by humans and LLMs.
Evaluates vision-language models, including with multi-turn Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Models often miss important context, hashtags, and semantic nuances while overemphasizing salient visual details.
Results highlight persistent challenges in context-aware multimodal understanding.

papers.abstract: Visual rule reasoning asks whether multimodal models can recover an abstract concept from a few examples. Existing studies either infer rules from visual examples but evaluate only classification or verbalization, or supervise executable generation with rules provided as input. Consequently, the relationship between visual rule understanding and reliable rule instantiation remains insufficiently explored. We present Bongard-Forge100k, a controlled benchmark, together with RuleForge, a backbone-agnostic framework that jointly learns visual rule understanding and rule-conditioned executable generation. The benchmark contains 108,797 problems: 86,000 for training, 19,297 for testing familiar rules, and 3,500 for testing held-out rule compositions. The framework progresses through rule-understanding training, joint understanding and scene-program supervision, and refinement via execution-grounded reinforcement learning with Understanding Replay. Executing generated programs under multiple random seeds provides verifiable feedback on executability, rule satisfaction, diversity, and robustness. With UniLIP as the primary backbone, RuleForge improves multiple-choice accuracy over the base model by 20.93 percentage points on familiar rules and 28.42 percentage points on held-out rule compositions, while increasing scene-level rule satisfaction on familiar rules from 2.91% to 70.99%. Additional experiments on InternVL3.5, Qwen3-VL, and Show-o2 demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed training data and framework across diverse multimodal architectures.
authors: Weifeng Xu, Yaxiong Wang, Zhedong Zheng
bullets: Introduces Bongard-Forge100k, a 108,797-problem benchmark covering familiar rules and held-out rule compositions.
Uses staged training: rule understanding, joint understanding with scene-program supervision, and execution-grounded reinforcement learning with Understanding Replay.
Evaluates generated programs through execution across random seeds for executability, rule satisfaction, diversity, and robustness.
With UniLIP, improves multiple-choice accuracy by 20.93 points on familiar rules and 28.42 points on held-out compositions.
Raises familiar-rule scene satisfaction from 2.91% to 70.99%; results extend across several multimodal backbones.

papers.abstract: Human handwriting is produced as an ordered sequence of pen movements, but an offline image keeps only the final ink. Handwriting trajectory recovery aims to restore the ordered stroke points and their pen-up/pen-down transitions. Existing image-trajectory pair datasets are recorded with digitizing tablets under controlled conditions, which limits writer coverage and stylistic diversity. Moreover, there is no benchmark that measures the visual grounding capabilities of general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for the stroke trajectory recovery task. In this work, we introduce inkGround, a benchmark for stroke trajectory recovery from full-page, camera-captured handwriting. inkGround pairs 537 page images (~18.7k words, ~163k strokes) with reference trajectories produced by a pretrained offline-to-online model, filtered by OCR agreement, and verified by human raters. Because these references are pseudo-labels that represent one plausible pen trajectory, we also evaluate VLMs on the IAM-OnDB dataset, which provides recorded pen trajectories. We cast the task as text-conditioned point grounding: given a page image and a target word, the model must locate the word and output its ordered stroke points. Outputs are scored by trajectory fidelity (DTW, Chamfer distance), readability of the rendered strokes (Accurate Rate, Correct Rate), and style similarity. We benchmark four open-source and three frontier closed-source VLMs with a shared in-context prompt. Closed-source models, notably Gemini-3.1-Pro, produce legible trajectories close to the reference, and this ranking also holds on IAM-OnDB.

Evaluates trajectory fidelity, rendered-stroke readability, and style similarity across four open-source and three closed-source VLMs.
Closed-source models—especially Gemini-3.1-Pro—generate legible trajectories close to references, with the ranking replicated on IAM-OnDB.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. However, existing proactive paradigms typically assume that the information required to answer a query is complete, leaving models to only wait or answer. In the real world, however, information is often incomplete due to uncertainty from either the video or the user. In proactive paradigms, such uncertainty can cause the model to wait forever or generate highly hallucinatory responses. We therefore argue that proactive interaction should be redefined with a third action: ask, allowing models to actively ask for missing information. To study when and what models should ask before answering, we introduce AskStream, the first multi-turn benchmark spanning video and user uncertainty for streaming video understanding, with four task categories and eight subtasks. It contains 438 videos with 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask, and answer. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, even the strongest model attains only 52.18% on our proposed Ask-F1 metric, highlighting substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty.
authors: Lu Wang, Zhuoran Jin, Longxiang Wang, Junhong Chen, Yupu Hao, Yao Xu, Daojian Zeng, Yubo Chen, Kang Liu, Guang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Existing systems often assume complete information, risking endless waiting or hallucinated answers when video or user intent is unclear.
The benchmark evaluates multi-turn interaction across video and user uncertainty with four categories and eight subtasks.
It includes 438 videos and 2,714 manually annotated frame-level windows labeled wait, ask, or answer.
Models remain substantially challenged: the strongest reported model reaches 52.18% on the Ask-F1 metric.
The benchmark covers both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, emphasizing proactive information seeking.

papers.title: AskStream: When and What to Ask Proactively under Uncertainty in Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: AskStream reframes proactive streaming video understanding as deciding whether to wait, ask for missing information, or answer under uncertainty.

papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) can process speech directly, but it remains unclear how well they use the non-lexical acoustic information that speech carries. We study this question through pain, using TAME-Pain, which contains pain-neutral Harvard sentences and spoken pain ratings recorded at different self-reported pain levels. We introduce HEAR, a four-stage diagnostic framework that traces pain-related information from the speech signal to the model's prediction, and apply it to seven closed-source and open-weight LALMs. On the Harvard sentences, where pain can only be inferred from the voice, all models perform at chance level, and same-speaker references or few-shot examples improve balanced accuracy by no more than six points. On the spoken ratings, the same models reach 87.5-99.7% balanced accuracy. Layer-wise probing of open-weight LALMs shows that pain can be decoded from early audio representations (74.1% balanced accuracy for binary prediction and 45.0% for three-class severity), but that this information, along with most pain-associated acoustic cues, decreases in deeper layers. In an acoustic perception test, weaker models cannot distinguish even large changes in these cues, whereas stronger models can but still fail to infer pain. Finally, we recover pain-related acoustic cues and directly reinject them as structured text into the prompt, which improves pairwise pain prediction by up to 32 points. These results indicate that current LALMs encode paralinguistic information in early layers that is largely unavailable when the model produces its answer.
authors: Wenqi Li, Xiangjue Dong, Sulaiman Vesal
bullets: On pain-neutral Harvard sentences, where pain is conveyed only through voice, all seven LALMs perform at chance; references and few-shot examples help by at most six balanced-accuracy points.
On spoken pain ratings, models achieve 87.5–99.7% balanced accuracy, suggesting performance depends strongly on task and available linguistic information.
HEAR traces pain information from audio to prediction: pain is decodable in early representations but declines in deeper layers, along with most associated acoustic cues.
Stronger models can perceive large acoustic changes yet still fail to infer pain; reinjecting recovered cues as structured text improves pairwise prediction by up to 32 points.

Table 11: Construction and validation of the audio perturbations. We select ten representative acoustic attributes spanning the four parameter groups across 88 features. Each manipulation aims to shift its target eGeMAPSv02 parameter(s) while leaving parameters of other feature families unchanged (parameters within one family are inherently correlated). Shifts are measured on 24 recordings, each from a different training speaker, as the perturbed recording minus its matching null resynthesis (same tool at zero strength), divided by that parameter’s mean within-speaker SD over the training speakers. Target shift is the median of this shift over the 24 recordings, oriented so that a leading − on a target parameter means it is expected to decrease, and averaged over the target parameters when a cue has several. Range: for each cue and direction, the candidate strength whose Target shift is closest to ±1 SD. Largest off-target feature: the parameter with the largest median absolute shift after excluding the target’s own family (e.g., all F0 parameters for the pitch cues). Its ratio to |Target shift| is flagged when above 0.5 but is only reported, not used for filtering. RMS level is matched to the original recording for every manipulation except Loudness. Filtering. A setting passes calibration if |Target shift| ∈ [0.5, 1.5] and none of the 24 recordings fails processing; passing settings are shown in bold, and non-bold settings are excluded. WORLD could not lower jitter, shimmer or breathiness (Target shift ≈ 0), so these cues were tested in the increase direction only, contrasting a 2× against the 1× strength. Pairs: test recordings (760 in total, from 10 held-out speakers) for which both perturbed versions of a cue were processed successfully; the effect of each bidirectional cue is estimated from the + versus − version of the same recording. Cues marked † were excluded from the analysis because more than 5% of their 1×/2× pairs showed no achieved change in the target parameter (jitter 10.0%, shimmer 8.9%, breathiness 9.3%). In total we generated 18,240 test-set versions for the 17 passing settings and 7 null resyntheses (4 failed, all Pauses), 2,280 2× WORLD versions, and 4,560 round-trip null resyntheses for the PSOLA and speech-rate cues. a Each sample is multiplied by (e/ẽ)k−1, where e is the smoothed Hilbert envelope, ẽ its median and k the exponent; k > 1 exaggerates and k < 1 flattens loudness fluctuations. b Non-speech stretches detected by WebRTC VAD are resampled to the given multiple of their length; speech is left unchanged. c One of the 24 calibration recordings also failed processing. d 760 minus 4 recordings whose perturbation failed and 1 recording whose + and − versions had identical target values.

papers.selection_reason: Studies audio large language models as multimodal systems and traces acoustic information through their reasoning.
papers.title: Do Audio LLMs HEAR Pain? Tracing Acoustic Evidence from Speech to Language Reasoning
papers.tldr: Current audio LLMs encode pain-related vocal cues early, but largely fail to use them for pain reasoning and prediction.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires models not only to acquire useful training experience, but also to decide when their current experience has ceased to be useful. Existing methods often focus on what experience to generate next, while paying less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced. Many also construct training targets through self-consistency or majority voting, making supervision depend on the model's own uncertain predictions. We address these two questions separately: training dynamics determine when to acquire new experience, while the answers to new tasks remain independently checkable. A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh a task pool when its learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers; we specify the task-generation contract, automatically verify chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules, and separately audit the generated answers. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, A-RSI raises the performance average from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.
authors: Yu Liu, Youxing Li, Yuedong Tan, Zhiwei Yang, Zihan Su, Hanqi Feng, Shaojie Zhang, Libin Liao, Zihao Wan, Chenxu Wu, Cong Cao, Fangfang Yuan, Yanbing Liu, Ziheng Chen, Pei Fu, Radu Timofte, Zongwei Wu, Nicu Sebe, Barnabas Poczos, Jian Luan
bullets: Addresses when to introduce fresh experience, complementing methods that focus on what experience to generate.
Uses reward variation and training accuracy to detect declining learning signals without validation or test scores.
Generates multimodal questions from a static library of model-authored programs with independently checkable answers.
Automatically verifies task properties and refresh rules, while separately auditing generated answers.
Raises average performance from 57.77 to 61.05 using 800 fresh tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses zero-data multimodal self-improvement and task refresh for multimodal LLMs, fitting multimodal instruction-tuning interests.
papers.title: A-RSI: Adaptive Task Refresh for Zero-Data Multimodal Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: A-RSI enables zero-data multimodal self-improvement by refreshing tasks when training signals weaken, improving average performance on an eleven-benchmark suite.

papers.abstract: The large-scale digitisation of medieval manuscripts creates a growing need for automated iconographic indexing. We evaluate two complementary paradigms for this task on 9,735 full-folio images annotated with 2,333 TIMEL concepts: generative Vision-Language Models (VLM) and supervised discriminative classifiers (SDC). The VLM experiments evaluate fine-tuning, structured JSON decoding, taxonomybased candidates generation, and deterministic reranking. The discriminative experiments evaluate flat, hierarchy-aware, and patch-attention heads over a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Our results highlight key functional differences: ML-Decoder (SDC) achieves the strongest overall retrieval performance (precision@1 of 0.696, MRR of 0.806), with loss calibration (Asymmetric Loss) serving as the primary performance lever. While SDCs provide superior precision and reliability within a closed vocabulary, VLMs offer strong semantic generalization and broad taxonomic coverage, particularly through structured JSON targets and verify-calibrate reranking (hierarchical F1 of 0.559). Furthermore, model behavior strongly depends on concept abstraction: SDCs excel at perceptually grounded descriptive concepts, whereas VLMs provide useful hypotheses for complex interpretative scenes. Finally, we find that enforcing explicit hierarchy within model architectures limits coverage compared to spatial feature aggregation. Overall, rather than competing approaches, SDCs and VLMs emerge as complementary components for future hybrid indexing systems combining structured retrieval with exploratory annotation assistance. As a methodological contribution, we define the soft F1 metric to provide a taxonomy-aware evaluation that credits semantically close predictions based on lowest common ancestors.
authors: Vincent Jolivet (ENC, CJM), Lucas Terriel (ENC), Chahan Vidal-Gor{\`e}ne (CJM, ENC)
bullets: Evaluates generative VLMs and supervised discriminative classifiers on 9,735 folio images annotated with 2,333 TIMEL concepts.
ML-Decoder achieves the strongest retrieval performance, with precision@1 of 0.696 and MRR of 0.806; Asymmetric Loss is the main performance lever.
VLMs show broader taxonomic coverage and semantic generalization, especially with structured JSON targets and verify-calibrate reranking.
Classifiers perform best on perceptually grounded concepts, whereas VLMs better support hypotheses for complex interpretative scenes.
The approaches are complementary: the study proposes hybrid systems and introduces taxonomy-aware soft F1 evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: VLM pipeline for TIMEL classification. All strategies share one backbone(Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, full SFT; a QLoRA Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline reported separately)and diverge only at three stages. Training-side augmentation (dynamic Albumentations and staticmosaic/pairmix/oversampling, both long-tail-oriented) feeds the SFT. Four output-encoding families differ in target representation and decoding constraint: (A) flat French labels, optionally trie-constrained (V5); (B) opaque tm-xxxx identifiers (V4, abandoned); (C) explicit root-to-leaf pathswith trie, minimum-label and beam constraints (V6/V6.1 and the staged HCoT variant V7); (D)the retained categorised-JSON target (V9), a bare TRL SFTTrainer decoded greedily. Predic-tions are parsed to a flat leaf set, optionally refined by post-processing (consistency, semantic/self-embedding remap, multimodal LLM-judge), then scored. The TIMEL taxonomy supplies trie pre-fixes (A-V5, C), JSON category keys and the consistency filter (D), and the ancestor sets used bythe hierarchical metrics.

papers.selection_reason: Compares generative vision-language models and supervised classifiers for structured visual annotation, contributing to multimodal model evaluation and use.
papers.title: Automatic Iconographic Annotation of Medieval Illuminations: Comparing Generative Vision-Language Models and Supervised Discriminative Classifiers
papers.tldr: The study finds that supervised classifiers are best for precise closed-vocabulary retrieval, while vision-language models add semantic breadth and exploratory value for medieval iconographic indexing.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs), which can process and generate diverse modalities within a single framework, have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm. However, when these models undergo continual learning on multiple tasks across different modalities, their learning and forgetting dynamics remain poorly understood. In this paper, we systematically investigate how architectural design and adaptation method shape intra-modal learning and cross-modal interference between the generation and understanding sides. Specifically, we report three findings. First, the severity of cross-modal interference decreases with the degree of modality-specific parameter isolation. Second, a within-model asymmetry: the generation side of a UMM is markedly more fragile than its understanding side. Third, what post-training adds is the first to be forgotten: purely post-training capabilities such as personalized generation collapse by 84\% to 90\%, while pretraining capabilities remain stable. Together, these results clarify how parameter isolation and post-training fragility shape UMMs' learning and forgetting dynamics, offering a starting point for developing continually evolving UMMs.
authors: Xinrui Wang, Zhihao Chen, Jia Tang, Alexandra Gomez-Villa, Bartlomiej Twardowski, Joost van de Weijer, Songcan Chen
bullets: Greater modality-specific parameter isolation reduces cross-modal interference.
The generation side is substantially more fragile than the understanding side.
Post-training capabilities, such as personalized generation, are forgotten first, while pretrained capabilities remain stable.
The findings provide design guidance for building continually adapting multimodal models.

papers.abstract: Humans routinely consume multimodal content, where textual and visual information is naturally interleaved. Although Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) can jointly generate text and images, multimodal interleaved generation remains largely underexplored. Progress in this area is hindered by two key limitations: (1) the lack of well-defined interleaved generation tasks and corresponding training data, and (2) the absence of fine-grained evaluation protocols that can reliably diagnose model performance across different capability dimensions. To this end, we present IntReal, comprising two complementary components: IntReal-100K, a real-world dataset of multimodal interleaved samples spanning four major categories, and the IntReal Evaluation Suite, which evaluates model performance across seven complementary dimensions using specialized expert models, enabling coarse-to-fine diagnosis. Extensive experiments validate our evaluation suite through low inter-metric redundancy (max pairwise absolute Spearman's $\rho \leq 0.42$ ), high agreement with human judgments (83.3% accuracy), and strong consistency across different expert evaluators (Spearman's $\rho > 0.9$ ), supporting the complementarity and reliability of our metrics. By benchmarking four families of UMMs, we show that IntReal Evaluation Suite reveals distinct strengths and weaknesses across models. Post-training experiments demonstrate the utility of IntReal-100K for improving interleaved generation and further show that training unimodal generation can also benefit interleaved generation. These findings suggest that interleaved generation can benefit from modality-specific optimization, rather than requiring joint text-image training at every stage.
authors: Shaohan Yu, Jie Qin, Wende Tan, Haiwen Diao, Limeng Qiao, Yueming Lyu, Chenyang Si
bullets: Addresses the lack of standardized tasks, training data, and fine-grained evaluation for generating interleaved text and images.
Provides IntReal-100K, a dataset spanning four major categories, plus an evaluation suite using specialized expert models.
The suite shows low redundancy between metrics, 83.3% agreement with human judgments, and strong consistency across expert evaluators.
Benchmarking four UMM families reveals distinct capability profiles; post-training with IntReal-100K improves interleaved generation.
Results suggest modality-specific optimization can benefit interleaved generation without joint text-image training at every stage.

papers.abstract: To solve problems in 3D space rather than merely describe images, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) need 3D spatiotemporal reasoning: reconstructing 3D geometry from occluded 2D views, anticipating physical dynamics, and executing precise, closed-loop actions. Prior studies test passive VQA on static images or symbolic planning, requiring no execution or supplying privileged coordinates while ignoring collision, statics, and timing. We introduce SpaceAct, an interactive benchmark evaluating 3D spatiotemporal reasoning via closed-loop physical action and active perception, with SAPA, a Spatiotemporal Active-Probing Agent framework. Built on interlocking bricks and mechanical puzzles, it has 108 verified instances across 36 task families in six categories, without privileged coordinates, and diagnostic modes (+plan, +state, no-camera, blind, L7 levers). In brick-bridging or aperture-threading, models rotate the camera to resolve occlusion, read in-scene rulers, output 6-DoF poses under swept-collision and statics checks, and self-correct via split-screen rollback feedback (dynamic tasks freeze time during deliberation and give five strobe frames). Across 10 frontier MLLMs on the 44 hardest instances, scores span 4.8-79.1 (seven solve at most 27.3% of 6-DoF tasks); for the top three, a reference plan (+plan) closes 44% of the gap while leaving collisions at 5.2 per episode, whereas adding exact 3D state (+state) closes 90% and cuts collisions to 0.5; for four others, +plan lifts the mean score from 10.9 to 35.3 and +state to 81.8; and 46% of failures are collision or observation loops. SpaceAct and SAPA advance evaluation to closed-loop physical interaction, showing that even with a valid plan, MLLMs remain bottlenecked by 3D visual grounding and action refinement, while offering a testbed for active multi-view exploration and explicit 3D grounding.
authors: Chenglong Shi, Zekai Yuan, Yue Song, Jon Pu, Will Wu
bullets: Benchmarks 3D spatiotemporal reasoning through active perception and physical action rather than passive image question answering.
Includes 108 verified brick and mechanical-puzzle instances across 36 task families, with no privileged coordinates and diagnostic settings for planning, state access, vision, and control.
SAPA uses camera rotation, in-scene measurement, 6-DoF action output, collision/statics checks, and feedback-based self-correction.
Across 10 MLLMs, performance ranges from 4.8 to 79.1; many models solve few 6-DoF tasks, and 46% of failures involve collision or observation loops.
Providing exact 3D state greatly improves performance and reduces collisions, while reference plans help less, highlighting 3D grounding as the main bottleneck.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The SpaceAct task suite and the SAPA active-perception agent. (a) The six task categories contain 36 task families and 108 verified instances in total (44 in the main matrix). (b) At each turn, the input comprises actively acquired RGB observations with rulers, task rules, the available tools, and a dynamic memory (a bounded history window plus a persistent note). A single MLLM call per turn jointly performs 3D localization (𝒢vis), physics identification (ℐphys), multi-step planning (𝒫plan), and frame-aware control (ℰctrl), returning a JSON response with a rationale, a memory update (note), and 1–5 tool calls; the four capabilities are a diagnostic decomposition, not four separate calls. The tool calls execute sequentially in swept substeps of at most 0.05 stud or 0.5°, without a motion planner, under collision/topology and static-equilibrium checks, and the simulation clock is frozen while the model deliberates. (c) Observations are RGB images with rulers and no coordinates; dynamic tasks provide five frames from the same viewpoint at 0.25-s intervals. The first violation truncates execution and skips the remaining calls, returning a 1280 × 640 split-screen rollback view (left: the violating contact; right: the last valid state). (d) The diagnostic conditions grouped by the operator of Eq. (3) that they replace or stress.

Figure 2: SpaceAct's four design principles (conceptual illustration). Active 3D grounding: the agent reads in-scene rulers and moves the camera to resolve occlusion, with no privileged coordinates. Physics-constrained action: the full swept motion path is checked for collisions and structures for static equilibrium, without a motion planner. Controlled-time dynamics: simulation time pauses while the model deliberates and during camera actions, and advances only with timed physical actions; five sameview frames expose the motion. Controlled failure diagnosis: split-screen rollback feedback pairs the contact with the last valid state, and separately run +plan and +state conditions isolate the bottleneck.

Figure 3: Inputs of the three controlled-diagnostic conditions (schematic), each run separately on the same instances. All conditions share the RGB observation, task and rules, history, and note; the model generates every action, and all actions run under the same execution protocol. +plan adds a reference high-level plan (turns and regions; distances are left to the model). +state supplies the reference plan as well, plus the coarse layout as text and the exact 3D pose of the payload at every turn.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) show strong performance in radiology report generation (RRG) and medical visual question answering (Med-VQA), producing free-form clinical descriptions and answers from medical images. However, they may generate clinically meaningful statements that lack visual evidence or contradict image content. We refer to these errors as visually irrelevant hallucinations and investigate them at the phrase level. We propose CLEAR (Counterfactual Localized Evaluation of Alignment and Response), a model-agnostic post-hoc framework for phrase-level hallucination risk estimation. CLEAR decomposes generated responses into visually assessable clinical phrases. For each phrase, phrase-conditioned grounding identifies a candidate visual region, which is selectively perturbed by a localized counterfactual intervention. CLEAR characterizes the intervention using two complementary auditing cues: response cues, capturing semantic and clinically meaningful changes in the generated response, and alignment cues, measuring changes in image-phrase compatibility. These cues are normalized and jointly modeled to estimate phrase-level hallucination risk. Across four datasets spanning RRG and Med-VQA, CLEAR outperforms state-of-the-art hallucination detection baselines across multiple medical and general-purpose VLMs. On MIMIC-CXR, CLEAR improves AUPRC from 85.10% to 90.23%. Its effectiveness is further validated on a GT-derived controlled VIH benchmark. These results establish visually irrelevant hallucination as an important fine-grained reliability failure mode in medical VLMs and demonstrate the value of model-agnostic visual-support auditing for more trustworthy multimodal clinical generation.
authors: Ke Zou, Nan Zhou, Tao Yang, Meng Liu, Linchao He, Zehui Liao, Ling Huang, Guangren Huang, Yidi Chen, Yi Zhang, Hu Chen, Huazhu Fu
bullets: Medical VLMs can produce clinically meaningful statements that are visually unsupported or contradict the image.
CLEAR is a model-agnostic, post-hoc framework that decomposes outputs into visually assessable phrases.
It grounds each phrase to a candidate region, perturbs that region, and combines response-change and image–phrase alignment cues to estimate hallucination risk.
Across four radiology report generation and Med-VQA datasets, CLEAR outperforms existing detection baselines across multiple VLMs.
On MIMIC-CXR, CLEAR raises AUPRC from 85.10% to 90.23% and is additionally validated on a controlled benchmark.

papers.abstract: Visual foundation models learn rich pathological morphology but lack explicit concept-level supervision. Vision--language pretraining can provide this supervision but requires costly image--text pairs. Here, we introduce GloSAGE, a semantic self-distillation framework that uses lesion profiles predicted by a pretrained visual teacher to construct structured pathology descriptions. Reliability-guided selection identifies image--text anchors, while Knowledge-Structured Pathology Text Synthesis and Evidence-Guided Negative-pair Construction account for partially observed lesions. Image--text alignment trains projection layers while retaining the frozen visual encoder; an intermediate Semantic Transfer Layer supplies features for downstream tasks. Developed on GloMillion and evaluated across seven glomerulus- and case-level cohorts, GloSAGE supported zero-shot lesion recognition, image--text retrieval, hard-negative discrimination and concept-intervention analyses. It outperformed its source visual model in most lesion-recognition tasks and improved lesion grading, while supporting competitive case-level disease classification, injury grading and baseline renal function estimation. Ablations supported the combined contributions of knowledge-structured text and evidence-guided negatives, and the intermediate transfer layer improved mean lesion-recognition ROC-AUC relative to the complete projection output. A frozen language model conditioned on GloSAGE features generated glomerular descriptions. These findings suggest that teacher-derived lesion profiles can provide annotation-efficient semantic supervision for extending a glomerular visual foundation model.
authors: Qiming He, Jing Li, Zihan Wang, Tian Guan, Yifei Ma, Zimo Zhao, Yanxia Wang, Hongjing Chen, Yexing Zhang, Yizhi Wang, Xinrui Chen, Xitong Ling, Minxi Ouyang, Yujie Xie, Lianghui Zhu, Yiqing Liu, Qingxia Hou, Shuyan Zhao, Xiaoqin Wang, Lili Ma, Qiang Huang, Zhiyuan Shen, Junru Cheng, Siqi Zeng, Chao He, Yonghong He, Zhe Wang
bullets: Addresses the lack of concept-level supervision in visual pathology foundation models without requiring costly image–text pairs.
Uses reliability-guided image–text anchors, knowledge-structured pathology text, and evidence-guided negative pairs to handle partially observed lesions.
Aligns images and text while freezing the visual encoder; an intermediate Semantic Transfer Layer supports downstream tasks.
Evaluated across seven glomerulus- and case-level cohorts for lesion recognition, retrieval, hard-negative discrimination, concept intervention, and clinical prediction.
Improved most lesion-recognition tasks and lesion grading over the source visual model, with competitive case-level performance; ablations supported both structured text and guided negatives.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of GloSAGE. (A) Development of GloSAGE through semantic self-distillation. A pretrained visual teacher predicts lesion profiles for glomerular images in GloMillion, and KEYS converts these profiles into knowledge-structured captions. Paired images and captions undergo image–text contrastive pretraining through PIRA with EDGE-guided negative construction. STL transforms pretrained visual features for downstream tasks. GloSAGE is evaluated across seven cohorts for semantic capabilities, clinical diagnosis, component contributions and language-related extensions. (B) Framework of KEYS, PIRA and EDGE. Reliability-guided selection identifies over 40,000 trustworthy visual–semantic anchors. KEYS transforms their lesion profiles into structured descriptions incorporating lesion hierarchies, subtypes and severity grades. PIRA aligns images encoded by the frozen visual encoder with descriptions encoded by PubMedBERT through trainable projection heads, while EDGE excludes unsupported or contradicted negative pairs. STL comprises the first visual projection layer and GELU activation and provides the downstream visual representation. (C) Evaluation of semantic enhancement through zero-shot lesion recognition, bidirectional retrieval, hard-negative discrimination and concept intervention. (D) Evaluation of the diagnostic benefits of semantic enhancement at the glomerular and case levels. Glomerular evaluations include the distribution of ROC-AUC across 27 lesion-recognition tasks (left) and performance on 15 tasks across four independent cohorts (middle). Case-level evaluations include kidney disease diagnosis, subtyping, injury grading and biomarker prediction. (E) Ablation results assessing the contributions of individual components. (F) Exploratory evaluation of language-related capabilities.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are advancing in multimodal understanding and reasoning, accelerating medical model development. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) uses evidence from the four examinations to determine disease location and nature, differentiate syndromes and guide treatment. This diagnostic process constitutes a complete chain of reasoning. We present Fu-TCM, a multimodal TCM LLM trained on data retained after cleaning and filtering an initial collection of approximately 7.12 million examples derived from classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases and publicly available datasets. The model was further optimized using Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization (BGPO), which explicitly targets syndrome differentiation through rewards for response format, intermediate TCM reasoning fields and final syndrome predictions. Fu-TCM-27B led all six benchmarks spanning TCM reasoning, text and vision, achieving a macro-average accuracy of 81.01% and surpassing the strongest reference model with complete results across all six benchmarks by 7.13 percentage points. Its largest margin was 11.90 points on Fu-bianzheng. Case-level analyses further showed a positive association between intermediate-field accuracy and final syndrome-selection accuracy in most evaluated models. These findings suggest that TCM syndrome differentiation may be computationally learnable and that structured reasoning supervision can improve performance across TCM tasks.
