papers.abstract: Short video platforms have become a primary channel for black and gray industry operations in internet finance, where inducements such as prompts to like, follow, join private chat groups, or click external links frequently steer users toward fraud. Because such videos are short, dynamic, and often convey intent through fleeting visual cues rather than stable text, a moderation system must guarantee detection recall and localize the offending segment so reviewers inspect only the relevant clip. Existing OCR+LLM pipelines transcribe on-screen text frame by frame and classify the transcript, but exploit only textual information. Many inducements are conveyed through visual cues OCR cannot observe, and keyframe-based localization cannot recover precise temporal boundaries. We explore OCR+MLLM, which augments the text pipeline with a Multimodal Large Language Model, and compare three routes: OCR+LLM, OCR+MLLM, and a large zero-shot MLLM, along detection, latency, token consumption, and deployment complexity. OCR preserves the text signal that guarantees recall, while the MLLM jointly performs OCR-grounded discrimination and temporal grounding, localizing both textual and non-textual inducements. We construct a dataset of 2,419 internet finance short videos (66.49 hours) with 3,194 annotated events across four categories, and study reward design for RL-based grounding under class imbalance. We report two findings: auxiliary reward terms are exploited through reward hacking, and stronger localization rewards degrade class-balanced detection. We therefore design a recall-weighted F2 localization reward with class-balanced resampling. Experiments show OCR+MLLM localizes better than the keyframe OCR+LLM baseline (mIoU 26.52 vs. 14.49) and detects non-textual inducements that text-only pipelines miss, while maintaining 67.0 percent macro recall.
bullets: Targets prompts to like, follow, join private groups, or click external links that may lead to fraud.
Combines OCR with a multimodal LLM for joint discrimination and temporal grounding of textual and visual cues.
Evaluates OCR+LLM, OCR+MLLM, and a zero-shot MLLM across detection, latency, token use, and deployment complexity.
Uses a recall-weighted F2 localization reward with class-balanced resampling after finding reward hacking and detection–localization trade-offs.
On 2,419 annotated videos, OCR+MLLM raises mIoU to 26.52 versus 14.49 for keyframe OCR+LLM and detects non-textual inducements missed by text-only methods.

papers.abstract: Deciding which member of an animal group produced a vocalization and where that vocalization was produced are central to studying social communication but are rarely evaluated with physically verified ground truth. Existing resources either localize sounds without identifying the caller, or recognize individuals from isolated vocalizations without reliance on the 3D candidate geometry. We close this gap with V33DA, a dataset-centered multimodal benchmark for spatial vocal attribution in social zebra finches: it comprises 33,625 verified events coupling 5-channel audio with three camera views, calibrated 3D pose for every visible candidate, and per-bird radio telemetry across 10 individuals and three experiments. Caller identity is verified from an on-body accelerometer-derived vibration signal; this channel is withheld from benchmark models and used only by an on-body reference ceiling. Given a detected vocalization and the visible candidate birds, the task is to select the caller. We evaluate it under three regimes: session-disjoint testing on familiar birds from held-out recording dates, held-out-experiment transfer to a new cohort, and leave-one-individual-out evaluation on a bird whose vocalizations are held out from training. Reference methods expose a consistent gap between in-domain accuracy and transfer to unseen individuals: methods that can exploit familiar vocal identity perform well on known callers but degrade sharply on unseen ones, whereas candidate-aware methods preserving explicit spatial reasoning transfer substantially better. The on-body reference stays near-perfect across regimes, confirming the internal consistency of the accelerometer-verified labels. We release V33DA with fixed protocols and code for the evaluated methods, and V33DA++, an unevaluated companion set of verified overlapping-call events and +/-2 s context windows.
authors: Maris Basha, Yuhang Wang, Xiaoran Chen, Longbiao Cheng, Luca Yapura, Anja T. Zai, Mathieu Salzmann, Richard Hahnloser

Evaluates session-disjoint, held-out-experiment, and leave-one-individual-out settings.
Finds that familiar-caller recognition degrades sharply on unseen birds, while candidate-aware spatial methods transfer better; releases V33DA, protocols, code, and V33DA++ context data.

papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

papers.selection_reason: Open MoE hybrid Mamba-Transformer LLMs with long-context training, multimodal capabilities, and efficient deployment.
papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
papers.tldr: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning are open hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE models optimized for efficient reasoning, long-context, multimodal, and agentic AI workloads.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) ground language in visual evidence, yet their semantic reasoning can be exploited through transferable black-box adversarial attacks. Existing attacks typically allocate perturbations using surrogate-model saliency, which may not reflect how an unseen MLLM semantically interprets or relies on different image regions. We introduce VISTA (Vulnerability-Informed Semantic Transfer Attacks), a black-box framework that identifies semantically vulnerable visual regions from an MLLM's responses without access to gradients, logits, parameters, or internal representations. VISTA supports two attack settings: (i) VISTA-Proxy, a pure-transfer setting that probes an open-source MLLM and transfers the resulting adversarial examples to unseen commercial MLLMs without querying them; and (ii) VISTA-Victim, a query-assisted setting that probes the target MLLM to capture model-specific semantic vulnerabilities. VISTA builds an Uncertainty-Based Multimodal Behavior (UBMB) map from response drift, conflict, misleading, and semantic shifts, then uses entropy-adaptive Sinkhorn routing and a surrogate ensemble to focus perturbations on vulnerable regions. Across GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, VISTA achieves up to 97 % attack success rate (ASR) while maintaining a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) above 30 dB. Notably, VISTA-Proxy achieves up to 93 % ASR without querying the final victim, demonstrating that response-derived semantic vulnerability can enable effective transfer across heterogeneous MLLMs.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between surrogate-model saliency and how unseen MLLMs actually interpret visual regions.
Builds an Uncertainty-Based Multimodal Behavior map from response drift, conflict, misleading, and semantic shifts.
Uses entropy-adaptive Sinkhorn routing with a surrogate ensemble to focus perturbations on vulnerable regions.
Supports pure-transfer VISTA-Proxy and query-assisted VISTA-Victim attack settings.
Reports up to 97% ASR with PSNR above 30 dB; VISTA-Proxy reaches up to 93% ASR without querying the final victim across GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6.

papers.abstract: A widely held assumption in knowledge distillation is that teacher and student representations must occupy a compatible or explicitly aligned feature space. We propose RPKD (Random Prototype Knowledge Distillation), which discards this assumption by comparing both networks against a shared bank of randomly initialized, frozen prototype vectors. Alignment is therefore carried out in an external reference space rather than in the teacher's native feature coordinates: the teacher side is projected by fixed random maps that carry no trainable parameters, and only the student adapts. Two branches handle the transfer: a logit branch aligning global prototype similarity distributions and a feature branch matching spatially-resolved prototype activation maps. Both operate within the same fixed prototype space, which can be interpreted as a random feature embedding that approximately preserves inter-sample similarity structure, so the prototype bank and the distillation objective stay unchanged across teacher-student pairs while only the input projections are instantiated per architecture. In low-category settings, decoupling the prototype vocabulary from the task label space yields richer supervision than the label space alone, an advantage absent from logit-based methods, whose supervisory signal collapses as class count shrinks. This advantage is especially relevant in real-world scenarios where the label space is typically constrained. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RPKD, achieving a maximum gain of +7.98% over OFA on CIFAR-100, +12.44% on ImageNet-100, and +1.28% on ImageNet-1K. Source code is available at https://github.com/HamzaEtcibasi/RPKD
bullets: Uses a frozen bank of randomly initialized prototype vectors as an external reference space.

Reports gains over OFA of up to 7.98% on CIFAR-100, 12.44% on ImageNet-100, and 1.28% on ImageNet-1K.

papers.abstract: Real-world forgery is inherently heterogeneous: it manifests not only as digital manipulation but also as physical spoofing, and is carried not only by images but also by videos. Despite substantial progress, a unified anti-forgery foundation model covering such a broad threat spectrum remains absent. In this paper, we present Venus-DefakerOne2, which substantially extends the forensic capability boundary along both the forgery-form and media-type dimensions. Trained on tens of millions of open-source and in-house samples, it incorporates two key designs. Tide-Style-Tuning alternates LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning to balance computational efficiency, generalization, and hard-sample fitting while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Entropy-based Test Adaptation determines the optimal prediction modality by analyzing prediction entropy. Venus-DefakerOne2 achieves new state-of-the-art performance across a comprehensive suite of benchmarks, including DeepFake faces (96.7%), AI-generated images (93.3%), tampered documents (87.6%), manipulated natural images (89.6%), physical spoofs (93.1%), and AI-generated videos (96.0%). It significantly outperforms both specialized expert models and its predecessor, DefakerOne, establishing itself as a powerful and versatile foundation model for binary-decision forensic tasks.

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors routinely achieve high aggregate accuracy while exhibiting substantial demographic disparities in their errors: false-positive rates differ by double digits across gender and skin tone. Most existing remedies require either full retraining with a fairness-aware objective or demographic-annotated training data, both impractical when only a pretrained checkpoint is available, while label-free post-hoc calibrators leave the detector's weights unchanged. We introduce FYC (FPR-disparity Weight Perturbation and Youden Calibration), a two-stage post-hoc method that perturbs a detector's weights under an FPR-disparity criterion, then calibrates a separate decision threshold for each demographic group - requiring no architectural changes and no full retraining. Evaluated against every detector benchmarked on AI-Face v2 across six intersectional gender x skin-tone groups, FYC outperforms the field on 18 of 21 reported fairness and utility metrics, including purpose-built fairness architectures, at a fraction of the training cost. We further identify why the choice of fairness criterion is critical: the original Demographic Parity objective used in prior weight-perturbation work is architecture-dependent and unpredictable, improving two of four evaluated architectures, leaving a third largely unchanged, and substantially degrading the fourth (PG-FDD), with no way to anticipate the outcome for a given checkpoint in advance. Conditioning the same objective on real images only - our FPR-disparity criterion - eliminates this unpredictability, improving fairness and accuracy jointly across all four architectures with no exceptions.
authors: Uzoamaka Ezeakunne, Taiwo Olabamipe, Deevesh Jain, Xiuwen Liu
bullets: Targets demographic disparities in false-positive rates across intersectional gender and skin-tone groups.
Uses two stages: FPR-disparity-guided weight perturbation, then separate Youden-calibrated thresholds per group.
Requires no architectural changes, full retraining, or demographic-annotated training data.
Outperforms benchmarked alternatives on 18 of 21 reported fairness and utility metrics across AI-Face v2 detectors.
Shows that conditioning the fairness objective on real images avoids the architecture-dependent unpredictability of Demographic Parity perturbation.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D maps enable robots to reason about previously unknown environments using natural language. However, existing systems typically segment every incoming image, associate detections with persistent 3D segments, and frequently perform costly Vision-Language (VL) inference. We present TRACKGRAPH, an online open-vocabulary system that maintains short-term 2D mask identity directly in the image stream before fusing segments into 3D. FastSAM masks and CLIP features are computed at sparse keyframes, while dense DINOv3 features are used to propagate masks at a high rate in between. The resulting tracked masks are fused into a class-agnostic 3D segment layer within a hierarchical scene graph, with 3D association handling tracking interruptions and long-term revisits. Compact multi-view CLIP embeddings enable open-vocabulary retrieval. Across Replica, ScanNet++, and HM3D, TRACKGRAPH achieves competitive open-vocabulary segmentation and retrieval against state-of-the-art mapping methods, including the highest synonym frequency on Replica (0.50). On the same NVIDIA A100, it is 1.7x faster and uses 3.3x less GPU memory than ViT-H OVI-MAP. Real-world quadruped deployments demonstrate onboard scene graph construction and object search at 7.5Hz, while recorded drone data is used to test the method under aerial viewpoints.
bullets: Addresses the high cost of per-frame segmentation, 3D association, and frequent vision-language inference in online mapping.
Computes FastSAM masks and CLIP features at keyframes, then propagates masks densely using DINOv3 features.
Fuses tracked masks into a class-agnostic hierarchical 3D scene graph, with 3D association supporting interruptions and revisits.
Achieves competitive segmentation and retrieval across Replica, ScanNet++, and HM3D; reports 1.7× faster runtime and 3.3× lower GPU memory than ViT-H OVI-MAP.
Demonstrates onboard scene-graph construction and object search at 7.5 Hz on a quadruped, with additional evaluation on aerial drone data.

papers.abstract: As robots transition from structured factory settings into homes, they are required to interact with an ever-increasing variety of objects. Many tasks require grasping, and often it is not sufficient to just pick up the target object. Consider a task like "pouring coffee" --- to facilitate the subsequent pouring, the robot should grasp the mug by its handle. Existing learning-based approaches for grasping either find robust and collision-free grasps that are largely agnostic to the task (e.g., picking up the mug by its rim), or leverage foundation models to propose task-appropriate grasp locations that lack fine-grained physical grounding (e.g., reaching for and missing the handle). In this work, we bridge these approaches with a real-to-sim-to-real framework. Based on a single RGB-D observation, we construct a digital twin of the environment, query a large foundation model to propose grasps that align with the object's affordances and task description, and then optimize the proposals to ensure robustness and plausibility before executing the result on the real robot. Our key insight is that the grasp proposals of the foundation model should be regarded as semantic priors that serve as seeds for local, gradient-free optimization. We leverage Bayesian optimization with Thompson sampling to draw batches of nearby poses, which are subsequently evaluated in parallel under domain-randomized physics rollouts. The resulting grasp is both task-oriented and physically feasible for execution by the robot arm. Our full zero-shot real-world transfer only takes a few minutes and improves task-oriented grasping success by up to 33% as compared to other state-of-the-art pipelines. Our code is available here: https://github.com/VT-Collab/GraspTwin/
bullets: Addresses the gap between task-agnostic robust grasps and semantically appropriate but physically imprecise foundation-model proposals.
Builds a digital twin from a single RGB-D observation and uses the task description and object affordances to generate grasp priors.
Refines these priors with gradient-free Bayesian optimization using Thompson sampling and parallel domain-randomized physics rollouts.
Transfers the optimized grasp to a real robot in a few minutes without task-specific training.
Improves task-oriented grasping success by up to 33% over other state-of-the-art pipelines in real-world experiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of GraspTwin. (Left) We convert from real to sim by constructing a digital twin from an RGB-D image of the robot’s environment. (Right) These proposals become the initial guesses for localized grasp optimization. We simulate grasp poses T in the digital twin with object perturbations ∆θ. Batch Bayesian optimization with Thompson sampling enables parallel evaluations for gradient-free optimization. The minimum-cost grasp pose T∗ is executed by the real robot.

These semantically-aware grasps seed local optimization while enforcing physical constraints (e.g., unintended collisions) and domain randomization. The resulting grasp pose is then executed by the real arm.

papers.abstract: Discrete visual tokens represent vision in a discrete form analogous to language, offering a native interface for multimodal modeling under a shared next-token prediction objective. However, quantization error is widely assumed to cause unavoidable semantic loss, fundamentally limiting the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and positioning continuous visual representations as an intrinsic upper bound. Using multimodal understanding as a proxy for semantic fidelity, we revisit this assumption and find quantization error unreliable, as discrete representations with substantially larger errors can achieve better understanding. Instead, the effective bit budget of discrete indices emerges as a key determinant of downstream performance. However, existing quantizers eventually saturate as additional codebooks contribute progressively less semantic information. As one approach to alleviating this saturation, we introduce Factorized Vector Quantization, which quantizes complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the visual feature with symmetric parallel codebooks. It continues to improve at larger bit budgets, ultimately matching continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding. Trained on industrial-scale multimodal data, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models, outperforming UniAR and Emu3-Chat by 22.8% and 59.2%, respectively, on a nine-metric average. To our knowledge, it is also the first discrete-representation model competitive with strong continuous-representation models such as Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained OCR tasks. We further identify the key principles and a practical recipe enabling this competitiveness. These results and insights support the potential of discrete visual representations to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models. Code and models are available at https://github.com/hustvl/FVQ
bullets: Quantization error is not a reliable predictor of semantic fidelity; larger-error discrete representations can perform better.
Effective bit budget, rather than quantization error alone, is a key driver of downstream understanding.
Existing quantizers saturate as added codebooks provide diminishing semantic information.
Factorized Vector Quantization uses complementary fixed-dimensional feature views with symmetric parallel codebooks to reduce this saturation.
The resulting model matches continuous-representation performance, including fine-grained OCR, and reports strong gains over prior discrete-representation models.

papers.abstract: Visual generation requires both high-level semantic knowledge and fine-grained pixel details. We propose a learning paradigm that assigns these roles to autoregressive pretraining for knowledge acquisition and diffusion post-training for high-fidelity rendering. Within this framework, we study the objective, representation, and scaling of knowledge acquisition and rendering. Controlled comparisons identify autoregression as the stronger pretraining objective for downstream rendering, improving both learning efficiency and final generation quality. We further find that AR-only generation quality does not necessarily correlate with final performance; semantic quality matters more. This motivates a purely semantic tokenizer trained with language supervision alone, without an image decoder or reconstruction loss. We establish compute-optimal scaling laws for knowledge acquisition and rendering, and find that autoregressive pretraining lowers the fitted asymptotic rendering loss compared with pixel diffusion models trained from scratch. Guided by the laws, we train a 3B-parameter text-to-image model with only 6,600 H100 GPU-hours, achieving 86 on GenEval and 87 on DPG-Bench and validating the proposed paradigm at scale.
bullets: Separates visual generation into knowledge acquisition and pixel-level rendering.
Finds autoregressive pretraining more effective than diffusion for learning knowledge that supports downstream rendering.
Shows semantic quality—not necessarily AR-only image quality—better predicts final generation performance.
Introduces a language-supervised semantic tokenizer without an image decoder or reconstruction loss.
Derives compute-optimal scaling laws and validates the approach with a 3B-parameter model trained using 6,600 H100 GPU-hours.

papers.abstract: Agile robots require spatiotemporal intelligence to interpret scenes, reason about interactions, and anticipate future events. Yet it remains unclear how well foundation vision models support these capabilities, particularly from a moving egocentric camera, which is a natural view for robots. To investigate this, we collect an annotated tennis dataset and train a suite of vision models on spatiotemporal tasks. Our dataset contains egocentric video synchronized with five allocentric videos, estimated global positions, labeled contact times, and annotated stroke types. We then evaluate seven prediction tasks from egocentric images: 2D ego player and 3D ball localization, future player and ball trajectories, forehand or backhand stroke anticipation, time to the next ego player ball contact, and 3D ball position at that contact. We compare image encoders, video encoders, and vision-language models with jointly trained prediction heads. The best performing models achieve mean current-frame localization errors of 0.14 m for the ego player and 0.54 m for the ball, future forecasting errors of 0.34 m for the ego player and 0.91 m for the ball over 1.1 s, and a mean contact-time prediction error of 0.14 s. Auxiliary depth information substantially improves 3D ball localization, suggesting that inferring metric depth remains a challenge. Longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, indicating that representations exploit scene context rather than rely solely on inter-frame motion. Finally, we propose a conditional diffusion model to generate whole-body kinematic tennis motion from vision encoder predictions on egocentric video at real-time rates, adapting movements as predictions are refined. These results move towards a deeper understanding of how foundation vision models can support real-time dynamic robots using egocentric video.
bullets: Introduces an annotated egocentric tennis dataset synchronized with five allocentric views, global positions, contact times, and stroke labels.
Evaluates seven tasks, including player/ball localization, trajectory forecasting, stroke anticipation, contact-time prediction, and contact-position estimation.
Best models reach 0.14 m ego-player and 0.54 m ball localization error, 0.34 m and 0.91 m forecasting error over 1.1 s, and 0.14 s contact-time error.
Auxiliary depth improves 3D ball localization; longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, suggesting reliance on scene context over motion alone.
A conditional diffusion model generates adaptive whole-body tennis motion from vision predictions at real-time rates.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Tongkun Guan, Zhibo Yang, Mingkun Yang, Haocheng Wang, Wei Shen, Xiaokang Yang
bullets: Targets perception degradation during MLLM post-training, where subjective dense captions make reliable rewards difficult.
Perception RL converts verified caption errors into fixed-label QA pairs with rule-based rewards, using chain and multiple-choice formats.
Perception Agentic RL handles unresolved dense cases through multi-turn tool use, with Coordinate Injection and grounding-aware process rewards to reduce spatial errors.
Uses shared cold-start SFT followed by single-turn and multi-turn perception RL.
Achieves 71.6% average accuracy across seven benchmarks, exceeding the same-tool base model by 15.7 points and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 5.2 points.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Perception RL: from perceptual errors to rewardable QA. (01) Perception tree construction: A hierarchical capability map and model probing reveal perceptual weaknesses, guiding specialized and general data-construction routes. Appendix ?? expands the displayed tree with additional skills and associated failure modes. (02) Rewardable QA construction: A multi-agent pipeline mines and verifies errors in the base model’s captions, then composes them into questions with unambiguous answers. MCQs combine unrelated errors, while chain QA connects correlated errors. (03) Rule-based reward for RL: The resulting QA pairs provide exact-match rewards for training the model’s visual perception. The error distribution and example errors are illustrative.

Fig. 1: PERCEPTRL: making real-world perception rewardable, and training it at two levels. Center: How it becomes rewardable. Open-ended captions contain useful perceptual information but are difficult to score with direct rule-based rewards. We extract and verify perceptual facts from these captions, then formulate QA pairs with fixed answer labels for rule-based training (top). The pipeline organizes tasks from multiple perception families (e.g., color, spatial position, counting, functional state, orientation), using a perception tree to guide data construction (Section 3.2). The difficulty axis is what divides the two levels. Level 1: Perception RL. A single look suffices here, so we train single-turn visual QA under a rule-based outcome reward. The left panel shows what this must fix: an error entering at the perception level is inherited by an otherwise correct reasoning chain, so the answer is wrong for a purely perceptual reason. Level 2: Perception Agentic RL. This tail, where objects are small, scenes are cluttered, or details require magnification, resists a single look, so the model inspects the image over multiple grounded turns with a code interpreter. The right panel illustrates how a grounding error, where a predicted crop or annotation misses its target, can affect subsequent observations. Its propagation and accumulation across successive tool interactions constitute coordinate drift. Coordinate Injection corrects these grounding errors during data construction, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity (Section 3.3).

Fig. 3: Perception Agentic RL: correcting and supervising spatial grounding during multi-turn visual inspection. (01) Coordinate drift. A misplaced annotation changes the visual evidence available to later turns. Subsequent spatial operations can inherit this error, leading to repeated or missed counts. (02) Coordinate Injection (CI). During trajectory construction, CI identifies the intended target of each spatial operation, corrects its coordinates using a VLM judge or the LocateAnything detector, and re-executes the code before the next turn. The corrected trajectories provide cold-start SFT data. (03) Grounding-aware process reward. During RL, a fidelity judge evaluates the predicted boxes and points against their intended targets in the original image. The resulting per-turn rewards complement the final-answer reward and supervise intermediate spatial accuracy (Equation 17).

Agentic QA is a strict subset selected from this pool after Level-1 training: the trained model generates eight rollouts per query, and queries with empirical accuracy < 5/8 are retained for Perception Agentic RL (Level 2).

papers.selection_reason: Improves MLLM fine-grained visual and spatial perception via RL and tool-use supervision.
papers.title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions
papers.tldr: PerceptRL improves fine-grained visual perception in MLLMs by turning verified caption errors into rewardable QA tasks and training multi-turn visual inspection with grounding-aware feedback.

papers.abstract: Unified conditional image generation requires a single model to preserve different aspects of a visual input while producing a target image that follows textual guidance. Pretrained video models provide a promising foundation by encoding visual transformations across time, yet existing approaches typically assign the condition and target to fixed temporal positions. We observe that condition-target relationships vary substantially across generation tasks, while video models naturally encode visual transformations at different temporal scales. This motivates us to model conditional generation through input-adaptive virtual temporal relations. We propose FrameForge, which captures two complementary aspects of such relations. Mixture of Temporal Experts (MoTE) models how far the target lies from the condition by dynamically selecting temporal RoPE experts with different virtual intervals. Chain of Temporal Reasoning (CoTR) models how the condition is transformed into the target through a latent intermediate state, with a reasoning-bottleneck attention mask encouraging information propagation through this pathway. Experiments on DreamBench, COCO2017, and GEdit-Bench show that FrameForge achieves superior performance in subject-driven generation, canny-to-image generation, and image editing among the compared methods.
authors: Yijing Lin, Zhendong Mao, Mengqi Huang, Yuxin Wang, Yongdong Zhang
bullets: Existing methods fix condition and target at predetermined temporal positions, limiting flexibility across tasks.
Mixture of Temporal Experts dynamically selects temporal RoPE intervals to model the target’s distance from the condition.
Chain of Temporal Reasoning uses a latent intermediate state and bottleneck attention to guide condition-to-target transformations.
Experiments on DreamBench, COCO2017, and GEdit-Bench report superior performance among compared methods for subject-driven generation, canny-to-image generation, and image editing.

papers.abstract: Long video understanding requires reasoning over hours of content that far exceed the context window of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Existing approaches compress video into fixed-length clips, yet events are fragmented and unrelated content is merged, yielding noisy retrieval. To overcome this challenge, we propose EMMA, an Event-driven Multimodal Memory system with Multi-Agent retrieval, which organizes memory around semantic events in three stages: (1) Event segmentation: a dual-stream detector adaptively locates event boundaries by fusing visual semantic drift with spoken transitions, rather than fixed windows. (2) Memory construction: built on the detected events, a three-level hierarchy of raw video, clip-level memory, and event-level memory stores content at progressively higher semantic abstraction. (3) Memory retrieval: a multi-agent framework collaboratively queries this hierarchy through query decomposition, tiered search, evidence validation, and answer generation, narrowing evidence from coarse events to precise clips. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements, showing the effectiveness of our event-aligned memory system. Code, prompt templates, and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/BAI-LAB/EMMA.
bullets: Targets noisy retrieval caused by fixed-length video chunking, which can fragment events and merge unrelated content.
Detects event boundaries using visual semantic drift and spoken transitions.
Builds a three-level memory hierarchy spanning raw video, clip-level memory, and event-level memory.
Uses multi-agent query decomposition, tiered search, evidence validation, and answer generation.
Experiments on three challenging benchmarks show substantial improvements, though the abstract does not specify metrics or limitations.

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is a necessary step in moving multimodal large language models (MLLMs) toward reasoning about the 3D physical world. Their visual pretraining data, however, is almost entirely 2D, so the visual tokens processed by MLLMs often lack inherent 3D structural information. A growing number of methods inject such structure by transferring representations from external vision or geometry models, and collectively establish that such transfer helps. Behind these methods lies a largely underexplored question: what makes a visual representation good for spatial understanding? To answer it, we first separate what is transferred from how it is transferred, and then trace the resulting differences back to properties of the representations themselves. What we transfer comes from 3D geometry models, self-supervised image and video models, vision-language models, and generative models, in the form of latent features or explicit depth and point maps. We transfer it either by distillation, using it as a supervision target, or by fusion, feeding it as an additional input. We find that a representation's 3D structure correlates strongly with how much it helps, measured by cross-view consistency for latent features and by depth and reconstruction accuracy for explicit geometry. We further show that the form of a representation dictates the mechanism it needs. Latent features gain as much from fusion as from distillation; explicit geometry gains little from fusion, and most of its distillation gain depends on a geometry decoding head. Guided by these findings, we distill both latent features and explicit geometry into a single MLLM. Taking only RGB video as input, it consistently improves over its base model on both static 3D and dynamic 4D spatial reasoning benchmarks.
bullets: MLLM visual tokens often lack 3D structure because pretraining is dominated by 2D data.
The study compares transferred representations from geometry, self-supervised, vision-language, and generative models, using distillation or fusion.
Representation quality correlates with spatial usefulness: cross-view consistency for latent features and depth/reconstruction accuracy for explicit geometry.
Latent features benefit similarly from fusion and distillation, while explicit geometry benefits mainly from distillation with a geometry decoding head.
Distilling both representation types into one RGB-video MLLM improves static 3D and dynamic 4D spatial reasoning over its base model.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates what makes visual representations effective for spatial understanding in MLLMs, finding that 3D structure correlates with performance and proposing a distillation method combining latent features and explicit geometry.
papers.title: What Makes a Good Visual Representation for Spatial Understanding in MLLMs?
papers.tldr: Visual representations with stronger 3D structure—and transfer mechanisms matched to their form—better enable MLLMs to understand spatial scenes.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) to solve complex visual problems, but also exposes them to CoT hijacking: an adversary implants a backdoor through poisoned fine-tuning so that a visual trigger induces a hijacking turn, redirecting an otherwise faithful reasoning chain to an attacker-chosen answer. However, since the hijack acts within the reasoning chain, existing multimodal backdoor defenses designed for MLLMs that answer directly struggle to detect it. Moreover, inspecting the chain itself does not reliably expose the hijack, since the hijacking turn can resemble honest self-correction in form. In this paper, we find that honest reasoning tends to revise its answer at high-entropy "aha moments", whereas a hijack can overturn a confident answer through a near-deterministic turn. To quantify this contrast, we formalize this phenomenon as belief inertia, the cumulative next-token entropy of a reasoning span minus the answer-belief revision it induces, with markedly lower values for hijacked spans than for honest reasoning spans. Since hijacking tokens are also image-dependent, we further improve detection by restricting the measure to image-dependent spans, yielding visual belief inertia (VBI). Building on this, we propose InertiaGuard, a training-free, test-time detector that flags a trace when its VBI falls below a threshold calibrated on a small set of clean traces. Across various attacks and benchmarks, InertiaGuard achieves higher detection performance than existing baselines, while generalizing to different model architectures and trigger types.
bullets: CoT hijacking redirects a model’s reasoning and answer after an attacker implants a backdoor triggered by an image.
Existing defenses struggle because hijacks occur inside reasoning chains and can resemble honest self-correction.
The paper defines belief inertia as reasoning-span token entropy minus the resulting answer-belief revision.
Visual belief inertia (VBI) focuses this measure on image-dependent spans, improving sensitivity to visual hijacks.
InertiaGuard is a training-free, test-time detector calibrated on a small set of clean traces and performs better than existing baselines across attacks, benchmarks, architectures, and trigger types.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CoT hijacking combines low belief inertia with strong image dependence. Each dot is a reasoning step (gray: clean; red: hijacking) sampled from a validation set. (a, b) Hijacking steps induce large belief revisions B at low entropy cost H , resulting in lower belief inertia than clean reasoning. (c, d) Because hijacking steps also exhibit strong image dependence, adding this criterion filters out most low-inertia clean steps while retaining hijacking steps.

Figure 2: Illustration of INERTIAGUARD. Although the model initially recognizes the stop sign, a trigger-induced hijacking turn redirects its answer from (b) to (a). To detect this redirection, INERTIAGUARD first identifies image-dependent steps, then compares the belief revision across spans containing these steps with their cumulative entropy. Because the hijacking span induces a large revision at little entropy cost, its belief inertia falls below the calibrated threshold, causing the trace to be flagged.

papers.abstract: Spherical data arise in many scientific applications. Often spherical transformers disregard the geometry of the underlying spherical domain, causing distortions and coordinate singularities near the poles. We introduce SO(3)-RoPE, a relative positional embedding that incorporates spherical geometry into transformer attention through unitary SO(3) representations. Our formulation is SO(3)-equivariant and compatible with FlashAttention, retaining efficiency of vanilla transformers. On shallow water dynamics prediction over a rotating sphere, our SO3ViT outperforms an S2Transformer baseline with lower errors and reduced runtime.
bullets: Addresses distortions and polar coordinate singularities in transformers for spherical data.
Introduces a relative positional embedding based on unitary SO(3) representations.
Provides SO(3)-equivariant attention while remaining compatible with FlashAttention.
SO3ViT achieves lower errors and reduced runtime than an S2Transformer baseline on shallow-water prediction.
Scope: evaluated on shallow-water dynamics over a rotating sphere.

Figure 3: SO3ViT has lower and more homogeneously distributed prediction errors than S2Transformer.
Table 1: Peak GPU memory during training and inference time. For every S2Transformer configuration, some SO3ViT configuration performs better in ℓ1 error, ℓ2 error, memory, and inference speed.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces SO(3)-RoPE, a relative positional embedding for spherical transformers that incorporates spherical geometry, contributing to spatial intelligence and geometric reasoning in foundation models.
papers.title: SO(3)-RoPE for Spherical Transformers
papers.tldr: SO(3)-RoPE builds spherical geometry into transformer attention, improving accuracy and runtime for rotating-sphere dynamics prediction.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are deployed as zero-shot judges of image aesthetics, and panels of several models are recommended, on thin evidence, as the way to make such judges reliable. On two human-rated datasets, EVA and PARA, we find that a panel of holistic judges never significantly beats its best member, whether the verdicts are averaged or fused by a learned combiner. What a panel is worth depends on what it is fed. We therefore have each model score each image on the five dimensions of a frozen, human-written rubric and fuse those scores, alongside each model's verdict, across model families with an out-of-fold combiner. The dimension scores measure what their labels claim: with the overall human score partialled out, a dimension prompt carries more attribute-specific information than the holistic prompt in 28 of 30 model-attribute cells. Fused, they beat the best single VLM in all ten three-family panels on EVA (against that best single model, +0.07 Spearman rho for the strongest trio and +0.10 for the pre-declared one, and +0.06 and +0.07 when averaged over twenty fold partitions; against the panel mean, the primary test gives +0.118 on its EVA design set), and on PARA they reach parity under Spearman rho and a small, non-significant loss under Kendall tau-b, where one model already captures 85% of the human noise ceiling. It is not a feature-count artefact: giving the same combiner an equal number of pure holistic columns, split from the same repetitions, does not reproduce it. The gain costs a few hundred labels, which do not transfer between datasets, and 4.8x the API calls on EVA; we report it with paired bootstraps and Kendall tau-b, alongside a failed pre-registration and the configurations that lost.
bullets: Holistic judge panels never significantly outperform their best member on EVA or PARA.
Models score five frozen, human-written rubric dimensions, and an out-of-fold combiner fuses these scores with holistic verdicts across model families.
Dimension prompts provide more attribute-specific information than holistic prompts in 28 of 30 model–attribute comparisons.
Dimension-aware fusion beats the best single VLM across all ten EVA three-family panels, while reaching parity or a small non-significant loss on PARA.
The approach requires a few hundred dataset-specific labels and 4.8× more EVA API calls; labels do not transfer between datasets.

papers.selection_reason: Studies vision-language model behavior and proposes a transferable rubric-based fusion method for VLM evaluation.
papers.title: Feed the Panel Dimensions, Not Verdicts: Rubric-Decomposed Fusion of Vision-Language Aesthetic Judges
papers.tldr: Feeding VLM panels rubric-based aesthetic dimensions—not just holistic verdicts—makes fusion reliably improve on the best individual judge on EVA, but offers little benefit on PARA.

papers.abstract: Relations compose through the entity they share - Alice is Bob's mother and Bob is Carol's father, so Alice is Carol's grandmother - and the order matters, since a father's mother is not a mother's father; verifying a composed relation means closing the loop. We show that if each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently (per-entity frame freedom), three things follow. In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact at all. The only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy $H = T_{ij} T_{jk} T_{ki}$ - a Wilson loop. And the only equivariant update of an edge is $U = \Psi(H)\, T_{ij}$ with $\Psi$ conjugation-equivariant. Edge attention by Wilson loops is therefore not one design among many but the unique form the symmetry permits. Three communities hold pieces of this form: the commuting-operator embeddings of knowledge graphs are its abelian (commuting) sector; AlphaFold's triangle update and the Edge Transformer have its shape - an edge updated through the third vertex - without its constraints; and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. We instantiate the equivariant sub-family on general relational graphs as holonomy attention. With no training and composition alone, it infers unobserved $S_4$ relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, at or slightly below specialist synchronization algorithms, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083; its holonomy score flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 where commuting scores are capped at 0.76 by a second selection rule, and it separates clusters without labels.
authors: Aakash Sarkar, Ananya Mukherjee, Motoshige Sato
bullets: In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact.
Triangle scores must depend on the holonomy of the composed edge transformations, while edge updates take a conjugation-equivariant Wilson-loop form.
The framework unifies commuting knowledge-graph embeddings, triangle-based edge updates, and lattice-QCD constructions as special or partial cases.
Holonomy attention infers unobserved S₄ relations on sparse corrupted graphs without training, achieving 0.88 accuracy and detecting corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99.
It also separates graph clusters without labels; the reported results concern composition-based inference on relational graphs.

(b) Accuracy on unobserved S4 relations versus corrupted fraction (14 entities, degree 8, four rounds; mean and sd, 10 instances). (c) Holonomy score trH/d of observed triangles at p=0.3 (discrete: permutation traces are integers). (d) The same score separates within- from cross-cluster triangles with no labels.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a theoretical framework connecting attention mechanisms to Lattice Gauge Theory, offering a novel perspective on relational reasoning and attention updates applicable to foundation models.
papers.title: Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops
papers.tldr: The paper argues that per-entity frame symmetry uniquely restricts relational attention to gauge-invariant Wilson-loop interactions over cycles.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning has substantially advanced video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, language-based reasoning traces do not provide a reliable mechanism for models to revisit relevant visual evidence, leading to visual forgetting and impairing their ability to reason over video content. Existing approaches maintain visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways: they either refer to evidence using textual coordinates, which specify symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself, or reinsert cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, preserving visual details at the cost of substantial context expansion. To address these limitations, we introduce VideoLVR, which constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, thereby providing visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. To supervise latent visual evidence generation, we introduce a visual token prediction objective that formulates visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, thereby unifying visual evidence reconstruction and text generation within the same token prediction framework. This shared prediction framework enables MLLMs to reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. We further extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. By efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context. Experiments on multiple video benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness, especially on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.
authors: Shilong Li, Xingyuan Bu, Hao Shi, Yun Xing, Weixin Feng, Qiangpeng Yang, Shilei Wen
bullets: Addresses the weakness of language-only reasoning traces, which can lose access to relevant video evidence.
Constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments instead of relying only on coordinates or pasted crops and frames.
Uses visual token prediction over an input-video-derived vocabulary to unify visual reconstruction and text generation.
Supports interleaved text and visual latent states, with a reinforcement-learning extension that jointly optimizes visual and text token actions.
Improves performance across multiple video benchmarks, particularly on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.

(c) At inference with the supervised model, each decoder hidden state is projected into a latent visual state and fed back as the input for the next decoding step, enabling autoregressive reasoning over latent visual evidence without additional visual observations.

papers.abstract: Visual world models increasingly support spatial reasoning by generating RGB views of unobserved states. However, RGB has become the default interface largely because it is well suited for visual generation, rather than necessarily being the most effective representation for downstream reasoning. Different spatial questions may benefit from different representations of the same imagined state: top-down geometry can facilitate global distance comparisons, while panoramic views provide broader context for reasoning about open space. To isolate the role of representation in spatial imagination, we introduce ImagiRep, a simulator-grounded benchmark of 922 questions spanning seven question types across two settings, Viewpoint Imagination and Cross-view Integration, providing oracle RGB and six alternative representations (e.g., depth, panoramic views, and top-down geometry) of the same unobserved state. This controlled comparison reveals that even accurate imagined RGB does not guarantee accurate spatial reasoning, and different questions benefit from different representations. Similar trends hold for representations derived from world-model-estimated states. Notably, estimated RGB alone can mislead spatial reasoning, while alternative representations retain complementary benefits. Building on these findings, we introduce GEARS, a lightweight test-time strategy for adaptive representation selection, outperforming existing spatial imagination methods and showing that reasoning about unseen states requires more than generating RGB views.
authors: Zengqi Zhao, Zun Wang, Shoubin Yu, Mohit Bansal, Yue Zhang
bullets: ImagiRep benchmarks 922 spatial questions across seven question types and two settings using RGB and six alternative representations of the same unseen state.
Different spatial questions benefit from different representations, such as top-down geometry for global distances and panoramas for open-space context.
Accurate imagined RGB does not guarantee accurate reasoning; estimated RGB can mislead, while alternative representations provide complementary information.
GEARS adaptively selects representations at test time and outperforms existing spatial-imagination methods.
The findings suggest that visual world models should represent unseen states beyond RGB generation.

papers.abstract: For reliable deployment, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) should recognize when an image provides insufficient evidence to answer a question and withhold unsupported answers. Yet refusal alone is not necessarily evidence of such recognition: models may refuse because of unrelated safety constraints or without identifying the missing evidence. We study how refusal on visually unanswerable questions is shaped by three sources of control: inference-time instructions, post-training, and internal activation interventions. Across three MLLMs on the MoHoBench benchmark, we systematically manipulate the meaning and placement of refusal instructions, compare supervised and preference-based post-training, and intervene on a refusal-related activation direction derived from naturally answered and refused examples. We find that refusal is highly sensitive to both the meaning and placement of instructions, with model-specific changes at the sample level that are obscured by aggregate refusal rates. Evidence-aware and general refusal instructions have stronger effects than an intentionally mismatched safety instruction. Post-training produces larger increases in refusal, but can also induce responses that combine refusal language with attempted answers. In contrast, activation intervention produces smaller yet transferable changes across prompt conditions, without evidence of indiscriminate refusal on tested visually answerable samples. These findings show that refusal is jointly shaped by external instructions, post-training, and internal representations, highlighting the need to disentangle evidence recognition from a model's learned propensity to refuse.

papers.abstract: When a multimodal model computes 17+35 from text or 91-39 from a rendered image, it produces the same answer, 52. Does it use one internal concept of number for both, or separate machinery for each path? Similarity metrics such as RSA or CKA cannot settle this question. They give the same score to identical and to rotated directions, and two representations can look alike only because both prepare the same output digits. We therefore use causal interventions. For four conditions (text or image, addition or subtraction), we learn a small subspace of Gemma4-12B-it's residual stream in which swapping coordinates swaps the model's answer. The subspaces answer three questions. First, do the conditions write numbers along the same directions? They do not. Reusing a subspace from text in an image on the same operation recovers only 53.2% of its causal effect. A single rotation and rescaling maps one subspace onto the other and raises recovery to 91.4%, so the conditions share one geometry expressed in different coordinates. Second, does this shared geometry only reflect the digit the model is about to print? To test this, we split each subspace into 9 directions that the output layer reads to choose the next digit and 13 directions that it cannot see. The 13 hidden directions still carry the number, yet changing them barely alters the digit being written. Third, what are these hidden directions for? A model must emit a multi-digit answer one digit at a time, so it can compute the full result early and keep it in reserve. When two numbers share their first digit, swapping the number in the hidden directions leaves the digit being written intact and redirects the next digit in 77.6% of cases. The model thus forms an abstract numerical concept upstream and unfolds it across time: multimodal representations share meaning through relational geometry across distinct coordinate frames.
authors: Oriol Juan Sabater, Alex Ferrando de las Morenas, Pau Rodr\'iguez, Xavier Suau
bullets: Text and image arithmetic use distinct subspaces, but a learned rotation and rescaling aligns them, recovering 91.4% of the causal effect.
Similarity measures alone cannot distinguish shared numerical concepts from representations that merely support the same output digits.
Numerical information exists in hidden directions not directly read by the output layer, beyond the directions controlling the next digit.
Swapping hidden numerical states redirects later digits in 77.6% of cases while preserving the current digit, indicating early computation of the full answer.
The evidence is limited to four conditions: text/image inputs paired with addition/subtraction in Gemma4-12B-it.

papers.abstract: Hyperbolic graph representation learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling hierarchical data. Unlike Euclidean space, which exhibits polynomial volume growth, hyperbolic space grows exponentially with radius, naturally accommodating tree-like structures without the geometric distortion known as Euclidean crowding. Despite strong empirical performance, the theoretical mechanisms underlying hyperbolic embeddings remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a geometric quantifcation research for Euclidean crowding, a generalization-theoretic explanation for the superiority of hyperbolic space on hierarchical data, and further develop an adaptive Euclidean-hyperbolic fusion learning framework toward bridging this gap. Specifically, we \textbf{first} establish a geometric quantification of Euclidean crowding by analyzing layer-wise minimum separation in node embeddings, proving that fixed-dimensional Euclidean embeddings of tree-like graphs inevitably exhibit layer-wise crowding that leads to weaker margin-based generalization bounds. \textbf{Second}, we provide a generalization-bound for the superiority of hyperbolic geometry on hierarchical data. \textbf{Third}, we propose EH-Fusion, a geometry-adaptive framework that lifts Euclidean GNN representations into hyperbolic space via exponential mapping and adaptively fuses both geometries based on node-level neighborhood expansion patterns. Extensive experiments validate our theoretical insights and demonstrate the effectiveness of EH-Fusion on benchmark datasets.
authors: Hao Chen, Jian Sun, Chuan Shi, Hongying Zhang
bullets: Quantifies Euclidean crowding through layer-wise minimum separation in embeddings of tree-like graphs.
Shows that fixed-dimensional Euclidean representations suffer increasing crowding and weaker margin-based generalization bounds.
Derives a generalization bound explaining hyperbolic geometry’s advantages for hierarchical data.
EH-Fusion maps Euclidean GNN representations into hyperbolic space and adaptively fuses both geometries using node-level neighborhood expansion.
Experiments on benchmark datasets support the theory and demonstrate EH-Fusion’s effectiveness.

Lower part: High-order degree growth information is extracted to capture local geometric characteristics and guide the adaptive aggregation of manifold-specific prediction probabilities.

Fig. 1. Euclidean crowding and its connection to generalization. In hierarchical data, the exponential growth of nodes with depth compresses pairwise distances in Euclidean space, reducing the geometric separation ∆ and the induced functional margin γ. This margin reduction leads to a looser margin-based generalization bound, whereas hyperbolic space can better preserve hierarchical distances with lower distortion.

papers.abstract: We present EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model which natively represents text, images, audio, video, and combinations thereof in a unified space. Our approach introduces improvements such as simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with modality and objective progression which ensure strong quality across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal evaluations. Notably, in comprehensive embedding benchmarks across all modalities, EmbeddingGemma 2 establishes a new Pareto frontier, outperforming both specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. Furthermore, our design offers flexibility for resource-constrained environments, supporting selective modality encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. We present ablations analyzing key decisions and release EmbeddingGemma 2 to promote further research.

papers.abstract: This report presents the implementation and validation of two end-to-end multimodal adaptation pipelines for 3D-aware visual question answering on a custom spatial dataset. The first pipeline fine-tunes HiSpatial-3B, which augments RGB observations with metric-scale 3D point maps; the second adapts Qwen3-VL through memory-efficient QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning. The completed engineering stack covers dataset conversion, image-annotation alignment, monocular geometry preprocessing, instruction construction, mixed-domain training, checkpoint management, batch inference, and automated evaluation. On the target spatial benchmark, HiSpatial adaptation increases overall accuracy from 1.73% before fine-tuning to 79.89% at 3,600 steps. On a separately collected styled split, accuracy improves from 14.9% to 55.1%, indicating transfer beyond the original training set. The Qwen3-VL pipeline is likewise implemented end-to-end for both 8B- and 32B-scale models using mixed-domain QLoRA adaptation. The resulting accuracy improves from 20.74% to 45.27% for Qwen3-VL-8B and from 30.79% to 47.60% for Qwen3-VL-32B. Together, these results establish two complementary and reproducible adaptation pipelines for geometry-aware and general-purpose multimodal spatial reasoning. These results establish a reproducible engineering foundation for subsequent work on metric 3D reasoning, spatial grounding, and domain-adapted multimodal systems, while also identifying training-data composition as a central factor in preserving general multimodal capability during specialization.
authors: Yu Zhang, Xiaogang Wang, Yuhang Cheng, Jingrui Li, Wenbo Chen
bullets: Fine-tunes HiSpatial-3B with RGB images and metric-scale 3D point maps, raising target-benchmark accuracy from 1.73% to 79.89%.
Applies memory-efficient QLoRA supervised fine-tuning to Qwen3-VL-8B and 32B, improving accuracy to 45.27% and 47.60%, respectively.
HiSpatial adaptation transfers to a separately styled split, increasing accuracy from 14.9% to 55.1%.
The engineering stack includes data conversion and alignment, geometry preprocessing, instruction construction, mixed-domain training, checkpointing, inference, and automated evaluation.
The report highlights training-data composition as important for retaining general multimodal capabilities during spatial specialization.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as an effective post-training paradigm for enhancing the video reasoning capability of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs). Despite its empirical effectiveness, we show that outcome-level optimization can introduce an undesirable shortcut amplification effect, whereby models increasingly favor text-prior answers even when they are not supported by the visual evidence. To characterize this behavior, we investigate the training dynamics of video RLVR through the lens of perceptual uncertainty, analyzing how predictive uncertainty evolves under video-conditioned and text-only contexts. Our analysis identifies a perceptual uncertainty collapse phenomenon, in which RL training continuously sharpens the model's answer distribution while the uncertainty reduction attributable to visual evidence progressively diminishes. A further gradient-direction analysis reveals that such confidence enhancement becomes increasingly less aligned with visually grounded uncertainty reduction and is instead dominated by text-prior compression. Motivated by these findings, we propose Bifocal Self-distillation Policy Optimization (BSPO), a self-distillation framework that regulates policy updates with two complementary distributional signals. Specifically, BSPO derives empirical reasoning principles from intra-group correct and incorrect rollouts to identify reasoning-sensitive tokens, and introduces shortcut-aware visual perturbation to penalize predictions that remain invariant when task-relevant visual evidence is weakened. By adaptively reweighting the original RL advantage, BSPO preserves the task-solving benefits of RLVR while promoting updates that are both reasoning-sensitive and visually grounded. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of BSPO in improving video reasoning performance and strengthening visual faithfulness.
authors: Jiafeng Liang, Xianhao Ou, Tao Ren, Rongchuan Mu, Runxuan Liu, Dandan Tu, Ming Liu, See-Kiong Ng, Bing Qin
bullets: RLVR may make models increasingly confident in text-prior answers unsupported by video evidence.
Perceptual uncertainty collapse occurs as visual evidence contributes less to uncertainty reduction during training.
Gradient analysis links this confidence growth more to text-prior compression than to visual grounding.
BSPO combines self-distillation from correct/incorrect rollouts with shortcut-aware visual perturbations to guide policy updates.
Experiments show improved video reasoning performance and stronger visual faithfulness.

papers.abstract: Current 3D scene understanding pipelines typically concatenate vast numbers of 3D object tokens with text tokens and feed the resulting sequence to a Large Language Model (LLM). However, existing 3D-LLMs for scene understanding encounter two major limitations: (i) excessive inclusion of task-irrelevant object data, introducing noise that reduces reasoning accuracy and increases hallucinations; and (ii) reliance solely on point cloud data, which inherently lacks the rich semantic information available in complementary 2D modalities, such as color, material properties, texture, and high-level contextual relationships. To address these challenges, we introduce 3D-SceneQ, a 3D LLM that unifies adaptive token pruning with multimodal semantic enrichment, markedly advancing scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding. Specifically, we propose a Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) module that adaptively selects task-relevant objects based on the intended meaning of user instructions, leveraging a learnable latent query to retain critical information while effectively suppressing irrelevant noise. In addition, we introduce a Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) module, which integrates 2D feature embeddings from pre-trained models into 3D representation to enrich object-level semantic information. Evaluations show that 3D-SceneQ outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks (e.g., +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D), demonstrating its remarkable capabilities in various 3D language reasoning tasks.
authors: Yongqi Shan, Lu Zhang, Jiazuo Yu, Yunzhi Zhuge, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Addresses noise from feeding large numbers of task-irrelevant 3D object tokens to LLMs.
Uses Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) to retain objects relevant to the user instruction.
Uses Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) to integrate pretrained 2D features into 3D representations.
Outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks, including +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D.
Targets 3D scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding tasks.

papers.abstract: Image quality assessment (IQA) aims to evaluate the perceptual visual quality of images. Recently, the rapid development of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has significantly advanced the IQA field. By integrating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and reinforcement learning (RL), these models can generate more accurate and interpretable results while relying on less training data. However, existing MLLM-based methods are predominantly constrained to holistic, image-level evaluations and lack the capability to produce fine-grained, localized assessments, which substantially limits their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose VGIQA, a novel IQA model endowed with both local and global quality assessment capabilities. VGIQA is trained via a two-stage paradigm comprising a cold-start phase followed by reinforcement learning. Driven by carefully designed local quality assessment reward functions, our model exhibits exceptional image quality understanding on VGSR-2K, a new dataset we propose specifically for local quality evaluation, significantly outperforming existing open-source MLLMs such as Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct. Furthermore, the local quality evaluation task can effectively enhance the model's performance on the degradation perception task.
authors: Weichang Wang, Liyu Chen, Shuyue Guan, Jie Hu, Fei Gao, Wei Li, Nannan Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing MLLM-based IQA methods that mainly provide holistic, image-level evaluations.
Uses a two-stage training strategy: cold-start training followed by reinforcement learning with local quality assessment rewards.
Introduces VGSR-2K, a dataset designed for local image-quality evaluation.
Reports strong local quality understanding and outperformance of the compared open-source MLLMs on VGSR-2K.
Finds that local quality assessment also improves degradation perception.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the proposed VGIQA framework. The framework follows a two-stage training paradigm. Stage 1 (Cold Start): The Qwen-based foundation model is initialized via SFT using CoT reasoning data distilled from Qwen3-VL-Plus [2] to establish structural formatting and inject IQA priors. Stage 2 (Multi-Task GRPO): Reinforcement learning jointly optimizes Local Quality Assessment, Degradation Perception, and Score Regression. Alongside a shared format reward, task-specific rewards are dynamically routed: a dedicated local reward exclusively supervises the local task (computing zero for non-local tasks), evaluating spatial bounding boxes via Hungarian Matching, negative DIoU, and F1 Score. Meanwhile, global tasks are optimized via verifiable score and classification/intensity rewards, unifying local-and-global quality evaluation.

Fig. 4: Overview of the VGSR-2K dataset construction pipeline. The dataset is curated via a rigorous human-in-the-loop pipeline. (1) Candidate Generation: Qwen3-VL-Plus [2] and Seed1.6-VL independently process LR-SR image pairs, yielding six candidate spatial bounding boxes. (2) Double-Blind Selection: Two annotator groups select the most consistent candidate; consensus establishes the baseline, while divergence prompts expert resolution. (3) Double-Blind Correction & Merging: Annotators refine baselines by adding or removing boxes. Corrections are merged via the Hungarian algorithm with a negative DIoU cost metric, extracting the MBR for matched pairs. (4) Final Review & Balancing: After expert review, pristine LR-HR image pairs are introduced as negative samples (with empty annotations) to calibrate spatial predictions and prevent trivial over-generation.

Fig. 2: Example applications of the proposed VGIQA framework. Built upon a Qwen-based foundation model, VGIQA achieves comprehensive quality understanding via multi-task reinforcement learning. While existing models (e.g., Q-Insight) are limited to holistic Score Regression and Degradation Perception, VGIQA explicitly bridges the gap in fine-grained Local Quality Assessment. Driven by novel visual grounding rewards, it adopts a rigorous "look and then judge" paradigm—precisely localizing spatial artifacts before formulating final judgments.

Fig. 1: Qualitative visualization of the local quality assessment results. Given a reference image, a distorted image to be evaluated, and a user query, VGIQA produces more reliable and accurate responses compared with the state-of-the-art RL-based IQA method Q-insight and the general large vision-language model Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct [1].

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction represents scene geometry and semantics in a unified voxel grid, enabling recognition beyond predefined categories. One approach reconstructs scenes with 3D Gaussians and converts them into voxel occupancy. However, Gaussian scale inflation and excessive overlap can distort voxel occupancy predictions, while semantic mixing can arise within Gaussians spanning multiple categories and during 3D--2D semantic feature alignment. We propose GCSR-OCC, which combines geometry calibration and multi-mode query-conditioned semantic routing for indoor occupancy prediction from a single RGB image. The Evidence-Conserving Gaussian-to-Occupancy operator (EC-G2O) uses kernel mass normalization, $p$-norm aggregation, and a learnable gain to suppress scale inflation and excessive local evidence accumulation while calibrating occupancy responses. Multi-mode Query-First Gaussian Semantic Routing (MM-QGSR) matches multiple semantic modes per Gaussian to text queries and aggregates query-specific evidence into voxels through a learnable text-conditioned router. Fine-grained subclass queries and smoothed semantic aggregation further refine voxel-level predictions. Without 3D semantic annotations, GCSR-OCC achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-vocabulary occupancy prediction on Occ-ScanNet, with 63.31% geometric IoU and 27.44% semantic mIoU. It also reduces geometric aggregation latency from 19.76 ms to 12.88 ms. Our code will be made publicly available.

Uses EC-G2O to normalize Gaussian evidence, aggregate it with a p-norm, and calibrate occupancy responses with a learnable gain.
Uses MM-QGSR to match multiple semantic modes per Gaussian to text queries and route query-specific evidence into voxels.
Adds fine-grained subclass queries and smoothed semantic aggregation for more precise voxel semantics.
Achieves 63.31% geometric IoU and 27.44% semantic mIoU on Occ-ScanNet, while reducing geometric aggregation latency from 19.76 ms to 12.88 ms without 3D semantic annotations.
