papers.abstract: We present a variational control framework that connects sampling-time guidance and reward-based model adaptation through a shared Jacobian pullback. Starting from terminal reward maximization with a path-space KL penalty, the Gibbs variational principle and Doob transform yield a correction to the generative dynamics. A local denoising approximation exposes the pullback that transports output preferences to the controlled variable. This construction gives Variational Optimal Guidance (VOG) in state space and extends to Distilled Variational Optimal Control (DVOC) by amortizing locally improved endpoints into model parameters. The resulting controls share a local variational rule: VOG acts through the denoising Jacobian, while DVOC realizes the parameter pullback by endpoint distillation. Under a linear MMSE model, VOG's exact correction lies in the data subspace. On ImageNet, VOG reduces DiT-XL/2 FID from 2.27 to 2.04 at 250 sampling steps and from 7.58 to 4.44 at 25 steps. After 20 updates on Z-Image-Turbo, DVOC improves HPSv3++ and four held-out evaluator scores over the untrained model, with the highest corresponding means among the trained methods compared. These results connect inference-time control and reward adaptation through a common geometric principle.
authors: Ruoyu Wang, Xinyi Ye, Yunshuo Shi, Liangyu Yuan, Beier Zhu, Chi Zhang

VOG reduces DiT-XL/2 FID from 2.27 to 2.04 at 250 steps and from 7.58 to 4.44 at 25 steps on ImageNet.
DVOC improves HPSv3++ and four held-out evaluator scores on Z-Image-Turbo after 20 updates; the abstract does not specify limitations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence. To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2). Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. These results establish EvidenceConnect as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.
authors: Lai Wei, Yatai Li, Liangbo He, Jun Lan, Renjie Gu, Linhan Cao, Junkai Lin, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Linghe Kong, Yue Wang, Zhuosheng Zhang, Weiran Huang
bullets: Targets the shared capability of connecting evidence: finding relevant visual facts, linking them to entities, recovering relations, and composing answers.
Generates comparison, aggregation, and multi-step visual questions from zoomed views of related regions within one image.
Filters data using agreement among independent VLMs and region-ablation tests to verify answer quality and evidence dependence.
Trains base VLMs with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) to obtain ZwZ2.
Although not tailored to downstream benchmarks, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with broader gains across several multimodal reasoning settings.

papers.title: Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception

papers.abstract: Embedding-level scaling expands the capacity of language models through lookup-based memory rather than by increasing model depth, width, or dense computation. Extending this idea to vision-language models (VLMs) is challenging because visual features are continuous, spatially structured, and query-dependent, unlike discrete text tokens that naturally support n-gram lookup. We introduce V-LUMEN, a visual lookup memory for VLMs. V-LUMEN discretizes visual features with a frozen codebook, builds spatially aware memory keys through spatial aggregation-based hashing, and modulates them with text-conditioned relevance signals; all addressing is non-parametric, and the retrieved embeddings are fused into the backbone through a gated residual pathway. On five reasoning-intensive benchmarks, V-LUMEN substantially improves a frozen Qwen3-VL-2B backbone and transfers zero-shot to three benchmarks whose images are disjoint from the training data. At a matched parameter budget, moving part of a LoRA or MoE adapter's capacity into V-LUMEN preserves accuracy on two backbones, indicating that external visual memory is an independent capacity axis rather than a stronger adaptation method. Because lookup cost is constant in table size and incurred only once at prefill, this capacity grows in storage rather than in per-token compute. Code is available at https://github.com/miso-choi/V-Lumen.
authors: Miso Choi, Daekeun Kim, Eunji Kim, Jungbeom Lee
bullets: Visual features are continuous, spatially structured, and query-dependent, making text-style lookup memory difficult to apply directly.
It discretizes visual features with a frozen codebook and creates spatially aware, text-conditioned memory keys.
Retrieved embeddings are integrated into the VLM through a gated residual pathway.
It improves a frozen Qwen3-VL-2B on five reasoning benchmarks and transfers zero-shot to three disjoint-image benchmarks.
At matched parameter budgets, V-LUMEN can replace part of LoRA or MoE capacity while preserving accuracy on two backbones.

papers.abstract: Streaming multimodal assistants must make response decisions while events are still unfolding. They need to recognize when the available evidence warrants a response, produce an appropriate continuation, and remain silent otherwise. Supervised fine-tuning learns from recorded assistant turns, but does not directly train on the response prefixes produced by the evolving policy itself. We introduce Live-OPSD, an on-policy self-distillation method that uses privileged hints available only during training to supervise the policy on its own outputs. The policy first generates a continuation from the streaming context alone. The same model then re-evaluates that continuation with a hint describing the relevant evidence, and the resulting distributions guide the unhinted policy. On Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, Live-OPSD attains an average score of 59.64 on LiveProBench, 5.26 points above the strongest continued-SFT baseline, and stays competitive on OVO-Bench (65.84). These results indicate that guiding the policy on its own outputs with privileged hints improves both when and how a streaming assistant responds.
authors: Kaixuan Du, Xin Wan, Dai Guan, Ming Chen, Xiaoxi Jiang, Guanjun Jiang
bullets: Streaming assistants must decide whether to respond, what to say, or remain silent as events unfold.
The method addresses a gap in supervised fine-tuning, which does not train on prefixes generated by the evolving policy.
It generates a continuation from streaming context, then re-evaluates it with training-only privileged evidence hints.
On Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, it scores 59.64 on LiveProBench—5.26 points above the strongest continued-SFT baseline—and remains competitive on OVO-Bench at 65.84.
The approach improves both response timing and content, within the evaluated streaming-assistant benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multimodal transformer models have driven unprecedented performance breakthroughs in modern document understanding. However, the inherent black-box nature of these models remains a major obstacle to their safe deployment in high-stakes sectors. Despite significant progress in explainability for vision and language tasks, explainable AI (XAI) research tailored to multimodal document understanding has received little attention. To address this gap, we present \ourframework{}, the first comprehensive explainability framework that adapts existing XAI methods and evaluation metrics to the multimodal (text, layout, and image) document understanding context, while introducing efficient multi-target adaptations of both methods and metrics for domain-specific tasks such as semantic entity recognition. Using \ourframework{}, we systematically evaluate 13 XAI methods across 3 document understanding tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 evaluation metrics, and find that only a few methods perform consistently across all evaluation criteria, with Occlusion emerging as the most faithful and interpretable method overall. Through a dedicated meta-evaluation, we observe moderate to strong agreement among several faithfulness and complexity metrics while identifying certain ones that produce unreliable results. Finally, through multiple dataset-wide diagnostic analyses, we uncover key insights into model behavior, including the contribution of individual modalities across tasks and labels, spatial attribution patterns around target entities, and potential dataset biases. Overall, this work serves as both a benchmark and a practical guide for future XAI research in multimodal document understanding. To support reproducibility, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/saifullah3396/docxeval/.
authors: Saifullah Saifullah, David Dembinsky, Stefan Agne, Andreas Dengel, Sheraz Ahmed
bullets: Addresses the limited XAI research for models combining document text, layout, and images, especially in high-stakes applications.
Adapts existing XAI methods and metrics to multimodal documents and develops efficient multi-target variants for tasks such as semantic entity recognition.
Systematically evaluates 13 XAI methods across 3 tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 metrics.
Finds that only a few methods perform consistently across evaluation criteria; Occlusion performs best overall.
Diagnostic analyses reveal modality contributions, spatial attribution patterns, and potential dataset biases; code is publicly released.

papers.abstract: Although the recent development of LLMs has paved the way for multi-modal interaction, minority languages face difficulties keeping pace. This work presents the first open Speech Language Model for Basque, designed for low-latency, end-to-end spoken interaction. Based on the LLaMA-Omni architecture, the system integrates a Latxa model as its backbone, transferring its Basque capabilities to the spoken modality by fine-tuning several modules. To address data scarcity, the English VoiceAssistant-400K corpus was translated into Basque, and the audio was synthesized using a Basque TTS. Evaluation results confirm the system's viability, achieving 3.86/5 in content quality, a 9.94% WER for spoken intelligibility, and a 3.07 UTMOS for audio quality. This work demonstrates that advanced spoken interaction systems can be developed using modular architectures and synthetic data even in low-resource languages.
authors: Andoni Sudupe, Inma Hernaez, Ander Arriandiaga, Christoforos Souganidis, Ibon Saratxaga, Eva Navas
bullets: Addresses the limited availability of advanced spoken-interaction systems for minority and low-resource languages.
Builds on LLaMA-Omni with Latxa as the Basque backbone, fine-tuning modules to transfer language capabilities to speech.
Expands scarce training data by translating VoiceAssistant-400K into Basque and synthesizing corresponding audio with Basque TTS.
Evaluation reports 3.86/5 content quality, 9.94% word error rate, and 3.07 UTMOS audio quality.
Demonstrates the viability of modular architectures and synthetic data for Basque speech interaction.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding on high-resolution screens fails mostly on small targets, and zooming in is a common training-free remedy. However, most existing zooming pipelines do not match the zoom to the target's size, accept the zoomed answer unconditionally and never revisit a wrong answer. To address these issues, we propose AdaGround, a training-free framework with three components: (1) Token-Normalized Adaptive Zooming, which sets the magnification, field of view and zoom depth of each sample from the model's own estimate of the target size; (2) Verifier-in-the-Loop Refinement, which uses one marked-click Yes/No verifier to keep or reject each zoom, choose between zoom chains, trigger re-grounding and, with an existence query, decide when to abstain; and (3) Compositional Structure Grounding, which composes spreadsheet cells from their headers. On Qwen3-VL models, AdaGround surpasses state-of-the-art training-free zooming methods and many trained GUI models, improving accuracy over the backbone by 7.4 to 20.6 points on OSWorld-G and ScreenSpot-Pro, and its gains carry over to held-out UI-Vision. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/AdaGround
authors: Bingchao Wang, Yongcheng Jing, Chengyu Wang, Jun Huang, Jie Yang, Wei Liu, Dacheng Tao
bullets: Targets zoom magnification, field of view, and depth to the model’s estimated target size.
Uses a marked-click Yes/No verifier to accept or reject zooms, select zoom chains, trigger re-grounding, and abstain when targets may not exist.
Composes spreadsheet-cell targets from their row and column headers.
On Qwen3-VL, improves over the backbone by 7.4–20.6 points on OSWorld-G and ScreenSpot-Pro, with gains transferring to held-out UI-Vision.
The framework is training-free and evaluated on high-resolution GUI grounding.

papers.title: AdaGround: Token-Normalized Adaptive Zooming with Verifier-in-the-Loop Refinement for GUI Grounding
papers.tldr: AdaGround is a training-free GUI grounding framework that adaptively zooms to target size and uses verifier-guided refinement to improve small-target localization.

papers.abstract: Leading GUI grounders score 93 to 96% on ScreenSpot-v2, and reported gaps between new and prior models are about a point. At this level the useful question is what the remaining errors are. Benchmarks count a click as correct only inside one annotated box, but interfaces often expose one action through several elements: a duplicated link, the label of a checkbox, the title next to a logo. The box is not wrong. The rule is incomplete. We call a click correct when executing it produces the same outcome as clicking the annotated target. A probe that executes and fingerprints about a thousand clicks per page turns this definition into outcome maps and an execution judge for live web applications, with no new annotation. We execute the predictions of three strong 7--8B grounders on a code forge and an online shop. About one in five and one in three of the clicks that box scoring rejects reach the intended outcome, and the shares remain one in seven and one in three when the instructions are rewritten as natural tasks. A blind audit of 11 models on ScreenSpot-v2 (three 7--8B grounders and eight 3B variants) finds the same effect on web screenshots, with two independent reviewers on a 60-unit subset. The share is highest for the strongest grounders. Training seeds and test-set sampling add noise that more runs and paired intervals control. Box scoring instead under-counts correct clicks, which repetition does not remove, and the audit-based correction of 0.2 to 1.8 points on ScreenSpot-v2 is as large as the gaps the field reports. The correction is needed in evaluation. In our 3B GRPO study, crediting equivalent clicks in the reward gives no stable gain over box rewards across three seeds and four test sets. We release the probe, the outcome maps, the audit and every prediction.

The authors execute clicks and fingerprint page outcomes to build outcome maps and an execution-based judge without new annotations.
Across a code forge, online shop, and ScreenSpot-v2 audit, roughly one-fifth to one-third of box-rejected clicks achieve the intended outcome.
Correcting ScreenSpot-v2 scores changes results by 0.2–1.8 points, comparable to reported model gaps.
Rewarding equivalent clicks in a 3B GRPO study produced no stable improvement over box-based rewards.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have made substantial progress in visual question answering, but complex visual reasoning often requires locating and comparing multiple pieces of question-relevant visual evidence. Existing methods that move intermediate reasoning into the visual latent space usually follow a single linear reasoning trajectory, which can be limiting when multiple visual hypotheses or competing evidence regions are relevant. We propose Latent Visual Contrastive Reasoning, a branch-aware latent reasoning framework that generates multiple question-conditioned latent visual branches as soft hypotheses over image tokens. To train these branches, our method uses bounding-box evidence annotations to build target evidence representations and introduces a soft contrastive branch-evidence alignment objective. This objective encourages evidence-relevant branches to align with annotated visual regions while contrasting them against negative evidence. We instantiate our method on Qwen2.5-VL backbones and train it with standard supervised fine-tuning. Experiments on perception-intensive visual reasoning benchmarks show that the proposed method achieves overall improvements over the corresponding backbone and single-path latent reasoning baselines at both 3B and 7B scales.
authors: Kegeng Tang, Jingbo Wang, Yangming Zhang, Huanshu Zhang, Shaogang Ren, Zihao Wang
bullets: Targets the limitation of single-path latent reasoning when questions require comparing multiple visual regions or competing evidence.
Generates multiple question-conditioned latent visual branches as soft hypotheses over image tokens.
Uses bounding-box annotations and a soft contrastive branch–evidence alignment objective to associate branches with relevant regions and reject negative evidence.
Implemented with Qwen2.5-VL backbones and standard supervised fine-tuning.
Reports overall gains over the backbone and single-path latent reasoning baselines on perception-intensive benchmarks at 3B and 7B scales.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overall framework of LVCR. Given an image-question pair, LVCR encodes the image and question into visual and textual tokens, and proposes multiple question-conditioned latent branches as candidate visual hypotheses over the image. These branches are contrastively aligned with answer-relevant visual evidence and separated from irrelevant regions. LVCR then ranks the branches using relevance scores computed by cosine similarity with the question representation, and injects the selected branch tokens into the MLLM decoder, which combines them with the original multimodal context to generate the final answer.

Fig. 3. Accuracy (%) of three branch injection strategies on V ∗, MMVP, and BLINK (aggregated). Ranked denotes our default LVCR strategy; Top-1 injects only the highest-ranked branch; Unranked injects all branches without ordering. Results are reported using LVCR-3B with K=4.

Fig. 2. Ablation study on the NCE loss coefficient using LVCR-3B with K=4. We compare the default setting with λNCE = 0.1 against a variant trained without the NCE loss, i.e., λNCE = 0. Removing the NCE loss leads to consistent performance drops on V ∗, MMVP, and BLINK, indicating that contrastive branch-evidence alignment helps latent branches capture questionrelevant visual cues.

papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) predicts the next item through its semantic ID (SID). Existing methods commonly fit SID vocabularies to pretrained language model (PLM) representations of item descriptions, incurring additional training costs and making vocabulary coverage dependent on the fitting domains. We observe that pretrained sparse autoencoders expose PLM features with human-interpretable semantic annotations, allowing feature indices to serve as a reusable SID vocabulary. However, reusing this vocabulary requires preserving item distinctions under compact token budgets and learning to favor target items over candidates with shared dominant features. It also requires extending feature interpretability from item content to retrieval decisions. To address these challenges, we propose API, a framework that Adapts the Pretrained Interpretable vocabulary for effective and explainable GR without additional vocabulary learning. Within API, Pretrained Interpretable IDs (PIDs) retain selected feature indices and relative activation strengths for item discrimination. With PIDs as supervision, the Semantic Prediction Adapter (SPA) learns user preferences from interaction histories through joint feature-index and strength prediction. SPA combines both predictions to score candidate items, with item-level supervision encouraging the observed next item to outrank its alternatives. API further explains candidate score differences through feature contributions paired with their pretrained semantic annotations. Extensive experiments show that API achieves competitive performance across backbones and decoding schemes, while preserving item distinctions under compact token budgets and enabling explainable retrieval.
authors: Ziluowen Luo, Ruochen Liu, Jun Yin, Hao Yan, Zhengxuan Hu, Xinze Shi, Chaozhuo Li, Chengqi Zhang, Senzhang Wang
bullets: Addresses the cost and domain-dependent coverage of fitting new semantic-ID vocabularies.
Uses Pretrained Interpretable IDs that preserve selected feature indices and activation strengths under compact token budgets.
Trains a Semantic Prediction Adapter to jointly predict feature indices and strengths from user histories.
Scores candidates using feature predictions and item-level ranking supervision, while attributing score differences to semantic features.
Experiments report competitive performance across backbones and decoding schemes, with preserved item distinctions and explainable retrieval.

papers.abstract: Multilingual multi-hop document question answering (MMHop-DocQA) requires locating and integrating evidence across complex layouts, document pages, and diverse languages. Existing approaches include single-pass processing and adaptive tool use, but learning to coordinate evidence acquisition, cross-page integration, and answer verification remains challenging. To address this challenge, we present DocSkill, an agentic framework with a learned skill-orchestration policy for adaptive evidence acquisition and reasoning. The policy selects, revisits, or skips skills according to the evolving evidence state. To construct supervision for skill orchestration, bounded Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) explores alternative skill trajectories offline. These trajectories provide demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We further introduce MMHop-DocBench, a multilingual multi-hop document QA dataset with training and test splits, containing 60K QA pairs across 10 languages and eight document domains. Its HopGen pipeline builds hierarchical page-element graphs to derive traceable cross-page evidence paths and generate grounded QA pairs with page- and element-level evidence annotations. Experiments show that DocSkill with Qwen3-VL-8B achieves 41.0 accuracy and 49.2 F1 on MMHop-DocBench, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 5.5 and 6.3 points, respectively, and achieving competitive performance on MMLongBench-Doc and DocBench.
authors: Jing Huang, Zhiya Tan, Changtao Miao, Shutao Gong, Yang Wang, Joey Tianyi Zhou, Jianshu Li, Ying Yan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reasoning across complex layouts, pages, and languages while coordinating evidence gathering and answer verification.
Uses a learned skill-orchestration policy that selects, revisits, or skips skills based on the evolving evidence state.
Generates orchestration supervision with offline bounded MCTS, followed by supervised fine-tuning and Direct Preference Optimization.
Introduces MMHop-DocBench: 60K QA pairs in 10 languages and eight domains, with traceable page- and element-level evidence annotations.
With Qwen3-VL-8B, reports 41.0 accuracy and 49.2 F1, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 5.5 and 6.3 points; also performs competitively on two other benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) process their entire input at every denoising step. Since visual tokens make up 89-97% of this input on the benchmarks we study, most of the decoding computation is spent repeatedly processing the same image. Visual token pruning methods partially relieve this burden by removing part of the visual tokens, but they lose the removed information and still process the remaining image at every step. To measure how often the image is actually needed, we compare LLaDA-V's predictions with and without the image at every decoding step and find that removing the image changes a token being unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average and at as few as 7.9%. We therefore propose LOWN, a decoding method that decides at every step whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask. LOWN predicts the masked tokens without the image and processes the image only when this prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. We further observe that the need for the image differs across benchmarks, so LOWN's adaptive decision is needed rather than a fixed schedule. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average. LOWN also generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, composes orthogonally with visual token pruning, and runs under key-value caching for further efficiency gains. Code and project page are available at https://hyeon9698.github.io/LOWN/
authors: Donghyeon Cho, Joowon Kim, Seungho Shin, Eunho Yang
bullets: DVLMs repeatedly process mostly redundant visual tokens at every denoising step.
The method compares image-free and image-conditioned predictions to certify when prior predictions can be reused.
It adaptively decides both whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask, without training or a tuned threshold.
Across ten benchmarks, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V’s score while using 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average.
It generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, combines with visual token pruning, and supports key-value caching.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive visual routing reduces decoding FLOPs for diffusion VLMs.
papers.title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs

papers.abstract: To generate landmark-based route instructions, models must understand both map geometry and human landmark preferences. Although large language models (LLMs) show great abilities in language tasks, the best way to structure map data for these models is not yet established. This paper proposes a structured text representation for landmark selection tasks in route navigation, utilizing SVG format to encode spatial features. The structured text maintains a geometric connection with rendered map images, allowing language models to directly access spatial and semantic data. Using a new dataset created from human-written route descriptions and OpenStreetMap data, we evaluate models on two tasks: landmark selection at turns and around destinations. Experiments with five LLMs show that the proposed structured text input performs as well as or better than image-based PNG inputs. In addition, task-specific fine-tuning enables smaller local LLMs to effectively leverage map layouts to achieve high selection accuracy. These results demonstrate that structured text is an efficient and lightweight interface for spatial reasoning in human-oriented navigation.
authors: Mifu Matsumoto, Yuki Nakanishi, Tomoya Hashiguchi, Hiroaki Ohshima
bullets: Addresses the challenge of representing map geometry and semantic information for landmark-based route instruction generation.
Encodes spatial features in structured SVG text while preserving alignment with rendered map images.
Evaluates landmark selection at turns and near destinations using a dataset combining human-written routes with OpenStreetMap data.
Across five LLMs, structured text performs as well as or better than PNG map inputs.
Task-specific fine-tuning allows smaller local LLMs to use map layouts effectively.

papers.abstract: Final-answer accuracy reports whether a vision-language model was right, but not whether its answer was grounded in the image, whether its stated reasoning reflects that evidence, or what the answer cost to produce. Those are the properties that decide whether a system can be deployed. We present PRISM-BENCH, a benchmark of 1,000 expert-curated questions spanning five under-represented reasoning categories, in which every item carries an idealized reasoning trace written by one human annotator and validated by another. The traces support two diagnostics that accuracy cannot provide. A perception probe, in which the model answers from a description it wrote itself, attributes roughly 85% of frontier-model failures to misperception and places the bottleneck at grounding. Trace alignment predicts answer correctness for all 25 systems tested (macro AUROC 0.66) and survives length control, so it measures reasoning content and not verbosity. We further introduce CORE, an efficiency-aware metric that reorders 24.2% of model pairs relative to accuracy while remaining uncorrelated with response length. Across 25 open and closed systems, including GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4.6, the best accuracy is 66.0%. On the four categories with a human baseline the best system trails humans by 18.4 points, and recent frontier gains fall on recognition and not on spatial grounding.
authors: Vansh Bhatia, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh, Parsa Ashrafi Fashi, Igor Gilitschenski, Vikram Appia, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Introduces 1,000 expert-curated questions across five under-represented reasoning categories, each with a validated ideal reasoning trace.
A self-description perception probe attributes roughly 85% of frontier-model failures to misperception, identifying grounding as the main bottleneck.
Trace alignment predicts correctness across all 25 evaluated systems, beyond effects of response length.
CORE, an efficiency-aware metric, reorders 24.2% of model pairs relative to accuracy while remaining uncorrelated with response length.
The best system reaches 66.0% accuracy, trails humans by 18.4 points where comparable, and recent gains emphasize recognition over spatial grounding.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Three deployment-relevant diagnostics that final-answer accuracy cannot provide. (a) Accuracy falls when a model must answer from its own image description instead of the image (drop annotated in red); the white figure inside each bar is the share of that model’s baseline failures that the model itself, judging in a fresh context, attributes to perception instead of inference. (b) For all 25 evaluated systems, responses that are correct align more closely with the human reasoning trace than responses that are incorrect (macro AUROC 0.66, and 0.665 after regressing out response length). (c) CORE reorders models relative to accuracy; dashed arrows connect matched thinking/instruct pairs, which spend more tokens for less accuracy.

Figure 3: (a) Overall accuracy for all 25 evaluated systems, shaded by family, against the 83.9% human baseline (red). Restricted to the four categories where both are measured, the best system trails humans by 18.4 points, and the open/closed gap is larger than any difference within the open families. (b) Best system of any kind versus the human baseline (red tick) per category. The deficit is concentrated in the two spatially grounded categories and nearly vanishes on multi-hop, where the reasoning is largely textual once the scene is read.

Figure 6: Navigation / map reading. Gemma-3-12B-It reads the label adjacent to the church and answers correctly in 74 tokens. Kimi-VL (140 tokens), Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (172) and Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct (316) all produce longer, more structured deliberations and all answer “Henry Street”. This item is a compact illustration of why we score cost alongside correctness: the cheapest response here is the only correct one, and a leaderboard ordered by accuracy alone would still rank three of these systems above Gemma overall.

Figure 9: Navigation / spatial orientation. The question asks which street is the odd one out and states explicitly that the criterion is not the name. The answer is Wilfred Ave, the only street running north–south while the others run east–west. Only OpenAI o3 checks orientation on the map. Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (1,861 tokens), Ovis2.5-9B and Gemma-3-12B all reason from the linguistic distinction between “Court” and “Avenue” despite the hint ruling it out, and Ovis2.5-9B visibly loops before committing. This is the linguistic shortcutting failure, and it is the pattern behind the ∼47% navigation scores in Table 2: the models read the map as text rather than as space.

Figure 2: The five reasoning categories, balanced at 200 items each. The categories mix functional reasoning patterns, such as multi-hop composition, with domain-specific grounding requirements, such as medical interpretation, because deployment demands both.

Figure 4: Visual coreference under occlusion. The question asks for the registration of the aircraft partially occluded behind the silver plane in the foreground. Gemini 2.5 Pro resolves it by enumerating the three visible aircraft, reading each registration, and matching against the referring expression. Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL-30B-Thinking and Ovis2.5-9B all answer N177XV, the registration of the foreground plane. This is the saliency bias described in Section E: the referring expression is never applied, and the most prominent entity is returned instead. Token budgets of 614, 296 and 753 show this is not a matter of insufficient reasoning length.

Figure 5: Handwriting / OCR reasoning. All five candidate words appear correctly in the handwritten passage, so the answer is “none of the above”, which requires transcribing every option correctly before concluding that nothing is missing. Qwen3-VL-8BInstruct does so. Gemini 2.5 Pro misreads one word and then constructs an elaborate, internally consistent argument for “based”; Gemma-3-12B and VL-Rethinker each settle on “favour”. This is the cascade pattern: the reasoning is valid given the misperception, so the trace looks sound and the error is invisible without the ground truth.

Figure 7: Multi-hop reasoning. Answering requires chaining what the scene shows (people playing a Wii boxing game) to a fact about the game (each player needs a remote and a nunchuck) to a count. Ovis2.5-9B, Gemma-3-12B and Skywork-R1V3-38B chain correctly. OpenAI o3 counts three players from the image and propagates that into three controllers, an error at the first hop that the subsequent reasoning faithfully preserves.

Figure 8: Scientific / medical reasoning. The nail finding is Beau’s lines, transverse ridges left by repeated arrest of nail-matrix growth, which point to cyclical chemotherapy. Only OpenAI o3 reaches this. Gemini identifies the pattern as Muehrcke’s lines and reasons fluently to nephrotic syndrome; Gemma-3-12B reasons to psoriasis; Qwen2.5-VL-7B concludes none of the options apply. Each wrong answer arrives with a confident, clinically phrased causal chain. This is the category with the highest rate of confidently wrong explanations, and the reason we treat it as the clearest safety concern for deployment.

Figure 10: The four-stage annotation loop. Duties are separated so that no annotator validates an item whose reasoning trace they wrote, and an item that fails Stage 4 returns to its author for revision instead of being silently accepted or discarded. Stage 2 produces the human reference length Lgt i that CORE uses and the reference content that trace alignment uses.

Table 7: Trace alignment for all 25 evaluated systems, sorted by gap. “Sim.” is the mean over gold trace steps of the maximum cosine similarity to any step of the model response. The gap is positive for every variant: responses that reach the correct answer track the human reasoning trace more closely than responses that do not.

Table 2: Accuracy (%) of all 25 evaluated systems across the five PRISM-BENCH categories, against the human baseline (5 annotators × 50 items per category). No system exceeds 66% overall, or 84% in any single category. The newest frontier systems lead on OCR yet remain near 47% on navigation, where humans reach 86%: recent gains concentrate on recognition rather than spatial grounding.
Table 1: PRISM-BENCH dataset statistics. The three answer-choice rows partition all 1,000 items; most are 4-way or wider multiple choice, and 11 items are open-ended or binary.

Table 6: Reflective-token analysis for 12 representative models. “Reflective tokens” counts hesitation and backtracking phrases (“Wait”, “Actually”, “Let me reconsider”) per response. More self-correction does not yield higher accuracy: Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking averages 17.0 reflective phrases and 1,812 tokens to reach 36.0%, while its instruct counterpart averages 2.6 phrases and 737 tokens to reach 40.0%.
Table 3: Perception-vs-reasoning probe on navigation and coreference. Accuracy falls when models answer from their own descriptions, and the large majority of failures are attributed to perception.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for diagnosing grounded and faithful multimodal reasoning, providing metrics beyond final answer accuracy for VLMs.
papers.title: PRISM-BENCH: Diagnosing Grounded and Faithful Multimodal Reasoning Beyond Final-Answer Accuracy
papers.tldr: PRISM-BENCH shows that multimodal reasoning quality depends on grounding, faithful reasoning, and efficiency—not final-answer accuracy alone.

papers.abstract: We propose Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Uni (NLD-Uni), a unified discrete diffusion large language model (DLLM) for visual understanding and generation tasks. Compared with prior unified diffusion models, NLD-Uni introduces two major innovations. First, we propose a unified cross-paradigm on-policy distillation (OPD) framework that successfully transfers the visual understanding ability of autoregressive VLMs and visual generation ability of continuous flow models, to a unified DLLM. Second, NLD-Uni incorporates a novel progressive self-refining diffusion process that gradually corrupts each token across multiple steps during training, as opposed to adopting the conventional masked diffusion formulation that directly corrupts a clean image token to an uninformative mask token. At inference, this design allows NLD-Uni to make intermediate commit to a token, enabling progressive self-refinement for better visual quality. Through extensive experiments, we show that NLD-Uni achieves state-of-the-art performance among unified DLLMs on diverse tasks including visual question-answering, multi-modal reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image generation, and image editing.
authors: Shufan Li, Hanrong Ye, Greg Heinrich, Yonggan Fu, Haotian Zhang, Sifei Liu, Aditya Grover, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Transfers capabilities from autoregressive vision-language models and continuous flow models into one unified diffusion model.
Uses cross-paradigm on-policy distillation to train visual understanding and generation abilities.
Introduces progressive self-refining diffusion, gradually corrupting tokens instead of replacing them directly with masks.
Enables intermediate token commitments during inference for progressive visual refinement.
Reports state-of-the-art unified-DLLM performance across VQA, multimodal reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image generation, and image editing.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | NLD-Uni supports diverse multimodal tasks by adopting an Elastic-MoT architecture with three elastic views of a single model. The VLM view uses the 8B understanding branch; the T2I view combines 4B understanding parameters with the 8B generation branch; and the interleaved view uses both full branches (16B). Each view loads only the parameters needed for its task. Yellow and green blocks denote understanding and generation layers, gray blocks indicate omitted layers, and blue arrows denote joint attention. Representative examples demonstrate visual reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image synthesis, and image editing guided by reasoning and localization.

Figure 3 | Overall Framework of NLD-Uni. NLD-Uni is a unified diffusion model whose input and output are both multimodal. Images in the input stream are represented by both continuous embeddings of a semantic encoder and discrete tokens of a VQ encoder. Images in the output stream are represented solely using VQ codes. NLD-Uni is trained to predict the clean token distribution given partially masked inputs. For image generation, we incorporate an intermediate masking state.

Figure 6 | On-Policy Distilling from Continuous Flow Models. Given a student output, we generate a teacher-refined output by adding noise to the student sample and re-denoise it with the teacher model. For reference, we also show an independent teacher generation. We observe that the teacher’s refinements are closely aligned to the student’s output while having better visual fidelity and source image preservation.

Figure 5 | On-Policy Distilling from Autoregressive VLMs. Top: Given a prompt and clean prefix blocks, we generate the current block with the student’s AR view by temporarily adopting a block size of 1. Left: AR on-policy distillation loss aligns the student’s AR distribution with a frozen AR teacher. Right: Consistency loss aligns the student’s diffusion view to its own AR view. The diffusion prediction is obtained by evaluating the student on randomly masked AR rollouts. We apply stop-grad to the AR target.

Figure 10 | The design of SBD formulation. (Left) SBD adopts a two-stream training process that concatenates clean blocks and noisy blocks in the sequence dimension. It applies AR CE loss on the clean blocks, and diffusion CE loss on the noisy blocks. (Right) SBD models use a specialized attention mask with a causal mask in the clean blocks and block-bidirectional mask in the noisy blocks. Each noisy block can attend to all other tokens in itself and all tokens in preceding clean blocks.
Figure 8 | Qualitative Results on Text-to-Image Tasks. Results are sampled at 1024× 1024 resolution.
Figure 9 | Qualitative Results on Image Editing Tasks. For each input-output pair, we present the input image on the left and the output image on the right.

Figure 11 | Visualization of Ball-Tree-Based Corruption Process. (Right) Ball-Tree is a balanced binary tree whose leaf nodes correspond to unique tokens in the vocabulary. The forward corruption process 𝑈𝑘|𝑘−1 increases the token age 𝑎 and decreases the node depth 𝑑. (Left) Each node has a geometric representation which is a high-dimensional ball in the VQ embedding space. Decreasing depth 𝑑 corresponds to increasing ball radius. In this visualization, the depth 𝐷 = 4 and maximum token age 𝐾 = 3.

Figure 12 | Visual Reconstruction Across Different Token Ages. To investigate whether the proposed age-based corruption process is semantically meaningful for visual generation tasks, we show reconstructed images at different token ages and compare them with the rectified flow process in the continuous latent space of Qwen-VAE. Results indicate that changes in the token age represent a smooth corruption process in the pixel space. In this visualization, all tokens are corrupted at the same rate, which corresponds to 𝜖 = 1.

Figure 13 | Image PSNR Across Different Token Ages. To investigate whether the proposed age-based corruption process is semantically meaningful for visual generation tasks, we plot the PSNR of reconstructed images at different token ages and compare them with the rectified flow process in the continuous latent space of Qwen-VAE. Results indicate that changes in the token age represent a smooth corruption process in the pixel space measured by PSNR. In the clean state, Qwen-VAE has better PSNR than NLD-Uni, suggesting its continuous VAE has better reconstruction capability.

Figure 15 | Comparison with MDM-Prime. Progression of Generated Images at Different Training Steps. The prompt is "Highly stylized, whimsical illustration of a fox wearing a tiny monocle and top hat, reading a miniature book in a cozy, mushroom-filled forest glade. Children’s book art, gentle colors, charming, adorable."
Figure 16 | Ablation Studies on distilling from AR VLMs. We report MathVista Acc throughout training steps.

Figure 14 | Additional Qualitative Illustrations of the Teacher Refinement Process. We show additional qualitative samples of teacher-refined student outputs. They generally align with the student roll-outs but have better visual fidelity and source image preservation. In some examples where the teacher over-edits, the refined student outputs are preferable to pure teacher generation.
Table 4 | Per-Category and overall scores on ImgEdit benchmark. *Off-policy indicates we use an independent teacher output as the target, as opposed to teacher-refined student output.

Table 3 | Text-to-Image Generation Performance on GenEval, DPG, and HPSv3. † LLaDa-2-Uni incorporates a pretrained 6B continuous diffusion decoder. *Half of the understanding layers are not loaded in T2I tasks due to the Elastic-MoT design.
Table 1 | Quantitative results on image-level understanding tasks. NLD-Uni is evaluated using a confidence-based diffusion sampler following [51].
Table 2 | Quantitative results on multi-modal reasoning benchmarks. *Denotes naively applying teacher score to student’s diffusion view using OPD-LM’s loss.
Table 5 | Training configurations across three stages. We use letters A-C to represent different dataset.

Table 7 | Ablation study of teacher choices. Results are sampled in AR view with a block size of one.

papers.abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.
authors: Alexa R. Tartaglini, Zhengxuan Wu, Thadd\"aus Wiedemer, Martin Wattenberg, Been Kim, Yuxuan Li
bullets: Simple symbols, such as a red heart, can implicitly steer VLM behavior toward recursive solutions on coding tasks.
Models’ stated interpretations and reasoning about symbols may differ substantially from the behavior those symbols induce.
Visual communication between models shows a generation–interpretation gap: intuitive shape-based cues often fail to steer other models.
In communication games, VLMs can creatively convey abstract concepts and stories, though some messages are unintuitive to humans.
The work highlights both the promise and challenges of human–VLM visual communication.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Simple visual symbols steer model behavior on a coding problem. A) Evaluation methodology. We append an image of a simple colored shape (e.g., a blue triangle) to a coding prompt (binary tree traversal) and instruct the model to look at the image while solving the problem. Across 𝑛 sampled generations, we compute the proportion of recursive solutions 𝑃(recursion) and measure the visual steering effect Δ𝑃(recursion) as the change in 𝑃(recursion) relative to the no-image baseline. B) Visual symbols steer toward recursion far more strongly than random noise or matching text descriptions. Star-patterned bars show average Δ𝑃(recursion) for Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7’s top three steering symbols (symbols shown below each bar), which nearly matches the effect of directly instructing the model to use recursion (light gray bars). By contrast, matching text descriptions (e.g., “an image of a pink heart”; hatched bars) and Gaussian noise images (dark gray bars) induce minimal to no steering. C) Models display different steering landscapes over a library of 288 visual symbols. Heatmaps show Δ𝑃(recursion) across 12 colors (𝑥-axis) for each model’s 8 highest- and 6 lowest-steering shapes (𝑦-axis; full heatmaps in Sec. B.2.1).

Figure 2 | Models generate creative visualizations to communicate concepts, but exhibit a generation–interpretation gap. A) Communication game methodology. A sender model generates a visualization to convey a target coding strategy (e.g., recursion), concept, or story to a receiver model, refining its visualization through multi-turn feedback. B) Multi-turn feedback enables models to converge on effective visualizations. Bars show the average number of turns to succeed using visual symbols (top bars) versus free-form PIL drawings (bottom bars). Symbol-based communication requires more communication turns to align sender and receiver than free-form drawing. C) Senders choose intuitive symbols to communicate recursion rather than the symbols that actually steer them. Top symbols selected by Claude Opus 4.7 as a sender (left, sized by selection frequency) compared to the symbols with the largest empirical steering effect Δ𝑃(recursion) (right). D) Models construct creative scenes using free-form code and abstract symbols. Examples show successful visualizations generated by Gemini 3.1 Pro to communicate the concept “art” (left) and a threesentence story about a knight removing a thorn from a dragon’s paw (right).

Figure 3 | Visual steering associations diverge from both human intuition and models’ own explicit interpretations. A) Optimizing symbol communication for model receivers reduces human legibility, whereas free-form drawings remain interpretable. Bars show human accuracy (%) at identifying the target coding strategy (recursion vs. iteration), concept, or story from visualizations on the first communication turn (blue; unsuccessful for the receiver) versus the final turn (red; successful), using visual symbols (top bars) or free-form PIL drawings (bottom bars). B) Models’ direct interpretations of visual symbols poorly predict their empirical steering effects. Each point represents one or more of the 288 visual symbols (sized by count), plotting the proportion of trials in which a model explicitly classifies the symbol as “recursion” (𝑥-axis) against its behavioral steering effect Δ𝑃(recursion) (𝑦-axis).

Figure 22 | Steering results for all binary choice semantic pairs. The labels along the 𝑥-axes indicate the direction of steering away from each model’s unsteered baseline preference (from 𝐴 to 𝐵), with icons below each bar showing the visual symbols that drive the shift.

Figure 4 | All shapes and colors in the visual symbol library. Each symbol shows an example of the color and shape indicated by the label; the library includes all 288 combinations of the 12 × 24 colors and shapes.

Figure 5 | Full steering heatmaps for inorder binary tree traversal, where the model is instructed to look at the image (“Explicit image instruction prompt,” Appendix B.1). Each heatmap is one model; rows are the 12 colors, and columns are the 24 shapes. Cell values are the steering effect (i.e. delta Δ𝑃(recursion) relative to that model’s text-only baseline), on a diverging scale from −1 (red, towards iteration) to +1 (blue, towards recursion).

Figure 6 | Recursion steering heatmaps aggregated across baseline-iterative coding problems: 𝑁 = 4 problems for Claude Opus 4.7, 𝑁 = 3 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 𝑁 = 4 for GPT-5.4. Because all problems for each model have baseline iterative solutions, the cell values show steering towards or away from recursion. Axes and color scale are as in Figure 5.

Figure 7 | Iteration steering heatmaps aggregated across baseline-recursive coding problems: 𝑁 = 2 problems for Claude Opus 4.7, 𝑁 = 3 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 𝑁 = 2 for GPT-5.4. Because all problems for each model have baseline recursive solutions, the cell values show steering towards or away from iteration. Axes and color scale are as in Figure 5.

Figure 15 | Placing images at the end of context rather than the beginning changes which symbols steer for recursion. A) The steering effect at the start and end of context decouple most strongly for Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.4. The 𝑦-axis shows the steering effect of visual symbols when placed at the start of context, while the 𝑥-axis shows the end of context. Gemini 3.1 Pro remains somewhat correlated. B) Top steering symbols appear to shift from more geometric to more semantic. Lines show the steering effect for four individual symbols when placed at the start, middle, and end of context (symbols are visualized next to their lines). Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.4 exhibit a marked shift where more intuitively “recursive” shapes like branching arrows or spirals begin to exert the strongest steering effect. Interestingly, this appears to line up with these models’ interpretations and choices in communication games. Gemini 3.1 Pro’s top steering shapes remain largely the same.
Figure 23 | Cross-model correlations (Pearson 𝑟) in visual steering on inorder binary tree traversal. Shapes are generally more correlated than colors.

Figure 31 | Example free-form vs. symbol library visualizations for short story communication. Visualizations generated by A) Claude Opus 4.7, B) Gemini 3.1 Pro, and C) GPT-5.4. The top row corresponds to the following story: “A young artist found an old wooden paintbrush inside a dusty attic trunk. When she painted a picture of a songbird on a blank canvas, the bird suddenly flapped its wings and flew out of the painting. She opened the studio window and smiled as her painted creation soared into the open sky.”; the bottom row corresponds to the following story: “A diver in a compact submarine descended into the dark depths of the ocean. Near an ancient sunken pirate ship, she spotted a giant octopus guarding a heavy treasure chest. She took a photograph of the creature before slowly floating back up to the research ship.” Interestingly, models appear to arrive at largely similar layouts for visualizing stories.

Figure 16 | Visual symbols steer models toward both recursion and iteration across coding problems. Bars show the mean shift away from each model’s unsteered baseline strategy (±1 SEM across problems and top-3 symbols, shown below each bar). A) Aggregated recursion steering across baseline-iterative problems (𝑁 = 4 for Claude Opus 4.7, 𝑁 = 3 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 𝑁 = 4 for GPT-5.4). B) Aggregated iteration steering across baseline-recursive problems (𝑁 = 2 for Claude Opus 4.7, 𝑁 = 3 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 𝑁 = 2 for GPT-5.4). On baseline-recursive problems, Claude Opus 4.7 responds strongly to Gaussian noise (indicating a less purely semantic influence), whereas Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.4 maintain the selective visual-symbol steering pattern from Sec. 3.

Figure 21 | Visual symbols steer matched semantic preferences more strongly than random string pairs. Bars show the mean shift away from each model’s unsteered baseline preference (𝑁 = 9 pairs per split). A) Steering on matched semantic pairs, like “summer” vs. “winter.” B) Steering on length-6 random strings.
Figure 24 | Recursion steering results for smaller models.

Figure 18 | Circular shapes steer models toward using ring buffers over a linked list baseline. Box plots depict the steering effect (Δ𝑃(Ring Buffer)) driven by individual shapes across doubly linked list vs. ring buffer coding problems (𝑁 = 3), computed the same way as Fig. 17. GPT-5.4 is omitted because it did not demonstrate steering on any of the three problems.

Figure 19 | Writing style steering heatmaps aggregated across 𝑁 = 5 topics for optimistic vs. melancholic (Claude Opus 4.7, top) and verbose vs. terse (Gemini 3.1 Pro, bottom). Warm colors tend to steer Claude Opus 4.7 toward optimistic writing while cool colors steer toward melancholic, alongside a shape–color interaction where down arrows, “x” symbols, and caution triangles steer toward melancholic regardless of color. Gemini 3.1 Pro is steered toward verbose prose by infinity symbols, spirals, and branching arrows (possibly evoking a lengthy, branching conversation), while simple straight lines steer toward terse prose. Axes and color scale are as in Figure 5.

Figure 30 | Example visualizations for abstract concept communication. A) Zero-shot communication. Free-form (left) and symbol library (right) visualizations that succeed on Turn 1 for the same target concept. B) Multi-turn communication. First-turn vs. final-turn free-form visualizations across refinement trajectories. Edits across turns are sometimes a bit opaque; i.e. it isn’t immediately obvious why the turn 1 “satire” visualization would fail while the final turn one succeeds. C) Unsuccessful visualizations. Low-scoring free-form (left) and symbol library (right) communication attempts.

Figure 29 | Example free-form visualizations for recursion vs. iteration steering. A) Multiturn communication. Three-turn refinement trajectories toward recursion, with receiver steering proportions (𝑛 = 10) shown below each image. B) Successful & unsuccessful visualizations. Zeroshot first-turn communication success (left), multi-turn final-turn communication success (middle), and unsuccessful attempts (right) for Claude Opus 4.7 (top), Gemini 3.1 Pro (middle row), and GPT-5.4 (bottom).

Figure 8 | The steering effect of text captions largely does not match that of images. A) Top three steering captions for each model. The colors of the text show the corresponding color. Captions are formatted as, e.g., “An image of a brown spiral.” B) The steering effect of captions decouples from the steering effect of images of visual symbols.
Figure 10 | Naturalistic animal images (𝑁 = 20) used to measure the ImageNet steering baseline.

Figure 11 | Disrupting shape structure via pixel shuffling disrupts visual steering at high enough percentages. A) Example pixel-shuffled stimuli. Progressive pixel shuffling (0% to 100%) preserves global color proportions while progressively destroying shape geometry and adding low-level noise (shown for the pink heart and blue triangle). B) Recursion proportion 𝑃(recursion) across pixel shuffle levels. Lines show 𝑃(recursion) on inorder binary tree traversal across five symbols (visualized next to their lines) for Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.4.

Figure 12 | Visual steering is highly sensitive to symbol orientation. A) Example rotated stimuli. Visual symbols rotated from 0◦ (prototypical upright orientation, outlined in bold) to 315◦ in 45◦ increments. B) Recursion proportion 𝑃(recursion) across rotation angles. Lines show 𝑃(recursion) on inorder binary tree traversal across the three orientation-dependent symbols for Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.4.

Figure 14 | Per-symbol steering across canvas position and symbol size. Lines track 𝑃(recursion) for each of the five symbols across Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.4. A) Sensitivity to canvas position (marginalized across symbol sizes). B) Sensitivity to symbol size (marginalized across canvas positions).
Figure 27 | Gemini 3.1 Pro’s choices in symbols for communicating recursion vs. its actual top steering symbols.
Figure 28 | GPT-5.4’s choices in symbols for communicating recursion vs. its actual top steering symbols.
Figure 26 | Claude Opus 4.7 choices in symbols for communicating recursion vs. its actual top steering symbols.

Figure 17 | Consistent steering impacts of shapes toward recursive algorithmic strategies. Box plots depict the distribution of steering effects (i.e. proportion shifts, Δ𝑃(Recursion)) driven by individual shapes across baseline-iterative coding problems (𝑁 = 4 for Claude Opus 4.7, 𝑁 = 3 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 𝑁 = 4 for GPT-5.4). papers.abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
authors: Matea Tashkovska, Na\"el Ouerghemi, Haozhe Qi, Alexander Mathis
bullets: Introduces 1,632 human-verified questions spanning body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning.
Evaluates 37 closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, alongside human evaluation.
Humans achieve 68.5% video-only accuracy, compared with 50.0% for the strongest evaluated MLLM, Qwen3.6-27B, in zero-shot evaluation.
Finds recurring errors in interpreting the wearer’s body, temporal events, repetition counts, and hand-side biases.
Provides aligned video–body-motion–language training data and a multimodal baseline to support future research.

papers.abstract: Are concepts and mechanisms unified across modalities in current AI models, or instead implemented separately for each one? We operationalize this broad question of modality unification by studying cross-modal steering: 1) finding vectors that successfully steer generation on tokens of one modality, which then 2) transfer zero-shot to steer generation when added to tokens of another modality. Our study goes beyond simple correlational alignment (e.g. representational similarity) because steering is fundamentally causal. We study cross-modal steering in several unified multimodal models (UMMs), since they possess shared parameters for language and image generation, focusing on these two modalities. Across diverse steered concepts such as emotion and object size, we show that steering vectors transfer zero-shot in both directions (text-to-image & image-to-text). Even for concepts that are highly unique to one modality (e.g. formal vs. colloquial language), steering vectors often induce a consistent, interpretable effect in the other modality, such as formal clothing and design. This transfer has a geometric signature too: despite a clear modality gap separating text and image representations, steering vectors with strong cross-modal transferability tend to point in similar directions for the same concept. Our findings shed light on how vision and language interact inside unified multimodal models and point towards more general, modality-agnostic approaches for controlling their behavior.
authors: Donghao Zeng (Mila, McGill University), Nishant Subramani (Carnegie Mellon University), Tamar Rott Shaham (MIT CSAIL), Benno Krojer (Mila, McGill University, Northeastern University)
bullets: Tests whether concepts and mechanisms are unified across language and vision models.

Suggests modality-agnostic methods for controlling multimodal model behavior.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, \emph{i.e.}, the misleading cues caused by spurious \textit{linguistic} correlations and salient yet irrelevant \textit{visual} observations. In this paper, we first introduce {S-MME}, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding.
authors: Xusheng Liang, Jianqiao Sun, Hao Zhang, Yulei Niu, Hengshuang Zhao, Jiawei Ma
bullets: Long-video QA is difficult because sparse frame sampling can miss decisive evidence, while spurious cues can still mislead models.
S-MME benchmarks shortcut-biased behavior from misleading language correlations and salient but irrelevant visual content.
CLEAR estimates bias using question-only and locally salient-clip views, then intervenes on hidden states at inference.
Experiments across five benchmarks show consistent gains in prediction and robustness across different MLLMs.
CLEAR is presented as a complementary test-time scaling approach; the abstract does not specify detailed limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of CLEAR. (a) The full-video path produces the final answer, while questiononly and salient-view probes reveal spurious linguistic correlations and salient-yet-misleading visual observations. The salient view is formed by selecting top-K locally relevant clips according to query-conditioned visual attention. (b) CLEAR extracts the hidden state of the shared decision token z at selected late decoder layers, and constructs residual vectors rql = hf l − hq l and rsl = hf l − hs l from the restricted-view probes to the full-video state. These residual vectors are injected into the full-video path to steer its hidden state away from shortcut anchors before final decoding.

Figure 2: Construction pipeline of S-MME. We first mine candidate questions with explicit long-video evidence requirements, then use restricted views to identify shortcut-consistent distractors, followed by human validation of answer uniqueness, evidence sufficiency, and shortcut plausibility.
Figure 4: Effect of intervention location. Latelayer intervention performs best, with the last block achieving the highest accuracy.

Figure 1: MLLMs often fail despite the presence of decisive evidence, either by following spurious linguistic correlations or by over-relying on salient but misleading visual observations. CLEAR diagnoses these shortcut-biased trajectories with controlled probes and steers the full-video representation toward evidence-consistent prediction.

papers.abstract: Despite rapid progress in visual understanding and document transcription, modern vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with a fundamental accessibility task: reading Braille from images. We introduce BrailleBench, a manually curated benchmark of 259 real-world Grade-1 and Grade-2 Braille images. We evaluate proprietary, open-weight, OCR-specialized, and tool-assisted multimodal systems and find that standalone general-purpose models perform poorly at directly transcribing Braille images, whereas tool-assisted systems perform much better. We design a synthetic Braille generation pipeline with diverse layouts and image perturbations. A 2B VLM model trained on our synthetic data reaches 87% exact match on Grade-1 and 61% on Grade-2 BrailleBench, outperforming standalone VLMs and achieving the highest Grade-2 exact match score among the evaluated systems. We further show that high accuracy on synthetic validation data does not guarantee high accuracy on real photographs in our experiments: models trained on prior synthetic data reach up to 96% on their synthetic validation set but at most 3.26% on Grade-1 BrailleBench. Our results identify an accessibility-relevant capability gap in multimodal systems and show that targeted synthetic supervision can improve real-world Braille transcription.
authors: Kartik Jangra, Atharva Gawane, Siddharth Pulipaka, Hemachandran Karah, Raj Dabre
bullets: BrailleBench contains 259 manually curated real-world Grade-1 and Grade-2 Braille images.
Standalone general-purpose VLMs perform poorly, while tool-assisted systems perform much better.
A synthetic Braille generation pipeline uses diverse layouts and image perturbations for training.
A 2B VLM trained on the synthetic data achieves 87% Grade-1 and 61% Grade-2 exact match on BrailleBench.
Synthetic validation accuracy may not transfer to real photographs: prior models reached up to 96% synthetically but at most 3.26% on Grade-1 BrailleBench.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our work. (1) BrailleBench contains manually verified real-world Braille images captured on diverse materials and under diverse conditions. (2) Standalone VLMs largely fail to transcribe them, often producing fluent but unrelated text, while tool-assisted harnesses succeed at a high inference cost. (3) Models fine-tuned only on synthetically generated Braille images transcribe real-world Braille with a single model call, without a tool loop. EM denotes exact match; G1 and G2 denote Grade-1 and Grade-2.

Figure 2: Synthetic training data generation pipeline. Text sampled from FineWeb at multiple granularities is translated to Braille with Liblouis, rendered as embossed Braille with randomized dot geometry, spacing, and paper textures, and degraded with augmentations that simulate real-world capture conditions. The resulting image–text pairs are used to fine-tune Qwen3.5-2B and Chandra-OCR-2 without any real-world Braille images.

Figure 4: Prediction outcomes by grade. Each image falls into exactly one category. Formatting only: differences that disappear after normalization; spacing only: only word spacing differs; partial error: at most half of the normalized reference characters need editing; large error: more than half; no output: empty outputs and refusals. Numbers on bars give exact match (%). Rows above the dotted line are the harnesses, our models, and the strongest standalone model. Exact counts are in Appendix E. For Claude Code Grade-2 (*), categories are recomputed from the predictions using the normalized-match transform in Table 1, retaining punctuation. Other rows retain the supplied counts under the original looser formatting normalization; their error-type splits are not directly comparable to this recomputed row. Exact match remains raw string equality for all rows.
Figure 7: Qwen3.5-2B performance during continual LoRA training on samples from our 276k corpus, following pretraining on 500k longer synthetic samples.

Figure 3: Models trained only on WMT-Train (Llama3.2-11B with LoRA; Qwen3.5-2B with full fine-tuning), evaluated on the in-distribution WMT validation set and on Grade-1 BrailleBench (both models reach 0% exact match on Grade-2). Both models score highly on synthetic validation but fail on real photographs. CER and WER use logarithmic axes; values above 1 come from long hallucinated outputs.

papers.abstract: Image and video generators can produce spatially consistent visual content, but how to use this capability to improve spatial understanding remains underexplored. We study this problem from two perspectives: geometric supervision during training and explicit geometric evidence during inference. To this end, we introduce a unified geometric understanding and generation model (GeoUG) that integrates depth and multi-view generation with spatial understanding. First, we design a multi-scale depth codec that enables metric-depth generation using a pretrained visual autoencoder, and show that joint training yields task-dependent gains in spatial understanding. Second, we introduce 3DCueBench to control geometric difficulty while balancing selected 2D cues, and find that generated depth provides larger reasoning gains on questions requiring fine-grained geometric discrimination. Building on this finding, we develop adaptive interleaved reasoning, in which GeoUG first drafts an answer and then decides whether to generate geometric evidence to confirm or revise it. We train this decision through reinforcement learning, balancing accuracy gains over retaining the draft against generation cost. GeoUG achieves circular accuracies of 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% on CV-Bench-3D, 3DCueBench, and DA-2K with fewer generation calls than always generating.
authors: Rui Yang, Yanwei Li, Sili Chen, Jingjia Huang, Yi Lin, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Studies how visual generation can support spatial understanding through training-time geometric supervision and inference-time geometric evidence.

Presents 3DCueBench to test geometric difficulty while controlling 2D visual cues.
Finds generated depth particularly helps fine-grained geometric reasoning.
Uses reinforcement-learned adaptive interleaved reasoning to decide when to generate evidence; reports 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% circular accuracy on three benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Emergent generative AI technologies, while remarkably beneficial across several tasks and domains, can suffer from unforeseen vulnerabilities and difficult-to-anticipate failure modes. Such failure modes can disparately affect vulnerable communities. This paper investigates two well-known vision language models (VLMs) and inspects how these models encode protected identities while generating images. We show that when VLMs are requested to transform human face images to reflect race identities (e.g., Hispanic, Black, White, or Asian) and sexual orientation (e.g., gay or straight), VLMs often comply with such requests. We demonstrate that compliance (and refusal) is non-deterministic, group-sensitive, and generated images are statistically distinguishable, often accentuating deep-seated stereotypes. We further show that representation biases introduced during image generation can re-emerge in textual reasoning and characterization tasks. Finally, we show that this worrisome finding is not limited to racial identity or sexual orientation, image generation can perpetuate bias around criminality, raising concerning possibilities of AI-assisted profiling.
authors: Soumyajit Datta, Arka Dutta, Ashiqur R. KhudaBukhsh
bullets: Examines two VLMs’ handling of requested racial and sexual-orientation transformations of human faces.
Finds that compliance and refusal vary across groups and requests.
Generated images are statistically distinguishable and may accentuate stereotypes.
Biases introduced during image generation can reappear in textual reasoning and characterization.
Similar concerns extend to criminality, suggesting risks of AI-assisted profiling.

papers.abstract: A robot policy needs to understand what a task is asking for in a scene, and how to move the robot to accomplish that task. To achieve these two skills, we introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches a small off-the-shelf vision-language model to control a robot via a simple tool harness. We use a pretrained 27B parameter model to bootstrap world understanding and reasoning, followed by supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks to teach it how to move the robot. Without observing real-world robot data during training, ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness and outperforming the MolmoAct2 VLA (33.3%), while running 3x faster and 17x cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Furthermore, ZAP also generalizes to an unseen embodiment as well as new objects, goals and strategies never seen during training. On a single-arm Franka, ZAP reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 percentage points ahead of the leading VLA/WAM baseline.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining task understanding with robot motion control without real-world robot training data.
Uses a pretrained 27B vision-language model, then supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks via a tool harness.
Achieves 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra while running 3× faster and costing 17× less.
Generalizes to unseen embodiments, objects, goals, and strategies; reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 points above the cited VLA/WAM baseline.
Scope: results are reported for the described harness and selected real-world benchmarks.
