papers.abstract: Global vision--language similarities compress an image and a caption into one vector, preserving semantics but not which word corresponds to which region or how those regions are arranged; a model can recognize every word and object yet prefer a compositionally incorrect caption. We argue that a frozen encoder retains this association structure, so the problem is to read it rather than to rebuild it beside the pretrained similarity. We introduce BindCLIP, a pairwise scorer built on one latent object: a balanced token--patch--depth optimal-transport coupling that places both candidate captions and several visual depths in a single plan. Semantic, entity, order, and spatial evidence are read as energies of this state, and exchanging the candidates permutes the plan, making the score exactly antisymmetric. A geometric refinement inside the coupling contracts moves that the candidates and the visual depths do not support. No task label, parser, relation inventory, or detector is used. One checkpoint and one inference path improve the official What'sUp, ARO, and SugarCrepe benchmarks over frozen global CLIP, with the strongest transfer on the relation splits. Controls rule out patch access and caption-length shortcuts, and an inference-time lesion localizes spatial arrangement to the coupling.
bullets: Addresses the failure of global image–caption similarity to capture word–region correspondences and spatial composition.
Builds one balanced token–patch–depth optimal-transport plan jointly over candidate captions and multiple visual depths.
Derives semantic, entity, ordering, and spatial evidence from coupling energies; candidate exchange yields an exactly antisymmetric score.
Uses no task labels, parsers, relation inventories, or detectors, and follows one checkpoint and inference path.
Improves frozen CLIP on What'sUp, ARO, and SugarCrepe, with strongest transfer on relation splits; controls identify spatial arrangement in the coupling.

Fig. 2. papers.title: BindCLIP: One Balanced Coupling For Compositional Vision Language Scoring
papers.tldr: BindCLIP reads compositional token–region structure from frozen vision–language encoders via a balanced optimal-transport coupling, improving relation-sensitive caption scoring without extra supervision.

papers.abstract: Expanding multilingual ASR systems to new languages is challenging when adaptation must preserve previously supported languages without replaying source-language training data. We study this problem in connector-based Speech LLMs, where a trainable connector maps speech representations into a frozen large language model. We evaluate target-update construction and merging strategies for adapting the connector while preserving source-language performance. In single-target expansion, target-only fine-tuning and standard TIES merging learn new languages but cause severe source-language forgetting, while SSU-Wanda+TIES gives the best source-preserving trade-off. In multi-target expansion, update merging provides stable source retention, whereas recursive expansion can improve target adaptation under favorable orders but is highly order-sensitive. These results show that multilingual ASR expansion requires balancing target acquisition, source retention, and interactions among target-language updates.
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
bullets: Problem: Add new languages to connector-based Speech LLM ASR without replaying source-language data or degrading existing languages.
Method: Compare target-update construction and merging strategies for adapting a trainable speech-to-LLM connector while keeping the LLM frozen.
Single-target finding: Target-only fine-tuning and standard TIES merging cause severe source-language forgetting; SSU-Wanda+TIES offers the best reported trade-off.
Multi-target finding: Update merging provides stable source retention, while recursive expansion can improve target adaptation but is highly order-sensitive.
Scope: Expansion requires balancing new-language acquisition, source retention, and interactions among target-language updates.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes source-aware adaptation and model merging strategies for multilingual Speech LLMs, specifically focusing on preserving source language performance while expanding to new target languages.
papers.title: Preserve to Expand: Source-Aware Adaptation and Model Merging for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
papers.tldr: Source-aware connector adaptation and model merging can expand multilingual ASR while reducing source-language forgetting, but success depends on the merging strategy and target-language order.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can control robots without robot-specific training, but how their capabilities compare and interact with post-trained vision-language-action (VLA) and world action model (WAM) policies across manipulation demands remains to be thoroughly evaluated. In this report, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness under the same visual and proprioceptive observation protocol as post-trained policies. We study two agent configurations: direct control, in which the agent generates waypoint commands directly, and harness with policy, in which it can also invoke a post-trained VLA or WAM policy for action execution. Under direct control, the agent achieves competitive overall performance relative to post-trained policies. It leads on short-horizon tasks and exhibits the least performance variation across generalization dimensions, whereas it underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon tasks, tabletop manipulation, and high-precision contact-rich tasks. In the harness with policy, invoking a post-trained VLA or WAM combines the complementary strengths of both components, raising overall task success to the level of the strongest compared post-trained policies while substantially reducing token cost. However, performance remains below the per-task upper bound of the standalone components due to suboptimal policy invocation, fixed-instruction execution without subgoals, and grasp disruption when the agent resumes control. Overall, our study characterizes the capability boundary of a frontier MLLM agent and suggests directions for improving future agent harness design. Project page: https://internrobotics.github.io/EBench-Astra-Tech-Report/
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
bullets: GPT-6-Astra is evaluated as a robot-control agent under the same visual and proprioceptive observations as post-trained policies.
Direct control performs competitively, especially on short-horizon tasks and across generalization dimensions.
It underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon, tabletop, and high-precision contact-rich manipulation.
A harness that invokes VLA or WAM policies combines complementary strengths, reaching the strongest standalone policies’ overall success level with lower token cost.
Remaining gaps stem from suboptimal policy invocation, fixed instructions without subgoals, and grasp disruption when control returns to the agent.
papers.selection_reason: Profiles frontier MLLM agents controlling robots directly and via VLA/WAM policies, directly relevant to embodied VLA and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
papers.tldr: Evaluating GPT-6-Astra on EBench shows that direct MLLM control is strong on short-horizon tasks, while combining it with VLA/WAM policies improves overall performance and reduces token cost but remains limited by imperfect policy orchestration.

papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown impressive capabilities in high-level reasoning and task planning for robots. However, specialized domains remain a challenge for VLMs' image interpretation and grounding abilities. We introduce TrySee, a modular closed-loop robot task planning pipeline integrating general-purpose VLM reasoning with domain-specific perception and established robotics components. The system consists of an inherently reactive cyclic planning pipeline, augmented with domain-specific modular vision preprocessing, to provide online grounding. Finally, a dynamic preprocessing selection mechanism contributes to the scalability of the pipeline. The system requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations and adapts through replaceable perception modules and motion planning. The approach is evaluated on planning tasks across 5 widely different domains, including a real-world robot disassembly task. The field tests in a brownfield environment demonstrate the approach's practicality in integrating VLM planning into specialized robotic systems with limited domain-specific training data.
authors: Elias Hofele, Thomas Trapp, David Timmermann, Tristan Schnell, Georg Heppner, Arne Roennau
bullets: Targets weak VLM image interpretation and grounding in specialized robotic domains.
Uses a reactive cyclic planning pipeline with online grounding and dynamically selected vision preprocessing.
Requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations.
Evaluated across five diverse domains, including real-world robot disassembly.
Field tests indicate practical integration in brownfield settings with limited domain-specific data.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop VLM-based robot task planning with domain-specific perception grounding, directly relevant to embodied VLA and multimodal LLM use.
papers.title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains
papers.tldr: TrySee combines general-purpose VLM reasoning with modular domain-specific perception and robotics components for adaptable closed-loop robot task planning.

papers.abstract: Social media enables cross-lingual communication, yet the meaning of user-generated content (UGC) is often distributed across text, images, and cultural knowledge, making translation challenging. Existing evaluations typically treat images as optional and assume textual information is sufficient, obscuring whether errors stem from missing visual evidence or inadequate cultural adaptation. We introduce \textbf{Culture-MMT}, a diagnostic benchmark for \textbf{distributed-evidence pragmatic reconstruction} in social-media translation. It contains 498 curated, de-identified UGC instances across 20 domains, categorized into Symbol, Visual, and Hybrid by their required evidence. We also develop a human-aligned domain-specific judge, Judger, and a controlled evaluation framework that systematically varies the evidence available to translators. Across 17 model configurations, real images improve performance by +0.280 on Visual and +0.197 on Hybrid, but only +0.050 on Symbol, while random images provide no comparable gains. Human-authored descriptions further show that jointly dependent cases remain more challenging even when visual facts are explicit. These results characterize culturally effective social-media translation as {meaning reconstruction from distributed evidence}, highlighting visual grounding and cultural-pragmatic adaptation as distinct model bottlenecks.
authors: Dingming Li, Yiwen Qiu, Linjuan Wu, Hongxing Li, Zixuan Wang, Xinze Lyu, Ye Guo, Daoxin Zhang, Zhe Xu, Weiming Lu, Yongliang Shen
bullets: Introduces 498 de-identified UGC instances across 20 domains, categorized as Symbol, Visual, or Hybrid by required evidence.
Provides Judger, a human-aligned domain-specific evaluator, plus a controlled framework that varies available evidence.
Across 17 model configurations, real images help most on Visual and Hybrid cases, but offer limited gains on Symbol cases; random images do not provide comparable benefits.
Human-authored descriptions show jointly dependent cases remain difficult even when visual facts are made explicit.
Findings distinguish visual grounding from cultural-pragmatic adaptation as separate translation bottlenecks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a diagnostic benchmark for visually grounded cultural translation, relevant to multimodal LLM evaluation and visual grounding.
papers.title: Beyond Words Alone: Disentangling Distributed Evidence for Visually Grounded Cultural Translation
papers.tldr: Culture-MMT diagnoses how text, images, and cultural knowledge jointly affect culturally effective social-media translation.

papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) are increasingly expected to assist users while observing continuous audiovisual streams. However, existing evaluations provide limited insight into how reliably these models connect stream evidence and user needs to timely, sustained interventions. We introduce \textbf{Omni-InteractScope}, a benchmark of 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets across eight task groups. It links input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs, covering event-timed tool invocation and query-free assistance alongside notifications, warnings, state tracking, and continuous responses. Our experimental results on the proposed benchmark reveal three critical limitations of current Omni-LLMs: (1) \textbf{Timely tool invocation remains unreliable}: all 12 evaluated models produce an on-time first response for at most 40\% of tool-invocation targets, and joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0\%. (2) \textbf{Query-free reminders remain poorly covered}: all evaluated models achieve lower timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders than on explicit questions, measured on their respective target sets. Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0\%. (3) \textbf{End-to-end guidance coverage remains limited}: nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and the remaining three cover only one to three sequences each. Targeted controls further show that tool-invocation scores alone do not establish event grounding and that reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency. These findings motivate developing and evaluating streaming assistants for timely action, initiative under general user needs, and coverage of entire response sequences.
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
bullets: Benchmark includes 1,479 human-annotated interactions, 1,790 temporal targets, and eight task groups spanning tools, reminders, warnings, tracking, and continuous responses.
Evaluates event timing, tool use, query-free assistance, reference-target recall, and full guidance-sequence coverage.
Across 12 models, on-time first responses for tool invocation reach at most 40%, while joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0%.
Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0%, and nine of 12 models complete none of the 26 guidance sequences.
Controls show that tool-use scores do not alone prove event grounding, while reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Omni-InteractScope, a benchmark for proactive and agentic interaction in continuous audiovisual streams using Omni-LLMs. This evaluates the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models in streaming contexts.
papers.title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
papers.tldr: Omni-InteractScope benchmarks whether Omni-LLMs can turn continuous audiovisual evidence and user needs into timely, sustained, proactive assistance, revealing major reliability gaps.

papers.abstract: Text-in-image translation aims to translate all textual content embedded in an image. In Text Image Translation (TIT), the output is translated text; In-Image Machine Translation (IIMT) additionally renders the translation back into the image. We introduce ImgMT, a massively multilingual dataset and benchmark mined from localized SVG illustrations on Wikimedia Commons, focusing on diagrams, maps, and infographics. ImgMT contains 35,612 aligned image pairs grouped into 1,855 image sets, spanning 129 languages, 20+ writing systems, and 4,886 language pairs. We propose a multi-level evaluation protocol that measures source-side text-region detection and OCR accuracy alongside target-side translation quality. We benchmark several multimodal large language models and a dedicated TIT system in English->X and X->English settings, and find that the source language and writing system substantially affect TIT quality. Finally, we show that ImgMT is not well suited for isolating the contribution of visual information in multimodal translation.
authors: \v{S}\'arka Uramov\'a, Petar Kirilov Petrov, Josef Jon, Ond\v{r}ej Bojar, Michal Nov\'ak
bullets: Mined from localized Wikimedia Commons SVGs, covering diagrams, maps, and infographics.
Contains 35,612 aligned image pairs organized into 1,855 image sets across 129 languages, 20+ writing systems, and 4,886 language pairs.
Evaluates source text-region detection, OCR accuracy, and target-side translation quality in a multi-level protocol.
Benchmarks multimodal large language models and a dedicated TIT system in English→X and X→English directions.
Finds that source language and writing system substantially influence translation quality; the dataset is unsuitable for isolating visual-information effects.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a multilingual benchmark for text-in-image translation and evaluates multimodal LLMs, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models and MLLM evaluation.
papers.title: ImgMT: Wikipedia-based Dataset For Evaluating Text-in-Image Translation
papers.tldr: ImgMT is a multilingual benchmark for evaluating text-in-image translation across diverse languages, writing systems, and visual formats.

papers.abstract: Monocular occupancy prediction in indoor scenes aims to recover a scene's 3D geometry and semantics from a single RGB image. Existing methods are restricted to a closed set of predefined categories, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen categories. This limitation is particularly critical in indoor scenes, where objects exhibit highly diverse and fine-grained semantic categories. We study open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction for indoor scenes and present OVM-Occ, a Gaussian-based occupancy framework with an instance-aware vision-language teacher. Specifically, we adopt Language-Embedded Gaussians as the intermediate scene representation, propose a geometry-aware deformable attention module to refine Gaussian semantic features, and construct instance-level vision-language embeddings to provide reliable semantic supervision. We further introduce geometry-aware decoupled semantic distillation to mitigate the interference between geometry learning and semantic learning. To evaluate open-vocabulary occupancy prediction performance, we introduce OpenOcc-ScanNet and OpenOcc-Replica, two extended benchmarks with more diverse and fine-grained semantic categories. Experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction for indoor scenes, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art approach by 12.2 mIoU and 0.6 IoU on the Occ-ScanNet dataset, with consistent gains under new open-vocabulary evaluation protocols.
authors: Shuyang Yu, Haibo Qin, Shaohan Hu, Wei Shan, Xiaoqing Guan, You Wang, Guang Li
bullets: Addresses the limited category generalization of existing closed-set monocular occupancy methods.
Represents scenes with Language-Embedded Gaussians and refines semantic features through geometry-aware deformable attention.
Uses instance-level vision-language embeddings and geometry-aware decoupled semantic distillation for semantic supervision.
Introduces OpenOcc-ScanNet and OpenOcc-Replica benchmarks with more diverse, fine-grained categories.
Reports gains of 12.2 mIoU and 0.6 IoU over the previous state of the art on Occ-ScanNet, with consistent improvements under new protocols.
papers.selection_reason: Open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction with geometry-aware vision-language distillation directly advances 3D scene perception and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: OVM-Occ: Open-Vocabulary Monocular Occupancy Prediction via Geometry-Aware Vision-Language Distillation
papers.tldr: OVM-Occ enables open-vocabulary 3D geometry and semantic occupancy prediction from a single indoor RGB image using geometry-aware vision-language distillation.

papers.abstract: Existing multi-agent collaboration (MAC) methods have primarily explored a group thinking collaboration topology, where agents independently generate solutions and aggregate their outputs. In this work, we investigate an alternative relay thinking topology, where reasoning ownership is dynamically transferred across agents, allowing subsequent agents to inherit and refine an evolving reasoning trajectory. We introduce Multi-Agent Confidence-guided Relay (MACR), a framework that enables dynamical relay collaboration among agents. The key challenge is determining when reasoning should be relayed and which agent should continue the process. method addresses this challenge through confidence-guided relay triggering and a bidding mechanism that selects the next agent based on its confidence. Experiments on four benchmarks show that method outperforms the strongest single-model strategies in accuracy, e.g., +3.3% on MathVista and +3.9% on MMStar, and remains on par with multi-agent strategies while consuming 6.0x less token overhead on HallusionBench and MMStar.Further analysis demonstrates that relay collaboration enables heterogeneous agents to progressively integrate complementary insights, combining heterogeneous capabilities across reasoning stages. Our source code is available at https://github.com/67L1/MACR.
authors: Xu Liu, Jungang Qiao, Guikun Chen, Xiaojuan Qi, Wenguan Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of group-based multi-agent collaboration, where agents reason independently before aggregation.
Uses confidence-guided triggering to decide when to relay reasoning and a confidence-based bidding mechanism to select the next agent.
Evaluated on four benchmarks, MACR outperforms the strongest single-model strategies, including gains of 3.3% on MathVista and 3.9% on MMStar.
Matches multi-agent strategies while using 6.0× less token overhead on HallusionBench and MMStar.
Relay collaboration helps heterogeneous agents combine complementary capabilities across reasoning stages.
papers.selection_reason: Confidence-guided relay collaboration among multimodal LLMs fits multimodal foundation-model reasoning.
papers.title: Multi-Agent Relay Thinking
papers.tldr: MACR introduces confidence-guided relay collaboration, enabling agents to dynamically pass and refine reasoning with lower token overhead than conventional multi-agent approaches.

papers.abstract: Understanding and operating with scientific charts is a standard approach in data analysis, and while humans are good at interpreting such charts, open vision-language models (VLMs) are known to perform poorly when it comes to question answering based on such data types. Motivated by an initial observation that many of their errors are due to inexact answering, we raise the following natural question: how much accuracy can we recover without changing the model at all? In this paper, we study this question by searching over inference programs and the code around a "frozen" version of the model. Using ideas from autonomous evolution (famously used in AlphaEvolve), we first start from a baseline inference program, and in each round we show an LLM judge the code together with a few failures on training questions, and ask for an improving evolutionary move. As usual in autonomous evolution approaches, the candidate programs are kept in a small pool ranked by training accuracy, and the next edit is performed on top-scorers from this pool. We run this approach on three VLMs and four popular benchmarks on scientific charts, and we measure the fraction of descriptive questions whose answer exactly matches the ground truth. The accuracy improves in all experimental settings. On average, it rises from 16.6% with the starting program to 41.3% with the evolved one, and the largest single increase is 55.2 percentage points. As a side benefit, our evolved program is 3.8x faster than the starting program, because short answers are easier to grade and faster to generate. Our results demonstrate that a large part of the observed errors arise due to the inference pipeline, and that optimizing it can improve the "frozen" VLM without the need to retrain it.
authors: Abhinav Sudhakar Dubey, Vidushi Goel, Kiran Rana, Shikhar Mathur, Vaggos Chatziafratis
bullets: Open VLMs often fail on scientific-chart questions, particularly through inexact answers.
The method evolves inference programs using an LLM judge, failure examples, and a pool of high-scoring candidate programs.
Evaluated across three VLMs and four scientific-chart benchmarks, accuracy improved in every setting.
Average exact-match accuracy increased from 16.6% to 41.3%, with a largest gain of 55.2 percentage points.
The evolved program was also 3.8× faster, suggesting inference-pipeline errors account for many failures.
papers.selection_reason: Autonomous evolution of inference programs improves frozen VLM chart analysis; relevant to multimodal LLM inference and optimization.
papers.title: Improving VLMs on Scientific Chart Analysis via Autonomous Evolution
papers.tldr: Autonomously evolving the inference program around a frozen VLM substantially improves scientific-chart question answering without retraining the model.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) ground a referring expression in one of two ways. They decode the box as coordinate tokens, which is precise but takes one sequential step per token, or they regress it from a hidden state with a small head, which takes one step but loses accuracy at high IoU. The two fail differently: a head usually finds the right object but places its edges loosely, while coordinate tokens place edges precisely. We therefore use the regression head as a speculative drafter for the model's own coordinate tokens. Locus writes the head's box as coordinate tokens and checks them with the same backbone by Jacobi iteration over a shared image prefix. The fixed point is the model's greedy coordinate-token answer, reached in about 5.60 sequential passes on average instead of 18.46 decoding steps; head and verifier are one set of weights, trained jointly. On the 8 RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg splits, verification raises Locus-2B's Acc@0.9 from 54.87 for its own head to 59.13, and the one-pass head is ahead at Acc@0.5 of every published model with at most 3B parameters except Florence-2-L. Against Jag, the strongest open regression-head model, at its own size and training budget, Locus ties at Acc@0.5 and, with typical acceptance, gains +4.52 points at Acc@0.9, with paired significance tests. Exact answers come 1.5x faster than vLLM greedy-decoding the same coordinate tokens with the same weights; a pure regression head remains faster still.
bullets: Uses the regression head to draft a box, then verifies and refines its coordinate tokens via Jacobi iteration with the same backbone.
Reaches the model’s greedy coordinate-token answer in about 5.60 sequential passes on average, versus 18.46 decoding steps.
On RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg splits, verification improves Locus-2B Acc@0.9 from 54.87 to 59.13.
The one-pass head achieves strong Acc@0.5 performance, while verified outputs provide more precise box edges.
Exact answers are obtained 1.5× faster than vLLM greedy decoding with the same weights, though pure regression remains faster.
papers.selection_reason: Draft-and-verify visual grounding improves VLM coordinate-token decoding; relevant to multimodal LLMs, spatial grounding, and inference efficiency.
papers.title: LOCUS: Locate Once, Check Until Settled. Draft-and-Verify Visual Grounding with a Box Head and Coordinate-Token Verification
papers.tldr: LOCUS combines a fast box-regression head with coordinate-token verification to improve high-IoU visual grounding while reducing sequential decoding passes.

papers.abstract: Text-steerable visual encoders condition a frozen Vision Transformer on a natural-language prompt and point at the matching image region, producing prompt-conditioned heatmaps and features. We audit the released SteerViT model and find that its steering interface turns language-driven pointing into demographic profiling. On counterfactual face mosaics and real multi-person photographs, "the person" selects a man more often than the base rate, crime words select Black people more often than occupation words do, "the man" among four women selects the Black woman 75.6% of the time on SocialCounterfactuals, and "the monkey" selects Black people. None of them is in the backbone's unsteered saliency, and the crime association is not in the frozen text encoder; the race effects grow with steering strength and enter through the last two cross-attention layers: giving the prompt to those layers alone reproduces them. Four other grounding models, CLIPSeg, Grounding-DINO, SAM 3, and Qwen2.5-VL, show no crime routing and weaker race routing. The model cannot refuse. Its patch softmax must place its mass somewhere, and its heatmap separates a groundable request ("the police officer") from one that is absent ("the pizza") or that would require a stereotyped demographic inference ("the criminal") only at chance (AUROC 0.52). We introduce SafeSteer, which adds a learned abstention output and counterfactual-invariance training on the same 23M steering parameters. SafeSteer separates should-point from should-abstain prompts at AUROC 0.997, generalizes to held-out sensitive and absent words (0.998; at a 0.5 threshold it refuses 99.8% of trained and 62% of held-out sensitive words) with no over-refusal of visible people on the benchmark, and removes most race routing while keeping localization and retrieval within 1 point of the released model. Code, benchmarks, and the curated mosaic sets will be released.
authors: Seyedarmin Azizi, Parsa Razmara, Sajjad Ghiasvand, Ardalan Aryashad, Tina Khezresmaeilzadeh
bullets: The released model profiles people: crime prompts disproportionately select Black individuals, and “the man” selects a Black woman in 75.6% of four-woman mosaics.
These effects are absent from unsteered saliency and the frozen text encoder, increasing with steering strength through the final two cross-attention layers.
SteerViT cannot recognize when a prompt is absent or requires a stereotyped inference, separating valid from unsafe requests at chance (AUROC 0.52).
SafeSteer achieves AUROC 0.997 on refusal detection and generalizes to held-out sensitive and absent words, while reducing race routing.
Localization and retrieval remain within 1 point of the released model, with no benchmark over-refusal of visible people.
papers.selection_reason: Bias and refusal audit of text-steerable visual encoders, with a learned abstention method.
papers.title: When Pointing Becomes Profiling: Social Bias and Refusal in Text-Steerable Visual Encoders
papers.tldr: SteerViT’s language-guided pointing can amplify demographic stereotypes, while SafeSteer adds effective refusal and largely removes race-based routing without materially harming localization.

papers.abstract: Training-free few-shot adaptation of vision-language models typically constructs a classifier from CLIP's final projected image representation, leaving intermediate representations unused. Combining them is not straightforward. Class scores from different representations differ in spread by orders of magnitude for the same query. Direct averaging allocates influence by numerical scale rather than predictive information. We propose Layer-Ensemble Gaussian Discriminant Analysis (LE-GDA), a method that fits regularized shared-covariance discriminants independently to intermediate and final representations extracted in one frozen encoder pass. LE-GDA standardizes each discriminant's class scores per query, selects a small representation multiset on labeled validation data, and combines it with the zero-shot classifier without gradient-based optimization. Across 11 datasets, four CLIP backbones, five shot counts, and three independently sampled K-shot training sets, LE-GDA achieves the highest mean accuracy of all evaluated methods on every backbone, raising the 16-shot mean from 78.01% to 79.54% over a matched GDA-CLIP (final-feature) baseline and improving that baseline for every backbone-shot combination. At one shot, LE-GDA retains a 1.20-point mean gain over the baseline even though covariance estimation is unavailable and per-query standardization is neutral. A control with richer per-class structure inside a single representation does not reproduce the gain, indicating that the benefit comes from combining representations. These results show that intermediate CLIP representations carry information beyond the final embedding and can improve training-free few-shot adaptation. Code and evaluation resources are available at https://github.com/pavodi-NM/le-gda.
authors: Pavodi Maniamfu, Vogel Kiketa, Zezina Kuzulu Kuetu, Jakin Mukendi Kabongo, David Mayoya Kutangila, Pescie Honore Kinkani Mampuya, L'Or Wolo Sieka
bullets: Addresses the underuse of intermediate CLIP representations and scale mismatches between their class scores.
Fits regularized shared-covariance discriminants independently in a single frozen encoder pass, then selects and ensembles representations using labeled validation data.
Combines the learned ensemble with CLIP’s zero-shot classifier without gradient-based optimization.
Across 11 datasets, four backbones, and five shot counts, it achieved the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods for every backbone.
Improved 16-shot mean accuracy from 78.01% to 79.54% over a matched final-feature GDA baseline, with a 1.20-point mean gain at one shot.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free few-shot adaptation of CLIP, a multimodal foundation model; combines intermediate representations.
papers.title: LE-GDA: Layer Ensemble Gaussian Discriminant Analysis for Training-Free Few-Shot CLIP Adaptation
papers.tldr: LE-GDA improves training-free few-shot CLIP adaptation by combining standardized class scores from intermediate and final representations with Gaussian discriminant analysis.

papers.abstract: Learning an unfamiliar visual category requires more than adapting a classifier: the model must connect its visual evidence to a useful semantic name. A pre-trained vision-language model can retain discriminative image features while providing a weak textual anchor for the target concept. We address this imbalance through context-grounded semantic anchoring. Our framework, SynerNet, learns concept-specific name embeddings, exposes them to compatible linguistic contexts, and conditions their representations on visual evidence. Difficulty-aware processing and adaptive objective weighting coordinate this adaptation while retaining the pre-trained backbone. On four VISTA-Beyond domains, SynerNet reaches a mean 16-shot accuracy of 74.35%, compared with 72.45% for few-shot name learning. Across 14 domains in the name-masked transfer setting, it improves mean accuracy from 45.17% to 46.74%. Ablations identify concept-specific name embeddings and cross-modal context integration as important components. These results support treating concept acquisition as the construction of visually grounded semantic anchors.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between strong pre-trained visual features and weak textual anchors for unfamiliar categories.
Learns concept-specific name embeddings, integrates compatible language contexts, and conditions representations on visual evidence.
Uses difficulty-aware processing and adaptive objective weighting while retaining the pre-trained backbone.
Achieves 74.35% mean 16-shot accuracy versus 72.45% for few-shot name learning, and 46.74% versus 45.17% in name-masked transfer.
Ablations highlight concept-specific embeddings and cross-modal context integration as important components.
papers.selection_reason: Context-grounded learning of novel visual concepts in vision-language models directly fits multimodal foundation model adaptation and semantic grounding.
papers.title: Seeing Before Naming: Context-Grounded Learning of Novel Visual Concepts
papers.tldr: SynerNet improves novel visual concept learning by grounding learned semantic names in both visual evidence and linguistic context.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation can transfer large multimodal models to compact models for autonomous driving, but uniform token-level matching can dilute planning-relevant semantics and amplify teacher errors. We propose RSKD, a semantic-consistency-guided distillation framework that routes supervision according to both the task importance of an answer phrase and its semantic consistency with the teacher prediction. Task-critical semantic phrases are localized in the ground-truth answer, and a phrase-level consistency score controls the balance between Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) distillation and ground-truth supervision. Teacher information is emphasized only where it is semantically consistent, while semantically inconsistent phrases receive stronger ground-truth supervision. We evaluate RSKD on DrivingVQA, LingoQA, and MapLMv2. RSKD improves over the compared student-based baselines on DrivingVQA and LingoQA and remains competitive on MapLMv2.
authors: Chuchu Xie, Yang Zhong, Kangan Qian, Hao Ye, Kun Jiang, Diange Yang
bullets: Uniform token-level distillation can dilute planning-relevant meaning and propagate teacher errors.
The framework identifies task-critical phrases in ground-truth answers and scores their semantic consistency with teacher predictions.
Phrase-level consistency dynamically balances JSD distillation against ground-truth supervision.
RSKD improves over compared student baselines on DrivingVQA and LingoQA, while remaining competitive on MapLMv2.
papers.selection_reason: Distillation framework for driving vision-language models with semantic consistency; fits multimodal foundation models and video-language understanding.
papers.title: RSKD: Grounding Semantic Consistency in Driving VLMs via Distillation
papers.tldr: RSKD improves distillation for driving vision-language models by emphasizing teacher guidance only when it agrees with task-critical semantics.

papers.abstract: Language-Only Vision-Language Model Selection (LOVM) aims to identify the Vision-Language Model (VLM) with the highest zero-shot accuracy on a target task using only textual information. We revisit the existing LOVM evaluation protocol and argue that ranking metrics, such as top-5 recall and Kendall's rank correlation, do not directly assess the performance of the selected model. We therefore adopt simple regret (SR), defined as the performance gap between the best and selected models, and introduce Outlier-Robust Normalized Regret (ORNR) to account for the varying performance ranges across tasks while reducing sensitivity to outliers. Building on this revised evaluation protocol, we propose Target-Conditioned Expected Source Regret (TC-ESR), a training-free method that selects the model with the lowest similarity-weighted mean regret across source tasks. Across 22 target tasks and 43 VLMs, TC-ESR achieves the lowest mean SR and ORNR among all compared methods. Separately, we identify two sources of target performance leakage in the prior ranking-based evaluation protocol and provide corrections that remove both.
authors: Hyuk Kwon, Jaebyeong Jeon, Hyeonseo Jang, Kibok Lee
bullets: Existing top-5 recall and Kendall correlation can reward good rankings even when the selected model performs poorly.
The authors use simple regret and introduce Outlier-Robust Normalized Regret (ORNR) to compare selection quality across tasks with different performance ranges.
Target-Conditioned Expected Source Regret (TC-ESR) is a training-free selector based on similarity-weighted regret across source tasks.
TC-ESR obtains the lowest mean simple regret and ORNR among compared methods.
The study identifies and corrects two sources of target-performance leakage in prior ranking-based evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Revisits evaluation and selection of vision-language models; technically meaningful for multimodal foundation model deployment and benchmarking.
papers.title: Good Rankings, Poor Choices? Rethinking Language-Only Vision-Language Model Selection
papers.tldr: The paper argues that LOVM selection should measure the regret of the chosen model, not just ranking quality, and proposes TC-ESR, which achieves the lowest regret across 22 tasks and 43 VLMs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while miss the implicit user intent (e.g., "where should I click next?" while a user navigate a website), meanwhile fail to update the state simultaneously as user requests might update continuously. These limitations make them less suited to intent-aware interaction in practical. To address these challenges, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a new benchmark serving as testbed for user intent interaction, with 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically tailors its interactions as these intents evolve. We further introduce StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent states with a fleixble lifecycles via a hierarchical memory to track the latest user intent and environmental state. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (i) StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over other baselines; (ii) existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intent and deciding when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and (iii) StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation over sustained interaction, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction.

papers.title: StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent
papers.tldr: StreamVibe introduces a benchmark and streaming agent that infer evolving implicit user intent and proactively respond during continuous video interaction.

papers.abstract: Latency-sensitive spoken agents must know not only which tool to call, but also when they have heard enough to act. Waiting for the turn to complete delays execution even when the request is already actionable. However, neither existing spoken agents nor spoken dialogue corpora define the earliest point at which a request becomes actionable. We introduce a synthetic spoken-dialogue pipeline that provides earliest-actionable-point supervision, marking when the observed speech grounds a tool and its required arguments. Through controlled task generation, speech synthesis and alignment, and gated annotation, we construct 26,694 dialogues totaling 786 hours across 48 domains, with disjoint training and test argument values. We additionally create an audio rendering of $\tau^2$-bench for external evaluation. We train an omni-modal language model on this corpus, enabling causal, chunk-level decisions and partial-transcript generation for downstream call completion. The model achieves tool-state macro-F1 scores of 0.48 and 0.47 on held-out dialogues and the external benchmark, respectively. For correct calls, the estimated mean lead over a turn-end cascade, using the same formatter, is 1.8-2.0 seconds in-domain and 1.1 seconds on $\tau^2$-bench. These results demonstrate a data-driven path toward spoken agents that act while listening. We will open-source the pipeline and the training scripts.
authors: Yizhou Peng, Chen Chen, Donghang Wu, Hexin Liu, Eng Siong Chng
bullets: Targets latency in spoken agents by detecting the earliest point where a tool and its required arguments are grounded.
Builds 26,694 dialogues spanning 48 domains, with 786 hours of speech and disjoint training/test argument values.
Trains chunk-level causal decisions and partial-transcript generation for downstream tool-call completion.
Reports tool-state macro-F1 of 0.48 on held-out dialogues and 0.47 on an external benchmark.

papers.title: Heard Enough to Act: Early Tool Calling in Spoken Dialogue Systems
papers.tldr: A synthetic spoken-dialogue dataset and omni-modal model enable agents to identify when a request is actionable and call tools before the user finishes speaking.

papers.abstract: Vision-language anomaly detectors describe normal and abnormal appearance with text, and their gains are commonly credited to the semantic content of these descriptions. This attribution is plausible in the zero-shot setting, but few- and full-shot detectors interpose a trained visual adapter, and in that setting it has not been isolated. Changing a description changes both its meaning and its geometry, so accuracy comparisons cannot separate the two. We ask what a fixed pair of text embeddings, or anchors, contributes to such a detector: semantic content, effective scale, or joint anchor geometry. For a single anchor pair, the answer is effective scale alone. The score reads the anchors only through their difference, and a trained adapter can rotate to follow any replacement direction, leaving that direction, and with it the linguistic content, unidentifiable. We prove that replacement anchors with the same difference-vector length permit exactly the same probability maps and attainable losses. Across seven medical datasets, three vision backbones, both supervision regimes, and three adapter families, scale-matched random and orthogonal anchors track correct prompts; breaking the scale match opens a gap that restoring it closes without text. The same pattern holds in MVFA and when MadCLIP's learned prompts are replaced by a text-free learned scale. When one adapter serves many categories, the answer expands to their joint arrangement. Rotating all category axes together changes nothing, as predicted. For the tested CLIP prompts, these axes are nearly collinear, and meaning-free rotations that spread them apart improve performance on both industrial benchmarks. Even under frozen zero-shot transfer, a random anchor frame transfers as well as the prompt frame: coordinate consistency, not meaning. What these detectors read from their prompts is scale and arrangement, not semantic content.
authors: Arda Baris Basaran, Mesut Ceylan, Elgar Fleisch, Filipe Barata
bullets: A single anchor pair contributes only through its difference-vector scale; its direction and semantic content are unidentifiable after adapter training.
Scale-matched random or orthogonal anchors reproduce correct-prompt behavior, while mismatched scale causes performance gaps.
With multiple categories, joint anchor arrangement matters: rotating all axes together has no effect, but spreading nearly collinear prompt axes can improve performance.
These findings hold across seven medical datasets, three vision backbones, two supervision regimes, and multiple adapter settings.
Even in frozen zero-shot transfer, coordinate consistency—not prompt meaning—explains comparable performance.
papers.selection_reason: Provides transferable insight into what text embeddings contribute in vision-language models, showing scale and geometry rather than semantic content drive CLIP-based detectors.
papers.title: Do Words Matter? What Text Contributes to Few and Full-Shot Vision-Language Anomaly Detection
papers.tldr: In few- and full-shot vision-language anomaly detection, prompt performance is driven by embedding scale and category geometry—not linguistic meaning.

papers.abstract: Erasing all furniture from a single room image to generate its empty counterpart is valuable for XR applications such as diminished reality and virtual staging. The challenge is twofold: inpainting the furniture regions with realistic content, and doing so without distorting the room's 3D geometry. Prompt-driven image editors, such as FLUX.2, handle realism impressively, but their structural faithfulness is inferior to explicit layout conditioned inpainting. To improve geometric consistency, we propose a training recipe for finetuning a LoRA on 2,500 furnished-empty room pairs. FLUX.2 with our LoRA adaptor significantly improves geometric consistency while retaining the high texture fidelity. This single-photo inpainter can be an effective building block for depth-aware and 3D-consistent XR pipelines.
authors: Prakhar Kulshreshtha, Brian Pugh, Zachary Nussdorfer, Salma Jiddi
bullets: Addresses single-image room defurnishing for diminished reality and virtual staging.
Targets the trade-off between realistic inpainting and structural faithfulness.
Finetunes a LoRA using 2,500 furnished–empty room pairs.
The adapted FLUX.2 significantly improves geometric consistency while retaining high texture fidelity.
Designed as a building block for depth-aware and 3D-consistent XR pipelines.
papers.selection_reason: Finetunes prompt-based image editor for geometry-consistent room defurnishing; relevant to spatial/geometric consistency in multimodal models.
papers.title: Finetuning Prompt-Based Image Editor for Geometry-Consistent Room Defurnishing
papers.tldr: A LoRA-finetuned FLUX.2 editor removes furniture from room images while better preserving the room’s geometry and realistic appearance.

papers.abstract: A chunky gold-tone chain necklace bought online for 2.43 USD was photographed four ways: worn with formal attire against a wood-panelled wall, worn at a party, worn with casual clothing in a recycling yard, and laid flat with no person present. We asked six frontier language models to estimate its price in 1,164 independent and sequential API sessions (4,604 logged rows) and compared estimates across settings. Among the four models that answered image prompts, the same necklace was priced 1.9 to 3.3 times higher in the formal photograph than in the flat-lay (all p < 0.01). Against the yard photograph, the ratio ranged from 1.23 (Grok 4.5, not significant) to 3.57 (Kimi K3), with Claude Fable 5 at 3.32. A text-only version of the task, in which the setting is described in words, produced formal-to-yard ratios of 2.2 to 3.9 in all six models, so the effect does not require pixels. Flat-lay estimates themselves were 7.8 to 18.7 times the receipt price, so part of any headline "outfit multiplier" computed against the receipt is baseline overestimate, not a context effect. A single instruction to ignore clothing and setting significantly reduced the effect in one model (ratio of ratios 0.77, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.91) and not detectably in the others; telling the model the photo came from a company website or a personal account changed nothing significant. Asked afterward whether a different outfit would have changed their number, Claude Fable 5 said yes in 24 of 24 sessions, GPT-5.6 in 69%, and GPT-4o in 18%, while GPT-4o also refused 79% of image estimation prompts. The study isolates a mechanism with one object and one wearer at about 10 sessions per model and condition; we outline the replication needed next, with multiple objects and a human benchmark. Data, code, and raw outputs are released.
bullets: The necklace’s formal-photo estimates were 1.9–3.3× higher than flat-lay estimates across responding models.
Formal settings also raised estimates relative to a recycling-yard scene, with effects varying by model.
Text-only descriptions produced similar context effects, indicating the bias does not require visual pixels.
Flat-lay estimates already exceeded the $2.43 receipt price by 7.8–18.7×, inflating receipt-based outfit multipliers.
An instruction to ignore context reduced the effect significantly in only one model; the study used one object and calls for replication across objects and human benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of context effects in vision-language model valuation; relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Does the Outfit Change the Price? Context Halo in Vision-Language Model Valuation of an Identical Low-Cost Necklace
papers.tldr: Vision-language models valued the same low-cost necklace substantially higher in formal social contexts than in a neutral flat-lay, showing a context-driven valuation bias.

papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP typically rely on independently parameterized transformer blocks across depth. We investigate the extent to which these blocks can instead be reused recurrently while preserving the transferable capabilities of CLIP. We study recursive transformer backbones in which a small set of $N$ transformer blocks is applied $M$ times per forward pass. By holding $N \cdot M$ fixed to the depth of a standard ViT-B, our models preserve computational depth while progressively increasing parameter sharing. We consider two recursive CLIP model families: rCLIP, where only the vision encoder is recursive, and r$^2$CLIP, where recurrence is also introduced in the text encoder. We study these models under both direct contrastive training and through knowledge distillation from a strong ViT-B/16 teacher pretrained on DFN-2B, using the substantially smaller CC3M and CC12M datasets. We evaluate the resulting models on zero-shot classification and cross-modal retrieval, and further study their adaptability through few-shot learning, visual grounding, and concept unlearning. Our results show that CLIP can tolerate substantial recurrent block reuse, although its effect depends on the encoder and downstream task. Recurrence also provides parameter efficiency by construction, since fewer distinct transformer blocks need to be stored and adapted. Our results establish recurrent block reuse as a practical design space for vision-language models and highlight its implications for knowledge transfer, downstream adaptation, and parameter efficiency.
authors: Szymon Mazurek, Alberto Presta, Micha{\l} Byra
bullets: Replaces independently parameterized transformer layers with a small set of blocks reused recurrently across depth while preserving total computational depth.
Introduces rCLIP with recursive vision encoding and r²CLIP with recurrence in both vision and text encoders.
Studies direct contrastive training and distillation from a strong ViT-B/16 teacher using smaller CC3M and CC12M datasets.
Evaluates zero-shot classification, cross-modal retrieval, few-shot learning, visual grounding, and concept unlearning.
Finds recurrence is a practical parameter-efficiency design space, but its benefits and costs depend on the encoder and downstream task.
papers.selection_reason: Recursive CLIP with recurrent block reuse; relevant to multimodal foundation models and parameter efficiency.
papers.title: Recursive CLIP: Vision-Language Distillation with Looped Transformer Blocks
papers.tldr: Recursive transformer blocks can substantially reduce distinct parameters in CLIP while retaining useful vision-language capabilities, though performance effects vary by encoder and task.

papers.abstract: Adapting general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) to medical visual question answering (VQA) is valuable for helping clinicians read images and make diagnoses, but annotated data are scarce and provide only short answers, without reasoning annotations. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) fits these labels but overfits to them and amplifies their biases, eroding out-of-domain (OOD) generalization. Reinforcement learning (RL) better preserves generalization but never uses the gold answer as a training target: GRPO-style algorithms learn from the contrast between correct and incorrect answers within a group of sampled responses, so all-correct or all-wrong groups give no correctness signal. Existing SFT-RL hybrids either apply SFT and RL in separate stages or switch between them per question, or need reasoning traces from experts or stronger models, which medical VQA data lack. We propose GRASP, which combines RL and SFT in every update using only short answers: RL lets the model explore its own reasoning, SFT teaches the gold answer after that reasoning to supply the direct supervision RL lacks, and their balance adapts to how well the model answers each question. Tuning only about 1% of the parameters with LoRA, GRASP outperforms all compared training objectives both in domain and on OOD open-ended questions across Qwen3-VL-8B, InternVL3-8B and Gemma 3-4B. On an OOD benchmark spanning eight imaging modalities, GRASP-trained InternVL3-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B beat all 10 compared general and medical VLMs in open-ended accuracy, including models trained on up to 2,600 times more data or with over 250 times more trainable parameters. We release MedTerse, a dataset of 12.9K short-answer questions, and our code at https://github.com/sea-comet/GRASP-MedVQA.
authors: Wanqi Dong, Wanyue Dong, Jingze Ge, Mehul Motani
bullets: Addresses SFT overfitting and RL’s weak signal when sampled responses are all correct or all wrong.
Uses RL to encourage self-generated reasoning, then applies SFT toward the gold short answer; their balance adapts to per-question performance.
Trains about 1% of parameters with LoRA and improves both in-domain and out-of-distribution open-ended VQA across three VLMs.
On an eight-modality OOD benchmark, GRASP-trained InternVL3-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B outperform 10 compared general and medical VLMs.
Introduces MedTerse, a 12.9K-question short-answer dataset, and releases the implementation.
papers.selection_reason: Hybrid RL-SFT post-training for medical VQA; directly relevant to multimodal LLM adaptation.
papers.title: GRASP: Group-Adaptive Hybrid RL-SFT Post-Training for Medical VQA without Reasoning Annotations
papers.tldr: GRASP combines group-adaptive reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning in every update to improve medical VQA from scarce short-answer data without reasoning annotations.

papers.abstract: Vision--language models applied to medical question answering can reach correct diagnoses without using the diagnostic image, inferring instead from the clinical vignette. We ask whether this is visible in how \emph{firmly} a model holds its answer: does a model defend a diagnosis derived from a blank placeholder as tenaciously as one derived from a real medical image? Crossing an image-substitution protocol with two levels of adversarial pressure on 60 Italian State Examination items, we find no evidence that ungrounded verdicts are more fragile. In a paired item-level analysis, fabricated consensus (L4) overturns 94.4\% of verdicts with the real image and 98.1\% without ($\Delta = +0.037$; one-sided 95\% upper bound $+0.105$); contentless doubt (L1) overturns 62.5\% and 51.8\% ($\Delta = -0.107$, 95\% CI $[-0.209, -0.001]$), the point estimate running opposite to the direction a grounding detector requires. The two levels nonetheless produce opposite \emph{dynamics}: under L4 the model flips once, always to the exact option argued for (110/110 first-turn flips), and then freezes, averaging 1.9 verdict changes over ten turns; under L1 it never settles, averaging 7.4 changes. Instability under contentless doubt tracks intrinsic item ambiguity rather than evidence availability, and so does not serve as a grounding signal. Flips are almost entirely corrupting (99/100 across both levels). The model is not unaware of the missing evidence---it flags the blank image at baseline on 35 of 60 items and abstains on 4--6---yet those abstentions do not survive contact with pressure. None of the epistemic signals a user could plausibly consult distinguishes a grounded diagnosis from a confabulated one.
authors: Federico Felizzi, Francesco Andrea Causio, Bianca Destro Castaniti, Olivia Riccomi, Michele Ferramola, Vittorio De Vita, Alessandro Tosi, Antonio Cristiano, Alessia Longo, Lorenzo De Mori, Chiara Battipaglia, Melissa Sawaya, Luigi De Angelis, Marcello Di Pumpo, Alessandra Piscitelli, Pietro Eric Risuleo, Giulia Vojvodic, Mariapia Vassalli, Nicolo Scarsi, Manuel Del Medico

Across 60 Italian State Examination items, blank-image and real-image verdicts showed no grounding-related difference in fragility.
Fabricated consensus typically caused one targeted flip followed by freezing, while contentless doubt caused persistent oscillation.
Instability under doubt reflected item ambiguity rather than access to visual evidence.
Models often noticed missing images initially, but their abstentions did not persist; nearly all flips were corrupting.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of visual grounding reliability in medical VLMs; relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Conviction Without Evidence: Verdict Stability Is Independent of Visual Grounding in Medical Vision--Language Models
papers.tldr: Medical vision–language models defend diagnoses based on blank images about as firmly as those based on real images, so verdict stability does not reveal visual grounding.

papers.abstract: Language models switch tasks from demonstrations, but vision still often relies on separate systems for restoration, editing, and stylization. A before--after example offers a shared instruction only if the transferable change can be separated from the scene that demonstrates it. We introduce CrossPair, which adapts a pretrained multimodal image editor to transfer diverse transformations from one exemplar pair. Exemplar-before, exemplar-after, and query images take fixed roles in its native VLM and VAE pathways: the VLM extracts operation semantics, while the VAE retains fine appearance and structure. A training-only, change-aware DINOv3 objective aligns feature-change directions across content-distinct scenes, guiding the output to follow the demonstrated relation without an inference-time encoder. We construct Transform-360K by grouping filtered pairs from conditional representations, restoration, editing, virtual try-on, and stylization under shared transformations. On Relation252K-derived seen and held-out transformations, \method improves target agreement and edit-direction similarity over released systems. Ablations show that the semantic and visual exemplar routes are complementary and that DINO relation alignment further strengthens transfer; Transform-360K training also improves aggregate held-out-operation scores.
authors: Yibo Zhao, Lifan Jiang, Senlin cheng, Tianrun Wu, Bolei Xu, Xiaobo Li, Can Ye, Xiaofei He, Dehai Zhao, Boxi Wu
bullets: Addresses the need for one generalist system across restoration, editing, stylization, and related image transformations.
Assigns the exemplar images and query fixed roles: the VLM captures operation semantics, while the VAE preserves appearance and structure.
Uses a training-only change-aware DINOv3 objective to align transformation directions across different scenes, without an inference-time encoder.
Introduces Transform-360K, a dataset grouping filtered image pairs by shared transformations.
Improves target agreement and edit-direction similarity on seen and held-out transformations; ablations support complementary semantic/visual routes and relation alignment.
papers.selection_reason: Adapts a multimodal image editor to transfer visual transformations via VLM/VAE pathways; relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: CrossPair: Unlocking Generalist Visual Transformation Learning in Image Editors
papers.tldr: CrossPair enables a pretrained multimodal image editor to transfer diverse visual transformations from a single before–after exemplar pair to a new image.

papers.abstract: Training a spatial VLM to answer which side an object lies on does not require it to preserve the metric displacement that determines that answer, while supervision for a distance estimate may leave categorical relations largely unconstrained. When post-training emphasizes one readout, improvements can therefore concentrate on that interface while transfer to others remains weak or even degrades; we call this observed specialization interface lock-in. ChronoReplay addresses it by replaying heterogeneous spatial supervision as chronologically ordered episodes, retaining source-native targets, and balancing supervision across families. Under the same observation access, a single ChronoReplay checkpoint improves OVO-S-Bench, OST-Bench, and UCS-Bench together, including a 13.41-point gain on OST-Bench, and achieves the highest three-benchmark mean among the supervision settings compared here. Same-data controls further separate the ingredients of this transfer: answer serialization redistributes gains across OST and UCS, family-balanced learning improves over ordinary joint SFT and natural turn weighting, and chronological replay exceeds a shifted-order control by about 2.41 OST points across two paired seeds. Adaptive frame selection then changes evidence access while keeping the trained model fixed, providing an additional inference-time gain at lower visual cost. Streaming spatial performance depends on what distinctions supervision preserves, how heterogeneous histories are organized during learning, and what causal evidence inference makes available at test time.
authors: Yihao Hu, Yitong Lin, Pan Wang, Zhihao Wen, Hang Wang, Yiwen Zhao, Deyuan Liu, Yutong Li, Mingda Wan, Yuchen Mao, Tao Lin
bullets: Single-interface post-training can cause interface lock-in, weakening transfer between categorical, metric, and other spatial readouts.
ChronoReplay replays heterogeneous, source-native supervision as chronologically ordered episodes with balanced spatial families.
One checkpoint improves OVO-S-Bench, OST-Bench, and UCS-Bench together, including a 13.41-point OST-Bench gain.
Answer serialization, family balancing, and chronological order each contribute to transfer; chronological replay beats shifted-order control by about 2.41 OST points.
Adaptive frame selection adds inference-time gains while reducing visual cost, with the model unchanged.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial VLM training with heterogeneous spatial supervision and chronological replay; directly targets spatial intelligence.
papers.title: ChronoReplay: One Answer Interface Is Not Enough for Streaming Spatial Intelligence
papers.tldr: ChronoReplay improves streaming spatial reasoning by preserving diverse spatial distinctions and replaying their supervision in chronological, balanced episodes.

papers.abstract: Spatial localization of surgical instruments through bounding-box annotations is a foundational component of surgical scene understanding, supporting detection, tracking, interaction analysis, and grounded vision-language applications. Yet existing annotations often cover selected frames, video subsets, or dataset variants rather than complete procedures. Manual extension is time-consuming and expert-dependent. Additionally, weakly supervised and detector-based pseudo-labels require task-specific training and may be imprecise. In this study, we design a scalable MLLM-based annotation framework that converts surgical frames and existing instrument-presence labels into accurate bounding boxes, and systematically analyze its reliability, cost, and design sensitivity. We instantiate the framework using six MLLMs and a multi-call configuration on laparoscopic cholecystectomy in Cholec80. Using a carefully designed stratification scheme, two annotators independently label 1,000 frames, and an expert surgeon reviews one annotation set to establish the reference. Results show that instrument-set F1 ranges from 88.2 to 92.7,whereas mIoU ranges from 0.180 to 0.735, showing that comparable recognition can conceal large localization differences. A structured multi-stage annotation pipeline achieves 0.784 mIoU, compared with 0.735 for the best single-call baseline and 0.814 human-human agreement. Using the best accuracy pipeline, we create and publicly release a spatial extension of Cholec80 comprising 285,977 bounding boxes across all 184,498 annotated frames from the 80 videos. The annotations and human references are made available on GitHub
authors: Mohamed Hamdy, Muraam Abdel-Ghani, Fatmaelzahraa Ahmed, Sifna Nasar, Mariam Ahmed, Khalid Al-Jalham, Abdulaziz Al-Ali, Shidin Balakrishnan
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited coverage of manually annotated surgical bounding boxes.
Evaluates six MLLMs and multi-call annotation designs on laparoscopic cholecystectomy frames from Cholec80.
Shows that similar instrument recognition F1 can hide substantial localization differences, with mIoU ranging from 0.180 to 0.735.
A structured multi-stage pipeline reaches 0.784 mIoU, approaching human-human agreement of 0.814.
Releases 285,977 bounding boxes covering all 184,498 annotated frames across 80 videos.
papers.selection_reason: MLLM-based framework converting presence labels to bounding boxes; directly relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial localization.
papers.title: From Presence Labels to Bounding Boxes: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Scale Surgical Instrument Localization?
papers.tldr: A scalable multimodal-LLM pipeline converts surgical instrument-presence labels into bounding boxes, achieving near-human localization quality and enabling a large public spatial extension of Cholec80.

papers.abstract: Modern surgical AI increasingly requires multimodal understanding rather than isolated perception, yet existing datasets remain largely limited to single-task supervision such as recognition or templated question answering. Current medical VQA resources often rely on synthetic templates, lack natural descriptive supervision, or provide sparse annotations that hinder reasoning about spatial relations and procedural context. We introduce MIS-VQA, a surgical vision-language dataset generated through an annotation-driven pipeline that converts heterogeneous surgical annotations into structured textual scene representations. Using EndoVis18 and CholecT50, we transform phase, instrument, interaction, triplet, and segmentation labels into unified contexts that guide large language models to generate clinically coherent question-answer pairs. MIS-VQA supports four response types-concise and detailed descriptions, perception-level grounding, and multi-step reasoning-enabling hierarchical evaluation from atomic visual grounding to compositional reasoning. To address annotation sparsity, we incorporate confidence-filtered segmentation and cross-annotation consistency checks, enabling spatially grounded supervision at scale. MIS-VQA establishes a unified benchmark for surgical vision-language understanding with spatial supervision and multi-tier reasoning evaluation. To demonstrate its utility, we introduce LLaVA-SurgXpert, a family of surgical vision-language models with visual encoders to analyze how visual representations influence multimodal reasoning. Experiments show consistent improvements over existing surgical VQA baselines while revealing capability gaps between perceptual grounding and higher-level reasoning hidden in prior benchmarks.
authors: Mohamed Hamdy, Iheb Zouari, Fatmaelzahraa Ahmed, Muraam Abdel-Ghani, Muhammed Arsalan, Ponnuthurai Suganthan, Khalid Al-Jalham, Abdulaziz Al-Ali, Shidin Balakrishnan
bullets: Addresses limitations of existing surgical VQA datasets, including synthetic questions, sparse annotations, and weak procedural or spatial supervision.
Builds unified scene contexts from phase, instrument, interaction, triplet, and segmentation annotations in EndoVis18 and CholecT50.
Provides four response types: concise and detailed descriptions, perception-level grounding, and multi-step reasoning.
Uses confidence-filtered segmentation and cross-annotation consistency checks to scale spatially grounded supervision.
Introduces LLaVA-SurgXpert models and reports improvements over existing surgical VQA baselines, while exposing gaps between grounding and higher-level reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Surgical vision-language dataset and MLLM family with spatial grounding and multi-step reasoning; relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial understanding.
papers.title: MIS-VQA: An Annotation-Driven Surgical Vision-Language Dataset for Complex Surgical Understanding
papers.tldr: MIS-VQA turns diverse surgical annotations into a structured vision-language benchmark for evaluating both spatial grounding and multi-step clinical reasoning.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary instance segmentation (OVIS) provides a promising solution for marine perception by recognizing and segmenting categories beyond predefined label spaces. Existing OVIS methods usually rely on vision-language alignment, where visual region features are matched with textual category embeddings to recognize both seen and unseen classes. However, this alignment assumption becomes fragile in underwater environments. Color attenuation, scattering, turbidity, and low contrast distort visual appearance, causing region features to deviate from their corresponding semantic concepts. As a result, the similarity between degraded visual features and textual classifiers becomes unreliable, which particularly weakens the recognition of unseen underwater categories that cannot be corrected by category-specific supervision. To address these issues, we propose GeoPrompt, a geometry-conditioned prompt learning framework for underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation. Our key insight is that geometric structure is more stable than visual appearance in degraded underwater scenes. Specifically, GeoPrompt introduces a geometry-guided visual adaptation module (GVAM) to extract depth-derived structural priors and inject them into multi-scale visual features. It further develops a geometry-conditioned prompt learning (GCPL) that generates geometry-aware textual classifiers from structural representations. These geometry-aware classifiers are integrated with fixed and image-conditioned textual classifiers to improve open-vocabulary semantic alignment. Experiments on the MARIS-OpenIS benchmark show that GeoPrompt achieves state-of-the-art performance and brings consistent improvements on underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation.
authors: Shanshan Han, Yuxi Wang, Can Qin, Yujie Chen, Cong Pan, Haitao Li, Guoqiang Zhong
bullets: Underwater degradation distorts visual features, making text-based recognition—especially for unseen categories—unreliable.
The method extracts depth-derived structural priors and injects them into multi-scale visual features.
It generates geometry-aware textual classifiers and combines them with fixed and image-conditioned classifiers.
Experiments on MARIS-OpenIS report state-of-the-art performance with consistent improvements.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-conditioned prompt learning injects depth-derived structural priors into vision-language segmentation, fitting geometry-aware multimodal models.
papers.title: GeoPrompt: Geometry-Conditioned Prompt Learning for Underwater Open-Vocabulary Instance Segmentation
papers.tldr: GeoPrompt improves underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation by using stable geometric cues to strengthen vision-language alignment.

papers.abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel at zero-shot reasoning, their spatial capabilities are primarily evaluated through static, passive observation. In complex, human-centric scenes, occlusion often hides crucial geometric evidence, and passive benchmarks force models to guess rather than recognize their own visual uncertainty. To bridge this gap, we introduce SATE-Bench, a novel interactive benchmark comprising 316 real-world scenes and 2,525 multi-turn QA pairs to evaluate visual self-awareness and active exocentric view-exploration. It combines a Passive multi-view control with an Active exploration setting, where models start from a severely occluded view and must iteratively query adjacent viewpoints until they gather enough evidence to fully ``sate'' the question, scored by a step-penalized efficiency reward. Evaluating state-of-the-art MLLMs reveals that they terminate exploration prematurely while reporting high confidence, and struggle with fine-grained 3D geometric tasks; matched-view controls further attribute the Active--Passive gap primarily to insufficient evidence acquisition. Moreover, fine-tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) shows that rewarding view-seeking increases active exploration but lowers overall accuracy, as models over-explore and fail to fuse expanding multi-view contexts across turns. These findings indicate that scaling passive multi-view perception does not intrinsically yield active spatial reasoning, highlighting the need for models that know where to look, how to integrate what they see, and when to stop. Code and data are available at https://gtc-gh.github.io/SATE-Bench/
authors: Tianchen Guo, Tengyue Zhang, Chen Liu, Ling Chen, Xin Yu
bullets: Introduces an interactive benchmark with real-world scenes and multi-turn questions, covering passive multi-view control and active exocentric exploration.
Models must query adjacent viewpoints from severely occluded views and are scored on answer quality and exploration efficiency.
State-of-the-art MLLMs often stop too early with high confidence and struggle with fine-grained 3D geometry.
Matched-view comparisons suggest the active–passive performance gap mainly stems from insufficient evidence acquisition.
GRPO-based view-seeking increases exploration but can reduce accuracy because models over-explore and fail to integrate views across turns.
papers.selection_reason: Interactive benchmark for MLLM human-centric spatial understanding and active view exploration, directly fitting spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Humans in Space: Can MLLMs Construct Human-Centric Spatial Understanding via Active Exocentric Exploration?
papers.tldr: SATE-Bench evaluates whether MLLMs can actively seek informative viewpoints and build reliable human-centric spatial understanding in occluded scenes.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning adapts pretrained models to new tasks, but identifying which weight changes support the resulting behavior remains difficult. Weight-space interpretability assigns semantic descriptions to these changes, called fine-tuning deltas. Such descriptions leave open how much task performance depends on the identified updates, particularly when other updates can support the same predictions. We address this gap by pairing reversion, which restores selected parameters to their pretrained values, with retention, which keeps only selected fine-tuning updates. We evaluate Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) models on synthetic financial charts, Flowers102, EuroSAT, and FGVCAircraft with ViT-L/14, and on Flowers102 with ViT-B/16, using a shared recipe that tunes the final six visual blocks. Our contributions are threefold. First, attention value-output (VO) updates alone recover 43-87% of the accuracy improvement, although reverting them leaves chart accuracy unchanged. Cross-entropy loss preserves this contrast on Charts and EuroSAT, while correct-class score margins reveal additional contributions. Second, VO weights recover more loss improvement than all ten equally sized, layer-matched random subsets in each setting.
