Conclusion: Integrating autoregressive language generation with diffusion-based continuous prediction improves quantitative medical image measurement while retaining prompt-conditioned task flexibility. Significance: HAD-VLM provides a unified approach to combining language interaction with anatomically grounded numerical prediction for quantitative medical image analysis.
authors: Dianye Huang, Jiamei Guo, Yue Zhou, Mingde Li, Yi Xiong, Wei Wang, Nassir Navab, Zhongliang Jiang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between continuous measurements and discrete token-based numerical prediction.
Uses a shared vision-language backbone with autoregressive text generation, visual prompt tuning, and diffusion-based prediction of caliper coordinates and measurement length.
Adds coordinate-length consistency and ensemble post-processing to refine estimates.
On four echocardiographic tasks, it reduces measurement errors by 21.4–37.6% versus a Vicuna-based autoregressive baseline and preserves medical question-answering performance.
Also improves X-ray vertebral measurement error from 11.4 to 6.7 pixels; evaluation is limited to the reported ultrasound, question-answering, and X-ray tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Unified vision-language model with diffusion-based continuous spatial measurement prediction; fits multimodal LLMs and geometry-aware VLMs.
papers.title: Beyond Discrete Tokens: Preserving Numerical Continuity in Medical Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: HAD-VLM combines language generation with diffusion-based continuous prediction to improve prompt-conditioned quantitative measurements in medical images.

papers.abstract: Location encoders map geographic coordinates to high-dimensional descriptors through contrastive alignment with paired Earth Observation imagery. We prove that this construction is structurally limited: any Lipschitz location encoder produces an output of intrinsic dimension at most 2, regardless of architecture or bandwidth, which forces the contrastive loss to strictly exceed its asymptotic optimum. Empirically, joint training also collapses the encoder's embedding covariance to low rank. Although dimension-limited, current location encoders sidestep this spectral collapse by training against a frozen image encoder, which we reinterpret as a covariance regularizer that supplies a high-rank target for the location encoder to fold onto. However, extending this approach to multimodal inputs is challenging, as location encoders should simultaneously map a single location to multiple, potentially incompatible, descriptors. We identify two requirements a regularizer must satisfy for location encoding in multimodal regimes: co-alignment across modalities, since adapters alone cannot align independently pretrained encoders; and high effective rank, since the location encoder inherits its target's spectrum. We propose LoCA (Location Contrastive Alignment), a two-stage pipeline that satisfies both. Stage 1 jointly trains Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 encoders with contrastive learning, producing a co-aligned, high-rank multimodal target. Stage 2 freezes the image encoders and trains a location and a tabular metadata encoder as projection adapters with multi-view contrastive learning. Against five state-of-the-art encoders on 17 tasks ranging from land cover and wildfire forecasting to geophysical, socio-economic, biodiversity and climate applications, LoCA achieves the most task wins, is the only model to outperform every other on a majority of tasks, and wins 68.8% of all per-task comparisons.
authors: Panagiotis Koromilas, Eleanna Vali, Diogenis Antonopoulos, Eleni Saka, Dimitris Christofis, Nikolaos Ioannis Bountos, Konstantin Klemmer, Ioannis Papoutsis, Yannis Panagakis, Mihalis A. Nicolaou
bullets: Standard Lipschitz location encoders have intrinsic dimension at most 2, causing low-rank embeddings and preventing optimal contrastive alignment.
Frozen image encoders act as covariance regularizers, but multimodal settings require targets that are both cross-modal aligned and high-rank.
LoCA first jointly aligns Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 encoders, then trains location and tabular metadata adapters with multi-view contrastive learning.
Across 17 geospatial, environmental, socioeconomic, biodiversity, and climate tasks, LoCA records the most task wins and wins 68.8% of per-task comparisons.
The approach is evaluated within the scope of the five compared state-of-the-art encoders and the listed downstream tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Studies multimodal alignment of location and Earth-observation encoders, contributing to spatial-geometric representation learning.
papers.title: LoCA: Enabling Multi-Modality in Geospatial Location Encoders
papers.tldr: LoCA enables multimodal geospatial location encoding by creating a co-aligned, high-rank image target before training location and metadata adapters, achieving the strongest overall results across 17 tasks.

papers.abstract: While multimodal contrastive models like CLIP and CLAP successfully learn shared representations, their embeddings typically exhibit a persistent \emph{modality gap}. We propose addressing this separation through a purely geometric approach: changing the embedding domain from the unit sphere, $S^{d-1}$, to the probability simplex, $\Delta^{d-1}$. Although both manifolds share the same intrinsic dimension, the simplex acts as a structural prior; its nonnegative, unit-mass constraints serve as a cross-modal calibration that forces both modalities to ground themselves in the same coordinate system. By attaching lightweight softmax adapters and using Total Variation similarity, we reduce the centroid $\ell_2$ gap by 97--99\% across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks. This confirms that simplicial geometry induces genuine semantic alignment, matching or exceeding the retrieval performance of standard unconstrained models.
authors: Shubham Gupta, Siva Reddy, Perouz Taslakian, Valentina Zantedeschi, Cem Subakan
bullets: The modality gap persists in shared embedding spaces learned by models such as CLIP and CLAP.
The method replaces unit-sphere embeddings with probability-simplex representations.
Softmax adapters and Total Variation similarity provide a shared, calibrated coordinate system for both modalities.
Across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks, the centroid ℓ₂ gap is reduced by 97–99%.
Retrieval performance matches or exceeds that of standard unconstrained models.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses the modality gap in multimodal models by using simplex-constrained representations and geometric priors, improving cross-modal alignment and retrieval.
papers.title: Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations
papers.tldr: Constraining multimodal embeddings to the probability simplex with lightweight adapters substantially closes the modality gap while preserving strong retrieval performance.

papers.abstract: Echocardiography is the cornerstone of cardiovascular diagnostics, yet its global utility is constrained by a critical shortage of experienced interpreters. Current artificial intelligence (AI) solutions remain limited, typically operating as opaque "black boxes" or focusing on narrow tasks that fail to capture the holistic, guideline-driven reasoning of a clinician. Here we introduce EchoChat, a generative multimodal vision-language model that performs comprehensive echocardiographic analysis to support clinician interpretation. By emulating the cognitive workflow of a cardiologist, EchoChat integrates vast medical knowledge with a chain-of-thought reasoning mechanism to explicitly ground its conclusions in visual evidence. Trained on echocardiography-instruction pairs from 46,358 examinations, our model establishes a new state-of-the-art across diverse cohorts from six international medical centers. It supports the broadest diagnostic scope of 33 cardiac conditions and findings, including 15 newly added conditions for which it achieves an average F1 of 73.7% across available external evaluations. It surpasses existing best-performing foundation models in cardiac condition recognition (improving average recall by 13.54% on shared tasks) and quantification (average R2 score increase of 0.275 on shared tasks). Furthermore, in a source-blinded echocardiographer reader study, echocardiography reports co-generated with EchoChat were rated higher in diagnostic accuracy and completeness by two senior echocardiographers, and improved diagnostic performance from 72.78% to 82.75% in terms of F1 score over routine-reader only reports. These results demonstrate that integrating clinical reasoning into multimodal AI can democratize specialist expertise and transform the standard of cardiovascular care.
authors: Yi Qin, Marawan Elbatel, Shanshan Song, Taoran Huang, Jiarong Guo, Ningshu Li, Lehan Wang, Chenxu Zhao, Jiexin He, Machteld J. Boonstra, Stephan van der Zwaard, Marielle C. van de Veerdonk, Pere Lopez-Gutierrez, Lydia Dux-Santoy, Andrea Guala, Enrique Almar-Munoz, Sebastian Johannes Reinstadler, Radek Debiec, Yi-Hang Zhu, Huiyu Zhou, Adrian P Cheong, Yike Guo, Agnes Mayr, Karim Lekadir, Yong Jiang, Nilesh J. Samani, Dacheng Tao, Folkert W. Asselbergs, Hongwen Fei, Alex PW Lee, Xiaomeng Li
bullets: Addresses the shortage of experienced echocardiography interpreters and limitations of narrow or opaque AI systems.
Integrates echocardiographic images, medical knowledge, and explicit reasoning to emulate a cardiologist’s workflow.
Trained on instruction pairs from 46,358 examinations and evaluates 33 cardiac conditions and findings.
Achieves strong external performance, including an average F1 of 73.7% for 15 newly added conditions, while improving recognition and quantification over prior foundation models.
In a blinded reader study, EchoChat-assisted reports improved diagnostic F1 from 72.78% to 82.75% and were rated more accurate and complete by senior echocardiographers.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a medically grounded multimodal vision-language model with comprehensive clinical reasoning, directly fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Multimodal Generative AI Assists Comprehensive Echocardiographic Interpretation
papers.tldr: EchoChat is a multimodal generative AI model that provides broad, evidence-grounded echocardiographic interpretation and improves report quality and diagnostic performance.

papers.abstract: Text-enhanced visible-infrared person re-identification (VI-ReID) exploits textual descriptions to compensate for appearance cues that are weak or unavailable under infrared imaging. Existing methods construct compensation from differences between modality-oriented textual representations, implicitly assuming that textual differences are visually complementary. We revisit this assumption through semantic superposition and show that dense textual residuals may entangle useful appearance variations with redundant, making direct residual fusion unreliable. We propose Superposition-Aware Residual Calibration, which transforms dense textual differences into selective and visually grounded complements. Low-Interference Sparse Residual Learning represents modality-oriented text embeddings as sparse activation strengths over a shared dictionary, selects positive strength differences, and suppresses both dictionary-level overlap and activation-weighted interference to reconstruct a compact, selectively controlled residual. Visual Complement and Counterfactual Calibration further calibrates the residual against identity-specific RGB-IR visual discrepancies, encouraging retained semantics to provide meaningful compensation while preserving the residual structure. Experiments on Tri-SYSU-MM01, Tri-RegDB, and Tri-LLCM show that SARC consistently improves the VI-ReID backbone and remains competitive with text-assisted methods. Mechanism analyses show that SARC produces more concentrated textual variations, reduces dictionary-level feature interference, and improves residual-visual-complement alignment for most samples. These results demonstrate that effective cross-modal compensation requires textual residuals to be selectively represented and explicitly calibrated, rather than directly treated as visual complements. Code and implementation details will be released upon publication.
authors: Xiaoyang Li, Mingming Lu, Wei Zhou, Hao Li, Canhui Zhang
bullets: Dense differences between modality-specific text representations can mix useful appearance cues with redundant or interfering semantics.
Low-Interference Sparse Residual Learning selects informative residual differences over a shared dictionary while suppressing overlap and activation-weighted interference.
Visual Complement and Counterfactual Calibration aligns retained textual semantics with identity-specific RGB–IR visual discrepancies.
Experiments on Tri-SYSU-MM01, Tri-RegDB, and Tri-LLCM show consistent backbone improvements and competitive performance among text-assisted methods.
Mechanism analyses report more concentrated textual variations, less feature interference, and better residual–visual-complement alignment for most samples.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses cross-modal person re-identification by reformulating textual residuals as visual complements. This contributes to spatial intelligence and multimodal fusion techniques.
papers.title: Are Textual Residuals Truly Complementary? Learning Visual Complements under Semantic Superposition for Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification
papers.tldr: SARC makes textual residuals more selective and visually grounded, improving text-enhanced visible-infrared person re-identification.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) read images through visual tokens, and under the small per-image budgets that efficient deployment requires, the fine text of documents, charts and infographics becomes illegible. Zooming in recovers the evidence, but the region must be chosen before the model answers. We find that MLLMs know where the evidence is, but not in a form that can be read before they answer: the answer tokens localize it from the middle layers on, whereas the attention available before answering does so only in the top layers, at a depth that varies across models, and diffusely. Supervising the pre-answer attention to point degrades reading, and the benefit of zooming is governed by each image's information gap. Building on these findings, we introduce ours, which lets an MLLM look where its answer would. A dedicated look token, processed in a single prefill and kept out of the answering pass, learns in hindsight to attend as the model's own correct answers do, extracting this knowledge into a concentrated pointer before any answer exists. Its hidden state then selects how to look, from no zoom to crops, square windows, windows that adapt to the pointer and foveated warps, supervised by the counterfactual outcome of every view. ours needs no box annotations, per-model layer search, external localizers or generation before the answer. On Qwen3-VL at three scales and five text-rich benchmarks, it surpasses the strongest baseline by 4.8-9.1 points at 98 visual tokens per view and attention-guided zooming by 11.1-17.0 points, while running faster than attention-guided and grounding-based zooming.
authors: Zhensheng Hu, Guanglong Xu, Guanqiang Hu
bullets: Small visual-token budgets make fine text in documents, charts, and infographics difficult to read.
Answer tokens localize relevant evidence earlier and more clearly than pre-answer attention, whose useful depth varies by model.
OURS uses a dedicated look token trained from correct-answer attention to produce a concentrated pointer before answering.
The pointer selects among no zoom, crops, adaptive windows, square windows, and foveated warps using counterfactual view outcomes.

On Qwen3-VL across three scales and five text-rich benchmarks, it improves over the strongest baseline by 4.8–9.1 points and attention-guided zooming by 11.1–17.0 points at 98 visual tokens per view, while running faster than both attention-guided and grounding-based zooming.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a mechanism for MLLMs to intelligently zoom into images before answering, optimizing visual token usage. This addresses spatial intelligence (understanding where to look) and efficient AI (token budget management).
papers.title: The Answer Knows Where to Look: Zooming before MLLMs Answer under Visual-Token Budgets
papers.tldr: OURS lets MLLMs identify where answer-critical visual evidence lies before answering, enabling effective zooming under tight visual-token budgets.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) are costly to pretrain, yet model families often repeat this process across backbone scales and sensing modalities. We investigate feature distillation as a more efficient way to reuse existing representations. First, we distill frozen CROMA and TerraMind teachers into smaller Vision Transformers through patch-level feature matching. Across nine PANGAEA tasks, distilled TerraMind Tiny, Small, and Base outperform their scale-matched released counterparts by 2.76, 3.02, and 1.87 mean IoU points, respectively; each also matches or exceeds the next-larger released model. Distilled CROMA-Base gains 2.05 points. TerraMind-Base required only 43 A6000 GPU-hours, approximately 0.5\% of the reported cost of independent pretraining. Second, we introduce TEDI, an unpaired multi-expert approach combining TerraMind for multispectral imagery and DINOv3 for high-resolution RGB. Separate patch embeddings route unpaired inputs into a shared Transformer trunk, removing the need for co-registered data. TEDI-Large achieves the highest single-model mean in our PANGAEA-9 comparison (62.51 mIoU), outperforming both teachers overall while retaining their modality-specific strengths. TEDI-Base reaches 61.75 mIoU with 72\% fewer parameters. These results show that distillation improves the GeoFM accuracy-compute frontier while consolidating complementary experts into a single versatile backbone.
authors: Mario Hamon, Pierre Adorni, Minh-Tan Pham
bullets: Distills frozen CROMA and TerraMind teachers into smaller Vision Transformers using patch-level feature matching.
Across nine PANGAEA tasks, distilled TerraMind and CROMA models improve over scale-matched released models and often reach the performance of larger ones.
TerraMind-Base distillation used approximately 0.5% of the reported cost of training an independent model.
TEDI combines TerraMind’s multispectral expertise with DINOv3’s high-resolution RGB features through separate patch embeddings and a shared Transformer trunk, without co-registered data.
TEDI-Large achieves the highest reported PANGAEA-9 single-model mean, while TEDI-Base offers a lower-parameter alternative with competitive performance.
papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates efficient feature distillation for geospatial foundation models, significantly reducing compute costs while maintaining or improving accuracy. This addresses both spatial intelligence (geospatial understanding) and efficient AI (distillation).
papers.title: Reuse, Don't Retrain: Efficient, Modality-Versatile Geospatial Foundation Models through Feature Distillation
papers.tldr: Feature distillation efficiently repurposes geospatial foundation models into smaller, multimodal models that match or outperform larger pretrained counterparts at much lower cost.

papers.abstract: People differ in how they perceive music, what associations they make with it, what they like about it, and how they respond to it. Computational models intended to simulate people in environments that include music should account for these differences. Although LLMs have been shown to reproduce aspects of human behavior, whether audio-language models (ALMs) can reproduce a specific person's responses to textual and musical stimuli remains underexplored. We introduce MusicTwins, a framework that combines persona summaries, personal memory, and post-training to generate person-specific responses. We construct persona representations from human writings, capturing background, views, personality, writing style, and a musical profile, and post-train Audio Flamingo Next through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Evaluation on ten held-out personas shows notable improvements for Audio Flamingo Next in persona fidelity, including personality, writing style, and responses to music, supporting MusicTwins as a foundation for training audio-language models to listen like their persona.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling individual differences in how people perceive and respond to music.
Builds persona representations from human writings, including background, views, personality, writing style, and musical profiles.
Post-trains Audio Flamingo Next using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, combined with persona summaries and personal memory.
Evaluation on ten held-out personas shows improved fidelity in personality, writing style, and responses to music.
The study focuses on reproducing person-specific responses to textual and musical stimuli.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a framework for training Audio-Language Models with specific personas, fitting Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: MusicTwins: Training Audio-Language Models to Listen like Their Persona
papers.tldr: MusicTwins adapts audio-language models to produce music responses that reflect a specific person’s personality, memories, style, and musical preferences.

papers.abstract: Photonic crystal fibers (PCFs) underpin critical applications in telecommunications, sensing, and high-power laser delivery, yet their design remains a manual, expert-intensive process that couples geometric intuition with deep waveguide physics. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising path toward automating PCF design, but can they truly reason about photonic physics from microscopy images, or do they merely recognize visual patterns? We introduce PCFBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs on the perception, reasoning, and decision steps of the photonic inverse-design loop. PCFBench spans 26 tasks organized into six categories of increasing cognitive demand (Geometry Perception, Physics Understanding, Text Generation, Multi-modal Reasoning, Inverse-Design Decision, and Code Generation), built from over 220K FDTD simulation samples across 18 structurally diverse fiber families. We evaluate both individual VLMs on isolated tasks and multi-agent systems (MAS) on the full sequential pipeline from perception to design. Our results reveal a striking perception-design gap: current models can identify fiber geometry with moderate success, yet consistently fail to translate that visual understanding into physics-aware design actions. Moreover, cascading agents through the pipeline exposes significant error propagation, where upstream perception mistakes compound into downstream design failures. These findings suggest that neither model scaling nor naive agent chaining suffices, and that closing the loop demands explicit physical grounding. PCFBench provides the community with a rigorous, multi-dimensional testbed to measure progress toward AI-assisted photonic engineering. The project is available at https://pcfbench.github.io/.
authors: Shengchao Chen, Ting Shu, Sufen Ren
bullets: Evaluates 26 tasks across six stages, from geometry perception and physics understanding to inverse-design decisions and code generation.
Built from over 220K FDTD simulation samples spanning 18 structurally diverse photonic crystal fiber families.
Tests both individual VLM capabilities and multi-agent systems across the full perception-to-design pipeline.
Models recognize fiber geometry with moderate success but often fail to convert visual understanding into physics-aware actions.
Sequential agent pipelines suffer from compounded upstream errors, indicating that physical grounding—not just scaling or agent chaining—is needed.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating VLM perception, geometry, and physics-aware reasoning for photonic inverse design, relevant to multimodal and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: PCFBench: How Far Can Large Vision-Language Models Go in Physics-aware Photonic Inverse Design?
papers.tldr: PCFBench benchmarks whether vision-language models can move beyond recognizing photonic crystal fiber geometry to making physics-aware inverse-design decisions, finding a substantial gap between perception and design.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially advanced Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) by enabling fine-grained emotion understanding through reasoning over multimodal evidence. However, they still exhibit systematic confusion between semantically adjacent emotions with highly overlapping multimodal cues. Existing approaches typically address these errors through global parameter adaptation, making confusion correction costly and inflexible. We instead observe that emotion confusion is highly localized and therefore better addressed through reusable pair-specific expertise. Building on this insight, we propose Confusion-Aware Skill Evolution (CASE), the first agent-skill framework for MER. CASE maintains a sparse, self-evolving library of pair-specific EmotionSkills that externalize affective expertise from model parameters, enabling the learned expertise to be continuously refined and readily transferred across diverse frozen MLLM backbones. During inference, CASE dynamically retrieves the appropriate EmotionSkill to reinforce boundary-aware reasoning while keeping the MLLM backbone frozen. Extensive experiments on CA-MER, DFEW, and EMER demonstrate the effectiveness and transferability of CASE across both general-purpose and emotion-specialized MLLMs. Notably, CASE improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B on the CA-MER benchmark from 46.80% to 59.13%, while achieving consistent gains across MLLMs.
authors: Siyu Wu, Zeyu Liang, Linghao Wang, Qiyun Zheng, Yi Yao, Ling Lo, Hongxia Xie
bullets: Targets systematic confusion between semantically adjacent emotions with overlapping multimodal cues.
Represents affective expertise as sparse, self-evolving pair-specific EmotionSkills rather than global model adaptations.
Retrieves relevant skills at inference time to support boundary-aware emotion reasoning.
Transfers across frozen general-purpose and emotion-specialized MLLM backbones.
Raises Qwen3-VL-8B’s CA-MER average accuracy from 46.80% to 59.13% and delivers consistent gains across evaluated MLLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Agent-skill framework for frozen multimodal LLMs in emotion recognition, contributing to multimodal LLM adaptation and externalized expertise.
papers.title: CASE: Confusion-Aware Skill Evolution for Frozen Multimodal Emotion Models
papers.tldr: CASE improves multimodal emotion recognition by using a reusable, dynamically retrieved library of pair-specific emotion skills while keeping the underlying MLLM frozen.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models used for decisions in histopathology rarely return calibrated probabilities over the candidates a user cares about. Decision-native models write a question and a candidate set chosen at run time into the input and return a normalised distribution from a small decision head in one forward pass. We build PathJev-P, a decision-native model for histopathology: MedGemma-1.5-4B with LoRA adapters and a decision head, trained on 40,000 patch states from three public collections whose expert labels are turned into typed questions with organ-specific candidate sets and a "none of these" option. In a comparison over 3 seeds with an analysis plan fixed before testing, on test sets without documented overlap with the training data of the backbone, PathJev-P is more accurate than a generative model trained with the same backbone, data and selection rule, the zero-shot pathology model CONCH and a general medical decision model (balanced accuracy 0.541 against 0.492, 0.345 and 0.213); its advantage over the generative model comes from two organs absent from training. The calibration advantage depends on how the generative model's probabilities are read out. With the summed candidate log-likelihood used in previous work, PathJev-P has the lower calibration error (ECE 0.204 against 0.279); with a length-normalised read-out of the same generative model, examined post hoc, the two have similar mean calibration error (0.201) and the generative model is better calibrated on the unseen organs, where PathJev-P remains over-confident. A supervised linear probe on a pathology foundation model is better calibrated in every setting. In a qualitative whole-slide demonstration, PathJev-P labels unsupervised tissue clusters with abstention and separates carcinoma from other tissue while running the model on a fraction of the tiles.
bullets: Addresses the lack of calibrated probabilities for user-defined diagnostic candidates in vision-language pathology models.
Uses MedGemma-1.5-4B with LoRA adapters and a decision head that outputs a normalized distribution in one forward pass.
Trained on 40,000 labeled patch states from three public collections, with organ-specific typed questions and a “none of these” option.
Achieved balanced accuracy of 0.541 versus 0.492 for a matched generative model, 0.345 for CONCH, and 0.213 for a general medical decision model.

Calibration depends on probability readout: PathJev-P is better than summed-log-likelihood generation, but comparable after length normalization and remains over-confident on unseen organs; a supervised linear probe calibrates better overall.
papers.selection_reason: Decision-native vision-language model built on MedGemma directly extends a multimodal LLM with a calibrated decision head.
papers.title: PathJev: Decision-Native Vision-Language Modelling for Histopathology
papers.tldr: PathJev-P makes histopathology decisions with run-time candidate sets and calibrated distributions, improving accuracy over several comparators but showing calibration limitations on unseen organs.

papers.abstract: Advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have driven substantial progress in multimodal embeddings. Recent methods exploit generative capabilities by augmenting embedded inputs with self-generated reasoning to produce more informative embeddings. However, conventional retrieval supervision for training embedding models specifies pairwise relevance relations without explicitly guiding the reasoning used for input augmentation. Such reasoning is neither directly observed nor uniquely determined by the input, allowing multiple plausible traces to introduce semantic cues of varying retrieval utility. Existing approaches largely optimize reasoning conditioned on the input alone, limiting the exploration of retrieval-relevant traces. We introduce PILOT, a framework that models reasoning as a latent variable and instantiates its prior and posterior distributions as distinct reasoning modes of a shared MLLM. The prior conditions only on the input, whereas the posterior uses additional training-time relational evidence to guide reasoning exploration. To translate the posterior's broader exploration into inference-time improvements, we derive an importance-weighted variational objective and instantiate it as a prior-posterior co-evolution framework that improves both modes under a shared inference-compatible reward while selectively transferring posterior trajectories to the prior according to their utility and prior reachability. On the 78-task MMEB-V2 benchmark, PILOT outperforms the primary baseline across all 12 task groups at both 2B and 7B parameters, improving overall scores by 3.2 and 3.3 points, respectively, with the largest gains in visual-document retrieval (+6.1 and +6.4 points). Our results show that relational supervision is most valuable not as a post-hoc reward but as a signal for shaping how reasoning is explored in training reasoning-enhanced embedding models.
authors: Tianyu Yang, Yijun Tian, Lars Benedikt Kaesberg, Jan Philip Wahle, Bela Gipp, Terry Ruas, Daniel Kurzawe
bullets: Existing embedding training specifies relevance relations but does not guide the latent reasoning used to augment inputs.
PILOT models reasoning with input-only prior and relation-informed posterior modes of a shared MLLM.
An importance-weighted variational objective enables prior–posterior co-evolution and selective transfer of useful, reachable posterior traces.
On MMEB-V2, PILOT improves over the primary baseline across all 12 task groups for both 2B and 7B models.
Overall gains are 3.2 and 3.3 points, with the largest improvements in visual-document retrieval: 6.1 and 6.4 points.
papers.selection_reason: Improves multimodal embeddings via privileged reasoning exploration from MLLMs, directly fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Beyond Post-Hoc Rewards: Privileged Reasoning Exploration for Multimodal Embeddings
papers.tldr: PILOT improves multimodal embeddings by using relational supervision to explore and transfer more retrieval-useful reasoning traces during training.

papers.abstract: While large vision-language models excel at optical character recognition, it remains unclear how their underlying vision encoders process text and its meaning, and whether they support anything resembling reading comprehension. We systematically study transformer-based vision encoders, using cross-modal alignment between rendered text and visual concepts together with probing and retrieval-based analyses as a controlled window into these broader capabilities. Our layer-wise analyses span orthographic, grammatical, and semantic organization, and reveal that strong cross-modal mapping emerges only in the deepest layers, after unimodal object and text recognition have already developed, coinciding with a progression from surface-level to semantic representations. Although this hierarchy is strongest in contrastively trained models, larger self-supervised models and text-rich training data partially support similar behaviors without explicit language supervision. Together, our results suggest that increasing model and training-data scale, as well as text-rich training data, can partially compensate for the absence of language supervision.
authors: Sugam Karki, Ra\'ul V\'azquez, Yova Kementchedjhieva
bullets: Studies how vision encoders process rendered text across orthographic, grammatical, and semantic levels.
Combines cross-modal alignment, probing, and retrieval analyses to examine representational hierarchy.
Finds object and text recognition emerge before strong text–concept mapping.
The hierarchy is strongest in contrastively trained models, but larger self-supervised models and text-rich data show partial similar behavior.
Results suggest scale and text-rich training can partly offset the lack of explicit language supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Systematically analyzes cross-modal alignment and representational hierarchy in Vision Transformers, revealing how text processing emerges in deep layers of VLMs.
papers.title: Reading Between the Layers: Cross-Modal Alignment and Representational Hierarchy in Vision Transformers
papers.tldr: Vision Transformers develop cross-modal text–concept alignment mainly in their deepest layers, where representations shift from visual form to semantics.

papers.abstract: Multimodal healthcare data contain relational information that extends beyond individual patient observations. Effective clinical outcome prediction therefore requires not only integrating information from multiple modalities, but also modeling the relationships between them. Standard fusion approaches do not explicitly capture these interactions, while existing graph-based approaches typically model only a subset of them. We propose DIGOM (Disentangled Interaction Graphs for Outcome prediction in Multimodal healthcare), a graph-based framework that jointly models three complementary interaction types: Intra-patient cross-modal, Cross-patient same-modal, and Cross-patient cross-modal interactions. DIGOM learns a sparse multiplex graph with disentangled views, each encoding interactions between pairs of modalities across patients. Discrete adjacency matrices with patient-adaptive connectivity are sampled via a differentiable mechanism, enabling end-to-end learning and allowing the model to select informative relationships without imposing a fixed number of neighbors. A regularization objective maintains overall graph sparsity, while message passing integrates this relational context into patient representations for outcome prediction. We evaluate DIGOM on two multimodal healthcare datasets, MIMIC-IV and NIH-TB, across five clinical prediction tasks. DIGOM achieves the highest AUROC on all five tasks while using fewer connections than existing multi-interaction approaches. Ablation studies reveal that each interaction type's contribution varies across tasks, highlighting the need to adapt relational structures per task. DIGOM also demonstrates greater robustness to missing modalities, suggesting learned relationships provide complementary information when modalities are unavailable. Post-hoc analyses further reveal task- and outcome-specific connectivity patterns in the learned graphs.
authors: Hakima Laribi, Olivier Lefebvre, Dan Poenaru, Martin Valli\`eres
bullets: Models intra-patient cross-modal, cross-patient same-modal, and cross-patient cross-modal relationships.
Uses differentiable sampling to learn patient-adaptive discrete connectivity without fixing the number of neighbors.
Combines sparse multiplex graph message passing with multimodal patient representations.
Achieves the highest AUROC across five tasks on MIMIC-IV and NIH-TB while using fewer connections than existing multi-interaction methods.
Shows improved robustness to missing modalities and task-specific interaction patterns.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a graph-based framework for multimodal healthcare outcome prediction, fitting Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: DIGOM: Disentangled Interaction Graphs for Outcome prediction in Multimodal healthcare
papers.tldr: DIGOM improves multimodal clinical outcome prediction by learning sparse, task-adaptive graphs that disentangle three types of patient and modality interactions.

papers.abstract: Visual grounding with vision-language models such as CLIP typically produces a single deterministic relevance map for an image-query pair, without indicating whether the localisation is reliable or whether the referent is present at all. We introduce \textbf{PROVE} (\textbf{Pro}babilistic \textbf{V}isual Grounding via Patch-Level \textbf{E}vidence), a post-hoc evidential adapter that maps frozen CLIP patch features to per-patch Beta distributions without modifying the backbone. PROVE casts grounding as per-patch membership: each patch accumulates positive and negative evidence for whether it belongs to the referent, so a query may match zero, one, or many patches. We train PROVE with an evidential objective on soft patch-coverage targets, and define a prior-pull objective that keeps absent-referent examples near an uninformative prior, so that vacuity serves as an absence signal without a dedicated presence classifier. During inference, a single forward pass yields, in closed form, a posterior-mean grounding map, a spatial vacuity map, and an image-level absence score. We evaluate PROVE on referring-expression benchmarks: it is competitive in localisation with state-of-the-art CLIP grounding methods, its uncertainty tracks localisation error and supports selective prediction under abstention, and its image-level score detects when the referent is absent altogether. Our evidential patch-membership modelling offers a simple, drop-in mechanism for probabilistic verification in frozen vision-language grounding systems.
authors: Mayank Nautiyal, Tianru Zhang, Li Ju, Ekta Vats, Prashant Singh
bullets: Addresses the limitations of deterministic relevance maps, which do not show localisation reliability or referent absence.
Uses a post-hoc evidential adapter that maps frozen CLIP patch features to per-patch Beta distributions for referent membership.
Trains on soft patch-coverage targets and pulls absent-referent examples toward an uninformative prior, using vacuity as an absence signal.
A single forward pass produces a grounding map, spatial uncertainty map, and image-level absence score.
On referring-expression benchmarks, PROVE is competitive in localisation; its uncertainty tracks error, supports abstention, and detects absent referents.
papers.selection_reason: Probabilistic patch-level visual grounding with CLIP is directly relevant to spatial understanding in multimodal models.
papers.title: PROVE: Probabilistic Visual Grounding via Patch-Level Evidence for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: PROVE adds probabilistic, uncertainty-aware visual grounding to frozen CLIP by modelling patch-level evidence and detecting when a referent is absent.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have significantly improved Visual Question Answering (VQA) performance, yet their reasoning over structured content such as tables remains inconsistent, often plagued by spatial misalignment and logical hallucinations. Existing approaches for improving table VQA typically rely on architectural modifications or expensive supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which impose high barriers to entry due to the need for large-scale, expert-annotated datasets and significant computational resources. In this work, we propose Self-RefineVQA, a training-free, inference-time self-correction framework that improves table VQA performance without additional labeled data or model updates. Inspired by human revision behavior, our method enables a single VLM to iteratively act as a generator, critic, and refiner, forming a closed self-feedback loop that corrects common reasoning errors through prompt-guided re-evaluation. Experiments on tabular VQA benchmarks demonstrate that Self-RefineVQA yields consistent accuracy gains in monolingual and cross-lingual understanding, with a particularly significant boost for small models, enabling lightweight models (e.g., 2B-7B parameters) to rival the performance of significantly larger counterparts. Furthermore, we provide a comparative complexity analysis demonstrating that while inference cost increases linearly, our framework offers superior data efficiency and a lower cumulative cost by eliminating the prohibitive annotation bottleneck of human labeling required for fine-tuning. Our results highlight the potential of prompt-based self-improvement as a scalable, accessible paradigm for reliable table reasoning in VLMs.
bullets: Targets spatial misalignment and logical hallucinations in VLM reasoning over document tables.
Uses one VLM as generator, critic, and refiner in a prompt-guided self-feedback loop.
Requires no labeled data, architectural changes, or model updates.
Improves accuracy across monolingual and cross-lingual tabular VQA, especially for small models.
Inference cost grows linearly with iterations, but avoids the annotation burden of supervised fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free self-correction framework for Table VQA using VLMs. This fits Multimodal Foundation Models (VLMs) and Spatial Intelligence (structured content reasoning).
papers.title: Cycle-of-Thought: Self-Evaluative Iterative Reasoning for Table Visual Question Answering in Document Images
papers.tldr: Self-RefineVQA improves table visual question answering through training-free, iterative self-critique and refinement at inference time.

papers.abstract: Locating relevant evidence in long inputs is a core capability of Multimodal Large Language Models. Prior studies attribute this capability to retrieval heads, a sparse set of attention heads that transfer information from the context to the output. However, these analyses are confined to a limited set of modalities and the corresponding models. Moreover, how retrieval heads can be leveraged to enhance the model calls for further exploration. In this paper, we ask whether this mechanism expands together with the input modalities of the model. Taking audio-visual input as a newly added modality, we construct paired inputs in which the same answer is either spoken or shown on screen. With the evidence content fixed, retrieval heads remain sparse in the new modality and are shared to a large extent across modalities. Across 18 language, vision-language, and omni-modal checkpoints, omni-modal models largely preserve the retrieval heads of their backbones. Ablating these heads eliminates nearly all audio-visual retrieval. The heads shared across modalities make up fewer than 2\% of all heads, yet ablating them also degrades document understanding, spatial perception, and visual mathematics. Building on these findings, we turn retrieval heads into a target of optimization by training their attention with a ranking objective. This raises the page Recall@1 of Qwen3-VL-8B on MMDocIR by 6.03 points and improves document retrieval across three model families. Functional attention heads can thus serve both as a lens on multimodal models and as a target for improving them.
authors: Jia Wang, Yuqing Li, Jiangnan Li, Zheng Lin, Mo Yu
bullets: Studies retrieval heads—the attention heads responsible for transferring relevant evidence to model outputs—across language, vision-language, and omni-modal models.
Using paired audio-visual inputs with identical evidence, finds that retrieval heads remain sparse and are substantially shared across modalities.
Across 18 checkpoints, omni-modal models largely preserve the retrieval heads of their language backbones; ablating them nearly eliminates audio-visual retrieval.
Fewer than 2% of shared heads also support document understanding, spatial perception, and visual mathematics.
Training retrieval-head attention with a ranking objective improves Qwen3-VL-8B's MMDocIR page Recall@1 by 6.03 points and benefits three model families.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes retrieval heads in Multimodal LLMs, demonstrating their sparsity and cross-modal sharing, and uses them to optimize retrieval performance in document understanding.
papers.title: A Broader Look into MLLM's Retrieval Heads
papers.tldr: Retrieval heads remain sparse and largely shared across modalities in multimodal LLMs, and optimizing them improves multimodal document retrieval.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) process images and text jointly, yet robustness evaluations often perturb these inputs separately or assess only predefined corruption levels. Such evaluations provide limited evidence of which modality is more susceptible to perturbations and whether smaller changes across both modalities can jointly expose failures. We present MoST, a black-box testing framework that characterizes modality sensitivity by comparing image-only, text-only, and joint perturbations. MoST uses multi-objective search to select and combine perturbations and adjust their severity, seeking prediction degradation while limiting changes to images and prompts. We evaluate MoST on four VLMs performing object localization on ImageNet and driving images. The models exhibit distinct sensitivities: textual perturbations dominate for some, whereas others are susceptible across both modalities. In several configurations, joint perturbations match or exceed the effectiveness of single-modality perturbations with smaller modifications to each input. In a human study, 60-76% of assessments across models judge the perturbed inputs sufficiently understandable to perform the task, and human localization is more accurate than that of the corresponding VLMs. These results show that evaluating modalities separately can overlook failure-inducing combinations and that modality sensitivity provides a more detailed account of VLM robustness than aggregate failure rates alone.
authors: Oliver Wei{\ss}l, Eduardo Breitembach, Andrea Stocco
bullets: Evaluates modality sensitivity through image-only, text-only, and combined perturbations with adjustable severity.
Tests four VLMs on object localization using ImageNet and driving images.
Finds model-specific vulnerabilities: text dominates for some models, while others are sensitive to both modalities.
Joint perturbations can match or exceed single-modality effectiveness while making smaller changes to each input.
Human evaluators generally found the perturbed inputs understandable, suggesting failures can occur without obvious loss of task clarity.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a black-box testing framework (MoST) to characterize modality sensitivity in VLMs, offering a methodological contribution to evaluating robustness in multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Search-Based Testing of Modality Sensitivity in Vision Language Models
papers.tldr: MoST uses black-box multi-objective search to reveal how vision-language models fail under image, text, and joint perturbations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves multimodal reasoning, but uniformly assigning a single response-level advantage to all tokens overlooks the distinct roles of visual observations and subsequent reasoning. Visual affinity alone is insufficient: predictive states may align with both image and prompt-context representations, and upweighting valid visual observations can amplify their negative-advantage updates when later reasoning fails. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{Outcome-Conditioned Visual Credit (OVC)}, a plug-in framework that separates visual-association measurement from token-level credit assignment and is adaptable to policy-optimization methods with uniform response-level advantage allocation. Relative Visual Encoding constructs a context-relative visual coordinate by contrasting each predictive state's affinity to image and prompt-context representations. Outcome-conditioned Evidence Calibration combines this coordinate with uncertainty-scaled predictive features and calibrates their contributions to outcome-discriminative evidence through mean contrasts between positive- and negative-advantage responses, scaled by regularized within-side variation. Visual association thus informs credit through observed outcome differences rather than directly determining update priority. Normalized Credit Allocation conditions the calibrated evidence on the response's advantage sign to produce positive token weights with unit global mean. These detached weights preserve advantage signs while modulating individual token-gradient contributions. OVC reuses existing rollouts without auxiliary reward models, process annotations, or inference-time modules. Instantiated through GSPO-token, OVC retains sequence-level clipping and consistently improves six-benchmark mean accuracy over GSPO across three models, with gains of 1.86-2.39 percentage points.
authors: Yuhang Han, Dingning Liu, Yujie Chen, Yaojie Zhang, Jingwei Song, Zequn Yang, Xuanming Shang, Li Ding, Zhijiang Guo, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: Uniform response-level advantages can misassign credit between visual observations and later reasoning tokens.
OVC separates visual-affinity measurement from token-level credit assignment using relative visual encoding and outcome-conditioned evidence calibration.
Normalized credit allocation produces positive, unit-mean token weights while preserving the original advantage sign.
The framework reuses existing rollouts and needs no auxiliary reward model, process annotations, or inference-time module.
With GSPO-token, OVC improves mean accuracy across six benchmarks and three models by 1.86–2.39 percentage points over GSPO.
papers.selection_reason: Token-level credit assignment for multimodal RLVR; improves multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: From Visual Affinity to Learning Credit in Multimodal Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: OVC improves multimodal RL credit assignment by using outcome-conditioned visual evidence to weight tokens without changing their advantage signs or requiring extra supervision.

papers.abstract: Geographic regions are multimodal: satellite imagery captures visual morphology, text conveys human-interpretable semantics, and map structures describe urban context. Existing geospatial contrastive methods typically align image-text or image-location pairs, underusing structured map data. We introduce GeoLEON-CLIP, a graph-anchored contrastive framework that aligns three views of each H3-indexed region: an OpenStreetMap-derived graph embedding, a satellite image crop, and a textual description. Frozen pretrained LEON graph embeddings provide a semantic anchor between vision and language. Frozen graph, image, and text encoders are connected by trainable residual projection heads and trained with a symmetric tri-modal contrastive objective. Experiments show strong graph-image and graph-text alignment; graph-image retrieval achieves the best cross-modal performance in a mixed-resolution pool. To evaluate the anchoring hypothesis, we propose chained cross-modal recall $\mathrm{R}@A@B$, which routes retrieval through the graph modality and compares it with direct retrieval under a matched candidate budget. At $\mathrm{R}@1@1$, image$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$text and text$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$image outperform direct image-text retrieval by 4.8 and 4.4 points, respectively, despite using a single intermediate cell. Downstream probes show task-dependent gains, with the largest improvements on Airbnb and Beijing housing. These results indicate that OpenStreetMap graph structure can anchor multimodal representations combining maps, imagery, and language.
authors: Radoslaw Malek, Szymon Soltysiak, Aleksandra Kawala-Sterniuk, Piotr Szymanski
bullets: Addresses the underuse of structured map data in geospatial multimodal representation learning.
Aligns H3-indexed regions across OSM-derived graph embeddings, satellite image crops, and textual descriptions.
Uses frozen pretrained encoders with trainable residual projection heads and a symmetric tri-modal contrastive objective.
Introduces chained cross-modal recall, routing image–text retrieval through the graph modality under a matched candidate budget.
Graph-mediated retrieval improves R@1@1 over direct image–text retrieval by 4.8 and 4.4 points; downstream gains are task-dependent and largest on Airbnb and Beijing housing.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a graph-anchored contrastive framework that aligns map, image, and text modalities for geographic regions, effectively modeling spatial relationships and multimodal integration.
papers.title: GeoLEON-CLIP: Graph-Anchored Multimodal Contrastive Learning for Geographic Region Representation
papers.tldr: GeoLEON-CLIP uses OpenStreetMap graph structure to anchor contrastive alignment among satellite imagery, text, and geographic regions, improving routed cross-modal retrieval and some downstream probes.

papers.abstract: 3D MLLMs recognize objects via pattern matching, which fails when geometrically similar objects require functional reasoning to disambiguate (e.g., dresser vs. wardrobe). Our per-sample Geometric Confusion Score (GCS) exposes this failure: baseline accuracy is 33.7% on ModelNet40's most ambiguous 20% versus 84.0% on its least ambiguous 20%. We identify a function-as-annotation pattern, in which functional language decorates a known identity instead of supporting inference, and hypothesize that reversing this information flow should concentrate improvements on the most ambiguous samples. PFIR (Part-level Functional Inference for Recognition) reverses that flow. Built on PartNeXt part segmentation, its data pipeline produces 507K QA pairs with functional CoTs (geometry $\to$ function $\to$ identity), and its progressive curriculum culminates in dual-objective GRPO: strict functional reasoning and descriptive grounding for Objaverse's diverse distribution. The two RL objectives yield nearly orthogonal task vectors ($\cos = 0.056$), enabling composition via Task Arithmetic. Under a strict dual OOD protocol (Objaverse $\to$ ModelNet40; XYZRGB $\to$ XYZ-only), PFIR raises zero-shot accuracy from 60.5% to 66.7%, with gains concentrated $2.6\times$ more on geometrically ambiguous samples---supporting part-level functional reasoning as an effective route to more generalizable 3D recognition. Code: https://github.com/this233/pfir-3d.
authors: Weihong Li, Hao Jiang, Yaohua Zha, Tao Dai, Shu-Tao Xia
bullets: Pattern-matching 3D MLLMs struggle to distinguish geometrically similar objects, with accuracy dropping sharply on highly ambiguous samples.
The method reverses the usual information flow: geometry → function → identity, using part-level segmentation and functional chain-of-thought supervision.
PFIR trains on 507K functional QA pairs with a progressive curriculum and combines functional reasoning with descriptive grounding through dual-objective GRPO.
Under Objaverse→ModelNet40 and XYZRGB→XYZ-only zero-shot evaluation, accuracy improves from 60.5% to 66.7%.
Improvements are concentrated 2.6× more on geometrically ambiguous samples, supporting part-level functional reasoning for recognition.
papers.selection_reason: Part-level functional reasoning in 3D MLLMs to improve generalizable 3D recognition; relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Beyond Pattern Matching in 3D MLLMs: Part-Level Functional Reasoning for Generalizable Recognition
papers.tldr: PFIR improves generalizable 3D object recognition by inferring function from parts before identifying the object, especially in geometrically ambiguous cases.

papers.abstract: Single-image 3D scene construction is a fundamental problem in 3D vision. Recent methods such as SAM-3Dfy enable end-to-end reconstruction of 3D assets and their scene layouts, but still struggle with fine-grained scene geometry and asset quality. Meanwhile, specialized 3D object generators provide detailed object geometry, while 3D foundation models offer strong and generalizable spatial understanding. We propose Easy-3Dfy, a compositional workflow that decouples object generation from scene layout estimation, allowing specialized models to fully exploit their respective strengths. An RPF-based aligner then bridges these capabilities by establishing geometric correspondence between object-local meshes and partial scene pointmaps, recovering object layout for scene composition. Without requiring complete scene-level supervision, the proposed workflow consistently outperforms SAM-3Dfy across multiple geometric metrics on Scene-Maker and 3D-FUTURE200. Our results demonstrate that explicit geometric composition can effectively combine high-quality object generation with strong spatial understanding, while enabling the workflow to benefit independently from advances in both 3D object generation and foundation models.
authors: Ziang Zhang, Wenyou Yi, Zehan Wang, Jiachen Xu, Xintong Han, Chunchao Guo, Zhou Zhao
bullets: Targets limitations in fine-grained scene geometry and asset quality in existing end-to-end methods such as SAM-3Dfy.
Uses specialized 3D object generators for object geometry and 3D foundation models for spatial understanding.
An RPF-based aligner matches object-local meshes with partial scene pointmaps to recover object layouts.
Requires no complete scene-level supervision and outperforms SAM-3Dfy across multiple geometric metrics on Scene-Maker and 3D-FUTURE200.
Its modular design can independently benefit from advances in object generation and foundation models.
papers.selection_reason: Single-image 3D scene construction via geometric composition, linking 3D object generation with spatial understanding from foundation models.
papers.title: Easy-3Dfy: Object-Level Geometric Composition for Single-Image 3D Scene Construction
papers.tldr: Easy-3Dfy improves single-image 3D scene reconstruction by separately generating detailed objects and estimating their spatial layout, then aligning them geometrically for composition.

papers.abstract: Screen Tables and Substrate Scopes are information-dense figures widely used in synthetic chemistry literature, yet automated extraction of structured reaction data from them remains challenging. We introduce RxnExBench, a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained reaction-level evaluation. Built from high-impact chemistry journals, it contains 3,565 expert-annotated reactions and 2,361 molecular structures. The dataset adopts a unified schema with 15 reaction roles and 26 core fields, supporting downstream AI-for-Chemistry tasks such as retrosynthetic planning, yield prediction, and reaction condition recommendation. RxnExBench further provides a reasoning-driven difficulty taxonomy, a modular annotation pipeline, and the Oracle-MolRec protocol, which disentangles molecular recognition from higher-level reasoning. Evaluation of 9 state-of-the-art VLMs shows that performance degrades substantially as schema complexity and reasoning demands increase. Under the Oracle-MolRec setting, results further reveal that accurate molecular recognition alone is insufficient, with multimodal integration and chemistry-aware reasoning remaining the primary bottlenecks. We release all data and code to facilitate future research in chemistry-aware multimodal understanding and AI-for-Chemistry dataset construction. The dataset and code will be released at https://github.com/opendatalab/RxnExBench.
authors: Jiaxing Sun, Junyuan Gao, Ruikang Zhang, Hao Zheng, Lingli Ge, Xiao An, Jiang Wu, Huazheng Zeng, Jiahe Song, Chen Zhu, Haote Yang, Jingchao Wang, Lu Chen, Yuanyuan Cao, Ruijie Zhang, Shengxin Lu, Weijia Li, Lijun Wu, Conghui He
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 3,565 expert-annotated reactions and 2,361 molecular structures from high-impact chemistry journals.
Uses a unified schema covering 15 reaction roles and 26 core fields for fine-grained reaction-level evaluation.
Adds a reasoning-based difficulty taxonomy, modular annotation pipeline, and Oracle-MolRec protocol to separate molecular recognition from reasoning.
Evaluation across 9 state-of-the-art VLMs shows performance drops with greater schema complexity and reasoning demands.
Data and code are released to support chemistry-aware multimodal understanding and AI-for-Chemistry research.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks vision-language models for structured multimodal chemical reaction extraction.
papers.title: RxnExBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Structured Chemical Reaction Extraction from Scientific Literature
papers.tldr: RxnExBench benchmarks how well vision-language models extract structured chemical reactions from dense literature figures, showing that chemistry-aware multimodal reasoning—not just molecule recognition—is the main challenge.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to ground generated text in the correct image regions, and existing explainability methods, such as attention maps and Logit Lens, often produce poor spatial explanations due to weak text-to-vision attention and sink tokens. We propose \textbf{Angular Relevance} ($R_L$), a simple visualization measure based on cosine similarity between visual token embeddings and unembedding-matrix rows. Because $R_L$ is invariant to token norm, it produces substantially sharper and more faithful heatmaps than attention maps or Logit Lens on out-of-the-box models. Without any training, $R_L$ yields competitive referring-expression segmentation (RES), outperforming prior diagnostic maps and CLIP-based training-free methods. To preserve localized object information during cross-modal mixing, we introduce \textbf{Angular Object-Aware Loss (AOL)}, an auxiliary loss that directly supervises visual token embeddings to align angularly with the vocabulary directions of their corresponding object concepts. Finetuning with AOL alongside the standard next-token prediction objective significantly sharpens object localization in heatmaps, showing that the VLM's own visual tokens can be used directly for grounding and improving RES, without training any segmentation heads and without degrading general VQA performance. We further demonstrate that the learned grounding also transfers to category-level segmentation of object categories not seen during training.
bullets: Addresses weak text-to-image grounding and poor spatial explanations from attention maps and Logit Lens.
Introduces Angular Relevance, a cosine-similarity measure between visual token embeddings and vocabulary unembedding directions.
Uses Angular Object-Aware Loss to supervise visual tokens toward the vocabulary directions of corresponding object concepts.
Achieves competitive referring-expression segmentation without training and improves localization after finetuning with AOL.
Grounding transfers to unseen object categories for category-level segmentation; scope is demonstrated in autoregressive VLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Improves visual grounding in autoregressive VLMs via angular supervision and auxiliary loss; directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Angular Supervision for Visual Object Grounding in Autoregressive Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Angular Relevance enables sharper, training-free visual grounding, while Angular Object-Aware Loss improves object localization and segmentation in autoregressive VLMs without adding segmentation heads or harming VQA.

papers.abstract: Effective multimodal reasoning requires a model to reliably utilize visual information while sufficiently exploring diverse reasoning paths. To achieve this goal, prior work combines visual dependency and token entropy to reshape sequence-level advantages, but scaling the contribution of token entropy by visual dependency can leave high-entropy tokens with low visual dependency underweighted, despite their important role in reasoning exploration. To address this limitation, we propose PEAR, an adaptive advantage reshaping method for improving perception and exploration in multimodal reasoning. PEAR retains visual dependency as the base signal and adds an entropy-based exploration gain only at high-entropy positions, with lower visual dependency leading to a larger additional gain. The fused signal is then mapped to positive token-level weights that reshape the sequence-level advantage. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B show that PEAR achieves the highest average performance among evaluated baselines across multimodal reasoning benchmarks, alongside leading results on textual reasoning and general multimodal benchmarks.
authors: Junxin Wang, Yingfeng Luo, Xiangchen Song, Weiqiao Shan, Runsong Zhao, Xinyu Liu, Shunjie Xing, Yifu Huo, Dingyang Lin, Qiuyu Gu, Yongyu Mu, Chenglong Wang, Changliang Li, Jingbo Zhu, Tong Xiao
bullets: Addresses the underweighting of high-entropy, low-visual-dependency tokens in prior advantage-reshaping methods.
Uses visual dependency as the base signal and adds an entropy-based exploration gain selectively at high-entropy positions.
Maps the combined signal to positive token-level weights for reshaping sequence-level advantages.
Evaluated on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, PEAR achieves the highest average performance among tested baselines across multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
Also reports leading results on textual reasoning and general multimodal benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Improves perception and exploration in large vision-language models via adaptive advantage reshaping.
papers.title: PEAR: Adaptive Advantage Reshaping for Perception and Exploration in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: PEAR improves multimodal reasoning by adaptively boosting high-entropy tokens that have low visual dependency, encouraging both better perception and broader exploration.

papers.abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $\Psi$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $\Psi$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $\Psi$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.
authors: Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Baihan Zhang, Yifan Liu, Lilian Chen, Atlas Kazemian, Rahul Venkatesh, Daniel Yamins
bullets: Interleaves images, text, geometry, and motion representations as composable “streams of thought” through a shared token interface.
Performs zero-shot multi-view spatial reasoning and benefits from explicit geometric intermediate reasoning.
Supports counterfactual simulation, such as predicting whether moving an object would block a path.
Reinforcement learning from task feedback improves intermediate-representation selection and visual question answering, with gains transferring to unseen benchmarks.
The abstract focuses on adaptive physical reasoning; specific limitations and quantitative results are not reported.
papers.selection_reason: Unified vision-language world model with geometric/spatial reasoning and counterfactual simulation directly fits world models, spatial intelligence, and 3D reasoning.
papers.title: $\Psi$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
papers.tldr: Ψ-0.6 is a unified vision-language world model that adaptively combines visual, linguistic, geometric, and simulated reasoning for flexible physical-world inference.

papers.abstract: Hyperbolic vision-language models are well suited to modeling the hierarchical structure of multimodal data, because hyperbolic volume grows exponentially with radius, enabling low-distortion representations of tree-like taxonomies from general to specific concepts. However, existing pretraining objectives for hyperbolic vision-language models entangle semantic alignment with entailment modeling, forcing radial coordinates to simultaneously encode semantic matching and hierarchical structure, leading to conflicting geometric constraints. In this paper, we introduce AURORA, a hyperbolic vision-language framework that decouples the objectives through angular alignment and a novel Radial-Angular Order Cone (RAOC) for entailment modeling. Angular alignment captures semantic similarity while preserving the radial structure for representing hierarchies. Unlike conventional entailment cones, RAOC determines angular allowance from relative parent-child radial gaps. It is incorporated into hierarchical entailment contrastive training to capture partial-order relations. We further introduce a norm regularization term that prevents undesirable radial degeneration for stable training. We train models on millions of image-text pairs and evaluate them across zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, hierarchical reasoning, and compositional understanding. Our model consistently outperforms strong Euclidean and hyperbolic vision-language baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of decoupling semantic alignment from hierarchical entailment modeling.
authors: Mingyang Gao, Yuwei Wu, Shiyu Luo, Wei Wu, Xiaomeng Fan, Qihao Lv, Haoyu Zhang, Rui Gao, Bingzhen Liu, Zhi Gao, Che Sun
bullets: Hyperbolic models can represent tree-like multimodal taxonomies efficiently, but existing objectives entangle alignment and hierarchy in radial coordinates.
AURORA uses angular alignment for semantic similarity while preserving radial structure for hierarchical organization.
Its Radial-Angular Order Cone (RAOC) models entailment using angular allowances based on parent–child radial gaps.
Hierarchical entailment contrastive training and norm regularization support partial-order learning and stable radial representations.
Evaluations on zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, hierarchical reasoning, and compositional understanding show consistent gains over Euclidean and hyperbolic baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Hyperbolic vision-language model decoupling alignment and entailment, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Separating Angular Alignment from Radial Ordering in Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: AURORA separates semantic similarity from hierarchical entailment in hyperbolic vision-language representations, improving performance across several multimodal understanding tasks.

papers.abstract: Complex text-to-image requests remain difficult to satisfy reliably. Verifying and repairing an image can fix an individual output, but a successful repair does not necessarily carry over to other requests. We present ImageRSI, a framework that keeps the image generator frozen and combines three components: five-dimensional verification and repair within each task, an experience library shared across tasks, and offline updating of the judge. Candidate experiences enter the library only after paired A/B validation, and the judge is updated with supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on accumulated image-judgment records and evaluated before reuse. We also introduce ImageReq-Bench, a benchmark of 961 requests built around hard cases in real-world image-generation requests, each paired with an evaluation checklist. ImageRSI achieves a Checklist Strict Accuracy (CSA) of 52.6% on MindBench (with Nano Banana Pro as the generator) and 65.66% on ImageReq-Bench, and we compare system outcomes across judge-training configurations.
authors: Shuo Han, Zhilin Wang, Peng Ling, Wenjia Gong, Yang Liu, Guanjun Jiang, Yukun Cao, Xike Xie
bullets: Targets unreliable satisfaction of complex text-to-image requests and limited transfer of successful repairs across tasks.
Uses a frozen image generator with five-dimensional verification and repair, a shared experience library, and an offline-updated judge.
Adds experiences only after paired A/B validation; trains and evaluates the judge on accumulated image-judgment records before reuse.
Introduces ImageReq-Bench, containing 961 difficult real-world image requests with evaluation checklists.
Reports 52.6% CSA on MindBench and 65.66% on ImageReq-Bench, and compares different judge-training configurations.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses agentic image generation with verification and self-improvement, relevant to multimodal foundation models and agents.
papers.title: ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation
papers.tldr: ImageRSI improves agentic image generation through verified repair, cross-task experience reuse, and offline judge updating, achieving strong checklist-based accuracy on two benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) can assess cognitive impairment (CI) from speech, yet their answers reveal neither which internal components control the decision nor how much CI information is accessible in their representations. We investigate both questions through CI-contrast neurons (CICNs), selected by class-contrastive activation frequency in decoder MLPs. Across eight open LALMs and two corpora (Pitt and PROCESS-2), we causally test CICNs against size- and layer-matched random masks and activity-matched controls. In three of the five models that meet our eligibility criteria, ablation of small CICN sets causes large, class-directed prediction shifts; speech-identified masks also control transcript-only decisions, and three of four primary Pitt masks retain specificity on PROCESS-2. Position-restricted interventions locate the influence before the final answer position, most strongly after the speech or transcript evidence under letter-labeled options, largely as a decision-direction shift. Beyond causal localization, supervised linear readouts of frozen CICN activations achieve 0.92--0.97 AUC within Pitt, versus 0.67--0.84 for the models' direct answers. Matched random and all-neuron readouts reach comparable performance; top-ranked CICNs show only an exploratory advantage at very small unit budgets. These results distinguish concentrated causal control over output decisions from broadly distributed diagnostic information for CI detection in LALMs.
authors: Xiutian Zhao, Luqi Sun, Bj\"orn Schuller, Berrak Sisman
bullets: The study identifies cognitive-impairment contrast neurons (CICNs) in decoder MLPs across eight open LALMs using two speech corpora.
Ablating small CICN sets produces large, class-directed prediction shifts in 3 of 5 eligible models, including transcript-only decisions.
Interventions localize influence before the final answer position, especially after speech or transcript evidence, mainly by shifting decision direction.
Frozen CICN activations support strong within-Pitt linear readouts (0.92–0.97 AUC), but matched random and all-neuron readouts perform similarly.
Findings separate concentrated causal control of outputs from broadly distributed information useful for CI detection; CICN unit-budget advantages remain exploratory.
papers.selection_reason: Causal interpretability of large audio-language models fits multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Concentrated Causal Influence, Distributed Diagnostic Information: Cognitive Impairment Decisions in Large Audio-Language Models
papers.tldr: In LALMs, a small set of neurons can causally steer cognitive-impairment decisions, while diagnostic information is broadly distributed across representations.

papers.abstract: This paper introduces Sense-Aligned Grounding Evaluation (SAGE), a unified 10-candidate image-selection benchmark that reformulates VWSD, VerSe, and WikiDiverse into a shared term-centric protocol covering noun-, verb-, and entity-centered grounding. SAGE includes confusable hard negatives and a context-swapped VerSe diagnostic to probe target-term grounding beyond direct caption--image compatibility. We further propose Gloss-Augmented Reasoning (GAR), a training-free framework combining definition grounding with constraint-guided semantic verification. Experiments show that strong VWSD performance does not transfer uniformly across grounding settings. With Gemma3-12B, definition augmentation improves all three subsets, while constraint-guided reasoning improves VWSD and yields particularly strong gains on VerSe, but is less effective on WikiDiverse. Combining the two signals achieves the best macro-average performance, improving Hits@1 from 65.90 to 71.22. These results show that SAGE supports both unified evaluation and fine-grained analysis of explicit semantic reasoning across grounding settings.
authors: Sunjae Kwon, Suhaas Kiran DG, Zonghai Yao, Talha Chafekar, Deepali Singh, Hong Yu
bullets: Recasts VWSD, VerSe, and WikiDiverse as a shared 10-candidate, term-centric benchmark covering nouns, verbs, and entities.
