The refinement stage then optimizes merge coefficients in the recovered low-dimensional subspace. Both stages use a style-aware kernel, allowing preference information to transfer between visually similar adapters. In simulated-user image-matching experiments, HimmBO achieves higher final similarity than all comparisons while reaching a given similarity with under one tenth of the image generations required by prior work. Its performance remains stable as the collection grows to 1080 adapters, while competing methods degrade substantially.
authors: Jinyuan Mao, Zhihao Shen, Chenxi Liu
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited scale of interactive adapter-merging methods for text-to-image models.
Uses level-set estimation on pre-generated images to identify an active adapter subset without generating new images.
Refines merge coefficients in the recovered low-dimensional subspace using a style-aware kernel that transfers preferences across similar adapters.
In simulated-user image-matching experiments, it achieves higher final similarity and reaches target similarity with fewer than one-tenth the image generations of prior methods.
Remains stable with collections of up to 1,080 adapters, whereas competing methods degrade substantially.
papers.selection_reason: Preference-driven adapter merging for text-to-image models is relevant to multimodal foundation model adaptation and efficiency.
papers.title: HimmBO: High-Dimensional Interactive Model-Merging Bayesian Optimization for Image Generation
papers.tldr: HimmBO efficiently optimizes image-generation adapter merges at large scale by screening relevant adapters without new image generation, then refining their coefficients with preference-based Bayesian optimization.

papers.abstract: Ambiguity is a central feature of natural communication: a sentence, image, or sound may remain underspecified until evidence from the other channels is considered. Yet current multimodal benchmarks mostly test perception, recognition, or reasoning over already determinate inputs, leaving unclear whether omni-modal large language models can resolve ambiguity distributed across text, vision, and audio. We introduce TRIAD, a benchmark for omni-modal ambiguity resolution. Each item is a text--image--audio triplet paired with a question and a set of answer options, and is constructed so that the full triplet determines a unique answer while removing any one modality makes the set of consistent options non-unique. TRIAD contains $327$ hand-written queries in $86$ scene groups and covers $18$ ambiguity categories across the three modalities. Evaluating $14$ omni-modal systems reveals that strong item-level performance does not translate into robust scene-level disambiguation: the best model still trails humans by over $20$ points in group accuracy. Removing answer options widens the gap further, driving model group accuracy to the single digits while humans remain robust. Leave-one-out and transcript/description counterfactuals further show that current systems often underuse audio cues when text and image are present. TRIAD reframes omni-modal evaluation around disambiguation rather than recognition, and provides a taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocol for measuring this capability.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Yidi Wang, Yile Li, Siqi Zeng, Yingjie He, Richeng Xuan, Zhichao hu
bullets: Introduces 327 hand-written text–image–audio queries across 86 scene groups and 18 ambiguity categories.
Each item has a unique answer only when all three modalities are available; removing one leaves multiple plausible answers.
Evaluations of 14 omni-modal systems show strong item-level results but substantially weaker scene-level disambiguation than humans.
Models rely insufficiently on audio, especially when text and images are present; removing answer options worsens performance sharply.
Provides an ambiguity taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocols for evaluating cross-modal disambiguation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an omni-modal ambiguity-resolution benchmark and diagnostic protocol for multimodal LLMs across text, image, and audio.
papers.title: TRIAD: Benchmarking Omni-Modal Ambiguity in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: TRIAD benchmarks whether multimodal large language models can resolve ambiguity that requires jointly using text, images, and audio.

papers.abstract: Long chain-of-thought reasoning improves vision-language models (VLMs), but it also exposes a temporal grounding failure: as generation unfolds, models may drift from image evidence while reinforcement learning still provides only a final-answer reward. We study this gap through visual revisit, a temporally localized reactivation of image evidence during reasoning. Across three VLM backbones, revisit peaks are predictive of correctness and causally linked to performance: masking them degrades accuracy more than masking non-peaks, while injecting revisit-like peaks into failed rollouts partially restores correct answers. Control analyses show that this signal is not explained by raw attention strength, uncertainty, logit margin, or hidden-state norm. We propose RECAP, a GRPO-compatible training method that turns detached revisit traces into a credit-assignment signal. RECAP uses revisit-conditioned advantage estimation, dynamic discounting, and gated value prediction to propagate final rewards through visually important reasoning steps, without extra rewards, additional rollouts, or inference-time changes. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, and LLaVA-OV-7B, RECAP consistently improves over GRPO and VPPO, yielding $+6.1$--$+6.5$ HallusionBench gains over the SFT base while preserving reasoning and text-only performance. Results on larger LoRA-tuned models, Chinese zero-shot benchmarks, visual perturbations, and human evaluation further demonstrate robust improvements in image-grounded reasoning.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Tailong Luo, Chenxin Li, Yingjie He, Zhenyu Yu, Fengyu Zhou, Jiachen Qian, Lei Wei, Shuang Chen, Jiachen Li, Eric Hanchen Jiang, Rongchao Zhang, Zhengtao Yao, Hoi Leong Lee, Guansu Wang, Kaiyue Zhou
bullets: Long chain-of-thought can cause VLMs to drift from visual evidence because training often rewards only the final answer.
Visual revisit peaks predict correctness and are causally important: masking them hurts accuracy, while adding them can recover some failed answers.
RECAP uses revisit-conditioned advantages, dynamic discounting, and gated value prediction within GRPO, without extra rewards, rollouts, or inference-time changes.
Across three VLM backbones, RECAP improves over GRPO and VPPO, including +6.1–+6.5 HallusionBench points over the SFT base.
Additional evaluations support robustness across larger LoRA-tuned models, Chinese zero-shot benchmarks, visual perturbations, and human judgments.
papers.selection_reason: Improves image-grounded reasoning in VLMs by leveraging visual revisit signals during long chain-of-thought, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: RECAP: Looking Once Is Not Enough for Vision-Language Reasoning
papers.tldr: RECAP improves vision-language reasoning by using moments when models revisit image evidence to better assign credit during reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Visual perception should be iterative and task-directed, with representations refined in response to the question and the need for further processing. While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly support extended reasoning, their visual tokens are still typically acquired in a single, task-agnostic encoder pass. This creates an evidence-acquisition bottleneck: models may reason longer without refining the visual evidence needed to answer the question. We propose LoopLook, a lightweight encoder-side recurrent perception framework that equips pretrained VLMs with adaptive visual depth. LoopLook recurrently revisits a middle-to-late window of the vision encoder, injecting question representations at each loop to guide visual refinement. A learned stopping mechanism adaptively determines the recurrent depth, while a token-wise Mixture-of-Looks (MoL) combines representations from different loops, allowing each visual token to selectively integrate information acquired across recurrent steps. Across four backbones and eight benchmarks, LoopLook consistently improves performance over the baseline, yielding gains of up to 8.6% on MMStar and 8.1% on HallusionBench. Our analysis shows that LoopLook progressively refines visual attention and adaptively allocates depth according to task difficulty. It also better preserves task-relevant visual information under reduced input resolution, while increasing time to first token (TTFT) by only 5.1-6.5%. By bringing recurrence from reasoning back into perception, LoopLook transforms visual perception from a one-shot glimpse into an adaptive process of recurrent refinement.
authors: Wencheng Ye, Anning Hu, Hongye Fang, Tianyi Wang, Junchi Yan
bullets: Addresses the evidence-acquisition bottleneck caused by one-pass, task-agnostic visual encoding.
Recurrently revisits a middle-to-late vision-encoder window, injecting question representations to guide refinement.
Uses learned adaptive stopping and token-wise Mixture-of-Looks to select and combine information across loops.
Improves results across four backbones and eight benchmarks, with gains of up to 8.6% on MMStar and 8.1% on HallusionBench.
Allocates more depth to difficult tasks, preserves relevant information at lower resolution, and increases TTFT by 5.1–6.5%.
papers.selection_reason: Adds recurrent question-guided visual refinement to pretrained VLMs, improving multimodal reasoning and perception.
papers.title: Loop to Look Better: Learning Adaptive Depth for Question-Guided Perception in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: LoopLook enables VLMs to adaptively revisit and refine visual representations based on the question, improving performance with modest inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly embedded in software systems. Testing them raises two problems. Mutating either input can change the expected answer, so an output change is not by itself a failure. Some failures appear only when both inputs are mutated; attributing them to the combination requires testing each mutation alone. We present VLTest, a black-box VLM testing approach. It generates image variants by editing VQGAN latent codes and text variants with a rewrite-expand-prune pipeline, filters variants likely to change the expected answer, and tests each variant alone before testing combinations, so every joint failure has four matched cells. A VLM judge confirms a failure only after checking that the input keeps the expected answer. On three tasks with eight VLMs, including two commercial API models, the oracle confirms 81.7% of the candidates, with 88.8% to 94.6% precision against human labels, and four-cell confirmation rejects 22.5% of joint candidates. Under the same budget, VLTest's generators find 1.8 to 2.5 times as many confirmed failures as SINVAD and TextFooler, and its joint tests find 91 to 197 attributed joint failures per 1,000 joint calls, 1.3 times as many as the same pairing applied to the baselines' variants.
authors: Bin Duan, Jintao Lin, Guowei Yang
bullets: Generates image variants via VQGAN latent-code editing and text variants through rewrite, expansion, and pruning.
Filters variants likely to preserve the expected answer, then tests image-only, text-only, and combined mutations in four matched cells.
Uses a VLM judge to confirm failures while checking answer preservation; it confirms 81.7% of candidates with 88.8–94.6% precision against human labels.
Across three tasks and eight VLMs, VLTest finds 1.8–2.5× more confirmed failures than SINVAD and TextFooler under the same budget.
Four-cell confirmation rejects 22.5% of joint candidates and enables attribution of failures specifically to image-text interactions.
papers.selection_reason: Black-box testing of vision-language models for joint image-text failures; relevant to VLM reliability and robustness.
papers.title: VLTest: Finding Joint Image-Text Failures in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: VLTest black-box tests vision-language models for reliable image-text and joint-input failures using matched single- and combined-mutation checks.

papers.abstract: Mixing requires not only applying processing but also assessing the resulting mix. Audio-language models can provide conversa- tional mixing advice, but existing evaluations do not separately test whether they can judge specific mixing issues. Since professional supervision for such judgments is scarce, we construct a curriculum of 11 vocal-mix issues at multiple severity levels and use it to train MixJudge, a language-queryable audio critic. MixJudge shows its ability to retrieve mixing issues, distinguish opposite issues, and order the severity of an issue. Moreover, its judgments transfer to menu selection: given a set of processing candidates, MixJudge often favors versions acoustically closer to a held-out professional version, demonstrating how explicit mixing judgment can support comparison and downstream mixing decisions.
authors: Kuan-Hsun Ho, Yuan-Chiao Cheng, Yen-Tung Yeh, Yi-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the lack of separate evaluation and professional supervision for specific vocal-mixing judgments.
Uses a curriculum covering 11 vocal-mix issues across multiple severity levels.
Can retrieve requested issues, distinguish opposing issues, and order issue severity.
Its judgments transfer to processing-menu selection, often favoring candidates acoustically closer to a held-out professional mix.
Scope: focuses on vocal-mix issues and comparative downstream selection; the abstract does not quantify performance.
papers.selection_reason: A language-queryable audio critic is a multimodal language model with transferable relevance to multimodal foundation-model evaluation and instruction following.
papers.title: MixJudge: Learning a Language-Queryable Critic for Vocal Mixing
papers.tldr: MixJudge is a language-queryable audio critic trained to identify, distinguish, and rank the severity of vocal-mixing issues, with judgments that help select better processing options.

papers.abstract: Complex camera motion is central to visual storytelling, yet translating cinematographic intent into controllable, executable camera trajectories remains challenging. We introduce FilmFlow, an agentic framework that converts natural-language instructions or reference videos into explicit camera trajectories for dynamic 3D environments. To generate these trajectories, a Director agent constructs executable camera plans by composing high-level motions from concurrent atomic operations that jointly control translation, rotation, and framing. The Director is supported by three specialized agents: an Interpreter that extracts scene-grounded cinematographic intent, a Scout that selects initial viewpoints, and a Critic that evaluates rendered results and provides visual feedback for iterative plan refinement. We also introduce CinemaBench, comprising 150 Blender scenes from self-created and licensed sources, with five camera instructions per scene for 750 text-directed tasks and 60 reference videos associated with a subset of scenes. CinemaBench supports evaluation of both text-directed camera generation and video reference-directed camera generation. Across a diverse set of evaluated baselines, FilmFlow achieves the strongest benchmark performance and the highest user preference, demonstrating effective spatial reasoning, temporal coordination, and visual composition for executable 3D cinematography.
authors: Yiming Zhang, Jiarui Guo, Haojia Wei, Yifei Liu, Yifan Yang, Hongjie Zhang, Xue Yang, Zhihang Zhong
bullets: Addresses the challenge of translating cinematographic intent into controllable camera motion in dynamic 3D scenes.
A Director agent composes high-level camera plans from concurrent atomic operations controlling translation, rotation, and framing.
Interpreter, Scout, and Critic agents extract intent, choose viewpoints, and iteratively refine plans using rendered visual feedback.
Introduces CinemaBench with 150 Blender scenes, 750 text-directed tasks, and 60 reference videos for evaluating 3D camera generation.
Reports the strongest performance across evaluated baselines and the highest user preference, indicating effective spatial reasoning, temporal coordination, and composition.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic system translating language into 3D camera trajectories, involving spatial reasoning and 3D-aware multimodal understanding.
papers.title: FilmFlow: Agentic System for 3D Virtual Film Cinematography
papers.tldr: FilmFlow is a multi-agent system that turns text or reference videos into executable, cinematographically coherent 3D camera trajectories.

papers.abstract: Shadows are observable consequences of latent physical causes, arising from the interaction between illumination, object geometry, and scene structure. A model that understands shadows should be able not only to read a shadow's direction, but also to infer where a shadow should fall when it is absent, and to judge whether a shadow is physically consistent with the scene. We introduce ShadowBench, built from real photographs, which poses these three questions to vision-language models (VLMs). From each scene, we build a correct-shadow, a shadow-removed, and a human-annotated wrong-direction state. Evaluating 19 open VLMs (2B to 78B) and frontier proprietary models, we find that VLMs read a visible shadow's direction well above chance and improve with scale, yet infer the absent direction only weakly and fall to chance at judging physical consistency even under a bias-free two-alternative test that removes the yes-bias of single-image naturalness questions. Only Gemini-3.1-pro exceeds chance on validity, and even then only modestly and far below humans. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) does not help. The missing ingredient is not reasoning but knowledge that image generation models (IGMs) already hold. Routing a VLM through an IGM lifts its inference well above its direct attempt and helps it flag the wrong-direction shadows it otherwise accepts. Cast-shadow direction is a single facet of illumination understanding, but the sharp gap it reveals between VLMs and IGMs suggests image-generation or reconstruction objectives as a route toward illumination-aware VLMs.
authors: Ryugo Morita, Shunsuke Kitada, Stanislav Frolov, Brian Bernhard Moser, Ko Watanabe, Riku Takahashi, Jinjia Zhou, Andreas Dengel
bullets: ShadowBench evaluates VLMs on visible-shadow direction, absent-shadow inference, and physical-consistency judgments using real photographs with correct, removed, and human-annotated wrong-direction shadows.
Across 19 open and frontier proprietary VLMs, visible-direction reading improves with scale, but absent-direction inference is weak and validity judgments are near chance.
Only Gemini-3.1-pro exceeds chance on validity, modestly and far below human performance; Chain-of-Thought does not help.
Routing VLMs through image-generation models improves missing-shadow inference and helps identify wrong-direction shadows.
The findings suggest image-generation or reconstruction objectives may provide useful illumination knowledge for VLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and improves VLM physical/spatial reasoning about cast shadows, fitting spatial intelligence in multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Where Did the Light Come From? Diagnosing Cast-Shadow Reasoning in VLMs and Borrowing the Missing Shadow Prior from Image Generation Models
papers.tldr: VLMs can read visible shadow directions but struggle to infer missing shadows or detect physically inconsistent ones, while routing through image-generation models substantially improves these abilities.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is usually tied to the pretrained backbone on which it is learned. We ask whether LoRAs trained independently for the same task on different pretrained backbones can be summed and applied unchanged to all contributing backbones. We call this construction LoRA superposition. Across seven ViT-B/16 CLIP backbones and eight image-classification tasks, the exact sum improves all 56 backbone-task pairs and achieves a mean accuracy gain of 30.21 percentage points over the unadapted backbone. The exact sum achieves a mean accuracy only 0.28 percentage points below that of individually trained solo LoRAs. In contrast, a leave-one-model-out (LOMO) sum produces a mean gain of only 0.06 percentage points over the unadapted backbones. Backbone-specific solo LoRAs are nearly orthogonal in parameter space, while pairwise cross-backbone responses are strongly concentrated on the diagonal. These results support a component-wise non-interference hypothesis, under which the frozen backbone acts as an implicit selector of its own component without explicit routing or cross-model alignment.
authors: Keigo Watanabe, Hiroshi Kera, Kazuhiko Kawamoto
bullets: Evaluates LoRA superposition across seven ViT-B/16 CLIP backbones and eight image-classification tasks.
The exact sum improves all 56 backbone–task pairs, with a mean gain of 30.21 percentage points over unadapted backbones.
Its accuracy is only 0.28 percentage points below that of backbone-specific solo LoRAs.
Leave-one-model-out sums provide almost no benefit, suggesting the contributing model-specific components are necessary.
Near-orthogonal LoRA parameters and diagonal cross-backbone responses support a component-wise non-interference explanation without routing or alignment.
papers.selection_reason: LoRA superposition across pretrained CLIP backbones; transferable parameter-efficient adaptation idea for foundation models.
papers.title: LoRA Superposition across Pretrained Models
papers.tldr: LoRAs trained separately on different pretrained backbones can be summed and reused across those backbones with nearly the same performance as individually trained adapters.

papers.abstract: Open-world geographic artificial intelligence (GeoAI) agents can transform public geospatial data into accessible decision support for real-world challenges, but must balance autonomous reasoning with reliable spatial analysis and human oversight. We present a topology-guided GeoAI agentic framework for urban flood screening that takes a place name, drawn region, or uploaded boundary and returns ranked candidate basins with an interactive map and report. A deterministic controller retrieves public elevation, rainfall, soil, land-cover, exposure, and infrastructure layers, extracts terrain depressions with discrete Morse theory, and ranks basins with a relative flood-priority score. The language model acts only at recorded decision points: selecting a persistence threshold from a precomputed candidate table, drafting recommendations from computed evidence, and reviewing each recommendation against the same evidence. Three human-in-the-loop checkpoints let users revise the threshold, factor weights, or recommendation. In a College Park, Maryland case study, the selected threshold reduced 278 raw terrain minima to 70 basins, with 77% of these basins' lowest points also identified as sinks by a separately computed eight-direction (D8) flow-routing model. Across four further study areas, agreement ranged from 61% to 83%. By combining open data, explicit spatial reasoning, traceable evidence, and human oversight, the framework enables transparent first-pass flood screening while keeping consequential recommendations inspectable and user-controlled.
authors: Yutian Tao, Haoan Feng, Xin Xu, Leila De Floriani
bullets: Accepts place names, drawn regions, or uploaded boundaries and returns ranked candidate basins with maps and reports.
Uses public elevation, rainfall, soil, land-cover, exposure, and infrastructure data to identify terrain depressions and compute relative flood-priority scores.
Restricts the language model to traceable decision points: threshold selection, evidence-based recommendations, and recommendation review.
Provides three human checkpoints for revising the persistence threshold, factor weights, or recommendations.
In the case studies, basin identification agreed with D8 flow-routing sinks for 61%–83% of basins, including 77% in College Park, Maryland.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a topology-guided GeoAI framework for spatial reasoning and flood screening, directly utilizing spatial intelligence concepts like topology and spatial analysis.
papers.title: A Topology-Guided GeoAI Agentic Framework for Urban Flood Screening
papers.tldr: A topology-guided GeoAI agent combines deterministic spatial analysis, constrained language-model reasoning, and human oversight to provide transparent first-pass urban flood screening.

papers.abstract: Scaling large language models has substantially improved linguistic fluency, yet reliable autonomous agents require more than fluent generation. In multi-turn inference, current agentic systems often produce semantically plausible but structurally ungrounded reasoning, especially under incomplete observations. We propose Structure-Grounded Uncertainty Reduction (SGUR), a training-free framework that complements token-level generation with active uncertainty reduction over structured hypothesis spaces. SGUR represents incomplete observations as a query graph and aligns them with candidate hypothesis graphs through a prior-weighted partial graph matching mechanism, where database-derived empirical priors assign greater importance to decision-relevant relations rather than treating all graph edges uniformly. The resulting inference state is iteratively refined by an active information-gain strategy that selects the next most informative node to query, systematically pruning the candidate space. We instantiate SGUR on a challenging PrimeKG-derived sequential medical diagnosis benchmark, demonstrating that structural grounding can partially substitute for model scale: starting from only two observed symptoms, SGUR achieves 92.5% Hit@3, outperforming the strongest Graph-RAG baseline by 9.4 percentage points while using approximately 5x fewer tokens. Notably, SGUR enables smaller backbone models to match or exceed the performance of models up to 10x larger, suggesting that structural grounding provides a more robust and efficient paradigm for scaling agent performance than relying exclusively on increasing model size.
authors: Amirhossein Aghaei, Liangyan Li, Shiyi Yang, Shaohua Wang, Yan Wang
bullets: Targets structurally ungrounded reasoning in agentic systems operating with incomplete observations.
Uses a query graph, prior-weighted partial graph matching, and active information-gain queries to prune hypotheses.
Evaluated on a PrimeKG-derived sequential medical diagnosis benchmark from two observed symptoms.
Reports 92.5% Hit@3, 9.4 percentage points above the strongest Graph-RAG baseline, with about 5× fewer tokens.
Findings suggest structural grounding can let smaller models match or exceed models up to 10× larger.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a structure-grounded framework using graph matching and active information gain for reasoning, which aligns with spatial intelligence and graph-based reasoning.
papers.title: Better Reasoning, Not Just Bigger Models: A Structure-Grounded Framework for Efficient and Reliable Inference
papers.tldr: SGUR improves efficient, reliable multi-turn reasoning by actively reducing uncertainty over structured hypothesis graphs instead of relying only on larger language models.

papers.abstract: LLMs have shown strong in-context learning (ICL) capability, but extending it to Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) remains challenging. Prior multimodal ICL methods often rely on ICL-specific datasets for additional training or task vector extraction, which can improve performance on the same ICL benchmark used for adaptation. However, they do not generalize well to other benchmarks and often induce forgetting in previously well-solved tasks. For this reason, we identify 'visual grounding' as the key bottleneck in multimodal ICL; MLLMs often fail to attend to task-relevant visual evidence in demonstrations, instead over-relying on textual cues and producing hallucinated outputs. To address this, we propose ProCoRe to enhance visual grounding through contrastive reinforcement learning on multimodal contrastive data for improving multimodal ICL. ProCoRe generates captions for contrastive image pairs, decomposes them into propositions, and optimizes contrastive rewards that encourage alignment with corresponding images while discouraging mismatched ones. Despite never seeing ICL-formatted training examples, ProCoRe improves average multimodal ICL classification accuracy by 5.6% and captioning ROUGE-L by 13.8% over the off-the-shelf Qwen-VL-3-8B model, outperforming ICL-data-dependent state of the arts across benchmarks. Finally, we introduce PICL, a personalized multimodal ICL captioning benchmark that tests whether MLLMs genuinely understand visual demonstrations rather than relying on pre-trained semantic priors.
authors: Minhyuk Seo, Minjae Lee, Chaeeun Lee, Wei Lin, Muhammad Jehanzeb Mirza, Tinne Tuytelaars, Jonghyun Choi
bullets: Problem: MLLMs often rely on textual cues instead of task-relevant visual evidence in demonstrations, causing hallucinations, poor cross-benchmark generalization, and forgetting.
Method: ProCoRe uses contrastive reinforcement learning on multimodal contrastive data, rewarding captions aligned with matching images and penalizing mismatches.
Results: It improves average multimodal ICL classification accuracy by 5.6% and captioning ROUGE-L by 13.8% over Qwen-VL-3-8B.
Scope: The method is evaluated across benchmarks and compared with ICL-data-dependent approaches.
Contribution: The authors introduce PICL, a personalized captioning benchmark designed to test genuine understanding of visual demonstrations.
papers.selection_reason: Improves multimodal in-context learning by enhancing visual grounding in MLLMs via contrastive reinforcement learning, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Visual Grounding First, Multimodal In-context Learning Follows
papers.tldr: ProCoRe improves multimodal in-context learning by strengthening visual grounding without training on ICL-formatted examples.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic mapping in dynamic real-world environments is essential for embodied intelligence and long-term autonomy. However, existing methods often involve a trade-off: lightweight online mapping is efficient but captures limited semantic context, while dense mapping provides richer semantics at higher computational cost and is more vulnerable to distractors. They also struggle to relocalize objects after scene changes. To address these challenges, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS), a unified system for online mapping, complex open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments. Motivated by the observation that indoor scenes are organized around stable semantic anchors, OASIS represents the environment using a sparse set of anchor nodes, each maintaining a unified multimodal representation that integrates semantic descriptions, visual features, and geometric states for reasoning, verification, and navigation. Its compact anchor-centric memory supports on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval, reducing redundant storage while improving retrieval reliability. To handle scene dynamics, OASIS further reuses transient observations collected during navigation to relocalize moved objects. Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, including standard retrieval benchmarks and navigation tasks under both static and dynamic settings, demonstrate that our system can perform complex open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation, while also enabling relocation of displaced objects after scene changes.
authors: Kaiyao Liao, Qingfeng Li, Chen Chen, Xiaoze Wu, Qing Sun, Jianwei Niu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–semantic richness trade-off in online mapping and the difficulty of relocalizing objects after scene changes.
Represents scenes with sparse anchor nodes that combine semantic, visual, and geometric information for reasoning, verification, and navigation.
Uses on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval to reduce redundant storage while supporting complex queries.
Reuses transient navigation observations to relocalize objects that have moved.
Validated in simulation and real-world settings across retrieval benchmarks and static/dynamic navigation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Anchor-centric multimodal memory for open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation in dynamic scenes; combines spatial understanding with embodied memory.
papers.title: OASIS: Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System for Open-Vocabulary Retrieval and Navigation in Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: OASIS enables efficient open-vocabulary object retrieval and navigation in dynamic environments using a sparse, multimodal memory built around stable semantic scene anchors.

papers.abstract: LLM correctors of ASR output are judged by aggregate WER, which hides what they fix and what they break. We decompose every WER change exactly into repaired tokens, damaged tokens and insertions, and use this to ask what the source audio adds to a corrector. We compare correction with and without the audio, for the model's own draft and for the output of an independent recogniser, on three corpora. With Gemini 2.5 Flash, text-only correction of its own draft breaks 13-32% of already-correct transcripts; with the audio, 1-3%. Damage falls in both settings. Repair falls against the own draft and rises against the recogniser. On medical dictation, kept insertions cancel the gain in net WER. The open-weight Voxtral, which rarely edits, does not show this pattern. Prompts differ between the two arms, so the contrasts bound the effect of the audio and do not isolate it.
authors: Vasiliy Kudryavtsev, Kirill Borodin, Nikita Vasiliev, Mikhail Gorodnichev, Grach Mkrtchian
bullets: Aggregate WER is decomposed into repaired tokens, damaged tokens, and insertions to expose correction trade-offs.
Gemini 2.5 Flash text-only correction damages 13–32% of already-correct outputs from its own draft; adding audio reduces this to 1–3%.
Audio reduces damage in both settings, but repairs decrease on the model’s own draft and increase on an independent recognizer’s output.
On medical dictation, retained insertions offset the net WER improvement.
Voxtral rarely edits and does not exhibit the same damage pattern; differing prompts mean the audio effect is bounded rather than isolated.
papers.selection_reason: Audio-grounded LLM correction of ASR output is a multimodal LLM application, and the repair-damage decomposition is a transferable evaluation method for multimodal language models.
papers.title: Text-Only LLM Correctors Break Correct Transcripts: A Repair-Damage Analysis of Audio Grounding in ASR Error Correction
papers.tldr: Audio grounding substantially reduces the tendency of Gemini 2.5 Flash to damage already-correct ASR transcripts, but its net benefit depends on the recognizer, domain, and retained insertions.

papers.abstract: Dynamic representations based on 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) have shown strong capabilities in reconstruction and rendering, yet current methods remain limited in supporting complex natural-language referring in dynamic scenes. Existing 4D Gaussian methods are primarily designed for rendering-oriented dynamic modeling, while current semantic extensions often rely on scene-specific semantic optimization or are evaluated on relatively simple query settings. In this paper, we study Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), a task for grounding temporally varying, multi-target or reasoning-intensive, and zero-target or distractor expressions in dynamic 4D scenes. To support this task, we introduce R4D-Bench-QA, a benchmark with structured query annotations. We further present ReferGaussian, a unified framework built upon 4DGS that converts low-level dynamic Gaussians into persistent, language-addressable entities for training-free referring inference. ReferGaussian organizes mask-supported Gaussian entities in an EntityBank, uses Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to decompose complex queries into trackable object phrases and structured referring constraints, and performs constraint-aware grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization. Experiments on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol demonstrate improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding without scene-specific semantic training. Project resources are available at https://chenbangpu.github.io/R4DGS/.
authors: Bangpu Chen, Yaxuan Li, Shirui Peng, Xiangtian Si, Liuxin Chu, Xitong Cao, Hongbo Jin, Jiayu Ding
bullets: Addresses temporal, multi-target, reasoning-intensive, and zero-target or distractor referring expressions in dynamic 4D scenes.
Introduces R4D-Bench-QA with structured query annotations for evaluating referring segmentation.
ReferGaussian converts dynamic Gaussians into persistent language-addressable entities stored in an EntityBank.
MLLMs decompose queries into object phrases and referring constraints, enabling constraint-aware grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization.
Shows improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol.
papers.selection_reason: Grounds referring language in dynamic 4D Gaussian scenes via MLLM-guided decomposition and spatial entity grounding; directly relevant to spatial intelligence and 3D vision.
papers.title: R4DGS: Referring Segmentation in 4D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: R4DGS introduces a benchmark and training-free framework for grounding complex language references to dynamic objects in 4D Gaussian Splatting scenes.

papers.abstract: Visual mathematical reasoning can fail before reasoning begins: when a vision-language model (VLM) misreads a diagram, subsequent reasoning proceeds from false premises. This perceptual bottleneck is especially pronounced in smaller models, while accurate textual descriptions can substantially narrow the gap to larger models. Because obtaining such descriptions at inference requires additional annotation or model calls, we propose minimal-edit corrective on-policy distillation. Using reference figure descriptions and verified reference solutions as training-only information, a teacher scores incorrect student rollouts under a minimal-edit objective, and only teacher-disfavored tokens contribute to the corrective loss. Correct rollouts receive task-reward reinforcement learning. This preserves on-policy supervision while avoiding full-response imitation. Across model scales, the method requires no descriptions at test time and meets or exceeds the corresponding base model supplied with a reference figure description at inference. It also improves perception-oriented performance, particularly low-level geometric perception, and transfers to external mathematics and perception benchmarks. Because the minimal-edit teacher evaluates corrections rather than generating its own solution, the method remains effective with a frozen same-size teacher, although its gains are smaller than with a larger teacher on most metrics.
authors: Wen Ye, Ailin Deng, Zirui Wang, Shixing Yu, Han Zhang, Tian Yun, Nikhil Mehta, Tarun Kalluri, Xuefei Cao, Xuezhe Ma, Hengduo Li
bullets: Targets perceptual errors in visual mathematical reasoning, especially for smaller VLMs.
A teacher scores incorrect student rollouts using reference descriptions and solutions available only during training.
Only teacher-disfavored tokens receive corrective loss; correct rollouts use task-reward reinforcement learning.
Improves perception and transfers to external math and perception benchmarks across model scales.
Works with a frozen same-size teacher, though larger teachers generally provide greater gains.
papers.selection_reason: Improves vision-language model reasoning via on-policy corrective distillation, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Edit, Don't Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: Minimal-edit on-policy distillation teaches VLMs to correct visual misreadings without requiring figure descriptions or extra model calls at test time.

papers.abstract: LLMs can act as scientific agents using tools to consult specialists and run experiments. Yet specialist information must enter their context, generally as text, images, audio or video: a bottleneck between models with rich, high-dimensional representations. We advocate direct representation exchange: a mindmeld conveying many properties, including information an LLM would not think to request. It should be extensible to new specialists, flexible across questions and tasks, and compositional across independently connected specialists without joint training. The Latent Interconnect Protocol (LIP) learns connectors mapping specialist representations into LLM internal states. Training only connectors keeps this practical as LLMs grow and evolve. We connect three protein and three small molecule specialists to Gemma 3 (4B and 12B parameters) and Kimi K2.6 (1T total, 32B active), freezing all pretrained models. Independently trained connectors provide useful information without changing the LLM or existing connectors, supporting familiar and new question types about unseen objects. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to cross-domain tasks without joint training. Task performance and compositionality generally improve with LLM capability, with especially strong gains in zero-shot task transfer. Limitations remain: current LLMs were not trained for specialist representations as native inputs; access does not ensure reliable interpretation, integration or use in reasoning. We call on specialist developers to provide consistent representation interfaces and, especially, on LLM developers to train models to receive, combine and reason with these inputs. These efforts could expand scientific agents' information while preserving conventional tools' flexibility. Data, pretrained connectors, and code for training, evaluation and interactive inference: https://github.com/PolymathicAI/AI-Mindmeld
authors: Siavash Golkar, Jake Kovalic, Shirley Ho
bullets: Addresses the bottleneck of passing specialist knowledge to LLMs only through text, images, audio, or video.
Trains lightweight connectors from protein and small-molecule specialists into the internal states of Gemma 3 and Kimi K2.6, while freezing all pretrained models.
Supports independently adding specialists without joint training or modifying existing connectors, including questions about unseen objects and new task types.
Demonstrates zero-shot cross-domain transfer; performance and compositionality generally improve with greater LLM capability.
Current LLMs may not reliably interpret, integrate, or reason over specialist representations because they were not trained to receive them natively.
papers.selection_reason: Latent interconnect protocol injecting specialist representations into frozen LLMs, relevant to multimodal LLM extension.
papers.title: AI Mindmeld: A Latent Interconnect Protocol
papers.tldr: AI Mindmeld introduces LIP, a connector-based protocol that lets frozen LLMs directly combine specialist model representations for flexible, compositional scientific reasoning.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained multimodal intelligence requires models to both understand a designated region and localize it from language. Existing methods learn these directions with separate objectives and task-specific annotations. We present Generalized CycleGRPO, the first unified reinforcement learning framework coupling region understanding and localization across spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal domains. Given a region, a multimodal large language model generates candidate descriptions and then localizes each description to reconstruct the input region. Reconstruction overlap provides a verifiable reward for captioning, while individual localization rewards improve the inverse mapping. A common region-space formulation extends this cycle from image masks and boxes to video intervals and timestamped spatial evidence, without reference captions or an external language-model judge during reinforcement learning. In videos, the cycle encourages descriptions that distinguish a target event from similar recurrences. We introduce DOVE (Distinctive Occurrence-level Video-caption Evaluation), a human-verified contrastive benchmark for this temporal distinctiveness. CycleGRPO improves SAMTok's overall gIoU from 57.5% to 68.2% on GroundingSuite and average gIoU from 71.2% to 78.7% on GRES. For temporal tasks, it achieves 51.9% tIoU on Charades and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE, compared with 45.6% and 14.8% for the Qwen3-VL initialization. These results establish region-text cycle consistency as a general self-evaluation principle for multimodal understanding and localization. Models, code, and DOVE are available at https://devinxzhang.github.io/Generalized-CycleGRPO-Page/.
bullets: Addresses the need for models to describe designated regions and localize them from language using a shared objective rather than separate task-specific supervision.
Generates a description for a region, relocalizes that description, and uses reconstruction overlap plus localization rewards for self-verifiable training.
Extends a common region-space formulation to image masks/boxes, video intervals, and timestamped spatial evidence without reference captions or an external judge during RL.
Introduces DOVE, a human-verified benchmark for evaluating whether video descriptions distinguish a target event from similar recurrences.
Reports improved spatial grounding and temporal localization, including 68.2% gIoU on GroundingSuite, 78.7% on GRES, 51.9% tIoU on Charades, and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE.
papers.selection_reason: Unified region-text cycle RL for fine-grained multimodal understanding and spatial grounding directly fits MLLM and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Generalized CycleGRPO for Fine-Grained Multimodal Understanding and Grounding
papers.tldr: Generalized CycleGRPO unifies multimodal region understanding and localization through reinforcement learning with region-text cycle consistency across images and videos.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models have achieved remarkable progress in multi-modal understanding, yet their capabilities in educational settings remain insufficiently evaluated. In AI-assisted language learning, models must interpret artistic imagery, understand its semantic, affective, and cultural content, and reason about visual context to support meaningful interaction. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on real-world images or domain-specific educational reasoning, providing limited coverage of artistic educational content. To address this gap, we introduce MUSE, a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models on artistic image understanding in situated educational applications. MUSE decouples image annotation from question generation, enabling diverse tasks with controllable difficulty while reducing annotation effort. It comprises twelve tasks spanning visual perception, semantic and affective interpretation, culture understanding, and compositional reasoning, together with diverse artistic images deliberately curated to center Singaporean and Southeast Asian multicultural contexts alongside Western art traditions, covering multiple themes and difficulty levels. Evaluation of open-source and proprietary models reveals substantial disparities across capability dimensions, particularly in affective interpretation and compositional reasoning. Our analysis further identifies common failure modes and key challenges for developing trustworthy multi-modal models for education. We hope MUSE will serve as a standardized benchmark for advancing multi-modal understanding in situated educational applications.
bullets: Addresses limited evaluation of multimodal models on artistic content in education, especially language-learning contexts.
Separates image annotation from question generation to support diverse, controllable-difficulty tasks with lower annotation effort.
Covers 12 tasks spanning visual perception, semantic and affective interpretation, cultural understanding, and compositional reasoning.
Includes multicultural artistic imagery centered on Singaporean and Southeast Asian contexts alongside Western art traditions.
Finds substantial capability gaps, especially in affective interpretation and compositional reasoning, and analyzes common failure modes.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating large vision-language models on multimodal artistic-image understanding, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: MUSE: Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models on Multi-Modal Understanding in Situated Education
papers.tldr: MUSE benchmarks large vision-language models on artistic image understanding for culturally situated educational applications.

papers.abstract: Language models' abilities to interpret tasks and generate programs offer a promising basis for 3D spatial reasoning. Yet following spatial instructions in 3D scenes requires programs to construct geometric references that language leaves implicit. In this work, we introduce VoxProg, which formulates 3D object placement through voxel programming: a language model translates task interpretations into executable programs over local voxel views of scene surfaces. Because these views index surface geometry on regular grids with explicit coordinates and neighborhood relations, an evidence program can isolate task-relevant regions and boundaries directly from scene meshes, and a downstream pose program can measure the resulting geometry to compute a target $SE(3)$ pose. Visual and numerical feedback from execution lets the model inspect intermediate selections and candidate placements to iteratively revise its code. To evaluate open-ended placement across functional use, geometric fit, and contextual arrangements, we introduce the 71-task VoxProg-Bench benchmark along with an evaluation suite pairing perceptual Intent Alignment and 3D Physical Validity. Across VoxProg-Bench and external benchmarks, VoxProg consistently outperforms relation-based, keypoint-based, and mesh-based baselines.
authors: Zhichao Zhai, Menglei Zhao, Guikun Chen, Zihao Yan, Kanzhi Wu, Wenguan Wang, Jun Xiao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of translating implicit spatial instructions into explicit geometric references for 3D placement.
Uses a language model to generate executable evidence and pose programs over local voxel views with coordinates and neighborhood relations.
Computes target SE(3) poses from selected scene geometry and revises programs using visual and numerical execution feedback.
Introduces the 71-task VoxProg-Bench and evaluation metrics for Intent Alignment and 3D Physical Validity.
Outperforms relation-, keypoint-, and mesh-based baselines across VoxProg-Bench and external benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Language-model-driven voxel programming for 3D object placement; directly relevant to spatial reasoning and 3D-aware multimodal understanding.
papers.title: VoxProg: 3D Spatial Reasoning through Voxel Programming
papers.tldr: VoxProg enables language models to perform 3D object placement by programming over voxelized scene surfaces with iterative execution feedback.

papers.abstract: Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.
authors: Yicheng Xu, Zhikai Xu, Ziyuan Chen, Yuhang Dong, Tao Zhang, Zhucun Xue, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
bullets: Targets embodied agents that must adapt to evolving environments, human needs, and physical and social constraints.
Combines a physics simulator with embodied NPCs, constrained dialogue, and an event-driven FSM for tracking actions, information, and task outcomes.
Enables frozen multimodal LLMs to act through executable skills using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback.
Introduces TARSphere-Bench with 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes and five paired evaluation conditions.
Evaluation of eight MLLMs finds task updates and human interaction challenging, with collisions and falls highlighting the need to measure execution safety.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a full-stack framework for long-horizon embodied agents using frozen MLLMs, relevant to embodied AI and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments
papers.tldr: TARSphere is a full-stack simulation, control, and benchmarking framework for evaluating long-horizon robot agents under changing physical and social conditions.

papers.abstract: Thermal cameras can watch over older people living alone without capturing faces, and multimodal large language models (LLMs) can judge a short video without task-specific training. We evaluate a production multimodal LLM, Gemini 3.8 Flash at temperature 0, as the decision stage of an event-triggered fall screener, used exactly as a deployed prototype uses it: one request per short thermal clip, with its sound track when there is one, and its predecessor Gemini 3.7 Flash on the same requests. On 438 staged falls and 563 non-fall windows that we located by hand in a public 32x24 thermal dataset, the deployed request called 69% of the held-out subjects' falls (67% over all subjects; bed falls excluded) and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying on the floor and getting up. Over 76 h of ordinary life in an occupied room, recorded at 160x120 with sound, it called none of 395 clips a fall (95% upper bound 1.2 false alarms per day) and caught 4 of the 9 staged falls the camera could see. One cautionary sentence in the prompt ("a person who goes out of view ... is not a fall") accounted for many of the misses: removing it raised sensitivity on the held-out subjects from 69% to 83% on 3.8 Flash and from 80% to 92% on Gemini 3.7 Flash, and in the home from 4 to 9 of the 9 visible falls, with no false call in ordinary living but at the price of calling deliberate lie-downs a fall. Sensitivity collapsed at 8x6 pixels (34%); identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows; and when the model called a fall, its explanation placed it within a second of the annotated landing 99% of the time. Two conventional detectors trained on the laboratory data caught nearly every held-out laboratory fall but raised 14.2 and 23.9 false alarms per day in the home. We release the frame-level fall annotations of the public dataset and every model answer on it.
authors: Marcos Junca (Senecta Inc.), Mauro Junca (Senecta Inc.)
bullets: Evaluated Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.7 Flash as deployed decision stages using one request per short thermal clip, with audio when available.
On staged laboratory data, Gemini 3.8 Flash detected 69% of held-out-subject falls and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying down and rising.
In 76 hours of occupied-home footage, it produced no false calls and detected 4 of 9 visible staged falls; the reported upper bound was 1.2 false alarms per day.
Removing a prompt warning about people leaving view substantially increased sensitivity, but caused deliberate lie-downs to be labeled as falls.
Performance fell to 34% sensitivity at 8×6 pixels; identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows, while detected falls were temporally localized accurately.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates a multimodal LLM for zero-shot event/action understanding in thermal video, fitting video understanding and multimodal LLM application.
papers.title: Asking a Multimodal LLM Whether Someone Fell: Zero-Shot Screening of Low-Resolution Thermal Video in a Laboratory and an Occupied Home
papers.tldr: A zero-shot multimodal LLM screened low-resolution thermal clips with no false alarms in tested ordinary home activity, but its fall sensitivity depended strongly on prompt wording, resolution, and whether falls went out of view.

papers.abstract: Learning across medical imaging modalities requires making use of images without paired text and accommodating new domains while retaining existing representations. We propose a medical vision-language technique built around an expandable bank of modality experts. Its Multiway Transformer combines shared visual computation with deterministically routed feed-forward experts and a separate text pathway. A modality-aware visual tokenizer supplies targets for masked pretraining on 19.4 million unpaired image rows across seven modalities; contrastive alignment then uses 3.23 million image-text pairs. Additional fundus and optical coherence tomography experts learn from paired data while the original image and text embedding paths remain frozen. With a ViT-Large backbone, the proposed technique achieves the best or tied-best result in 24 of 25 benchmark settings across nine modalities: 10 of 11 zero-shot classification benchmarks, all 10 linear probes, and all four retrieval benchmarks. Mean balanced accuracy is 0.674 for zero-shot classification and 0.856 for linear probing, and mean bidirectional retrieval recall is 20.70%. A separate three-seed sequential experiment with matched adaptation data yields fundus and OCT retrieval gains of 14.95 and 9.31 percentage points, with no measured loss on preceding fundus or pathology tasks. The preservation argument requires unchanged existing computation paths and inference conditions, and feature-identity checks verify retention on evaluated inputs. The proposed technique provides a modular approach to learning and expanding medical vision-language representations.
authors: DM BAPPY, Eunsu Kim, Hanjoo Lee, Sung Hak Lee, Sangjeong Ahn
bullets: Addresses unpaired multimodal medical images and continual adaptation to new domains without disrupting prior capabilities.
Uses a Multiway Transformer with shared visual computation, deterministically routed modality experts, a separate text pathway, and a modality-aware visual tokenizer.
Pretrains on 19.4M unpaired image rows across seven modalities, then aligns vision and language using 3.23M image-text pairs.
Achieves the best or tied-best performance in 24 of 25 benchmarks across nine modalities, including zero-shot classification, linear probing, and retrieval.
Sequential fundus and OCT adaptation improves retrieval by 14.95 and 9.31 percentage points, with no measured loss on preceding evaluated tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Expandable multimodal medical vision-language model with modality experts and continual expansion without forgetting.
papers.title: Expandable Modality Experts for Medical Vision-Language Learning
papers.tldr: An expandable bank of modality-specific experts enables medical vision-language models to learn new imaging domains while preserving existing representations.

papers.abstract: Compositional zero-shot learning (CZSL) aims to recognize novel combinations of previously observed objects and attributes. Prior work showed that large-scale vision-language models encode decomposable semantic structures that can be recomposed to enable generalization. The Geodesically Decomposable Embeddings (GDE) framework formalizes this by identifying directions in the tangent space at the Frechet mean of the embedding distribution, which encode primitive visual concepts. Unseen attribute-object compositions can be synthesized through vector addition of these primitives. We revisit the assumption that compositional generalization requires explicit attribute-object pair re-composition. By means of new compositional scoring functions and extensive evaluations, we show that directly using the decomposed primitives suffices for recognizing unseen compositions. In that, we gain insights on how the geometry of the embedding manifold (Euclidean, spherical, or hyperbolic) and dataset structure affect compositional reasoning. Across models (CLIP, DINOv2, MERU, HyCoCLIP), we show that compositional structure consistently emerges as primitive representations, enabling inference on CZSL benchmarks (MIT-States, VAW-CZSL, UT-Zappos50K, Clothing16K) and group robustness on Waterbirds and CelebA. Code: https://github.com/nis-research/Compositionality-with-Primitives.
authors: Puru Vaish, Meelad Dashti, Christoph Brune, Pascal Mettes, Tatiana Tommasi, Nicola Strisciuglio
bullets: Reexamines whether explicit recomposition of attribute-object pairs is necessary for compositional generalization.
Introduces new compositional scoring functions that directly use decomposed primitives.
Analyzes how Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic geometry and dataset structure influence compositional reasoning.
Finds consistent primitive-based compositional structure across CLIP, DINOv2, MERU, and HyCoCLIP.
Demonstrates inference on four CZSL benchmarks and group robustness on Waterbirds and CelebA.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes compositional structure and embedding geometry of vision-language foundation models, relevant to multimodal foundation model research.
papers.title: Compositionality with Primitives: A Unified View from Euclidean to Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Decomposed primitive representations alone can support compositional zero-shot recognition, across embedding geometries, vision-language models, and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Large pretrained models such as CLIP are widely used as frozen feature extractors. However, their embeddings inherit spurious correlations from training data, introducing bias into the features. A growing body of research has sought to address this issue through post hoc debiasing, leaving the backbone untouched. We discover that despite differing mechanisms, these methods require the bias feature to be identified and expressed in text. This dependency is not innocuous. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate that this requirement incurs an unforeseen penalty in certain scenarios. For example, on the UrbanCars benchmark, having two co-occurring bias attributes, the recent methods underperform a vanilla classifier on biased frozenbackbone features, and even providing ground-truth bias identities does not close the gap. We show that the pattern that such methods seek is readily observable in the frozen geometry. Specifically, cross-class training pairs placed closest together by the frozen encoder almost always share a spurious attribute, regardless of the bias type, without requiring access to the bias labels. Based on this, we propose a novel approach to identify such pairs and learn a single linear map that transforms the features to perform post-hoc debiasing. The proposed approach achieves competitive performance across all datasets without access to bias attribute annotations or any LLMs.
authors: Divyaansh Mertia, Chirag Bhutra, Himanshu Shekhar, Shubham Bagwari, Pratik Mazumder
bullets: Existing post-hoc methods depend on identifying and expressing bias features in text.
This dependency can hurt performance: on UrbanCars, recent methods underperform a vanilla classifier, even with ground-truth bias identities.
Cross-class pairs that are closest in frozen embedding space usually share a spurious attribute, across bias types.
The proposed method identifies these pairs and learns one linear feature transformation for debiasing.
It achieves competitive performance across datasets without bias annotations or LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Post-hoc debiasing of CLIP features directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Rethinking Post-hoc Debiasing of Large Pretrained Models
papers.tldr: Post-hoc debiasing methods can be hindered by requiring text-specified bias attributes, while frozen feature geometry enables annotation- and LLM-free debiasing through a learned linear map.

papers.abstract: Pixel language models process text as rendered images instead of a finite vocabulary, which gives them strong cross-lingual transfer abilities. However, not much is known about how these abilities are influenced by larger-scale pretraining. In this paper, we train a family of MPIXEL models along three axes of variation: more languages, more scripts, and larger model capacity under fixed per-language compute. In evaluations on five tasks covering 83 languages, we find that scaling acts locally: each axis improves the added languages and scripts, while increased capacity mitigates the curse of multilinguality from pretraining on more languages. Transfer to unseen scripts improves with multilingual pretraining, but does not further improve with scaling. On typologically distant low-resource languages, our models outperform subword and character-level baselines across many writing systems. We also show that larger pixel models reserve more layers for visual processing, and that cross-lingual alignment weakens as more languages are added. Overall, our findings characterize how multilingual scaling improves pixel language models.
authors: Ilker Kesen, Jenny Kunz, Kasra Malihi, Desmond Elliott
bullets: Evaluates MPIXEL models across more languages, more scripts, and larger capacity under fixed per-language compute.
Across five tasks and 83 languages, each scaling axis primarily benefits the corresponding languages or scripts.
Larger models mitigate the curse of multilinguality, but transfer to unseen scripts does not improve further with scaling.
Pixel models outperform subword and character-level baselines on many typologically distant, low-resource languages.
Scaling increases visual-processing layers, while cross-lingual alignment weakens as more languages are added.
papers.selection_reason: Scaling multilingual pretraining of pixel language models, a multimodal LLM variant.
papers.title: Scaling Multilingual Pretraining of Pixel Language Models
papers.tldr: Scaling multilingual pretraining improves pixel language models mainly for the languages and scripts directly added, while larger capacity reduces interference from multilinguality.

papers.abstract: Multimodal inputs may be missing or degraded, raising distinct questions of evidence availability and trust. We introduce a reliability-aware Gaussian Product-of-Experts (PoE) in which an input-dependent reliability weight tempers each modality's latent precision, while missing experts are omitted. We characterize how reliability and availability affect posterior information and expert influence. Across two clinical multimodal tasks, the full framework remains competitive with complete inputs and achieves its clearest mean-AUROC advantage under modality absence, particularly on HAIM-MIMIC-MM. Ablations show a substantial gain from missing-aware training and an additional HAIM improvement from reliability weighting under matched PoE, missing-aware, and consistency training. Unseen test-time corruptions are used diagnostically and reveal modality-dependent reliability-weight and latent-uncertainty responses, including failure under severe degradation. Thus, reliability weighting provides an explicit evidence-control mechanism, while learning dependable quality signals remains an open challenge.
authors: Patitapaban Palo, Abhisek Tiwari, Mattia Carletti, Anshul Thakur, Xiao Gu, David A. Clifton
bullets: Addresses both modality availability and trust in incomplete or corrupted multimodal evidence.
Uses input-dependent reliability weights to temper each modality’s latent precision and omits missing experts.
Analyzes how reliability and availability change posterior information and expert influence.
Across two clinical tasks, remains competitive with complete inputs and shows its clearest mean-AUROC benefit under modality absence, especially on HAIM-MIMIC-MM.
Unseen severe corruptions reveal modality-dependent uncertainty responses and failure modes.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses multimodal learning with incomplete evidence using a reliability-aware Gaussian Product-of-Experts framework, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Reliability-Aware Probabilistic Fusion for Multimodal Learning with Incomplete Evidence
papers.tldr: A reliability-aware Gaussian Product-of-Experts improves multimodal inference when inputs are missing or degraded, while exposing challenges in learning dependable quality signals.

papers.abstract: In this report, we introduce pplx-embed-v2-late, a pair of 0.6B and 9B multilingual and multimodal late-interaction models. Both models achieve state-of-the-art results within their respective size classes across a range of text, image, and visual document retrieval benchmarks. On visual document retrieval tasks, pplx-embed-v2-late-0.6b is competitive with models several times larger than itself. The models are trained via representation distillation from an 18B teacher. Consequently, they share an embedding space that supports asymmetric deployment: documents can be indexed with the 9B model and queried with the low-latency 0.6B model. Both models are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/perplexity-ai/pplx-embed-v2.
authors: Markus Krimmel, Louis Milliken, Ekaterina Glazkova, Maximilian Schall, Antoine Chaffin, Sedigheh Eslami, Jonas Golde, Denis Bykov, Claire Beamer, Jeremy Yang, Bo Wang
bullets: Provides 0.6B and 9B models for text, image, and visual document retrieval.
Uses representation distillation from an 18B teacher.
The models share an embedding space, enabling documents to be indexed with the 9B model and queried with the lower-latency 0.6B model.
Reports state-of-the-art results within their size classes across several retrieval benchmarks.
The 0.6B model is competitive with substantially larger models on visual document retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Multilingual multimodal late-interaction embedding models for text, image, and document retrieval; directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: pplx-embed-v2-late Technical Report
papers.tldr: pplx-embed-v2-late introduces multilingual, multimodal late-interaction retrievers that combine strong retrieval performance with flexible large-document/small-query deployment.

papers.abstract: Biometric recognition often degrades under partial facial vis- ibility, where conventional facial cues are occluded. The forehead region remains consistently visible and contains distinctive crease patterns that can serve as a complementary biometric trait. We present a unified eval- uation of forehead-crease recognition across explainable zero-shot rea- soning, domain-adaptive learning, and trait-specific modeling. FIRE en- ables interpretable zero-shot verification using multimodal large language models, while pretrained face-recognition models are adapted to the fore- head domain through margin-based learning. Under open-set evaluation, the best zero-shot model GPT-4o+FIRE achieves 18.22% EER, while Edge-Forehead achieves 8.30% EER and 54.01% TMR@0.1% FMR. The results show that although MLLMs offer interpretable zero-shot verifi- cation, trait-specific learning remains more effective for robust forehead- crease biometric recognition.
authors: Geetanjali Sharma, Aryan Jain, Dev Nagaich, Aditya Nigam, Raghavendra Ramachandra
bullets: Forehead creases provide a complementary biometric cue when other facial regions are occluded.
FIRE supports interpretable zero-shot verification with multimodal large language models.
Pretrained face-recognition models are adapted to the forehead domain using margin-based learning.
Edge-Forehead achieves 8.30% EER and 54.01% TMR at 0.1% FMR, outperforming the best zero-shot result.
GPT-4o+FIRE reaches 18.22% EER, indicating weaker robustness despite interpretability.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates the use of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for zero-shot forehead-crease biometric recognition, fitting Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: Balancing Foundation Models and Trait-Specific Learning for Forehead-Crease Recognition
papers.tldr: Trait-specific models recognize forehead creases more reliably than interpretable zero-shot multimodal models under open-set evaluation.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image generation models do not explicitly receive the syntactic structure of the prompt, i.e., which word modifies which and where each phrase attaches. Consequently, they often struggle to bind attributes to the correct objects, to depict spatial relations and counts correctly, and to render syntactically ambiguous prompts in the intended interpretation. Existing syntax-based control methods mainly address attribute binding and have limited ability to control spatial relations and counts or to specify the interpretation of syntactically ambiguous prompts. They rely on phrase-structure or dependency grammars and require additional rules or constraints on the tree structure to extract modification relations between words or to specify a syntactic interpretation. We propose CCG Diffusion, a training-free method that controls image generation using Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG). In CCG, the category of each word carries rich syntactic information: it specifies what the word combines with and what phrase it forms. Modification relations between words can therefore be read directly from a CCG parse. Moreover, prepositional phrase (PP) attachment ambiguity, a representative syntactic ambiguity, can be resolved simply by fixing the preposition's category. CCG Diffusion applies the same two CCG-based mechanisms, prompt rewriting and attention guidance, both to controlling attribute binding, spatial relations, and counts and to resolving PP ambiguity. On two architecturally different backbones, Stable Diffusion and Sana, CCG Diffusion achieves the highest scores among the compared methods in attribute binding and 2D spatial relations and significantly outperforms all of them in PP ambiguity resolution.
authors: Ryosuke Yamaki, Daichi Mochihashi, Nobutaka Shimada, Seitaro Shinagawa, Tadahiro Taniguchi
bullets: Addresses failures caused by text-to-image models lacking explicit prompt syntax.
Uses CCG parses to derive word-combination and modification relations directly, avoiding extra tree constraints.
Combines prompt rewriting and attention guidance to control attributes, spatial relations, counts, and PP-attachment interpretations.
Works with Stable Diffusion and Sana, achieving the best compared scores for attribute binding and 2D spatial relations.
Significantly outperforms compared methods on resolving prepositional-phrase ambiguity.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CCG Diffusion, a training-free method to control text-to-image generation using syntax to handle spatial relations and ambiguity, fitting Multimodal Foundation Models and Spatial Intelligence.
papers.title: CCG Diffusion: Combinatory Categorial Grammar-Driven Compositional and Syntactically Disambiguated Text-to-Image Generation
papers.tldr: CCG Diffusion uses Combinatory Categorial Grammar to guide text-to-image models toward syntactically correct attribute binding, spatial relations, counts, and interpretations of ambiguous prompts without training.

papers.abstract: Promptable segmentation models such as SAM 3 achieve remarkable open-vocabulary performance but require dedicated architectures, large-scale annotation engines, and task-specific training. We ask a different question: can a general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) segment images directly, without an added segmentation head, mask decoder, or training? We present LLMSeg, a training-free pipeline that turns a vision-capable LLM into a text-prompted image segmenter. LLMSeg decomposes segmentation into three LLM-driven stages. First, detect localizes all instances matching a free-form text query and describes their coarse morphology. Next, segment traces each instance using closed periodic B-splines confined to its detected box. These splines define an outer boundary and optional hole loops. Finally, refine iteratively proposes focus boxes around residual errors and retraces confined splines. The process ends when the mask stabilizes or the pass budget is exhausted. The output is a binary mask with inspectable intermediate geometry. We evaluate LLMSeg across ten referring and reasoning segmentation splits (ReasonSeg and RefCOCO/+/g). We also evaluate open-vocabulary instance segmentation (LVIS, COCO, and SA-Co), semantic segmentation, and zero-shot detection (ODinW13 and RF-100VL). With an off-the-shelf Gemini-3.7-Flash backend, LLMSeg is competitive with and often surpasses the specialist SAM 3 model on identical items. It reaches 71.5 cIoU on ReasonSeg val without additional segmentation-specific training. Backend model updates can improve accuracy without retraining the pipeline. The code is available at https://abdullahamdi.com/llmseg .
bullets: Addresses whether MLLMs can directly produce image masks without segmentation-specific architecture, annotations, or training.
Uses three stages: detect queried instances, trace confined closed B-splines with optional holes, and refine residual errors iteratively.
Produces binary masks with inspectable intermediate geometric representations.
Evaluated on referring, reasoning, open-vocabulary instance, semantic segmentation, and zero-shot detection benchmarks.
With Gemini-3.7-Flash, it reports 71.5 cIoU on ReasonSeg validation and is competitive with or often surpasses SAM 3 on identical items.
papers.selection_reason: Develops LLMSeg, a training-free pipeline that enables vision-capable LLMs to perform image segmentation using B-splines, demonstrating strong open-vocabulary performance without task-specific training.
papers.title: LLMSeg: Training-Free Text-Prompted Image Segmentation with B-Splines
papers.tldr: LLMSeg turns a general-purpose vision-language model into a training-free text-prompted image segmenter using iterative B-spline geometry instead of a segmentation head or decoder.
