papers.abstract: Unlike question answering, where a query specifies a perceptual target, open-ended detailed captioning must determine what evidence to acquire and how to integrate it into a coherent global description. We propose Observation-Adaptive Video Captioner (OACap), a caption-centered agent that turns unsupported or missing information into targeted observation requests, uses spatiotemporal tools to acquire evidence, and iteratively verifies and revises the caption. OACap captions consistently improve performance across general video-understanding benchmarks using a fixed text-only reader. To better diagnose the information they preserve, we introduce Factual-Semantic Captioning Bench (FSCap-Bench). Its Core-Support Factuality Score (CSFS) combines claim precision with importance-aware fact coverage and responds as expected to four controlled perturbation types on 93.0-98.3% of valid caption pairs. Its Cross-Modal Semantic Round-Trip Score (CSRS) measures semantic preservation through a video-caption-video-caption round trip by matching atomic facts from source and recovered captions. Together, they connect downstream textual-memory utility with factual and semantic preservation.
authors: Hao Shi, Hong Yan, Xiaoyang Zhang, Qing Cui, Chao Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deciding what evidence to observe for open-ended, detailed video captioning.
Uses a caption-centered agent that identifies missing or unsupported information, gathers targeted spatiotemporal evidence, and revises captions iteratively.
Improves captioning performance across general video-understanding benchmarks with a fixed text-only reader.
Introduces FSCap-Bench with CSFS for importance-aware factual coverage and CSRS for cross-modal semantic preservation.
CSFS responds appropriately to four controlled perturbations in 93.0–98.3% of valid caption pairs.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an active observation agent for detailed video captioning, relevant to video understanding and multimodal agents.
papers.title: OACap: Caption-Guided Active Observation for Detailed Video Captioning
papers.tldr: OACap actively requests and verifies visual evidence to produce more detailed, factually supported video captions, while FSCap-Bench evaluates their factual and semantic preservation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are now routinely tested on theory of mind: whether they can work out what another person sees, knows, and means. A common design asks the model to report that perspective and then to act for the person, and reads a correct report beside a wrong action as a failure to use the perspective. That reading rests on a quiet assumption: that asking for the report leaves the action unchanged. We show that it does not. In a rendered Director Task, a partition hides the largest block from a director who asks for "the largest block". Asking first which blocks the director can see raises the share of replies that choose this hidden block by 12 to 88 percentage points on six GPT models and by 17 on Qwen3.8-27B, even though the models mostly report correctly which blocks the director sees. Reasoning traces and prompt rewordings suggest why: the question shifts how the request is read, from the director's view toward the model's own. When the prompt states what the director knows and refers to, fewer than 1% of replies pair a correct report with a hidden-block choice. Any evaluation that elicits a perspective report before the action it scores needs a baseline without the question, and we deliver one: paired prompts that differ only in that question, a design any perspective-taking benchmark can adopt.
authors: Jiaxuan Guo, Xingyu Ren, Kejia Zhang, Jingxin Yang, Youran Sun, Haizhao Yang
bullets: In a rendered Director Task, a partition hides the largest block from a director requesting “the largest block.”
Asking models to report the director’s visual perspective first increased hidden-block choices by 12–88 percentage points across six GPT models and by 17 points on Qwen3.8-27B.
Models generally reported the director’s visibility correctly, suggesting the question changed how they interpreted the request rather than simply revealing a lack of perspective-taking.
Explicitly stating what the director knows and refers to reduced correct-report/hidden-choice pairings to below 1%.
The authors recommend paired prompts with and without the perspective question as a baseline for perspective-taking benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates perspective-taking behavior in vision-language models, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Asking What a Director Sees Can Change What Vision-Language Models Choose
papers.tldr: Asking vision-language models what a director can see can change their subsequent choice, making standard theory-of-mind evaluations confound perspective reporting with action.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires more than access to geometric tools: a reasoner must decide when direct observation is sufficient and when to reconstruct, measure, or change reference frames. We present SpatialBrain, a framework that retains experience about these decisions while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed. The key distinction is between evidence about a scene and experience about how to reason with that evidence. 3DFusionMemory fuses current-scene observations into queryable spatial relations. A Spatial Skill Library provides reusable tool procedures, and Spatial Cognition associates task conditions with experience about when and how to use memory and skills. Completed trajectories are abstracted into process records and consolidated between task blocks, allowing later decisions to draw on earlier execution without transferring scene coordinates or reference answers. Across five spatial-reasoning benchmarks, SpatialBrain improves on direct answers from the same backbone on four and ties on the fifth. Component comparisons, experience-coverage curves, and traced resource decisions characterize how the framework accumulates and uses these resources.
authors: Yifan Zhou, Ziyang Gong, Xiaojun Ye, Yifei Liu, Donggang Li, Xiaolong Zhou, Zhihang Zhong, Xue Yang
bullets: Separates scene evidence from experience about reasoning strategies.
Uses 3DFusionMemory to build queryable spatial relations from current observations.
Provides a Spatial Skill Library and Spatial Cognition for selecting reusable procedures and resources.
Abstracts completed task trajectories into process records for consolidation across task blocks.
Improves over direct answers from the same backbone on four of five benchmarks and ties on one.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial reasoning framework with a vision-language backbone, queryable 3D spatial relations, and reasoning experience growth; fits spatial intelligence.
papers.title: SpatialBrain: Spatial Intelligence Growing from Experience
papers.tldr: SpatialBrain improves spatial reasoning by retaining experience about when and how to use spatial memories and tools while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed.

papers.abstract: Multimodal ocean modeling remains challenging due to substantial heterogeneity in data structures, physical semantics, and spatiotemporal characteristics across satellite imagery, gridded oceanographic fields, and buoy observations. Existing approaches largely focus on task-specific ocean modeling, while learning transferable representations from heterogeneous observations remains an open problem. To address this challenge, we propose YingLan, a multimodal ocean foundation model that integrates physics-attribute-conditioned dynamic encoding, Spatiotemporal Increment Coupling (STIC), and ocean-state evolution-aware pretraining. Specifically, the dynamic encoding mechanism generates adaptive input projections conditioned on physical semantics and observation characteristics, enabling flexible representation of heterogeneous ocean variables. STIC models multiscale spatiotemporal dependencies through cross-scale interactions of latent temporal increments. The pretraining strategy further combines masked observation reconstruction with temporal evolution objectives to facilitate the learning of coherent ocean-state representations across different prediction horizons. YingLan is implemented using MindSpore and trained on Huawei Ascend 910B NPUs, demonstrating its compatibility with domestic AI computing infrastructure. In a seven-day sea surface salinity (SSS) forecasting task conducted in the Shenzhen coastal waters, YingLan achieves an average RMSE of 0.687508 PSU, corresponding to relative error reductions of 0.58%, 5.31%, and 12.42% compared with LangYa, XiHe, and GloNet2, respectively. These results provide initial evidence of the model's effectiveness in regional ocean forecasting, while broader cross-task and cross-regional evaluations remain necessary to assess its generalization capabilities.
authors: Sen Jia, Siqi Wei, Junyu Wang, Zijun Lv, Pan Liu, Meng Xu, Xiyou Fu, Yuxi Sun, Qiang Liu, Shuyu Zhang, Lin Mu
bullets: Addresses heterogeneity across satellite imagery, gridded ocean fields, and buoy observations.
Uses physics-attribute-conditioned dynamic encoding to adapt inputs to differing physical semantics and observation characteristics.
Introduces Spatiotemporal Increment Coupling (STIC) to capture multiscale temporal and spatial dependencies.
Pretrains with masked observation reconstruction and ocean-state evolution objectives.
In Shenzhen coastal waters, it achieves 0.687508 PSU RMSE for seven-day SSS forecasting, with reported reductions versus three comparison models.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes YingLan, a multimodal foundation model for oceanography that integrates heterogeneous observations (satellite, buoy) using physics-conditioned encoding and spatiotemporal coupling.
papers.title: YingLan: A Multimodal Ocean Foundation Model for Unified Representation Learning from Heterogeneous Observations
papers.tldr: YingLan is a multimodal ocean foundation model that learns unified representations from heterogeneous observations and shows improved seven-day coastal salinity forecasting in an initial regional evaluation.

papers.abstract: Managed and wild bees sustain roughly a third of the global food products, yet colonies face mounting stress from climate-change including extreme weather patterns, altered parasite and disease patterns. Timely assessment of colony condition such as understanding colony strength, brood area, honey and pollen storage, comb usage, is essential to adaptive management. However, manual hive frame inspection is slow, costly, and quality depends on scarce expertise. We present an artificial targeted intelligent system framework focusing on edge deployable pipeline that turns hive frame photographs into interpretable and action-oriented inspection report. The pipeline includes an object detector to detect biologically-meaningful comb-cell classes; detections are distilled into structured fact schema; facts are converted into constrained factual text; the text triggers a grounded knowledge-base for interpretations and recommendations. Knowledge-base entries are required to be triggerable by evidence expressed in the fact schema. We built our system based on open source FAIRHiveFrames-1K dataset and favour reproducible, edge-deployable models over large general purpose frontier models. We additionally release FAIRHiveText-1K dataset that turns FAIRHiveFrames-1K dataset into interchangeable facts and text interpretation of the facts, making it easy for further LLM-based research into this area. We also propose a pathway to develop the grounded knowledge-base that will be helpful in providing interpretable and actionable reports from the facts.
authors: Asaduz Zaman, Mohaimenul Azam Khan Raiaan, Malika Nisal Ratnayake
bullets: Addresses the slow, costly, and expertise-dependent nature of manual hive-frame inspection.
Detects biologically meaningful comb-cell classes and distills detections into a structured fact schema.
Generates constrained factual text that triggers interpretable recommendations from a grounded knowledge base.
Prioritizes reproducible, edge-deployable models over large general-purpose language models.
Introduces FAIRHiveText-1K and outlines a pathway for developing evidence-triggered knowledge-base entries.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a system for intelligent beekeeper assistance using computer vision and knowledge-grounded language models, fitting embodied AI and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Computer Vision and Knowledge-Grounded Language Models for Intelligent Beekeeper Assistance
papers.tldr: An edge-deployable computer-vision and knowledge-grounded language pipeline converts hive-frame images into evidence-based, actionable beekeeper reports.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have shown strong potential for robot manipulation by jointly learning visual dynamics and executable actions. However, their video and action objectives do not explicitly constrain the 3D geometry that is crucial for precise manipulation. Recently, geometry-aware WAMs introduce depth or 4D prediction branches, whereas representation alignment methods supervise intermediate WAM features with pretrained 3D foundation models. Yet we find that such pointwise alignment benefits the video features but degrades action learning, since dense geometric feature targets overly restrict compact action features. To address this limitation, we propose Relational Geometry Forcing (RGF), which transfers geometric priors from a frozen 3D foundation model by aligning pairwise feature relations instead of pointwise features. Specifically, RGF applies three complementary relational objectives, where intra-frame and cross-view relations transfer scene geometry and multi-view correspondence to the video features, while action-temporal relations couple action dynamics to geometric scene evolution. Applied only during training, RGF requires no explicit geometry branch or extra inference module. Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate the effectiveness of Relational Geometry Forcing, showing consistent gains across diverse manipulation scenarios and WAM paradigms.
authors: Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Jiabing Yang, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Jianhua Yang, Jianlou Si, Jun Huang, Jing Liu, Nianfeng Liu, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: WAMs lack explicit constraints on the 3D geometry needed for precise manipulation.
Pointwise alignment with 3D foundation-model features can help video representations but hurt compact action representations.
RGF aligns intra-frame, cross-view, and action-temporal feature relations to transfer geometry, correspondences, and scene-action dynamics.
The method is training-only and adds no explicit geometry branch or inference module.
Experiments in simulation and the real world show consistent gains across diverse manipulation settings and WAM paradigms.
papers.selection_reason: Relational geometry forcing for world action models targets manipulation, action-conditioned world dynamics, and geometry-aware multimodal reasoning.
papers.title: Relational Geometry Forcing for World Action Models
papers.tldr: Relational Geometry Forcing improves world action models for precise robot manipulation by transferring 3D geometric structure through relational rather than pointwise feature alignment.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) understand music, yet struggle to locate a described moment in time. We ask whether this reflects missing temporal information or a bottleneck in how the time span is extracted. Using a paired-query probe built from Slakh2100 stem activations, we attach a state query (e.g., ``only piano and bass are playing'') and a change query (e.g., ``the guitar drops out, leaving piano and bass'') to the same span and vary how much preceding audio the model is shown. Across frozen LALMs, three ways of extracting the span ask different questions: full-track prompting asking whether the model can say when; windowed yes/no scoring asking whether it verifies the moment when handed the segment, and whether it needs what came before; attention asking whether it can find the moment on its own. State queries score above baseline without context, while change queries improve with preceding context in most short-segment models; 30s padded encoders show no comparable recovery. Prompting and attention expose almost none of this. Prompting failures thus understate what LALMs can verify, though not what they can locate, by an amount set by query type and encoder.
bullets: LALMs struggle to identify when a described musical moment occurs, raising questions about missing temporal information versus extraction bottlenecks.
A paired-query probe compares state descriptions (what is playing) with change descriptions (what just stopped) over the same audio span and varying preceding context.
State queries perform above baseline without context, while change queries usually benefit from preceding audio in short-segment models.
Full-track prompting and attention reveal little of this contextual ability; windowed yes/no scoring exposes more verification capacity.
Thirty-second padded encoders do not show comparable recovery, indicating that effects depend on query type and encoder design.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of temporal information extraction in frozen audio-language models; meaningful for multimodal model understanding.
papers.title: Heard But Not Said: Prompting Understates Temporal Information of Musical Moments in Frozen Large Audio-Language Models
papers.tldr: Frozen large audio-language models can often verify musical states, but prompting and attention substantially understate their ability to use temporal context and locate musical changes.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.
authors: Hong Ting Tsang, Boyi Zhang, Haoyu Huang, Jiaxin Bai, Yufei Li, Yisen Gao, Zhongwei Xie, Hongyu Luo, Jeff Z. Pan, Yangqiu Song
bullets: Evaluates 923 questions across persona-grounded histories spanning 11–24 sessions and four modalities.
Targets meaningful spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media.
Uses matched controls to isolate failures in representation, retrieval, delivery, and reading.
Finds modality-dependent representation loss, substantial residual reading errors even with gold evidence, and weak abstention.
Moves evaluation beyond a single leaderboard score toward component-level diagnosis.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for long-term memory and cross-modal reasoning in omni-modal conversational agents; directly relevant to LLM memory and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: MOSAIC: An Omni-Modal Benchmark for Long-Term Memory and Cross-Modal Reasoning in Conversational Agents
papers.tldr: MOSAIC is an omni-modal benchmark that diagnoses where conversational agents fail when remembering and reasoning over long-term text, image, video, and audio histories.

papers.abstract: Thermal cameras enable robots to perceive human activities in darkness while revealing less personally identifiable appearance information and fewer details of the surrounding environment than RGB cameras. As vision-language models (VLMs), originally developed for RGB imagery, are increasingly integrated into embodied systems for scene understanding and high-level planning, thermal sensing offers a promising way to extend activity perception to low-light and privacy-sensitive settings. However, the failure modes of VLMs in thermal human activity understanding for human-robot interaction (HRI) remain underexplored. We fill this gap by evaluating seven locally deployable VLMs, including models developed for physical AI and robotics, on two person-centric thermal datasets. Our diagnostic tasks examine fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and the ability to withhold unsupported answers. Paired RGB recordings serve as a performance reference, while controlled variations in frame sampling, thermal input presentation, and reasoning are used to assess whether the observed errors can be mitigated. Our results show that models can recognize broad activity categories but struggle with fine-grained actions such as coughing, sneezing, and yawning. They also produce inaccurate event timelines and hallucinate actions involving objects. Simple thermal input preprocessing and additional reasoning offer only limited, model-dependent gains. Abstention behavior also varies across models even under explicit instructions, limiting their reliability for practical robotic use.
bullets: Thermal sensing supports activity understanding in darkness while exposing less personal appearance information than RGB.
The evaluation covers fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and withholding unsupported answers on two person-centric thermal datasets.
Models recognize broad activities but often miss coughing, sneezing, and yawning, and generate inaccurate timelines.
Models frequently hallucinate actions involving objects; preprocessing and extra reasoning provide only limited, model-dependent improvements.
Variable abstention behavior limits reliability for practical robotic use, despite evaluation across locally deployable and robotics-focused VLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates vision-language models for thermal human activity understanding in HRI, directly relevant to embodied perception and multimodal foundation models in physical environments.
papers.title: Failure Modes of Vision-Language Models for Human Activity Understanding in Thermal HRI
papers.tldr: A study of seven vision-language models finds that, although they recognize broad activities in thermal imagery, they remain unreliable for fine-grained actions, timelines, object-related events, and abstention in HRI.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate why vision-language models (VLMs) produce errors by decomposing them into two sources: visual-representation failures, in which the visual evidence required for the correct answer is not encoded, and visual-utilization failures, in which this evidence is encoded but not successfully used. We propose to estimate the visual-utilization failure rate using lightweight probes and derive theoretical bounds on the true rate that account for probe imperfections. We introduce VELens (Visual Evidence Lens), a rank-based probe that traces visual evidence for both a target object and its ground-truth attribute, such as color, material, or shape, across VLM layers. We evaluate VELens on over 6,000 images using LLaVA-1.6-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Our method achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.95 and 0.91, respectively, and outperforms alternative probes in both low-resource and unseen-attribute settings. Using it to diagnose errors, we estimate that visual-utilization failures account for 84.4% of LLaVA errors and 70.0% of Qwen errors, with conservative lower bounds of 77.5% and 61.0%, respectively. Overall, our study identifies visual utilization as the dominant bottleneck in VLMs and suggests that a central opportunity for improvement lies in developing better mechanisms to locate, route, and use the visual information they already encode.
authors: Anat Veikherman, Mor Ventura, Nitay Calderon, Lihi Zelnik-Manor, Roi Reichart
bullets: Decomposes VLM errors into visual-representation failures and visual-utilization failures.
Introduces VELens, a rank-based probe that traces object and attribute evidence across model layers.
Uses lightweight probes with theoretical bounds to estimate utilization-failure rates despite probe imperfections.
Evaluated on over 6,000 images with LLaVA-1.6-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B; VELens achieves ROC-AUCs of 0.95 and 0.91 and outperforms alternative probes.
Estimated utilization failures account for 84.4% of LLaVA errors and 70.0% of Qwen errors, with conservative lower bounds of 77.5% and 61.0%.
papers.selection_reason: Decomposes VLM errors into representational versus utilization failures using a visual evidence probe; directly relevant to diagnosing and improving MLLMs.
papers.title: Encoded but Unused: Bounding the Sources of VLM Errors
papers.tldr: The paper finds that most VLM errors arise from failing to use visual evidence that is already encoded, rather than failing to encode it.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at 2D recognition but often fail to maintain consistent 3D relations across sparse viewpoints, leading to spatial hallucinations under occlusion and perspective changes. Existing methods commonly fuse all frames with dense geometry, incurring substantial computation and context overhead while encouraging blind reliance on imperfect estimators. We present Think-Capture, a query-conditioned framework that first identifies task-critical objects and then acquires their geometry on demand. A 3D toolkit lifts zero-shot masks into a common coordinate frame, and a Symbolic 3D State Abstraction compresses object and camera states into structured text. Hierarchical Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trains the VLM on cases in which geometry either helps or misleads, teaching it when to use tool evidence and when to fall back on visual cues. Think-Capture-4B reaches 54.4% on MindCube-Tiny (+21.5 points over its backbone), 39.1% on the MMSI-Bench positional subset (+7.9), and 42.8% on ViewSpatial (+5.2). It also remains robust under coordinate and mask perturbations. The full stack fits one 24 GB GPU and serves as an asynchronous high-level reasoner on an Agibot G1. Our code is available at https://github.com/819346675/Think-Capture.
authors: Junjie Wang, Zhihao Yuan, Yunhan Tang, Sheng Xu, Jiaqi Mao, Xiaoyu Ye, Yueru Luo, Xu Yan, Chun-Mei Feng, Zhen Li
bullets: Targets spatial hallucinations caused by occlusion, perspective changes, and sparse viewpoints.
Identifies task-critical objects, lifts their zero-shot masks into a shared 3D frame, and compresses geometry into structured text.
Uses hierarchical GRPO to teach the VLM when to trust geometric tools and when to rely on visual evidence.
Think-Capture-4B improves over its backbone by 21.5, 7.9, and 5.2 points on MindCube-Tiny, MMSI-Bench positional, and ViewSpatial, respectively.
The system remains robust to coordinate and mask perturbations, fits on one 24 GB GPU, and runs as an asynchronous reasoner on an Agibot G1.
papers.selection_reason: Query-conditioned active 3D geometry acquisition for VLM spatial reasoning; strongly fits spatial intelligence and 3D-aware multimodal modeling.
papers.title: Think-Capture: Active 3D Geometry Acquisition for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Think-Capture improves VLM spatial reasoning by selectively acquiring and symbolically representing 3D geometry when it is useful, rather than densely processing every view.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering from low-altitude UAV imagery must deliver timely and accurate judgments to support disaster response under limited edge computing resources. Routine questions may be answered through direct decisions, whereas more challenging questions may benefit from step-by-step reasoning. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving models' visual understanding and generative reasoning capabilities, with limited exploration of efficient direct decision-making and its adaptive coordination with generative reasoning. We develop Disaster-S1 based on a vision-language model adapted to the disaster domain. Trained for option discrimination, it outputs a probability distribution over answer options in a single multimodal forward pass for fast decision-making. We further propose DisasterRoute, a dual-system routing framework that combines prediction confidence with disaster evidence to decide whether to accept the initial answer or invoke the disaster reasoning model DisasterVL for review. By allocating inference computation on demand, the framework retains the efficiency of direct decision-making and improves overall question-answering accuracy through selective review. Experiments on DisasterBench show that Disaster-S1 achieves superior accuracy with low latency, while DisasterRoute further improves accuracy through selective review at substantially lower latency than full reasoning.
authors: Tan Zhang, Xing Deng, Lu Zhang, Xiaofeng Zhu, Ping Hu
bullets: Targets timely UAV-based disaster QA under limited edge-computing resources.
Disaster-S1 performs fast option discrimination in a single multimodal forward pass.
Routes answers using both prediction confidence and disaster evidence.
Invokes DisasterVL selectively for review instead of applying full reasoning to every question.
On DisasterBench, selective review improves accuracy while maintaining substantially lower latency than full reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Dual-system routing between fast direct VQA decisions and generative reasoning; relevant to multimodal LLM deployment and selective computation allocation.
papers.title: DisasterRoute: Evidence-Guided Dual-System Routing for Visual Disaster Question Answering
papers.tldr: DisasterRoute efficiently improves visual disaster question answering by routing only uncertain or insufficiently supported answers to a slower reasoning model.

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable end-to-end visual grounding via language prompts and generative decoding, demonstrating largely improved zero-shot and open-vocabulary detection capabilities. As a result, VLMs are rapidly being deployed at the edge in safety-critical real-world systems. However, the physical adversarial robustness of edge VLMs has not been systematically studied, and the fundamental differences in output with modern object detectors create methodological challenges for fair evaluation. To compare the two families directly, we evaluate every selected representative model on one outcome: whether an adversarial patch worn on a person evades detection of the model. We report this by introducing a unified metric, conditional attack success rate (cASR), counted only on images the model still localizes under a matched gray occluder, and partition every failure into omission (no box), substitution (a box on the patch), and displacement (a box on neither). We benchmark the physical adversarial vulnerability of compact grounding VLMs against a range of object detectors, and find that the VLMs can be as vulnerable as the detectors. We disclose that failure mode is largely associated with the output format of a model rather than its architecture family. Of the three, only omission is visible to a downstream system; displacement and substitution return confident, well-formed boxes, making them potentially more dangerous failures. Further, we find that, under distribution shift, VLMs that primarily failed by omission instead shift to failing more by displacement/substitution. Thus, a grounding VLM can inherit the detector's vulnerability while showing the possibility to adopt more dangerous failure modes. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ericliang1/physical-adversarial-robustness.
authors: Eric Liang, Alan Luo, Kaiwen Yuan
bullets: Evaluates whether an adversarial patch worn by a person evades detection across representative VLMs and object detectors.
Introduces conditional attack success rate (cASR), measured only when the model localizes the person under a matched gray occluder.
Categorizes failures as omission, substitution, or displacement to account for differences in model outputs.
Finds failure modes are more closely linked to output format than architecture family; substitution and displacement can remain invisible to downstream systems.
Under distribution shift, VLMs that mainly omit detections may shift toward substitution or displacement failures.
papers.selection_reason: Targeted study of physical adversarial robustness in grounding VLMs with a unified failure-mode evaluation framework; directly relevant to multimodal LLM-based perception.
papers.title: A Unified Evaluation Framework of Physical Adversarial Robustness in the Edge VLM Era
papers.tldr: A unified evaluation shows that compact grounding VLMs can be as physically vulnerable to adversarial patches as object detectors, while sometimes producing more dangerous, confident mislocalizations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress in general visual understanding, yet they still struggle with fine-grained instance-level consistency verification, where the goal is to determine whether two images depict the exact same physical object under varying viewpoints, illumination, and backgrounds. This task requires both global semantic perception and precise examination of subtle local evidence, since semantically similar objects may differ only in small suspicious regions. To address this challenge, we propose LocalAgent, a collaborative agentic framework that integrates the complementary strengths of a generalist MLLM and lightweight specialist verifiers. The MLLM first reasons globally to identify suspicious local regions, which are then delegated to a Local Evidence Verifier (LEV) toolkit for fine-grained appearance and geometric matching. LEV comprises Local Appearance Consistency (LAC), which estimates appearance similarity under illumination and color changes, and Local Geometric Correspondence (LGC), which estimates spatial correspondence under viewpoint changes. LEV returns structured scalar evidence that the MLLM integrates for the final decision. We further introduce an auxiliary-capped reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) strategy, in which answer correctness dominates auxiliary tool-use and format signals, enabling the policy to learn when verification is necessary. Experiments show that LocalAgent improves mean accuracy by 4.9% over the strongest CoT-RFT baseline while invoking a verifier on only 12.13% of samples and preserving the general multimodal capabilities of the underlying MLLM. The open-source repository is available at https://github.com/Firefly-zoo/LocalAgent-main.
authors: Jiachen Guo, Xinshan Zhu, Boyun Wang, Yanyan Liang, Jun Wan, Feng Lin, Ajian Liu
bullets: Targets instance-level consistency under viewpoint, illumination, and background changes, where differences may appear only in small regions.
The MLLM identifies suspicious areas and delegates them to lightweight Local Evidence Verifiers for detailed analysis.
LAC evaluates local appearance consistency, while LGC measures local geometric correspondence; their structured evidence guides the final decision.
An auxiliary-capped reinforcement fine-tuning strategy teaches the model when verification is necessary while prioritizing answer correctness.
Reports a 4.9% mean-accuracy gain over the strongest CoT-RFT baseline, with verifier use on only 12.13% of samples.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic MLLM framework combining global visual reasoning with local geometric/appearance verifiers for fine-grained instance consistency; fits VLM and spatial reasoning interests.
papers.title: LocalAgent: Collaborative Agentic Verification for Fine-Grained Instance-Level Consistency
papers.tldr: LocalAgent combines global MLLM reasoning with targeted local appearance and geometric verification to improve fine-grained identification of whether two images show the same physical object.

papers.abstract: Sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) communicate through short click sequences called codas, whose structure includes the rhythmic pattern of inter-click intervals (ICI) and the spectral composition of the clicks. In this paper, we propose the Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoder (DCCE), which explicitly encodes rhythm and spectral information with separate encoders before fusing them. We evaluate DCCE on three coda-understanding tasks: social unit, coda type, and individual identification. We compare DCCE against strong baselines from literature under a common linear-probe protocol and analyze the role of each channel and training objective through ablations. On 1,383 codas, shared partitions and validation-only layer selection support three random splits and three recording-date-disjoint folds. DCCE with unit pairing and type supervision achieves mean random-split macro-F1 of 0.901/0.865/0.597 for unit/type/identity. Raw ICI remains strongest for type (0.987), and ICI plus temporal mel statistics is a strong identity reference (0.724). An auxiliary identity objective improves spectral-branch identity prediction but does not improve the mean fused-identity score in this configuration. Date-grouped evaluation and four year holdouts expose generalization limits. The results support task-dependent combinations of timing and spectral information, without establishing independent biological channels or general architectural superiority. Code, notebooks, and complete results are available at https://dcce-research-site.vercel.app.
authors: Jo\~ao Victor Quintanilha, Emma Virnelli, Shuo Zhang
bullets: Evaluates social-unit, coda-type, and individual-identification tasks on 1,383 codas using linear probes across random splits and date-disjoint folds.
Combines separate inter-click-interval and spectral encoders through contrastive training and fusion, with ablations of channels and objectives.
Achieves mean random-split macro-F1 of 0.901 for unit, 0.865 for type, and 0.597 for identity under the reported configuration.
Raw ICI is strongest for coda type, while ICI plus temporal mel statistics is a strong identity reference.
Date-grouped evaluation and year holdouts expose generalization limits; results do not establish independent biological channels or universal architectural superiority.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a dual-channel contrastive encoder (DCCE) for audio data to understand whale communication, representing a multimodal technical contribution.
papers.title: Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoding of Sperm Whale Coda
papers.tldr: DCCE separately encodes sperm whale coda rhythm and click spectra, improving some understanding tasks while revealing strong task and recording-date generalization limits.

papers.abstract: We introduce MixAgent, an agentic pipeline for music post-production that follows the workflow of audio engineers to build interpretable and editable mixing plans guided by a reference song. A grouping agent first routes related input tracks, such as drum recordings, into subgroups. A planning agent then uses retrieved examples to choose and order audio effects, such as volume control and reverb, for tracks, subgroups, and the full mix. To refine the mix, a detector identifies what needs correction, and a critic proposes numerical parameter adjustments from tracks to the full mix. In our experiments, prompting recent multimodal models to listen and revise often worsens the mix, making reliable correction a central challenge. We therefore build MixCritic, a dataset of 45,657 repair critiques derived from parameters fitted to professional mixes, and train the critic with supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization on rendered audio outcomes. On MedleyDB, learned refinement reduces error by 19% relative to the initial mix, with preference optimization reducing it by 8.4% over supervised training alone. Retrieved examples further improve effects selection, and a human listening test shows that MixAgent gets higher quality ratings than mixes produced by Qwen3-Omni, Gemini 3.8 Flash and GPT-4o-audio.
authors: Jaywon Koo, Junghyun Koo, Marco A. Martinez-Ramirez, Wei-Hsiang Liao, Seungheon Doh, Qiyu Wu, Vicente Ordonez, Yuki Mitsufuji
bullets: Groups related tracks, plans and orders effects using retrieved examples, and supports edits from individual tracks to the full mix.
Uses a detector to identify mixing problems and MixCritic to propose numerical parameter corrections.
MixCritic is trained on 45,657 critiques derived from professional mixes, with supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization.
On MedleyDB, refinement reduces error by 19% from the initial mix; preference optimization adds an 8.4% improvement over supervised training alone.
Human listeners rate MixAgent mixes higher than mixes from several multimodal models; reliable automated correction remains challenging.
papers.selection_reason: Utilizes multimodal models (audio) in an agentic pipeline (MixAgent) for music post-production, including a critic trained on preference optimization.
papers.title: Agentic Music Post-Production
papers.tldr: MixAgent is an interpretable, reference-guided agentic system for music mixing that plans effects and learns to refine mixes through audio-based critiques.

papers.abstract: Many problems in signal processing, machine learning, and neuroimaging provide several jointly observed measurements of one process, each mixing a component common to all of them with a component private to itself, and require the common component to be recovered without supervision. This problem has been studied in several communities, largely independently. Statisticians proposed canonical correlation analysis (CCA), introduced by Hotelling in 1936. Information theorists proposed two notions of common information, due to G\'acs and K\"orner and to Wyner. Engineers developed subspace methods for sensor arrays and multiuser communications to design multiview receivers. This tutorial presents the main results and tools each community developed for this problem in a single exposition, and explains the connections that emerge where they meet, distinguishing exact equivalences from special cases and analogies. We develop the information-theoretic foundation from first principles. We then introduce CCA and its extension to several views, followed by the engineering thread from blind multiuser detection to CCA as a blind receiver. Next, we turn to nonlinear CCA, covering kernel, deep, and probabilistic formulations, the conditions under which the common factor is identifiable, and connections to self-supervised learning. We conclude with a discussion of further extensions and open directions. The exposition is self-contained, so that readers from each of these communities can follow the parts developed by the others.
bullets: Addresses unsupervised recovery of components shared across multiple measurements while separating view-specific components.
Connects Gács–Körner and Wyner common information, classical and multiview CCA, and engineering subspace methods.
Develops the information-theoretic foundations and explains exact equivalences, special cases, and analogies across communities.
Covers kernel, deep, and probabilistic nonlinear CCA, including common-factor identifiability and links to self-supervised learning.
Concludes with extensions and open research directions; it is a tutorial rather than a report of new experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Tutorial on Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) and its extensions to deep and probabilistic formulations, connecting information theory and signal processing to self-supervised learning. Relevant to multimodal foundation models for alignment and representation learning.
papers.title: From Common Information to Canonical Correlation Analysis and Beyond: Bridging Information Theory, Signal Processing, and Machine Learning
papers.tldr: A self-contained tutorial unifies common-component recovery across information theory, signal processing, statistics, and machine learning through CCA and its nonlinear extensions.

papers.abstract: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.
authors: Md Khalid Syfullah, Alvi Ataur Khalil
bullets: The study tests classically simulated 4- and 8-qubit quantum circuits within LLaVA-OneVision.
Quantum layers are evaluated through insertion and replacement at four model locations on Visual Spatial Reasoning.
Insertion after the visual projector achieves 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 points above classical full fine-tuning.
Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer preserves 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters.

Earlier replacements can hurt accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably reduce training or computation; security robustness is assessed across six attack settings, while generalization remains open.
papers.selection_reason: Explores quantum-enhanced layers in a vision-language model for spatial reasoning, relevant to multimodal foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?
papers.tldr: Quantum layers can improve or compress vision-language models, but their benefits depend strongly on where they are used and do not yet establish broad security gains.

papers.abstract: Few-shot image classification (FSIC) frequently suffers from visual ambiguity, where background clutter and RGB appearance similarities hinder discriminative feature matching in data-scarce settings. To mitigate this, we propose DAFIC, a geometry-guided framework that incorporates monocular depth into representation learning, episodic adaptation, and dense support-query matching. DAFIC first learns geometry-aware token representations through RGB-D self-supervised pre-training. Subsequently, the Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation (DGA) module uses depth-derived geometry to refine patch representations with geometry-enriched class context while suppressing background interference. Spatial Bidirectional Patch Matching (SBiM) then performs bidirectional dense matching on the refined features, reducing sensitivity to spurious correspondences and background clutter. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks show that DAFIC achieves strong performance against existing methods, with ablation and robustness analyses supporting the effectiveness of coupling geometry-conditioned episodic adaptation with bidirectional matching for few-shot visual recognition.
authors: Zhiqi Miao, Estefan\'ia Talavera, Weichuan Zhang, Jiapan Guo
bullets: Addresses visual ambiguity from background clutter and similar RGB appearances in data-scarce classification.
Uses RGB-D self-supervised pre-training to learn geometry-aware token representations.
Applies Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation to refine patch features with class context while suppressing background interference.
Uses Spatial Bidirectional Patch Matching for more robust dense support-query correspondence.
Experiments on four benchmarks, including ablation and robustness analyses, support the framework’s effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Depth-guided geometric adaptation for few-shot classification incorporates geometric priors into visual representations.
papers.title: Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation for Few-shot Image Classification
papers.tldr: DAFIC improves few-shot image classification by using monocular depth to make feature adaptation and dense patch matching more geometry-aware and less sensitive to clutter.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering requires models to assign attributes and relations to the correct objects, a problem known as visual binding. Structured prompts make these assignments explicit through labeled fields. Yet an improvement from the full prompt does not reveal which labels help or how they interact. First, we isolate field-label effects across ten models and six tasks by holding the image and claim fixed. These comparisons reveal differences that overall accuracy can hide. With a relation label present, adding object-role labels helps Qwen3 but hurts Qwen2 on Spatial. Second, we compare auxiliary hints that preserve or swap the question's role assignments against a no-hint baseline. Across two image sets, Qwen3's advantage with preserving hints mainly reflects errors caused by swapped hints. Preserving hints remain near baseline. Field order further affects the harm. Third, we test clearer hint wording and direct selection of the relation shown in the image. Clearer hints improve text matching but do not consistently improve visual judgments. In contrast, relation selection partly reduces errors for some hints in Qwen3 and GPT-4.1-mini.
authors: Xiaoyu Ma, Zheyuan Zhang, Kaiwen Shi, Yanfang Ye
bullets: Structured prompts expose visual-binding errors that overall accuracy can obscure.
Object-role labels interact differently with models: they help Qwen3 but hurt Qwen2 on Spatial when relation labels are present.
For Qwen3, preserving hints stays near the no-hint baseline, while swapped hints account for much of the apparent benefit of preserving hints.
Clearer hint wording improves text matching but does not consistently improve visual judgments.
Selecting the relation shown in the image partly reduces hint-related errors for some cases in Qwen3 and GPT-4.1-mini.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of compositional prompt cues in visual question answering directly concerns multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Beyond Correct Answers: How Compositional Cues Shape Visual Judgments
papers.tldr: Visual prompt structure can substantially alter visual judgments, but its effects depend on the model, task, hint correctness, and field order.

papers.abstract: Most unified multimodal models treat images and text asymmetrically: a pretrained language model generates text, an attached diffusion head generates images, and outputs that contain both are produced in a fixed order, so the first output cannot adapt to the second. We ask whether both modalities can instead be generated by one process that is trained on them jointly from scratch. Pretrained encoder spaces hold both modalities in one continuous form and carry knowledge learned at scale, and recent work finds them effective as generative targets for vision and language. We therefore model the joint distribution directly in these spaces. We introduce JUICE (Joint Unified multimodal modeling In Continuous Encoder spaces), a single flow matching Transformer over frozen image and text representations, in which each modality has its own noise level. Which modalities are clean and which are generated then decides the task: image generation, captioning, visual question answering, or joint generation. Controlled pretraining runs test each design choice. At equal guidance, generating text as continuous states leaves image generation intact (48.41 GenEval, against 47.86 for a model trained only for text-to-image generation), while captions lose some exact wording. Training on joint and conditional denoising together beats either alone, and semantic encoder spaces beat VAE latents and raw pixels as targets. At 2.1B parameters, with no language model initialization and at 224x224, JUICE reaches up to 0.88 on GenEval and 73.1 on VQAv2. By sampling both modalities from the joint distribution (coupled sampling), it can also draw a route on a map while writing out the matching moves. On mazes with several valid solutions, joint success rises from 54.6% with independent sampling to 93.7%, and no modality has to go first. On visual spatial planning, JUICE solves 99.8% of maps at its training sizes.
authors: Jiahan Li, Huangyuan Su, Shengbang Tong, Shusheng Yang, Ruihan Guo, Suozhi Huang, Hexu Zhao, Pratyusha Sharma, Sherry Yang, Jiatao Gu, Rob Fergus, Kyunghyun Cho
bullets: Addresses the asymmetry of prior unified models, where one modality is generated first and cannot adapt to the other.
Uses frozen image and text representations, modality-specific noise levels, and a shared flow-matching Transformer.
Supports image generation, captioning, visual question answering, and joint generation by varying which modalities are clean or generated.
Joint and conditional denoising together improves performance; semantic encoder spaces outperform VAE latents and raw pixels as targets.
Coupled sampling greatly improves multimodal consistency on mazes, raising joint success from 54.6% to 93.7%; JUICE reaches up to 0.88 GenEval and 73.1 VQAv2.
papers.selection_reason: Joint multimodal generation in continuous encoder spaces is a general multimodal foundation modeling contribution.
papers.title: JUICE: Unified Multimodal Modeling in Pretrained Representation Spaces
papers.tldr: JUICE jointly generates images and text in pretrained encoder spaces with a single flow-matching Transformer, enabling flexible multimodal generation and coordinated outputs without a fixed modality order.

papers.abstract: We present Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR, a family of audio-language models that builds upon its predecesor Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR with improved speech recognition and expanded capabilities in speaker-diarized transcription and general audio understanding. The family retains support for 30 languages and 16 Chinese dialects, together with instruction-controlled capabilities including historical-context conditioning, hierarchical hotword customization, and native transcription polishing. Speaker-diarized ASR produces structured outputs containing speaker labels, timestamps, and recognized text, maintaining consistent speaker labels across turns and the representation of overlapping speech. The general audio understanding capabilities cover audio-, speech-, and music-captioning, temporal grounding and sound event detection, as well as audio question answering and multiple-choice reasoning. These tasks broaden the application scope from recognizing spoken words to interpreting speakers, acoustic events, and their temporal relations. To accommodate different deployment requirements, the family includes variants for asynchronous file transcription, low-latency streaming, interactive voice input, and non-streaming recognition, with speaker-diarized transcription and general audio understanding available in certain variants. Evaluations span conventional ASR, multilingual and dialectal speech, speaker-diarized transcription, and general audio understanding, demonstrating the capabilities of the Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR family across transcription and broader audio analysis tasks.
authors: Chuanmeng Bian, Daren Chen, Peixin Chen, Zhigao Chen, Chong Deng, Zhiyun Fan, Zhifu Gao, Bo Gong, Qing Gu, Jiajun He, Yawei Hu, Yunjie Ji, Wei Ju, Jingbei Li, Xiangang Li, Xu Li, Zengxi Li, Zheng Li, Chengdong Liang, Baiji Liu, Yaming Liu, Ying Liu, Bin Ma, Yiping Peng, Yuezhang Peng, Zhendong Peng, Yu Pu, Yang Shi, Xin Shu, Jian Tang, Biao Tian, Peiyao Wang, Tianzi Wang, Wen Wang, Wupeng Wang, Cheng Wen, Yuzhong Wu, Zijian Xia, Yunchong Xiao, Nan Yang, Jianwei Yu, Jixing Yu, Binbin Zhang, Lei Zhang, Sitong Zhao, Guangdong Zhou, Yuan Zhou, Jianheng Zhuo

Adds speaker-diarized transcription with labels, timestamps, consistent identities, and overlapping-speech representation.

papers.title: Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR Technical Report

papers.abstract: Recent studies have explored the potential of multimodal large language models for robot control, yet the models' embodied capabilities remain insufficiently characterized across models, tasks, and execution settings. We conduct a multidimensional comparative evaluation on RoboColiseum across four tracks: Instruction Following, Spatial Reasoning, General Manipulation, and Robustness. We implement Agent2Act, a control harness that integrates GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon into the evaluation environment through shared observation, action execution, and feedback interfaces. Under common task settings and scoring criteria, all four models exhibit a consistent capability profile: high instruction-following scores, with three approaching perfect performance; strong spatial reasoning; and general manipulation scores below those of the other three tracks. Within the evaluated configurations, Astra leads instruction following and robustness, while Opus leads spatial reasoning, general manipulation, and overall performance. These results reveal complementary strengths across models and a persistent gap between task understanding and reliable physical execution. Component comparisons on selected tasks further show that harness design affects task success, planning cost, and execution time. Additionally, case studies with Astra examine whole-body coordination, manipulation across robot embodiments, precision manipulation, dexterous-hand manipulation, and real-robot tasks, providing further insight into the model's capabilities and limitations across embodied tasks.
bullets: Evaluates GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon across instruction following, spatial reasoning, manipulation, and robustness.
All models perform strongly on instruction following and spatial reasoning, but general manipulation is consistently weaker.
Astra leads instruction following and robustness; Opus leads spatial reasoning, manipulation, and overall performance in the tested configurations.
Harness design influences task success, planning cost, and execution time.
Astra case studies examine whole-body coordination, cross-embodiment manipulation, precision and dexterous manipulation, and real-robot tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-model evaluation of frontier multimodal LLMs for embodied robot control, including instruction following, spatial reasoning, manipulation, and robustness.
papers.title: Frontier LLMs Enter the World of Robotics: A Cross-Model Evaluation on RoboColiseum
papers.tldr: A cross-model RoboColiseum evaluation finds that frontier multimodal LLMs understand robot tasks well but still struggle with reliable physical manipulation, with performance varying by model and harness design.

papers.abstract: General-purpose multimodal models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, demonstrate broad capabilities in embodied manipulation. Our analysis indicates that this generality is accompanied by strong spatial perception, as Astra can determine where to interact with task-relevant entities amid visual distractors. Because spatial perception connects high-level reasoning to the physical scene, we investigate scaling visual grounding to strengthen the perceptual foundation of general embodied operation. We develop a unified data pipeline that combines robot manipulation recordings with complementary visual data from diverse sources. After automatically annotating the robot recordings, the pipeline converts the collected data into verifiable grounding supervision. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on approximately 1.5 million samples produced by this pipeline yields ACE-Brain-0.6. The model outperforms GPT-6 Astra on four of seven public grounding benchmarks, with an overall average score of 75.41 compared with Astra's 73.68. Under a fixed Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuning setup, aggregate grounding performance improves steadily as successive data releases expand the training collection to cover a broader range of grounding scenarios. These results show that scaling verifiable grounding supervision from diverse sources can strengthen the spatial perception of an open 9B model for general embodied operation.
bullets: Motivation: spatial perception links high-level reasoning with interaction in physical scenes.
Method: a unified pipeline combines robot manipulation recordings and diverse visual data, automatically annotates them, and converts them into verifiable grounding supervision.
Training: Qwen3.5-9B was fine-tuned on approximately 1.5 million generated samples.
Results: ACE-Brain-0.6 outperforms GPT-6 Astra on four of seven public grounding benchmarks, with average scores of 75.41 versus 73.68.
Scope: performance improves as successive data releases broaden grounding scenarios under a fixed fine-tuning setup.
papers.selection_reason: Scales verifiable visual grounding to strengthen spatial perception of physical foundation models for embodied operation.
papers.title: ACE-Brain-0.6: Scaling Spatial Grounding for Physical Foundation Models
papers.tldr: ACE-Brain-0.6 strengthens spatial grounding in an open 9B multimodal model by scaling diverse, verifiable supervision from robot and visual data.

papers.abstract: Foundation models offer a promising basis for robotic agents, but long-horizon tasks require them to sustain coherent reasoning and reliable physical execution across interdependent stages. We introduce Embodied Playground, a benchmark for evaluating how foundation-model agents coordinate physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning throughout such tasks. Agents must track task progress, satisfy intermediate constraints, and revise their plans using execution feedback as earlier actions shape subsequent decisions. The playground comprises 410 task environments spanning basic manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities, with variations in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. We curate EP-100, a representative selection of 100 tasks across five suites and 16 task types, together with the EP-Easy and EP-Hard difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection. A shared protocol specifies observation and tool access, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent checks of goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity. Embodied Playground provides a unified framework for studying whether foundation-model agents can sustain effective reasoning and action over extended task horizons. https://winniechen2002.github.io/Agent-bench-website/
bullets: Covers 410 environments involving manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities.
Tests coordination of physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning under interdependent actions and execution feedback.
Provides EP-100, EP-Easy, EP-Hard, and EP-20 task selections spanning five suites and 16 task types.
Uses a shared protocol with observation/tool constraints, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent validity checks.
Evaluates task progress, intermediate constraints, plan revision, goal completion, rule compliance, and physical validity.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for foundation-model agents on long-horizon physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning in embodied environments.
papers.title: Embodied Playground: A Long-Horizon Agentic Robotics Benchmark for Physical, Strategic, and Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: Embodied Playground benchmarks whether foundation-model agents can sustain reliable reasoning and physical action across long-horizon robotic tasks.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.
bullets: Controlled results across 22 benchmarks show that merely increasing inference-time reasoning yields modest gains.
A capability layer standardizes tool access and renders tool outputs as model-readable evidence.
Persistent memory stores images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts across reasoning steps.
A coding interface enables computations that combine outputs from multiple tools.

Across eight open and proprietary backbones, it improves average scores by 9.7–12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, with substantially lower token cost than maximum-effort alternatives in one comparison.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal tool-use harness with persistent agentic memory and evidence composition for MLLMs.
papers.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
papers.tldr: OpenVLHarness improves visual-agent reasoning by combining heterogeneous tool use with persistent multimodal memory for iterative evidence gathering and composition.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models have substantially improved in language understanding, in-image text rendering, and visual composition, while their safety mechanisms do not always keep pace with these capabilities. This creates a cross-modal attack surface in which harmful semantics can remain inconspicuous in a serialized prompt yet emerge through image-level composition. We propose CollageAttack, an automated single-prompt black-box jailbreak that shifts semantic assembly into the image plane by combining context-relevant scenes, scene-grounded textual carriers, and spatially distributed text fragments. Experiments across multiple open-weight and commercial T2I models show that CollageAttack achieves attack success rates of up to 86.0%, outperforming the strongest baseline on the same model by 18.5 percentage points, while consistently producing more harmful outputs and preserving the source intent. We further find that distributed textual fragments can reconstruct the intended semantics after generation, with visual composition producing stronger communicative impact than text alone. These results reveal a cross-modal safety gap in which harmful meaning emerges from the composition of individually less explicit elements.
bullets: Targets a cross-modal safety gap: harmful semantics can be inconspicuous in serialized prompts but emerge through image composition.
Uses an automated, single-prompt, black-box attack combining context-relevant scenes, scene-grounded text carriers, and spatially distributed text fragments.
Evaluated across multiple open-weight and commercial T2I models, reaching attack success rates of up to 86.0%.
Distributed fragments can reconstruct the intended meaning after generation, with visual composition strengthening its communicative impact.
Shows that individually less explicit elements can combine into harmful outputs while preserving the source intent.
papers.selection_reason: CollageAttack investigates cross-modal alignment flaws in T2I models by exploiting spatial text composition, contributing to the understanding of spatial reasoning and safety in multimodal models.
papers.title: CollageAttack: Exploiting Cross-Modal Alignment Flaws in T2I Models through Spatial Text Composition
papers.tldr: CollageAttack jailbreaks text-to-image models by hiding harmful meaning across spatially composed visual and textual elements that evade prompt-level safety checks.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities, with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supporting complex multi-hop reasoning by retrieving evidence distributed across documents. Graph-based approaches exploit connections among evidence, and hypergraph-based retrieval further preserves higher-order entity associations within documents and connects documents through shared entities. However, existing hypergraph retrievers often rely on predefined structural expansion or diffusion, which may miss query-dependent interactions needed to identify relevant evidence. They also leave connections among retrieved evidence implicit, requiring LLMs to reconstruct these connections before reasoning. Therefore, we propose HyperReCo, a framework for retrieving and connecting evidence with a hypergraph neural network (HyperGNN). We represent each document as a hyperedge over its extracted entities, with shared entities connecting the hyperedges. Through hypergraph message passing with joint supervision over documents and entities, the HyperGNN learns query-dependent interactions to retrieve complementary evidence. We further introduce Gradient-Guided Hyper-Path Decoding (GGHD), which uses gradient attribution to interpret the learned interactions and translate them into explicit hyper-paths that help LLMs combine complementary facts for multi-hop reasoning. Experiments on six benchmarks show that HyperReCo achieves the best retrieval performance among the compared methods on all three multi-hop QA datasets, together with strong downstream QA performance. Case studies and further analyses demonstrate the utility of decoded hyper-paths for connecting retrieved evidence.
bullets: Addresses the need to model query-dependent interactions among evidence spread across documents.
Represents documents as hyperedges over extracted entities, with shared entities linking documents.
Jointly supervises document and entity representations to retrieve complementary evidence.
Uses Gradient-Guided Hyper-Path Decoding to convert learned interactions into explicit reasoning paths.
Achieves the best retrieval performance among compared methods on all three evaluated multi-hop QA datasets, with strong downstream QA performance.
papers.selection_reason: HyperReCo proposes a hypergraph neural network for retrieving and connecting evidence in LLMs, contributing to multimodal reasoning and retrieval-augmented generation techniques.
papers.title: HyperReCo: Retrieving and Connecting Evidence with Hypergraph Neural Networks for LLM Multi-hop Reasoning
papers.tldr: HyperReCo uses a query-aware hypergraph neural network to retrieve complementary evidence and explicitly connect it into hyper-paths for improved LLM multi-hop reasoning.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence has recently been assessed through generative tasks such as spatially grounded image editing, yet language-guided generation of spatially consistent views from partial multi-view observations remains underexplored. We introduce MindView, a benchmark for generative multi-view spatial intelligence with 1,500 samples from 513 scenes across three indoor datasets. Its seven tasks form two families: geometry-dominant tasks specify changes in camera position and orientation, while semantics-dominant tasks require inferring target viewpoints by grounding referred objects and interpreting spatial relations and reference-frame cues. Evaluation of eleven generators reveals substantial room for improvement on MindView. A paired context analysis further shows that all eleven generators obtain lower overall scores under the expanded context setting. These findings motivate us to investigate whether task-specific supervision can improve target-view generation and whether models can use additional multi-view evidence effectively. We therefore fine-tune BAGEL on the MindView training dataset, improving its overall score by 24.3 points and yielding gains across all seven MindView tasks. Beyond these generation gains, the fine-tuned model also yields higher scores on three spatial-understanding benchmarks without training on their annotations, suggesting that learning to generate spatially grounded views may benefit spatial understanding. To improve evidence utilization under expanded context, we propose MindCue, a training-free spatial evidence selector guided by a target-view hypothesis. MindCue reverses the drop in overall score under expanded context and outperforms the standard-context baseline. Overall, MindView provides a concrete testbed for generative multi-view spatial intelligence.
authors: Yanbo Wang, Siqi Luo, Siyu Zhang, Chenming Zhu, Wenzhao Zheng, Qian Yu, Juncheng Yan, Bin Fu, Tai Wang, Yu Qiao, Yihao Liu, Jiwen Lu
bullets: Introduces 1,500 samples from 513 indoor scenes across seven tasks in geometry- and semantics-dominant families.
Evaluates 11 generators and finds substantial room for improvement, with performance declining when more context is provided.
Fine-tuning BAGEL on MindView improves its overall score by 24.3 points and benefits all seven tasks.
The fine-tuned model also improves three spatial-understanding benchmarks without using their annotations.
MindCue, a training-free target-view-guided evidence selector, reverses the expanded-context performance drop and surpasses the standard-context baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and a method (MindCue) for generative multi-view spatial intelligence, directly aligning with the spatial intelligence subtopic.
papers.title: MindView: Benchmarking Generative Multi-View Spatial Intelligence
papers.tldr: MindView benchmarks how well generative models infer and produce spatially consistent target views from partial multi-view observations, revealing major gaps and showing that task-specific fine-tuning and evidence selection help.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive models (ARMs) face a "Sequentiality Bottleneck" in reasoning, while diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallelism but lack semantic coherence. To addresses both limitations, we propose Collaborative Reasoning Asymmetric Learning (CoRAL), a hybrid framework via an Asymmetric Planner-Executor (APE) architecture: a DLM Planner generates K diverse reasoning trajectories in parallel, while a large ARM Executor selects the optimal plan and synthesizes the final answer. To train the Planner effectively, we introduce Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT (RDC), which integrates outcome-based rewards into the diffusion process to steer it toward goal-directed reasoning. Experiments on vision-language benchmarks show that CoRAL significantly outperforms prior diffusion-based methods and achieves competitive performance against strong ARMs, achieving both superior efficiency and quality.
authors: Wei Cai, Jian Zhao, Yuchen Yuan, Xuelong Li
bullets: Targets the sequentiality bottleneck of autoregressive reasoning and the semantic-coherence limitations of diffusion language models.
Uses an Asymmetric Planner-Executor architecture: a diffusion planner generates K diverse reasoning trajectories in parallel, while an autoregressive executor selects and completes the best plan.
Introduces Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT to steer diffusion-generated reasoning toward goal-directed solutions using outcome-based rewards.
On vision-language benchmarks, CoRAL outperforms prior diffusion-based methods and is competitive with strong autoregressive models in both efficiency and quality.
papers.selection_reason: Hybrid diffusion-autoregressive framework for efficient multimodal reasoning directly fits multimodal large language model reasoning.
papers.title: Beyond the Sequentiality Bottleneck: A Hybrid Diffusion-Autoregressive Framework for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: CoRAL combines parallel diffusion-based planning with autoregressive execution to improve the efficiency and coherence of multimodal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Collaborative perception enables agents to retrieve the scene semantics and geometry beyond the field of view of any individual agent. This broader scene understanding enhances transportation safety and improves efficiency in multi-robot systems. However, existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods rely on dense 3D voxel annotations and are limited to recognizing objects within a predefined set of semantic classes. To overcome these limitations, we present CoGaussian, an open-vocabulary Gaussian-based collaborative semantic occupancy prediction framework. CoGaussian represents a scene as a set of foundation model-aligned sparse 3D Gaussians, which serve as a compact representation for communicating and fusing geometric and semantic information across multiple agents. On the Semantic-OPV2V benchmark, our method outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of open-vocabulary collaborative scene understanding.
authors: Om Shivam Verma, Shaya Farahmand, Lingjun Zhao, Lu Gan
bullets: Addresses the limits of existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods, which require dense 3D voxel annotations and fixed semantic classes.
Represents scenes with sparse 3D Gaussians aligned to foundation models.
Uses Gaussians to communicate and fuse geometric and semantic information across agents.
Evaluated on Semantic-OPV2V, where it outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent methods.
