papers.title: From Views to Worlds: Active Exploration over 3D Worlds for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: V2W turns VLMs from passive image viewers into active 3D-world explorers by letting them gather spatial evidence through reconstructed geometry, camera poses, and language-grounded semantics.

papers.abstract: 3D manipulation policies derive actions from explicit scene geometry rather than color images alone, enabling them to reason over metric distances, object relations, and robot-scene reachability. This geometric interface is also a vulnerability: commodity RGB-D sensors return missing measurements, boundary artifacts, and plausible but wrong surfaces around transparent, reflective, thin, or textureless objects. We study this failure under realistic depth corruption and observe a sharp depth-noise cliff across modern 3D policies, even when they are trained with matched noisy depth. This residual gap motivates a spatial-encoding approach: corrupted depth becomes entangled with the token coordinates and geometry features consumed by the action expert. We propose Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding (NISE), a 3D policy architecture that learns trustworthy geometry features even facing imperfect depth. NISE uses Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision to shape shared policy features with calibrated multi-view depth, and Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention to carry position uncertainty into deployed attention rather than treating every lifted token as exact. Across simulated benchmarks with sensor-realistic corruption and real-robot tasks involving transparent and reflective materials, NISE improves depth-noise robustness while preserving clean-depth performance, supporting 3D policies designed for commodity RGB-D deployment rather than clean-depth benchmarks alone.
authors: Zhiyuan Yang, Jiaju He, Ruiteng Zhao, Anqi Cheng, Haiyue Zhu, Kezhi Mao
bullets: Commodity RGB-D sensors produce missing, distorted, or incorrect geometry, causing a sharp performance drop in modern 3D policies.
NISE learns trustworthy spatial features using Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision with calibrated multi-view depth.

The approach targets deployment with imperfect commodity RGB-D sensors, beyond clean-depth evaluation.

papers.abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

papers.abstract: Enabling humanoid robots to participate effectively in social interactions is important for their integration into human-centered environments. Existing methods, however, typically map pre-generated speech directly to continuous motion trajectories but have limited awareness of complex social environments and lack explicit high-level semantic action planning. We introduce SocialCoAct, a unified agent-centered framework for VLM-based egocentric social co-action. We formulate egocentric social co-action as an end-to-end agent task and develop SocialCoAct-Agent, which transforms egocentric observations and dialogue history into verbal responses and atomic action sequences, aligns each action with its corresponding utterance span, and executes the resulting behaviors in MuJoCo and on a physical humanoid robot. To evaluate the VLM capabilities required by this task, we construct SocialCoAct-Bench from continuous egocentric recordings of natural multi-party interactions. The benchmark comprises 423 human-verified multiple-choice questions across three subtasks: Long Episode Understanding (LEU), Speaker Intention Understanding (SIU), and Coordinated Action Planning (CAP). Across a diverse set of closed-source and open-weight VLMs, including general and egocentric models, the highest overall accuracy is 77.54%, while accuracy on the hard subset reaches only 46.51%. Extended reasoning improves Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B by 19.62 and 17.02 percentage points, respectively, but reduces inference throughput by 53.6$\times$ and 20.2$\times$. Visual-input ablations further show that the benefits of visual context vary across models. SocialCoAct provides a foundation for developing and evaluating VLM-based humanoid agents that coordinate context-aware speech and action in complex social interactions. The codebase and benchmark will be made publicly available upon publication.

papers.tldr: SocialCoAct introduces an egocentric VLM framework and benchmark for humanoid robots to understand social interactions and coordinate context-aware speech with physical actions.

papers.abstract: Best-of-N methods improve text-only LLM reasoning by sampling multiple trajectories before selecting an answer. For Vision-Language Models (VLMs), answer frequency and model confidence alone can be insufficient, as sampled generations also vary in their engagement with the visual input. We find that distributional confidence and visual attention are complementary indicators of rollout quality. Each is limited on its own, while trajectories that show strong signals in both are more likely to be correct. Motivated by this, we introduce VisConf, a rollout-quality score that multiplicatively combines visual engagement with candidate-calibrated Self-Certainty, penalizing rollouts that are weak in either signal. We incorporate Rank-Weighted Consensus (RWC), a tuning-free aggregation rule that converts within-question VisConf ranks into answer-level vote weights. Across three VLMs on MathVista, MMMU-Pro, and MMStar, VisConf with RWC consistently outperforms strong BoN baselines. Our analysis shows particularly large gains when correct trajectories are present but underrepresented in the candidate pool.
authors: Muhammad Usman, Muhammad Qasim Ayub, Usman Ahad, Muhammad Tahir
bullets: VLM rollout quality depends on complementary signals: attention to visual input and distributional confidence.

Rank-Weighted Consensus converts within-question VisConf rankings into tuning-free answer vote weights.
Across three VLMs and three multimodal benchmarks, VisConf with RWC consistently outperforms strong Best-of-N baselines.
Gains are especially large when correct trajectories exist but are underrepresented among sampled candidates.

papers.title: VisConf: Quality-Aware Consensus for Best-of-N in Vision-Language Model Reasoning
papers.tldr: VisConf improves Best-of-N VLM reasoning by selecting and weighting answers using both visual engagement and calibrated confidence.

papers.abstract: Concept erasure removes harmful, private, or copyrighted concepts from text-to-image models while preserving their other abilities. Leading models such as FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 are trained with flow matching, and erasure methods for them fine-tune the model toward a guided teacher's velocities under a Euclidean loss. Yet the squared distance is only one member of a larger family: Bregman divergences are exactly the losses under which flow matching recovers the correct velocity field, and each member shapes differently what is erased and what is preserved. We introduce BEM (Bregman erasure matching), which is, to our knowledge, the first to learn this divergence through bi-level optimization, so that the fine-tuned model forgets the concept on unseen prompts while its unrelated generations stay unchanged. In the experiments we target the suppression of nudity, violence, real identities, and copyrighted characters. Under the evaluation protocol of GEM, BEM removes more of the concept than GEM on most settings, cutting the unsafe rate on bloody gore from 53.9% to 14.4% and the FID on nudity from 8.64 to 6.64, while retention holds on some concepts and degrades on others.
bullets: Targets concept erasure in models such as FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3, where existing methods use Euclidean velocity matching.
Uses bi-level optimization to learn a Bregman divergence that balances forgetting the target concept with retaining other abilities.
Evaluated on nudity, violence, real identities, and copyrighted characters under the GEM protocol.
Outperforms GEM on most settings, including reducing bloody-gore unsafe rate from 53.9% to 14.4% and nudity FID from 8.64 to 6.64.

papers.title: BEM: Learning Bregman Divergences for Concept Erasure in Flow Matching Models
papers.tldr: BEM learns task-specific Bregman divergences to erase harmful or protected concepts from flow-matching text-to-image models while preserving unrelated generation capabilities.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate strong performance on multiple-choice question answering (MCQA), yet their reliability under biased conditions remains underexplored. We investigate length bias, the systematic preference for longer answer options, through controlled benchmarks spanning fine-grained visual domains. LVLMs consistently favor longer options even when visually inconsistent, with accuracy dropping 2--38\% when correct answers are shorter and increasing 1--70\% when longer. This bias persists across model scales. Through layer-wise mechanistic analysis, we reveal that length bias emerges from late-layer suppression of visual evidence in favor of language-side length priors. Blurry-image experiments show that bias intensifies when visual evidence weakens, while abstention tests reveal that LVLMs struggle to refuse incorrect predictions. We propose and evaluate multiple inference-time mitigation strategies; while these provide partial improvements, none achieves deployable bias mitigation without relying on oracle information unavailable at inference time. These results underscore that inference-time interventions are insufficient, pointing to the need for architectural solutions and bias-aware training.

Layer-wise analysis links the bias to late-layer suppression of visual evidence in favor of language-based length priors.
The bias becomes stronger with blurry images, while models also struggle to abstain from incorrect predictions.
Inference-time mitigation methods offer only partial improvements and require unavailable oracle information for reliable deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates length bias and robustness in large vision-language models for multiple-choice QA.
papers.title: Investigating Length Bias and Robustness in LVLMs for Multiple-Choice Question Answering
papers.tldr: LVLMs exhibit persistent length bias in multiple-choice visual QA, often overriding visual evidence, and current inference-time fixes only partially mitigate it.

papers.abstract: We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine-grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). We address these challenges with HumanSkill-4D, a training-free framework that shares a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars. For each avatar, a semantic memory links body-part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks and show that HumanSkill-4D outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.

bullets: Targets ambiguous references to adjacent body parts, garments, and visually similar motions.

An MLLM selects regions by appearance, relation, or function, while composable operators identify matching motion intervals.
Selections are traceable and extensible through category choices and operator programs.
On three human-annotated benchmarks, it outperforms baselines in part, 3D, and 4D referring segmentation, with minutes of per-avatar setup.

papers.title: HumanSkill-4D: Training-Free Language Querying of Animatable Gaussian Avatars in Space and Time
papers.tldr: HumanSkill-4D enables training-free language-based selection of avatar regions and motion intervals by combining multimodal reasoning with geometric operations.

papers.abstract: Recent 3D Large Language Models (3D-LLMs) have shown strong performance on scene question answering with extensive post-training. Yet, existing benchmarks rarely evaluate how 3D-LLMs respond to referential ambiguity, insufficient scene evidence, or false presuppositions, obscuring whether their responses are grounded in 3D evidence. In this work, we introduce UNICORNS, a benchmark for evaluating the reliability of 3D-LLM responses across four evidence conditions. UNICORNS contains 11,387 questions across 557 ScanNet scans, covering eight challenge categories alongside answerable controls. A response passes only if it satisfies the required response behavior and contains no scene claim unsupported by the available evidence. Evaluation of six open-sourced 3D-LLMs reveals a pronounced performance gap: even the strongest zero-shot model achieves 61.22% accuracy on answerable controls, but only 40.94% across the eight challenge categories. To address this gap, we further propose HORN, an obligation-aware post-training method combining group-relative task rewards, leaf-conditioned obligation rewards, and supervised control replay. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HORN reaches $75.1 \pm 1.0\%$ across the challenge categories and $77.2 \pm 0.8\%$ overall, outperforming all baselines without degrading answerable-control accuracy. Our findings enable a systematic evaluation and improvement of evidence-grounded 3D reasoning for 3D-LLMs (code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/unicorns-6B38/).
authors: Yifei Zhao, Fanyu Zhao, Han Zhang, Yixuan Lin, Yuyang Hou, Bin Wu, Ruike Cao, Li Xiao, Yinsheng Li

papers.title: Do 3D Large Language Models Really Use 3D Evidence?
papers.tldr: UNICORNS reveals that 3D-LLMs often fail to ground answers in available 3D evidence, while HORN substantially improves reliable reasoning without hurting answerable-question performance.

papers.abstract: We introduce Long Listening Thoughts (LLT), a framework for constructing post-training datasets that improves audio reasoning by pairing deliberate perceptual grounding with explicit cognitive behaviors. On audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks, large audio-language models (LALMs) are limited primarily by perceptual errors, yet existing post-training datasets rely on audio descriptions of limited diversity. Through a four-stage pipeline, LLT (1) builds multi-aspect dense audio descriptions spanning semantic, acoustic, and temporal information, (2) generates more challenging questions, (3) synthesizes incorrect reasoning traces, and (4) extends short reasoning traces into long ones via a thought-continuation strategy that elicits cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. Using LLT, we synthesize 1.6M reasoning traces and train Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with a two-stage pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). This improves accuracy on MMAU Test-mini (71.5 to 78.2), MMAR (56.7 to 63.7), and MMSU (60.6 to 66.0).
authors: Jaeyeon Kim, Chao-Han Huck Yang, Luoyi Zhang, Chan-Jan Hsu, Fernando Ruiloba Portilla, Jinchuan Tian, Shinji Watanabe, Carlos Busso
bullets: Targets perceptual errors and limited-diversity descriptions in existing audio post-training data.
Builds dense semantic, acoustic, and temporal descriptions, then creates challenging questions and incorrect reasoning traces.
Extends short traces into longer cognitive reasoning sequences through thought continuation.
Synthesizes 1.6M traces and trains Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with supervised fine-tuning followed by direct preference optimization.
Reports accuracy gains on MMAU Test-mini, MMAR, and MMSU.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training framework for large audio-language models that improves auditory reasoning; fits multimodal foundation models and multimodal LLM extension to audio.
papers.title: Long Listening Thoughts: Eliciting Open Auditory Reasoning with Deliberative Perception and Cognitive Refinement
papers.tldr: LLT improves audio reasoning by combining detailed perceptual grounding with long, explicit reasoning traces that include verification and backtracking.

papers.abstract: In multimodal learning, modality imbalance often lets one modality dominate optimization and keeps the model from fully exploiting cross-modal interactions. Balance-oriented methods such as the Multimodal Competition Regularizer (MCR) perform well by alleviating this imbalance during training. These dynamic balancing methods, however, mainly adjust modality contributions and do not consider how imbalance affects the formation of synergistic information during fusion. Synergy is a major source of multimodal advantage, because it is predictive gain that cannot be recovered from unimodal evidence alone. We propose the Multimodal Synergistic Competition Regularizer (MSCR), a fusion method that jointly promotes balanced modality utilization and the discovery of synergistic information. MSCR has two complementary objectives. An anti-dominance objective suppresses excessive unimodal influence and leaves room for synergistic information, and a synergy objective encourages the fused predictor to outperform a non-synergistic unimodal reference. An adaptive gate further concentrates the regularization on samples that need stronger collaborative modeling. Experiments on five benchmarks show that MSCR consistently improves performance over MCR and strengthens synergistic capability. It raises conditional recovery, the accuracy of the fused prediction on samples that the unimodal predictors misclassify, as well as the share of the model's output that InterSHAP attributes to cross-modal interactions. Its gain in conditional recovery persists when the fusion module is Transformer-based. Code is available at https://github.com/chenxinyu991-collab/MSCR.
authors: Xinyu Chen, Liangjian Wen, Jiang Duan, Dongkai Wang, Yong Dai, Jiayu Bai, Jianzhuang Liu, Zhen Tian, Guoping Qiu, Zhao Kan
bullets: Addresses modality dominance and the underdevelopment of cross-modal synergy during fusion.
Uses anti-dominance and synergy objectives, with an adaptive gate targeting samples needing stronger collaboration.
Evaluated on five benchmarks, MSCR consistently outperforms the MCR baseline.
Improves conditional recovery and the share of predictions attributed to cross-modal interactions.
Conditional-recovery gains persist with Transformer-based fusion modules.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal fusion regularizer balancing modality utilization and synergy, transferable to multimodal foundation model training.
papers.title: MSCR: Jointly Balancing Utilization Across Modalities and Discovering Synergistic Information
papers.tldr: MSCR improves multimodal fusion by balancing modality use while explicitly encouraging synergistic information that unimodal predictors cannot provide.

papers.abstract: Jointly pretrained multimodal encoders are a common way to combine modalities, while alternatives integrate their information during downstream training or inference. When does each approach win? We compare three paradigms, instantiated with public checkpoints, across 16 paired datasets in five domains and multiple training-label budgets. JOINT trains a fusion head on frozen, jointly pretrained encoders. DECOUPLED trains a fusion head on frozen, independently pretrained encoders. AGENT gives a frozen LLM task instructions, labelled examples, available sample text, and supervised unimodal readouts. No paradigm dominates the complete 144 dataset-budget combinations: DECOUPLED wins 54, JOINT 44, and AGENT 46 by mean utility. ScienceQA, MELD, and MetMeme shift from AGENT to fusion as supervision increases. Between the fusion paradigms, JOINT leads on four of five QA datasets across all evaluated budgets, while higher unimodal 5-NN accuracy is associated with a relative shift toward DECOUPLED across eight classification datasets (Spearman $\rho=-0.67$). We test whether representation and task diagnostics predict these preferences on held-out datasets before fitting their candidate systems. A two-step cascade combines these diagnostics with task and budget metadata to select AGENT or fusion, then JOINT or DECOUPLED. Under leave-one-group-out evaluation, it selects the winner in 71.4% of cells versus 54.2% for metadata-only routing, with mean relative regret 0.028 versus 0.057. Using geometry, supervised representation diagnostics, and text-label matching together yields higher accuracy and lower regret than using any one of these sources with metadata. These results connect paradigm preferences to supervision budget, task format, and unimodal 5-NN accuracy. Target-task diagnostics thus support selecting among the three paradigms before candidate fitting.
authors: Yi Fang, Gaurav Srivastava, Sirui Ding, Xuan Wang
bullets: Compares JOINT, DECOUPLED, and AGENT across 16 paired datasets, five domains, and varied label budgets.
DECOUPLED wins 54, JOINT 44, and AGENT 46 of 144 dataset-budget combinations by mean utility.
More supervision shifts some tasks from AGENT toward fusion; JOINT generally leads on QA, while stronger unimodal 5-NN accuracy favors DECOUPLED on classification.
A diagnostic cascade selects the paradigm winner in 71.4% of held-out cells, improving over 54.2% for metadata-only routing.
Combining geometry, supervised representation diagnostics, and text-label matching gives the best routing accuracy and regret among tested diagnostic sources.
papers.selection_reason: Compares multimodal alignment paradigms and selection diagnostics, directly relevant to multimodal foundation model design.
papers.title: Joint, Decoupled, or Agent: When Each Multimodal Alignment Paradigm Wins
papers.tldr: No multimodal alignment paradigm consistently wins; task diagnostics and supervision budget can guide whether to use AGENT, JOINT, or DECOUPLED.

papers.abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) generative models have made significant progress in producing high-fidelity images from natural-language prompts. Alongside this progress, numerous benchmarks have been developed to evaluate capabilities such as attribute binding, numeracy, spatial reasoning, and commonsense reasoning. In this work, we propose a new perspective on T2I evaluation by casting it as a constraint-satisfaction problem. We introduce a logical framework that formally specifies the benchmark domain, including objects, attributes, and relations, alongside the constraints that generated images must satisfy. We evaluated four state-of-the-art T2I models across 9 classes of constraints ranging from a single-object-attribute to multi-object relationships constraints involving logical operators ($\forall, \exists, count, \rightarrow$). Our results reveal a substantial gap between single-object and complex conditional multi-object relationship constraint classes, with the best-performing model achieving 98% accuracy on the former and just 53% on the latter. We assess compositional generalisation, finding that the best-performing model`s accuracy drops from 84% on single-constraint prompts to 20% when satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously. Identifying unsatisfiable constraints is also challenging, with the best model correctly recognizing only 23% of such prompts. Building on this framework, we introduce \textbf{LogicVal}, an evaluation methodology that combines neural visual detection with logical reasoning to assess constraint satisfaction in generated images. On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores ranging from 0.88 to 0.98, indicating strong alignment with human judgments. These findings underscore the value of logic-based evaluation for characterizing T2I model capabilities and limitations.
authors: Savitha Sam Abraham, Marjan Alirezaie, Hossein Rahnama
bullets: Reframes T2I evaluation as constraint satisfaction over objects, attributes, and relations.
Tests nine constraint classes, including logical operators such as ∀, ∃, counting, and implication, across four T2I models.
Performance drops from 98% on single-object attributes to 53% on complex conditional multi-object relations.
Compositional generalization declines from 84% for single constraints to 20% for multiple constraints; unsatisfiable prompts are recognized correctly only 23% of the time by the best model.
On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.88–0.98 against human judgments.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LogicVal, a benchmark for evaluating logical and spatial reasoning in Text-to-Image models using constraint satisfaction.
papers.title: LogicVal:A Logic-Formalized Benchmark for Constraint Satisfaction in Text-to-Image Generation
papers.tldr: LogicVal evaluates text-to-image models as logical constraint solvers, revealing major weaknesses in complex, multi-constraint, and unsatisfiable prompts.

papers.abstract: Generative AI is becoming an important medium for artistic creation, yet existing interactions often assume that creators can specify intentions in advance and accurately communicate them through text prompts. Artistic intentions, however, may be vague, latent, or recognizable only after seeing concrete visual possibilities. We propose a human-AI co-creation paradigm beyond explicit intent expression. By expanding model exploration, we expose artists to diverse visual possibilities, allowing them to identify previously unarticulated preferences through observation, comparison, and selection. We then integrate artists' curatorial judgments into reinforcement learning, assigning different learning strengths based on preferences over generation trajectories, so recognized directions are more strongly reinforced and the model gradually adapts to individual aesthetics. This creates a continuous "explore-identify-shape-re-explore" loop in which artistic intent is progressively discovered, externalized, and shaped. Through three user studies, we examine latent-preference discovery, personalized preference alignment, and the externalization of vague, difficult-to-express creative intentions.
authors: Renye Yan, Jialun Zhong, Jikang Cheng, Yi Gao, Yanzeng Li, Ling Liang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of text-prompt interactions that assume artists can specify intentions in advance.
Expands model exploration to present diverse visual possibilities, enabling artists to identify latent preferences through comparison and selection.
Uses artists’ curatorial judgments in reinforcement learning, with preference-dependent learning strengths for different generation trajectories.
Establishes an iterative “explore–identify–shape–re-explore” loop that adapts the model to individual aesthetics.
Three user studies investigate latent-preference discovery, personalized alignment, and externalization of difficult-to-express intentions.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a human-AI co-creation loop using reinforcement learning to shape artistic intent, integrating multimodal generation with user feedback.
papers.title: Beyond Explicit Intent: Discovering and Shaping Artistic Intent through Human-AI Co-Creation
papers.tldr: A human-AI co-creation framework helps artists discover vague creative intentions through visual exploration and progressively shapes generation toward their evolving preferences.

papers.abstract: Native multimodal large language models (native MLLMs) jointly encode visual and linguistic sequences within a unified autoregressive Transformer, emerging as a promising paradigm for multimodal understanding. Unlike conventional ViT-based MLLMs relying on external vision encoders, ViT-free native MLLMs tokenize pixel patches directly, potentially suffering severe visual token redundancy. A pilot study confirms this: unlike ViT-based models that degrade under compression, ViT-free MLLMs tolerate aggressive compression with near-lossless or even improved performance. Yet existing compression methods target ViT-based settings, leaving native MLLMs, which stand to gain the most, unexplored. To close this gap, we introduce an analysis pipeline centered on token discriminability and cross-dimensional heterogeneous redundancy, revealing that (i) redundancy is distributed independently and heterogeneously along height and width axes, and (ii) early-layer visual tokens are indiscriminable and uniformly redundant. Guided by these findings, we propose PACE (Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs), the first visual token compression framework tailored for native MLLMs with Multimodal-RoPE. Leveraging dimensional decoupling of positional encoding, PACE decomposes attention into two orthogonal spatial saliency estimates along height and width, gated by a positional attention signal, yielding direction-aware importance with negligible overhead. It further casts token budget allocation as Pareto optimization over performance preservation, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage, jointly identifying optimal compression depths and retention ratios. Experiments show PACE maintains near-lossless performance at only 25%-50% visual token retention, even improving several benchmarks, while delivering over 2x FLOPs reduction.
authors: Lei Tian, Chunzheng Zhu, Kai Wu, Yifan Zhang, Haihua Yang
bullets: Native MLLMs tokenize image patches directly, creating substantial visual-token redundancy that existing ViT-oriented compression methods do not address.
Analysis finds redundancy is heterogeneous and independently distributed across height and width, while early-layer tokens are broadly indiscriminable.
PACE estimates direction-aware spatial importance by decoupling Multimodal-RoPE attention along height and width with negligible overhead.
It allocates token budgets through Pareto optimization across performance, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage.
Experiments report near-lossless performance at 25–50% visual-token retention, with improvements on several benchmarks and over 2× FLOPs reduction.
papers.selection_reason: Visual token compression framework for native MLLMs, directly relevant to token pruning/eviction and multimodal LLM efficiency.
papers.title: PACE: Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs
papers.tldr: PACE efficiently compresses visual tokens in native MLLMs, retaining 25–50% of tokens with near-lossless or improved performance and over 2× lower FLOPs.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer binary clinical questions with a yes or no token, leaving the decision threshold implicit and fixed. We derive a continuous score from a single forward pass by renormalizing the probabilities of the yes and no tokens, allowing the threshold to be adapted to clinical needs without retraining. We evaluated this approach with MedGemma and Gemma-3 (4B and 27B) on six medical imaging datasets. The default threshold was frequently misaligned with the task: for identifying normal chest radiographs, MedGemma-27B labeled every image as abnormal, whereas a validation-selected threshold yielded a sensitivity of 0.945 and a specificity of 0.696. Normalization achieved the highest AUROC on four of six datasets (CheXpert: 0.819 vs. 0.777 for raw and 0.743 for text-elicited probabilities), and a single decision required 53-79 ms on one GPU. This simple post-hoc method turns medical MLLMs into fast classifiers with adjustable operating points. Code: https://github.com/TruhnLab/llm-threshold-calibration
authors: Patrick Wienholt, Frederik Hauke, Christiane Kuhl, Jakob Nikolas Kather, Sven Nebelung, Daniel Truhn
bullets: Medical MLLMs’ default yes/no threshold can be poorly calibrated for binary clinical tasks.
The method renormalizes yes and no token probabilities from one forward pass to produce a continuous decision score.
Validation-selected thresholds can substantially improve task-specific operating points; for normal chest radiographs, sensitivity was 0.945 and specificity 0.696.
Normalization achieved the best AUROC on 4 of 6 medical imaging datasets, including 0.819 on CheXpert.
Inference took 53–79 ms per decision on one GPU; evaluation covered MedGemma and Gemma-3 models.
papers.selection_reason: Post-hoc decision-score calibration for medical MLLMs; fits multimodal large language models.
papers.title: Single-Pass Decision Scores Enable Rapid Classification with Adjustable Thresholds in Medical Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A single-pass yes/no probability normalization turns medical multimodal LLMs into fast classifiers with tunable decision thresholds, without retraining.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual understanding requires distinguishing subtle differences in local attributes and spatial relations, yet remains challenging for existing vision-language models. Unified multimodal models (UMMs) offer a new opportunity through generation pathways that preserve rich visual information complementary to understanding. However, existing generation-assisted understanding methods mainly rely on generative supervision or explicit generation and have not systematically explored direct use of native generation-side representations. To address this gap, we systematically analyze what generation-side representations offer for fine-grained understanding, finding that they are more sensitive to fine-grained semantic changes, capture task-relevant changes missed by understanding-side representations, and depend on correct spatial organization for this advantage. Guided by these findings, we design GAFU, a post-training framework that unlocks native generation-side information for fine-grained understanding. It compresses generation-side visual representations into compact \(G\) tokens that preserve fine-grained visual details, enabling task-conditioned retrieval by the understanding pathway. Experiments show that GAFU consistently outperforms SFT baselines trained on the same data across diverse visual understanding tasks and UMM architectures, with maximum relative improvements of 20.00\%, 17.94\%, and 8.62\% on VStar-Bench, OmniSpatial, and VSR-Bench, respectively. Overall, GAFU converts complementary information from the generation pathway into gains in fine-grained visual understanding, providing an effective path toward synergy between generation and understanding in UMMs.
authors: Tengju Ru, Weitong Lian, Zecong Tang, Zhiheng Liu, Lingyi Meng, Haoran Li, Kaixuan Wang, Bohao Li, Xihui Liu
bullets: Fine-grained understanding of subtle attributes and spatial relations remains difficult for vision-language models.
Generation-side representations are more sensitive to fine-grained semantic changes, but their benefit depends on correct spatial organization.
GAFU compresses these representations into compact G tokens that preserve visual detail and support task-conditioned retrieval by the understanding pathway.
Across multiple tasks and UMM architectures, GAFU outperforms same-data SFT baselines, with reported maximum relative gains of 20.00%, 17.94%, and 8.62%.
The approach is evaluated within unified multimodal models and focuses on improving fine-grained visual understanding through generation-understanding synergy.
papers.selection_reason: Unlocks generation-side representations for fine-grained spatial understanding in unified multimodal models.
papers.title: What Generation Knows: Unlocking Fine-Grained Understanding in Unified Multimodal Models
papers.tldr: GAFU harnesses native generation-side representations in unified multimodal models to improve fine-grained visual understanding.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled them to act as autonomous agents, creating and editing 3D models via code or direct software manipulation. In practical workflows, these models must infer object shapes, materials, spatial layouts, and lighting from diverse references while strictly following instructions to reconstruct, modify, or design 3D content. However, existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of such open-ended requests across real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce BlenderWorld, the first comprehensive benchmark dedicated to evaluating frontier models on realistic 3D creation tasks. BlenderWorld comprises 223 tasks spanning architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization, driven by text, image, video, and structured specification inputs. To rigorously assess these complex deliverables, we establish a unified evaluation protocol: we render the submitted Blender projects from multiple viewpoints and evaluate them against 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics alongside holistic visual quality scores. Benchmarking thirteen frontier models reveals that GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest overall fused score of 79.9, followed by Opus-5 (73.0) and GPT-5.6-Sol (67.7). Ultimately, our findings reveal a critical bottleneck: while current models can parse broad instructions, they still profoundly struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence and accurate structural reproduction in Blender, leaving substantial headroom for future 3D-native agentics.
authors: Xinyu Fang, Yuchi Wang, Weihao Yu, Rongyao Fang, Zhaohai Li, Zhixun Li, Tiancheng Gu, Xilin Wei, Yuhang Zang, Hongsheng Li, Dahua Lin, Guofeng Zhang, Shuai Bai, Zhibo Yang, Dayiheng Liu
bullets: Introduces 223 open-ended tasks across architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization.
Uses text, image, video, and structured specifications as task inputs.
Evaluates rendered Blender projects from multiple viewpoints with 2,651 binary rubrics and holistic visual-quality scores.
Among 13 frontier models, GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest reported fused score, followed by Opus-5 and GPT-5.6-Sol.
Results show broad instruction understanding but substantial weaknesses in structural accuracy and 3D spatial consistency.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for MLLM agents on 3D creation, emphasizing spatial coherence; fits spatial intelligence and 3D foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: BlenderWorld: Benchmarking Visual Agents for 3D Creation from Real-World References
papers.tldr: BlenderWorld benchmarks multimodal agents on realistic Blender-based 3D creation and finds that models still struggle with fine-grained spatial coherence and faithful reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Although reinforcement learning (RL) effectively trains Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents, the mechanisms behind these capability gains are poorly understood. Across four diverse agent environments, we investigate whether the task-success gains from multi-turn RL are accompanied by improved grounded visual question answering about the environment. To assess this, we design environment-specific grounded VQA tasks that reveal improvements in grounded visual understanding. Representational probing shows that vision-encoder probe accuracy remains relatively stable, while LLM-layer probe accuracy improves. Attention analysis further reveals that LLM layers pay more attention to visual tokens during RL training. To test whether increased attention to visual tokens contributes to VQA gains, we introduce a lightweight plug-and-play intervention using a fixed attention bias. Without updating model parameters or computing gradients, this intervention partially restores VQA gains on the untrained model. These results reveal better utilization of visual information as a key mechanism behind the gains from RL.
authors: Ziqian Zhang, Junjie Liao, Zhining Zhang, Wentao Zhu
bullets: Across four agent environments, multi-turn RL gains are evaluated through environment-specific grounded visual question answering.
Vision-encoder probe accuracy stays relatively stable, while probe accuracy in LLM layers improves after RL.
Attention analysis shows that LLM layers attend more to visual tokens during RL training.
A fixed attention-bias intervention partially recovers VQA gains without parameter updates or gradients.
The findings suggest RL teaches VLMs where to attend, but not how to perceive visual content.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of RL-induced attention changes in VLMs; fits multimodal LLM understanding.
papers.title: RL Teaches VLMs Where to Attend but Not How to Perceive
papers.tldr: RL improves VLM agents mainly by helping their language-model layers use visual information more effectively, rather than by improving visual perception itself.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence, the capacity to represent and reason about physical space, underlies embodied perception and real-world visual understanding. Existing benchmarks probe it through spatial relations, perspective-taking, and mental modeling. What remains underexamined is whether a model can maintain a coherent scene representation across views, since pairwise comparison alone cannot reveal which view departs from the truth. We thus introduce Same Space or Not (SSoN), a benchmark of cross-view contradiction resolution comprising 1,000 questions from seven indoor scene sources and six categories of controlled 3D edits. Each question presents three views of an unchanged scene and one view of an edited variant. Models must identify the inconsistent view and explain the contradiction without a designated trusted reference or a marked target. Our pipeline iteratively translates human review into generation constraints. Automated checks and exhaustive human validation screen out both trivial visual shortcuts and questions lacking sufficient evidence for a unique answer. Humans achieve 83.3% accuracy, compared with 39.7% for the strongest vision-language models (VLMs), falling to 34.9% when a valid visual explanation is also required. We investigate prompting, camera information, and 3D reconstruction as interventions. On a 100-question intervention set with a 24% baseline, prompting and 3D reconstruction remain below 50% answer accuracy, except when ground-truth camera information is supplied, which reaches 61% answer accuracy but only 48% True solve accuracy. On a held-out 201-question test set, Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves 21.89% accuracy, 33.33% after answer-only fine-tuning, and 41.79% after fine-tuning on both rationales and answers. These results identify cross-view contradiction resolution as a substantial weakness of current VLMs that can be partly addressed by targeted supervision.
authors: Huizi Cao, Guanyu Xu, Zhixuan Liang, Ming Yin, Jiuxiang Gu, Manling Li, Mengdi Wang, Shilong Liu
bullets: Introduces a 1,000-question benchmark spanning seven indoor-scene sources and six controlled 3D-edit categories.
Requires identifying an inconsistent view among four without a trusted reference, marked target, or reliance on trivial visual cues.
Humans achieve 83.3% accuracy, versus 39.7% for the strongest tested VLMs and 34.9% when valid explanations are required.
Prompting and 3D reconstruction generally remain below 50% accuracy; ground-truth camera information improves answer accuracy to 61% but true solving to 48%.
On a held-out test set, Qwen2.5-VL-7B improves from 21.89% to 41.79% with fine-tuning on both answers and rationales.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for cross-view spatial reasoning directly targets spatial intelligence in VLMs.
papers.title: Same Space or Not: Benchmarking Spatial Intelligence Through Cross-View Contradictions
papers.tldr: SSoN reveals that current vision-language models struggle to detect and explain contradictions across views of the same 3D scene, though targeted rationale-and-answer supervision improves performance.

papers.abstract: Enterprises run schema-guided structured field extraction on documents with frontier multimodal models, and accuracy keeps improving as new models and systems arrive. Two things have not kept pace: the evidence for each extracted value, meaning the location of the document it was read from, and how far to trust the value and that evidence. Neither is a component of most extraction systems today, so we build them as a framework that attaches to an existing extractor and leaves it untouched. We present VERDICT, a plug-in framework that uses a small Vision--Language Model (VLM) to ground/localize the evidence once per document over a fixed external extractor's output, then calibrates value and evidence confidence. Fine-tuning the VLM for evidence localization substantially improves visual evidence quality and, more importantly, expands VERDICT's selective-prediction operating range. At a strict confidence threshold $0.80$, VERDICT with the fine-tuned VLM gives usable precision--coverage trade-offs for both value and evidence confidence across the in-distribution and out of distribution datasets, whereas the frozen setting often collapses to little or no coverage. Running an open-weight VLM for localization rather than a closed API makes its internal states available to the calibrator, and they are worth more than output log-probabilities: in-distribution AUROC rises from $0.730$ to $0.914$ for value confidence and from $0.681$ to $0.906$ for evidence confidence. This advantage does not survive a distribution shift. We show that the signal is displaced rather than destroyed, and that labeling roughly $120$ fields from the target dataset takes evidence confidence from $0.641$ to $0.905$ on one dataset and from $0.675$ to $0.829$ on the other.
authors: Harikrishnan P M, Goutham Vignesh, Siva Prasad, Zishan Ahmad, Mahesh Basveshwar Deshmukhe, Varun V, Rohit Agrawal, Vishal Vaddina
bullets: A small VLM localizes evidence for each extracted field and calibrates confidence in both the value and its supporting evidence.
Fine-tuning the VLM improves evidence quality and expands selective-prediction coverage at strict confidence thresholds.
Open-weight VLM internal states substantially outperform output log-probabilities for in-distribution confidence estimation.
This advantage weakens under distribution shift, but target-domain labeling of roughly 120 fields restores evidence-confidence quality.
The framework is evaluated across in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets, with scope limited by reduced cross-distribution calibration transfer.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-based evidence localization in document layouts is a multimodal spatial grounding contribution.
papers.title: VERDICT: Visual Extraction-Result Decoder with Integrated Confidence and Traceable Evidence
papers.tldr: VERDICT adds calibrated value confidence and traceable visual evidence to existing document extractors without modifying them.

papers.abstract: In certain real-world scenarios, obtaining labeled data is excessively expensive, motivating increasing interest in adapting models without annotations. Vision-language models (VLMs) provide pseudo-labels for unlabeled images through image-text similarity, enabling adaptation without manual labeling. The previous unsupervised vision-language model adaption methods assume access to an adaptation vocabulary containing all class names. However, a complete vocabulary is difficult to construct in real-world scenarios, as unlabeled data may contain classes that are overlooked or fall outside the current task scope. Thus, we propose Vocabulary-Incomplete Unsupervised Vision-language model Adaptation (VI-UVA), where only a subset of class names are available during adaptation. The vocabulary incompleteness induces an adaptation bias toward provided classes, which degrades omitted-class recognition. To address this issue, we propose Label Space Reconstruction (LSR), which reconstructs a latent label space from the unlabeled data and incorporates it into prompt tuning, thereby extending adaptation beyond the incomplete vocabulary and mitigating the adaptation bias. Furthermore, we derive an omitted-class semantic discrepancy bound for LSR and identify the key factors affecting the bound. Extensive experiments across eight benchmarks demonstrate that LSR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Si Qin, Jiawei Tang, Yaxin Hou, Yan Chen, Yutong Xie, Chen Li, Yuheng Jia
bullets: Existing unsupervised VLM adaptation assumes all relevant class names are available, which can bias adaptation toward known classes.
The proposed VI-UVA setting uses only a subset of class names during adaptation.
Label Space Reconstruction (LSR) infers a latent label space from unlabeled images and integrates it into prompt tuning.
The method derives a bound on omitted-class semantic discrepancy and analyzes factors influencing it.
Experiments on eight benchmarks show LSR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.
papers.selection_reason: Unsupervised VLM adaptation with incomplete vocabulary via label space reconstruction, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Vocabulary-Incomplete Unsupervised Vision-Language Model Adaptation
papers.tldr: VI-UVA enables unsupervised vision-language model adaptation when the available class vocabulary is incomplete by reconstructing omitted classes from unlabeled data.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models answer questions about images and also generate images with one shared set of weights. This creates a post-training risk that single-purpose models do not have: fine-tuning one capability can damage another that works in a different modality. We measure this cross-modal forgetting for LoRA post-training of Janus-Pro-7B. Every target is chosen by how poorly the base model already handles it, from a poetic register to a language it barely speaks, so that retention is tested against a real intervention; we then evaluate the capabilities we never trained, first after a single run and then after chaining three. A single run looks entirely safe: nothing we did not train degrades on four public benchmarks or in free-form English, even when the adapter cuts held-out Welsh perplexity by 76% with a relative weight change under 2%. That safety belongs to the run, not to the recipe. Chaining three runs destroys the capability learned one run earlier and raises general-text perplexity by one to two orders of magnitude above the never-adapted model, on the very measures that stayed flat before. The cause is in the objective, which constrains only the modality being trained and leaves the other head unconstrained: cutting the learning rate to one fifth does not prevent the collapse, while anchoring the other head removes the damage to the capabilities we never trained, at no cost to what is learned. What is learned also stays inside its own modality, with Welsh acquired from text closing only 3% of the English-Welsh gap in image generation.
authors: Francesco Colasurdo, Ivan Slobozhan, Joaquin Vanschoren, Anna Vettoruzzo
bullets: The study measures whether adapting one modality harms capabilities in another for Janus-Pro-7B.
A single LoRA run caused no observed degradation on four benchmarks or free-form English, despite substantially improving held-out Welsh perplexity.
Chaining three runs erased a capability learned earlier and increased general-text perplexity by one to two orders of magnitude.
Reducing the learning rate did not prevent collapse; anchoring the other modality’s head did, without sacrificing the trained capability.
Knowledge transfer across modalities was weak: text-based Welsh learning closed only 3% of the English–Welsh gap in image generation.
papers.selection_reason: Studies cross-modal forgetting in unified multimodal post-training and proposes anchoring to prevent collapse, relevant to multimodal foundation models and continual learning.
papers.title: Cross-Modal Forgetting and Transfer in Unified Multimodal Post-Training
papers.tldr: LoRA post-training of unified multimodal models appears safe after one run but can cause severe cross-modal forgetting when three runs are chained, which is prevented by anchoring the untrained head.

papers.abstract: Characters, locations, and actions recur throughout a movie, so many of its moments differ only in fine-grained details. Grounding such a moment in a full-length movie requires resolving that detail rather than matching the attributes it shares with other moments, yet existing temporal movie grounding benchmarks rarely test this. We introduce CoM$^2$-Bench, a benchmark of confusable query pairs, where the two queries in each pair share most attributes but differ in a single distinguishing detail within a full movie, posing a challenge for recent temporal grounding approaches. To locate where grounding breaks down, we analyze a retrieve-then-localize pipeline, in which a retriever first selects a short candidate chunk and a localizer then performs temporal grounding within it. Separating the two stages lets us attribute each failure to either retrieval or localization. We find that retrieval is the major bottleneck: state-of-the-art retrievers often select a moment's confusable counterpart, because their choices follow the content the two moments share rather than the detail that tells them apart. To address these failures, we propose a simple, training-free remedy, Agentic Window Search (AWS): an MLLM agent $\textit{Decomposes}$ the query into attribute-level sub-queries, then $\textit{Inspects}$ each candidate window against them and $\textit{Expands}$ the window when evidence is cut off at its edge. AWS works with existing retrievers and localizers without additional training, raising mIoU from 18.5 to 26.8.
authors: Dong-Hee Kim, Seonwoo Choi, Changbeen Kim, Juyeon Ko, Youngju Choi, Il Hyeon Mun, Hyunwoo J. Kim, Donghyun Kim
bullets: Introduces paired queries that share most attributes but differ in one distinguishing detail.
Evaluates retrieve-then-localize pipelines on full-length movies and separates retrieval from localization failures.
Finds retrieval is the main bottleneck: systems often select a confusable counterpart based on shared content.
Proposes training-free Agentic Window Search, which decomposes queries, inspects candidate windows, and expands truncated windows.
Improves mIoU from 18.5 to 26.8 when used with existing retrievers and localizers.
papers.selection_reason: Temporal grounding benchmark and MLLM agent for confusable movie moments, relevant to video-language understanding.
papers.title: Grounding Confusable Movie Moments
papers.tldr: CoM²-Bench exposes fine-grained confusions in movie moment grounding, while Agentic Window Search improves retrieval and localization without training.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as general-purpose multimodal assistants, making multimodal safety alignment an important challenge. Safety depends on the interplay between textual and visual content, with visual context often playing a critical role. However, VLMs may fail to use visual information appropriately, either overlooking safety-relevant visual content or over-interpreting sensitive visual content, leading to unsafe responses or over-refusal. Existing multimodal safety alignment datasets largely follow the response-preference paradigm, which teaches models how to respond but provides limited supervision on how visual context should inform the safety judgment, making it difficult to balance safety and over-refusal. To address this limitation, we introduce ContraSafe-VL, a Contrastive Safety preference dataset for Vision-Language Models. For each fixed textual query, ContraSafe-VL constructs paired visual contexts that result in multimodal queries with different safety labels, providing direct supervision for how visual context should inform multimodal safety judgments. It further provides response preference pairs based on harmlessness and helpfulness to encourage models to generate responses that are both safe and helpful. Experiments across three VLM architectures and multiple benchmarks demonstrate that training with ContraSafe-VL improves cross-modal safety recognition and achieves a better safety--over-refusal trade-off while preserving general multimodal capabilities. The dataset will be publicly released.
authors: Di Wu, Yanyan Zhao, Xin Lu, Hao Yang, Taotao Zhang, Yunzhen Zhao
bullets: Addresses VLM failures to notice safety-relevant visual content or overreact to benign sensitive content.
Pairs the same textual query with different visual contexts that receive different safety labels.
Adds harmlessness- and helpfulness-based response preference pairs.
Experiments across three VLM architectures and multiple benchmarks show improved cross-modal safety recognition and a better safety–over-refusal trade-off.
The dataset is intended for public release and aims to preserve general multimodal capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Contrastive safety preference dataset for vision-language model alignment, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: ContraSafe-VL: A Contrastive Safety Preference Dataset for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: ContraSafe-VL improves VLM safety alignment by teaching models how contrasting visual contexts change safety judgments while preserving helpfulness.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, making it better aligned with human-AI collaborative creation than single-turn editing. However, constructing high-quality multi-turn training data remains challenging, as conventional sequential rollout accumulates errors and introduces visual-quality drift across editing turns. To address this challenge, we introduce MTEdit, a multi-turn image editing dataset built through a pipeline centered on packed trajectory canvas (PTC) generation. By jointly generating multiple editing states within a unified visual context, this pipeline reduces visual-quality drift across turns. Covering both step-wise and context-aware editing scenarios, MTEdit comprises 500K multi-turn image editing trajectories, with up to 8 turns and an average of 5.38 turns per trajectory, making it one of the most extensive datasets for multi-turn image editing. We further introduce MTEdit-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate both scenarios by assessing models' ability to follow editing instructions, maintain content consistency, resist visual-quality drift, and effectively use historical context across turns. Using MTEdit, we fine-tune Qwen-Image-Edit-Causal to obtain Qwen-Image-MTEdit. On MTEdit-Bench, we evaluate a broad range of closed-source and open-source image editing models, including Qwen-Image-MTEdit. Experimental results show that Qwen-Image-MTEdit achieves the best performance among the evaluated open-source models, demonstrating the effectiveness of MTEdit in improving models' multi-turn image editing capabilities.
bullets: Targets visual-quality drift and error accumulation in sequential multi-turn editing data generation.
Introduces packed trajectory canvas generation, which jointly creates multiple editing states in one visual context.
Provides 500K trajectories covering step-wise and context-aware editing, with up to 8 turns.
Introduces MTEdit-Bench for instruction following, content consistency, drift resistance, and historical-context use.
Fine-tuned Qwen-Image-MTEdit performs best among the evaluated open-source models on MTEdit-Bench.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-turn image editing with instruction following and fine-tuning of a multimodal image model aligns with multimodal instruction tuning.
papers.title: MTEdit: Packed Trajectories Beat Rollouts for Multi-Turn Image Editing
papers.tldr: MTEdit uses packed trajectory canvases to build large-scale, higher-consistency multi-turn image-editing data and improve model performance.

papers.abstract: Many of the most important datasets in the physical sciences live natively on the sphere, and these data often carry no preferred position or orientation. Using methods that do not reflect this symmetry leads to far higher simulation requirements, which can be catastrophic for scientific analyses (forcing reliance on cheap, imperfect models that bias results). We present a novel spherical implementation of a gauge equivariant mesh architecture that is specifically designed for the Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (\healpix{}) of the sphere. The $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-equivariant convolution is built from steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features. The architecture supplies the exact symmetry, so the network does not spend training data learning it. The convolution operations are constructed to give provably exact equivariance, given a band-limit. Our full CNNs can achieve SO(3)-invariance error at per-cent-level and lower, which is controlled through well-understood hyperparameters. On benchmarks, our technique gives the most accurate dense gradient regression and competitive cosmic microwave background foreground removal and denoising. The improved simulation efficiency matters most in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulations are expensive and neural compressors require large training sets, so a fixed budget forces analyses with less accurate simulators. In cosmology lensing SBI, our technique yields the tightest posteriors at matched simulation count. This approach is a novel method that will enable new convolutional neural network analyses, including generative and inference tasks, for processes and data on the sphere.
authors: Joshua Williamson, Niall Jeffrey, Lorne Whiteway
bullets: Targets spherical physical-science datasets with no preferred position or orientation, where ignoring symmetry can require costly simulations.
Implements a gauge-equivariant architecture on HEALPix using steerable filters, parallel transport, and spin-weighted features.
Provides provably exact SO(3) equivariance under a band-limit, with full-network invariance errors at the percent level or lower.
Achieves strong benchmark performance in dense gradient regression, competitive CMB foreground removal and denoising, and tighter cosmological-lensing SBI posteriors at matched simulation counts.
Scope: equivariance and exactness depend on the band-limit, while full-network invariance is controlled by hyperparameters.
papers.selection_reason: Develops an SO(3)-equivariant CNN for spherical data, explicitly incorporating geometric symmetry to avoid relearning invariance, directly relevant to spatial intelligence and geometric reasoning.
papers.title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere
papers.tldr: An SO(3)-equivariant CNN for spherical data encodes rotational symmetry exactly, reducing the need to learn it from simulations and improving scientific inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Recent large audio language models (LALMs) have extended their capabilities beyond lexical speech understanding to tasks requiring paralinguistic and non-linguistic audio understanding, such as emotion recognition. However, these models still struggle to reliably utilize acoustic information, particularly when it co-occurs with spoken linguistic content. Existing benchmarks do not clearly distinguish acoustic perception from higher-level reasoning, making it difficult to identify the source of these failures. To address this issue, we introduce VocalGrad, a benchmark designed to evaluate LALMs' ability to perceive low-level acoustic variations. VocalGrad formulates this problem as a simple binary classification of temporal change direction, enabling evaluation largely independent of higher-level reasoning or semantic understanding. Our benchmark results reveal a substantial gap in acoustic perception between human annotators and state-of-the-art LALMs: while human annotators achieve high accuracy, LALMs perform at near-chance levels. We further conduct linear probing to identify structural bottlenecks in these models. Our analysis reveals two distinct failure modes: for some categories, task-relevant information is preserved in internal representations but not utilized by the language model head; for others, the information becomes progressively less linearly decodable across model layers. Overall, our results reveal substantial limitations of LALMs in modeling acoustic variation under controlled settings and expose representation differences not observable from text outputs.
bullets: Existing benchmarks conflate acoustic perception with semantic reasoning, obscuring the source of model failures.
VocalGrad evaluates temporal change direction through binary classification, minimizing reliance on language understanding.
State-of-the-art LALMs show a substantial human–model gap and perform near chance on the benchmark.
Linear probing identifies two failure modes: relevant information is either unused by the language-model head or becomes less linearly decodable across layers.
The benchmark exposes acoustic-representation limitations not visible from text outputs.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and analysis of acoustic perception in audio language models, relevant to multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: VocalGrad: Evaluating Acoustic Perception in Audio Language Models
papers.tldr: VocalGrad shows that large audio language models struggle to perceive low-level acoustic changes, often performing near chance despite strong human accuracy.

papers.abstract: End-to-end visual generation with pixel-space loss has recently achieved competitive performance without the need for learned image tokenizers. In this work, we study whether language-informed supervision can provide a richer training signal than pixel loss for visual generation. We introduce LILIE (pronounced "lily"), a Language-Informed and Lossless Image Encoder. LILIE is an invertible image transform trained such that a vision-language model can recover captions from noised features. The encoder uses a normalizing flow transformer trained jointly with a vision-language model via next token prediction. We then use the encoder to extract a simple language-informed loss for text-to-image generation. We train JiT models with LILIE loss, reducing gFD by 14 points (66.84 $\to$ 53.01) against a pixel-only baseline on the GPIC dataset. Our code, encoders, and generative models are available at https://suchiragarwal.com/lilie.
authors: Suchir Agarwal, Keshigeyan Chandrasegaran, Ziyu Chen, Kyle Sargent, Juan Carlos Niebles, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu
bullets: Motivation: Pixel loss may provide a poorer training signal than supervision aligned with image semantics and language.
Method: Train an invertible normalizing-flow image encoder jointly with a vision-language model to recover captions from noised features.
Application: Use the encoder to define a language-informed loss for JiT text-to-image models.
Result: On GPIC, LILIE loss reduces gFD from 66.84 to 53.01 versus a pixel-only baseline.
Scope: The approach is evaluated on the GPIC dataset; broader applicability is not established in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Language-informed loss for visual generation using a vision-language model; transferable to multimodal foundation model training and generation.
papers.title: A Language-Informed Loss for Visual Generation
papers.tldr: LILIE uses language-informed, invertible image features to improve text-to-image generation beyond pixel-space loss.

papers.abstract: Object hallucination in vision-language models (VLMs) is usually measured by checking each object a caption names against the image. Most benchmarks and detectors alike treat every object mention as a claim that the object is present. This assumption fails when a caption names an object without asserting it, as in "a bench for people to sit on", which mentions people without claiming that any are in the image. We call such mentions non-assertive. Treating them as hallucinations inflates the error rates attributed to models that use such language. To separate them from real hallucinations, we introduce NAME-Bench (Non-Assertive Mention Evaluation Benchmark), 25,497 object mentions from captions that five VLMs generate for COCO images. Each mention is labelled concrete (asserted and present), hallucinated (asserted and absent), or non-assertive, and non-assertive mentions are further divided into four subtypes: depictive, purpose, negation and hedged. All the hallucination detectors that we evaluate flag non-assertive mentions as hallucinations, at rates between 14% and 80%. Adding non-assertive mentions to detector training as negatives largely corrects this on LLaVA-1.5. On the four newer VLMs, a comparable correction takes five to ten times more data, and the detectors then catch fewer real hallucinations. These findings show that current detectors conflate mentioning an object with asserting it, and that this conflation is harder to undo on the four newer VLMs than on LLaVA-1.5. Hallucination evaluation should therefore separate what a caption asserts from what it merely mentions.
authors: Hsin-Ling Hsu, Neeraja Kirtane, Kuan-Hao Huang
bullets: Introduces NAME-Bench, containing 25,497 object mentions from VLM captions on COCO images.
Labels mentions as concrete, hallucinated, or non-assertive; non-assertive cases include depictive, purpose, negation, and hedged mentions.
All evaluated detectors incorrectly flag non-assertive mentions as hallucinations at rates of 14%–80%.
Training with non-assertive examples improves correction on LLaVA-1.5, but newer VLMs require 5–10× more data and then detect fewer real hallucinations.
The findings expose a persistent mismatch between object mentioning and object assertion in hallucination evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Rethinks object hallucination evaluation in vision-language models; relevant to multimodal LLM reliability and benchmarking.
papers.title: Not Every Mention Is a Claim: Rethinking Object Hallucination Detection in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Object hallucination detectors often mistake merely mentioned objects for falsely asserted ones, so evaluation should distinguish mentions from claims.

papers.abstract: Medical Vision-Language Models (Med-LVLMs) have shown strong performance in Medical Visual Question Answering (MVQA), yet they may still produce factually inconsistent responses. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can mitigate this issue by incorporating external clinical evidence; however, retrieval is often guided by a single modality, potentially overlooking the joint semantics of medical images and clinical questions. We introduce a multimodal RAG framework that learns a joint query representation through a Gated Multimodal Unit, enabling evidence retrieval to leverage information from both modalities while keeping the underlying Med-LVLM frozen. We evaluate the proposed approach on benchmark datasets. Results show that the multimodal query representation consistently outperforms a reference Med-LVLM and remains competitive with state-of-the-art methods. Our findings demonstrate the potential of multimodal query representations for more effective evidence retrieval in Medical VQA.
authors: Daniela Jimenez-Pano, Hugo Jair Escalante, Delia Iraz\'u Hern\'andez-Far\'ias
bullets: Medical VQA models can generate factually inconsistent answers.
Single-modality retrieval may miss the joint meaning of medical images and questions.
The proposed RAG framework uses a Gated Multimodal Unit to combine both modalities into a query representation.
Evaluations on benchmark datasets show consistent gains over a reference Med-LVLM and competitiveness with state-of-the-art methods.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal RAG with gated joint query representation for medical VQA; relevant to multimodal LLM retrieval and grounding.
papers.title: Enhancing RAG-based Medical VQA with Gated Multimodal Representations
papers.tldr: A gated multimodal query improves evidence retrieval for Medical VQA while keeping the underlying Med-LVLM frozen.

papers.abstract: Recent image generators exhibit rich visual priors that can support dense visual perception. However, existing approaches typically encode multiple perception tasks into a shared parameterization, making joint training sensitive to the mixture and weighting of heterogeneous data and prone to cross-task interference. To address this issue, we introduce ReVision, an instruction-conditioned parameter generation framework built on a frozen multimodal understanding model and a frozen image generator. Given an image and a free-form instruction, the understanding model jointly encodes them into a multimodal image--instruction representation, which a trainable parameter generator maps to transient low-rank updates for the generator. Each image--instruction pair induces a distinct set of transient prediction parameters, enabling instance-specific adaptation while both pretrained backbones remain unchanged. ReVision requires no task-specific heads, explicit task identifiers, or stored adapters. A shared RGB output interface unifies segmentation, depth estimation, and surface-normal prediction. Across diverse dense prediction benchmarks, ReVision achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods while supporting flexible task specification through natural-language instructions. Our analysis further reveals substantial gradient disagreement across tasks, highlighting the conflict introduced when heterogeneous objectives share a single parameterization. Meanwhile, the generated updates exhibit structured task- and input-dependent organization in weight space, further validating instance-level parameter generation for multi-task perception.
authors: Yitong Yang, Yinglin Wang, Xuexin Liu, Wei Chen, Zhaoyang Xu, Jiaxin Lin, Rui Chen, Shuting He, Kai Wang
bullets: Addresses cross-task interference and sensitivity to heterogeneous data mixtures in jointly trained dense perception models.
Uses a frozen multimodal understanding model to encode an image and natural-language instruction, then generates transient low-rank updates for a frozen image generator.
Supports segmentation, depth estimation, and surface-normal prediction through a shared RGB output interface without task-specific heads, task IDs, or stored adapters.
Achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods across diverse dense prediction benchmarks while enabling flexible natural-language task specification.
Gradient analysis shows substantial task conflict, while generated updates exhibit structured task- and input-dependent organization in weight space.
papers.selection_reason: Instruction-conditioned parameter generation for dense perception tasks including depth and surface-normal prediction, directly relevant to spatial intelligence in multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: ReVision: Reprogramming Image Generators for Dense Visual Perception
papers.tldr: ReVision adapts a frozen image generator to multiple dense perception tasks by generating instruction- and image-specific low-rank parameter updates, avoiding shared-parameter task interference.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now perceive, describe, and reason about images and audio, yet time series understanding remains underestimated: most work uses LLMs as forecasters and classifiers, reasoning studies are few and narrow, and no suite trains and evaluates the full range of capabilities. In this paper, we build the first such suite, with 337K training and 44K evaluation samples across three progressive capabilities, Perceive, Solve, and Reason, and use it to ask how time series should enter an LLM that must master all three, and in what order. We find that a dedicated encoder is essential: with one, a 4B model surpasses GPT-4o on every perception attribute we test, whereas textualizing the series costs 8--10 points in reasoning accuracy. The capabilities then build on one another: learning them in order beats mixing the same data and rivals reasoning-only training with over three times the reasoning data, but only when an encoder is used. Analyses further reveal that capabilities are transferred through distinct network depths rather than simply stacked, and that a stage converged on its own benchmark is not necessarily ready for the next. Distilled into a simple recipe, these findings yield 4B TS-LLMs that, without any target-domain data, outperform four recent 7B TS-LLMs on seven of eight out-of-domain metrics, by up to 11 points. We therefore advocate treating time series as a first-class modality for LLMs, read through dedicated encoders and taught to perceive before they reason.
authors: Xin Qiu, Junlong Tong, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Introduces a suite with 337K training and 44K evaluation samples spanning Perceive, Solve, and Reason capabilities.
Finds that dedicated encoders are essential: textualizing time series reduces reasoning accuracy, while a 4B model exceeds GPT-4o on tested perception attributes.
Shows that ordered capability training outperforms mixing the same data and can rival reasoning-only training with over three times the reasoning data.
Reports that capability transfer occurs across distinct network depths, and benchmark convergence at one stage does not guarantee readiness for the next.
The resulting 4B models outperform four recent 7B time-series LLMs on seven of eight out-of-domain metrics without target-domain data.
papers.selection_reason: Develops Time Series-LLMs with a dedicated encoder, treating time series as a first-class multimodal modality.
papers.title: Perceive, Solve, Reason: Progressive Capability Formation in Time Series-LLMs
papers.tldr: A dedicated time-series encoder and progressive training from perception to solving to reasoning substantially improve LLM-based time-series understanding.

papers.abstract: Compact medical vision-language models (VLMs) can answer clinical questions correctly without reliably using the image, relying instead on question wording or learned priors. Standard knowledge distillation copies a teacher's answer preference on the original image, but it leaves unchecked whether that preference is conditional on the visual evidence required by the question. We study this missing target as medical visual evidence dependency: support for the correct answer should decrease when the matched evidence is absent. We introduce Evidence-Conditioned Dependency Distillation (ECDD), which pairs each training image with a control matched to the evidence level and distills the teacher's drop in answer margin across the pair. A lower bound objective transfers positive dependency by penalizing only shortfalls, while original-image supervision preserves task accuracy. The same formulation applies when the evidence is a queried clinical region, a surgical instrument, or whole-image visual content.
