Across three medical VQA settings, ECDD keeps original-image accuracy competitive with distillation and alignment baselines while making answer support more sensitive to evidence removal. Under the DME headline objective, for example, the positive-case margin response to target rather than random masking rises from 0.786 with KD to 2.023 with ECDD, while original-image accuracy differs by 0.11 points. These results suggest that medical VLM distillation should transfer both the teacher's answer preference and its dependence on visual evidence.
authors: Qizhen Lan, Yiling Ma, Ruiqi Chen, Mengchen Fan, Xi Xiao, Lin Zhao, Liang He, Baocheng Geng, Pulin Che, Tianyang Wang, Xiaoqian Jiang
bullets: Targets a failure mode where compact medical VLMs answer correctly from question wording or priors without using the image.
Pairs each image with an evidence-matched control and distills the teacher’s answer-margin drop when relevant evidence is removed.
Uses a shortfall-only lower-bound objective to encourage positive visual dependency while preserving original-image task accuracy.
Supports evidence at the level of clinical regions, surgical instruments, or whole-image content.

Across three medical VQA settings, ECDD increased sensitivity to evidence removal while maintaining competitive accuracy; under the reported DME objective, the margin response rose from 0.786 with KD to 2.023 with ECDD, with a 0.11-point accuracy difference.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces distillation of visual-evidence dependency in medical vision-language models, directly relevant to multimodal LLM training and reliability.
papers.title: When Evidence Vanishes: Distilling Visual-Evidence Dependency in Medical Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: ECDD distills not only a teacher’s answer preference but also its dependence on the visual evidence needed to support that answer.

papers.abstract: LLMs and LVLMs are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous hardware, ranging from data-center GPUs to resource-constrained edge devices. Their fixed-size architectures limit the ability to reuse a single model across deployment settings with different compute, latency, and model-size targets. We introduce HydraLLM, an elastic MQA-based architecture. Its number of active attention heads determines the effective widths of the embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward layers, and the output head, forming a nested family of subnetworks within a single parameter set. We introduce a static-to-elastic conversion pipeline that, starting from a pre-trained model checkpoint, includes importance-driven weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation. We extend this principle to multimodal inference through an elastic projection module whose output width follows the active text width. HydraLLM covers a wider range of active parameter configurations than FFN-only elastic architectures. With 75% of heads active, HydraLLM achieves 2.2 percentage points higher TriviaQA accuracy than a state-of-the-art nested baseline configuration which has 17.25% more parameters. With 50% of heads active, our multimodal model achieves a CLIPScore comparable to that of the 7$\times$ larger Gemma 3 4B model. With only 25% of heads active, HydraLLM increases token-generation throughput by 75.3% over the full-width configuration.
authors: Oscar Kemme, Janek Haberer, Ali Hojjat, Olaf Landsiedel
bullets: Uses the number of active attention heads to jointly control embedding, attention, feed-forward, and output widths.
Converts pretrained checkpoints into elastic models through importance-based weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation.
Adds an elastic multimodal projection whose width matches the active text-model width.
Reports higher TriviaQA accuracy than a larger-parameter nested baseline at 75% active heads, comparable CLIPScore to a much larger Gemma 3 4B model at 50%, and 75.3% higher token throughput at 25%.
papers.selection_reason: Elastic width slicing for efficient LLM/LVLM inference, fitting efficient AI and foundation-model topics.
papers.title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: HydraLLM turns one text or vision-language model into a flexible family of width-adjustable subnetworks for different hardware and efficiency targets.

papers.abstract: In-air handwriting recognition based on radio frequency (RF) signals offers a promising solution for human-computer interaction, yet existing methods are often limited by predefined writing planes, constrained writing styles, and small recognition vocabularies. To address these limitations, we propose m^2VLMs, a modality mapping architecture that bridges millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar sensing and large vision-language models (VLMs), and develop mmPencil, a 3D in-air handwriting word recognition system. mmPencil reconstructs 3D handwriting trajectories from mmWave signals using a multi-stage spatial trajectory reconstruction algorithm and maps them into visual representations through a spatial-to-visual mapping algorithm, enabling VLMs to recognize handwriting while reducing sensitivity to writing styles and environmental factors. We collect and release a 3D mmWave handwriting dataset containing 7,664 samples of 200 words from 12 users across 22 writing scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that mmPencil achieves robust word recognition under variations in writing position, range, angle, speed, size, direction, and user movement. It achieves 97.60% accuracy on 200 word classes for seen users and 92.50% zero-shot accuracy on 50 word classes for unseen users, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.
authors: Yifan Guo, Zhu Wang, Qian Qin, Yangqian Lei, Qiwen Gan, Zhuo Sun, Chao Chen, Bin Guo, Zhiwen Yu
bullets: Addresses limitations of RF handwriting recognition, including fixed writing planes, constrained styles, and small vocabularies.
Reconstructs 3D handwriting trajectories from mmWave signals and maps them into visual representations for VLM recognition.
Introduces a dataset of 7,664 samples covering 200 words, 12 users, and 22 writing scenarios.
Reports 97.60% accuracy for seen users and 92.50% zero-shot accuracy for unseen users across the evaluated word classes.
Demonstrates robustness to changes in position, range, angle, speed, size, direction, and user movement.
papers.selection_reason: Modality mapping from mmWave radar to visual representations for VLMs is transferable to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: mmPencil: Toward Writing-Style-Independent In-Air Handwriting Recognition via mmWave Radar and Large Vision-Language Model
papers.tldr: mmPencil uses mmWave radar and a vision-language model to recognize 3D in-air handwriting across diverse writing styles and conditions.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly advanced instruction-driven perception through the "Embedding-as-Mask" paradigm. However, extending this capability to Remote Sensing (RS) reasoning segmentation remains exceptionally challenging under cluttered geographical contexts and extreme scale variations, often leading to Spatial Fidelity Degradation and Target Misidentification. We identify a critical yet underexplored bottleneck: the sequential alienation of the segmentation token [SEG] from its initial visual grounding within the autoregressive generation paradigm. Produced only at the end of long reasoning chains, [SEG] relies on visual evidence that has been progressively diluted by linguistic abstraction and autoregressive noise. This information decay is particularly catastrophic for RS targets with minuscule pixel footprints, where even marginal fidelity loss leads to localization failure. To address these bottlenecks, we propose GeoReason, a novel framework designed to fortify logical deduction and preserve spatial integrity. First, we introduce an Anticipatory Prior mechanism that injects the [SEG] token directly into the initial user query, shifting it from a terminal output to a primary condition. This paradigm shift transforms the token into a persistent spatial anchor, preventing information decay during long-form linguistic inference. Second, we enhance visual reasoning via a Location-aware Chain-of-Thought (CoT) that enforces coarse-to-fine localization using bounding boxes, coupled with a Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment (PTA) Loss that explicitly aligns the latent segmentation token with physical RS textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GeoReason consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanc0126/GeoReason.
authors: Cheng Fan, Han Wu, Tingzhang Luo, Minjing Dong, Yehui Tang, Jianyuan Guo
bullets: Addresses spatial fidelity degradation and target misidentification in cluttered, scale-variable remote-sensing scenes.
Introduces an Anticipatory Prior that places the [SEG] token in the initial query as a persistent spatial anchor.
Uses Location-aware Chain-of-Thought for coarse-to-fine localization with bounding boxes.
Adds a Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment loss to align segmentation representations with physical image textures.
Reports consistent improvements over existing methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: MLLM reasoning segmentation with spatial fidelity and location-aware CoT; fits MLLM and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: GeoReason: Bridging Logical Reasoning and Spatial Fidelity in Remote Sensing Segmentation
papers.tldr: GeoReason improves remote-sensing reasoning segmentation by preserving visual grounding during long-form reasoning and refining target localization.

papers.abstract: As climate change intensifies, floods are becoming more frequent and destructive, making accurate flood understanding an urgent priority. However, existing vision-language models perform poorly on flood-related tasks, suffering from attentional bias and inaccurate descriptions of flood magnitude. To bridge this gap, we construct the first large-scale remote sensing flood multi-modal benchmark that supports language-level flood understanding and pixel-level flood segmentation. The benchmark contains 131,200 flood image patches and corresponding 443,100 textual descriptions for flood severity and evolution. Based on this benchmark, we propose FloodVLM-Pix, a language-guided pixel-level flood understanding model that includes a flood prior module and a multi-temporal flood pixel decoder to achieve accurate flood understanding. The flood prior module automatically distills sub-region flood spatial priors and inputs priors into FloodVLM-Pix, solving the attentional bias problem in flood language understanding. The flood pixel decoder introduces a novel general-specific feature fusion mechanism to address performance degradation caused by interference (e.g., clouds or mountain shadows) during flood segmentation. Experiments on FloodVL-Pix demonstrate that FloodVLM-Pix improves both flood description quality and pixel-level flood segmentation performance compared with state-of-the-art VLMs and flood segmentation models. Our code and data will be released at https://github.com/Haomiaoyanmeng/FloodPix.
authors: Chengyang Zhang, Zhihao Wang, Zhiyu Long, Xueqian Wang, Quanming Yao, Wei Wu, Gang Li
bullets: Introduces a large-scale remote-sensing flood multimodal benchmark with 131,200 image patches and 443,100 textual descriptions.
Addresses attentional bias in flood-language understanding using a flood prior module that distills sub-region spatial flood priors.
Uses a multi-temporal flood pixel decoder with general-specific feature fusion to reduce interference from clouds and mountain shadows.
Reports improved flood description quality and pixel-level segmentation performance over existing vision-language and flood-segmentation models.
Scope is remote-sensing flood understanding, covering both language-level descriptions and pixel-level masks.
papers.selection_reason: Language-guided VLM for flood understanding and segmentation; fits multimodal LLM and vision-language understanding.
papers.title: FloodVLM-Pix: Language-Guided Pixel-Level Flood Understanding
papers.tldr: FloodVLM-Pix combines language-guided flood understanding with pixel-level segmentation to improve descriptions of flood severity and evolution and delineate flooded regions more accurately.

papers.abstract: Recent closed-source image generation systems can produce diverse visual content from simple compositions to information-dense graphics, yet open-weight text-to-image models still struggle with dense text and intricate layouts. To narrow this gap, we introduce MOSS-Image, an open generation system that combines high-fidelity visual synthesis with intent-aware composition. First, we pretrain a 5B single-stream diffusion transformer (DiT) from scratch with a carefully designed recipe, enabling bilingual long-form text rendering and precise layout control. Second, we develop an intention-aware agentic prompt enhancement (PE) module that translates diverse user requests into detailed content and layout specifications. Together, they enable MOSS-Image to generate text-rich and layout-coherent images. We further introduce LongLongTextBench (LLTB) for evaluating long-form English and Chinese text rendering, and RealLayoutArena (RLA) for end-to-end layout-rich generation. MOSS-Image achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-weight models on LLTB, with an average text coverage of 96.3%. On RLA, MOSS-Image ranks second in the end-to-end system comparison, while its backbone ranks first among generators evaluated with shared enhanced prompts. We will release the model, training recipe, and evaluation framework to support further research and promote the text-to-image community.
bullets: Addresses open-weight models’ difficulties with dense text and intricate visual layouts.
Pretrains a 5B single-stream diffusion transformer from scratch for text rendering and layout control.
Uses an intention-aware agentic prompt-enhancement module to convert user requests into detailed content and layout specifications.
Introduces LongLongTextBench and RealLayoutArena for evaluating text rendering and layout-rich generation.
Reports state-of-the-art open-weight performance on LLTB, with 96.3% average text coverage, and strong RLA results. “],
papers.selection_reason: Open text-to-image DiT with layout and long-text control; fits multimodal foundation model interests.
papers.title: MOSS-Image Technical Report
papers.tldr: MOSS-Image is an open-weight text-to-image system designed to generate text-rich images with accurate layouts and bilingual long-form text.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) repeatedly process hundreds of visual tokens across decoder layers, incurring substantial computation and memory costs. Existing inference-time visual token pruning methods often irreversibly remove low-ranked tokens, although the set of visual tokens receiving high query-conditioned attention can change across decoder depth. Recoverable routing preserves skipped tokens for later reconsideration, but re-admits them with stale representations after bypassing intermediate transformations. We further find that replacing stale re-admitted states with their current-depth oracle states from a full-token reference trajectory substantially improves grounding performance. We therefore propose CatchUp, a training-free framework for depth-aware visual-token re-admission. CatchUp repeatedly re-evaluates query-conditioned visual relevance, processes only selected visual tokens through each decoder interval, and preserves deferred tokens for later re-admission. Upon re-admission, CatchUp approximates missed representation evolution using reference-to-current transition signals from semantically and spatially related visual tokens. Across three referring-expression grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention in both benchmark groups at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets. At a 64-token budget with 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, CatchUp retains 92.17% of the full model's performance on average across six multimodal benchmarks while reducing end-to-end latency by 8.0%. Code is available at https://github.com/pej0918/CatchUp
bullets: Problem: Irreversible visual-token pruning can discard tokens that become relevant later, while recoverable routing may re-admit them with stale representations.
Method: Re-evaluates query-conditioned token relevance at each decoder interval, processes only selected tokens, and preserves deferred tokens for later re-admission.
Key idea: Uses transition signals from semantically and spatially related tokens to approximate the representation evolution missed by skipped tokens.
Results: Across three grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets.
At 64 tokens, it uses 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, retains 92.17% of full-model performance on average, and reduces end-to-end latency by 8.0%.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free depth-aware visual token re-admission for efficient LVLMs; directly targets token pruning/eviction and MLLM efficiency.
papers.title: CatchUp: Depth-Aware Re-Admission of Visual Tokens for Efficient Large Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: CatchUp is a training-free method that efficiently prunes and later re-admits visual tokens across decoder depth while approximating their updated representations, preserving LVLM performance with lower latency.

papers.abstract: Spatial context prediction requires visual grounding and spatial reasoning to identify vacant regions relative to objects in a scene. Spatial relationships and physical constraints remain challenging for large vision-language models (VLMs). Recursive reasoning has demonstrated strong performance on discrete and abstract reasoning tasks, motivating its use for improving spatial context prediction in natural images. Weight sharing enables higher accuracy with a small trainable parameter count. We introduce Spatial-TRM, a compact recursive model with frozen vision-language features, a convex region decoder, and just 11.2M trainable parameters. This weight-tied reasoner supports six spatial relationships, three reference frames, and open-vocabulary anchor objects. On the RoboSpatial-Home benchmark, Spatial-TRM achieves 29.51% context accuracy, a gain of 9.02 percentage points (44.0% relative) over a separately trained single-step model with the same parameter count. Including the frozen encoders, the model has 877.8M total parameters, approximately $15\times$ fewer than the reported 13B size of RoboPoint. These results show that repeated refinement improves spatial context prediction from pretrained vision-language features at a fixed trainable parameter count on this benchmark.
authors: Wajeeha Tahir, Anna Tegon, Lionnus Kesting, Gamze \.Islamo\u{g}lu, Krist\'of Karacs, Luca Benini, Thorir Mar Ingolfsson
bullets: Targets spatial context prediction: identifying vacant regions relative to objects while handling spatial relationships and physical constraints.
Combines frozen vision-language features, a convex region decoder, and a compact 11.2M-parameter recursive reasoner.
Supports six spatial relationships, three reference frames, and open-vocabulary anchor objects.
Reaches 29.51% context accuracy on RoboSpatial-Home, improving by 9.02 percentage points over a same-size single-step model.
The reported gains are demonstrated on RoboSpatial-Home and do not establish broader generalization beyond this benchmark.
papers.selection_reason: Recursive spatial reasoning for VLMs in spatial context prediction.
papers.title: Look, Reason, Draw a Region: Recursive Refinement for Spatial Context Prediction
papers.tldr: Spatial-TRM uses recursive, weight-shared refinement over frozen vision-language features to predict spatial regions with few trainable parameters.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer questions about whole images well, yet they still struggle with fine-grained region understanding. A key reason is that text-only supervision never specifies which regions support an answer. To close this gap, we present Xiaomi-Lens-0, a 4B MLLM built on Qwen3.5 that predicts masks from its own visual representations. Specifically, a lightweight decoder combines vision-encoder patch features with visual latents, the language model's mask-token states, so mask supervision reaches the shared backbone without an additional segmentation encoder. Because each latent decodes to a mask, the model can interleave reasoning with region-specific latents and thus think with visual latents, while grounded reasoning traces supervise the regions it visits during chain-of-thought. As a result, across all eight RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg splits, Xiaomi-Lens-0 gains 5.6 points on average over Qwen3.5 in referring comprehension and achieves the highest segmentation cIoU among compared models. Moreover, it surpasses Qwen3.5 across all perception benchmarks. Homepage: \href{https://seerray-lab.github.io/Xiaomi-Lens-0}{this https URL}
authors: Pei Fu, Yike Liu, Yue Sun, Hanmo Wang, Xiuwen Xi, Ruoceng Zhang, Shaojie Zhang, Chao Jiang, Hang Li, Bingrui Liu, Zhenbo Luo, Heng Qu, Changjian Xu, Ming Xu, Jian Luan
bullets: Addresses the gap between strong whole-image question answering and weak region-level understanding caused by insufficient region-grounded supervision.
Uses a lightweight decoder that combines vision patch features, visual latents, and mask-token states to predict region masks without a separate segmentation encoder.
Supports region-specific visual latents and grounded reasoning traces, allowing reasoning to reference and supervise the regions it visits.
Improves referring comprehension by an average of 5.6 points over Qwen3.5 across eight RefCOCO-family splits and achieves the highest reported segmentation cIoU among compared models.
Surpasses Qwen3.5 across all reported perception benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: MLLM with mask prediction and grounded reasoning for fine-grained region understanding.
papers.title: Xiaomi-Lens-0 Technical Report
papers.tldr: Xiaomi-Lens-0 is a 4B multimodal model that improves fine-grained image understanding by generating segmentation masks from its own visual and language representations.

papers.abstract: Relational out-of-distribution errors are easy to describe and hard to evaluate cleanly. An image may be natural, a caption may be fluent, and all mentioned objects may be common, yet the caption may describe the wrong relation in the image. Many evaluations intended to test this behavior can be solved without checking the pairing at all, because negatives differ in caption style, template, length, object frequency, or image statistics. We propose counterfactual pairing cycles, a blocked evaluation primitive that reuses the same two images and the same two captions on both sides of the comparison, changing only which image is paired with which caption. This makes image-only, text-only, and additive component shortcuts cancel exactly in finite samples. The same contrast also gives a training loss for relational outlier exposure and a diagnostic for bilinear vision-language scores. Across synthetic controls, GQA, and COCO, cycles separate coarse image-caption matching from directional role-binding failures, while also identifying geometric size relations that remain strongly visible in global features. In a shortcut-contaminated COCO outlier-exposure stress test, a model selected by a near-perfect shortcut validation AUROC retains substantial relational signal but remains below cycle training on exact cycles; cycle training improves CycleAcc from 0.882 to 0.927. The main lesson is simple: to test whether a model understands a pairing, the benchmark should keep the parts fixed, change the pairing, and ask only about coupling. The official implementation is available online.
bullets: Existing relational OOD evaluations can be solved through image-only, text-only, or additive shortcuts.
The proposed blocked cycles reuse two images and two captions, changing only the image–caption assignment so these shortcuts cancel.
The same contrast supports a training loss for relational outlier exposure and diagnoses bilinear vision-language scores.
Experiments on synthetic controls, GQA, and COCO separate coarse matching from directional role-binding failures and reveal persistent global-feature sensitivity to geometric size.
Cycle training improves CycleAcc from 0.882 to 0.927 in a shortcut-contaminated COCO stress test, though performance remains imperfect.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluation and training method for relational vision-language understanding; relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Can the Parts Fool the Test? Counterfactual Pairing Cycles for Relational OOD
papers.tldr: Counterfactual pairing cycles cleanly test relational vision-language understanding by keeping images and captions fixed while swapping their pairings.

papers.abstract: Making a conference poster is visual coding in miniature: an entire paper must be compressed onto a single page, which exercises summarization, visual design, and code implementation at once, using nothing beyond the paper itself. Yet benchmarks for this task in the context of visual coding remain scarce: existing resources are small and annotated only with layout boxes, so evaluation must fall back on VLM-as-judge or human checklists rather than objective render-and-compare, and the generation methods they support design layouts from scratch, leaving human-crafted posters unusable as either a retrievable design library or as verified supervision. We introduce RAP (Reconstruct A Poster), a dataset and benchmark for paper-to-poster generation as a visual coding task. RAP contains 25K+ verified paper-poster pairs from various machine learning conferences held between 2022 and 2026, annotated with a three-level content taxonomy, plus a held-out benchmark of 150 test papers each paired with its human poster. A fully automated derendering pipeline turns each poster into styled HTML/CSS of typed, refillable slots, so every sample is a paper-poster-markup triplet verifiable by rendering against the source poster. The corpus serves both inference and training: PosterRAG, a training-free multi-agent pipeline, retrieves an exemplar and refills its slots without touching layout or styling, while an SFT+RL recipe trains a dedicated model from the same triplets. An online demo is available at https://reconstruct-a-poster.github.io/.
authors: Haonan Han, Yukang Lin, Minliang Lin, Haoxian Tan, Jun-Yan He, Rui Yang, Zhi-Qi Cheng, Jie Hu, Guanglu Wan, Xiu Li
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of objective benchmarks for paper-to-poster visual coding, where prior resources rely mainly on layout boxes and subjective evaluation.
Provides 25K+ verified paper–poster pairs from machine learning conferences, with a three-level content taxonomy and a 150-paper held-out test set.
Uses automated derendering to convert posters into styled HTML/CSS with typed, refillable slots, enabling render-and-compare verification.
Supports both retrieval-based inference through PosterRAG and model training with an SFT+RL recipe.
Scope is centered on machine learning conference posters from 2022–2026 and human-crafted layouts.
papers.selection_reason: Paper-to-poster generation with declarative markup and multimodal LLM pipelines; relevant to multimodal generation and visual coding.
papers.title: RAP: A Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars
papers.tldr: RAP introduces a large, render-verifiable dataset and benchmark for generating conference posters from papers by reusing human-crafted poster layouts encoded as editable HTML/CSS.

papers.abstract: This paper presents the overview of the runs related to the Ad-hoc Video Search (AVS) and Video Question Answering (VQA) tracks of TRECVID 2025 on behalf of the CERTH-ITI team. For the AVS track, we introduce a two-stage framework built on foundation models. In the first stage, multiple vision-language models (VLMs) encode both the input query, augmented through LLM-generated rephrasings, and the candidate video shots, producing weighted similarity scores for initial retrieval. In the second stage, we utilize a Multimodal-LLM(MLLM)-based reranking module that evaluates the semantic alignment between each shot among the top-N highest-ranked ones and the original query, generating updated relevance scores for reordering these shots. This MLLM-driven reranking significantly improves contextual matching and produces more accurate final rankings without requiring any model training. Regarding the VQA track, we fine-tune an audio-visual MLLM model on the provided TRECVID training dataset and we implement an inference-time scaling technique to enhance the multimodal understanding capabilities of the MLLM. For the open-ended Answer Generation (AG) task, we aggregate multiple model responses per question via a majority vote. The responses are generated with greedy sampling from different random frame subsets of the video and they are ranked based on the number of votes. For the Multiple-Choice (MC) task, instead of voting, we use mean pooling on the logits assigned by the fine-tuned model to each candidate response. Through the combination of fine-tuning and frame subset ensembling we achieve the highest score across 3 metrics in the VQA AG task and the second highest in the VQA MC task.
authors: Andreas Goulas, Damianos Galanopoulos, Ioannis Patras, Vasileios Mezaris
bullets: AVS uses LLM-generated query rephrasings and multiple VLMs for initial video-shot retrieval, followed by MLLM-based reranking of the top-N shots.
The AVS reranker assesses semantic alignment with the original query and requires no additional model training.
VQA fine-tunes an audio-visual MLLM on TRECVID training data and applies inference-time scaling over different random frame subsets.
For answer generation, responses are aggregated by majority vote; for multiple choice, candidate logits are averaged.
The approach achieves the highest score on three VQA answer-generation metrics and the second-highest score on the multiple-choice task.
papers.selection_reason: MLLM-based video QA and reranking for video search; relevant to video understanding and multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: MLLM Frame Subset Ensembling for Audio-Visual Video QA and MLLM-based Reranking for Ad-hoc Video Search in TRECVID 2025
papers.tldr: The CERTH-ITI team combines foundation-model retrieval and MLLM reranking for AVS with frame-subset ensembling for VQA, achieving top performance in several TRECVID 2025 tasks.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD) aims to detect anomalies in previously unseen classes using auxiliary images, with applications such as industrial visual inspection and medical imaging. Recent vision-language-model-based approaches improve ZSAD by aligning textual and visual representations, while distributional prompting further models prompt variability for unseen categories. However, existing methods do not explicitly combine normality-referenced distributional modeling with hierarchy-specific prompt specialization, limiting their ability to model anomalous semantics relative to normality while addressing both image-level detection and fine-grained localization. We propose Hierarchical Knowledge-Guided Distributional Prompt Learning (HiDist), a normality-referenced hierarchical distributional prompt framework for ZSAD. HiDist models each prompt token with a diagonal Gaussian distribution and generates stochastic prompt variations through Monte Carlo sampling. Rather than learning normal and anomalous distributions independently, anomalous prompt distributions are parameterized as deviations from learned normal references, explicitly encoding their dependency. The resulting distributions are specialized into global and local representations for image-level detection and pixel-level localization, respectively, while an adapted global visual representation guides hierarchical alignment. Experiments on seven industrial and medical datasets demonstrate strong cross-dataset performance across anomaly detection and localization tasks. Extensive ablation and representation analyses further support the effectiveness of the proposed distributional modeling and hierarchy-specific representation learning.
authors: Jiyul Ham, Seongho Yoon, Yonggon Jung, Sangjae Lee, Jun-Geol Baek
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling anomalous semantics relative to normality in unseen categories.
Represents prompt tokens as diagonal Gaussian distributions and generates variations via Monte Carlo sampling.
Parameterizes anomalous distributions as deviations from learned normal references rather than learning them independently.
Specializes distributions into global and local representations for detection and localization, guided by adapted visual features.
Shows strong cross-dataset performance on seven industrial and medical datasets, supported by ablation and representation analyses.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language prompt learning for zero-shot anomaly detection; relevant to multimodal foundation models and distributional prompting.
papers.title: Knowledge-Guided Distributional Prompt Learning with Visual Hierarchy for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection
papers.tldr: HiDist improves zero-shot anomaly detection by learning hierarchy-specific, normality-referenced prompt distributions for both image-level detection and pixel-level localization.

papers.abstract: Generating complete, coherent, and usable 3D indoor scenes from natural language requires strong \textbf{design intelligence}: the ability to design high-quality scenes and critique their quality. However, existing approaches either rely on general-purpose models lacking domain-specific design experience or learn from static scenes. In this work, we introduce \textbf{Scene-Designer}, an agentic framework that learns design intelligence through complementary design and critique experiences. We construct two datasets: \textbf{Scene-OTA-35K}, which provides Observation--Thought--Action supervision for learning scene design and efficient error correction, and \textbf{Scene-OTC-15K}, which provides Observation--Thought--Critic supervision for learning scene quality critique across physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence. Based on these experiences, we propose \textbf{Scene-GRPO}, a Critic-guided GRPO framework that improves design decisions and reduces unnecessary trial-and-error corrections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Scene-Designer achieves superior performance in physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, while the learned Scene-Critic significantly outperforms general-purpose models in scene critique. Moreover, test-time Critic guidance further improves scene generation, showing that the Critic can provide useful guidance beyond training. Additional analysis suggests a trend of mutual enhancement between scene design and critique abilities.
authors: Xuanyu Liu, Hongyan Feng, Miao Pan, Sunlai Chen, Lizhou Liang, Bing Sun, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang
bullets: Targets the lack of domain-specific design intelligence in natural-language 3D scene generation.
Introduces Scene-OTA-35K for design and error-correction supervision, and Scene-OTC-15K for critique across physical validity, functionality, and layout coherence.
Proposes Critic-guided Scene-GRPO to improve design decisions and reduce unnecessary trial-and-error corrections.
Experiments show stronger physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, while the learned Scene-Critic outperforms general-purpose models in critique.
Test-time Critic guidance further improves generation, suggesting mutual enhancement between design and critique abilities.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic 3D scene generation from language with learned design and critique; relevant to multimodal LLM agents and spatial generation.
papers.title: Scene-Designer: Learning Design Intelligence for Agentic 3D Scene Generation
papers.tldr: Scene-Designer trains an agentic 3D scene generator to design and critique coherent indoor environments through complementary design and critique experiences.

papers.abstract: Multimodal data are commonly fused into latent representations that improve downstream task performance but are not interpretable, limiting their application in domains that require explainable model decisions. Vision-language alignment has made image embeddings interpretable through language, but requires vast image-caption training data. However, captioned data are typically not available for multimodal embeddings, as relevant features cannot directly be observed and annotated from embeddings alone. Here, we propose a framework to language-align any embedding space that can be linked to interpretable auxiliary data. Captioning functions convert auxiliary data into partial captions; a soft contrastive loss weights pairs by the similarity of their properties that each caption describes; and a rank-based concept retrieval task evaluates alignment against the auxiliary data rather than the captions. We apply this framework to multimodal Earth embeddings to facilitate explainable predictions for two species distribution modelling tasks: S2BMS and SatBird. AlphaEarth embeddings beat previous state-of-the-art models on 6/7 metrics, while our framework language-aligns domain-specific concepts of the embedding space, outperforming previous Earth observation vision-language models on average concept retrieval for both datasets. Finally, aligned concepts recover species-habitat associations ($\rho$=0.44) and relate habitat descriptions to species predictions, showing that abstract embeddings can be interrogated in the language of domain experts.
authors: Gabriel\.e Tij\=unaityt\.e, Thijs L. van der Plas, Mohamed-Bachir Belaid, Rob Knapen, Maciej J. Soja, Ioannis N. Athanasiadis
bullets: Addresses the limited interpretability of multimodal embeddings and the lack of captioned training data for domain-specific features.
Uses auxiliary-data captioning, similarity-weighted soft contrastive learning, and rank-based concept retrieval to align embeddings with interpretable concepts.
Applied to multimodal Earth embeddings for two species distribution modelling tasks, S2BMS and SatBird.

AlphaEarth embeddings outperform prior state-of-the-art models on 6 of 7 reported metrics, while the alignment framework surpasses prior Earth-observation vision-language models in average concept retrieval.
Aligned concepts recover species–habitat associations and connect habitat descriptions to species predictions, supporting expert-interpretable analysis.
papers.selection_reason: Framework for language-aligning multimodal embeddings is transferable to multimodal foundation model research.
papers.title: Domain-specific language alignment of multimodal embeddings towards explainable predictions
papers.tldr: A framework aligns arbitrary multimodal embeddings with domain-specific language using auxiliary data, enabling more interpretable and explainable predictions without requiring image-caption pairs.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering (VQA) models are known to suffer from the bias issue, which refers to overfitting the regularities of frequent patterns. Previously, researchers only consider the language bias. Recently, the multimodal bias is noticed. However, what multimodal bias is remains unclear. In this paper, we investigate the multimodal bias in counting and non-counting questions. We find that they have distinct underlying mechanism, so their biases come from distinct reasons. We provide valuable interpretations of VQA counting mechanism: \textbf{quantity information stems from the magnitude of the multimodal features in specific dimensions.} Thus, counting bias stems from the vision side and propagates to multimodal features through modality fusion, while the non-counting bias stems from primarily language bias and slightly vision bias. Thus, we propose a method to deal with them differently: Variational and Decomposed method for mitigating Bimodal Bias (VDB). It extracts bimodal bias affected by different proportion of vision and language sides. We introduce variational bias models utilizing the principle of Variational Auto-Encoder to learn mainly language bias with slight vision effect, and a bimodal bias model for bimodal bias combining language and vision sides. Extensive experiments on VQACPv2, VQACPv1, and GQAOOD datasets demonstrate the rationality of our claim and the effectiveness of our method. We also provide explanation for the compromised performance on VQAv2.
bullets: Analyzes multimodal bias in counting versus non-counting VQA questions.
Finds that counting information is encoded in the magnitude of specific multimodal feature dimensions, linking counting bias to vision and modality fusion.
Attributes non-counting bias mainly to language, with a smaller visual contribution.
Introduces VDB, combining variational language-dominant bias models with a bimodal bias model.
Experiments on VQACPv1/v2 and GQAOOD support the bias analysis and method’s effectiveness; the paper also explains compromised VQAv2 performance.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates and mitigates bimodal bias in VQA, relevant to Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: Variational and Decomposed method for Mitigating Bimodal Bias in Robust Visual Question Answering
papers.tldr: VDB mitigates VQA bias by separately modeling counting bias as vision-driven and non-counting bias as primarily language-driven.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained alignment between text and video object trajectories is a core challenge in multimodal understanding. Existing embedding models excel at global retrieval, yet their single global representation entangles multiple objects and their spatiotemporal dynamics, limiting direct object-level grounding. To address this issue, we propose VTrajEmbed, an embedding model that decomposes a video into object trajectories and aligns each trajectory embedding with text for object-level grounding through retrieval. Our main contributions: (1)Slow-Fast Trajectory Encoding, a dual-branch architecture that establishes trajectory representations by densely sampling low-resolution frames for high-frequency motion cues and sparsely selecting high-resolution frames for scene context, aggregated by a shared LLM backbone; (2)Mask-Guided Contrastive Learning, a training objective built upon these representations that couples an intra-group loss and a batch-level bidirectional loss under a relation mask, excluding unverified relations and preventing confirmed matches from becoming false negatives; (3)Text2Traj-Bench, a trajectory-level text-video benchmark with model-assisted construction and human-verified query--trajectory relations. Experimental results show that VTrajEmbed-5B improves text-to-trajectory and trajectory-to-text R@1 over Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B by 15.48 and 18.05 percentage points, respectively, and achieves 49.48% average R@1 across five global retrieval benchmarks, compared with 42.86% for Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B.
authors: Ruizhi Chen, Zining Fan, Yudi Guo, Jiang Liu, Zhiyu Lin, Zhongjiang He, Shouqian Shi, Hao Sun
bullets: Addresses global embeddings’ tendency to entangle multiple objects and their spatiotemporal dynamics.
Uses Slow-Fast Trajectory Encoding to combine dense low-resolution motion cues with sparse high-resolution scene context.
Introduces Mask-Guided Contrastive Learning with relation masking to handle verified matches and unknown relationships.
Provides Text2Traj-Bench, a human-verified trajectory-level text–video benchmark.
VTrajEmbed-5B improves text-to-trajectory and trajectory-to-text R@1 over Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B by 15.48 and 18.05 percentage points, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes VTrajEmbed for aligning text with video object trajectories, a relevant technical contribution to Video Understanding and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: VTrajEmbed: Aligning Text with Video Object Trajectories via Spatiotemporal Embeddings
papers.tldr: VTrajEmbed enables object-level text–video grounding by aligning text with individual video trajectories rather than a single global video representation.

papers.abstract: Blindness and low vision limit many people's ability to complete daily tasks, motivating AI assistants that provide useful guidance. Yet, existing benchmarks do not adequately test whether vision models can provide effective everyday assistance. In particular, i) existing benchmarks primarily rely on visual and textual inputs, with limited support for other modalities that are increasingly available in egocentric wearable devices such as gaze, inertial measurements, spatial trajectories, and others; and ii) existing evaluations emphasize scene understanding and question answering, with limited coverage of goal-conditioned guidance for blind and low-vision users across everyday tasks. To bridge this gap, we introduce VISTA (Visually Impaired Scene and Task Annotations), a multimodal egocentric benchmark for goal-oriented assistance for blind and low-vision users. VISTA contains $\sim$1,000 egocentric recordings captured with Project Aria glasses; each recording provides synchronized sensor streams, six of which serve as model inputs, and three different types of annotation, covering ten task categories (TC), from object localization to hazard detection. We evaluate 14 representative vision-language models zero-shot on VISTA and design a lightweight multimodal model baseline that integrates all six modalities. Experimental results show that, although existing models can often describe egocentric scenes, they remain limited in generating goal-directed assistive guidance. VISTA thus provides a benchmark for evaluating multimodal models that could improve everyday accessibility.
authors: No\'e Mosca, Mohamed Rayan Barhdadi, Muhammad Hamza, Joshua Yeh, Suryodaya Bikram Shahi, Zhiyan Li, Selim-Antoine Lali, Weiyue Li, Hasan Kurban, Erchin Serpedin, Gang Luo, Yue Zhang, Minghan Li, Mengyu Wang
bullets: Addresses gaps in benchmarks that lack wearable sensor modalities and goal-conditioned assistive guidance.
Includes ~1,000 Project Aria egocentric recordings with synchronized streams, six model-input modalities, and three annotation types.
Covers ten task categories, including object localization and hazard detection.
Evaluates 14 vision-language models zero-shot and introduces a lightweight baseline integrating all six modalities.
Finds that existing models can describe scenes but remain limited in producing effective goal-directed guidance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VISTA, a multimodal egocentric benchmark for goal-oriented assistance, directly relevant to Embodied AI and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: VISTA: A Multimodal Egocentric Benchmark for Goal-Oriented Perception and Assistance to Blind and Low-Vision Users
papers.tldr: VISTA is a multimodal egocentric benchmark for evaluating AI-generated, goal-directed assistance to blind and low-vision users in everyday tasks.

papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, perceiving surrounding objects is not enough: failing to understand how they move and interact over time can lead to dangerous decisions. Evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) therefore requires testing whether they connect past spatial observations to future consequences. Yet existing benchmarks often assess edge cases through basic perception questions or test temporal understanding in simple scenarios, leaving complex spatiotemporal reasoning underexplored. We introduce STRIDE (SpatioTemporal Reasoning In Driving Edge Cases), an object-centric benchmark for long-tail, safety-critical driving scenarios. STRIDE covers six task families: spatial perception, spatial understanding, temporal memory, temporal extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness. It pairs multiple-choice questions probing individual spatiotemporal judgments with related free-form visual question answering (VQA) requiring detailed scene explanations and justifications of driving decisions. We prioritize scenes with unusual object behaviors and complex traffic interactions, generate reference answers from structured dataset annotations through automated procedures, and use limited language-model assistance and human verification to ensure annotation quality. Across 12 proprietary, open-weight, and driving-specialized models, even the best performer, GPT-6-Astra, achieves only 43.4% average multiple-choice accuracy, versus an approximately 20% random-choice baseline. Further analysis reveals that strong performance in describing driving scenes does not necessarily translate to accurate safety-critical judgments, and that models struggle more with reconstructing object motion than recalling past positions. STRIDE thus exposes spatiotemporal driving limitations that aggregate VQA scores can conceal.
authors: Lieqi Liu, Rui gao, Jia-Chen Gu, Wenbo Hu, Zhaobin Mo, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar, Wei Wang, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Targets long-tail, safety-critical scenarios that existing perception and simple temporal benchmarks underrepresent.
Covers six task families, including spatial reasoning, temporal memory and extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness.
Combines multiple-choice judgments with free-form VQA requiring scene explanations and driving-decision justifications.
Across 12 models, the best reported average multiple-choice accuracy is 43.4%, compared with an approximately 20% random-choice baseline.
Finds that descriptive scene understanding does not guarantee accurate safety judgments, with motion reconstruction especially challenging.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces STRIDE, a benchmark for spatiotemporal reasoning in driving edge cases, highly relevant to VLMs and Video Understanding.
papers.title: STRIDE: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Driving Edge Cases
papers.tldr: STRIDE benchmarks whether vision-language models can reason about object motion, interactions, and future consequences in complex driving edge cases.

papers.abstract: Pathology foundation models (FMs) are trained predominantly on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images but are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for immunohistochemistry (IHC), where cross-hospital differences can impair grading. However, systematic comparisons of correction methods for cross-hospital IHC grading remain limited. To address this gap, we benchmark label-free transformations applied to input images before frozen-FM encoding and to features after frozen-FM encoding using UNI and Virchow2, three IHC markers, and six directed cross-hospital transfers, yielding 12 settings. Among the evaluated input-space methods, our proposed method FIX achieved the largest macro-F1 improvement over no correction, outperforming well-known stain normalization techniques. Among feature-space methods, a simple feature-wise standardization achieved the best improvement over no correction, outperforming CORAL. Under patient-averaged tile-level evaluation, combining FIX with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 and quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) by 0.181 and 0.208, respectively, and reduced ordinal error by 0.209 relative to no correction. These results show that input- and feature-space transformations can provide complementary benefits for cross-hospital IHC grading with frozen pathology FMs.
authors: Jongwoon Lee, Jhair Gallardo, Christopher Kanan
bullets: Cross-hospital variation can impair IHC grading when H&E-trained foundation models are used as frozen feature extractors.
The study benchmarks input-space corrections and feature-space corrections with UNI and Virchow2 across three IHC markers and six directed hospital transfers.
FIX achieved the strongest improvement among input-space methods, while feature-wise standardization outperformed CORAL in feature space.
Combining FIX with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 and QWK and reduced ordinal error under patient-averaged tile-level evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes input and feature space corrections for cross-hospital pathology foundation models, relevant to Multimodal Foundation Models and domain adaptation.
papers.title: Input- and Feature-Space Correction for Cross-Hospital IHC Grading
papers.tldr: Label-free corrections applied before and after frozen pathology foundation models improve cross-hospital IHC grading, with complementary gains from combining both.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) for visual question answering (VQA) often pass long visual-token sequences to the language model, making visual-token pruning attractive but risky for medical images, where answers may depend on localized boundary and texture evidence. We study training free pre-decoding pruning and treat pruning as a subspace stable evidence preservation problem. The retained tokens should remain close to the dominant visual evidence subspace induced by the full token set. To this end, we propose \emph{Subspace-Transition Token Pruning} (\method{}), which estimates each token's spectral support from principal component space and constructs a compact representation subspace. To better reflect medical image structure, \method{} further uses a bounded token-grid transition prior to promote boundary and texture sensitive tokens. We evaluate \method{} on the closed-ended SLAKE and OmniMedVQA benchmarks and on RadImageNet-VQA, which provides both closed-ended and open-ended evaluations, using Lingshu-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones. \method{} delivers consistently strong performance on both the closed-ended and open-ended RadImageNet-VQA evaluations. These results show that \method{} is an effective training free pruning framework for medical domain VQA.
authors: Mengchen Fan, Qizhen Lan, Xi Xiao, Lin Zhao, Liang He, Tianyang Wang, Xiaoqian Jiang, Pulin Che, Baocheng Geng
bullets: Medical VQA often uses long visual-token sequences, but pruning can remove localized evidence needed for accurate answers.
MedSTP estimates tokens’ support in principal-component space to preserve the dominant visual evidence subspace.
A bounded token-grid transition prior promotes tokens capturing medical-image boundaries and textures.
Evaluated on SLAKE, OmniMedVQA, and RadImageNet-VQA with Lingshu-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B.
It shows consistently strong performance on both closed- and open-ended RadImageNet-VQA evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses token pruning in medical VLMs using subspace stability, directly relevant to Multimodal Foundation Models and Efficient AI.
papers.title: MedSTP: Preserving Subspace and Transition Evidence for Medical VQA Token Pruning
papers.tldr: MedSTP is a training-free medical VQA token-pruning method that preserves dominant visual evidence while retaining boundary- and texture-sensitive tokens.

papers.abstract: Existing video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) organize observations primarily in time, but embodied spatial reasoning requires organizing them in space. Consequently, their visual representations can remain locally consistent across nearby frames while lacking a persistent spatial context that is stable across viewpoints and time. We exploit depth and camera pose, which are naturally available to embodied agents, to explicitly establish this spatial correspondence. We introduce Cambrian-BEV, which extends Cambrian-S with a parameter-free geometric tokenization scheme that back-projects visual patch features from each frame into a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) coordinate frame and averages features that fall within the same spatial cell. Thus, observations of the same physical location, regardless of viewpoint or time step, are aggregated into a common spatial token. In addition to providing a persistent scene representation, this formulation acts as an efficient compression mechanism: 128 frames containing approximately 100K DINOv3 patch features are consolidated into a fixed 27$\times$27 grid of only 729 BEV tokens, cutting LLM prefill time by $2.9\times$ and peak memory by $3.6\times$. Cambrian-BEV requires no architectural modification beyond BEV tokenization and uses a frozen DINOv3 vision encoder with a trainable multimodal projector and LLM. On VSI-Bench, our model reaches 63.48, $+8.5$ points over an identically fine-tuned frame-token control with $12.6\times$ fewer visual tokens, with particularly large gains on room size ($+24.5$) and relative direction ($+34.1$). On ReVSI, it reaches 44.68, $+4.5$ over the corresponding control.
authors: Faizan Siddiqui, Nirav Savaliya, Sahith Reddy Chada, Enna Sachdeva
bullets: Addresses the lack of stable spatial context in video MLLMs that primarily organize observations over time.
Back-projects visual patch features using depth and camera pose into shared BEV coordinates, averaging features within spatial cells.
Compresses 128 frames and roughly 100K patch features into 729 BEV tokens without architectural changes beyond tokenization.
Reduces LLM prefill time by 2.9× and peak memory by 3.6×.
Outperforms the matched frame-token control on VSI-Bench and ReVSI, with especially strong VSI-Bench gains in room-size and relative-direction reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: BEV tokenization compresses video MLLM visual tokens while improving embodied spatial reasoning, combining spatial intelligence, token merging, and video understanding.
papers.title: Thinking from Above: Efficient Spatial Reasoning with Bird's-Eye-View Visual Tokens
papers.tldr: Cambrian-BEV improves embodied spatial reasoning by aggregating multi-view video features into a compact, persistent bird’s-eye-view representation.

papers.abstract: Answering complex spatial reasoning questions from egocentric video requires determining what evidence is needed, acquiring targeted observations, and combining them through multiple reasoning steps. Existing vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to perform this process reliably. Agentic systems address this challenge by querying external vision and geometry tools, but training their reasoning leaves these tools unchanged, so inaccurate observations can still lead to incorrect answers. We introduce EgoP$^{2}$C, a framework that internalizes a plan-perceive-compose process within a single VLM. To this end, we first train specialized Planner and Perception teachers using separate adapters (Dual-LoRA), then fine-tune the corresponding experts in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) student under their supervision. We subsequently train the student on trajectories generated by its current policy using a segment-level extension of multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), assigning different trajectory segments to different supervisors. The Planner teacher supervises which evidence-seeking questions to ask, when to stop gathering evidence, and how to compose the final answer. The Perception teacher supervises the video-grounded answers to those questions. At inference, the student executes this adaptive workflow end-to-end, without external spatial tools. Across three spatial reasoning benchmarks, EgoP$^{2}$C students built from Qwen3-VL-8B and SenseNova-SI-1.3-8B outperform their base models by an average of 9.2 and 7.5 percentage points, respectively. Across both backbones, EgoP$^{2}$C reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8-66.3% and achieves $1.29$-$1.49\times$ speedups over their shared Dual-LoRA teacher.
authors: Chaoyu Li, Arka Sadhu, Yuliang Li, Hyo Jin Kim, Yuning Chai, Pooyan Fazli
bullets: Addresses unreliable multi-step spatial reasoning caused by inaccurate external tool observations.
Uses Planner and Perception teachers with Dual-LoRA to supervise a mixture-of-experts student.
Applies segment-level multi-teacher on-policy distillation to train the student on its own trajectories.
The resulting workflow adaptively asks evidence-seeking questions, stops gathering evidence, and composes final answers.
Across three benchmarks, it improves base-model accuracy by 9.2 and 7.5 points, reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8–66.3%, and achieves 1.29–1.49× speedups over the teachers.
papers.selection_reason: Internalizes plan-perceive-compose reasoning for egocentric video spatial understanding, fitting spatial intelligence and video-language reasoning.
papers.title: EgoP$^{2}$C: Internalizing Plan-Perceive-Compose for Spatial Reasoning in Egocentric Video
papers.tldr: EgoP²C teaches a single VLM to plan, selectively perceive, and compose answers for spatial reasoning in egocentric video without external tools.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly serve as judges in training and evaluation pipelines, often assessing answers together with explanations. Although AI judges are sensitive to textual factors, it remains unclear whether ordinary plausible explanations can sway judgments requiring visual verification. We introduce JUPE, a visual-question-answering (VQA)-style benchmark that fixes answers while varying explanations. Across 14 MLLM judges, ordinary explanations that sound plausible mislead judges, with effects comparable on average to deliberately persuasive arguments. Plain justifications and chain-of-thought rationales reduce rejection of incorrect answers by 12.7 and 13.8 percentage points, respectively. We call this failure plausibility capture. Using signal detection theory, we find a significant mean shift in decision criterion toward acceptance, without a clear change in mean discriminability. Explanations sway judgments across domains, explanation generators, and judging protocols, while tested mitigations offer limited, model-dependent protection. Such shifts can inflate performance estimates when judges evaluate answers with explanations.
authors: Anglin Cai, Zhiqi Wang, Xiaozhi Yang, Yurun Lin, Dongwon Lee, Yuchen Yang
bullets: JUPE is a VQA-style benchmark that holds answers fixed while varying their explanations.
Across 14 MLLM judges, ordinary plausible explanations were nearly as influential as deliberately persuasive arguments.
Plain justifications and chain-of-thought rationales reduced rejection of incorrect answers by 12.7 and 13.8 percentage points, respectively.
The effect reflects a shift toward accepting answers rather than improved ability to distinguish correct from incorrect answers.
The vulnerability persisted across domains, explanation generators, and judging protocols; mitigations were limited and model-dependent.
papers.selection_reason: Studies explanation sensitivity of multimodal LLM judges, directly relevant to multimodal large language models.
papers.title: A Plausible Explanation Is Enough to Mislead Multimodal Judges
papers.tldr: Plausible explanations can make multimodal LLM judges accept incorrect answers even when visual verification is required.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are usually chosen from leaderboards, which give one ranking for every application. On questions about objects that a scene suggests but does not contain, however, the model with the lowest error on the POPE hallucination benchmark is not the one with the lowest error on such questions. For yes/no questions about object presence, we show that the best model for a target domain can be predicted without running any candidate on that domain, given 650 to 1,200 labeled target items that calibrate a detector. We measure each model's reliance on a cue, a feature such as scene context or text in the image, by editing 100 labeled source images so that the cue suggests the wrong answer, and comparing with a matched control edit. Reliance predicts which VLMs are misled by physical sticker attacks (Spearman .93 on nine models not used to design the score) and which hallucinate on unedited COCO photographs, beyond what their tendency to answer yes explains. Shift-Reliance Alignment (SRA) scores a model by its source error on the labeled source questions plus its reliance multiplied by the shift. The shift is the proportion of target questions on which the cue misleads, and a detector estimates it on the unlabeled target images. SRA selects the model with the lowest score. In pre-registered tests on new images where most questions mislead, it lowered the error of the selected model from 30.4% under selection by source error to 18.8% on Objects365 and OpenImages but, against its prediction, not on COCO. On CueDial, a benchmark we release that varies how often a cue misleads, selection by model confidence falls more than 40 percentage points behind the best model when overlaid text denies a visible object, and SRA stays within 3 points.
bullets: Leaderboard rankings can fail when target questions rely on misleading scene context or image text.
SRA measures each model’s cue reliance using edited labeled source images and estimates how often that cue misleads in unlabeled target images.
With 650–1,200 labeled target items for detector calibration, SRA predicts target model errors without evaluating every candidate on the target domain.
Cue reliance strongly predicted vulnerability to sticker attacks and hallucinations on COCO images beyond models’ general tendency to answer yes.

In preregistered tests, SRA reduced selected-model error from 30.4% to 18.8% on Objects365 and OpenImages; it did not improve selection on COCO and stayed within 3 points of the best model on CueDial.
papers.selection_reason: Ranks and selects VLMs by cue reliance for hallucination robustness, contributing to multimodal foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: Shift-Reliance Alignment: Ranking Vision-Language Models by the Cues They Trust
papers.tldr: Shift-Reliance Alignment selects vision-language models for a target domain by estimating which visual cues mislead them, often outperforming selection by standard source-domain error.

papers.abstract: Retrieval is a fundamental task in multimodal systems: given an image or text query, the goal is to find the most relevant images or texts in a collection, often using a shared embedding space. Reliable retrieval requires these embeddings to capture not only which concepts are present, but also how they are composed. One key compositional challenge is attribute--object binding: encoding which attributes belong to which objects. Existing benchmarks provide a limited view of this capability, typically covering a subset of modality pairings, simple two-object swaps, or small attribute sets. Consequently, it remains unclear how robustly current models preserve attribute--object bindings across different modality pairings and more complex settings. We therefore introduce SABER, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute--object binding across all four image and text modality pairings, spanning diverse attribute types and scenes with up to ten objects. Evaluating models on SABER reveals substantial binding failures in both CLIP-style dual encoders and recent MLLM-based embedders. These findings motivate us to ask how binding can be improved efficiently. While multimodal supervision may be effective, collecting suitable images is difficult and costly. Text, on the other hand, is well suited to binding supervision: it is cheap to generate, supports a broader range of attributes and enables precisely controlled hard negatives. We thus finetune an MLLM-based embedder exclusively on synthetic attribute-binding text. Despite the absence of image supervision, the gains transfer to cross-modal and image--image retrieval while preserving general multimodal embedding performance. Our model achieves SOTA results on SABER while also improving on negation and instance-retrieval benchmarks, demonstrating broader benefits of our binding-focused supervision.
authors: Netanel Y. Tamir, Michael Green, Issar Tzachor, Or Shimshi, Dvir Samuel, Or Patashnik, Rami Ben-Ari
bullets: Introduces SABER, a controlled benchmark covering all four image/text retrieval pairings, diverse attributes, and scenes with up to ten objects.
Finds substantial binding failures in both CLIP-style dual encoders and MLLM-based embedders.
Fine-tunes an MLLM-based embedder exclusively with synthetic text designed to teach attribute–object binding and hard negatives.
Improvements transfer to cross-modal and image–image retrieval despite no image supervision, while preserving general embedding performance.
The approach achieves state-of-the-art SABER results and also improves negation and instance-retrieval benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates and improves attribute-object binding in vision-language and MLLM-based embedders, relevant to multimodal foundation model capabilities.
papers.title: Stuck on Shuffle: On Attribute-Object Binding in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: SABER exposes widespread attribute–object binding failures in vision-language embedders and shows that synthetic text-only supervision can improve binding across retrieval modalities.

papers.abstract: Recent works augment Vision-Language Models with geometry features from pretrained 3D models, expecting that the geometric signal will boost spatial reasoning. However, we find that simply fusing geometry features and training on standard spatial QA yields only marginal improvements on high-level multi-hop tasks. We attribute this gap to a training-signal problem: standard spatial QA can be largely answered from visual features and language priors, so the geometry pathway receives weak gradients and fails to integrate with the visual features. To provide a training signal that requires geometry, we propose \textbf{novel-view semantic rendering} as an auxiliary training task that requires the model to predict the semantic layout of an unobserved viewpoint, inspired by humans' ability to mentally simulate novel viewpoints during spatial reasoning. This task encourages joint use of both pathways: geometry provides pose-dependent visibility, while vision provides semantic content. Our auxiliary task yields consistent improvements over the geometry-augmented baseline across all three benchmarks (up to +1.6 on VSI-Bench, +2.2 on ReVSI, +2.9 on our 3D-Point-QA dataset) and our full model surpasses prior open-source methods on VSI-Bench and on ReVSI. Project page: https://yuqunw.github.io/Render2Reason/.
bullets: Simply adding pretrained 3D geometry features provides limited gains because standard spatial QA can rely on vision and language priors.
The proposed auxiliary task predicts the semantic layout from an unobserved viewpoint, requiring mental-style spatial simulation.
Geometry supplies pose-dependent visibility while visual features provide semantic content, encouraging pathway integration.
The method improves over the geometry-augmented baseline by up to 1.6 on VSI-Bench, 2.2 on ReVSI, and 2.9 on 3D-Point-QA.
It surpasses prior open-source methods on VSI-Bench and ReVSI.
papers.selection_reason: Improves spatial understanding in VLMs via novel-view semantic rendering.
papers.title: Render to Reason: Novel-View Semantic Prediction Improves Spatial Understanding in VLMs
papers.tldr: Novel-view semantic rendering gives geometry-augmented VLMs a stronger training signal, improving spatial reasoning across three benchmarks.

papers.abstract: When the visual style of text is considered, a wide variety can be observed in font, color, and size. However, when a word is read, its meaning is independent of the style in which it has been written or rendered. In this paper, we investigate whether, and how, the style in which a word is visualized in an image impacts the description that a Large Visual Language Model (LVLM) provides for the concept to which that word refers. Specifically, we investigate how functional text styles (readability-oriented, e.g., black sans-serif) versus decorative styles (display-oriented, e.g., colored cursive/script) affect LVLMs' descriptions of a concept in terms of the attributes of that concept. Our experiments study the situation in which the LVLM is able to correctly identify the concept referred to by a visual text, i.e., by a word or words rendered as an image, and in which the visual text style should not influence the attribute-based description that the LVLM produces. Our experimental results reveal that even when the concept is correctly identified, text style influences the model's attribute-based descriptions of the concept. Our findings demonstrate non-trivial style leakage from text style into semantic inference and motivate style-aware evaluation and mitigation for LVLM-based multimedia systems.
authors: Xiaomeng Wang, Martha Larson, Zhengyu Zhao
bullets: Studies whether font, color, and size affect attribute-based descriptions beyond the word’s meaning.
Compares functional, readability-oriented styles with decorative, display-oriented styles.
Focuses on cases where the LVLM correctly identifies the concept represented by the visual text.
Finds that text style still influences the model’s semantic attribute descriptions.
Motivates style-aware evaluation and mitigation for LVLM-based multimedia systems.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the impact of visual text style on descriptions generated by Large Visual Language Models (LVLMs), revealing style leakage effects. This is an empirical study relevant to LVLM robustness and evaluation.
papers.title: Revealing the Impact of Visual Text Style on Attribute-based Descriptions Produced by Large Visual Language Models
papers.tldr: Even when large visual language models correctly read a word in an image, its visual text style can bias the attributes they describe for the referenced concept.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) inherit their visual and linguistic capabilities from Vision-Language Models (VLMs), yet most VLAs are built from off-the-shelf VLMs that are not adapted to the embodied domain, limiting their downstream performance. In this work, we propose EmbodiedMidtrain to bridge the gap between VLMs and VLAs. We first characterize the data distribution gap between them, showing that VLA data occupy compact regions that are largely separated from the broader VLM distribution, while the degree of alignment varies substantially both across and within VLM data sources. Then, we build a mid-training data engine that leverages a lightweight learnable proximity estimator to select the most VLA-aligned candidates from a large VLM pool, and produce EmbodiedMidtrain-1M, a VLM dataset that we further use to mid-train the VLM before downstream VLA fine-tuning. Experiments on both simulated robot manipulation benchmarks and real-world tasks show consistent VLA performance gains over off-the-shelf checkpoints across VLM backbones and VLA action heads. These gains extend to downstream tasks not used to guide data selection. Further analysis reveals that mid-training provides a stronger initialization for VLA fine-tuning, with gains emerging from the earliest steps and widening throughout training. Moreover, the data engine captures both dataset-level and sample-level alignment signals, favoring spatial reasoning over text-centric tasks while preserving the diversity of the VLM data. We will release all code, data and models for future research.
authors: Yiyang Du, Zhanqiu Guo, Haochen Zhang, Annabella Macaluso, Xin Ye, Liu Ren, Yonatan Bisk, Chenyan Xiong
bullets: VLA data occupy compact regions largely separated from broad VLM data, with alignment varying across and within sources.
A lightweight learnable proximity estimator selects VLA-aligned samples from a large VLM pool.
The resulting EmbodiedMidtrain-1M dataset is used for VLM mid-training before downstream VLA fine-tuning.
Improvements appear across VLM backbones, VLA action heads, simulated benchmarks, and real-world tasks, including tasks not used for data selection.
Mid-training yields a stronger initialization, with gains appearing early and increasing during fine-tuning; selection favors spatial reasoning while retaining data diversity.
papers.selection_reason: Mid-training VLMs for VLA models, directly relevant to vision-language-action and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: EmbodiedMidtrain: Bridging the Gap between Vision-Language Models and Vision-Language-Action Models via Mid-training
papers.tldr: EmbodiedMidtrain adapts VLMs to embodied data before VLA fine-tuning, consistently improving robot manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Time-series data generated continuously across industrial, environmental, and especially health domains produce multimodal signals whose scale and heterogeneity make their processing and interpretation particularly challenging. Time-Series Language Models (TSLMs) promise scalable interpretation of these signals, yet remain bottlenecked by a fundamental lack of text-annotated time series pairs that are signal-grounded, reproducible, and extensible across modalities and schemas. Existing paired corpora are either closed or limited in scale and modality coverage. Annotation with large language models could scale them up, but its outputs cannot be regenerated exactly, which prevents others from re-deriving, extending, or auditing the resulting corpus. To address this, we release TimeCap, an open deterministic captioning pipeline with three reusable extractor tiers and a cross-channel synthesis layer that operates directly on the signal with no language model in the loop, extensible to new schemas by writing channel definitions alone. This positions TimeCap as a reproducible mechanism for future dataset generation rather than a one-off release. Applying TimeCap to OpenMHC, the MyHeart Counts wearable dataset, yields MHCap, the largest open caption layer for multimodal wearable time-series data. MHCap spans 19 Apple HealthKit channels and 7,005,763 captions over 908,944 person-days. To showcase the impact of the corpus, we train OpenTSLM, a time-series language model, on MHCap and benchmark on health-outcome prediction. Caption-augmented training (OpenTSLM-Cap) outperforms a label-only baseline on 29 of 32 per-user binary evaluations across 8 tasks.
bullets: Addresses the shortage of signal-grounded, reproducible text–time-series pairs for training and evaluating TSLMs.
Uses three reusable extractor tiers plus cross-channel synthesis directly on signals, without an LLM in the captioning loop.
Supports new data schemas through channel definitions alone, making the pipeline extensible and auditable.
Applied to OpenMHC, it produces MHCap with 7,005,763 captions across 19 HealthKit channels and 908,944 person-days.
Caption-augmented OpenTSLM training outperforms label-only training on 29 of 32 per-user binary evaluations across 8 health tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Releases TimeCap, a pipeline for captioning wearable health time-series data, and OpenTSLM, a time-series language model trained on the resulting corpus. This contributes to the development of TSLMs, fitting 'Multimodal Large Language Models'.
papers.title: TimeCap: A Scalable Open-Source Pipeline for Captioning Wearable Health Time-Series Data
papers.tldr: TimeCap is a deterministic, open-source pipeline that generates reproducible captions for multimodal wearable health time series, enabling large-scale training of time-series language models.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual understanding requires models to recognize small details within complex images.
