Multimodal on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) addresses this challenge by using a teacher conditioned on evidence-centered crops to supervise a student conditioned on original images along student-generated trajectories. Ideally, teacher corrections, the distributional changes from the student toward the privileged teacher, should be driven by task-relevant visual evidence. However, the designs that make the teacher effective also introduce other interference. Using a lagged or frozen teacher improves training stability but introduces a model-state gap from the evolving student, while cropping enhances task-relevant evidence but also loses the visual context. These two sources of interference make the teacher corrections not purely rely on the visual evidence. We introduce Evidence-Aligned multimodal on-policy self-Distillation (EAD), which retains the crop-conditioned teacher as the target but constructs a separate evidence reference for weighting the corrections. To exclude the effect of lagged model-state from this reference, EAD measures prediction changes using the current student. To avoid crop-induced context changes, EAD masks the evidence region in the original image while preserving the other visual context. The change from the student's masked-image prediction to its original-image prediction provides a controlled reference for the direction in which the visual evidence shifts the student's prediction. EAD weights each teacher correction by its cosine alignment with the reference, i.e., retaining aligned corrections and downweighting the rest. Retaining only 6\% of the supervision mass of dense OPSD, EAD consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods.
bullets: Addresses interference in on-policy self-distillation from lagged teacher states and evidence-centered crops that remove context.
Uses a crop-conditioned teacher for supervision while building an independent evidence reference with the current student.
Compares predictions on masked-region and original images to isolate how the visual evidence changes the student’s prediction.
Weights teacher corrections by cosine alignment, retaining evidence-consistent updates and downweighting others.
Uses only 6% of dense OPSD’s supervision mass while consistently outperforming prior state-of-the-art methods.
papers.selection_reason: Improves fine-grained visual understanding in multimodal models via evidence-aligned self-distillation, relevant to multimodal LLM training.
papers.title: Evidence-Aligned Multimodal On-Policy Self-Distillation for Fine-Grained Visual Understanding
papers.tldr: EAD improves fine-grained visual understanding by filtering multimodal self-distillation signals according to whether they align with task-relevant visual evidence.

papers.abstract: Traditional change detection (CD) identifies changes between bi-temporal remote sensing images, while semantic change detection (SCD) assigns predefined land-cover classes. However, mapping all changes may not meet a user's specific needs. Referring change detection (RCD) enables selective retrieval through category prompts. However, existing category-prompted RCD uses the queried category to specify the destination of a change and returns only a binary mask of the corresponding regions. Users may instead request a particular transition and paired semantic maps to understand what changed into what. Such requests require explicit source and target reasoning beyond target-class localization. To address these needs, we propose query-guided semantic change parsing (QSCP), which supports category names, synonyms, and intent-bearing sentences and returns a query-specific mask with paired temporal semantic maps. QSCP parses requests into intents and semantic slots, composes bidirectional visual evidence, and predicts both temporal states with a query-conditioned decoder. On SECOND, QSCP outperforms RCDNet on synonym, sentence, and transition queries and improves end-to-end semantic prediction over evaluated semantic baselines. WHU-CDC experiments further assess cross-dataset transfer and consistency across equivalent expressions without target-domain training. Code is available at https://github.com/qianyuancs/QSCP
bullets: Addresses the limitation of target-class-only retrieval, which cannot explicitly reason about change sources and destinations.
Parses queries into intents and semantic slots, combines bidirectional visual evidence, and uses a query-conditioned decoder.
Outputs a query-specific change mask together with semantic maps for both temporal states.
Outperforms RCDNet on synonym, sentence, and transition queries on SECOND, while improving end-to-end semantic prediction over evaluated baselines.
WHU-CDC experiments examine cross-dataset transfer and consistency across equivalent expressions without target-domain training.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a query-guided semantic change parsing method for remote sensing, utilizing VLMs for spatial reasoning and source-target transition understanding.
papers.title: QSCP: Beyond Class-Name Prompts for Query-Guided Semantic Change Parsing
papers.tldr: QSCP advances query-guided change detection by interpreting category, synonym, and sentence queries to identify specific transitions and produce paired semantic maps over time.

papers.abstract: Vision-language verifiers and routers must distinguish errors repairable by more reasoning from those caused by visual evidence never reaching the language model. This distinction lacks ground truth because annotators see full-resolution images while models receive preprocessed tensors. We introduce AliasForge to create cases where the relevant fact is provably absent from the interface. Fixed-point resampling makes the pre-rounding resize an exact integer linear map that can send nonzero integer perturbations to zero. Hiding a label-flipping perturbation there produces images with opposite step-correctness labels but bit-identical interface states. Every verifier therefore has the same output law on both members, giving pair-balanced accuracy exactly one half and zero gain from language-side repair. We prove that every fixed-point downscaler has such null vectors and bound their smallest size at the most common ratios, which rules out an 8-bit fit whenever the bound exceeds 255. From the resize configuration alone, a lattice criterion supplies realizable collisions and certifies their absence within the specified construction family. It resolves all 20 screened configurations, 17 as constructible and 3 as non-constructible. We construct certified pairs across three architectures and certify four additional processors, with zero decision-logit gap on all 18 scored pairs and none of the 18 controls. The pairs also screen routers that waste computation on re-attention or further reasoning. On natural items, per-item routing headroom exists, but no tested interface-only router improves over stopping. Our fiber ceiling bounds the headroom recoverable from the interface. Code: https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/aliasforge.
bullets: Constructs label-flipping image pairs with bit-identical preprocessed interface states, forcing pair-balanced verifier accuracy to exactly 50%.
Shows every fixed-point downscaler has null vectors and provides a lattice criterion for certifying collision existence or absence within the construction family.
Resolves 20 screened resize configurations: 17 constructible and 3 non-constructible; also certifies pairs across three architectures and four additional processors.
All 18 scored pairs show zero decision-logit gap, while 18 controls do not; tested interface-only routers gain nothing from extra reasoning on these cases.
On natural items, routing headroom exists per item, but no tested interface-only router improves over stopping; a fiber ceiling bounds recoverable interface information.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes vision-language preprocessing interfaces and constructs certified input collisions affecting VLM verifiers and routers, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Certified Interface Aliases: Exact Collisions in Vision-Language Preprocessing, and When They Exist
papers.tldr: AliasForge proves that vision-language preprocessing can create exact, certified image collisions that make some visual facts unrecoverable by any language-side reasoning or routing.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models still struggle to understand 3D spatial relations across views and update spatial judgments as the observer moves. A common approach fuses 3D reconstruction features into visual tokens, but aligning these features with pretrained semantic representations remains challenging under limited spatial supervision. We propose DK-VLM with Dual-Kernel Attention, which computes attention from both a visual token's input position and its geometric position in the scene. A semantic kernel retains the pretrained model's native attention and positional encoding, while a separate geometric kernel uses estimated 3D points and camera poses to directly modulate attention through point displacements and relative view transformations. Then, a learned gate fuses their outputs. Geometry thus enters attention as position rather than as fused reconstruction features. We further introduce Reference-Frame Composition (RC) supervision to train the model to update its reference frame across successive judgments. It provides stepwise turn and heading targets derived from verified single-step annotations. Among the compared methods, DK-VLM-8B achieves the highest average score across six spatial benchmarks and the highest overall scores on VSI-Bench (74.33) and ReVSI-32 (58.28). RC supervision further improves multi-step spatial reasoning, while the full model preserves general video understanding. Project page: https://sumuru789.github.io/DK-VLM-website/.
authors: Han Su, Meng Tian, Tianyu Huang, Mingyu Gao, Lennox Wei, Dongxu Li, Jianhua Han, Hang Xu, Xiaohe Wu, Wangmeng Zuo
bullets: Targets VLMs’ difficulty with 3D relations across views and changing observer positions.
Uses Dual-Kernel Attention: semantic attention preserves pretrained behavior, while geometric attention uses 3D points and camera poses.
A learned gate fuses semantic and geometric attention outputs instead of directly fusing reconstruction features into visual tokens.
Introduces Reference-Frame Composition supervision with stepwise turn and heading targets for multi-step reasoning.
DK-VLM-8B reports the best average score across six spatial benchmarks, including 74.33 on VSI-Bench and 58.28 on ReVSI-32; it also preserves general video understanding.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-as-position attention for spatial reasoning in VLMs; directly fits spatial intelligence.
papers.title: DK-VLM: Geometry as Position for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: DK-VLM improves multi-view 3D spatial reasoning by injecting scene geometry into attention as positional information and training explicit reference-frame updates.

papers.abstract: Time Series Language Models (TSLMs) enable language-based understanding and reasoning over temporal data, yet a fundamental question remains: what information should their time-series representations preserve, and what variation should they factor out? Existing TSLMs typically expose the language model to a single representation, imposing a fixed inductive bias across downstream tasks. We instead introduce complementary representations as a design principle for time-series reasoning. Our model combines two visual views: line plots preserve absolute measurements and the observed coordinate frame, while normalized delay embeddings factor out positive amplitude rescaling and offsets while exposing temporal structure. Dedicated visual encoders integrate both views into a shared language model through visual tokens and multi-level feature fusion. Evaluation-time interventions verify that the two views exhibit distinct invariance profiles, while single-view ablations show that their combination is particularly beneficial beyond basic perception, with the large gains in prediction and reasoning. Built on Qwen3-VL-8B, our dual-view model improves overall TSRBench accuracy from 44.5% with line plots alone to 53.2%, substantially exceeding the strongest evaluated dedicated TSLM baseline at 36.7%. It further achieves 89.9% accuracy on TSExam and 86.8% numerical accuracy on multivariate ChatTS alignment. Together, these results demonstrate that complementary representations provide an effective design principle for general-purpose TSLMs, enabling models to exploit temporal structure without sacrificing access to the original measurement frame.
authors: Hedi Zisling, Liran Nochumsohn, Ilan Naiman, Mihir Parmar, Omri Azencot
bullets: Line plots retain absolute measurements and the original coordinate frame.
Normalized delay embeddings remove positive amplitude scaling and offsets while highlighting temporal structure.
Dedicated visual encoders fuse both views into a shared language model through visual tokens and multi-level features.
Evaluation-time interventions confirm that the views provide distinct invariance profiles; ablations show their combination especially benefits prediction and reasoning.
The model raises TSRBench accuracy from 44.5% to 53.2%, and reports 89.9% on TSExam and 86.8% numerical accuracy on multivariate ChatTS alignment.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal LLM with complementary visual representations for time-series reasoning.
papers.title: Twice Upon a Time: Complementary Representations for Time-Series Reasoning
papers.tldr: A dual-view time-series representation combining line plots with normalized delay embeddings substantially improves language-model-based temporal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Spatial instructions describe how to move objects, transform regions, or modify their surroundings. When several operations are applied in sequence, each acts on a configuration shaped by earlier changes. How accurately can large language models (LLMs) predict the resulting spatial state? We introduce Grid-Bench, an executable benchmark in which eight families of operations transform discrete worlds represented as two-, three-, and four-dimensional grids. Given an initial grid, explicit rules, and an event history expressed as text, a model predicts the complete final grid. Reference execution makes every predicted value checkable, supporting comparisons across spatial operations, history lengths, and workloads. Evaluating six LLMs shows that complete-state accuracy falls sharply as histories grow, with substantial divergence among models that perform similarly on single events. Models with similar exact-match accuracy can nevertheless differ substantially in the number of incorrect cells on shared instances. Even over long histories, some models recover many correct changes beyond what copying the initial state would yield. Grid-Bench makes both complete recovery and these differences in returned states directly measurable across a range of spatial conditions.
authors: Zixiang Xu, Zirui Song, Wanrong Zheng, Chiyu Zhang, Yue Huang, Yuyang Peng, Kexin Zhang, Jinkun Chen, Xiuying Chen, Xiangliang Zhang, Yan Liu, Laurent Itti, Frank Shyu, Xiaoqiang Luo, Sandeep Pandey, Xi Liu, Luke Simon, Xiyang Hu, Yue Zhao
bullets: Benchmarks eight operation families across 2D, 3D, and 4D grid worlds.
Provides an initial grid, text-based rules, and event histories; models must output the complete final grid.
Reference execution makes every predicted cell verifiable across history lengths and workloads.
Six LLMs show sharply declining complete-state accuracy as histories grow, with differing error patterns despite similar exact-match scores.
Some models recover many correct changes in long histories, outperforming simple copying of the initial state.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for LLM spatial state prediction over discrete grids directly targets spatial reasoning.
papers.title: Grid-Bench: Can LLMs Predict How Discrete Worlds Change?
papers.tldr: Grid-Bench evaluates how accurately LLMs execute sequences of spatial transformations and reconstruct final states in discrete grids.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence lets an agent perceive and act in the physical world, and many of its judgments must be made at interaction rates: which spatial relation holds, how far an object is, or where to place it. Vision-language models (VLMs) produce these answers by free-form text generation, paying for autoregressive decoding and answer parsing even though the output space is compact: one of a few options, a scalar, or a 2D point. In light of this, we introduce MJev-Spatial, a System 1 multimodal decision model that tackles all three types of spatial understanding tasks within a unified classification framework. Specifically, MJev-Spatial treats each candidate as a class and scores it using the backbone's pretrained query and key projections, without adding parameters. The candidates are the given options for choice tasks, or value bins and image regions refined through coarse-to-fine classification for numerical and point prediction, respectively. At inference, each classification decision takes a single forward pass and generates no answer tokens. To train on heterogeneous spatial data efficiently, we supervise all coarse-to-fine stages jointly with teacher forcing in one forward pass, and combine this with length-aware global batching and cross-GPU load balancing, raising training throughput by 30.8% over the original batching strategy. Built on Qwen3.5-4B and trained on 12.3M question-answer pairs converted from existing spatial datasets, MJev-Spatial achieves the highest overall score (65.64%) among eight tested models, ranks first on seven of twelve benchmarks, and outperforms its unmodified autoregressive base model on all twelve, while running 2.5 times faster than the fastest autoregressive baseline and 5.6 times faster than the base model.
authors: Luozheng Qin, Yuhan Zhu, Changhai Zhou, Qian Qiao, Jun Gao, Yuhua Zhou, Harry Zhang, Xiangyu Zeng, Yuxuan Liu, Kaijie Chen, Andrew Chen, Pony Ma
bullets: Targets three spatial tasks: choice-based relations, numerical distance estimation, and 2D point prediction.
Scores candidates with pretrained query/key projections, adding no parameters and requiring one forward pass per decision.
Uses coarse-to-fine classification for value bins and image regions, with jointly supervised stages and efficient heterogeneous-data batching.
Trained on 12.3M converted question-answer pairs, it ranks first on 7 of 12 benchmarks and achieves a 65.64% overall score across eight models.
Runs 2.5× faster than the fastest autoregressive baseline and 5.6× faster than its autoregressive base model; scope is spatial understanding tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Unified classification framework for spatial understanding tasks (relations, distance, points) in a multimodal decision model.
papers.title: MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching
papers.tldr: MJev-Spatial converts spatial reasoning into fast, unified classification, achieving strong benchmark performance while avoiding autoregressive answer generation.

papers.abstract: Real desktop automation is neither purely visual nor purely programmatic. Agents must understand user-facing interfaces while efficiently manipulating files, scripts, and system state. However, native GUI/code coordination cannot be obtained by prompt-level tool composition. In our preliminary experiments, naively adding a code tool degrades a GUI agent, revealing that GUI/code routing must be internalized through training on high-quality hybrid data. We present OS-Helix, an end-to-end trained multimodal computer-using agent that unifies GUI actions and code execution in one action space. To construct the required supervision, we introduce application-artifact composition, pairing desktop applications with authentic file artifacts to instantiate executable Ubuntu states, and a decoupled instruction/evaluator generation pipeline that produces environment-grounded tasks whose final states can be verified regardless of the solution modality. We cold-start the policy with SFT on filtered hybrid data and further improve it through online RL in live desktop environments. For RL, we propose Step-balanced GSPO, which aggregates importance weight by action step rather than raw assistant tokens to prevent long code actions from dominating heterogeneous-action optimization. On OSWorld-Verified, OS-Helix-27B and OS-Helix-35B-A3B achieve relative improvements of 35.0% and 33.7% over their matched Qwen3.5 hybrid baselines, while OS-Helix-27B-RL further improves by 42.9% to reach 66.44% success. Ablations provide evidence consistent with contributions from learned GUI/code coordination, scalable verifiable supervision, and action step balanced optimization, while demonstrating cross-platform transfer on WindowsAgentArena. Our project homepage is at https://os-copilot.github.io/OS-Helix/.
authors: Bowen Yang, Kaiming Jin, Zichen Ding, Zhenyu Wu, Zehao Li, Zhoumianze Liu, Kanzhi Cheng, Fangzhi Xu, Yanan Sun, Qiushi Sun, Yu Qiao
bullets: Naively adding code tools can hurt GUI agents, motivating learned GUI/code routing rather than prompt-level composition.
The agent unifies GUI interaction and code execution in a single action space and is trained with SFT followed by online RL in live desktops.
Application-artifact composition and decoupled instruction/evaluator generation create executable, verifiable hybrid tasks.
Step-balanced GSPO weights action steps instead of raw tokens to prevent long code actions from dominating RL optimization.
On OSWorld-Verified, OS-Helix-27B-RL reaches 66.44% success; results also support transfer to WindowsAgentArena.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end trained multimodal computer-using agent with unified GUI/code action space and RL optimization, relevant to multimodal agent foundation models.
papers.title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents
papers.tldr: OS-Helix trains a multimodal agent to coordinate GUI actions and code execution natively, achieving substantial gains on desktop automation benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Physical understanding is crucial for decision making, yet vision models struggle to infer properties such as damping that govern how materials behave. Audio encodes such properties directly, because an object's acoustic response to impact reveals its damping through measurable decay. We probe frozen encoders for the quality factor $Q$, a dimensionless measure of how many oscillations an object completes before its ring dies away, and report how well each embedding orders impacts by $Q$ using the Spearman rank correlation $\rho$, for which $\rho=1$ is a perfect ordering and $\rho=0$ an unrelated one. Audio embeddings reach $\rho=0.73$ and retain most of that advantage on materials withheld from training, while a single video frame taken at the moment of impact, encoded by CLIP, supports only $\rho=0.28$. Having established where the signal lives, we ask how much of that gap vision can recover. We distill a frozen audio teacher into a frozen CLIP backbone through a trained projection head and find that this recovers a useful fraction of the audio advantage. Because pooled correlations on this task are dominated in practice by category identity, we also evaluate under a leave-one-material-out protocol in which the held-out material is withheld from the projection head as well as the probe. Distillation with a four-frame input improves the correlation there from 0.234 to 0.338 (+0.053 over the matched four-frame baseline, 14 of 17 materials), a gain that no category-level strategy can produce. Widening the visual input to four frames spanning the impact supplies half of that improvement at no acoustic cost, which indicates that part of what a single frame misses is visible dynamics.
authors: Zainab Afolabi, Vadim Selyutin, Zhao Gao, Babs Khalidson, Mohamed Ghoneim
bullets: Audio encoders rank impacts by quality factor with Spearman ρ=0.73, retaining most of their advantage on unseen materials.
A single impact-frame encoded by CLIP reaches only ρ=0.28, showing limited visual access to damping cues.
Distilling a frozen audio teacher into a frozen CLIP backbone recovers a useful portion of the audio advantage.
Under leave-one-material-out evaluation, four-frame distillation improves correlation from 0.234 to 0.338 across 14 of 17 materials.
Four frames alone provide half the improvement, indicating that visible impact dynamics—not just category identity—carry relevant information.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-modal distillation of physical damping structure from audio into vision; transferable to learned physical dynamics and multimodal representations.
papers.title: How Much Physics Can Vision Learn from Audio? Probing and Distilling Damping Structure
papers.tldr: Audio embeddings capture damping structure far better than single-frame vision, while distilling audio knowledge and using short video clips helps vision recover part of the gap.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can elicit specialized visual capabilities in vision-language models (VLMs), yet jointly optimizing heterogeneous objectives often introduces cross-capability gradient conflicts. Training experts independently mitigates this interference, but direct reward optimization may entangle specialized knowledge with reward-hacking biases. This paper proposes Skill-Decoupled On-Policy Expert Distillation (SCOPED), which trains capability-specific experts and extracts explicit skills through reward-guided reflection. During on-policy distillation, these skills guide expert supervision while remaining unavailable to the unified student, encouraging it to internalize procedural knowledge without explicit skills at inference time. Across eight multimodal benchmarks, SCOPED consistently outperforms the backbone and mixed-capability RL, demonstrating the effectiveness of skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation for integrating independently acquired capabilities. Further analyses reveal interference during joint capability optimization and suggest that skill augmentation promotes more consistent expert trajectories, greater attention to task-relevant visual evidence, and better preservation of specialized expertise in the unified student. All code and data are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/SCOPED.
authors: Yuqi Xiong, Chunyi Peng, Zhipeng Xu, Qing Yang, Zhenghao Liu, Zulong Chen, Yu Gu, Ge Yu
bullets: Motivation: jointly optimizing heterogeneous capabilities can cause cross-capability gradient interference, while direct reward optimization may encourage reward-hacking biases.
Method: train capability-specific experts, extract skills through reward-guided reflection, and use those skills to guide on-policy distillation into a unified student.
The student receives skill-guided supervision during training but not the explicit skills at inference, encouraging it to internalize procedural knowledge.
Across eight multimodal benchmarks, SCOPED outperforms the backbone and mixed-capability RL.
Analyses indicate reduced interference, more consistent expert trajectories, stronger attention to relevant visual evidence, and better preservation of specialized expertise.
papers.selection_reason: Skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation for unified vision-language models is directly relevant to multimodal LLM training and capability integration.
papers.title: Skill-Decoupled On-Policy Expert Distillation for Unified Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: SCOPED unifies specialized visual capabilities by distilling independently trained experts into one VLM while keeping their explicit skills hidden at inference.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance through instruction tuning, yet real-world applications often require them to continually acquire new capabilities from sequential tasks, i.e., Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT). In typical MLLMs, a projector is employed to align visual representations with the language model. However, existing methods primarily protect the language model from forgetting while continuously updating the projector across tasks. Such asymmetric adaptation can cause substantial representation drift in the projector, increasing the mismatch between the projector and language model and consequently exacerbating catastrophic forgetting. To address this issue, we propose Compatible Routing (CART), which explicitly coordinates the adaptation of the projector and language model. Specifically, CART maintains task-specific experts for both modules and combines them through weighted mixtures. CART jointly infers their weights by considering both expert relevance and cross-module compatibility, thereby promoting coordinated adaptation between the two modules. To further control model growth, we introduce relevance-guided expert consolidation, which merges experts exhibiting similar relevance profiles across samples within each module. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CART achieves state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Ling-Xiang Zhang, Tao Hu, Da-Wei Zhou
bullets: MCIT requires MLLMs to learn sequential multimodal tasks without losing previously acquired capabilities.
Existing methods mainly protect the language model while continually changing the projector, causing representation drift and cross-module mismatch.
CART maintains task-specific experts for both the projector and language model, then jointly routes them using expert relevance and cross-module compatibility.
Relevance-guided consolidation merges experts with similar sample-level relevance profiles to limit model growth.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, though the abstract provides no specific datasets or numerical results.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses continual instruction tuning for multimodal LLMs with coordinated projector and language model adaptation.
papers.title: CART: Compatible Routing for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
papers.tldr: CART reduces catastrophic forgetting in multimodal continual instruction tuning by coordinating projector and language-model adaptation through compatible expert routing.

papers.abstract: Interactive agents repeatedly choose among a finite set of actions, labels, or ordinal outcomes. Generating a free-form response for each choice adds latency and complicates the interface between a model and its environment. We present Intern-Decision, a family of 0.8B, 2B, and 4B multimodal decision models that return structured choices and candidate probabilities from text and optional images. Our autoregressive masked language modeling objective places one decision placeholder per field in a complete assistant JSON skeleton. Ground-truth symbols appear only in supervision, while all fields are evaluated in a single causal forward pass using the backbone's native language-model head. The 4B model achieves a 90.02% unweighted average accuracy across seven evaluation suites, compared with 88.74% for Jev v1.13.0. For a fixed 289-token request with three fields on one RTX 4090, mean latency is 44.16 ms for the 4B model and approximately 33--34 ms for the smaller models. On a separate 96-case known-distribution pilot, temperature scaling reduces expected multiclass Brier from 0.628 to 0.550 and expected calibration error from 0.213 to 0.089. A confidence-based handoff study on 111 public Jevbench-Hard items improves accuracy from 82/111 (73.87%) to 97/111 (87.39%) by routing 42 items to Atria-Dawn-Preview. We also describe qualitative game, visual interface, and browser demonstrations. These results support compact decision models as a practical component of larger agent systems.
authors: Tong Zhu, Zhe Xu, Zefeng He, Yunkai Chai, Xuyang Hu, Dehong Zheng, Yun Luo, Yafu Li, Qi Zhang, Yu Cheng
bullets: Supports text and optional images, returning structured choices and candidate probabilities for finite-action decisions.
Places one decision placeholder per field in a complete JSON response and evaluates all fields in one causal forward pass.
Offers 0.8B, 2B, and 4B models; the 4B model reports 90.02% average accuracy across seven evaluation suites.
The 4B model reports 44.16 ms mean latency for a fixed three-field request on one RTX 4090.
Temperature scaling improves calibration in a 96-case pilot, while confidence-based handoff raises Jevbench-Hard accuracy from 73.87% to 87.39%.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a multimodal decision model with an autoregressive masked LM objective for efficient structured choice generation.
papers.title: Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Making with Autoregressive Masked Language Modeling
papers.tldr: Intern-Decision uses masked autoregressive language modeling to make fast, structured multimodal decisions with calibrated confidence and optional escalation to a stronger model.

papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language pre-training supports zero-shot chest X-ray diagnosis, but standard objectives treat every off-diagonal image-report pair in a batch as a negative. In radiology, recurring findings across patients mean that instance mismatch need not imply semantic incompatibility, creating false-negative supervision that we term a semantic conflict. A training-trace audit shows that pair-observations selected by the online mask used during training are enriched for report-derived finding agreement, although this proxy analysis does not establish clinical equivalence. Fixed thresholds can become miscalibrated as similarity distributions evolve, while soft reweighting leaves residual repulsive gradients. We therefore propose Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning (SCCL), which tracks modality-specific similarity distributions with exponential-moving-average (EMA) statistics, derives adaptive thresholds, and hard-masks flagged candidates before softmax normalization. Inclusive (OR) and consensus (AND) rules define two SCCL teachers, whose bidirectional cross-modal rankings are consolidated through standard distillation into a single deployable student, SCCL-DT. Across five public chest X-ray benchmarks, SCCL-DT achieves a mean zero-shot AUC of $0.850$, compared with $0.837$ for the strongest evaluated baseline in our comparison. Code will be made publicly available soon.
authors: Ting Liu, Haoran Lai, HaobinChen, Ming Liu, S Kevin Zhou
bullets: Addresses false-negative supervision caused by treating all mismatched image-report pairs as incompatible.
Uses EMA-tracked modality-specific similarity distributions to set adaptive thresholds and hard-mask conflicting candidates before softmax.
Combines inclusive (OR) and consensus (AND) teachers through bidirectional ranking distillation into a deployable student.
Reports mean zero-shot AUC of 0.850 across five public chest X-ray benchmarks, versus 0.837 for the strongest evaluated baseline.
The agreement signal is proxy-based and does not establish clinical equivalence; code is planned for public release.
papers.selection_reason: Contrastive vision-language pretraining with semantic-conflict-aware hard-negative handling; technically transferable to multimodal foundation model alignment.
papers.title: SCCL-DT: Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning with Dual-Rule Teacher Distillation for Zero-Shot Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
papers.tldr: SCCL-DT improves zero-shot chest X-ray diagnosis by identifying and masking semantically conflicting contrastive negatives, then distilling two rule-based teachers into one student.

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that depth recurrence can be retrofitted into pretrained language models. In this work, we adapt this paradigm for visual understanding, using depth recurrence to reduce the parameter footprint of a pretrained vision-language model (VLM). To this end, we prune layers from the language backbone of the VLM and loop over a subset of the remaining layers. At each step of the loop, a linear adapter merges the block's output with the token representations from the preceding layers and projects the fused representation back into the block. As the pruning impacts the original model performance, we propose a three-stage recovery training: first, we leverage a language-only pretraining to recover the performance of the language backbone, followed by an alignment of the vision-language projector, and a full fine-tuning of the model via visual instruction tuning. In the first and the last stage, we distill the outputs of the pretrained non-recurrent model into the recurrent model, which further improves the recovery. We evaluate the proposed approach on the TinyLLaVA-1.4B backbone without introducing any new vision-language data during retrofitting. Our experiments demonstrate that the retrofitted recurrent model outperforms the unpruned baseline trained with the same recovery data while storing 23.3% fewer language parameters. We further show that the proposed retrofitting recurrence outperforms the setup of converting a recurrent LM into a VLM on the same data. Additionally, our ablations show how design choices, such as the adapter between recurrences and a larger recurrent block, lead to the improved performance of our approach. Finally, we find that our proposed model gains on reasoning-oriented benchmarks, whereas its performance on basic visual understanding benchmarks remains on par with the baseline.
authors: Madhav Iyengar, Andreas Geiger, Hilde K\"uhne
bullets: Prunes the language backbone and repeatedly applies a subset of its layers, using linear adapters to merge representations across recurrences.
Uses three-stage recovery: language-backbone training, vision-language projector alignment, and visual instruction tuning.
Distills outputs from the original non-recurrent model during the first and final recovery stages.
On TinyLLaVA-1.4B, the retrofitted model outperforms an equally recovered unpruned baseline without adding vision-language data.
Improvements are strongest on reasoning benchmarks; basic visual understanding remains comparable to the baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces VLM parameters via recurrence, fitting both multimodal foundation models and efficiency.
papers.title: Retrofitting Recurrent Vision-Language Models from Pretrained Backbones
papers.tldr: A pretrained vision-language model can be made recurrent and 23.3% smaller in language parameters while matching or improving performance through structured recovery training and distillation.

papers.abstract: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9% to 11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%.
authors: Zhuoming Liu, Jinhong Lin, Lin Zhang, Yiwu Zhong, Yin Li
bullets: Addresses the context bottleneck caused by memory methods that retrieve or append historical video observations to current inputs.
Uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to consolidate incoming observations into fixed-size LoRA parameter updates while keeping current observations as input.
Introduces MaLoW-Instruct, a streaming-video instruction dataset with 381K question-answer pairs across 56K videos.
Achieves 3.9%–11.8% higher performance than prior memory approaches on OVO-Bench’s backward split, with modest latency overhead.
Also improves action success on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%, suggesting applicability to vision-language-action models.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming VLM memory via LoRA weights; improves video understanding and VLA action success.
papers.title: Memory as Weights: Internalizing Long-Term History for Streaming Videos
papers.tldr: MaLoW turns long-term video history into evolving LoRA weights, enabling streaming VLMs to retain context without repeatedly reloading past observations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can act unsafely when individually benign images and texts are interpreted jointly. Beyond implicit reasoning risk, where reasoning drifts toward harm, we identify intent-level risk, where cross-modal ambiguity silently commits the model to a hazardous premise that path-level optimization alone cannot correct. We propose SAFE-PRO, which uses a Risk-Conditioned Uncertainty (RCU) signal, combining predictive entropy with a learned cross-modal risk score, to decide when to ask safety-grounded clarifying questions and where to apply path optimization, under a reward that prioritizes safety and penalizes over-refusal. We also build SSUI-Dialog, a multimodal multi-turn dataset with dual-intent supervision, and theoretically analyze gradient variance and unsafe-completion risk under RCU. Across seven benchmarks and two base MLLMs, SAFE-PRO consistently improves safety over SRPO, roughly halves its over-refusal, and surpasses GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet in average single-turn safety.
authors: Wei Cai, Jian Zhao, Yuchen Yuan, Xuelong Li
bullets: Identifies intent-level risk: benign images and text can jointly imply hazardous premises that ordinary reasoning optimization may miss.
Uses Risk-Conditioned Uncertainty to trigger safety-grounded clarification and guide path optimization.
Introduces SSUI-Dialog, a multimodal multi-turn dataset with dual-intent supervision.
Theoretically analyzes RCU’s effects on gradient variance and unsafe-completion risk.
Across seven benchmarks and two base MLLMs, improves safety over SRPO, roughly halves over-refusal, and exceeds GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet in average single-turn safety.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses cross-modal safety in multimodal LLMs with proactive inquiry and uncertainty-based routing.
papers.title: When Reasoning Is Not Enough: Proactive Inquiry for Cross-Modal Safety in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: SAFE-PRO improves cross-modal safety in multimodal LLMs by asking targeted clarifying questions when uncertainty and hidden intent-level risk are high.

papers.abstract: Arabic calligraphy is a high-stakes cultural visual domain for Muslim communities, yet VLM evaluations rarely test its fine-grained script traditions. We audit 12 VLMs on a cleaned 1,195-image six-way benchmark using numeric, visual-cue, and Diwani-first prompts. In this closed-set setting, the best numeric-prompt accuracy is 60.9% for closed/API models and 47.2% for open-weight models. The main failure is default-label collapse: every numeric run is dominated by a single label taking 33-63% of predictions, against an 18.8% majority-class baseline. For 8 of 12 models the default is Thuluth; GPT-4o labels 52.9% of all images as Thuluth although it is only 18.1% of the set. Prompting helps unevenly: visual cues move accuracy by more than 10 points for some models but hurt others, and foregrounding Diwani often relocates the default rather than removing it. Arabic calligraphy recognition is therefore a compact, culturally grounded stress test for VLM robustness and for measuring which visual traditions become legible to automated systems.
authors: Niaz Mohaiman Abtahi, Evan Maksud, Reyana Shahid
bullets: The audit evaluates 12 VLMs on a cleaned 1,195-image, six-way Arabic calligraphy benchmark.
Best numeric-prompt accuracy reaches 60.9% for closed/API models and 47.2% for open-weight models.
All numeric-prompt runs show default-label collapse, with one label receiving 33–63% of predictions versus an 18.8% majority-class baseline.
Prompt strategies have inconsistent effects: visual cues help some models by over 10 points but hurt others, while Diwani-first prompts often shift rather than eliminate the default.
The benchmark serves as a culturally grounded stress test for VLM robustness and the visual traditions recognized by automated systems.
papers.selection_reason: Audits VLMs for calligraphy recognition, fits MLLM evaluation.
papers.title: When Models Misread Ink: Auditing VLMs for Arabic Calligraphy Recognition
papers.tldr: VLMs struggle to reliably distinguish Arabic calligraphy styles, often collapsing predictions onto a culturally prominent default label.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used to interpret religious, educational, and culturally sensitive visual content, yet their reliability on citation verification remains underexplored. We introduce Visual Sanad, a controlled benchmark for testing whether VLMs falsely accept incorrect Qur'anic verse attributions when the same quote-reference pair is rendered under different visual framings. The benchmark contains 2,400 rendered images built from 100 English Qur'an verses, four factual states per verse, and six visual conditions ranging from plain text to decorative and authority-framed layouts. All quote-reference pairs were source-checked and human-audited before rendering. Across 24 full model-prompt runs, we observe a sharp capability split. Proprietary API-served VLMs range from near-perfect citation verification to moderate false acceptance, whereas recent open-weight VLMs often show weak discrimination and default to VALID on most images. De-biased prompting can reduce false acceptance, but often by shifting the decision threshold toward INVALID rather than by producing strong citation discrimination. Visual Sanad therefore exposes a culturally grounded multimodal factuality failure: fluent VLMs may treat displayed religious citations as self-authenticating unless they have strong citation-verification ability.
authors: Niaz Mohaiman Abtahi, Reyana Shahid, Evan Maksud
bullets: Introduces a controlled benchmark of 2,400 rendered images based on 100 English Qur'an verses and four factual states.
Tests citation verification across six visual framings, from plain text to decorative and authority-framed layouts.
Finds a sharp capability split: proprietary VLMs range from near-perfect verification to moderate false acceptance, while many open-weight models default to VALID.
De-biased prompting can lower false acceptance but may simply shift models toward INVALID rather than improve discrimination.
Highlights a culturally sensitive multimodal factuality failure: displayed citations may be treated as self-authenticating.
papers.selection_reason: Audits VLMs for citation verification, fits MLLM evaluation.
papers.title: Visual Sanad: Auditing Vision-Language Models for False Acceptance of Qur'anic Citations
papers.tldr: Visual Sanad shows that vision-language models may falsely accept incorrect Qur'anic citations, especially when visual design conveys authority.

papers.abstract: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.
authors: Agnese Chiatti, Matteo Matteucci, Viola Schiaffonati
bullets: Studied 56 AI-literate participants across 392 video question-answering trials.
After each response, participants rated task-specific trust and chose to reject, verify, or fully delegate to AI.
Higher post-interaction trust strongly predicted delegation, but trust and delegation were not equivalent.
Verification was the most common policy and often occurred alongside high trust.
Delegation increased with task order, motivating enacted delegation traces as a framework for studying human-AI oversight.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates human delegation and trust in interaction with multimodal AI (Video QA), relevant to multimodal model evaluation and user interaction.
papers.title: Following Delegation Traces to Study Human Oversight in Interaction with Multimodal AI
papers.tldr: An online study shows that trust predicts how people delegate to multimodal AI, while observed delegation behavior captures experience-related factors that trust ratings miss.

papers.abstract: Recent post-training approaches have shown that self-supervised speech encoders can be adapted to learn a single utterance-level speech attribute through knowledge distillation. In this work, we investigate whether a single speech encoder can simultaneously preserve multiple complementary utterance-level speech representations. We propose a multi-attribute multi-teacher distillation framework that learns semantic, speaker, language, and emotion representations from four frozen teacher models using a shared SSL backbone and attribute-specific branches. Experiments on multilingual semantic retrieval, speaker verification, language identification, and speech emotion recognition show that the proposed model achieves performance close to dedicated single-task students while requiring only a single shared encoder. Furthermore, the learned layer aggregation strategies reveal that different speech attributes naturally emerge at different depths of the SSL encoder, providing new insights into the organization of speech representations.
authors: Maryem Bouziane, Salima Mdhaffar, Yannick Est\`eve
bullets: Addresses whether one self-supervised speech encoder can preserve multiple complementary utterance-level attributes.
Uses four frozen teacher models, a shared SSL backbone, and attribute-specific branches.
Evaluated on multilingual semantic retrieval, speaker verification, language identification, and emotion recognition.
Performance is close to dedicated single-task student models while using one shared encoder.
Layer aggregation results suggest different attributes emerge at different SSL encoder depths.
papers.selection_reason: Learns multiple speech attribute representations in a shared SSL encoder via multi-teacher distillation, relevant to multimodal representation learning.
papers.title: Learning Speech Attribute Representations via Multi-Teacher Distillation
papers.tldr: A multi-teacher distillation framework enables one speech encoder to retain semantic, speaker, language, and emotion representations with near-single-task performance.

papers.abstract: Vision--language pre-training has enabled substantial progress in image--text retrieval and zero-shot recognition by learning transferable cross-modal representations. However, sentence-level alignment remains insufficient for compositional matching, where captions can describe the same objects and attributes while differing in how these elements are bound. To address this limitation, we propose Flow-CLIP, which refines global image-text alignment through image-conditioned changes in token--patch evidence. Global Compatibility Calibration (GCC) learns a sentence-level similarity metric, while Image-Conditioned Evidence Refinement (ICER) incorporates visual patch context into token queries and uses the resulting change in local matching evidence to adjust the global score. We further introduce Cross-Image Margin Ranking (CIMR), which compares the same positive--negative caption pair across matched and mismatched images, encouraging a larger ranking margin when the image supports the correct description. Experiments on compositional matching and attribute--object binding benchmarks show that Flow-CLIP improves binding accuracy over pretrained CLIP and learned global alignment through local evidence refinement, while cross-image ranking supervision mitigates reliance on language priors. Code will be released at link.
authors: Minghong Wei, Enguang Zhu, Pu Cao, Lu Yang, Qing Song
bullets: Targets sentence-level alignment failures where captions mention the same elements but bind attributes and objects differently.
Combines Global Compatibility Calibration (GCC) with Image-Conditioned Evidence Refinement (ICER) to adjust global scores using changes in local visual evidence.
Uses Cross-Image Margin Ranking (CIMR) to reduce reliance on language priors by comparing caption pairs across matched and mismatched images.
Improves binding accuracy over pretrained CLIP and learned global alignment on compositional matching and attribute–object binding benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Improves compositional image-text matching, a multimodal foundation model technique.
papers.title: Flow-CLIP: Image-Conditioned Residual Scoring for CompositionalImage-Text Matching
papers.tldr: Flow-CLIP improves compositional image–text matching by refining global similarity with image-conditioned token–patch evidence and cross-image ranking.

papers.abstract: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.
authors: Dongjie Cheng, Ruifeng Yuan, Ran Wei, Ning Song, Yongqi Li, Wenjie Li
bullets: Addresses the limits of fixed visual-imagination pipelines, such as novel-view synthesis, for diverse reasoning tasks.
Uses tools and skills to help the VLM decide whether and how to imagine, formulate generation requests, and interpret visual evidence.
Introduces co-evolution of tools, skills, and execution code from feedback while keeping model weights fixed.
Improves over direct reasoning with the same VLM across seven spatial, temporal, causal, and perceptual benchmarks.
Reports relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA; the strongest variant outperforms five evolving baselines across five benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: VWM-driven agentic reasoning for spatiotemporal and spatial tasks fits world models, video understanding, and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness
papers.tldr: CoWorld Reasoner equips a VLM with an evolving, tool-based video world-model harness for flexible visual imagination and stronger spatiotemporal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Language priors in MLLMs can override visual evidence, impairing visual perception. Existing benchmarks assume shared priors across models and rely solely on accuracy. However, cross-model prior agreement falls below 80%, and over 15% of items can be answered correctly without any image, causing accuracy to overestimate prior resistance. To address these limitations, we introduce ViSiP-Bench, a benchmark grounded in rare-but-real scenarios across six prior categories, with a model-aware dynamic prior induction protocol and three metrics that more precisely and continuously measure prior resistance than accuracy alone. Evaluating 24 models reveals that prior adherence is pervasive, does not improve with scale, and larger models tend to either strongly override their priors or firmly adhere to them. We therefore propose MAPS, which identifies each model's strongest priors and fine-tunes on factually grounded knowledge to soften excessive prior reliance without disrupting general capabilities.
authors: Li Ma, Yan Zhuang, Jiawen Deng, Fuji Ren
bullets: Existing evaluations overestimate prior resistance because they assume shared priors and rely only on accuracy.
ViSiP-Bench covers six prior categories using rare-but-real scenarios, model-aware dynamic prior induction, and three continuous resistance metrics.
Across 24 models, prior adherence is widespread and does not consistently improve with model scale.
Larger models tend to either strongly override or firmly follow their language priors.
MAPS identifies each model’s strongest priors and fine-tunes on factually grounded knowledge while aiming to preserve general capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and mitigation for language priors in MLLMs.
papers.title: Seeing is Believing: Benchmarking and Mitigating the Interference of Language Priors on Visual Perception in MLLMs
papers.tldr: ViSiP-Bench exposes how language priors distort MLLM visual perception, while MAPS reduces excessive prior reliance through targeted factual fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Embodied spatial intelligence requires more than visual recognition: models must localize entities, reason about their relations, and express this knowledge in action-relevant forms. Yet joint training can conflate the knowledge needed at different stages because supervision is fragmented across incompatible geometric and semantic outputs. We introduce Anvil, a unified framework for data generation, training, and benchmarking for embodied spatial intelligence. (1) Anvil-Gen is a heterogeneous data flywheel that combines form-specific generation, cross-stage consistency verification, and failure-driven recollection across 11 Ground--Relation--Act forms. (2) Anvil-Ben provides scene-aligned supervision for learning diverse embodied spatial capabilities and scene-linked assessments that distinguish stage competence from error propagation. (3) Anvil-MOPD is a 9B student that consolidates heterogeneous spatial knowledge through distillation from specialist teachers. Semantic-first-fault routing targets teacher supervision to the student's earliest decisive failure, while stage normalization controls the loss scale across native outputs of different lengths. We construct 5.8M source-grounded records spanning 160K images, reserving 580K spatial records for held-out evaluation and using the remaining 5.22M records for training. On average across seven public benchmarks, Anvil-MOPD outperforms Qwen3.5-9B and RynnBrain-8B by 9.29 and 11.03 percentage points, respectively, while reaching 80.67% on VABench-Point. Controlled studies support targeted coverage, selective transfer, and feedback-guided repair as complementary framework components.
authors: Weilin Ruan, Bohan Zhou, Jinghao Li, Yangkai Wei, Wenqian Li, Peiran Dong, Yingjie Xu, Leyi Wu, Haojian Huang, Binghui Xie, Han Yang, Kaiwen Zhou, Yinchuan Li, Ying-Cong Chen, James Cheng
bullets: Addresses fragmented supervision that can mix distinct geometric and semantic reasoning stages.
Anvil-Gen generates and verifies data across 11 Ground–Relation–Act forms, then recollects failure cases.
Anvil-Ben provides scene-aligned supervision and evaluations that separate stage competence from propagated errors.
Anvil-MOPD is a 9B student distilled from specialist teachers using earliest-failure routing and stage-normalized losses.
Across seven public benchmarks, it reports average gains of 9.29 and 11.03 percentage points over Qwen3.5-9B and RynnBrain-8B, respectively; it reaches 80.67% on VABench-Point.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Anvil, a framework for embodied spatial intelligence and robot manipulation, combining data generation, training, and benchmarking.
papers.title: Anvil: Scaling Embodied Spatial Intelligence through Knowledge Recirculation
papers.tldr: Anvil builds embodied spatial intelligence by recirculating verified, failure-driven knowledge across localization, relation reasoning, and action-oriented stages.

papers.abstract: Partial shape matching is a crucial yet underexplored problem in 3D vision, with significant relevance to real-world scenarios where shapes are often only partially observed. Existing feature descriptors face difficulties in this setting, as traditional representations either struggle with the boundaries of partial shapes or heavily depend on the shape's spatial position. While existing approaches have employed DINO features for partial shape matching, these features are not inherently suited for handling partial observations. In this work, we propose a method to refine DINO features using LoRA-based self-supervised learning, enabling the generation of feature descriptors that are robust to partiality. Our features substantially improve performance on partial shape matching compared to traditional or vision foundation features. Additionally, when integrated into existing partial shape matching pipelines, we achieve state-of-the-art results on partial shape matching and left-right prediction benchmarks.
authors: Viktoria Ehm, Dongliang Cao, Riccardo Marin, Daniel Scholz, Weikang Wang, Florian Bernard, Daniel Cremers
bullets: Addresses partial 3D shape matching, where boundaries and spatial-position dependence challenge existing descriptors.
Refines DINO features through self-supervised learning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA).
Produces geometry-aware descriptors designed to handle partial observations.
Improves partial shape matching over traditional and general vision-foundation features.
Achieves state-of-the-art results when integrated into existing pipelines on partial shape matching and left-right prediction benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Self-supervised geometry-aware refinement of DINO features for partial 3D shape matching; relevant to 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Teaching DINOv3 About Partial 3D Geometry: A Self-Supervised Geometry-Aware Approach
papers.tldr: A LoRA-based self-supervised adaptation makes DINO features more robust for matching partially observed 3D shapes.

papers.abstract: We study how vision-language models (VLMs) can learn to think and actively explore in 3D space. Instead of providing multi-view images, videos, or 3D representations to the model, we preserve the native visual encoding of VLMs, i.e., a single image, one at a time, just like humans, and treat the 3D representation only as an environment with which the model can interact through actions (e.g., move left) and observations (rendered images). Each rollout begins from an initial first-person view and a visual question. The model can then iteratively reason, navigate, and reorient its viewpoint before committing to a final answer. Following an initial trajectory-supervised finetuning, we apply reinforcement learning (RL) with rewards driven primarily by final-answer correctness. Crucially, RL provides no direct supervision over which viewpoints the model should visit or which exploration actions it should take. Instead, the model must learn an effective exploration policy solely from the extent to which its interactions improve performance. Across six 3D benchmarks, our model ACT3D achieves an average accuracy of 53.2% that improves its base Qwen model by 22.0% and surpasses proprietary Gemini 3.6 Flash. ACT3D also outperforms existing open-source 3D methods while using 50-70% fewer input frames, and generalizes to unseen domains with an average improvement of 5.9% over its supervised initialization. Further analysis reveals adaptive, question-conditioned exploration. Performance gains over the base model increase from 0.6% on questions answerable from the initial view to 16.3% on those requiring extensive exploration. ACT3D searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary exploration, and acquires complementary viewpoints for spatial comparisons. These findings demonstrate that outcome-based RL enables VLMs not only to reason over visual evidence, but also to learn when and how to acquire it.
authors: Yijiang Li, Bingyang Wang, Nuno Vasconcelos
bullets: Uses one rendered image at a time, with actions such as moving and reorienting, rather than preloaded multi-view or 3D inputs.
Combines trajectory-supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning driven mainly by final-answer correctness, without viewpoint or action labels.
Achieves 53.2% average accuracy across six 3D benchmarks, improving its base Qwen model by 22.0% and using 50–70% fewer input frames than existing open-source methods.
Learns question-conditioned exploration: it searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary movement, and gathers complementary views for spatial comparisons.
Generalizes to unseen domains, improving 5.9% over supervised initialization; gains are largest for questions requiring extensive exploration.
papers.selection_reason: VLM agent learns to actively explore 3D environments via actions and RL; directly fits embodied vision-language navigation and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: Learning to Think and Explore in 3D World
papers.tldr: ACT3D trains a vision-language model to actively navigate 3D environments and gather only the visual evidence needed to answer questions.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal semantic segmentation benefits from complementary sensors, but this benefit is fragile when some modalities are degraded or missing at test time. Many existing methods rely on dedicated fusion modules or multi-branch cross-modal encoders, and the fusion often becomes unreliable when modalities are absent, leading to substantial performance drops. We propose \textbf{FuseAdapt}, a parameter-efficient framework that performs fusion within the adaptation space of a frozen vision foundation model (VFM), exploring whether VFM priors can serve as an effective shared backbone for multi-modal segmentation. Instead of attaching a standalone fusion network, FuseAdapt assigns each modality a lightweight adaptation branch and performs \emph{adaptation-space fusion} by keeping Q/V low-rank adaptation private to each modality and routing only FFN low-rank residual activations across modalities inside the frozen backbone. The pretrained VFM remains fixed while modality-specific corrections and explicit cross-modal interaction are learned through the adaptation paths. To handle missing modalities, we further introduce \textbf{Predictive Modality Modeling (PMM)}, a direct representation-level objective for cross-modal redundancy. During training, PMM masks a target modality and predicts its embedding from the visible ones, supervised by a teacher target computed under full-modality input. PMM is used only during training and adds no inference-time overhead. Across three multi-modal segmentation benchmarks (MCubeS, DELIVER, MUSES), FuseAdapt consistently improves both modality-complete and modality-incomplete segmentation with a small trainable budget, yielding up to +3.01 mIoU under full modalities and +12.56 mIoU under missing modalities over prior state-of-the-art. Project page: https://devinxzhang.github.io/FuseAdapt-Page/.
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when modalities are absent or corrupted at test time.
Uses modality-specific low-rank adaptation branches inside a frozen vision foundation model.
Fuses modalities by routing only FFN adaptation residuals across modalities while keeping Q/V adaptations private.
Introduces Predictive Modality Modeling to reconstruct masked modality embeddings during training without inference overhead.
Improves complete- and incomplete-modality segmentation across three benchmarks, with gains of up to 3.01 and 12.56 mIoU, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient multimodal fusion in a frozen vision foundation model; relevant to efficient adaptation and spatial segmentation.
papers.title: FuseAdapt: Parameter-Efficient Multimodal Fusion for Semantic Segmentation with Missing Modalities
papers.tldr: FuseAdapt enables robust multimodal semantic segmentation with missing sensors by learning lightweight cross-modal adaptations within a frozen vision foundation model.

papers.abstract: Audio-enabled large language models (AuLLMs) allow users to interact with them simply by talking to them, without the need for an intermediate transcription. This expands the model's accessibility and capabilities by encoding non-verbal cues. However, using non-verbal cues may lead to biased behaviour based on the attributes inferred (or assumed) from them. In this work, we focus on the gender attribute and show that models' perception of it can be unlearned using adversarial methods without a loss in performance on other benchmarked tasks. Such models are useful in situations where gender inference is unwanted. However, in other practical settings, gender perception (without bias) may be desired.As a less radical measure, we distil the gender-agnostic model, creating a model that perceives gender but responds similarly to the gender-agnostic teacher, unless explicitly asked.We apply our newly proposed methods to three AuLLMs and obtain satisfactory results in the gender-unlearning part and partially satisfactory results in the distilling part.
authors: Adnan Al Ali, Jind\v{r}ich Libovick\'y, Anne Lauscher
bullets: Audio-enabled LLMs can infer gender from non-verbal cues, potentially causing biased behavior.
Adversarial training is used to unlearn gender perception while preserving performance on other benchmarked tasks.
Distillation creates models that retain gender perception but aim to respond like a gender-agnostic teacher unless gender is explicitly requested.
The methods are evaluated on three audio-enabled LLMs.
Gender unlearning achieves satisfactory results; distillation is only partially satisfactory.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses bias mitigation in audio-enabled LLMs via adversarial training and distillation, relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Bias Mitigation in Audio-Enabled LLMs through Adversarial Training and Distillation Methods
papers.tldr: The paper reduces gender-related bias in audio-enabled LLMs through adversarial unlearning and selective distillation, with strong unlearning results but only partial success in distillation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves multimodal reasoning, but group-relative policy optimization broadcasts a single sequence-level advantage to every token of a response, although errors usually localize to a few decisive steps. Recent self-distilled variants refine credit with a teacher--student likelihood gap. However, this signal cannot tell whether it relies on the image or on a language shortcut, and is applied uniformly even when the teacher is uninformative. To address this, we propose Pairwise token contrast and Adaptive trajectory ConfidencE (PACE). Pairwise token contrast scores each response under four teacher views, crossing a correct or incorrect answer hint with the image present or removed, and compares the two hints for every token, which cancels shifts shared by both hints and reveals whether the token's support relies on the image. Adaptive trajectory confidence measures how well the teacher predicts each response given the correct hint and the image, normalizes this score within the batch, and uses it to set how far the token contrast redistributes credit within that response. PACE achieves the best average accuracy on three backbones and ranks first on all evaluated multimodal reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. Experiments show that both components matter: replacing pairwise token contrast with a single-view signal underperforms our method, while adaptive trajectory confidence adds further improvement.
authors: Yiran Zhang, Hanbo Huang, Jielan Li, Zhen Zhao, Shiyu Liang, Hongxia Hao
bullets: Addresses sequence-level credit assignment, where one advantage is applied uniformly despite errors being localized.
Uses pairwise token contrast across correct/incorrect hints with and without the image to distinguish visual support from language shortcuts.
Uses adaptive trajectory confidence to control how strongly token-level credit is redistributed for each response.
Achieves the best average accuracy across three backbones and ranks first on evaluated multimodal reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct.
Both pairwise contrast and adaptive confidence contribute to the gains.
papers.selection_reason: Token-level credit assignment for multimodal RLVR; directly relevant to multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Enhancing Multimodal RLVR with Pairwise Token Contrast and Adaptive Trajectory Confidence
papers.tldr: PACE improves multimodal RLVR by assigning image-grounded, token-level credit and adapting its strength to teacher confidence.

papers.abstract: Distilling vision-language features into 3D Gaussian Splatting yields a language map that can be queried with arbitrary text. In deployment, however, a small set of user-specified targets must be reliably located, which current distilled maps often miss, while open-vocabulary queryability for other words must remain intact. We propose a training-free, target-aware refinement of an already-distilled language map. Guided by a text-promptable segmenter, the visual embedding inside each detected target region is blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient sets the amount of injected prior, while non-target regions are left untouched. Injecting too much overwrites appearance cues and general queryability, so we seek, for each target, the smallest coefficient that still lets it win, and we obtain every coefficient in closed form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. We further identify a failure mode of injection in language-goal localization. Text embeddings share a common component, and injecting them makes the standard cosine read-out query-agnostic, which a centering step in the read-out removes. Across three benchmarks, the refinement consistently improves open-vocabulary segmentation, roughly doubling the base mIoU on Replica, and localizes language goals more reliably than the base map. It also transfers as a plug-in to off-the-shelf field-based and object-level language maps and supports a real-world demonstration in which a legged robot navigates to natural-language goals. Project page and code: https://lab-of-ai-and-robotics.github.io/target-aware-langmap/
authors: Sibaek Lee, Kyeongsu Kang, Seongbo Ha, Yewon Jeon, Joonyeol Choi, Daegeol Ko, Jaehyuk Hur, Taemin Choi, Minsu Kim, Hyungjoo Ahn, Wonsok Yoo, Hyeonwoo Yu
bullets: Addresses missed user-specified targets in distilled 3D language maps without sacrificing other-word queryability.
Uses a text-promptable segmenter to blend target-region visual embeddings with target text embeddings, leaving non-target regions unchanged.
Computes the smallest effective blending coefficient in closed form, avoiding tuning hyperparameters.
Centers the read-out to remove query-agnostic effects caused by shared components in text embeddings.
Improves open-vocabulary segmentation across three benchmarks, roughly doubling base mIoU on Replica, and transfers to other language maps and real-world robot navigation.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free refinement of 3D language maps for target localization.
papers.title: Training-Free Target-Aware Refinement of 3D Gaussian Language Map
papers.tldr: A training-free refinement makes 3D Gaussian language maps reliably detect specified targets while preserving open-vocabulary querying and improving language-goal navigation.

papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) have made substantial progress in audio understanding. However, in high-throughput applications requiring frequent selection, judgment, and scoring, autoregressive text generation introduces additional computational overhead and response latency. To address this limitation, we introduce Qwen-Audio-Jev by augmenting Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next with a dedicated Jev decision head. The model unifies selection, binary judgment, and scoring through three decision primitives: CHOICE, NOUL, and SCORE. Given audio, a natural-language question, and an explicit answer specification, it directly produces a task-conditioned probability distribution or a numerical score through typed decision readouts. Evaluation across 18 labeled configurations covers all three primitives: for CHOICE, Qwen-Audio-Jev achieves accuracies of 78.70% on MMAU-mini and 84.06% on MMSU; for NOUL, it achieves an equal error rate of 6.50% on the VoxCeleb1-O speaker verification benchmark; and for SCORE, the model achieves a normalized mean absolute error of 0.1062 on NISQA overall quality assessment, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.8210 and 0.8074, respectively. Compared with the original Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next, Qwen-Audio-Jev achieves an approximately 20x inference speedup. It demonstrates its potential for efficient, high-throughput audio decision-making in applications such as large-scale audio screening, speaker verification, and automated quality assessment.
authors: Ying Fang, Zhifu Gao, Qing Gu, Jiajun He, Kangqi Jing, Xiangang Li, Yu Pu, Wupeng Wang
bullets: Supports three typed decision primitives: CHOICE, NOUL, and SCORE, conditioned on audio, a question, and an answer specification.
Evaluated across 18 labeled configurations for audio understanding, speaker verification, and quality assessment.
Reports 78.70% and 84.06% accuracy on MMAU-mini and MMSU, 6.50% EER on VoxCeleb1-O, and 0.1062 normalized MAE on NISQA.
