Achieves approximately 20× faster inference than Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next, targeting high-throughput audio applications.
papers.selection_reason: Audio LLM with a decision head for efficient audio understanding, fitting multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Qwen-Audio-Jev: A Unified Interface for Audio Decisions
papers.tldr: Qwen-Audio-Jev adds a dedicated decision head to enable fast, unified audio selection, judgment, and scoring without autoregressive text generation.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) have made strong progress in multimodal understanding, yet most treat audio as monaural semantic content, limiting their ability to reason about where sounds originate and how they relate to the visual scene. Recent spatial audio-visual studies address parts of this problem, but often focus on specific abilities, such as spatial correspondence or direction and distance reasoning. In this work, we introduce HLR-AVSceneQA, a comprehensive benchmark with a hear-localize-reason hierarchy that evaluates whether models can recognize what is heard, localize sound sources in egocentric and allocentric views, and use these localized sources to reason about how they relate to the visual scene. We further introduce HLR-LLM, which augments a strong audio-visual foundation model with a binaural spatial audio branch alongside its monaural semantic audio pathway. We train HLR-LLM with a curriculum that incorporates final-stage chain-of-thought supervision for multi-step spatial reasoning. Experiments show that existing AV-LLMs remain limited in spatial grounding and relational reasoning, while HLR-LLM substantially improves spatial audio-visual scene understanding without compromising semantic audio-visual perception.
authors: Kim Sung-Bin, Lee Jung-Mok, Jinwoo Jung, Oh Hyun-Bin, Hyeonggon Ryu, David Harwath, Tae-Hyun Oh
bullets: Addresses AV-LLMs’ limited spatial grounding beyond monaural audio semantics.
Introduces HLR-AVSceneQA, a hierarchical benchmark covering recognition, egocentric/allocentric localization, and scene-relative reasoning.
Presents HLR-LLM with binaural spatial audio and monaural semantic audio pathways.
Uses curriculum training with final-stage chain-of-thought supervision for multi-step spatial reasoning.
Experiments show improved spatial audio-visual understanding without compromising semantic perception; existing AV-LLMs remain limited in spatial grounding and relational reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Spatially aware audio-visual LLM with binaural spatial branch and spatial reasoning benchmark, fitting multimodal LLM and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Hear, Localize, and Reason: Spatially Aware Scene Understanding for Audio-Visual LLMs
papers.tldr: HLR-AVSceneQA and HLR-LLM enable audio-visual models to hear, localize, and reason about sounds in relation to visual scenes.

papers.abstract: Decision trees can make vision-language model (VLM) classification interpretable by replacing a single prediction with a sequence of root-to-leaf questions. However, the accuracy cost of this greedy, non-backtracking procedure remains unclear. We introduce \textbf{MYOPIA}, a benchmark comprising four LLM-generated, human-refined decision trees for GTSRB, MNIST, CIFAR-10, and MSCOCO, together with matched prompts, diagnostic protocols, and an evaluation harness. Across GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, and LLaMA-3.2 11B Vision, tree traversal underperforms zero-shot prompting in all 12 dataset--model pairs; paired bootstrap analyses consistently favor zero-shot. Our diagnostics characterize interacting failure modes associated with this gap. Models often recall tree-encoded class attributes more accurately than they ground the same attributes in images: the mean label--image accuracy gaps are 9.5, 13.8, and 12.6 points for GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, and LLaMA, respectively. Incorrect local decisions then irreversibly exclude the correct class, while answer extraction introduces additional model-dependent loss. A node-level audit of the four trees finds that split entropy is weakly but consistently associated with lower node accuracy, whereas depth, branching factor, and within-node grounding differences are less stable. \textbf{MYOPIA} therefore provides a framework for diagnosing hierarchical visual classification and motivates testing tree designs that prioritize perceptual answerability and recovery from early errors. Code is available at https://github.com/islammesabah/VLM_Classification.
authors: Islam Mesabah, Sary Elmansoury, Gerrit Gro{\ss}mann, Peter Neigel, Sebastian J. Vollmer
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of four human-refined decision trees for GTSRB, MNIST, CIFAR-10, and MSCOCO, with prompts, diagnostics, and an evaluation harness.
Tests GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, and LLaMA-3.2 11B Vision across 12 dataset–model pairs; tree traversal underperforms zero-shot prompting in every pair.
Models recall tree-provided class attributes better than they ground those attributes in images, producing model-dependent label–image accuracy gaps.
Local decision errors can permanently remove the correct class, while answer extraction adds further losses.
Higher split entropy is weakly associated with lower node accuracy; effects of depth, branching factor, and within-node grounding are less consistent.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and analysis of tree-based reasoning in VLMs, relevant to multimodal LLM capabilities.
papers.title: MYOPIA: Understanding the Limits of Tree-Based Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: MYOPIA shows that greedy decision-tree reasoning consistently reduces VLM image-classification accuracy compared with zero-shot prompting, largely because visual grounding errors cause irreversible class elimination.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models have advanced video understanding, but existing benchmarks mainly evaluate whether models can interpret observed visual content. In real-world scenarios, assistants must additionally anticipate what assistance is needed and decide when to provide it. To address this gap, we introduce \textsc{P$^3$IBench}, a benchmark for proactive video understanding in real-life streaming scenarios. It evaluates three complementary capabilities: daily perception, risk prediction and intervention. We benchmark 12 representative open-source and proprietary video-language models, including streaming and adapted non-streaming systems. Our evaluation shows that current models struggle to make well-calibrated response decisions. Finally, we construct additional proactive training data and train \textsc{P$^3$I-Assistant-4B}, achieving improvements on several tasks, though gains remain uneven across capabilities. Together, these findings show that effective proactive assistance requires not only visual understanding, but also precise response timing and appropriate restraint.
authors: Boyu Cui, Junhao Luo, Zhihao Wang, Linghan Chen, Zejun Li, Jiwen Zhang, Siyuan Wang, Zhongyu Wei
bullets: Existing video benchmarks focus mainly on interpreting observed content, not anticipating assistance needs or deciding when to respond.
The benchmark measures daily perception, risk prediction, and intervention.
It evaluates 12 open-source and proprietary video-language models, including streaming and adapted non-streaming systems.
Current models struggle with well-calibrated response decisions and appropriate restraint.
Training P$^3$I-Assistant-4B with additional proactive data improves several tasks, but gains vary by capability.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for proactive video understanding with video-language models, directly fitting video understanding and multimodal LLM topics.
papers.title: From Perception to Prediction and Intervention: Benchmarking Proactive Video Assistants in Real-Life Scenarios
papers.tldr: P$^3$IBench evaluates whether video assistants can perceive situations, predict risks, and intervene appropriately in real-life streaming scenarios.

papers.abstract: When a vision-language model is finetuned on class-imbalanced data, rare-class recall can fall well below the model's own zero-shot performance. In this regime, we uncover a surprising matched-prompt penalty whereby the standard choice of reusing the descriptive finetuning prompt at inference can yield lower rare-class recall than using a different descriptive prompt. We call this inference-time strategy cross-prompt inference. We evaluate diverse VLMs across six datasets and find that cross-prompt inference consistently recovers rare-class recall, with varying trade-offs in frequent-class recall. The effect reflects a train-eval prompt interaction rather than prompt quality alone, and does not arise with non-descriptive prompt changes. It is strongest when imbalance and visual confusability produce substantial rare-class suppression, and is weak or absent when such suppression does not occur. Using Tuning Contribution (TuCo), which decomposes a model's computation into pretrained and finetuning parts, we find that cross-prompt inference reduces reliance on finetuning-induced computation and shifts the model toward its pretrained component. Reducing that finetuning contribution also substantially reduces the cross-prompt advantage. These results show that rare-class knowledge suppressed by imbalanced finetuning can remain accessible under a different inference prompt.
authors: Emanuel Ben Baruch, Sivan Biham, Alon Shoshan, Yochai Zvik, Avi Ben-Cohen
bullets: Imbalanced finetuning can suppress rare-class recall below the model’s zero-shot performance.
Reusing the finetuning prompt at inference may worsen rare-class recall relative to a different descriptive prompt.
Across diverse VLMs and six datasets, cross-prompt inference consistently improves rare-class recall, sometimes trading off frequent-class recall.
The effect depends on train–evaluation prompt interaction and is strongest under severe imbalance and visual confusability.
TuCo analysis suggests cross-prompt inference shifts reliance away from finetuning-induced computation toward pretrained representations; reducing that finetuning contribution weakens the benefit.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes inference-prompt effects in imbalanced VLM finetuning, relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Cross-Prompt Inference Mitigates Rare-Class Suppression in Imbalanced VLM Finetuning
papers.tldr: Using a different descriptive prompt at inference can recover rare-class recall lost during imbalanced VLM finetuning.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) receive image-generation supervision that exposes them to visual information not fully documented in text. Can learning to generate images expand what pretrained models know? We introduce Knowledge Transfer Probing (KTP), a controlled protocol that supplies new knowledge through image-generation training and tests its accessibility through text-only question answering. Across seven knowledge categories and three UMMs, we observe direct but uneven transfer from visual supervision to language. Motivated by these observations, we successively introduce Textual Alignment and Interleaved Image--Text Alignment, which connect generation and answering through shared knowledge and interleaved responses, respectively. Guidance on selected entities can improve knowledge access on other entities without QA supervision, with additional gains from interleaved alignment. Further analysis shows that knowledge correctly reproduced in images is often more accessible through text, although substantial gaps remain between the two forms of access. These findings support visual generation as a source of knowledge beyond textual supervision, and motivate joint investigation of training data design and model architecture to make this knowledge more broadly accessible.
authors: Wenkai Li, Wenyi Hong, Zhuoyi Yang, Jie Tang
bullets: KTP tests whether image-generation supervision makes visual knowledge accessible through text-only question answering.
Across seven knowledge categories and three models, the study finds direct but variable transfer from visual supervision to language.
Textual Alignment and Interleaved Image–Text Alignment improve access to generated knowledge, including for unguided entities.
Knowledge reproduced correctly in images is generally more accessible through text, but notable gaps remain.
The findings motivate better training-data design and model architectures for broader cross-modal knowledge access.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates knowledge transfer from image generation to language in UMMs using a controlled protocol (KTP).
papers.title: Can Visual Generation Expand What Unified Multimodal Models Know?
papers.tldr: Visual-generation training can transfer new knowledge to language in unified multimodal models, but the transfer is uneven and incomplete.

papers.abstract: Human face-to-face conversation requires coordinating speech, gestures and expressions across both speaking and listening. We present ELLSA 2, an end-to-end full-duplex dialogue model that jointly optimizes speech interaction and streaming gesture-expression generation. An autoregressive, chunk-wise synthesizer combines pretrained acoustic features with distinct listening and speaking hidden states from the dialogue backbone and speech synthesizer, enabling continuous non-verbal generation even when the model is verbally silent. To translate dialogue understanding into vivid semantic gestures, we introduce contextual semantic calls and template guidance, separating whether to invoke an available semantic gesture from how to realize it. We also establish a curated data and evaluation pipeline for dialog-aware co-speech gesture generation and investigate reference-based multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as automatic judges. Experiments show that ELLSA 2 remains highly competitive with open-source full-duplex speech interaction models and outperforms cascaded baselines across dialog-aware gesture and expression metrics. Semantic template guidance further significantly improves semantic gesture quality. Strong system-level correlations with human judgments support these reference-based scores as useful preliminary metrics for full-duplex and semantic gesture assessment. Together, these results advance dialogue modeling from spoken responses toward coordinated multimodal interaction.
authors: Siyin Wang, Wenyi Yu, Terumi Chiba, Xianzhao Chen, Xiaohai Tian, Jun Zhang, Lu Lu, Chao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coordinating speaking, listening, speech, gestures, and expressions during face-to-face interaction.
Uses an end-to-end autoregressive, chunk-wise synthesizer with separate listening and speaking states, allowing nonverbal generation even during verbal silence.
Introduces contextual semantic calls and template guidance to separate selecting semantic gestures from realizing them vividly.
Establishes a curated data and evaluation pipeline and explores reference-based MLLM judges for dialog-aware gesture and expression assessment.
Reports strong competitiveness against open-source full-duplex models, improved gesture and expression metrics over cascaded baselines, and further semantic-gesture gains from template guidance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ELLSA 2, a full-duplex dialogue model generating speech, gestures, and expressions jointly.
papers.title: Full-Duplex Interaction with Speech, Expressions and Gestures
papers.tldr: ELLSA 2 enables full-duplex dialogue with continuous speech, gesture, and facial-expression generation, producing more contextually appropriate nonverbal behavior than cascaded systems.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has brought strong gains to language model reasoning, but its improvements on visual tasks remain less consistent. One difficulty is that visual task failures can arise from different sources: the same benchmark may be limited by perception for one model and by reasoning for another. We introduce Perception and Reasoning Attribution (PARA), which measures the remaining perceptual and reasoning headroom of each model--benchmark pair by comparing how many current errors are recovered with more accurate visual information versus a stronger reasoner. Across 4 vision-language models and 17 multimodal benchmarks, PARA broadly agrees with the expected characteristics of existing benchmarks while revealing substantial model-specific variation. More importantly, it shows that RL gains become smaller as perceptual headroom increases, but larger when reasoning explains more of the recoverable errors, suggesting that current RL exploits reasoning headroom more effectively than perceptual headroom. Motivated by this gap, we analyze how existing RL objectives affect visual perception and find that reward- and token-level signals influence visual attention only indirectly. We therefore propose GRAD, a group-relative attention distillation objective that uses the best rollout in each group to directly guide the visual attention of weaker rollouts. GRAD consistently improves performance across two model scales and seven benchmarks, and further complements existing RL methods.
authors: Zeyuan Yang, Zhuohao Chen, Jiaben Chen, Yao Zhang, Maohao Shen, Chuang Gan
bullets: Visual-task failures vary by model: the same benchmark may be perception- or reasoning-limited.
PARA estimates remaining perceptual and reasoning headroom by comparing error recovery with better visual information versus stronger reasoning.
Across 4 VLMs and 17 multimodal benchmarks, PARA finds that RL benefits reasoning headroom more effectively than perceptual headroom.
The authors find existing reward- and token-level RL signals affect visual attention only indirectly.
GRAD distills visual attention from the best rollout to weaker group rollouts, consistently improving results across two model scales and seven benchmarks while complementing existing RL methods.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses perception vs reasoning bottlenecks in VLMs and proposes attention distillation; fits multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Perception or Reasoning? Diagnosing and Tackling Reinforcement Learning Bottlenecks in VLMs
papers.tldr: PARA diagnoses whether VLM errors stem from perception or reasoning, while GRAD improves visual attention to make reinforcement learning more effective on perception-limited tasks.

papers.abstract: Residential design aims to transform existing homes into functional living spaces while satisfying diverse design preferences and physical constraints. However, existing floorplan generation methods typically assume empty building boundaries as input, whereas renovation requires reasoning over existing floorplans. Furthermore, floorplan renovation and furniture layout are commonly addressed as separate tasks, overlooking their inherent spatial dependency. Consequently, practical residential design must preserve immutable structural components while transforming editable spatial elements. It must also optimize furniture placement under design objectives and physical constraints. To address these challenges, we formulate residential design as a design-point-guided conditional generation task and propose RenoLayout, a framework that translates a pre-design residential state together with a design-point set into an executable Geometry-as-Code program. To enable controllable supervision, we construct a Design Map comprising 123 fine-grained design points covering structural renovation and furniture layout. We further introduce Difference-Grounded Design-Point Annotation to derive design-point sets automatically from before--after design pairs with VLM-based consistency verification. RenoLayout is trained using a three-stage CPT--SFT--RL pipeline, progressively improving spatial reasoning, instruction following, and constraint compliance. We also introduce the RenoLayout Benchmark, a set of 200 real-world before--after renovation cases with complete furniture layouts. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first benchmark for unified residential design. These cases include design-critical structural and building-service constraints.
authors: Jingguo Liu, Yuanqing Liu, Chong Zhang, Yue Yang
bullets: Addresses the gap between methods that generate empty-boundary floorplans and practical renovation of existing homes.
Models renovation and furniture layout jointly while preserving immutable structural components and satisfying physical constraints.
Introduces a 123-point Design Map and VLM-verified annotation method to derive design guidance from before–after examples.
Trains the framework with a three-stage CPT–SFT–RL pipeline for spatial reasoning, instruction following, and constraint compliance.
Provides the RenoLayout Benchmark with 200 real-world renovation cases containing complete furniture layouts and design-critical constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Unified floorplan renovation and furniture layout with spatial reasoning and constraint compliance; directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: RenoLayout: Unified Floorplan Renovation and Furniture Layout for Constraint-Aware Residential Design
papers.tldr: RenoLayout unifies residential floorplan renovation and furniture placement by generating executable Geometry-as-Code designs from existing layouts, design points, and structural constraints.

papers.abstract: Multimodal long-document question answering requires models to seek sparse evidence across pages and modalities, understand heterogeneous document content, and reason over the collected evidence. Even advanced vision-language models (VLMs) can overlook sparse evidence and struggle with cross-modal reasoning in a single pass. Existing document agents further introduce multi-step interaction, but some still rely on predefined workflows or coarse-grained actions, limiting the flexibility and granularity of document reasoning. We introduce DocPilot, an agentic document framework that supports expressive orchestration and makes complex document solving learnable by small language models (SLMs). DocPilot orchestrates evidence seeking through page-level navigation and fine-grained evidence localization, and integrates local visual inspection, code-based numerical reasoning, and cross-modal reasoning for multimodal understanding. To transfer these capabilities to small models, we propose curriculum-based agentic training that progresses from single-ability learning to adaptive orchestration through supervision from data-grounded reasoning traces and executable interaction trajectories. Across MMLongBench-Doc, DocBench, FinRAGBench-V, and MADQA, DocPilot achieves strong gains with frontier VLM backbones, while DocPilot-4B delivers competitive performance against substantially larger models, demonstrating strong effectiveness and generalization across diverse long-document reasoning settings. The code is available at https://github.com/HKUSTDial/DocPilot.
authors: Zhuowen Liang, Xiaotian Lin, Yuyu Luo, Haixun Wang, Nan Tang
bullets: Targets sparse, heterogeneous evidence and cross-modal reasoning challenges in long documents.
Uses page-level navigation, fine-grained evidence localization, local visual inspection, code-based numerical reasoning, and cross-modal reasoning.
Trains small language models with a curriculum that advances from individual abilities to adaptive orchestration.
Supervision combines data-grounded reasoning traces with executable interaction trajectories.
Shows strong gains with frontier VLMs and competitive performance from DocPilot-4B across four diverse benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic orchestration of VLMs for long visual document reasoning fits multimodal LLM interests.
papers.title: DocPilot: Interactive Agent Orchestration and Training for Long Visual Document Understanding
papers.tldr: DocPilot improves long visual-document QA by flexibly orchestrating evidence search, visual inspection, numerical reasoning, and cross-modal reasoning, while training small models to perform these capabilities.

papers.abstract: Most vision-language models (VLMs) treat the vision encoder as a static feature extractor: it encodes an image once, independently of the question, and leaves subsequent reasoning to the language model. Yet different questions may require different visual operations and processing depths. We present AdaLoop, a framework for question-conditioned visual recurrence in VLMs. AdaLoop adapts visual computation to the question and reuses the encoder's transformations across multiple iterations, with the pretrained vision weights frozen. We also introduce VisRO, a procedural dataset and generation pipeline for training and evaluating vision-centric reasoning. On six VisRO tasks, AdaLoop outperforms standard fine-tuning and question-conditioned single-pass baselines with matched training data and optimizer updates. These gains hold across three VLM families on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution examples. Our findings suggest that pretrained vision encoders can contribute to reasoning through task-directed, iterative visual computation.
authors: Xinran Nicole Han, Yiyang Lu, Katelyn Gan, Todd Zickler
bullets: Addresses the limitation of one-pass, question-independent visual encoding in VLMs.
Adapts visual processing depth and operations to each question through visual recurrence.
Introduces VisRO, a procedural dataset and pipeline for vision-centric reasoning tasks.
Outperforms matched standard fine-tuning and single-pass baselines across six VisRO tasks, three VLM families, and both in- and out-of-distribution examples.
Shows that frozen pretrained vision encoders can support iterative, task-directed reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a framework for iterative visual computation in VLMs, reusing the vision encoder conditioned on the question. This architectural innovation allows for deeper visual reasoning and is relevant to advancing multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: AdaLoop: Thinking with the Vision Encoder
papers.tldr: AdaLoop enables VLMs to perform question-conditioned, iterative visual reasoning by reusing a frozen vision encoder across multiple computation steps.

papers.abstract: Detailed captions transfer visual information into vision-language model supervision, but quality is easily conflated with length: long single-pass outputs still miss small objects, text, and spatial relations or promote uncertain observations into confident claims. We formulate fine-grained captioning as recoverable visual information transfer, in which a teacher acquires missing evidence under a finite observation budget and converts it into reusable supervision. ZoomCap uses a draft caption to route conditional knowledge retrieval, OCR-sensitive reading, coverage-gap recovery, and adaptive visual zooming, allocating deeper crops only to the most complex eligible region, deriving spatial relations from grounded geometry, and fusing non-duplicate evidence. We also introduce FactCycle, which scores caption-derived atomic claims on two blind anchors--source image (truthfulness) and reconstruction (realizability)--separating fabrication from generator loss claim by claim; human and multi-judge comparisons complement this fact-level view. Against Qwen3.5-397B-A17B captions, ZoomCap achieves an 81.9% human tie-adjusted preference score with a teacher over 10x smaller, and FactCycle counts 52.4 transferred claims per image vs. 31.5 for ScaleCap. The evidence also transfers: in continual pre-training, ZoomCap-450K improves the 11-benchmark average by 1.31-2.38 points over the strongest competing corpus and Ling-Tiny-VL-v3 gains 1.4 points on a production document/OCR monitor suite (1.5 on perception) at 60B tokens; in medical pre-training, 2.64M ZoomCap-captioned images improve five VQA benchmarks by 3.04 points (vs. 1.76 for same-image Gemini-3.1-Pro captions).
authors: Hao Shi, Jiafeng Wang, Yuzhuo Fu, Tao Zhang, Jian Bai, Juelu Zhang, Qing Cui, Chao Huang
bullets: Targets missed small objects, text, spatial relations, and overconfident unsupported claims in long single-pass captions.
Routes a draft caption to conditional retrieval, OCR-sensitive reading, coverage recovery, adaptive region zooming, and grounded spatial reasoning under a fixed observation budget.
Introduces FactCycle, which evaluates atomic claims against both the source image and reconstructed scene to distinguish fabrication from information loss.
Achieves an 81.9% human tie-adjusted preference score and transfers 52.4 claims per image versus 31.5 for ScaleCap.
ZoomCap-based pre-training improves general, document/OCR, and medical VQA performance across the reported benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for transferring visual information to VLMs via evidence-routed zooming. This improves the spatial reasoning capabilities of multimodal models by grounding them in specific visual details.
papers.title: ZoomCap: Evidence-Routed Visual Zooming for Recoverable Visual Information Transfer
papers.tldr: ZoomCap uses evidence-guided visual zooming and claim-level verification to produce more detailed, reliable captions that transfer effectively to vision-language model training.

papers.abstract: Multimodal document retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has focused largely on retrieval, yet its answers depend on how well a vision-language model reads the retrieved pages. We find that evidence in retrieved pages remains underused even when the correct pages are retrieved. On SciEGQA oracle pages, five prior methods give the generator 0.7K to 2.7K visual tokens per query on average under a common image processor, yet raising the page-only budget from 1K to 32K improves accuracy by 15.22 points. At a fixed 16K budget, adding ground-truth crops improves accuracy by 3.75 points over page-only input. We study what the generator needs from retrieved pages through two requirements: Loud, making full use of visual token capacity, and Clear, refining the page so that its evidence becomes prominent. For Loud, increasing either the visual token budget or visual fidelity, the image resolution those tokens preserve, improves accuracy with the other held fixed, and full-page scaling outperforms repetition and tiling at matched budgets. For Clear, suppressing surrounding content improves accuracy without enlarging selected regions, and adding OCR of these regions to page images outperforms either input alone. We implement both as Loud and Clear (LoC), which combines higher-resolution pages with OCR from query-relevant regions without ground-truth annotations or additional training. LoC outperforms eight prior methods on SciEGQA, ViDoRe-v3, and MMLongBench-Doc, improving over the strongest, ColQwen3, by 8.88, 3.09, and 4.22 points with the same retriever and generator. It also outperforms its page-only variant under the same visual token budget. These results locate a bottleneck beyond retrieval: how the retrieved pages are given to the generator.
authors: Eunchan Jo, Seounghyun Jang, Sangwoo Mo
bullets: Retrieval is not the only bottleneck: generators often underuse evidence on correctly retrieved pages.
Accuracy improves with larger visual-token budgets, higher image fidelity, and full-page scaling rather than repetition or tiling.
Highlighting relevant regions and combining their OCR with page images makes evidence clearer than either input alone.
LoC combines higher-resolution pages with OCR from query-relevant regions, requiring no ground-truth crops or additional training.
It outperforms eight prior methods across SciEGQA, ViDoRe-v3, and MMLongBench-Doc, including its page-only variant at the same visual-token budget.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses how vision-language models use visual evidence in multimodal document RAG, directly relevant to multimodal LLM reading and reasoning.
papers.title: Loud and Clear: Making Visual Evidence Count in Multimodal Document RAG
papers.tldr: LoC improves multimodal document RAG by presenting retrieved-page evidence more visibly and clearly to the vision-language generator, substantially boosting answer accuracy without extra training or annotations.

papers.abstract: Panoramic 3D reconstruction enables the holistic recovery of complete 360 $^\circ$ scene geometry, offering significant benefits for robotics and AR/VR applications. However, directly estimating geometry from ERP images is inherently challenged by spherical distortions. To reduce spherical projection distortions, a common strategy is to decompose panoramas into distortion-free perspective views, but independently processing these views often introduces cross-view geometric inconsistencies. To address these challenges, we introduce GeoPano, a feed-forward framework for single-view panoramic 3D reconstruction that recovers a geometrically accurate and consistent point cloud from a single panorama. Our approach is driven by two key innovations: First, we propose a panoramic-aware attention aggregator, featuring a streamlined attention architecture equipped with a novel Pano-Attention mechanism, which explicitly exploits the intrinsic spherical geometry of the panorama to guide cross-view interactions, thereby suppressing geometric inconsistencies. Furthermore, we formulate a hybrid supervision strategy to jointly enforce fine-grained local details in perspective space and global structural coherence in spherical space. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous SOTA approaches in reconstruction accuracy, geometric consistency, and visual fidelity.
authors: Jing OU, Zidong Cao, Liaoyuan Fan, Zhuoxiao Li, Shuai Zhang, Yinrui Ren, Dongli Wu, Haoang Li, Hui Xiong, Wufan Zhao
bullets: Addresses ERP spherical distortions and inconsistencies caused by independently processing perspective views.
Uses a panoramic-aware attention aggregator with a Pano-Attention mechanism for geometry-guided cross-view interaction.
Combines perspective-space supervision for local detail with spherical-space supervision for global structural coherence.
Experiments report improved reconstruction accuracy, geometric consistency, and visual fidelity over prior state-of-the-art methods.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a framework for 3D reconstruction from panoramas that explicitly handles spherical geometry. This contributes to spatial intelligence by improving geometric reasoning and 3D-aware understanding in multimodal models.
papers.title: GeoPano: Towards Geometrically Accurate 3D Reconstruction from a Single Panorama
papers.tldr: GeoPano reconstructs geometrically consistent 3D point clouds from a single panorama by modeling spherical geometry and combining local and global supervision.

papers.abstract: On-screen text can describe what a video shows, or it can frame what the video is supposed to mean. Current benchmarks treat both alike, testing whether a model can read the text rather than whether it should trust it. We study claim deference, multimodal large language models' tendency to let an on-screen claim override conflicting visual evidence. We introduce VisualTrust, a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases across 14 claim-fact classes. Each case pairs a question with three versions of the same video: one with no claim, one with an accurate claim, and one with a misleading claim that alters a single grounded fact. The option the misleading claim supports is the trap answer. Across seven open-weight and four proprietary models, mean accuracy falls from 90.1% without a claim to 51.9% with a misleading claim. Among initially correct responses, 42.8% flip to the trap answer and only 0.6% become other errors. Strong no-claim accuracy does not ensure resistance. We also introduce DEAR (Decoupled Evidence Arbitration and Reading), a training-free agent for video question answering that separates evidence arbitration from reading. An independent check reports conflicting evidence, a selector weighs it without a fixed modality priority and blinds what it withholds, and the reader answers from the resulting video in a fresh context. On 500 videos across three proprietary models, DEAR raises accuracy under misleading claims from 47.2--64.0% to 81.8--85.2% and reduces trap-answer selection from 34.4--50.8% to 11.6--15.0%, while preserving no-claim accuracy.
authors: Huachao Zhu, Junjielong Xu, Sicheng Li, Liang Yang, Mingtao Chen, Zhichao Hu, Li Jiang, Pinjia He
bullets: Introduces a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases spanning 14 claim–fact classes and three versions of each video.
Misleading claims reduce mean accuracy from 90.1% to 51.9%; 42.8% of initially correct answers flip to the trap answer.
Evaluates seven open-weight and four proprietary models, finding that strong performance without claims does not imply claim resistance.
Proposes DEAR, a training-free agent that separates evidence arbitration from reading and answers from a fresh context.
Across 500 videos and three proprietary models, DEAR raises misleading-claim accuracy to 81.8–85.2% and reduces trap answers to 11.6–15.0%.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and training-free method for video reasoning with multimodal LLMs under misleading on-screen claims; relevant to multimodal robustness and video understanding.
papers.title: VisualTrust: Video Reasoning under On-Screen Claim Framing
papers.tldr: VisualTrust shows that multimodal models often let misleading on-screen claims override video evidence, while DEAR substantially improves resistance without reducing no-claim accuracy.

papers.abstract: Spoken Dialogue Models (SDMs) typically share a speech-token space for generation and synthesis, leading to long autoregressive sequences and costly inference. Lower-rate speech tokenizers shorten sequences but may introduce compression-quality trade-offs and costly replacement without breaking this coupling. To address this limitation, we propose CoSTA, a compatibility-preserving post-hoc framework that decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder. CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations via mean-initialized vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, followed by deterministic expansion back to the original speech-token space before synthesis. On bilingual speech-dialogue benchmarks, CoSTA achieves approximately $1.7\times$ expanded speech-token generation speed, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput while preserving response quality. Analyses show more sustained interaction under limited budgets and a practical trade-off among compression, decoding efficiency, and quality. Further experiments demonstrate cross-architecture transfer and complementarity to low-rate tokenization.
authors: Yingzhuo Deng, Chong Li, Bingxin Liu, Yi Shu, Tianyu Peng, Can Xie, Siyao Song, Shuo Ren, Jiajun Zhang
bullets: Addresses long autoregressive sequences and costly inference caused by tightly coupled generation and synthesis token spaces.
Decouples the token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder.
Uses vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, then deterministically expands compressed tokens before synthesis.
Reports approximately 1.7× faster expanded speech-token generation, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput on bilingual benchmarks.
Supports sustained interaction under limited budgets, transfers across architectures, and complements low-rate tokenization.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient speech-token compression for spoken dialogue models; relevant to efficient inference and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: CoSTA: Compressed Speech Token Adaptation for Efficient Spoken Dialogue Models
papers.tldr: CoSTA makes spoken dialogue generation more efficient by using compressed speech tokens while preserving the original synthesis pipeline and response quality.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc image explanations usually show where a model looks using spatial heatmaps or indicate which channels matter using global channel scores. These separate views are limiting for multispectral data because channel relevance is often spatially localized and physically meaningful. We introduce Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), a full-grid attribution method over position-channel players (g,c). For each spatial position, SSI fixes the observed surrounding context, defines a conditional game over the channels at that position, and applies the Shapley value to this local game. The result is a full spectral-spatial attribution matrix rather than a single heatmap or a global channel ranking. SSI has a clear local interpretation. It satisfies Shapley fairness within each position, and aggregating its channel attributions exactly recovers the position-level contextual contrast obtained by replacing that position with the baseline. SSI also differs from context-averaged Owen-style hierarchical accounting, which uses the same position-channel grouping but averages over external spatial coalitions. On HLS Burn Scar, SSI outperforms an MC-Owen estimator across retained attribution metrics while using only about 6% of its evaluation budget. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn Scar under both per-channel mean and zero baselines, SSI achieves the best joint deletion and insertion AUC over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines, yields the strongest spectral hit rates and channel deletion, and leads spatial localization on both annotated datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/AtheavenMa/Spectral-Spatial-Interpretation.
authors: Haotian Ma, Ruqi Yang, Philip Townsend
bullets: Addresses the limitation of separate spatial heatmaps and global channel scores when channel relevance varies across locations.
Defines a conditional local game over channels at each position while holding surrounding context fixed.
Provides Shapley fairness locally and exactly recovers each position’s contextual contrast when channel attributions are aggregated.
Across three datasets and two baselines, SSI achieves the strongest reported deletion/insertion, spectral, channel, and spatial-localization metrics.
On HLS Burn Scar, it outperforms an MC-Owen estimator using about 6% of its evaluation budget.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Spectral-Spatial Interpretation for multispectral data, a method for attribution that explicitly models spatial and channel relationships, relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Spectral-Spatial Interpretation
papers.tldr: SSI explains multispectral model predictions by assigning Shapley-based importance to each spatial position–channel pair, producing a detailed spectral-spatial attribution map.

papers.abstract: Spatial agents have access to reconstruction and segmentation tools, yet inconsistent predictions and fragmented object identities can prevent their outputs from becoming reliable 3D scene information. A simple oracle experiment exposes this perception bottleneck: replacing tool-predicted perception with ground-truth 3D bounding boxes raises an agent to nearly full score across five object-centric VSI-Bench tasks, while retaining the same reasoning tools. Motivated by this finding, we believe the devil of spatial reasoning lies in 3D itself, and introduce DeSpatial(Devil of Spatial), which explicitly decomposes spatial understanding into perception and reasoning. DeSpatial has a shared 3D perception tool to reconcile independent perception outputs into a unified, metric, gravity-aligned 3D scene. This perception tool has two core components: a) a joint segmentation--depth co-refinement module that consolidates masks of the same object and removes projection artifacts caused by inconsistent segmentation and depth within a single frame; b) a cross-view instance fusion module that consolidate voxel-overlapping instances but not allowed to merge same-frame instances. This fusion module additionally fuses spatially disjoint fragments caused by insufficient multi-view observations, by checking their 3D structure and source mask appearance. After receiving the complete and unified 3D scene information, the agent chooses reasoning or computational tools to solve the spatial problem. DeSpatial achieves leading performance on VSI-Bench, MindCube-Tiny, and ViewSpatial, with additional long-video results on VSI-SUPER, revealing the bottleneck of spatial understanding lies in a precise 3D perception itself.
authors: Yifei Liu, Xiaolong Zhou, Ziyang Gong, Yifan Zhou, Yuanyuan Gao, Yuning Gong, Yuchen Yang, Hongjie Zhang, Xue Yang, Xiao Sun, Zhihang Zhong
bullets: An oracle experiment finds that ground-truth 3D boxes nearly solve five object-centric VSI-Bench tasks, exposing perception as the main bottleneck.
DeSpatial explicitly separates 3D perception from downstream reasoning and computation.
Its shared perception tool builds a metric, gravity-aligned scene using joint segmentation–depth refinement and cross-view instance fusion.
The system prevents erroneous merges while reconnecting fragmented instances using 3D structure and mask appearance.
It achieves leading performance on VSI-Bench, MindCube-Tiny, and ViewSpatial, with additional long-video evaluation on VSI-SUPER.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic spatial reasoning decomposed into unified 3D perception and reasoning; directly relevant to spatial intelligence and 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: DeSpatial: The devil of Agentic Spatial Reasoning Lies in 3D Itself
papers.tldr: DeSpatial shows that reliable agentic spatial reasoning depends primarily on accurate, unified 3D perception rather than reasoning alone.

papers.abstract: Improving the reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) often relies on post-training with supervision from stronger models. Two common strategies are supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which trains on teacher-generated demonstrations, and on-policy distillation (OPD), which provides teacher feedback on trajectories generated by the student itself. While OPD can be more data-efficient by supervising student-generated trajectories, it is unclear how the teacher's supervision at each state affects the student's learned behavior. To study this question, we conduct a controlled comparison of OPD and filtered SFT across data budgets and tasks where the teacher exhibits different levels of reliability, and analyze how these differences shape student accuracy and completion behavior. Across the two tasks, we find that OPD is effective only when the teacher remains reliable on student-generated trajectories. On ChartQA, where the teacher completes 99% of its solutions, OPD trained on only 10% of the data comes within 1.4 accuracy points of full-data SFT. In contrast, on Geometry3K, where the teacher fails to complete 22% of its solutions, OPD underperforms SFT by 7.9 points, with most of the gap explained by incomplete responses. More strikingly, starting OPD from an SFT student reduces its completion rate from 76% to 62%, effectively erasing the completion behavior learned through SFT. Filtering teacher demonstrations for completeness alone recovers much of SFT's advantage. These results show that on-policy supervision can transfer not only teacher knowledge but also persistent failure modes on student-visited states. Code is available at https://github.com/ffy208/opd-inherits-teacher-vlm.
authors: Frank F. Yang, Kefei Yan, Yiren Wang, Yiyang Wang
bullets: OPD is compared with filtered supervised fine-tuning across tasks, data budgets, and teacher reliability levels.
On ChartQA, a teacher with 99% completion enables 10%-data OPD to approach full-data SFT within 1.4 accuracy points.
On Geometry3K, a teacher with 22% incomplete solutions makes OPD trail SFT by 7.9 points, largely due to incomplete responses.
Initializing OPD from an SFT student reduces completion from 76% to 62%, while filtering incomplete demonstrations recovers much of SFT’s advantage.
The findings indicate that OPD inherits persistent teacher failures on states visited by the student.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates on-policy distillation for vision-language models, analyzing how teacher reliability affects student behavior, which is relevant to multimodal model training.
papers.title: Do As I Do, Not As I Say: On-Policy Distillation Inherits the Teacher in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: On-policy distillation transfers a teacher’s failure modes as well as its knowledge, working well only when the teacher reliably completes student-generated trajectories.

papers.abstract: Large multimodal models have achieved remarkable progress by scaling model capacity and training on massive paired multimodal data. However, this paradigm introduces a fundamental bottleneck: aligned multimodal datasets are expensive to curate, difficult to scale across diverse modality combinations, and increasingly constrain further progress. We introduce Modality Self-Play (MSP), a training framework for multimodal foundation models based on proxy-mediated modality composition. Instead of relying on paired cross-modal data, MSP uses anchor-supporting proxy textual descriptions of unseen modalities as semantic bridges during training. Given an observed modality (e.g., image or audio), the model generates proxy descriptions for complementary unseen modalities, which are then encoded and aligned with the observed modality through learned bridges, enabling cross-modal interaction without real paired non-text supervision. Our central hypothesis is that proxy text, combined with contrastively trained pretrained encoders, provides sufficient semantic structure for multimodal composition to emerge. We show that MSP enables zero-shot modality composition: models trained only with a real anchor modality and accompanying proxy descriptions can integrate and reason over multiple modalities at inference time despite never observing real paired non-text data during training. Empirically, MSP achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on multiple multimodal benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate that learned bridges improve alignment, while anchor-supporting proxy descriptions enable effective cross-modal composition. MSP removes the need for real paired non-text (e.g., audio-vision) supervision, while continuing to rely on modality-text pairs, pretrained contrastive encoders, and modality-distribution bridge calibration.
authors: Robert Moseley, Md Kaykobad Reza, Ameya Patil, Edward Ayrapetian, Salman Asif
bullets: Addresses the cost, limited scalability, and modality coverage of curated paired multimodal datasets.
Uses an observed anchor modality to generate proxy descriptions of complementary unseen modalities.
Encodes and aligns observed modalities and proxy text through learned modality bridges and pretrained contrastive encoders.
Enables zero-shot multimodal composition and reasoning at inference despite no real paired non-text supervision during training.
Reports state-of-the-art or competitive benchmark performance; results still depend on modality-text pairs and bridge calibration.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses the training of multimodal LLMs without paired cross-modal data using a self-play framework, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: MSP: Modality Self-Play for Training Multimodal LLMs Without Paired Cross-Modal Data
papers.tldr: MSP trains multimodal LLMs to compose unseen modalities without paired non-text data by using proxy text as a semantic bridge.

papers.abstract: Existing long-document QA benchmarks rarely combine large-scale human-authored questions with detailed visual evidence annotations, limiting diagnosis of evidence localization and interpretation failures. We present VELD-QA, a large-scale benchmark for Visual Evidence grounding and question answering in Long Documents. It contains 15,000 fully human-authored question-answer pairs across 5,859 real-world PDFs totaling 372,445 pages, balancing chart, table, and complex-layout tasks. Human annotations identify supporting pages and evidence elements and describe cited visual content, enabling separate retrieval and interpretation evaluation. We evaluate nine vision-language models under four evidence settings and seven retrieval-augmented and agentic systems. Our analysis identifies bottlenecks in evidence localization and interpretation. Retrieval-based methods substantially underperform the oracle setting with ground-truth supporting pages; full-document access does not close the gap. Localization alone is insufficient: oracle accuracy peaks at 81.7%, highlighting persistent visual interpretation and reasoning challenges. Enriching inputs with our visual-element annotations narrows the performance gap by 17-24%, demonstrating value beyond evaluation and motivating data enrichment for multimodal document QA. Our code is available at https://github.com/oracle-samples/veld-qa.
authors: Zhivar Sourati, Marianne Menglin Liu, Rongguang Wang, Zheng Wang, Yazhe Hu, Lan Guo, Yuying Wang, Mengqing Guo, Bhavesh Dnyaneshwar Gore, Shubham Pathak, Ramapriya Ranganath, Sandeep Sharma, Tao Sheng, Sujith Ravi, Dan Roth

Annotates supporting pages, evidence elements, and cited visual content, enabling separate evaluation of retrieval and interpretation.
Evaluates nine vision-language models and seven retrieval-augmented or agentic systems across four evidence settings.
Results reveal major bottlenecks in evidence localization and visual interpretation; full-document access does not eliminate the gap to oracle evidence.

papers.title: VELD-QA: A Large-Scale Dataset for Visual Evidence Grounding and Question Answering in Long Documents
papers.tldr: VELD-QA is a large-scale benchmark that evaluates both visual evidence localization and reasoning for question answering over long, visually complex documents.

papers.abstract: Negation is a fundamental aspect of language understanding and it is important vision-language models (VLMs) are able to process it effectively. We investigate how VLMs process negation by analysing attention patterns of different models. We draw comparisons between human gaze and attention in models when processing affirmative vs negated statements. We compare object level model attention to human eye-fixations in both binary and multary settings, evaluating with both synthetic and realistic datasets. We find models generally do not follow human-like attention patterns when resolving negation, suggesting they rely on mechanisms outside of attention. While layerwise analysis shows that PaliGemma2-3B shifts object attention to the alternative under negation, our headwise ablations suggest this is a byproduct rather than a negation processing mechanism. Additionally, we find that LLaVA-1.5-7B displays a spatial bias towards left-side objects. Our evaluation of models on downstream tasks shows that all models have a discrepancy between affirmative and negated questions highlighting the need to better understand the underlying processing of negation to close this performance gap. Code available at https://github.com/otmive/negation_attention
authors: Beth Pearson, Michael Wray, Martha Lewis
bullets: The study compares model object attention with human eye fixations across affirmative and negated statements.
It evaluates binary and multary settings using both synthetic and realistic datasets.
PaliGemma2-3B shifts attention toward the alternative object under negation, but ablations suggest this is not the underlying negation mechanism.
LLaVA-1.5-7B shows a spatial bias toward objects on the left.
All evaluated models perform differently on affirmative versus negated downstream questions, highlighting a persistent negation-processing gap.
papers.selection_reason: Directly studies attention and reasoning in vision-language models, fitting multimodal LLM analysis.
papers.title: Probing Negation Understanding in Vision-Language Models With Object Attention
papers.tldr: Vision-language models’ object-attention patterns generally do not resemble human gaze when processing negation, revealing unresolved differences in how they handle affirmative versus negated statements.

papers.abstract: Map generation tasks feature extensive non-structural vectorized data (e.g., points, polylines, and polygons) and thus pose significant challenges to common pixel-wise generative models. Conventional approaches use multiple stages, first segmenting these features at the pixel level and then performing vectorized post-processing, with errors and complexity compounding at each stage. Motivated by the recent success of auto-regressive language modeling, we propose the first map foundation model, named Map Auto-Regressor (MARS), that is capable of generating both multi-polyline road networks and polygon buildings in a unified manner. For training MARS, we collected to our knowledge the largest multi-class map extraction dataset totaling 3.4M examples, which we call MAP-3M. Across four road and building datasets, MARS outperforms or matches the performance of multistage baselines. Additionally, we develop a "Chat with MARS" capability that enables interactive human-in-the-loop map generation and correction, supported by the auto-regressive nature of our end-to-end approach. We release our MAP-3M dataset and project demo page at (1) https://huggingface.co/datasets/bag-lab/MAP-3M and (2) https://huggingface.co/spaces/bag-lab/MARS, respectively.
authors: Qi Zhang, Suvam Bag, Rupanjali Kukal, Lucas Thai, Jacob Kovarskiy, Mike Bianco, Xiaojie Guo, Raphael Tang, Mikael Figueroa, Rishi Madhok, Nikolaos Karianakis, Fuxun Yu
bullets: Addresses the complexity and error accumulation of conventional pixel-wise, multistage map-generation pipelines.
Unifies generation of multi-polyline roads and polygon buildings in an end-to-end autoregressive framework.
Trained on MAP-3M, a 3.4M-example multi-class map extraction dataset.
Across four road and building datasets, matches or surpasses multistage baselines.
Supports interactive human correction through a “Chat with MARS” capability; the dataset and demo are released publicly.
papers.selection_reason: Autoregressive map foundation model generating vectorized road networks and buildings; directly relevant to spatial layout understanding and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: MARS - A foundational map auto-regressor
papers.tldr: MARS is an autoregressive foundation model that directly generates vectorized road networks and building polygons, avoiding multistage pixel segmentation and post-processing.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal generation covers discrete, continuous, and hybrid paradigms. Discrete approaches with single-codebook visual tokenizers align naturally with text modeling but have limited representational capacity. Continuous and hybrid approaches retain richer visual representations, but they model text and images in heterogeneous spaces with different training objectives, potentially introducing optimization conflicts between modalities with misaligned representation spaces. These choices expose a central question: how to efficiently model high-capacity visual representations alongside textual content in a shared optimization space within a single backbone. We present Intern Lumina U2, to our knowledge the first diffusion language model to represent multi-codebook visual tokens in a fully discrete space. Each visual position is represented by a group of codes from complementary codebooks, increasing its representational capacity while preserving compatibility with discrete text modeling. At the input, the embeddings are concatenated at each position; at the output, a lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head predicts the codes within each position sequentially, while the diffusion backbone processes all positions in parallel. Built on the unified 4D representation of AToken, Intern Lumina U2 supports image, video, and 3D inputs within a single backbone and achieves leading performance among unified models in visual understanding, image generation, and image editing. We further build a full-stack training, inference, and evaluation system on both Ascend and NVIDIA platforms to verify the cross-platform effectiveness of our model. We also improve the inference efficiency through a stability-aware sampling strategy, which combines confidence-plateau-guided unmasking approach with drift-triggered cache refreshing mechanisms, accelerating image generation by 4.45x.
authors: Qian Yu, Zongyang Qiu, Juncheng Yan, Hongliang Li, Qi Qin, Keqi Wang, Siqi Luo, Junkui Ju, Yapeng Mi, Tiantian Lu, Tian Liu, Pengyu Xie, Chenhao Ji, Minghui Zhang, Yiang Zhao, Siyu Yan, Haiying Xu, Yanbo Wang, Jianghan Shen, Yuandong Pu, Jiayi Lei, Borui Zhang, Jinxin Shi, Bo Zhang, Yuhang Zang, Shenglong Ye, Lixin Gu, Hongjie Zhang, Linghan Liu, Xinyuan Chen, Yuewen Cao, Lihe Zhang, Xiaohong Liu, Junjun He, Qiangwei Liu, Qi Zhang, Yu Cheng, Tianfan Xue, Hui Xiong, Chang Xu, Yu Qiao, Yihao Liu, Bin Fu

Represents each visual position with complementary code groups, concatenating their embeddings and predicting codes sequentially with a lightweight head while denoising positions in parallel.
Built on AToken’s unified 4D representation to support image, video, and 3D inputs.
Reports leading performance among unified models for visual understanding, image generation, and image editing.
A stability-aware sampling strategy reportedly accelerates image generation by 4.45×, with cross-platform validation on Ascend and NVIDIA systems.

papers.title: Intern Lumina U2: A Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation
papers.tldr: Intern Lumina U2 is a diffusion language model that uses multiple discrete visual codebooks to unify text, image, video, and 3D understanding and generation in one backbone.

papers.abstract: Image-to-text (I2T) understanding and text-to-image (T2I) generation are dual tasks in unified multimodal models (UMMs). Reconstructive post-training couples these tasks, but existing reconstruction-based methods remain perception-centric and provide limited supervision for reasoning about structure, intent, and transformation. We propose ReasonUni, a reasoning-augmented reconstructive post-training framework that extends this coupling beyond perception. Given an original image and an editing instruction, the UMM first reasons about what and how to edit and describes the target state, then generates the corresponding target image conditioned on this understanding output. To jointly optimize both modules, we introduce TreeGRPO, a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that samples multiple reasoning paths and candidate images per path, then aggregates visual rewards to update both modules under a unified objective. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains in both understanding and generation, showing that reasoning-augmented reconstruction yields genuine mutual gains for UMMs.
authors: Feize Wu, Zhiyuan Yan, Yuhuan Hong, Yuwei Niu, Zongjian Li, Zheyuan Liu, Bin Lin, Jinbo Yan, Jie Qin, Xudong Mao, Limeng Qiao, Guanglu Wan, Li Yuan
bullets: Targets the limited structural, intentional, and transformational reasoning in reconstruction-based multimodal training.
Given an image and editing instruction, the model reasons about the edit, describes the target state, and generates the target image.
Introduces TreeGRPO, which samples multiple reasoning paths and candidate images and uses visual rewards to train both modules jointly.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks report consistent gains in both multimodal understanding and image generation.
The abstract does not specify numerical results, datasets, or detailed limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Reasoning-augmented reconstruction for unified multimodal understanding and generation models.
papers.title: ReasonUni: Reasoning-Augmented Reconstruction Advances Unified Multimodal Models
papers.tldr: ReasonUni improves unified multimodal models by adding explicit editing reasoning to image reconstruction and jointly optimizing reasoning and generation with tree-structured reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly used for driving-scene understanding, yet their defensive reasoning under weakly structured Global South traffic remains unclear. We introduce BD-HazardVLM, a diagnostic benchmark of 500 Bangladesh road-scene images, comprising 375 from RSUD20K and 125 from TFP-BD, annotated for hazard presence, primary hazard category, risk timing, severity, defensive actions, visible evidence, and hallucination- and Western-road-bias traps. We evaluate Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, and MiniCPM-V-4.6 using a shared zero-shot task definition and structured output schema. Binary hazard-presence accuracy ranges from 88.0 percent to 89.2 percent, essentially matching the 89.0 percent majority-class baseline. Fine-grained reasoning is substantially weaker: category accuracy remains below 40 percent, risk-timing accuracy ranges from 1.6 percent to 12.4 percent, and exact defensive-action matching remains below 2 percent. Although InternVL3-8B achieves the highest severity accuracy at 61.2 percent, it has zero recall on the 58 high-severity cases. Qwen exhibits severe category mode collapse, while all models show weak latent-hazard anticipation and near-zero self-reported trap recognition. For the evaluated models, these findings show that coarse hazard recognition does not imply reliable fine-grained defensive-driving reasoning and motivate geographically diverse safety evaluation.
authors: Abdullah Al Maruf, Md. Sajedul Islam, Tanmoy Mridha, Irfan Hossain Bhuiyan
bullets: Benchmarks 500 Bangladesh road-scene images with annotations for hazards, categories, timing, severity, defensive actions, evidence, and bias or hallucination traps.
Evaluates Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, and MiniCPM-V-4.6 under a shared zero-shot structured-output setup.
Hazard-presence accuracy is 88.0–89.2%, roughly matching the 89.0% majority-class baseline.
Category accuracy stays below 40%, risk-timing accuracy is 1.6–12.4%, and exact defensive-action matching is below 2%.
Models show weak anticipation and trap recognition; InternVL3-8B has the best severity accuracy but misses all high-severity cases.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic benchmark probing vision-language models for defensive-driving hazard reasoning, relevant to multimodal LLM evaluation and embodied driving perception.
papers.title: BD-HazardVLM: Probing Vision-Language Models for Latent Defensive-Driving Hazards in Bangladesh Road Scenes
papers.tldr: BD-HazardVLM shows that vision-language models can detect obvious hazards in Bangladesh road scenes but struggle with fine-grained, anticipatory defensive-driving reasoning.

papers.abstract: Visual latent reasoning compresses rendered derivations into compact intermediate states, reducing textual reasoning overhead. Existing approaches differ in how they represent these states: continuous methods avoid vocabulary constraints, whereas discrete methods improve accuracy through quantization into a finite codebook. Our analysis of representative continuous and discrete systems identifies two functional requirements: answers must rely on latent states, and those states must carry valid, problem-specific reasoning. Continuous latents influence answers despite collapsed reasoning content, whereas discrete latents retain recoverable intermediate reasoning that answer prediction largely bypasses. To address these challenges, we propose Continuous Anchored Latent Reasoning (CALR), which connects latent formation with answer use through functional anchoring. With reference latents from information-balanced compression, CALR couples latent-mediated answer supervision with derivation-level semantic anchoring: the former routes answer supervision through intermediate states, while the latter grounds their decoded content in problem-specific derivations. A parallel-to-autoregressive curriculum develops sequential reasoning by conditioning subsequent latent blocks on generated prefixes. Evaluations on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks across model families show substantial accuracy gains. Under matched budgets, CALR gains 26.0 percentage points over a comparable continuous latent reasoning method. Further analyses show that its latents support answer prediction and carry problem-specific intermediate reasoning.
bullets: Continuous latents can affect answers without preserving meaningful reasoning, while discrete latents may preserve reasoning that answer prediction bypasses.
CALR uses information-balanced reference latents and functional anchoring to connect latent formation with answer use.
It combines latent-mediated answer supervision with derivation-level semantic anchoring.
A parallel-to-autoregressive curriculum trains sequential reasoning by conditioning later latent blocks on generated prefixes.
Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CALR improves accuracy, including a 26.0-point gain over a comparable continuous method under matched budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Visual latent reasoning method for multimodal LLMs with functional anchoring and reduced reasoning overhead.
papers.title: CALR: Continuous Anchored Latent Reasoning via Render-of-Thought Compression
papers.tldr: CALR improves continuous latent reasoning by anchoring compressed latent states to both answer prediction and problem-specific derivations.

papers.abstract: We describe our submission to the MedReason 2026 challenge, covering multiple-choice (MCQ) and open-ended (OE) medical visual question answering (VQA) under fully offline, containerized inference. Our first finding is that MCQ retrieval must compare answer \emph{semantics} rather than answer labels: labels are independently assigned per question, so copying a retrieved neighbor's label transfers no useful information, whereas scoring each current option's text against correct-answer text from similar training cases raises retrieval-only accuracy from 20.0\% to 57.5\% on a 200-case retrieval-excluded development holdout. Our second finding attributes the submitted system's accuracy: holding the task-specific MCQ Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter fixed and varying the number \(k\) of in-prompt retrieved examples changes accuracy by at most one case --- 187/200 (93.5\%) at both \(k=0\) and the adapter's training-time \(k=1\), 188/200 (94.0\%) at the packaged runtime's default \(k=3\) --- and the submitted confidence-gated override adds no net accuracy on top of \(k=3\), selecting the VLM in 198/200 cases. With the final MCQ adapter fixed, retrieval changes accuracy by at most one case, and gating provides no net gain. On 20 OE cases, token-F1 and RaTEScore~\cite{zhao2024ratescore} decrease as \(k\) grows, but paired sign tests on token-F1 differences are nonsignificant (\(p \ge 0.29\)); a single-annotator comparison found 6/20 wrong-anchor errors for the final configuration and 14/20 for an earlier configuration that jointly differed in routing, adapter, and prompting. The system reaches 94.0\% MCQ accuracy on the development holdout and 93.20\% on the organizer's official pre-evaluation, versus 29.43\% for the off-the-shelf reference baseline, while both of the organizer's open-ended scores are lower than that baseline's (ground-truth agreement 1.245 versus 1.588, visual accuracy 1.995 versus 2.696, each out of 4).
