A task-specific MCQ LoRA adapter reaches 93.5–94.0% accuracy; changing retrieved-example count or applying confidence gating has negligible effect.
The final system scores 94.0% on the development holdout and 93.20% on official pre-evaluation, versus 29.43% for the reference baseline.
For 20 open-ended cases, increasing retrieval generally lowers token-F1 and RaTEScore, but token-F1 differences are not statistically significant.
Open-ended scores trail the baseline on both ground-truth agreement and visual accuracy, indicating weaker performance outside MCQ.
papers.selection_reason: Medical visual question answering with VLM LoRA adaptation and retrieval; relevant to multimodal LLM methods.
papers.title: Option-Aware Retrieval and Task-Specific VLM Adaptation for Medical VQA
papers.tldr: An offline medical VQA system achieves strong multiple-choice performance by retrieving answer semantics rather than labels, while retrieval provides little added value after task-specific VLM adaptation and open-ended performance remains weaker.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks that distribute harmful intent across text and images, making unimodal safety mechanisms insufficient. We investigate whether this vulnerability can be mitigated directly in the multimodal key-value (KV) memory formed during prefill, without modifying model parameters at inference time. We introduce SPARK, a two-stage framework for targeted KV-memory repair. Stage 1 uses a disposable diagnostic adapter to identify harm-associated directions in multimodal key and value representations. Stage 2 projects out these directions, learns a lightweight residual repair, and anchors repaired keys with an image-structural prior to preserve visual grounding. Rather than applying the intervention uniformly, SPARK mixes repaired and original memory using a head-wise coefficient g_h* determined by intervention-relevant subspace energy E_h, requiring no explicit harm classifier at inference. Across LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Chameleon-7B, Qwen2-VL-7B, and InternVL2-4B, SPARK reduces multimodal attack success while preserving general capability. On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, image-only jailbreak attack success falls to 4.7%, while MMMU remains within 0.6 points of the undefended model (47.8 vs. 48.4) with near-baseline language quality. On MM-SafetyBench, attack success decreases from 39.2% to 12.4%. Even under white-box adaptive joint prompt-image attacks, attack success is limited to 20.3%, compared with 54.6% for the undefended model. These results suggest that multimodal jailbreak behavior can be substantially mitigated by selectively repairing intervention-relevant KV subspaces at prefill, particularly when harmful evidence is carried by the visual modality.
bullets: Targets jailbreaks that distribute harmful intent across text and images, which unimodal defenses may miss.
Uses a disposable diagnostic adapter to identify harm-associated key/value directions, then projects them out and applies a lightweight residual repair.
Mixes repaired and original memory per attention head using intervention-relevant subspace energy, without an inference-time harm classifier.
Across four VLMs, it reduces attacks while preserving general performance; on LLaVA-OneVision-7B, image-only attack success is 4.7% and MMMU remains 47.8 versus 48.4 undefended.
Under adaptive joint prompt-image attacks, attack success is 20.3% versus 54.6% for the undefended model.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces SPARK, a framework for repairing multimodal KV memory at inference time to mitigate jailbreaks in vision-language models without modifying parameters.
papers.title: SPARK: Representation-Level KV Memory Alignment for Safer Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: SPARK selectively repairs harmful directions in a VLM’s prefill KV memory to reduce multimodal jailbreaks without changing model parameters or substantially harming capability.

papers.abstract: We propose to finetune vision-language models to generate more pragmatically optimal referring expressions by transforming observations of incremental listener comprehension, in the form of gaze scanpaths, into learning signals. During training, referring expressions are sampled from the speaker policy being optimized, conditioned on images and target referents; then, a neural listener estimating human gaze behavior maps from images and sampled referring expressions to scanpaths, each represented by a sequence of fixations, with each fixation corresponding to a word in the referring expression. We experiment with several approaches to convert fixation sequences and target referents into token- and sequence-level rewards, which are used to optimize policy parameters. Through evaluation with human listeners, we find that speaker policies trained with gaze-estimating listeners result in significantly more pragmatically-optimal references than base models, reducing sequence length from 15.4 down to 4.0 words while increasing referential success from 75.2 up to 80.0%. Our work demonstrates a promising opportunity for learning to generate utterances through language-based interaction, not only from the explicit signal of communicative success, but also from implicitly-available observations of a listener's process of comprehension.
bullets: Uses estimated human gaze behavior as an implicit learning signal for pragmatic reference generation.
A neural listener predicts fixation sequences from images and sampled referring expressions.
Token- and sequence-level rewards derived from gaze and target referents optimize the speaker policy.
Human evaluation found descriptions shortened from 15.4 to 4.0 words while referential success rose from 75.2% to 80.0%.
The approach explores learning from listeners’ comprehension processes, beyond explicit communication-success feedback.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method to finetune vision-language models using estimated listener gaze as a signal for generating pragmatic referring expressions, bridging multimodal understanding and interaction.
papers.title: Learning to Refer from Estimated Listener Gaze
papers.tldr: Fine-tuning referring-expression generators with listener gaze scanpaths produces shorter and more successful descriptions.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large vision-language models have led to impressive performance in visual question answering and multimodal reasoning. However, it remains unclear whether these models genuinely perform grounded visual reasoning or rely on superficial patterns and dataset biases. In this work, we introduce MagiC, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate grounded multimodal cognition, assessing not only answer accuracy but also the quality of step-by-step reasoning and its alignment with relevant visual evidence. Our benchmark includes approximately 5,500 weakly supervised QA examples generated from strong model outputs and 900 human-curated examples with fine-grained annotations, including answers, rationales, and bounding box groundings. We evaluate 15 vision-language models ranging from 7B to 70B parameters across four dimensions: final answer correctness, reasoning validity, grounding fidelity, and self-correction ability. MagiC further includes diagnostic settings to probe model robustness under adversarial visual cues and assess their capacity for introspective error correction. We introduce new metrics such as MagiScore and StepSense, and provide comprehensive analyses that reveal key limitations and opportunities in current approaches to grounded visual reasoning.
authors: Chengfei Wu, Ronald Seoh, Bingxuan Li, Liqiang Zhang, Fengrong Han, Dan Goldwasser
bullets: Evaluates grounded multimodal cognition across answer correctness, reasoning validity, grounding fidelity, and self-correction.
Combines approximately 5,500 weakly supervised QA examples with 900 human-curated examples annotated with answers, rationales, and bounding boxes.
Assesses 15 vision-language models ranging from 7B to 70B parameters.
Includes adversarial visual-cue and introspective error-correction diagnostics.
Introduces MagiScore and StepSense, revealing limitations and opportunities in grounded visual reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for grounded visual reasoning and reasoning-grounding fidelity in vision-language models; directly evaluates multimodal LLM capabilities.
papers.title: MagiC: Evaluating Multimodal Cognition Toward Grounded Visual Reasoning
papers.tldr: MagiC benchmarks whether vision-language models genuinely reason from visual evidence rather than exploiting superficial patterns.

papers.abstract: Generating novel views from limited observations requires preserving both the appearance and spatial structure of a scene. Although recent approaches exploit fine-grained geometric cues, they do not explicitly model high-level semantic and spatial properties such as object identity, attributes, and inter-object relationships. In this work, we investigate whether 3D language understanding can provide complementary supervision for novel-view generation. We introduce Ask4NV, built on a pretrained unified multimodal model with a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture. Our model incorporates camera geometry into both VAE and ViT representations and leverages understanding features during generation through joint self-attention with a modality-aware attention masking strategy. Experiments demonstrate strong image quality and geometric consistency in novel-view generation, alongside competitive 3D language understanding. Further analysis shows that joint training improves cross-view correspondence in VAE representations and similarity in a 3D-aware feature space.
authors: Jahyeok Koo, Hyeonseo Yu, Seungho Jang, Jaewoo Jung, Jiwon Kang, Seokju Cho, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Targets the challenge of preserving both scene appearance and spatial structure from limited observations.
Introduces Ask4NV, built on a pretrained unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers model.
Encodes camera geometry in VAE and ViT representations and integrates understanding features via masked joint self-attention.
Achieves strong image quality and geometric consistency while maintaining competitive 3D language understanding.
Joint training improves cross-view correspondence and 3D-aware feature similarity.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates using 3D language understanding (spatial questions) to supervise novel-view generation. This combines 3D reasoning with generative models, relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Can Learning to Answer Spatial Questions Improve Novel-View Generation?
papers.tldr: Ask4NV uses 3D language understanding and camera-aware multimodal modeling to improve the visual quality and geometric consistency of novel-view generation.

papers.abstract: Achieving general spatial intelligence requires a unified understanding of both static 3D and dynamic 4D. However, we find that existing models struggle to excel at both: 3D post-training can weaken dynamic understanding, while 4D-specialized models often lack strong static 3D reasoning. Our analysis reveals that this spatial--dynamic interference is highly non-uniform across parameter groups, with the balance between static and dynamic capabilities particularly sensitive to changes in late-layer MLPs. To address this interference, we propose DynThinker, a unified framework for jointly strengthening static and dynamic spatial reasoning. Decoupled Exponential Moving Average (D-EMA) applies configurable group-wise averaging to constrain drift in interference-sensitive pretrained parameters while preserving flexibility for capability enhancement. Spatial-Dynamic Fusion (SDF) complements D-EMA by selectively integrating spatial and temporal priors from a dynamic geometry encoder into intermediate VLM representations under semantic guidance. Across ten metrics spanning nine static 3D and dynamic 4D benchmarks, DynThinker achieves the highest average score among all evaluated models. Notably, DynThinker achieves 56.0 on ReVSI, 67.2 on DSR-Bench, and 51.2 and 40.1 under the sample-wise and group-wise evaluation protocols of DSI-Bench, respectively, setting new state-of-the-art results among the compared open-source models across all four evaluations within a unified model.
authors: Qihang Cao, Haoyuan Li, Zihan Guo, Sensen Gao, Zihui Gao, Huixin Zhang, Fan He, Jianhua Han, Hang Xu, Xiaodan Liang, Jia-Wang Bian
bullets: Existing models face a trade-off: improving static 3D reasoning can harm dynamic understanding, while 4D-specialized models may underperform on static tasks.
The interference is non-uniform across parameters and is especially sensitive to late-layer MLP changes.
Decoupled Exponential Moving Average (D-EMA) stabilizes interference-sensitive parameter groups while allowing capability improvements elsewhere.
Spatial-Dynamic Fusion (SDF) selectively injects temporal and spatial priors from a dynamic geometry encoder into intermediate vision-language representations.
Across ten metrics on nine benchmarks, DynThinker obtains the highest average score among evaluated models and sets open-source results on four reported evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified framework (DynThinker) for static 3D and dynamic 4D spatial reasoning in VLMs, addressing the interference between these capabilities through decoupled EMA and spatial-dynamic fusion. This directly addresses spatial reasoning and geometry-aware multimodal models.
papers.title: DynThinker: Unifying Static 3D and Dynamic 4D Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: DynThinker unifies static 3D and dynamic 4D spatial reasoning by mitigating interference between the two capabilities.

papers.abstract: Existing geometry-aware Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly rely on external 3D encoders to provide structural priors, but executing these additional encoder paths at inference introduces substantial latency and computational overhead. We propose GeoThinker-$F$, an efficient framework that internalizes spatiotemporal perception by transforming causal MLLM hidden states into predictive latent world representations. Our key insight is that intermediate semantic representations contain sufficient information to predict useful representations of current geometry and future semantics, without requiring an exact reproduction of features from a dedicated 3D encoder. To realize this idea, GeoThinker-$F$ adopts a decoupled two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, the MLLM backbone is frozen while lightweight Latent Frame Prediction (LFP) heads learn from an offline 3D geometry expert and next-frame semantic targets. In the second stage, the external expert is removed, and the model is jointly optimized to generate and selectively integrate its self-predicted priors through a specialized Spatial-Grounded Temporal (SGT) Fusion module. Extensive evaluations show that GeoThinker-$F$ eliminates runtime dependence on external 3D geometry encoders while maintaining competitive performance across diverse spatial intelligence benchmarks. It achieves up to a $3.6\times$ inference speedup, reducing latency from $1.45\,\mathrm{s}$ to $0.40\,\mathrm{s}$ while retaining strong spatial reasoning performance.
authors: Haoyuan Li, Qihang Cao, Huanyuan Zhou, Xin Hu, Sijia Chen, Zihan Guo, Kun Xiang, Yunshuang Nie, Tao Tang, Xinlong Zheng, Jia-Wang Bian, Xianming Liu, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Addresses the latency and computational overhead caused by external 3D geometry encoders in geometry-aware MLLMs.
Transforms intermediate MLLM hidden states into predictive representations of current geometry and future semantics.
Uses two-stage training: lightweight latent frame prediction heads first learn from geometry and next-frame semantic targets, then the external expert is removed during joint optimization.
Introduces Spatial-Grounded Temporal Fusion to selectively integrate self-predicted spatial-temporal priors.

papers.selection_reason: Geometry-aware MLLM with predictive world representations and faster spatial intelligence inference.
papers.title: GeoThinker-$F$: Endogenous Predictive World Representations for Fast Spatial Intelligence
papers.tldr: GeoThinker-F internalizes spatial and temporal world representations in an MLLM, removing external 3D encoders and achieving up to 3.6× faster inference while maintaining strong spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal code intelligence connects the symbolic world of programs with the visual world their execution creates. Interest in this capability is burgeoning, as models are increasingly asked to produce charts, webpages, animations, and semi-structured documents. Recently, proprietary models have pushed far ahead, producing interactive artifacts even from a text description or a screenshot alone. Yet their data and training remain closed, and open progress is held back by the quantity and quality of available data and by the pipelines and methods for producing it. Quality is the harder of the two, since a sample must be correct as a program, well built, and above all visually right once rendered. No existing signal covers all three. Execution often returns just a pass or fail, code similarity does not map to the visual output, and task-specific verifiers do not generalize. To push open progress further, we start from the data side with PrismaForge, a hierarchical data pipeline centered on a synthesized rubric that decomposes these factors into checkable criteria. The same rubric serves as both filter and reward: it curates the supervised corpus, then drives reinforcement learning on visual-coding tasks. Leveraging PrismaForge for data synthesis and filtering, we build PrismaCoder-2M, the most diverse open dataset for multimodal code intelligence and the largest to date. On the model side, we train PrismaCoder-9B and PrismaCoder-35B on this data and release both. They lead the open state of the art by a wide margin and rival leading proprietary systems. Our analyses further show that the proposed rubric-based pipeline improves multimodal coding performance across model backbones. We release our code and data at https://qiushisun.github.io/PrismaCoder-Home/.
authors: Qiushi Sun, Jingyang Gong, Yang Liu, Qiaosheng Chen, Zhangyue Yin, Zixian Huang, Hanxu Hu, Jing Xiong, Fangzhi Xu, Haochen Tan, Haoli Bai, Lifeng Shang, Xiaoguang Li, Ben Kao, Qipeng Guo, Lingpeng Kong, Jiahui Gao
bullets: Addresses the lack of unified evaluation for code correctness, implementation quality, and rendered visual fidelity.
Introduces PrismaForge, a hierarchical pipeline whose synthesized rubric acts as both a data filter and RL reward.
Builds PrismaCoder-2M, described as the largest and most diverse open dataset for multimodal code intelligence.
Trains and releases PrismaCoder-9B and PrismaCoder-35B, which the abstract reports lead open systems and rival proprietary models.
Analyses indicate the rubric-based pipeline improves multimodal coding across model backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal code intelligence models and rubric-based data pipeline for visual coding tasks.
papers.title: PrismaCoder: Pushing the Boundaries of Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis
papers.tldr: PrismaCoder improves open multimodal code intelligence by using synthesized, decomposed visual-quality rubrics to curate data and guide reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models have made significant progress in referring expression comprehension (REC), yet most REC benchmarks still focus on final-target localization. Complex queries often involve intermediate visual references with different dependencies on prior grounding, but final-only evaluation leaves this process unexamined. To address this gap, we formulate trajectory-level REC, in which models receive an ordered sequence of grounding steps constructed from a single complex query and localize the target regions associated with each step. We instantiate this setting in ReferFlow-Bench, which characterizes structured region transitions through four trajectory types, namely Refinement, Shift, Reset, and Mixture. Experiments show that current models struggle to consistently ground intermediate visual references across successive steps. We further propose ReferFlow, which decouples interleaved text-latent trajectory generation from coordinate decoding. Specifically, Stateful Region Latent Reasoning represents each target region as an object-indexed state composed of continuous latents, with explicit visual and spatial supervision to preserve region information for subsequent grounding. Trajectory-Aware Parallel Decoding then recovers all coordinate blocks in parallel through four geometry-constrained refinement rounds, with each block conditioned on its corresponding trajectory prefix, thereby reducing within-box sequential dependencies and eliminating cross-box autoregression. We further apply Grounding-Aware GRPO to promote consistent grounding across steps and learn adaptive trajectory generation from complex REC queries. ReferFlow achieves leading performance on general REC benchmarks and ReferFlow-Bench.
authors: Tianyi Gao, Han Fang, Xin Wei, Yaoyao Zhong, Zhaoyan Pan, Weijie Zhu, Hongbo Sun, Zhiyu Lin, Kaicheng Yang, Jinglin Xu, Ye Yuan, Hao Li, Hao Sun, Jingmin Xin
bullets: Introduces trajectory-level REC, evaluating ordered grounding steps rather than only the final target.
Presents ReferFlow-Bench with four region-transition types: Refinement, Shift, Reset, and Mixture.
Uses stateful region latent reasoning to preserve visual and spatial information across grounding steps.
Employs trajectory-aware parallel coordinate decoding with geometry-constrained refinement to reduce sequential dependencies.
Grounding-Aware GRPO encourages consistent multi-step grounding; ReferFlow achieves leading performance on general REC benchmarks and ReferFlow-Bench.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses complex referring expressions in MLLMs using trajectory-level grounding and geometry-constrained refinement, advancing spatial reasoning capabilities.
papers.title: ReferFlow: Beyond Final-Target Localization for Complex Referring Expressions
papers.tldr: ReferFlow extends referring expression comprehension from final-target localization to step-by-step grounding of intermediate visual references, improving trajectory-level reasoning.

papers.abstract: Document understanding systems are typically evaluated as separate components via layout analysis, optical text recognition, reading-order prediction, and image captioning. This separation leaves scientific figures, captions, and visual semantics weakly connected, and fails to measure whether a model can produce a single page-level parse that is both structurally faithful and semantically accessible. We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a unified dataset for document parsing with visual element description generation. Given a page image, models are required to output an ordered list of layout elements containing bounding boxes, semantic labels, reading-order indices, recognized textual content, and alternative text descriptions for visual elements. The benchmark is built from 2,402 documents, comprising 18,163 continuous pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances. Besides, we further propose a plug-and-play space-awareness enhancer that reuses multi-layer visual features and injects grid-aware spatial guidance into vision-language tokens for layout-aware generation. Experiments across end-to-end VLMs and pipeline parsers show that existing systems still struggle to jointly recover reading order and visual semantics, while our enhanced model achieves strong joint performance. These results highlight the need to move beyond isolated document parsing modules toward unified models that jointly read, parse, and describe complex documents. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yufanchen96/RPD
authors: Yuheng Chen, Yufan Chen, Zhuojun Cai, Ruiping Liu, Junwei Zheng, Jiale Wei, Di Wen, Weijia Fan, Kunyu Peng, Jiaming Zhang, Rainer Stiefelhagen
bullets: Targets the limitations of evaluating layout analysis, OCR, reading order, and image captioning as separate tasks.
Requires page-level outputs combining ordered layout elements, bounding boxes, semantic labels, recognized text, and visual-element descriptions.
The dataset contains 2,402 documents, 18,163 pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances.
Adds a plug-and-play space-awareness enhancer that injects grid-guided spatial information into vision-language tokens.
Experiments show existing systems struggle to jointly recover reading order and visual semantics, while the enhanced model achieves strong joint performance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a unified document parsing dataset and a space-awareness enhancer for VLMs, explicitly incorporating grid-aware spatial guidance into vision-language tokens.
papers.title: Read, Parse, Describe: Unified Document Parsing with Visual Element Description Generation
papers.tldr: Read-Parse-Describe introduces a benchmark and spatially enhanced model for jointly parsing document structure, text, reading order, and visual semantics from page images.

papers.abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) holds that increasingly capable models converge toward a common representation. However, recent studies have shown different views on aligning representations via their neighborhoods, spanning trees, and distances. We show that these views can differ because the alignment criteria behind them sit at different points of one lattice, and we formalize this explanation as the Lattice Representation Hypothesis (LRH). Under the LRH, the convergence claimed by the PRH is agreement at the top of the lattice, whereas its evidence comes from neighbor overlap, a criterion near the bottom. The Aristotelian Representation Hypothesis (ARH) restricts convergence to local neighborhoods because calibration keeps the growth of neighbor overlap with model size but largely removes that of centered kernel alignment. We show that this removal can come from calibrating a maximum over layers, so global convergence remains open. Back into Plato's Cave (BPC) infers coarse shared structure from the collapse of neighbor overlap on larger evaluation sets, whereas we trace it at least partly to a fixed number of neighbors covering shorter distances. We show that the spanning-tree overlap used by Structure over Geometry (SOG) mostly repeats one-nearest-neighbor overlap. The LRH also extends to independently trained models, whose training procedure and objective decide the criteria met reliably across runs. We prove this claim for the training procedure in a linear autoencoder and for the objective in a finite contrastive Gibbs model. Experiments on dozens of pretrained vision and language models and thousands of runs of both theoretical models support these conclusions. We hope this work paves the way toward a general theory of representation hypotheses, with a framework to analyze them and compare their evidence. Project page: https://eethanshi.github.io/LRH
authors: Dai Shi, Andi Han, Xiaoyu Li, Luke Thompson, Jos\'e Miguel Hern\'andez-Lobato
bullets: Different alignment criteria—neighbor overlap, distances, centered kernel alignment, and spanning-tree overlap—occupy different levels of a representation-criteria lattice.
The Lattice Representation Hypothesis (LRH) reframes the Platonic Representation Hypothesis as convergence at the lattice’s strongest criterion, while existing evidence often tests weaker criteria.
The Aristotelian Representation Hypothesis (ARH) limits reliable convergence to local neighborhoods; calibration can preserve neighbor overlap while removing centered-kernel alignment.

Some reported effects are reinterpreted: large-set neighbor-overlap collapse can reflect fixed-neighbor, shorter-distance coverage, and spanning-tree overlap largely duplicates one-nearest-neighbor overlap.
Experiments across pretrained vision/language models and theoretical linear-autoencoder and contrastive-Gibbs settings support the framework; global convergence remains unresolved.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical framework for representation alignment across vision and language models, plausibly transferable to multimodal foundation model analysis.
papers.title: From Plato to Aristotle: Toward a General Theory of Representation Hypotheses
papers.tldr: The paper proposes a lattice-based framework explaining why representation-alignment studies support different, often local, forms of convergence rather than a single global shared representation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are moving onto edge devices, but little is known about how much energy they draw on single-board computers with NPU or GPU accelerators, or where that energy goes. We measure total-system energy, latency, and thermal behavior of Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and its text-only sibling on a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-10H NPU and on a Jetson Orin Nano Super, on both CPU and accelerator, and separate the fixed energy of each request from the energy that grows with output length. Because the accelerators use different quantization and serving software, we compare deployment stacks rather than silicon. Three findings stand out. First, NPU offloading makes the Pi a much more efficient VLM platform: it cuts energy per generated token by about two-thirds, leaves the host CPU largely free, and avoids the thermal throttling that the CPU backend reaches in sustained use. Second, an image adds both fixed and per-token energy, but at typical response lengths generating the answer costs far more than processing the image. Third, the Jetson GPU favors short responses through its lower fixed cost per request, whereas the Pi NPU favors longer ones through its lower cost per output token; their energy curves cross near 40 output tokens.
authors: Junlin Liao, Harshit Kondle, Di Liu, Zonghua Gu
bullets: Measures system energy, latency, and thermal behavior across Raspberry Pi 5 CPU/NPU and Jetson Orin Nano Super CPU/GPU deployments.
Separates fixed per-request energy from energy that scales with generated output length, while comparing deployment stacks rather than hardware alone.
Pi NPU offloading reduces energy per generated token by about two-thirds and prevents the thermal throttling seen with sustained CPU inference.
Image inputs increase both fixed and per-token energy, but answer generation typically dominates total energy at common response lengths.
Jetson GPU has lower fixed request cost; Pi NPU has lower per-token cost, with energy curves crossing near 40 output tokens.
papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the energy efficiency, latency, and thermal behavior of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on edge hardware, directly addressing efficiency and multimodal deployment.
papers.title: Seeing at the Edge: Energy Characterization of Vision-Language Model Inference on Edge Platforms
papers.tldr: NPU acceleration makes Raspberry Pi 5 inference for a 2B vision-language model substantially more energy-efficient and thermally stable, while Jetson GPU is better for short responses.

papers.abstract: We present several advances on neural operators by viewing the action of operator layers as the minimizers of Bregman regularized optimization problems over Banach function spaces. The proposed framework allows interpreting the activation operators as Bregman proximity operators from dual to primal space. This novel viewpoint is general enough to recover classical neural operators as well as a new variant, coined Bregman neural operators, which includes the inverse activation operator and features the same expressivity of standard neural operators. Numerical experiments support the added benefits of the Bregman variant of Fourier neural operators for training deeper and more accurate models.
authors: Abdel-Rahim Mezidi, Jordan Patracone, Saverio Salzo, Amaury Habrard, Massimiliano Pontil, Remi Emonet, Marc Sebban
bullets: Recasts neural-operator layers as minimizers of Bregman-regularized problems on Banach function spaces.
Interprets activation operators as Bregman proximity operators mapping dual spaces to primal spaces.
Recovers classical neural operators and defines a new Bregman neural operator with an inverse activation operator.
The Bregman variant retains the expressivity of standard neural operators.
Experiments indicate improved training of deeper and more accurate Fourier neural operator models.
papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the energy efficiency, latency, and thermal behavior of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on edge hardware, directly addressing efficiency and multimodal deployment.
papers.title: A Bregman Proximal Viewpoint on Neural Operators
papers.tldr: A Bregman-optimization perspective generalizes neural operators and introduces a Bregman variant that supports deeper, more accurate Fourier neural operator models.

papers.abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has shown strong effectiveness for text-based LLMs and LLM systems, but its application to audio-visual understanding systems requires suitable textual interfaces through which multimodal reasoning can be exposed to text-based optimizers. We investigate how the design of textual interfaces affects prompt optimization for multimodal reasoning, on the audio-visual question answering task. We compare three interface designs, including a direct inference system consisting of a single omni-modal large language model (OmniLLM), a captioner-reasoner system, and an agentic architecture in which a primary agent orchestrates subagent OmniLLMs. Experiments with Qwen3-Omni and Gemini show that direct prompt optimization provides model-dependent gains; the captioner-reasoner system and the agentic system expose more interpretable optimization interfaces but are harder to optimize, where error analysis of cases affected by optimization is conducted. Our study highlights textual interface design as an important factor in making prompt optimization effective for omni-modal reasoning systems. Our implementation details are specified in GitHub repo.
authors: Yi Wang, Tianzi Wang, Tong Lei, Dahan Wang, Peter Bell
bullets: Studies prompt optimization for audio-visual question answering through text-based interfaces.
Compares a direct OmniLLM, a captioner–reasoner pipeline, and an agentic system with subagent OmniLLMs.
Finds direct optimization produces model-dependent gains, while more interpretable interfaces are harder to optimize.
Uses Qwen3-Omni and Gemini, with error analysis of optimization-affected cases.
Highlights interface design as a key factor in optimizing omni-modal reasoning systems.
papers.selection_reason: Studies textual interface design and prompt optimization for omni-modal audio-visual QA, fitting multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Designing Textual Interfaces To Enhance Llm Reasoning On Audio-Visual Question Answering
papers.tldr: Textual interface design strongly influences how effectively automatic prompt optimization improves audio-visual question answering with multimodal LLM systems.

papers.abstract: Visual world knowledge is a core capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), underpinning knowledge-intensive visual question answering and fine-grained visual reasoning. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in two key respects. First, their category coverage is narrow: most benchmarks span only a small number of categories across a few domains, falling far short of the open-ended scale of real-world visual entities. Second, their task construction is often insufficiently rigorous: models can answer correctly using coarse-grained cues, vague associations, or elimination strategies without truly mastering precise concepts, making it difficult to accurately assess their knowledge of fine-grained entities. We introduce VisualWorldBench, a taxonomy-grounded multi-task benchmark built on a hierarchical taxonomy of 21,291 leaf-node classes across 8 visual domains, with 32,541 evaluation instances whose ground-truth labels cover 15,479 categories across four complementary tasks: closed-set recognition, contrastive selection, precise localization, and open-world naming, covering different directions of knowledge retrieval and varying degrees of answer openness to comprehensively evaluate visual world knowledge. Most questions are constructed from taxonomically proximate categories, forcing precise discrimination among fine-grained entities. Experiments reveal that the strongest closed-source model achieves only 80.4% average accuracy, exposing capability gaps hidden under conventional benchmarks. We further construct VisualWorldBench-50K, a training resource covering 50K+ categories. Fine-tuning on VisualWorldBench-50K yields over 21 percentage points improvement on VisualWorldBench, with consistent transfer to public fine-grained recognition and visual knowledge benchmarks.
authors: Chen Chen, Zheming Liang, Jiaqi Wang
bullets: Covers 21,291 leaf-node classes across 8 visual domains, with 32,541 evaluation instances spanning 15,479 categories.
Uses four tasks—closed-set recognition, contrastive selection, precise localization, and open-world naming—to test varied knowledge retrieval abilities.
Emphasizes taxonomically similar categories, requiring precise discrimination rather than coarse cues or elimination strategies.
The strongest evaluated closed-source model reaches 80.4% average accuracy, indicating limitations on fine-grained visual knowledge.
VisualWorldBench-50K covers 50K+ categories; fine-tuning improves benchmark performance by over 21 percentage points and transfers to other benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Fine-grained multi-task benchmark and training resource for visual world knowledge in MLLMs.
papers.title: VisualWorldBench: A Fine-Grained Multi-Task Benchmark for Evaluating Visual World Knowledge in MLLMs
papers.tldr: VisualWorldBench evaluates fine-grained visual world knowledge in MLLMs across broad taxonomies and complementary tasks, revealing substantial capability gaps and supporting effective fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large vision language models (LVLMs) has made geolocation inference from images highly accurate and accessible. This poses serious privacy risks: a passive adversary with black-box LVLM access can infer a user's location from a single photo with no metadata. Existing protection methods rely almost exclusively on adversarial perturbation, which introduces perceptible visual artifacts and utility degradation. We identify the visual-geolocation asymmetry: geolocation-decisive clues, such as street signs, tend to be visually peripheral but dominate location inference. Exploiting this asymmetry, we propose GeoCloak, an agentic framework for semantics-preserving geolocation privacy protection. It acts as a clue-aware planner that analyzes each image to identify geolocation-relevant clues, dispatches targeted semantic edits to directly suppress peripheral clues, and autonomously configures adversarial perturbation to further suppress residual geolocation features, all under iterative utility-aware feedback. We evaluate GeoCloak on four diverse datasets spanning 108 countries and 576 cities against five LVLMs and three inference methods. GeoCloak reduces overall city-level accuracy from 41.2% to 9.9%, approximately half of the best-performing baseline, while achieving substantially superior utility preservation both qualitatively and quantitatively. We hope this work takes a meaningful step toward practical, semantics-preserving geolocation privacy protection, giving users greater control over the location information inadvertently embedded in their shared images.
authors: Yixin Wu, Mingjie Li, Yun Shen, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang
bullets: Targets the risk that black-box vision-language models can infer locations from ordinary photos without metadata.
Exploits the asymmetry that geolocation-critical clues, such as street signs, are often visually peripheral.
Uses an agentic planner for clue detection, targeted semantic edits, adaptive perturbation, and utility-aware iteration.
Evaluated across four datasets covering 108 countries and 576 cities, with five LVLMs and three inference methods.
Reduced city-level geolocation accuracy from 41.2% to 9.9% while preserving utility better than the evaluated baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic manipulation of geolocation clues in LVLMs, relevant to spatial/geolocation understanding and multimodal model robustness.
papers.title: GeoCloak: An Agentic Framework for Semantics-Preserving Geolocation Privacy via Peripheral Clue Manipulation
papers.tldr: GeoCloak protects image geolocation privacy by identifying and editing peripheral location clues while preserving overall image semantics.

papers.abstract: In recent years, with advances in multimodal interaction technologies and the growing demand for intelligent emotional support, Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation (MESC) has emerged as an important task. However, existing systems still suffer from shallow responses and inappropriate support strategies due to weak semantic feedback, cross-dimension reward compensation, and coarse reasoning supervision. To address these challenges, we propose FACES, a fine-grained gated semantic alignment framework for MESC. Specifically, FACES integrates multi-source rewards to construct multidimensional semantic and functional alignment signals, employs a non-compensatory gated fusion mechanism to reduce cross-dimension reward offset, and leverages structured Chain-of-Thought (CoT) anchors to perform token-level credit assignment. Under a controlled response-length protocol, FACES improves the average MLLM-based evaluation score from 3.61 to 4.04 and achieves an 80.22% pairwise win rate over SOTA. Human evaluation under the same protocol yields a 75.3% preference rate. Results on three external datasets further support transferability. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/OCT-ARR/arr.
authors: Hang Ren, Peidong Wang, Yichen Gao, Wen Zhang, Jiayang Yu, Xiaocui Yang, Shi Feng
bullets: Targets shallow responses and inappropriate support strategies caused by weak semantic feedback, reward compensation, and coarse reasoning supervision.
Combines multi-source rewards into multidimensional semantic and functional alignment signals.
Uses non-compensatory gated fusion to reduce cross-dimension reward offset and structured CoT anchors for token-level credit assignment.
Under controlled response length, improves the average MLLM evaluation score from 3.61 to 4.04, with an 80.22% pairwise win rate and 75.3% human preference rate.
Results on three external datasets support transferability; code and dataset are publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal emotional support conversation framework with gated semantic alignment and CoT supervision.
papers.title: FACES: Fine-grained Gated Semantic Alignment for Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation
papers.tldr: FACES improves multimodal emotional-support responses through fine-grained reward alignment, gated fusion, and structured reasoning supervision.

papers.abstract: Chemistry evaluation has moved past multiple-choice probes toward open-ended expert problems, yet the benchmarks that define the current frontier still score answer endpoints alone. Such scoring conflates memorized facts with stepwise derivation, treats visual and textual inputs as interchangeable, and confounds long-horizon planning with stepwise execution. These blind spots prevent any diagnosis of where the reasoning chain breaks in a model. We present ChemArgus, a competition-level chemistry benchmark drawn from chemistry competition material, textbooks, and research papers, whose scoring replaces the answer endpoint with three measurement properties. Fine-grained scoring grades every subquestion point by point with partial credit, so a score lands at the level of the step rather than the outcome. Multimodal capability is priced on every problem containing a real image, paired with a controlled text description, so visual understanding is measured against text on identical tasks. Diagnostic attribution reads paired metrics that share one scoring unit and differ only in context construction, so a gap between two scores isolates a single cause, namely integration, propagation, or local reasoning. GPT-5.6-Sol scores 23.2% on unassisted whole-problem solving against 28.8% and 30.4% under the two sequential metrics, a gap measuring the integration burden. Through rubric partial credit and these cause-isolating score gaps, ChemArgus shows not only whether a model answers chemistry correctly but where its reasoning chain fails, so that every score it reports doubles as a diagnosis, a readout of the chain rather than a verdict, aiming to guide language models step by step on their path toward chemistry expertise, one corrected step at a time, each step priced by the rubric, point by point.
authors: Hanyao Guo, Mo Cui, Zihan Tan, Leixin Sun, Yichun Wang, Yinan Shen, Guojun Zhu, Jia Jiang, Erhao Chen, Zui Chen, Wenzhe Gao, Zhihao Yu, Qijun Wang, Yetian Zhu, Jiande Chen, Chuhang Pei, Yao Jiang, Yichen Fan, Pinhan Wang, Xiaorui Pan, Qianyi Zhu, Yang Liu, Mang Ye, Guancheng Wan
bullets: Targets blind spots in endpoint-only evaluation, including memorization versus derivation, visual versus textual understanding, and planning versus execution.
Uses point-by-point rubric scoring with partial credit to evaluate intermediate subquestion steps.
Pairs real-image problems with controlled text descriptions to measure multimodal understanding on equivalent tasks.
Compares sequentially constructed metrics to attribute score gaps to integration, propagation, or local reasoning.
For GPT-5.6-Sol, reports 23.2% on unassisted whole-problem solving versus 28.8% and 30.4% on the two sequential metrics, illustrating an integration gap.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and diagnostic methodology for multimodal LLM reasoning, separating visual and textual understanding.
papers.title: ChemArgus: Automated Scientific Diagnostics for Lab-Grade Multimodal Chemistry Reasoning: A Frontier Benchmark
papers.tldr: ChemArgus is a diagnostic multimodal chemistry benchmark that identifies which reasoning steps and capabilities cause models to fail, rather than scoring only final answers.

papers.abstract: This work presents a compact and reproducible pipeline for synthesizing and curating image-based instruction-response pairs for DCVLR. We draw from the Cauldron collection and use Magpie-style instruction and response synthesis with Qwen2.5-VL-7B Instruct to create concise, image-conditioned instruction pairs. The pipeline consists of instruction synthesis, conditioned on input images and controlled via a system prompt, sanitization, tagging, and filtering of the instructions based on the score obtained by a reward model (DeBERTa-v3). We retain samples with positive scores to maximize the quality of the generated instructions. We observe that score distributions have a median and mean reward score of ~ 1.53 and ~ 1.75 respectively, indicating that most generated instructions are of good quality. The resulting dataset contains diverse instructions in the math, spatial, and social reasoning domains.
authors: Eleni E. Kasoura, Dimitrios Damianos, Georgios Paraskevopoulos, Vassilios Katsouros
bullets: Starts from the Cauldron image collection and generates concise instruction-response pairs with Qwen2.5-VL-7B Instruct using Magpie-style synthesis.
Sanitizes and tags generated instructions before filtering them with a DeBERTa-v3 reward model.
Retains samples with positive reward scores; the abstract reports mean and median scores of approximately 1.75 and 1.53.
The resulting dataset covers math, spatial, and social reasoning domains.
The work is presented as a DCVLR competition submission with an emphasis on compact, reproducible data construction.
papers.selection_reason: Synthetic instruction-data pipeline for image-conditioned multimodal instruction tuning, relevant to multimodal LLM training.
papers.title: Instruction Mining From Images: Constructing a Synthetic Dataset for Multimodal Learning ILSP DCVLR Competition Submission
papers.tldr: A compact pipeline uses vision-language generation and reward-based filtering to build a synthetic dataset of diverse image-conditioned instructions for multimodal learning.

papers.abstract: Adapting a single vision-language model to medical image parsing requires training choices that reflect the demands of each task. We study task-specific adaptation with Qwen3.5-9B for FLARE 2026 Task 3, covering six task families and seven imaging modalities. Our system couples a shared, frozen 4-bit backbone with LoRA adapters selected from the input question. We customize adapter ranks and prompts, rebalance rare classification targets, and supplement regression training with dermatology classification examples. On the fixed internal holdout, the task-specific adapters achieve a dataset-macro balanced accuracy of 0.7791 for classification, a dataset-macro micro-F1 of 0.6286 for multi-label classification, a counting mean absolute error (MAE) of 11.73, a dataset-macro detection F1 of 0.8914, a dataset-macro regression MAE of 9.78, and a report-generation CRIMSON score of 0.8204. On the organizer's 1,703-example hidden-validation set, the submitted system achieves 0.8496 classification balanced accuracy, 0.5338 sample-averaged multi-label F1, and 14.5950 regression MAE. The final 30.1 GB container averages 3.1 seconds per case, including model loading, and produces identical outputs across repeated verification runs. The benefits vary across tasks, supporting the use of task-specific adapter configurations and image budgets within a shared medical vision-language model. Code is available at https://github.com/TahaSabir0/FLARE26-Hexapus.
authors: Taha Sabir, Alberto Montero Molina, Thinh Quang Ly, Veronika Dmitrenko, Mohammad Yaqub, Tausifa Jan Saleem
bullets: Uses a shared 4-bit backbone with adapters selected from the input question, plus task-specific ranks, prompts, and image budgets.
Addresses class imbalance and augments regression training with dermatology classification examples.
On an internal holdout, reports classification balanced accuracy of 0.7791, detection F1 of 0.8914, regression MAE of 9.78, and report-generation CRIMSON of 0.8204, among other task metrics.
On 1,703 hidden-validation examples, achieves 0.8496 classification balanced accuracy, 0.5338 sample-averaged multi-label F1, and 14.5950 regression MAE.
The final 30.1 GB container averages 3.1 seconds per case; results indicate that task-specific adapter configurations benefit some tasks differently.
papers.selection_reason: Task-specific LoRA adaptation of a multimodal LLM for medical image parsing; fits multimodal LLM adaptation.
papers.title: Multimodal Medical Image Parsing with Task-Specific Low-Rank Adapters
papers.tldr: A shared frozen Qwen3.5-9B vision-language model with question-selected, task-specific LoRA adapters supports diverse medical image parsing tasks across six task families and seven modalities.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models suffer significant accuracy drops under common corruptions. While test-time adaptation (TTA) successfully mitigates these shifts in CLIP-like contrastive models, its application to generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains underexplored and uniquely challenging due to their sequential token generation. In this work, we demonstrate that representation-based TTA fails to recover performance in MLLMs. Our experiments reveal that even when violating standard TTA assumptions by leveraging target data offline, sample-blind feature alignment recovers only marginal accuracy. We attribute this failure to the nature of corruption shifts: unlike CLIP-like architectures, which benefit from a shared domain-shift direction within a single pooled classification embedding, MLLM visual token sequence shifts are nearly orthogonal and span the full embedding space.These findings bound what any sample-blind, position-shared correction at a single encoder site can achieve, establishing that representation-space interventions alone might be insufficient to ensure corruption robustness in MLLMs.
authors: Miko{\l}aj Pi\'orczy\'nski, Wojciech Masarczyk, Damian S\'ojka, Sebastian Cygert, Bart{\l}omiej Twardowski
bullets: MLLMs experience substantial accuracy drops under common corruptions, and standard TTA strategies do not transfer reliably from CLIP-like models.
Even with offline access to target data, sample-blind feature alignment provides only marginal recovery.
MLLM corruption shifts are nearly orthogonal across visual tokens and span the embedding space, unlike the shared shift direction in pooled CLIP representations.
These results limit the effectiveness of position-shared, single-layer representation corrections for MLLM robustness.
The findings suggest that representation-space interventions alone may be insufficient for corruption robustness in generative MLLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes test-time adaptation limits for multimodal LLMs, directly relevant to test-time learning and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: On the Limits of Representation-Based Test-Time Adaptation for Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Representation-based test-time adaptation is fundamentally limited for improving corruption robustness in multimodal LLMs because their visual-token shifts are diverse rather than aligned.

papers.abstract: We introduce SEA-HELM Audio, a Southeast Asian (SEA) multilingual evaluation framework that extends the text-based SEA-HELM benchmark to assess performance degradation in cascaded automatic speech recognition and large language model (ASR-LLM) pipelines. Using synthesized speech, we compare speech-input and text-input performance across five languages (Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil) on multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following tasks. We evaluate open-weight and commercial ASR-LLM systems using identical verifiers and quantify the speech gap as the difference between text and speech accuracy. Results show substantial degradation, with accuracy drops of 9.00 to 18.50 percentage points for multiple-choice reasoning and 20.00 to 42.86 points for instruction following. Tamil exhibits the largest degradation, exceeding 40 percentage points. Our findings highlight the limitations of text-only benchmarks in predicting voice-agent reliability and demonstrate the value of SEA-HELM Audio for evaluating multilingual voice-agent systems.
authors: Yixian Tan, Aulia Adila, Jonathan Heng, Kunat Pipatanakul, Donghang Wu, Anocha Sutaveephamochanon
bullets: Extends the text-based SEA-HELM benchmark to evaluate cascaded ASR–LLM pipelines.
Compares synthesized speech and text inputs across Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil.
Assesses multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following using identical verifiers across open-weight and commercial systems.
Speech causes 9.00–18.50 percentage-point drops on reasoning and 20.00–42.86-point drops on instruction following.
Tamil shows the largest degradation, exceeding 40 percentage points, challenging text-only estimates of voice-agent reliability.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates multilingual ASR-LLM voice-agent pipelines, relevant to multimodal LLM systems.
papers.title: SEA-HELM Audio: Evaluating Multilingual ASR-LLM Pipeline Performance Across SEA-HELM Subsets
papers.tldr: SEA-HELM Audio measures how much multilingual ASR–LLM systems lose when processing speech instead of text, revealing substantial performance degradation across Southeast Asian languages and tasks.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. We introduce Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (ARP-CD), a training-free framework for constructing contrastive negatives directly in representation space. ARP-CD uses the attention mass assigned to visual tokens at the answer-prediction position to guide bounded gradient updates of the language model's input visual hidden states. These updates reduce visual attention and produce a negative input, whose predictions are contrasted with those of the original branch throughout generation. Experiments across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks show that ARP-CD outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model--benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while improving general video understanding. Further analyses show that attention-guided perturbation directions improve negative quality and that the resulting negatives provide effective contrastive references for correcting the original predictions.
authors: Zhixin Cai, Ruoqi Yuan, Xinchen Yang, Zhuofan Chen, Jun Bai, Chuantao Yin, Wenge Rong
bullets: Targets unsupported video-grounded responses in Video LLMs.
Uses visual-token attention at the answer position to guide bounded gradient updates to visual hidden states.
Contrasts predictions from the perturbed negative branch with the original branch during generation.
A training-free method evaluated across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks.
Outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model–benchmark settings while improving general video understanding.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses hallucination reduction and video understanding in Video LLMs via contrastive decoding.
papers.title: Mitigating Video Hallucinations via Attention-Guided Representation Perturbation
papers.tldr: ARP-CD reduces Video LLM hallucinations by using attention-guided, representation-space perturbations to create stronger contrastive negatives during decoding.

papers.abstract: Interpreting an ambiguous utterance in real-world interactions often requires context beyond a single utterance. When the utterance refers to objects in a visual scene, it is necessary to maintain and update the set of plausible referents as context accumulates, without assuming that the available information identifies a unique object. However, prior work on interactive visual grounding, which localizes objects referred to by linguistic expressions, has focused on identifying a unique object once sufficient dialogue context becomes available. To address this gap, we propose Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG), a task for estimating the set of objects consistent with the given dialogue context. We further introduce CandVG, a benchmark that evaluates how the candidate set changes across dialogue turns. Our evaluation of vision-language models shows that stronger visual grounding capability does not necessarily yield better CSVG performance. In particular, models have difficulty predicting the complete candidate set, owing to challenges in candidate generation and premature commitment to a small set of candidates in early turns. Nevertheless, we find that this limitation can be partially mitigated in the evaluated large-scale models using instructions designed for CSVG.
authors: Shun Inadumi, Lee Sangmyeong, Koichiro Yoshino
bullets: Ambiguous referring expressions may remain compatible with multiple scene objects as dialogue unfolds.
Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG) estimates the full set of plausible referents rather than selecting one object.
CandVG benchmarks how candidate sets change across dialogue turns.
Stronger conventional visual grounding does not necessarily improve CSVG performance.
CSVG-specific instructions partially mitigate incomplete candidate generation in evaluated large-scale models.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a visual grounding task for ambiguous dialogue, evaluating vision-language models and spatial referent understanding.
papers.title: Recognizing Dialogue Ambiguity via Candidate Set Visual Grounding
papers.tldr: CSVG reframes visual grounding as tracking all objects consistent with ambiguous dialogue, revealing that current vision-language models often miss candidates and commit too early.

papers.abstract: Hyperspectral imaging distinguishes RGB-similar objects, but a pretrained vision-language-action model needs a state its frozen decoder can use. SPECTRA-VLA provides a native-width spectral upgrade without retraining the visual encoder or action decoder. A learned continuous residual enriches each target token through its own normalized false-color reference; projection, norm control and validation-calibrated injection regulate the change. Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category balanced accuracy rises from 0.812 to 0.883. With identical residuals and scale, own-token addition improves reuse of an external category-derived probe on frozen decoder logits: 0.701 versus 0.590 with pooled replacement, at similar image-disjoint recognition. Five grouped tests covering the same 86 acquisitions recover within-category spectral shape with $R^2=0.802/0.337$ from continuous and posterior-code states. Category-matched spectral swaps further show that own-token composition approximately doubles the target-specific recovery increment after frozen decoding. Spectral enrichment and receiving-token preservation thus work together at the pretrained interface.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of making hyperspectral distinctions usable by a pretrained model without retraining its visual encoder or action decoder.
Uses native-width residual enrichment based on each token’s normalized false-color reference, with projection, norm control, and validation-calibrated injection.
Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category-balanced accuracy increases from 0.812 to 0.883.
Own-token addition improves external category-probe reuse over pooled replacement (0.701 vs. 0.590) under identical residuals and scale.
Grouped tests recover within-category spectral shape, while spectral swaps indicate that own-token composition approximately doubles target-specific recovery after frozen decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, adapting frozen interfaces to hyperspectral data without retraining, a core interest in Embodied AI.
papers.title: SPECTRA-VLA: Base-Fine Hyperspectral Token Transfer at Frozen Vision-Language-Action Interfaces
papers.tldr: SPECTRA-VLA transfers hyperspectral information into a frozen vision-language-action model by enriching each visual token with a calibrated, token-specific residual.

papers.abstract: Recent work has explored visual reasoning through image generation, where models solve visual-reasoning problems by directly generating solution images. Intuitively, iterative samplers such as flow matching are well suited to this task, since each sampling step may resemble one reasoning step. However, in this work, from a circuit complexity perspective, we show that this intuition is misleading. We prove that as long as the model outputs satisfy certain mild regularity conditions, the trajectory of the vanilla flow-matching sampler can be simulated by a constant number of sequential rounds of parallel model evaluations. Consequently, additional sampling steps cannot increase the expressive power of a constant-depth backbone model under the standard complexity-theoretic model of transformers. We then reveal that self-conditioning, which conditions the model on the previous step's estimate of the final image, plays a previously unrecognized role in removing this bottleneck. Controlled experiments on diverse visual-reasoning tasks show that flow matching with self-conditioning achieves higher accuracy and greater reasoning depth than vanilla flow matching, and its performance improves with more sampling steps. Theoretically, we prove that with self-conditioning, a constant-depth backbone can achieve expressive power equivalent to that of space-bounded Turing machines. Our study suggests a design principle for future visual reasoning research: carry more information between sampling steps, so that additional steps translate into deeper reasoning.
authors: Zeyang Zhang, Linxiang Gao, Meiqi Gu, Xingyan Chen, Minrui Luo, Kaifeng Lyu, Tianxing He
bullets: Vanilla flow-matching trajectories can be simulated with only a constant number of parallel model-evaluation rounds under mild regularity conditions.
Therefore, adding sampling steps alone does not increase the expressive power of constant-depth transformer backbones.
Self-conditioning passes the previous estimate of the final image between steps, removing this computational bottleneck.
Experiments across diverse visual-reasoning tasks show higher accuracy, greater reasoning depth, and continued improvement with more sampling steps when self-conditioning is used.
The theory shows that self-conditioned constant-depth backbones can match the expressive power of space-bounded Turing machines.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes self-conditioning in flow matching for visual reasoning, providing a transferable technical insight for deep sequential reasoning in generative models.
papers.title: Self-Conditioning Enables Deep Sequential Reasoning in Flow Matching
papers.tldr: Self-conditioning allows flow-matching samplers to use additional steps for genuinely deeper visual reasoning, overcoming a limitation of vanilla flow matching.

papers.abstract: Modern vision-language models can accept multi-image contexts, but aggregate accuracy rarely reveals where a multi-image reasoning pipeline fails. We study a controlled schema-application task in which a model must locate two target characters in a 16-image sequence, identify their visual attributes, consult an item-specific visual codebook, and compose two ordered nonce code names. We introduce a within-item 2-by-2 factorial Oracle design: Oracle-A supplies a verified textual schema, Oracle-B supplies a verified ordered target-appearance representation, and both interventions retain the original images and final question. Across 72 new items and 1,188 analyzed model responses, Oracle-B increased strict exact accuracy by 54.6 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 46.3 to 63.0) and outperformed Oracle-A by 60.6 points (Holm-adjusted p-value no greater than .0002). An auxiliary retrieval diagnostic reached only 49.1% ordered-appearance accuracy even after removing code-name generation. Providing both Oracle sources yielded 100% accuracy across all models. These results localize the dominant recoverable deficit to upstream ordered instance recovery rather than primarily to downstream schema use and composition.
authors: Yiliu Xu, Xinjin Li, Yu Ma
bullets: The task requires locating two characters across 16 images, identifying their attributes, consulting a visual codebook, and composing ordered nonce names.
A within-item 2×2 design independently supplied a verified textual schema and verified ordered target-appearance representation while retaining the original images and question.
Providing ordered target appearances increased strict exact accuracy by 54.6 percentage points; it outperformed schema provision by 60.6 points.
An auxiliary diagnostic achieved only 49.1% ordered-appearance accuracy, while supplying both Oracle sources produced 100% accuracy across all models.
Findings are scoped to this controlled schema-application task and its 72 new items and 1,188 analyzed responses.
papers.selection_reason: Oracle-intervention analysis of multi-image VLM schema application; fits multimodal LLM understanding.
papers.title: What Breaks in Multi-Image Schema Application? Factorial Oracle Interventions Reveal an Instance-Information Bottleneck
papers.tldr: A factorial Oracle study finds that multi-image schema reasoning fails mainly because models cannot reliably recover the ordered appearances of target instances, rather than because they cannot apply the schema.

papers.abstract: Real-world engineering drawings are often large-format and information-dense. Answering practical engineering questions therefore requires both fine-grained understanding of engineering information and complex reasoning over objects, relations, and evidence distributed across different regions or views. Existing benchmarks cover a range of engineering-drawing understanding tasks involving local regions, individual views, specific elements, or more constrained visual settings. However, systematic evaluation of understanding over realistic, large-format engineering drawings remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce LED-BENCH, a multidisciplinary benchmark designed to evaluate fine-grained understanding and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings, spanning the mechanical, architectural, and transportation domains. Extensive evaluation of 11 representative multimodal large language models, including 8 proprietary models and 3 open-source models, reveals substantial remaining difficulty: GPT-5.6 Sol achieves 52.65% average accuracy, performance varies across engineering domains, and all evaluated models perform worse on questions requiring broader evidence integration. These results highlight fine-grained understanding, evidence integration, and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings as persistent challenges for current multimodal models.
authors: Ke Li, Tianyi Wang, Enning You, Chaoqun Wan, Zhen Huang, Shuxian Liang, Xian-Sheng Hua
bullets: Covers mechanical, architectural, and transportation engineering domains.
Tests reasoning over objects, relations, and evidence distributed across regions and views.
Evaluates 11 multimodal large language models, including proprietary and open-source systems.
Models struggle particularly with questions requiring broad evidence integration; GPT-5.6 Sol reaches 52.65% average accuracy.
Results identify fine-grained understanding, evidence integration, and complex reasoning as persistent challenges.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for MLLM understanding of large-format engineering drawings; fits multimodal LLM evaluation and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: LED-BENCH: A Benchmark for Large-format Engineering Drawing Understanding
papers.tldr: LED-BENCH evaluates multimodal models on fine-grained understanding and complex reasoning over realistic, large-format engineering drawings.

papers.abstract: A spatial answer depends on the reference frame specified in language and its supporting visual evidence. Item accuracy alone obscures whether correctness persists when either changes. We introduce Frame Evidence, a benchmark of 320 matched triplets and 960 Chinese multiple-choice questions from captured and rendered scenes. One family compares three grounded reference frames over fixed images. The other pairs image deletion annotated as insufficient with answer-preserving addition. Joint metrics require correct answers across all three frames and paired evidence variants. Across 20 configurations on 288 held-out questions, GPT three-shot reaches 50.00\% item accuracy, but the best three-frame group accuracy is 5/48 (10.42\%), reached by GPT two-shot. Few-shot prompting and task-specific adaptation improve item accuracy without consistently improving joint correctness. Input controls show where images support matched success, while repeated executions reveal answer instability beneath similar scores.
authors: Chunxi Luo, Qishuai Ding, Xingchen Peng, Hengwei Ye, Ke Zhang, Wenxin Lian, Tianyi Lu, Chunlong Yu, Zhenya Lin
bullets: Introduces 320 matched triplets and 960 Chinese multiple-choice questions from captured and rendered scenes.
Tests three grounded reference frames with fixed images, plus image deletion and answer-preserving addition variants.
Uses joint metrics requiring correct answers across all reference-frame and evidence variants.
Across 20 configurations, GPT’s best three-frame group accuracy was 5/48 (10.42%), despite 50.00% item accuracy in one setting.
Few-shot prompting and task adaptation improved individual answers but did not consistently improve joint correctness; repeated runs exposed instability.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for reference frames and visual evidence in multi-image spatial reasoning; fits spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Frame Evidence:A Benchmark for Reference Frames and Visual Evidence in Multi-Image Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: Frame Evidence shows that high item accuracy can hide poor consistency across reference frames and supporting visual evidence in multi-image spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires scalable 3D environments that are both photorealistic and semantically grounded, yet existing indoor datasets are dominated by room-scale captures and costly LiDAR acquisition. Online real-estate platforms offer abundant panoramas of diverse multi-room homes, but sparse viewpoints and texture-poor regions make reconstruction severely under-constrained. We introduce Holi-Spatial 360, a generative reconstruction and data curation framework for converting these panoramas into annotated multi-room 3D environments. Because reconstruction quality bounds subsequent generation, our Correspondence-Guided Geometric Optimization converts feed-forward reconstruction priors into reliable cross-view constraints and builds a coherent 3D Gaussian Splatting representation as 3D spatial memory. Adapted single-image and video priors then restore appearance and complete continuous trajectories while preserving observed content. The reconstructed scenes support arbitrary RGB-D rendering and an automated curation pipeline that combines end-to-end 3D grounding with VLM-based verification. Holi360 contains over 1K multi-room 3DGS scenes, more than 100K instance annotations, and 2M spatial question-answer pairs. We also introduce the Holi360 benchmark to evaluate the spatial understanding of VLMs in real-world, multi-room indoor environments. Experiments demonstrate superior reconstruction and curation quality under sparse panoramic inputs, while fine-tuning VLMs on Holi360 substantially improves spatial reasoning capabilities.
authors: Yuanyuan Gao, Zhirui Liu, Yuning Gong, Yifei Liu, Yifan Zhan, Kuixuan Jiao, Xiaolong Zhou, Yifan Yang, Hongjie Zhang, Xue Yang, Dan Xu, Zhihang Zhong
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of scalable, photorealistic, semantically grounded indoor 3D data and the under-constrained nature of sparse panoramas.
Uses correspondence-guided geometric optimization to turn reconstruction priors into cross-view constraints and build coherent 3D Gaussian Splatting spatial memory.
Applies image and video generation priors to restore appearance and complete continuous trajectories while preserving observed content.
Provides RGB-D rendering and automated 3D curation with grounding and VLM-based verification.
Introduces over 1K scenes, 100K+ instance annotations, 2M spatial QA pairs, and a benchmark; fine-tuning on the data improves VLM spatial reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Generative reconstruction of multi-room 3D environments and benchmark for VLM spatial reasoning, directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Holi-Spatial 360: Generative Reconstruction from Sparse Panoramas for Spatial Rendering and Intelligence
papers.tldr: Holi-Spatial 360 reconstructs richly annotated multi-room 3D environments from sparse real-estate panoramas and uses them to improve spatial reasoning in vision-language models.

papers.abstract: Post-training often improves the performance of large audio-language models on audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks. However, these improvements may reflect adaptation to specific question formats, such as multiple-choice questions, rather than genuine advances in audio understanding and reasoning capabilities. To investigate what LALMs actually learn from post-training, we conduct controlled experiments that disentangle improvements in audio understanding from adaptation to specific question formats. Across different models and post-training methods, we find that much of the reported improvement persists even without informative audio, but largely disappears when the question format changes. These findings suggest that post-training often teaches models to exploit task-specific textual cues and answer patterns rather than developing generalizable audio understanding and reasoning capabilities.
authors: Hua-Hsuan Chen, Xuanjun Chen, Wei-Chung Lu, Chih-Kai Yang, Yu-Xiang Lin, Sung-Feng Huang, Haibin Wu, Hung-yi Lee
bullets: Reported benchmark improvements may be driven by adaptation to multiple-choice and other task-specific formats.
Controlled experiments separate audio understanding from question-format adaptation across models and post-training methods.
Much of the improvement persists when informative audio is removed.
The gains largely disappear when the question format changes.
The findings question whether standard benchmarks measure genuine audio reasoning progress.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes post-training of large audio-language models, directly relevant to multimodal LLM understanding and evaluation.
papers.title: What Does LALM Post-training Learn? Rethinking Audio Understanding and Reasoning Capabilities
papers.tldr: Post-training gains in large audio-language models often reflect learning question formats and answer patterns rather than genuine, generalizable audio understanding or reasoning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal in-context learning (ICL) is an important capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Its performance is closely tied to the demonstrations it uses, making demonstration retrieval a core problem for ICL. Common methods use fixed scoring methods to retrieve all the demonstrations at once, which may introduce redundancy and noise. Context-aware retrieval methods have emerged to address this problem by allowing incremental retrieval from a growing context. However, none of them lets the MLLM learn how to judge what new demonstrations it needs and then carry out progressive retrieval on its own. To this end, we introduce ActICL, which trains an MLLM agent to acquire and use an ICL context via tool-augmented reasoning. An ActICL agent analyzes its own information gaps during iterative reasoning and tool-use actions. Based on these gaps, it performs targeted retrieval to acquire a set of initial candidates. It can then use the existing context to further filter the candidates and refine the context, or it can iteratively perform a new retrieval. When the agent judges that the context is sufficient for the task, or when the resource limit is reached with the user request met, it sends the acquired context to an answering model, either the agent itself or another MLLM. We use a two-stage post-training procedure that jointly optimizes the agent's acquisition and answering. With an adaptive number of demonstrations, ActICL improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over standard similarity-based retrieval across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points compared to the strongest prior baseline. The contexts acquired by ActICL agents can also be used effectively by frontier models. When GPT-5.6-Sol performs 4-shot ICL, ActICL's contexts improve its performance by 3.5 points over standard retrieval, averaged over three benchmarks.
authors: Yanshu Li, Ruixiang Tang, Junyi Jessy Li, Elias Stengel-Eskin
