bullets: Fixed, one-shot demonstration retrieval can introduce redundant or noisy context.
ActICL uses tool-augmented reasoning for adaptive, progressive retrieval and context refinement.
A two-stage post-training procedure jointly optimizes demonstration acquisition and answer generation.
It improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over similarity-based retrieval across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points over the strongest prior baseline.
ActICL-generated contexts also improve GPT-5.6-Sol’s 4-shot ICL performance by 3.5 points across three benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Trains MLLM agents for progressive demonstration retrieval in multimodal in-context learning, directly relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: ActICL: Post-Training for Agentic Multimodal In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: ActICL trains an MLLM agent to iteratively identify information gaps and retrieve only the demonstrations needed for effective multimodal in-context learning.

papers.abstract: Native multimodal pre-training trains a single model from scratch on text and multimodal data, enabling it to understand both language and visual inputs. However, how visual signals shape scaling behavior and support capabilities beyond visual understanding remains unclear. We investigate this question through controlled visual-content ablations across model sizes and training budgets. Specifically, we replace image embeddings with content-free padding token embeddings. Retaining visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples without materially changing the lowest text-only loss at a given compute budget, the optimal balance of model size and training data, or aggregate language scores. The relative multimodal loss benefit grows approximately as a power law of compute. To test benefits beyond understanding images, we evaluate spatial reasoning from text descriptions alone. Both conditions improve with model and data scaling. During training of the largest model, visual gains are most sustained in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, which involve maintaining object configurations or composing spatial updates; gains in spatial relations, geometry, and physical commonsense are less consistent. These findings identify visual content as a scalable anchor for multimodal learning, with benefits that extend beyond visual inputs while preserving aggregate language performance.
authors: Haoyuan Wu, Aoqi Wu, Jiani Hu, Bei Yu
bullets: Controlled ablations replace image embeddings with content-free padding embeddings across model sizes and compute budgets.
Retaining visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples, with benefits growing approximately as a power law of compute.
Visual content does not materially change the lowest text-only loss, optimal model/data balance, or aggregate language scores.
Text-only spatial reasoning benefits most consistently in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, while gains in geometry and physical commonsense are less consistent.
papers.selection_reason: Native multimodal pretraining analysis showing visual content benefits spatial reasoning, fitting multimodal and spatial intelligence interests.
papers.title: More Than Seeing: Vision as Scalable Anchors in Native Multimodal Pre-Training
papers.tldr: Visual content acts as a scalable anchor in native multimodal pre-training, improving multimodal learning and some text-only spatial reasoning without reducing overall language performance.

papers.abstract: MLLM-based detectors formulate vision-language grounding as autoregressive coordinate generation, yet in dense scenes, they often collapse into a box repetition loop, repeatedly emitting identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted. We trace this failure to historical-answer attention takeover: Under full-history autoregression, repeated coordinate tokens in the growing answer history attract disproportionate attention, crowding out the attention sinks needed to attend to new visual evidence. % To break this loop, in this paper, we propose \textbf{Compressed Window Auto-Regression} (WinAR). This new mechanism partitions a long answer sequence into consecutive generation windows and restricts full token-level autoregression to the current window only while compressing each previous window into a fixed set of latent tokens that condition subsequent decoding. This design reduces the repeated exposure to raw historical coordinates that triggers the attention takeover, yet preserves cross-window dependencies essential for coherent multi-object generation. On RSDense, which contains 200-2,000 objects per image, our model WinARDet improves RexOmni F1-score (IoU=0.5) from 32.16 to 39.36 over the baseline, while reducing the redundancy rate from 35.48% to 13.00%. WinARDet also generalizes across decoding strategies and output formats, including parallel box decoding and polygon generation, providing a practical paradigm for long-horizon vision-language grounding across scene densities.
authors: Chenxu Wang, Hangyi Kuang, Bo-Wen Yin, Yuxuan Li, Quan-Sheng Zeng, Yang Zhang, Xu Guo, Xiang Li, Qibin Hou
bullets: Dense-scene autoregressive detectors can repeatedly emit identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted.
The proposed Compressed Window Auto-Regression limits token-level attention to the current generation window.
Each previous window is compressed into fixed latent tokens, preserving cross-window dependencies while reducing historical-coordinate interference.
On RSDense, WinARDet raises F1 at IoU 0.5 from 32.16 to 39.36 and lowers redundancy from 35.48% to 13.00%.
The approach also extends to parallel box decoding and polygon generation across varying scene densities.
papers.selection_reason: Novel compressed window autoregression for MLLM-based dense vision-language grounding, relevant to multimodal LLMs and token efficiency.
papers.title: WinARDet: Compressed Window Auto-Regression for Long-Horizon Vision-Language Grounding
papers.tldr: WinARDet prevents repetitive box-generation loops in dense-scene vision-language grounding by compressing past decoding windows into latent tokens.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models must reconcile conflicting text and images. Prior work has characterized the resulting behavior in terms of modality biases--e.g., a "blind faith in text"--but why preferences vary across models, domains, and input conditions remains unclear. We develop a predictive account from a Bayesian perspective, positing that VLMs combine conditionally independent evidence from each modality with prior beliefs, subject to modality-specific biases. The resulting two-parameter cue combination model accurately predicts VLM preferences under unseen combinations of input degradation and transfers to new forms of unreliability without refitting. Separating evidence strength from integration bias explains how VLMs can follow text even while weighting visual evidence more heavily, reconciling reports of text and vision dominance under a single combination rule.
authors: Josh Barua, Kyle Mahowald, William Rudman
bullets: Models combine conditionally independent visual and textual evidence with prior beliefs.
The framework separates evidence strength from integration bias, clarifying seemingly contradictory text- and vision-dominance findings.
It predicts model preferences for unseen combinations of input degradation.
The model transfers to new types of unreliability without refitting.
It offers a unified account of why modality preferences vary across models, domains, and conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Bayesian account of VLM evidence integration relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Vision-Language Models Integrate Conflicting Evidence Like Biased Bayesian Observers
papers.tldr: A two-parameter Bayesian cue-combination model explains how vision-language models integrate conflicting text and image evidence with modality-specific biases.

papers.abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) organize information across different modalities to support multimodal Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which aims to improve the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The effectiveness of these multimodal Graph RAG methods largely depends on the quality of the constructed MMKGs. However, most existing methods construct MMKGs without explicit guidance on graph quality, while reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods that rely on final-answer correctness may provide only indirect feedback on MMKG quality. To address these limitations, we propose MMKG-R1, a novel MMKG-quality-driven RL framework for training an MLLM as a multimodal knowledge constructor. To be specific, MMKG-R1 introduces multiple quality-aware rewards to directly evaluate both the quality of information extracted from individual knowledge sources and the quality of the assembled MMKG. These rewards are then used to guide the RL training. Experiments across multiple datasets show that MMKG-R1 constructs MMKGs that improve downstream question-answering accuracy.
authors: Zongyu Wu, Yilong Wang, Xiaochen Wang, Minhua Lin, Yuan Zhong, Fenglong Ma, Xiang Zhang, Suhang Wang
bullets: Targets the lack of explicit guidance for MMKG quality in existing construction methods.
Trains an MLLM as a multimodal knowledge constructor with reinforcement learning.
Uses rewards that assess both extracted information from individual sources and the assembled graph.
Experiments on multiple datasets show improved downstream question-answering accuracy.
The abstract does not specify quantitative gains or detailed limitations.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based MLLM training for multimodal knowledge graph construction, relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: MMKG-R1: Constructing Multimodal Knowledge Graphs via Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: MMKG-R1 uses quality-aware reinforcement learning to train an MLLM to construct better multimodal knowledge graphs for improved multimodal Graph RAG question answering.

papers.abstract: Existing illumination estimation methods primarily recover lighting distributions for rendering, but typically leave the contributions of individual physical light sources at specific scene locations implicit. We address this gap by leveraging the scene understanding capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to connect local illumination with its physical sources. We introduce LAMP, a framework for point-conditioned, source-aware illumination reasoning from a single RGB image with marked query points. LAMP constructs a shared inventory of active light sources, ranks contributing sources for each query, and predicts their 3D query-to-source directions. We supervise these relationships using procedurally controlled indoor scenes, reusing independently rendered source responses to derive contribution targets across lighting configurations and obtaining exact directions from source and query positions. On the Infinigen test set, fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B increases dominant-source 3D PCK@0.5m from 0% to 70.6%, with 94.5% of directions within 12.5 degrees of ground truth among correctly localized sources. Combined with a lightweight network predicting dense RGB irradiance, LAMP achieves probe-rendering quality comparable to prior lighting-estimation methods while additionally localizing individual physical sources in 3D and explicitly attributing local illumination to them.
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit source attribution in conventional illumination-estimation methods.
Builds a shared inventory of active light sources, ranks their contributions per query point, and predicts 3D query-to-source directions.
Trains on procedurally controlled indoor scenes with source-response contribution targets and exact geometric directions.
On Infinigen, fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B reaches 70.6% dominant-source 3D PCK@0.5m; 94.5% of correctly localized directions are within 12.5° of ground truth.
Combined with dense RGB irradiance prediction, achieves probe-rendering quality comparable to prior methods while adding explicit 3D source localization and attribution.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-based 3D source-aware lighting estimation with spatial reasoning, relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: LAMP: 3D Source-Aware Lighting Estimation at Multiple Points
papers.tldr: LAMP uses vision-language models to identify and localize the physical light sources contributing to illumination at multiple 3D query points from a single RGB image.

papers.abstract: Emerging decision models such as JEV provide typed interfaces that map task instructions and observations directly to choices, judgments, and scores. As these models are increasingly used for automated decision-making, understanding their reliability under adversarial manipulation becomes critical. We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of decision models across textual and visual inputs. Our benchmark covers practical decision-making scenarios and a diverse suite of attacks, including semantics-preserving text perturbations, image perturbations, and prompt injection in both modalities. We curate evaluation sets through external validity checks and cross-model candidate selection. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text tasks and 17 on vision tasks, including 24 and 12 held-out models, respectively, that are excluded from candidate selection. Our experiments reveal several key findings. First, attacks expose vulnerabilities beyond the models used for construction and selection, although optimized image perturbations transfer weakly to many targets even with multiple surrogates. Second, relative model robustness varies across tasks and attack types, and resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. Third, label-consistency checks substantially reduce measured attack success across text and image settings, highlighting the importance of validating apparent failures. The benchmark is available at https://yifan-lan.github.io/DecisionRobust/.
authors: Yifan Lan, Zhongye Liu, Yurui Chang, Hanyu Wang, Yongkang Du, Lu Lin, Jinghui Chen
bullets: Evaluates robustness across textual and visual inputs using semantics-preserving perturbations, image attacks, and multimodal prompt injection.
Tests 30 text-model configurations and 17 vision-model configurations, including held-out models for external evaluation.
Finds vulnerabilities transfer beyond benchmark-construction models, while optimized image attacks often transfer weakly.
Shows that robustness depends on the task and attack type; perturbation resistance does not guarantee prompt-injection resistance.
Label-consistency checks substantially lower measured attack success, underscoring the need to validate apparent failures.
papers.selection_reason: Robustness benchmark for multimodal decision models across text and vision; relevant to multimodal foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision
papers.tldr: DecisionRobust benchmarks how reliably JEV-style decision models withstand text, image, and prompt-injection attacks across diverse decision tasks.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have been widely applied in embodied agents and robotics for vision tasks. However, MLLMs suffer from limitations in spatial reasoning and perception. Post-training techniques have shown promise for improving these capabilities; yet, there are limited data-driven surveys of such approaches. In this survey, we consider approaches to fine-tuning pretrained MLLMs for spatial reasoning tasks, ranging from supervised to reinforcement learning, with an emphasis on the datasets used. We investigate themes of dataset construction, data modality and annotation, and evaluation of the resulting models. Based on these themes, we categorize research into three groups: dataset design, dataset construction and evaluation. We find four main methods for constructing fixed spatial annotations: rules and templates, LLM prompting, procedural generation, and human-in-the-loop. We also observe substantial variation in evaluation approaches, including different scoring methods, tolerance metrics, and benchmark types. Finally, we identify opportunities for future research in unified dynamic annotation, efficient spatial reasoning, standardization of evaluation, expanded spatial range, and human-centered spatial interactions.
authors: Mahdieh Mallahnezhad, Masoud Jafaripour, Mohamadali Tofigh, Sheila Schoepp, Osmar R. Zaiane
bullets: Reviews supervised- and reinforcement-learning approaches for fine-tuning pretrained MLLMs on spatial reasoning tasks.
Categorizes research into dataset design, dataset construction, and evaluation.
Identifies four fixed-annotation strategies: rules and templates, LLM prompting, procedural generation, and human-in-the-loop methods.
Highlights substantial variation in scoring, tolerance metrics, and benchmark types.
Proposes future directions including dynamic annotation, efficient reasoning, standardized evaluation, broader spatial ranges, and human-centered interaction.
papers.selection_reason: Survey of data-centric spatial reasoning fine-tuning for MLLMs.
papers.title: Towards a Data-Centric Understanding of Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A data-centric survey organizes how datasets and annotations shape post-training for spatial reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs).

papers.abstract: Aerial and remote sensing video is increasingly evaluated like web video, by posing multiple-choice questions to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) over sampled frames and reporting accuracy. This paper argues that this recipe measures the wrong aspect, and supports the claim with a convergent meta-analysis of a broad set of published results, organized in four evidence tiers, in which a claim becomes a position only when collected evidence agrees. Parameter scale exhibits a median of +3.4 accuracy points per tenfold increase on aerial benchmarks, far below a human gap of at least 19 points, whereas acquisition conditions control perception, as 315 of 318 evaluations in 19 within-paper contrasts lose accuracy when conditions such as altitude, view, object size or time horizon become harder. No aerial benchmark in the corpus combines video input with per-task human and random baselines, competence collapses from answering to acting in closed-loop navigation, and the same MLLMs score higher on the aerial benchmark than on ground spatial ones, but lower on studies that test cross-view geometry. From these findings the current study derives five falsifiable principles and proposes the AVU-Card, a reporting card for aerial video benchmarks
authors: Georgios Angelidis, Aggelos Psiris, Maria Vakalopoulou, Georgios Th. Papadopoulos, Giorgos Sfikas, Iraklis Varlamis
bullets: A convergent meta-analysis synthesizes published aerial and remote-sensing video results across four evidence tiers.
Model parameter scaling yields limited gains: a median +3.4 accuracy points per tenfold increase, versus a human gap of at least 19 points.
Perception degrades in 315 of 318 within-paper contrasts when altitude, viewpoint, object size, or time horizon becomes harder.
Current benchmarks lack video-input evaluations with both task-specific human and random baselines, and competence drops sharply from answering to closed-loop navigation.
The paper proposes five falsifiable principles and the AVU-Card for reporting aerial video benchmark properties.
papers.selection_reason: Meta-analysis of MLLM aerial video understanding and geometry, relevant to spatial and video evaluation.
papers.title: The Gap Is in the Geometry: A Convergent Meta-Analysis of Multi-Facet Aerial and Remote Sensing Video Understanding
papers.tldr: Aerial video benchmarks often measure acquisition-condition sensitivity rather than genuine spatial understanding, motivating geometry-focused evaluation and standardized reporting.

papers.abstract: Constructing robust GUI agents relies on multimodal visual grounding: the ability to precisely map natural language intents to actionable on-screen components. Despite abundant desktop, web, and mobile benchmarks, high-fidelity resources tailored for diverse environments are surprisingly scarce. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Screen Referring Grounding Dataset (ScreenRef), a comprehensive GUI grounding dataset consisting of GUI screenshots paired with natural language referring expressions and box or point annotations. Spanning desktop, web, and mobile domains, ScreenRef comprises 586K screenshots and over 633K referring expression instances, covering tasks such as text recognition, visual matching, spatial understanding, and refusal scenarios. To boost the model's grounding performance, we propose the Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning (D2RL) method to address the limited generalization of supervised fine-tuning and the sparse reward problem in reinforcement learning. Utilizing ScreenRef, we train Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct via sequential SFT and D2RL training, yielding GroundGUI-8B. GroundGUI-8B achieves 95.2% on ScreenSpot-V2, 63.9% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 65.4% on OSWorld-G, 86.8% on MMBench-GUI L2, and 38.3% on UI-Vision. Among 8B-scale models, it produces substantial gains over models trained on open-source datasets, with performance comparable or even superior to models trained on closed-source data. Code, models, and datasets are available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/GroundGUI.
authors: Qingsong Xie, Jiahao Tian, Jiacheng Tang, Zhifeng Li, Madalina Ciobanu, Navan Preet Singh, Qingqing Mao, Ritankar Das
bullets: ScreenRef contains 586K GUI screenshots and over 633K referring-expression instances across desktop, web, and mobile environments.
The dataset supports text recognition, visual matching, spatial understanding, and refusal scenarios using box or point annotations.
The proposed D2RL method targets limited generalization from supervised fine-tuning and sparse rewards in reinforcement learning.
GroundGUI-8B, trained from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, reports strong results across five GUI grounding benchmarks.
The work provides the ScreenRef dataset, trained models, and code publicly.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces GroundGUI, a method for GUI grounding using a large dataset (ScreenRef) and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning. This advances multimodal VLMs (Qwen3-VL) in spatial understanding and grounding tasks.
papers.title: GroundGUI: GUI Grounding by High-Quality Data and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: GroundGUI improves GUI grounding by combining a large, diverse annotated dataset with sequential supervised and distillation-to-reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Video-based remote physiological measurement (RPM) has broad applications, while Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide a promising opportunity to enable end-to-end physiological monitoring for future human-aware intelligent systems. However, existing RPM methods rely on task-specific models and cannot be seamlessly integrated with the multimodal understanding and interaction capabilities of VLMs. We revisit RPM with VLMs and provide empirical evidence for two major bottlenecks: generic visual semantic representations fail to preserve fine-grained physiological cues; while discrete token prediction in autoregressive generation is inherently misaligned with continuous numerical measurement. To address these challenges, we propose VITAL (Visual-physiological Token Alignment for Language Models), a visual-physiological token alignment framework for RPM and preserving general vision tasks. VITAL retains the original visual pathway for semantic understanding and introduces an independent physiological pathway to jointly model semantic and physiological information. Moreover, we propose a structured numerical alignment approach to improve the reliability of generative heart rate estimation by enhancing numerical relationship modeling. Extensive experiments show that VITAL improves cross-domain estimation performance on multiple rPPG datasets while preserving the general visual understanding capability of VLMs, demonstrating its effectiveness as a unified visual-physiological model. Code will be released.
authors: Xiao Yang, Zekun Zhang, Yuxuan Fan, Duoxun Tang, Ziyang Liu, Dengbo He, Kaishun Wu, Jiyao Wang
bullets: VLM-based RPM is limited by generic visual features that miss fine-grained physiological cues.
Autoregressive discrete-token prediction is poorly aligned with continuous physiological measurements.
VITAL adds an independent physiological pathway alongside the original semantic visual pathway.
Structured numerical alignment improves the reliability of generative heart-rate estimation.
Experiments report improved cross-domain performance on multiple rPPG datasets while preserving general visual understanding.
papers.selection_reason: Extends VLMs with a physiological pathway, relevant to multimodal foundation model design.
papers.title: Why Do VLMs Fail at Remote Physiological Measurement? Rethinking with Physiological Grounding and Numerical Alignment
papers.tldr: VITAL equips VLMs with dedicated physiological representations and numerical alignment to improve remote heart-rate measurement without sacrificing general visual understanding.

papers.abstract: Modern image generation largely relies on specialized generative models that leave the process of image construction implicit in learned parameters. We explore an alternative: general-purpose coding agents that construct images through executable programs. Our study of zero-shot drawing on AgentDrawBench, a 200-prompt benchmark, reveals a distinctive capability profile. Agents excel at preserving structure and satisfying precise visual constraints, achieving competitive results in domains where compositional accuracy matters more than photorealistic appearance, while remaining limited in perceptual richness. Their visual expressiveness varies with the drawing interface, and a qualitative study on reconstruction shows how procedural skills extracted from human demonstrations support different artistic media. We then examine code as an external visual language of thought: a structured, executable representation that agents can construct and inspect. We test it in visual question answering task and find reconstructed visual code retains substantial information for question answering and, in some domains, supports higher accuracy than the original image. These abilities raise a further question: do agents draw on a shared internal representation of scene content beyond a particular drawing program? We explore an internal visual language-of-thought hypothesis, in which a shared, compositionally structured representation supports visual operations across drawing languages. Cross-harness drawings and images assembled from independent single-pixel queries exhibit related layouts and tones. Agents also maintain self-generated room arrangements across viewpoints after visible drawings are removed. These results demonstrate that the coding agent would maintain a consistent and coherent world inside its imagine even before the harness gets involved and the generation starts.
authors: Hengguang Zhou, Yuanhao Ban, Jiaqi Feng, Xiaohuan Pei, Justin Cui, Cho-Jui Hsieh
bullets: On the 200-prompt AgentDrawBench, agents perform well when compositional accuracy and precise constraints matter more than photorealism.
Their expressiveness depends on the drawing interface, while procedural skills from human demonstrations transfer across artistic media.
Executable visual code retains substantial information for visual question answering and can outperform the original image in some domains.
Cross-harness and single-pixel experiments suggest agents maintain a shared, compositionally structured internal representation of scenes.
The findings indicate coherent scene understanding before image generation begins, though perceptual richness remains a limitation.
papers.selection_reason: Explores code as visual language of thought and internal scene consistency, transferable to multimodal and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: How Far Can Coding Agents Go in Visual Generation?
papers.tldr: Coding agents can generate structurally precise, executable visual representations and preserve scene information, but their visual richness remains limited.

papers.abstract: Current scaling law formulations suggest that increasing the number of unique samples in a dataset improves model performance, while repeated exposure to the same samples provides diminishing value. In this work, we examine this assumption for image self-distillation models. Through systematic experiments across diverse datasets, namely Maxar, SATLAS, Waymo, nuPlan, Ego4D, ImageNet, and YFCC15M, we demonstrate that the effects of sample repetition on downstream performance are non-trivial and dataset-dependent. We identify settings where repeatedly training on a smaller random subset can outperform training on a larger set of unique samples. This finding highlights a limitation of existing scaling laws. To address this gap, we propose a modified version of a Chinchilla-style scaling law that explicitly accounts for two factors: the number of unique samples and repetition per sample. This formulation provides a framework for understanding data-compute trade-offs and improves prediction in some regimes where repetition plays a central role, although its benefits are not consistent across datasets. Finally, we examine how subset selection and augmentation affect downstream performance.
authors: Alvard Barseghyan, Ani Vanyan, Hakob Tamazyan, Hrant Khachatrian
bullets: Finds that sample repetition has non-trivial, dataset-dependent effects across seven diverse image and video datasets.
Shows that repeatedly training on a smaller random subset can outperform training on more unique samples in some settings.
Proposes a Chinchilla-style scaling law incorporating both unique-sample count and repetition per sample.
The modified law improves prediction in some repetition-dominated regimes, but gains are inconsistent across datasets.
Also studies the effects of subset selection and data augmentation on downstream performance.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a modified scaling law for image self-distillation models that accounts for sample repetition, addressing a gap in current understanding of data efficiency for foundation models.
papers.title: Data Density Scaling Laws for Image Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: Image self-distillation does not follow a simple “more unique data is always better” rule: repetition can sometimes outperform larger unique datasets, motivating repetition-aware scaling laws.

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has become a widely adopted approach for aligning vision-language models (VLMs), yet the security of multimodal preference data remains largely unexplored. Existing preference poisoning attacks either corrupt explicit supervision signals or require visible triggers, making them detectable under human inspection. We introduce DPOison-VL, the first clean preference poisoning attack against VLM-DPO, which manipulates model alignment solely through imperceptible perturbations on a small fraction of training images, while leaving all prompts, responses, and preference annotations semantically intact. We formulate poison construction as a bilevel optimization and derive a gradient alignment surrogate that efficiently steers image perturbations toward the attacker-specified preference. We further introduce a preference displacement score for principled poison selection with provable first-order optimality under a fixed poison budget, and derive a sufficient condition for preference inversion. Extensive experiments across diverse attack tasks, different VLM architectures and scales, and baseline comparisons demonstrate that DPOison-VL achieves up to 98\% ASR with only 2\% poisoned data and exhibits cross-model transferability, while largely preserving clean accuracy and general utility. Our findings reveal a critical vulnerability in VLM-DPO, where imperceptible image perturbations in preference training data can silently redirect alignment.
bullets: Targets the largely unexplored security of multimodal preference data without altering prompts, responses, or preference labels.
Constructs poisons via bilevel optimization and a gradient-alignment surrogate to steer model preferences toward attacker-specified outcomes.
Uses a preference displacement score to select effective poisons under a fixed budget and derives a sufficient condition for preference inversion.
Reports up to 98% attack success with 2% poisoned data, cross-model transferability, and largely preserved clean accuracy and utility.
Scope: evaluates poisoning across multiple attack tasks, VLM architectures, scales, and baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Preference poisoning attack on VLM-DPO; relevant to multimodal foundation model alignment and security.
papers.title: DPOison-VL: Clean Preference Poisoning in Vision-Language Direct Preference Optimization
papers.tldr: DPOison-VL shows that imperceptible perturbations to a small fraction of preference-training images can silently redirect VLM alignment during DPO.

papers.abstract: 3D part assembly aims to reconstruct a complete shape from a set of unassembled parts by predicting a rigid SE(3) transformation for each part. Because the placement of a part is rarely determined by its own geometry, the task demands reasoning over the entire part set, and existing methods, which rely on pairwise relations or iterative generation and verification, scale poorly to objects with many parts. We present LLM2R, which casts part assembly as sequence modeling with a pretrained decoder-only large language model (LLM): a Point-BERT encoder and a Q-Former compress each part into a block of geometric tokens, the blocks of all parts are concatenated, and a causal LLM adapted with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) processes the sequence in one forward pass. Causal attention, however, lets the hidden states of a part observe only the parts that precede it. LLM2R therefore appends a block of learnable summary tokens after the last part: these tokens follow every part, so their states aggregate the whole assembly at a constant token cost, and a part-aware pose head fuses each part's states with them before predicting its rotation and translation. One architecture thus handles semantic and geometric assembly and predicts all poses in a single non-autoregressive pass. LLM2R achieves the highest part accuracy and success rate on all three PartNet categories, the best rotation error, translation error, and part accuracy on PartNeXt, and the lowest translation error and fastest inference on Breaking Bad, where only a fracture-specialized method is more accurate. Its advantage grows with the number of parts: at 100 parts it exceeds GARF by 33.5 points in part accuracy on Breaking Bad and Assembler by 29.1 points on PartNet, and it transfers zero-shot to unseen categories with more than 16 points higher part accuracy than the strongest of three baselines.
authors: Zhouhan Zhong, Qiuhong Shen, Xingyi Yang, Jinyi Xu, Xinchao Wang
bullets: Problem: Pairwise and iterative assembly methods struggle as the number of parts grows because placement depends on the full set.
Method: Point-BERT and a Q-Former encode each part into geometric-token blocks, which a LoRA-adapted causal LLM processes in one pass.
Key design: Learnable summary tokens aggregate information from all parts and are fused with each part’s states to predict rotation and translation.
Results: LLM2R achieves leading or competitive accuracy, pose errors, success rate, and inference speed across PartNet, PartNeXt, and Breaking Bad.
Scope: It transfers zero-shot to unseen categories and its advantage increases for assemblies with many parts.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-based 3D part assembly with geometric token sequence modeling; relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: LLM2R: From Large Language Models to 3D Reassemblers
papers.tldr: LLM2R reframes 3D part assembly as one-pass sequence modeling with an LLM, enabling scalable prediction of all part poses using global assembly context.

papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs are typically trained by first aligning a vision encoder with a language model via projector training on large image-caption datasets, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model. Despite its widespread use, the role of the projector training stage remains poorly understood. We find that (i) using only $10$ to $20\%$ of the data for training the projector already recovers most downstream performance gains, and (ii) projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving performance. These results suggest that projector training mainly performs a coarse alignment, which many different projectors achieve equally well. Motivated by these findings, we propose PORTAL, a training-free projector initialization that requires neither paired image-caption data nor gradient-based optimization, but only per-modality summary statistics. PORTAL computes an optimal-transport-based map between Gaussian approximations of the vision and language feature distributions on a shared principal subspace, so that the projector training stage can be skipped entirely. Without any paired data, PORTAL matches the standard pipeline trained on 558k image-caption pairs across six LLM backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks. It outperforms that pipeline in $3$ of $7$ (vision encoder, LLM) settings and reaches an average $98\%$ of its score across the other four.
authors: Fabian Gr\"oger, Na\"el Ouerghemi, Shuo Wen, Maria Brbi\'c
bullets: Using only 10–20% of projector-training data recovers most downstream gains.
Projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated with little performance loss.
PORTAL maps Gaussian approximations of vision and language features via optimal transport on a shared principal subspace.
It uses only per-modality summary statistics and requires neither paired image-caption data nor gradient optimization.
Across six backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks, PORTAL matches the standard 558k-pair pipeline; it outperforms it in 3 of 7 settings and averages 98% of its score in the other 4.
papers.selection_reason: Core multimodal LLM alignment research; analyzes projector training and proposes a training-free initialization.
papers.title: Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Projector training in multimodal LLMs mainly provides coarse alignment, enabling PORTAL to replace it with a training-free, statistics-based initialization that nearly matches the standard pipeline without paired data.

papers.abstract: Target-aware multimodal instruction selection requires useful examples and an appropriate balance of supervision. Sample-level rankings can overrepresent similar content without optimizing this balance; group-level methods face coarse units, predefined set-level validation signals, and costly or inaccurate mixture search. We propose CLIVO, a target-aware framework connecting fine-grained semantic allocation, automatically learned validation objectives, and differentiable mixture search. Specifically, semantic clusters provide independently adjustable shares at the hundred-cluster scale. Correlations between per-example merged-proxy losses and real probe performance identify target-relevant validation examples; learned nonnegative weights combine their losses into an objective. A single backward pass through the merged proxy supplies gradients for all shares, avoiding an additional mixture-response regression model. Selecting 100K instructions from an 8M pool, CLIVO attains 97.2% of the full-data four-target average score with only 1.25% of the data. It improves on the strongest evaluated selection baseline by 1.16 points using random within-cluster sampling; combining learned quotas with sample ranking increases this advantage to 1.55 points. Analyses show that finer units benefit most targets, short-trained experts preserve mixture responses, sample weighting retains useful validation information, and direct search consistently reduces the learned objective. CLIVO also supports interpretable allocation, modular selection, and reuse across targets and granularities.
authors: Yuhan Wang, Rui Hu, Batian Di, Tan Jiang, Dongsheng Ma, Leichao Dong, Yuanzi Li, Yalin Feng
bullets: Addresses redundancy in sample-level ranking and inefficiency or coarseness in group-level instruction selection.
Uses fine-grained semantic clusters with independently adjustable shares, learned nonnegative validation-example weights, and gradient-based mixture search.
Selects 100K instructions from an 8M pool while reaching 97.2% of the full-data average score across four targets using 1.25% of the data.
Outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline by 1.16 points with random within-cluster sampling and by 1.55 points when combined with sample ranking.
Supports interpretable, modular allocation and reuse across targets and granularities; scope includes the evaluated multimodal instruction-selection setting.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes differentiable instruction mixing for multimodal instruction tuning, directly relevant to multimodal LLM training and data selection.
papers.title: CLIVO: Differentiable Cluster-Based Instruction Mixing with Learned Validation Objectives
papers.tldr: CLIVO selects a small, target-aware instruction mixture by learning validation objectives and differentiably optimizing semantic-cluster quotas.

papers.abstract: Geospatial reasoning links VLMs to real-world action and decision making. Reliable reasoning requires accurate spatial information and effective spatial representations. However, current VLMs obtain this information mainly from language and vision. At larger geographic scales, limited visual observations make it difficult to establish accurate spatial references and recover precise spatial relations. This leads to a bottleneck for VLM spatial perception and reasoning. This paper proposes that geospatial vector geometry can become a native spatial modality within a VLM and introduces GeoVec-VLM. First, we develop a structured geometry representation that preserves the spatial structure and arrangement of vector objects, building an explicit spatial basis. Second, we introduce a geometry interaction strategy that brings this basis into multimodal computation, where it interacts with visual content and language references according to the queried spatial relations. Together, these designs allow perception and reasoning to operate on shared geometric references. Across five spatial reasoning tasks, GeoVec-VLM improves mean accuracy by about 11\% relative to the strongest baseline, maintains its gains under geographic transfer, and shows greater geometric consistency. Our results show that geospatial vector geometry offers a promising internal spatial basis for VLM spatial reasoning. https://github.com/TXFR/GeoVector-VLM
authors: Huang Fei, Boyi Chen, Hao Xue, Yang Yue, Yehong Xu, Xiaofang Zhou
bullets: Current VLMs struggle with precise spatial references at large geographic scales because visual observations are limited.
The model uses a structured geometry representation that preserves vector-object arrangements as an explicit spatial basis.
A geometry interaction strategy combines this basis with visual content and language references based on queried spatial relations.
Across five spatial reasoning tasks, it improves mean accuracy by about 11% over the strongest baseline and retains gains under geographic transfer.
The model also demonstrates greater geometric consistency, supporting vector geometry as an internal basis for VLM reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces geospatial vector geometry as a native spatial modality for VLMs, directly advancing spatial reasoning in multimodal models.
papers.title: Geospatial Vector Geometry as a Native Spatial Modality for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: GeoVec-VLM integrates geospatial vector geometry as a native spatial modality to improve large-scale spatial perception and reasoning in vision-language models.

papers.abstract: We present Co-DSL, a framework in which users and LLMs co-design reusable spatial concepts for layout generation. In the first stage, our system allows users to create a library of personalized operations. To add a concept, a user provides a description, which the LLM converts into an initial implementation. The user can then observe the concept's execution behavior over example scenarios and provide lightweight feedback to the LLM, which revises the concept's implementation logic. In the second stage, given a library, an LLM can author a layout program that meets a new layout request from a user. Executing a layout program instantiates a concept-graph, a declarative composition of library concepts. In this way, we require the LLM only to specify which concepts should hold, while we use a solver to search for a layout that satisfies them. Across five spatial layout domains, we find that Co-DSL libraries let LLMs capture layout patterns that are challenging for prior fixed-operation systems, and demonstrate that our concept-graph representation is needed for LLMs to reliably compose concepts together. We further find that Co-DSL lets LLMs author generative layout programs that expose high-level parametric controls users can manipulate to explore a distribution of related layouts without re-prompting.
authors: R. Kenny Jones, Jiajun Wu, Maneesh Agrawala
bullets: Users describe personalized spatial operations; the LLM implements and revises them based on lightweight feedback and observed examples.
For new requests, the LLM authors a layout program represented as a concept graph, specifying which concepts should hold.
A solver searches for layouts satisfying the composed concepts, reducing the need for the LLM to generate exact layouts directly.
Across five spatial layout domains, the framework captures patterns beyond fixed-operation systems and reliably composes concepts.
Generated programs expose parametric controls for exploring related layouts without repeated prompting.
papers.selection_reason: Human-LLM co-design of reusable spatial concepts for layout generation, relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Co-DSL: Human-LLM Co-design of Reusable Spatial Concepts for Layout Generation
papers.tldr: Co-DSL lets users and LLMs collaboratively create reusable spatial concepts that LLMs compose into solver-generated layouts with high-level controls.

papers.abstract: A GUI agent decides which action to take and where to take it; we ask how a small grounding model should receive the action type. Fine-tuning Qwen2-VL-2B with LoRA on Android in the Wild, we compare a flat baseline with five ways of supplying the type under matched data, compute, and decoding: an auxiliary loss, a hard-routed action word, an additive learned embedding, a prepended learned token, and the type written into the prompt. With five seeds, an episode-clustered bootstrap, and seed-level paired tests, the ranking on a mixed stream is clear: the auxiliary loss, the additive embedding, and the prompt word each gain five to seven hit@0.10 points over the baseline, while hard routing and the prepended token are not distinguishable from it. Much of that gain is protection from a preprocessing choice of ours rather than a spatial prior. Our serializer clamps the off-screen touch point AITW records for type events to the origin; that class degrades the baseline's click grounding, and removing it lifts the baseline by nearly seven points, after which no mechanism's hit rate beats it and the intervals exclude a two-point effect, though the auxiliary loss still shortens the average miss; on a stream of taps and swipes none helps. Whether this generalizes beyond one serialization is open. For deployment, the pipeline's margin over the baseline with predicted rather than gold types is not established (+0.016, 95% interval [-0.017, +0.052]), and a wrong type collapses every model conditioned at inference. The prepended token does not help at the shared learning rate, where its rows barely move from initialization; trained ten times faster it reaches the level of the other three, with a margin three seeds do not establish. We also document a silent failure: injecting conditioning through inputs_embeds makes Qwen2-VL fall back to 1-D positions for image tokens, costing nine points.
bullets: Fine-tuning Qwen2-VL-2B with LoRA compared five conditioning mechanisms against a flat baseline under matched settings.
Auxiliary loss, additive embedding, and prompt-word conditioning initially improved mixed-stream hit@0.10 by 5–7 points; hard routing and a prepended token did not.

Clamping off-screen touch points to the origin caused much of the apparent gain: after removing this artifact, no method outperformed the baseline, though auxiliary loss reduced average miss distance.
No method helped on taps and swipes; predicted action types gave no established deployment margin, and wrong types degraded all conditioned models.
A separate inputs_embeds implementation issue caused 1-D image-token positions and a nine-point performance loss; generalization beyond this serialization remains open.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates how to condition GUI grounding models on action types, relevant to spatial intelligence and multimodal models.
papers.title: Decoupling What from Where: How Should a Small GUI Grounding Model Receive the Action Type?
papers.tldr: For a small GUI grounding model, action-type conditioning appears helpful mainly because of a preprocessing artifact, not a robust spatial benefit.

papers.abstract: Generative vision-language models (VLMs) such as Qwen-VL and LLaVA achieve strong zero-shot performance on tasks overlapping with their pretraining distribution, yet fail on specialized domains where the required discriminative features were never learned, a regime we term distant out-of-distribution (OOD). Standard adaptation methods cannot overcome this representational absence because they operate within the encoder's existing feature space. However, VLMs retain a robust descriptive capacity even when discrimination collapses: a model that cannot classify a medical scan can still articulate its visual patterns. Exploiting this asymmetry, we introduce Inductive Visual Logic (IVL), a training-free framework that constructs classification knowledge from the model's surviving descriptive ability. IVL extracts visual traits from few-shot support images through dual-mode prompting, combining semantic descriptions with primitive visual observations, and organizes them into per-class trait dictionaries. At inference, hierarchical filtering identifies spatially grounded trait evidence for classification. Across multiple distant-OOD benchmarks, IVL achieves the highest aggregate accuracy under two VLM backbones while producing interpretable, trait-traceable predictions.
bullets: Addresses distant OOD settings where required discriminative features are absent from the VLM’s learned representation.
Uses dual-mode prompting to extract semantic and primitive visual traits from few-shot support images.
Builds per-class trait dictionaries and applies hierarchical, spatially grounded trait filtering at inference.
Achieves the highest aggregate accuracy across multiple distant-OOD benchmarks with two VLM backbones.
Produces interpretable predictions that can be traced to visual traits.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free framework for VLM adaptation to distant OOD domains by extracting spatially grounded visual traits, bridging descriptive and discriminative capabilities.
papers.title: Inductive Visual Logic for Few-Shot Out-Of-Distribution Adaptation in VLMs
papers.tldr: IVL enables few-shot adaptation to distant OOD visual domains by turning VLMs’ descriptive abilities into interpretable classification rules without training.

papers.abstract: There has been significant work on understanding the In-Context Learning capabilities of Large Language Models, especially on the induction circuit. For a few-shot classification task, the induction circuit leverages linear representations of each labeled example in-context in order to classify an unlabeled query. However, few works focus on how those linear representations are built in the first place. Leveraging the expressivity of the vision modality compared to text, we uncover a Shared Discriminative Geometry (SDG) inside Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs). It is a low-dimensional space, shared across all image classification tasks, in which in-context images are compressed into linearly separable representations later used to perform classification. We observe that this is the result of the model performing a dimensionality reduction of vision representations in early layers. In order to explain this phenomenon: (1) We show analytically that linear self-attention can perform a dimensionality reduction by projecting in-context data onto its principal components, with each layer implementing one gradient descent step toward this objective. (2) We provide evidence that trained LVLMs reduce the dimensionality of vision representations in early layers via a similar mechanism.
bullets: Addresses how linear representations for in-context classification are formed, not just how they are used.
Identifies a Shared Discriminative Geometry (SDG) where in-context images become linearly separable.
Finds that vision representations undergo dimensionality reduction in the model’s early layers.
Analytically shows linear self-attention can project in-context data toward principal components through layer-wise gradient steps.
Provides evidence that trained LVLMs use a similar dimensionality-reduction mechanism.
papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic analysis of in-context learning in large vision-language models, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Are In-Context Images Worth 10 Dimensions?
papers.tldr: LVLMs compress in-context images into a shared, low-dimensional geometry that enables linear classification across image tasks.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, yet the visual and textual evidence supporting the generated responses remains difficult to identify. Faithful token attribution explains an LVLM's response by assigning scores that rank image and prompt tokens by how much the model relies on them, such that removing higher-ranked tokens causes the likelihood of the generated response to drop more rapidly. However, existing token-attribution methods have been developed mainly for text-based language models, and our empirical study reveals two challenges when complex multimodal sources are involved. First, the joint image-text attribution can underrepresent visual evidence relative to text, obscuring the image regions supporting the response. Second, visual evidence may influence the generated response through multiple intermediate reasoning paths, while existing methods trace only a limited subset of these paths, causing important visual contributions to be underestimated. Motivated by these insights, we introduce VTrace, a multimodal token-attribution framework that traces input contributions through intermediate reasoning and calibrates attribution scores across modalities. VTrace constructs pairwise attributions that highlight token-specific contributions and aggregates all forward attribution paths in closed form to account for both direct and indirect contributions. Cross-modal calibration then rescales image and text attribution scores using modality contributions estimated from response-likelihood changes, enabling a unified ranking of input tokens. Evaluations against seven baselines across six visual reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the superior attribution faithfulness. Project page: https://vtrace-attribution.github.io/.
bullets: Existing attribution methods can understate visual evidence and miss contributions flowing through intermediate reasoning steps.
VTrace computes pairwise token attributions and aggregates all direct and indirect forward paths in closed form.
It calibrates image and text scores using modality contributions inferred from response-likelihood changes.
Evaluated against seven baselines on six visual reasoning benchmarks, VTrace achieves stronger attribution faithfulness.
Scope: the method focuses on identifying input-token evidence supporting LVLM responses.
papers.selection_reason: Faithful token attribution for vision-language reasoning, relevant to multimodal foundation model interpretability.
papers.title: Tracing the Evidence: Faithful Token Attribution Through Vision-Language Reasoning
papers.tldr: VTrace improves faithful evidence tracing in vision-language models by capturing indirect reasoning paths and balancing image–text token attributions.

papers.abstract: Advancing spatial intelligence in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is bottlenecked by the scarcity of complex, scalable 3D question-answer (QA) data. While manual annotation is labor-intensive, directly utilizing LLMs to synthesize these QA pairs often fails due to their inherent deficiencies in spatial and geometric computation. We introduce Exemplar2VQA, a scalable exemplar-driven visual question answering generation framework that rapidly synthesizes large-scale spatial QA pairs in simulated environments via multi-agent coding. By equipping collaborative agents with a meticulously designed library of geometric utilities, Exemplar2VQA bypasses LLMs' spatial reasoning flaws through deterministic code execution. Crucially, the framework exhibits remarkable versatility: taking diverse static object-centric spatial query templates as exemplars, it seamlessly and autonomously scales them into massive, high-fidelity synthetic datasets. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL (3B/7B) exclusively on Exemplar2VQA-generated synthetic indoor data yields significant performance improvements across various diverse benchmarks. Furthermore, its effectiveness is not limited to in-domain indoor datasets but also robustly extends to outdoor and mixed-scene benchmarks. These results establish Exemplar2VQA as a scalable and powerful paradigm for bridging the sim-to-real gap in Embodied AI. Our code is at https://github.com/yingjiayu12/Exemplar2VQA
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and high annotation cost of complex 3D spatial QA data.
Uses collaborative agents with deterministic geometric code execution to avoid LLM spatial-reasoning errors.
Expands diverse static object-centric spatial query templates into large synthetic datasets in simulated environments.
Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL models on the generated indoor data improves performance across multiple benchmarks.
Shows transfer beyond indoor scenes to outdoor and mixed-scene settings, supporting sim-to-real applications.
papers.selection_reason: Scalable spatial QA generation framework that directly targets spatial intelligence in MLLMs.
papers.title: Exemplar2VQA: A Scalable Exemplar-Driven Visual Question Answering Generation Framework via Multi-Agent Coding
papers.tldr: Exemplar2VQA uses multi-agent coding and geometric utilities to efficiently generate scalable, high-quality 3D spatial VQA data from exemplars, improving MLLM spatial intelligence across indoor, outdoor, and mixed-scene benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Current explanation methods for contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP mainly identify important regions without showing how to change the input in order to get a target prediction. We introduce Mask-guided Adaptive Counterfactual Explanations (MACE), a targeted visual counterfactual method designed specifically for CLIP zero-shot classification. MACE constructs an editable region from either source attribution or source-target attribution differences and expands the mask only when needed to reach a specified target class. A latent diffusion inpainting model then modifies the selected region, while a frozen CLIP model provides modification guidance and anchors the remaining image content to the original input. We evaluate MACE on ImageNet, Food-101, Oxford Pets, and CUB-200. The source-mask variant achieves the highest target top-1 success rate across all four datasets, while the difference-mask variant produces the smallest pixel level and perceptual changes and the best realism scores. Both variants improve proximity and realism over a Stable Diffusion-only baseline using the same generative backbone. These results show that adaptive mask-guided editing produces effective CLIP counterfactuals. They further reveal a tradeoff between counterfactual validity and source-image preservation.
bullets: Addresses the lack of targeted visual counterfactual explanations for CLIP, beyond merely identifying important regions.
Builds an editable mask from source or source–target attribution and expands it only as needed to reach the target class.
Uses latent-diffusion inpainting guided by a frozen CLIP model while anchoring unedited content to the input.
Evaluated on ImageNet, Food-101, Oxford Pets, and CUB-200; source masks maximize target success, while difference masks minimize visual changes and improve realism.
Finds a tradeoff between achieving the target prediction and preserving the source image.
papers.selection_reason: Counterfactual explanation method for CLIP, relevant to multimodal foundation model interpretability.
papers.title: Targeted Visual Counterfactual Explanations for Contrastive Vision-Language Model
papers.tldr: MACE generates targeted, realistic image edits that steer CLIP toward a chosen class while preserving the original content.

papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of text-to-image (T2I) generation, robust evaluation becomes critical yet challenging, as traditional metrics fail to capture fine-grained alignment and generative artifacts. While large multimodal models (LMMs) are increasingly adopted as evaluators, existing benchmarks typically study semantic understanding, quality perception, and authenticity identification in isolation, while largely neglecting responsibility detection. This leaves a gap in unified and comprehensive validation. To bridge this gap, we introduce SQUARE-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark that systematically evaluates LMM capabilities as evaluators of AI-generated images across four aspects: Semantics, Quality, Authenticity, and Responsibility. SQUARE-Bench introduces a granular taxonomy of 38 sub-dimensions to evaluate nearly 10K AI-generated images sampled from 22 diverse models, ranging from legacy to state-of-the-art generators, complemented by over 3K real-world images. The images are annotated with curated question-answering pairs. Extensive experiments on 23 LMMs reveal that top proprietary models, such as Gemini-3-Pro, already outperform the individual human expert baseline. However, the performance gap between models remains significant, exhibiting notable disparities in fine-grained inference and domain-specific robustness. Beyond benchmarking, we conduct a proof-of-concept study of LMM-guided iterative editing, in which dimension-specific LMMs provide diagnostic feedback to fixed image editors. The resulting guided system yields selective improvements in semantics, authenticity, and responsibility, while exhibiting a consistent visual-quality trade-off. SQUARE-Bench can serve as both a diagnostic tool for characterizing LMM evaluator capabilities and studying their use in T2I generation refinement. The benchmark and dataset will be released upon publication.
bullets: Addresses the lack of comprehensive evaluation benchmarks that include responsibility detection alongside existing assessment capabilities.
Evaluates 23 LMMs on nearly 10K AI-generated images from 22 generators and over 3K real images using 38 fine-grained sub-dimensions.
Finds that leading proprietary models can surpass an individual human expert baseline, but substantial gaps remain in fine-grained reasoning and domain robustness.
A proof-of-concept LMM-guided editing system improves semantics, authenticity, and responsibility selectively, while consistently trading off visual quality.
The benchmark is intended both to diagnose LMM evaluator capabilities and to support T2I generation refinement.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for evaluating large multimodal models as AI-generated image assessors, relevant to multimodal foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: Evaluating the Evaluators: Diagnosing Large Multimodal Models for AI-Generated Image Assessment
papers.tldr: SQUARE-Bench provides a unified benchmark for assessing how well large multimodal models evaluate AI-generated images across semantics, quality, authenticity, and responsibility.

papers.abstract: Multimodal model merging aims to consolidate task experts into a single model that retains their complementary capabilities. Most unimodal model merging methods combine expert updates within individual layers, and multimodal approaches largely follow this design. However, an expert update changes the representations passed to subsequent layers, allowing its influence to propagate across depth and affect how visual and textual information interact. When visual and language updates are combined, later updates act on inputs already modified by earlier ones, coupling their effects. This poses two challenges: (1) how to characterize the multimodal influence of individual expert updates across depth, and (2) how to jointly combine expert updates based on their multimodal influence. To address these challenges, we propose TAC-Merge for tracing and coordinating cross-layer influence in multimodal model merging. It contains two modules, i.e., multimodal influence mapping (MIM) and coupled merge control (CMC). MIM constructs graphs of update effects and uses Ricci curvature together with expert predictions to define a shared fusion objective. CMC models interactions among coefficient adjustments and jointly optimizes regional weights to synthesize one shared model. Experiments across diverse multimodal tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of TAC-Merge in consolidating complementary expert capabilities and supporting generalization to unseen tasks.
bullets: Addresses cross-layer propagation and coupling between visual and textual expert updates.
Uses multimodal influence mapping (MIM) to build update-effect graphs and define a shared fusion objective with Ricci curvature and expert predictions.
Uses coupled merge control (CMC) to jointly optimize regional merge weights and synthesize one shared model.
Experiments across diverse multimodal tasks show consolidation of complementary capabilities and generalization to unseen tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-layer influence tracing for merging multimodal expert models; relevant to multimodal foundation model development.
papers.title: Tracing and Coordinating Cross-Layer Influence for Multimodal Model Merging
papers.tldr: TAC-Merge improves multimodal model merging by tracing how visual and language expert updates influence later layers and jointly coordinating their combination.

papers.abstract: Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8.
authors: Xin Gao, Yifan Yang, Xin Li, Pan Wang, Yan Li, Muzhao Tian, Mingxi Cheng, Bei Liu, Kai Qiu, Qi Dai, Dong Chen, Yue Dong, Leandros Tassiulas, Rex Ying, Ji Li, Chong Luo
bullets: Targets editable, verifiable code generation for slides, posters, dashboards, and similar visual artifacts.
Represents designs as attributable design graphs covering canvas elements and their relationships.
Uses deterministic code/rendering verifiers for parsable properties and a VLM judge with sample-specific Visual Graph Rubrics for non-parsable visual qualities.
Optimizes the reward channels with reinforcement learning and per-channel normalization to improve planning, aesthetics, and correctness.

On a benchmark separating correctness from visual quality, AesCode improves visual quality over same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points for its 8B and 32B models, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces AesCode, a framework for generating code for visual artifacts using a VLM judge and decoupled cross-modal rewards to improve spatial planning and aesthetic quality.
papers.title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards
papers.tldr: AesCode improves code-generated visual artifacts by combining reference-image aesthetic guidance with graph-grounded, decoupled rewards for correctness and visual quality.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have advanced rapidly, but most remain optimized for single-image inputs. Multi-image reasoning is costly because each image adds many visual tokens, increasing encoding and attention demands. Existing techniques that address the above issue, including visual token pruning, token merging, visual token compression, learned resampling, hierarchical compression, retrieval-augmented visual reasoning, and memory-based architectures, have largely been designed for single-image scenarios, where redundancy is primarily spatial and local. Multi-image reasoning introduces additional challenges: redundancy may occur across images, task-relevant evidence may be sparse or distributed, and aggressive per-image compression can remove details needed for comparison, counting, temporal reasoning, retrieval, or evidence grounding. Moreover, existing token-reduction methods are often either (i) training-free but inference-inefficient, typically relying on accessing attention matrices to get token-importance that may be impractical to access with memory-efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention, or (ii) training-dependent, requiring the base MLLM to be retrained or adapted to a new compressed-token paradigm. In this work, we study scalable multi-image reasoning and understanding without retraining the base model and without accessing attention matrices at inference time. To this end, we propose mmVB, a lightweight plug-and-play module that assigns query-conditioned per-image token budgets via cross-image context, adding only 1.6M trainable parameters while reducing visual input tokens by 9x. This reduction yields 5x faster time-to-first-token and 7x fewer prefill FLOPs, while maintaining 94.4% of full-resolution accuracy across eight multi-image reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Aimon Rahman, Joymallya Chakraborty, Vidit Bansal, Abhishek Dan
bullets: Multi-image inputs are expensive because each image contributes many visual tokens, with relevant evidence potentially sparse or distributed across images.
mmVB uses cross-image context to assign query-conditioned, per-image token budgets.
The lightweight plug-in adds 1.6M trainable parameters and reduces visual input tokens by 9×.
It delivers 5× faster time-to-first-token and 7× fewer prefill FLOPs while retaining 94.4% of full-resolution accuracy across eight benchmarks.
The approach targets multi-image reasoning without modifying or retraining the base model.
papers.selection_reason: Query-conditioned visual token budgeting for efficient multi-image MLLM reasoning, directly relevant to token pruning and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Visual Tokens on Demand: Visual Budgeting for Scalable and Efficient Multi-Image Reasoning in Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: mmVB enables efficient multi-image reasoning by dynamically allocating visual-token budgets across images without retraining the base multimodal LLM or accessing attention matrices.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in visual perception and spatial reasoning, leading to growing interest in using them as high-level planners for embodied AI. However, physical tasks require models to integrate spatial information, reason over temporal states, and generate multi-step plans under various constraints, raising the question of whether current VLMs can reliably support such reasoning and planning independently of execution. We introduce Plan-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating the high-level reasoning and multi-step planning capabilities of VLMs relevant to embodied worlds, while isolating the influence of action execution. It covers three complementary dimensions, spanning 16 subclasses and 699 curated samples. Extensive evaluation of 28 VLMs reveals room for improvement, with even the strongest model achieving only 75.0% accuracy. We further find that model scaling generally improves these capabilities. Ablation studies also indicate larger models show increasing potential as high-level planners. Overall, Plan-Bench provides a lightweight probe for evaluating VLMs' reasoning and planning capabilities relevant to embodied environments and assessing their potential as decision makers for physical tasks. Our benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/MinneFeng/Plan-Bench.
authors: Juntong Feng, Qingan Liu, Jingru Dong, Yue Zhu, Weiming Zheng, Yujie Cheng, Xinzhe Han, Shuai Hao, Yunzhi Zhuge, Haiwen Diao, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Evaluates VLM planning independently of action execution in embodied-world scenarios.
Covers three dimensions, 16 subclasses, and 699 curated samples.
Evaluation of 28 VLMs finds substantial room for improvement; the best reaches 75.0% accuracy.
Larger models generally perform better and show greater potential as high-level planners.
Provides a lightweight benchmark and code for assessing embodied reasoning and planning.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for VLM high-level reasoning and multi-step planning in embodied worlds, directly relevant to embodied decision making.
papers.title: Plan-Bench: Can Existing VLMs Go Well Beyond Perception to Reason and Plan in Embodied Worlds?
papers.tldr: Plan-Bench shows that current VLMs still struggle with reliable multi-step reasoning and planning for embodied tasks, despite benefits from scaling.

papers.abstract: Visual reasoning is an important capability for vision-language models (VLMs) to understand visual evidence, spatial structure, constraints, and state changes. Existing evaluations mainly rely on real-world data or procedurally generated tasks. Real-world data preserve natural complexity, while procedural games provide controllable generation and verifiable solutions. However, it remains unclear whether abilities measured in toy games correspond to real-world visual reasoning and whether game examples can support transfer. We introduce Game2Real-Bench, a benchmark that studies these connections across four capability groups, including fine-grained perception, spatial reasoning, constraint reasoning, and sequential planning. We construct 1,000 procedurally generated game samples with executable verification and curate 400 real-world samples aligned by shared reasoning requirements rather than visual similarity. We evaluate 25 representative VLMs and observe strong game-to-real consistency, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.935. We further study one-shot game-to-real transfer on four models. Constraint reasoning improves for several models, while fine-grained perception declines with game demonstrations. We also construct Game2Real-Dataset with nearly 24K verified game samples across 18 tasks and 65 QA families. Our benchmark, dataset, and code are available at https://github.com/QingAnLiu/Game2Real-Bench.
authors: Qingan Liu, Juntong Feng, Yue Zhu, Yujie Cheng, Xinzhe Han, Shuai Hao, Yunzhi Zhuge, Haiwen Diao, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Evaluates VLMs across fine-grained perception, spatial reasoning, constraint reasoning, and sequential planning.
Pairs 1,000 procedurally generated, executable-verified game samples with 400 real-world samples sharing reasoning requirements.
Reports strong game-to-real consistency across 25 VLMs, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.935.
One-shot game-to-real transfer improves constraint reasoning for several models but can hurt fine-grained perception.
Also releases nearly 24K verified game samples spanning 18 tasks and 65 QA families.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark studying VLM visual and spatial reasoning, including game-to-real transfer of reasoning capabilities.
papers.title: Game2Real-Bench: Do Toy Games Reveal and Transfer to Real-World Visual Reasoning?
papers.tldr: Game2Real-Bench finds that performance on verified toy-game tasks strongly reflects real-world visual reasoning, but game demonstrations transfer unevenly across capabilities.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) that segment from language must pass the location of the referent to a pixel decoder. The dominant interface compresses it into the hidden state of a single [SEG] token, a d-dimensional vector with no spatial index, and leaves the decoder, which never sees the expression, to recover the referent's extent. We show that the VLM already computes a better signal: the [SEG] token's attention over the image tokens, which is defined on the patch grid by construction. Probing a frozen segmentation VLM, we find that this attention yields 18 to 22 more gIoU than the [SEG] hidden state when read by the same probe, that it gains nothing from the image where the hidden state does, and that it is concentrated in the late layers. Building on these findings, we introduce AttnSeg, which replaces the [SEG] embedding with this attention as the decoder's prompt. A learned, signed combination of the attention heads forms a dense spatial prompt, and an attention-guidance objective supervises it directly.
