A two-stage recipe first trains the VLM to localize without the decoder, then trains the decoder to refine, within the budget of standard fine-tuning. Applied to Sa2VA, AttnSeg improves ReasonSeg by 6.4 gIoU and GS-Eval by 10.2 at 4B (4.2 and 9.6 over the same model fine-tuned on the same data), and by 8.8 and 11.3 at 14B. The gains reach 13 to 18 gIoU on object parts, multiple objects, and single objects, where the referent must be singled out, and are negligible on stuff regions, which the decoder already recovers unaided. Code and models are available at https://eslambakr.github.io/attseg_project_page/
authors: Eslam Abdelrahman, Hamza Omar Alkaf, Yuheng Li, Siddharth Srinivasan Iyer, Nanxuan Zhao, Eli Shechtman, Krishna Kumar Singh, Mohamed Elhoseiny
bullets: The standard [SEG] embedding discards spatial information, forcing the pixel decoder to infer the referent’s extent.
[SEG]-token attention over image patches is a stronger localization signal, yielding 18–22 higher gIoU with the same probe and concentrating in late layers.
AttnSeg learns a signed combination of attention heads as a dense spatial prompt and directly supervises it with attention guidance.
A two-stage training recipe separates VLM localization from decoder refinement within standard fine-tuning.
On Sa2VA, AttnSeg improves ReasonSeg and GS-Eval, especially for single objects, multiple objects, and object parts; gains are negligible for stuff regions.
papers.selection_reason: Uses VLM attention as a spatial prompt for segmentation, improving spatial grounding and fitting multimodal LLM and spatial intelligence topics.
papers.title: Segment Where You Look: Attention as the Interface Between Language Models and Segmenters
papers.tldr: AttnSeg improves language-guided image segmentation by using the VLM’s spatial [SEG]-token attention instead of its non-spatial hidden state as the decoder interface.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric and multi-view relationships that remain implicit in RGB observations. Geometry foundation models recover this structure from RGB, but existing methods either fuse the estimated features with visual tokens and learn to use them from question answering alone, or align VLM latents with geometry features. Capturing geometry, however, does not ensure its use: zeroing the aligned latents of a released feature-alignment model leaves its accuracy unchanged. We introduce GeoReader, a framework that learns geometric representations for the VLM that reads them. First, we train lightweight Geometric Readers to produce continuous input tokens, supervising them with geometry descriptions decoded by a frozen VLM, so that the Readers express geometry in a form the target model can already read. We then freeze the Readers to preserve this interface while fine-tuning the VLM on spatial QA, with geometry injection conditioned on the question. Geometry descriptions serve only as training targets: at inference, the VLM answers directly from the continuous geometric tokens without generating a geometry chain of thought. With geometry predicted from RGB images, our approach reaches 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and, with a multi-source QA mixture, an average of 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B. These results suggest that a useful geometric representation is one the receiving model can use, not merely one from which geometry can be reconstructed.
authors: Rong Li, Shijie Li, Jiangyong Huang, Lingdong Kong, Jiaming Zhou, Dongyue Lu, Zeying Gong, Baoxiong Jia, Junwei Liang, Siyuan Huang
bullets: Targets VLM difficulty with metric and multi-view relationships implicit in RGB observations.
Trains lightweight Geometric Readers to convert geometry into continuous tokens aligned with representations the frozen VLM can interpret.
Fine-tunes the VLM for question-conditioned geometry use while keeping the Readers fixed; no geometry chain-of-thought is needed at inference.
Achieves 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny and averages 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks in the reported Qwen-based settings.
Shows that reconstructible geometry features are insufficient unless the receiving VLM actually uses them.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces geometry-aware continuous tokens to improve spatial reasoning in VLMs, fitting spatial intelligence and geometry-aware multimodal modeling.
papers.title: GeoReader: Learning Latent Geometry for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: GeoReader teaches vision-language models to directly use learned geometric tokens for stronger spatial reasoning from RGB images.

papers.abstract: Reliable robot autonomy requires reasoning about the world from partial and noisy observations. However, many perception systems model only visible scene regions, rely on fixed semantic categories, and assume reliable sensor measurements. These assumptions break under occlusion, novel object encounters, and sensor degradation. In this paper, I present a research vision for incompleteness-aware scene understanding. I organize this vision around three fundamental challenges: incomplete evidence, incomplete knowledge, and incomplete sensor reliability. I discuss my research contributions toward addressing these challenges through amodal perception, semantic occupancy forecasting, open-world scene understanding, label-efficient learning, and uncertainty-guided multi-modal fusion. Building on these contributions, I outline future research directions toward belief-centric 4D scene representations. These representations aim to jointly model geometry, semantics, motion, and uncertainty. I also discuss active sensing and safe adaptation strategies that allow robots to reduce uncertainty through interaction. The goal is to develop calibrated and actionable scene representations that support reliable autonomy in dynamic, open-world environments.
bullets: Identifies three challenges: incomplete observations, incomplete semantic knowledge, and uncertain sensor reliability.
Proposes addressing them with amodal perception, semantic occupancy forecasting, open-world understanding, label-efficient learning, and uncertainty-guided multimodal fusion.
Envisions belief-centric 4D scene representations combining geometry, semantics, motion, and uncertainty.
Highlights active sensing and safe adaptation as ways for robots to reduce uncertainty through interaction.
Focuses on calibrated, actionable representations rather than assuming complete visibility or fixed categories.
papers.selection_reason: Incompleteness-aware spatial scene understanding and belief-centric 4D representations for robot autonomy, relevant to embodied AI, spatial intelligence, world models, and 3D vision.
papers.title: Perception Beyond the Visible: Incompleteness-Aware Scene Understanding for Robot Autonomy
papers.tldr: A research vision for robot perception that explicitly models missing evidence, unknown objects, and unreliable sensors to enable safer autonomy in dynamic open-world environments.

papers.abstract: Combining pretrained models is a common strategy for building AI systems, whether by aligning a vision encoder with a language model or merging fine-tuned checkpoints. However, finding compatible pairs typically requires costly empirical search, as compatibility is known only after alignment or merging. We propose COMPASS (COMPatibility ASsessment Score), a theoretically motivated diagnostic that estimates whether a model pair will be compatible prior to alignment or merging. Building on the observation that representational convergence is most robust at the level of local neighborhoods, COMPASS decomposes model compatibility into two cheap-to-compute axes: a pair-specific ease, defined as the $k$-NN overlap between the two encoders, and a paradigm-level ceiling, capturing the maximum overlap their training paradigms allow. Together, these two axes provide a ranking of candidate model pairs and prescribe how to act on each pair: (i) prioritize pairs that already agree and whose paradigms are compatible, (ii) invest additional compute on pairs with compatible paradigms but low initial agreement, (iii) switch the pretraining paradigm when it cannot support sufficient agreement, or (iv) deprioritize pairs that score poorly on both axes. We apply COMPASS to $72$ cross-modal alignment experiments and $392$ task-arithmetic model merges and show that compatibility estimates by COMPASS strongly correlate with downstream success, achieving average Pearson correlation of $0.91$ on cross-modal alignment tasks and $0.70$ on model merging.
authors: Fabian Gr\"oger, Petar Damjanovi\'c, Maria Brbi\'c
bullets: Addresses the costly trial-and-error needed to identify compatible model pairs.
Measures compatibility using two axes: pair-specific k-NN overlap and a training-paradigm compatibility ceiling.
Ranks candidate pairs and recommends whether to proceed, spend more compute, change the paradigm, or deprioritize the pair.
Across 72 cross-modal alignment experiments and 392 model merges, COMPASS correlated strongly with downstream success.
Reported average Pearson correlations were 0.91 for alignment and 0.70 for merging.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes COMPASS, a diagnostic tool to assess model compatibility for alignment/merging based on representational convergence (k-NN overlap), a spatial/structural metric.
papers.title: To Align or Not To Align: Check Your COMPASS Before You Train
papers.tldr: COMPASS cheaply predicts whether pretrained model pairs will align or merge successfully before expensive training or merging.

papers.abstract: Visual agents must turn video observations into timely decisions to track progress and choose what to do next. Building on the emerging System One paradigm, we introduce VideoJev, a family of models that cast video understanding and interaction as structured decision tasks. We adapt pretrained multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by replacing autoregressive answer decoding with a shared head that scores temporal intervals and textual options against video evidence. These scores yield event spans or answer choices, unifying temporal grounding and multiple-choice video question answering. This combines the semantic flexibility of MLLMs with efficient decisions that agents can use directly. As an interaction unfolds, new goals and intermediate results prompt further queries about the same visual history. VideoJev therefore reuses visual computation through Cached inference for queries as they arrive and Joint inference for multiple queries in a single forward pass. Across three temporal grounding benchmarks, VideoJev-4B and VideoJev-35B-A3B improve mean mIoU over their backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, respectively, with measured inference speedups of $2.8$-$3.1\times$. On four video QA benchmarks, both achieve performance comparable to their backbones in Thinking mode, with measured inference speedups exceeding $100\times$. These results offer a unified, reusable decision interface for composing structured visual judgments into complex, open-ended workflows.
authors: Yuhan Zhu, Xiangyu Zeng, Qingyi Si, Chenxu Yang, Yifei Li, Luozheng Qin, Junhao Zhou, Dingyu Yao, Jun Zhang, Chuanyu Qin, Zhiqiu Zhang, Yuandong Yang, Yuqi Xu, Tianyu Zhang, Hongcheng Guo, Jiaqi Wang, Nan Duan, Limin Wang
bullets: Frames video understanding and interaction as structured decisions over temporal intervals or textual answer choices.
Adapts pretrained multimodal language models with a shared scoring head instead of autoregressive answer generation.
Supports cached inference for sequential queries and joint inference for multiple queries over the same video history.
Improves temporal-grounding mean mIoU over backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, with 2.8–3.1× inference speedups.
Matches backbone performance on four video-QA benchmarks in Thinking mode while exceeding 100× inference speedups.
papers.selection_reason: Unifies video understanding and interaction as structured decision tasks with efficient cached inference, fitting video understanding and multimodal LLM topics.
papers.title: VideoJev: System One Model for Video Understanding and Interaction
papers.tldr: VideoJev turns video understanding into efficient, reusable scoring decisions for temporal grounding and multiple-choice QA, enabling fast interactive visual agents.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) aims to understand human emotions by integrating information from multiple modalities such as speech and text. Psychological studies suggest that emotions exhibit latent hierarchical structured relationships in their semantic representations. However, most MER approaches rely on Euclidean representations, which capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions but do not explicitly provide a geometric prior for organizing hierarchical emotional structures. To mitigate this gap, we propose GeoMER, a joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic modeling framework that introduces hyperbolic emotion-core routing to capture higher-level, abstract emotional representations for MER. The proposed framework jointly models token-level cross-modal semantic interactions and latent emotion representations in two complementary geometric spaces. Specifically, GeoMER consists of a Euclidean Multimodal Fusion Module (EuclFusion) for multimodal representation fusion and a Hyperbolic Geometric Core Routing (HypGeoRoute) module that performs geometry-aware core assignment and aggregation in a hyperbolic manifold to capture more abstract feature representations. The HypGeoRoute module complements the Euclidean token-level modeling. We experiment on the IEMOCAP multimodal MER benchmark and demonstrate that the proposed method achieves the best performance, with 83.54% weighted accuracy and 83.35% unweighted accuracy, outperforming Euclidean baselines, including MemoCMT.
authors: Ting Zhu, Huizhi Liang, Boguslaw Obara, Shufei Duan, Varun Ojha
bullets: Targets the lack of explicit geometric structure in predominantly Euclidean multimodal emotion recognition methods.
Uses EuclFusion for token-level cross-modal semantic fusion and HypGeoRoute for geometry-aware emotion representation routing in hyperbolic space.
Evaluated on the IEMOCAP benchmark, achieving 83.54% weighted accuracy and 83.35% unweighted accuracy.
Reports the best performance among evaluated methods, outperforming Euclidean baselines including MemoCMT.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes GeoMER, a multimodal emotion recognition framework using a joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic geometry, which fits the 'Spatial Intelligence' subtopic regarding geometry-aware multimodal models.
papers.title: GeoMER: A Joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic Geometry Framework for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
papers.tldr: GeoMER combines Euclidean multimodal fusion with hyperbolic emotion-core routing to model both fine-grained interactions and hierarchical emotion structures.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) have significantly promoted using text-to-image (T2I) models to generate images with specific affective intentions. However, the emotional effects conveyed by generated images frequently deviate from target expectations, and it remains unclear whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reliably interpret the emotion of AI-generated visual content. Existing affective benchmarks are predominantly built on natural images, while affective studies of generated images have largely focused on emotions expressed in portraits, lacking a unified benchmark for studying the emotions expressed and evoked by generated images. We therefore introduce EmoGenie, a benchmark of emotion for AI-generated images that evaluates capabilities in T2I generation and MLLM understanding across expressed and evoked emotions. It comprises 6,400 images generated by eight T2I models using 800 emotion-targeted prompts, annotated with question-answer (QA) pairs, termed EmoGenie-QA, and continuous human ratings, termed EmoGenie-Assess. EmoGenie-QA contains 90,000 closed-set questions in single-image and image-pair settings, as well as 1,057 open-ended questions for emotion description. EmoGenie-Assess benchmarks continuous affective and aesthetic prediction using 13,175 mean opinion scores (MOSs) aggregated from human ratings in terms of valence, arousal, dominance, and aesthetic quality. We further develop EmoProbe, which combines emotion question answering with response-aligned, dimension-specific regression heads for continuous score prediction. Experimental results show that EmoProbe achieves superior results on emotion-related QA tasks, while its affective and aesthetic predictions correlate better with human ratings, demonstrating its state-of-the-art capabilities of unified coarse-to-fine affective understanding for AI-generated images.
authors: Zixuan Xing, Lancheng Gao, Shengyan Li, Huiyu Duan, Zhaolin Cai, Guangtao Zhai, Xiongkuo Min
bullets: Addresses the gap between intended and conveyed emotions in text-to-image generation and the limited evaluation of MLLMs on generated imagery.
Provides 6,400 images from eight T2I models and 800 emotion-targeted prompts, with QA annotations and continuous human ratings.
EmoGenie-QA covers closed-set single-image and image-pair questions plus open-ended emotion descriptions.
EmoGenie-Assess evaluates valence, arousal, dominance, and aesthetic quality using human mean opinion scores.
EmoProbe combines emotion QA with dimension-specific regression heads and shows stronger alignment with human ratings across affective and aesthetic tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and evaluation of emotion in T2I generation using MLLMs, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: EmoGenie: Benchmarking and Evaluating Expressed and Evoked Emotion in T2I Generation with MLLMs
papers.tldr: EmoGenie introduces a unified benchmark and model for evaluating both emotions expressed by and evoked by AI-generated images, enabling coarse-to-fine affective understanding.

papers.abstract: World models have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied AI, yet existing systems often remain fragmented in the modalities they model and the functions they support. In particular, visual dynamics, geometric structure, and executable action are commonly coupled through separate interfaces or downstream modules rather than being jointly represented and evolved within a shared dynamics model. In this work, we present Thinker-WM, a unified multimodal world model that jointly models and generates RGB, metric depth, and robot action through a shared intermediate Unified Dynamics Transformer with modality-specific encoders and decoders. The model performs multimodal unification at the representation level: appearance, geometry, and action are transformed into a common dynamic representation and jointly evolved by shared parameters, while their distinct output structures are preserved. The same parameterization supports multiple functions, including joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics. To examine whether the shared representation captures action-related information, we introduce a lightweight motion probe that shows the frozen visual representation contains recoverable motion information. Thinker-WM is trained on a heterogeneous corpus comprising approximately 20K hours of egocentric video, 10K hours of real-robot data, and 1K hours of simulation data, including approximately 4K hours of real-robot data with aligned depth supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance across embodied world-model evaluations. Thinker-WM ranks first on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad and WorldArena, while controlled studies further demonstrate the benefits of action conditioning, geometric interaction, and multi-function training within the shared representation.
authors: Thinker Team, Peng Gao, Jichao Jiao, Chen Liao, Daqin Luo, Yiming Ma, Baiyu Pan, Hailin Shi, Jiyuan Wang, Xiangming Xu, Xiongwei Zhao
bullets: Addresses fragmented world models that handle modalities and functions through separate interfaces or modules.
Uses modality-specific encoders and decoders around a shared Unified Dynamics Transformer that jointly evolves RGB, metric depth, and action representations.
Supports joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics.
A motion probe indicates that frozen visual representations retain recoverable action-related motion information.
Trained on heterogeneous egocentric-video, real-robot, and simulation data; the abstract reports top results on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad, and WorldArena.
papers.selection_reason: Unified multimodal world model jointly modeling RGB, depth, and robot action for embodied intelligence, with strong relevance to world models, embodied action, and spatial representation.
papers.title: Thinker-WM: A Unified World Model with Shared Multimodal Representations for Embodied Intelligence
papers.tldr: Thinker-WM unifies visual appearance, depth geometry, and robot actions in one shared world model for prediction, generation, and control-related tasks.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) appears highly effective, with existing methods retaining over 95% of unpruned performance on common VQA benchmarks using a quarter of the visual tokens or fewer. However, our extensive evaluation of ten methods across three MLLM families and five ability groups reveals a critical gap: strong general performance often comes at the cost of severe degradation on fine-grained tasks such as OCR and visual grounding. We trace these failures to two limitations of the prevailing paradigm of retaining the highest-ranked native patches. A single importance ranking overlooks the complementary evidence required by different tasks, while sparse patch selection disrupts both image content and spatial integrity. To address these limitations, we propose Bifocal, a training-free, two-stage pruning method built on a mixed-granularity framework. It allocates separate budgets to query-focused and image-intrinsic evidence, complemented by a pooled coarse representation of the entire image. Before the LLM, Bifocal matches question words to visual regions through a soft conjunction balanced against norm-debiased image saliency, while selecting image-intrinsic evidence to maximize representational coverage. Inside the LLM, it further prunes tokens using density-adjusted text-to-image attention. With roughly a quarter of the original visual tokens, Bifocal is the only evaluated method to retain over 90% of unpruned performance in every ability group across all three models, and ranks first on average in all nine model-budget settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Bifocal
authors: Peiran Yin, Hao Wu, Zihao Yang, Fengyu Zhou, Yijuan Liang, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Existing pruning methods can retain strong overall performance but substantially harm OCR and visual grounding.
Bifocal uses mixed-granularity pruning with separate query-focused and image-intrinsic token budgets plus a pooled whole-image representation.
It matches question words to regions, balances this with norm-debiased image saliency, maximizes coverage, and applies density-adjusted text-to-image attention pruning inside the LLM.
Using roughly one-quarter of the visual tokens, it retained over 90% of unpruned performance in every evaluated ability group across three MLLM families.
The method was evaluated across ten pruning methods, five ability groups, and nine model-budget settings; code is publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free visual token pruning for MLLMs, directly relevant to efficiency and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Bifocal: Training-Free Mixed Granularity Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Bifocal is a training-free visual-token pruning method that preserves fine-grained and general MLLM abilities by combining query-focused, image-intrinsic, and coarse image evidence.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for remote sensing understanding, yet reliable reasoning remains challenging when tasks require fine-grained visual grounding and multi-step inference. Existing approaches typically rely on either costly pre-constructed reasoning trajectories or self-generated signals such as response consistency, which can reinforce shared errors and provide unreliable supervision. We introduce \textbf{Reasoning--Diagnosis Self-Evolution (ReDiS)}, a framework that separates reasoning exploration from candidate evaluation while allowing the two processes to evolve jointly. ReDiS instantiates two role-specific experts from a shared multimodal backbone: a \textbf{Reasoner} that explores diverse visual evidence--answer candidates and a \textbf{Diagnoser} that jointly evaluates the complete candidate set and provides credibility-aware feedback. As the Reasoner evolves, it exposes new candidate distributions and failure modes; the Diagnoser adapts to these changes and, in turn, reshapes the learning signal for subsequent exploration. To handle groups in which all sampled answers are incorrect and group-relative advantages vanish, we further introduce \textbf{Failure-Triggered Recovery (FTR)}, which provides minimal outcome-level correction without prescribing intermediate reasoning trajectories. Experiments on LHRS-Bench, MME-RS, and CHOICE show consistent improvements over Qwen3.5 backbones at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B scales. ReDiS improves category-averaged accuracy by 6.47 percentage points at 0.8B, while ReDiS-4B achieves the highest average performance among the compared remote sensing MLLMs.
authors: Yi Liu, Wentao Jiang, Shuo Ni, Zhiming Luo, Di Wang, Zengmao Wang, Jing Zhang, Bo Du
bullets: Targets unreliable multi-step reasoning and fine-grained visual grounding in remote sensing.
Uses a shared multimodal backbone to create separate Reasoner and Diagnoser roles that co-evolve.
Introduces Failure-Triggered Recovery to provide outcome-level correction when all sampled answers are wrong.
Evaluated on LHRS-Bench, MME-RS, and CHOICE across 0.8B, 2B, and 4B Qwen3.5 backbones.
Reports a 6.47-point category-averaged accuracy gain at 0.8B; ReDiS-4B has the highest average performance among compared models.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolution framework for multimodal reasoning in remote sensing MLLMs.
papers.title: ReDiS: Reasoning-Diagnosis Self-Evolution for Multimodal Reasoning in Remote Sensing
papers.tldr: ReDiS improves multimodal remote-sensing reasoning by jointly evolving a candidate-generating Reasoner and credibility-aware Diagnoser, with recovery for fully incorrect candidate groups.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities for remote sensing reasoning, yet they frequently generate visually unsupported reasoning that contradicts the visual evidence. Existing post-training methods optimize primarily for final-answer correctness, providing limited supervision for identifying and correcting hallucinations that arise during the reasoning process. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{FaithRS}, a hallucination-aware self-reflection framework for faithful reasoning in remote sensing. We first construct \textbf{SFHD-43K}, a dataset of 43K structured, fine-grained hallucination annotations, and train a detector to identify hallucination types, underlying causes, and supporting visual evidence. FaithRS then incorporates this diagnostic feedback into a Safe Detector-Guided Corrective Rollout framework, where a safety-aware gate selectively determines whether and how to revise the response. Training is driven by a composite reward that jointly optimizes answer accuracy, reasoning faithfulness, hallucination reduction, format compliance, and revision safety. Experiments with Qwen3.5 backbones (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) show consistent improvements across four remote sensing benchmarks, with gains of up to 11.64 points.
authors: Yi Liu, Jing Zhang, Xiang Feng, Xiaoyu Tian, Haonan Guo, Di Wang, Zengmao Wang, Bo Du
bullets: Addresses reasoning that contradicts visual evidence, beyond optimizing only final-answer correctness.
Introduces SFHD-43K, a dataset with 43K structured, fine-grained hallucination annotations.
Uses a hallucination detector to identify error types, causes, and supporting visual evidence.
Applies a safety-aware detector-guided corrective rollout with rewards for accuracy, faithfulness, hallucination reduction, format compliance, and safe revision.
Experiments across four remote-sensing benchmarks and three Qwen3.5 backbones report improvements of up to 11.64 points.
papers.selection_reason: Hallucination-aware faithful reasoning for remote sensing MLLMs.
papers.title: Hallucination-aware Faithful Reasoning in Remote Sensing
papers.tldr: FaithRS improves the faithfulness of remote-sensing MLLM reasoning by detecting visual hallucinations and selectively correcting them during self-reflection.

papers.abstract: City-scale 3D grounding is commonly formulated as candidate ranking, which requires precomputed instance proposals and becomes inefficient in large outdoor scenes. We propose Urbex, an agentic vision-language framework that instead casts grounding as active spatial search. Urbex represents a city-scale 3D scene as an interactive multi-view environment, allowing a VLM agent to query landmarks, zoom into local regions, render oblique views, and commit a grounded bounding box. We optimize this tool-use policy with reinforcement learning on CityRefer, using smooth localization rewards and lightweight shaping rewards for efficient exploration. Experiments show that Urbex achieves the best Hit@1 and IoU on CityRefer, supports candidate-free grounding without ground-truth boxes, and is substantially faster than the strongest city-scale ranking baseline. Zero-shot results on STPLS3D-Refer further indicate improved cross-scene robustness.
authors: Yu Wang, Rui Dai, Wei Chen, Yi Wang, Bo Dang, Kaikui Liu, Xiangxiang Chu, Yansheng Li
bullets: Represents scenes as interactive multi-view environments for landmark queries, zooming, oblique rendering, and bounding-box prediction.
Trains the vision-language tool-use policy with reinforcement learning using localization and exploration-efficiency rewards.
Achieves the best reported Hit@1 and IoU on CityRefer while grounding without candidate boxes.
Runs substantially faster than the strongest city-scale ranking baseline.
Shows improved zero-shot cross-scene robustness on STPLS3D-Refer.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic VLM spatial grounding in city-scale 3D scenes; active spatial search and RL-optimized tool use.
papers.title: Urbex: Agentic Spatial Grounding for City-Scale 3D Scenes
papers.tldr: Urbex reframes city-scale 3D grounding as efficient, agentic spatial search rather than ranking precomputed proposals.

papers.abstract: Practical remote sensing applications often require both understanding and generation capabilities for the same geographic scene. However, most existing methods address either understanding or generation in isolation, while existing unified remote sensing models' generative ability is limited to text-to-image. To bridge this gap, we propose Omni-RS, a unified framework supporting four remote sensing understanding tasks and five generation tasks. Specifically, we introduce the "Scene-Guided Two-Stage Training" strategy, which first adapts a multimodal large language model to remote sensing understanding and then uses its hidden states to guide a diffusion transformer for image generation. To enable joint learning across diverse generation tasks, we construct UniGen, a unified multi-task generation dataset, by organizing heterogeneous remote sensing data into a unified format. Furthermore, we introduce "Detailed Visual Conditioning", which uses visual conditions encoded by a VAE to guide the generation process, thereby supporting additional generation tasks that require reference images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Omni-RS performs exceptionally well in understanding tasks and has achieved outstanding results in a variety of generative tasks.
authors: Pan Yin. Shuai Yang, Yuanhao Liu, Datao Tang, Jialin Li, Hao Wang, Pei Liu, Kaiyu Li, Cong Zhao, Xiangyong Cao
bullets: Addresses the gap between remote-sensing models that handle understanding or generation separately.
Uses Scene-Guided Two-Stage Training: adapts a multimodal language model, then guides a diffusion transformer with its hidden states.
Introduces UniGen, a unified dataset format for joint learning across heterogeneous generation tasks.
Adds Detailed Visual Conditioning via VAE-encoded visual inputs to support reference-image generation.
Reports strong performance across both understanding and diverse generative tasks, without specific metrics in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Unified remote sensing understanding and generation via MLLM and diffusion, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Omni-RS: Unifying Multi-Task Understanding and Generation in Remote Sensing
papers.tldr: Omni-RS unifies four remote-sensing understanding tasks with five image-generation tasks through scene-guided multimodal training and visual conditioning.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have been widely adopted for document parsing and optical character recognition (OCR), as they can accurately extract page-level elements. However, downstream applications such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) also require coherent document-level structure. Although these models indicate heading levels using different numbers of preceding ``\#'' symbols, page-by-page prediction often lacks document-level consistency. In practice, input-resolution and context-length constraints make it infeasible for a VLM to jointly process all page images in documents containing tens or hundreds of pages. To address this limitation, we propose a VLM-based framework that incrementally reconstructs heading hierarchies with a \emph{level-wise multimodal memory}. The memory retains a compact subset of all previously processed pages, selected by anchors. Our framework supports flexible anchor selection, and in this work we select the most recent node at each level, allowing the VLM to observe the visual, textual, and layout patterns of headings at every level. For comprehensive evaluation, we also introduce the Complex and Long Document Heading Hierarchy Reconstruction Benchmark (CLDoc-HHRBench), comprising 250 documents and 11,212 pages with expert-verified annotations. Experiments on CLDoc-HHRBench and three existing benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
authors: Qian Chen, Xianyin Zhang, Lifan Guo, Chi Zhang
bullets: Addresses inconsistent heading-level predictions caused by page-by-page processing and VLM context or resolution limits.
Maintains visual, textual, and layout information from selected anchor pages at each heading level.
Uses the most recent node at every level as anchors, while supporting flexible anchor-selection strategies.
Introduces CLDoc-HHRBench, a benchmark of 250 documents and 11,212 pages with expert-verified annotations.
Shows effectiveness on CLDoc-HHRBench and three existing benchmarks; specific quantitative results are not reported in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language model document parsing with multimodal memory for long-document structure fits VLM-based multimodal understanding.
papers.title: Heading Hierarchy Reconstruction for Complex and Long Documents with Level-Wise Multimodal Memory
papers.tldr: A VLM framework incrementally reconstructs consistent heading hierarchies in long, complex documents using compact level-wise multimodal memory.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong zero-shot reasoning across diverse domains, but their potential for Human-Object Interaction (HOI) remains unexplored. Unlike traditional HOI approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets and fixed interaction taxonomies, MLLMs offer flexible reasoning, making them well-suited for dynamic, real-world scenarios. In this work, we present the first systematic study of MLLMs for HOI recognition and detection within a pipeline that combines an external object detector for entity localization with zero-shot multimodal reasoning for interaction understanding. We introduce a benchmark framework for principled zero-shot evaluation, consisting of (i) a unified taxonomy of zero-shot prompting strategies, and (ii) a methodology that transforms token-level logits into interaction scores, enabling fair comparison with specialized HOI models under standard metrics. To support prompt-based evaluation, we additionally construct new question-answer annotations for standard HOI datasets, transforming them into a format suitable for MLLMs. Building on this, we propose two visual prompting strategies, namely Objects as Context and Black Other Objects, that guide MLLMs to target objects while preserving scene context. Experiments on HICO, HICO-DET, and V-COCO demonstrate state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, achieving 53.50 mAP on HICO and 23.69 mAP on HICO-DET. Overall, our work provides a principled benchmarking framework for MLLMs in HOI, opening the door to new models and datasets and enabling flexible open-world interaction understanding.
authors: Oriol Rabasseda, Zenjie Li, Kamal Nasrollahi, Sergio Escalera
bullets: Addresses HOI understanding without relying on extensive labeled data or fixed interaction taxonomies.
Combines an external object detector for localization with zero-shot multimodal reasoning for interaction understanding.
Introduces a unified taxonomy of prompting strategies and converts token-level logits into interaction scores for standard evaluation.
Adds question-answer annotations to HICO, HICO-DET, and V-COCO for prompt-based MLLM evaluation.
Proposes Objects as Context and Black Other Objects visual prompts; reports 53.50 mAP on HICO and 23.69 mAP on HICO-DET.ada

papers.title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Zero-Shot Human-Object Interaction
papers.tldr: This work establishes a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on zero-shot human-object interaction recognition and detection, achieving strong performance through structured prompting and logit-based interaction scoring.

papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (OLLMs) are susceptible to cross-modal hallucinations under audio-visual interference. We find that, for a substantial fraction of incorrect joint predictions, the question-relevant unimodal branch can still recover the correct answer, suggesting that task-relevant evidence can remain recoverable from the relevant modality even when it is not reflected in the joint prediction. We refer to this recoverable failure pattern as \emph{modality misrouting}. We propose CaRe (Conflict-aware Residual Intervention), a training-free inference-time method for identifying and correcting modality misrouting. CaRe uses a text-only modality probe to identify a candidate modality-specific counterfactual branch, and flags potential misrouting when its prediction conflicts with the original joint prediction. For such cases, CaRe computes a residual direction from the discrepancy between the counterfactual and fused representations and uses it to steer the original multimodal state toward the relevant modality evidence, while retaining both modalities in the original audio-visual inference path. The intervention strength is adapted based on the confidence of the counterfactual branch. Experiments on CMM and AVHBench across two OLLMs show that CaRe consistently outperforms the evaluated inference-time hallucination-mitigation baselines.
authors: Yu Mi, Licheng Pan, Jiayi Zhu, Qirui Liu, Yitong Qiao, Changtong Xu, Tao Wei, Fei Sun, Zhixuan Chu, Kui Ren
bullets: Audio-visual interference can cause incorrect joint predictions even when the question-relevant unimodal branch predicts correctly.
CaRe is a training-free, inference-time method that uses a text-only modality probe to find conflicting modality-specific predictions.
It derives a residual direction between counterfactual and fused representations to correct the multimodal state while preserving both modalities.
Intervention strength is adapted according to the counterfactual branch’s confidence.
Across CMM and AVHBench on two OLLMs, CaRe consistently outperforms the evaluated inference-time mitigation baselines.

papers.title: Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations by Correcting Modality Misrouting in Omnimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: CaRe reduces audio-visual hallucinations in omnimodal LLMs by detecting modality misrouting and steering joint representations toward recoverable relevant-modality evidence.

papers.abstract: In this paper, our goal is to represent text embeddings as sketches for three main reasons. First, to visualize text representation and to explore their potential their potential for AI explainability. Second, to investigate the potential benefits of the sketch-based representation for information retrieval. Third, to explore their potential for reasoning, drawing inspiration from the concept of mental imagery. We propose a sketch-based visual grounding framework that transforms text representations into visual topographic sketches. Our approach aims to emphasis the semantics content encoded in the text embeddings through the corresponding sketch. Evaluations are conducted on the MS-COCO dataset to examine the utility of these sketches for text retrieval. The comparative study of SBERT and Sketch-based method reveals that SBERT retains an advantage in strict top-1 retrieval accuracy while achieving comparable performance to the sketch-based method in top-5 retrieval. A cascaded approach combining SBERT and the sketch-based method outperforms SBERT alone, suggesting that the Sketch-based representation could offer significant potential for information retrieval if trained directly on text.
bullets: Represents text embeddings as sketches to make semantic content more visually interpretable and explore AI explainability.
Investigates whether visual, sketch-based representations can support information retrieval and reasoning inspired by mental imagery.
Evaluated on MS-COCO for text retrieval using SBERT and the proposed sketch-based method.
SBERT performs better at strict top-1 retrieval, while sketch-based retrieval is comparable at top-5.
Combining SBERT with the sketch-based method in a cascade outperforms SBERT alone; direct training on text is identified as future potential.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a sketch-based visual grounding framework that transforms text embeddings into topographic sketches, offering a novel spatial representation for multimodal information retrieval.
papers.title: Beyond Black Boxes: Visual Grounding for Text Embeddings
papers.tldr: A sketch-based visual grounding framework turns text embeddings into semantic topographic sketches, supporting interpretability and retrieval, with a cascaded system improving over SBERT alone.

papers.abstract: A medical vision-language model may analyze a given CT scan and correctly detect both kidneys in view. Continuing this conversation, if a user provides a prescription with an opposite direction, medical VLMs often sycophantically choose to realign their diagnosis. In this work, we study regressive sycophancy under fabricated evidence, where a model abandons a correct answer when pushback comes with a fake document. We test four open VLMs on 400 VQA-RAD yes/no questions in 19,200 multi-turn conversations, with and without a fabricated prescription. Without a disclosure that documents are synthetic, the models abandon 80.1% of 6,488 correct answers. Notably, under one script each, the same prescription raises the flip rate of Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 45.9% to 89.6% and lowers that of Qwen3-VL-8B from 77.7% to 50.9%. A model rejected the prescription while still preserving the correct answer in 915 of 3,232 conversations with the prescription (28.3%), and 40% of these flipped in later turns. System-prompt sentences that disclose the documents as synthetic lower one model's flip rate from 77.8% to 47.3%. Thus, we conclude that awareness about a forgery does not prevent a model from adopting its answer.
authors: Sadif Ahmed, Soumya Swagata Biswas, Rifat Shahriyar, Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider
bullets: Evaluates four open VLMs on 400 VQA-RAD yes/no questions across 19,200 multi-turn conversations with or without fabricated prescriptions.
Without synthetic-document disclosure, models abandoned 80.1% of 6,488 initially correct answers.
Prescription effects varied substantially by model and conversation script, increasing one model’s flip rate while decreasing another’s.
Even when a model rejected the prescription, 40% of preserved answers later flipped in subsequent turns.
A system prompt identifying documents as synthetic reduced one model’s flip rate, but did not eliminate the behavior.
papers.selection_reason: Studies failure modes of multimodal LLMs under fabricated evidence, relevant to multimodal foundation model behavior and reliability.
papers.title: Seeing Through the Forgery Is Not Enough: Regressive Sycophancy under Fabricated Evidence in Medical Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Medical VLMs frequently abandon correct CT interpretations when confronted with fabricated prescriptions, and simply recognizing the forgery does not reliably prevent this regressive sycophancy.

papers.abstract: Do vision-language models use depth information to judge which object is closer, or rely on image-plane cues? We investigate this question through controlled depth--cue conflicts, representation analysis, and interventions. Among the many image-plane cues relevant to depth perception, we focus on apparent size and vertical position. We compare depth judgments under cue-consistent and cue-conflict conditions in both rendered scenes and real-world photographs. Across model families and scales, depth judgments systematically shift toward misleading cues. Yet the correct depth order remains decodable from the queried objects' visual representations, including when the model answers incorrectly. Image and category controls support interpreting this signal as image-dependent depth information beyond the two target cues. Strengthening the model's own depth readout through object-level write-back can correct conflict decisions without updating model parameters or using ground-truth depth annotations. Interventions show that the effect of this correction depends on the direction and target tokens of the written signal, while its strength varies across architectures and domains. Together, these findings reveal a mismatch between a model's ability to represent depth and use this information when deciding the answer. VLMs can retain useful depth information while allowing competing image-plane cues to exert greater influence on their answers.
bullets: The study examines depth judgments under conflicts involving apparent size and vertical position.
Across model families, scales, rendered scenes, and real photographs, answers systematically shift toward misleading cues.
Correct depth order remains decodable from object representations even when the model answers incorrectly.
Object-level write-back can strengthen depth readout and correct decisions without parameter updates or ground-truth depth labels.
Correction effects depend on the written signal’s direction and target tokens, and vary by architecture and domain.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates depth representation and cue use in vision-language models via controlled conflicts and interventions, directly fitting spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Seeing Depth but Choosing Cues in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Vision-language models can represent correct depth information but often let misleading image-plane cues dominate their judgments.

papers.abstract: Table reasoning with language models typically assumes access to clean textual tables. In practice, tables are often serialized into text, which can corrupt cell contents, distort structural relationships, and discard visual cues, leaving the model to reason over incomplete evidence. In contrast, table images retain this information, but using it requires both accurate perception and reasoning grounded in the relevant cells. To address this, we propose MERIT (Multimodal Evidence Reasoning over Image Tables), a three-stage framework for learning to reason over table images, with serialized tables serving as optional auxiliary inputs (if provided). Our analysis identifies visual evidence acquisition as a bottleneck, motivating table-specific encoder adaptation through reconstruction, localization, and color-conditioned supervision. Building on the adapted representations, supervised fine-tuning teaches explicit evidence selection and reasoning using verified trajectories. Finally, reinforcement learning refines the policy with separate rewards for evidence correctness, calculation, final answers, and output format. By providing feedback on intermediate steps, the framework targets retrieval and computational errors that final-answer supervision alone does not distinguish. We evaluate the approach on table question answering and fact verification, analyze the contributions of visual inputs and training components, and assess generalization to additional datasets with different table structures and visual presentations.
authors: Haoyang Jiang, Zhuotong Fan, Mingyang Yi, Ju Fan, Lanqing Hu, Xiao Zan
bullets: Addresses information loss and structural corruption caused by serializing tables into text.
Adapts a table-specific visual encoder using reconstruction, localization, and color-conditioned supervision.
Uses supervised fine-tuning with verified evidence-and-reasoning trajectories.
Applies reinforcement learning with separate rewards for evidence, calculations, answers, and formatting.
Evaluates visual inputs, training components, and generalization across varied table structures and presentations.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a multimodal evidence-reasoning framework over table images, relevant to multimodal LLM reasoning and instruction tuning.
papers.title: MERIT: Multimodal Evidence Reasoning over Image Tables
papers.tldr: MERIT is a three-stage framework that combines table-image perception, explicit evidence selection, and stepwise reasoning for more reliable table question answering and fact verification.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering models often produce plausible responses even when the available visual evidence is insufficient to support a valid answer. Although prior work has introduced benchmarks and abstention mechanisms for unanswerable visual questions, it remains unclear which signals derived from a frozen vision-language model reliably indicate answerability on unseen image-question pairs. We systematically evaluate answerability signals on a stratified 10K subset of UNK-VQA using frozen InstructBLIP, covering predictive uncertainty, cross-modal alignment, visual grounding, visual dependence, internal representations, and learned probes. Answerability discrimination remains weak, with test AUROC largely confined to 0.50-0.54. CLIP alignment yields the highest point estimate but does not significantly outperform generation confidence under paired bootstrap analysis. Targeted removal of question-relevant visual evidence causes substantially larger changes in answer confidence than same-size random masking, yet intervention sensitivity provides essentially no answerability discrimination. Increasing probe capacity, combining multiple signals, and adding reason-aware supervision do not provide robust improvements, while post-freeze cross-validation yields similarly weak discrimination. Selective-answering analysis shows limited usable coverage under low-risk operating criteria. Failure-mode analysis shows that the relative utility of individual signals varies across perturbation mechanisms. Taken together, these results show that, on our UNK-VQA subset with frozen InstructBLIP, visual dependence, uncertainty, semantic alignment, and static representations are not robust standalone proxies for answerability. Our findings emphasize the need to distinguish a model's reliance on visual evidence from whether that evidence is sufficient to support an answer.
authors: Minjun Kim, Hyunmin Song, Changwon Lim
bullets: Evaluates answerability signals across uncertainty, cross-modal alignment, grounding, visual dependence, representations, and learned probes.
Discrimination is weak, with test AUROC generally around 0.50–0.54.
CLIP alignment has the highest point estimate but does not significantly outperform generation confidence.
Removing question-relevant visual evidence changes confidence more than random masking, yet intervention sensitivity remains uninformative for answerability.
More powerful probes, signal combinations, reason-aware supervision, and post-freeze cross-validation yield no robust gains; useful selective-answering coverage is limited.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes answerability signals in a frozen vision-language model, relevant to multimodal LLM behavior and reliability.
papers.title: Visual Dependence Does Not Imply Answerability: A Systematic Analysis of Answerability Signals in Frozen InstructBLIP
papers.tldr: On UNK-VQA with frozen InstructBLIP, common signals—including visual dependence, uncertainty, alignment, and representations—do not reliably distinguish answerable from unanswerable questions.

papers.abstract: Time-series analysis is increasingly studied in multimodal settings, yet most benchmarks pair temporal signals with text or with visualizations derived from the same signal. This leaves open whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can integrate time series with real-world visual evidence. We introduce MMTA (multimodal temporal analysis), a benchmark of tri-modal tasks with diverse cross-modal complementarity patterns among time series, text, and vision. MMTA spans nine domains -- robotics, autonomous driving, human action, manufacturing, AR assistance, healthcare, recommendation, finance, and climate -- under video+TS and image+TS layouts, with a 3,524-sample test split covering classification and forecasting. The benchmark standardizes heterogeneous real-world sources into a shared schema with domain-specific prompts, provenance documentation, and success-weighted metrics that penalize both wrong answers and failed generations. Evaluating eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs reveals a shared bottleneck: representing time series as text creates very long token sequences and weakens fine-grained alignment with visual evidence, especially in long-video settings. We then introduce TimeOmni-v, a multimodal LLM extension with a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and a forecasting head. TimeOmni-v improves long-video classification and time-series inference efficiency, showing that MMTA not only exposes representation and grounding failures but also motivates targeted model design.
authors: Ziyang Zhang, Shenyi Li, Yilin Wang, Ziyun Cui, Bowen Zhou, Wen Wu, Chao Zhang
bullets: Introduces tri-modal classification and forecasting tasks across nine domains using video+time-series and image+time-series layouts.
Standardizes heterogeneous sources with shared schemas, domain-specific prompts, provenance documentation, and success-weighted metrics.
Evaluates eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs, finding that text-based time-series representations produce long token sequences and weak visual alignment, especially for long videos.
Proposes TimeOmni-v with a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and forecasting head.
TimeOmni-v improves long-video classification and time-series inference efficiency, though the abstract does not report quantitative results.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a tri-modal benchmark and a multimodal LLM extension integrating time series, text, and vision, directly fitting multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: MMTA: Benchmarking Multimodal Temporal Analysis with Time Series, Text, and Vision
papers.tldr: MMTA benchmarks whether multimodal LLMs can jointly reason over real-world time series, text, and visual evidence, exposing temporal representation and grounding challenges and motivating TimeOmni-v.

papers.abstract: Understanding facial behaviour in video requires answering three fundamental questions: when a key facial expression occurs, where the model attends on the face at that moment, and why that evidence is necessary rather than merely correlated. Today's multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can label and describe video, but they rarely provide faithful explanations, especially for small facial movements that change over time. We present VideoFace-X-LLM, a framework for explainable facial video understanding comprising two key components. First, we introduce ExplainFace, a weakly supervised video-text corpus for facial behaviour understanding, automatically constructed from CelebV-HQ videos and validated through human evaluation and a two-model audit (at most 2.3% contradictions), demonstrating consistent gains across two backbone architectures. Second, H-TCC (Hierarchical Temporal Spatial Causal Concepts), which finds the key temporal moments (When), the facial regions (Where), and verifies its causal necessity (Why) through targeted occlusion. Fine-tuning on ExplainFace raises appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87% (+13.39), with gains of +4.38 on actions, +6.77 on temporal emotion, and +11.84 F1 on deepfake detection. We also measure the explanations pointing lift, face/edge lift, stability, an Adebayo sanity check, and a necessity test rather than only showing examples. Our models, code, and corpus are available on request for research use.
authors: Anubhav Kataria, Shreya Ghosh, Jingwen Ye, Abhinav Dhall
bullets: Targets faithful explanations for small, evolving facial movements that existing MLLMs often describe without causal grounding.
Introduces ExplainFace, a weakly supervised video–text corpus built from CelebV-HQ and validated by humans and a two-model audit with at most 2.3% contradictions.
Uses H-TCC to identify key moments, relevant facial regions, and causal necessity through targeted occlusion.
Fine-tuning improves appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87%, with additional gains for actions, temporal emotion, and deepfake detection.

papers.selection_reason: Explainable facial video understanding with MLLMs; fits video understanding and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: When, Where, and Why: Hierarchical Causal Explainability for Video Face Understanding with MLLMs
papers.tldr: VideoFace-X-LLM combines weakly supervised data and hierarchical causal analysis to explain when, where, and why facial behaviours occur in video.

papers.abstract: We introduce Diffuplex, a full-duplex spoken language model based on discrete diffusion that achieves an unprecedented balance between linguistic intelligence and response efficiency. With thinking mode, Diffuplex delivers 13.0 tokens per forward pass, reaching an average of 1872 tokens per second and substantially surpassing the frontier autoregressive (AR) models in decoding speed. Without thinking, Diffuplex matches the first-audio latency of existing full-duplex models while achieving markedly stronger linguistic intelligence. This capability is enabled by separating when to say from what to say at the training level, rather than compressing both into a single autoregressive timeline. During inference, Diffuplex continuously tracks the user speech through an AR interaction policy, while independently generating and refining response content through parallel diffusion. Consequently, semantic computation is no longer bounded by the perception audio frame rate, allowing intelligence and responsiveness to improve simultaneously. Taken together, these results establish a new paradigm for spoken agents that can sustain real-time dialogue while devoting parallel computation to intelligent response generation. Training code and checkpoints will be avaliable soon.
authors: Chen Chen, Pin-Jui Ku, Ankita Pasad, Ante Juki\'c, Zhehuai Chen, Boris Ginsburg
bullets: Targets the trade-off between spoken-agent responsiveness and linguistic intelligence in full-duplex conversation.
Separates when to speak from what to say during training instead of using one autoregressive timeline.

papers.title: Full-duplex Spoken Language Modeling with Discrete Diffusion
papers.tldr: Diffuplex uses discrete diffusion to separate response timing from content generation, enabling real-time full-duplex dialogue with faster decoding and stronger linguistic intelligence.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models often exhibit object hallucination, generating claims that are not supported by the input image. To mitigate this issue, we propose Evidence-Guided Visual Claim Admission (EGVCA), a training-free framework that admits a semantic claim only when it receives sufficient image-dependent support. EGVCA measures this support by comparing the claim likelihood under the observed image and a visual-null input. For captioning, it controls semantic expansion without altering token generation. For binary visual question answering, it combines atomic visual support with the image-induced change in the model's native Yes--No margin. Experiments on CHAIR, POPE, and MME across three LVLM backbones show that EGVCA substantially reduces object hallucination while preserving caption quality. It achieves the highest POPE F1 in eight of nine backbone--sampling settings and improves the native MME total score on all three backbones. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of claim-level admission as a simple alternative to token-level distribution correction.
authors: Hyeonggeun Han, Taehyun Cho, Sangwoo Hong
bullets: Targets object hallucination: models generate claims unsupported by the input image.
Compares claim likelihood with the observed image against a visual-null input to measure image-dependent support.
Controls semantic expansion for captioning and combines atomic support with image-induced Yes–No margin changes for binary VQA.

Achieves the highest POPE F1 in eight of nine backbone–sampling settings and improves native MME total scores on all backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free hallucination mitigation for LVLMs; directly relevant to multimodal LLM reliability.
papers.title: From Token Correction to Claim Admission: Training-Free Hallucination Mitigation for Large Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: EGVCA reduces hallucinations in large vision-language models by admitting claims only when the image provides sufficient evidence, without training or changing token generation.

papers.abstract: Can vision-language models turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action? This requires inferring object geometry, anticipating the effects of rotation, and refining actions through visual feedback. We introduce RoTA-Bench to evaluate these abilities through interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Given a target silhouette, a model observes a rotated object and chooses successive rotations to recover the target projection within a limited action budget. Our automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D objects from 2D icons and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. Empirically, we find that (i) a substantial human-model gap persists: GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on only 17% of tasks, whereas 20 undergraduate participants collectively complete the test set four times with a 100% success rate; (ii) image-space and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, the model more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%); and (iii) fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history: removing it leaves 96.8% of the model's actions at a coarse 30-degree step size and sharply reduces observed task success. These findings highlight the challenge of converting visual evidence into precise 3D control, beyond recognizing or matching individual images.
authors: Qingchuan Ma, Yuexiao Ma, Xiang Meng, Yixuan Zou, Tianyu Xie, Wang Chen, Yuhui Zeng, Yuhang Wu, Xiawu Zheng, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Models iteratively rotate a 3D object to match a target 2D silhouette under a limited action budget.
The benchmark contains 674 solvable tasks, including a stratified 100-task test set built from 2D icons and reversible initialization.
GPT-5.6-Sol succeeded on 17% of tasks, while undergraduate participants achieved 100% success across repeated test-set completion.
Models sometimes improve silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment more often than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%).
Removing interaction history led 96.8% of model actions to use coarse 30° rotations and sharply reduced task success.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates VLMs' interactive 3D spatial reasoning via projection alignment, directly fitting spatial intelligence.
papers.title: RoTA-Bench: Evaluating 3D Spatial Reasoning through Interactive Projection Alignment
papers.tldr: RoTA-Bench evaluates whether vision-language models can use visual feedback to perform precise 3D rotation-based alignment, revealing major gaps in spatial reasoning and control.

papers.abstract: Although chain-of-thought prompting has improved multimodal reasoning, it is still difficult to produce correct final answers, as the reasoning can drift away from the image. Besides, the trace is already fixed when the answer is generated, leaving no room for self-correction. Considering the image is still available at the final-answer step, we think it is reasonable to fix the answer there without rewriting the reasoning. As such, the problem becomes to correct the final answer using the image under fixed reasoning. Unlike methods that improve trace generation through training, resampling, or decoding-time grounding, we repair the final-answer readout while keeping the reasoning trace fixed. The motivation is based on our finding that a wrong option can become prematurely committed in the reasoning while the correct option still has stronger image support in middle-to-deep layers. Thus, we propose Text-to-Visual Evidence Reallocation (TVER), a training-free method for final-answer repair. Specifically, TVER selects answer-related text and question-matched image patches, and moves bounded attention from text to patches. Furthermore, the patches are chosen in a middle-to-deep layer window based on question relevance. Our method improves answers across benchmarks and backbones, with gains in both multiple-choice and open-answer evaluations.
authors: Yulan Pan, Xiaoyu Xu, Zhihong Shen
bullets: Addresses answer errors caused when reasoning drifts from the image or prematurely commits to a wrong option.
Uses a training-free final-answer repair step rather than retraining, resampling, or modifying the reasoning trace.
Selects answer-related text and question-relevant image patches, then reallocates bounded attention from text to patches.
Chooses patches from a middle-to-deep layer window based on question relevance.
Improves performance across benchmarks and backbones in both multiple-choice and open-answer settings.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free final-answer repair for multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning directly fits multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: The Image Still Has a Say: Final-Answer Repair for Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
papers.tldr: TVER repairs multimodal chain-of-thought answers by redirecting final-answer attention toward image evidence while leaving the reasoning trace unchanged.

papers.abstract: Reliable video reasoning requires models to produce correct answers and expose supporting visual evidence. Open-o3-Video enables verifiable reasoning by embedding timestamps and object-level bounding boxes into reasoning traces, but is restricted to frames from an initial sparse sampler. We introduce Open-o3-Video-v2, which formulates video reasoning as a unified agentic evidencegrounded process. The model identifies missing information, acquires additional observations, grounds the moments and objects supporting its reasoning, and writes this evidence into the trajectory before continuing or answering. To support this behavior, we construct STGR-v2-CoT135K, including 52K multi-turn agentic grounded reasoning trajectories, and STGR-v2-RL-13K for reinforcement learning. We further propose Clue-Seek GRPO (CS-GRPO), which tracks how tool calls change accumulated evidence, rewards clue coverage and step-wise gains, and penalizes excessive, repetitive, or uninformative retrieval. On V-STaR, Open-o3-Video-v2-4B achieves 40.4% mAM and 56.3% mLGM, outperforming its Qwen3-VL-4B backbone by 8.5% and 12.6%, respectively. It also delivers consistent gains across general video understanding, long-video reasoning, and temporal grounding benchmarks. These results show that active evidence acquisition and verifiable object-level grounding are complementary for reliable video reasoning. The code and models are released at https://msalab-pku.github.io/projects/Open-o3-Video-v2.
authors: Jiahao Meng, Zhongyuan Bao, Yue Tan, Haiquan Wen, Renrui Zhang, Anna Wang, Jason Li, Yanwei Fu, Yunhai Tong, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Frames video reasoning as an agentic process: identify gaps, retrieve additional observations, ground relevant moments and objects, then answer.
Introduces STGR-v2-CoT135K and STGR-v2-RL-13K datasets for multi-turn grounded reasoning and reinforcement learning.
Proposes Clue-Seek GRPO, rewarding evidence coverage and useful retrieval while penalizing repetitive or uninformative tool calls.
The 4B model achieves 40.4% mAM and 56.3% mLGM on V-STaR, with gains over its Qwen3-VL-4B backbone and across multiple video benchmarks.
Code and models are publicly released.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic video reasoning with verifiable spatio-temporal evidence; fits video understanding and multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Open-o3-Video-v2: Seek, Ground, and Reason with Verifiable Spatio-Temporal Evidence
papers.tldr: Open-o3-Video-v2 improves reliable video reasoning by actively seeking missing visual evidence and grounding answers in verifiable timestamps and object regions.

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents navigating and interacting with the physical world. As observations arrive incrementally, agents must reason in a streaming manner. Yet streaming understanding must also be closed-loop: task-relevant evidence may require both recalling past observations and actively acquiring new views. Existing streaming approaches largely emphasize processing incoming observations, leaving task-driven active exploration underexplored. We introduce MemAct, a framework for streaming spatial understanding with memory and action. A shared vision--language model incrementally writes structured historical memory, retrieves records and past frames on demand, and acquires additional evidence through movement and turning. Retrieved evidence and action observations inform subsequent decisions, enabling the agent to continue exploring or answer within a unified reasoning loop. We develop the MemAct suite, a data generation pipeline and collection across real and simulated environments, with approximately 1M training examples for spatial reasoning, memory writing, retrieval, and exploration. Its MemAct-bench comprises 20,000 main QA pairs evaluating current-observation understanding, historical evidence use, and active exploration, plus 2,000 separate Timing questions. MemAct combines supervised fine-tuning for memory and interaction with counterfactual action optimization using cumulative evidence gains, action costs, and terminal answer quality to improve exploration and stopping decisions. Experiments show that MemAct outperforms existing spatial understanding and streaming baselines and approaches frontier multimodal models on MemAct-bench while retaining streaming inference efficiency.
authors: Yuxi Wei, Wei Huang, Qirui Chen, Lu Hou, Xiaojuan Qi
bullets: Addresses the gap between passive streaming observation and task-driven exploration that acquires missing evidence.
Uses a shared vision-language model to write structured memories, retrieve past frames, and guide movement or turning.
Introduces MemAct data and benchmarks spanning current observations, historical evidence, active exploration, and timing.
Trains memory and interaction with supervised fine-tuning plus counterfactual action optimization for evidence gain, action cost, and answer quality.
Outperforms existing spatial and streaming baselines, approaches frontier multimodal models, and maintains streaming inference efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming spatial understanding with embodied memory and active exploration; directly fits embodied memory, spatial intelligence, and vision-language-action.
papers.title: MemAct: Streaming Spatial Understanding with Memory and Active Exploration
papers.tldr: MemAct enables embodied agents to understand spaces over time by combining structured memory, on-demand retrieval, and active exploration in a unified streaming loop.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly used to identify and describe places, yet their recognition and knowledge of specific cultures remain poorly understood, particularly in underrepresented regions such as the Philippines. This study introduces the Tanawpamana Dataset, a repository of Philippine heritage site images with metadata based on the Talapamana registry of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts of the Philippines. We also introduce the Tanawpamana Benchmark, comprising 4,046 tasks designed to evaluate models' recognition and knowledge of heritage sites. Evaluating seven vision-language models, we find that they struggle more with fine-grained visual discrimination among similar heritage sites than with coarse recognition, and that their geographic knowledge is weaker when inferred from image inputs than from text.
authors: Ivan Yuri De Leon, Hiroki Ouchi, Sakriani Sakti
bullets: Introduces a dataset of Philippine heritage-site images with metadata from the NCCA’s Talapamana registry.
Provides 4,046 benchmark tasks assessing heritage-site recognition and knowledge.
Evaluates seven vision-language models on visual and geographic understanding.
Models perform worse on distinguishing visually similar sites than on coarse recognition.
Geographic knowledge is weaker from images than from text inputs.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks vision-language models on cultural heritage recognition, fitting multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: Tanawpamana: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models on Philippine Cultural Heritage Sites
papers.tldr: Tanawpamana benchmarks vision-language models on Philippine heritage sites and reveals weaknesses in fine-grained visual and image-based geographic understanding.

papers.abstract: Dual-encoder vision-language models systematically fail at negation, scoring ''a cat without a dog'' nearly identically to ''a cat with a dog.'' We show that this failure is inherent to the single-embedding framework. Under contrastive training, single-embedding methods can at best ignore the negated concept (dilution) but never penalize its presence (rejection). We propose Know-Thy-Not (KTN), a training-free method that introduces an image-side rejection dimension to penalize the negated concept directly in the visual representation. We also introduce COCO-Confusion, the first benchmark requiring genuine rejection to succeed. Across 9 backbones, KTN improves COCO-Confusion mAP by up to +25.6 over vanilla VLMs and +9.6 over the strongest existing method.
authors: DoYoung Kim, Changkyu Choi, Ad\'in Ram\'irez Rivera, YunSeok Choi, Jee-Hyong Lee
bullets: Problem: Dual-encoder models treat prompts like “a cat without a dog” similarly to “a cat with a dog,” failing to penalize the negated concept.
Analysis: Single-embedding contrastive models can dilute a negated concept but cannot directly reject its presence.
Method: KTN adds an image-side rejection dimension to penalize the negated concept, without training.
Benchmark: COCO-Confusion is introduced to test genuine negation-based rejection.
Results: Across 9 backbones, KTN improves mAP by up to 25.6 points over vanilla models and 9.6 points over the strongest existing method.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses negation failure in dual-encoder vision-language models with a training-free rejection mechanism; relevant to multimodal foundation model robustness.
papers.title: Know-Thy-Not: Training-Free Targeted Negation in Dual-Encoder Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: KTN enables dual-encoder vision-language models to truly reject negated concepts without retraining, substantially improving targeted-negation understanding.

papers.abstract: Sampling multiple reports creates an inference problem: how should sampled evidence be converted into a final decision, and does a better structured decision yield a better report? We study these questions through a framework that separates the decision signal, scoring objective, and feasible decision set, followed by text realization. On MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, controlled comparisons across 13 generator configurations per benchmark under grouped development/test evaluation reveal three findings. First, changing the objective under fixed evidence and rule capacity changes predictions and their held-out metric trade-offs. Second, relaxing candidate constraints has objective-dependent effects under shared signals and frozen scores. Diagnostics connect the IU macro-oriented assertion increase to near-zero label thresholds and show that limited candidate coverage coexists with selection headroom. Third, a controlled realization study with SFT-Qwen3-VL-8B shows that decision-level gains can be attenuated, amplified, or reversed. Change decomposition reveals that realization can remove incorrect assertions while losing correct findings, so target fidelity and reference accuracy need not improve together. Finding gains also do not consistently improve reference-based report quality. These results motivate separate evaluation of decision rules, candidate constraints, and realized reports.
authors: Kun Zhao, Haoteng Tang, Chenghua Lin, Liang Zhan
bullets: Studies how sampled report evidence is converted into structured decisions and then realized as text.
Separates decision signals, scoring objectives, feasible candidate sets, and realization for controlled analysis.
Across MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, objectives and candidate constraints alter predictions and metric trade-offs.
Realization with SFT-Qwen3-VL-8B can amplify, attenuate, or reverse decision-level gains.
Finding improvements do not consistently improve reference-based report quality, motivating separate evaluation stages.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes decision rules and text realization for radiology report generation with a vision-language model, relevant to multimodal LLM applications.
papers.title: From Sampled Evidence to Radiology Reports: Objectives, Constraints, and Realization
