papers.tldr: A framework for radiology report generation shows that evidence selection, decision objectives, candidate constraints, and text realization each independently shape—and may distort—final report quality.

papers.abstract: Can a vision-language model tell left from right? Modern VLMs solve visual puzzles and follow hour-long videos, yet when asked whether the camera moved left or right, most do no better than a coin flip. Adding camera-motion data or geometric representations has been tried, separately, and neither closes the gap. We argue that camera-motion understanding needs two conditions at once: the representation must couple off-screen camera motion with on-screen flow dynamics, and it must be interpreted by the language model rather than trained as a standalone pose or depth estimator. We propose CameraVLM, which pairs a motion-state representation with state-language alignment. Camera tokens capture how the camera moves off screen, flow tokens capture how the subject and background move on screen, and a two-stage training strategy keeps language in the loop so that both are learned together with camera-motion semantics. With only 9B parameters, CameraVLM outperforms all open-source and camera-motion-specific models by a wide margin across three benchmarks and more than 20 baselines, and matches or surpasses GPT-6 Astra as well as human viewers in a 48-participant study. Project page: https://3dagentworld.github.io/CameraVLM/
authors: Chong Cheng, Ran Zhang, Xinyuan Li, Alan Zhao, Hao Wang, Xi Wang
bullets: Vision-language models often perform near chance when identifying whether a camera moved left or right.
The approach combines camera tokens for off-screen motion with flow tokens for subject and background dynamics.
A two-stage training strategy aligns these motion representations with language while keeping camera-motion semantics in the loop.
Using 9B parameters, CameraVLM outperforms open-source and camera-motion-specific models across three benchmarks and over 20 baselines.
It reportedly matches or exceeds GPT-6 Astra and human performance in a 48-participant study.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CameraVLM, a vision-language model for understanding camera motion by coupling off-screen motion with on-screen flow, directly advancing spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: When Left Is Right? Camera-Motion Understanding beyond Screen
papers.tldr: CameraVLM improves left-versus-right camera-motion understanding by jointly modeling off-screen camera motion, on-screen optical flow, and language semantics.

papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial audio reasoning requires a model to associate changing acoustic observations with the correct source and recover its spatial state at a queried time or interval, a challenge intensified by overlapping speech and source motion. To study this problem, we introduce Sonic-Bench, comprising 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips and 28.8K target-specific question-answer pairs across 480 simulated indoor scenes. The benchmark covers localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in single- and dual-source settings. We further propose SonicWorld, which integrates physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features into persistent source states through learned transitions and recurrent updates, and projects them into an Omni LLM for spatial reasoning. Compared with Spatial-Omni on the Sonic-Bench test split, SonicWorld improves direction accuracy from 31.98% to 34.69% and reduces azimuth error from 57.22{\deg} to 48.01{\deg}. In zero-shot transfer to Spatial LibriSpeech, SonicWorld retains strong localization performance, achieving 73.98% direction accuracy and 19.29{\deg} azimuth error, compared with 27.14% and 70.74{\deg} for Spatial-Omni.
authors: Chenlong Wei, Hanling Wang, Mingjin Lou, Yufan Shi, Yandong Sun, Sheldon Yu, Xiaohui Zhu, Xiaobo Jin, Yiwei Wang
bullets: Introduces Sonic-Bench with 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips and 28.8K target-specific QA pairs across 480 simulated indoor scenes.
Covers source localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in single- and dual-source settings.
Combines physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features with learned transitions and recurrent updates, then feeds source states into an Omni LLM.
On Sonic-Bench, improves direction accuracy and azimuth error over Spatial-Omni.
Transfers zero-shot to Spatial LibriSpeech while retaining strong localization performance.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial audio reasoning with latent source dynamics and an Omni LLM, fitting spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: SonicWorld: Source-Centric Latent Dynamics for Spatial Audio Reasoning
papers.tldr: SonicWorld enables source-aware spatial audio reasoning by maintaining persistent latent states for moving and overlapping sound sources.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) support simultaneous listening and speaking, but often lag behind half-duplex spoken language models (HD-SLMs) in general capabilities. We propose Dialogue-to-Duplex (D2), a framework that converts pretrained HD-SLMs into high-capability FD-SLMs at fine temporal granularity. D2 adapts the original audio encoder to streaming through decoder-free representation distillation and learns full-duplex interaction through supervised fine-tuning. We systematically study the effects of chunk size on full-duplex interaction, general capabilities, and inference computation. We apply D2 to two distinct HD-SLM architectures, Qwen3-Omni and LLaMA-Omni 2. At a 12.5Hz update rate, Qwen3-Omni-D2 achieves 99.2% turn-taking success with 521-ms latency, 99.5% interruption success, and a state-of-the-art VoiceBench score of 70.1.
authors: Cheng-Kuang Chang, Alexander H. Liu, Brian Kingsbury, Hilde Kuehne, Rogerio Feris, Samuel Thomas, James Glass, Kai-Wei Chang
bullets: Addresses the capability gap between full-duplex and half-duplex spoken language models.
Uses decoder-free representation distillation to make the audio encoder streamable, followed by supervised fine-tuning for duplex interaction.
Studies how chunk size affects interaction quality, general capabilities, and inference computation.
Applied to Qwen3-Omni and LLaMA-Omni 2; Qwen3-Omni-D2 reaches 99.2% turn-taking success, 521 ms latency, and 99.5% interruption success at 12.5 Hz.
Qwen3-Omni-D2 achieves a VoiceBench score of 70.1, reported as state of the art.
papers.selection_reason: Converts half-duplex spoken language models into full-duplex multimodal LLMs, fitting multimodal LLM extension.
papers.title: D2: High-Capability Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models from Half-Duplex Backbones
papers.tldr: D2 converts half-duplex spoken language models into capable, low-latency full-duplex models that can listen and speak simultaneously.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) provide an interface for interleaved text-image generation, where generated visual states can directly inform subsequent reasoning and synthesis. However, existing systems are still primarily demonstrated on short trajectories or simplified visual content. We develop a large UMM natively trained on interleaved multimodal data, with strong capabilities in image synthesis, text rendering, complex composition, and multimodal planning, and study how to extend these native capabilities to substantially longer autoregressive trajectories. The main challenge is that generated images continuously accumulate in context: irrelevant or imperfect visual states interfere with future synthesis, while previously established characters and scenes must still be recovered after long intervals. We introduce a visual-memory framework that maintains persistent visual references, selectively retrieves scene-relevant historical states while preserving the complete semantic history, and uses few-step self-rollout to adapt the model to imperfect generated histories. We further introduce LongMIG-Bench for evaluating long-horizon text-to-multi-image and image-to-multi-image generation. Our model achieves high-fidelity long-horizon interleaved generation with strong character and scene consistency, demonstrating how visual memory can scale native interleaved generation to substantially longer trajectories.
authors: Ziqiao Peng, Yutao Cui, Wang Lin, Zhong-Yu Li, Qingwen Gu, Tianhui Song, Chengyou Jia, Guozhen Zhang, Xuerui Qiu, Qixun Wang, Miles Yang, Zhao Zhong, Yonglong Tian, Hongyan Liu, Jun He
bullets: Addresses interference from accumulated or imperfect images while preserving recurring characters, scenes, and semantic history.
Uses persistent visual references, selective retrieval of relevant past visual states, and few-step self-rollout adaptation.
Introduces LongMIG-Bench for long-horizon text-to-multi-image and image-to-multi-image evaluation.
Demonstrates high-fidelity generation with strong character and scene consistency.
Scope: focuses on extending native interleaved generation to longer autoregressive trajectories.
papers.selection_reason: Unified multimodal model for long-horizon interleaved text-image generation with persistent visual memory; relevant to multimodal foundation models and long-context interleaved reasoning.
papers.title: Scaling Unified Multimodal Models to Long-Horizon Interleaved Generation
papers.tldr: A visual-memory framework enables unified multimodal models to generate coherent text-image sequences over substantially longer horizons.

papers.abstract: Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering (VQA) requires reasoning that extends beyond visible image content, demanding external commonsense and factual knowledge. While recent work leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) as knowledge sources, the question of how deeply such guidance should be integrated into a vision language architecture remains underexplored. In this work, we generate structured reasoning guidance, visual focus concepts, distractor elements and external knowledge using Llama~3.3~70B and systematically compare two integration strategies within a unified frozen ViT + FLAN-T5 framework on the OK-VQA benchmark: decision level late fusion and attention-matrix injection. Contrary to the prevailing assumption that deeper integration is superior, we find that shallow late fusion achieves the strongest results (39.4% exact match, +10.0 over the no guidance baseline), outperforming deep attention modification (31.8%) under data scarce fine-tuning. We further contribute an LLM based augmentation pipeline that expands training data more than tenfold via question paraphrasing. Our findings indicate that integration depth must be matched to the data regime.
authors: Aneerban Saha, Vijay Kumar, Sameer Madhav D., Priyam Srivastava, Dhruv Bansal
bullets: Studies how deeply LLM-generated knowledge should be integrated into vision-language models for knowledge-based VQA.
Uses Llama 3.3 70B to generate reasoning guidance, visual focus concepts, distractors, and external knowledge.
Compares late decision-level fusion with attention-matrix injection in a frozen ViT + FLAN-T5 framework on OK-VQA.
Late fusion achieves 39.4% exact match, 10.0 points above the no-guidance baseline, versus 31.8% for deep attention modification.
Introduces an LLM-based question-paraphrasing pipeline that expands training data more than tenfold; results suggest integration depth should match the data regime.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates LLM-guided knowledge integration strategies in vision-language VQA, directly relevant to multimodal LLM architecture and instruction/reasoning design.
papers.title: Rethinking LLM-Guided Visual Question Answering: Does Deeper Knowledge Integration Really Help?
papers.tldr: For knowledge-based VQA under data-scarce fine-tuning, shallow LLM guidance via late fusion outperforms deeper attention-based integration.

papers.abstract: Visual in-context learning (ICL) enables vision-language models (VLMs) to adapt at test time via demonstration examples, but its effectiveness depends critically on the examples selected. Recent counterfactual selection methods improve ICL by constructing demonstrations that expose how individual attribute changes affect the answer. However, they require multi-stage pipelines involving attribute extraction, caption engineering, and composed image matching. We propose a simpler alternative grounded in a key observation: a model's own prediction errors are natural counterfactual demonstrations that directly encode its failure modes. Our method, SMILE (Self-Mined Visual In-Context Learning from Errors), builds a model-specific pool of hard negatives offline by recording the target VLM's own mistakes. At test time, the prediction serves as a direction signal that surfaces, in the semantic embedding space, the past mistakes most likely to recur for the current query. This prediction-conditioned identification provides a unified mechanism for both closed-set classification and open-ended visual question answering without task-specific design. Across four benchmarks and four VLMs, SMILE delivers an average task-score gain of +3.09 points over the SOTA baseline at 5x lower latency. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/SMILE/
bullets: Visual ICL depends heavily on selecting effective demonstrations, while prior counterfactual methods require complex multi-stage pipelines.
SMILE offline-mines hard negatives from the target VLM’s own prediction errors to capture model-specific failure modes.
At test time, the model’s prediction guides semantic retrieval of likely recurring mistakes for the current query.
The same mechanism supports both closed-set classification and open-ended visual question answering without task-specific design.
Across four benchmarks and four VLMs, SMILE gains an average of 3.09 task-score points over the SOTA baseline with 5× lower latency.
papers.selection_reason: Improves visual in-context learning for VLMs by mining the model's own errors as demonstrations; directly relevant to multimodal LLM adaptation.
papers.title: The Value of Being Wrong: Self-Mined Visual In-Context Learning from Errors
papers.tldr: SMILE improves visual in-context learning by retrieving a model’s own past mistakes as prediction-conditioned counterfactual demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models, exemplified by GPT-6 Astra, raise the prospect of general-purpose embodied reasoning and planning. Using Internet videos for embodied pretraining calls for reliable physical-scale annotations. Yet visual geometry foundation models often recover scene structure and camera motion without reliable metric scale. We show that uncertain size priors of familiar objects can jointly constrain a reconstruction's shared scale. Building on this insight, we present UniMetric, a universal and training-free metric scale recovery framework for geometry foundation models, without additional sensors or task-specific metric supervision. Specifically, Metric Prior Acquisition elicits object height intervals from a vision-language model. Semantic-Geometric Alignment measures reconstructed object heights along the estimated support-surface normal in each frame and converts the priors into scale intervals. Global Scale Recovery reconciles these intervals through a convex objective, yielding a jointly feasible scale when they overlap and a unique compromise otherwise. The estimated sequence-level scale is applied uniformly to reconstructed points and camera translations. Controlled experiments with real VLM priors show that combining observations improves scale accuracy with exact relative object heights. To evaluate metric accuracy on GFM reconstructions without ground-truth scale alignment, we introduce MetricBench, covering twelve embodied, driving, and roadside subsets with sensor-derived ground truth. Across nine geometry foundation models, UniMetric reduces mean depth Abs Rel, reconstruction Chamfer distance, and trajectory error by 54.2%, 83.8%, and 65.6%, respectively, improving every model on all three tasks at the suite level. We release the UniMetric code and MetricBench data.
authors: Lei Yang, Yuner Zhang, Ziyang Liu, Ziying Song, Kai WU, Yiyang Gao, Jiangtao Su, Yiming Li
bullets: Addresses the lack of reliable physical-scale annotations in geometry foundation model outputs.
Elicits object-height intervals, aligns reconstructed objects with support-surface geometry, and converts them into scale intervals.
Reconciles multiple observations with a convex global objective to estimate one sequence-level scale, applied to points and camera translations.
Introduces MetricBench, a sensor-grounded benchmark spanning 12 embodied, driving, and roadside subsets.

Across nine geometry foundation models, reduces mean depth Abs Rel, Chamfer distance, and trajectory error by 54.2%, 83.8%, and 65.6%, respectively. In scope: requires familiar objects with usable size priors and overlapping or reconcilable scale constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free metric scale recovery for visual geometry foundation models using VLM object priors and geometric alignment; directly relevant to spatial/geometric reasoning in multimodal systems.
papers.title: UniMetric: Universal Metric Scale Recovery for Visual Geometry Foundation Models
papers.tldr: UniMetric is a training-free framework that recovers metric scale for visual geometry foundation model reconstructions using uncertain object-size priors from a vision-language model.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
authors: Zhe Sun, Liang An, Jiayu Yao, Ronglai Qian, Jianing Cai, Ziwei Huang, Qing Fan, Zhiyuan Yang, Yujun Cai, Hongli Cao, Yiwei Wang, Xiaoyan Wang
bullets: Targets underwater signal recognition for vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing.
Contains 375,051 traceable records spanning detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise under modeled propagation conditions.
Provides three-level labels, 13 leaf classes, templated multi-turn dialogues, and source/channel metadata.
On a balanced 2,600-record evaluation, nine open LALMs achieve only 2.0%–13.1% leaf accuracy; waveform input helps source routing more than fine-grained recognition.
Includes a silent-audio control, gated coarse-to-fine evaluation, and a released training partition for future adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks large audio-language models, which are multimodal LLMs with an additional audio modality; relevant to multimodal foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition
papers.tldr: UA-Bench is a large synthetic benchmark showing that open large audio-language models struggle with fine-grained underwater acoustic recognition without task-specific adaptation.

papers.abstract: Recent work has investigated Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs), models which can take multiple modalities and their combinations as input, as a way forward to have systems really capable of interacting with their environment. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for OLLMs, however, remains an open problem: existing methods largely target at most two modalities at a time, require access to model internals, or re-invocation of the evaluated model. We propose a model-agnostic UQ framework that scores a Chain-of-Thought response entirely through external omni-modal embeddings, measuring the grounding of the reasoning in the multimodal input and its internal coherence. Our contribution is the family of signals and an empirical characterisation of when it is reliable, rather than any single estimator: we find the geometric scores to be largely redundant with one another (mean within-split rank correlation 0.91-0.94) but strongly complementary to answer-dispersion baselines, and their reliability to depend on the generator and the modality. The resulting confidence estimates require no access to logits, hidden states or gradients of the evaluated model and no additional inference from it; they do require segmenting the reasoning trace with an auxiliary model and, for the aggregated score, a labelled calibration set that we show can be as small as 25 examples (although we also show that such a set buys little over fixing one signal a priori). On UNO-Bench, with both a closed and an open model, our scores yield small gains over self-consistency (systematic with the closed generator, mixed with the open one) and are competitive with self-verbalisation and internal-state baselines, especially in open-ended, omni-modal questions where previous state-of-the-art baselines struggle.
authors: Iacopo Ghinassi, Hy Nguyen Gia La, Luke Ong
bullets: Targets uncertainty quantification for inputs combining multiple modalities, beyond methods limited to two modalities.
Scores Chain-of-Thought grounding in multimodal inputs and internal coherence using external omni-modal embeddings.
Geometric signals are highly redundant with each other but complementary to answer-dispersion baselines; reliability varies by generator and modality.
On UNO-Bench, results provide small, systematic gains over self-consistency for a closed model and mixed gains for an open model, while remaining competitive with other baselines.
Requires an auxiliary model to segment reasoning traces; aggregated scoring may use a small labelled calibration set, though its benefit is limited.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty quantification for omni-modal LLMs using external embeddings; fits multimodal large language models.
papers.title: Estimating Uncertainty of Omnimodal Large Language Models via External Omnimodal Embeddings
papers.tldr: An external-embedding framework estimates uncertainty in omni-modal LLM reasoning without accessing model internals or rerunning the evaluated model.

papers.abstract: The rapid spread of face forgeries on the Web challenges the credibility of visual content. In practical Web environments, manipulated media originate from evolving generation pipelines and undergo diverse processing during dissemination, making reliable authenticity assessment under unseen manipulations and visual changes a critical challenge. We observe that a standard LoRA-adapted CLIP detector exhibits uneven patch-level decision dependence, concen trating a disproportionate share of class-specific relevance on a small fraction of visual patches. To improve robustness to variations in such highly dependent evidence, we propose EviStress, a two-stage framework for generalizable face forgery detection with textual explanations. In the first stage, Evidence-Targeted Patch Perturbation (ETPP) estimates patch dependence from global, relational, and semantic cues and assigns positively correlated perturbation probabilities, explicitly stress-testing highly dependent visual evidence during training. We further introduce Discriminative Variation Preservation (DVP), which constrains the residual between clean and perturbed representations to retain authenticity discriminative information. In the second stage, Intrinsic Evidence Instruction Tuning (IEIT) transfers the adapted CLIP encoder into LLaVA as its vision tower and performs parameter-efficient multimodal instruction tuning, enabling authenticity prediction and textual explanation directly from the learned forgery-sensitive representation without an external detector. Experiments demonstrate improved cross-dataset and cross-method generalization and corruption robustness, with the multimodal model providing authenticity predictions and human-readable explanations.
authors: Jiuyao Jing, Xuanyu Yi, Yu Zheng, Chunlei Peng
bullets: Targets the brittleness of CLIP-based detectors that rely disproportionately on a small number of image patches.
Uses Evidence-Targeted Patch Perturbation to identify and perturb highly dependent evidence during training.
Applies Discriminative Variation Preservation to retain authenticity-related information in perturbed representations.
Transfers the adapted CLIP encoder into LLaVA with parameter-efficient instruction tuning for prediction and explanation.
Reports improved cross-dataset, cross-method generalization and corruption robustness, with human-readable authenticity explanations.
papers.selection_reason: Uses evidence-targeted patch perturbation and multimodal instruction tuning on CLIP/LLaVA to produce predictions with textual explanations; transferable to robustness and interpretability of multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: EviStress: Evidence Stress Learning for Generalizable Face Forgery Detection with Textual Explanations
papers.tldr: EviStress improves face-forgery detection under unseen manipulations and visual corruption by stress-testing highly influential visual evidence and generating textual explanations.

papers.abstract: Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation often requires integrating visual findings with task-specific evidence rather than relying on direct visual recognition alone. While tool-augmented medical agents can supply such evidence via external modules, they often lack explicit mechanisms for learning when auxiliary evidence is needed and for preventing inapplicable quantitative evidence from entering diagnostic reasoning. To address this, we propose X-Ragent, a post-training framework for tool-augmented reinforcement learning that decouples learned auxiliary-evidence seeking from validity-gated quantitative measurement acquisition for evidence-grounded CXR reasoning. We construct Rad-CoT, a 7.7K-sample corpus combining causally ordered tool-augmented trajectories with report-style diagnostic reasoning, and use it to initialize Qwen3-VL-8B via agentic supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We then optimize the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using an accuracy-gated reward that applies process-level terms for measurement consistency and auxiliary-tool cost only to correct trajectories, preventing plausible process behavior from compensating for an incorrect diagnosis. Across three CXR benchmarks, X-Ragent achieves the strongest results, including an 8.6-point improvement on the fully held-out ChestAgentBench. By seeking evidence selectively and admitting only valid measurements, X-Ragent supports more faithful and evidence-grounded CXR reasoning.
authors: Yi Wang, Zhenlong Yuan, Yuchan Guo, Maolei Huang, Zijian Song, Dapeng Zhang, Rongbin Tan, Jiyuan Wang, Zhiyuan Wang, Fangfang Lin, Shuhan Song, Huawei Cao
bullets: Addresses tool-augmented CXR agents that lack selective evidence-seeking and safeguards against inapplicable measurements.
Uses reinforcement learning to decouple auxiliary-evidence acquisition from validity-gated quantitative measurement use.
Builds Rad-CoT, a 7.7K-sample corpus, and initializes Qwen3-VL-8B with agentic supervised fine-tuning.
Optimizes with GRPO using accuracy-gated process rewards for measurement consistency and tool cost.
Achieves the strongest results across three CXR benchmarks, including an 8.6-point gain on held-out ChestAgentBench.
papers.selection_reason: Post-trains a multimodal LLM with tool-augmented reinforcement learning and instruction tuning; technically transferable to general multimodal reasoning agents.
papers.title: X-Ragent: Tool-Augmented Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Grounded Chest X-Ray Reasoning
papers.tldr: X-Ragent improves chest X-ray reasoning by learning when to seek auxiliary evidence and admitting quantitative measurements only when valid.

papers.abstract: Interacting with unfamiliar objects requires understanding how their parts connect and move. We introduce ViewStruct, a framework for jointly predicting connectivity and articulation in objects and scenes. Given an RGB image with aligned part segmentation and depth, optionally supplemented by images or video, ViewStruct predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters. Its view-grounded representation links predictions to observed regions and expresses joint geometry in a gravity-aligned, view-relative frame, without requiring category-specific canonical orientations. A pretrained vision--language model is adapted to predict structure in seconds, without requiring observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation. Experiments demonstrate improved structural prediction over evaluated baselines and transfer to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos, despite task-specific training exclusively on synthetic data. Simulated manipulation experiments further demonstrate the utility of predicted joints for generating robot motion trajectories.
authors: Wenjing Bian, Ranran Huang, Andreas Geiger
bullets: Predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters from RGB, aligned segmentation, and depth, with optional additional images or video.
Represents joint geometry in gravity-aligned, view-relative coordinates without requiring category-specific canonical orientations.
Adapts a pretrained vision–language model for inference in seconds, without observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation.
Outperforms evaluated baselines and transfers to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos.
Predicted joints support simulated robot manipulation trajectory generation; training is task-specific and exclusively synthetic.
papers.selection_reason: Predicts part articulation and connectivity from images/depth and demonstrates utility for generating robot motion trajectories; view-grounded spatial representation is transferable to embodied manipulation and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: ViewStruct: View-Grounded Articulation and Connectivity Inference
papers.tldr: ViewStruct infers object part connectivity and articulation from visual inputs using a view-grounded representation that transfers beyond synthetic training categories and assets.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards commonly assigns one sequence advantage to an entire response. This outcome-level signal distinguishes overall response quality but leaves changes in visual-evidence use across generated tokens implicit. We introduce VAttnPO (Visual Attention-Guided Policy Optimization), which uses answer-conditioned visual attention to refine token-level credit while preserving the verifier-derived trajectory-mean advantage. A frozen old policy constructs a visual reference by teacher forcing the known correct answer and produces a visual distribution for each rollout token. VAttnPO measures their agreement in visual-attention space using Jensen--Shannon divergence, rather than reading guidance from teacher output-token distributions or introducing an attention-matching objective. Trajectory centering, relative-position weighting, and credit balancing turn this agreement into a zero-mean, position-aware correction to the GRPO sequence advantage. Token intervention, visual-index permutation, and trajectory analysis provide diagnostic evidence linking this signal to model behavior, visual correspondence, and generation position. On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, VAttnPO raises six-task image AVE from 70.97 with GRPO to 73.50 and scores higher on every reported structured, video, and MME metric. Gains over GRPO also hold on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and InternVL3-8B-Instruct.
authors: Lihao Zheng, Zhenwei Shao, Zhou Yu, Yan Yang, Haoyi Sun, Qian Wang, Ning Mao, Pan Zhou
bullets: Problem: Sequence-level advantages do not reveal how visual evidence contributes across individual generated tokens.
Method: A frozen old policy compares rollout-token visual attention with attention from teacher-forced correct answers using Jensen–Shannon divergence.
The resulting signal is trajectory-centered, position-aware, and balanced before correcting the GRPO sequence advantage.
Diagnostics examine token interventions, visual-index permutations, and generation-position effects.
On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, image AVE improves from 70.97 with GRPO to 73.50; gains also hold across other reported models and metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Visual-attention-guided policy optimization for multimodal LLMs; fits MLLM training/reasoning.
papers.title: VAttnPO: Visual Attention-Guided Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: VAttnPO improves multimodal RL by converting answer-conditioned visual-attention agreement into token-level credit while retaining sequence-level verifier rewards.

papers.abstract: Visual contrastive decoding corrects answers using the prediction difference between the original image and a reference condition, yet the same contrast also turns supported abstentions into incorrect answers. We find that abstentions are lost at two stages: contrastive decoding with candidate filtering can exclude the abstention token before any comparison takes place, and the reference branch's response to the abstention instruction is removed when the reference prediction is subtracted. We therefore propose instruction-preserving decoding, which keeps the effect of the abstention instruction on the original-image prediction intact while leaving the contrast strength freely adjustable. Using a perturbed image and an image-free prediction as references, we obtain IP-VCD and IP-M3ID. On decision utility (DU), which credits both correct answers and supported abstentions, both methods outperform all compared non-IP baselines on every one of nine models on VizWiz, and IP-VCD also leads on eight of nine models on Food-101. Candidate measurements and paired per-question comparisons show that computing the instruction effect and the visual contrast term separately lets contrastive decoding support both correct answers and supported abstentions.
authors: Haonan Zhang, Ting Jin, Wenzhong Tang, Shuai Wang
bullets: Visual contrastive decoding can wrongly eliminate supported abstentions during candidate filtering or reference subtraction.
The proposed method preserves the abstention instruction’s effect on the original-image prediction while keeping contrast strength adjustable.
Two variants use perturbed-image and image-free references: IP-VCD and IP-M3ID.
Both outperform non-instruction-preserving baselines on decision utility across nine models on VizWiz; IP-VCD leads on eight of nine models on Food-101.
Separate measurement of instruction effects and visual contrast supports both correct answers and supported abstentions.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces instruction-preserving decoding for VQA to handle abstention tokens correctly, improving decision utility on standard benchmarks.
papers.title: Lost in Contrast: Instruction-Preserving Decoding for Reliable Visual Question Answering
papers.tldr: Instruction-preserving decoding improves visual question answering by retaining valid abstentions while using visual contrast to correct unreliable answers.

papers.abstract: Visual token compression has emerged as a critical technique for reducing the inference cost of Vision-Language Models. Existing methods select tokens based on text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed combination of both---treating the relevance-diversity balance as a universal constant independent of the input. We conduct a systematic analysis to challenge this assumption. At the dataset level, grid-searching the optimal relevance-diversity weight per benchmark reveals substantial cross-task variation. More critically, we further maximize per-sample answer likelihood to recover sample-level oracle weights, finding that their distributions not only differ markedly across benchmarks but also exhibit high within-benchmark variance. Based on these observations, we propose SAVER, a framework for Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction. We first derive a Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens to infer a sample-specific relevance-diversity weight, and then apply this weight to jointly select tokens via a Weighted Text Centroid (WTC) for relevance scoring and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (VMCG) for diversity. SAVER requires no additional training and achieves sample-aware balancing entirely at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, retaining 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B with only 11.1% of the original visual tokens, and further generalizing to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
authors: Yihang Huang, Peisong Wen, Chenhao Zhou, Difu Feng, Qianqian Xu
bullets: Fixed relevance–diversity weights vary substantially across tasks and even among samples within the same benchmark.
SAVER infers a sample-specific weight from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens using a Geometric Intent Prior.
It combines Weighted Text Centroid relevance scoring with Visual Marginal Coverage Gain diversity selection.
The training-free method retains 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B while using 11.1% of the original visual tokens.
It also generalizes to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
papers.selection_reason: Sample-aware visual token reduction for VLMs balancing relevance and diversity at inference time.
papers.title: When 1+1 Backfires: Rethinking Relevance-Diversity Balancing for Sample-Aware Visual Token Reduction
papers.tldr: SAVER improves visual token compression by adapting the relevance–diversity trade-off to each input sample at inference time.

papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) representation learning is challenged by noisy signals, inter-subject variability, and heterogeneous electrode montages in different datasets and recording settings. Recent self-supervised EEG pretraining methods improve transferability by converting heterogeneous recordings into unified token or sequence representations, but channel-aware designs may still encode montage- or dataset-specific regularities. We propose HyBRA, a self-supervised framework based on hyperbolic global-local brain-region aggregation. HyBRA maps heterogeneous channel observations into a fixed regional token space by combining electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances. A channel-evidence injection branch preserves fine-grained discriminative cues during aggregation. The resulting tokens are processed by a Region-Time Transformer and pretrained with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals. HyBRA outperforms the compared methods in average balanced accuracy on six benchmark datasets. Under a controlled six-fold evaluation on OpenBMI-MI, HyBRA matches CSBrain in balanced accuracy, improves AUROC by 1.84 percentage points and AUPRC by 5.23 percentage points, and uses 96.8\% fewer parameters. Matched comparisons on TUAB and TUEV show higher balanced accuracy for hyperbolic matching than for Euclidean distance or cosine similarity.
authors: Xin Liu, Feng Lu, Wei Li
bullets: Maps variable EEG channels into fixed regional tokens using electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances.
Preserves fine-grained channel information through a channel-evidence injection branch.
Uses a Region-Time Transformer with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals for pretraining.
Outperforms compared methods in average balanced accuracy across six benchmark datasets.
On OpenBMI-MI, matches CSBrain in balanced accuracy, improves AUROC by 1.84 and AUPRC by 5.23 percentage points, while using 96.8% fewer parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Uses hyperbolic geometry for self-supervised EEG representation learning. The hyperbolic aggregation method is transferable to spatial reasoning tasks involving hierarchical data.
papers.title: HyBRA-EEG: Hyperbolic Global-Local Brain-Region Aggregation for Self-Supervised EEG Representation Learning
papers.tldr: HyBRA is a self-supervised EEG representation-learning framework that uses hyperbolic global-local brain-region aggregation to improve robustness across heterogeneous electrode montages and datasets.

papers.abstract: An ordered visual code lets a short prefix stand in for an image, and the training loss decides what that prefix contains. Under pixel reconstruction the first bits go to the directions of highest variance, and we prove that a caption can then be independent of the entire first half of a code that is rate-optimal for pixels at every length. In the rate-distortion sense a caption is therefore not the low-rate code of its image, unless the code is built to make it one. We study that construction and what it costs. We cast captioning and text-to-image generation as successive refinement under a distortion measure that changes along the code, from caption log-loss in the early stages to pixel distortion in the last, so that each stage is compared with its own optimum. Putting words first then costs nothing among the caption stages exactly when the captions form a summarization chain, and it costs the pixels at most the caption uncertainty left in a pixel-optimal reconstruction, which is large for short prefixes and small at full length. We build RUNG, an ordered code whose prefixes are supervised by a summarization ladder of captions and whose full length reconstructs the image; generation extends the code past the prompt and captioning truncates it. With data and capacity held fixed, ordering by language instead of reconstruction raises prefix-caption information 2.9 times and GenEval from 0.76 to 0.83, at a measured cost of 2.8 dB PSNR at a quarter of the code and 0.1 dB at full length. RUNG-XL (3.4B) reaches 0.88 GenEval and 87.6 DPG-Bench in 32 network evaluations and 0.91 GenEval when errors are redrawn at the rung where they appear; its coarse and fine captions agree 94.1% of the time, and it edits images without inversion.
bullets: Pixel-optimal codes prioritize high-variance visual information, so short prefixes may contain little caption-relevant content.
The paper formulates captioning and image generation as successive refinement with caption loss early and pixel distortion late.
RUNG supervises code prefixes with a hierarchy of captions, then uses the full code for image reconstruction.
With fixed data and capacity, language-first ordering raises prefix-caption information 2.9× and GenEval from 0.76 to 0.83.
The approach costs 2.8 dB PSNR at one-quarter code length but only 0.1 dB at full length; RUNG also supports editing without inversion.
papers.selection_reason: Builds an ordered visual code supervised by captions and reconstructs images; novel multimodal representation with language-vision trade-offs.
papers.title: Making Language the Low-Rate Code of Vision: Successive Refinement from Words to Pixels
papers.tldr: RUNG orders visual codes around language first, improving caption alignment and text-to-image generation while largely preserving full-resolution reconstruction quality.

papers.abstract: Basic probabilistic models form the basis of modern deep learning largely by defining the final activation layer of a network and allowing the networks outputs to be interpreted through a probabilistic lens. By increasing the complexity of these final activation layers to include features such as spatial regularisation, allow for these models to improve in performance without requiring significantly more data. The challenge however is to ensure that these more complex probabilistic graphical models adapt well to being used in tandem with deep learning, that is, ensuring they converge and have meaningful derivatives. The goal of this paper is to show two algorithms with provable convergence properties to allow this type of regularisation for image and signal classification models. Through both rigorous mathematical analysis and in silico experiments, we can show the differing performance between these solution types.
bullets: Motivates richer probabilistic output layers to add spatial regularization without substantially increasing data requirements.
Addresses the challenge of obtaining meaningful derivatives and convergence when pairing graphical models with deep networks.
Introduces two solution approaches for pairwise conditional random fields with convergence guarantees.
Evaluates the approaches through mathematical analysis and in silico experiments, showing differences in their performance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces convergent differentiable approaches for CRFs with spatial regularization. This contributes to the class of differentiable probabilistic models for spatial reasoning.
papers.title: DeepFlow: Two Convergent Differentiable Approaches for Pairwise Conditional Random Fields
papers.tldr: DeepFlow presents two provably convergent differentiable algorithms for incorporating pairwise CRF-style spatial regularization into deep image and signal classifiers.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models answer questions about images they were never shown, a failure called mirage. Such an answer can be correct without being justified by the evidence, and the difference matters wherever a model's output is checked by someone who did not see its input. We locate the failure in the training objective: cross-entropy separates a model that reads the image from one that ignores it by only the conditional mutual information between answer and image, and no training example rewards declining. We formalise support completion, TIDE, which also shows each training question with a blank image, a same-domain wrong image and an out-of-domain image, with targets that decline, and prove that under TIDE every image-blind predictor is suboptimal by at least 1.04 nats per example, that the optimum declines exactly on the counterfactual kinds while keeping its behaviour on valid images, and that for any finite model the error of its answer-or-decline decision, declining on valid input plus answering on invalid input, is bounded below by how well its representation separates valid from invalid evidence. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B under a frozen held-out protocol with two judges, the three-condition predecessor of TIDE reduced the invalid-evidence mirage rate from 0.759 to 0.097 and the blank-image rate from 0.700 to 0.003 at a false-abstention cost of 0.126; label-free grounding raised the rate to 0.859, a likelihood-advantage contrast moved it only to 0.718 because its empty-image term carries no gradient, and grounding applied after support completion re-opened the mirage. The four-condition protocol on three base models, with seeds and component ablations, is in progress and not reported here.
authors: Alfaj Uddin Ahmed, Md. Shaown Miah, Md Arid Hasan, Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, Sayeed Shafayet Chowdhury
bullets: Mirage occurs when models answer questions about unseen or irrelevant images, even if the answer happens to be correct.
The proposed support-completion objective presents valid, blank, same-domain wrong, and out-of-domain image conditions, with decline targets for invalid evidence.
Theory shows image-blind predictors are suboptimal under TIDE and links decision errors to how well representations separate valid from invalid evidence.
On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, a three-condition predecessor reduced invalid-evidence mirages from 0.759 to 0.097 and blank-image responses from 0.700 to 0.003, with a false-abstention cost of 0.126.
The full four-condition evaluation across three base models is still in progress; reported results use a predecessor protocol and two judges.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses a core failure mode of vision-language models via a new training objective, directly relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Teaching Vision-Language Models to Decline: Support Completion Against Mirage
papers.tldr: TIDE trains vision-language models to decline when an image does not support an answer, substantially reducing unsupported image-question responses while preserving valid-image behavior.

papers.abstract: 3D scene graph generation requires understanding both object semantics and metric spatial relations. However, existing open-vocabulary methods often struggle with spatial predicates because language similarity reflects semantic co-occurrence rather than explicit geometry. We propose GHOST, a Geometry-constrained Hybrid diffusion framework for Open-vocabulary 3D Scene graph generaTion. GHOST jointly models continuous node geometry and discrete edge predicates, following a geometry-to-constraint-to-predicate denoising process to ensure geometrically consistent relation prediction. It introduces language-grounded constraint induction, which maps predicate embeddings to differentiable geometric constraints that guide both layout refinement and predicate reweighting. A Geometry-Topology Collaborative Denoiser further couples node and edge reasoning through noise-adaptive interaction and orientation-aware modeling. Experiments on 3DSSG demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both closed-set and open-vocabulary settings, including over 17-point gains over RelationField on spatial predicates.
authors: Changqun Feng, Wangxiandi Yin, Xin Hu, Ruiting Dai, Feiyang Yang, Jielei Wang, Tao He
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between language similarity and explicit 3D spatial geometry in open-vocabulary relation prediction.
Uses a geometry-to-constraint-to-predicate denoising process to jointly model continuous node geometry and discrete edge predicates.
Induces differentiable geometric constraints from predicate embeddings to refine layouts and reweight relation predictions.
Employs a Geometry-Topology Collaborative Denoiser with noise-adaptive interaction and orientation-aware modeling.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on 3DSSG, including over 17-point gains over RelationField on spatial predicates.
papers.selection_reason: Open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation with geometry-constrained spatial reasoning fits 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: GHOST: Geometry-Constrained Hybrid Diffusion for Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Graph Generation
papers.tldr: GHOST improves open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation by coupling language-grounded geometric constraints with diffusion-based joint reasoning over objects and spatial relations.

papers.abstract: Visual artifacts such as charts, technical diagrams, webpages, and document pages underpin scientific, commercial, and engineering workflows. Editing these artifacts requires direct modification, dependency-aware updates, preservation of unaffected content, and compliance with domain constraints. We define this capability as Visual Artifact Operation (VAO). Prior benchmarks test parts of this problem, including cascading updates in charts. We study direct edits, dependent updates, and preservation across visual domains and pixel, code, and agent paradigms under one image-only protocol. We introduce Visual Artifact Operation Bench (VAO-Bench), comprising 1,573 manually screened tasks across nine artifact categories and three difficulty levels. VAO-Bench uses executable artifacts and deterministic rendering to trace reference transformations and annotate direct edits, dependent updates, and preservation constraints. All systems receive the same source image and instruction; we evaluate pixel-space editors, code-generating multimodal systems, and tool-using agents on direct-edit accuracy, dependency-aware update, content preservation, domain validity, and visual quality. Experiments show that executable-code systems better support dependent updates, while pixel-space editors offer faster execution and strong visual quality. Explicitly stating dependencies improves both paradigms, identifying implicit-update inference as a central bottleneck. VAO-Bench provides a reproducible foundation for dependable visual artifact editing across generation paradigms.
authors: Shun Guo, Shuizhou Shi, Boao Wang, Wei Xiong, Siyu Sun, Jiangtong Li, Jie Li
bullets: Defines Visual Artifact Operation as direct editing, dependency-aware updates, preservation of unaffected content, and domain-valid outputs.
Introduces 1,573 manually screened tasks spanning nine artifact categories and three difficulty levels.
Uses executable artifacts, deterministic rendering, and a shared image-only protocol to assess multiple system paradigms.
Code-based systems handle dependent updates better, while pixel editors execute faster and produce strong visual quality.
Explicit dependency instructions improve both paradigms; inferring implicit updates remains a key bottleneck.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks instruction-guided visual editing across multimodal systems, relevant to multimodal foundation model capabilities.
papers.title: Pixels or Code? Benchmarking Instruction-Guided Visual Artifact Operation
papers.tldr: VAO-Bench evaluates how well pixel, code, and agent systems perform instruction-guided edits to visual artifacts, revealing a trade-off between dependency handling and execution speed or visual quality.

papers.abstract: Current image-text evaluation often relies on a global score, which gives limited insight into which semantic details are supported by the image. Explainable metrics provide rationales, but the visual evidence supporting those rationales can still be difficult to verify. We introduce VisExMEM, a reference-free evaluator that decomposes captions into atomic claims, localizes visual evidence, verifies each claim, and averages claim-level support into a global score. Explanations use the same evidence and decisions. We train Qwen3.5-based 4B and 9B models on 100K samples with multi-task SFT, counterfactual refinement, and evidence-aware GDPO. Across eight benchmarks, VisExMEM-9B achieves the highest descriptive composite among open-source evaluators in our comparison, exceeding VQAScore by 11.7 points while remaining competitive with GPT-5.6 Sol. We also introduce AGITA-Bench, containing 600 human-annotated image-text pairs and 8.7K atomic claims for global and claim-level evaluation. For untuned Qwen3.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol controls, decomposed prompting raises the same composite by 3.6-5.1 points relative to holistic prompting. Human evaluation shows that VisExMEM explanations outperform prior explainable metrics and approach GPT-5.6 Sol.
authors: Subhadeep Roy, Christoph Leiter, Steffen Eger
bullets: Addresses the limited interpretability and verifiability of global image-text evaluation scores.
Decomposes captions into atomic claims, localizes supporting evidence, verifies each claim, and averages support into a global score.
Uses shared evidence and decisions to generate explanations, improving their faithfulness.
Across eight benchmarks, VisExMEM-9B reports the highest descriptive composite among compared open-source evaluators and remains competitive with GPT-5.6 Sol.
Introduces AGITA-Bench with 600 human-annotated image-text pairs and 8.7K atomic claims for global and claim-level evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a multimodal evaluation metric that grounds explanations in visual evidence, contributing to spatial intelligence and multimodal foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: VisExMEM: Visual Evidence-Based Explainable Multimodal Evaluation Metric
papers.tldr: VisExMEM is a reference-free multimodal metric that evaluates captions by verifying atomic claims against localized visual evidence and producing evidence-grounded explanations.

papers.abstract: Speech-driven visual grounding in remote sensing (RSVG) removes the typing bottleneck of text-based interaction and is intended to preserve prosodic intent, enabling hands-free target acquisition in time-critical missions. The direct-audio paradigm, mapping raw speech straight to a bounding box and bypassing automatic speech recognition (ASR), was recently adopted by RSTalker, but what such grounders actually learn about language remains unmeasured. SemEcho grafts a frozen Whisper speech pathway onto a VLTVG grounding host so that speech and text share one decoder, making the paired text, free by construction since speech corpora in this task are synthesized from DIOR-RSVG expressions, a training-time teacher and a fair, same-host text upper bound. On this instrument we dissect three semantic injection channels (feature-mimicry distillation, word-level CTC supervision, and two-stage ASR pretraining) with linear semantic probes, and release Audio-DIOR-R (80,973 training clips; 10 timbres x K=3; Qwen3-TTS synthesis with online sox noise lambda in [0, 0.4]) and Audio-DIOR-Comp, a re-split holding out 17 attribute-category combinations under a 2x2 acoustic-semantic protocol. Our anatomy yields four findings. (i) Whether direct alignment beats a domain-trained ASR cascade is decided by recognizer quality: against a weak in-domain cascade (CTC 0.53) direct wins by 9.0 Acc@0.5 points with transcription errors concentrated on spatial-relation words, but a strong in-domain cascade (CTC 0.029) reaches the text upper bound (80.8 vs. 81.0) and beats even the strongest direct model by 8.8 points; the anti-ASR premise holds only against weak recognizers.
bullets: Speech-driven remote-sensing grounding aims to enable hands-free target acquisition while preserving prosodic intent.
SemEcho combines a frozen Whisper speech pathway with a VLTVG grounding host, using paired text as training-time semantic supervision and an upper bound.
It evaluates feature-mimicry distillation, word-level CTC supervision, and two-stage ASR pretraining with linear semantic probes.
The study introduces Audio-DIOR-R and Audio-DIOR-Comp for acoustic and compositional evaluation.
Against a weak in-domain ASR cascade, direct grounding gains 9.0 Acc@0.5 points; a strong cascade nearly matches the text upper bound and exceeds the strongest direct model by 8.8 points.
papers.selection_reason: Speech-driven visual grounding with spatial-relation understanding fits multimodal spatial intelligence.
papers.title: From Sound to Sense: An Anatomy of Semantic Supervision for Speech-Driven Visual Grounding in Remote Sensing Imagery
papers.tldr: SemEcho provides a controlled framework for measuring semantic supervision in direct speech-driven visual grounding and finds that strong ASR can outperform direct audio grounding, challenging the anti-ASR premise.

papers.abstract: Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) is widely used to encode relative positions in Transformers. In multi-view settings, however, patch coordinates are defined independently in each image: the same 3D point can therefore have different coordinates across views, making them insufficient for establishing cross-view correspondences. We introduce WorldRoPE, a probabilistic world-centric RoPE for multi-view attention. At each layer, WorldRoPE back-projects each patch token into a set of volumetric Gaussian primitives in a shared world frame. These primitives represent multiple plausible 3D supports for a token, jointly capturing alternative depth hypotheses, depth uncertainty, and the finite spatial extent of its patch frustum. When a key token's support is projected into a query view, it induces a distribution over where that key may appear in the query image. WorldRoPE integrates the rotary operator over this distribution in closed form, combining rotations at the projected primitive centers according to their mixture weights with covariance-dependent attenuation. This makes attention less sensitive to uncertain key locations in the query view, without rasterizing or warping token features. The formulation reduces to deterministic RoPE when the support collapses to a point. Across layers, the predicted geometry guides cross-view attention, while the updated features refine the geometry used at the next layer. Experiments on novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D geometry reconstruction demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRoPE for multi-view Transformers.
authors: Mijeong Kim, Kyujin Lim, Bohyung Han
bullets: Per-image patch coordinates cannot reliably establish correspondences for the same 3D point across views.
Each token is back-projected into volumetric Gaussian primitives capturing alternative depths, uncertainty, and patch-frustum extent.
The method integrates RoPE over the induced projected-location distribution using mixture weights and covariance-based attenuation.
It guides cross-view attention with predicted geometry while allowing updated features to refine geometry across layers.
Experiments show effectiveness for novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D geometry reconstruction.
papers.selection_reason: World-centric RoPE for multi-view attention; fits 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: WorldRoPE: Probabilistic World-Centric Rotary Embedding for Multi-View Attention
papers.tldr: WorldRoPE enables geometry-aware cross-view attention by representing uncertain 3D token locations as probabilistic supports in a shared world frame.

papers.abstract: Test-time agentic computation can improve multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection, but indiscriminate computation may duplicate resolved work, introduce noisy evidence, and perturb correct predictions. We propose that such computation should be residual: allocate additional computation only to requirements unresolved by the base model and, after a localized failure, recompute only the affected states. We instantiate this formulation in ReTAC, a training-free multiagent framework for video spatial reasoning. ReTAC organizes supplementary computation around unresolved requirements. It plans ordered steps to acquire missing spatial evidence and combines the observations with compatible native evidence for reasoning. In addition, it uses stage-aligned verification to localize failures to planning, perception, or reasoning. Dependency-based recovery recomputes only affected states while reusing unaffected ones. Extensive experiments show that ReTAC achieves the highest overall score among the compared methods across three mainstream MLLMs and two widely adopted benchmarks. Further analyses show that gains from additional computation depend not only on how much is used, but also on where it is allocated and which valid intermediate states are preserved.
authors: Yike Wu, Keyan Chen, Qixiong Wang, Xi Xiang, Maofei Que, Xiaolong Jiang, Xiaoqin Zhang, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Addresses redundant, noisy, or disruptive computation in MLLMs during video spatial reasoning.
Uses a training-free multiagent framework that plans steps to gather missing spatial evidence and combines it with native evidence.
Applies stage-aligned verification to identify whether failures arise from planning, perception, or reasoning.
Uses dependency-based recovery to recompute affected states while preserving valid intermediate results.
Achieves the highest overall score among compared methods across three MLLMs and two benchmarks, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Residual test-time agentic computation for video spatial reasoning; fits spatial intelligence and test-time learning.
papers.title: ReTAC: Residual Test-Time Agentic Computation for Video Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: ReTAC improves video spatial reasoning by directing test-time agentic computation only toward unresolved requirements and localized failures.

papers.abstract: Current ASR models perform well on general benchmarks but still struggle with acoustically ambiguous words. Visual context can aid recognition in screen-based scenarios, yet existing benchmarks provide limited insight into the benefits of different types of visual evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ScreenASR-Bench , a tiered benchmark with three progressively challenging levels: Explicit Textual Evidence (ETE), based on direct on-screen text; Explicit Visual Evidence (EVE), using visible content rather than on-screen text; and Implicit Semantic Evidence (ISE), requiring scene-level inference. Extensive experiments on ASR models, Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) and Omni models show that incorporating visual context substantially improves recall over the audio-only setting across all three model families. The gains are largest for ETE and smallest for ISE, indicating that models leverage direct visual evidence more effectively than indirect semantic cues. To facilitate future research on visually grounded speech recognition, we publicly release ScreenASR-Bench.
authors: Mingwei Fu, Zheshu Song, Zhikai Zhou, Shen Huang, Shidong Shang, Mengxiao Zhu
bullets: Targets acoustically ambiguous words in screen-based ASR scenarios.
Introduces three tiers: Explicit Textual Evidence, Explicit Visual Evidence, and Implicit Semantic Evidence.
Tests ASR, Large Audio-Language, and Omni models with visual context.
Visual input improves recall across all model families, with the largest gains for direct on-screen text and the smallest for scene-level inference.
The benchmark is publicly released to support research on visually grounded speech recognition.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for visually grounded ASR with multimodal models; relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: ScreenASR-Bench: A Tiered Benchmark for Speech Recognition with Visual Context
papers.tldr: ScreenASR-Bench evaluates how progressively indirect visual context helps speech recognition beyond audio alone.

papers.abstract: World-action models should preserve the intended manipulation across equivalent descriptions of a spatial goal. We evaluate this consistency in 864 rollouts from three models across four RoboLab scenes, holding initial states and task goals fixed. Describing relations through the reference object rather than the object-to-move lowers the rate of reaching a stable placement by 12.2 percentage points on average. The effect of instruction rephrasing varies across spatial relations, so aggregate scores can hide sensitivity to wording. Standalone tests of the policies' language understanding identify relation reversals and show that adding images can disrupt otherwise correct text-only interpretations. Rollout analysis also distinguishes spatial placement from instruction following: moving the wrong object can satisfy the requested relation, and rates of stable placement fall from 43.2% at any time to 21.8% at episode end. These findings motivate a more thorough evaluation of world-action models' steerability, language understanding, and grounding. Evaluations should test consistency across equivalent instructions, verify that the intended object moved, and check whether the requested arrangement persists to the end of the rollout.
authors: Ali-Adeeb Abbas, Esmaeil Seraj, Behrad Toghi, Taskin Padir
bullets: Evaluates instruction consistency across 864 rollouts, three models, and four RoboLab scenes with fixed initial states and goals.
Reference-object phrasing reduces stable-placement success by 12.2 percentage points on average, with sensitivity varying by spatial relation.
Standalone language tests reveal relation reversals; adding images can disrupt interpretations that are correct from text alone.
Rollout analysis separates spatial placement from instruction following: the wrong object may be moved, and end-of-episode stability is lower than transient success.
Findings call for evaluations that test equivalent instructions, verify object identity, and assess whether arrangements persist to episode end.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates spatial instruction grounding in world-action models for manipulation, relevant to VLA and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Same Goal, Different Words: Spatial Instruction Sensitivity in World-Action Models
papers.tldr: World-action models can produce different—and sometimes incorrect—manipulations for equivalent spatial instructions, revealing weaknesses in language grounding and steerability.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image models have made remarkable progress in visual fidelity and instruction following, yet complex compositional generation remains challenging. Existing agentic approaches address this limitation through iterative generation and editing, adapting their actions based on interaction history. However, they typically fix the continuation state (i.e., the image from which refinement proceeds) to the latest image. Since iterative editing is not necessarily monotonic, the agent may continue refining from the latest image even when it has already degraded. In this work, we introduce GenRevisit, an agentic framework that extends action selection to joint continuation-state and action selection. The agent can not only use interaction history to adjust editing instructions but also select an image candidate to edit, jointly deciding where to continue from and how to refine. We train GenRevisit with SFT followed by agentic reinforcement learning. To address the coarse credit assignment of final outcome reward in GRPO, which assigns the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, we further propose Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA) to redistribute positive advantage according to each action's contribution to reducing the remaining objective. On GenEval2, GenRevisit achieves GM scores of 84.3 and 74.4 with Qwen-Image-2512 and Z-Image-Turbo, surpassing the strongest baselines using the same generators by 12.7 and 10.9 points respectively. GenRevisit achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval, GenEval++, and GenEval2 among baselines.
authors: Zixu Wang, Xiaoran Zhao, Yahui Liu, Feng-ao Wang, Junhao Xiao, You Shu, Bing Liu, Yiting Liu, Songlei Jian, Zhiliang Tian, Dongsheng Li
bullets: Addresses degradation caused by always refining the latest image in iterative editing.
Jointly selects a continuation image from interaction history and the next editing action.
Uses supervised fine-tuning followed by agentic reinforcement learning.
Introduces Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA) to assign credit based on each action’s contribution.
Achieves state-of-the-art results among baselines on GenEval, GenEval++, and GenEval2; on GenEval2, it improves GM scores by 12.7 and 10.9 points with two generators.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses compositional image generation using an agentic framework. It involves training image generation models with RL and SFT, which falls under multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Look Back to Move Forward: Learning to Revisit for Agentic Compositional Image Generation
papers.tldr: GenRevisit improves agentic compositional image generation by jointly choosing which prior image to revisit and how to edit it.

papers.abstract: Situated 3D Question Answering requires models to interpret a 3D scene relative to an agent's pose. Existing methods commonly convey that pose through a natural-language situation description, which may be unavailable or costly to obtain in real-world deployments. While some methods additionally incorporate numerical pose, we find that randomly shuffling the agent pose causes little performance degradation, indicating limited functional dependence on the numerical pose. To address this gap, we introduce EgoAlign, a simple 3D language model that represents a scene in an agent-centric coordinate frame, together with a dedicated egocentric alignment stage comprising four complementary tasks: object category recognition, egocentric direction prediction, metric distance estimation, and spatial relation prediction. This stage teaches the model to consistently interpret scene geometry relative to the agent's pose before task-specific fine-tuning. EgoAlign achieves the strongest performance on SQA3D, Real-3DQA, and MSQA among compared methods while remaining highly efficient. More importantly, removing textual situation descriptions yields comparable or better downstream performance, whereas shuffling EgoAlign's numerical pose causes substantial degradation. These results show that EgoAlign establishes agent-centric spatial context directly from numerical pose without requiring textual situation descriptions.
authors: Yiyang Li, Tianyi Ma, Zehong Wang, Yanfang Ye
bullets: Addresses the cost and unavailability of natural-language situation descriptions in real-world 3D deployments.
Represents scenes in an agent-centric coordinate frame and uses four alignment tasks: category recognition, egocentric direction, metric distance, and spatial relation prediction.
Achieves the strongest reported performance among compared methods on SQA3D, Real-3DQA, and MSQA while remaining efficient.
Removing textual situation descriptions preserves or improves performance, while shuffling numerical pose substantially degrades it.
Demonstrates that numerical pose can directly establish the agent-centric context needed for situated 3D understanding.
papers.selection_reason: Agent-centric 3D language model for situated spatial reasoning, directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: EgoAlign: Situated 3D Understanding without Situation Descriptions
papers.tldr: EgoAlign enables situated 3D question answering by learning agent-centric spatial context directly from numerical pose, without textual situation descriptions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer many geometric and physical reasoning questions correctly, yet still behave inconsistently in interaction, for example, abandoning a correct answer when confronted with a confident but incorrect user assertion. Standard single-turn accuracy cannot distinguish such capitulations from beneficial corrections because it scores each response in isolation. We introduce GRIP, a controlled benchmark with 34 procedurally generated reasoning domains, 100,000 images, and 600,000 questions spanning geometric, spatial, visual, and physical reasoning. Each scene is generated by deterministic code, and every answer is derived directly from the underlying scene state, providing exact ground truth without human annotation. On GRIP, we propose Dual-Loop Evaluation. A closed loop probes each image with a five-step compositional question ladder to localize where reasoning fails. An open loop then re-elicits the model's answer under controlled challenges, including peer-model responses and unsupported user assertions. Because ground truth is known exactly, answer changes can be signed as corrections (wrong-to-right) or capitulations (right-to-wrong), separating two failure modes: rule absence and rule fragility. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/bilaljawaid980/GRIP-Benchmark, with further details at https://bilaljawaid980.github.io/grip-benchmark/.
authors: Bilal Jawaid, Hamza Hanif, Muhammad Maaz Uddin, Anas Zafar, Inad Alqurashi, Aizan Zafar, Osama Farooqui, Sheheryar Khan, Ferhat Sadak, Shaina Raza, Rizwan Qureshi
bullets: Introduces a procedurally generated benchmark covering 34 geometric, spatial, visual, and physical reasoning domains.
Uses 100,000 images and 600,000 questions with exact ground truth derived from deterministic scene states.
Applies Dual-Loop Evaluation: compositional question ladders diagnose reasoning failures, while controlled challenges test answer stability.
Separates rule absence from rule fragility by labeling answer changes as corrections or capitulations.
Provides the benchmark publicly; the abstract does not report model-specific performance results or limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and evaluation protocol for spatial, geometric, and physical reasoning in vision-language models.
papers.title: Geometric Parrots: Rule Absence vs. Rule Fragility in Spatial and Physical Reasoning for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: GRIP evaluates whether vision-language models lack spatial and physical reasoning rules or abandon correct answers under confident but unsupported challenges.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) extend LLMs to process heterogeneous modalities (e.g., vision, audio, and IMU signals) alongside language, enabling a broader range of multimodal tasks. Yet we find that these models often fail to express information from non-textual modalities even when they perceive it correctly. We term this disconnect knows-but-cannot-say. To investigate this phenomenon, we introduce Token-level Modality Alignment (TMA), which measures the alignment between individual modality representations and response representations. Our analysis shows that non-textual representations are less aligned with response tokens and receive less attention than textual representations, suggesting a potential explanation for uneven modality preferences. Motivated by these findings, we propose OmniCatalyst, a simple perceive $\rightarrow$ infer strategy that complements the original modality inputs with self-generated text, making non-textual knowledge more accessible. Across seven Omni-LLMs, OmniCatalyst consistently improves performance (+7.29%) and yields more balanced modality preferences, with further gains from diverse training strategies. Further analysis demonstrates that the knowledge extraction phases increase TMA, suggesting that improved alignment makes non-textual information more accessible during response generation. In summary, our findings uncover how Omni-LLMs can better express modality knowledge through language. Our code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/OmniLLM.
authors: Na Min An, Taekyung Kim, Jaemyung Yu, Hyunjung Shim, Dongyoon Han
bullets: Identifies a “knows-but-cannot-say” gap between multimodal perception and language responses.
Introduces Token-level Modality Alignment (TMA) to measure alignment between modality representations and response tokens.
Finds that non-textual modalities receive less response-token alignment and attention than text.
OmniCatalyst uses a perceive → infer strategy to supplement original inputs with generated textual knowledge.
Across seven Omni-LLMs, it consistently improves performance by 7.29% and balances modality preferences; gains are linked to increased TMA.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses multimodal LLMs (Omni-LLMs) and the issue of modality alignment (knows-but-cannot-say). Proposes TMA and OmniCatalyst, which are relevant to multimodal reasoning and instruction following.
