authors: Andrew Perrault (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA), Anmol Takiar (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA), Dominik Wienecki (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA), Arnab Nandi (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA)
bullets: Benchmarks documentation and view acceptability across 11 Blender environments modeling unconstrained tasks such as solar installation and vehicle repair.
Evaluates 26 vision-language models on whether views provide suitable proof-of-work and whether task-relevant state can be understood.
Models generally solve documentation when answers are visible as text, but struggle with measurements, small parts, and spatial relationships.
Acceptability judgments are difficult because human raters disagree; leading models perform similarly to an individual non-author rater.
Model rankings on rendered documentation frames transfer to real images for the three tested questions.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating VLMs on documenting physical work, testing spatial relations and scene understanding.
papers.title: RealityBench: Simulated Environments to Evaluate a Vision Language Model's Ability to Document Human Physical Work
papers.tldr: RealityBench uses simulated physical-work environments to show that vision-language models struggle with visual proof-of-work quality, measurements, fine details, and spatial relations despite handling text-in-frame documentation well.

papers.abstract: We show that continuous bitstream diffusion (CoBit), originally developed for language modeling, provides a unified framework for joint and conditional multimodal generation using the same training and sampling protocol. Across image-text, speech-text and protein sequence-structure modeling, models are trained separately from scratch, but each uses a single input projection, transformer backbone, bitwise prediction head and binary score-matching objective shared across its modalities. Within each setting, a single checkpoint supports joint generation and the conditional directions included in training by changing which parts of the bitstream are observed. We first validate the approach on MNIST-Sum, a controlled image-text task pairing raw binary images with equations encoded as text, achieving near-perfect conditional accuracy and high joint consistency without learned tokenizers. We then apply the same protocol at larger scale to speech-text and protein sequence-structure modeling. Trained without text pretraining, a single speech-text model performs speech synthesis, recognition, continuation, and unconditional co-generation. Jointly generated speech and text achieve 3.5% word error rate between the generated text and automatic transcriptions of the generated speech. In protein modeling, a single CoBit checkpoint supports forward folding, inverse folding, and joint sequence-structure generation. For jointly generated proteins spanning 100-500 residues, computational refolding of CoBit's sequences yields structures that agree with the generated backbones at a mean self-consistency TM-score of 0.911. Together, these results show that CoBit provides a common generative framework for substantially different modalities and forms of cross-modal dependence, without introducing a domain-specific objective or sampling procedure.
authors: Georgios Batzolis, Georgios Kontos, Bruno Trentini, Pranam Chatterjee, Micha Livne, Mark Girolami, Luca Ambrogioni
bullets: A shared architecture uses one input projection, transformer backbone, bitwise prediction head, and binary score-matching objective for each multimodal setting.
A single checkpoint supports multiple generation directions by varying which portions of the bitstream are observed.
On MNIST-Sum, CoBit achieves near-perfect conditional accuracy and high joint consistency without learned tokenizers.
The speech-text model supports synthesis, recognition, continuation, and co-generation; generated speech and text achieve 3.5% word error rate.
For proteins, one checkpoint handles forward folding, inverse folding, and joint generation, with generated structures reaching a mean self-consistency TM-score of 0.911 after refolding.
papers.selection_reason: Unified continuous bitstream diffusion for joint and conditional multimodal generation across image-text, speech-text, and protein; relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Multimodal Co-Generation With Continuous Bitstream Diffusion
papers.tldr: Continuous bitstream diffusion enables one unified model and sampling procedure for joint and conditional generation across image-text, speech-text, and protein sequence-structure modalities.

papers.abstract: We present CoPlanVLM, which uses a Vision Language Model (VLM) to translate a single natural-language instruction and image into coordinated paths for a team of two robots. While VLMs offer a flexible, natural-language interface for commanding robot teams, their weak spatial reasoning has greatly limited VLM-based path planning. CoPlanVLM improves the VLM's spatial reasoning and path planning abilities through three components: (1) an image overlay marking both free space and obstacles, (2) task classification that selects the most appropriate low-level planner and reasoning prompt for each instruction, and (3) task-specific chain-of-thought reasoning that prompts the VLM to identify key objects, allocate roles, and verify routes are collision-free before committing to a plan. Together, these components enable the team to complete complex coordinated maneuvers requiring both robots and divide large tasks between robots to increase efficiency. CoPlanVLM also supports detailed maneuvers involving specific routes, loops, and coverage of large areas, as well as tasks requiring directional reasoning such as north/south or left/right. We validate CoPlanVLM in both Gazebo simulation and on physical Turtlebot 4 hardware. CoPlanVLM attains an average success rate of 84.4% compared to 50.0% for the closest baseline. On trials where both methods succeed, CoPlanVLM's paths are 27% shorter on average. Project code is available at https://github.com/AICPS/CoPlanVLM.
authors: David R. Martin, Jared Paquet, Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque, Pramod Khargonekar, Kyle Volle, J. Humberto Ramos, Scott Nivison
bullets: Addresses weak VLM spatial reasoning for multi-robot path planning.
Uses free-space/obstacle overlays, task classification, and task-specific chain-of-thought reasoning.
Supports role allocation, collision-free route verification, coordinated maneuvers, task division, and directional or coverage-based instructions.
Validated in Gazebo and on Turtlebot 4 hardware, achieving 84.4% average success versus 50.0% for the closest baseline.
When both methods succeed, its paths are 27% shorter on average.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-based coordinated path planning for robot teams with spatial reasoning enhancements from language and image input.
papers.title: CoPlanVLM: Coordinated Path Planning for a Robot Team using Vision Language Models
papers.tldr: CoPlanVLM combines visual overlays, task-specific planning, and structured VLM reasoning to generate coordinated paths for two robots from a single instruction and image.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing accurate camera poses and floor-plan layouts from sparse, unposed, wide-baseline RGB panoramas remains a challenging open problem. Direct multi-room floor-plan prediction is especially difficult in this setting: pose, geometry, semantics, and global layout structure are tightly coupled, yet a complete floor-plan is hard to learn as a single global output. Our key insight is to keep the model's predictions strictly local. Multi-view Ordered Wall Instance Segmentation (MOIS) is designed around this concept. Each panorama column predicts only the wall it observes plus the next two adjacent walls in clockwise order. The global wall partition, room layouts, and shared coordinates emerge from deterministic aggregation of overlapping local predictions. Building on MOIS, we propose Multi-view floor-plan Feed-Forward Network (MvFFN), which jointly predicts coarse camera poses, dense global geometry, and per-wall semantic outputs. A downstream Layout Chaining (LC) post processing pipeline then assembles these predictions into multi-room floor-plans with shared global coordinates, consistent wall identities, and connected room structure. The dense MOIS predictions recover cross-view wall identity and local within-room connectivity more accurately than composed modular baselines, and the assembled layouts substantially outperform prior methods on wall and junction level accuracy. We also introduce the ZInD-CrossView dataset, which augments ZInD with globally unique wall instances and cross-view segmentation labels for this task.
authors: Yuguang Li, Yichuan Deng, Zixuan Liu, Ivaylo Boyadzhiev, Xiuyuan Wu, Xinyu Zou, Linda Shapiro, Alex Colburn
bullets: Addresses the coupled challenges of camera pose, geometry, semantics, and global structure in multi-room reconstruction.
MOIS predicts each panorama column’s observed wall and its next two clockwise adjacent walls, keeping predictions local.
MvFFN jointly estimates coarse poses, dense global geometry, and per-wall semantics.
Layout Chaining aggregates overlapping local predictions into globally coordinated, connected floor plans.
Experiments report improved wall and junction accuracy over prior methods; the work also introduces the ZInD-CrossView dataset.
papers.selection_reason: Jointly reconstructs camera poses and floor-plan layouts from panoramas, advancing spatial layout understanding.
papers.title: MvFFN: Multi-view Floor plan Feed-forward Network for Unposed Wide-Baseline Panorama Layout Reconstruction
papers.tldr: MvFFN reconstructs multi-room floor plans from sparse, unposed wide-baseline panoramas by combining local wall predictions with deterministic global layout assembly.

papers.abstract: Speech large language models (LLMs) are often built using pretrained acoustic encoders as an audio interface to an LLM decoder. However, LLMs scale poorly with input sequence length, while acoustic encoders tend to produce substantially longer sequences than typical textual inputs. This motivates learning to compress encoder outputs while preserving task-oriented information. To this end, we introduce ASSET, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework that learns to adaptively compress encoder outputs by first partitioning them into variable-duration segments and then pooling each segment into a continuous audio token. We use group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to train a segmenter with task performance feedback and a token-rate penalty. In automatic speech recognition (ASR) experiments, ASSET achieves performance comparable to a transcript-assisted character-boundary oracle with approximately 25% fewer audio tokens on English LibriSpeech, while improving on a phone-boundary oracle at a similar token rate on Mandarin AISHELL. Exploratory experiments on non-ASR tasks further illustrate how learned segmentation changes when the framework is adapted to tasks beyond transcription.
authors: Cihan Xiao, Yuan Tseng, Matthew Wiesner, Desh Raj, Leibny Paola Garcia Perera, Sanjeev Khudanpur, David Harwath
bullets: Addresses the sequence-length mismatch between long acoustic-encoder outputs and speech LLM inputs.
Learns variable-duration segments and pools each into a continuous audio token.
Trains the segmenter with GRPO using task-performance feedback and a token-rate penalty.
Matches a transcript-assisted character-boundary oracle with about 25% fewer tokens on English LibriSpeech.
Outperforms a phone-boundary oracle at a similar token rate on Mandarin AISHELL; non-ASR behavior is explored but not fully characterized.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based adaptive compression of speech encoder outputs into fewer audio tokens for speech LLMs; relevant to token efficiency and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: ASSET: Adaptive Speech Segmentation via Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ASSET uses reinforcement learning to adaptively segment and compress speech encoder outputs into fewer task-relevant audio tokens while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multi-modal large language models have shifted toward the "thinking with images" paradigm to improve reasoning faithfulness, yet existing methods rely heavily on explicit coordinate- based grounding. We identify two fundamental limitations in this approach, i.e., a semantic gap where sparse regressions miss high-dimensional latent structures, and a resolution gap due to the granularity mismatch between patch-level tokens and pixel-level coordinates. To address these, we propose TiCO (Thinking with images without COordinates). It reformulates visual reasoning as a semantic evidence discovery process within the latent space, and evidence is injected as token-level regions without pixel coordinates. Specifically, TiCO utilizes a dedicated probe token to estimate similarity distributions and performs importance sampling over spatially connected components to generate diverse, semantically dominant evidence rollouts. Extensive experiments across multiple high-resolution and general visual reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our TiCO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art coordinate-based methods with significantly improved inference efficiency.
authors: Meng Cao, Haoze Zhao, Yi Wang, Ian Reid, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Coordinate-based visual reasoning suffers from semantic gaps in sparse regressions and resolution gaps between patch tokens and pixels.
TiCO reformulates reasoning as semantic evidence discovery in the model’s latent space.
A dedicated probe token estimates similarity distributions, while importance sampling over connected spatial components produces diverse evidence rollouts.
Evidence is injected as token-level regions rather than coordinate-based locations.
Experiments on high-resolution and general visual reasoning benchmarks show improved performance and inference efficiency over coordinate-based methods.
papers.selection_reason: Coordinate-free visual reasoning for MLLMs directly targets multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Thinking with Images without Coordinates
papers.tldr: TiCO improves visual reasoning by discovering and injecting semantically meaningful image evidence without relying on pixel coordinates.

papers.abstract: Purpose : To develop and evaluate CAPTOR, a deep-learning vision-language foundation model for oncologic chest-abdomen-pelvis (CAP) CT interpretation. Materials & Methods : CAPTOR (Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis foundaTion model for Oncologic Radiology) is a contrastive vision-language model, trained using a pretraining strategy for oncologic CAP CT (in single- or multiple-series acquisitions), on a multicenter retrospective dataset from North America, Europe and Asia, predominantly from tumor lesion examinations. CAPTOR was compared with state-of-the-art CT foundation models on three downstream tasks: disease detection, survival prediction using TumorImagingBench and image retrieval. Classification and retrieval were both evaluated on held-out internal and public test sets, stratified by anatomical coverage and indication. Bootstrap resampling was used to estimate confidence intervals, and pairwise comparisons were performed using permutation tests. Results : CAPTOR was trained and tested on 25,512 and 10,794 CT-report pairs respectively. TumorImagingBench datasets comprised between 134 and 421 studies each. CAPTOR outperformed all baseline models, on the classification task, on the CAP subset (AUC 0.767, 95%CI: 0.734-0.793, vs. 0.695, 95%CI: 0.645-0.736 for the next-best, p<0.001) and oncologic subset (AUC 0.784, 95%CI: 0.759-0.805, vs. 0.734, 95%CI: 0.703-0.767 p<0.001), ranked first on three of the four oncologic prognostic benchmarks, and achieved superior retrieval performance on CAP and oncologic subsets. Conclusion : A foundation model trained on oncology-enriched CAP CT data outperformed relevant state-of-the-art models in its target clinical context, underscoring the importance of clinically aligned pretraining. We release our preprocessing, training and inference code : https://github.com/Guerbet-AI/CAPTOR and model weights : https://huggingface.co/Guerbet-AI/CAPTOR
authors: S\'el\'ena Jean-Mactoux, Sophie Loizillon, Ghina Jardali, Amandine Cromb\'e, Nathalie Lassau, Alexandre B\^one
bullets: Uses contrastive vision-language pretraining on multicenter oncologic CAP CT-report pairs, including single- and multiple-series acquisitions.
Evaluated for disease detection, survival prediction, and image retrieval across internal and public test sets.
Achieved the best classification performance on CAP and oncologic subsets, and ranked first on three of four prognostic benchmarks.
Showed superior image retrieval performance on CAP and oncologic subsets.
Preprocessing, training, inference code, and model weights are publicly released.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language foundation model for 3D oncologic CT, fits multimodal and 3D foundation model interests.
papers.title: CAPTOR: a vision-language foundation model for Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis Oncologic CT
papers.tldr: CAPTOR is an oncology-focused vision-language foundation model for chest-abdomen-pelvis CT that outperformed existing CT foundation models across detection, prognosis, and retrieval tasks.

papers.abstract: ScanRefer Multiple queries require spatial disambiguation: several instances of the target class are present, and the referencer must pick one. When per-query logits were never logged, a common substitute is cross-epoch agreement. On the full ScanRefer validation set (9,508 queries; GeoClassifier with ground-truth proposals), object-level softmax is similarly miscalibrated on Unique and Multiple (ECE 0.068 vs. 0.102; the scene-bootstrap gap interval includes zero). Fixed-final agreement on the same checkpoints reports ECE 0.041 vs. 0.272 (gap +0.231). Modal-vote agreement is 0.045 vs. 0.318. Most Multiple errors are same-class wrong-instance (45.6%); geometric miss (H2) is 59.6%, and wrong-category (H1) is 16.7%. A non-monotone H1 pattern does not appear under the default fixed-final protocol, and we retract it. Logit-free thresholds rank spatially hard queries poorly. If only agreement was logged, calibrate abstention on Multiple and report wrong-instance rates with H1.
authors: Micha{\l} Zakrzewski, Mariia Shpir, Taras Rumezhak, Volodymyr Karpiv
bullets: The study evaluates 9,508 ScanRefer validation queries using a GeoClassifier with ground-truth proposals.
Object-level softmax calibration is similar on Unique and Multiple queries, while fixed-final and modal-vote agreement show much larger calibration gaps on Multiple.
Most Multiple errors select the wrong instance of the correct class (45.6%); geometric misses account for 59.6% and wrong-category errors for 16.7%.
Logit-free agreement thresholds rank spatially difficult queries poorly, and the previously suggested non-monotone H1 pattern is retracted under the default protocol.
When only agreement is available, the abstract recommends calibrating abstention specifically on Multiple queries and reporting wrong-instance rates alongside H1 errors.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of spatial disambiguation in 3D referring expressions; relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Agreement versus Softmax under Spatial Disambiguation
papers.tldr: For ScanRefer spatially ambiguous queries, cross-epoch agreement appears substantially less reliable than object-level softmax for calibration, especially on Multiple queries.

papers.abstract: Under a fixed context budget, which objects and relations should a 3D scene-grounded VLM see first? On ScanNet indoor referring benchmarks (Dai et al., 2017), matching the query to object category names outperforms pairwise geometry scoring at every reported K. The gaps are largest at high recall. Analytic pairwise cues beat per-object cue scoring and query-agnostic kNN graphs, including on paraphrases. MiniLM and BGE-small still score higher on those splits. We evaluate token-budgeted candidate retrieval with axis-aligned boxes, a token-ratio metric, training-free baselines, two small encoders that match q to each object's category name, and QCRR (Query-Conditioned Relation Retrieval), a deterministic pairwise-geometry scorer. Across ScanRefer gt_val plus a custom 20% scan-id split of Nr3D and Sr3D (35,504 queries; not official ReferIt3D val), additive noun matching reaches R@10 0.864 on ScanRefer against QCRR's 0.626; MiniLM and BGE-small reach 0.911 to 0.913 on ScanRefer and 0.941 to 0.947 on Nr3D. A corrected 3DGraphLLM harness (native Acc@0.25 0.67 on the full graph, n=300 ScanRefer queries) shows that context selection changes downstream accuracy under a matched object budget (Random 0.44, QCRR 0.56, MiniLM 0.67, oracle 0.70). Semantic retrieval beats hand-designed geometry on that harness. We will release the protocol, retriever implementations, and per-query outputs so new selectors can be swapped in without rewriting the analysis.
authors: Micha{\l} Zakrzewski, Mariia Shpir, Taras Rumezhak
bullets: Evaluates token-budgeted candidate retrieval using object category names, pairwise geometry, kNN graphs, and small text encoders.
On ScanRefer, additive noun matching reaches R@10 0.864 versus 0.626 for QCRR; MiniLM and BGE-small reach 0.911–0.913.
Semantic retrieval also performs better on Nr3D and Sr3D splits, including paraphrased queries.
In a corrected 3DGraphLLM harness, downstream Acc@0.25 is 0.67 with MiniLM, versus 0.56 with QCRR and 0.44 with random selection.
The evaluation uses custom splits and a limited harness; results are scoped to the reported ScanNet-based benchmarks and budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Token-budgeted context selection for 3D scene-grounded VLMs; directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Token-Budgeted Candidate Retrieval for 3D Scene-Grounded VLMs: Category Names vs. Pairwise Geometry
papers.tldr: For token-limited 3D scene-grounded VLMs, category-name matching retrieves relevant objects more effectively than pairwise geometry, improving downstream accuracy under matched context budgets.

papers.abstract: Explaining a vision--language model (VLM) prediction requires tracing training-example influence to the multimodal evidence that mediates it, yet existing attribution methods largely operate only at the sample level. Recent latent-mediated influence methods provide feature-level attribution in language models, but lack the multimodal and spatial structure needed to ground influence in VLMs. We introduce MOSAIC (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization). It learns a shared sparse image--text latent space whose concepts are 1) sparse within each modality, 2) supported on contiguous image regions, 3) aligned to the phrases that describe them, and 4) approximately decorrelated. It then applies EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these concepts and localize their contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. We evaluate MOSAIC on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering. The learned features are more localized and coherent without degrading task behavior, and ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency. We find that visual evidence can substantially reorganize training-data attribution while preserving more of the shared latent structure. MOSAIC thus connects where model behavior comes from with what multimodal evidence carries that influence.
authors: Laura Yao, Shixing Yu, Jie Peng, Promit Ghosal, Kyra Gan, Tianlong Chen
bullets: Addresses the lack of spatially and multimodally grounded training-sample attribution for vision-language models.
Learns a shared sparse image–text latent space with localized, phrase-aligned, and approximately decorrelated concepts.
Uses EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these latent concepts.
Evaluated on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering.
Influence-ranked latent ablations alter outputs more than activation- or frequency-ranked ablations, while preserving task behavior.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces multimodal latent influence attribution for vision-language models; directly relevant to multimodal LLM interpretability.
papers.title: Cross-Modal Latent Influence: Patch-Level Training Sample Attribution for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: MOSAIC traces VLM predictions from training examples to the specific image regions and text phrases that mediate their influence.

papers.abstract: Digital libraries increasingly host scientific publications whose figures encode primary research findings, yet making this visual content searchable, accessible, and reusable remains an open challenge. Large language and multimodal models (LLMs/LMMs) provide the possibility to automate many figure parsing tasks such as determining data trends or extracting data from plots. In this work, we consider if these models can reliably support task-oriented visual data analysis when presented with synthetic, but realistic, scientific figures that contain multiple charts. Our Visual Question Answering (VQA) process scaffolds our tasks along a four-level description model from basic conceptual answers to interpretive and analytical understanding. Additionally, we outline our process for synthetically generating our single and multi-panel (charts in which there are multiple panels present) plots and testing the data with various LMMs using quantitative analysis. In general, we find LMMs become less accurate with increasing figure complexity as the number of panels, number of plot elements, and difficulty of questions increase. Finally, because LMM accuracy is expected to change rapidly, our analysis also considers cost relative to performance as a metric to inform future user decisions. We provide the detailed question-answer pairs used in this analysis, along with the code used to generate random plots, question-answer pairs and detailed bounding-box metadata for chart elements. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ReadingTimeMachine/LLM_VQA_MultiPanel and https://huggingface.co/datasets/ReadingTimeMachine/visual\_qa\_multipanel
authors: Daniel J. Evans, J. P. Naiman, JooYoung Seo, J. Stephen Downie
bullets: Introduces a multi-panel chart VQA benchmark organized into four levels, from basic descriptions to interpretive and analytical questions.
Generates synthetic but realistic scientific plots, question–answer pairs, and bounding-box metadata for chart elements.
Evaluates multiple LMMs quantitatively while considering both accuracy and cost.
Finds performance generally worsens with more panels, plot elements, and difficult questions.
Releases the benchmark data and plot-generation code publicly.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-panel chart VQA dataset and LMM evaluation, relevant to multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Do you "see" what I "see"? A Multi-panel Visual Question Answer Dataset for Large Language Model Chart Analysis
papers.tldr: This study evaluates how well large multimodal models answer increasingly complex questions about synthetic single- and multi-panel scientific charts, finding that accuracy declines as visual and question complexity grow.

papers.abstract: Existing jailbreak attacks have exposed serious safety weaknesses in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Most prior attacks rely on specially constructed visual inputs to carry or support harmful intent. In this paper, we uncover a different vulnerability: task-relevant scene semantics alone can shift an MLLM from refusal to compliance, even when the visual input introduces no additional attack instructions and the original task intent remains unchanged. We formalize this failure as a scene-grounded visual safety vulnerability and introduce SceneSafetyBench to investigate it across eight risk categories and nine white- and black-box MLLMs. Our analysis reveals that this failure is associated with how task-relevant visual evidence influences downstream safety representations, suggesting that visual grounding alone cannot fully explain the observed safety shift. Building on this finding, we propose Scene-Grounded Attacks (SGA), which preserve the original task while constructing validated scene-grounded queries and combining their independent responses. Across nine target MLLMs, SGA achieves an average attack success rate (ASR) of 86.17%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 8.55 percentage points and achieving the highest ASR on eight models. Our results identify scene semantics as an overlooked attack surface in MLLMs and highlight a growing tension between stronger visual grounding and robust multimodal safety alignment.
authors: Tongxi Wu, Yuyang Cheng, Jiacheng Xian, Hu Huang, Zhihao Wu, Menglin Yang, Jian Zhang, Yang Gao
bullets: Identifies a scene-grounded visual safety vulnerability: task-relevant visual content can shift safety behavior without adding attack instructions or changing task intent.
Introduces SceneSafetyBench, covering eight risk categories and nine white- and black-box MLLMs.
Finds that task-relevant visual evidence affects downstream safety representations beyond what visual grounding alone explains.
Proposes Scene-Grounded Attacks (SGA), which preserve the original task and combine responses from validated scene-grounded queries.
SGA reaches an average 86.17% attack success rate, exceeding the strongest baseline by 8.55 percentage points and achieving the highest ASR on eight models.
papers.selection_reason: Scene-grounded safety failures in MLLMs; directly relevant to multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Scenes as an Attack Surface: Uncovering Scene-Grounded Safety Failures in MLLMs
papers.tldr: Scene semantics alone can turn MLLM refusals into harmful compliance, revealing a new attack surface that Scene-Grounded Attacks exploit effectively.

papers.abstract: Training on broad, unfiltered data enables high-quality image generation, but can also teach models concepts that should not be generated; restricting the training data ensures safety, but reduces quality because examples containing unsafe concepts also provide useful knowledge that is not itself unsafe. Existing approaches largely address this trade-off post hoc through concept unlearning, which can lead to catastrophic forgetting as the number of concepts to remove grows. We instead ask whether unsafe concept knowledge can be compartmentalized during pretraining so that access to it can be disabled at inference. We introduce Pristine Models, a novel text-to-image generation architecture with an attention mechanism that encourages the separation of safe and unsafe knowledge into independently parameterized branches. The branch-specific parameters are learned during training, while the unsafe branch can be detached at inference. On ImageNet, Pristine Models enable safer generation while retaining much of the utility of full-data pretraining, achieving higher image quality and better text alignment than training only on safe data or applying post-hoc concept removal. We further scale our approach to CC12M, demonstrating that it remains effective in a substantially larger and more diverse open-world pretraining setting.
authors: Anirudh Sundara Rajan, Krishna Kumar Singh, Richard Zhang, Yong Jae Lee
bullets: Motivation: filtering unsafe concepts from training data can reduce useful visual knowledge, while post-hoc unlearning may cause increasing catastrophic forgetting.
Method: an attention-based architecture learns safe and unsafe knowledge in independently parameterized branches during pretraining.
At inference, the unsafe branch can be detached to restrict generation of unsafe concepts.
On ImageNet, the approach retains more utility than safe-only training or post-hoc concept removal, with higher image quality and better text alignment.
The method also remains effective when scaled to the larger, more diverse CC12M dataset.
papers.selection_reason: Text-to-image foundation model with compartmentalized safe/unsafe knowledge; relevant to multimodal foundation model safety.
papers.title: Pristine Models
papers.tldr: Pristine Models compartmentalize unsafe and safe knowledge during text-to-image pretraining, enabling safer inference without sacrificing as much generation quality or text alignment.

papers.abstract: Positional embeddings encode the spatial position of each image patch in a Vision Transformer (ViT), allowing the model to distinguish different spatial arrangements of visual content. However, we know little about how the choice of embedding shapes a vision transformer's internal representation. In this work, we show that Absolute Positional Embeddings (APE) and Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) encode spatial position through different internal mechanisms: APE stores position in explicit features, while RoPE builds it inside attention and rebuilds it when it is withheld. Specifically, in APE models, sparse autoencoders recover causal row- and column-specific features, whereas interventions on RoPE reveal distinct rotary components that separately encode row and column information. Additionally, causal interventions selectively disabling RoPE's row or column rotations show that decodable row and column information can be independently removed and, once rotations are restored, partly reconstructed, in part by axis-specialized attention heads. Both mechanisms are causally important for classification: permuting APE's positional features across patches reduces top-1 accuracy by 24--31 points, and ablating the rotations of RoPE's primary rebuilding head reduces it more than ablating those of any other head. Our findings show that the choice of positional encoding fundamentally changes how spatial information is organized and processed inside Vision Transformers. More broadly, our work demonstrates how mechanistic analysis can reveal how models construct, reconstruct, and maintain structured representations, providing a basis for targeted interventions in vision models.
authors: Mahmoud Mannes, Nikhil Maturi, Parva Mehta, Jiwon Jeong, Aravind Singaram Kannappan
bullets: APE represents position in explicit, patch-specific features, while RoPE encodes it through attention-based rotary components.
Sparse autoencoders identify causal row- and column-specific features in APE models; interventions reveal separate row and column rotations in RoPE.
When RoPE rotations are removed, spatial information can be partly reconstructed, with some attention heads specializing in particular axes.
Causal disruption of APE positional features lowers top-1 accuracy by 24–31 points, while ablating RoPE’s key rebuilding head causes the largest impact among heads tested.
The study shows that positional-encoding choice fundamentally shapes how spatial information is organized and processed.
papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic analysis of positional encodings in ViT; transferable to spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: How Vision Transformers Represent Position: A Mechanistic Comparison of Absolute and Rotary Positional Encodings
papers.tldr: APE and RoPE enable spatial reasoning in Vision Transformers through fundamentally different, causally important internal mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Dense visual text requires image generators to reproduce long strings across multiple regions with correct placement and legibility. As short-string rendering improves, evaluation must test sustained performance across more demanding scenes. We introduce UltraText Bench, a bilingual benchmark for prompt-only generation of dense visual text. It contains 432 prompts spanning 24 real-world scene categories and three difficulty levels, split equally between English and Chinese. Each human-reviewed prompt supplies exact strings for four to twelve text regions, paired with structured references for their content, placement, and visual attributes. We use the Q-Judger vision-language model to assess each image against the complete reference, reporting text fidelity, text clarity, spatial quality, and scene quality. Across 24 model configurations, these dimensions reveal different strengths: Z-Image-Turbo gains 3.81 clarity points over Z-Image-Base while losing 14.76 fidelity points under the reported settings. Performance also varies with workload; Qwen-Image-2512's English composite falls from 86.50 at L1 to 42.86 at L3. Ten participants took part in human evaluation of the automatic scores. Repository: https://github.com/LINs-lab/UltraText_Bench.
bullets: Covers 432 human-reviewed prompts across 24 real-world scene categories and three difficulty levels, evenly split between English and Chinese.
Each prompt specifies exact text for 4–12 regions, including content, placement, and visual attributes.
Uses the Q-Judger vision-language model to score text fidelity, clarity, spatial quality, and scene quality.
Results across 24 model configurations show distinct trade-offs and substantial performance degradation as text workload increases.
Automatic-score evaluation included human assessment from 10 participants.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a comprehensive benchmark for visual text rendering in image generation, contributing to the evaluation of multimodal generative models.
papers.title: UltraText Bench: A Comprehensive Bilingual Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Text Rendering in Image Generation
papers.tldr: UltraText Bench evaluates how well image generators render dense bilingual text across multiple regions, measuring fidelity, clarity, layout, and overall scene quality.

papers.abstract: Existing attacks on unlearned diffusion models assume that the erased concepts are known in advance and focus on recovering them. In practice, however, model providers may not disclose which concepts have been removed, and even with access to the original base model, an adversary may still lack a clear target to attack. In this paper, we aim to answer the following critical but overlooked questions: which concepts have been erased from the model, and how many have been erased in total? To this end, we present Tracer, a framework that rapidly and accurately identifies erased concepts and estimates their number. Tracer efficiently identifies erased concepts without generating and classifying images. By combining lightweight spectral analysis of weight footprints, it enables efficient search over large candidate vocabularies. To distinguish multiple erased concepts, we introduce a footprint coverage objective that guides sequential discovery. Tracer estimates the number of erased concepts by detecting a sharp decline in candidate confidence as the selected concepts account for the erasure footprint, without requiring labeled examples for calibration. The framework requires only lightweight linear algebra and limited forward probes, with no prior knowledge of the unlearning algorithm. Experiments across text-to-image and text-to-video backbones and diverse unlearning methods demonstrate that Tracer identifies erased concepts and estimates their number in seconds, achieving 150 to 137,000 times and 133 to 20,000 times speedups over MIA and brute-force search on image and video models, respectively, with substantially higher identification accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the overlooked problem of identifying erased concepts when the provider does not disclose them.
Uses lightweight spectral analysis of model-weight footprints to search large candidate vocabularies efficiently.
Introduces footprint coverage for sequentially distinguishing multiple erased concepts.
Estimates the total number of erased concepts from a confidence drop, without labeled calibration data.
Works across text-to-image and text-to-video models, substantially outperforming MIA and brute-force search in speed and identification accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses a critical issue in diffusion model unlearning, contributing to the safety and interpretability of foundation models, which is a relevant subfield of multimodal AI.
papers.title: Your Unlearning Gives You Away: Identifying Erased Concepts in Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: Tracer quickly discovers which concepts were erased from diffusion models and estimates how many were removed, without generating images or knowing the unlearning method.

papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs report strong performance on scientific reasoning benchmarks, yet most treat perception and reasoning as a single measurable process. We introduce a five-task diagnostic experiment across physics and geometry benchmarks that isolates failures to perception, reasoning, or both. Incorrect diagram interpretation degrades performance even on problems models solve correctly from text alone, and accuracy generally rises from raw images to human-authored captions. Recovery under corrected captions is high for some models, separating perception-blocked failures from genuine reasoning bottlenecks. Which reasoning error follows a perception failure depends on domain: physics failures resolve into calculation errors, geometry into conceptual misapplication. As a discussion beyond our core experiments, InternS1-mini, despite heavy scientific pretraining and thinking capabilities, falls below the weakest model from experiments on every task, with reasoning traces frequently truncating before completion.
bullets: Incorrect diagram interpretation harms performance even when models solve the same problems from text alone.
Human-authored captions generally improve accuracy over raw images.
Corrected captions reveal which failures are perception-blocked versus genuine reasoning failures.
Perception failures tend to become calculation errors in physics and conceptual misapplication in geometry.
InternS1-mini underperforms all evaluated models across tasks, often truncating its reasoning traces.↩
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses perception vs reasoning failures in multimodal physics and geometry reasoning, directly relevant to MLLMs and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Lost in Perception: Isolating Perceptual and Reasoning Failures in Multimodal Physics and Geometry Reasoning
papers.tldr: A five-task diagnostic shows that multimodal physics and geometry errors often stem from diagram perception, while remaining failures reflect domain-specific reasoning bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: Compositional Zero Shot Learning aims to recognize unseen compositions by recombining learned primitives. Recent methods rely on vision language models and attempt to explicitly model contextual variations of primitives through multiple representations. However, such approaches are limited by fixed variant capacity and competition between abstract and concrete semantics. In this work, we present a new perspective that views primitive variations as the context-driven activation of concrete visual cues rather than independent entities. Based on it, we propose CLEAR, a CLoze-style rEAsoning-based Re-ranking framework inspired by human perceptual processes. CLEAR extracts conditional variants from the primitive candidate set in a coarse-to-fine manner, performs cloze-style reasoning to infer high-level semantics, and re-ranks predictions to correct biases toward salient concrete primitives. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CLEAR consistently improves the Base Model and outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the challenging C-GQA and MIT-States datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/buptLwz/CLEAR.
bullets: Addresses limitations of fixed primitive-variant capacity and conflicts between concrete and abstract semantics.
Models primitive variations as context-driven activation of concrete visual cues rather than independent representations.
Uses coarse-to-fine variant extraction, cloze-style reasoning, and prediction re-ranking.
Reportedly improves its base model and outperforms state-of-the-art methods on C-GQA and MIT-States.,
papers.selection_reason: Compositional zero-shot learning via vision-language models with cloze-style multimodal reasoning, fitting multimodal foundation model interests.
papers.title: From Model Patterns to Abstract Semantics in Compositional Zero-Shot Learning
papers.tldr: CLEAR improves compositional zero-shot recognition by reasoning from concrete visual cues to abstract semantics and re-ranking predictions.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have intensified the need to understand how different modalities share, preserve, and complement information. Mutual Information (MI), the Information Bottleneck (IB), and Partial Information Decomposition (PID) provide complementary perspectives, yet existing studies often treat them as isolated tools. This survey presents an information-theoretic perspective connecting these principles as progressively refined views of multimodal information processing: MI characterizes inter-modal dependency, IB explains task-oriented information preservation under compression, and PID decomposes preserved information into redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy. We review 170 recent studies (2018--2026) and 12 foundational works, organizing multimodal learning around four challenges: cross-modal alignment, information-efficient fusion, interaction-type characterization, and scaling to multimodal foundation models. Rather than using application domains as primary taxonomy axes, we interpret healthcare, robotics, recommendation systems, affective computing, and wireless communications as empirical validations of these information principles. Beyond taxonomy, we organize existing multimodal paradigms within a single information-theoretic coordinate system -- the Generalized Multimodal Information Lagrangian -- in which they occupy exact or approximate parameter corners, and whose unoccupied regions name candidate method families the literature has not yet built. We further discuss how emerging multimodal foundation models instantiate these principles at scale and identify open challenges including scalable information estimation in high-dimensional settings, standardized evaluation across information-theoretic methods, combinatorial complexity of multimodal PID, and the transition from post-hoc information analysis toward information-aware multimodal learning.
authors: Liangjian Wen, Linjie Li, Jiang Duan, Yong Dai, Jianzhuang Liu, Zhao Kang
bullets: Reviews 170 recent studies and 12 foundational works through four challenges: alignment, efficient fusion, interaction characterization, and multimodal scaling.
Frames MI as inter-modal dependency, IB as task-relevant compression, and PID as the decomposition of information into redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy.
Introduces the Generalized Multimodal Information Lagrangian to position existing paradigms and highlight unexplored method families.
Interprets applications across healthcare, robotics, recommendation, affective computing, and wireless communications as validations of shared information principles.
Identifies open issues in scalable information estimation, standardized evaluation, multimodal PID complexity, and information-aware learning.
papers.selection_reason: Survey unifying information-theoretic views of multimodal learning, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Dependency, Compression, and Synergy: A Unified Information-Theoretic View of Multimodal Learning
papers.tldr: This survey unifies mutual information, the information bottleneck, and partial information decomposition into a common framework for understanding dependency, compression, and synergy in multimodal learning.

papers.abstract: Clinical prognosis requires integrating structured measurements, physiological waveforms, longitudinal history, and population context. We introduce PRISM (Population-Retrieved Inference for Structured Multimodal Prognosis), a multimodal language model that combines per-feature numerical tokenization, recency-weighted aggregation of longitudinal ECGs, and a dual-modality population memory bank. Retrieval operates in representation space: the model receives mean-pooled embeddings of similar training-cohort encounters, while no individual retrieved record enters the prompt. On the 1,443-task MDS-ED benchmark, PRISM achieves AUROCs of 86.2% for diagnosis, 93.1% for deterioration, 91.8% for ICU admission, and 92.8% for mortality. These results use a 96-hour pre-arrival window unavailable to reported baselines. With benchmark-window inputs only, PRISM reaches 0.8895 AUROC, compared with 0.8937 for UniPACT and 0.8889 for MDS-ED. A matched-input compact fusion model using the same five evidence streams and frozen encoders reaches 0.7652 AUROC, versus 0.9092 for PRISM. Replacing numerical EHR encoding with text serialization reduces AUROC by 3.66 points; removing pre-arrival history reduces it by 1.97 points; and zeroing retrieval reduces it by 0.99 points. Genuine retrieval outperforms random-neighbor retrieval by 0.97 macro-average points, although a paired task-level sign test does not establish a uniform advantage (p=0.067). On the external MC-MED cohort, supervised fine-tuning reaches 0.8611 AUROC, compared with 0.8227 for locally trained gradient boosting and 0.7841 for source-only PRISM. These results support structure-aware multimodal integration and supervised external adaptation.
bullets: Addresses clinical prognosis across diagnosis, deterioration, ICU admission, and mortality using heterogeneous evidence.
Uses per-feature numerical tokenization, recency-weighted ECG history, and representation-space retrieval from a population memory bank without prompting individual records.
On MDS-ED, reports AUROCs of 86.2%–93.1% using a 96-hour pre-arrival window; with benchmark-window inputs, performance is comparable to reported baselines.

Ablations show declines from text-based numerical encoding, removing pre-arrival history, and removing retrieval; genuine retrieval improves average performance, though uniform superiority is not statistically established.
On external MC-MED data, supervised fine-tuning outperforms locally trained gradient boosting and source-only PRISM.
papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces PRISM, a multimodal language model for clinical prognosis that integrates heterogeneous evidence (waveforms, structured measurements) via a population memory bank and retrieval-augmented generation. This aligns with the 'Multimodal Foundation Models' topic, specifically the 'Multimodal Large Language Models' subtopic, as it extends LLMs to handle non-text modalities and retrieval-based context.
papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Language Model with Heterogeneous Evidence Integration for Clinical Prognosis
papers.tldr: PRISM integrates structured clinical data, waveforms, longitudinal history, and population retrieval to improve multimodal prognosis, with performance depending on input scope and supervised adaptation.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex voice agents make many small, closed decisions, which current systems answer by slow autoregressive decoding. We propose DuplexJev, which feeds ASR-encoder hidden states through a small connector into a frozen LLM and reads each question as a single-token distribution over its options. Nothing is decoded, and an 8-GPU node answers 80 decisions about eight utterances in about 0.1 s. With a last-layer connector, spoken QA stays close to reading the transcript (90% vs. 91%). DuplexJev also hears the speaker: gender and emotion accuracy both reach 90% (from 55% and 28%) with a cross-attention connector, whose spoken QA drops by only 1 point (83% to 82%). We train decisions with cross-entropy on the read-out answer token, instead of the usual transcript distillation, whose teacher never hears the voice, and keep distillation for content. Encoders and LLMs are interchangeable; we release weights, training recipe, a batched-inference pipeline for full-duplex serving and a bilingual spoken-QA set.
bullets: Maps ASR-encoder representations into a frozen LLM and reads each question as a single-token option distribution.
Uses answer-token cross-entropy for decision supervision while retaining distillation for speech content.
Handles spoken QA, speaker gender, and emotion, with cross-attention improving paralinguistic recognition while slightly reducing QA accuracy.
Batches 80 decisions over eight utterances in about 0.1 seconds on an 8-GPU node.
Provides interchangeable encoder/LLM components, released weights and recipe, a full-duplex inference pipeline, and a bilingual spoken-QA set.
papers.selection_reason: Extends a frozen LLM with speech encoder features for batched single-token decisions; fits multimodal LLMs and efficient inference.
papers.title: Batched Speech Decisions Without Decoding: Single-Token Supervision Lets a Frozen LLM Hear Beyond the Transcript
papers.tldr: DuplexJev enables a frozen LLM to answer many speech-based decisions in parallel from ASR hidden states without autoregressive decoding.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide limited support for sign language interaction. Unifying sign language translation (SLT) and generation (SLG) to enable sign language as both input and output can reduce switching between separate models during sign-text interaction. We present SignGPT, a unified, pose-based framework for gloss-free SLT and SLG. SignGPT integrates part-aware hierarchical representations of body, hand, and facial motion into a shared language model and employs asymmetric multi-token prediction and progressive training for bidirectional modeling. We evaluate SignGPT on How2Sign (ASL) and Phoenix-2014T (DGS) through benchmark comparisons, qualitative analyses, and component ablations. An exploratory study with 12 Deaf ASL signers assesses an LLM-mediated sign-to-sign response pipeline, highlighting the potential of unified modeling to support sign language conversation (SLC).
bullets: Targets limited LLM support for sign language and the need to combine translation and generation.
Uses part-aware hierarchical representations of body, hand, and facial motion within a shared language model.
Applies asymmetric multi-token prediction and progressive training for bidirectional modeling.
Evaluated on How2Sign (ASL) and Phoenix-2014T (DGS) with benchmark comparisons, qualitative analysis, and ablations.
A 12-person Deaf ASL signer study explores its potential for sign-to-sign conversational interaction.
papers.selection_reason: Unifies sign language translation and generation through an LLM with multimodal pose understanding; fits multimodal large language models.
papers.title: SignGPT: Toward LLM-Mediated Sign Language Interaction through Gloss-Free Translation and Generation
papers.tldr: SignGPT unifies gloss-free sign language translation and generation in one pose-based, LLM-mediated framework to support bidirectional sign-text and sign-to-sign interaction.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive generation of interleaved text and acoustic tokens is a common approach to spoken-response generation in speech large language models. Although this design enables streaming generation with explicit textual guidance, generated acoustic tokens become part of the context for subsequent text predictions. Given identical speech inputs, we observe markedly lower answer accuracy for the internal text generated in speech-to-text-and-speech (S2TS) mode than for speech-to-text (S2T) responses. We term this discrepancy the \emph{output-mode gap} (OMG). To reduce OMG, we propose \emph{Joint-Output On-Policy Distillation} (JO-OPD), which distills the model's stronger S2T policy into joint generation using student-generated S2TS trajectories. At each text position, the S2T teacher provides soft targets from a text-only projection of the student's preceding outputs, while the student predicts from the corresponding full interleaved history. A preservation objective further regularizes native non-text predictions. Experiments on Step-Audio-2-mini and Baichuan-Audio-Instruct reveal OMG across two interleaved generation architectures. On Step-Audio-2-mini, JO-OPD reduces OMG from 42.87 to 16.26 percentage points on Spoken-MQA and from 29.72 to 13.04 points on speech-rendered GSM8K, with little change in S2T accuracy and substantially larger reductions than matched SFT baselines. ASR-based evaluation further shows a 7.49-point improvement in spoken-answer accuracy on Spoken-MQA.
bullets: The output-mode gap arises because generated acoustic tokens remain in the context and degrade later text predictions.
JO-OPD uses student-generated S2TS trajectories and soft targets from an S2T teacher based on text-only histories.
A preservation objective regularizes the model’s native non-text predictions during distillation.
On Step-Audio-2-mini, the gap fell from 42.87 to 16.26 points on Spoken-MQA and from 29.72 to 13.04 points on speech-rendered GSM8K.
S2T accuracy changed little, while ASR evaluation showed a 7.49-point Spoken-MQA improvement; results cover two interleaved-generation architectures.
papers.selection_reason: Speech language models with interleaved text and audio generation are multimodal LLMs, and the distillation method targets a core multimodal generation challenge.
papers.title: Reducing the Output-Mode Gap in Speech Language Models via Joint-Output On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: JO-OPD narrows the accuracy gap between speech-to-text-and-speech and speech-to-text generation by distilling a stronger text-only policy into interleaved speech generation.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) allow a single model to perform clinical image analysis tasks ranging from diagnosis classification to report generation. However, joint adaptation is challenged by heterogeneous output formats, conflicting task gradients, and imbalanced training data. Hence, we present \textbf{Two-Stage Mixture-of-LoRA}, a framework built on MedGemma-1.5-4B. The framework uses a shared-specific Mixture-of-LoRA architecture comprising one shared LoRA and six task-specific expert LoRAs, together with a two-stage training procedure. In Stage 1, we jointly train the shared LoRA and all task-specific expert LoRAs on all tasks. In Stage 2, we first freeze the backbone, the shared LoRA, and all non-target experts, and refine one task expert at a time. Classification and regression then receive an additional modality-balanced continuation, in which smaller modality groups are repeated to match the largest group. In the FLARE 2026 Task 3 test sets, the proposed method achieves 0.85 balanced accuracy for classification, 0.48 micro-F1 for multi-label classification, 0.79 detection F1, and 17.39 regression MAE. Code is available at https://github.com/YuanYL03/MICCAI-FLARE-2026-Challenge-Task3-2D.
bullets: Addresses heterogeneous outputs, conflicting task gradients, and imbalanced data in joint medical VLM adaptation.
Uses one shared LoRA plus six task-specific expert LoRAs.
Jointly trains all adapters, then separately refines each task expert while freezing the others.
Adds modality-balanced continuation training for classification and regression.
On FLARE 2026 Task 3 test sets, reports 0.85 balanced accuracy, 0.48 micro-F1, 0.79 detection F1, and 17.39 regression MAE across task types.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-task medical vision-language model adaptation via Mixture-of-LoRA; fits multimodal LLM adaptation.
papers.title: Two-Stage Mixture-of-LoRA for Multi-Task Medical Vision-Language Learning
papers.tldr: Two-Stage Mixture-of-LoRA adapts MedGemma-1.5-4B to diverse medical vision-language tasks using shared and task-specific LoRA experts refined in two stages.

papers.abstract: A central challenge in de novo protein design is generating proteins with desired structural and functional properties. Existing design models typically require a dedicated input representation for each property, limiting the design objectives they support. We develop Prompteina, the first all-atom structure generation model that supports new and broader design objectives specified in natural language, analogous to text-to-image generation. To train Prompteina, we construct Prompteina-Data, a paired text--protein structure dataset of 1.8M structures and 50M+ captions describing global and residue-specific structural and functional properties. We adapt Proteina-Complexa, a pretrained structure generation model, through text-conditioned pretraining and finetuning that aligns residues with their corresponding text. Prompteina outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and generates proteins that more closely match descriptions of their intended functions. In binder design, it leads baselines on at least 13 of 20 targets and improves interface confidence by 14\% over the strongest baseline. With iterative in silico feedback, Prompteina's gain over non-iterative generation is 57\% larger than the next-best baseline on the hardest targets. Finally, we experimentally validate Prompteina designs against GM2A, a target with no reported de novo binders. We identify nine binders, with the strongest at an apparent $K_{\mathrm{D}}$ of 107 nM. These results establish natural language as an effective and powerful conditioning interface for protein structure generation.
authors: Joseph Lee, Yanjing Li, Bo Qiang, Gregory Lau, Allyson Ettinger, Noah A. Smith, Rory Donovan-Maiye, David Baker, Hanna Hajishirzi, Pang Wei Koh
bullets: Addresses the limited range of objectives supported by protein design models requiring property-specific input representations.
Introduces Prompteina, an all-atom structure generator conditioned on natural-language descriptions of global and residue-specific properties.
Trains on Prompteina-Data, containing 1.8M protein structures and over 50M paired captions, with text–residue alignment.
Outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and leads on at least 13 of 20 binder-design targets; iterative feedback further improves performance.
Experimental validation against GM2A identified nine binders, with the strongest showing an apparent KD of 107 nM.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a text-conditioned all-atom 3D structure generation foundation model, directly fitting multimodal foundation models and 3D foundation models.
papers.title: Designing Protein Structures from Natural Language
papers.tldr: Prompteina enables natural-language-guided generation of protein structures and produces designs that better satisfy structural and functional goals, including experimentally validated binders.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly analyze and reason about images, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations faithfully encode the structured relations required for such reasoning. We introduce EICS (Evaluation-Invariant Concept Stability), a metric for testing whether representations consistently encode concepts under controlled one-concept interventions, and CASP-VL (Causally controlled Spatial Perturbations for Vision-Language models), a benchmark of causally controlled spatial perturbations derived from Visual Genome scene graphs. Across multiple VLM architectures, we find that spatial relations are represented substantially less faithfully than lexical information, even when the same models score well above chance on compositional benchmarks. Further analysis shows that the relation is identifiable at the predicate's own tokens but is lost when the sentence is aggregated into a global representation, whether through the (EOS) token or by mean pooling. These findings reveal a systematic failure invisible to output-based evaluation: VLMs do not preserve, in the representation used downstream, relational information that is present in their own input.
bullets: Introduces EICS, a metric for testing concept stability under controlled one-concept interventions.
Introduces CASP-VL, a benchmark of causally controlled spatial perturbations derived from Visual Genome scene graphs.
Across multiple VLM architectures, spatial information is represented less faithfully than lexical information.
Spatial relations remain identifiable at predicate tokens but are lost when representations are aggregated via EOS tokens or mean pooling.
The failure is hidden by output-based and compositional benchmark performance.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates spatial relation representations in VLMs; directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: When VLMs Destroy What They Know: Spatial Representations Fall Below Lexical Priors
papers.tldr: VLMs can recognize spatial relations in outputs yet fail to preserve them reliably in their global internal representations.

papers.abstract: Comics are one of the great visual records of the twentieth century: hundreds of thousands of pages in which a mass readership saw its leaders, its wars and its heroes. Most of this record has never been studied as a whole; comics scholarship proceeds one book at a time. We argue that artificial intelligence, including generative models, can change this to the benefit of the medium itself. We propose PAGE, a framework that makes artificial intelligence an instrument for comics research. It parses every scan into panels, text and a bibliographic record; annotates each page with a vision-language model that follows a written codebook, as a human coder would; grounds samples of these readings in human annotation; and explains change across an archive, with estimates controlled for publisher and genre. We demonstrate the framework on 3,929 American comic books (1938--1956) and 87 volumes of Japanese manga, in three studies, each resting on a different capability. The first pairs text search with visual reading to recover how a mass medium portrayed political power. The second measures the page's visual form across an industry and recovers the hand of individual artists. The third follows who speaks across two comics traditions, checked against human annotation. Beyond research, the same instruments can make archives searchable by what is drawn, open comics to blind and low-vision readers, and help preserve fragile collections and credit uncredited artists. We outline a research agenda in which artificial intelligence strengthens the study, preservation and reach of the medium.
bullets: Addresses the limits of book-by-book comics scholarship across vast American comics and Japanese manga archives.
Parses scans into panels, text, and bibliographic records, then applies codebook-guided vision-language annotation grounded in human checks.
Demonstrates three studies of political representation, visual form and artists’ styles, and speaking roles across comics traditions.
Applies the framework to 3,929 American comic books from 1938–1956 and 87 manga volumes.
Potentially supports searchable archives, accessibility for blind and low-vision readers, preservation, and attribution of uncredited artists.
papers.selection_reason: Uses vision-language models for large-scale comics analysis and annotation, relevant to multimodal foundation model applications.
papers.title: Studying Comics at Scale with Artificial Intelligence: The PAGE Framework and Three Studies of American Comics and Japanese Manga
papers.tldr: PAGE uses AI to study comics at archival scale by parsing, annotating, validating, and interpreting their visual and textual content.

papers.abstract: When solving complex spatial reasoning tasks, ordinary humans naturally revisit the scenes from task-relevant viewpoints and mentally reconstruct the spatial layouts from those viewpoints. But can Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) proactively think in the same way? We term this ability Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM), an intrinsic component of visual intelligence that remains substantially underdeveloped in current LVLMs. To bridge this gap, we introduce SpatialASM, a scalable framework to internalize ASM into LVLMs through training-time spatial simulation. SpatialASM employs an allocentric novel-view generator to ground hypothetical viewpoints in visual evidence and produces two complementary forms of supervision: i) explicit ASM trajectories that teach LVLMs when and how to adaptively invoke view planning and imagination during spatial reasoning, and ii) automatically-constructed perspective-taking tasks that further strengthens viewpoint-conditioned scene imagination. On seven benchmarks spanning relatively perception-oriented spatial understanding to more challenging tasks requiring multi-image, cross-view and viewpoint-transformation reasoning, SpatialASM yields performance gain on LVLMs of four LVLM backbones in spatial reasoning while retaining their original general vision capabilities. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves average accuracy across the seven spatial benchmarks. And the synthesis of ASM trajectories provides a scalable pathway to alleviate the scarcity of spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision for eliciting active viewpoint exploration and mental scene simulation.
authors: Yuhong Liu, Shenxi Wu, Junyi Chi, Beichen Zhang, Xuanlang Dai, Jiaqi Wang, Yuhang Zang, Dahua Lin
bullets: Targets the underdeveloped ability of LVLMs to revisit scenes from task-relevant viewpoints during spatial reasoning.
Uses training-time spatial simulation with an allocentric novel-view generator grounded in visual evidence.
Provides explicit Active Spatial Mentalization trajectories and automatically constructed perspective-taking tasks as supervision.
Improves average accuracy across seven spatial benchmarks and four LVLM backbones while preserving general vision capabilities.
Offers a scalable way to reduce reliance on scarce spatial chain-of-thought supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Enhances LVLMs' active spatial mentalization, viewpoint planning, and spatial reasoning, fitting spatial intelligence.
papers.title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: SpatialASM trains vision-language models to actively plan viewpoints and mentally simulate scenes, improving spatial reasoning across diverse benchmarks.

papers.abstract: How well can vision-language models (VLMs) reason about what is missing from an image? We study this question with OccludeBench, a manually curated benchmark for recovering fully occluded objects from the visual evidence that remains. OccludeBench distinguishes direct cases, where the hidden object must be recovered from a specific physical cue such as a shadow or reflection, from inferential cases, where it can be inferred from broader scene context. Across five VLMs, accuracy averages 42.7% on direct cases versus 62.7% on inferential cases, exhibiting a 20.0-point gap. Humans attain higher accuracies of 63.4% versus 68.5% for direct and inferential images, respectively, with no significant gap. To locate this failure, we introduce OccludeTrace, a four-stage diagnostic that isolates where the visual reasoning process breaks down. The bottleneck emerges when models must recover the relevant object from the projection within the full image: they succeed on only 50% of failed examples, compared with 91% of examples they answer correctly. Extended reasoning, tool use, and few-shot prompting yield inconsistent improvements and do not reliably eliminate the gap. In contrast, an inpaint-then-confront intervention, which prompts models to first generate a candidate hidden object and then evaluate that hypothesis against the visible physical cue, reduces the gap to a statistically non-significant difference for both models with image-generation capabilities. Together, our results establish a tractable, controlled diagnostic for isolating how VLMs reason about visual content that is missing from an image.
authors: Jasin Cekinmez, Addison J. Wu, Ryo Mitsuhashi, Linrong Cai, Xingyu Fu, Zhuang Liu
bullets: Benchmark separates direct cases, relying on shadows or reflections, from inferential cases based on broader scene context.
Across five VLMs, accuracy was 42.7% on direct cases versus 62.7% on inferential cases; humans showed no significant gap.
OccludeTrace identifies recovering the hidden object from its projection in the full image as the main bottleneck.
Extended reasoning, tool use, and few-shot prompting provide inconsistent improvements.
Inpaint-then-confront reduces the direct–inferential gap to a statistically non-significant difference for models with image-generation capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: VLM benchmark for recovering occluded objects; relevant to multimodal LLM and spatial/visual reasoning.
papers.title: OccludeBench: Can VLMs Find What's Missing?
papers.tldr: OccludeBench shows that VLMs struggle to recover fully occluded objects from direct physical cues, and an inpaint-then-confront strategy can reduce this reasoning gap.

papers.abstract: Memes play a central role in modern online communication, especially in contexts of political conflict where visual and textual cues combine to convey persuasive messages. We study persuasive technique detection in Ukrainian memes using vision-language models (VLMs). We introduce UkrMeme, a dataset of 200 organically produced Ukrainian wartime memes annotated for persuasion techniques, and PTM-UA, a Ukrainian translation of a subset of the Propaganda 950 benchmark that preserves original visual content while translating meme text. We evaluate VLMs in a zero-shot prompting setup across image, text, and multimodal inputs using hierarchical F1 metrics. Finally, we compare Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) and model-generated token attributions and analyze the semantic categories of evidence emphasized by each explanation method.
authors: Nazar Andrushko, Vera Schmitt, Veronika Solopova
bullets: Introduces UkrMeme, a dataset of 200 organically produced Ukrainian wartime memes annotated for persuasion techniques.
Presents PTM-UA, a Ukrainian translation of part of Propaganda 950 that retains the original visuals.
Evaluates VLMs with zero-shot prompts using image-only, text-only, and multimodal inputs.
Uses hierarchical F1 metrics and compares Layer-wise Relevance Propagation with model-generated token attributions.
Analyzes which semantic evidence categories different explanation methods emphasize.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates vision-language models for multimodal persuasion detection, directly relevant to multimodal LLM understanding.
papers.title: UkrMeme: Multimodal Explainable Persuasion Detection in Ukrainian Memes
papers.tldr: UkrMeme evaluates vision-language models for explainable persuasion-technique detection in Ukrainian wartime memes using new Ukrainian datasets and attribution analyses.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on speech-text tasks, but standard audio encoders produce hundreds of tokens for even short audio clips. Because self-attention scales quadratically in sequence length, this inflates inference-time compute substantially. Current training-free token compression methods prune or merge tokens based solely on coarse attention or feature similarity. However, treating audio tokens as generic, isotropic features smooths over spectral transitions, destroying fine-grained phonetic transitions essential for decoding speech. In contrast, speech signals exhibit highly structured temporal patterns where information density peaks at acoustic transitions. We propose AudioTETRIS, a training-free, two-stage framework that uses the audio encoder's representation geometry as an acoustic prior for token importance before applying attention-based compression. Instead of discarding encoder structure after the encoding stage, AudioTETRIS propagates this prior directly into the LLM decoder to compute a per-token fused score. This score drives progressive top-$k$ token selection across decoder layers without requiring additional training or auxiliary models. Evaluated on Qwen2-Audio-7B, Phi-4-Multimodal, and Audio Flamingo 3, AudioTETRIS retains near-uncompressed performance on several speech tasks using only 25% of audio tokens, matches or surpasses full-token accuracy at moderate compression rates, and consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines.
authors: Shreya Sajid, Anna Vettoruzzo, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Targets the high inference cost caused by hundreds of audio tokens and quadratic self-attention.
Uses encoder representation geometry to identify transition-rich, information-dense tokens.
Fuses acoustic-prior and decoder attention signals into per-token importance scores.
Progressively selects top-k tokens across decoder layers without training or auxiliary models.
Evaluated on three audio LLMs, it retains near-uncompressed speech-task performance and outperforms training-free baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free token elimination for audio LLMs using acoustic transition priors; fits token pruning and multimodal LLM efficiency.
papers.title: AudioTETRIS: Token Elimination via Transitional Importance Signals for Efficient Audio LLMs
papers.tldr: AudioTETRIS efficiently compresses audio tokens by preserving acoustically important transitions, maintaining near-full performance with only 25% of tokens.

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models (MLLMs) exhibit promising spatial reasoning capabilities, yet the internal mechanisms supporting them remain poorly understood. We uncover S-Space, a linear representation subspace in which object-token representations encode continuous coordinates along horizontal, vertical, and distance axes. Although we identify these axes by differentiating spatial-answer scores with respect to object-token activations, S-Space is intrinsic rather than induced by specific data or prompts, remaining readable under non-spatial questions. We show that S-Space functions as an internal spatial workspace of MLLMs. Perception encodes object locations into it, forming spatial representations that can be directly read out to support accurate spatial judgments. Internal reasoning transforms it for changing viewpoints. Verbal responses selectively access it, evidenced by causal interventions that alter spatial judgments while largely preserving non-spatial responses. Case studies further show that S-Space assigns locations to unseen entities and the observer, and connects physical directions with abstract linguistic meanings, suggesting both the capabilities and limitations of large-scale language training. Finally, we use S-Space as a diagnostic tool for spatial reasoning failures. Direction-word readouts reveal systematic coupling between cardinal and image-relative reference frames. More importantly, a perception-computation decomposition exposes a key bottleneck: MLLMs can form capable spatial representations, yet fall short in the spatial transformations required to reason reliably across viewpoint changes.
authors: Zhiyuan Shi, Xiang Li, Xingzhuo Guo, Shangchen Miao, Weiliang Chen, Qiyu Dai, Jinshan Ren, Jiangran Lyu, Fangfu Liu, Mingsheng Long, Jialong Wu
bullets: Object-token representations encode continuous horizontal, vertical, and distance coordinates in a linear subspace.
The subspace is intrinsic and remains readable across prompts, including non-spatial questions.
Perception writes locations into S-Space, reasoning transforms them across viewpoints, and verbal responses selectively read from it.
Causal interventions show that modifying S-Space changes spatial judgments while largely preserving non-spatial responses.
Diagnostics indicate that unreliable spatial reasoning stems mainly from deficient viewpoint-related spatial transformations, not representation formation.
